cards.title: Prove the runtime OS edge safe: leaf contracts, model checking, fault injection, checked mode
cards.body: Owner direction: find a way to prove the safety of the unsafe runtime layer, holistically. #6701 c4-c6 shrink the trusted base, make misuse unwritable through ownership and range types, and remove Linux hazards by design. This card proves what remains: every runtime syscall leaf against a written contract. Kernel-enforced confinement (a default seccomp allowlist) is a separate owner ballot. A public claim that the edge is proven needs a passing adversarial review per AGENTS.md. Limit: this proves Jet against the kernel documented behaviour, not kernel bugs.
cards.checkSteps: each item has a case or gate that fails when broken

criteria.text: Every runtime syscall leaf carries a machine-checkable contract (precondition, postcondition, frame: which bytes and fds it may touch, with no arithmetic overflow), and a symbolic checker written in Jet with no external solver proves each leaf IR against it; a leaf without a passing proof record fails the build.

Machine-code translation check: the syscall number and argument registers emitted for every leaf at O0/O1/O2 match a committed table derived from the kernel syscall_64.tbl, and a mismatch fails the gate.

Model-based differential testing: a pure-Jet model of the fd table and mappings runs at least one million random operation sequences against the real kernel with no divergence; a fault-injection test mode makes every leaf return each documented errno (EINTR, EAGAIN, ENOMEM, EMSGSIZE, truncated control data), and every error path is exercised; the Wayland wire and XKB parsers are fuzzed with no hang or panic.

Checked runtime mode: extend --checked-alloc with a shadow ledger of open fds and mappings that checks every leaf call against it (owned and open, in range, not after close); the cases and golden suites pass in this mode.

Drift gates: the unsafe-site ratchet can only fall, every leaf has a contract and a proof record, and jet audit foreign stays clean; a dated adversarial review in Docs/audits tries to break the claim and passes before any public text calls the edge proven.

cards.title: A range-typed Int(lo..hi) argument is rejected for a plain Int parameter (E0108); no explicit widening exists
cards.body:
Found by WaylandLead (#6701 c5, range-typed OS-edge params). Seed a0_039:
plain: fn(value: Int) -> Int { value * 2 }
ranged: fn(size: Int(1..1073741824)) -> Int { plain(size) }   // E0108
Int{size} and size.raw() are rejected too; only arithmetic (size + 0) widens. A value of a refined range type is always a valid Int, so widening to the unrefined type should be implicit (or have one ratified explicit spelling). Repro: $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/WaylandLead/probe/range_widen_repro.jet.
cards.checkSteps: jet run of the repro prints 10 on O0, O1 and O2; a case under tests/cases covers the call, a return and an assignment of a range value to Int

log.text: c2 sweep by G5DevX-1 on dev 16f96f3c7a. Narrow form: git grep -nE "wrapping\([a-z_]+ \+ 0\)" -- Core Compiler Tools tests hits only Core/Sys/Sys.jet (14 sites), all removed by G5DevX-range1b2, so 0 hits on its tree. Broad form: git grep -nE "[A-Za-z_)\]] \+ 0\b"; every other hit is Float arithmetic (+ 0.5 and the like), index symmetry (base + 0, start + 0 in generated lexer rows), Int + 0 on an Int, comments, or awk/shell text, none of them a widening workaround. Meets after range2 (b15) and range1b2 (b16) land and the range-widening cases pass at O0/O1/O2.

Main sweep 2026-11-12: still E0108 on seed-b13 (repro $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/sweep/r6704/main.jet). spec.md says safe widening is implicit, so Int(lo..hi) to Int is implicit with no new spelling; routed to G5DevX-1 as G5DevX-range1.

criteria.text: Passing, returning or assigning an Int(lo..hi) value where Int is expected type-checks and runs with the same value on O0, O1 and O2 (case under tests/cases).

Safe widening is one rule applied at every place a value meets a declared type: call and Core-call arguments, returns, local and place assignment, struct-literal fields, list and map items, and returned field reads. A ranged Int or a narrower fixed-width integer passes where Int is expected at each place, at O0, O1 and O2, and narrowing stays refused. Proof: the tests/cases range-widening case covers every position and its refused case. No `+ 0` widening workaround remains in Core, Compiler, Tools or tests.

cards.title: Wayland window and ui stack: measured best against every alternative
cards.body: Owner order (2026-11-08): the native Wayland window is good enough for now (the compositor-paced frame loop ran "buttery smooth" at 240 Hz). Land the deterministic functionality first, then hill-climb this card until it is near perfect. The window and ui stack must beat every strong alternative on the same compositor and display, idle and under a full-machine load. The alternatives are GTK4 (frame clock), Qt 6 (QQuickWindow), SDL3, winit with softbuffer, a Chromium/Electron requestAnimationFrame page, and a hand-written C wl_surface.frame + wp_presentation loop as the machine ceiling. The xkb keymap is measured against libxkbcommon. Peer programs stay outside the tree. Each loss is fixed at its root in the runtime leaves or the loop, never by dropping a feature (AGENTS.md performance gate).
cards.plan: Start after the Wayland functionality (frame loop, CSD, HiDPI and fractional scale, cursors, clipboard, multi-window, keyboard) and X11 have landed. Build the same bouncing-square program and a resize/HiDPI/text scene in each alternative, measure every metric in the criteria, rank the losses in Pareto order and fix them.

log.text: HELD by owner order 2026-11-11 (no small optimizations until the language is mostly stable; architecture and regression fixes go first, per #5479 c5-c8). These criteria stay open and unworked: c1 (owner order 2026-11-11 (no micro-optimization until the language is mostly stable; #5479 c); c2 (owner order 2026-11-11 (no micro-optimization until the language is mostly stable; #5479 c); c3 (owner order 2026-11-11 (no micro-optimization until the language is mostly stable; #5479 c); c4 (owner order 2026-11-11 (no micro-optimization until the language is mostly stable; #5479 c).

criteria.text: A same-program comparison table, recorded with its commit and commands, covers Jet and each alternative on: presented-interval p50/p99 and missed frames at the display's refresh (idle and under a full-machine load), input-to-photon latency, CPU time per frame and wakeups per second, time to first presented frame, RSS and binary size.
Jet is at or better than every alternative on every metric of that table, and within the hand-written C ceiling, or each remaining loss has its own card naming its root.

Live resize, fractional scale (125% and 150%), cursor shape, clipboard and multi-window are compared the same way: no stretched or blank frames during resize and crisp output at fractional scale, with the same metrics as criterion 1 where they apply.
The Jet xkb keymap matches libxkbcommon on the oracle and beats it on keymap compile time (compositor keymap fd to ready Keymap), per-key cost and memory, or each loss has its own card.

cards.title: Safe read-only file maps expose bytes another process can change, and fault with SIGBUS when the file shrinks
cards.body: Found by the D-MAP-WRITE1 adversarial review (Docs/audits/2026-11-08-D-MAP-WRITE1-review.md). files.map gives safe code a borrowed byte view of a MAP_PRIVATE read-only mapping. Private mapping is not a snapshot: an external write changed an already borrowed byte from 3 to 9 (probe Current.jet). An external truncate makes the next access of a borrowed byte die with Fault [SIGBUS] and exit 135 (probes Shrink.jet and CFreeLead's MapShrink.jet); the shared flock is advisory and does not prevent it. Safe Jet must not observe a borrowed value changing under it, and an I/O failure in safe code must surface as a typed error or a registered, explained fault, never a raw signal death. This holds whatever D-MAP-WRITE1 decides.
cards.plan: Decide the I1 contract for read-only maps: copy-on-read, or a view the runtime keeps stable (e.g. MAP_PRIVATE plus a seal or lease where the kernel offers one), or an Unsafe-only borrowed view with a safe copying API. Then make the truncation case a typed IOError or a registered fault with what/why/fix text and a UI snapshot, with one meaning on every tier. A choice that changes public API or behavior goes to an owner ballot first.

criteria.text: A case proves that a safe borrowed view of a mapped file cannot observe a byte change made by another process after the borrow (or the safe API no longer hands out such a view), on every applicable tier.

A case truncates a mapped file from another process during safe access; the program gets a typed error or a registered fault with its diagnostic code, what/why/fix text and UI snapshot, never an unexplained SIGBUS exit, on every applicable tier.

(was #2790 c1) Implementation-only closure: mapped files use the existing read-only view ownership mechanism, return checked view-shaped types through nested Option/Result/Shared carriers, root every borrowed result in the receiver mapping, and route O0, O1, O2 and web where applicable behavior through the same mmap Prelude kernels [precut audit: no dev test, golden, case or snapshot proves this today] (was #4620 c11)
criteria.evidence: dev fbd660ba2f (G9Web-6706c4): Examples Systems/Files/FilesMapViews returns mapped windows through Option, Result, a named pair, a list and a Shared carrier (guard_read gives View<U8>? from SharedGuard<MappedFile>, read by a task through a handle copy), each rooted in the receiver map, through the one mmap Prelude kernel. The web target returns a typed IOError (ENOSYS). Lander ran on seed-b14: golden FilesMapViews PASS 3 (o0, o1, o2), golden FilesMapAdvise PASS 3, ui mapped_window_outlives_its_map PASS 1 (E2305), and DiagnosticRows --check rc 0 after the E2305 page regeneration.

cards.title: Element and module-storage reassignment drops the old Close value without closing it (xs[i] = v, m[k] = v, module storage)
cards.body: Found by AllocLead while tracing #6707. With seed a0_040, `xs[i] = v` and `m[k] = v` drop the replaced element without running its close. Assigning to module storage does the same, from reading the code; that path has not been run. Field writes and Shared guard writes correctly close before they drop. Fix: one replace-then-close-then-drop path for every assignment target, with a case for each target on every tier.

cards.title: ICE: `o := Box?(Val(make("o0")))` crashes sema.body totality ("has no checked type")
cards.body: Found by AllocLead with seed a0_040. An Option of a boxed value built inline in a local binding crashes the compiler in sema.body totality with "has no checked type" instead of checking. Under I2 and I3 this must be either a checked program or a registered diagnostic. Add a case under tests/cases.

criteria.text: Comparing a value with None checks in sema on every type: a FileLock? (from files.try_lock) compared with None runs true or false on O0, O1 and O2, and a value whose type can never be None (for example the plain FileLock that `try_lock(p) ?? panic(..)` yields) is E0109 in sema, never an ir.build ICE. A case pins both sides.

cards.title: FFI attribute accepts and ignores unknown arguments
cards.body: The seed accepts `#FFI(c, concurrent)` and silently ignores the unknown argument `concurrent` (found by BallotLead-2 while probing the #6689 thread ballots). Sema must reject every FFI argument it does not define, with a registered diagnostic (what/why/fix and a UI snapshot), so a misspelt or unsupported option never compiles silently.

cards.title: Generic call to a trait method returning `T? Never!` loses the optional and fails in the backend (ICE)
cards.body: Found by SqliteLead on the b6c compiler (#6695 slice 8). A generic call `fn<H: Host>` to a trait method declared `-[]> T? Never!` loses the optional, and the backend rejects it: `ir.build unlowered: ... binder got of type ?[U8] bound to a value of type [U8]`. The smallest repro is the trait `Src{grab -[]> [U8]? Never!; grab2 -> Int? Never!}`, called generically. It works without `Never!`. That breaks I2 (a backend rejection of checked code must not happen) and the one-mechanism promise for effect rows. A workaround is in core.db: VdbeAux.jet Host.vtab_take_errmsg is declared without `Never!`; remove it once fixed. Criteria: a regression case in tests/cases compiles and runs on O0/O1/O2; the workaround is removed.

cards.title: jet build --os=web of checked FFI.C code exits 101 (web host lacks the inline FFI symbol) instead of a checked refusal
cards.body: Found by the fresh adversarial review of the #6689 ballots (FFIReview, 2026-11-09). `jet build --os=web --allow=FFI.C main.jet` on the carrier example passes checking and then exits 101, because the web host lacks jet_inline_jet_ffi_digits. That breaks I2 and I3: sema must refuse a C import on a target without C (a registered diagnostic with what/why/fix and a UI snapshot), so codegen never meets it. Repro: $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/FFIReview/2026-11-09-ffi-ballots-review.md. Criteria: the web build refuses with a registered diagnostic, a UI snapshot exists, no exit 101, and the native build is unchanged.

cards.title: CoreModuleCheck reads the checked tree's CoreSourceParts.tsv

cards.title: Release cut in 10 minutes or less: faster golden and cases suites
cards.body: Owner order (2026-11-09): the whole seed-cut process (preflight, self-host chain, packs, the golden/ui/cases gates, tag and publish) takes at most 10 minutes of wall-clock time. Today a fresh cut takes about 37 minutes: chain ~3, packs ~2, golden ~10.6, ui ~2, cases ~20 (the suites run one after another with 4 shards x --jobs; the baseline side and the retries add more). Speed it up without weakening the gate. Every row still runs or is soundly reused by content identity; no dropped rows, no easier tier, I9 parity is kept, and timeouts are not hidden as flakes.
cards.plan: 1. Profile one fresh admit: wall time per phase, and per-row cost split by compile, link, run and harness overhead; find the slowest rows and the idle cores. 2. Find the levers: concurrency (shards and jobs sized to cores and memory, the three suites run concurrently), baseline rows reused from the previous seed's recorded evidence instead of rerunning the release side, fine-grained input-hash reuse of candidate rows, compiler start-up and per-row compile cost (cached Core and Prelude artifacts, one compile shared by the O0/O1/O2 rows where the meaning allows), fewer process spawns, and timeout and retry policy. 3. Implement in Tools/release and the testkit, and measure the result on a real admit.

criteria.text: A fresh release admit of a dev commit with no reuse of candidate rows from an earlier admit, on this workstation, runs from the preflight to publish in at most 10 minutes of wall-clock time, with its timestamped log as evidence.

The gate keeps its strength. Nothing is cached or reused between runs and nothing is built incrementally (owner 2026-11-09): every run starts from source. Within ONE run, each test worker may parse and check Core once and share that checked Core in memory across the rows it runs (owner 2026-11-09, the vitest model); each row still compiles and runs its own fresh native program on the candidate. A proof run shows the shared-Core verdicts are byte-identical to per-row cold compiles on every row. OWNER 2026-11-09 (later): the release (previous seed) column runs only on the rows that fail on the candidate, the release's known-failing rows, and rows whose files changed since the baseline commit, with gains and losses judged exactly as before; every candidate row still runs. There are no new skips and no dropped tiers, and the compiler front end itself also gets at least 2x faster cold (owner: both).
The flaky-timeout rate under the new concurrency is no higher than today's: retried TIMEOUT rows are counted and reported.

cards.title: core.ui renderer is the fastest 2D renderer: gauntlet cells against Blend2D, Skia raster, tiny-skia and cairo/pixman, with an asm-parity ceiling
cards.body: Owner 2026-11-09: 'we should be the fastest renderer especially since we have top to bottom full control over the whole language stack.' Today a 900x600 frame (a full gradient, ~15 shapes, ~7 text lines) takes ~140 ms at O0 and ~55 ms at O2. Under the AGENTS.md performance gate, core.ui's rasterizer (Core/Ui/Draw.jet and the font rasterizer) gets required cells in the GUI-applications area. For each workload, Jet/peer must be below 1.00 against every matched CPU 2D renderer (Blend2D, Skia's raster backend, tiny-skia, cairo/pixman), and Jet/ceiling at most 1.00 against a hand-written SIMD reference (asm-parity) doing the same work, on every tier (O0 included, since  is what users run) and in both cycles and bytes. The workloads: solid and gradient fills, anti-aliased paths and shapes (rects, rounded rects, circles, polygons), alpha blending (straight and premultiplied), anti-aliased glyph text, image blits and scaling, and full-frame redraw at 1080p and 4K. Use the whole stack: SIMD in the runtime or Core through vetted internals, compiler codegen (bounds-check elimination, vectorizing span loops) and data layout. Fix compiler-side gaps at their root in the compiler, not by hand-unrolled Jet. Semantics and pixels are identical on every tier.
cards.plan: 1. Gauntlet cells plus peer harness: same scenes, same pixels (compared as images), peers built at their best settings. 2. asm-parity ceiling references with the best known technique (AVX2/AVX-512 span fill and blend, analytic coverage rasterization). 3. Profile Jet per workload; split the gap into rasterizer algorithm, codegen and runtime. 4. Close the gap: algorithm first (span and coverage pipelines like Blend2D's), then codegen defects as compiler cards. 5. Gate: every cell passes both stages.

cards.title: Codegen: pixel-loop throughput (fill leaf through a &struct field place, slow U64 arithmetic at O2, O0 indexed stores ~3 ns/element)
cards.body: Found by WaylandLead3 while speeding up the core.ui rasterizer (#6718); repro in Micro.jet from the renderer lane. (1) The O2 fill leaf doesn't fire for stores through a &struct field place: 1.15 ns/B vs 0.07 ns/B for a local. (2) U64 arithmetic takes ~10 ns/iteration even at O2, no faster than O0. (3) An O0 indexed store costs ~3 ns/element, so per-pixel Jet code can't redraw 1080p in a few ms at O0 (jet run). Fix each at its root in the compiler (IR/backend), not with library workarounds. The same semantics on every tier (I9).

cards.title: Games: Jet ships every primitive needed to build a full high-resolution 3D game (no engine)
cards.body: Owner order (2026-11-09): Jet is to be the best language for making games, so it must be capable of rendering full high-resolution 3D games. Do not build a 3D rendering engine now, but ship all the tools and primitives needed to make one: GPU device, swapchain and presentation on the native window, buffers, textures, render passes and pipelines, shaders written in Jet (D-GPU-SHADER-SURFACE1), GPU compute, 3D math (vectors, matrices, quaternions, SIMD), image and mesh asset loading, raw and relative input, audio, frame pacing and GPU timing. Related cards: #c0ce571w (shader stages and pipelines), #c0li0kor (GPU kernels), #c084tcrl (device providers), #c0776o2m (game platform layer), #c0ba141x (linking model: GPU drivers need the platform loader). First step: a gap map against code, then ballots for every public API.

criteria.text: A dated gap map (Docs/research) lists each primitive a high-resolution 3D game needs and, for each, what Jet has today, proven by code, an example or a probe, and what is missing, the dependencies, the owner gates and the related cards.
Every missing public API or new syntax has a Tower ballot that has passed adversarial review before it reaches the owner.

An executable example draws a lit, textured, depth-tested 3D mesh of at least 100k triangles at 2560x1440 through the GPU in a native window, using only shipped primitives and no engine code in Core, with golden-tested output (headless image hash) on every applicable tier.
Gauntlet cells measure the GPU path (frame time and draw submission cost) against C with Vulkan and Rust with wgpu, with an asm-parity ceiling reference, per the performance gate.

cards.title: core.ui GPU acceleration in native Jet, with the same look native and in the browser
cards.body: Owner 2026-11-09, on the Showcase: 'it would also be excellent if it can be gpu accelerated - again with native jet support, not some additional dsl or sub language, but native jet', and 'we want this to look the same whether it is running in a native app or in a browser'. Standing direction: one unified GPU language built into core Jet (ratified markers: #Shader for graphics, D-GPU-SHADER-SURFACE1=B; Kernel for compute, D-GPU-COMPUTE-LAUNCH1), working on any GPU out of the box, with no per-vendor or per-OS DSLs. Conflict: D-GPU-UI1=A keeps desktop defaults on software (a static single file, no driver loading), so a GPU default on desktop needs a new owner ballot that revises it, tied to the linking-model ballot #c0ba141x (GPU drivers need the platform loader). Open technical questions for the ballot: GPU rasterization isn't bit-identical across vendors, so 'same look' must be defined (bit-identical through the software path vs perceptually identical through the GPU), and how a static musl binary reaches the system Vulkan/WebGPU driver.

criteria.text: An adversarially reviewed owner ballot (revising D-GPU-UI1) decides the desktop and web GPU default for core.ui, the fallback, the driver-loading model, and what 'the same look native and in the browser' means, with same-program alternatives.
core.ui draws through the GPU from native Jet code only (#Shader/#Kernel), with no shader-language source, per-vendor path or DSL in the repository, on Linux native and in the browser.
The same Showcase program renders the same look native and in the browser, proven by headless checksums or a perceptual-difference bound the ballot fixes, on every applicable tier.

cards.title: I1: branch lowerings carry a move from one path onto the other, so values leak (same class as the ?? fallback leak)
cards.body: ReplMem's audit after fixing ir_or_fallback (ReplMem-1): these lowerings in Compiler/JetIR lower user code inside a branch without saving and joining binding ownership, so a .move() on one path disowns the binding on the other path too and the value is never dropped. ir_short_circuit (&&/|| right side), ir_condition .And, ir_optional_call (x?.f(y.move())), ir_range_switch and ir_mixed_switch (arm fall-through), the require/require_eq message branches and the contract message (BuildContracts.jet), and contract post clauses under present. Fix them all through the shared save/restore plus ir_meet_paths join, as for the valued if and ??. Separate residual: about 12 MB per REPL turn inside jet_eval_native_load (the per-compile native session's image and stub buffers).

criteria.text: Each listed lowering saves ownership before its branch and joins the paths after it, through the shared join, with one regression case per shape (an ordinary program whose lock or descriptor count proves the drop), at O0, O1 and O2 and in an AOT build, failing on the base compiler.
criteria.evidence: ReplMem-2 landed on dev 0e3254d092; batch post42a census rc=0; rerun with the batch compiler: cases trait/closure/union/generic/memory_semantics/repl filters all FAIL 0 (integ/post42a/rerun); five *_keep_the_* cases fail on s12 per the author

criteria.text: The jet_eval_native_load residual is found and fixed: the REPL peak grows by less than 1 MB per turn over 30 turns, measured.
A census confirms that no other lowering in Compiler/JetIR lowers user code inside a branch without saving and joining ownership.

I1 use-after-free in safe Jet, found by G1Lead4 on seed-t21, 2026-11-11 ($JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/G1Lead-4/out/miscompile-push-break.jet). Inside `loop item in items { path: "dir/{item}"; loop _ in 0..<2 { out.push(path); break } }`, `out` ends up holding freed text (it prints `got  ,got  ,got  ` instead of `dir/c,dir/b,dir/a`): the break path frees `path` after push has moved or shared it into `out`. Same class as c-branch moves, a move on one control path carried onto another. The fix is in the shared lowering of moves and drops across break and continue edges, not in this loop shape. The repro becomes a case printing the right list on O0/O1/O2, plus variants with continue, a labeled outer break, `?? return` and a `match` arm exit, all under the leak and sanitizer checks.
criteria.evidence: G3Ctx-15 a32aeb5757: a break edge carries its own ownership to the loop's exit, so the push-then-break pattern no longer frees a held value. cards.title: I1: boxed trait values are never dropped, so every trait value leaks its payload
cards.body: ReplMem (2026-11-09): a trait-value row (Compiler/JetIR BuildTypes.jet:286) is a Pointer row with no drop and no clone, so a boxed trait value has no drop glue and its payload leaks. A strong_count probe leaks one per binding. In the compiler, Pipeline.jet's compiler_queries (a JetEvalCompilerQueryHost trait value) holds a Shared context whose eval_config.native keeps the whole JetEvalNativeSession (about 3.25 MB image plus the child) alive on every compile: the REPL residual of about 12 MB per turn. The fix gives trait values drop glue that dispatches on the payload's implementer, keeping today's observable copy and alias semantics as the spec states them, and handles move-receiver dynamic calls.

Today jet --version prints 'Jet 0.1.0' (COMPILER_VERSION, never updated), the identity says jet@0.0.1#<hash>, and the releases are named a0_NNN, so a tester can't tell compilers apart. Existing published a0_NNN tags and seeds stay as history; the first release with the new spelling is the one after a0_042.

cards.title: Core range fill: one call fills a span of a list or buffer (owner: no ballot)
cards.body: OWNER RULING 2026-11-09 (chat): no ballot; build it with an idiomatic Jet API design. The UI canvas's full redraw is ~15 ms at 2560x1440 (36 ms at 3440x1362), and 74% of it is per-byte fill stores, about a 5.2 ms floor, because Jet has no range-write primitive. Add a whole-span fill on lists and buffers that the runtime lowers to memset/word stores, with one meaning on every tier (I9). The canvas fill uses it. Target: a full redraw ≤ 6 ms at 2560x1440 O2. It needs a paired perf cell (the plain loop against the fill) per the performance gate, plus an example with golden output.

log.text: Spelling decision (Main, 2026-11-10, within the owner ruling that a public whole-span fill needs no ballot). xs.fill(range, value) is the plain form. xs.fill_repeat(range, pattern) repeats a multi-element pattern across the span, for RGBA pixels and gradient rows. Neither clamps: a range outside 0..len stops with the same bounds fault as range indexing, and an empty pattern stops the same way; a span that is not a whole number of patterns ends with a partial pattern. Both methods share the one fast path that replaces the internal xs.__fill, and every caller moves in one cutover. G6Lead is building it.

Landed in train 2 (dev c057ea659d): 75ae287c5f makes core.ui opaque fills write in place through xs.__fill and deletes the stitch rebuild; a5a8142d89 gives the program one built-in face. WaylandLead3-10cr measured a full 2560x1440 redraw at 4.9-5.2 ms on its compiler (it was 223-240 ms). Still open: __fill is internal, so the public spelling, the perf pair and the example remain; criteria 1-4 track them.

criteria.text: A public, idiomatic whole-span fill on lists and byte buffers (not a double-underscore internal) lowers to memset or word stores, with one meaning on O0, O1, O2 and web (I9).
criteria.evidence: Landed on dev (train t12c, 4a5c0ec793..aaca1c8db2 (dev 00a2b37a42)), SUB G6Lead-6731a + G6Lead-6731b. Every test line of the SUB passes with the compiler built from the landed tree ($JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/integ/t12c/REPORT.md: census rc=0, ratchets rc=0; reruns noted there for load timeouts). fill and fill_repeat are public [T] methods with one shared fast path; __fill and its route are removed.

criteria.text: core.ui's canvas fill uses it, and a full redraw at 2560x1440 on O2 takes at most 6 ms, measured on a landed compiler.
A paired perf cell compares the plain per-element loop with the fill, per the performance gate, and the fill strictly beats it.
criteria.evidence: Landed on dev (train t12c, 4a5c0ec793..aaca1c8db2 (dev 00a2b37a42)), SUB G6Lead-6731a. cards.title: sema accepts a &&self implementation of a trait method declared self; calling it twice through a trait value hangs
cards.body: Found by ReplMem (#6727): a trait method declared with a borrowed self receiver accepts an implementation whose receiver is &&self (consuming). Called twice through a trait value, the program hangs on s12. The trait method's declared receiver must bind its implementations: sema rejects a receiver mismatch with a registered diagnostic (what/why/fix and a UI snapshot), and the IR then never has to guess ownership from the implementations.

criteria.text: Sema rejects an implementation whose receiver differs from the trait method's declared receiver, with a registered diagnostic and a UI snapshot; a case proves a call through a trait value twice no longer hangs.
criteria.evidence: d9c9b7ebea: jet test Compiler --profile ui --filter trait_impl_receiver_must_match_the_trait -> PASS 1; cases nested_impls/impl_receiver_follows_the_trait_declaration -> PASS 1 (Lander holdsweep $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Lander/holds/5-6732-c1.out)

cards.title: Acronyms in caps in every file and folder name (Core/Net/TLS.jet, not Tls.jet): one cutover plus a guard
cards.body: OWNER HARD REQUIREMENT (2026-11-09): acronyms are all caps in types AND file names, Title Case otherwise (Core/Net/TLS.jet, not Core/Net/Tls.jet). S66 and D-ONCE-CASE1 already require this for type names (E0358) and name the lexicon for file names, but nothing enforces file names. A census of dev (lexicon Compiler/JetFoundation/Data/Syntax/Acronyms.jet) finds 156 distinct file and folder names with a word-cased acronym (642 path hits), e.g. Ast.jet, Cbor.jet, Cli/, Db/, Http/, Tls.jet, CanonicalJson.jet. Greenfield cutover: rename every one and migrate every import, module path mapping, reference, generated artifact and doc in one commit stack; no aliases.

log.text: Owner: 'That is a hard requirement.' Starts after the post-a0_042 held-SUB batch lands, so the renames don't conflict with the held stacks.

criteria.text: A committed guard (a closed-list check beside tests/guards/closed_lists) fails on any tracked path whose PascalCase file or folder word spells a lexicon acronym in any other case, and the guard's census over dev is empty (receipt).

Every in-repository import, module mapping, test, example, golden, generated table and doc reference follows the rename in the same stack; the case, ui and golden suites pass on O0/O1/O2 and the self-host chain reaches its fixed point.

OWNER 2026-11-09: every folder in the repository is TitleCase with acronyms in capitals, top level included: tests/ becomes Tests/ and every lowercase folder under it (cases, guards, fixtures, ui, ...) and elsewhere follows. The only exceptions are names a tool requires (.git, .agents, .jet, src/ where ratified), each listed with the code that requires it. The AGENTS.md line 'tests/ keeps its lowercase name' is replaced in the same cutover, and the guard from c1 also refuses lowercase folders.

cards.title: User-visible text is never all lowercase, and every text is American English
cards.body: OWNER HARD REQUIREMENTS (2026-11-09): (1) The owner hates all-lowercase text in readouts, UI and anything a user sees (CLI output such as jet --version's 'release status: prerelease', HUD labels, reports, help). User-visible labels and readouts use Title Case or sentence case; acronyms in caps. Identifiers, paths, flags, code and machine formats (JSON keys) keep their spelling. (2) American English everywhere, never British: behavior not behaviour, color not colour, initialize not initialise, license not licence, and so on. A census of dev finds 129 files with British spellings.

criteria.text: A committed spelling guard (a British-to-American word list with exceptions for quoted external names) fails on British spellings in tracked text, source comments, diagnostics and docs; its census over dev is empty (receipt).

Every CLI readout, diagnostic heading, report, help text and UI label starts with a capital (Title Case for labels and headings, sentence case for prose), acronyms in caps; a guard over the CLI, diagnostic registry and Core.Ui label sources holds it, and the UI snapshots and goldens are regenerated in the same stack.

cards.title: MIT crypto and TLS: rewrite core.crypto and core.net.tls from the specifications, with the same module boundaries, replacing the Apache-2.0 mbedtls translation
cards.body: Owner ruling 2026-11-09: keep the mbedtls translation (#6694) for now, then rewrite it from scratch, preserving the module boundaries, so that it can be MIT. Work from the RFCs, FIPS and SP 800 documents, never from mbedtls or another non-MIT source. Starts after G1.

log.text: BoardPlanner review 2026-11-09 (dev 6a06b917cb). Owner 2026-11-09: the rewrite starts after G1, so it waits on the mbedtls port #6694.

criteria.text: core.crypto and core.net.tls contain no file derived from mbedtls: every file is MIT, written from the cited specifications (RFC, FIPS, SP 800), and the public and private module boundaries are unchanged.
The rewrite passes the same vectors (NIST CAVP plus the fetched Wycheproof), the interop matrix and the constant-time checks as #6694.

The full mbedtls surface that Core does not use is complete in Jet: every mbedtls test-suite vector, interop with OpenSSL and the old mbedtls build on every TLS 1.2 and 1.3 version, suite and curve, client certificates and the remaining X.509 and PSA features, with constant-time checks on every secret-dependent primitive (moved from #6694 c2-c4 by owner order 2026-11-09).

cards.title: Moving a task &&name capture inside the task body is a false E0121 at the capture mark
cards.body: Found by WaylandLead3 on a0_042. owned: Box{..}; child: task &&owned { consume(owned) } with consume(b: &&Box) reports 'owned was consumed by consume, so it can't be used here' at the capture mark, with no later use. The same happens for 'mine: owned' and 'owned :=' inside the body. The capture hands ownership into the task, so a move inside the body is the task's own last use. Repro: $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT-style scratch file a.jet (copied into the card's case when fixed).

criteria.text: Moving a task &&name capture inside the body (a call taking &&, a let binding, a := rebinding) checks clean, with a cases row per form that fails on a0_042 and runs at O0, O1 and O2 with the value dropped exactly once (a lock or strong_count proof).
A real use of the captured name after the body's move still reports E0121 at the later use, with its UI snapshot unchanged or updated.

A value taken by a task &&name capture runs its Close exactly once when the task drops it: plain and grouped tasks, at O0, O1 and O2, the same as a local or a call-taken value. On seed-b14 it never runs (G6Meta-4 repro: $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/G6Meta/p6749/plain.jet prints no "close group"), which is an I1 leak. Proof: a cases row per form, printing the close line, fails on a0_042 and passes on every tier.

cards.title: Every registered diagnostic code has a UI snapshot (397 uncovered)
cards.body:
I4 says every diagnostic has a registered code, what/why/fix text and a UI snapshot; without the snapshot it isn't done.

A sweep on 2026-11-11 (G8Scope-3, seed-b8, dev fe4c65249b) found 977 codes registered in Compiler/Prelude/Diagnostics.jet. 582 are carried by a tests/ui or tests/ui_lint snapshot ([Exxxx] or /e/Exxxx). 397 are carried by none.

The list is $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/G8Scope/ecodes/missing.txt and the sweep script is lanes/G8Scope/ecodes.sh.

By range: E00 60, E01 8, E02 4, E03 28, E04 17, E06 4, E07 3, E08 1, E09 37, E11 5, E12 81, E13 32, E14 4, E18 4, E20 2, E21 13, E22 6, E23 9, E24 8, E26 11, E27 5, E28 4, E29 14, E30 3, E31 3, E32 4, E33 7, E34 3, E35 2, E36 12, E42 3.

criteria.text: Classify each of the 397 uncovered codes as emitted (a compiler, runtime or tool path reports it) or dead (no path does). The classification is checked in as a generated report from a Jet tool, never by hand, and it lists each emitting site as file:line.
Every dead code is removed from Compiler/Prelude/Diagnostics.jet and from every in-repository reference, in one cutover.

Every emitted code has a tests/ui (or tests/ui_lint) snapshot that triggers it from user source and shows its what, why and fix text. A code that only a tool or the runtime emits gets a tests/cases case that asserts the code and its text instead.
A checked gate makes the rule permanent: a Jet tool run by LaneCheck fails when a registered code has no snapshot or case carrying it, and names the code.

Every snapshot in the directories tests/guards/diagnostics_snapshots.jet lists is compared against a live producer run in a suite that runs by default. The guard fails when a snapshot has no producer, and orphans are re-rendered from their producer or deleted (sweep list in the evidence). Proof: the guard passes on dev, and a planted orphan snapshot makes it fail.

dc_snapshot_texts (tests/guards/diagnostics_coverage.jet) and kit_ui_coverage (JetTestKit Ui.jet) credit only producer-checked snapshots. The E0979 (jetpack_jetos) and E1327 (module-eval-diagnostics) snapshots match their live producers' text, with no decision ids. Proof: jet test tests/guards/diagnostics_coverage.jet, plus the producer tests for E0979 and E1327, all passing.

cards.title: A package's authority.allow takes a scoped grant with the same meaning as jet run --allow
cards.body: `jet run --allow='FS.Read("<path>")'` confines reads to that path (spec.md, reference/cli.md, tests/cases/authority/run_allow_read_path_confines_reads_to_the_granted_paths.case). The package model refuses the same scoped grant in a manifest's `authority.allow` and accepts a scope only in `deny` or on FFI. Its message also wrongly calls the grant "a parameterized memory denial" (Jetpack Blocks/Authority.jet:315). Examples/Modules/Packages/PluginFailure/package.jet and tests/run/Foundations/Capabilities put `FS.Read("<dir>")` in allow, so their manifests fail to parse. One meaning per form (I8): a scoped grant in allow means what the flag means. Found by G6Meta-73's manifest round trip.

log.text: Decision by Main within the card's approved scope (2026-11-11): a scoped path in a manifest's authority.allow is resolved against the directory that holds the manifest, while a scoped path in --allow is resolved against the working directory where it is typed. The grant's meaning (kernel confinement, no escape by .. or symbolic link) is identical. Reason: an author's grant must not change with where the user runs the program; working-directory resolution would turn FS.Read(".") into a grant of the user's current directory. G6Meta-76 implements it, with a two-directory case.

criteria.text: The package model accepts a scoped FS.Read/FS.Write grant in authority.allow, and a run of that package is confined exactly as `--allow` confines it (same E1803 refusal and wording). Proof: a tests/cases/authority case running a package whose manifest grants FS.Read("<dir>") in allow, with a read inside and a read outside the grant.

The two example manifests parse and their goldens pass. A scope the model still refuses gets a correct, registered message with a UI snapshot. Proof: jet test Compiler --profile golden --filter PluginFailure, and the Capabilities run case.

cards.title: Effects-on-types follow-ups: write charging, lambda rows, comptime input effects, host-read inventory, explain effects
cards.body: The open criteria of #6129 and #6551, moved here when G8 closed (owner order, 2026-11-11). Each keeps its original text, finding and proof. Each criterion names its source criterion.

log.text: Decision for c6, made by Main within the ratified D-NET-HOSTREADS1 scope (denials are truthful), 2026-11-12 01:3x. No owner ballot is needed: these are effect declarations on existing Core API, not new syntax or new behavior. The rule: a host read whose value can change what the program does or prints is declared under its own effect; a read that is an internal nonce or the process's view of itself, and cannot change observable behavior, is exempt and listed as such in the inventory. Applied: H3 declare Time, Rand and Env on the core.service entry points that read them. H4 drop the timestamp from the JSON coercion audit (it adds a hidden clock read for no user value). H5 declare Env on the TUI terminal reads (TERM, COLUMNS and similar change the output). H6 and H7 exempt the temp-name and atomic-write pid nonces. H8 declare Env on path.home(). H9 exempt the PATH lookup as part of Exec, which resolves a program by name, and the Exec docs say so. H10 exempt /proc/self introspection. G5DevX-1 codes H3, H4, H5 and H8 and flips the exempt rows in host-reads.md.

cards.title: Peer floor, enforced structurally: Jet is faster and uses less peak memory than every other language
cards.body: Owner order 2026-11-11 late. A Jet program must be faster and use less peak memory than the same program in any other language. Only highly optimized hand-written machine code is exempt, and Jet aims as close to it as it can. A loss to any peer on wall time or peak memory is a codegen, runtime or Core failure. It is fixed generally, structurally and robustly in the mechanism every program uses, never per cell, so that the result holds for programs nobody measured. The machine ceiling stays the hill-climbing stage (G13): its ratio is reported, but it holds no cell until the owner opens it.

log.text: Main 2026-11-12, found by G11Speed-4 measuring c3: the gauntlet's run tier reuses each compiled peer's binary-only row (rust, c, zig, go), comparing jet run (a cold compile plus the run) with a prebuilt binary. That is mismatched evidence, and it contradicts the ratified run-cell rule: jet run time-to-answer is gated, after an edit and on a repeat run, against lua, luajit, python3 and node; the hello cell must come within 0.5 ms of a minimal hand-written program; the first run after install is reported only. The manifest's report_contract.peer_measurement ratio_tiers [aot, run], which reuses peer rows for every Jet tier, is the defect. G11Speed-4 is fixing the manifest contract and run.mjs so run-tier ratios use only the interpreted peers and compiled peers gate aot and build time. The c3 census waits for that fix and runs on b12. Sieve smoke on b11: aot beats all 5 peers on wall and peak; jet run is 0.73 s / 271 MB, all front end over Core (load 280 ms, comptime.bodies 210 ms, core_demand 140 ms, finalize 130 ms), which is the #6759 root.

criteria.text: The perf gate encodes the peer floor: on the canonical manifest it fails every required cell where Jet/peer is at or above 1.00 on wall time or on peak memory for any matched peer, names the cell, peer, metric and ratio, and reports the asm-ceiling ratio without failing on it. A unit test plants one time loss and one memory loss and expects both refusals.
criteria.evidence: G11Speed-G40 landed on dev 6ca4d72969 (tool-only: Tools/gauntlet/harness run.mjs, status.mjs, measurement-manifest.test.mjs, matrix.json). Lander5 loop 2026-11-12 02:3x on HEAD 70cfb9499a plus the patch (seed-b10 jet@a0.0.45#c089d4d3), rc 0 on each: node --test --test-name-pattern="the peer floor fails a planted wall-time or peak-memory loss" Tools/gauntlet/harness/measurement-manifest.test.mjs (tests 1 pass 1 fail 0); --test-name-pattern="a cell passes on the peer floor; its ceiling ratio is reported only" (1/1, fail 0); --test-name-pattern="the matrix encodes the peer floor and the reported machine ceiling" (1/1, fail 0); node --test Tools/gauntlet/harness/status.test.mjs (10/10); node --test Tools/gauntlet/harness/integrated-gate.test.mjs (6/6). The gate fails a cell at Jet/peer >= 1.00 on wall or peak memory for any matched peer, names cell/peer/metric/ratio, and reports the ceiling ratio without failing. Out: $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Lander/loop/out/G11Speed-G40/{1..6}.out.

criteria.text: Every required cell measures peak memory for Jet and every matched peer with the same method. A cell or peer without a memory reading is reported as uncovered and fails the gate.
criteria.evidence: G11Speed-G40 landed on dev 6ca4d72969. Lander5 loop on HEAD 70cfb9499a plus the patch (seed-b10), rc 0: node --test --test-name-pattern="a missing peak-memory reading for Jet or a peer is uncovered" Tools/gauntlet/harness/measurement-manifest.test.mjs (tests 1 pass 1 fail 0): a missing Jet or peer runtime_peak_rss_kb reading is reported uncovered and blocks. --test-name-pattern="the matrix encodes the peer floor and the reported machine ceiling" (1/1): runtime_peak_rss_kb is a required comparison metric in every mode, measured by the one harness method for Jet and every peer. Out: $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Lander/loop/out/G11Speed-G40/{2,4}.out.

criteria.text: A loss census on the current compiler lists every cell, peer and metric where Jet loses. It groups the losses by root (the codegen, runtime or Core mechanism responsible), and each root is on a card with its general fix.

Structural coverage beyond the cells: a generated or curated corpus of at least 30 programs that use the language's features in varied ways (the gauntlet programs and their peer twins) is measured against the peers on wall time and peak memory, and its losses join the census, so that a fix that only helps a measured cell is caught.

The loss census is empty: on the canonical manifest and the coverage corpus, Jet beats every matched peer on wall time and peak memory, each fix proven on a second program that uses the feature differently.

Peak memory is measured per program, not per harness. The gauntlet's peak_rss readings no longer inherit the timer's own high-water mark across exec: each reading is the measured process's own exact VmHWM, read at its exit, for every peer and Jet alike. Proof: the Jet hello binary reads under 1 MB through both the gauntlet timer and GNU time; coreutils true reads within 5% of its exact /proc VmHWM at exit; the timer's own overhead on wall time is reported for one cell; and the hello cell's rss is re-judged under the fixed timer. (Found 2026-11-12: timer.py's ru_maxrss gave every reading a floor of about 15.3 MB.)

ScriptBench peak memory is measured per program too. Its rss column comes from hyperfine's memory_usage_byte, which reads hyperfine's own high-water floor: Jet hello (exactly 0.19 MB) and coreutils true (exactly 2.47 MB) both read 3.66 MB, so every rss row under about 3.7 MB is the harness floor. Bench.jet reads each run's exact VmHWM at exit through the G51 launcher. Proof: the hello and true rows read within 5% of their /proc VmHWM, and the ScriptBench rss rows are re-judged.

cards.title: Compile-time folding bakes vDSO reads: rt.clock_mono_ns() in a local became one build's constant
cards.body: Found by G4Ports-1, 2026-11-11, root of the run-cold-context parity failure. sema's comptime-local folding treated an initializer as pure when the seccomp filter saw no syscall. vDSO reads such as clock_gettime never trap, so 'now: rt.clock_mono_ns()' in Core/Http/Client.jet __client_until held one build's reading: every 500 ms HTTP send failed at once in a process older than that. The same latent bake sits in the Tls, Db, Server, Web and Wayland deadlines. Fix: G4Ports-clock.

log.text: c2 amended (Main, 2026-11-13). G10Safe-runtime-reads2 gave the live cell IO, and IO then spread into every Db write signature (Core/Db/Db.jet execute and rollback), which broke corelib. An effect row is the wrong tool for a read whose effect is invisible to the caller. Such reads are now run-time-only (RUNTIME_ONLY_READS), which already exists and is consulted by the same never-fold rule, so this adds no second mechanism. Bindings whose effect is real to the caller (watcher poll IO, task_cpu_ns Time) still carry rows. A keep-going sweep over Core, Compiler, Jetpack, Tools, Examples and tests found 0 IO and 0 Time violations.

Main ruling 2026-11-12 (c2 scope): the goal is that no ambient read is baked into the image; an effect row is one means. task_identity keeps an empty row (context is an implicit input, D-CONTEXT-EFFECT1=F) but joins a sema run-time-only set (the c3 never-computed-while-compiling rule), avoiding a Context row cascade into Compiler trace functions. os_family may stay reviewed-pure only if a case shows a cross-target fold yields the target family; otherwise it joins the run-time-only set. The census names each reviewed entry with its reason.

criteria.text: Sema folds a local at compile time only when the solved effect row of its initializer is empty. An initializer that reaches Time, Rand or any other effect is never folded, whatever syscall path it takes (vDSO included), and seccomp is only a backstop. Proof: a #Test that fails on the base compiler (two clock reads in one process equal) and passes on the fix, a second test for another vDSO-backed read, and the run-cold-context PortBars parity cases 2, 5, 6 and 7 passing.
criteria.evidence: 32cf234624: jet test Core/Http/Client.jet -> 1 passed 0 failed; jet test Core/Net/Tls.jet -> 6 passed 0 failed (Lander holdsweep $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Lander/holds/7-6758-c1.out)

criteria.text: Every runtime binding that reads ambient state is never computed while compiling. It either declares the effect it reads (so the empty-row rule refuses to fold it, as clock_mono_ns does), or it is a run-time-only read (RUNTIME_ONLY_READS) when an effect row would spread into user signatures that never perform that effect. live_load and replace reach every Db write, so they are run-time-only reads. Found by G4Ports-1, 2026-11-12: live_load, task_identity, simd_lanes, os and os_family, clipboard_get and event_pop had empty rows. Proof: a census #Test lists every jet.runtime binding with an empty row and no run-time-only listing, and fails unless that list matches the reviewed pure list. A comptime case shows each read runs at run time on O0, O1 and O2 as a local, and is E0643 as a module value.

A computation whose result carries a raw address or a pointer (RawOf, RawAddressOf, PtrFromAddr), or a local value whose body runs #Unsafe code, is never computed while compiling, whatever its effect row says: a compile-time address has no runtime frame. Module values take the raw rule only, because Core has 171 #Unsafe blocks and a refused module value is an E0643 build error. Found 2026-11-12: a1e1b740f6 folded addr: leak(), so the expired-stack sentry reported R0801 instead of R0802. Proof: jet test Compiler --profile cases tests/cases/custom/sentry_fault_kinds_hold_at_every_tier.case (expired-stack R0802, provenance R0801, quarantine R0802, at O0, O1 and O2), and tests/cases/custom/sentry_faults_are_tier_parity.case, both PASS.
criteria.evidence: 21b423faed: jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter custom/sentry_fault -> PASS 2/2 (Lander holdsweep $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Lander/holds/8-6758-c3.out)

cards.title: Cold compile of a small script is about 1-4 s, and comptime.bodies is its largest phase
cards.body: Measured by G4Ports-1, 2026-11-11, on seed-b9, from the #5072 port twins (PortBars runs each twin from source, so every case pays a cold compile). jetc-trace, a 148-line file: jet run 1063 ms, against a 3 ms run of the built binary and node's 24 ms. Its phases: comptime.bodies 0.29 s (4 comptime programs built and run), load 0.26, sema.finalize 0.19, register 0.07, ir.build+opt+x64 0.07, link about 0.01. run-cold-context: jet run -- --help takes 4108 ms against node's 40 ms. Its phases: comptime.bodies 1.26 s (31 programs, 381 functions), sema.finalize 0.80, load 0.60, ir.opt 0.40, register 0.23, ir.build 0.08, x64 0.08. The port bar measures exactly what the 30M lines/s cold-compile target is about: the cost is general compile cost, not twin code.
cards.plan: Steps 1b and 1c of the owner-ordered speed program; the full ordered plan is the plan of #5479. Owner: G11Speed-4, after 1a. 1b: c10 (D-CORE-LAYERS1 reach rule and Core layers), slices S1-S6. 1c: c1, c5, c2, c4 and c9, then c8 and c3.

log.text: Main 2026-11-12 (c10, tactical finding): D-CORE-LAYERS1=A fixes the four-layer table, with encoding, data, compute and crypto in layer 1 under files. criteria.text: comptime.bodies costs one compile-and-run for the whole compilation, not one per comptime program: every comptime body of a compilation is built into one image at O0 and run in one child, keeping each body's own failure report (collect-all) and its I9 meaning. Proof: the phase trace of jet run for the jetc-trace and run-cold-context twins shows a single comptime child, and comptime.bodies falls at least 4x from 0.29 s and 1.26 s on seed-b9, with every comptime case and golden unchanged.

Core load and sema.finalize for a script that imports a few Core modules cost time in proportion to the Core code the script reaches, not to all of Core. Proof: the phase trace of run-cold-context shows load plus sema.finalize under 0.3 s (1.40 s on seed-b9), with a second program that imports a different Core subset showing the same scaling.
The jetc-trace and run-cold-context PortBars speed rows (wall time and peak memory, each case compiling from cold) pass against the node originals.

Peak memory of a cold jet run scales with the code reached, as wall time does. Measured by Lander5 on seed-b10, 2026-11-12 01:36: every orchestrator twin peaks at 344-379 MB against 6.6-48 MB for its original (integrate10 379 against 6.6 MB, native-c-compiler 360 against 48 MB), which fails the port memory bar for every twin. Proof: on the batch compiler, jet run of a hello-plus-x.abs() script peaks at no more than node's peak for the same script on the same host, and the PortBars memory rows of batch10, streamb10, integrate10, integ-land4, lane-commit and native-c-compiler pass (Jet at or below the original's peak).

The type-level comptime precheck builds no more than one child per compilation. Today run-cold-context builds 2 (the user constant NUL alone, then the Core SSL field defaults cert_profile and conf) before comptime.bodies builds its one. The precheck values that feed types are batched into one image and one child, keeping each value's own failure report and its I9 meaning. Proof: the jet run phase trace for run-cold-context shows at most one precheck child and one comptime.bodies child, with every comptime case and golden unchanged.

Owner target 2026-11-12: every landed Jet tool twin (#5072) runs its job dramatically faster than its original and as close as physically possible to hand-optimized machine code for the same job, on wall time and peak memory, each case compiling from cold. cards.title: EncodingCause as an error type ICEs: runtime routes name a mangled handle-drop and record-get symbol the runtime does not export
cards.body: Found by Lander5 in the b10 merged cases run, 2026-11-11: 36 case rows end in ERROR, an internal compiler error with exit 101. Every encoding stream case is hit (corelib cbor, csv, xml, json and jsonl streams, corelib_parts_encoding_streams, corelib_parts_encoding_surface xml, encoding_hostile_io, encoding_parity, encoding_cause_is_a_failure_domain). The fault: runtime route jet_rt_handle_drop_jet_x3ccorelib_x3e_score_dencoding_c_c_encoding_cause, and jet_rt_record_get_..._encoding_cause_kind, which the Jet runtime does not export (it exports jet_rt_handle_drop_encoding_cause). Bisect: jet build of the text_and_file_readers_keep_distinct_checked_layouts fixture gives rc 0 on seed-b7 and seed-b8 (776b3d1191), and rc 101 on seed-b9 (c805093fd9) and seed-b10. The only b8..b9 commit touching EncodingCause is 892727fd3a (TlsLead #6615 S13: EncodingCause becomes an error type, with #[Error, Equatable] and a JET_CORE_ERROR_TYPES row). Its own deferred lines were rc 1 on b9 and b10. A backend rejection of checked code is an I2 internal error.

criteria.text: A Core type that becomes an error type keeps one runtime symbol for each of its handle and record routes: codegen and the runtime derive the name from the same source (the runtime's export table, or one mangling function used by both), so no route names a symbol the runtime does not export. Proof: the 36 encoding case rows from b10 pass on the next batch compiler, TlsLead-6615s13b-h's deferred lines pass, and a #Test or case declares a second Core error type and builds a program that drops and reads it on O0, O1 and O2.

cards.title: jet test packages profile ignores the memory limit: package_jobs runs 4+ children of about 5.5 GB each and is OOM-killed under any cap below about 22G
cards.body: Found by G5DevX-1, 2026-11-11 23:56: jet test Compiler --profile packages under a systemd-run scope with MemoryMax 12G or 14G was OOM-killed. The journal says the kernel OOM killer killed processes in the unit, and OOMPolicy=stop then sent SIGTERM to the parent jet, which gave rc 143 with no output. That happens even for a 2-package filter. Compiler/test.jet package_jobs() runs max(PACKAGE_JOBS=4, cpus/4) package children at once, and its own comment budgets about 5.5 GB each. It never reads the profile memory setting or the cgroup memory.max, while the corpus pool does. The job count should come from the same memory budget the corpus pool uses, and never exceed the number of selected packages.

log.text: c1 (JetLSP packages 39/39 under a 10G scope, plus the job-count #Test) and c2 (the census jetpack-areas row fits its lanes, no exit 137) are met. All criteria met.

criteria.text: jet test Compiler --profile packages sizes its concurrent package children from the cgroup memory.max and the profile memory setting, through the same budget function as the corpus pool, and never runs more children than the selected packages. Proof: jet test Compiler --profile packages --filter Compiler/JetLSP under a 10G MemoryMax scope passes with 39 rows, 39 passed, plus a #Test of the job count for given memory, CPU and package numbers.
criteria.evidence: G5DevX-package-jobs-memory landed as afca453b51: Compiler/test.jet package_jobs sizes concurrent package children from a quarter of the CPUs, lowered to the PACKAGE_MEMORY claims that fit the cgroup memory.max and the profile memory setting through JetTestKit's kit_claim_jobs, the same budget function as the corpus pool, and capped at the runs there are. b11 deferred pass (Lander5, 2026-11-12) on the batch tip with seed-b11 jet@a0.0.45#3667b9a1 (built at 19333b2bb3). systemd-run --user --scope -p MemoryMax=10G -p MemorySwapMax=0 jet test Compiler --profile packages --filter Compiler/JetLSP: rc 0, '39 rows, 39 passed, 0 failed' (deferred-b11/159.out; without the patch the same scope was OOM-killed, rc 143). jet test Compiler/JetTestKit/Tests/Core.jet --filter 'claimed runs': 1 passed, 0 failed (the #Test of the job count for given memory, CPU and run numbers; deferred-b11/158.out). The SUB's other two lines are outside c1 and route to G5DevX-1: the whole-JetTestKit run (242 pass, red only on the judge's skip flag) and jet build Compiler/ (rc 137 at its 10G scope cap, rerun under 24G in b12).

cards.title: Debug display of a value holding Shared<T> passes sema and then ICEs in ir.build
cards.body: Found 2026-11-12 by Lander5. On seed-b10 (jet@a0.0.45#c089d4d3), jet build --profile dev Compiler at dev 7446243b8b exits 101 with: ir.build unlowered: jet_driver_recheck_differences: display of Shared<SemaLookupCounters> at JetDriver/Source/Driver/BodyComptime.jet:17421. The line is "{our_graph:Debug}" != "{their_graph:Debug}". Sema accepted a :Debug interpolation of a value that holds Shared<SemaLookupCounters>, but lowering has no display for Shared, so checked code reaches an internal error. That breaks I2 and I3. G4Ports-1 is changing the call site to avoid it; this card covers the root.

log.text: Both criteria are met.

Workaround G4Ports-ctfix (BodyComptime.jet): the JET_RECHECK_VERIFY comparison now skips the modules and registration_graph rows of SemaGraphResult, because their types hold Shared<SemaLookupCounters>. When c1 lands, restore the full comparison of those two rows in jet_driver_recheck_graph_rows in the same SUB, so the recheck verifies the registration graph again.

criteria.text: Either :Debug display works for every type sema accepts in an interpolation, Shared<T> included (rendered as its inner value, the same on O0, O1 and O2), or sema refuses the interpolation with a registered diagnostic that has a UI snapshot. A case covers a struct field of type Shared<T> under :Debug. jet build --profile dev Compiler no longer has a path to ICE 101 on it.
criteria.evidence: G6Meta-89 landed on dev 5e488a6cbc: sema refuses :Debug of a struct with a Shared<T> field with E0112, and the ui row tests/ui/debug_display_of_a_shared_field_is_refused.jet passes 1/1 on seed-b13 ($JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Lander/loop/out/direct-G6Meta-89/1.out).

criteria.text: Intake gap: ec6bdb7feb (G4Ports-ctrecheck) changed compiler sources and landed without a compiler build check, so the ICE surfaced only at the b11 build. Every compiler-input SUB at intake gets at least jet check of each touched compiler module on the train compiler, and the train's build catches the rest before landing. The Lander's intake does this, shown by its intake rule and one rejected sample.

Then Land.jet receipt and check-gate accepted it, and the admit reached the release gate before it was stopped by hand (no publish). cards.title: Diagnostic coverage credits orphan snapshot text that no producer still prints
cards.body: Found by G5DevX-1 on 2026-11-12 during the #3720 c79 id sweep. tests/fixtures/jetpack-diagnostics is read only as snapshot text: tests/guards/diagnostics_coverage.jet:147 (dc_snapshot_texts) and Compiler/JetTestKit Ui.jet:682 (kit_ui_coverage) both credit it as rendered coverage, but neither checks that a producer still prints it. Live producers have moved on. JetOS/Source/LoadValidate.jet:18 E0979 now renders 'a bare host selects system.<host> in ./package.jet…', while the snapshot still holds the old decision-id text and ./config.jet. EnvModel ModuleEval/EnvPlanBuilder.jet:372 E1327 renders 'an environment image projects…', while module-eval-diagnostics/E1327.stderr holds a decision-id line and an old Fix. The jetpack_jetos cases are opt-in (-- --ignored), so nothing re-renders them. This breaks I4: a snapshot that no producer run checks is not evidence. Fix at the root, sweeping every snapshot directory first: tests/guards/diagnostics_snapshots.jet (which owns the snapshot-directory list, line 14) requires every listed snapshot to be compared against a live producer run in some suite that runs by default; orphan fixtures are re-rendered from their producer or deleted; dc_snapshot_texts and kit_ui_coverage count only producer-checked snapshots. Every stale text is re-blessed from its live producer, with no ids, in the same batch.

cards.title: I9: a built binary keeps strings past their last use (memory_semantics/strings_free_at_their_last_use passes on jet run, fails after jet build)
cards.body: Reproduced by G11Speed-4 on 2026-11-12 on seed-b13 against origin/dev; not marked known-failing. jet run at O0, O1, O2 and default passes. The built binary (jet build --optimize=full, then run it) exits 70: 'Stop [E3001]: panic: last use: peak grew 97536 kB, more than 1.5 strings of 50000000 bytes' at main.jet:31 in measure. Drop at last use holds when run from memory but not in the built artifact: one meaning across tiers (I9) is broken. Repro: $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/G11Speed/work/gen/devred/.

log.text: Answered the owner question on D-COMPTIME-SIZE1 (q197tdsb). c3 (read-only placement), c4 (length folding) and new c5 (unread bytes not emitted) are fixes built without a vote. The ballot is to be rewritten around the one remaining owner choice: optional compressed storage for large read data in size-targeted builds, with measured options and an adversarial review, before it goes back to the owner. Option A (report only) is withdrawn as the recommendation.

criteria.text: memory_semantics/strings_free_at_their_last_use tests strings made at run time (their size comes from a run-time input, so the compiler can't fold them), keeps its peak assertion, and passes for jet run at O0/O1/O2 and for the binary jet build --optimize=full produces. The compile-time rule is unchanged: no size bound makes a computable value fall back to run time.
criteria.evidence: G11Speed-G50c landed on dev ad118e5f34: the case reads its size from STRING_BYTES at run time, and its jet test line passes on seed-b13 at O0/O1/O2 (sweep g50c-6769). The --optimize=full binary (232,544 bytes) runs with STRING_BYTES=50000000, rc 0, printing one string live at each peak (sweep g50c-6769b, $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Lander/loop/out/meet-g50c-6769b/1.out). No compiler change: the compile-time rule is unchanged.

criteria.text: The owner rules on ballot D-COMPTIME-SIZE1 (a very large build-time constant in a binary: do nothing, a lint, or a compact encoding), and the ratified option's build criteria are added here.

A build-time constant's payload is mapped read-only: immutable folded data lands in a read-only ELF segment, not a writable one. Found by the D-COMPTIME-SIZE1 review on seed-b13. Proof: readelf of a built binary holding a large folded String shows its bytes in a non-writable PT_LOAD, and a case asserts it.

A consumer that needs only a large constant's length does no run-time scan of it. In the ballot program, `big.len()` of a folded 50 MB String folds to its constant, and the emitted IR holds no Unicode scalar count over it. Proof: jet inspect decisions shows the folded length, and a case checks the IR.

Bytes of a build-time value that no run-time code reads are not emitted. In the D-COMPTIME-SIZE1 program (two 50 MB repeats used only for their lengths), the --optimize=full binary holds neither run and is within 10% of the size of the same program reading its size at run time (136,272 bytes on seed-b13). Proof: a case builds it, asserts the binary size bound and the output 100000000, and readelf shows no 50 MB run.

Build-time evaluation costs no more than running the same code: building the D-COMPTIME-SIZE1 Collatz table at compile time takes at most the time and peak memory of the same code run at run time plus the compiler's own floor. Measured by the ballot review on seed-b13, 2026-11-12: 12 s and 4.1 GB at compile time against 1.24-1.29 s and 596 MB at run time ($JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/ballots/probes/D-COMPTIME-SIZE1/review/runtime.txt).

cards.title: Tests fail under machine load: a wall-clock step limit turns slow into failed
cards.body: Owner, 2026-11-12: a test that fails under load, rather than passing more slowly, is a reliability defect. In the a0.0.45 admit of dev 2844b04984 (run beside a train build, landings and probes), about 200 rows across candidate chunks 2-5 and 8 were TIMEOUT or ERROR. 82 golden, 20 ui and 59 cases rows passed only on retry. Five browser_bidi and web_app rows ERRORed with an empty 'free-port probe failed', because the probe's own wall-clock timeout was reported without its reason. The root: JetTestKit gives every step a 60 s wall-clock timeout (Compiler/JetTestKit/Source/Exec.jet KitOptions timeout: 60, process.cmd(...).timeout), so a loaded host's slowness is judged as failure. The admit retry masks it instead of fixing it.

criteria.text: A test step's limit judges the work, not the host's load: JetTestKit bounds each step by the CPU time of the step's process tree (unaffected by other load). The wall-clock limit stays only as a hang guard, set far enough out that a loaded host can't reach it on a working step. A hit on either limit reports TIMEOUT with the limit kind, the CPU and wall seconds used, and the step. A Core.jet #Test proves a CPU-bound step that exceeds the CPU limit is TIMEOUT (cpu) and that a step sleeping past its wall guard is TIMEOUT (wall).

Every helper inside a test step that has its own deadline reports a deadline miss with its reason, never as an ERROR with an empty message. This covers the free-port probe (kit_steps_free_ports, StepsTokens.jet) and any readiness or port wait in the case harness. A case forces the free-port probe past its deadline and checks the TIMEOUT reason.

Load sweep: the corpus rows that were TIMEOUT, ERROR, or passed only on retry in the a0.0.45 admit are run again while a load generator holds every core busy (for example stress-ng at 2x the core count). Every row passes, and each failure found on the way is fixed at its root: either the harness limit, or a product deadline. A product deadline in Jet's runtime or Core (a BiDi handshake, a service delivery wait, a readiness wait) waits on its event or uses the user's own deadline, never a fixed wall time that load can exhaust. The rows, the generator and the result are recorded.

The release gate stops masking load sensitivity: a row that fails and then passes on retry is reported in REPORT.md as a flaky row with its two outcomes, and fails the gate unless it carries a disposition that names an owning card.

A build action's time limit judges the action's work, not the host's load, the same as test steps (c1). It bounds the action by the CPU time of its process tree and keeps a wall-clock limit only as a far-out hang guard. Today, on G6Meta-7-r5's CHAIN line 13 (b14, 08:13), jet build --profile dev Compiler failed with E3505 'Build action runtime ran past its time limit of 600000ms' at a 10.9G peak while the deferred pass and a 30G probe loaded the host, while the unloaded base passed. Proof: that build passes with every core held busy by a load generator, and a case shows a looping action still stops at its CPU limit with E3505.

cards.title: A string or byte literal body after an effect row lexes as a typed head, so escapes and holes are wrong
cards.body: Found by G12Docs-4 (G12Docs-69) on seed-b13: h: fn() -[]> String { "a\nb" } prints a literal backslash-n. Compiler/JetLexer/Source/Lexer/Payload.jet string_head_modes reads Ident { followed by a string as a typed head (raw text, holes, undecoded escapes), and its only exemption for a return type, returned_type_at, recognizes just ) -> before the type. After an effect arrow -[E]> the body String { ... } becomes the typed head String{...}: \n stays raw, \u{41} becomes \u plus a hole, and interpolation breaks. The [U8] { byte head has the same gap. char literals, return, parenthesized and if bodies are unaffected. It is wrong output with no diagnostic.

criteria.text: A function body that is a string, byte or interpolated literal lexes as a body after every return-type form: -> T, an effect arrow -[E]> T with one or several effects, generic, list, map, optional, fallible and qualified return types. Its escapes decode and its holes interpolate exactly as in the same body after -> T. A case covers each literal kind (escapes, \u{...}, interpolation, byte strings) with and without an effect row, at O0, O1 and O2, and a real typed head written as a body expression still lexes as a typed head.

The typed-head decision is made in one place from the parser's knowledge of the return-type position, not from a lexer token-pattern guess that each new return-type spelling must extend. The tests/ and Examples corpus show no output change other than the fixed cases, by the golden profile at O0, O1 and O2.

cards.title: I9: string interpolation of a Display type prints a struct dump while compiling but its Display text at run time
cards.body: A user struct with impl Display interpolated as "{value}" prints its Display text at run time (default level and --optimize=none) but the derived dump (Failure { query: query, code: 7 }) when the same interpolation runs under #run. One spelling, two meanings across tiers (I9). Repro: $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/G6Meta/r6/diag/d.jet on seed-b13. Found by G6Meta-4 in the G6Meta-36 query program, which now calls .display() explicitly as a stopgap.

criteria.text: The root is named and fixed: interpolation while compiling formats a value through the same Display path as run time, in one shared runtime mechanism, not a second formatter. A case interpolates a Display struct, an enum with Display, a nested field and a value without Display, and prints identical text under #run and at run time on O0, O1 and O2.

The stopgap explicit .display() calls in the G6Meta-36, 40 and 43 query programs and 43 fixture main.jet are reverted to plain "{err}", and inspect_facts_program_store_is_the_build_query still passes on every tier.

options.name: Public schemas from first write flow
options.detail: Studio and CI share stable JSON immediately.
options.code: jetos plan --json

options.name: Internal GUI schema first
options.detail: Faster GUI iteration, but CI cannot trust the same artifact.
options.code: internal schema

options.name: Public after read-only Studio (recommended)
options.detail: Stabilize once projection fields prove out, before activation handoff.
options.code: public before switch flows

comparisons.note: Plans are useful because CI and humans inspect the same object.

decisions.title: Declarative containers and microVMs
decisions.gist: Choose how jetos declares containers and microVMs under one proof model.
decisions.explainer: Best hybrid: one proof-backed workload model with explicit isolation backends.
decisions.story: Walter runs Postgres in a container and a risky service in a microVM. Both need network, storage, secrets, health checks, and rollback proof, but they should not become two unrelated config languages.
decisions.detail: Hybrid review 2026-07-07: recommended option combines the beginner/default path with expert control where that preserves one semantic mechanism. Best hybrid: one proof-backed workload model with explicit isolation backends.

options.name: Hybrid: workload declarations with container/microVM profiles (recommended)
options.detail: One workload.<name> mechanism declares isolated workloads. The backend enum selects Container or MicroVM; shared fields cover image/package, ports, mounts, secrets, health, resources, proof, and rollback. Backend-specific knobs live under nested profiles. Beginners see one concept; experts control isolation depth.

options.name: Separate `containers` and `microvms` trees
options.detail: Matches ecosystem words and keeps backend specifics obvious, but duplicates policy/proof fields.
options.code:
containers.db { image: image.postgres }
microvms.sandbox { memory: 2048.MiB }

options.name: Packages only
options.detail: Treat containers/VMs as packages launched by services. Reuses service machinery, but hides isolation/proof semantics.
options.code: services.db.exec: package.postgres_container.run

comparisons.note: Powerful but split modules; Jet can unify proof concepts.

decisions.title: Hardware profiles and specialisations
decisions.gist: Choose the surface for hardware scans, reusable device profiles, and boot-selectable variants.
decisions.explainer: Best hybrid: generated local truth, reusable device knowledge, and boot-selectable variants without duplicating hosts.
decisions.story: Earl installs on a laptop with NVIDIA and a desktop with GPU passthrough. He needs hardware facts generated once, community profiles applied explicitly, and specialisations selectable at boot without duplicating a host.
decisions.inWild:
jet os init devhost
// emits what? how do variants compose?
decisions.detail: Hybrid review 2026-07-07: recommended option combines the beginner/default path with expert control where that preserves one semantic mechanism. Best hybrid: generated local truth, reusable device knowledge, and boot-selectable variants without duplicating hosts.

options.name: Hybrid: scanned hardware modules plus reusable profiles and specialisations (recommended)
options.detail: Hardware scan emits hardware.<host> source. Systems import that source and can apply first-party/community hardware profile packages. Specialisations are named boot variants over the same host and generation, with option-priority/explain output showing what changed.

options.name: Inline hardware in system
options.detail: All facts live in system.<host>. Fewer modules, but generated hardware and authored policy mix noisily.
options.code: system.devhost { hardware.gpu: .Nvidia }

options.name: Profile packages only
options.detail: Hardware profiles are packages users add. Good sharing, weak for local scan facts and drift reporting.
options.code: packages: [hardware.nixos-hardware.framework-13]

comparisons.note: hardware-configuration.nix + nixos-hardware + specialisations are separate conventions.

decisions.title: Declarative disks and impermanence
decisions.gist: Choose how disk layouts, encryption, filesystems, and persisted paths are declared.
decisions.explainer: Best hybrid: guided beginner install and expert disko/impermanence power share one storage source truth.
decisions.story: Inez wants btrfs subvolumes, LUKS, an ephemeral root, and a precise persist list. The installer must show exactly what will be destroyed and what survives rollback before touching a disk.
decisions.detail: Hybrid review 2026-07-07: recommended option combines the beginner/default path with expert control where that preserves one semantic mechanism. Best hybrid: guided beginner install and expert disko/impermanence power share one storage source truth.

options.name: Hybrid: storage tree consumed by installer and activation (recommended)
options.detail: One storage tree declares disks, partitions, encryption, filesystems, mounts, ephemeral roots, and persistence. The installer uses the same source for destructive actions; activation uses it for mounts and persistence proof. Guided install can draft storage source, never own hidden disk state.

options.name: Separate `disk` and `impermanence` modules
options.detail: Mirrors existing tools. Clear boundaries, but persistence and mount truth can drift.
options.code:
disk.main { ... }
impermanence.persist: ["/var/lib"]

options.name: Installer-generated only
options.detail: Installer records disk facts outside source. Fast first install, but not reproducible or reviewable.
options.code: jet os install --guided

comparisons.note: Community tools solve each half separately; Jet can make one proof-backed source.

decisions.title: Declarative theming
decisions.gist: Choose the source surface for wallpaper, palette, fonts, cursor, and per-app theme projection.
decisions.explainer: Best hybrid: one reusable theme source with exact host/app control and Studio preview over the same facts.
decisions.story: Doris wants one wallpaper and palette to drive GTK, Qt, terminals, editors, and the display manager, with per-app opt-outs and Studio preview. It should be first-party source, not community glue.
decisions.detail: Hybrid review 2026-07-07: recommended option combines the beginner/default path with expert control where that preserves one semantic mechanism. Best hybrid: one reusable theme source with exact host/app control and Studio preview over the same facts.

options.name: Hybrid: reusable theme profiles with inline host overrides (recommended)
