options.technical: Single user field on deploy.target. Activation uses the same account as SSH. No first-class connect/activate split in the default surface.

options.name: Forbid root SSH
options.detail: Connect user must be non-root. Activation is always root for system profiles. Gain: strong SSH policy. Loss: labs and recovery hosts that need root SSH become second-class or blocked.
options.technical: Sema rejects connectUser == root. System activation always escalate to root through a declared privilege path.

options.name: SSH config owns identity
options.detail: Jet stores only the host label. OpenSSH config picks the user. Activation privilege stays implicit. Gain: familiar for operators. Loss: Jet cannot type-check or prove the full authority graph from source.
options.technical: Conflicts with D-JOS-FLEETTARGET1 proof-visible authority. Would reintroduce inventory outside Jet source.
options.code:
# ~/.ssh/config
Host web1
  User deploy

# Jet source has no connect/activate users
fleet.prod { hosts: { web1: system.web } }

comparisons.note: Profiles set user for activation and sshUser for the SSH login. Docs recommend a wheel user for SSH and root for activation.
D-JOS-FLEETTARGET1 already requires typed target and privilege facts in source and proof. This ballot picks the beginner default shape.
comparisons.code:
# from D-JOS-FLEETTARGET1=A
# host target/authority fields are proof-visible

recommendation.why: Split identities match real remote deploy practice and keep root SSH optional. Beginners get a safer default while experts can still write root for both.

whyNot.reason: One user field pushes beginners toward root SSH and hides the privilege boundary.
A hard ban on root SSH blocks valid lab and recovery setups that Jet should still allow explicitly.
Authority outside Jet source breaks typed proof and conflicts with D-JOS-FLEETTARGET1.

recommendation.tradeoff: First deploy needs keys and a privilege path on the host. Accepted: that setup cost is the price of a safe default, and preflight names the missing piece.

reviewPasses.base: Compared split users, one user, forbid-root SSH, and SSH-config identity. Recommended split connect and activate with wheel-plus-root defaults.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: Also tested sudo-only without typed activate user and agent-forwarding only. Folded those into A and D as incomplete authority graphs.
reviewPasses.hybrid: Kept optional root-for-both inside A instead of a separate hybrid row, so one mechanism covers beginner and expert.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Strengthened B for tiny fleets and C for hard policy shops. B still weakens SSH defaults; C over-blocks recovery hosts.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Attacked missing NOPASSWD or key setup as silent hangs. Preflight must fail closed with a clear diagnostic before switch.

decisions.title: JetOS install trust without App Store gatekeeping
decisions.gist: How jetos stops malware while still letting people install and run software they choose or build.
decisions.lesson: Apple treats central review and signing locks as security. Those locks also block owner-built apps, peer share, plugins, and fast local tools. jetos already has generations, Flatpak policy, hangar hashes, and Studio risk gates. This choice sets the default trust law for installs. It must protect beginners and keep owner freedom. The same law covers any future jetos device class unless a later ballot changes it.
decisions.story: Maya builds a small drawing app on her jetos laptop and wants her friend to try it tonight. She also wants her parents' laptop to resist random malware from a download. She needs one system that allows her share and still protects the family machine.
decisions.inWild:
# Maya shares a local package with a friend (must work without Jet review):
$ jet pack ./doodle
$ jet install ./doodle.jetpkg
# friend sees capability prompt, not a rejection

# Studio Apps install from catalog:
# Install "Music Player" -> sandboxed; Photos access needs an explicit grant

# After a bad install:
$ jet os generations rollback
# previous generation returns; provenance still names the package

options.name: Capability-first freedom
options.detail: Anyone may install software they choose or build. Third-party and foreign apps start with almost no power. The user grants files, network, devices, or agents later. Hangar hashes and optional publisher signatures feed trust UI. They never block an owner-built local install. Generations and rollback repair bad installs. There is no central review and no category ban.
options.technical: Default runtime policy for user apps and Flatpak refs is deny-by-default capabilities with explicit grants in Studio or Jet config. System hangar closures keep supply-chain integrity (hash, sign/verify, locks). Owner-local packages and jet run paths skip notarization. Catalog ranking may prefer signed publishers; ranking is not a hard gate. Family or enterprise lock modules may tighten policy as expert opt-in.
options.code:
# config.jet — beginner default stays free to install, tight to run
apps.flatpak.permissions.default: .Deny

# friend installs Maya's package
$ jet install ./doodle.jetpkg
grant needed: Documents (read)
# after grant, app runs; no Jet notary step

options.name: Notarization gate
options.detail: Only packages signed by Jet-approved keys or a central notary may run. Unsigned code is blocked unless a hard developer mode is on. That blocks many casual malware installs. Owner-built and peer-shared software become second-class. This repeats the App Store shape jetos is trying not to copy.
options.technical: Hard gate at activation: signature required against a Jet trust root. Local unsigned installs fail closed outside developer mode. Catalog and peer share both hit the same gate.
options.code:
$ jet install ./doodle.jetpkg
error: package is not notarized by Jet
hint: enable developer mode, or submit for review

options.name: Warn-only open install
options.detail: People may install and run anything with full host power. Unknown publishers only show warnings. Maximum freedom and simple plumbing. One hostile package can own the machine. Beginners get alerts instead of real limits.
options.technical: No default capability jail for GUI apps. Trust UI is advisory. Generations still roll back if the user notices damage in time.
options.code:
$ jet install ./free-game.jetpkg
warning: unknown publisher
# proceeds with full user powers

options.name: Curated beginners, free experts
options.detail: The default profile installs only from a curated catalog under sandbox rules. An expert profile unlocks free install. Safer default story. It teaches that real power lives in another mode. Beginners may never learn grants. The catalog risks becoming a soft App Store.
options.technical: Two named profiles in config. Beginner profile rejects non-catalog refs. Expert profile matches option A or C. Mode switch is explicit.
options.code:
profile: .Beginner
$ jet install ./doodle.jetpkg
error: beginner profile allows catalog apps only
hint: switch profile to .Expert

options.name: Disposable VM per app
options.detail: Every GUI app runs in a disposable microVM with gated portals. Strong isolation for hostile binaries. High cost in battery, memory, and desktop fit. Terminal tools and light apps pay a heavy tax. Portal grants are still required, so this does not replace a capability model.
options.technical: App launch always goes through a microVM or equivalent strong boundary. Portals mediate files and devices. Native hangar system services stay outside this path.
options.code:
$ jet install music-player
# launches inside app-vm; Documents access via portal prompt

comparisons.note: Central review and signing locks block whole categories. Security and rent seeking stay hard to separate.
comparisons.code: # no peer install path without Apple approval

comparisons.note: Apps can ship widely. Permissions start tight. Users grant more later. Closest open model to option A.
Hardened Android with stronger sandbox defaults and user control. Still a phone OS with store pressure around it.
comparisons.code: # install unknown apps allowed; sandbox remains

comparisons.note: Bad system changes roll back. Provenance and immutability help recovery. They do not replace app capability grants.

recommendation.why: Capability-first freedom matches jetos goals. Beginners get real limits by default. Owners can build and share without Jet review. Hangar identity, Studio risk gates, and generations already cover supply chain and recovery. The store stays a discovery surface, not a notary.

whyNot.reason: A notarization gate recreates App Store lock-in and blocks the kid-builds-and-shares story.
Warnings without capability limits leave beginners open to full-host malware.
A beginner-only catalog becomes a soft store and hides grants behind an expert mode.
Always-on microVMs add heavy cost and still need the same grant model for portals.

recommendation.tradeoff: Users can approve too many grants. Studio risk classes and clear prompts must keep that rare. Expert family locks can tighten later without changing the default.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared capability defaults, notarization, warn-only installs, split beginner profiles, and per-app VMs. It recommended capability-first freedom.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review also tested mandatory antivirus scanning and web-of-trust-only installs. Those folded into identity signals and expert policy under option A, not separate defaults.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review kept option A and added catalog ranking by signatures, generation rollback, and optional family locks. Those stay helpers, not hard gates.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened notarization with fast local developer mode and strengthened curated beginners with one-click expert escape. Each still blocks or hides owner freedom.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review tested peer-share malware, users who grant everything, and signed-but-hostile publishers. Sandbox defaults, rollback, provenance, and honest trust UI repair those cases, so option A remains.

decisions.title: One text for the jetos boot default: the record and the code disagree
decisions.gist: Which bootloader and kernel a fresh jetos machine starts with.
decisions.lesson: One ratified decision now has two texts. The board record for D-JOS-BOOTKERNEL1=A reads systemd-boot with a Linux long-term kernel. The syntax record, the jetos plan, and the shipped code all read Limine with the CachyOS kernel. A second ratified decision from the same day, D-JOS-KERNELSRC1=A, carries a first-party CachyOS kernel package, which the long-term kernel text does not allow. Three boot cards are queued against the Limine text. One owner line ends the split.
decisions.story: Sam installs jetos on a spare laptop. The machine must boot, roll back to the last generation, and show a menu that names each one. Sam does not choose a bootloader. Jet does, once, and every later card builds on that answer.

options.name: systemd-boot with the long-term kernel
options.detail: The default boot path is systemd-boot and the kernel is the Linux long-term release. This is what the ratified board record says today. It is the quiet, conservative answer, and it matches what most declarative Linux systems ship. The cost is that three queued cards, the syntax record, the jetos plan and the shipped code all say something else, so all of them change.
options.technical: Keeps the D-JOS-BOOTKERNEL1=A record as stored. Requires amending docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:4501, docs/plans/epoch-7/native-jetos.md, and the shipped jetos boot code, and reworking cards #909, #409 and #910. D-JOS-KERNELSRC1=A must also be reopened, because it ratifies a first-party CachyOS kernel package.

options.name: Limine with the CachyOS kernel
options.detail: The default boot path is Limine and the kernel is the CachyOS package. This is what the syntax record, the plan and the code already say, and it is what the sibling kernel decision from the same day ratifies. It also gives jetos a faster desktop kernel by default. The cost is that the stored decision text is wrong today and must be corrected so one text exists.
options.technical: Amends the D-JOS-BOOTKERNEL1 record to match its own rendered form at docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:4501. Agrees with D-JOS-KERNELSRC1=A, the first-party CachyOS kernel package with exact source, config, patches and hashes. Cards #909, #409 and #910 proceed as written. Expert override of the kernel package and boot entry fields is unchanged either way.

comparisons.note: Ships systemd-boot as the modern default and a long-term kernel, with GRUB still available.
Ships Limine as an option beside its own tuned kernel, which is the pairing option B names.
Uses GRUB2 with boot loader specification entries, so menu entries are files rather than a generated script.

recommendation.why: It is the answer already written into the syntax record, the plan and the shipped code, and the only one that agrees with D-JOS-KERNELSRC1=A from the same day. Choosing it corrects one stored sentence. Choosing the other rewrites four places and reopens a second ratified decision.

whyNot.reason: It contradicts D-JOS-KERNELSRC1=A, which ratifies a first-party CachyOS kernel package on the same day and the same card. It also forces a rewrite of the spec, the plan, the code and three queued cards.

recommendation.tradeoff: A tuned desktop kernel carries more patches than a long-term release, so jetos owns more upstream tracking. That is accepted because the kernel package is first-party and already ratified with exact source and hashes.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft set the stored decision text against the rendered spec text and recommended the rendered form, because the code and the sibling kernel decision both agree with it.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested a third answer, GRUB, and a fourth, no default with an install-time prompt. Both were dropped: no card, plan or line of code asks for either, and a prompt moves a settled choice onto the beginner.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review asked whether the loader and the kernel can be decided apart. They can, but nothing on the board wants that split, so the menu stays two coherent pairings.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review made the conservative answer as strong as it can be. A long-term kernel with systemd-boot is the least surprising pairing for a declarative system, and NixOS ships it.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review asked whether the stored record is right and the spec is the error. It could be, which is exactly why this needs an owner line rather than an agent judgement, and the ballot names both texts.

decisions.title: wasm32-wasi as a user-facing server target
decisions.gist: Whether `jet build` gains a server-side WebAssembly target.
decisions.lesson: WebAssembly (wasm) is a portable binary format. WASI is the system interface that lets a wasm program run outside a browser. Some hosting platforms run only wasm, because it starts fast and the host can sandbox it. Today `jet build --target=wasm32-wasip1` fails with E3302, because Jet ships no standard library for that target. Jet's browser target (`--target=web`) is separate and stays. This choice decides whether Jet promises a server wasm target, records a no, or routes wasm work through plugins.
decisions.story: Priya runs a platform team. Her company hosts tenant code on a wasmtime fleet, where every handler is one wasm module. She likes Jet and wants tenants to write handlers in it. She copies the build command from her platform docs and gets E3302. She must now tell her tenants whether Jet will ever build for this platform.
decisions.inWild:
# Priya follows her platform's docs:
$ jet build handler.jet --target=wasm32-wasip1
Error E3302: Target `wasm32-wasip1` is not available.
 Why: rustc doesn't have the standard library for this target compiled in, or the target triple is not recognised.
 Fix: Run `jet self doctor --target=wasm32-wasip1` to see what's missing, or `rustup target add wasm32-wasip1` to install it.

# She retries with a space instead of `=` (open defect, card #1899):
$ jet build handler.jet --target wasm32-wasip1
built: build/handler        # native binary — the flag was silently ignored

# Her wasm host then rejects build/handler: not a wasm module.

options.name: Full supported server target (wasm32-wasip2)
options.detail: Jet ships wasm32-wasip2 as a real server target: stdlib port, CI lane, and full tier parity (I9). Preview 2 carries wasi-sockets, so a Jet server can actually listen and serve, which preview 1 could not. The gain is every platform that deploys wasm server-side becomes a Jet platform. The cost is a stdlib port and a permanent CI lane, paid up front.
options.technical: Target triple wasm32-wasip2; sockets via wasi-sockets, filesystem via wasi-filesystem, entropy rides the existing CryptoEntropy wasi shims. E3302 retires for this triple. The example matrix and golden corpus gain a wasip2 column per I5/I9; no carve-out.
options.code:
$ jet build server.jet --target=wasm32-wasip2
built: build/server.wasm
$ wasmtime serve build/server.wasm
listening on 0.0.0.0:8080

options.name: Recorded non-goal for v1.x
options.detail: Jet says no, in writing. Native binaries are Jet's server story; a container wraps them when a platform needs isolation. The build error for wasi triples then names this decision, so nobody waits for a port that will not come. Gain: one server path, the whole standard library everywhere Jet claims to run, and no I9 carve-out. Loss: teams on wasm-only platforms cannot deploy Jet there in v1.x. The record names a revisit trigger: WASI preview 2 sockets settle and real user demand appears.
options.technical: No new target. The decision record lists the revisit trigger. E3302 gains a triple-specific message for `wasm32-wasi*` that cites D-WASISRV1 instead of suggesting `rustup target add`, which would mislead here. Card #1899 (space-form `--target` silently ignored) is fixed separately; a recorded no makes the correct rejection reachable by both spellings.
options.code:
# Today the error suggests installing a target Jet cannot use:
$ jet build server.jet --target=wasm32-wasip1
Error E3302: Target `wasm32-wasip1` is not available.
 Fix: Run `jet self doctor --target=wasm32-wasip1` to see what's missing, or `rustup target add wasm32-wasip1` to install it.

# After this option ships, the same command names the decision:
$ jet build server.jet --target=wasm32-wasip1
Error E3302: Target `wasm32-wasip1` is not available.
 Why: server-side WebAssembly is a recorded non-goal for v1.x (D-WASISRV1). Jet servers ship as native binaries.
 Fix: build a native binary with `jet build server.jet`, or package it in a container for your platform.

options.name: WASI only through the plugin surface
options.detail: Jet keeps sandboxed wasm where it already exists: `target: plugin` packages, which build as WASM Components and run fully sandboxed. A native Jet server loads tenant plugins and calls them. Gain: the sandbox case is served today, with a hard capability boundary — plugins are deny-by-default with zero host capabilities (E1258). Loss: a plugin cannot open a socket or read a file, so it can never be a server by itself. Platforms that want one wasm module per service still get nothing.
options.technical: No new target. Plugins compile via `rustc --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` plus `wasm-tools component` (E1259) and export all-`Int` or all-`Float` functions in v1 (E1260). E1258 and I1 forbid widening plugin capabilities, so this option cannot grow into a server story later without a new decision.
options.code:
# jetpack.toml of the sandboxed part:
[package]
name = "scorer"
target = "plugin"

$ jet build
built: build/scorer.wasm      # WASM Component, zero host capabilities

# A native Jet server embeds it:
plugin := Plugin.load("build/scorer.wasm")
result := plugin.call("score", [42])

# A plugin that touches the OS does not build:
Error E1258: A plugin can't use any effect.

options.name: Preview target under an I9 carve-out
options.detail: Jet ships the target now, marked preview, with an owner-ratified I9 carve-out that lists what is missing. A program that avoids the missing parts builds and runs today. Gain: early adopters and wasm platforms get a real artifact now, and the port grows in public. Loss: a beginner's program passes the toolchain, then stops at the first `core.net` call. Carve-out lists also grow stale, and recent tier drift (the `#Todo` AOT defect) shows how such gaps leak raw internals to users.
options.technical: The carve-out names the excluded modules (`core.net`, `core.exec`, threads) and the diagnostic that rejects them at compile time, in the E3301 style. CI runs the supported subset under wasmtime. The carve-out expires when WASI preview 2 sockets land or the owner renews it.
options.code:
$ jet build tool.jet --target=wasm32-wasip1
warning: wasm32-wasip1 is a preview target (D-WASISRV1 carve-out): core.net, core.exec, and threads are unavailable
built: build/tool.wasm
$ wasmtime run --dir=. build/tool.wasm
processed 3 files

# The first socket call is a compile-time stop:
$ jet build httpd.jet --target=wasm32-wasip1
Error: `net.listen` is not available in a wasm32-wasip1 build (preview carve-out D-WASISRV1).
 Fix: build a native binary with `jet build httpd.jet`, or keep this program off `core.net`.

comparisons.note: Go 1.21 shipped `GOOS=wasip1` as a port, not a first-class target. `net.Listen` fails at run time because WASI preview 1 has no sockets. Server use never arrived; the port serves plugins and scripts.
comparisons.code:
$ GOOS=wasip1 GOARCH=wasm go build -o main.wasm .
$ wasmtime run main.wasm
panic: listen tcp :8080: operation not permitted

comparisons.note: Rust keeps `wasm32-wasip1` at tier 2. The standard library compiles, but sockets and threads return errors at run time. Real servers on wasm use host worlds such as `wasi:http` instead of the target's own stdlib.
comparisons.code:
$ cargo build --target wasm32-wasip1   # builds
// std::net::TcpListener::bind(...) -> Err(Unsupported) at run time

comparisons.note: Wasm platforms answer the socket gap by owning the socket in the host: `wasmtime serve` speaks the `wasi:http` proxy world and hands the program one request at a time. Any future Jet server target would take this shape, not a ported `core.net`.
comparisons.code:
$ wasmtime serve app.wasm
Serving HTTP on http://0.0.0.0:8080/

recommendation.why: A full wasip2 target serves users where they already deploy instead of telling them Jet does not go there. The sockets objection dissolves at preview 2, and the owner accepts the up-front stdlib and CI cost for user benefit.

whyNot.reason: A recorded non-goal cuts out every team whose platform is wasm-first, for no user-facing gain.
Plugin-only WASI serves embedding, not deployment; a server team cannot ship its whole program as someone else's plugin.
A preview target under an I9 carve-out ships two meanings of the same program, which is the drift I9 exists to prevent.

recommendation.tradeoff: A permanent stdlib port and CI lane for one more target. Accepted by owner direction: more work up front for the benefit of users.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared a full standard-library port, a recorded non-goal, and a plugins-only route. It recommended the non-goal because WASI preview 1 cannot carry Jet's server standard library.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added the preview target under an I9 carve-out as a fourth option. A separate 'export a component from any package' variant folded into the plugin option, because both are host-embedded wasm.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review moved the improved E3302 message into the non-goal option, so a no still teaches. The error now names the decision, the native path, and stops suggesting `rustup target add`.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened the full target with the `wasi:http` host-world shape and the existing `CryptoEntropy` shim. It gave the preview option an explicit carve-out list with an expiry rule.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked the non-goal with the serverless cold-start case and the polyglot-host case. The plugin surface, the container path, and the recorded revisit trigger absorb both, so the recommendation stands.

decisions.title: Named results for task.all
decisions.gist: Whether task.all branches can be named, so results come back as named fields instead of positions.
decisions.lesson: task.all runs several branches at the same time and returns every result. Today the results are positional: the third result is whatever the third branch was. When several branches return the same type, a reordered branch list silently swaps results. Names remove that failure class. JavaScript is adding Promise.allKeyed for exactly this reason, and its users welcomed it.
decisions.story: Maya builds a status dashboard. She fetches the build state, the deploy state, and the alert state concurrently. All three are String. A teammate adds a fourth fetch and sorts the branches alphabetically. The build column now shows deploy text. No error fired anywhere.

options.name: Named branches, record result
options.detail: A branch may be written name: expression. When branches are named, task.all returns a value with those fields, and you read results.build. Positional branches keep working exactly as today. Reads like a record literal, so there is nothing new to learn.
options.technical: Grammar: task.all block accepts either all-positional or all-named branches (mixing is an error with a registered diagnostic). Named form types as an anonymous record whose fields are the branch names; failure semantics per branch are unchanged (D-CONC-FAIL1). Parity across parser, sema, TIR, AOT, JIT, interpreter, web (I9).

options.name: Keep positional, lean on destructuring
options.detail: No grammar change. The idiom is to destructure results into named bindings right at the call. Zero new surface, but when two branches share a type, a swapped branch still compiles and runs wrong — the names live one line away from the branches instead of on them.
options.technical: Documentation and example work only. The swap-bug class remains undiagnosable by sema because positions carry no intent.

options.name: Library join over a record of tasks
options.detail: No change inside task.all. You build an ordinary record whose fields are running tasks, then join the record to await all fields. Keeps the grammar frozen, but it creates a second way to await a group, and it makes raw Task values something beginners hold and pass around.
options.technical: Requires Task-typed record fields, a generic join over records (comptime field walk), and rules for a Task value that escapes its scope. Two join spellings then exist: task.all and join(record).

comparisons.note: Await Dictionary is Stage 3 precisely because positional Promise.all mis-wires results as call sites grow.
comparisons.code: const {build, deploy} = await Promise.allKeyed({build: fetchBuild(), deploy: fetchDeploy()});

comparisons.note: No named form. errgroup collects by closure side effects; result wiring is manual and positional.

decisions.title: The password-hash row that no program can call
decisions.gist: What happens to `crypto.password_hash_with_salt`, a public core function that the compiler refuses on every call?
decisions.lesson: A password hash needs a salt: random bytes mixed in so two equal passwords hash differently. Jet makes the salt for you in `crypto.password_hash`. A second function lets the caller pass the salt. The compiler rejects every call to it with E2702, because a caller-chosen salt can be fixed and predictable. The function is still listed as public, so the conformance census, which must run every public function, cannot cover it.
decisions.story: Mara reads the core library page, sees `password_hash_with_salt`, and writes a test that stores a known salt so her fixture is stable. The compiler refuses the call. She reads E2702, switches to `crypto.password_hash`, and her fixture now changes on every run. The census that checks every public function on every run mode hits the same wall and cannot record a result for the row.

options.name: Delete the row
options.detail: The function leaves the public core surface. `crypto.password_hash` keeps making the salt. Fixed-salt tests use `expert.argon2id` inside `#Unsafe`, which already exists for that job. Gains: no public function that always fails; the census covers every row. Loss: none found.
options.technical: Remove the `(core.crypto, password_hash_with_salt)` row from CORE_CALLS, module_items.rs, and fixed_sigs.rs. Remove its E2702 arm in core_call.rs, its ledger entry, and its core-library table row. Replace the crypto_release_entropy_seam UI fixture with one that shows the unknown-item path. The DeterministicEntropy reason class stays for the `expert.argon2id` literal checks.

options.name: Keep the row, count it as an exclusion
options.detail: The function stays public and always rejected. The census lists it as an owner-ratified excluded row. Gains: no source change. Losses: a documented function that cannot be called; every new reader hits the wall Mara hit; the exclusion list grows by one permanent entry.
options.technical: Add `core.crypto	password_hash_with_salt	always-rejected (E2702)` to tests/conformance/exclusions.tsv with this decision id as the ratifying reference.

options.name: Make the row callable inside #Unsafe
options.detail: The function stays public. A call outside `#Unsafe` is still E2702; inside an audited `#Unsafe` block it runs with the caller's salt. Gains: one name for the expert case. Losses: two ways to do the same expert job (`expert.argon2id` already exists); the safe-looking name becomes an expert door.
options.technical: The E2702 arm in core_call.rs reads the enclosing `#Unsafe` fact and returns None inside it. A Prelude symbol `jet_crypto_password_hash_with_salt` is added. The census gains a witness that wraps the call in `#Unsafe`.

comparisons.note: The caller always supplies the salt; the crate documents `SaltString::generate` as the right source. There is no compile-time refusal.
comparisons.code:
let salt = SaltString::generate(&mut OsRng);
let hash = Argon2::default().hash_password(password.as_bytes(), &salt)?;

comparisons.note: `hashpw` accepts any salt bytes; `gensalt()` is the documented source. Misuse is a runtime fact, not a compile error.

recommendation.why: Jet is greenfield and the expert path already exists. A public function that always fails teaches nothing and blocks the census. Deleting it leaves one safe door and one audited expert door.

whyNot.reason: B keeps a permanent trap on the public page and a permanent hole in the census.
C adds a second expert spelling for the job `expert.argon2id` already does, against the one-mechanism rule.

recommendation.tradeoff: Designed away: fixed-salt tests keep a home in `expert.argon2id` inside `#Unsafe`, so deleting the row removes no capability. No remaining loss was found.

decisions.title: Should native UI expose application and window lifetimes?
decisions.gist: Should Jet expose independently managed native windows within one application?
decisions.lesson: Current GTK presentation owns one window and blocks in its loop. Two independent windows need identities and separate close states. This choice adds window lifetime, not a second UI tree. Existing native behavior still needs proof regardless of the vote.
decisions.story: User compares a main application window with a settings window. Closing settings must not destroy the main view or its state.
decisions.inWild:
// https://v3.wails.io/features/windows/basics/
app := application.New(application.Options{Name: "Inbox"})
main := app.Window.NewWithOptions(
    application.WebviewWindowOptions{Title: "Main"})
settings := app.Window.NewWithOptions(
    application.WebviewWindowOptions{Title: "Settings"})
main.Show()
settings.Show()
app.Run()
decisions.detail:
This extends the current native backend contract and respects the approved UI architecture. Tray, printing, mobile expansion, and a new renderer are not part of this vote.

The design pass placed shared work at application scope and removed per-window event loops. Card #3004 separately owns proof of the existing native feature.

options.name: One app with owned windows
options.detail: Add typed application and window handles over the existing UI tree. Settings can close while the main window keeps working. Window state has stable identity and clear ownership. Each open native window consumes host resources.
options.technical:
Add UiApplication and UiWindow handles. application creates an application model. window(title, view) creates an owned window description. run acquires the host and enters its single loop.

Window operations include show, hide, focus, and request_close. A close request can be cancelled before disposal. A closed handle returns a typed error.

Default application completion follows its last closed window. Explicit application shutdown closes owned windows and releases their callbacks and work scopes.

Shared work belongs to application scope, not whichever window was created last. One selected host serves that application; avoid a latest-window global.

Reuse UiNode and existing event/state mechanisms. Unsupported hosts report unavailability. Linux-first support does not create a new execution-mode exception.

options.name: One native window with internal views
options.detail: Keep a single native window and switch settings inside it. The application has one native focus and close state. Settings cannot have an independent native lifetime.
options.technical: Keep the current native presentation contract. Express settings through the existing reactive view tree. Do not claim that two blocking backends are a public multi-window manager.

comparisons.note: Wails separates its application loop from window objects. Each window has its own identity and close lifecycle.
comparisons.code:
// https://v3.wails.io/features/windows/basics/
app := application.New(application.Options{Name: "Inbox"})
main := app.Window.NewWithOptions(
    application.WebviewWindowOptions{Title: "Main"})
settings := app.Window.NewWithOptions(
    application.WebviewWindowOptions{Title: "Settings"})
main.Show()
settings.Show()
app.Run()

recommendation.why: Owned windows give the requested independent lifetimes while preserving one UI tree, one event model, and one application loop.
gains: Settings can close while the main window keeps working.
Window state has stable identity and clear ownership.

losses.loss: Each open native window consumes host resources.
losses.mitigation: Independent OS windows need separate native handles and compositor state.

whyNot.reason: An in-window view cannot be focused or closed as a separate native window.

recommendation.tradeoff: Pay for each window the application explicitly creates; keep the one-window path small.

decisions.title: Inspect exact generated code without exposing backend failures
decisions.gist: How should experts inspect the exact machine code Jet produced?
decisions.lesson: Assembly names processor instructions. Disassembly decodes the bytes in a built program. Jet currently shows generated Rust and compiler decisions, but not exact machine output. This choice adds observation only. Normal execution, safety checks and compiler-error policy stay unchanged.
decisions.story: Priya audits add_registers before using it in a hot loop. She needs the selected registers and actual instructions, not a guessed Rust wrapper.
decisions.inWild:
cargo asm --asm mycrate::add_registers
cargo asm --disasm mycrate::add_registers
# https://github.com/pacak/cargo-show-asm
decisions.detail:
This adds the inspect code view and explicitly amends D-OBSERVE-LIVE1 and D-RECORD1 for opt-in machine capture and bounded artifact records. D-INSPECT-DECISIONS1 remains the sole explanation record. I2 and I3 are unchanged. D-FFI-ASM1 and D-FFI-ASMOPS1 remain binding.

The fresh build failed E0282 in MIRRust.rs:10455. Current examples are grounded in command registration, not a successful new execution. Implementation must wait for #3010.

Imported law: D-INSPECT-DECISIONS1 keeps one source of compiler explanations. I2 keeps backend failures internal, with exit 101. I3 keeps user checking in sema. D-FFI-ASM1 and D-FFI-ASMOPS1 keep the existing unsafe assembly and operand contract. #3010 owns the current compiler build repair. The Rust compiler could not infer a map type; no new Jet binary was produced.

options.name: Inspect the exact build
options.detail: Add one source-linked code view beside compiler decisions. Shows actual instructions and bridge operands. Shares build identity with explanations. Works from terminals and editors. Exact output requires a retained matching artifact.
options.technical:
Add code to the existing inspect registry. Scope is file/package, live session or retained run, using existing inspection selection rules. --symbol selects an exact semantic symbol; ambiguity returns candidates without guessing. --view accepts asm, disasm, mir, backend-ir or bridge. Default text shows assembly and identity; --json returns the same records. No new top-level command or backend-selection flag is introduced. A separate explicit capture flag is defined below.

Inspection reads artifacts only. It never builds, links, runs the program or invokes package hooks. Missing output names the existing build/run action that can produce it. AOT disasm means bytes from the final linked artifact. JIT disasm means bytes from the identified live or retained generation. Compiler assembly is separately labelled pre-link and cannot stand in for final bytes.

Each record carries schema, source span and hash, symbol identity, target triple, CPU features, ABI, profile, compiler/toolchain/backend identity, artifact hash, build/run identity and generation. Instruction rows carry address or offset, bytes, text and available source locations. MIR, backend IR and bridge templates keep stage labels. Bridge rows show checked input/output/clobber facts. Reasons link to D-INSPECT-DECISIONS1 records, never new analysis.

Inlining, merging and stripped symbols produce explicit mappings or unavailable fields. Missing, unsupported, stale, redacted and expired output remain distinct. Retention uses existing bounded record budgets. Redacted bytes cannot be labelled exact. No source, artifact or native log leaves the local machine automatically. Raw native stderr remains an internal failure attachment, not a Jet user diagnostic.

Instruction count, spills, vectorization and static throughput are separate derived evidence with producer and model identity. They are unavailable when no trustworthy producer exists. llvm-mca estimates never become measured runtime. Register allocation stays backend-owned; this ballot adds observation, not optimizer override switches.

Exact selectors: file scope uses the current requested build inputs. --live <pid> selects an observed process and atomically snapshots its current generation. New --run <record-id> --generation <n> selects retained machine output. A run ID without a generation returns a generation index, not guessed bytes. These selectors are mutually exclusive. Explicit retained-run scope uses recorded source identity; it does not pretend that old code represents edited source.

New run --observe --capture-code explicitly stores bounded machine artifacts and prints run ID plus generation on tool stderr. --observe alone and ordinary dev do not enable machine capture. Program stdout and exit status remain unchanged by capture failures. Normal run adds no artifact retention. Inspection itself never starts capture or executes code. Inline-asm run capture remains blocked on #3017; a proposed transcript is not a live receipt.

Proposed retained-run transcript:

```text
jet run --observe --capture-code examples/features/lowlevel/inline_asm.jet
# Tool stderr: observed run r42, generation 1.
jet inspect code --run r42 --generation 1 --symbol add_registers --view disasm --json
# run=r42, generation=1, stage=jit-final, status=available.
```

Availability law: missing means no matching artifact was produced or indexed. Stale means an indexed candidate differs from current requested source, target, CPU features, ABI, profile, compiler, toolchain or backend identity. Expired means the index identifies an evicted artifact. Unsupported means the selected producer cannot supply this view. Redacted means policy withheld bytes. Unavailable means the artifact exists but lacks a reliable symbol mapping. None of these states returns claimed exact bytes.

Exit status is 0 only when every selected row is available; 1 means an unavailable row; 2 means an invalid or ambiguous request. Internal compiler failures retain exit 101. JSON contains status, stage, identity, ranges, reason and recovery. Stale rows also carry expected and actual identity fields. Missing text says: No matching artifact; build this file first. Stale text names the differing field and the same recovery action.

Illustrative absent records:

```json
{"status":"missing","ranges":[],"recovery":"jet build examples/features/lowlevel/inline_asm.jet"}
{"status":"stale","ranges":[],"expected":{"source_hash":"new"},"actual":{"source_hash":"old"},"recovery":"jet build examples/features/lowlevel/inline_asm.jet"}
```

The hash words above are explanatory labels, not real hashes. Production records contain full hashes.

Stage table: mir is checked Jet intermediate representation; backend-ir is the backend instruction representation; bridge is generated foreign-wrapper source and operands. These are not final executable bytes. asm is pre-link compiler instruction text. An object file before linking contains pre-link bytes. Linking can change addresses, merge bodies or remove code. Only disasm from a final linked artifact or identified JIT generation claims exact artifact or captured-generation bytes.

A symbol may map to several disjoint ranges or inlined ranges inside callers. Each range names its owning artifact and caller, origin symbol and sharing status. Merged code may share a range across symbols. Stripped output without retained source mapping returns unavailable, not an approximate name match. Ambiguous source names return candidate semantic IDs and exit 2 with no bytes.

Terms: AOT compiles before execution; JIT compiles during execution. MIR and backend IR are intermediate code forms. ABI defines calling and value-layout rules. A target triple names processor, operating system and platform conventions. CPU features name optional instructions. A symbol identifies a source function. A bridge adapts a foreign call. A clobber is a destroyed register. A generation identifies one compilation in a running process. An artifact is a produced code file or captured code block.

Inlining places a function body inside its caller. Merging shares identical machine code. Stripping removes symbol metadata. Register allocation assigns temporary values to processor registers. Static throughput estimates use a processor model, not elapsed-time measurements. Producer and model identity state which tool and assumptions made derived evidence.

Exact AOT selection adds --artifact <sha256> or --build <record-id>. File/package, artifact/build, live and retained-run scopes are mutually exclusive. File scope must match the complete D-RECORD1 target-input-closure SHA-256. That closure includes dependencies, generated inputs, foreign objects, linker configuration and relevant environment, not only the displayed fields. Multiple matches return candidate artifact/build IDs and exit 2. An exact artifact request uses that artifact’s recorded identity, never current-source claims.

Final linked bytes are not proof that an instruction executed. A loader can relocate them. Label AOT output final-linked-artifact and JIT output captured-code-generation. Loaded bytes require an identified process-memory snapshot. Executed ranges require separate trace evidence. This view never infers execution from presence.

This explicitly amends D-OBSERVE-LIVE1: --observe remains a viewer by itself; --capture-code is a separate opt-in producer. It cannot be enabled merely by JET_OBSERVE or ordinary dev. Capture/index/retention failure yields a bounded tool-side unavailable receipt and cannot change program streams or exit status. The option is valid only with explicit run --observe. Machine capture adds bounded copy time and storage; it is unsuitable as an unqualified timing baseline.

This explicitly extends D-RECORD1 with an evictable code-artifact record. It atomically links a whole artifact hash to source closure, build/run ID and generation. Existing retention limits include bytes and index entries. Bounded tombstones retain the reason for eviction; after a tombstone expires, the honest state is missing rather than expired. An artifact larger than the available budget is not partially retained. It produces exhausted-budget with required bytes and limit. Recovery must change the budget or capture scope; it must not recommend an identical retry.

Every returned range has complete bytes and its own content identity. An incomplete whole-artifact record cannot claim exactness. Saved/referenced retention protection follows the existing record law. Capture offers no new unlimited storage category.

# Source-linked bytes, instructions, target, profile and artifact hash.

options.name: Export exact artifact files
options.detail: Export the same exact artifacts as files for external tools. Fits external tooling. Users join artifacts with separate source and decision records.
options.technical:
Extend emit with --code-artifact for the same exact final AOT, live and retained JIT artifacts as A. Export bytes, disassembly text and identity manifests to files. Source-linked decision records remain separate. The exact selectors, input-closure identity, bounded capture, status/exit behavior and privacy rules are identical to A. Export reads artifacts only; it does not build or run. A raw JIT code block is labelled as raw code, not passed off as a loadable object.

Existing pre-link assembly/object export, when available, remains separately labelled. This option differs in the public workflow and file-based correlation, not in artifact coverage. It adopts the same explicit observe/record amendments and opt-in capture cost as A.

objdump -d -Mintel exported-image
# Manifest states whether bytes are final-linked or pre-link.

# Export captured JIT bytes, disassembly and identity manifest.

options.technical: Keep emit --rust and inspect decisions unchanged. Experts use objdump, debugger disassembly and compiler tooling on produced artifacts. Jet does not promise a stable artifact discovery, source-symbol map or bridge projection beyond existing contracts. This preserves current public scope but leaves the demonstrated visibility gap.

# https://github.com/pacak/cargo-show-asm

gains: Shows actual instructions and bridge operands.

External tools cannot supply missing Jet bridge and source identity.

decisions.title: How should Jet code launch a checked GPU function?
decisions.gist: How should Jet code launch a checked GPU function?
decisions.lesson: A kernel is a small GPU function. #Kernel(.parallel) marks independent runs. F32 means a 32-bit floating-point number. Launch pairs input elements by index and stores answers in a Tensor, an owned array. Adding [1,2,3] and [4,5,6] produces [5,7,9]. Default selection requires a real GPU, never an implicit CPU substitute.
decisions.story: Add xs=[1,2,3] and ys=[4,5,6], both F32 tensors, to produce [5,7,9]. A beginner supplies the function and inputs. An expert uses the same call to choose output storage, grid, stream and device. Both alternatives execute the authored body, not a hidden built-in substitute.
decisions.detail:
Both alternatives have identical values, errors, controls and performance. A gives every kernel one shared command, compute.launch. B offers .launch after a kernel name. Both forms resolve the same proved declaration and lower to the same operation; B needs no generated per-function class. This is a discovery/spelling choice, not two execution engines.

In fn add(left: F32, right: F32) F32 -> left + right, the colon introduces each input type, the final F32 is the result type, and -> introduces the returned expression. The tuple (xs, ys) supplies the two inputs. For [1,2,3] and [4,5,6], index 0 computes 1+4, index 1 computes 2+5, and index 2 computes 3+6: [5,7,9]. Extent means the shared input shape; here it is [3], not [3,3].

Omitting device selects a compatible real GPU. compute.device_vulkan() supplies the existing Vulkan device request; compute.device_cpu() explicitly requests CPU reference execution. compute.device_auto() has the same compatible-real-GPU meaning as omission. This preserves the existing .Auto placement law; neither form silently executes a GPU-required launch on the CPU. No available device or required capability means a typed failure before work is submitted. The example uses ?? panic("{err}"): success yields the Tensor; failure exposes err to the handler and stops with its detail instead of discarding it.

The ordinary call allocates a fresh output owned by its returned Tensor. Inputs are borrowed read-only until the completed call returns. An expert output: ^buffer transfers a preallocated output into the call and receives that same storage back as the returned Tensor; there is no deep output copy. Aliasing an output with any input storage is rejected before submission. A failed call does not hand out partly written data.

Every Tensor input must have the exact same shape and F32 element layout. No broadcasting or implicit narrowing occurs. Empty inputs return an empty Tensor without claiming device submission.

Expert example: gpu :: compute.device_vulkan(); queue :: compute.stream_new_on(gpu) ?? panic("{err}"); out :: compute.launch(add, inputs: (left: xs, right: ys), device: gpu, stream: queue, grid: [3]) ?? panic("{err}"). The stream orders work on that device. grid states the logical invocation shape and must equal the common input shape. Any output buffer must match that shape and F32 layout.

The stream must belong to the selected device. All checks happen before submission; grid is not a hardware block-size guess. Removing these overrides restores inferred shape and compatible-real-GPU selection. The operation still returns completed output, so no pending token or escaping resource loan is introduced.

compute.placement(out) is the existing human-readable placement report; compute.device(out) names the selected device. Keep that access model and extend its authored-program facts rather than returning a second receipt object. Actual provider/program/profile evidence must come from submitted work, never from the requested device label. The runtime card also records actual dispatch/readback proof.

Typed source inputs and Tensor metadata must retain F32 element facts; do not pass ordinary Float/F64 through a hidden narrowing cast.

This launch contract maps each Tensor<F32> input to one F32 parameter at the same logical index. It returns one F32 per index. It accepts a directly resolved, proved #Kernel declaration, including an imported declaration, not a stored function value or closure.

This ballot does not invent an unchecked whole-resource parameter or implicit invocation-index variable. The existing kernel proof must cover every admitted body, helper, bound and effect. Existing precision, ownership, raw-unsafe and CPU-reference laws remain intact. Any additional public resource declaration requires its exact signature and owner approval before implementation.

These are proposed call excerpts, not a claim that current Jet has launch. The full executable fixture supplies typed inputs and imports. Compiler checking establishes bounds, captures, effects, races, synchronization and output coverage; the shared lowered program carries those facts to provider adapters, which execute rather than rediscover language rules.

decisions.title: How should a Jet function declare its graphics stage?
decisions.gist: How should a Jet function declare its graphics stage?
decisions.lesson: A vertex function runs for each triangle corner. Its UV image coordinates are blended across the triangle; a fragment function uses them to color each covered pixel. F32 is a 32-bit floating-point number. A marker is a #Name(...) label above a function that tells Jet its checked GPU role. Every option performs the same work.
decisions.story: Use identical mesh, texture, sampler and target inputs in every option. The mesh has corners (-0.5,-0.5), (0.5,-0.5), (0,0.5), UVs (0,1), (1,1), (0.5,0), and a one-pixel opaque red texture. On a black 64-by-64 target, an interior pixel is red and a corner pixel remains black. The snippets isolate stage declarations; the implementation fixture supplies complete resource setup.
decisions.detail:
Only the place and spelling of stage identity differ. A and B label the function declaration; C checks the function when it is wrapped for a pipeline. All use one checked device-program representation and the existing core.game backend. No parallel core.graphics family, window loop, scene model or foreign shader-string language is authorized.

A/B functions remain ordinary callable Jet bodies for CPU reference work with explicitly CPU-backed resources. Their declared GPU role is fixed. C can check the same otherwise-compatible function for different roles at separate wrapping sites, without editing its declaration. In C, game.vertex_stage or game.fragment_stage checks that function and every helper it calls; role errors are reported at the wrapper with the failing body location. All three preserve ordinary source type errors and the same safe subset.

The mesh supplies vertex inputs. The vertex function runs once per corner; the renderer blends its floating UV values over covered pixels and calls fragment for each. A pipeline joins the stages, resources and destination. game.draw submits that work and returns its existing ComputeStream handle. compute.stream_sync(queue) is the named completion boundary before readback or presentation may observe the result.

An expert may pass stream: queue to batch several draws and synchronize once. The queue retains resources and their access leases until completion, even if the caller drops local handles. Submission alone does not mean pixels are ready or displayed.

VertexOut<V> contains position: [F32#4] and varyings: V. The fragment's first input must match V. For this fixture, position is x,y,z,w: after division by w, x/y range from -1 to 1, z from 0 to 1; positive y points up. The shown z=0,w=1 places the triangle on the near plane without perspective scaling. Texture UV uses its documented top-left origin. The shared contract, not individual adapters, owns coordinate conversion.

Texture2D and Sampler are typed backend resources. The supplied fixture uses a one-pixel linear RGBA8 texture and nearest, clamped sampling, so sample returns four normalized F32 color values. Routine bindings/locations derive deterministically from checked types; explicit layout overrides must agree with them.

The initial shared profile uses triangle lists, no multisampling or culling, counterclockwise front faces and the top-left edge-fill rule.

Pixel centers are half-integer coordinates. Floating varyings use perspective-correct interpolation; integer varyings use flat interpolation from the first vertex. Viewport and readback rows start at the top left.

Texture and target are linear RGBA8 UNORM: four unsigned normalized eight-bit channels, with no automatic sRGB conversion.

Output channels clamp to [0,1] and quantize by nearest-even rounding. The shared lowering owns this conversion, not a vendor default. Other formats, interpolation modes and sampling profiles require explicit supported declarations; this fixture never silently selects them. Enumerate further resource/override signatures for owner approval rather than slipping them into a backend implementation.

The snippets assume mesh, tex, samp and target are already supplied by the common fixture. An undeclared tex is an ordinary source error. Omitting a required texture from resources is a pipeline-creation failure before draw.

Stage/type/layout mismatches fail when the pipeline is created. Every draw revalidates live handles, selected device, target and resources before queue submission. Wrong-device, closed, invalid or incompatible resources fail before submission with source context. A later device loss reports through compute.stream_sync; no partly completed target is presented as valid. ?? panic("{err}") yields success or stops while retaining the original error detail in the handler message; it is not fallback rendering.

Headless means no display window, not no GPU. A headless machine with a supported real GPU can draw to an offscreen target and read pixels back. Missing GPU capability fails before draw. CPU reference work occurs only in an explicit application branch that calls the same stage bodies with CPU-backed reference resources; it is not GPU rasterization or an automatic substitute.

No backend silently narrows Float/F64 to F32 or accepts unchecked host effects, captures, races, derivatives or synchronization. Required platform proof observes actual device work; an unsupported-device error cannot stand in for successful coverage. These stage, pipeline and resource APIs are proposals, not claims about current runnable Jet.

decisions.title: Turn expensive bug checks on only where needed
decisions.gist: Should one switch enable expensive bug checks in your code and its libraries?
decisions.lesson: A deep check inspects data to find a bug, such as a wrong stored tree size. Today, ordinary debug checks can run automatically during development. These extra checks stay off until requested. Required safety checks stay on. A package is a named library or application; a function is a named operation.
decisions.story: A tree library updates a cached node count incorrectly. The developer wants a thorough walk to locate the bug, without making every normal request walk the tree.
decisions.detail: A approves an optional argument to the existing DebugOnly marker and one compiler switch. The switch may target existing packages or functions. B approves no new spelling and uses ordinary package settings. Both preserve required contracts, memory safety and type safety. Neither lets a successful optional check justify otherwise unsafe code.

options.name: One switch, with optional targeting
options.detail: Mark in-memory checks once, then enable all or selected names. Existing package settings still support checks with file or database access. Jet checks for invalid operations even when these checks are off. Target costly checks instead of enabling everything. Enabled checks take time; changing selection can require recompilation. Interactive sessions keep their starting selection; a different selection needs another session. Unverifiable prebuilt code needs rebuilding or is refused, even with checks off.
options.technical:
## Selection

`#DebugOnly(.deep) { ... }` marks optional, read-only bug checks. No switch means every deep check is disabled, in every profile. `--deep-checks` selects all authored deep checks in the program and its Jet libraries. It does not affect foreign libraries or separate build tools.

`--deep-checks=<scope>` limits selection. The grammar is `<package>` or `<package>::<name>(.<name>)*`. The package is its exact declared package.jet name; subsequent names follow the authored module and declaration path. Use dots after the single package separator: `tree::balance.rebuild`. Owner-qualified methods use `tree::balance.Tree.rebalance`; a default method body written in a trait uses that trait as its owner. Same-owner/name implementations are selected together. Diagnostics print copyable matching scopes and the matched declaration locations; they never expose generated backend names.

For example, `tree` selects that package; `tree::rebalance` selects deep checks inside that function. A module selects its descendants. Same-named package instances, overloads and generic instances are all selected, not silently guessed between. Compiler diagnostics identify the matched declarations. Anonymous nested bodies belong to their nearest named function. There are no new per-check labels, patterns or registry. Several occurrences take the union; a bare occurrence selects all. Every supplied scoped occurrence must match at least one declaration containing a deep check.

An empty, unknown or unmatched occurrence is a registered blocking error: neither compilation nor execution proceeds, even if another occurrence matches or a bare switch is also present. A selected declaration with no deep checks is an unmatched scope, not silent success.

Selection uses the declaration that contains the check, not whoever calls it. Calling a selected function does not enable unrelated checks in its callees. A scope selects every marked block within its named declaration; one block needs no public identifier. The example is a package named tree; tree::run selects its shown function. A separately declared library uses its own package and function names in the same way.

## Checking and effects

All deep bodies type-check when disabled. Captured program state is read-only; only fresh, nonescaping locals may be mutated. No initialization, reference, ownership transfer, refinement, permission or optimizer assumption escapes. No return or error propagation may leave the enclosing function; break/next cannot target an outside loop. Local helper returns and local-loop control remain allowed.

External effects, including file/database access, time, randomness and logging, are rejected transitively. Ordinary authorized code outside this diagnostic scope remains available for those jobs. Private memory work follows ordinary memory rules. Assert may report failure through Panic, but the marker grants no Panic permission. Enabled checks obey surrounding effect restrictions. Disabled bodies add no reachable memory or Panic effect. Required Pre/Post contracts and ordinary safety checks are never removed. These restrictions belong to `.deep`, not ordinary active DebugOnly code.

Independent #3043 fixes facts escaping removed code.

## Compilation and reuse

The switch applies to run, dev, test, build, emit, check, debug, repl, eval and notebook. Compiler wrappers propagate the resolved selection. Both debugger engines inherit it. The existing compiler-options input gains one typed deep_checks request with off, all or scoped forms. CLI and embedded callers use that same input; resolution to declaration/site identity occurs once inside the compiler. Entry points without an options input use off, not ambient environment.

Thread the existing options boundary through selection-capable compile/check facade calls and migrate affected callers in one cutover. Do not introduce separate globals, a second selector parser or parallel compile APIs. Exercise an embedded caller selecting the same checks without a CLI. REPL and notebook sessions select it at creation and keep it for their lifetime. A different selection requires a new session. Creating that session does not reset the existing session, migrate its in-memory values or silently replay prior cells.

Each may retain its own compiled units. A dev process likewise keeps its launch selection; restart it to change selection under its existing lifecycle. D-CLI1 applies: before standalone `--` it is a compiler option; after it, an application argument.

Cache and resident identities use the resolved selected check sites in each affected semantic body, unit and artifact. Equivalent selector lists reuse the same identity. Recompile changed units and their affected dependents, not unrelated packages. Already compiled matching code is reused. Per-function targeting does not promise sub-unit compilation. Already launched binaries retain their compiled choice; there is no runtime flag that recreates removed code.

Rebuilding uses admitted source and ordinary authority. Only run may delegate declared environment preparation to Jetpack; --no-prepare forbids it. Other commands gain no preparation permission. Locked mode preserves pins and dependency identities. Existing E0983, E0603 and E1334 resolution failures keep their causes and repairs. An incompatible prebuilt unit without admitted rebuild source gets a registered blocking diagnostic naming the unit and compiled/requested selections. Missing, unreadable or unsupported selection identity is never assumed to mean off.

It is a cache miss requiring admitted-source rebuilding, or a blocking refusal if that is unavailable. This applies even to default-off requests; no legacy artifact reader or guessed compatibility is introduced. This creates no new resolver, download path or prebuilt format.

## Profiles and delivery

Deep selection is independent of ordinary DebugOnly eligibility. Bare DebugOnly is on for dev, debug, test, ci, small, no-os, default, fast, fuzz, coverage and package-defined profiles. It is off for explicit release and hardened. This fact is shared by all execution engines; optimization alone does not change it. Hardened sentries remain separate.

AOT, default run, interpreter and applicable web use one selected meaning. New marker/flag/scopes require registration, diagnostics and snapshots. Preserve the read-only tree fixture and its valid/corrupt, on/off outputs. No speed advantage over B is claimed; any later performance-motivated replacement still requires its paired strict performance gate.

Build with the setting on to check that branch for invalid operations.
options.technical:
Use D-CONF-KEY1 and D-CONF-MERGE1 as exercised by examples/features/packages/typed_settings. The setting belongs to the declaring package and defaults false; current contribution/Force rules still apply. Do not assume an application CLI setting reaches separately configured dependencies.

Libraries expose ordinary read-only predicates where callers need checks; the application authors and enables those calls, or explicitly binds a library-supported setting through its existing configuration contract. The predicate remains ordinary typed Jet. The branch follows the existing comptime checking law: an unselected arm is not promised the always-type-check behavior of DebugOnly, so the author must exercise both setting values.

No marker argument, global deep flag or new invariant API is added. Selected values already fold before execution and participate in instance identity. Ordinary code/effect/safety checking remains in force; a setting is not permission to rely on erased initialization or skip a required guard.

options.technical:
## One producer, one existing inspector

`jet emit --asm add.jet --symbol add` compiles current source when needed and emits pre-link compiler assembly beside mapped Jet source. Reuse existing target, profile, CPU/features and package defaults. Source emission accepts the existing --target, --profile, --symbol, --json and -o conventions. --view belongs to inspect code, not emit --asm; combining it with source emission is an invalid request. No new top-level command, execution mode or backend selector is added.

Source emission returns the approved pre-link asm stage, not final linked bytes. Exact inspect code uses the approved file/package, --artifact <sha256>, --build <record-id>, --live or retained-run selectors. It does not add a filesystem-path meaning to --artifact. Live and retained-run selectors continue under D-CODE-INSPECT1. Artifact/live/retained inspection never builds, links, runs, replays or starts capture. Input scopes are exclusive. The semantic symbol must match exactly; ambiguity returns candidates rather than choosing. A source file need not have been built or recorded before emission.

## Reuse and authority

Reuse cached compiler assembly only when every input affecting that requested stage, its producer and its source map matches. Include source and dependency inputs, generated inputs, target, CPU/features, ABI, profile, compiler/toolchain/backend and relevant environment where they affect compiler assembly. Inputs used only by downstream linking do not invalidate pre-link assembly. Exact final-linked artifact selection still matches its full approved closure, including foreign objects and linker settings. The compiler records actual stage dependencies; it may not guess an input is irrelevant.

A final executable is not a substitute for compiler assembly. Reuse existing immutable stored artifacts; no duplicate capture is required just to view them.

On a miss, perform only the ordinary authorized build-time work required for the selected source and target. This may evaluate compile-time code, resolve already admitted packages, produce generated inputs and run declared permitted build hooks. It grants no new preparation, download, network or execution permission. Source preparation keeps the command's existing rules. Record the authorization and actions. Never start the application entry or event loop. Tool progress goes to stderr; requested text/JSON goes to stdout or -o.

## Optional saved runs

Keep `jet run --observe --capture-code add.jet` and `jet inspect code --run <record> --generation <n>`. Capture remains explicit and bounded. Ordinary run/dev and --observe alone do not gain code capture. A later read can only show a retained generation that was actually recorded. Capture/storage failures remain tool-side and cannot alter the program's output or exit status. D-RECORD1 eviction and complete-artifact/tombstone rules remain unchanged.

`--live <pid>` observes one atomically identified current generation. It never substitutes a newer generation when the requested one disappears. `-o` explicitly saves a selected view and its identity. Reuse immutable retained data where its ownership and lifetime permit. Keeping code after its process or generation disappears still requires stored bytes; that optional storage and privacy cost is disclosed before capture/export. There is no promise of free recording or recovery of unrecorded history. Generic --replay data is not a native code image.

## Exact meaning and failure

Retain D-CODE-INSPECT1 stage and availability law, including pre-link asm, jit-final and the final-linked-artifact/captured-code-generation distinctions. No stage/status renaming is part of A. Inspector --view keeps asm, disasm, mir, backend-ir and bridge. A source compiler listing is not final linked instructions. Non-native targets never fabricate host assembly; keep the approved unsupported or explicitly applicable portable behavior.

Records retain every approved field: schema, source span/hash and input identity, semantic symbol/instantiation, target, CPU/features, ABI, profile, compiler/toolchain/backend, artifact hash, build/run identity and compilation generation. Exports preserve those fields, plus applicable producer and source-map identity. An artifact hash alone cannot replace run/generation identity. A --run request without --generation returns the approved generation index, never guessed bytes. Maps link Jet spans through actual lowering to instruction ranges, including inline assembly.

Show real bridges and operand facts where present, not an invented wrapper. Inlining, merging, stripping, missing generic instances and removed bodies retain their actual relationships. Never force noinline, guess a source line or rebuild a historical image as if it were the original. Stored code is not proof that it executed.

Preserve available, missing, stale, expired, unsupported, redacted and unavailable, with the approved invalid/ambiguous request and internal-failure handling. Missing means no matching produced/indexed artifact. Unavailable includes an existing artifact without reliable mapping; it is not renamed unmapped or missing-code. Keep exhausted-budget for oversized capture and its required-bytes/limit repair. Preserve existing source-build authorization diagnostics instead of adding a competing code-view status vocabulary.

Exit 0 requires every selected row to be available. Unavailable output exits 1; invalid/ambiguous requests exit 2; internal compiler failure exits 101. Lost or optimized-away code reports its actual mapping or unavailable reason. An absent semantic symbol identifies the selector and candidates, not fabricated bytes or a pointless rebuild. Stale names differing identity fields. Expired names an evicted record while its tombstone remains; after that it is missing.

Privacy redaction, unsupported views, denied build work, exhausted budgets and export failures retain their concrete causes and safe recovery. No incomplete export or partial capture is marked complete. Derived instruction/spill/throughput evidence keeps producer/model identity and cannot be called measured runtime. Reasons link to D-INSPECT-DECISIONS1 rather than new analysis. No source or native log leaves the machine automatically.

All existing inspection consumers keep the same protocol. The added source producer uses that record/renderer and ordinary registered compiler/build errors. It adds no alternate reader or compatibility branch.

Sources: D-CODE-INSPECT1, D-OBSERVE-LIVE1, D-RECORD1, D-INSPECT-DECISIONS1; https://docs.rs/cargo-show-asm/latest/cargo_show_asm/.
