decisions.title: Const generics: a compile-time Int as a type parameter
decisions.gist: May a compile-time number be a type parameter, and how is it spelled?
decisions.lesson: A generic type takes a type parameter: `Pair<T>`. Some types need a number: a 64-byte packet, a 3x3 matrix. Today a constant can size an array field, but `Packet<64>` cannot be written, so each size is a separate struct. A slice does not help: the size must live in the type so a 64-byte frame cannot pass as a 32-byte one. This ballot asks whether a compile-time `Int` may be a type parameter (option D: no) and how to spell it. Running code never builds a type.
decisions.story: Omar writes firmware. His radio frames come in 32, 64, and 128 bytes. He wants one `Packet` type and one `checksum` function. Today he copies the struct three times. With `Packet<@N: Int>` he writes it once, and passing a `Packet<64>` where a `Packet<32>` is expected is a compile error at the call.

options.name: Compile-time sigil: struct Packet<@N: Int>
options.detail:
A value parameter is written with the `@` that S57 gives compile-time names: `struct Packet<@N: Int> { data: [U8#@N] }`, used as `Packet<64>` or `Packet<@lanes>`. Type parameters like `T` are also compile-time, so here `@` marks 'value, not type'; that widens the sigil's meaning. It cannot be misread as a trait bound (`<T: Add>`, which constrains T to implement Add). Inside the body `@N` shadows any outer `@N` constant.

Only `Int` for now; the `: Int` is written so later kinds (`Bool`, `U32`) fit the same slot. Any Int is legal; a negative or zero size fails only where it sizes an array, as `[U8#0]` does today. A bare argument is a literal or `@name`; anything else takes parentheses, `Packet<(@lanes * 16)>`, like `[Float#(@lanes * 2)]`. Inside a generic body arguments are a bare `@N` or fully closed; `Packet<(@N * 2)>` is rejected, so type equality never needs algebra.

`Packet<64>` and `Packet<(@lanes * 16)>` are the same type. One compiled copy per distinct value, like `<T>`. At a call site the value is inferred from the argument, or written explicitly (D-GENERIC-CALL1=A). Value and type parameters mix in declaration order with optional defaults: `Matrix<T, @R: Int, @C: Int = @R>`. `impl<@N: Int> Wire for Packet<@N>` and `impl Wire for Packet<64>` overlap; the existing coherence rule rejects that.

Narrow amendment to S26: a compile-time Int may parameterize an existing type constructor. `Meta.Const` (D-META-GATE1) governs declaring `<@N: Int>`; instantiating a dependency's `Packet<64>` is always allowed.
options.technical: Generic parameter list accepts `@name: Int`. Arguments: literal, `@const`, or a parenthesized comptime Int expression; a bound value parameter may appear only bare. Sema instantiates per distinct value; `[T#@N]` sizes resolve after instantiation and reject non-positive sizes there. A runtime value in the slot is a teaching diagnostic.

options.name: Plain name: struct Packet<N: Int>
options.detail: Rust and Swift shape without a keyword; uniform with the unsigiled `T`. `<N: Int>` looks exactly like a trait bound `<T: Add>` until the reader knows `Int` is not a trait, and the body writes `N`, unlike every other compile-time constant in Jet. The parser cannot tell the kind without name resolution, which Jet's parser does not do today.
options.technical: Disambiguate by resolving the bound: if it names a type rather than a trait, the parameter is a value. Requires name resolution before the parameter kind is known.
options.code:
struct Packet<N: Int> { data: [U8#N] }     // reads like a trait bound <T: Add>
p :: Packet<64>{data: [U8#64]{}}

options.name: Keyword: struct Packet<const N: Int>
options.detail: Rust's spelling, recognized at once by Rust readers, and the body stays unsigiled like `T`. It reserves `const` for one position (I7 has no contextual keywords) when `@` already carries the meaning.
options.technical: Reserve `const` (I7). Parameter kind is known at the parser without name resolution.
options.code:
struct Packet<const N: Int> { data: [U8#N] }   // new reserved word
p :: Packet<64>{data: [U8#64]{}}

options.name: No const generics: keep per-size types
options.detail: Keep S26 as written. Sizes stay array facts (`[U8#64]`); one struct per size by hand, or a generated sibling file per size from `fn build`. Zero grammar change and no monomorphization by value. Cost: `checksum` is written once per size, and a shared field or method cannot be generic over the count.
options.technical: Status quo. Alternatives considered and refused here. A trait with an associated constant (`struct Packet<S: Size>`, typenum style) needs one marker type per size and cannot infer from a literal. A `#N` size parameter reuses the array-size marker but keys the whole feature to arrays.

comparisons.note: A keyword marks a value parameter; only integers, bool, char today.
comparisons.code: struct Packet<const N: usize> { data: [u8; N] }

comparisons.note: Types are values; a function takes a comptime size and returns a struct type. Jet refuses this route.
comparisons.code: fn Packet(comptime n: usize) type { return struct { data: [n]u8 }; }

comparisons.note: Non-type template parameters have existed since the start; the type is written before the name.
comparisons.code: template <std::size_t N> struct Packet { std::array<uint8_t, N> data; };

comparisons.note: Value generics use a plain `let N: Int` marker; only Int today.

recommendation.why: `@` already marks a compile-time name in Jet, so `<@N: Int>` needs no new word and cannot be read as a trait bound; the sigil's meaning widens to 'value, not type'. Inside the body `@N` looks like every other constant. The amendment to S26 stays narrow: a number parameterizes an existing type, no type is computed, and arithmetic over bound parameters is refused so equality stays by value.

whyNot.reason: It reads as a trait bound until the reader knows Int is not a trait, and the parser needs name resolution to know the parameter kind.
Familiar to Rust readers, but it reserves a word for one position when `@` already carries the meaning.
One function per size forever; generated sibling files hide the count in a build step instead of the type.

recommendation.tradeoff: Jet takes on monomorphization by value and a second kind of generic parameter. Only Int is allowed, which covers sizes and counts and keeps the type checker away from arbitrary values.

losses.loss: A second kind of generic parameter to learn.
losses.mitigation: A number and a type cannot share one parameter kind without types-as-values.

losses.loss: Only Int values for now.
losses.mitigation: A scope choice: sizes and counts are the shipped need; `Bool` or `U32` can follow in the same slot.

losses.loss: No arithmetic over a bound parameter in a type argument.
losses.mitigation: Deciding `Packet<(@N * 2)>` equals `Packet<(2 * @N)>` needs symbolic algebra.

reviewPasses.beginner: Fresh agent: completion-beginner-constgen1. Skill: rli5. A stateless fresh reader flagged the unexplained `[U8#@N]`, the trait-bound comparison, and call-site inference; all repaired in option A.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Anthropic. Adversarial model family: Anthropic. Fresh agent: completion-adversarial-constgen1. decisions.detail:
## Shared publication contract

D-BUILD-GENVALUE1 already selects Generated item values and b.generate(name, value). This decision adds the shared-preparation entry point, not another template engine. The example assumes make_commands returns that existing Generated type.

Publication returns the normal checked result or a source diagnostic. A generated value is inert until published. Returning it from a helper neither publishes declarations nor executes their runtime bodies.

Names identify generated modules within the current package and input snapshot. Duplicate names, conflicting declarations, illegal target scopes and dependency cycles fail explicitly. Every published declaration retains template, capture and publication provenance.

Standard publication is additive. It cannot replace an existing body, signature or type. Advanced changes require the separate opt-in and transformation contract. Generated source still follows normal visibility, effect and safety checks.

Typed template holes retain their selected meaning only inside templates. An ordinary prepared value is referenced normally outside a template. The advanced control ballot distinguishes captured syntax from compiler metadata queries.

Materialization uses #3421's canonical generated root. Source navigation must work whether physical materialization is requested or a virtual generated document is used. Materialized output is drift-checked rather than treated as independent handwritten source.

Both examples add the same commands module. Its function runs only when the application calls it. Cold and warm preparation publish the same logical declarations with the same effects. The target program cannot change through an imported module's ambient state.

options.name: Program publisher
options.detail: Name the current program before publishing. The receiving program is visible. The common operation needs a receiver lookup.
options.technical: compiler.program() returns the current preparation program handle. Its generate method has the same name, Generated input and failure rules.

decisions.detail:
## What this vote changes

This vote chooses the prep boundary grammar and @PHASE() query spelling. The phase, Runtime, effect, generation and artifact rules below preserve prior owner selections. They are stated to make the complete behavior visible, not to reopen those selections.

## Shared contract

Both choices run ordinary Jet functions, conditions and loops during shared preparation. AOT, default run and interpreter receive the same prepared meaning. Web participates when the program reaches web. A saved AOT artifact does not prepare again when launched.

Prepared values use ordinary names. Compiler-owned metadata remains under callable @ roots. Metadata roots use uppercase names and lowercase members. No extra @ appears merely because a value was prepared.

Generation remains explicit. Evaluating or returning a Generated value does not publish it or execute its generated body. D-BUILD-GENVALUE1 remains the typed item-template contract. Build remains AOT artifact production, not a second shared-preparation meaning.

Runtime barriers use #Runtime(.NoEager) and #Runtime(.Only) on functions, methods or explicit blocks. Neither has a bare shorthand or module-wide default. NoEager prevents automatic eager evaluation but allows an explicit prep call. Only rejects calls during preparation or AOT build execution. Both permit ordinary runtime optimization. These are phase boundaries, not optimizer barriers.

## Failure and effect rules

Preparation may call ordinary helpers under their inferred effects and approved host policy. Invalid phase crossings get source diagnostics before code generation. A pure-result cache cannot suppress observable effects. Each logical invocation observes effects once and in order, even when its pure computation is reused.

Compiler scheduling may wait for declared inputs. It must diagnose dependency cycles rather than guess a result. Preparation of an ordinary application cannot acquire advanced privileges by importing a module.

## Examples and acceptance

calculate_lanes returns 8 in both examples. The program prints 8 on each applicable execution mode. Launching the emitted AOT binary prints 8 without repeating preparation IO. Replacing the call with an ordinary loop remains legal inside braces.

The implementation registers every selected spelling in Syntax.rs. It migrates parser, formatter, editor, diagnostics, examples and current explanations together. Historical ballots are not rewritten. New public grammar outside this decision remains owner-gated.

The compiler-owned @PHASE() query reports Preparation, Build or Runtime at its evaluation site. The result follows language phases, never optimizer decisions. A phase-only branch is checked according to the selected phase and cannot smuggle runtime state into preparation.

## Reader key and direct proof owners

The binding operator :: gives the calculated value a name. A block without a value expression yields Unit, meaning no value. Under B, prep f() + 1 prepares the entire sum. Use (prep f()) + runtime_value to put only f inside preparation.

#3521 proves legal explicit NoEager calls and rejected Only calls, source diagnostics and saved-artifact startup. #3525 proves cycle rejection. #3506 and #3532 prove effects occur once in order on cold and warm runs. @PHASE() returns Preparation, Build or Runtime as defined above.

## Ordinary prepared values in generic uses

The latest owner selection supersedes repeated sigils on ordinary prepared values. Keep Packet<@N: Int> for the selected compile-time binder. Use N in [U8#N] and lanes in Packet<lanes>. This is one ordinary-value naming rule, not a new generic mechanism. #3505 owns the clean parser, checker, formatter and example cutover. D-CONSTGEN1 remains immutable history; typed template holes retain their separately scoped meaning.

decisions.title: Complete reflection contract and callable record shape
decisions.gist: Which record shape should Jet’s complete reflection contract use?
decisions.lesson: Both options approve complete typed facts for types, callables, programs, source, packages, local state and runtime values. Queries use ordinary typed Result errors; missing facts never become empty lists. Runtime retention is explicit. The choice is whether callable facts share one signature record or repeat its fields. The complete field schema appears below.
decisions.explainer: Both options approve complete typed facts for types, callables, programs, source, packages, local state and runtime values. Queries use ordinary typed Result errors; missing facts never become empty lists. Runtime retention is explicit. The choice is whether callable facts share one signature record or repeat its fields. The complete field schema appears below.
decisions.story: A tool author compares one function, method and closure signature. They need typed parameters and honest missing-fact errors. A runtime inspector separately requests retained metadata.

decisions.detail:
## Complete fact contract

This decision approves complete checked reflection, not only a signature cleanup. @TYPE(T), @FUNCTION(f), @METHOD(T, name) and @CLOSURE(value) are callable queries. @PROGRAM(), @PACKAGE() and @SOURCE() expose the corresponding checked snapshot. Ordinary prepared values do not acquire metadata sigils.

The existing selected callable-root convention is fixed. This ballot does not reopen dot-of spelling. Function overloads require an unambiguous selected callable or an explicit typed selection; a bare ambiguous name is an error.

CallableSignature contains ordered params, return_type, effects, calling_convention and generic_bindings. Each parameter exposes name, label, type, default, zone, mutability and source. Defaults distinguish absent, available checked expression and unavailable evaluation. They never execute merely because metadata is read.

Callable records also expose stable identity, visibility, captures, attributes, source, documentation and checked body availability. Closure captures expose binding identity, type, capture mode and lifetime constraints. Compile-time metadata can inspect structure without retaining runtime closure values.

Type metadata covers every compiler Type variant. It includes generics, constraints, traits, methods, fields, enum cases, aliases, numeric dimensions, representation and target layout. Type identity is not a formatted name. Recursive graphs use stable references, not infinite expansion.

Program metadata covers declarations, references, calls, typed expressions, scopes, locals, control flow, effects, obligations and memory facts. Package metadata includes resolved imports, dependencies, settings, contributions and provenance. Source metadata includes exact snapshot identity, spans, comments, documentation and expansion origins.

Use the canonical checked semantic index for program facts. No second ownership analysis or mutable private store is exposed. #3175 supplies bounded local obligations. #3199 and #3202 own facade and diagnostic-origin consistency. #3181 owns the versioned schema cutover.

## Availability, privacy and runtime

A query returns a typed fact or an explicit unavailable, unsupported, stale, invalid, denied or truncated result. Empty collections mean checked emptiness only. Target-dependent facts name their target. Phase-dependent facts name their checked phase and source version.

Preparation can read complete facts within its approved workspace and visibility authority. Reflection does not grant foreign-file or private-dependency access. Opted-in transformations can operate only on explicitly registered targets.

Runtime exposes type and value facts retained for requested roots. It does not ship the complete compiler heap. Runtime type tables name their retention scope and completeness. Erased values preserve actual type identity and lawful access. Dead-code elimination must retain explicitly requested metadata without retaining unrelated metadata by default.

D-ENUM-CASEMETA1 remains binding. Exported reflection captures intentionally disclose the complete lawful captured graph. Ordinary copies preserve captured contents. Shared mutable and noncopyable graphs are refused as specified, not silently approximated.

## Same-program result

Both options report advance's ordered parameter types, defaults and return type identically. Only the member path differs. A method and closure with equivalent callable contracts produce equivalent signature facts. A program without runtime reflection receives no new runtime table allocation.

Every field family receives a named delivery owner and behavioral witness under #3509. Current source models define implementation reuse, not permission to omit requested facts. The contract card implements the owner-visible schema below in the executable registry before consumers implement it. It cannot silently choose different public shapes.

## Reader key and failure witnesses

:: binds a value. @FUNCTION asks for compiler metadata; a dot reads one typed member. An effect describes an operation such as filesystem access. Calling convention describes how a function passes arguments across its selected ABI. The example is pure and has no world-touching effect.

#3523 and #3199 own these query/result witnesses: unavailable before its checked phase; unsupported for a named unimplemented fact; stale after source edits. They also cover invalid checked input, denied private scope and explicitly truncated bounded output. No such result is accepted as complete feature delivery. #3524 proves requested retention and absence of unrelated runtime metadata.

@PROGRAM() means the current authorized checked program snapshot. @PACKAGE() means its lexical package. @SOURCE() means the lexical source snapshot, not an implicit caller capture. Querying another scope requires an explicit authorized handle. These queries do not add host file access.

## Closed query and error schema

These are proposed public types, not claims about current CallableSignatureFact fields. The existing producer currently has string types/defaults and lacks return-type and calling-convention members. #3522 extends the same checked source instead of creating a parallel analysis.

Every fact-query root listed below returns its success type with the ordinary Jet failure carrier: T !MetadataError. This is the existing Result mechanism, not a new wrapper or implicit empty result. An ordinary call may propagate that typed error; ? makes propagation explicit in the examples. Querying an invalid source cannot publish recovered facts as success.

MetadataError is an error record with kind: MetadataFailure, query: String and source: ?SourceSpan. MetadataFailure has exactly six cases: Unavailable, Unsupported, Stale, Invalid, Denied and Truncated. Each case has the following typed payload, not an arbitrary string map.

- Unavailable: required_stage: CompilerStage; reason: String.
- Unsupported: capability: String.
- Stale: requested: SnapshotId; current: SnapshotId.
- Invalid: diagnostics: [CompilerDiagnostic].
- Denied: scope: ScopeId; reason: String.
- Truncated: limit: Int; observed: Int.

Truncated contains no partial fact payload and is never a successful complete result. A bounded query may be retried with an explicit larger limit. An empty successful list means the compiler proved there were no rows. Optional fields mean known absence, not missing analysis. Error text must not disclose denied private content.

CompilerStage is Parsed, Resolved, Typed, Prepared or Emitted. It describes fact availability within compilation, not a new user execution phase. @PHASE() remains Preparation, Build or Runtime. SnapshotId, TypeId, DeclarationHandle, ScopeId, NodeId and ValueHandle are opaque compiler-issued identities. They cannot be constructed by user casts or strings.

The roots and success types are @TYPE(T): TypeInfo, @FUNCTION(f): FunctionInfo, @METHOD(T, name): MethodInfo and @CLOSURE(value): ClosureInfo. @PROGRAM(): ProgramInfo, @PACKAGE(): PackageInfo and @SOURCE(): SourceInfo use the current authorized lexical snapshot. @VALUE(value): ValueInfo and @TYPES(): TypeCatalog provide runtime value and retained-table inspection. Explicit authorized handles select other snapshots through the same root's handle overload.

@METHOD accepts an unambiguous typed method handle as its second argument when a name selects several overloads. A query never guesses the first overload. @VALUE can inspect an erased value without replacing its actual TypeId with the static container type.

## Record notation and cardinality

The following schema uses [T] for an ordered list and ?T for known optionality. The ordinary T !MetadataError carrier marks a field that needs a later checked stage or unretained fact. These are exact field names and types. Records are immutable value projections; references resolve only through the same checked snapshot or a retained captured graph.

SourceSpan has source: SourceId, start: Int and end: Int, using half-open byte offsets. SourceId contains package: PackageId, path: ?String and digest: String. PackageId contains name: String, version: String and digest: String. Digests identify checked content, not the current contents of a mutable file path.

CallableSignature has params: [ParameterInfo], return_type: ?TypeId, effects: [EffectInfo], errors: [TypeId], failure: FailureInfo, calling_convention: CallingConvention and generic_bindings: [GenericBinding]. It also has returned_views: [ViewProvenanceFact] and policies: [PolicyFact]. An absent return_type means no returned value, not an unknown inferred type.

ParameterInfo has name: String, label: String, type: TypeId, default: ?DefaultInfo, zone: ParamZone, access: AccessConvention, variadic: Bool and source: SourceSpan. DefaultInfo has expression: CodeRef, value: PreparedValue !MetadataError and source: SourceSpan. Reading a default never executes it; its value can be unavailable while its checked expression is present.

FunctionInfo has identity: DeclarationHandle, name: String, signature: CallableSignature, visibility: Visibility, attributes: [AttributeInfo], source: SourceSpan and documentation: [CommentInfo]. It also has body: CodeRef !MetadataError. MethodInfo adds receiver: ParameterInfo and owner: TypeId. ClosureInfo adds captures: [CaptureInfo].

CaptureInfo has binding: DeclarationHandle, name: String, type: TypeId, mode: CaptureMode, source: SourceSpan and constraints: [ObligationFact]. CaptureMode uses the existing checked capture modes rather than inferring capture from a name. Under option B, CallableSignature's fields appear directly on each callable record; all their types and meanings remain identical.

EffectInfo has identity: DeclarationHandle, name: String and source: ?SourceSpan. FailureInfo has carrier: TypeId, source: FailureSource and errors: [TypeId]. GenericBinding has parameter: DeclarationHandle and argument: GenericArgument. GenericArgument is Type(TypeId), Value(PreparedValue) or Measure(MeasureInfo). PreparedValue uses the existing typed compile-time value algebra, never pre-stringified data.

ParamZone, AccessConvention, Visibility, CallingConvention, FailureSource and CaptureMode project their existing checker enums exactly. Their canonical declarations and public case spellings are included in the generated schema. No string catch-all or unchecked extension case is permitted. A new enum case requires the normal public-contract review.

## Type, field and layout records

TypeInfo has identity: TypeId, name: String, form: TypeForm, source: ?SourceSpan and attributes: [AttributeInfo]. It has fields: [FieldInfo], cases: [CaseInfo], methods: [MethodInfo], traits: [TraitInfo], generic_bindings: [GenericBinding] and layout: LayoutInfo !MetadataError. These lists are complete for the requested retained type graph or the root query fails. A scalar's empty fields list is genuinely empty.

TypeForm mirrors every checked type form: Int, Float, Bool, String, Char, List, Map, Shared, Option, Result, Function, Named, Apply and TraitObject. It also includes Tuple, FixedList, IntN, InlineRange, Float32, Tagged, Union, Quantity and Measure. These cases project the exact algebra in crates/jet-foundation/src/AST/types.rs, not a reduced string taxonomy.

Child types in that algebra become TypeId references. Named and applied declarations become DeclarationHandles plus ordered GenericArguments. Fixed lengths use MeasureInfo; dimensions use the existing canonical dimension algebra. Tagged facts separate identity-bearing tags from non-identity annotations. Function forms reference CallableSignature. Type identity follows existing sema equality, including callable labels and zones.

FieldInfo has identity: DeclarationHandle, name: String, type: TypeId, visibility: Visibility, default: ?DefaultInfo, attributes: [AttributeInfo], source: SourceSpan and offset: Int !MetadataError. CaseInfo has identity: DeclarationHandle, name: String, payload: [FieldInfo], discriminant: PreparedValue !MetadataError and source: SourceSpan. Active-case inspection and captured payloads preserve D-ENUM-CASEMETA1's ratified access and copy rules.

TraitInfo has identity: DeclarationHandle, parameters: [GenericBinding], required_methods: [MethodInfo], associated_types: [TypeId] and constraints: [ObligationFact]. LayoutInfo has target: TargetId, size: Int, alignment: Int and abi: AbiInfo. Layout values describe the selected target, never the compiler host by accident. Runtime variants retain the selected target identity.

## Program, source, package and local facts

ProgramInfo has snapshot: SnapshotId, stage: CompilerStage, declarations: [SymbolDef], scopes: [ScopeInfo], references: [ReferenceFact] and calls: [CallFact]. It also has typed_nodes: [CheckedNode] !MetadataError, state_graphs: [StateGraph] !MetadataError, fact_registry: [FactDefinition] and derivations: [DerivationFact] !MetadataError.

SymbolDef, ReferenceFact, CallFact, StateGraph, FactDefinition and DerivationFact are the existing canonical semantic-index record families. Export their complete checked fields and nested cardinalities through one versioned schema, not a second thinner facade. #3199 and #3181 own the exact typed/JSON agreement and version identity. Existing ratified fields stay mandatory; unavailable producer phases use the specified failure carrier.

ScopeInfo has identity: ScopeId, parent: ?ScopeId, declarations: [DeclarationHandle] and source: SourceSpan. CheckedNode has identity: NodeId, kind: CheckedNodeKind, type: ?TypeId, source: SourceSpan, children: [NodeId] and facts: [ObligationFact]. CheckedNodeKind is the closed typed expression/statement/item algebra exported from the existing checked semantic representation. It never exposes mutable Rust nodes.

ObligationFact uses the complete #3175 checked-local schema, including source version, expression point, binding/place identity and before/after state. All approved initialization, move, view, lifetime, cleanup, narrowing, sendability and typestate variants are preserved. A fact points to its checker derivation; no renderer synthesizes a proof.

SourceInfo has identity: SourceId, text: String, comments: [CommentInfo], documentation: [CommentInfo] and expansions: [ExpansionInfo]. CommentInfo has text: String, span: SourceSpan and kind: CommentKind. CommentKind is Line, Block or Documentation. ExpansionInfo has generated: SourceSpan, template: ?SourceSpan, caller: ?SourceSpan, captures: [SourceSpan] and publisher: ?SourceSpan.

AttributeInfo has identity: DeclarationHandle, arguments: [PreparedValue], source: SourceSpan and origin: AttributeOrigin. AttributeOrigin is Written or Expanded with its ExpansionInfo. Reading expanded attributes never claims they were directly written by the user.

PackageInfo has identity: PackageId, root: SourceId, dependencies: [DependencyInfo], imports: [ImportInfo], settings: [SettingInfo], profiles: [ProfileInfo] and targets: [TargetInfo]. DependencyInfo, ImportInfo, ProfileInfo and TargetInfo extend the existing canonical package-model records without dropping existing fields. #3523 owns their complete checked projection.

SettingInfo has name: String, type: TypeId, default: PreparedValue, selected: PreparedValue and contributions: [ContributionInfo]. ContributionInfo has value: PreparedValue, source: SourceSpan, kind: ContributionKind and selected: Bool. ContributionKind is Declaration, Profile or CommandLine. Build inputs and outputs retain existing typed BuildPlan records and their source/package provenance.

## Runtime values and retention

ValueInfo has type: TypeId, active_case: ?DeclarationHandle, fields: [ValueFieldInfo] and value: ValueHandle. ValueFieldInfo has field: DeclarationHandle, type: TypeId and value: ValueHandle. ValueHandle follows the existing lawful typed-access, capture and copy rules. It is not a raw address or a way to access arbitrary memory.

TypeCatalog has snapshot: SnapshotId, target: TargetId, roots: [TypeId], types: [TypeInfo] and scope: RetentionScope. RetentionScope is RequestedRoots or WholeProgram. A successful catalog is complete for its declared scope; it cannot imply that unretained program types do not exist.

Explicit runtime query use requests its statically known type/value roots. compiler.metadata.retain(types, facts) additionally retains named roots. compiler.metadata.retain_program(facts) requests the whole checked program catalog. Both run during preparation and preserve normal visibility and host authority. They are read-only retention requests, not advanced transformation grants.

The facts argument is a list of MetadataFamily values: Types, Callables, Program, Source, Packages, LocalState or All. Retaining LocalState preserves static checked facts, not live runtime variable contents. Retaining Source intentionally includes source text and comments within approved scope. The compiler refuses denied content rather than silently stripping a supposedly complete capture.

Runtime queries for an unretained family return Unavailable with the required stage and a retention reason. They do not reopen source files or start a compiler. A program that makes no runtime query and no retention request gets no metadata table allocation.

## Concrete unavailable access

This uses Jet's existing Result deconstruction. program is a ProgramInfo from a Parsed compiler event. Its typed_nodes field is unavailable until type checking completes. Both callable-layout options behave identically.

```jet
if program.typed_nodes == {
    .Ok(nodes) -> print(nodes.len())
    .Err(error) -> print(error.kind)
}
// Prints MetadataFailure.Unavailable, not 0.
```

The query/result types above are part of this ballot's shared contract, not an implementation choice left for #3520. Canonical existing record algebras remain in their executable homes. That reuse is not permission to invent new public fields without an owner decision.


Bounded root queries accept the optional named limit argument as ?Int. Absence requests all rows in the authorized scope. A reached policy or explicit bound returns Truncated; observed counts rows actually observed, not an invented total. Retrying cannot widen visibility or host authority.

@PHASE() is a total compiler-known Phase value, not a fallible fact query. It retains the exact Preparation, Build and Runtime cases from D-PREP-SURFACE2.

options.name: Shared signature
options.detail: Give every callable one typed signature member. All callable kinds share one schema. Parameter access adds one member hop.
options.technical: FunctionInfo, MethodInfo and ClosureInfo reference CallableSignature. The record contains ordered typed parameters, return type, effects, calling convention and generic bindings.

options.name: Flat callable records
options.detail: Repeat signature fields on each callable record. Common parameter access is shorter. Equivalent fields need coordinated definitions.
options.technical: Each callable record directly contains the same typed fields. A generated schema must enforce equivalence across functions, methods and closures.

comparisons.note: The compiler separates a signature from its definition. This is compiler-internal practice, not a stable Rust reflection API. https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/nightly-rustc/rustc_type_ir/ty_kind/struct.FnSig.html

recommendation.why: Extend the existing CallableSignatureFact producer into one complete typed public signature. Reuse its semantic facts without pretending its current string fields are complete.
gains: All callable kinds share one schema.

losses.loss: Parameter access adds one member hop.
losses.mitigation: A named shared record requires a member access; flattening duplicates its public fields.

whyNot.reason: B shortens access but spreads one contract across several records.

recommendation.tradeoff: A named shared record requires a member access; flattening duplicates its public fields.

decisions.title: Complete advanced API with checked change sets or editors
decisions.gist: Should the complete advanced API publish change sets or scoped edits?
decisions.lesson: Both options approve type construction, code parsing, caller capture, insertion, specialization, compiler workspaces and build control. Existing code and signatures may change. Authorization comes from D-META-OPTIN2; host permissions stay separate. This choice assembles edits explicitly or in a private draft. Both recheck affected callers before accepting anything.

decisions.detail:
## Contract status and authority

The owner already requested the full advanced capability set. This ballot selects its common public API and editing model. Both A and B include the type, code, specialization, workspace and build interfaces below. These are proposals, not claims of existing behavior. D-META-REFLECT2 supplies the common fact model. D-META-OPTIN2 separately gates authorization.

Existing Generated templates remain fixed by D-BUILD-GENVALUE1. Existing safety, shared phases and host-policy decisions remain binding. No required capability is deferred by choosing either option.

## Common power and limits

Both alternatives implement the complete advanced scope. This includes first-class types, code values, caller-code capture, source insertion and existing-program rewrites. Signature and nominal type changes are allowed, not quietly reduced to body-only edits.

The selected operation is available only through an authorized compiler.advanced session. A session records root authorization, registered targets, source versions, target layout and provider identities. It cannot change the authorization record itself. Imported code cannot register itself or acquire a session through ambient state.

External host policy and language safety remain binding. A transformation can intentionally change an application's declared API or effects. The receipt must expose those contract changes and recheck every consumer. This does not promise equivalence with the original application. Enterprise policy cannot be deleted by editing application syntax.

## Code values and capture

The existing generate item-template expression continues to produce Generated values. Its typed template holes remain scoped to the template. Compiler metadata queries keep callable @ roots. Ordinary prepared values outside templates use ordinary names.

New code values have explicit kinds: expression, statement sequence and declaration sequence. Parsed fragments retain syntax, source and capture maps. Checked fragments additionally carry a snapshot-bound type and effect result. Parsed code cannot masquerade as checked code.

The advanced session exposes code.parse_expression, code.parse_statements and code.parse_items. Each takes text, a source identity and explicit captures. They invoke the real Jet lexer and parser. They do not introduce a second string-template language. Strings are accepted only through these explicit advanced operations.

code.of(handle) retrieves checked code for an authorized declaration or expression. code.caller() is legal only inside a registered expansion callback. The callback receives invocation code and a capture context. Reusing captured caller bindings requires an explicit capture map.

Default insertion is hygienic. Introduced names get fresh identities. Captured names retain their lexical identities. Capturing a caller binding requires that binding's handle, not a coincidentally matching string. Scope insertion names an authorized target scope and an exact before, after or replacement position.

code.serialize(fragment) preserves kind, syntax, identities and origins. code.deserialize(bytes) checks the schema and resolves captures against the selected snapshot. Unsupported versions, unresolved captures and stale checked facts fail. Deserialization never authorizes new files or trusts serialized type proofs.

## Types and procedure specialization

The session's types service exposes primitive, tuple, array, function, struct, enum and apply constructors. These use existing Jet type forms and normal generic constraints. type_of(value) returns a first-class type value rather than its display name.

A type value may be bound by ordinary preparation and used in a type position in authorized code. For example, Packet :: prep { make_packet_type() } then packet: Packet is a use of the resulting type. Every type-position use is checked after preparation produces the type value.

Structural type constructors preserve structural identity. Nominal struct and enum constructors require a declaration identity in the registered target scope. Repeated evaluation of one declaration keeps identity. Distinct declarations with equal fields remain distinct. Recursive definitions use explicit declare/define operations and reject unresolved cycles or infinite layout.

The procedures service exposes of_call, bake and specialize. of_call takes a checked call handle and returns its selected procedure identity. bake binds named arguments and returns a callable with the remaining signature. specialize selects type/value arguments through the ordinary generic checker.

A registered specialization callback may validate constraints or produce adjusted type arguments. It returns explicit checked inputs to the same specialization engine. It cannot mark an invalid constraint as proved. Compile-time captures and runtime captures remain distinct and obey normal lifetime rules.

## Transaction operations

A mutable ChangeSet builder supports add, remove, replace_body, replace_signature, replace_type and insert. Its methods append operations in order. Commit consumes and seals the builder; subsequent mutation is rejected. Program snapshots and checked code remain immutable. Each target names its source version and declaration or scope identity. Replacements carry the parsed or checked code/type value appropriate to that operation. Signature and type replacements require explicit acknowledgement of changed public contracts.

Commit rejects overlapping conflicting edits, stale targets, unauthorized scopes and invalid generated code. It checks names, types, effects, visibility, ownership, safety and affected callers. Failed transactions publish no partial declarations or artifacts. Successful commits return a new immutable snapshot and complete transformation receipt.

Alternative B offers the same operations through scoped candidate fields and methods. Its commit produces the same receipt and recheck result. Neither option exposes Rust AST pointers or lets callers write inferred facts.

## Sessions and build control

compiler.advanced.session() obtains the authorized current session. session.workspace(name, inputs) creates an isolated compilation workspace. Inputs include source, imports, settings, compile-time arguments and target configuration. Workspace policy can narrow inherited authority but cannot widen it.

A workspace supports add_source, generate, compile, run_prepared and events. Session options configure output kind, target, link inputs, metadata retention and backend selection within supported targets. The existing BuildPlan remains the AOT artifact mechanism. Advanced build control configures it rather than creating a competing linker pipeline.

Events cover file discovery, imports, parsing, typed declarations, checked fixed points, diagnostics, target completion and artifact writes. Shared preparation events exist on every applicable execution mode. Link and artifact-write events exist only for AOT builds. Event ordering is logical and deterministic, independent of cache hits.

Callbacks may await declared producer inputs and yield while compilation proceeds. Dependency cycles fail with source diagnostics. Prepared global state persists within its named session. Cross-session transfer requires explicit immutable transferable values; an implicit no-reset switch cannot leak mutable state across unrelated builds.

Generated data is registered through workspace.add_data(name, bytes, alignment). Target layout validates alignment and relocation requirements. Native helper execution uses a separate host executable/workspace path. It still requires ordinary effect and host authorization. A metaprogramming grant is not an FFI or process grant.

## Beginner, expert and proof

Beginners keep additive generation and read-only checks without these APIs. Experts register only the transformations they need. Both examples add fee to price and update run atomically. The before program prints 4; the changed program prints 6. The new public signature is an intentional contract change, not an equivalence claim.

Additional witnesses must change a signature and its callers atomically, create a recursive legal type, bake arguments and reject stale transactions. The closure matrix also covers caller hygiene, serialization, workspaces, event order and native-host boundaries. Every public operation is owned by a delivery card before implementation starts.

## Exact example and reader key

A snapshot is one immutable version of the checked program. A change set records edits to that version. The affected dependency closure means changed declarations and every consumer whose checked facts depend on them. A receipt records the accepted source versions, changes and rechecking result.

A code value represents code rather than executing it. A first-class type can be calculated and then used in a type position. A capture map explicitly binds names in inserted code to existing declarations. Hygienic insertion keeps new names from accidentally capturing unrelated bindings. Nominal types have declaration identity, not merely matching fields.

In both examples, only() requires exactly one parsed declaration. The selected declaration exposes parsed signature and body components. set_signature under B corresponds exactly to replace_signature under A. The acknowledge argument explicitly accepts a public contract change; ordinary sema still checks it.

s.captures(name, handle) constructs a one-entry capture map. The captured price handle keeps declaration identity across this atomic signature change. The parser does not infer a new capture merely from matching text. Prelude print remains a normal lexical prelude reference.

The receipt reports price changed from (Int) -> Int to (Int, Int) -> Int. It also reports the changed run body and unchanged Console effect on run. No Console effect is added to price. Leaving run unchanged rejects the transaction for its missing argument. Nothing partially publishes.

The provider runs only after the root's manifest and explicit registration pass D-META-OPTIN2. A later attempt to read a forbidden host file is denied by #3418 despite that metaprogram authorization.

## Operation and failure owners

#3529 owns code parsing, hygiene, capture, serialization and stale capture rejection. #3528 owns type construction, nominal identity, recursion and invalid-layout diagnostics. #3541 owns baking, selected procedure identity and specialization constraints.

#3530 owns stale targets, edit conflicts, unauthorized scopes, invalid changed code and complete atomic rechecking. #3525 owns producer barriers and cycle failures. #3527 owns workspace isolation, events, build options and data emission. #3531 owns host execution and persistent-state boundaries.

#3526 owns authorization and self-enablement refusal. #3418 and #3419 own host denial and approval presentation. #3532 owns invalidation; #3533 owns receipts, source navigation and diagnostics. #3539 refuses closure if any public operation lacks an exercised witness.


The examples define the registered transform callback. Registration supplies s after checking the root, provider and named targets. An import does not call transform. The callback may return a checked preparation error through ordinary error propagation; it cannot obtain an unauthorized session itself.

## Audited safety origin

Advanced authorization does not grant permission to manufacture an Unsafe approval. I1 requires an applicable user-written audited #Unsafe region or vetted library/memory internals. Parsed source identities are compiler-verified handles, not proof supplied by text. Moving a checked node cannot widen its safety authority. #3530 owns attempted marker, text and serialized-proof forgery witnesses.

## Complete callback registration

Root preparation uses compiler.advanced.register(provider, targets: [(@FUNCTION(price)?).identity, (@FUNCTION(run)?).identity]). Each target is a compiler-issued DeclarationHandle carrying package identity, declaration identity and source digest. A display string is not an authority token. The callback receives one authorized Session and returns a normal checked preparation result.

compiler.advanced.register_expansion(provider, targets: [(@FUNCTION(entry)?).identity]) registers a call-expansion provider for the selected declaration. The provider receives Session and ExpansionRequest, then returns a CodeFragment or source-bound error. ExpansionRequest contains target, call_source, call_syntax, caller_scope, explicit_captures and the current checked-fact availability. The selected provider runs at that declaration's call sites before the replacement is checked. Ordinary calls remain ordinary when no provider is registered.

compiler.advanced.register_specialization(provider, targets: [(@FUNCTION(generic_entry)?).identity]) registers a specialization provider. It receives Session and SpecializationRequest, then returns SpecializationInputs or a source-bound error. The request contains the selected declaration, original type/value arguments, constraints and caller source. Returned inputs contain adjusted type/value arguments and explicit constraint diagnostics. The ordinary specialization checker still proves every constraint.

Both registration forms use the same root approval, pinned provider identity, declared targets and deterministic event scheduler. They cannot self-register from an imported module. Duplicate identical registrations are idempotent; competing providers for one target and callback kind are rejected unless composed explicitly into one provider.

code.caller() exposes only the active ExpansionRequest's call syntax and capture context. It fails outside that callback. session() likewise fails outside an active approved provider scope. Returned handles cannot widen the provider's target grant or outlive their checked snapshot. No unregistered implicit macro expansion is introduced.

#3529 owns register_expansion dispatch and its capture failures. #3541 owns register_specialization dispatch and its constraint failures. #3526 owns typed target authorization for every registration form. The ordinary typed template engine remains the same mechanism beneath Generated values and advanced fragments.


## Lookup and source identity types

session.program().function(name) resolves one unambiguous function in that authorized snapshot and returns its DeclarationHandle. candidate.function(name) returns a scoped CandidateDeclaration with identity, signature and body. Its identity is the stable DeclarationHandle used in capture maps. Missing or ambiguous lookups produce a source-bound error, never a first-match selection.

Reflection roots return their typed result records under D-META-REFLECT2. Registration uses each FunctionInfo.identity after normal error propagation. Parsed-code calls use SourceInfo.identity as their verified origin. The parser creates a new derived source identity from the actual fragment bytes; it cannot pretend those bytes were handwritten in the original file.

options.name: Explicit change sets
options.detail: Read a stable snapshot, then submit explicit replacements. Conflicts and changed contracts remain inspectable. Edits require an explicit change set.
options.technical: Program snapshots and checked code remain immutable. A mutable ChangeSet builder records explicit versioned operations, never edits compiler nodes. Commit consumes and seals it, then checks and atomically publishes the complete affected program.
options.code:
use core.compiler as compiler
fn transform(s: compiler.advanced.Session) {
    f :: s.program().function("price")
    new_price :: s.code.parse_items("fn price(x: Int, fee: Int) -> Int { return x + fee }", source: (@SOURCE()?).identity, captures: [])?
    new_run :: s.code.parse_statements("print(price(4, 2))", source: (@SOURCE()?).identity, captures: s.captures("price", f))?
    edits :: s.changes()
    edits.replace_signature(f, new_price.only().signature, acknowledge: true)
    edits.replace_body(f, new_price.only().body)
    edits.replace_body(s.program().function("run"), new_run)
    receipt :: s.commit(edits)?
}

options.name: Scoped candidate editor
options.detail: Edit a private candidate, then commit the whole candidate. Tree algorithms can edit a local tree directly. The full edit history needs a separate receipt.
options.technical: The editor grants mutable candidate handles only inside one scope. Handles cannot escape. Commit derives the complete change set and atomically checks the affected dependency closure.
options.code:
use core.compiler as compiler
fn transform(s: compiler.advanced.Session) {
    candidate :: s.edit()
    f :: candidate.function("price")
    new_price :: s.code.parse_items("fn price(x: Int, fee: Int) -> Int { return x + fee }", source: (@SOURCE()?).identity, captures: [])?
    new_run :: s.code.parse_statements("print(price(4, 2))", source: (@SOURCE()?).identity, captures: s.captures("price", f.identity))?
    f.set_signature(new_price.only().signature, acknowledge: true)
    f.body = new_price.only().body
    candidate.function("run").body = new_run
    receipt :: candidate.commit()?
}

recommendation.why: Explicit changes preserve a stable basis for analysis, conflict detection and review. They still permit body, signature and type transformations.
gains: Conflicts and changed contracts remain inspectable.

losses.loss: Edits require an explicit change set.
losses.mitigation: Making the explicit review record primary requires constructing it; B instead derives that record from a mutable candidate.

whyNot.reason: B helps tree editing but introduces scoped mutable handles and a second edit-history representation.

recommendation.tradeoff: A makes the edit record primary. B avoids manual recording but needs a scoped mutable candidate.

surface.gist: Should the complete advanced API publish change sets or scoped edits?
surface.lesson: Both options approve type construction, code parsing, caller capture, insertion, specialization, compiler workspaces and build control. Existing code and signatures may change. Authorization comes from D-META-OPTIN2; host permissions stay separate. This choice assembles edits explicitly or in a private draft. Both recheck affected callers before accepting anything.

current.note: Current extensions cannot apply this change. Both options preserve captured identities and reject stale serialized code (#3529). Nominal types keep declaration identity; illegal recursive layouts fail (#3528). Events are deterministic and session state stays isolated (#3527, #3531). Native-host permissions remain separate. options.name: Explicit change sets
options.gist: Read a stable snapshot, then submit explicit replacements.
gains: Conflicts and changed contracts remain inspectable.
losses: Edits require an explicit change set.

proposed.code:
use core.compiler as compiler
fn transform(s: compiler.advanced.Session) {
    f :: s.program().function("price")
    new_price :: s.code.parse_items("fn price(x: Int, fee: Int) -> Int { return x + fee }", source: (@SOURCE()?).identity, captures: [])?
    new_run :: s.code.parse_statements("print(price(4, 2))", source: (@SOURCE()?).identity, captures: s.captures("price", f))?
    edits :: s.changes()
    edits.replace_signature(f, new_price.only().signature, acknowledge: true)
    edits.replace_body(f, new_price.only().body)
    edits.replace_body(s.program().function("run"), new_run)
    receipt :: s.commit(edits)?
}

options.name: Scoped candidate editor
options.gist: Edit a private candidate, then commit the whole candidate.
gains: Tree algorithms can edit a local tree directly.
losses: The full edit history needs a separate receipt.

proposed.code:
use core.compiler as compiler
fn transform(s: compiler.advanced.Session) {
    candidate :: s.edit()
    f :: candidate.function("price")
    new_price :: s.code.parse_items("fn price(x: Int, fee: Int) -> Int { return x + fee }", source: (@SOURCE()?).identity, captures: [])?
    new_run :: s.code.parse_statements("print(price(4, 2))", source: (@SOURCE()?).identity, captures: s.captures("price", f.identity))?
    f.set_signature(new_price.only().signature, acknowledge: true)
    f.body = new_price.only().body
    candidate.function("run").body = new_run
    receipt :: candidate.commit()?
}

recommendation.why: Explicit changes preserve a stable basis for analysis, conflict detection and review. They still permit body, signature and type transformations.
gains: Conflicts and changed contracts remain inspectable.

losses.loss: Edits require an explicit change set.
losses.mitigation: Making the explicit review record primary requires constructing it; B instead derives that record from a mutable candidate.

whyNot.reason: B helps tree editing but introduces scoped mutable handles and a second edit-history representation.

recommendation.tradeoff: A makes the edit record primary. B avoids manual recording but needs a scoped mutable candidate.

decisions.title: Opt-in for type construction and existing-code transformations
decisions.gist: Should a checked package opt-in suffice, or must every invocation repeat it?
decisions.lesson: Standard mode permits reflection and additive generation. Advanced mode also permits type construction, caller-code insertion, explicit parsing and replacement of existing contracts. Both options require root approval and explicit provider registration. They share dependency denial, revocation, cache isolation and audit rules. Host permissions remain separate. A stores consent in the approved package; B repeats it per invocation.
decisions.explainer: Standard mode permits reflection and additive generation. Advanced mode also permits type construction, caller-code insertion, explicit parsing and replacement of existing contracts. Both options require root approval and explicit provider registration. They share dependency denial, revocation, cache isolation and audit rules. Host permissions remain separate. A stores consent in the approved package; B repeats it per invocation.
decisions.story: A package author needs the same example to work during preparation and across applicable execution modes. This choice fixes the public contract before implementation.
decisions.inWild:
cargo build --features metaprogramming
Cargo makes feature selection explicit, but features are not a security boundary. Jet authorization must not inherit that assumption. https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/features.html
decisions.detail:
## Fixed owner direction

The owner explicitly requested full Jai-level capabilities with powers above level 5 gated by metaprogramming opt-in. Neither option removes that requested scope. This decision chooses authorization placement, not whether advanced capabilities will exist.

Standard mode includes ordinary preparation, complete lawful read-only facts and explicit additive Generated publication. It also includes ordinary existing generics and project-defined checks. It forbids first-class type construction, caller-code insertion, arbitrary code parsing and replacement of existing program contracts.

Unrestricted means the complete checked metaprogramming API, not unrestricted operating-system access. Type safety, memory safety, explicit Unsafe regions and enterprise host policy still apply. Advanced metaprograms cannot forge inferred facts or erase external approval records.

## Exact configuration and registration

The manifest member is metaprogramming: unrestricted inside the invocation root package. Omission means standard. An explicit metaprogramming: standard has the same meaning. Unknown values fail rather than falling back. There is one compiler binary and one mode-aware compilation path.

compiler.advanced.register(transform, targets: [(@FUNCTION(price)?).identity, (@FUNCTION(run)?).identity]) registers a provider callback from an explicitly imported module. Registration names the provider's content identity and declared targets. Repeated identical registration is idempotent; conflicting identities under one name are errors. Merely importing a module runs no provider.

A callback receives an authorized session. Its targets must remain within the root's registered workspace and permitted dependency scopes. A dependency may expose a provider, but its own manifest cannot enable it in the root. The root must register it explicitly under the approved policy.

Existing #3418 trust policy decides whether the root and provider are approved. Existing #3419 owns consent presentation. A previously unapproved or changed privileged provider cannot silently run. Noninteractive operation fails closed with an actionable request for approval. A known approved root does not need redundant per-invocation consent under A.

Option B adds --metaprogramming=unrestricted to check, run, dev and build. Editor analysis requires the equivalent explicit session grant. The flag cannot enable a package whose manifest remains standard. Neither option allows a provider to edit its own mode, trust record or external policy.

## Effects, caching and artifacts

The privilege grant is distinct from file, process, network, native-code and sensitive-data authority. Those operations still use inferred effects and approved host policy. A denial stops the operation and records its actual source; no empty success fallback is allowed.

Cache keys include the mode, provider identities, settings, target and relevant grants. Standard mode cannot reuse an advanced result as if it were standard. Revoking authorization invalidates affected preparation artifacts. Existing audit retention policy controls receipts; a metaprogram cannot delete them.

An AOT binary launches without re-running preparation or obtaining compiler privileges. This does not erase ordinary runtime permissions required by its application code. A dev session reload must re-evaluate approval when provider code, mode or grants change.

## Same-program comparison

Both examples register transform and allow the same checked edits after root approval. Without the manifest member, registration fails before the provider executes. Under B, omitting the flag also fails. A dependency's identical manifest member does not enable the parent.

Beginners need no opt-in for read-only reflection or additive generation. Experts choose unrestricted once under A and register only required providers. Tests must exercise denial, dependency self-enablement, revocation, editor behavior and cold/warm execution. No unchecked compiler escape is introduced.

## Reader key and shared policy commitments

The invocation root is the package the user asks Jet to compile. A provider is an imported Jet function explicitly registered to transform named targets. Its content identity is the digest of its code and relevant dependencies. Ambient state means privileges acquired without an explicit passed or registered grant.

This ballot selects the exact opt-in, registration and invalidation rules stated here. The owner already selected advanced power behind opt-in. Existing #3418 and #3419 govern project trust and consent; this vote does not silently expand host rights. The complete transformation in D-META-CONTROL2 defines transform in both examples.

The same transform changes price's signature and updates run in one transaction. The result prints 6 rather than 4. Registration declares price and run as its only targets. Attempting to rewrite a third declaration fails. Attempting a denied file or process operation still fails before that effect occurs.

An approved root and unchanged approved provider may run under A without repeated prompts. An unapproved or changed provider requires interactive approval under the trust policy. Noninteractive compilation refuses it and explains which root/provider requires approval. Approval of a root never approves a dependency provider that was not explicitly registered.

Under B, the editor initialization field metaprogramming is the string unrestricted. Omission or standard permits passive diagnostics but prevents advanced provider execution. The package manifest and trust checks must still agree. Under A, editor execution uses the approved package request without an extra session flag. Revocation immediately prevents subsequent provider execution in either mode.

## Failure coverage

#3526 proves unknown mode values, missing requests, dependency self-enablement, undeclared targets, changed providers and revoked approval fail before privileged code runs. #3419 owns the actual interactive consent surface; #3418 owns a denied host effect. #3532 proves cache isolation and revocation invalidation. #3533 proves editor denial and actionable source locations.

#3521 proves saved AOT artifacts do not prepare at startup. #3527 proves a child workspace cannot widen its parent's grants. #3539 exercises the standard-versus-advanced matrix rather than accepting configuration parsing as proof.


The package file uses the existing top-level record grammar. metaprogramming is a new member next to name and version. No package wrapper keyword or second manifest grammar is proposed.

## Dependency targets and approval ownership

Registration uses compiler-issued DeclarationHandles, not unqualified strings. Handles carry package identity, declaration identity and checked source digest. The root's own declarations are eligible under its approved unrestricted request. Dependency declarations are ineligible unless explicitly granted below.

A root package may add metaprogramming_targets entries. Each record names package identity, source_digest and an exact declarations list. These records use the existing package-record and list grammar. No glob or transitive grant is implied. A conceptual entry is { package: "vendor.math", source_digest: "sha256:...", declarations: ["vendor.math.clamp"] }; the stored digest must be complete and verified.

The invocation-root owner approves this grant under #3418's project trust policy. A dependency cannot supply or approve its own parent grant. Enterprise policy may prohibit dependency transformation. The provider must also register the exact target handles; either missing approval or missing registration denies the edit. Changing the dependency digest invalidates the grant and requires approval again.

Approved edits apply only to the root's compilation workspace snapshot. They never rewrite the dependency cache or another project's source. Receipts retain original package identity, source digest, approved declarations and transformed snapshot identity. Private facts still need the corresponding explicit authorized scope; possession of a display name grants nothing.

#3526 owns exact grant matching, wrong-digest refusal, unauthorized dependency targets and registration checks. #3530 owns unchanged dependency storage and affected-consumer rechecking. #3532 keys the grant and transformed snapshot into cache identity. This grants complete checked dependency transformation without permitting dependency self-enablement.

options.name: Approved package opt-in
options.detail: Authorize the root package and explicitly register providers. Approved projects avoid repeated flags. Ordinary invocations can execute previously approved providers.
options.technical: Only the invocation root manifest can request unrestricted mode. Existing project trust and enterprise policy must approve that root. Registration is explicit in root preparation; import alone remains inert.

options.name: Package plus invocation
options.detail: Require the package request and an execution grant on each invocation. This limits accidental execution but adds CLI and editor setup.
options.technical: The same root authorization and provider registration apply. Every compile, run, dev, check and editor compilation also requires an invocation-level unrestricted grant.

comparisons.note: Cargo makes feature selection explicit, but features are not a security boundary. Jet authorization must not inherit that assumption. https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/features.html

recommendation.why: A makes explicitly approved project behavior work consistently in commands and editors. B adds stronger per-invocation refusal, at the cost of repeated execution grants.
gains: Approved projects run without a repeated flag.

losses.loss: Ordinary invocations can execute previously approved providers.
losses.mitigation: Avoiding repeated execution consent lets approved configuration activate providers on later invocations.

whyNot.reason: B can refuse advanced execution per invocation, but adds a grant to every CLI and editor workflow.

recommendation.tradeoff: A accepts durable activation, not merely a missing reminder. B provides finer control over each execution.

decisions.title: Package settings use ordinary typed brace defaults
decisions.gist: Should package settings use Jet’s ordinary constructor-default form?
decisions.lesson: A setting declares a type and default. Braces reuse Jet’s ordinary typed-default form, not arbitrary constructor execution. Allowed values remain Bool, Int, Char, String and fieldless enums. A rejects old equals declarations and offers a fix. Profile contributions and command-line overrides do not change.
decisions.explainer: A setting declares a type and default. Braces reuse Jet’s ordinary typed-default form, not arbitrary constructor execution. Allowed values remain Bool, Int, Char, String and fieldless enums. A rejects old equals declarations and offers a fix. Profile contributions and command-line overrides do not change.
decisions.story: A package author changes tls from true to false, then overrides it in a profile. Both choices preserve the result; A also migrates the declaration spelling.
decisions.detail:
## Exact scope

This decision covers declarations inside package settings blocks. It does not change profile contribution syntax or --set key=value. Configuration files do not gain package setting declarations. Scaffolds without settings require no invented setting block.

A chooses name: Type{default}. B retains name: Type = default. The tls and api_base examples produce identical typed values and normalized settings identity. This is a declaration-default form, not a general permission to execute arbitrary constructors in manifests.

The legal setting domain remains Bool, signed 64-bit Int, Char, String and fieldless enums. Floats, aggregates, user-defined effectful constructors and arbitrary preparation code remain rejected. Qualified fieldless enum names use ordinary type-name resolution within that existing domain.

The default must be a valid pure value of the declared type. Empty braces, wrong types, out-of-range integers and payload enum cases fail with a source-bound diagnostic. The normal declaration parser may understand more expressions than package settings permit; semantic validation preserves the smaller domain.

## Overrides and identity

Existing contribution precedence, conflict handling, provenance and validation remain unchanged. Profiles still use key: value. CLI overrides still use --set key=value, including strings containing another equals sign. Every profile is validated, including inactive profiles.

Unknown setting keys remain errors. A declaration supplies both its type and default. Reading the selected setting produces the same typed compile-time value before code generation. Equivalent values keep equivalent normalized cache identity and provenance across the syntax migration.

## Parser and complete cutover

Reuse ordinary lexer and typed-default parsing facilities. Do not add another quote-and-brace scanner. Character literals containing braces, comments, raw strings and triple strings must not corrupt package block boundaries. Nested ordinary token forms receive normal source locations even when settings later reject their value types.

If A wins, migrate all current package examples, fixtures, diagnostics, fix suggestions and explanations in one cutover. Old equals syntax is rejected with a constructor-form fix; it is not retained as a compatibility alias. Historical ballots and immutable audit evidence are not rewritten.

## Same-program proof

Both examples select true and the same URL. An existing profile can select false without changing its spelling. A CLI URL containing equals remains one string. Run the existing typed-settings package under AOT, default run and interpreter, with and without overrides.

The parser proof also covers a closing-brace Char, raw strings, triple strings, comments, invalid types and malformed constructors. Prove normalized semantic identity, diagnostics and package source provenance. No runtime filesystem read is introduced. Beginners see the ordinary declaration shape; experts retain existing explicit override controls.

The current package file is a top-level record, not a package declaration. Preserve settings: { ... } and its existing separators. Only each setting’s typed default changes. examples/features/packages/typed_settings/package.jet is the migration witness.

options.name: Ordinary constructor defaults
options.detail: Use the same typed-default form as ordinary declarations. One familiar form declares defaults. Existing settings declarations must migrate.
options.technical: The package parser reuses the ordinary typed-default token/parser contract. A setting still admits only the currently selected closed pure-value domain.

options.name: Keep equals defaults
options.detail: Keep the current settings-only separator. Existing setting files stay unchanged. Settings retain a separate declaration form.
options.technical: The current manifest grammar remains canonical. Constructor defaults remain ordinary-language syntax but are not accepted in settings declarations.

comparisons.note: Jet already parses brace defaults for parameters and fields. This is local executable practice, not an external adoption claim.

recommendation.why: Use A. Settings are declarations, so their defaults should look like other Jet defaults. Reuse the parser without broadening allowed values.
gains: One familiar form declares defaults.

losses.loss: Old equals declarations must migrate.
losses.mitigation: One canonical syntax requires migrating old declarations; accepting both would preserve the inconsistency.

whyNot.reason: B avoids migration but keeps a settings-only rule the owner must remember.

recommendation.tradeoff: One canonical syntax requires migrating old declarations; accepting both would preserve the inconsistency.

decisions.title: Which executable should a package image use?
decisions.gist: Which executable should `from: packages.<name>` put in an OCI image?
decisions.lesson: A package can expose several executables, but the image record names only its package. Jet must choose one file before it can build the image. This choice keeps the existing image syntax and OCI contents rule. It defines how the package reference selects its executable.
decisions.explainer: D-JPK-IMAGE1=A ratified `from: packages.<name>` as a package image source, but it did not say which executable to take when a package exposes several. The current consumer guesses a flat filename, which no longer identifies a build. This ballot decides the existing reference's meaning; it adds no syntax.
decisions.story: Mira packages `pulseops`. Its checked outputs include `cli` and `pulseops`, while `defaults.run` selects `cli`. She declares `from: packages.pulseops` and needs to know which executable the image will contain before she publishes it.
decisions.inWild:
[package]
name = "pulseops"
default-run = "cli"

[[bin]]
name = "cli"
path = "src/main.rs"

[[bin]]
name = "pulseops"
path = "src/server.rs"

# cargo run picks cli when a package has multiple binaries.
# https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html#the-default-run-field
decisions.detail: The existing image form identifies a package, not one of its executable outputs. Both options keep `module image.server { kind: .Oci, from: packages.pulseops }` unchanged. Both use the default build profile, current toolchain, native backend, and selected package member. Neither scans identity directories or falls back to `.jet/build/<name>`.

options.name: Use the package's ordinary default build
options.detail: Use the exact executable that the package's normal build selects without a named output. That selection follows the existing canonical entry and checked `defaults.run` rules. If the ordinary build cannot select one, the image fails with the same missing-or-ambiguous selection. Beginners keep the short package reference; experts choose the package default once for all ordinary consumers.
options.technical: Resolve the same checked package entry and executable target used by a bare `jet build`. The default build profile, current native toolchain, and native backend complete the artifact identity. Resolve the path from those checked facts; do not search for the first matching identity directory. The OCI `target` field and image projection rules remain unchanged.

options.name: Use the package-named executable output
options.detail: Select only the checked top-level `outputs.<name>` entry whose key exactly matches the package name in `packages.<name>`, and only when it is `.Executable`. Ignore `defaults.run`. If no matching executable exists, fail instead of choosing another output. Experts can keep the package's ordinary default separate from its image executable; beginners must name the output to match the package.
options.technical: For `from: packages.pulseops`, require exactly the package's checked top-level `outputs.pulseops` executable. Use that output's checked entry, output target name, default build profile, current native toolchain, and native backend to resolve one artifact identity. A missing, non-executable, or ambiguous match is an image error; never scan, choose another output, or read the retired flat path.

comparisons.note: Cargo's official guide says `default-run` picks one binary when a package has several. This is a comparison for package defaults, not image behavior: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html#the-default-run-field
comparisons.code:
[package]
default-run = "cli"

[[bin]]
name = "cli"

[[bin]]
name = "pulseops"

# cargo run picks cli.

recommendation.why: A reuses the package's existing no-selector build choice. It avoids a second image-only naming rule and gives beginners one package-level default.

whyNot.reason: B fails unless an image's package declares a matching executable output, even when its normal build already selects a different one.

recommendation.tradeoff: An image follows the package default; choosing another executable requires changing that default rather than adding a hidden image-specific choice.

decisions.checkInstructions: Wait for the owner to ratify before implementing either mapping. After ratification, test one executable; two outputs where `defaults.run` differs from `outputs.<package>`; no usable default; a missing or non-executable B match; and a workspace member. Verify the chosen artifact stays under its member's identity-qualified `.jet/build` root with the default profile, current toolchain, and native backend. Preserve environment images, OCI contents, platform, and entrypoint rules. Never scan identity paths or read flat paths.
