decisions.title: Which executable should a measured service use?
decisions.gist: How should a service probe get the executable path from its build receipt?
decisions.lesson: `jet budget` already builds an exact executable before readiness timing begins. The hidden service probe receives only a service name, while its saved command still names the old flat path. Choose how the probe uses the built file without compiling during readiness.
decisions.explainer: The http_ready receipt pairs a BuildArtifact with a ServiceProbe. `jet budget` captures the authoritative `built:` path first, then measures the service. Today the probe does not receive that path. This choice decides whether Jet replaces the command's executable or passes the path to a wrapper.
decisions.story: Mira measures an HTTP service. The build prints its new executable path before the timer starts, but the service command still names `build/run`. She wants the probe to start the same program without adding compilation time.
decisions.inWild:
[Service]
ExecStart=/opt/http_ready/run serve
# systemd.service(5), ExecStart=
# https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/latest/systemd.service.html
decisions.detail: This choice applies to `jet budget check` and `jet budget update` when a ServiceProbe and exactly one BuildArtifact refer to the same target. The build already completes before readiness timing. Neither option may scan identity directories, reconstruct a flat path, or compile inside the timed service start.

options.name: Start the exact built program
options.detail: For one matching BuildArtifact, the probe runs its exact `built:` file and keeps the service command's remaining arguments. The old first item is not read. With no matching artifact, the declared command runs unchanged. A custom wrapper in the first item is skipped.
options.technical: `jet budget` passes the path returned by its own build invocation to the hidden service probe. The probe uses that path as argv[0] and preserves run[1..]. A missing or ambiguous artifact must fail before readiness timing; it must not search `.jet/build`.
options.code:

decisions.title: Unprefixed immutable aggregate tables
decisions.gist: How should unprefixed module names represent fixed-size tables?
decisions.lesson: An unprefixed name has no marker before its letters. A module global is usable throughout its file. `::` prevents reassignment, not every change allowed by a type. `fn run` starts the program. AOT (ahead-of-time) compiles before launch; JIT compiles while running; an interpreter runs source. All three must return the same digest and reject bad initializers before `fn run`. An address is a location a pointer can keep naming. CoreLib constants never use `@`.
decisions.explainer: Choose whether a fixed table may have one plain file-wide name, must be repeated locally, or needs an explicit static marker. This decision changes global initialization and storage guarantees, not the SHA-256 algorithm.
decisions.story: Rina adds SHA-256 tables to CoreLib. A beginner wants to read the first word; an expert wants the hash of empty bytes. They need the same result in all three execution modes, without an `@` name.
decisions.detail: The current compiler accepts scalar or string module initializers under D-ENTRY-SCRIPT1=C. Fixed-size list literals are distinct from growable `[Int]` lists. The owner chooses which ordinary-name table rule to add, while the existing CoreLib naming requirement stays unprefixed snake_case.

options.name: Plain fixed-size value
options.detail: Use a plain `::` name at file scope. Every function in the file can read it. The first-word example returns `1779033703`; the hash of empty bytes is `e3b0c44298fc1c149afbf4c8996fb92427ae41e4649b934ca495991b7852b855`.
options.technical:
`sha256_iv :: [Int#8]{...}` has the explicit fixed-size type `[Int#8]`. A bare `[1, 2]` instead infers growable `[Int]`; see `CheckerInfer/expr.rs:5971-6023,6207-6208` and `examples/features/collections/fixed_arrays.jet:11-23`. Passing `[Int#8]` to `sha2_256(iv: [Int])` makes an owned list copy. The helper copies that list into mutable state (`Core/crypto/crypto.jet:835-841`). The binding root is read-only, not the `[Int]` type everywhere. Writes and mutable aliases through this name are forbidden. `~sha256_iv` makes an independent writable copy (D-SHAPE-COPY1=A).

A admits nonempty typed fixed-list and named-tuple literal trees. Leaves are Int, Float, Bool, Char, immutable String, or fixed-width integer literals such as `U8{1}`. A fixed list must have an explicit `[T#N]` type, directly or through a fully expanded alias. For example, `(words: [Int#2]{1, 2}, ready: true)` is admitted. Aliases to growable `[Int]`, maps, or records are rejected. `List<Int>` is not an alias for `[Int]`.

Names, calls, operators, indexing, comprehensions, maps, records, references, effects, and untyped empty `[]` fail before `fn run`. For example, `[U8#1]{U8{some_name}}` fails because its leaf reads a name. The 64-word round table (`Core/crypto/crypto.jet:716-781`) follows the same rule. A permits shared read-only backing where values stay unchanged, but promises neither an address nor copy-free speed.

The beginner reads word zero; the expert passes the IV copy to the hash helper. SHA-224 changes both IV and inclusive `[0..27]` truncation to 28 bytes (`Core/crypto/crypto.jet:154-155`). AOT, JIT, and interpreter preserve values and failure phase (AGENTS.md I9). The expected empty-input hex is a standard SHA-256 test vector, not proof from `tests/pkg.rs`. The Jet API is at `Core/crypto/crypto.jet:61-66,151-155`.

options.name: Local fixed-size value
options.detail: Put the ordinary `::` table inside each function that needs it. The code returns the same first word and digest, but no other function can name that local table. Repeated construction is possible, not guaranteed.
options.technical:
Each function keeps its own `[Int#8]` binding, and the hash helper copies it to its `[Int]` parameter. Calls have no guaranteed shared address. An optimizer may share backing when behavior stays unchanged; repeated physical construction is a possible cost, not a promise. Local expressions may compute values and fail when called.

The 64-word SHA-256 round table would live inside the hash helper. SHA-224 needs its own IV plus inclusive `[0..27]` truncation to 28 bytes. Beginner and expert outputs match A and C. AOT, JIT, and interpreter preserve the same result and error phase (AGENTS.md I9; D-ONCE-TIER1 at docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:6749-6750).

options.name: Explicit read-only static
options.detail: Proposed only: extend `#Static` to a plain module name. A pointer can then keep naming one location. The SHA-256 code shown here receives a value copy and cannot observe that address.
options.technical:
Proposed syntax only: `#Static name :: literal`. Unlike current `#Static @name`, this marker attaches to an ordinary name and changes storage only. S57 still reserves `@` for names that demand compile-time evaluation. C admits A's closed, nonempty fixed-list and named-tuple literals and expanded aliases. Computed initializers remain inside functions.

C promises one read-only object with a stable address per loaded module instance. All applicable execution modes preserve that identity (AGENTS.md I9). An ordinary value read or `~` copy cannot mutate the object. The sample hash widens `[Int#8]` to `[Int]` by copy, so it cannot observe the address. A real pointer consumer could. SHA-224 uses a separate IV and inclusive `[0..27]` truncation to 28 bytes. Current `#Static @name` remains available outside CoreLib (examples/features/comptime/static_constant.jet).

comparisons.note: Rust `const` behaves like a copied value and does not promise one address. `static` names one storage location, and immutable statics may use read-only memory. The Reference generally prefers constants unless large data, interior mutability, or one address is needed. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/items/constant-items.html and https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/items/static-items.html.

recommendation.why: A gives every function in a file one plain name. The fixed table widens by copy for the SHA routine, so the routine needs no shared address.

whyNot.reason: Each function must repeat its local table; the module-level name serves all functions while producing the same digest.
The SHA call only reads a copied value and cannot observe C's stable address. Use an address promise only when a real pointer consumer needs it.

recommendation.tradeoff: A shares one file-wide value but offers no stable address and keeps computed table construction inside functions.

decisions.title: How should buffered file handles be closed?
decisions.gist: How should buffered file handles be closed?
decisions.lesson: Jet opens files as typed reader or writer handles. They close automatically when their scope ends. The public files.close(Int) call instead takes a bare number, but no execution mode uses that number as a shared file handle. Compiling its implementation currently stops with an internal error. Both options remove that broken call and keep writers able to report flush errors.
decisions.explainer: Choose whether automatic closing alone is the public rule, or whether typed handles also need a way to close early.
decisions.story: Rina creates a file, writes one line, and flushes it. She needs the file closed safely, without guessing a numeric descriptor.
decisions.detail: Jet already promises automatic close on every exit path in docs/spec/reference/core-library.md:482-512. Core/files/files.jet:79-102 declares integer fd fields and close(Int), but the compiled handles are owned buffered objects, JIT uses table slots, and the interpreter uses opaque handles. core.sys.close_fd is a separate unsafe system operation. Neither option treats an arbitrary Int as a file handle or promises that dropping a buffered writer reports a flush error.

options.name: Automatic close only
options.detail: Retire files.close(Int) and its obsolete integer-descriptor example. Keep typed open/create/append, explicit writer.flush() for reported write errors, and automatic close on scope exit. The file contains x followed by a newline.

options.name: Typed early close too
options.detail: Retire files.close(Int), and add consuming reader.close() and writer.close() methods to release handles before scope exit. The caller flushes first to observe buffered write errors. Closing consumes the handle, so later use is rejected; close itself returns unit and does not promise OS close-error reporting. The file contains the same line.

comparisons.note: Rust File closes when its owned value is dropped. Flush is a separate fallible operation. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/fs/struct.File.html.

recommendation.why: A matches the existing typed-handle promise and keeps the flush error visible without inventing a meaning for numbers.

whyNot.reason: The shown file finishes at scope exit, so an additional public close method supplies no useful behavior here.

recommendation.tradeoff: A cannot release a handle early without ending its ownership scope.

decisions.checkInstructions: After owner ratification, remove the integer close declaration, exports, fixed signature, fixture, and generated views together. If B wins, implement consuming typed reader and writer close across AOT, default run, and interpreter and test early release, rejected reuse, and flush errors. For A, test automatic close on ordinary and early-return paths. Rebuild before focused file and crypto tier tests; never map the integer to an OS descriptor.

decisions.title: Prove that hot code has no hidden costs
decisions.gist: Which hidden costs should experts be able to forbid, with a compile error as proof?
decisions.lesson: A function can already forbid allocation (`!Mem.Alloc`), reference counting (`!Mem.Rc`), and panics (`!Panic`). The check follows every call it reaches, including dependencies. This extends the same form to other hidden costs. A hot loop could then prove it never collects, locks, notifies, or makes a dynamic call.
decisions.story: Rosa writes an audio callback that must finish in two milliseconds. C++ gives her control but no proof. She wants the build to fail if any code she reaches might lock, collect, or allocate.

options.name: Full cost family
options.detail: Add six denials. `!Mem.Gc` forbids collection, and `!Lock` forbids locks and blocking waits. `!Notify` forbids reactive update code, and `!Dyn` forbids dynamic dispatch. `!Mem.Check` forbids runtime alias checks. `!Mem.Copy(above: N)` forbids implicit copies above N bytes. Each works like `!Mem.Alloc`: it follows every reachable call and reports the full path.
options.technical: These are new rows in the effect registry and use the transitive fact check of D-MEM-FACTS1 and D-AUTHORITY-MEM1. Open-world dispatch needs a sealed target set or signed summary, as today. They are also the lock mechanism for D-AUTOPIN1.

options.name: Memory only
options.detail: Only the two memory denials are added.
options.technical: Two new registry rows.

options.name: Keep today's three
options.detail: No change.
options.technical: No change.

comparisons.note: `#![no_std]` removes the allocator for a whole crate; no per-function lock or dispatch proof. https://docs.rust-embedded.org/book/intro/no-std.html
Effect types can forbid effects per function. https://koka-lang.github.io/koka/doc/book.html#sec-effect-types

recommendation.why: Experts get what C and C++ cannot give: a compile-time proof that hot code has no hidden cost. It reuses the existing checker.

whyNot.reason: B leaves locks and dynamic calls, common hot-loop costs, unprovable.
C gives the new automatic features no way to prove absence.

recommendation.tradeoff: A few more effect names buy proven absence of cost.

decisions.title: Every automatic choice can be seen and locked
decisions.gist: Should every automatic compiler choice be reportable and lockable by experts?
decisions.lesson: Jet makes many choices for you: where code runs, how data is stored, and when memory is collected. Some are visible today, such as `--explain-partition` and `jet gc report`. Others are silent. This rule makes every automatic choice visible and lockable. A lock that no longer holds becomes a compile error, never a silent fallback.
decisions.story: Kenji tunes a game loop until it never allocates. Months later a teammate adds a log line. With a lock, the build fails and names the line. Without one, the frame rate quietly drops and nobody knows why.
decisions.inWild:
$ go build -gcflags=-m
./main.go:8:2: moved to heap: p
./main.go:12:6: can inline add
// Go can print escape and inlining decisions but offers few locks. Source: go.dev/doc/gc-guide#Escape_analysis.

options.name: One law: choose, explain, lock
options.detail: Every automatic decision is sound by default. `jet inspect choices` and editor hovers show it with its reason. A marker or effect denial locks it. If a later change breaks the lock, the build fails with the fact that changed. This applies to storage form, browser or server placement, collection, copies, inlining, and update notifications.
options.technical: It generalizes the existing precedents: the `#Local`/`#Shared` pins, `#Target` with `--explain-partition`, `jet bind --freeze`, `#Policy(copies: .Explicit)`, and `jet gc report`. The facts come from the existing structure and policy fact planes. No second mechanism is added.

options.name: Report only
options.detail: Reports everywhere, locks nowhere beyond today's.
options.technical: Adds the report plane only.
options.code:
$ jet inspect choices src/game.jet
game.jet:12  stats: thread-safe storage  (sent to a task at :18)

options.name: Per feature, as today
options.detail: No general law.
options.technical: No change.
options.code: // today: some flags, some markers, some silent choices

comparisons.note: `-gcflags=-m` reports escape and inlining; `//go:noinline` is a narrow lock. https://go.dev/doc/gc-guide
`#[inline(never)]`, `#[repr(C)]`, and `#[cold]` lock specific choices. https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/attributes/codegen.html

recommendation.why: Beginners get magic, and experts read each choice and lock it. The compiler never changes a locked choice behind their back.

whyNot.reason: B lets a later edit silently undo an expert's tuning.
C leaves choices invisible and controls inconsistent.

recommendation.tradeoff: Every automatic feature costs a report and a lock, and experts never fight the magic.

decisions.title: Keep live state when a type changes during development
decisions.gist: When a type changes during `jet dev`, should the running program keep its state?
decisions.lesson: Hot swap replaces edited code without restarting. Jet swaps body-only edits today. Changing a struct field forces a clean restart, so game or form state is lost. Jet already writes `migration` blocks for stored data. The same rules could convert live values in place.
decisions.story: Noah tunes a boss fight twenty minutes into a level. He adds a `speed` field to `Player`. Today `jet dev` restarts and he replays the level. He wants the running game to keep going with the new field.

options.name: Migrate live values
options.detail: Added fields take their declared default. Removed fields are dropped. Renames and type changes use `migration` blocks. When no rule applies, `jet dev` restarts and names the field that blocked the swap.
options.technical: It extends D-HOTSWAP1's type-surface check. Live values of changed types are walked from the resident roots and rewritten through the D-MIGRATE1 migration chain before the swap commits.

options.name: Keep state only for added fields
options.detail: Only additions with defaults are migrated.
options.technical: Subset of A.
options.code:
// adding speed: state kept
// renaming health -> hp: restart

options.name: Restart, as today
options.detail: No change.
options.technical: No change.
options.code: // jet dev restarts on any field change

comparisons.note: `code_change` converts state on hot upgrade. https://www.erlang.org/doc/system/appup_cookbook.html
Hot reload keeps state but cannot change some types. https://docs.flutter.dev/tools/hot-reload
comparisons.code: // hot reload keeps state; hot restart resets it

recommendation.why: Developers keep their place in a game or form while changing types, using rules they already write for stored data.

whyNot.reason: B loses state on renames, a very common edit.
C loses state on every type edit.

recommendation.tradeoff: Rare bad migrations in development buy uninterrupted iteration.

decisions.title: The compiler decides which cached data a write makes stale
decisions.gist: Should the compiler decide which cached queries a write makes stale, instead of hand-written keys?
decisions.lesson: A cache must learn when its data changed. TanStack Query uses hand-written keys for this. Jet's live database queries already use compiler-recorded read sets with no keys. Jet's web query and store modules still take key strings and invalidation lists. This ballot picks one rule for both.

options.name: Read and write sets everywhere
options.detail: Each query records what it reads: database tables or rows, and link fields. Each action records what it writes. When a write commits, every overlapping query refreshes. Keys disappear from the query, store, and server-action APIs. `app.invalidate` remains for sources the compiler cannot see, such as webhooks.
options.technical: It extends D-LIVEQUERY1 and D-EFFDBREAD1 footprints to D-DX-SERVERFN1 actions, `core.web.query`, and `core.web.store`. Typed queries (`core.data` plans) give table and column precision. Raw SQL gives only a coarse database-wide write. It retires the revalidation keys and invalidation lists.

options.detail: Automatic by default, with keyed APIs kept.
options.technical: Both paths feed one cache.

options.name: Keep keys
options.detail: No change.

whyNot.reason: B keeps two mechanisms, and keys can drift from the code.

decisions.title: Stopping a change while someone reads, when links alias
decisions.gist: When two links may reach the same data, how should Jet stop a write during a read?
decisions.lesson: Jet's rule is: while something is being changed, nobody else may be looking at it. A view is a window into another value without copying. The compiler proves this for names and views today. Links let two names reach one value, and sometimes only the running program knows whether they do. Swift checks what it can early and the rest at runtime. This ballot picks Jet's approach once D-MEMREF1 passes.
decisions.story: Ana writes a trip planner. Two routes can link to the same shop. Her restock step reads one shop's items and adds them to the other. When both routes reach one shop, the loop reads a list that it is growing.

options.name: Prove early, check the rest
options.detail: Where the compiler sees every path, it proves there is no conflict, as it does now. Where two links might reach one value, it adds a small runtime check at the lend or loop. A conflict stops the program with the source location. Experts can forbid runtime checks in a function with a denial and fix the code instead.
options.technical: It mirrors Swift's static and dynamic exclusivity enforcement. Counted link storage carries an access flag; the proven-free path lowers to a plain pointer with no flag. The denial spelling follows D-DENY-COST1 (`!Mem.Check`). It extends the E0204 and E0212 rules to links. Code uses the `@` link spelling that the owner chose for D-MEMREF1.

options.name: Reject what cannot be proven
options.detail: The compiler rejects any lend or loop where two links might reach one value.
options.technical: Sema treats every pair of same-type links as possibly overlapping unless it proves otherwise.

options.name: Loops read a snapshot
options.detail: When a long read goes through a link, Jet copies the data first.
options.technical: Lowering inserts a copy for iteration and views over counted link storage.

comparisons.note: Static plus dynamic exclusivity enforcement since Swift 5. https://www.swift.org/blog/swift-5-exclusivity/
comparisons.code: // Simultaneous accesses to 'x', but modification requires exclusive access

comparisons.note: `RefCell` checks borrows at runtime and panics on conflict. https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/cell/struct.RefCell.html
comparisons.code: cell.borrow_mut(); cell.borrow(); // panics: already mutably borrowed

recommendation.why: Correct code with aliasing links compiles, conflicts can never corrupt memory, and every runtime check is listed so experts can remove it.

whyNot.reason: B rejects correct code whenever two links might alias, which object graphs do often.
C hides a copy in every long read and silently misses writes.

recommendation.tradeoff: A rare located runtime stop replaces both corruption and over-strict compile errors.

decisions.title: When a link outlives the value it points to
decisions.gist: What should happen when a link outlives the variable it points to?
decisions.lesson: A link is free when its target provably outlives it. Otherwise the target must stay alive. Go does this silently with a garbage collector. Rust refuses to compile. Jet's `#Policy(gc)` and `jet gc report` already expose collector work, but Jet has no stored link today. This ballot picks the link lifetime default and expert controls. It applies once D-MEMREF1 passes.
decisions.story: Leo writes `new_player()` and returns a link to a local. In Rust he would fight a lifetime error. In Go it just works, but he never learns it cost a heap allocation. He wants it to work first and then see how to make it free.

options.name: Keep it alive, report it
options.detail: When the compiler cannot prove the owner outlives a link, it stores the target in counted memory from the start. It never moves memory at runtime. Cyclic types also get cycle collection. `jet gc report` lists each case with a concrete fix, and `jet fix` applies mechanical fixes. A CI budget can cap the count. Experts forbid the cost with `!Mem.Rc` or `!Mem.Gc` and use `Shared.Weak<T>` back links (`c.downgrade()`, `w.upgrade()`). Cross-task cycles need the thread-safe collector from D-MEMREF-TASK1.
options.technical:
Escape analysis in sema chooses counted storage per binding at compile time. The E0221 type analysis stops being an error. Instead it selects cycle collection only for types that can form cycles, using the existing private collector (D-DEP-GC1).

Under a `!Mem.Gc` denial, a possibly cyclic type is an error again, as E0221 is today. Thread-crossing cyclic types keep E0221 until a thread-safe collector is proven. `#Policy(gc)` stops changing what a store means.

This supersedes the scope design of D-OPTGC1 and the type-level rejection form of D-SHARED-CYCLE1=C. It keeps D-OPTGC1's report-and-fix goal.

options.name: Reject it, with a fix
options.detail: Links must be provably free. Otherwise the compiler rejects the code and names a fix.
options.technical: Sema reports an E2305-style diagnostic for every unprovable link. There is no counted storage and no collector for links.

options.name: Automatic only in a GC scope
options.detail: Outside a `#Policy(gc)` scope, B's errors apply. Inside it, A's automatic behavior applies.
options.technical: Keeps D-OPTGC1's scope ladder and applies it to links.

comparisons.note: Reference counting plus a cycle collector only for types that can form cycles. https://nim-lang.org/docs/mm.html
Reference counting plus a generational cycle collector. https://docs.python.org/3/library/gc.html
Automatic reference counting; cycles need `weak`. https://docs.swift.org/swift-book/documentation/the-swift-programming-language/automaticreferencecounting/
Rejects dangling references at compile time. https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch04-02-references-and-borrowing.html

recommendation.why: Ordinary links compile safely, as in Go. Experts still see every hidden cost and can forbid it, so the collector can be driven to zero.

whyNot.reason: B brings back lifetime errors, the most cited Rust pain point.
C makes one line legal or illegal because of a setting elsewhere.

recommendation.tradeoff: Beginners avoid lifetime errors, and experts pay nothing they did not allow; concurrent cycles remain fail-closed until their collector is safe.

decisions.title: Links that cross into another task
decisions.gist: What should happen when a link is sent into another task?
decisions.lesson: A task can run on another thread. Two threads changing one value at once is a data race. Today `Shared<T>` always takes a lock, even in single-threaded code, and `Cell` cannot cross at all. Reactive values already switch automatically: a fast local form by default, and a thread-safe form when they cross. This ballot applies to links once D-MEMREF1 passes.
decisions.story: Omar builds a web server with a hit counter. Locally, one thread runs everything and locks are wasted. In production, request tasks share the counter. He wants one piece of code that is fast in the first case and safe in the second.

options.name: Switch automatically, allow pins
options.detail: If any link to a type can reach another task, links to that type use atomic counts and one lock step per statement. `#Transact` groups several writes. Otherwise they use the fast local form. `jet inspect` lists each switch with the task that caused it. `#Local` forbids crossing; `#Shared` forces the thread-safe form.
options.technical: It reuses D-DATARACE1's representation choice and `#Local`/`#Shared` pins for reactive boxes. A task capture copies the link, never the binding, so E1101's mutable-binding rule does not apply. Sendability is checked on concrete types at each generic use, so each crossing has one answer. Code uses the `@` link spelling that the owner chose for D-MEMREF1.

options.name: Mark it to cross
options.detail: Links to unmarked types stay local. Crossing requires `#Shared` on the type.
options.technical: Sema reports a crossing of an unmarked link type as E1102.

options.name: Links never cross
options.detail: Tasks exchange values through channels and `freeze` only.
options.technical: Sema rejects any link in a task capture, task result, or channel message.

comparisons.note: `Rc` versus `Arc` chosen by the user. https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch16-03-shared-state.html
Actors and `Sendable` checks decide what may cross. https://docs.swift.org/swift-book/documentation/the-swift-programming-language/concurrency/

recommendation.why: The same code is fast in one thread and safe across many. Experts see each switch and can pin it.

whyNot.reason: B adds a marker that restates what the compiler already knows.
C forces redesign of common shared-state code such as counters and caches.

recommendation.tradeoff: Automatic storage choice trades one visible report for no manual lock decisions.

decisions.title: How to spell data held by reference
decisions.gist: Which spelling should Jet use for a field or name that holds a live link instead of a copy?
decisions.lesson: Jet keeps four verbs: read (plain), write (`&`), move (`^`), and copy (`~`). Today a stored value owns a copy unless it uses a special type. The new model adds a checked live link: every path sees the same changes. The compiler chooses its storage, so users write no lifetime notes. All options share this meaning; this ballot picks the spelling.
decisions.story: Maya ports a Python game editor to Jet. Her scene nodes share children and point to a parent. In Jet today the field stores a copy, and a list of `Shared` nodes fails with E0221. She wants to write 'this is the same node' in one short mark, as she would in C++ or Go.

options.name: `@` means at: a live link
options.detail: A value slot holds its own data. An `@T` slot holds a live link: reading through it shows the latest change from any path. `@p` links to a named place, or to a field or item of one. `@Player{hp: 3}` makes a new object held by link. Fields and methods follow the link on their own. You can write through a link only when you hold it with write access: a `:=` name, a writable field path, or `&` lending.
options.technical:
`@T` is a checked live-link type, and `@x` forms one from a place or a new value. A proven owner lifetime can use today's view representation; otherwise D-MEMREF-LIFE1 chooses counted storage. D-MEMREF-EXCL1 handles aliases, and D-MEMREF-TASK1 handles task crossings.

Read access is transitive: an unmarked read parameter cannot write through any link it reaches. `~c` copies the target value; storing a link in a value slot copies under D-MEM-COPYSEM1. `a == b` compares values, while `a.same(b)` compares identity. Existing `T`, `&T`, and `^T` parameters stay.

Prefix `@` in code now means a link, which supersedes D-ONCE-AT1's prefix assignment. The compile-time and compiler-fact uses of prefix `@` move to the spellings chosen on card #3662. Infix `@` in package references is decided there too. Raw pointers keep `*T`, `*x`, and `p.*` behind `#Unsafe`.

This supersedes the D-MEM1/S3 stored-reference ban. It replaces the spellings of D-MEM-VIEWRET1, D-SHARED-API1, D-CONC-SHARE1, D-LOCALCELL1, and D-PIN3's field form. It retires D-OPTGC1's scope identity.

options.name: `shared` keyword
options.detail: Same meaning as A, spelled with the `shared` word Jet already has. The `Shared<T>` type becomes the `shared T` prefix, the way `?T` names an optional. `shared Player{hp: 3}` makes a new object, exactly as today.
options.technical: It keeps D-CONC-SHARE1's `shared` word. `shared x` on an existing place changes from 'copy x into a new cell' to 'link to x'. `Shared<T>` retires into the prefix. Prefix `@` keeps its compile-time meaning, so card #3662 would not be needed.

options.name: `*` means link
options.detail: Same meaning as A, spelled with the pointer glyph. `*p` links to a place, and `*Player{hp: 3}` makes a new object. Unchecked raw pointers move to `mem.Ptr<T>` values that still require `#Unsafe`.
options.technical: It reassigns D-CAP9's raw `*T` type and `*x` expression to checked links. Raw pointers become `mem.Ptr<T>`, and `p.*` stays their dereference. Prefix `@` keeps its compile-time meaning.

comparisons.note: Per-field `*T`, automatic heap escape, garbage collected. Praised for simplicity; complaints are nil pointers and no read-only pointers. https://go.dev/doc/faq#stack_or_heap
Chooses per type: struct copies, class shares. Runtime plus compile-time exclusivity checks. https://docs.swift.org/swift-book/documentation/the-swift-programming-language/classesandstructures/
Per-field `&'a T` needs lifetimes; shared ownership needs `Rc<RefCell<T>>`. https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch15-05-interior-mutability.html
`T&`, `T*`, and `shared_ptr<T>` give full control with no dangling check. https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/memory/shared_ptr

recommendation.why: `@` reads as "at p", fits Jet's one-glyph access family, and leaves raw pointers alone. Compile-time `@` moves to its own spellings on card #3662.

whyNot.reason: B spends a whole word on a very common need, and `shared p` silently changes meaning.
C makes links read as C pointers and forces raw pointers to change spelling.

recommendation.tradeoff: Jet moves compile-time `@` elsewhere so links get the cleanest glyph.

decisions.title: Automatic optimistic updates
decisions.gist: Should the compiler generate optimistic UI updates from server actions?
decisions.lesson: An optimistic update shows a change before the server confirms it and undoes it if the server disagrees. Today Jet's store takes a hand-written apply function and field list, and rollback is manual. When an action only changes data the client already holds, the compiler could run the same code on the client first.
decisions.story: Lina adds 'add to cart'. Users wait half a second for each click. She writes an optimistic patch and a rollback, and they drift from the server code within a month. She wants the server action itself to drive the instant update.

options.name: Automatic when safe, opt out per action

fn add_item(cart: &Cart, id: Int) { cart.items.push(id) }

app.action("add", add_item)                   // shows the item at once
app.action("pay", pay, optimistic: false)     // never guess a payment

$ jet inspect choices app.jet
app.jet:3  add: optimistic (writes only cart.items)
app.jet:4  pay: waits for the server (has Net effect)

options.detail: Same mechanism as A, off by default.
options.technical: Same checks as A.

options.name: Manual, as today
options.detail: No change.

decisions.title: Complete the raw pointer tools behind #Unsafe
decisions.gist: Which raw pointer operations should audited `#Unsafe` Jet provide for C and Zig level work?
decisions.lesson: Raw pointers are the expert escape hatch. Jet has raw pointer values and fields, taking an address, following a pointer, `from_addr`, and volatile access, all inside `#Unsafe`. It lacks null, offset, cast, raw allocation, and pointer-plus-length slices. Experts do pointer math through `Int` addresses, which drops the tracking that dev-mode checks use.
decisions.story: Priya wraps a C sensor library. It returns a pointer to four readings that she must free. She needs null checks, indexing, a safe window over the four values, and a free call, all visible to a reviewer in one audited block.

options.name: Complete typed set, tracking kept
options.detail: Add optional pointers: `?mem.Ptr<T>`, where null is `None`. Add `p.offset(n)` in elements, `p.byte_offset(n)`, and `p.cast<U>()`. Add `mem.alloc_raw(size:, align:)` and `mem.free_raw(^p)`. Add `mem.window(p, len)` for a checked window, plus `mem.copy` and `mem.fill`. All require `#Unsafe` and keep the pointer's origin. Dev-mode checks and hardened builds then still verify range, liveness, and alignment.
options.technical: Each operation preserves allocation provenance for D-MEM-SENTRY1 and D-HARDENED1 instead of laundering through `Int`. The `?` optional representation uses the null niche. D-MEMREF1 gives `@` to checked links, so raw pointers keep `*T`; `mem.Ptr<T>` names the same type in module calls.

options.name: Null and offset only
options.detail: Only optional pointers and element offset are added.
options.technical: The remaining operations keep today's `Int` round trip.

options.name: Keep today's set
options.detail: Raw pointer support stays as shipped.
options.technical: No change.

comparisons.note: Optional pointers, many-item pointers, slices. https://ziglang.org/documentation/master/#Pointers
`ptr.add`, `cast`, `slice::from_raw_parts`, `std::alloc`. https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.pointer.html

recommendation.why: Experts get every common C and Zig pointer operation, and none of them escapes the audit gate or the runtime checks.

whyNot.reason: B still forces integer pointer math for casts, slices, and allocation.
C loses dev-mode tracking whenever experts do pointer math.

recommendation.tradeoff: A larger audited toolset replaces untracked integer arithmetic.

decisions.title: Plain data that updates the screen
decisions.gist: Should changing data through a link update everything that displays it, with no signal wrapper?
decisions.lesson: Today reactive state lives in `Signal<T>` boxes read with `.get()` and changed with `.set()`. Stores also list changed field names by hand. The compiler already knows every place that writes shared data, so it could notify readers exactly there. Screens and live queries would update when plain data changes. This applies once D-MEMREF1 passes.
decisions.story: Jun builds a to-do app. In Svelte, `todo.done = true` updates the checkbox. In Jet today he wraps each field in a signal or lists field names in a store call. He wants plain data that just updates the screen.

options.name: Links are observable
options.detail: Reads through a link inside a tracked context (render, computed, effect, or live query) subscribe to the fields they read. Writes notify exactly those readers. `#Transact` delivers several writes as one update. Data never read in a tracked context has no notification code. Experts use `untracked { }` for reads that should not subscribe and `!Notify` to prove a function has no update code.
options.technical: Sema already records every write site to link storage. Codegen emits a notify at those sites only for types that sema proves are read in a tracked context, and a notify is a null check when no one subscribes. `#Transact` commit is the batch boundary, the same commit that invalidates live queries (D-LIVEQUERY1). `Signal<T>` becomes `@T` held in a tracked context; `computed` and `effect` stay. It supersedes D-SIGNAL1's box-only surface. Code uses the `@` link spelling that the owner chose for D-MEMREF1.

options.name: Add observable links, keep Signal
options.detail: Observable links are added beside the signal library.
options.technical: Two reactive storage paths share one tracking runtime.
options.code:
count :: reactive.signal(0)            // still works
todo := @Todo{done: false}              // also reactive

options.name: Keep Signal only
options.detail: No change.
options.technical: No change.
options.code:
count :: reactive.signal(0)
count.set(count.get() + 1)

comparisons.note: Fine-grained stores update only readers of a changed field. https://docs.solidjs.com/concepts/stores
`$state` proxies make plain writes reactive. https://svelte.dev/docs/svelte/$state
Queries are reactive subscriptions; mutations are transactions. https://docs.convex.dev/functions/query-functions

recommendation.why: Plain data updates the screen, like Svelte or Solid, without runtime proxies. The compiler knows each write, so unwatched data costs nothing.

whyNot.reason: B keeps two ways to hold reactive state.
C keeps signal ceremony and hand-written field lists that can drift.

recommendation.tradeoff: One migration buys reactive plain data with no proxy cost.

decisions.title: Pages that resume instead of re-running
decisions.gist: Should web pages resume from server state and ship per-route code, instead of re-running components?
decisions.lesson: Server-rendered pages usually re-run component code in the browser to attach handlers. This step, called hydration, delays the first click. Resumable pages ship only the state each handler reads and load a handler's code on first use. Jet's app graph already knows each route's handlers and what they read.
decisions.story: Tomas runs a store on slow phones. His product page renders fast but ignores taps for two seconds while hydration runs. He wants the page to respond at once without tuning split points by hand.

options.name: Resumable by default, bundles from the app graph
options.detail: Each route's bundle holds only code reachable from its handlers. The page carries the state those handlers read. Handler code loads on first interaction and is prefetched on hover. `.split()` and `.island()` become locks on a choice instead of requirements.
options.technical: It uses the D-WEBAPP1 graph, the D-WASM1 partition, and per-handler read sets from sema. The serialized state uses `#Codable` wire types. Hydration-mismatch laws stay for server-rendered markup.
options.code:
fn run() -> App {
    web.app()
        .route("/", home)              // bundles and resume state are derived
        .route("/orders/:id", order)
}

$ jet inspect choices --web app.jet
/            12 KB  resumes: cart.count
/orders/:id  31 KB  resumes: order, cart.count  (handlers load on first use)

options.name: Per-route bundles only
options.detail: Bundles come from the graph; hydration stays.
options.technical: Graph reachability only.
options.code:
$ jet inspect choices --web app.jet
/  12 KB  (hydrates on load)

options.name: Manual, as today
options.detail: No change.
options.technical: No change.
options.code:
.island()
.split("widget")

comparisons.note: Resumability with lazy handlers. https://qwik.dev/docs/concepts/resumable/
Server components plus hydration of client components. https://nextjs.org/docs/app/building-your-application/rendering

recommendation.why: The compiler already knows what each handler needs, so pages can respond immediately without manual tuning.

whyNot.reason: B still re-runs component code before the page responds.
C leaves speed to manual split points.

recommendation.tradeoff: A small deferred load on first use buys instant page response.

decisions.title: Secrets can never reach the browser
decisions.gist: Should secret values be unable, at compile time, to reach browser code, responses, or logs?
decisions.lesson: Web apps leak secrets when server code sends them to the client. Jet already has built-in `Secret` and `Credential` tags, and it splits server and browser code. Tag policies deny named sinks. Browser and response boundaries are not default `Secret` sinks today. This ballot decides whether to add them.
decisions.story: Mia returns an `Account` from a server action. A teammate later adds an `api_key` field to `Account`. Nothing fails, and the key ships to every browser. She wants the build to fail at the line that sends it.
decisions.inWild:
experimental_taintUniqueValue('Do not pass the key to the client', user, user.apiKey);
// React's taint API marks values that must not reach client components, at runtime. Source: react.dev/reference/react/experimental_taintUniqueValue.

options.name: Built-in Secret tag with default sinks
options.detail: Core extends its existing `Secret` policy to browser, response, and log sinks. A tagged value reaching one is a compile error with the path. `#Scrub(Secret)` releases a value on purpose, and the release is listed for review.
options.technical: It adds `Browser`, `Response`, and `Log` as registered sinks next to `Html` in the tag checker (`Taint.rs`), and connects the D-WASM1 partition and D-DX-SERVERFN1 wire types to them. User tags can deny the same sinks.

options.name: Sinks only, keep policies app-defined
options.detail: Registers Browser, Response, and Log sinks. Each app attaches them through its own tag policy.
options.technical: Only sink vocabulary changes; no default Secret policy.
options.code:
tag Private { deny: [Browser, Response, Log] }
#Private api_key: String

options.name: No change
options.detail: No change.
options.technical: No change.
options.code:
api_key :: #Secret "token"
// no browser or response error today

comparisons.note: Runtime taint API for server components. https://react.dev/reference/react/experimental_taintUniqueValue
Compile-time information-flow labels for Java. https://www.cs.cornell.edu/jif/

recommendation.why: Secret leaks become compile errors in every app by default, using the tag checker Jet already has.

whyNot.reason: B protects only apps that remember to declare the tag.
C lets secrets reach browsers silently.

recommendation.tradeoff: An explicit scrub for deliberate releases buys compile-time leak prevention.

decisions.title: Worst-case stack and heap per entry point
decisions.gist: Should the build report and enforce worst-case stack and heap use for each entry point?
decisions.lesson: Embedded devices have fixed memory. A stack overflow there causes silent corruption or a reset. C toolchains estimate stack use per function, and separate tools add up the call chains. Jet knows every call, so the build can compute totals and fail when a limit is crossed. Recursion and dynamic calls need a stated bound.
decisions.story: Kai ships firmware for a sensor with 8 KB of RAM. A new logging call in an interrupt handler overflows the stack in the field. He wants the build to fail with the call chain that caused it.

options.name: Compute, report, and enforce
options.detail: The build combines backend frame sizes with Jet's call graph. `jet inspect memory` prints worst-case stack and heap for each entry point. `!Mem.Stack(above: N)` enforces a stack limit. `!Mem.Alloc(above: N)` keeps its current meaning: the total heap any call path may allocate. Recursion needs `#MaxDepth(n)`, and dynamic calls need a sealed target set.
options.technical: Frame sizes come from the backend's stack-size output per target. The sum uses sema's sealed call graph, as D-MEM-FACTS1 already requires for memory facts.

options.name: Report only
options.detail: Reporting without limits.
options.technical: Same computation as A.
options.code:
$ jet inspect memory firmware.jet
on_tick  stack 212 B

options.name: Nothing
options.detail: No change.
options.technical: No change.
options.code: // no stack report

comparisons.note: `-fstack-usage` per function. https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc/Developer-Options.html
Whole-program worst-case stack analysis. https://www.adacore.com/gnatpro/toolsuite/gnatstack

recommendation.why: Embedded developers get a build-time guarantee against stack overflow, next to today's heap limit, using the same effect-row form.

whyNot.reason: B lets a later edit overflow the stack without failing the build.
C leaves stack safety to outside tools after the build.

recommendation.tradeoff: Declared recursion bounds buy a proven stack limit.

decisions.title: Game systems run in parallel from their access
decisions.gist: Should game systems run in parallel automatically, based on which data each reads or writes?
decisions.lesson: Game engines split each frame into systems. Bevy runs systems in parallel when their data does not conflict, and it checks that at runtime. Jet already derives frame schedules from checked accesses (D-RESOURCE-SCHEDULE1) for built-in resources. User systems already state access through `T` and `&T` parameters, so the compiler can schedule them.
decisions.story: Iris has twelve systems in her game. They run one after another on one core while seven cores idle. She does not want to hand-order parallel groups that go stale whenever a system changes.

options.name: Parallel by default, expert schedules on request
options.detail:
Default: the compiler builds a conflict graph from each system's parameter access and runs non-conflicting systems at the same time. Conflicting systems keep source order. Commands, events, and logs merge in declaration order at each stage end, so output is repeatable.

Expert control: `schedule: .Serial` runs systems one at a time in source order. `schedule: .Manual(stages)` places systems by hand; the compiler rejects a stage whose systems conflict. `jet inspect choices --frame` explains every choice. `.after()` still adds an order by hand.
options.technical: It extends D-RESOURCE-SCHEDULE1 from built-in resources to user systems and keeps the serial source-order plan as the reference. Link parameters follow D-MEMREF-TASK1 storage.

options.name: Manual groups only
options.detail: Users must declare every parallel group; there is no automatic default. Conflicts are errors.
options.technical: Uses the same conflict check without deriving groups.
options.code:
scene.systems_parallel([[move_all], [aim, sound]])
// error if aim and sound conflict

options.name: Serial, as today
options.detail: No change.
options.technical: No change.
options.code: scene.on_frame(frame -> { print(frame.index) })

decisions.title: Old clients keep working after a deploy
decisions.gist: Should the compiler check that old clients still work with the new server's data types?

decisions.story: Eva renames `total` to `total_cents` in an order response. Users with the page already open see blank totals until they reload. She wants the build to catch this and keep old clients working.

options.technical: It extends D-MIGRATE1 and D-MIGRATE2 snapshots to D-DX-SERVERFN1 wire types. Requests carry a release identity, and generated adapters apply the migration chain.

options.name: Check only
options.detail: The build catches breaks but does not adapt.
options.technical: Snapshot diff only.
options.code: // error: `Order.total` was removed; old clients still read it

options.name: No check
options.detail: No change.
options.technical: No change.

comparisons.note: Field-number evolution rules. https://protobuf.dev/programming-guides/proto3/#updating

whyNot.reason: B forces client and server to deploy together, which web apps cannot guarantee.

decisions.title: Report an existing target and an unsupported request as IOError kinds
decisions.gist: How should IOError report that a target already exists, or that this system cannot do the request?
decisions.lesson: IOError has a fixed list of kinds, such as NotFound and PermissionDenied. Programs match a kind to choose a recovery. Safe file code must spot two more cases. The target already exists, or this system cannot do the request. Today both arrive as Other, so code must compare operating-system numbers. Whichever option wins, messages still say what happened, why, and how to fix it.
decisions.story: Sam writes a staging step. It creates pkg.partial.1, and if that name is taken it tries pkg.partial.2. Later it swaps a new tree into place, and on Windows it must fall back to a slower safe path. Sam should not memorize error numbers for three systems to write either branch.
decisions.detail:
Need: card #3593 items 2, 4, 7, and 9. Exclusive create, directory creation, refusing rename, rename swap, and extended-attribute writes each have an expected failure. The caller must recover from it, not just report it. D-IOERROR-TREE1=A made IOError a closed list of kinds sharing one IOContext. It also says os_code is audit data, never portable control flow. So matching os_code is not offered as an option.

Rust call sites that branch on an existing target. Store/Ingest.rs:241-243 and Recipe.rs:1531-1533. Provider/remote.rs:1259-1262 and 1302-1305. Store/Lifecycle/Directory.rs:223-226. The Core provider itself does this in FSWriteOps.rs:86.

Rust call sites that branch on an unsupported request. Recipe.rs:1733-1736 and 1764-1767 treat rename exchange as unsupported and fall back. Store/Ingest.rs:1435-1439 and Envelope.rs:436-445 report extended attributes as unsupported on a platform.

The tree has grown before: D-PROCESS-RESOURCE1 added ResourceLimit, and the source also carries Protocol. D-ENUM-EVOLUTION1 keeps enums closed and lets callers choose an else arm. So a match with an else arm keeps compiling. A match that lists every kind without else must add the two new kinds.

options.name: Two new kinds
options.detail: IOError gains AlreadyExists(IOContext) and Unsupported(IOContext). An existing target at a name the caller asked Core not to replace reports AlreadyExists. A request this operating system or file system cannot perform reports Unsupported. Both keep the same context record: operation, resource, os_code, and cause. Beginners keep using plain propagation; experts match the kind.
options.technical:
Add IOError.AlreadyExists(IOContext) and IOError.Unsupported(IOContext) to the one Prelude definition (CoreLib/JetStd/Open.rs) and every tier copy. The shared mapper sends EEXIST, ERROR_FILE_EXISTS, and ERROR_ALREADY_EXISTS to AlreadyExists. It sends ENOTSUP, EOPNOTSUPP, ENOSYS, and ERROR_NOT_SUPPORTED to Unsupported. A call whose flag is rejected with EINVAL maps it to Unsupported only where that call documents it, such as rename swap.

Display text states what happened, why, and the fix. For example: store/pkg already exists; this call refuses to replace it; choose a new name or pass if_exists: .Replace. UI snapshots cover both kinds (I4). AOT and default jet run share the mapper (I9).

options.name: A reason field on the context
options.detail: The list of kinds stays as it is. IOContext gains reason: ?IOReason, a closed enum with AlreadyExists and Unsupported. Both cases arrive as Other with the reason set. Callers match Other and then test the reason.
options.technical: Add pub enum IOReason { AlreadyExists, Unsupported } and IOContext.reason: ?IOReason. Every adapter for files, sockets, TLS, and codecs must set or clear the new field. Kinds are unchanged.

comparisons.note: Rust names both cases in io::ErrorKind, and the Jetpack source branches on them. Official docs: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/io/enum.ErrorKind.html.

Python raises FileExistsError as its own class for an existing target. Unsupported flags raise OSError with an errno the caller must read, which is the weaker shape. Official docs: https://docs.python.org/3/library/exceptions.html#FileExistsError.

recommendation.why: Programs already choose recovery by matching an IOError kind. Two more kinds keep that one habit for existing targets and unsupported requests, on every platform and for every stream adapter.
gains: One match shape covers every expected file failure.
No platform numbers in ordinary code.

losses.loss: Code that matched Other for these cases must change.
losses.mitigation: The failures move to a named kind, so an old catch-all match on Other sees fewer cases.

losses.loss: Matches listing every kind without else need two new arms.
losses.mitigation: A closed list of kinds grows only by naming the new kinds.

whyNot.reason: B hides a failure kind inside Other, so callers check two places for one fact, and every non-file adapter must maintain a field it never uses.

recommendation.tradeoff: The closed IOError list grows by two kinds, and every Core file call that can hit them documents which one it returns.

gains: Recovery code matches a kind, like every other file failure.

decisions.title: Add file identity, link count, owner, and exact times to Stat
decisions.gist: How should Stat report file identity, link count, owner, and exact change times?
decisions.lesson: Two paths can name the same file. The system gives each file an identity: a device number plus a file number. Safe tools compare identities to spot swapped or shared files. Today Stat has millisecond times and no identity, so files.samefile always fails. Whichever option wins, Core owes these fields on Linux, macOS, and Windows, with a stated value where a platform lacks one.
decisions.story: Priya ports the Jetpack store to Jet. Before sealing a package, the store checks that no file is hard-linked to a file outside the store. It also records each file's identity and exact change time in a table. If an attacker swaps a file between two checks, the identities differ and the seal stops. Priya cannot write any of these checks with today's Stat.
decisions.inWild:
# Python: https://docs.python.org/3/library/os.html#os.stat_result
a, b = os.lstat("a.txt"), os.lstat("b.txt")
same = (a.st_dev, a.st_ino) == (b.st_dev, b.st_ino)
# Go: https://pkg.go.dev/os#SameFile
same := os.SameFile(infoA, infoB)
# Rust: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/os/unix/fs/trait.MetadataExt.html
let same = (a.dev(), a.ino()) == (b.dev(), b.ino());
decisions.detail:
Need: card #3593 item 1. The Jetpack port needs file identity, hard-link count, owner id, and nanosecond times. The mapping receipts list 16 files that cannot be ported without them.

Identity comparisons in the Rust source. Store/Ingest.rs:325 and Store/Cleanup.rs:1089. Store/Reuse.rs:819-820, 871-872, 1078, and 1923-1924. Store/Lifecycle/Directory.rs:428-429 and Recipe.rs:2063. RuntimePolicy/Lock/unix.rs:110-111. Provider/remote.rs:1590-1591 and 1866-1870. jet-store/src/lib.rs:2050.

Identity as a key or table entry. Store/Closure.rs:307 and 382. Store/Archive.rs:2463 and Store/Reproducibility.rs:1436. Store/Reuse.rs:2621. jet-pkg-model/src/SealWalk.rs:18-20, 55-57, and 101. jet-pkg-model/src/Authority.rs:255.

Link count: Overlay.rs:76, Provider/remote.rs:1547, Store/Archive.rs:2474, Store/Ingest.rs:337, and jet-pkg-model/src/Authority.rs:1637. Owner id: Store/Broker.rs:894 and 1457. Disk allocation: Store/Closure.rs:310 and 383.

Nanosecond modified and changed times. Store/Ingest.rs:628-632 and Store/Nar.rs:1922-1929. Store/Reproducibility.rs:1451-1458 and Store/Closure.rs:1545. jet-pkg-model/src/Envelope.rs:1294-1298 and SealWalk.rs:114.

The group id appears only in CLI/studio_transactions.rs:1538, which is not ported by design. So no group field is proposed. SealWalk prints the file number into a persisted hashed table, so the number must be exact. Jet Int is exact, so 64-bit and 128-bit file numbers fit.

options.name: Identity value and exact times
options.detail: Stat gains an id field holding one FileId value, plus links, owner, and size_on_disk. The time fields become modified, changed, and created, each an Instant with nanosecond precision. They replace modified_ms and created_ms in the same change. files.samefile compares two ids and stops failing. A beginner compares info.id values. An expert reads id.device and id.inode for tables.
options.technical:
New plain-data type: pub struct FileId { pub device: Int, pub inode: Int }. It has equality and hashing, so it works as a Set or Map key. Stat adds id: FileId, links: Int, owner: ?Int, and size_on_disk: Int. It adds modified: Instant, changed: Instant, and created: ?Instant. It removes modified_ms and created_ms in the same cutover (E1). getmtime and Path.mtime derive milliseconds from modified.unix_ns. Signatures stay files.stat(path) -[FS]> Stat !IOError and files.samefile(a, b) -[FS]> Bool !IOError.

stat still never follows a final link.

Unix: st_dev, st_ino, st_nlink, st_uid, st_mtim, st_ctim, st_blocks times 512. created comes from statx birth time when present, else None. Windows: device is the volume serial number, and inode is the file id (128-bit where the file system provides it). links is NumberOfLinks, owner is None, changed is ChangeTime, and size_on_disk is AllocationSize. AOT and default jet run share the same provider values.

options.name: Flat number fields
options.detail: Stat gains device, inode, links, owner, modified_ns, changed_ns, created_ns, and size_on_disk as plain numbers. modified_ms and created_ms stay. A same-file check compares device and inode together every time.
options.technical: Stat adds device: Int, inode: Int, links: Int, owner: ?Int, modified_ns: Int, changed_ns: Int, created_ns: ?Int, and size_on_disk: Int. Existing fields stay. files.samefile compares device and inode inside Core. Platform sources match option A.

options.name: Separate identity call
options.detail: Stat stays unchanged. A new files.identity(path) call returns a record with device, inode, links, owner, and nanosecond times. Callers that need both use two calls.
options.technical: New files.identity(path) -[FS]> FileIdentity !IOError, reading the same metadata again. Stat is unchanged. files.samefile compares two identity records.

comparisons.note: Python puts st_dev, st_ino, st_nlink, st_uid, and nanosecond times on one stat result. Callers compare two fields for identity. Official docs: https://docs.python.org/3/library/os.html#os.stat_result.
comparisons.code:
a = os.lstat("a.txt")
print(a.st_dev, a.st_ino, a.st_nlink, a.st_uid, a.st_mtime_ns)

comparisons.note: Go hides identity behind os.SameFile, which compares device and file number for the caller. Option A keeps that one-comparison benefit and still shows the numbers. Official docs: https://pkg.go.dev/os#SameFile.

Rust exposes dev, ino, nlink, uid, and nanosecond parts through a Unix-only extension trait, with a separate Windows trait. The Rust Jetpack code uses both. Official docs: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/os/unix/fs/trait.MetadataExt.html.

recommendation.why: One FileId value turns the common same-file and swapped-file checks into one comparison. Instant fields keep exact times in the existing time type without a second spelling for the same fact.
gains: Same-file and swapped-file checks become one comparison.
Exact times match what the disk stored.

losses.loss: Readers of modified_ms and created_ms must change.
losses.mitigation: Keeping both spellings would give one fact two names, which the one-mechanism rule forbids.

whyNot.reason: Every identity check must remember the device field. Comparing only inode numbers silently matches unrelated files on different disks, and modified time keeps two spellings.
The second lookup can observe a different file than the first. That is exactly the swap these checks exist to catch.

recommendation.tradeoff: A few callers move from millisecond fields to Instant fields in the same change, and owner stays None on Windows because Windows owners are not numbers.

surface.lesson: Two paths can name the same file. The system gives each file an identity: a device number plus a file number. Safe tools compare identities to spot swapped or shared files. Today Stat has millisecond times and no identity, so files.samefile always fails. Whichever option wins, Core owes these fields on Linux, macOS, and Windows, with a stated value where a platform lacks one.

current.note: Stat has no identity and only millisecond times. files.samefile always returns an error (Core/files/files.jet:1041-1047). Read from source; not run.

wild.note: Python exposes device, file number, link count, owner, and nanosecond times on every stat result. See https://docs.python.org/3/library/os.html#os.stat_result.

a, b = os.lstat("a.txt"), os.lstat("b.txt")
same = (a.st_dev, a.st_ino) == (b.st_dev, b.st_ino)
print(a.st_nlink, a.st_uid, a.st_mtime_ns, a.st_ctime_ns)

options.name: Identity value and exact times
options.gist: Stat gains one comparable identity value, counts, owner, and nanosecond Instant times.
gains: One comparison answers whether two paths name the same file.
Times keep full precision in one existing time type.
Identity values work as set and map keys.

// PROPOSED; NOT RUN.
info :: files.stat("store/pkg/bin/tool")
id :: files.identity("store/pkg/bin/tool")  // a second lookup
print(id.device, id.inode, id.links, id.modified_ns)

Exact times match what the disk stored.

The file can change between the two lookups, which is the race these checks catch.

decisions.title: Open files with safety options and work with their bytes
decisions.gist: How should a program create a file only if new, refuse links, set permissions, and handle raw bytes?
decisions.lesson: Safe tools often need a brand-new private file, or a file that is not a planted link. They also read and write raw bytes, rewind, and force data onto the disk. Today files.create always replaces, files.open follows links, and handles only move text lines. Whichever option wins, handles gain byte reads and writes, rewind, disk sync, and facts about the opened file.
decisions.story: Omar ports the Jetpack store. A download lands in a staging file that must not already exist and must be private from its first byte. He writes the bytes, forces them to disk, and later hashes the published file in 64 KiB chunks. The file must not be a link an attacker planted. Today he cannot express any of these steps in Jet.
decisions.detail:
Need: card #3593 items 2, 3, 6, and 8. The port needs exclusive create with an explicit mode and no-follow opens. It also needs byte reads and writes, rewind, handle sync, handle mode, and handle stat.

Exclusive create sites in the Rust source. BuildDebug.rs:551 and EnvFiles.rs:401, 826. Image.rs:299, 343, 1114, and 1533. NixIndex.rs:1409, Recipe.rs:2324, and Services.rs:1141. Shell.rs:431, CLI/tool.rs:2507, and Provider/native.rs:688, 749. RuntimePolicy/ExecutableLease.rs:1490 and 1541. Store/Broker.rs:1592 and Store/Ingest.rs:228. Store/Cache.rs:1808, 2695, and 2895. Store/Nar.rs:487 and 1977.

Explicit creation mode: Secrets.rs:343-347, Store/Archive.rs:2603-2604, and EnvFiles.rs:400-404. No-follow opens: NixIndex.rs:1471-1473 and Recipe.rs:2045-2049. Also CLI/cc.rs:1510-1513, RuntimePolicy/Lock/unix.rs:65 and 72, and jet-pkg-model/src/Envelope.rs:543-551.

Byte loops: Store/Reuse.rs:1032-1041 and 2417-2425, and Store/Nar.rs:489-490. Rewind: Store/Reuse.rs:1021 and 2416. Handle mode: Overlay.rs:694-697, Provider/remote.rs:1586, and Store/Archive.rs:2606-2608. Handle stat: Store/Reuse.rs:1077-1078 and RuntimePolicy/Lock/unix.rs:101-112. Handle sync: sync_all in 39 files, for example Store/Ingest.rs:231 and Store/Nar.rs:1980.

Already ratified: D-NETIO-CONTRACT1=A and D-NETIO-CONTRACT2=B make FileReader and FileWriter implement core.io Reader and Writer. That fixes read(limit), write(bytes), and write_all(bytes). This ballot does not re-decide them; every option includes them. D-FILES-HANDLE-ABI1=A and D-CORE-FILECLOSE1=A keep handles opaque and closed at scope exit.

Not new API. set_len is used only by test fixtures: EnvHook.rs:1092, Provider/fetch.rs:979, and Provider/script_registry.rs:2418, 2451. Also jet-pkg-model/src/Authority.rs:1949 and Envelope.rs:1445. The existing files.truncate(path, size) covers them once its provider sets the length directly instead of rewriting the file.

Close-on-exec: every handle is opened close-on-exec, as the Rust code does (O_CLOEXEC throughout). Passing one to a child is D-CORE-PROCINHERIT1, drafted with the process ballots.

options.name: Named choices on open and create
options.detail: files.create gains if_exists (Replace or Refuse), mode (permission bits for a new file), and links (Follow or Refuse). files.open and files.append gain links; append also gains mode. Leaving them off keeps today's behavior. FileReader gains chunks, seek, and stat. FileWriter gains fsync, set_mode, and stat. Both also gain the ratified byte methods read, write, and write_all.
options.technical:
files.open(path, links: LinkPolicy{.Follow}) -[FS]> FileReader !IOError. files.create(path, if_exists: CreateIfExists{.Replace}, mode: ?Int{None}, links: LinkPolicy{.Follow}) -[FS]> FileWriter !IOError. files.append(path, mode: ?Int{None}, links: LinkPolicy{.Follow}) -[FS]> FileWriter !IOError. New enums: CreateIfExists { Replace, Refuse } and LinkPolicy { Follow, Refuse }.

if_exists: .Refuse is O_EXCL or CREATE_NEW and reports IOError.AlreadyExists (D-CORE-FILEERROR1). mode applies at creation, before the process umask, and has no effect on an existing file. links: .Refuse uses O_NOFOLLOW on Unix. On Windows it opens the reparse point itself and rejects it. A final link reports IOError.InvalidInput naming the path and the fix.

FileReader methods, all -[FS]>. read(limit: Int) -> [U8] !IOError, where an empty list means end of file. chunks(size: Int) is a loop source of [U8] that composes read. seek(offset: Int) !IOError moves to an absolute byte offset. stat() -> Stat !IOError describes the opened file.

FileWriter methods, all -[FS]>. write(bytes: [U8]) -> Int !IOError and write_all(bytes: [U8]) !IOError. fsync() !IOError flushes buffered bytes, then syncs the file. set_mode(mode: Int) !IOError changes the opened file, using the set_mode readonly mapping on Windows. stat() -> Stat !IOError.

All handles are close-on-exec. The defaults table gains one row for files.create. AOT and default jet run share one provider path (I9).
options.code:
// PROPOSED; NOT RUN.
use core.files as files

fn stage(path: String, bytes: [U8]) -[FS]> Int !IOError {
    out :: files.create(path, if_exists: .Refuse, mode: 0o600)
    out.write_all(bytes)
    out.fsync()
    input :: files.open(path, links: .Refuse)
    total := 0
    loop chunk in input.chunks(65536) -> total = total + chunk.len()
    Ok(total)
}

options.name: Separate function per choice
options.detail: Each behavior gets its own function: create_new(path, mode) for exclusive create and open_no_follow(path) for link refusal. Combinations need more names, such as create_new_no_follow. Handle methods match option A.
options.technical: New functions: create_new, open_no_follow, create_no_follow, create_new_no_follow, and append_no_follow. A mode parameter appears on the create forms. Handle methods and error kinds match option A.
options.code:
// PROPOSED; NOT RUN.
out :: files.create_new_no_follow(path, 0o600)
out.write_all(bytes)
out.fsync()
input :: files.open_no_follow(path)

options.name: One options record
options.detail: A new files.open_with(path, FileOptions{...}) takes every choice as a field: read, write, append, create, mode, and follow_links. It returns one read-write handle type. open, create, and append remain for simple use.
options.technical: New plain-data FileOptions with read, write, append, and follow_links as Bool fields. It also has create: CreateRule { No, IfMissing, New, Truncate } and mode: ?Int. New handle type FileHandle has both reader and writer methods. Conflicting fields are rejected at run time with IOError.InvalidInput.
options.code:
// PROPOSED; NOT RUN.
out :: files.open_with(path, FileOptions{write: true, create: .New, mode: Val(0o600), follow_links: false})
out.write_all(bytes)
out.fsync()

comparisons.note: Rust's OpenOptions record is the praised expert design, and the Jetpack source uses it everywhere. Its reported cost is that impossible combinations fail only at run time. Official docs: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/fs/struct.OpenOptions.html.

Python folds exclusive create into the mode string x. Link refusal and permissions need the lower os.open call with flag bits. Official docs: https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html#open and https://docs.python.org/3/library/os.html#os.open.
comparisons.code: fd = os.open(path, os.O_WRONLY | os.O_CREAT | os.O_EXCL | os.O_NOFOLLOW, 0o600)

comparisons.note: Go takes flag bits and a permission value on one OpenFile call. Official docs: https://pkg.go.dev/os#OpenFile.

recommendation.why: The existing open, create, and append calls stay the only doors. Labeled choices keep beginner calls unchanged, and experts can combine exclusive create, permissions, and link refusal in one readable call.
gains: Beginner calls stay unchanged.
Experts combine choices in one call.

losses.loss: Bare calls still follow a planted final link.
losses.mitigation: Refusing by default would break ordinary writes through linked files, such as linked dotfiles.

whyNot.reason: Three choices already need five names, and each later choice doubles the family. The stdlib laws prefer labeled options when the result is the same.
It adds a second door beside create and open. Its Boolean fields let a record describe impossible combinations that fail only at run time.

recommendation.tradeoff: Links are still followed by default, as in every other tool. Code that must refuse them says links: .Refuse, and directory handles (D-CORE-FILEDIR1) never follow.

surface.gist: How should a program create a file only if new, refuse links, set permissions, and handle raw bytes?
surface.lesson: Safe tools often need a brand-new private file, or a file that is not a planted link. They also read and write raw bytes, rewind, and force data onto the disk. Today files.create always replaces, files.open follows links, and handles only move text lines. Whichever option wins, handles gain byte reads and writes, rewind, disk sync, and facts about the opened file.

current.note: create replaces silently, open follows links, and handles only read or write text lines (Core/files/files.jet:96-102). Read from source; not run.
current.code:
// CURRENT (Core/files/files.jet); not run.
out :: files.create("store/.tmp/pkg.nar")   // replaces an existing file
files.set_mode("store/.tmp/pkg.nar", 0o600) // second step; readable meanwhile
input :: files.open("store/pkg.nar")        // follows a planted link
line :: input.read_line()                    // text lines only

wild.note: Rust sets each choice on one options value before opening. See https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/fs/struct.OpenOptions.html.

options.name: Named choices on open and create
options.gist: The existing calls gain labeled choices with safe defaults; handles gain byte methods.
gains: Bare calls behave exactly as today.
Each choice reads aloud at the call.
Choices combine without new function names.
losses: Bare calls still follow a planted final link.

proposed.code:
// PROPOSED; NOT RUN.
out :: files.create("store/.tmp/pkg.nar", if_exists: .Refuse, mode: 0o600)
out.write_all(bytes)
out.fsync()                        // bytes are on the disk now
input :: files.open("store/pkg.nar", links: .Refuse)
print(input.stat().size)           // facts about the opened file
loop chunk in input.chunks(65536) -> hasher.update(chunk)
input.seek(0)                      // read again from the start
first :: input.read(65536)         // [] means end of file
// Existing name: Err(IOError.AlreadyExists)
// Final link:    Err(IOError.InvalidInput) "store/pkg.nar is a link"

options.gist: Each safety choice gets its own function name beside open and create.
gains: Each name states one behavior.
No labels to learn.
losses: Names multiply with every combination of choices.
Adding a later choice doubles the family again.

options.name: One options record
options.gist: A new open_with call takes a record listing every choice, like Rust.
gains: One call can express any combination.
losses: A second door beside open and create.
The record allows contradictions, such as read-only plus create.

gains: Beginner calls stay unchanged.
