decisions.title: Rename that can refuse or swap, and folder sync for durable renames
decisions.gist: How should rename refuse or swap an existing target, and how does a rename survive power loss?
decisions.lesson: Rename moves a name in one step. Store tools also need to refuse an existing target, or swap two names at once. A rename survives power loss only after the folder holding it is flushed to disk. Today rename always replaces, and fsync is documented for files only. Whichever option wins, Windows rename behavior is written down and matches the other systems.
decisions.story: Ravi publishes a built package into the store. Two builds may finish together, so the second must fail instead of replacing the first. A new toolchain must replace the old one in a single swap, so no reader sees a missing folder. After a power cut, the published name must still be there.
decisions.detail:
Need: card #3593 item 9. The port needs directory fsync so renames are durable, and atomic rename exchange. It also needs a written Windows rule for replacing and write-through renames. Refusing an existing target is the same mechanism, and the Rust code needs it too.

Rust call sites for refuse and swap. Store/Lifecycle/Directory.rs:294-343 publishes without replacing, using linkat. Recipe.rs:1686-1770 swaps with renameat2 RENAME_EXCHANGE or renameatx_np RENAME_SWAP. It falls back when the system reports the swap unsupported (1733-1736 and 1764-1767). Recipe.rs:1641-1684 renames between held folders.

Rust call sites for Windows rename. Secrets.rs:374-392, CLI/tool.rs:2566-2580, and ToolchainUpdate.rs:1921-1938 all use MoveFileExW with MOVEFILE_REPLACE_EXISTING|MOVEFILE_WRITE_THROUGH.

Rust call sites for folder sync. Store.rs:493-499 and Store/Journal.rs:1048. Store/Archive.rs:2642-2645 and Store/Cache.rs:78. NixIndex.rs:1504, Overlay.rs:732, and Transition.rs:1054. RuntimePolicy/ExecutableLease.rs:1611, ToolchainUpdate.rs:1755-1766, and jet-store/src/lib.rs:2038-2041. Several of these skip the sync on Windows today because Rust cannot open a folder there without a special flag.

Not covered here. Windows delete-at-reboot (ToolchainUpdate.rs:1940-1956) is a different operation and is listed separately. files.write_atomic already flushes the file and its folder on Unix; the Windows folder flush is an implementation fix under the fsync rule below.

options.name: A conflict rule and explicit folder sync
options.detail: files.rename(from, to) gains if_exists with three values. Replace is today's behavior. Refuse fails with AlreadyExists when the target is present. Swap exchanges the two names in one step; both must exist. files.fsync(path) accepts a folder on every system, which makes an earlier rename inside it durable. Directory.rename from D-CORE-FILEDIR1 uses the same rule.
options.technical:
files.rename(from, to, if_exists: RenameIfExists{.Replace}) !IOError -[FS]>. New enum RenameIfExists { Replace, Refuse, Swap }. files.fsync(path) !IOError -[FS]> keeps its signature and now documents folders.

Linux and Android. Replace is renameat. Refuse is renameat2 RENAME_NOREPLACE; if the file system rejects the flag, files fall back to link then unlink, and folders report Unsupported. Swap is renameat2 RENAME_EXCHANGE, and EINVAL, ENOSYS, or ENOTSUP report IOError.Unsupported.

macOS. Refuse is renameatx_np RENAME_EXCL, and Swap is RENAME_SWAP, with the same Unsupported mapping.

Windows. Replace is MoveFileExW with MOVEFILE_REPLACE_EXISTING|MOVEFILE_WRITE_THROUGH. Refuse is MoveFileExW with MOVEFILE_WRITE_THROUGH only, where ERROR_ALREADY_EXISTS maps to AlreadyExists. Swap reports IOError.Unsupported. fsync of a folder opens it with FILE_FLAG_BACKUP_SEMANTICS and calls FlushFileBuffers.

Errors: AlreadyExists and Unsupported come from D-CORE-FILEERROR1. Swap with a missing name reports NotFound. AOT and default jet run share one provider (I9).

options.name: Durable rename by default
options.detail: rename gains the same if_exists rule. It also flushes the source and target folders before returning. A durability: .Later label skips the flush for speed.
options.technical: files.rename(from, to, if_exists: RenameIfExists{.Replace}, durability: RenameDurability{.Now}) !IOError -[FS]>. .Now calls the folder fsync from option A for both parent folders.

options.name: Separate verbs
options.detail: rename keeps replacing. files.rename_new(from, to) refuses a taken name, and files.swap(a, b) exchanges two names. fsync accepts folders as in option A.
options.technical: files.rename_new(from, to) !IOError -[FS]> and files.swap(a, b) !IOError -[FS]>, each with option A's platform mapping. Directory handles gain the same two extra verbs.
options.code:
// PROPOSED; NOT RUN.
files.rename_new("store/pkg.partial", "store/pkg")
files.swap(next, live)
files.fsync("store")

comparisons.note: renameat2 puts refuse and swap behind one call with a flag, which option A mirrors with a named rule. Official man page: https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/rename.2.html.
MoveFileExW takes flags for replacing and for write-through. Windows has no atomic swap of two names. Official docs: https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/win32/api/winbase/nf-winbase-movefileexw.

Python offers os.rename and os.replace, with no refuse or swap rule and no folder sync helper. Callers open a folder and call os.fsync themselves on Unix. Official docs: https://docs.python.org/3/library/os.html#os.replace.

recommendation.why: One rename with a readable conflict rule covers replace, refuse, and swap. Folder sync stays a separate, visible step, so only code that publishes durably pays for it.
gains: One move operation with three clear rules.
Folder sync works on every system.

losses.loss: Swap can report Unsupported, so callers need a fallback.
losses.mitigation: Windows and some file systems have no atomic swap of two names.

losses.loss: A durable rename needs a second fsync call.
losses.mitigation: Flushing inside every rename would slow every caller who does not need durability.

whyNot.reason: It hides disk flushes, often milliseconds each, inside every rename, including quick scratch moves in loops.
It splits one move into three verbs with the same shape. The stdlib laws ask for one method with a named rule, and directory handles would repeat all three.

recommendation.tradeoff: Durable publishing takes two visible steps. files.write_atomic stays the one-step durable door for whole files.

surface.lesson: Rename moves a name in one step. Store tools also need to refuse an existing target, or swap two names at once. A rename survives power loss only after the folder holding it is flushed to disk. Today rename always replaces, and fsync is documented for files only. Whichever option wins, Windows rename behavior is written down and matches the other systems.

current.note: rename always replaces, and there is no swap. fsync is documented for files only, and the Windows provider cannot open a folder that way. Read from Core/files/files.jet:430 and core-library.md:388; not run.

wild.note: Linux renameat2 takes a flag to refuse or to swap. See https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/rename.2.html.

options.name: A conflict rule and explicit folder sync
options.gist: rename gains if_exists (Replace, Refuse, Swap); fsync accepts folders on every system.
gains: Bare rename behaves exactly as today.
Refuse and swap read aloud at the call.
Durability costs time only where asked.
losses: Swap can report Unsupported, so callers need a fallback.

options.name: Durable rename by default
options.gist: Same conflict rule, but every rename also flushes its folders unless told not to.
gains: Beginners get durable renames without knowing about folder sync.
losses: Every rename pays disk flushes, even in loops.
The cost hides inside a call that looks cheap.

options.name: Separate verbs
options.gist: New rename_new and swap calls sit beside rename; fsync accepts folders.
gains: Each verb names one behavior.
losses: Three calls with the same shape for one move.
Directory handles would need the same three verbs.

proposed.code:
// PROPOSED; NOT RUN.
files.rename_new("store/pkg.partial", "store/pkg")   // refuses a taken name
files.swap("store/pkg.new", "store/pkg")
files.fsync("store")

gains: One move operation with three clear rules.
Folder sync works on every system.

losses.loss: Swap can report Unsupported, so callers need a fallback.
losses.mitigation: Windows and some file systems have no atomic swap.

losses.loss: A durable rename needs a second fsync call.
losses.mitigation: Flushing inside every rename would slow callers who do not need it.

whyNot.reason: It hides disk flushes inside every rename, including quick scratch moves.
It splits one move into three same-shaped verbs, against the one-method rule.

recommendation.tradeoff: Durable publishing takes two visible steps; files.write_atomic stays the one-step door.

decisions.title: Hold a directory open and work inside it without following links
decisions.gist: How should a program hold a directory open and create, open, rename, and remove entries inside it safely?
decisions.lesson: Each path-based call looks up every folder name again. If someone swaps a folder for a link between two calls, later writes land somewhere else. Safe tools hold the directory open and name entries relative to it, never following links. Today every Core call re-reads the full path. Whichever option wins, entry names cannot climb out with .., and listing and disk sync work on the held directory.
decisions.story: Lena runs a shared package store. Another local user can create links in a directory the store also writes. Lena's staging code creates a private folder, writes files into it, and renames it into place. If the store walked full paths each time, a well-timed link would make it overwrite a file outside the store.
decisions.detail:
Need: card #3593 items 3 and 4. The port needs no-follow traversal from a held root directory. It needs opens, creates, mkdir, rename, unlink, listing, and sync relative to that handle.

Rust call sites. Store/Lifecycle/Directory.rs:39-81 defines the pinned directory API, with the Unix body at 133-357 and the Windows body at 504-700. Recipe.rs:1471-1530 walks components, and 1554-1567 makes private directories. Recipe.rs:1641-1684 renames between held directories, and 1786-1864 removes entries without following links.

More call sites. Provider/remote.rs:1058-1340 holds checkout directories. NixEval/Authority.rs:121-170 and jet-pkg-model/src/Authority.rs:1705-1745 walk authority roots without following links. Overlay.rs:628-729 creates and removes overlay members. RuntimePolicy/Lock/windows.rs:124-196 pins lock parents on Windows.

Related ballots. Creation labels (if_exists, mode) come from D-CORE-FILEOPEN1. The rename conflict rule comes from D-CORE-FILERENAME1. AlreadyExists comes from D-CORE-FILEERROR1. Passing a Directory to a child process is D-CORE-PROCINHERIT1.

options.name: A Directory handle
options.detail: files.open_directory(path) opens and holds a directory. The last part of the path must be a real directory, not a link. Its methods take a relative name made of plain parts separated by slashes. Each part is opened without following links, and .., ., empty parts, and absolute paths are refused. The methods mirror the path calls: open, create, open_directory, create_directory, list, entry_stat, rename, remove, remove_directory, and fsync.
options.technical:
New opaque provider-owned handle Directory with read-only .path (D-FILES-HANDLE-ABI1 pattern), closed at scope exit and close-on-exec. files.open_directory(path) -[FS]> Directory !IOError. Unix uses O_DIRECTORY|O_NOFOLLOW|O_CLOEXEC. Windows uses FILE_FLAG_BACKUP_SEMANTICS with reparse points rejected, as in Directory.rs:664-679.

Methods, all -[FS]>. open(name) -> FileReader !IOError requires a regular file. create(name, if_exists: CreateIfExists{.Replace}, mode: ?Int{None}) -> FileWriter !IOError. open_directory(name) -> Directory !IOError. create_directory(name, mode: ?Int{None}) -> Directory !IOError reports AlreadyExists when present.

More methods. list() -> [DirEntry] !IOError returns name order. stat() -> Stat !IOError describes the held directory. entry_stat(name) -> Stat !IOError never follows. rename(from, to, into: ?Directory{None}, if_exists: RenameIfExists{.Replace}) !IOError. remove(name) !IOError unlinks a non-directory. remove_directory(name) !IOError removes an empty directory. fsync() !IOError.

Unix uses openat, mkdirat, renameat or renameat2, unlinkat, fstatat with AT_SYMLINK_NOFOLLOW, and fdopendir. Windows opens members relative to the held handle and denies delete sharing on held parents. A refused name reports IOError.InvalidInput naming the part and the fix. AOT and default jet run share one provider (I9).
options.code:
// PROPOSED; NOT RUN.
use core.files as files

fn publish(store: Directory, name: String, bytes: [U8]) !IOError -[FS]> {
    stage :: store.create_directory("{name}.partial", mode: 0o700)
    out :: stage.create("payload", if_exists: .Refuse, mode: 0o444)
    out.write_all(bytes)
    out.fsync()
    stage.fsync()
    store.rename("{name}.partial", name, if_exists: .Refuse)
    store.fsync()
}

options.name: A within label on path calls
options.detail: Path calls such as create, open, create_dir, rename, remove, stat, and list_dir gain within: a root path. Core confines each lookup under that root and refuses links. No handle is held, so the root is looked up again on every call.
options.technical: Linux resolves with openat2 and RESOLVE_BENEATH|RESOLVE_NO_SYMLINKS. Other systems walk each part from the root on every call. About twelve path functions gain within: ?String{None}.
options.code:
// PROPOSED; NOT RUN.
files.create_dir("pkg.partial", within: root, mode: 0o700)
out :: files.create("pkg.partial/payload", within: root, if_exists: .Refuse)
files.rename("pkg.partial", "pkg", within: root, if_exists: .Refuse)

options.name: Extend FileScope
options.detail: The FileScope from D-FILES-SCOPE1, made from an Authority value, also holds a directory open. It gains the same methods as option A's Directory.
options.technical: files.scope(authority) opens the first granted root and holds it. FileScope gains the Directory methods. Trusted code must build an Authority value first.

comparisons.note: Go's os.Root is the closest praised design: a held directory whose methods refuse escapes. Go 1.25 widened it with more methods. Go follows links that stay inside the root; option A never follows, as the Jetpack store requires. Official docs: https://pkg.go.dev/os#Root.
cap-std's Dir is a held directory with open, create, create_dir, rename, and remove methods. Official docs: https://docs.rs/cap-std/latest/cap_std/fs/struct.Dir.html.
Python passes a raw dir_fd number to each call. It works but exposes descriptor numbers, which Jet handles never do. Official docs: https://docs.python.org/3/library/os.html#dir-fd.
comparisons.code: fd = os.open("payload", os.O_WRONLY | os.O_CREAT | os.O_EXCL, 0o600, dir_fd=store_fd)

recommendation.why: Holding the directory is what makes every later call safe. A handle with familiar method names gives that guarantee without changing any path call a beginner uses.
gains: Swapped folders cannot redirect writes.
Path calls stay as they are.

losses.loss: One new handle type to learn.
losses.mitigation: Only a held value can keep pointing at the same directory between calls.

whyNot.reason: Looking up the root path on every call lets the root itself be swapped between calls. It also adds a label to about twelve functions.
It ties holding a folder to a permission value built for restricted plugins, so one type does two unrelated jobs.

recommendation.tradeoff: Experts gain a new Directory type. Beginners keep plain path calls and never see it.

surface.gist: How should a program hold a directory open and create, open, rename, and remove entries inside it safely?
surface.lesson: Each path-based call looks up every folder name again. If someone swaps a folder for a link between two calls, later writes land somewhere else. Safe tools hold the directory open and name entries relative to it, never following links. Today every Core call re-reads the full path. Whichever option wins, entry names cannot climb out with .., and listing and disk sync work on the held directory.

current.note: Every call re-walks the full path, so a swapped folder or link redirects later calls. Read from Core/files/files.jet; not run.

wild.note: Go's os.Root holds a directory and refuses names that escape it. See https://pkg.go.dev/os#Root.

root, err := os.OpenRoot("/var/jet/store")
err = root.Mkdir("pkg.partial", 0o700)
f, err := root.OpenFile("pkg.partial/payload",
    os.O_WRONLY|os.O_CREATE|os.O_EXCL, 0o600)
_, err = root.Open("../etc/passwd") // error: escapes root

options.gist: files.open_directory returns a held Directory whose methods act on names inside it.
gains: Later swaps of outer folders cannot redirect any call.
Method names match the path calls people know.
Links inside are never followed.
losses: One new handle type to learn.

stage :: store.create_directory("pkg.partial", mode: 0o700)
out :: stage.create("payload", if_exists: .Refuse, mode: 0o600)
out.write_all(bytes)
out.fsync()
stage.fsync()
store.rename("pkg.partial", "pkg", if_exists: .Refuse)
store.fsync()                                     // the rename is durable
loop entry in store.list() -> print(entry.name)
store.open("../etc/passwd")   // Err(IOError.InvalidInput): escapes

options.gist: Path calls gain a within label that confines lookups under a root path.
gains: No new type.
losses: The root path is looked up again on every call.
Many path functions gain one more label.

root :: "/var/jet/store"
files.create_dir("pkg.partial", within: root, mode: 0o700)
out :: files.create("pkg.partial/payload", within: root, if_exists: .Refuse)
out.write_all(bytes)

files.fsync(root)

options.name: Extend FileScope
options.gist: The restricted-code FileScope handle also holds a directory open.
gains: Reuses an existing handle type.
losses: Trusted code needs a permission value just to hold a folder.
One type does two different jobs.

scope :: files.scope(Authority.from_rights(["FS.Write:/var/jet/store"]))
stage :: scope.create_directory("pkg.partial", mode: 0o700)
out :: stage.create("payload", if_exists: .Refuse, mode: 0o600)

recommendation.why: Holding the directory is what makes every later call safe. A handle with familiar method names gives that guarantee without changing any path call.
gains: Swapped folders cannot redirect writes.
Path calls stay as they are.

losses.mitigation: Only a held value can keep pointing at the same directory between calls.

It ties holding a folder to a permission value meant for restricted plugins.

decisions.title: Make files.lock a system lock that a crash releases
decisions.gist: How should programs take a cross-process file lock that a crash always releases, and try it without waiting?
decisions.lesson: A lock keeps two processes from changing the same store at once. The operating system can hold an advisory lock for a process and drop it when the process ends, even after a crash. Today files.lock only creates a marker file, so a crash leaves it behind forever. Whichever option wins, the lock is exclusive and passes to a child only when asked.
decisions.story: Theo's machine loses power while Jetpack is installing a package. With a marker-file lock, the next Jetpack run finds the marker and refuses to start until Theo deletes it by hand. With a system lock, power loss released it, and the next run simply proceeds. Jetpack's cleanup also needs to ask whether a lease is still in use without waiting.
decisions.detail:
Need: card #3593 item 5, plus item 6 for locks. The port needs a system advisory lock with try_lock, unlock, and release on crash. Today core.files.lock only creates an exclusive marker file (FSRuntimeOps.rs:158-172), and its owner deletes the marker on drop.

Rust call sites. RuntimePolicy.rs:129-205 acquires with a 30-second wait (LOCK_WAIT at :21) or without waiting. RuntimePolicy.rs:217-236 probes whether a lock is held, idle, or absent. RuntimePolicy/Lock/unix.rs:160-180 uses flock with LOCK_EX|LOCK_NB and LOCK_UN. RuntimePolicy/Lock/windows.rs:249-281 uses LockFileEx and UnlockFileEx.

More call sites. RuntimePolicy/Lock/unix.rs:101-130 and windows.rs:215-247 check that the locked file is still the one at the path. RuntimePolicy.rs:778-783 asserts that the lock file is never unlinked. Unlinking would let a second process lock a new file at the same name.

Close-on-exec. The Rust lock files are close-on-exec (Lock/unix.rs:132-144 and windows.rs:162-165). RuntimePolicy.rs:197-205 deliberately passes a lease lock to launched descendants, so the lock lives as long as the process tree. In Jet every lock stays close-on-exec, and passing it to a child is D-CORE-PROCINHERIT1 (spec.keep_open), drafted with the process ballots. This ballot adds no inheritance switch.

Only exclusive locks are proposed, because no ported caller takes a shared lock. The only other flock user, CLI/studio_transactions.rs:1494-1516, is not ported by design.

options.name: System lock behind files.lock
options.detail: files.lock(path) opens or creates the lock file and waits for an exclusive system lock. A timeout label bounds the wait. files.try_lock(path) returns the lock, or None when another process holds it. The lock ends at scope exit, at close(^lock), or when the process ends for any reason. Release never deletes the lock file.
options.technical:
files.lock(path, timeout: ?Duration{None}) -[FS]> FileLock !IOError waits until acquired, or reports IOError.TimedOut after the bound. files.try_lock(path) -[FS]> ?FileLock !IOError returns None only for contention; other failures stay errors. FileLock keeps its read-only .path and scope-exit release (D-FILES-HANDLE-ABI1).

The provider creates a missing lock file with mode 0o600, opens it close-on-exec, and never follows a final link. On Unix it uses flock LOCK_EX, with LOCK_NB for try_lock. On Windows it uses LockFileEx with LOCKFILE_EXCLUSIVE_LOCK, plus LOCKFILE_FAIL_IMMEDIATELY for try_lock, and denies delete sharing.

After acquiring, the provider checks that the path still names the locked file by comparing identities. If not, it releases and retries, as in Lock/unix.rs:101-130. Waiting uses the operating system's blocking call when no timeout is set, and short polling when one is set.

The marker-file deletion on drop is removed (E1). A caller that held a marker lock now gets real mutual exclusion. The defaults table gains one row: bare lock waits without limit, and timeout: overrides it. AOT and default jet run share one provider (I9).

options.name: A second, separate lock kind
options.detail: files.lock keeps creating a marker file. New calls files.system_lock(path) and files.try_system_lock(path) give the system lock. Callers choose which kind they want.
options.technical: New SystemLock type beside FileLock, with the same provider behavior as option A. FileLock stays a marker whose owner deletes the file on drop.

options.name: Lock methods on open files
options.detail: FileReader and FileWriter gain lock(), try_lock() returning Bool, and unlock(). A program opens a file first, then locks it. files.lock is retired.
options.technical: Handle methods lock() !IOError, try_lock() -> Bool !IOError, and unlock() !IOError. The lock state lives on the handle and ends when the handle closes.

comparisons.note: Rust added File::lock, try_lock, and unlock backed by flock or LockFileEx. It puts locks on open files, like option C, and reports contention as a distinct error value. Official docs: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/fs/struct.File.html#method.try_lock.
Python's fcntl.flock raises BlockingIOError when LOCK_NB finds the lock held. The caller must know the flag bits. Official docs: https://docs.python.org/3/library/fcntl.html#fcntl.flock.

recommendation.why: The existing lock call becomes the safe one. Crashes release it, try_lock reports busy as None instead of an error, and no second lock kind appears for callers to choose between.
gains: Crashed runs never leave a stuck lock.
One lock kind for all code.

losses.loss: A bare lock call can wait a long time.
losses.mitigation: Any default timeout would fail some legitimate long jobs, so the bound is the caller's timeout: choice.

whyNot.reason: Two lock kinds make every caller choose, and the old marker kind still breaks after every crash.
Beginners must open a file before locking, and a Boolean try_lock result is easy to ignore.

recommendation.tradeoff: Lock files stay on disk after release. That is what keeps every process locking the same file.

surface.gist: How should programs take a cross-process file lock that a crash always releases, and try it without waiting?
surface.lesson: A lock keeps two processes from changing the same store at once. The operating system can hold an advisory lock for a process and drop it when the process ends, even after a crash. Today files.lock only creates a marker file, so a crash leaves it behind forever. Whichever option wins, the lock is exclusive and passes to a child only when asked.

current.note: files.lock creates a marker file that must not exist. After a crash the marker stays, and every later lock fails (FSRuntimeOps.rs:158-172). Read from source; not run.

wild.note: Rust's File gained lock and try_lock backed by the operating system. See https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/fs/struct.File.html#method.try_lock.

options.name: System lock behind files.lock
options.gist: files.lock waits for a system lock; files.try_lock returns None when another process holds it.
gains: A crash or kill releases the lock.
Existing lock calls keep their spelling.
Checking without waiting is one call.
losses: A bare lock call can wait a long time.

options.name: A second, separate lock kind
options.gist: files.lock stays a marker file; a new call gives the system lock.
gains: Existing marker behavior never changes.
losses: Two lock kinds with different crash behavior.
The marker kind still sticks after a crash.

proposed.code:
// PROPOSED; NOT RUN.
marker :: files.lock("build.lock")                       // marker file
lock :: files.system_lock("store/.locks/hangar")        // system lock
held :: files.try_system_lock("store/.locks/hangar")

options.name: Lock methods on open files
options.gist: Programs open a file first, then call lock, try_lock, and unlock on it.
gains: Can lock a file that is already open.
losses: Two steps for the common case.
try_lock returns a Boolean the caller must remember to check.

recommendation.why: The existing lock call becomes the safe one. Crashes release it, try_lock answers busy or free without an error, and no second lock kind appears.
gains: Crashed runs never leave a stuck lock.
One lock kind for all code.

losses.loss: A bare lock call can wait a long time.
losses.mitigation: Any default timeout would fail some legitimate long jobs; timeout: sets a bound.

whyNot.reason: Two lock kinds make every caller choose, and the old kind still breaks after crashes.
Beginners must open a file first, and a Boolean result is easy to ignore.

recommendation.tradeoff: Lock files stay on disk after release; that is what keeps two processes on one file.

decisions.title: List, read, and write extended attributes without following links
decisions.gist: How should Core list, read, and write a file's extended attributes?
decisions.lesson: Extended attributes are small named byte values stored beside a file, such as a macOS download quarantine mark. Package tools must see them, because they can change how a file behaves. Core has no way to read or write them today. Whichever option wins, names are text, values are bytes, and Windows reports no attributes.
decisions.story: Ines packages a macOS app that carries a user attribute its loader reads. The store must refuse such attributes by default, keep them when the package opts in, and ignore security and quarantine marks. With no Core call, the Jet port cannot even see that the attribute exists.
decisions.detail:
Need: card #3593 item 7. The port needs to list, read, and write extended attributes without following links.

Rust call sites. jet-pkg-model/src/Envelope.rs:278-299 lists names without following links. Envelope.rs:303-317 refuses unexpected names. Envelope.rs:319-345 hashes selected values. Envelope.rs:347-445 reads one value with lgetxattr or XATTR_NOFOLLOW. Envelope.rs:246-261 excludes security and quarantine prefixes before any value is read.

More call sites. Store/Ingest.rs:1335-1357 refuses attributes during ingest. Store/Ingest.rs:1360-1389 copies allowed attributes. Store/Ingest.rs:1392-1439 lists names, 1443-1520 reads values, and 1554-1633 writes values with lsetxattr. Envelope.rs:287-291 returns no names on Windows, and Ingest.rs:1629-1633 refuses writes on unsupported platforms.

Not proposed: removing an attribute. No ported caller removes one. The same naming would add it later if a caller needs it.

Naming follows the stdlib laws: plain words, no abbreviations. So the calls say extended_attribute, not xattr.

options.name: Three calls that never follow links
options.detail: files.extended_attribute_names(path) lists names. files.extended_attribute(path, name) returns one value, or None when the name is absent. files.set_extended_attribute(path, name, value) writes one value. All three act on the path itself; a final link is never followed, like files.stat.
options.technical:
files.extended_attribute_names(path) -[FS]> [String] !IOError returns names in sorted order. files.extended_attribute(path, name: String) -[FS]> ?[U8] !IOError. files.set_extended_attribute(path, name: String, value: [U8]) !IOError -[FS]>. A name that is not valid UTF-8 fails the list with IOError.InvalidInput, following the strict text rule of D-BYTESDECODE1=A.

Linux uses llistxattr, lgetxattr, and lsetxattr. macOS uses listxattr, getxattr, and setxattr with XATTR_NOFOLLOW. A file system without support returns [] and None, and set reports IOError.Unsupported (D-CORE-FILEERROR1). Windows returns [] and None, and set reports IOError.Unsupported, matching Envelope.rs:287-291.

The kernel omits names the process may not list, such as trusted.* for normal users. A permission failure on one value is IOError.PermissionDenied. AOT and default jet run share one provider (I9).

options.name: One map of every attribute
options.detail: files.extended_attributes(path) returns every name with its value as one map. files.set_extended_attributes(path, map) writes each entry. Neither follows a final link.
options.technical: files.extended_attributes(path) -[FS]> [String: [U8]] !IOError reads every listed value. files.set_extended_attributes(path, values: [String: [U8]]) !IOError -[FS]> writes each entry.

options.name: Follow links by default
options.detail: The same three calls as option A, but they read and write through a final link. A links: .Refuse label, shared with D-CORE-FILEOPEN1, acts on the link itself.
options.technical: Signatures match option A plus links: LinkPolicy{.Follow}. The default uses listxattr and getxattr without the no-follow flag.
options.code:
// PROPOSED; NOT RUN.
names :: files.extended_attribute_names(path, links: .Refuse)

comparisons.note: Python splits list, get, set, and remove into four calls, each with a follow_symlinks switch that defaults to following. Official docs: https://docs.python.org/3/library/os.html#linux-extended-attributes.
The widely used xattr crate makes its plain calls act on the link itself, and adds get_deref for following. That matches option A's default. Official docs: https://docs.rs/xattr/latest/xattr/.
comparisons.code: for name in xattr::list(path)? { let value = xattr::get(path, &name)?; }

recommendation.why: Listing names first lets callers skip protected attributes before reading them. Acting on the link itself matches files.stat and closes a link-swap trick.
gains: Protected names are never read by accident.
Same link rule as files.stat.

losses.loss: Copying all attributes takes a short loop.
losses.mitigation: A copy-all call would also read the protected values that every current caller skips.

whyNot.reason: It reads every value, including protected security values that may need extra rights or must stay unread.
Its default follows links, which is the unsafe choice for every caller the port has.

recommendation.tradeoff: Windows and file systems without support report no names and refuse writes with IOError.Unsupported.

surface.gist: How should Core list, read, and write a file's extended attributes?
surface.lesson: Extended attributes are small named byte values stored beside a file, such as a macOS download quarantine mark. Package tools must see them, because they can change how a file behaves. Core has no way to read or write them today. Whichever option wins, names are text, values are bytes, and Windows reports no attributes.

current.note: core.files has no extended-attribute call, so the port cannot check or copy them. Read from Core/files/files.jet; not run.

wild.note: Python has list, get, and set calls, each with a follow_symlinks switch. See https://docs.python.org/3/library/os.html#linux-extended-attributes.
wild.code:
names = os.listxattr("pkg/bin/tool", follow_symlinks=False)
value = os.getxattr("pkg/bin/tool", "user.origin", follow_symlinks=False)
os.setxattr("copy/tool", "user.origin", value, follow_symlinks=False)

options.name: Three calls that never follow links
options.gist: Separate calls list names, read one value, and write one value on the path itself.
gains: Callers skip names they must not read.
Acts on a link itself, like files.stat.
Missing names return None, not an error.
losses: Copying all attributes takes a short loop.

options.name: One map of every attribute
options.gist: One call returns every name with its value; another writes a whole map.
gains: Copying all attributes is two calls.
losses: Reads every value, including protected security values.
No way to skip one name before reading it.

options.name: Follow links by default
options.gist: Same three calls, but they read through links unless told not to.
gains: Matches most tools' default.
losses: The default reads a link's target, not the link.
Every safe caller must add a label.

recommendation.why: Names first lets callers skip protected attributes before reading them. Acting on the link itself matches files.stat and closes a swap trick.
gains: Protected names are never read by accident.
Same link rule as files.stat.

losses.loss: Copying all attributes takes a short loop.
losses.mitigation: A copy-all call would read protected values that callers skip.

whyNot.reason: It reads every value, including protected ones that may need extra rights.
Its default follows links, the unsafe choice for every caller Jet has.

recommendation.tradeoff: Windows and file systems without support report no names and refuse writes.

decisions.title: Raw bytes through a child process's pipes
decisions.gist: How should a program send raw bytes into a child process and read raw bytes back out?
decisions.lesson: A child process talks through pipes: input, output, and errors. Jet child pipes carry text today: write a string, loop over lines. Tools that pass archives need raw bytes. Files and sockets already share one byte shape: read up to a limit, write every byte. Whichever option wins, the reference page and one golden example must show a byte round trip.
decisions.story: Priya ports the Jetpack binary cache to Jet. It uploads a NAR archive by piping bytes into ssh, and it checks a downloaded tarball by reading gzip output 512 bytes at a time. With text-only pipes she cannot write either step, and the port may not work around Core.
decisions.detail:
Need: Tower #3594 item 1. Card text: "Binary stdin/stdout/stderr streaming on ProcessChild (today only line streams); Provider and Store feed and read NAR/tar bytes through child processes."

Rust call sites that require it:
```text
byte input into a child:
  crates/jetpack/src/Store/Cache.rs:2380-2384   ssh_put write_all(bytes)
  crates/jetpack/src/Store/Cache.rs:2406-2410   ssh_append write_all(bytes)
  crates/jetpack/src/Store/Cache.rs:2469-2473   s3_put write_all(bytes)
  crates/jetpack/src/Image.rs:857-862           curl request body
bounded byte output (kill the child past the bound):
  crates/jetpack/src/Store/Cache.rs:2513-2558   run_bounded_output
  crates/jetpack/src/Image.rs:946-975
streamed tar headers from gzip output:
  crates/jetpack/src/Provider/fetch.rs:317-334, 356-364
```

Current Jet surface: ProcessStdin has write(text) and close(). The output handles have only lines(). See crates/jet-sema/src/Sema/CheckerCoreLib/process_ui.rs:364-402.

Governing law: D-NETIO-CONTRACT1=A made io.Reader and io.Writer the one byte-stream contract. D-NETIO-CONTRACT2=B fixed read(limit), write, write_all, one IOError, and inherent close. D-FOUND-LIFECYCLE1=A already shows child.stdin.write_all and child.stdin.close. The core.files ballot D-CORE-FILEOPEN1 uses the same read(limit) and chunks(size) spellings.

options.name: Pipes are byte streams
options.detail: The child's input pipe becomes an io.Writer and its output and error pipes become io.Readers, exactly like files and sockets. read(limit) returns up to limit bytes and an empty list at end of input. chunks(size) is the loop form. write_all(bytes) writes every byte. The existing text write keeps working under the name write_text, the same name TCP and TLS use. lines() stays.
options.technical:
```text
ProcessStdin (existing field handle, now an io.Writer):
  write(bytes: [U8]) -> Int !IOError
  write_all(bytes: [U8]) !IOError
  write_text(text: String) !IOError     // renamed from write(text)
  close()                               // unchanged
ProcessStdoutStream / ProcessStderrStream (now io.Readers):
  read(limit: Int) -> [U8] !IOError     // [] = end of input
  chunks(size: Int{65536})              // loop source of non-empty [U8]
  lines()                               // unchanged
```

A limit or size below one is IOError.InvalidInput before any read. A pipe read failure inside a chunks loop ends the loop. child.wait() then reports it through the existing output_read_error path. The error type is the one core IOError from D-NETIO-CONTRACT2.

Effects stay the same as today’s pipe calls; no new effect appears. Mixing lines() and read() on one pipe reads one shared buffer in call order. A .Capture pipe is not a stream; read and chunks on it follow the rule lines() follows today.

Tiers: one Prelude implementation over the existing ProcessReader and ProcessStdin carriers. AOT, the JIT host, and the MIR evaluator all call it (I9).

Cutover with no alias (E1): rename every child.stdin.write(text) call in the same change. Known sites:
```text
Core/process/process.jet:53 (stdin_text)
tests/jit_run.rs:421
tests/process_sessions.rs:54-112, 578-604
tests/corelib_parts/platform.rs:448, 789, 897-901, 1245-1249
tests/agent_workloads/adapters/mcp_resource.jet:37
Docs/spec/reference/core-library.md:1371
```

options.name: Bytes in the receipt
options.detail: Keep the pipes text-only. A captured run also stores raw bytes as receipt.output_bytes and receipt.errors_bytes, bounded by output_limit. A new helper process.stdin_bytes(spec, bytes) feeds a whole byte list, closes input, and waits. Nothing streams.
options.technical: ProcessReceipt gains output_bytes: [U8] and errors_bytes: [U8]; process.stdin_bytes(spec: ProcessSpec, bytes: [U8]) !IOError -[Exec, Time.Wait]>. The output limit applies to bytes; crossing it ends the run with IOError.ResourceLimit as today.
options.code:
// PROPOSED; NOT RUN.
receipt :: process.cmd(["gzip", "-dc", path])
    .stdout(.Capture)
    .output_limit(1_073_741_824)
    .run() ?? return
inspect(receipt.output_bytes)

spec :: process.cmd(["ssh", host, "tee -- {key}"])
process.stdin_bytes(spec, nar) ?? return

options.name: A separate byte handle
options.detail: Add a .Bytes stream mode. A child spawned with it exposes a new ProcessByteReader field with its own read and chunk calls. Text handles keep their current names.
options.technical: ProcessStreamMode gains .Bytes; ProcessChild gains stdin_bytes, stdout_bytes, and stderr_bytes fields of new types ProcessByteWriter and ProcessByteReader, present only when the matching mode is .Bytes.

comparisons.note: Popen pipes are byte file objects; read(n) returns b'' at end. Official docs: https://docs.python.org/3/library/subprocess.html#subprocess.Popen.stdout. Praised for one file-object model; the documented complaint is deadlock when one pipe is not drained, which A keeps visible as the existing drain duty.
comparisons.code:
child = subprocess.Popen(cmd, stdin=subprocess.PIPE, stdout=subprocess.PIPE)
child.stdin.write(nar)
child.stdin.close()
while chunk := child.stdout.read(65536):
    inspect(chunk)

comparisons.note: ChildStdin implements Write and ChildStdout implements Read, the same traits as File and TcpStream. Official docs: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/process/struct.ChildStdout.html. This is the model D-NETIO-CONTRACT1 chose for Jet streams.

recommendation.why: A reuses the byte contract that files, sockets, and TLS already follow. It streams any size and lets the program stop a bad child early.

whyNot.reason: B holds whole archives in memory and cannot stop a child at the first bad header.
C gives one pipe two handle types and a second byte vocabulary.

recommendation.tradeoff: One rename of the text write buys a single byte contract for every stream.

surface.gist: How should a program send raw bytes into a child process and read raw bytes back out?
surface.lesson: A child process talks through pipes: input, output, and errors. Jet child pipes carry text today: write a string, loop over lines. Tools that pass archives need raw bytes. Files and sockets already share one byte shape: read up to a limit, write every byte. Whichever option wins, the reference page and one golden example must show a byte round trip.

current.note: Today the input pipe takes only text and the output pipe gives only lines. Archive bytes cannot pass through.

wild.note: Python pipes are byte streams: read up to n bytes, write bytes. Source: https://docs.python.org/3/library/subprocess.html#subprocess.Popen.stdout
wild.code:
child = subprocess.Popen(["gzip", "-dc", path],
                         stdout=subprocess.PIPE)
while chunk := child.stdout.read(65536):
    inspect(chunk)
child.wait()

options.name: Pipes are byte streams
options.gist: Child pipes use the same read and write calls as files and sockets.
gains: One byte shape for files, sockets, and child pipes.
Streams large archives with bounded memory.
Generic copy helpers accept a child pipe directly.
losses: Existing text writes move from write to write_text.

options.name: Bytes in the receipt
options.gist: Capture keeps raw output bytes; a helper feeds whole input bytes.
gains: Short programs need no loop.
losses: The whole archive sits in memory.
Cannot stop a child early on a bad header.
No way to feed input piece by piece.

proposed.code:
// PROPOSED; NOT RUN.
receipt :: process.cmd(["gzip", "-dc", path])
    .stdout(.Capture)
    .output_limit(1_073_741_824)
    .run() ?? return
inspect(receipt.output_bytes)

spec :: process.cmd(["ssh", host, "tee -- {key}"])
process.stdin_bytes(spec, nar) ?? return

options.name: A separate byte handle
options.gist: A new byte mode returns a different handle type for the same pipe.
gains: Existing text calls keep their names.
losses: Two handle types describe one pipe.
Byte calls differ from files and sockets.

recommendation.why: A reuses the byte contract that files, sockets, and TLS already follow. It streams any size and lets the program stop a bad child early.
gains: One byte contract across files, sockets, and child pipes.
Memory stays bounded for archives of any size.

losses.loss: Existing text writes move to write_text.
losses.mitigation: The shared byte contract already uses write for bytes, and one name cannot mean both.

whyNot.reason: B holds whole archives in memory and cannot stop a child at the first bad header.
C gives one pipe two handle types and a second byte vocabulary.

recommendation.tradeoff: One rename of the text write buys a single byte contract for every stream.

decisions.title: Replace the running program with another program
decisions.gist: How should a Jet program hand its whole process to another program, the way a shell's exec does?
decisions.lesson: Replacing a process means the running program becomes another program. It keeps the same process number and terminal, and no parent stays behind waiting. Jetpack's env and use commands hand the terminal to a verified tool this way. Jet can only start a child and wait. Whichever option wins, Windows needs a documented stand-in, because Windows cannot swap a running program.
decisions.story: Marco types `jetpack use -- python3`. Jetpack checks the verified environment, then should disappear so python3 owns his terminal, his Ctrl+C, and his shell's job list. The Jet port can only run python3 under a waiting Jet parent.
decisions.detail:
Need: Tower #3594 item 2. Card text: "exec: replace the current process image (jetpack env/use shell handoff)."

Rust call sites that require it:
```text
crates/jetpack/src/Shell.rs:207-215        exec_command (replace_process = true)
crates/jetpack/src/Shell.rs:761-772        CommandExt::exec on Unix
crates/jetpack/src/Shell.rs:773-790        non-Unix: status() and return the code
crates/jetpack/src/CLI/run_enter_dev.rs:2081, 2622   warm env/use handoff
```

Current Jet surface: ProcessSpec has run, run_checked, spawn, and plan. process.exit(code) ends the program through the explicit exit boundary (D-FAIL-EXIT1). Nothing replaces the program.

Law checks: Law 1 rejects abbreviations outside len, fmt, args, and mem, so the method is not named exec. D-AGENT-EXEC1 keeps authority-bound runs inside a captured receipt, so replace refuses them. D-PROCESS1 keeps process.cmd shell-free, and replace keeps that rule.

options.name: A replace call on the spec
options.detail: Add spec.replace_process() beside run and spawn. On success it never returns. On failure it returns the IOError and the program keeps running with its state intact. Jet flushes its own output buffers first. Deferred cleanup and exit handlers do not run, because the program is gone.
options.technical:
```text
ProcessSpec.replace_process() -[Exec, Time.Wait]> Never !IOError
```

Used from the spec: argv, cwd, env, env_remove, env_clear, and handles kept with keep_open (D-CORE-PROCINHERIT1). A replaced program uses the real streams, so any stream set to .Capture or .Stream is refused. An unset stdin gives the new program a closed input, the same default run uses.

Refused before replacing, with IOError.InvalidInput naming the setting: .Capture or .Stream, .terminal(), .detached(), .timeout(...), .output_limit(...), and .under(authority). A receipt cannot exist without a parent, so these settings have no honest meaning.

CPU, memory, and open-file limits apply to the new program on Unix through the existing setrlimit path. The Windows stand-in applies them through its Job Object, with today’s refusals.

Unix: resolve the executable, flush Jet stdout and stderr buffers, then execve. Close-on-exec closes every other Core handle. Defers, scope guards, and atexit handlers do not run.

Windows stand-in: start the child with inherited console and handles, wait, then end with the child's exit code. It skips defers and atexit, matching Unix. Effects include Time.Wait because of this wait.

Errors: IOError.NotFound when the executable is missing, IOError.PermissionDenied when it cannot run, and IOError.InvalidInput for refused settings.

Tiers: one Prelude implementation. The resident JIT host and MIR evaluator run inside the jet binary, so replace there ends the jet process itself. That is the same observable result as AOT (I9).

options.name: A separate exec function
options.detail: Add process.exec(argv, env:) shaped like Python's os.execvpe. It takes a plain argument list and an optional environment map and never sees a ProcessSpec.
options.technical:
```text
process.exec(argv: [String], env: ?[String: String]{None}) -[Exec, Time.Wait]> Never !IOError
```

Working directory, handle passing, and limits would need their own labels or stay unavailable.

options.name: No replace; keep forwarding
options.detail: Add nothing. A handoff runs the tool as a child, waits, and exits with its code. Core also places that child in its own process group, so terminal input needs D-CORE-PROCGROUP1 to work at all.
options.technical: No new API. The Jet port keeps a parent process for the whole tool session.
options.code:
// CURRENT PATTERN; NO CHANGE.
receipt :: process.cmd([tool, ...rest])
    .stdin(.Inherit).stdout(.Inherit).stderr(.Inherit)
    .run() ?? return
process.exit(receipt.code)

comparisons.note: CommandExt::exec reuses the Command builder and returns only an error. Official docs: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/os/unix/process/trait.CommandExt.html#tymethod.exec. It is Unix-only; Jetpack falls back to status() elsewhere.

os.execvpe is a free function separate from subprocess. On Windows it starts a new process and exits without waiting, a documented surprise for shells. Official docs: https://docs.python.org/3/library/os.html#os.execvpe
syscall.Exec takes an absolute path, argv, and environment. Official docs: https://pkg.go.dev/syscall#Exec. It is not offered on Windows.

recommendation.why: A adds one method to the builder that already owns arguments, environment, and working directory. The handed-off tool gets the real terminal and process number.

whyNot.reason: B adds a second command description beside ProcessSpec and an abbreviated name.
C leaves an extra parent that changes signals, job control, and the process number.

recommendation.tradeoff: Cleanup after a successful replace is skipped so the tool truly owns the process.

surface.gist: How should a Jet program hand its whole process to another program, the way a shell's exec does?
surface.lesson: Replacing a process means the running program becomes another program. It keeps the same process number and terminal, and no parent stays behind waiting. Jetpack's env and use commands hand the terminal to a verified tool this way. Jet can only start a child and wait. Whichever option wins, Windows needs a documented stand-in, because Windows cannot swap a running program.

current.note: Today the Jet program stays alive as a parent and forwards the child's exit code.
current.code:
spec :: process.cmd([tool, ...rest])
    .stdin(.Inherit).stdout(.Inherit).stderr(.Inherit)
receipt :: spec.run() ?? return
process.exit(receipt.code)
// Jet stays behind as an extra parent process.

wild.note: Rust's exec replaces the process and returns only an error. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/os/unix/process/trait.CommandExt.html#tymethod.exec

options.name: A replace call on the spec
options.gist: The same ProcessSpec that runs a child can replace the program.

decisions.title: Keyboard and Ctrl+C for a child that shares the terminal
decisions.gist: When a child process shares your terminal, should Jet give it the keyboard and Ctrl+C while it runs?
decisions.lesson: A process group is a set of processes that receive signals together. A terminal sends keys and Ctrl+C only to one foreground group. Jet starts every child in its own group, so stopping the child also stops its helpers. A child that reads the terminal from a background group is paused by the system. Whichever option wins, the group stop behavior stays.
decisions.story: Ana runs `jetpack enter`. Jetpack starts an interactive bash with her project tools, waits, and deletes its scratch files when bash exits. In a Jet port, bash would start in a background group and stop at its first prompt.
decisions.detail:
Need: Tower #3594 item 3. Card text: "Child process-group/session placement (Unix process_group(0), Windows CREATE_NEW_PROCESS_GROUP) and Windows Job Object containment plus GenerateConsoleCtrlEvent (Services supervision, RuntimePolicy)."

What Core already does:
```text
Unix: every std child gets process_group(0)
  crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/CoreLib/Top/Process.rs:328-347, 745-751
Windows: every non-detached child joins a kill-on-close Job Object
  crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/CoreLib/Top/Process.rs:493-513
kill / terminate / interrupt signal the whole group
  crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/CoreLib/Top/Process.rs:2560-2575, 3031-3077
```

So Services placement (Services.rs:3035-3047, 2659-2660) is already the Core default on Unix. This ballot covers the missing piece: an interactive child that inherits the terminal.

Rust call sites that run interactive children in the caller's group:
```text
crates/jetpack/src/Shell.rs:775    run_command: cmd.status() on an inherited terminal
crates/jetpack/src/Shell.rs:899    enter: interactive bash/zsh/fish, cleanup after exit
```

No Core code calls tcsetpgrp today, a search of crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/CoreLib found none. [INFERENCE] By POSIX job control, a background-group read from the controlling terminal raises SIGTTIN and stops the child. A pty smoke run was not possible in this environment.

Left to the other ballots: saving a child and stopping its group from another command is D-CORE-PROCIDENT1. The Windows graceful stop needs no new name; see the technical note.

options.name: Hand over the terminal automatically
options.detail: Keep every child in its own group. When the child's input is inherited and Jet's input is a terminal, Jet makes the child's group the terminal's foreground group. When the child finishes or stops, Jet takes the terminal back. No new name appears.
options.technical:
Rule: the handoff happens when spec.stdin is .Inherit, stdin is a terminal, and the child is not detached. It applies to run, run_checked, spawn, and the helpers that call them.

Unix: the child calls setpgid(0, 0) and tcsetpgrp(0, getpid()) before exec, with SIGTTOU blocked. Jet also calls tcsetpgrp after spawn to close the race. After wait, Jet reclaims the terminal with SIGTTOU ignored for that call. If the child stops itself with Ctrl+Z, Jet reclaims the terminal and wait keeps waiting, like a shell without job control.

A second spawn that asks for the terminal while another child owns it fails before spawn. The error is IOError.InvalidInput naming the owning child id. Pipelines give the terminal to the first step's group.

Windows: a child that inherits a console stays in the console's Ctrl+C group, inside its Job Object. Other children get CREATE_NEW_PROCESS_GROUP. Their terminate() then sends CTRL_BREAK_EVENT to that group before the job kill. That matches the existing meaning of terminate; it adds no name.

Effects and errors: unchanged signatures and rows. Tiers: one Prelude spawn path for AOT, the JIT host, and the MIR evaluator (I9).

options.name: An explicit placement option
options.detail: Add ProcessSpec.group(placement) with a new ProcessGroup enum. The default .Own keeps today's behavior. .Caller keeps the child in Jet's own group, like Rust's plain Command.
options.technical:
```text
ProcessSpec.group(placement: ProcessGroup) -> ProcessSpec
enum ProcessGroup { Own, Caller }
```

With .Caller, kill and terminate reach only the direct child, and Windows skips the Job Object.
options.code:
// PROPOSED; NOT RUN.
spec :: process.cmd(["bash", "-i"])
    .stdin(.Inherit).stdout(.Inherit).stderr(.Inherit)
    .group(.Caller)
receipt :: spec.run() ?? return

options.name: Refuse; use a terminal session
options.detail: Refuse .stdin(.Inherit) before spawn when Jet's input is a terminal. The error points to .terminal(), the ratified terminal session (D-PROCESS-SESSION1), which relays bytes through a pseudo-terminal.
options.technical: New IOError.InvalidInput before spawn for inherited terminal input. No new name; interactive tools move to the existing terminal session relay.

comparisons.note: The reference shell puts each job in its own group and gives it the terminal. Manual: https://www.gnu.org/software/libc/manual/html_node/Launching-Jobs.html. This is the model option A follows.

A plain Command child stays in the caller's group; process_group(0) opts into a new one. Docs: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/os/unix/process/trait.CommandExt.html#tymethod.process_group. Jetpack uses both forms today.
comparisons.code:
Command::new("bash").status()?;          // caller's group
cmd.process_group(0); cmd.spawn()?;      // own group

comparisons.note: CREATE_NEW_PROCESS_GROUP disables Ctrl+C for the new group but allows Ctrl+Break. Docs: https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/console/generateconsolectrlevent

recommendation.why: A fixes the pause without a new name and keeps the group stop that protects against leftover helpers. It follows how job-control shells have worked for decades.

whyNot.reason: B keeps the pause as the default and drops the group stop when chosen.
C makes every interactive tool pay for a byte relay and a new error.

recommendation.tradeoff: Jet lends the terminal to the child during the run and takes it back afterward.

Whichever option wins, the group stop behavior stays.

wild.note: Job-control shells give each job its own group, then hand it the terminal. Source: https://www.gnu.org/software/libc/manual/html_node/Launching-Jobs.html

decisions.title: Save a child's identity and stop it safely later
decisions.gist: How should a program save a child's identity, then safely stop that child later from another command?
decisions.lesson: The system reuses process numbers after a process ends. A saved number alone can later point at a stranger's program. Jetpack's services save the number plus the process start time and check both before stopping anything. Jet can stop a child only through the live handle from spawn. Whichever option wins, Windows children need a named group so another command can reach them.
decisions.story: Sam runs `jetpack services up`, and a supervisor starts his database. A day later he runs `jetpack services down` in a new terminal. By then the saved process number could belong to his editor. The port must stop the database, never the editor.
decisions.inWild:
# psutil: https://psutil.readthedocs.io/en/latest/#psutil.Process.create_time
proc = psutil.Process(saved_pid)
if proc.create_time() == saved_start:
    proc.terminate()
decisions.detail:
Need: Tower #3594 item 6. Card text: "core.sys: process start-identity query for pid-reuse guards on macOS/Windows." It also covers the cross-command part of item 3: "Windows Job Object containment plus GenerateConsoleCtrlEvent (Services supervision, RuntimePolicy)."

Rust call sites that require it:
```text
crates/jetpack/src/Services.rs:1153-1157      ProcessState { pid, start_identity }
crates/jetpack/src/Services.rs:2062-2215      start identity: Linux /proc stat, macOS proc_pidinfo,
                                              BSD ps lstart, Windows GetProcessTimes
crates/jetpack/src/Services.rs:2549-2569      process_matches_start guard
crates/jetpack/src/Services.rs:2685-2720      publish pid + start after spawn
crates/jetpack/src/Services.rs:3639-3702      down_one: verify, then stop
crates/jetpack/src/Services.rs:4035-4131      group TERM/KILL; Windows job open by name,
                                              Ctrl+Break, TerminateJobObject
crates/jetpack/src/Services.rs:2425-2545      named Job Object create/open/query
crates/jet-pkg-model/src/Prelude/SecretsCrypto.rs:2345-2348, 2490-2498   own start time in a lock
```

Current Jet surface: ProcessChild.id() returns a bare number. core.sys has pid(), getpgid(pid), and #Unsafe kill(pid, signal). core.watcher.process_pid(pid) watches liveness by number only. Core Windows children join a private, unnamed Job Object (Process.rs:493-513), which no other command can open.

options.name: A saved identity with a built-in check
options.detail: child.identity() returns a ProcessIdentity: the number, an opaque start token, and an optional group token. It is plain data, so JSON can save it. Later, process.find(identity) returns a RunningProcess only when the same process is still alive. RunningProcess has terminate, kill, and interrupt, which act on the whole group like ProcessChild.
options.technical:
```text
#Codable pub struct ProcessIdentity { pub pid: Int, pub start: String, pub containment: ?String }
ProcessChild.identity() -[Env]> ProcessIdentity !IOError
process.identity(pid: Int) -[Env]> ?ProcessIdentity !IOError
process.find(saved: ProcessIdentity) -[Exec, Env]> ?RunningProcess !IOError
RunningProcess.terminate() / kill() / interrupt() !IOError
RunningProcess.identity() -> ProcessIdentity
```

The start token is compared only for equality; its text is platform-tagged and stable across runs. Linux uses the stat starttime field in clock ticks. macOS uses proc_pidinfo start seconds and microseconds. Windows uses GetProcessTimes creation time. Other Unix targets without an exact source refuse with IOError.Unsupported, the variant D-CORE-FILEERROR1 proposes. If that ballot loses, the error is IOError.Other with the platform named in its cause, as limit refusals are today.

process.find returns None when no process has that number or the start token differs. On Windows it also returns a value while the named Job Object still has live members after the leader exits.

Unix stop calls signal the negative process group, which Core already creates for every child. Windows terminate sends CTRL_BREAK_EVENT to the group, kill calls TerminateJobObject, and interrupt sends CTRL_BREAK_EVENT too.

To make Windows reachable, Core names each child's Job Object with a random Local name and stores it in containment. process.identity(pid) for a process Jet did not start has containment None.

Errors: IOError.PermissionDenied when the system refuses the query or signal, and the refusal above for unsupported targets. Tiers: one Prelude implementation for AOT, the JIT host, and the MIR evaluator (I9).

options.name: A start-time query only
options.detail: Add sys.process_start(pid) that returns an opaque start token, or None when no such process exists. Callers save it beside the number, compare it later, and stop the group with the existing #Unsafe sys.kill. Windows Job Objects stay private.
options.technical:
```text
sys.process_start(pid: Int) -[Env]> ?String !IOError
```

The token sources match option A. There is no stop call and no Windows group reach.

comparisons.note: psutil keeps creation time inside Process and uses it in is_running to detect reuse. Docs: https://psutil.readthedocs.io/en/latest/#psutil.Process.is_running. It is praised because callers rarely write the check by hand.
A pidfd pins one live process and avoids reuse for that process. It cannot be saved to a file or signal a whole group. Manual: https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/pidfd_open.2.html
comparisons.code:
int fd = pidfd_open(pid, 0);
pidfd_send_signal(fd, SIGTERM, NULL, 0);

recommendation.why: A makes the safe path the only path: a saved identity cannot stop a reused number. It also reaches Windows groups without unsafe code.

whyNot.reason: B leaves the reuse check to every caller and stopping behind #Unsafe.

recommendation.tradeoff: One new value type buys a reuse check that every stop goes through.

Whichever option wins, Windows children need a named group so another command can reach them.

current.note: Today a later command has only a bare number, with no reuse check and no safe stop call.

wild.note: psutil pairs a process number with its creation time and checks it before acting. Source: https://psutil.readthedocs.io/en/latest/#psutil.Process.create_time

options.name: A saved identity with a built-in check
options.gist: Save an identity value; finding it later checks reuse and returns a stoppable handle.
gains: The reuse check cannot be forgotten.
Stopping reaches the whole group with no #Unsafe.
Works the same on Unix and Windows.
losses: A short gap remains between the check and the stop.

options.name: A start-time query only
options.gist: Add one call that reports a process's start token; callers compare and signal themselves.
gains: Smallest addition; mirrors the Rust code.
losses: Every caller must remember the comparison.
Stopping still needs #Unsafe sys.kill.
Windows groups stay unreachable from another command.

recommendation.why: A makes the safe path the only path: a saved identity cannot stop a reused number. It also reaches Windows groups without unsafe code.
gains: No caller can signal a reused process number.
Group stop needs no #Unsafe block.

losses.loss: A short gap remains between the check and the stop.
losses.mitigation: Portable systems offer no single call that checks identity and signals a whole group.

whyNot.reason: B leaves the reuse check to every caller and stopping behind #Unsafe.

recommendation.tradeoff: One new value type buys a reuse check that every stop goes through.

decisions.title: Pass one open file or lock to a child process
decisions.gist: How should a program pass one open file or lock to a child process?
decisions.lesson: A child normally starts with only input, output, and errors open. Jetpack sometimes needs one more: a verified program file the child runs, or a lock that stays held until every descendant exits. Jet closes every other file in a child and has no way to keep one. Whichever option wins, the plan and receipt list each file a child received.
decisions.story: Lena ports Jetpack's Nix projection. It opens verified tools and store objects, then runs unshare with /proc/self/fd paths so nothing can swap the files. It also hands a lease lock to the launched tree. Jet closes all of them in the child.
decisions.inWild:
# Python: https://docs.python.org/3/library/subprocess.html#subprocess.Popen
fd = os.open("/usr/bin/mount", os.O_RDONLY)
subprocess.run(["unshare", "--", f"/proc/self/fd/{fd}"], pass_fds=[fd])
decisions.detail:
Need: Tower #3594 item 4. Card text: "Hand an inherited file descriptor to a child (clear FD_CLOEXEC) (Store Broker, Services)."

Rust call sites that require it:
```text
crates/jetpack/src/Shell.rs:340-366, 595-626          verified tools passed as /proc/self/fd/N
crates/jetpack/src/Store/Reuse.rs:1653-1682, 1931-1932 snapshot dir and projection files
crates/jetpack/src/Store/Reuse.rs:2399, 2507-2509, 2654-2677   executable wrappers
crates/jetpack/src/RuntimePolicy.rs:197-206            lease lock inherited by the launched tree
crates/jetpack/src/RuntimePolicy/Lock/unix.rs:146-157  clear FD_CLOEXEC on the lock
crates/jetpack/src/RuntimePolicy/Lock/windows.rs:283   SetHandleInformation inherit flag
```

The receiving side, where a broker adopts an inherited listening socket (Store/Broker.rs:494-503, CLI/shared_store.rs:42-45), belongs to core.net card #3595. It is not part of this ballot.

Coordination: the core.files ballots keep every Core file handle close-on-exec by default. They name this ballot as the only way to pass one. Accepted handle types are FileReader, FileWriter, FileLock, and the proposed Directory (D-CORE-FILEDIR1).

options.name: Keep chosen handles open in the child
options.detail: Add spec.keep_open(^handle). The spec takes ownership of the handle, and every child it starts receives that handle open. The optional at: label places it at a chosen descriptor number on Unix, so the child can use a /dev/fd path. The parent copy closes when the spec is dropped. Every other Core handle stays closed in children.
options.technical:
```text
ProcessSpec.keep_open(handle: ^KeepOpen, at: ?Int{None}) -> ProcessSpec
KeepOpen = FileReader | FileWriter | FileLock | Directory   // core.files handles
```

The handle is consumed with ^, so the program cannot also read or close it. A spec may keep several handles. Each pinned number must be 3 or greater and unique within the spec. Numbers 0 to 2 are the standard streams and are refused with IOError.InvalidInput before spawn.

Unix: the child receives a duplicate at the pinned number, or at its current number when at is None. Close-on-exec is cleared only in the child, between fork and exec. The parent's own descriptor stays close-on-exec, so concurrent spawns in other tasks never see it.

Windows: the handle joins the child's explicit inherit list through PROC_THREAD_ATTRIBUTE_HANDLE_LIST. A pinned number is refused before spawn with IOError.Unsupported, the variant D-CORE-FILEERROR1 proposes. If that ballot loses, the error is IOError.Other with the platform named in its cause, as limit refusals are today.

Plan and receipt: ProcessPlan and ProcessReceipt list kept handles by kind, path, and pinned number. D-CORE-PROCREPLACE1 honors kept handles. Authority-bound specs (.under) refuse keep_open before spawn because the authority boundary lists no handle grant.

Effects: no new effect; spawn already carries Exec. Tiers: one Prelude spawn path for AOT, the JIT host, and the MIR evaluator (I9).

options.name: Mark a handle as inheritable
options.detail: Add handle.set_inheritable() and handle.descriptor(). The handle stays open in every child started later, from any task, until the program clears the flag or closes the handle.
options.technical:
```text
FileReader/FileWriter/FileLock.set_inheritable() !IOError
FileReader/FileWriter/FileLock.descriptor() -> Int
```

The flag is process-wide state on the descriptor, as in Rust Jetpack today.
options.code:
// PROPOSED; NOT RUN.
tool :: files.open("/usr/bin/mount") ?? return
tool.set_inheritable()
fd :: tool.descriptor()
spec :: process.cmd(["unshare", "--", "/dev/fd/{fd}"])
child :: spec.spawn() ?? return

options.name: Raw descriptors under #Unsafe
options.detail: Extend the existing #Unsafe POSIX controls in core.sys, which already include pipe and close_fd, with open_fd and set_close_on_exec. Callers manage raw numbers by hand.
options.technical:
```text
sys.open_fd(path: String) -[FS, Env]> Int !IOError          // #Unsafe
sys.set_close_on_exec(fd: Int, on: Bool) -[FS, Env]> !IOError  // #Unsafe
```

Unix only; Windows refuses.

comparisons.note: pass_fds names the descriptors one child keeps; close_fds closes the rest by default. Docs: https://docs.python.org/3/library/subprocess.html#subprocess.Popen. The complaint is that numbers stay raw; A hides them unless at is used.

Socket activation passes descriptors starting at 3 and tells the child how many. Manual: https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/latest/sd_listen_fds.html. Fixed low numbers are why A offers at.
Jetpack clears FD_CLOEXEC on the parent's descriptor, which exposes it to every concurrent spawn. Docs: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/os/unix/process/trait.CommandExt.html

recommendation.why: A passes the chosen handles only to children of that one spec and records them. Every other child stays closed, and no raw number appears in safe code.

whyNot.reason: B leaks the handle to every child any task starts until someone clears it.
C puts #Unsafe raw numbers into ordinary tool code and skips Windows.

recommendation.tradeoff: Pinned numbers are a Unix feature; plain inheritance works everywhere.

Whichever option wins, the plan and receipt list each file a child received.

current.note: Today Jet closes every file handle in the child, so the lock ends with this program.

wild.note: pass_fds keeps listed descriptors open in the child and closes the rest. Source: https://docs.python.org/3/library/subprocess.html#subprocess.Popen
wild.code:
fd = os.open("/usr/bin/mount", os.O_RDONLY)

               pass_fds=[fd])

gains: Nothing leaks to unrelated children.

gains: Full control for experts.

No Windows support.

gains: Only that spec's children receive the handle.
Audit records show every passed handle.

decisions.title: Catch Ctrl+C for one part of a program
decisions.gist: How should a program catch Ctrl+C for one part of its run, then put the old behavior back?
decisions.lesson: Ctrl+C and service stop requests arrive as signals. Today process.on_signal turns a signal into cancellation of the whole program, for the rest of the run. A full-screen dashboard instead needs to notice the signal, restore the screen, pick its exit code, and leave the old behavior in place. Whichever option wins, on_signal keeps its current meaning for services.
decisions.story: Kai ports the bare `jetpack` dashboard. It switches the terminal to raw mode and an alternate screen. On Ctrl+C it must restore the terminal, exit with code 0, and stop catching Ctrl+C. Today on_signal cancels the whole program and never lets go.
decisions.inWild:
// Go: https://pkg.go.dev/os/signal#Notify
stop := make(chan os.Signal, 1)
signal.Notify(stop, os.Interrupt, syscall.SIGTERM)
defer signal.Stop(stop)
decisions.detail:
Need: Tower #3594 item 5. Card text: "Scoped SIGINT/SIGTERM handler with a pollable flag and restore of the previous handler (on_signal registers a policy only)."

Rust call sites that require it:
```text
crates/jetpack/src/CLI/dashboard.rs:154-163    install guard before raw mode
crates/jetpack/src/CLI/dashboard.rs:218-226    loop checks the flag each pass
crates/jetpack/src/CLI/dashboard.rs:358-418    SignalGuard: set flag, restore previous handlers on drop
crates/jetpack/src/CLI/dashboard.rs:278-279    exit code 0 after a signal
```

Current Jet surface: process.on_signal(signal) -[Exec]> registers a permanent callback. It cancels the root task at the next wait point (crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/CoreLib/Top/Process.rs:42-54). Registration replaces, never restores (Top/Interrupt.rs:272-289).

Ratified law: D-FOUND-LIFECYCLE1=A made signals cancel the root task. It rejected its option B, a shared Boolean flag that every loop polls. This ballot keeps that ruling: no option adds a shared flag, and on_signal is unchanged. The card's "pollable flag" is met by a receiver the readiness table already polls.

Naming drift found while drafting: the checker resolves ProcessSignal to Term, Hup, and Int (crates/jet-sema/src/Sema/CheckerItems.rs:2396-2399; runtime carrier JetStd/CommonTypes.rs:16-20). The Core export table and the reference page list Interrupt, Terminate, Hangup, Child, User1, and User2 (crates/jet-foundation/src/CoreModuleExports.rs:475; core-library.md:1276). This ballot uses the documented plain names. Reconciling the two tables is separate work and needs no new name.

options.name: Signals arrive on a receiver
options.detail: Add process.signals(kinds). It returns a Receiver<ProcessSignal>. While that receiver exists, the listed signals arrive on it as values instead of their earlier effect. The program reads them with receive, a loop, or the readiness table. Closing or dropping the receiver puts the earlier behavior back.
options.technical:
```text
process.signals(kinds: [ProcessSignal]) -[Exec]> Receiver<ProcessSignal>
```

The list must be non-empty and may not contain .Child; an invalid list panics as a programmer error, like other Core argument misuse. The receiver works with receive(), loop signal in stop, and if { signal, stop -> ... } arms.

Scope rule: receivers nest. The newest live receiver for a kind wins. Dropping it restores whatever was active before it: an older receiver, an on_signal registration, or the system default. Restores happen in reverse creation order.

Buffering: an operating system merges repeats of a pending signal. The receiver keeps that rule and holds at most one pending value per listed kind. No accepted value is dropped beyond that merge.

Platform mapping is the one on_signal already uses (Top/Interrupt.rs). On Windows, .Interrupt is Ctrl+C and .Terminate covers Ctrl+Break and console close. Kinds a target cannot deliver are rejected the same way on_signal rejects them today, before the call runs.

Tiers: the existing single handler in Top/Interrupt.rs gains a stack of receiver slots. AOT, the JIT host, and the MIR evaluator share it (I9).

options.name: A one-shot signal wait
options.detail: Add process.wait_signal(kinds). It catches the listed signals only while it waits and returns the first one. Combine it with task.race to stop other work.
options.technical:
```text
process.wait_signal(kinds: [ProcessSignal]) -[Exec, Time.Wait]> ProcessSignal
```

The earlier behavior returns as soon as the wait ends or is cancelled.

options.name: A scoped cancellation guard
options.detail: Add process.cancel_on(kinds). It returns a guard; while the guard lives, the listed signals cancel the current task instead of the root task. Dropping the guard restores the earlier behavior.
options.technical:
```text
process.cancel_on(kinds: [ProcessSignal]) -[Exec]> SignalGuard
```

Cancellation follows D-CANCELMODEL1: the task unwinds at its next wait point and runs cleanup.

comparisons.note: signal.Notify sends chosen signals to a channel, and signal.Stop restores the default. Docs: https://pkg.go.dev/os/signal#Notify. It is praised for fitting select. The common complaint is an unbuffered channel missing a signal, which A avoids by keeping one pending value per kind.
signal.signal returns the previous handler so the caller can restore it by hand. Docs: https://docs.python.org/3/library/signal.html#signal.signal
comparisons.code:
previous = signal.signal(signal.SIGINT, handler)
try:
    run_dashboard()
finally:
    signal.signal(signal.SIGINT, previous)

recommendation.why: A reuses the receiver and readiness table Jet already teaches. Signals become ordinary values inside one scope, and dropping the receiver restores the old behavior.

whyNot.reason: B reopens a gap after each wait where a second Ctrl+C kills the program.
C unwinds a whole task and needs an extra task just to keep running.

recommendation.tradeoff: Services keep on_signal; code that must keep running gets a scoped receiver instead.

surface.gist: How should a program catch Ctrl+C for one part of its run, then put the old behavior back?
surface.lesson: Ctrl+C and service stop requests arrive as signals. Today process.on_signal turns a signal into cancellation of the whole program, for the rest of the run. A full-screen dashboard instead needs to notice the signal, restore the screen, pick its exit code, and leave the old behavior in place. Whichever option wins, on_signal keeps its current meaning for services.

current.note: Today a signal cancels the whole program, and the setting never ends.

wild.note: Go delivers chosen signals to a channel; Stop restores the earlier behavior. Source: https://pkg.go.dev/os/signal#Notify
wild.code:
stop := make(chan os.Signal, 1)
signal.Notify(stop, os.Interrupt, syscall.SIGTERM)
defer signal.Stop(stop)
select {
case <-stop:
case <-done:
}

gains: Uses the channel wait Jet already has.
Dropping the receiver restores the old behavior.
The program picks its own exit code.
losses: An unread receiver swallows Ctrl+C until it drops.

options.name: A one-shot signal wait
options.gist: A call waits for the next chosen signal; race it against the work.
gains: One call; combines with task.race.
losses: Between two waits the old behavior returns.

options.name: A scoped cancellation guard

gains: Keeps the cancellation meaning of on_signal.
losses: The whole task unwinds, not just the loop.
Choosing an exit code needs an extra child task.

gains: No second waiting mechanism beside channels.
