decisions.title: Ask whether input, output, or errors is a terminal
decisions.gist: How should a program ask whether its input, output, or error stream is connected to a terminal?
decisions.lesson: A terminal is an interactive screen and keyboard; a pipe or file is not. Programs check this before prompting, coloring text, or drawing progress. Jet's output and error handles answer with is_tty(), but the input handle has no check. A prompt cannot tell whether a person is there. Whichever option wins, all three handles answer the same way.
decisions.story: Noor ports Jetpack's trust prompt. When input comes from a pipe in CI, the prompt must print a plan and exit instead of waiting forever. Jet can check output but not input, so the port cannot decide.
decisions.detail:
Need: Tower #3598 item 1. Card text: "core.term: is_terminal for stdin/stdout/stderr (CLI output, prompts)."

Rust call sites that require it:
```text
crates/jetpack/src/Output.rs:568, 607            color and progress on stderr
crates/jetpack/src/Output.rs:916, 1004, 1047, 1076   prompts refuse without a terminal
crates/jetpack/src/Trust.rs:976, 1058, 1159      trust gates
crates/jetpack/src/NixFallbackPolicy.rs:263      stdin and stdout interactive
crates/jetpack/src/CLI/dashboard.rs:139, 148, 577
crates/jetpack/src/CLI/parse.rs:605
crates/jetpack/src/CLI/run_enter_dev.rs:3770
crates/jetpack/src/CLI/tool.rs:864
```

Current Jet surface: Stdout and Stderr already have is_tty() -> Bool. See crates/jet-sema/src/Sema/CheckerCoreLib/core_types.rs:3569-3577 and Codegen/TIR/subset/handles.rs:209, 214. StdinHandle has only lines() and read_line() (core_types.rs:3561-3567). The runtime already owns jet_term_stdin_is_terminal (crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Term.rs:69-82), so only the method is missing.

Law checks: Law 1 allows only len, fmt, args, and mem as abbreviations for new names. Predicates take the is_ prefix. D-COREIO1=A gave core.io ownership of terminal facts; the is_tty spelling appears only in its implementation note.

options.name: is_terminal() on all three handles
options.detail: Add is_terminal() to the input handle and rename is_tty() to is_terminal() on the output and error handles in the same change. All three answer from the one runtime check Jet already uses for color and prompts.
options.technical:
```text
StdinHandle.is_terminal() -> Bool
Stdout.is_terminal() -> Bool      // renamed from is_tty()
Stderr.is_terminal() -> Bool      // renamed from is_tty()
```

The answer comes from jet_term_stdin_is_terminal, jet_term_stdout_is_terminal, and jet_term_stderr_is_terminal (Prelude/Term.rs:69-82). Those use the platform isatty or console-mode check through Rust's IsTerminal. There is no error path and no new effect, the same as is_tty() today.

Tiers: the handle route table gains StdinIsTerminal next to the renamed StdoutIsTerminal and StderrIsTerminal. AOT, the JIT host, and the MIR evaluator share one Prelude function each (I9).

Cutover with no alias (E1):
```text
Examples/features/io/terminal_parity.jet:33-34
tests/conformance/corpus/core/term/stdout.jet:6
tests/conformance/corpus/core/term/stderr.jet:6
crates/jet-sema/src/Sema/CheckerCoreLib/core_types.rs:3575
crates/jet-codegen/src/Codegen/TIR/subset/handles.rs:209, 214
crates/jet-codegen/src/Codegen/TIR/routes.rs:1745-1795
Docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:3802
```

options.name: Add is_tty() to input
options.detail: Add StdinHandle.is_tty() -> Bool and leave the output and error names alone.
options.technical:
```text
StdinHandle.is_tty() -> Bool
```

Same runtime check as option A; no rename.

options.name: One module function
options.detail: Add term.is_terminal(stream) with a new TermStream enum of Stdin, Stdout, and Stderr. The handle methods stay as they are.
options.technical:
```text
enum TermStream { Stdin, Stdout, Stderr }
term.is_terminal(stream: TermStream) -> Bool
```

comparisons.note: IsTerminal replaced the atty crate in Rust 1.70 with one method on every standard stream. Docs: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/io/trait.IsTerminal.html
Every file object has isatty(); the name is an abbreviation Python kept from C. Docs: https://docs.python.org/3/library/io.html#io.IOBase.isatty
Streams carry an isTTY property that is undefined for pipes. Docs: https://nodejs.org/api/tty.html#readstreamistty

recommendation.why: A gives all three streams one plain predicate, matching the naming law and Rust. The rename touches a handful of calls in one change.

whyNot.reason: B adds a new abbreviated name that the naming law rejects.
C adds a second spelling and an enum beside methods that already exist.

recommendation.tradeoff: A small rename now keeps one plain name for every stream.

decisions.title: Parse JSON under caller-chosen size and depth limits
decisions.gist: How should a program parse JSON while choosing smaller size and nesting limits than the defaults?
decisions.lesson: Parsing untrusted JSON uses memory and stack that grow with its size and nesting. Jet's parse always allows 16 MiB of input and 256 levels of nesting. Protocol servers need smaller limits they choose, such as 1 MiB and 64 levels. The JSON reader already accepts a limits value. Whichever option wins, an over-limit input reports a Limit error naming the limit.
decisions.story: Omar ports Jetpack's MCP server. Each message may be at most 1 MiB by default and nest at most 64 levels, and the user can tighten both. Jet's parse accepts 16 MiB and 256 levels, so a hostile client gets far more room than the protocol allows.
decisions.detail:
Need: Tower #3598 item 3. Card text: "core.encoding.json: parse with a caller-supplied byte limit (MCP, CompilerExtension, FFI)."

Rust call sites that require it:
```text
crates/jet-pkg-model/src/MCP.rs:28-33, 145-175   max_message_bytes 1 MiB default, 16 MiB hard; depth 64
crates/jet-pkg-model/src/MCP.rs:280-291          decode: size check, parse_json_with_limit, depth check
crates/jet-pkg-model/src/CompilerExtension.rs:415-418, 543-546   JSON::parse, 1 MiB and depth 64
crates/jet-pkg-model/src/FFI.rs:4695             Cargo metadata at 16 MiB
crates/jet-foundation/src/JSON.rs:9-49           parse_json_with_limit, MAX_JSON_DEPTH 64
```

Current Jet surface: json.parse(text) and json.decode(text) take no limits. The parser checks the whole input against a fixed max_item_bytes of 16,777,216 and nesting against a fixed max_depth of 256. See Core/encoding/json.jet:60-72, 394, 425, and 498-502.

Ratified law: D-ENCSTREAM-SURFACE1=A. EncodingLimits is the one shared limits carrier for every codec, with safe() defaults and field ranges. Readers take limits with a safe() default; max_total_bytes counts wire bytes and max_depth bounds nesting. The defaults table in stdlib-api-laws.md names "A limits value" as the explicit control for codec readers and writers. D-CORE-JSON-DUP1=A (reject duplicate keys) is unchanged.

options.name: Limits on parse
options.detail: Give json.parse and json.decode an optional limits label with the safe() default. A caller lowers max_total_bytes to cap input size and max_depth to cap nesting. The bare call behaves exactly as today. Errors use the existing EncodingError with kind Limit.
options.technical:
```text
json.parse(text: String, limits: EncodingLimits{EncodingLimits.safe()}) -> DataTree !EncodingError
json.decode(text: String, limits: EncodingLimits{EncodingLimits.safe()}) -> DataTree !EncodingError
```

The limits are validated in field order before parsing, per D-ENCSTREAM-SURFACE1. The first invalid field returns kind Limit, byte offset 0, an empty path, and a reason naming the field, value, and range.

max_total_bytes, when Val(n), rejects input longer than n bytes before parsing. It reports kind Limit at byte 0, with a reason naming max_total_bytes and n. When None, the existing whole-input bound stays max_item_bytes, which is today's 16 MiB check.

max_depth bounds array and object nesting, with the root container at depth 1. It fails at the opening bracket's byte offset and path. max_item_bytes also bounds each decoded string and key. The buffer and expansion fields are validated but unused, as the law says.

The compatibility aliases loads and load keep their one-argument form. Effects: none; parse stays pure. Tiers: Core/encoding/json.jet is the one implementation that AOT, the JIT, and comptime already share (I9).

options.name: A byte-limit sibling
options.detail: Add json.parse_limited(text, max_bytes:). It checks the length, then parses with today's fixed nesting limit.
options.technical:
```text
json.parse_limited(text: String, max_bytes: Int) -> DataTree !EncodingError
```

max_bytes must be positive. Nesting stays at 256.

options.name: No change
options.detail: Add nothing. Each caller checks text length before json.parse and builds its own error. Nesting stays fixed at 256.
options.technical: No new API.

comparisons.note: JsonDocument.Parse takes JsonDocumentOptions with MaxDepth, next to the reader options. Docs: https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/system.text.json.jsondocumentoptions.maxdepth. Size is capped by the caller's stream.
Go caps size by wrapping the input, and encoding/json has no depth option. Docs: https://pkg.go.dev/net/http#MaxBytesReader. The missing depth control is a known complaint.
Jetpack's own protocol parser takes a caller byte limit with a fixed depth of 64. Source: crates/jet-foundation/src/JSON.rs:18-23.

recommendation.why: A reuses the ratified limits value that the JSON reader already takes. Size and nesting become adjustable with the same error every codec reports.

whyNot.reason: B adds a second parse name and still cannot lower nesting.
C leaves every server writing its own size error with fixed nesting.

recommendation.tradeoff: Three short lines of limits setup buy exact, standard bounds.

Different shape from the JSON reader.

Nesting cannot be lowered.

recommendation.why: A reuses the ratified limits value that the JSON reader already takes. Size and nesting become adjustable with the same error every codec reports.
gains: Whole-value and streaming JSON share one limit vocabulary.

losses.loss: Callers set fields on a limits value.

decisions.title: Non-prefix uses of `@` and the reserved machine form
decisions.gist: Should references and command filenames keep `@`, and should the future infix machine form stay reserved?
decisions.lesson: Package references use `target@provider#version`; host selectors use `host@root`. Optional command files are `@run.jet`, `@build.jet`, `@dev.jet`, and `@test.jet`. These marks do not request compile-time evaluation. D-ONCE-AT1 also reserves a future infix location form, not an implemented feature. Prefix links are settled; this ballot only decides the other uses.
decisions.story: Noor sees a provider separator in a package reference, a marked command filename, and a link in source code. She needs their contexts explained, not a claim that they do the same job.
decisions.inWild:
npm install @scope/pkg@1.2.0
// npm uses `@` for scopes and versions in package specifiers. Source: docs.npmjs.com/cli/using-npm/package-spec.

options.name: Keep them all
options.detail: Keep package references, host selectors, and optional command home files unchanged. Preserve only D-ONCE-AT1's infix location reservation; this does not approve a machine feature or its final grammar. Prefix `@` in expressions means a link.
options.technical: D-JPK-REF1, D-JPK-OSHOST1, and card #1866 remain unchanged. A future location feature still needs its own ballot. No compile-time prefix form survives.

options.name: Keep references; drop the machine reservation
options.detail: Non-code uses stay; the infix code reservation is released.
options.technical: It releases D-ONCE-AT1's location reservation.

options.name: Keep only links on `@`
options.detail: Use `target from provider#version` for package references and `host from root` for host selectors. Quote them as single CLI arguments. Rename all four command homes to `command.cmd.jet` and release the infix location reservation. Prefix links stay unchanged.
options.technical: Replace the D-JPK-REF1 and D-JPK-OSHOST1 separators and card #1866's filename set in one cutover, including parsers and scaffolding. Whitespace-delimited `from` separates the reference components; paths containing whitespace need the existing quoted-string or CLI argument handling. Remove D-ONCE-AT1's future location reservation.
options.code:
exact = "acme/tool from github#v1.2.0"
"host from root"
run.cmd.jet  build.cmd.jet  dev.cmd.jet  test.cmd.jet
leader :: @p

comparisons.note: `@scope/pkg@version`. https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/using-npm/package-spec
Flake references use `:` and `#`. https://nix.dev/manual/nix/latest/command-ref/new-cli/nix3-flake

recommendation.why: Keeping the established references and filenames avoids unrelated migration. Retaining a reservation approves no new feature; any future infix syntax still needs review.

whyNot.reason: B simplifies the reservation, but gives up the established location spelling before a concrete feature can be judged.
C churns package references and scaffolding for a small consistency gain.

recommendation.tradeoff: Avoid unrelated churn while accepting context-dependent meanings and a still-unbuilt reservation.

decisions.title: Where build facts such as the target OS live
decisions.gist: Where should build facts such as the target OS, profile, and settings live?
decisions.lesson: `@build` supplies the target OS, profile, package identity, declared settings, and build stamps. These reads need no error handler; some fields can be absent. This ballot moves only their home. A bare `build` name could be hidden by Jet's existing `fn build` entry. Command filenames belong to D-AT-INFIX1.
decisions.story: Kai reads the target OS in five places and a typed `api_base` setting in two. He wants one short, obvious home for these facts.

options.name: `compiler.build.*`
options.detail: `compiler.build` holds `os`, `profile`, `package`, `settings`, and `stamp`. Settings remain typed values declared by the package. Valid reads need no error handler, but absent stamp data stays optional. Undeclared settings remain compile errors, not missing runtime fields.
options.technical: Move package name/version, OS, profile, declared settings, and stamp git/dirty/toolchain/at paths without changing their values or types. D-CONF-MODULE1 owns settings; the registered COMPILER_BUILD_FACT paths own the complete family. Optional data is not a query failure. Examples assume D-COMPILER-NS1 A. B substitutes `__if`, `__loop`, `__const`, `__fn`, and `__compiler`; C substitutes `#if`, `#loop`, `#N`, `#fn`, and `#compiler`. Values keep ratified `prep` and plain names; fence and splice choices are independent.

options.name: Bare `build.*`
options.detail: Open `core.compiler.build` as the prelude name `build`. User declarations win, as for other prelude aliases. In a file declaring `fn build`, use an explicit module alias for fact reads; the entry function and home filename stay unchanged.
options.technical: Extend the existing prelude alias machinery to this compiler-owned record. Emit the normal shadowing lint when a declaration wins; never reserve or rename the build entry.

options.name: Inside the package view
options.detail: Add a `build` field to the existing package view. It holds A's complete build record, including settings and stamps.
options.technical: Extend the existing CompilerPackage view, not PackageInfo, with the build record. Acquiring that view still returns CompilerPackageError, even when only a total build fact is wanted.

comparisons.note: `cfg!` and `env!` for target and package facts. https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/conditional-compilation.html
`@import("builtin")` exposes target facts. https://ziglang.org/documentation/master/#Compile-Variables

recommendation.why: Build facts sit beside other compiler facts without inheriting package-query failures. Qualifying the name also avoids the existing `fn build` collision.

whyNot.reason: B saves nine characters but needs another alias where `fn build` hides it.
C makes total facts fallible and mixes target facts into package facts.

recommendation.tradeoff: Eight extra characters over `@build` buy a clear namespace.

decisions.title: One sigil for compiler facts and metadata
decisions.gist: Which sigil should mark every fact the compiler knows, such as build, type, and package facts?
decisions.lesson: Jet reads compiler facts: the target OS, a type's fields, the package version. `prep` already marks code that runs before the program. `@` now means a link. A sigil marks facts the compiler knows (this family). `@` marks links (D-MEMREF1).
decisions.story: Mo reads `if os == .Linux` in a game and cannot tell whether `os` is a variable or a build fact. A sigil tells him the compiler supplied it.

#endif

options.detail: `$` marks every compiler fact. Config files keep `$NAME` for environment variables (D-ONCE-DOLLAR1); both mean 'supplied by the build, not the program'. Markers keep `#`, links keep `@`.
options.technical: Amends D-ONCE-DOLLAR1 to allow `$` in code for compiler facts. The retired `$` compile-time mark (E0003) is replaced by this meaning.

options.name: Lowercase `#`
options.detail: Lowercase `#name` is a fact; PascalCase `#Name` stays a marker. Amends D-ONCE-HASH1.
Prefix `%` marks facts; infix `%` stays remainder.

comparisons.note: `#if`, `#file`: https://docs.swift.org/swift-book/
`@` builtins: https://ziglang.org/documentation/master/#Builtin-Functions
`#` directives and `ODIN_OS`: https://odin-lang.org/docs/overview/#directives
`$` marks a reassignable local (26:32, Roc talk https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=12yVcgQHAK0). https://www.roc-lang.org/functional.
`#` marks compile-time names in macros (50:46, Skip/Hack talk https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=J31LlAUtoos). https://raw.githubusercontent.com/skiplang/skip/master/docs/blog/2018-07-24-macros.md.

recommendation.why: `$` is free in Jet code, easy to type, and already means 'supplied by the build' in config files, so one idea covers both.

whyNot.reason: B stacks a fourth meaning onto `#` and relies on letter case.
C collides visually with the remainder operator and has no precedent.

recommendation.tradeoff: Pasting Jet into shells needs single quotes in exchange for a clean dedicated sigil.

decisions.title: Spelling a compile-time number parameter
decisions.gist: How should a type declare a compile-time number parameter, such as a buffer size?
decisions.lesson: A number parameter lets one type describe different sizes: `Packet<64>` or `Packet<32>`. D-CONSTGEN1 ratified `<@N: Int>`, but it is not implemented here. #3505 chooses plain `N` uses. The proposed replacement marks the declaration with `prep`. `[U8#N]` means a fixed array of N bytes. This ballot also covers generic functions.
decisions.story: Mia writes a firmware `Packet<64>` type. Reading the declaration, she must tell a number parameter from a type parameter at a glance.

options.name: `<prep N: Int>`
options.detail: Only the declaration carries `prep`; uses write plain `N`. Both types and functions may take Int parameters. Closed expressions remain parenthesized at use sites; bound number arguments remain bare, as D-CONSTGEN1 requires.
options.technical:
Preserve D-CONSTGEN1's value identity, defaults, inference, Int restriction, and rejection of runtime arguments. #3505 owns plain-name uses. In declaration parameter lists only, recognize `prep` followed by a name and colon. Existing `<prep>` and `<prep: Trait>` still mean type parameters; call arguments keep their angle grammar.

This extends the current parser, which accepts only names and trait bounds. Examples assume D-COMPILER-NS1 A. B substitutes `__if`, `__loop`, `__const`, `__fn`, and `__compiler`; C substitutes `#if`, `#loop`, `#N`, `#fn`, and `#compiler`. Values keep ratified `prep` and plain names; fence and splice choices are independent.

options.name: `<N: Int>`
options.detail: The compiler decides from `Int` being a type, not a trait, that `N` is a number.
options.technical: It relies on sema's type-versus-trait lookup to classify the parameter.

comparisons.note: `comptime n: usize`. https://ziglang.org/documentation/master/#Compile-Time-Parameters
`const N: usize`. https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/items/generics.html#const-generics

recommendation.why: `prep` tells a reader this parameter is a number known before running, with the same word used everywhere else.

whyNot.reason: B reads like a trait bound, which the owner already rejected.

recommendation.tradeoff: Four letters buy an unmistakable number parameter.

decisions.title: Spelling a fence that expands one line into several
decisions.gist: How should a fence that expands one line into several be spelled?
decisions.lesson: A fence repeats the entire containing statement once per entry. `@[ t1..t3 ]@ :: task work()` makes three bindings; `print(@[ "a", "b" ]@)` prints twice. Multiple fences advance together and must have equal lengths. Literal range `0..3` expands to four entries; parentheses preserve one range. The proposed delimiters restore D-EACH1's shape, but `:>` currently has a retired-arrow diagnostic meaning.
decisions.story: Tom starts eight transfer tasks and joins each one. He wants one line for the spawns and one for the joins, not sixteen near-identical lines.

options.detail: Keep statement repetition, paired entries, numbered names, and literal-range expansion. `print(<: (0..3) :>)` prints one range. Nonliteral and descending ranges stay single entries.
options.technical: Add longest-match `<:` and `:>` fence tokens. The old `:>` Arrow token currently serves retired-arrow diagnostics; reclaim it for closing fences and update that teaching path and formatter. This requires a coordinated lexer/parser cutover, not merely a registry rename. Existing comparisons `<`, `<=`, `<=>`, `>` and generic `<T>` stay distinct because none needs the adjacent pairs `<:` or `:>`. Preserve D-FENCE-RANGE1 and existing statement expansion.
options.code:
<: t1..t8 :> :: task transfer(from, to, 100)
<: t1..t8 :>.join() ?? panic("transfer failed")
print(<: "a", total(1, 2) :>)
print(<: 0..3 :>)
print((0..3))

options.name: `each[ … ]`
options.detail: `each` is a contextual word before `[`.
options.technical: The parser treats `each[` as a fence opener; a user binding named `each` cannot be indexed.
options.code:
each[ t1..t8 ] :: task transfer(from, to, 100)
each[ t1..t8 ].join() ?? panic("transfer failed")
print(each[ "a", total(1, 2) ])
print(each[ 0..3 ])
print((0..3))

options.name: Retire fences
options.detail: Retire fences. Homogeneous repeated work can use lists and loops; separate names and incompatible entry types need explicit statements. This removes source-level expansion, not just its spelling.
options.technical: Retire D-EACH1, D-FENCE-GLYPH1, and D-FENCE-RANGE1. Migrate each fence to an equivalent loop or explicit statements while preserving repetition order and evaluation count.
options.code:
handles :: [
    task transfer(from, to, 100), task transfer(from, to, 100),
    task transfer(from, to, 100), task transfer(from, to, 100),
    task transfer(from, to, 100), task transfer(from, to, 100),
    task transfer(from, to, 100), task transfer(from, to, 100),
]
loop handle in handles -> handle.join() ?? panic("transfer failed")
print("a")
print(total(1, 2))
loop n in 0..3 -> print(n)
print((0..3))

comparisons.note: seq-macro repetition. https://docs.rs/seq-macro

recommendation.why: `<: :>` preserves statement expansion without reserving a user name. It restores the original shape, but reclaiming the retired-arrow token needs explicit lexer work.

whyNot.reason: B takes away ordinary indexing on a variable named `each`.
C loses separately named and mixed-type expansion, which lists cannot generally replace.

recommendation.tradeoff: A glyph pair keeps fences unambiguous.

decisions.title: How code reads facts about a type, function, or value
decisions.gist: Should compiler facts be read as sigil members on the thing, or through a query that returns a record?
decisions.lesson: Code reads facts such as a type's fields or a function's effects. Examples use `$`, standing for whatever glyph D-COMPILER-NS1 picks. This ballot picks only the path shape. Build and package facts are decided in D-BUILD-FACT3. Family map: `prep` marks code that runs before the program (ratified). A sigil marks facts the compiler knows (this family). `@` marks links (D-MEMREF1).
decisions.story: Ada writes a serializer that loops over a type's fields. She wants to read the fields in the fewest steps, and see at a glance that they come from the compiler.
decisions.inWild: const fields = @typeInfo(T).@"struct".fields;

options.name: Sigil members on the subject
options.detail: Every fact is a `$` member of the thing it describes. Subjectless facts use sigil roots (`$phase`, `$program`). `T.reflect()` and `@TYPE(T)` are removed.
options.code:
prep loop field in T.$fields {
    print(field.$name)
}
range :: Severity.$range
effects :: send_report.$effects
origin :: value.$origin
phase :: $phase

options.name: Sigil query returns a record
options.detail: Sigil queries return records; facts are ordinary fields.

options.name: `.reflect()` method
options.detail: One reserved method returns the record.

comparisons.note: Zig returns one record from a builtin. See https://ziglang.org/documentation/master/#typeInfo.

Skip macros read facts and splice names with a sigil: `#thisClassName`, `this.#field` (Skip/Hack talk https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=J31LlAUtoos). https://raw.githubusercontent.com/skiplang/skip/master/docs/blog/2018-07-24-macros.md.

recommendation.why: Members keep the sigil exactly where a compiler fact is read, with the fewest steps and no handler for known subjects.

whyNot.reason: B turns every fact read into a call, a handler, and a field.
C drops the sigil the owner asked for.

recommendation.tradeoff: A few sigil roots join member reads to keep every fact short and marked.

decisions.title: Choosing a branch or repeating declarations before the program runs
decisions.gist: How should code pick a branch or repeat declarations before the program runs?
decisions.lesson: `@if` selects a branch while building. The selected branch gets full checks; discarded branches still get name checks. `@loop` repeats statements or declarations, including methods and tests. D-PREP-SURFACE2 introduced only `prep { }`, not `prep if` or `prep loop`. This ballot extends that word without changing branch checking.
decisions.story: Lena's app calls different platform APIs on Linux, macOS, and Windows. Names must resolve in every branch, but only the chosen branch needs full platform and type checks.

options.name: `prep if` and `prep loop`
options.detail: `prep if` evaluates its condition while building and keeps only the chosen arm. The other arms get name checks only, as `@if` does today. `prep loop` repeats statements, impl items, marker-body items, or tests over a closed list known while building.
options.technical: It respells S57's `@if`/`@loop` and D-STRUCT-ONCE1's declaration templates without changing their meaning. It amends D-PREP-SURFACE2's line that prep adds no condition or loop form. That line still holds inside `prep { }` blocks, where ordinary `if` and `loop` run while building. Examples assume D-COMPILER-NS1 A. B substitutes `__if`, `__loop`, `__const`, `__fn`, and `__compiler`; C substitutes `#if`, `#loop`, `#N`, `#fn`, and `#compiler`. Values keep ratified `prep` and plain names; fence and splice choices are independent.

options.name: Plain `if` and `loop` fold when known
options.detail: A known condition keeps only the taken arm, with name-only checks on discarded arms. Otherwise ordinary runtime checking applies to every arm. A top-level `loop` over a known list repeats declarations; nested template loops follow the same rule.
options.technical: The checking rule changes with the condition's phase. D-STRUCT-ONCE1 reversed an earlier same-day ruling that erased `@if` in favor of plain `if`.

comparisons.note: Known conditions prune branches; `inline for` unrolls. https://ziglang.org/documentation/master/#inline-for
`if constexpr` discards the untaken branch in templates. https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/if

decisions.title: Marking a function that runs while building
decisions.gist: How should a function that runs while building, such as a literal hook, be marked?
decisions.lesson: A literal hook constructs a value from a written number: for example, `1` becomes a Rational with denominator one. D-FOUND-LITERAL1 uses `@fn from_literal` inside a `Literal.Int` or `Literal.Float` implementation. The hook runs while building and cannot perform effects such as I/O. This ballot changes its mark, not its purity rules.
decisions.story: Ana writes a money type so `12` can mean twelve cents. She wants the hook to say plainly that it runs while building.

options.name: `prep fn`
options.detail: `prep fn` replaces every currently legal `@fn` method declaration. The compiler keeps checking that literal hooks have no effects such as I/O.
options.technical: Respell D-FOUND-LITERAL1 without widening the allowed declaration sites. Cover both Literal.Int and Literal.Float hooks, including decimal text input. Preserve the existing is_comptime flag and purity checks; ordinary runtime functions do not become compile-time functions merely because they are pure. Examples assume D-COMPILER-NS1 A. B substitutes `__if`, `__loop`, `__const`, `__fn`, and `__compiler`; C substitutes `#if`, `#loop`, `#N`, `#fn`, and `#compiler`. Values keep ratified `prep` and plain names; fence and splice choices are independent.

options.name: Plain `fn`
options.detail: The Literal.Int or Literal.Float implementation identifies `from_literal` as a compile-time hook without an extra mark. Purity checks remain mandatory.
options.technical: Infer the existing compile-time requirement from the literal capability and remove its explicit declaration mark. Other methods retain ordinary function behavior; this alternative does not infer arbitrary compile-time functions from purity.

comparisons.note: `consteval` functions. https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/consteval

recommendation.why: The mark tells a reader when the body runs, using the word Jet uses everywhere else for build time.

whyNot.reason: B hides when the body runs behind a site rule.

recommendation.tradeoff: One word buys a visible build-time function.

decisions.title: Decode gzip and Zstandard streams through a byte reader
decisions.gist: How should a program decode a large gzip or Zstandard stream without holding all of it in memory?
decisions.lesson: gzip and Zstandard shrink bytes for storage and download. Today Core decodes them only as one whole buffer, at most 64 MiB. Packages can be larger, and they arrive over time. D-NETIO-CONTRACT1 already defines io.Reader: read(limit) returns up to limit bytes, and [] means the end. Whichever option wins, Core owes bounded memory, checksum checks, and typed IOError failures.
decisions.story: Priya ports two Jetpack paths to Jet. A LuaRocks source tarball must be checked entry by entry before extraction. A Nix package arrives as zstd over HTTP and must be hashed as it lands. Today both need the whole file in memory and stop at 64 MiB, and Rust Jetpack avoids that only by running gzip -dc in a child process.
decisions.detail:
Need: card #3596 items 1 and 2. The card asks for a full streaming zstd decoder and "Streaming gunzip (whole-buffer 64 MiB today)." D-CORE-ZSTDSOURCE1 decides who decodes zstd blocks. This ballot decides the API both codecs share.

Rust call sites. Store/NixCache.rs:745-777 wraps the counted, hashed HTTP body in a zstd decoder. It feeds read_nar_stream_with_mode, then reads once more to refuse bytes after the NAR. Provider/fetch.rs:317-345 runs gzip -dc and scans the tar headers from the child's stdout. Provider/fetch.rs:274-315, luarocks.rs:614-692, and script_registry.rs:1048-1132 unpack .tar.gz files through tar child processes.

The mapping receipt for fetch.rs records: "missing streaming gunzip reader for registry tarballs." A Jet port without this API must hold whole archives in memory or keep shelling out to gzip.

Ratified law applied. D-NETIO-CONTRACT1=A defines core io.Reader and io.Writer traits and says codecs implement or wrap them. D-NETIO-CONTRACT2=B makes every stream report core IOError and conform through explicit adapters. D-IOERROR-TREE1=A gives IOContext with operation .Codec. D-CORE-COMPRESS1=A gives each codec one home, now core.archive.gzip and core.archive.zstd. L-A asks for a whole-value call over a streaming path, and L-D asks presets to compose the expert primitive. Encoding readers are the naming precedent (encoding.*.reader).

Cross-stream. D-CORE-FILEOPEN1 makes FileReader an io.Reader, D-CORE-PROCBYTES1 does so for child stdout, and NetCryptoBallots' D-CORE-HTTPBODYLIMIT1 does so for HTTP bodies. The reader here wraps any of them. Unsupported cases use IOError.Unsupported from D-CORE-FILEERROR1.

options.name: Reader adapters
options.detail: gzip.reader(&source) and zstd.reader(&source) borrow any io.Reader and return a reader that yields decoded bytes. Because the source is borrowed, the caller can still read its byte count or hash afterwards. The whole-buffer decompress calls keep their names, 64 MiB cap, and error enums, but run on the same decoder. So one decoder serves both doors.
options.technical:
```text
gzip.reader<R: io.Reader>(source: &R) -> GzipReader<R>
zstd.reader<R: io.Reader>(source: &R, max_window: Int{134_217_728}) -> ZstdReader<R>
GzipReader, ZstdReader implement io.Reader:
  read(limit: Int) -> [U8] !IOError      // [] = end of decoded data
  chunks(size: Int{65536})               // loop source of non-empty [U8]
```

Read rules. read never returns more than limit bytes, and a limit below one is IOError.InvalidInput. [] comes only when the source ended exactly at a member or frame boundary. A source that ends early is IOError.InvalidInput with cause "truncated". Errors from the source pass through unchanged. The adapter never closes its source.

gzip rules (RFC 1952). It decodes every concatenated member, as gzip -dc does. It reads FEXTRA, FNAME, FCOMMENT, and FHCRC. It checks CRC-32 and ISIZE for each member. Bytes after the last member that do not start a member are IOError.InvalidInput. Memory is the 32 KiB window plus one input chunk.

zstd rules (RFC 8878). It decodes every frame, skips skippable frames, and checks declared content sizes and content checksums. A frame whose window exceeds max_window is IOError.Unsupported, and the cause names the size and the max_window fix. A frame that needs a dictionary is IOError.Unsupported. The default cap of 128 MiB matches libzstd's default decode limit. Memory is the window plus one 128 KiB block.

Errors use IOContext{operation: .Codec, resource: Val("gzip" or "zstd"), cause}. Causes name the member or frame number, for example "gzip: CRC-32 mismatch in member 2".

Whole-buffer doors. gzip.decompress, zstd.decompress, and the _text and _file helpers become presets over these readers. They keep the 64 MiB cap and GzipFileError or ZstdFileError. Two behaviors change on purpose: gzip.decompress now reads multi-member files, and zstd.decompress now reads compressed blocks. archive.decompress and D-CORE-ARCHIVE-BOUND1's decompress_bounded (zlib) are unchanged.

Defaults table row: gzip.reader and zstd.reader read the whole stream, every member or frame, with a zstd window of at most 128 MiB; override with max_window:. AOT, jet run, and the interpreter run the same Core source (I9).

options.name: Push decoder
options.detail: gzip.decoder() and zstd.decoder() return a mutable decoder. The caller passes compressed chunks to feed and gets decoded bytes back, then calls finish to check the last checksum. No reader type is needed. To pass the output to a tar or NAR reader, the caller writes an adapter.
options.technical:
```text
gzip.decoder() -> GzipDecoder
zstd.decoder(max_window: Int{134_217_728}) -> ZstdDecoder
feed(&self, chunk: [U8]) -> [U8] !IOError
finish(&self) -> [U8] !IOError
```

feed returns all output its input produces. A zstd RLE block or a gzip run can turn a few bytes into megabytes, so bounded memory needs an extra max_output label on feed and a way to resume. Whole-buffer calls become presets over the decoder.

options.name: Copy helper
options.detail: gzip.decode_stream(from: &reader, to: &writer) and zstd.decode_stream copy every decoded byte to an io.Writer and return the count. It is one line for file-to-file work. A caller that needs to inspect decoded bytes as they arrive must decode to a temporary file and read it again.
options.technical:
```text
gzip.decode_stream<R: io.Reader, W: io.Writer>(from: &R, to: &W) -> Int !IOError
zstd.decode_stream<R: io.Reader, W: io.Writer>(from: &R, to: &W, max_window: Int{134_217_728}) -> Int !IOError
```

The same format rules as A apply. The decoded stream is never exposed as a reader.

comparisons.note: compress/gzip and archive/tar are both readers, so gzip output feeds tar directly. Multistream decoding is the default. Docs: https://pkg.go.dev/compress/gzip#Reader.Multistream.

flate2 and zstd provide Read adapters. flate2 splits single-member GzDecoder from MultiGzDecoder, a split option A avoids by always reading all members, as gzip -dc does. Docs: https://docs.rs/flate2/latest/flate2/read/struct.MultiGzDecoder.html.
comparisons.code:
let gz = flate2::read::MultiGzDecoder::new(file);
let tar = tar::Archive::new(gz);

comparisons.note: zlib.decompressobj is the push style of option B. Python caps output per call with max_length to stay bounded. Docs: https://docs.python.org/3/library/zlib.html#zlib.Decompress.decompress.

recommendation.why: Readers compose. The same adapter feeds a tar reader, a hash, or a NAR check, with memory bounded by the read limit. It reuses the ratified reader contract instead of adding a second streaming style.
gains: gzip, zstd, tar, and HTTP bodies chain with no glue.
Bounded memory for any stream length.

losses.loss: Checksum and malformed failures share IOError.InvalidInput.
losses.mitigation: D-NETIO-CONTRACT2 gives every byte stream one closed IOError tree; the cause text names the check.

whyNot.reason: Every consumer must write feed loops, and a small input can expand without bound unless each call adds a limit.
Tar and NAR checks must read decoded bytes as they arrive, so a copy helper forces a temporary file.

recommendation.tradeoff: Codec errors lose their own enum at the stream boundary, in exchange for readers that chain.

wild.note: Go wraps any reader in a gzip reader and copies decoded bytes as they arrive. Docs: https://pkg.go.dev/compress/gzip#NewReader.

options.gist: gzip.reader and zstd.reader wrap any io.Reader and are io.Readers themselves.
gains: Decoders chain into tar, hashing, and NAR readers.
Memory stays bounded by the read limit and window.

packed :: files.open("rock.tar.gz")
tar :: gzip.reader(&packed)            // an io.Reader
loop chunk in tar.chunks(65536) -> hasher.update(chunk)

nar :: zstd.reader(&body)              // body: HTTP response reader

// Bad CRC: Err(IOError.InvalidInput) "gzip: CRC-32 mismatch in member 1"

decisions.title: Write the full Zstandard decoder in Jet or wrap libzstd
decisions.gist: Should Core decode real Zstandard data with a decoder written in Jet, or through the approved libzstd C library?
decisions.lesson: Zstandard (zstd) is a compression format. Nix caches send packages as zstd files. Core's zstd decoder reads only stored and repeated-byte blocks, so real cache files fail. Rust Jetpack uses libzstd, a C library D-CODECS1 approved as a bridge; I6 calls such bridges temporary. Whichever option wins, Core owes a full streaming decoder, typed errors, a window-size limit, and one result on every run mode.
decisions.story: Priya ports the Jetpack Nix cache client to Jet. A signed package arrives from a Nix binary cache as a .nar.zst file. Her Jet code must unpack it to check its hash, but Core stops at the first compressed block. She needs to know whether Core will parse these untrusted bytes in Jet or hand them to libzstd, the C library Rust Jetpack uses today.
decisions.detail:
Need: card #3596 item 1. The card says: "core.archive.zstd decodes only raw/RLE blocks, whole-buffer, capped at 64 MiB. Store/NixCache.rs streams real zstd NARs. The Jet port needs a full streaming decoder in Core. This is the approved-bridge question for zstd under I6." This ballot answers only who decodes the blocks. The API shape is D-CORE-CODECSTREAM1, and it is the same under both options.

Rust call sites. The product path is Store/NixCache.rs:745-777: a zstd Decoder wraps the counted, hashed HTTP body and feeds the NAR reader, then checks for trailing bytes. Test-only uses are the level-19 encoder at NixCache.rs:427-446 and decode_all at NixCache/Tests.rs:114. NixIndex.rs:2569-2775 hand-writes a stored-block zstd codec and xxh64, which Core already has. Its decoded limit is 256 MiB (NixIndex.rs:23), above the whole-buffer cap.

Dependency facts. crates/jetpack/Cargo.toml:33-34 pins zstd 0.13 with the note "D-CODECS1: owner-approved native standard-cache zstd stream codec". The file crates/jet-jit/Cargo.toml:37-38 pins the same crate, but no zstd:: call exists under crates/jet-jit. The generated FFI bridge reaches zstd only through the parquet feature list (jet-pkg-model/src/FFI.rs:2254).

Ratified law. D-CODECS1=A shipped gzip and zstd through the bridge, with an I6 sign-off per dependency. D-DEP1 says every bootstrap wrap carries a native-ize obligation. D-CORE-SOURCE-AUTHORITY1=A makes Jet source the authority for Core behavior, with only unexpressible operations in a small kernel. D-CORE-COMPRESS1=A keeps zstd a stream codec beside the archive containers. Gzip already went the Jet way: D-CORE-ARCHIVE-BOUND1=A bounds one shared Jet inflater.

The owner's 2026-09-28 rule on #3665-#3670 keeps only policy-free leaves in Rust, such as syscalls and vetted engines. Option B fits that rule as a vetted engine. Option A removes the need for the leaf. Neither option changes the whole-buffer encoder, which stays a stored-block writer. Rust uses a real encoder only in tests, so committed fixture files replace it.

options.name: Decoder written in Jet
options.detail: Core/archive/zstd.jet implements the whole Zstandard frame format from RFC 8878 in Jet. That covers compressed blocks, entropy tables, and checksums. No new dependency is added. The decoder serves both the streaming reader and the whole-buffer calls, so there is one decoder. The zstd crate pin in jet-jit, which has no users, is removed.
options.technical:
Scope is RFC 8878 decoding. It covers frame and block headers, raw, RLE, and compressed blocks, and literals with Huffman tables, including treeless reuse. It also covers sequences with FSE tables in predefined, RLE, compressed, and repeat modes, and repeat offsets. It checks window and content sizes and the XXH64 content checksum, reusing xxh64 in zstd.jet, and skips skippable frames. Frames that need a dictionary fail with IOError.Unsupported naming the dictionary id (D-CORE-FILEERROR1).

Memory is the window plus one 128 KiB block. The window cap and the reader API come from D-CORE-CODECSTREAM1. The decoder is ordinary Core source, so AOT, jet run, the interpreter, and web run the same code (I9, D-CORE-SOURCE-AUTHORITY1).

Proof owed. The RFC 8878 test frames plus committed .zst fixtures made by the reference zstd tool at levels 1, 3, 19, and 22 with long windows. Differential fuzzing compares Jet output to the zstd tool as a development-only oracle, never a runtime dependency. A paired performance cell times decoding one real NAR against Rust Jetpack's libzstd path. Any loss is carded under the strict gate.

options.name: Leaf over libzstd
options.detail: Core/archive/zstd.jet keeps the API, the window limit, error meaning, and messages. A small Rust leaf wraps the zstd crate, which builds libzstd from C source. It turns input chunks into output chunks and returns only numeric status codes. The leaf is linked into the generated bridge, the JIT host, and the interpreter.
options.technical:
Leaf surface: decoder_new(window_log_max) -> handle; decoder_step(handle, input, output_capacity) -> (consumed, produced, status); decoder_free(handle). It calls ZSTD_decompressStream with ZSTD_d_windowLogMax set from the Jet limit. Jet maps each status code to one IOError kind, so no backend text is parsed.

The approval is D-CODECS1 with the existing zstd 0.13 pin. The bridge keeps D-DEP1's native-ize obligation, so a later Jet decoder is still owed. Web builds need libzstd compiled for wasm32. Without that, web needs a named I9 exception.

Proof owed: the same fixtures as A plus a check that the leaf never allocates past the Jet window limit.

comparisons.note: The klauspost/compress zstd package is a decoder written entirely in Go, with no C library. It shows a memory-safe language can own a full decoder. Docs: https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/klauspost/compress/zstd.
comparisons.code:
d, err := zstd.NewReader(body, zstd.WithDecoderMaxWindow(128<<20))
_, err = io.Copy(out, d)

comparisons.note: Python added compression.zstd to its standard library as a wrapper over libzstd, like option B. Docs: https://docs.python.org/3.14/library/compression.zstd.html.
comparisons.code:
from compression import zstd
with zstd.open("pkg.nar.zst") as f:
    data = f.read()

comparisons.note: Rust has both shapes: the zstd crate binds libzstd, while ruzstd is a decoder written in Rust. Jetpack uses the libzstd binding today. Docs: https://docs.rs/zstd/0.13 and https://docs.rs/ruzstd.
comparisons.code:
let d = zstd::stream::read::Decoder::new(body)?;      // libzstd
let d = ruzstd::decoding::StreamingDecoder::new(body)?; // pure Rust

recommendation.why: Cache files come from the network, and safety is Jet's first priority. A Jet decoder keeps that parsing memory-safe, gives every run mode one source, and ends the bridge's temporary status.
gains: Memory-safe parsing of untrusted cache downloads.
One decoder source for AOT, jet run, and the interpreter.

losses.loss: Decoding may start slower than libzstd.
losses.mitigation: libzstd has years of hand tuning; any new decoder starts behind it, and the speed gate measures it.

losses.loss: Core must write and fuzz a large decoder.
losses.mitigation: Real files use entropy-coded blocks; no smaller part of the format reads them.

whyNot.reason: It puts C parsing of network bytes into every Jet program that reads zstd. The dependency law also marks such bridges temporary, so the work returns later.

recommendation.tradeoff: Core takes on a large decoder and must prove its speed, instead of borrowing libzstd's.

decisions.title: Read and write tar archives entry by entry with kind, mode, and link target
decisions.gist: How should a program read and write tar archives entry by entry, seeing each entry's kind, mode, and link?
decisions.lesson: A tar archive is a list of entries. Each entry has a header, then its bytes. The header holds a name, a kind such as file or link, a mode (permission bits), and a size. Today Core's tar helpers work on one whole buffer and return only names and bytes. Whichever option wins, Core owes bounded memory, long names, true sparse-file sizes, and typed IOError failures.
decisions.story: Priya ports the Jetpack source providers to Jet. Before unpacking a LuaRocks or CPAN tarball, Jetpack refuses links, devices, unsafe names, and oversized entries, including sparse files that expand later. It also writes deterministic OCI image layers. Today Rust shells out to tar -tvzf and parses its text, and Core cannot even report an entry's kind.
decisions.detail:
Need: card #3596 item 3, "Streaming tar reader/writer with mode, type and link headers (Store/Archive.rs, Image OCI layers)". One correction: Store/Archive.rs writes Jet's own jet-hangar-archive-v1 format (Archive.rs:24), not tar. It needs no tar API. Its mode, kind, and link needs match this entry shape only by analogy.

Reader call sites. Provider/fetch.rs:274-315 lists entries with tar -tf and -tvf. It refuses unsafe names and non-file, non-directory kinds, and caps the entry count at 4,096. It caps each entry at 64 MiB and the total at 256 MiB (fetch.rs:12-15). fetch.rs:356-423 parses raw tar headers from gzip -dc output, including PAX and GNU sparse logical sizes, to stop sparse bombs.

luarocks.rs:653-692 refuses symlinks and hard links by kind. luarocks.rs:614-633 and script_registry.rs:1048-1132 extract through tar child processes. The test script_registry.rs:2410-2460 builds sparse archives that must be refused by logical size.

Writer call site. Image.rs:1597-1653 builds deterministic ustar OCI layers. It uses file entries with mode, mtime 0, and uid and gid 0. It silently truncates names longer than 100 bytes (Image.rs:1614), a defect a Core writer removes.

Ratified law applied. D-CORE-COMPRESS1=A: core.archive owns containers, so the new calls sit beside tar_add and tar_get with the same tar_ prefix. D-NETIO-CONTRACT1/2: the reader wraps and is an io.Reader, and failures are IOError. F2: next() returns ?TarEntry. D4: kinds are an enum, never flags. D-BYTESDECODE1: non-UTF-8 names fail loudly. L-A: the whole-buffer helpers stay as presets over the stream. Extraction to disk composes this reader with D-CORE-FILEDIR1's Directory handle, which refuses .. and absolute names.

options.name: Entry reader and writer
options.detail: archive.tar_reader(&source) returns a reader. next() returns the next entry header, or None at the end. The reader itself then yields that entry's bytes, and calling next() again skips any unread rest. archive.tar_writer(&sink) adds files, folders, and links with deterministic headers, and finish() writes the end marker.
options.technical:
```text
archive.tar_reader<R: io.Reader>(source: &R) -> TarReader<R>
  next(&self) -> ?TarEntry !IOError
  read(limit: Int) -> [U8] !IOError; chunks(size: Int{65536})   // current entry
archive.tar_writer<W: io.Writer>(sink: &W) -> TarWriter<W>
  add_file(name: String, body: [U8], mode: Int{0o644}, modified: Instant{epoch}) !IOError
  add_directory(name: String, mode: Int{0o755}, modified: Instant{epoch}) !IOError
  add_symlink(name: String, target: String) !IOError
  add_hardlink(name: String, target: String) !IOError
  finish() !IOError
pub struct TarEntry { pub name: String, pub kind: TarKind, pub mode: Int, pub size: Int, pub modified: Instant }
pub enum TarKind { File, Directory, Symlink(String), Hardlink(String), CharDevice, BlockDevice, Fifo }
```

Reading. Formats are ustar, GNU, and PAX. PAX and GNU long names, long link targets, and PAX size and mtime are applied inside the reader. They are never returned as entries. Sparse files in GNU and PAX formats come back as .File. Their size is the logical size, and holes read as zeros. So a size check counts what extraction would write.

Checks. The header checksum is verified. Numbers may be octal or base-256 and are exact Int values. Names and link targets are at most 4,096 bytes and must be UTF-8. One PAX record set is at most 1 MiB. A violation is IOError.InvalidInput. Volume, multi-volume, and unknown type flags are IOError.Unsupported (D-CORE-FILEERROR1).

End and names. next() returns None at the first all-zero header. A source that ends inside an entry is IOError.InvalidInput with cause "truncated". Names are returned as stored. size is 0 for every kind except File, and mode keeps only the 0o7777 bits. Memory is one header, one PAX set, and the caller's read limit.

Writing. Output is deterministic: uid and gid 0, empty user and group names, ustar magic, and mtime from modified, default the Unix epoch. Names over 100 bytes and link targets over 100 bytes use PAX records. Names must be relative with no .. part, the same rule tar_add uses today, or IOError.InvalidInput. Mode must be within 0o7777. finish() writes two zero blocks and does not close the sink.

Presets. tar_add, tar_get, and tar_names_json keep their names and 64 MiB and 4,096-entry caps but run on this reader and writer. tar_add's long names switch from GNU ././@LongLink records to PAX, so one long-name format remains. Defaults table row: tar_writer writes epoch-0 times and owner 0; override with modified:.

options.name: Visitor callback
options.detail: archive.tar_each(&source, visit) calls visit once per entry with the header and a body reader. Unread bodies are skipped. archive.tar_write(&sink, items) writes a finished list of items. Early stop means returning an error from the callback, and results must be gathered in outer mutable state.
options.technical:
```text
archive.tar_each<R: io.Reader>(source: &R, visit: fn(TarEntry, &TarBody) !IOError) !IOError
archive.tar_write<W: io.Writer>(sink: &W, items: [TarItem]) !IOError
```

Format, check, and determinism rules match A. TarItem holds an entry and its bytes, so the writer needs all items in memory before it starts.

options.name: List, then read by name
options.detail: archive.tar_list(path) returns every TarEntry from a plain tar file. archive.tar_read(path, name) opens the file again and returns one entry's bytes. A .tar.gz must first be decoded to a temporary file, because both calls seek. The writer is a list-based tar_write as in B.
options.technical:
```text
archive.tar_list(path: String) -[FS]> [TarEntry] !IOError
archive.tar_read(path: String, name: String) -[FS]> [U8] !IOError
```

Format and check rules match A. The listing holds every header in memory, and the second call re-opens the path.

comparisons.note: archive/tar returns one Header per Next call and exposes Typeflag, Mode, Size, and Linkname. It expands sparse files, reading holes as zeros. Docs: https://pkg.go.dev/archive/tar.
comparisons.code:
hdr, err := tr.Next()
fmt.Println(hdr.Typeflag, hdr.Mode, hdr.Size, hdr.Linkname)

comparisons.note: The tar crate yields entries whose headers carry entry type, mode, and link name, and each entry is a reader. Docs: https://docs.rs/tar/latest/tar/struct.Entry.html.

tarfile has a stream mode, r|gz, that yields members in order without seeking. Python 3.12 added extraction filters because member names are unsafe by default. Docs: https://docs.python.org/3/library/tarfile.html#extraction-filters.

recommendation.why: Jetpack checks each header and hashes each body while the archive streams from gzip. A reader that returns one typed entry at a time does that in bounded memory, like Go and Rust.
gains: Link and device entries are visible before any extraction.
Deterministic image layers from the same entry type.

losses.loss: Name safety is the caller's check.
losses.mitigation: Tar stores names verbatim; only the code that writes files knows the target folder.

whyNot.reason: A callback makes early stop and results awkward, and its writer holds every entry in memory.
It cannot read a gzip stream without a temporary file, and two passes let the file change in between.

recommendation.tradeoff: Callers write a short loop and check names, in exchange for full headers and bounded memory.

surface.gist: How should a program read and write tar archives entry by entry, seeing each entry's kind, mode, and link?
surface.lesson: A tar archive is a list of entries. Each entry has a header, then its bytes. The header holds a name, a kind such as file or link, a mode (permission bits), and a size. Today Core's tar helpers work on one whole buffer and return only names and bytes. Whichever option wins, Core owes bounded memory, long names, true sparse-file sizes, and typed IOError failures.

current.note: The helpers need the whole archive in memory and report no kind, mode, or link (Core/archive/archive.jet:279-445). Read from source; not run.

wild.note: Go reads one header at a time; the reader then yields that entry's bytes. Docs: https://pkg.go.dev/archive/tar#Reader.

options.name: Entry reader and writer
options.gist: tar_reader yields one typed entry at a time; tar_writer adds typed entries to any writer.
gains: Kind, mode, size, and link target on every entry.
Memory stays bounded for any archive size.
Chains after gzip.reader with no temporary file.
losses: Callers must check names before writing files to disk.

options.name: Visitor callback
options.gist: One call runs a function for each entry; the writer takes a finished entry list.
gains: Bodies are skipped automatically when unread.
No loop to write by hand.
losses: Stopping early or returning a value needs extra state.
The writer needs every entry in memory first.

options.name: List, then read by name
options.gist: A listing call returns every header; a second call reads one entry from a file.
gains: Simplest way to inspect an archive.
losses: Needs a seekable file, so gzip input needs a temporary file.
The file can change between the two calls.

recommendation.why: Jetpack checks each header and hashes each body while the archive streams from gzip. A reader that returns one typed entry at a time does that in bounded memory, like Go and Rust.
gains: Link and device entries are visible before any extraction.
Deterministic image layers from the same entry type.

losses.loss: Name safety is the caller's check.
losses.mitigation: Tar stores names verbatim; only the code that writes files knows the target folder.

whyNot.reason: A callback makes early stop and results awkward, and its writer holds every entry in memory.
It cannot read a gzip stream without a temporary file, and two passes let the file change in between.

recommendation.tradeoff: Callers write a short loop and check names, in exchange for full headers and bounded memory.

decisions.title: Load a sandbox component chosen at run time against a declared interface
decisions.gist: How should a host load a sandbox component chosen at run time, and still call it with checked types?
decisions.lesson: A sandbox component is a WebAssembly file that runs isolated, with only the rights its host lends. Today plugin.load needs the path written in the source, so the compiler can read the component's interface. Jetpack finds build plugins and compiler extensions only at run time. Whichever option wins, Core owes typed calls or errors, fail-closed imports, and today's fuel, memory, and time limits.
decisions.story: Priya ports jetpack-bin to Jet. When a package declares a build plugin, Jetpack verifies the component's digest from a signed manifest, then must run its build export. The compiler also hands Jetpack a compiler-extension path to analyze. Neither path exists when Jetpack is compiled, so today's plugin.load refuses both.
decisions.detail:
Need: card #3598 item 4, "dynamic-path WASM Component instantiation with bounded fuel/memory (core.plugin.load needs a literal artifact)". The users are the compiler-extension and build-plugin hosts in jetpack-bin, which use wasmtime today. This ballot covers the run-time path only. The fuel, memory, and time override is D-CORE-PLUGINLIMITS1.

Rust call sites. crates/jetpack-bin/src/main.rs:20-23 includes the two host files. main.rs:49-128 reads the manifest and component with size caps, checks both digests, and runs the build export. main.rs:133-193 decodes a snapshot and runs analyze. The hosts are jet-pkg-model Prelude/BuildPlugin.rs:52-124 and Prelude/CompilerExtension.rs:99-249. Tests are jetpack-bin/tests/build_plugin_e2e.rs and compiler_extension_e2e.rs.

What both hosts do. They link zero imports, so a guest that asks for any capability fails to instantiate. Each has one export taking list<u8> and returning list<u8>: build or analyze. Limits are 10,000,000 fuel, 16 MiB memory, 10,000 table slots, and 2,000 ms per call (BuildPlugin.rs:13-19; CompilerExtension.rs:39-51). Plugin.rs:52-57 uses the same numbers for application plugins.

The gap study (#3670) calls CompilerExtension.rs "Not Core" and BuildPlugin.rs a jetpack-only leaf. That is right for the protocol: snapshot schema and response validation stay in the Jetpack and compiler model. The owner rule still forbids Jetpack from keeping its own sandbox host. So the Jet port needs Core to load a run-time path, and this ballot adds only that.

Ratified law applied. D-DEP-WASM1=A: Wasmtime 25 runs components, with fuel, epoch, memory, table, wire, and import limits mandatory, and non-plugin builds never link it. D-PLUGIN1=A and D-FOUND-SANDBOX1=A: the guest declares needs, and the host lends one Authority at plugin.load.

D-PLUGIN-EXPORT1 and D-PLUGIN-VERSION1 freeze the literal-artifact interface, and E1257 reports a changed export. D-SCRIPT-PLUGIN-CLOSE1: close(^plugin). D-MODEL-SIGNATURE1 bound a model output to a source trait through models.open<Trait>, the precedent for option A. The spec says there is no dynamic export lookup (Docs/spec/spec.md:3863-3867), which option B would break. D-DX5-HOOK1 keeps the compiler-extension world import-free.

options.name: Declared interface trait
options.detail: plugin.load gains an optional type argument. plugin.load<BuildStep>(path, policy) accepts a path computed at run time. The interface comes from the Jet trait instead of a frozen artifact snapshot. At load, Core checks that the file exports every trait method with the same component type. The literal form, plugin.load("x.wasm", policy), is unchanged.
options.technical:
```text
plugin.load<I>(path: String, authority: Authority, sha256: ?String{None}) -> Plugin<I>
```

The interface. I must be a trait whose methods take self and use exportable shapes: the D-PLUGIN-EXPORT1 scalars, [U8], and closed Component Model shapes (E1260). The expected world is generated from I by the same generator that builds sandbox worlds. Method names map to WIT export names by the existing rule.

The load check. Every method must be exported with the same component type. Extra exports are ignored and cannot be reached. A missing or changed export gives the E1257 message at run time and names the export and trait. If sha256 is given, Core hashes the exact bytes it read and refuses a mismatch before compiling them. This closes the check-then-load race the build host guards against (main.rs:84-99).

Unchanged from plugin.load: path resolution under the lent Authority with the no-follow resource root, import preflight against the guest's declared needs and that Authority, and the failure-reporting contract. A component with no declared needs gets no imports, which gives the build and compiler-extension worlds their zero-import sandbox. Close is D-SCRIPT-PLUGIN-CLOSE1. Limits are today's defaults unless D-CORE-PLUGINLIMITS1 changes them. The effect row stays that of plugin.load.

Without a type argument, a non-literal path stays E1257 at compile time. Its fix text gains "or name an interface trait: plugin.load<Trait>(path, authority)". I4 needs UI snapshots for the compile error and the run-time mismatch. I9: AOT, jet run, and the interpreter share one Core check in Core/plugin/plugin.jet, the home #3670 assigns to plugin policy.

options.name: Call exports by name
options.detail: plugin.load_dynamic(path, policy) returns a DynamicPlugin. call(export, bytes) runs the named export if it takes and returns bytes. No trait is written, but export names are text checked only at run time. This goes against the spec's rule of no dynamic export lookup.
options.technical:
```text
plugin.load_dynamic(path: String, authority: Authority, sha256: ?String{None}) -> DynamicPlugin
DynamicPlugin.call(export: String, input: [U8]) -> [U8] !PluginError
```

Only list<u8> to list<u8> exports can be called. A missing export or another shape is a run-time error. Imports, limits, and close match A. The spec text at Docs/spec/spec.md:3863-3867 must be amended.

options.name: Keep a Rust host
options.detail: Core does not change. jetpack-bin keeps BuildPlugin.rs and CompilerExtension.rs as a Rust Wasmtime host behind its hidden subcommands. Jet code starts that host as a child process and exchanges bytes over stdin and stdout, as the compiler does today.
options.technical: The Rust host stays in crates/jetpack-bin with its own Wasmtime 25 pin. Its limit constants stay copies of Plugin.rs:52-57, the duplicate #3670 flags. Byte pipes to the child need D-CORE-PROCBYTES1. No Core source changes.

comparisons.note: bindgen! generates a typed host type from a WIT world at compile time. instantiate then checks any run-time file against it. Option A is the Jet form of this, with a trait in place of a WIT file. Docs: https://docs.wasmtime.dev/api/wasmtime/component/macro.bindgen.html.
comparisons.code:
bindgen!({ path: "wit/build.wit", world: "build-plugin" });
let step = BuildPlugin::instantiate(&mut store, &component, &linker)?;

comparisons.note: Extism calls plug-in functions by text name with byte input and output, like option B. Docs: https://extism.org/docs/concepts/plug-in.
D-MODEL-SIGNATURE1 already binds a run-time model output to a source trait through a type argument. Option A reuses that shape for components.

recommendation.why: A trait gives run-time paths the same typed calls that literal paths get today. The load checks the file once, so later calls need no string lookups. It follows the model precedent, models.open<Trait>.
gains: Build plugins and compiler extensions run through Core.
Export mistakes in host code fail at compile time.

losses.loss: A wrong file is found only when loaded.
losses.mitigation: The file is chosen at run time, so the compiler never sees it.

whyNot.reason: Text export names move typos to run time and break the spec's rule against dynamic export lookup.
The owner rule forbids working around a missing Core API inside Jetpack, and it keeps duplicate limits.

recommendation.tradeoff: Hosts write a small trait for each component interface, in exchange for typed calls.

surface.gist: How should a host load a sandbox component chosen at run time, and still call it with checked types?
surface.lesson: A sandbox component is a WebAssembly file that runs isolated, with only the rights its host lends. Today plugin.load needs the path written in the source, so the compiler can read the component's interface. Jetpack finds build plugins and compiler extensions only at run time. Whichever option wins, Core owes typed calls or errors, fail-closed imports, and today's fuel, memory, and time limits.

current.note: A path held in a variable is refused, because the interface comes from a literal artifact (jet-sema core_call.rs:7714-7735). Read from source; not run.

wild.note: Wasmtime's bindgen! fixes the interface at compile time and loads any file at run time. Docs: https://docs.wasmtime.dev/api/wasmtime/component/macro.bindgen.html.

options.name: Declared interface trait
options.gist: plugin.load<Trait>(path, policy) checks the file's exports against a Jet trait at load time.
gains: Calls stay typed; a wrong export name fails to compile.
One load call for literal and run-time paths.
Optional sha256 pins the exact bytes loaded.
losses: A file missing an export is found only when loaded.

options.name: Call exports by name
options.gist: A dynamic handle calls any byte-to-byte export named by a text string.
gains: No trait to declare.
Matches both Jetpack hosts exactly.
losses: A misspelled export name fails only at run time.
Only one value shape: bytes in, bytes out.
Breaks the rule of no dynamic export lookup.

proposed.code:
// PROPOSED; NOT RUN.
use core.plugin as plugin

policy :: Authority.from_rights(["FS.Read:{component_path}"])
step :: plugin.load_dynamic(component_path, policy)
response :: step.call("build", request) ?? return Err(failed(component_path))
close(^step)

options.name: Keep a Rust host
options.gist: Core stays unchanged; Jetpack keeps its Rust Wasmtime host and runs it as a child process.
gains: No new Core API.
losses: Jetpack keeps private sandbox code outside Core.
Limits and errors stay duplicated in Rust.

proposed.code:
// PROPOSED; NOT RUN.
host :: process.cmd([jetpack_bin, "__build-plugin-host", manifest, component,
    manifest_digest, component_digest]).stdin(.Stream).stdout(.Capture)
child :: host.spawn() ?? return Err(failed(component))
child.stdin.write_all(request)
receipt :: child.wait() ?? return Err(failed(component))

recommendation.why: A trait gives run-time paths the same typed calls that literal paths get today. The load checks the file once, so later calls need no string lookups. It follows the model precedent, models.open<Trait>.
gains: Build plugins and compiler extensions run through Core.
Export mistakes in host code fail at compile time.

losses.loss: A wrong file is found only when loaded.
losses.mitigation: The file is chosen at run time, so the compiler never sees it.

whyNot.reason: Text export names move typos to run time and break the spec's rule against dynamic export lookup.
The owner rule forbids working around a missing Core API inside Jetpack, and it keeps duplicate limits.

recommendation.tradeoff: Hosts write a small trait for each component interface, in exchange for typed calls.

decisions.title: Let a host set a sandbox component's fuel, memory, and time limits
decisions.gist: How should a host choose the fuel, memory, and time limits for one loaded sandbox component?
decisions.lesson: Fuel counts the work a guest does; when it runs out, the call stops. Today every component gets fixed limits: 10 million fuel, 16 MiB memory, 10 thousand table slots, and 2 seconds per call. The compiler states its own limits for each extension run. Whichever option wins, those defaults stay, and a guest over a limit stops with a typed budget error.
decisions.story: Priya ports the compiler-extension host to Jet. Each snapshot the compiler sends declares the limits that extension may use. The Rust host ignores them and applies its own copies of the defaults. The gap study says to pass the limits in instead, but Core offers no way to set them.
decisions.detail:
Need: card #3598 item 4 asks for component instantiation "with bounded fuel/memory" for the jetpack-bin hosts. The bounds exist today, but only as Rust constants. D-CORE-PLUGINPATH1 covers loading a run-time path, and this ballot covers the limits alone.

Rust call sites. The constants live in Prelude/Plugin.rs:52-57, Prelude/BuildPlugin.rs:13-19, and Prelude/CompilerExtension.rs:44-51, with the same values three times. jet-pkg-model CompilerExtension.rs:148-177 defines ResourceLimits, which every snapshot declares (CompilerExtension.rs:1029-1075). But analyze_with_host (CompilerExtension.rs:865-923) calls the default-limit analyze, so declared limits are checked in the response yet never applied to the guest.

Prelude/CompilerExtension.rs:184-249 already accepts fuel and timeout per call. The e2e test compiler_extension_e2e.rs:240-260 uses a short timeout and huge fuel to prove the timeout path. Card #3670 says to remove the duplicated constants and pass the limits in. That needs a Core way to pass them.

Ratified law applied. D-DEP-WASM1=A makes fuel, epoch, memory, table, wire, and import limits mandatory. D-CORE-DOCTRINE1 D2 requires every magic default to appear in the defaults table with an explicit override. D-AUTHORITY-NAME1=A says an Authority can only be narrowed, never widened, which rules out option B for raises. C2: an uncommon option is a label.

options.name: Limits value at load
options.detail: plugin.load gains an optional limits: label taking a plugin.Limits value. Each field defaults to today's number, so a bare load behaves exactly as now. The limits apply to every call on that component. Fuel is refilled and the timer restarts before each call. Memory and tables are capped for the component's whole life.
options.technical:
```text
pub struct Limits {
    pub fuel: Int              // default 10_000_000; refilled before each call
    pub memory_bytes: Int      // default 16_777_216; at most 4 GiB (wasm32)
    pub table_elements: Int    // default 10_000
    pub timeout: Duration      // default 2000ms; per call
}
plugin.load(path, authority, limits: Limits{Limits.default()})
plugin.load<I>(path, authority, sha256: ?String{None}, limits: Limits{Limits.default()})
```

A field of zero or less, or memory above 4 GiB, is refused before the component is read. That error is the user-error kind. A guest that runs out of fuel, memory, table space, or time stops the current call with the budget-exhausted kind. The error names the limit and the export. The instance, memory, and table counts stay fixed at one each, and so does the 16 MiB wire cap. Those are safety constants, not tuning.

The defaults live once in Core/plugin/plugin.jet, the home #3670 assigns. The three Rust copies are deleted in the same cutover. The build-plugin request and response caps (64 KiB and 4 MiB) stay host policy in Core/build/build.jet. Defaults table row: plugin.load uses the four defaults; override with limits:. I9: one Core value, marshalled to the Wasmtime leaf on every run mode.

options.name: Limits inside Authority
options.detail: Authority gains budget fields set with with_budget. plugin.load reads the limits from the Authority it already receives. Because an Authority can only narrow, a budget can only go down from the defaults.
options.technical: Authority.with_budget(fuel: ?Int, memory_bytes: ?Int, table_elements: ?Int, timeout: ?Duration) -> Authority. A value above the holder's current budget is refused, like widening a right (E0712). The defaults become the root budget. This amends D-AUTHORITY-NAME1's rights-only Authority to also carry resource numbers.

options.name: Fixed limits only
options.detail: The four limits stay fixed Core constants with no override. Hosts cannot apply limits the compiler declares, and tests of the timeout path must wait the full two seconds and burn full fuel.
options.technical: The constants move once to Core/plugin/plugin.jet under #3670. There is no API change. The compiler's declared ResourceLimits become documentation only, or they are removed from the snapshot.

comparisons.note: Wasmtime sets memory and table caps on the store and fuel with set_fuel. Rust Jetpack refills fuel and arms an epoch timer per call. Docs: https://docs.wasmtime.dev/api/wasmtime/struct.Store.html#method.set_fuel.
Extism puts memory pages and a timeout in the plug-in manifest the host passes at load, like option A's single limits value. Docs: https://extism.org/docs/concepts/manifest.

recommendation.why: Defaults stay safe for beginners, and a host that must apply declared limits writes them in one labeled value. Raises stay visible in the source, where review sees them.
gains: Hosts apply the limits the compiler declared.
Timeout tests run fast with a short limit.

losses.loss: A host can raise limits for a guest.
losses.mitigation: Heavier legitimate guests need more, and the raise is written at the load call.

whyNot.reason: Authority can only narrow, so a heavier guest could never get more fuel. Budgets are also not rights.
The compiler-extension host could not apply the limits the compiler declares, and D2 requires an override for every default.

recommendation.tradeoff: Hosts can raise limits, in exchange for applying declared limits without a Rust host.

Today every component gets fixed limits: 10 million fuel, 16 MiB memory, 10 thousand table slots, and 2 seconds per call. The compiler states its own limits for each extension run. Whichever option wins, those defaults stay, and a guest over a limit stops with a typed budget error.

current.note: The limits are Rust constants with no Jet control (Prelude/Plugin.rs:52-57). Read from source; not run.

wild.note: Wasmtime hosts set fuel and memory on each store; Rust Jetpack does this per call (Prelude/CompilerExtension.rs:195). Docs: https://docs.wasmtime.dev/api/wasmtime/struct.StoreLimitsBuilder.html.

options.gist: plugin.load takes an optional limits: value; every field defaults to today's number.
gains: Bare loads keep today's safe limits.
One labeled value sets fuel, memory, tables, and time.
Every raise is visible where the component loads.
losses: A host can raise limits and give a guest more.

options.gist: The lent Authority also carries fuel, memory, and time budgets.
gains: One value crosses the boundary.
losses: Authority only narrows, so limits could never rise.
Mixes resource numbers into the rights set.

policy :: Authority.from_rights(["FS.Read:{path}"])
    .with_budget(fuel: 5_000_000, timeout: 1000ms)   // lower only
extension :: plugin.load<Analyzer>(path, policy)
