decisions.title: Publish the model descriptor, checked model package, and model error in core.models
decisions.gist: Should core.models publish its model descriptor, checked package, and error types, so the compiler, runtime, and tools share them?
decisions.lesson: A model package pins a machine-learning model: its files, their SHA-256 digests, tensor shapes, and meaning. Programs only call models.open<Trait>. The checks behind it live in Rust (jet_rt::model), and the Jet port of the package loader needs the same types. Whichever option wins, the checks move into Jet under Core/models and give one answer at compile time and run time.
decisions.story: Priya ports jet-pkg-model's Model.rs to Jet. It turns a package's .Model output into a checked model package, and it verifies every file's digest. The compiler loader, the JIT host, and generated programs all run that same check today through Rust types. Her Jet port has no Jet type to return and no Jet error to report.
decisions.inWild:
# MLflow: https://mlflow.org/docs/latest/python_api/mlflow.models.html#mlflow.models.get_model_info
info = mlflow.models.get_model_info("models:/search-embedder/3")
# ONNX Runtime reads the tensor contract from a loaded session: https://onnxruntime.ai/docs/api/python/api_summary.html
print([(i.name, i.type, i.shape) for i in session.get_inputs()])
decisions.detail:
Need: card #3598 item 5, "core.models: ModelPackage/ModelDescriptor/ModelError runtime (jet_rt::model) for jet-pkg-model Model.rs." The mapping receipt for Model.rs names the same gap. It says jetpack only re-exports these types, and the real consumers are the compiler and runtime.

Rust call sites. jet-pkg-model/src/Model.rs:9 re-exports jet_rt::model. Model.rs:21-69 builds a ModelPackage from package facts, and Model.rs:127-150 verifies files through the no-follow package-root resolver. jet-driver/src/Loader.rs:79-103 calls from_facts for every .Model output at compile time.

At run time, jet-jit runtime_host.rs:17566 calls ModelPackage::load. jet-codegen MIRRust.rs:4814 emits a ModelDescriptor literal, and MIRRust.rs:5157 checks it with ModelPackage::from_descriptor. The types themselves are jet-rt/src/model/mod.rs:337-355 (ModelDescriptor), 438-446 (ModelPackage), 923-1003 (the check), and 1703-1716 (ModelError, 12 variants).

Why a decision is needed. Core/models/models.jet says the module does not fabricate model handles and has no functions. So any Jet home for these types is new Core surface. The Rust split between ModelDescriptor and ModelPackage is real: one holds declared fields, and the other is the checked result with derived identity. That makes them distinct types (T3), not two spellings.

Ratified law applied. D-MODEL-PACKAGE1=A: models are typed, versioned packages whose identity cannot drift. D-MODEL-BACKEND1=A: ONNX Runtime stays a pinned provider leaf, and nothing here moves it. D-MODEL-SIGNATURE1=A: models.open<Trait> and embed keep their T !Err results, and no core.models.Embedder is added. D-PACKAGE-MODEL1=A: core.compiler owns the typed package view, which can hold a ModelDescriptor for .Model outputs instead of defining another. I9 and the owner's 2026-09-28 rule put validation, limits, and error meaning in Jet under Core/.

options.name: Public read-only types
options.detail: core.models exports three types. ModelDescriptor holds the declared fields of one .Model output. ModelPackage is the checked result, and only models.check can make one. ModelError is a closed enum. check is pure, and ModelPackage.verify(root) hashes the files. models.open<Trait> keeps its ratified shape and runs the same check inside.
options.technical:
```text
pub struct ModelDescriptor { package, output, signature: ?String, version, license,
    graph: ModelFile, weights: ModelFile, tokenizer: ModelFile, adapter: ?ModelFile,
    inputs: [TensorSpec], outputs: [TensorSpec], provider, preprocessing, pooling,
    normalization, meaning, metric, custom_operators: Bool,
    max_context: ?Int, max_batch: ?Int, max_buffer_bytes: ?Int }
pub struct ModelFile { pub path: String, pub sha256: String }
pub struct TensorSpec { pub name: String, pub dtype: TensorType, pub shape: [TensorDim] }
pub enum TensorDim { Fixed(Int), Named(name: String, min: Int, max: Int) }
models.check(descriptor: ModelDescriptor) -> ModelPackage !ModelError
ModelPackage.verify(&self, root: String) -[FS]> !ModelError
```

ModelPackage has read-only fields: name, output, signature, version, license, files (deduplicated), inputs, outputs, and limits. It also has embedding_identity() -> EmbeddingIdentity !ModelError. Its fields cannot be set from outside, so holding one proves the check ran (T2).

ModelError variants carry the same fields as today's Rust enum. They are MissingPackage, MissingOutput, WrongKind, Declaration, Provenance, Artifact, SignatureMismatch, UnsupportedProvider, CustomOperatorsDenied, ResourceLimit, BufferLimit, and Cancelled. Messages follow the what, why, and fix format (F3).

Ownership. Reading a package.jet into a ModelDescriptor stays with the package model, the Jet port of Model.rs and D-PACKAGE-MODEL1's view. Core needs no package parser. The ONNX provider leaf receives a checked ModelPackage and file bytes only. I9: the compiler loader, the JIT host, generated programs, and the interpreter call the same Core/models source. The Rust jet_rt::model checks are deleted in that cutover.

options.name: Private Core types
options.detail: The same types and checks move into Core/models as private code. models.open<Trait> stays the only public door. The Jet compiler and the Model.rs port reach the check through a compiler-only path. Tools read raw .Model fields from the core.compiler package view.
options.technical: Core/models/models.jet gains non-pub ModelDescriptor, ModelPackage, and ModelError plus the check. The Jet port of Model.rs lives outside Core, so it needs a new compiler-only visibility rule to call them, or it keeps its own copy. Failures reach programs only as the text inside models.open's !Err.
options.code:
// PROPOSED; NOT RUN.
use core.compiler as compiler

facts :: compiler.package() ?? return
fields :: facts.outputs["search_encoder"].fields   // raw text fields
print(fields["license"], fields["weights_sha256"])

options.name: Keep them in Rust
options.detail: jet_rt::model keeps the descriptor, package, errors, and checks in Rust. The Jet port of Model.rs sends package fields to a Rust leaf and parses the text result.
options.technical: A new leaf function takes the encoded fields and returns O:<package> or E:<kind>:<message>, the wire shape Plugin.rs uses. This keeps validation, limits, and error meaning in Rust, against the owner's 2026-09-28 rule, and every run mode must link the Rust checks.

options.name: Remove models from Core
options.detail:
Delete `core.models` and every Core hook for model packages. The owner wants AI support as a library, not Core. If checked model loading is still wanted, it ships as a first-party package outside Core. Its name avoids "model", for example `jetpack.inference`.

Cutover: delete Core/models. Remove its Core registry and dispatcher rows (crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Core.jet:17-19,408-410). Remove model sema (ComputeModels.jet:739-790) and the Rust, web, and JIT lowerings. Remove Jetpack CoreImports and PackageModel model projection. Regenerate tables and update tests/conformance/exclusions.tsv:12 and the model fixture. Old `use core.models` gets a teaching error pointing to the package.
options.technical: The package decides whether the `.Model` package output kind survives. Keeping it moves jet_rt/model and jet-pkg-model model code into that package. Dropping it also removes PackageOutputKind.Model and fixture assets. The ML battery (crates/jetpack/batteries/ml) is already outside Core.

comparisons.note: MLflow separates model metadata (ModelInfo and signature) from loading, so a tool can audit a model it never runs. Docs: https://mlflow.org/docs/latest/python_api/mlflow.models.html#mlflow.models.get_model_info.

ONNX Runtime exposes tensor names, types, and shapes only after creating a session. Option A offers the declared contract before any session exists. Docs: https://onnxruntime.ai/docs/api/python/api_summary.html.

recommendation.why: The owner wants AI out of Core. A first-party package keeps checked loading for those who need it without growing Core or overloading "model".
gains: One model check for compile time and run time.
Typed failures a program can match.

losses.loss: Three public types must stay stable.
losses.mitigation: Code outside Core must name them, and only public types can be named there.

whyNot.reason: A grows Core's public surface for a feature the owner wants outside Core.
B still keeps model loading inside Core.
C keeps model checks in Rust inside Core's runtime.

recommendation.tradeoff: Existing model users migrate to a package in exchange for a Core without AI.

decisions.title: One table for which IP addresses count as public
decisions.gist: Which IP addresses should Core count as public when a program checks a network destination?
decisions.lesson: Some addresses reach only a home network, a provider's internal services, or the machine itself. A program that fetches outside URLs must refuse those, or an attacker can reach internal services. Core's ip.is_global misses several such ranges, including carrier NAT and documentation ranges. Whichever option wins, one written table decides, and every Core check uses it.
decisions.story: Ana ports the Jetpack provider fetcher, which downloads packages from URLs that registries supply. A hostile registry could point a URL at 100.64.0.1 or at a cloud metadata address. The Rust fetcher refuses those with one table. Core's is_global accepts several of them, so the port would silently weaken the check.
decisions.inWild:
# Python: https://docs.python.org/3/library/ipaddress.html
ipaddress.ip_address("100.64.0.1").is_global  # False
# IANA registries: https://www.iana.org/assignments/iana-ipv4-special-registry/ and
# https://www.iana.org/assignments/iana-ipv6-special-registry/
# Rust jet_net (today): crates/jet-net/src/lib.rs:681-713
jet_net::is_public_ip(ip)
decisions.detail:
Need: card #3595 item 3, "public-IP classification must match jet_net::is_public_ip (including CGNAT and other special ranges)." The request side of item 3 is D-CORE-HTTPDEST1.

Rust call sites. jet_net::is_public_ip (lib.rs:681-713) is used by resolve_public_addresses (lib.rs:654-676) and directly by Provider/fetch.rs:550-555 for IP-literal hosts. resolve_public_addresses serves NixIndex.rs:494-496, Store/NixCache.rs:1758-1760, and Provider/fetch.rs:159. A mixed answer with any non-public address is refused (lib.rs:674-676).

Current Jet surface. Core/net/ip.jet:62-83 defines is_global as not private, loopback, link-local, multicast, reserved (only 0/8 and 240/8), or unspecified. It returns true for 100.64/10, 192.0.0/24, 192.0.2/24, 198.18/15, 198.51.100/24, 203.0.113/24, and 241-255.x.

ipv6_is_global (ip.jet:453-455) returns true for 2001:db8::/32, IPv4-mapped private addresses, NAT64, and most other prefixes outside 2000::/3. Examples/features/net/network_core_contract.jet:6 prints is_global(240.0.0.1).

Differences between the Rust table and IANA, for the owner: Rust marks 192.0.0.9 and 192.0.0.10 non-public (IANA: reachable). Rust marks 64:ff9b::/96 non-public (IANA: reachable). Rust marks 2002::/16, 2001::/32, and 3fff::/20 public. IANA marks 6to4 and Teredo "not applicable" and 3fff::/20 as documentation, not reachable.

Not balloted: Core has two IP value types, net.IPAddr from DNS and ip.IPv4/IPv6 structs. That is existing drift; the HTTP destination policy applies the table internally, so Jetpack needs no public IPAddr predicate.

options.name: The Rust check's table, made Core's one rule
options.detail:
ip.is_global and ip.ipv6_is_global take exactly the rule in jet_net::is_public_ip (crates/jet-net/src/lib.rs:681-713).

IPv4 is public unless it falls in a listed range. The list is 0/8, 10/8, 100.64/10, 127/8, 169.254/16, 172.16/12, 192.0.0/24, and 192.0.2/24. It continues with 192.168/16, 198.18/15, 198.51.100/24, 203.0.113/24, and 224/3. IPv6 is public only inside 2000::/3, and never in 2001:db8::/32. An IPv4-mapped IPv6 address uses the IPv4 rule.

The HTTP destination policy in D-CORE-HTTPDEST1 uses this same table. A DNS answer counts as public only when every address in it is public.
options.technical:
No new name. The existing pub fns keep their signatures: is_global(addr: IPv4) -> Bool and ipv6_is_global(addr: IPv6) -> Bool. Their bodies become the table above; the narrower helpers (is_private, is_reserved, is_carrier_grade_nat, and others) keep their meanings. The table lives once in Core/net/ip.jet. The Rust jet_net check is deleted when the port lands; until then a table test pins both to the same answers.

Documentation: core-library.md gains a core.net.ip section with the table. Examples/features/net/network_core_contract.jet keeps its output (240.0.0.1 stays non-public). Pure functions: no effects. Tiers: plain Jet source, identical on every path (I9).
options.code:
// PROPOSED; NOT RUN.
use core.net.ip as ip
print(ip.is_global(ip.parse_ipv4("100.64.0.1")?))   // false
print(ip.is_global(ip.parse_ipv4("8.8.8.8")?))      // true
print(ip.ipv6_is_global(ip.parse_ipv6("::ffff:10.0.0.1")?))   // false
print(ip.ipv6_is_global(ip.parse_ipv6("64:ff9b::a00:1")?))    // false
print(ip.ipv6_is_global(ip.parse_ipv6("2606:4700::1")?))      // true

options.name: The IANA registry, with Rust updated first
options.detail: is_global and ipv6_is_global follow the "Globally Reachable" column of the IANA IPv4 and IPv6 special-purpose address registries. jet_net::is_public_ip changes to the same table before the parity run.
options.technical: Registry snapshot pinned in Core/net/ip.jet with its retrieval date. IPv6 becomes allow-by-default outside listed ranges, so new special ranges are public until the table is updated.
options.code:
// PROPOSED; NOT RUN.
use core.net.ip as ip
print(ip.is_global(ip.parse_ipv4("100.64.0.1")?))   // false
print(ip.is_global(ip.parse_ipv4("192.0.0.9")?))    // true (IANA)
print(ip.ipv6_is_global(ip.parse_ipv6("64:ff9b::a00:1")?))    // true (IANA)

options.name: IANA reachability plus a strict fetch check
options.detail: `is_global` follows a dated copy of the IANA special-purpose registries, so it answers "can this address be reached?". A separate `is_public_destination` answers "is it safe to fetch?". It starts from the Rust table and also refuses 6to4, Teredo, and NAT64 addresses that map to private IPv4. HTTP fetches, provider downloads, and redirects use only the strict check.
options.technical: New pub fns is_public_destination(IPv4) and ipv6_is_public_destination(IPv6) in Core/net/ip.jet. The IANA table carries its registry date; updating it is a normal Core change. Rust Jetpack gains the same strict check so the parity run compares identical answers.
options.code:
// PROPOSED; NOT RUN.
use core.net.ip as ip
a :: ip.parse_ipv6("2002:c0a8:0101::1")?          // 6to4
print(ip.ipv6_is_global(a))                        // IANA: reachable
print(ip.ipv6_is_public_destination(a))            // false: refused
n :: ip.parse_ipv6("64:ff9b::a00:1")?             // NAT64 to 10.0.0.1
print(ip.ipv6_is_public_destination(n))            // false
http.get("http://[2002:c0a8:0101::1]/")          // refused: not public

comparisons.note: is_global follows the IANA registries; is_private and is_global are both false for 100.64/10. Docs: https://docs.python.org/3/library/ipaddress.html.
Ipv4Addr::is_global is still unstable because the right table was disputed. Tracking issue: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/27709.
netip.Addr has IsPrivate, IsLoopback, and similar checks but no single public test; SSRF filters combine them. Docs: https://pkg.go.dev/net/netip#Addr.IsPrivate.

recommendation.why: Reachability and fetch safety are different questions. IANA answers the first; a stricter check refuses 6to4, Teredo, and NAT64 paths into private networks.
gains: One table for every destination check in Core.
The parity harness sees the same answers on both sides.

losses.loss: 6to4 and Teredo IPv6 addresses still count as public.
losses.mitigation: Refusing them changes the Rust answers the parity run compares; tighten both sides together later.

whyNot.reason: A keeps 6to4 and Teredo as public and ignores the published registry.
B makes fetch checks follow IANA, so NAT64 can still reach private IPv4.

recommendation.tradeoff: Two named checks buy standard reachability and strict fetch safety.

decisions.title: Keep HTTP requests on checked public or loopback addresses
decisions.gist: How should an HTTP client refuse private addresses and keep using the addresses it already checked?
decisions.lesson: A host name can resolve to a private address, or change its answer between a check and the connection. A careful client resolves once, checks every answer, and connects only to those checked addresses. Jetpack does this for package caches and indexes. Core's HTTP client resolves names itself and has no such check. Whichever option wins, "public" means the one table from D-CORE-NETPUBLIC1.
decisions.story: Mei ports the Jetpack Nix cache and index clients. Each resolves the configured endpoint once and refuses any private answer. Each then sends every request to those checked addresses so a changed DNS answer cannot redirect it. Core's HTTP client resolves names on its own, so the port cannot keep this protection.
decisions.inWild:
# Go: https://pkg.go.dev/net#Dialer (Control runs after resolution)
&net.Dialer{Control: checkPublic}
# curl: https://curl.se/docs/manpage.html#--resolve
curl --resolve cache.example:443:203.0.113.7 https://cache.example/x
# Rust reqwest: https://docs.rs/reqwest/latest/reqwest/struct.ClientBuilder.html#method.resolve_to_addrs
Client::builder().resolve_to_addrs("cache.example", &addrs)
decisions.detail:
Need: card #3595 item 3, "Request over pre-resolved, pinned public-only socket addresses - jet_net::get_stream_pinned + resolve_public_addresses." The table itself is D-CORE-NETPUBLIC1.

Rust call sites. Store/NixCache.rs:696-700 and 1329-1333 send over the endpoint's pinned addresses; resolve_endpoint_addresses (NixCache.rs:1726-1783) resolves once, public-only for HTTPS and loopback-only for plain HTTP. NixIndex.rs:345-437 and 489-517 do the same and cache one checked answer per authority for the client's life. Provider/fetch.rs:158-165 resolves public addresses for every hop and pins curl with --resolve. jet_net::get_stream_pinned (lib.rs:738-755) builds a ureq agent whose resolver returns the fixed list.

Current Jet surface. HTTPClient has cookies, redirects, protocols, timeouts, raw_encoding, proxy, tls, allow_http_downgrade, and retries (net_text_time.rs:800-818). None sets addresses or a destination rule. core.net has dns_a and dns_aaaa (net.jet:357-367) but no general resolve; D-NETDNS2 ratified net.resolve_ip, which is not built.

Prelude study (HTTP.rs rows "resolve" and "DNSEntry/DNSCache"): resolution is a leaf and cache lifetime is policy. The study does not cover a public destination rule, so this is new surface.

Ratified law checked: D-NETDNS2=A (system resolver by default), D-NETERROR1=A, D4 (enum option), D2 (defaults table), D-NET-HANDLE-ABI1 (no raw sockets exposed).

options.name: A destination rule on the client
options.detail: HTTPClient gains destinations(rule). .Any is the default and keeps today's behavior. .Public resolves each host once per client and refuses the request unless every address in the answer is public by the D-CORE-NETPUBLIC1 table. It then connects only to those addresses and reuses them for later requests to the same host and port. .Loopback does the same with loopback addresses. The rule also applies to IP-literal hosts and to every redirect hop. HTTPS still sends the original host name for SNI and certificate checks.
options.technical:
New closed enum HTTPDestinations { Any, Public, Loopback }. HTTPClient.destinations(rule: HTTPDestinations) -> HTTPClient. Refusal: HTTPError.Policy(reason:) naming the host and the first refused address, raised before any connection. A resolution failure stays HTTPError.Resolve(host:).

Pinning: the client keeps a map from (scheme, host, port) to the checked address list for its lifetime, shared by clones, as NixIndex.rs:345-422 does. The ordinary DNS cache TTL (HTTP.rs:1746-1785) does not apply to a pinned entry. Proxies: with .Public or .Loopback, an environment proxy is ignored; an explicit .URL proxy must itself pass the rule.

Defaults table row: "Client.new().destinations | .Any | .Public, .Loopback". Effects unchanged: Net, Time.Wait. The Prelude port moves resolve (HTTP.rs:1739-1745) behind this check. One path serves AOT, default jet run, and the interpreter (I9).

options.name: The caller resolves and pins addresses
options.detail: Add a public resolver call (D-NETDNS2's net.resolve_ip), a classification call for net.IPAddr, and HTTPClient.connect_to(host, port, addresses). The client then connects to the given addresses for that host.
options.technical: net.resolve_ip(host) -[Net, Time.Wait]> [IPAddr] !NetError uses the ratified D-NETDNS2 name, which is not built yet. net.ip_is_global(IPAddr) -> Bool is new. HTTPClient.connect_to(host: String, port: Int, addresses: [IPAddr]) -> HTTPClient works like curl --resolve.

options.name: A resolver function on the client
options.detail: HTTPClient gains resolver(function). The transport calls it for every connection instead of the system resolver. jet_net uses this mechanism through ureq today (lib.rs:748-754).
options.technical: HTTPClient.resolver(f: (String, Int) -[Net, Time.Wait]> [IPAddr] !NetError) -> HTTPClient. The client caches nothing on its own; pinning is up to the function.

comparisons.note: Dialer.Control is the praised SSRF hook because it sees the address actually dialed. Docs: https://pkg.go.dev/net#Dialer.
comparisons.code: Control: func(network, address string, c syscall.RawConn) error

comparisons.note: --resolve pins a host to fixed addresses while keeping the host name for TLS. Docs: https://curl.se/docs/manpage.html#--resolve.
A requests wrapper that refuses non-public destinations by policy at connect time. Project: https://github.com/JordanMilne/Advocate.

recommendation.why: Jetpack's caches and index use the same rule everywhere: HTTPS goes to checked public addresses and plain HTTP stays on loopback. One client setting gives that rule to every request and redirect.
gains: NixCache, NixIndex, and the provider fetcher each become one line.
The check happens where the connection is made, so it cannot be skipped.

losses.loss: A long-lived client keeps a stale address after DNS changes.
losses.mitigation: Pinning is the point: a new answer could be a private address, so a new client must opt in.

whyNot.reason: Pinning by hand misses redirect hops to new hosts, and a forgotten host silently falls back to normal resolution.
A resolver function makes every caller rewrite the same check and pinning, and hides the rule from receipts.

recommendation.tradeoff: Programs rebuild a client to pick up new DNS answers instead of trusting a fresh lookup.

surface.gist: How should an HTTP client refuse private addresses and keep using the addresses it already checked?
surface.lesson: A host name can resolve to a private address, or change its answer between a check and the connection. A careful client resolves once, checks every answer, and connects only to those checked addresses. Jetpack does this for package caches and indexes. Core's HTTP client resolves names itself and has no such check. Whichever option wins, "public" means the one table from D-CORE-NETPUBLIC1.

current.note: The client resolves each host inside the transport; a program cannot check or pin the addresses it uses. Read from source; not run.

wild.note: Go's Dialer.Control runs after resolution and before connect, so an SSRF filter can check the real address. See https://pkg.go.dev/net#Dialer.

gains: One line makes every request and redirect public-only.

losses: A long-lived client keeps a stale address until it is rebuilt.

gains: Mirrors the Rust code step by step.

gains: Any resolution policy is expressible.
losses: Each caller rewrites the public check and the pinning.

decisions.title: Limit which hosts an HTTP client may follow a redirect to
decisions.gist: How should a program limit which hosts its HTTP client may follow a redirect to?
decisions.lesson: A redirect tells a client to fetch a different address instead. A download tool that trusts one server must not follow a redirect to another server. Today the client redirect policy only caps the number of hops. Jetpack must turn redirects off and follow each hop by hand. Whichever option wins, Core still refuses HTTPS-to-HTTP hops and strips credentials when the origin changes.
decisions.story: Omar ports the Jetpack toolchain updater. It downloads signed manifests from one configured server and must refuse a redirect that leaves that server. The provider fetcher must also refuse hosts outside each provider's allow list. Today the Jet client follows any redirect, so both ports would need hand-written redirect loops.
decisions.inWild:
# Go: https://pkg.go.dev/net/http#Client (CheckRedirect)
client.CheckRedirect = func(req *http.Request, via []*http.Request) error { ... }
# Rust reqwest: https://docs.rs/reqwest/latest/reqwest/redirect/struct.Policy.html
Policy::custom(|attempt| if attempt.url().host_str() == Some("example.org") { attempt.follow() } else { attempt.stop() })
# curl: --max-redirs 5 --proto-redir =https (https://curl.se/docs/manpage.html#--proto-redir)
decisions.detail:
Need: card #3595 item 2, "Bounded fetch with an explicit redirect-policy callback - jet_net::fetch_bounded_with_redirect_policy." The byte bound is D-CORE-HTTPBODYLIMIT1; this ballot covers the redirect rule.

Rust call sites. ToolchainUpdate.rs:1010-1016 passes resolve_toolchain_redirect (ToolchainUpdate.rs:962-991), which refuses any hop whose scheme, host, or port differs from the configured origin. Provider/fetch.rs:143-206 follows up to five hops by hand; every hop must pass check_url (fetch.rs:209-218), an allow and deny list of provider hosts on HTTPS port 443. Provider/native.rs:672 and 773 call get_stream_follow_redirects with any host allowed. The jet_net helpers are lib.rs:802-890.

Current Jet surface. HTTPRedirectPolicy has one variant, .Follow{max, same_origin_credentials} (core_types.rs:2972-2995, core-library.md:655). Requests also take redirects(n) (net_text_time.rs:785-791). Core/http/client.jet:26-30 declares a second RedirectPolicy enum {Disabled, Limited, All}; the Prelude port removes that duplicate.

Prelude study (HTTP.rs row "send_following_redirects"): two redirect implementations exist today and must become one Jet implementation. That is implementation. Choosing a host rule is new public surface, so it is balloted here.

Ratified law checked: D4 (options are enums), D2 (defaults table row), D-NETERROR1 (typed errors). The same_origin_credentials Bool is existing D4 drift and is left alone here.

options.name: Allowed hosts written in the policy
options.detail: HTTPRedirectPolicy.Follow gains a to: field that names where a hop may go. .AnyHost is the default and keeps today's behavior. .SameOrigin allows only hops that keep the scheme, host, and port of the first request. .Hosts(list) allows only hops whose host and port appear in the list. Core resolves the Location header, checks it against the rule, and refuses a bad hop with HTTPError.Redirect before it connects. The existing rules still apply: no HTTPS-to-HTTP hop without allow_http_downgrade, and credentials are stripped when the origin changes.
options.technical:
New closed enum RedirectTarget { AnyHost, SameOrigin, Hosts([String]) }. HTTPRedirectPolicy.Follow becomes { max: Int, same_origin_credentials: Bool = true, to: RedirectTarget = .AnyHost }. The true default is what the Rust transport already uses (HTTP.rs:326-333). A Hosts entry is "host" or "host:port"; a bare host means the scheme's default port. Hosts compare case-insensitively after IDNA normalization in core.net.url. An empty Hosts list refuses every hop.

Refusal: HTTPError.Redirect(reason:) naming the refused URL; the response that carried the Location is drained and closed. The hop count check is unchanged. Relative Location values resolve with core.net.url join, one rule for both the Rust transport (HTTP.rs:2645-3020) and client.jet session_follow (client.jet:188-217). The Prelude HTTP port (#3665) merges those two.

Defaults table row: "Client.new().redirects | up to 10 hops, any host | .Follow{max:, to:}". Effects unchanged: Net, Time.Wait. One Prelude path serves AOT, default jet run, and the interpreter (I9).

options.name: A callback approves each hop
options.detail: HTTPRedirectPolicy gains .Check{max, allow}. Core calls allow with the current URL and the resolved next URL; false refuses the hop with HTTPError.Redirect.
options.technical: Variant Check{ max: Int, allow: (URL, URL) -> Bool }. The callback must be pure; effects inside it are refused by the checker. Downgrade and credential rules still apply after the callback allows a hop.

options.name: Follow hops by hand
options.detail: Keep the surface as it is. A caller sends each request with redirects(0), reads Location, joins it with core.net.url, checks the rule, and repeats. This is how Provider/fetch.rs:143-206 works today with curl.
options.technical: Uses existing HTTPRequest.redirects(n), HTTPResponse.header(name), and URL.join. The caller owns method rewriting on 303, body replay on 307/308, credential stripping, and downgrade refusal.

comparisons.note: CheckRedirect is a callback; praised for power, but callers often forget to stop cross-host hops. Docs: https://pkg.go.dev/net/http#Client.
Policy::limited(n) is data; Policy::custom is a callback for anything else. Docs: https://docs.rs/reqwest/latest/reqwest/redirect/struct.Policy.html.
Redirect rules are flags: hop count and allowed protocols. Jetpack's hardened curl uses --max-redirs 0 and loops itself (fetch.rs:221-239). Docs: https://curl.se/docs/manpage.html.

recommendation.why: Every Jetpack redirect rule is either same origin or an allowed host list. A data rule checked inside Core covers both, keeps the existing safety rules on every hop, and shows up in receipts.
gains: Toolchain updates and provider downloads get safe redirects in one line.
The redirect rule is visible data, not hidden code.

losses.loss: Unusual rules, such as path prefixes, still need a hand loop.
losses.mitigation: A closed list of rule kinds cannot express arbitrary code, and no Jetpack caller needs more.

whyNot.reason: A callback hides the rule from receipts and makes every caller rewrite the same-origin check that most need.
Hand loops repeat the joining, downgrade, and credential rules in every caller, and one slip leaks a token.

recommendation.tradeoff: Rare rules outside same origin and host lists use a hand loop instead of a callback.

current.note: The redirect policy caps hops but accepts any host. Keeping hops on one origin means a hand-written loop. Read from source; not run.

wild.note: Go lets the caller vet each hop in CheckRedirect. See https://pkg.go.dev/net/http#Client.

options.name: Allowed hosts written in the policy
options.gist: The redirect policy names where hops may go: any host, the same origin, or a host list.
gains: The rule is plain data that logs and receipts can show.
Core checks each hop before connecting to it.
Covers every Jetpack redirect rule without callbacks.
losses: A rule outside the three kinds needs a hand loop.

options.name: A callback approves each hop
options.gist: The policy carries a function that sees each hop and returns allow or refuse.
gains: Any rule a program can compute is expressible.
losses: Receipts cannot show the rule; it is code.
Each caller rewrites the common same-origin check.

options.gist: No new policy; programs turn redirects off and loop over Location headers themselves.
gains: No new Core surface.
losses: Every caller re-implements joining, downgrade, and credential rules.
Easy to forget stripping credentials on a cross-origin hop.

decisions.title: Stream a large HTTP response body under a caller-chosen byte cap
decisions.gist: How should a program stream an HTTP response body larger than 64 MiB under its own byte cap?
decisions.lesson: A response body arrives in pieces, so a program can save it without holding it in memory. A byte cap stops a bad server from sending forever. Today every response stops at a hidden 64 MiB limit, and explicit limits stop at 1 GiB. Jetpack downloads archives up to 16 GiB. Whichever option wins, the cap is written down and an over-cap body fails.
decisions.story: Mei ports the Jetpack Nix cache client. It downloads a signed package archive of several gigabytes, hashes it, and unpacks it while it streams. Today the Jet HTTP client stops every body at 64 MiB, so the port cannot fetch real packages. She needs to set the cap from the signed file size and hand the body straight to the decoder.
decisions.inWild:
# Go: https://pkg.go.dev/io#LimitReader
body := io.LimitReader(resp.Body, limit+1)
# Python requests: https://requests.readthedocs.io/en/latest/user/advanced/#body-content-workflow
for chunk in r.iter_content(chunk_size=65536): ...
# Rust jet_net (today): crates/jet-net/src/lib.rs:730-797
response.take(limit + 1).read_to_end(&mut body)
decisions.detail:
Need: card #3595 item 1, "Streaming GET response body with a caller-set byte cap (default body limit is 1 MiB) - jet_net::get_stream, get_stream_follow_redirects."

Rust call sites. Store/NixCache.rs:696-777 streams a Nix archive through a hashing reader and a zstd decoder, capped by the signed FileSize. MAX_NAR_BYTES is 16 GiB (Store/Nar.rs:22). Provider/native.rs:662-716 and 772-790 stream artifacts up to 512 MiB into a staging file (native.rs:35). ToolchainUpdate.rs:993-1019 fetches toolchain artifacts up to 512 MiB (ToolchainUpdate.rs:31). Store/Cache.rs:2251-2272, Store/NixCache.rs:1329-1355, and NixIndex.rs:355-389 read small bounded bodies; the existing bytes(limit) already covers those.

Current Jet surface. Body has bytes(limit), text(limit), json, chunks(size), and copy_to(^writer, limit) (net_text_time.rs:1034-1053, method_calls.rs:5200-5252). Explicit limits are clamped to 1 GiB (HTTPMessage.rs:884-889). The transport cuts every body at 64 MiB (HTTP.rs:73) and refuses a larger Content-Length as InvalidFraming (HTTP.rs:4271-4273). The card's "1 MiB" is the text() default from D-HTTP-MSG1; the binding limit for streams is the hidden 64 MiB.

Prelude study (prelude-core-gap.json, HTTP.rs row "Client limits constants"): the limit constants are policy that must become one set in Core/http/client.jet. That move alone does not decide how a caller raises the streaming cap, so this ballot decides it.

Ratified law checked. D-HTTP-MSG1 keeps text() and the explicit limit forms. D-NETIO-CONTRACT1=A and D-NETIO-CONTRACT2=B define one core.io.Reader that fails with IOError. D-IOERROR-TREE1=A fixes the IOError variants. The bounded buffering law (spec.md:2032) says body limits reject over-limit input. Peer draft D-CORE-CODECSTREAM1 (ArchivePluginBallots) adds zstd.reader and gzip.reader over any io.Reader; NixCache.rs:745-775 needs exactly that composition.

options.name: Cap set on the body, which reads like a file
options.detail:
HTTPResponse.body gains an optional labeled cap: resp.body(limit: n). The cap applies to every way of reading that one-pass body: chunks, copy_to, and the core.io.Reader read(limit) from D-NETIO-CONTRACT1/2. A Content-Length above the cap fails before any byte is delivered. A bare resp.body() keeps a 64 MiB cap, now written in the defaults table instead of hidden in the transport.

In-memory reads keep their own explicit limits: text(), bytes(limit), and json stay as D-HTTP-MSG1 ratified them and never exceed 1 GiB. copy_to(^writer) drops its second argument because the body cap already bounds it.
options.technical:
Signature: HTTPResponse.body(limit: Int = 67108864) -> Body. HTTPRequest.body() on the server gains the same label. Body implements core.io.Reader: read(limit: Int) -[Net, Time.Wait]> [U8] !IOError, [] at end. Through the reader, an over-cap body is IOError.InvalidInput with operation Read, the URL as resource, and cause "HTTP body exceeds N-byte limit". Inherent calls keep HTTPError.BodyTooLarge(limit). A negative limit fails the first read with HTTPError.BodyTooLarge(limit), as jet_http_consume_limit does today (HTTPMessage.rs:884-889).

Streaming reads (chunks, copy_to, read) accept any nonnegative Int cap. The 1 GiB clamp stays only on reads that collect into memory (bytes, text, json). The body checks against HTTP_RESPONSE_BODY_LIMIT (HTTP.rs:3934, 4091, 4272, 4423, 4515) are removed; the Jet-side cap is the one bound. The HTTP/2 frame-queue bound at HTTP.rs:1249 gets its own constant. Framing checks stay: a body shorter or longer than its Content-Length is HTTPError.InvalidFraming.

Cutover (E1): copy_to(^writer, limit) becomes copy_to(^writer) in the checker (method_calls.rs:5230-5240), the Prelude (HTTPMessage.rs:861-882), and every caller. The defaults table in stdlib-api-laws.md gains the row "resp.body() | 64 MiB streaming cap | resp.body(limit:)". One Prelude path serves AOT, default jet run, and the interpreter (I9). D-CORE-CODECSTREAM1 (ArchivePluginBallots draft) supplies zstd.reader over any io.Reader.

options.name: Cap on each streaming call
options.detail: chunks(size) gains limit:, and copy_to keeps its limit argument without the 1 GiB clamp. Body stays its own one-pass type and does not implement core.io.Reader. A bare chunks(size) keeps the 64 MiB default.
options.technical: Body.chunks(size: Int, limit: Int = 67108864) -> HTTPBodyChunks; Body.copy_to(^writer: FileWriter, limit: Int) -> Int !HTTPError. The transport cap is removed as in A. Composition with stream codecs needs an adapter that turns HTTPBodyChunks into a reader.

options.name: One cap for the whole client
options.detail: HTTPClient gains body_limit(n). Every body read from that client stops at n. One-shot helpers keep the 64 MiB default.
options.technical: HTTPClient.body_limit(limit: Int) -> HTTPClient. The client stores the cap and hands it to each response body. In-memory reads keep their explicit limits as today.
options.code:
// PROPOSED; NOT RUN.
client :: http_client.Client.new().body_limit(16.gib)
resp :: client.send(http_client.request("GET", nar_url)) ?? return
out :: files.create("stage/pkg.nar.zst") ?? return
resp.body().copy_to(^out) ?? return

comparisons.note: resp.Body is an io.Reader; callers bound it with io.LimitReader or http.MaxBytesReader. Official docs: https://pkg.go.dev/io#LimitReader.
stream=True plus iter_content lets the caller count bytes; there is no built-in cap. Docs: https://requests.readthedocs.io/en/latest/user/advanced/#body-content-workflow.
comparisons.code:
with requests.get(url, stream=True) as r:
    for chunk in r.iter_content(65536): ...

comparisons.note: bytes_stream() yields chunks; no body cap exists, so callers count. Docs: https://docs.rs/reqwest/latest/reqwest/struct.Response.html#method.bytes_stream.
comparisons.code:
let mut s = resp.bytes_stream();
while let Some(chunk) = s.next().await { total += chunk?.len(); }

recommendation.why: One cap on the body bounds every read path. A body that is a Core reader lets the archive decoder chain onto it without glue. Small reads keep their own tighter limits.
gains: One cap per download, chosen where the response is handled.
Package archives stream through decoders with no adapter.

losses.loss: copy_to callers drop their second argument.
losses.mitigation: Keeping both limits would give one body two caps that can disagree.

whyNot.reason: Per-call caps leave the body outside the shared reader contract, so stream decoders need glue, and two calls can set different caps.
Jetpack reads 1 MiB metadata and 16 GiB archives from the same server, so a client-wide cap is either too loose or too tight.

recommendation.tradeoff: A few copy_to callers change shape so that each body has exactly one cap.

resp, err := http.Get(narURL)
defer resp.Body.Close()
body := io.LimitReader(resp.Body, limit+1) // caller-chosen cap
n, err := io.Copy(out, body)
if n > limit { return errTooLarge }

options.gist: resp.body(limit:) sets one cap; the body is a Core reader every stream helper accepts.
gains: One cap covers every way of reading the body.
Stream decoders and file copies take the body directly.
A bare resp.body() keeps a written 64 MiB default.
losses: copy_to loses its separate limit argument in the same change.

options.gist: Each streaming call takes its own cap; the body stays a separate stream type.
gains: The cap sits next to the loop that reads.
No change to how the body is taken.
losses: Stream decoders cannot take the body without glue code.
Two calls on one body can disagree about the cap.

decisions.title: Take over a listening socket opened by the service manager
decisions.gist: How should a service take over a listening socket that its service manager opened for it?
decisions.lesson: A service manager such as systemd can open a socket before a service starts and hand it over at start. The service then accepts connections without binding the socket itself. Jetpack's shared-store broker works this way. In Core today, a listener comes only from binding. Whichever option wins, Core checks that the handed-over socket really is a listening socket before use.
decisions.story: Luis ports the Jetpack shared-store broker. An administrator installs it as a systemd socket unit, so systemd owns /run/jet/shared-store.sock and starts the broker per connection. The Rust broker turns descriptor 3 into a listener with unsafe code. Core has no way to receive that socket, so the port cannot run under the ratified install design.
decisions.inWild:
# systemd: https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/latest/sd_listen_fds.html
int n = sd_listen_fds(1);  /* descriptors 3 .. 3+n-1 */
# Go: https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/coreos/go-systemd/v22/activation#Listeners
listeners, err := activation.Listeners()
# Python: https://docs.python.org/3/library/socket.html#socket.fromfd
sock = socket.fromfd(3, socket.AF_UNIX, socket.SOCK_STREAM)
decisions.detail:
Need: card #3595 item 4, "Adopt an inherited listening socket (socket activation, fd 3) for non-JetOS dev services (see #329 for the JetOS twin)."

Rust call sites. Store/Broker.rs:490-507 (serve_shared_store_fd) turns a raw descriptor into a UnixListener with unsafe code and accepts one connection. CLI/shared_store.rs:36-56 reads --fd and defaults to 3. The systemd units are generated at Broker.rs:286-299 (ListenStream socket unit) and Broker.rs:360-365 (ExecStart ... broker --fd 3). The only caller is this broker; Services.rs:1806-1926 reserves socket paths for dev services but hands no descriptor to them, so the card's "dev services" wording names no second user today.

Current Jet surface. core.net offers tcp_listen, tcp_listen_addr, and unix_listen (core-library.md:2803, 2831; net.jet:109-116, 312-319). There is no way to receive a listener.

Ratified law checked: D-JPK-MULTIUSER-IMPL1=A (root-owned socket-activated verifier with peer credentials), D-NET-LISTENER-ABI1=A (listeners are opaque handles; no public descriptor construction), D-NETERROR1=A. The sending side (a parent passing a handle to a child) is D-CORE-PROCINHERIT1 in ProcessBallots; this ballot is the receiving side. #329 covers the JetOS service manager, which can speak the same convention.

options.name: Take the sockets the manager declared
options.detail: net.inherited_listeners() returns every listening socket the service manager handed over, as a list of InheritedListener values. Each value is .Unix{name, listener} or .TCP{name, listener}, where name comes from the manager (for example the systemd FileDescriptorName). Core checks that each handed-over descriptor is a stream socket in listening state, marks it close-on-exec, and clears the handover variables so children do not see them. A second call returns an empty list. Without a handover, the list is empty.
options.technical:
New closed enum InheritedListener { Unix{ name: ?String, listener: UnixListener }, TCP{ name: ?String, listener: TCPListener } }. net.inherited_listeners() -[Net, Env]> [InheritedListener] !NetError.

Protocol: the sd_listen_fds convention (https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/latest/sd_listen_fds.html). LISTEN_PID must equal the current process id, or the list is empty. LISTEN_FDS descriptors start at 3; LISTEN_FDNAMES supplies names. Each descriptor must report SO_ACCEPTCONN = 1 and SO_TYPE = SOCK_STREAM, with family AF_UNIX or AF_INET/AF_INET6. Any other descriptor fails the call with NetError.InvalidInput naming its position. The call unsets LISTEN_PID, LISTEN_FDS, and LISTEN_FDNAMES, like sd_listen_fds(1).

Platforms: Linux and other Unix hosts whose manager uses this convention. macOS launchd uses a different, name-based call and Windows has no handover; both return an empty list. The listener types stay the ones D-NET-LISTENER-ABI1 made opaque; no descriptor number is exposed. One Prelude path serves AOT, default jet run, and the interpreter (I9).

Jetpack cutover: the generated unit keeps ExecStart=... hangar shared broker, and the --fd 3 flag (CLI/shared_store.rs:39-44, Broker.rs:361) is removed.

options.name: Adopt a socket by descriptor number
options.detail: net.unix_listener_from_descriptor(n) and net.tcp_listener_from_descriptor(n) check that n is a listening socket of the right family and take ownership of it.
options.technical: unix_listener_from_descriptor(descriptor: Int) -[Net]> UnixListener !NetError; tcp_listener_from_descriptor(descriptor: Int) -[Net]> TCPListener !NetError. The same socket checks as A run. Core cannot tell whether another part of the program already owns the number.

comparisons.note: sd_listen_fds checks LISTEN_PID, returns the count, and optionally unsets the variables. Docs: https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/latest/sd_listen_fds.html.
activation.Listeners wraps each passed descriptor as a net.Listener. Docs: https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/coreos/go-systemd/v22/activation.
The listenfd crate reads the same convention without unsafe in user code. Docs: https://docs.rs/listenfd.
comparisons.code:
let mut fds = ListenFd::from_env();
let listener = fds.take_unix_listener(0)?;

recommendation.why: The handover convention already says which descriptors belong to the service and what they are called. Reading it in Core keeps descriptor numbers out of program code, as the ratified listener design requires.
gains: The broker takes its socket with no unsafe code and no numbers.
Children never see the handover variables.

losses.loss: Supervisors without the LISTEN_FDS convention cannot hand over sockets.
losses.mitigation: Without a convention, only a raw number identifies the socket, and D-NET-LISTENER-ABI1 removed numbers from public code.

whyNot.reason: It brings descriptor numbers back into public code, and Core cannot stop two parts of a program adopting one number.

recommendation.tradeoff: Only the widely used LISTEN_FDS handover is supported, in exchange for no descriptor numbers in programs.

surface.gist: How should a service take over a listening socket that its service manager opened for it?
surface.lesson: A service manager such as systemd can open a socket before a service starts and hand it over at start. The service then accepts connections without binding the socket itself. Jetpack's shared-store broker works this way. In Core today, a listener comes only from binding. Whichever option wins, Core checks that the handed-over socket really is a listening socket before use.

current.note: Listeners come only from binding a path or address; there is no way to receive one. Read from source; not run.

wild.note: The go-systemd package reads the systemd handover and returns ready listeners. See https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/coreos/go-systemd/v22/activation#Listeners.

options.name: Take the sockets the manager declared
options.gist: One call reads the service manager's handover and returns checked, typed listeners.
gains: No descriptor numbers in program code.
Each socket is checked before it is trusted.
Child processes do not inherit the handover by accident.
losses: Works only with managers that use the LISTEN_FDS handover.

options.name: Adopt a socket by descriptor number
options.gist: The program names a descriptor number; Core checks it and wraps it as a listener.
gains: Works with any supervisor that passes a known number.
Matches the Rust --fd flag exactly.
losses: Descriptor numbers return to public code.
Two parts of a program can adopt the same number.

recommendation.why: The handover convention already says which descriptors belong to the service and what they are called. Reading it in Core keeps descriptor numbers out of program code, as the ratified listener design requires.
gains: The broker takes its socket with no unsafe code and no numbers.
Children never see the handover variables.

losses.loss: Supervisors without the LISTEN_FDS convention cannot hand over sockets.
losses.mitigation: Without a convention, only a raw number identifies the socket, and D-NET-LISTENER-ABI1 removed numbers from public code.

whyNot.reason: It brings descriptor numbers back into public code, and Core cannot stop two parts of a program adopting one number.

recommendation.tradeoff: Only the widely used LISTEN_FDS handover is supported, in exchange for no descriptor numbers in programs.

decisions.title: Learn which user is on the other end of a Unix socket
decisions.gist: How should a Unix-socket server learn which user account is on the other end of a connection?
decisions.lesson: On one machine, a server can ask the kernel which user connected to its Unix socket. The kernel records this at connect time, so the client cannot fake it. Jetpack's shared-store broker uses the user number to decide who may read or write. Core's Unix sockets have no such query. Whichever option wins, platforms without the query report Unsupported.
decisions.story: Luis ports the Jetpack shared-store broker. For each connection, it reads the connecting user's number from the kernel. It then checks that user's enrollment record and grants read or write rights. The Rust code does this through an unsafe getsockopt call. Core's Unix streams offer no way to ask.
decisions.detail:
Need: card #3595 item 5, "Unix-socket peer credentials (SO_PEERCRED) for the shared-store broker."

Rust call sites. Store/Broker.rs:519 reads peer_uid for every connection, then authorize_peer (defined at Broker.rs:927, called at 526 and 533) checks enrollment and rights. peer_uid is Broker.rs:820-866 (Linux SO_PEERCRED through unsafe getsockopt) and 868-873 (other Unix: unsupported). The test at Broker.rs:2607-2690 proves the number is the kernel's view across a user namespace.

Current Jet surface. UnixStream has read, write, shutdown, and close (net.jet:317-355, core-library.md:2831-2834) and nothing about the peer.

Ratified law checked: D-JPK-MULTIUSER-IMPL1=A ("socket-activated transient verifier with peer credentials"), D-DBG-AUTH1 (same-user attach), D-NETERROR1=A (Unsupported and PermissionDenied variants exist in NetError, core_types.rs:2902-2917). Process identity is ProcessBallots' D-CORE-PROCIDENT1.

options.name: Ask the stream for its peer
options.detail: net.unix_peer(stream) returns UnixPeer{user, group}: the user and group numbers the kernel recorded when the client connected. The server compares them with its own policy. There is no process id in the result, because a process id can be reused by an unrelated process. D-CORE-PROCIDENT1 covers process identity.
options.technical:
New plain-data record UnixPeer { user: Int, group: Int } with equality. net.unix_peer(stream: UnixStream) -[Net]> UnixPeer !NetError.

Linux and Android: getsockopt(SOL_SOCKET, SO_PEERCRED), the ucred recorded at connect() time. macOS, iOS, FreeBSD, NetBSD, OpenBSD, and DragonFly: getpeereid(). Windows AF_UNIX has no peer credential: NetError.Unsupported. A closed stream: NetError.Closed. Numbers are the kernel's view from the server's user namespace, which is what the broker test at Broker.rs:2607-2690 relies on.

No raw descriptor is exposed. Effects: Net only. One Prelude path serves AOT, default jet run, and the interpreter (I9).

options.name: An admission rule on the listener
options.detail: unix_listen and the inherited-listener path take a peers: rule, .Anyone by default, or .SameUser, or .Users(list). Core checks each accepted connection and closes refused ones.
options.technical: Enum UnixPeers { Anyone, SameUser, Users([Int]) }. The accept loop skips refused connections. The server cannot learn which allowed user connected.
options.code:
// PROPOSED; NOT RUN.
use core.net as net
listener :: net.unix_listen(path, peers: .Users(config.enrolled_users)) ?? return
stream :: net.unix_accept(listener) ?? return   // only enrolled users arrive

options.name: Raw socket option under #Unsafe
options.detail: An expert unix_socket_option(stream, level, name, size) returns raw bytes. The caller knows the platform numbers and struct layout.
options.technical: unix_socket_option(stream: UnixStream, level: Int, name: Int, size: Int) -[Net]> [U8] !NetError, callable only in #Unsafe.

comparisons.note: peer_cred returns UCred{uid, gid, pid: Option}; pid is optional because not every platform has it. Docs: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/os/unix/net/struct.UnixStream.html#method.peer_cred.
x/sys/unix exposes the raw Linux ucred; callers write platform branches themselves. Docs: https://pkg.go.dev/golang.org/x/sys/unix#GetsockoptUcred.
Python needs getsockopt with a hand-written struct layout. Docs: https://docs.python.org/3/library/socket.html#socket.socket.getsockopt.

recommendation.why: The broker needs the user number itself to look up enrollment and choose read or write rights. A small record read from the stream gives exactly that on every Unix host, with no unsafe code.
gains: The broker port keeps its access rules without unsafe code.

losses.loss: No process id is reported.
losses.mitigation: A process id can belong to a new process by the time it is used, so it is not identity.

whyNot.reason: The broker must know which enrolled user connected to pick rights, so a yes/no admission rule is not enough.
Raw options push platform numbers and byte layouts into every caller and force #Unsafe for a routine check.

recommendation.tradeoff: Callers that want the connecting process use the process-identity surface instead of a raw process id.

surface.gist: How should a Unix-socket server learn which user account is on the other end of a connection?
surface.lesson: On one machine, a server can ask the kernel which user connected to its Unix socket. The kernel records this at connect time, so the client cannot fake it. Jetpack's shared-store broker uses the user number to decide who may read or write. Core's Unix sockets have no such query. Whichever option wins, platforms without the query report Unsupported.

current.note: A Unix stream exposes only its path; there is no peer identity query. Read from source; not run.

wild.note: Rust's UnixStream::peer_cred returns the kernel-recorded user, group, and process. See https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/os/unix/net/struct.UnixStream.html#method.peer_cred.
wild.code:
let cred = stream.peer_cred()?;
if cred.uid != allowed_uid { return Err(denied()); }

options.name: Ask the stream for its peer
options.gist: One call returns the connecting user and group numbers the kernel recorded.
gains: The server decides access with ordinary code on plain numbers.
Works on Linux, macOS, and the BSDs with one name.
losses: No process id, so it cannot find the connecting process.

options.name: An admission rule on the listener
options.gist: The listener takes an allowed-user rule and silently refuses other users' connections.
gains: Unwanted users never reach program code.
losses: The broker still needs the number to look up enrollment.
A refused client sees a closed socket with no reason.

proposed.code:
// PROPOSED; NOT RUN.
use core.net as net
listener :: net.unix_listen(path, peers: .Users(config.enrolled_users)) ?? return
stream :: net.unix_accept(listener) ?? return   // only enrolled users arrive

options.name: Raw socket option under #Unsafe
options.gist: An expert call reads any socket option as bytes inside an audited unsafe block.
gains: Reaches every platform-specific option.
losses: Every caller decodes platform byte layouts itself.
Jetpack would need #Unsafe for an ordinary check.

recommendation.why: The broker needs the user number itself to look up enrollment and choose read or write rights. A small record read from the stream gives exactly that on every Unix host, with no unsafe code.
gains: The broker port keeps its access rules without unsafe code.

losses.loss: No process id is reported.
losses.mitigation: A process id can belong to a new process by the time it is used, so it is not identity.

whyNot.reason: The broker must know which enrolled user connected to pick rights, so a yes/no admission rule is not enough.
Raw options push platform numbers and byte layouts into every caller and force #Unsafe for a routine check.

recommendation.tradeoff: Callers that want the connecting process use the process-identity surface instead of a raw process id.

decisions.title: Send a child process's output straight into a file
decisions.gist: How should a program send a child process's output and errors straight into files it opened?
decisions.lesson: A child process writes output and errors. Today Jet can pipe them back to the program, capture them in the receipt, or share the program's own terminal. A supervisor that starts a long-running service needs a fourth choice. The service writes into log files directly, with no copy loop in the supervisor. Whichever option wins, the plan and receipt name each file a child writes to.
decisions.story: Ravi ports Jetpack Services. The supervisor starts a database and sends its output and errors into two log files in the service folder. Rust hands the open files to the child. Jet has no output choice that takes a file, so the ported line does not compile.
decisions.detail:
Need: the Jetpack port (#3590) of Services and the JetOS proofs. A child writes output and errors into files the program opened.

Rust call sites that require it:
```text
crates/jetpack/src/Services.rs:3026-3029            service output and errors into log files
crates/jetpack/src/JetOS/vm_proof.rs:127-129         VM phase output into files
crates/jetpack/src/JetOS/nixos_backend.rs:1284-1285  QEMU errors into a file
Jetpack/Services/Source/Supervisor/Lifecycle.jet:192-219  the port already writes .stdout(.File(^stdout))
```

Current Jet surface. ProcessStreamMode has three unit variants: Stream, Inherit, and Capture (crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/CoreLib/JetStd/CommonTypes.rs:7-10). The checker and the three tiers list the same three names (Codegen/TIR/tir_to_mir_types.rs:2145, crates/jet-jit/src/Process.rs:1791-1801). No choice takes a file.

The only workaround is .Stream plus a copy loop in a task. The port rule forbids working around a missing Core API. The loop also stops when the parent stops.

Beginner path: open the log with files.create and pass it with .File(^log). Expert path: open with files.append, a mode, and links: .Refuse (D-CORE-FILEOPEN1). Two children, or output and errors, can then share one log without overwriting each other.

Related ballots. The ownership rule matches keep_open from D-CORE-PROCINHERIT1: the spec takes the handle with ^. D-CORE-PROCREPLACE1 keeps a .File stream across the replace. D-CORE-FILECLOSE1 makes writers buffered, so the handoff flushes first.

Seen nearby but not part of this ballot: nixos_backend.rs:1284 discards output with Stdio::null(). Jet has no discard choice either.

options.name: A file output choice
options.detail: ProcessStreamMode gains File(FileWriter). The stdout and stderr settings accept it, and the spec takes the writer with ^. Every child the spec starts writes into that file from its first byte. Jet flushes bytes the program already wrote first, so they stay in order. The program's copy closes when the spec is dropped. The receipt text for that stream is empty, as with .Inherit.
options.technical:
```text
enum ProcessStreamMode { Stream, Inherit, Capture, File(FileWriter) }   // Core dot-literal enum
ProcessSpec.stdout(mode: ProcessStreamMode) -> ProcessSpec   // signature unchanged
ProcessSpec.stderr(mode: ProcessStreamMode) -> ProcessSpec   // signature unchanged
```

Ownership. .File(^out) consumes the writer, so the program cannot write to it or close it afterward. The stdin setting rejects .File at compile time. Reading child input from a file is not part of this ballot.

Append or replace comes from how the writer was opened: files.create replaces, and files.append appends. A spec that is dropped without spawning closes the file.

Order. At spawn Jet flushes the writer's buffer before the child starts. A flush failure returns that IOError from spawn, and no child starts.

Limits. output_limit counts only captured streams. A .File stream is not counted, and the file grows as the child writes.

Unix (Linux and macOS). The child receives a duplicate on descriptor 1 or 2 between fork and exec. The parent's descriptor stays close-on-exec, so other children never see it.

Windows. The handle is duplicated as inheritable and listed alone in PROC_THREAD_ATTRIBUTE_HANDLE_LIST. It becomes hStdOutput or hStdError, and no other handle leaks.

Plan and receipt. ProcessPlan and ProcessReceipt name the stream as a file with the writer's path.

Other settings. .detached() keeps the file. .under(authority) follows the rule .Inherit has today: a non-detached authority-bound spec refuses it before spawn with IOError.InvalidInput. Captured output is what the redactor reads (ProcessPolicy.rs:299-313). replace_process keeps the file as the new program's output.

Errors and effects. Failures are IOError from the flush or from spawn; no new error kind. No new effect: spawn already carries Exec, and opening the writer carries FS. One Prelude spawn path serves AOT, the JIT host, and the MIR evaluator (I9).
options.code:
// PROPOSED; NOT RUN.
stdout :: files.create(stdout_path) ?? return
stderr :: files.create(stderr_path) ?? return
spec :: process.cmd(run).cwd(data_dir)
    .stdout(.File(^stdout))
    .stderr(.File(^stderr))
child :: spec.spawn() ?? return
// The service writes both logs itself; no copy loop.

options.name: Core opens the file by path
options.detail: ProcessStreamMode gains Path(String). Core creates or replaces the named file when the child starts. The program never holds the file.
options.technical:
```text
enum ProcessStreamMode { Stream, Inherit, Capture, Path(String) }
```

The file is created or replaced with default permissions and follows links. An open failure is returned by spawn. Append, mode, and link refusal would need their own labels, copying files.create and files.append.
options.code:
// PROPOSED; NOT RUN.
spec :: process.cmd(run).cwd(data_dir)
    .stdout(.Path(stdout_path))
    .stderr(.Path(stderr_path))
child :: spec.spawn() ?? return

options.name: Separate builder calls
options.detail: Add spec.stdout_to(^writer) and spec.stderr_to(^writer). The output choice keeps its three plain words.
options.technical:
```text
ProcessSpec.stdout_to(writer: ^FileWriter) -> ProcessSpec
ProcessSpec.stderr_to(writer: ^FileWriter) -> ProcessSpec
```

A later .stdout(mode) call replaces an earlier stdout_to, and the reverse. The last call wins.
options.code:
// PROPOSED; NOT RUN.
stdout :: files.create(stdout_path) ?? return
stderr :: files.create(stderr_path) ?? return
spec :: process.cmd(run).cwd(data_dir)
    .stdout_to(^stdout)
    .stderr_to(^stderr)
child :: spec.spawn() ?? return

comparisons.note: An *os.File assigned to Stdout is handed to the child directly, with no copy goroutine. Docs: https://pkg.go.dev/os/exec#Cmd. This is the shape A takes.
comparisons.code:
log, _ := os.Create(stdoutPath)
cmd := exec.Command(run[0], run[1:]...)
cmd.Stdout = log
cmd.Start()

comparisons.note: Stdio::from(File) moves the file into the command, like the ^ handoff in A. Docs: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/process/struct.Stdio.html

recommendation.why: A puts the file where every other output choice already lives. It reuses the ^ handoff from keep_open, and the program opens the file with the options it needs.
gains: Output files follow the same handoff rule as keep_open.
The port's existing line works as written.

losses.loss: The program cannot write to that file handle afterward.
losses.mitigation: Two owners of one handle would mix bytes; open the file again to write more.

whyNot.reason: B opens files by name inside spawn, so append, mode, and link rules need a second copy of the file options.
C adds a second way to set output, and the later call silently replaces the earlier one.

recommendation.tradeoff: The output choice carries an owned file, so one setting decides where each stream goes.

decisions.title: Wait for one key press for a limited time
decisions.gist: How should a full-screen program wait for keys: a timed read, keys on a receiver, or both?
decisions.lesson: A full-screen dashboard reads single key presses and redraws between them. #Live already switches the terminal to raw key input and restores it on exit. Inside it, term.read_key() waits forever. A timed read waits a set time, then returns. A reactive read delivers keys as values on a receiver, waited on beside signals and timers. The owner asked for both; this ballot settles how they share input.
decisions.story: Kai ports the bare `jetpack` dashboard. It redraws the store summary while a load runs, quits on q or Escape, and stops on a service stop request. Rust reads keys with a 100 ms limit. In Jet, read_key blocks until someone presses a key, so the screen freezes. Kai wants a plain timed loop, and a loop that stops at once on a stop request.
decisions.detail:
Owner direction (2026-09-30, question on this ballot): "I want to support both reactive & timed." Option A now does that. The earlier timed-only option is C, and the receiver-only option is B. The earlier poll-then-read option is dropped, because A's timed call already returns the key in one step.

Need: card #3598 and the dashboard port (Jetpack/CLI/Source/Dashboard/DashboardSnapshot.jet:93-106, 244-329). The port calls term.enable_raw_mode() and term.read_key_timeout(...). Neither exists.

Raw mode is already covered. #Live { } (D-TERM1, Docs/spec/spec.md:3007-3045) enters unbuffered, no-echo input and restores it on return, error, and panic. The port should wrap its loop in #Live instead of calling enable_raw_mode. So this ballot proposes no new raw-mode API.

The gap is a time limit and a way to wait on keys beside other events. term.read_key() (Core/term/term.jet:111, Prelude/Core/TermKey.rs:230-239) blocks until bytes arrive. At end of input it returns Unknown, so a loop cannot tell a closed terminal from a strange key.

One mechanism (I8). Both spellings in A sit on one key queue in the Prelude. The timed call is the beginner path. The receiver is the expert path, and it uses the same receiver and wait table as D-CORE-PROCSIGNAL1=A signals.

Why one queue matters. crossterm offers both styles, but its docs forbid mixing poll/read with EventStream. Jet removes that trap: every reader takes from the same queue, so mixing styles never loses or steals a key.

Rust call sites that rely on a timed read:
```text
crates/jet-repl/src/Term.rs:32-38                 raw mode "min 0 time 1": reads wait at most 100 ms
crates/jetpack/src/CLI/dashboard.rs:172-278       loop redraws and retries the store between keys
crates/jet-cli/src/Help/Interactive.rs:764-765    Key::Idle drives resize checks
```

Signals. In raw mode Ctrl+C arrives as a key, not as a signal. A stop request still arrives as a signal on the receiver from D-CORE-PROCSIGNAL1.

Beginner path: term.read_key() inside #Live, unchanged, or term.read_key_within(wait) for a redraw loop. Expert path: term.keys() in the wait table beside signals and timers.

options.name: Both, sharing one key queue
options.detail: Add term.read_key_within(wait) for timed loops and term.keys() for reactive loops. Both take keys from the one queue that #Live owns. Each key goes to exactly one reader, so the two styles mix safely. read_key() stays as it is.
options.technical:
```text
term.read_key_within(wait: Duration) -[IO, Time.Wait]> Key? IOError!
term.keys() -[IO]> Receiver<Key> IOError!
```

One queue. Each #Live block owns one key queue. read_key, read_key_within, and every receiver from term.keys() take keys from it. A receiver reads input only while the program waits on it, so it never holds a key that another reader asked for. Each key goes to exactly one reader, in arrival order.

Timed results. Val(key) is one key, decoded by the same table as read_key (Prelude/Core/TermKey.rs). None means no key arrived within wait. A wait of zero checks without waiting.

Reactive results. The receiver yields each Key through receive(), try_receive(), a loop, or a `key, keys ->` arm in the wait table. It closes when its #Live block ends.

Errors. IOError.InvalidInput for a negative wait. Both calls return IOError.InvalidInput outside #Live, or when #Live could not switch the terminal, so a failed #Live is visible. When input reaches its end, read_key_within returns IOError.Closed and the receiver closes. IOError.Cancelled when the task is cancelled during a timed wait.

Linux: poll on descriptor 0 with the time limit, then one read. macOS: select, because macOS poll does not support terminal devices. Windows: wait on the console input handle and skip focus, mouse, and resize records. Both calls use this one kernel.

AOT, the JIT host, and the MIR evaluator call the one key-queue kernel in the Prelude (I9).

options.name: Keys on a receiver only
options.detail: Add only term.keys(). A timed wait is the wait table with an `after` arm. read_key() stays as it is and shares the same key queue.
options.technical:
```text
term.keys() -[IO]> Receiver<Key> IOError!
```

Same queue, errors, and closing rules as A. There is no timed call; a loop that wants a time limit writes the wait table.

options.name: Timed read only
options.detail: Add only term.read_key_within(wait). It returns one key, or None when no key arrived in time. Closed input is an error. Stop requests are checked between reads.
options.technical:
```text
term.read_key_within(wait: Duration) -[IO, Time.Wait]> Key? IOError!
```

Same results, errors, and platform kernel as the timed call in A.

comparisons.note: crossterm has both styles: poll and read for timed loops, and EventStream for reactive ones. Its docs forbid mixing them in one program. A keeps both and removes that rule with one shared queue. Docs: https://docs.rs/crossterm/latest/crossterm/event/index.html

curses window.timeout sets how long getch waits; -1 means no key. Docs: https://docs.python.org/3/library/curses.html#curses.window.timeout. The timed call in A returns None instead of a magic number.
comparisons.code:
stdscr.timeout(250)
key = stdscr.getch()   # -1 when no key arrived

comparisons.note: Go delivers signals on a channel so a select can wait on them beside timers. Jet's receiver follows this shape for signals (D-CORE-PROCSIGNAL1=A); B and A add keys to the same wait. Docs: https://pkg.go.dev/os/signal#Notify

recommendation.why: A gives beginners one timed call and experts the shared wait table. One key queue feeds both, so mixing styles never loses or steals a key.
gains: Timed and reactive loops both work.
Mixing both styles is safe, unlike crossterm.

losses.loss: Two spellings can wait for a key with a time limit.
losses.mitigation: A timed call without the wait table is the point of the beginner path.

whyNot.reason: B makes every simple timed key loop learn receivers and the wait table.
C cannot wait on keys beside signals, so stop requests arrive up to one wait late.

recommendation.tradeoff: Two spellings over one key queue, in exchange for a simple timed path and a full reactive one.

decisions.title: Read a link inside a held folder after its path is gone
decisions.gist: How should a program read a link inside a folder it holds open once the folder's path stops working?
decisions.lesson: A held folder is a Directory handle from files.open_directory. It keeps working after its path is renamed or vanishes. Jet can already list it and inspect entries without following links. It cannot read where a link inside it points. Passing held files to a child is already solved by keep_open with a pinned number. Whichever option wins, the lease check must pass after the helper exits.
decisions.story: Lena ports Jetpack's executable leases. A short helper builds a sealed folder of links in a private mount, and Jetpack holds that folder open. The helper exits, and the folder's /proc path dies with it. Before each launch Jetpack must check that every link still names its pinned file. The port cannot read those links.
decisions.inWild:
# Python: https://docs.python.org/3/library/os.html#os.readlink (dir_fd)
fd = os.open(root, os.O_RDONLY | os.O_DIRECTORY)
for name in os.listdir(fd):
    target = os.readlink(name, dir_fd=fd)
decisions.detail:
Need: card #3593 and the Store lease port. The brief asked for the descriptor number of an open handle, to build /proc/self/fd/<n> paths for a child.

The child side is already covered. D-CORE-PROCINHERIT1 A pins a handle at a chosen number with keep_open(^handle, at: Val(slot)). The port already does this. It allocates process-unique slots from 64 up and hands children /proc/self/fd/<slot> paths (Store/Source/Reuse/CacheLease.jet:13-33, 57-73, 152-204; Environment/Source/Shell/NixProjection.jet:137-141, 298-306). No parent descriptor number is needed for that.

The remaining gap is on the parent side:
```text
Jetpack/Store/Source/Reuse/LeaseSnapshot.jet:350-360   holds /proc/<keeper>/root<mount>, then the keeper exits
Jetpack/Store/Source/Reuse/CacheLease.jet:598-610      validate lists wrapper.path and reads each link by path
crates/jetpack/src/Store/Reuse.rs:2507-2509            Rust reads through /proc/self/fd/<dirfd> instead
```

After the keeper exits, the /proc/<pid>/root path is gone, so every later lease check fails in the port. Rust avoids that by reading through its own descriptor path.

Current Jet surface. D-CORE-FILEDIR1 gives Directory list, entry_stat, open, create, rename, remove, and fsync, all by relative name without following links. It has no read_link.

Beginner path: files.read_link(path) for ordinary paths, unchanged. Expert path: a held Directory for paths that may move or vanish.

options.name: Read a link through the held folder
options.detail: Add Directory.read_link(name). It returns the text stored in the link named name inside the held folder. It uses the same name rules as the other Directory methods and never follows a link.
options.technical:
```text
Directory.read_link(name: String) -[FS]> String IOError!
```

Names are plain parts separated by slashes. .., ., empty parts, and absolute names are refused with IOError.InvalidInput. Each earlier part is opened without following links. The last part must be a link.

Result: the link text exactly as stored, not resolved. A missing entry is IOError.NotFound. An entry that is not a link, and link text that is not valid text, follow the rules files.read_link has today.

Linux and macOS: readlinkat on the held descriptor after the no-follow walk. Windows: open the entry relative to the held handle with FILE_FLAG_OPEN_REPARSE_POINT and read a symbolic-link target. A junction or other reparse kind is IOError.InvalidInput naming the kind.

No new effect: FS, as for the other Directory methods. AOT and default jet run share one provider (I9).

options.name: A process-local path for a handle
options.detail: Add handle.view_path() on Directory, FileReader, and FileWriter. It returns /proc/self/fd/<n> on Linux or /dev/fd/<n> on macOS. Ordinary path calls then work through it.
options.technical:
```text
Directory/FileReader/FileWriter.view_path() -> String IOError!
```

Windows has no such path and returns IOError.Unsupported (D-CORE-FILEERROR1). The path is valid only in this process and only while the handle is open.

options.name: The raw descriptor number
options.detail: Add handle.descriptor() -> Int. Callers build /proc/self/fd paths by hand, as Rust Jetpack does.
options.technical:
```text
Directory/FileReader/FileWriter.descriptor() -> Int
```

Unix only; Windows returns IOError.Unsupported.

comparisons.note: os.readlink and os.listdir accept a held directory descriptor, so no path is rebuilt. Docs: https://docs.python.org/3/library/os.html#dir-fd. A gives the same without a raw number.
comparisons.code:
fd = os.open(root, os.O_RDONLY | os.O_DIRECTORY)
target = os.readlink("tool", dir_fd=fd)

comparisons.note: cap_std::fs::Dir::read_link reads a link relative to a held directory, the shape of A. Docs: https://docs.rs/cap-std/latest/cap_std/fs/struct.Dir.html#method.read_link
comparisons.code:
let dir = Dir::open_ambient_dir(root, ambient_authority())?;
let target = dir.read_link("tool")?;

recommendation.why: A adds the one missing Directory method, so the lease check reads links through the held folder. No path or number escapes that could name the wrong file.
gains: The lease check works after the helper exits.
Held folders keep one no-follow name rule.

losses.loss: Only link reading is added; other path-only tools stay out.
losses.mitigation: A general path to a handle names the wrong file in children, so each need gets a method.

whyNot.reason: B hands out a path that silently names the wrong file in a child or after close.
C puts raw numbers in ordinary code, the thing keep_open was chosen to avoid.

recommendation.tradeoff: One more Directory method instead of a general escape hatch.
