decisions.title: Remove the helper copy a Windows self-update leaves behind
decisions.gist: How should Jetpack remove the helper copy that a Windows self-update leaves behind?
decisions.lesson: On Windows a running program cannot delete its own file. Jetpack's self-update runs a helper copy of jet.exe that swaps in the new version, then exits. Rust Jetpack asks Windows to delete the helper at the next restart. Windows allows that only for administrators, so per-user installs keep the copy. Whichever option wins, a leftover helper copy never blocks an update.
decisions.story: Amara installs Jet for her own Windows account and runs a toolchain update. The helper swaps in the new jet.exe and exits. Rust asks Windows to delete the helper at restart, fails without administrator rights, and ignores the error. A .jet-update-<pid>.helper.exe copy stays beside jet.exe after every update.
decisions.detail:
Need: card #3593 and the toolchain update port. Jetpack/Recipe/Source/Toolchain/UpdateInstall.jet:6-8 and 460-463 call files.delete_at_reboot(helper), which Core does not have.

Rust flow (crates/jetpack/src/ToolchainUpdate.rs):
```text
1801-1853   copy jet.exe to .jet-update-<pid>.helper.exe beside it and start the helper
2136-2139   the helper swaps in the new jet.exe, then schedules its own deletion
1940-1956   schedule_delete = MoveFileExW(path, NULL, MOVEFILE_DELAY_UNTIL_REBOOT)
```

Microsoft documents that delay-until-reboot needs the administrators group or LocalSystem. A per-user install gets an access error, which Rust ignores. So in the common case the copy is never removed.

Current Jet surface. files.list_dir and files.remove exist (-[FS]>). On Windows, removing a file whose program is still running fails, so a running helper protects its own copy.

Linux and macOS never create a helper: Unix can replace a running program's file. This ballot changes nothing there.

Beginner path: nothing to write; updates clean up after themselves. Expert path: the same sweep function, which tests can call on a scratch folder.

options.name: The next update removes old helper copies
options.detail: No new Core call. At the start of every Windows toolchain update run, Jetpack removes old helper copies beside jet.exe. A copy that is still running refuses removal and is skipped. The helper stops scheduling anything.
options.technical:
The sweep lists the folder that holds jet.exe with files.list_dir. It removes only regular files whose names match exactly: .jet-update-, then digits, then .helper.exe. It never follows a link, and files.remove on a link removes only the link.

Errors from one removal are dropped. A running helper, a locked file, or missing rights leave that copy for the next run. The update itself continues.

Port change: delete UpdateInstall.jet:460-463 and call the sweep before the new helper is created. Effects: FS, already on the update path. No Core change, so AOT and default jet run behave the same (I9).

options.name: A Core call that removes a file at restart
options.detail: Add files.remove_at_reboot(path). Windows deletes the file during the next restart. Other systems refuse. The port renames its call from delete_at_reboot, because Core's verb is remove.
options.technical:
```text
files.remove_at_reboot(path: String) IOError! -[FS]>
```

Windows: MoveFileExW(path, NULL, MOVEFILE_DELAY_UNTIL_REBOOT). Without administrator rights it returns IOError.PermissionDenied. A relative path is IOError.InvalidInput, because the list is read at boot with no working folder.

Linux and macOS: IOError.Unsupported (D-CORE-FILEERROR1). Unix has no restart delete list and can remove a running program's file directly.

Windows deletes by name at restart. A different file placed at that path before restart is deleted instead. One Prelude provider serves AOT and default jet run (I9).

comparisons.note: Rust Jetpack calls MoveFileExW with MOVEFILE_DELAY_UNTIL_REBOOT and ignores the result. Docs: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/winbase/nf-winbase-movefileexw

recommendation.why: A removes the copy for every user with calls Core already has. It keeps an administrator-only Windows request out of Core.
gains: Per-user installs stop collecting helper copies.
Core needs no new call.

losses.loss: One helper copy stays until the next update run.
losses.mitigation: The helper is still running when it finishes, and Windows keeps a running program's file.

whyNot.reason: B fails without administrator rights, the usual per-user install, so copies still pile up.

recommendation.tradeoff: One leftover copy until the next update, instead of a Windows-only Core call.

decisions.title: Where build and package facts live under the fact sigil
decisions.gist: Should build and package facts be their own sigil roots, or sit under one compiler root?
decisions.lesson: D-BUILD-FACT2 chose `compiler.build.*`, a plain word the owner now rejects. This amendment keeps its contents and only picks the root. Examples use `$`, standing for the glyph D-COMPILER-NS1 picks. Family map: `prep` marks code that runs before the program (ratified). A sigil marks facts the compiler knows (this family). `@` marks links (D-MEMREF1).
decisions.story: Lin switches an API URL per build profile. She wants the shortest clear way to read the profile and package version.
decisions.inWild:
if cfg!(target_os = "linux") { }
let v = env!("CARGO_PKG_VERSION");

options.name: Own roots
options.detail: `$build` holds target, profile, settings, and stamps; `$package` holds name, version, and license. Contents match D-BUILD-FACT2.

options.name: One compiler root
options.detail: Every fact hangs under `$compiler`.

comparisons.note: Rust reads build facts through `cfg!` and `env!`. See https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/conditional-compilation.html.

recommendation.why: The sigil already says 'compiler fact', so a second `compiler` word only adds length.

whyNot.reason: B repeats what the sigil already says on every read.

recommendation.tradeoff: Two short roots beat one long path.

decisions.shortAuthorizedBy: Owner, 2026-09-30: "clean them up so that they have one single decision each ... I really want a sigil".

decisions.title: Metadata parameters on marker and fact declarations
decisions.gist: Should the fixed metadata on a marker or fact declaration carry the fact sigil?
decisions.lesson: A marker declaration lists where it may attach and whether it repeats. These are facts for the compiler, not arguments for callers. Today they use `@`, which now means a link. Examples use `$`, standing for the glyph D-COMPILER-NS1 picks. Family map: `prep` marks code that runs before the program (ratified). A sigil marks facts the compiler knows (this family). `@` marks links (D-MEMREF1).
decisions.story: Kai declares a marker. He needs to tell which parameters callers pass and which ones only instruct the compiler.
decisions.inWild:
@attached(member, names: arbitrary)
macro AddFields() = #externalMacro(module: "M", type: "F")

options.name: Sigil metadata
options.detail: Sigil parameters are compiler metadata; plain parameters are what callers pass.
options.code:
marker AddFields($sites: [.Type], $repeatable: false, prefix: String) { }
fact Flow($holds: .Value, $safe: .Gain, $gates: [])

options.name: Reserved plain names
options.detail: A fixed list of names means metadata in marker and fact lists.
options.code:
marker AddFields(sites: [.Type], repeatable: false, prefix: String) { }
fact Flow(holds: .Value, safe: .Gain, gates: [])

comparisons.note: Swift macro roles are compiler metadata in attributes. See https://docs.swift.org/swift-book/documentation/the-swift-programming-language/macros/.

Skip macros read facts and splice names with a sigil: `#thisClassName`, `this.#field` (Skip/Hack talk https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=J31LlAUtoos). https://raw.githubusercontent.com/skiplang/skip/master/docs/blog/2018-07-24-macros.md.

recommendation.why: The owner wants compiler metadata marked. The sigil separates it from caller parameters without reserving words.

whyNot.reason: B reserves ordinary names and hides which parameters the compiler reads.

recommendation.tradeoff: One sigil in declarations buys visible metadata.

decisions.title: Match a case's fields by name, at any depth
decisions.gist: May a pattern name a case's fields, like `.FailedToFetch{url: u, cause: c}`, including inside another pattern?
decisions.lesson: A case with named fields is built by name: `AppError.FailedToFetch{url: raw, cause: err}`. Matching it works only by position: `.FailedToFetch(u, c)`. Writing the names is a parse error, both at the top of an arm and inside `.Err(…)`. So the reader must remember field order. Struct destructuring already uses names, and one shipped example already writes the named form.
decisions.story: Kai wraps a fetch error with `AppError.FailedToFetch{url: raw, cause: err}`. To report it he writes `.Err(.FailedToFetch{url: u, cause: c})`, the same shape. The parser answers "Expected `,` between pattern bindings".

options.name: Names at any depth
options.detail:
After a case declared with named fields, a pattern may list fields in braces: `.FailedToFetch{url: u, cause: c}`. A bare `url` binds a name `url`, as in struct destructuring. A field's pattern may be any pattern, such as `cause: .BadUrl(why)`. Listing only some fields needs `..` at the end, as struct destructuring does (E0326).

The form works wherever a pattern can go: an arm head, inside `.Err(…)` or `.Val(…)`, or deeper. The positional form keeps working. One pattern uses one form; mixing names and positions in the same braces is an error. Braces on a case with unnamed fields, like `BadUrl(String)`, are an error whose fix shows the positional form.
options.technical:
The parser gains one variant-pattern shape in both parsers, the Rust one and the Jet compiler's Patterns.jet. It maps onto the existing payload slots by field name, so checking, exhaustiveness and code generation are unchanged. decisions.gist: What should read C headers for Jet bindings, so real libraries like SQLite and SDL import completely?
decisions.lesson: To call a C library, Jet must read its header file: types, functions, constants, and macros. Jet's binder is a small parser of its own that maps simple declarations and skips the rest. Zig reads headers with a full C front end. `jet cc` already ships a pinned Clang in the Jetpack toolchain.
decisions.story: Dev wants to port a game from C to Jet one file at a time. SDL3's headers have unions, callbacks, and macros. Jet's binder skips most of them, so he would hand-write hundreds of declarations before running anything.
decisions.detail:
Interop wedge status: `jet cc` and `jet c++` exist and use the pinned Jetpack toolchain (crates/jet-cli/src/CLI.rs:1333-1349). `#Export(c)` exists. Foreign builds are on #1347, and cross toolchains are on #758, #1058, and #1060. Header import is the weakest link.

Conflicts: I6 governs compiler crate dependencies and new stdlib dependencies. A adds no crate dependency; it runs the toolchain's Clang as a tool, as `jet cc` already does. Binding output stays a generated `#Bindgen` module, checked by ordinary sema before use.

options.technical: Clang JSON AST plus macro expansion for constants; per-target sysroots from the Jetpack toolchain; results cached in jet-store by header digest and target.

options.name: Keep the focused parser

decisions.title: Values that must finish in a named way, such as commit or rollback
decisions.gist: Should a type list the methods that finish it, like commit or rollback, so forgetting one is a compile error?
decisions.lesson: Some values must not just disappear. A database transaction must end in commit or rollback. Today `#SingleUse` makes a value end exactly once, but any consuming call counts, and errors only say "owes consume". This ballot lets a type name its finishing methods and what runs when an error exits early. It is not a general rule system: effects, call order, and permissions keep their own tools.
decisions.story: Omar writes a payment handler. On one early return he forgets to roll back the transaction, and Jet compiles it, because transactions are plain values (card #4151). He wants the compiler to say "commit or rollback is missing here", and wants errors to roll back without a hand-written branch at every `?`.
decisions.detail:
What the marker does, and only this. `#MustFinish(commit, rollback, on_fail: rollback)` on a type says how a value of that type may end. The compiler tracks each value through four states.

- Created: it must still finish.

- Borrowed (`&txn.charge(...)`) or read: it must still finish.

- Finished: one listed method took it (`^txn.commit()`). Done; any later use is the existing use-after-move error.

- Handed on: passed with `^` to another function, or returned. The receiver now must finish it, by a listed method, by handing it on again, or by returning it. A wrapper function cannot make the duty disappear.

Every path that leaves the scope while the value must still finish is a compile error naming the missing methods. The listed methods are alternatives (commit OR rollback). If a type needs two steps in order, its API expresses that with typestate (`#State`/`#Transition`) or one method that does both.

What it is not. It does not add effects, permissions, value checks, or call-order rules. Those keep their tools: effect rows `-[IO]>` and `#FX`, typestate `#State`/`#Transition`, taint `#Input`/`#Scrub`, and capability authority. `#MustUse` stays separate: it only forbids ignoring a returned value, and reading the value satisfies it.

How `#SingleUse` is replaced. Today `#SingleUse` (D-LIN1) means: end exactly once, by passing with `^`, returning, or `#Unsafe("reason") { consume(x) }`. Any consuming method ends it, and the error says "owes consume" (E0140-E0143).

`#MustFinish(...)` keeps that same exactly-once check and changes three things. Among the type's own consuming methods, only the listed ones finish the value. Errors name those methods. And `on_fail:` can finish it automatically on error exits. Each `#SingleUse` type migrates by listing its consuming methods, for example `#MustFinish(close)`. Abandoning a value keeps the audited gate, `#Unsafe("reason") { consume(x) }` (D-DROP-WORD1=A).

`on_fail: m` runs `m` on a value that is still owned and unfinished when a failure leaves the scope. Failures are `?` propagation, `return Err(...)`, panic unwinding, and task cancellation. It never runs on a value already handed on. For example, if `^txn.commit()` fails, the value was handed to `commit` and counts as finished whether `commit` returns or fails. Mojo's explicit destructors follow the same rule.

`on_fail` does not run on abort, process kill, or power loss. `m` must be one of the listed methods and take only `^self`. If `m` itself fails, its error is attached as a note to the error already leaving; the value counts as finished. Without `on_fail`, every error exit must finish the value by hand, as `#SingleUse` requires today. An early success return is never finished automatically; that is the mistake the marker exists to catch.

Tasks: D-CONC-UNIT1=A already gives task handles the same single-use duty, and D-CONC-JOIN1=A lets reading a task's result count as joining. Under A, Core declares `Task<T>` as `#MustFinish(join, detach)`, and reading the result still counts as `join`. Behavior is unchanged; only the messages name `join` or `detach`.

Unbound spawns keep their scope-end join (D-CONC-SPAWN1). Containers of such values must finish each element, and generic code keeps the D-LIN1 rules.

Spelling: `#MustFinish` is new, chosen by the drafter to pair with `#MustUse` and to say plainly what is required. The earlier draft's `#Owes` is a metaphor; the owner may keep it, and nothing else depends on the name.

Conflicts: E0140 to E0143 merge into one diagnostic family with new snapshots (I4). Receivers follow D-CAP-RECEIVER1=D (`&txn.charge`, `^txn.commit`). In option B's example, `err` names the failure inside a `??` block (D-FAIL-BIND1=A). Card #4151 (transactions) is the first user.

The earlier option "Core marks buffered writers and locks too" is not lost. If A wins, which Core types adopt the marker is a separate ballot, because it changes beginner file code.

options.name: Named finishing methods
options.detail: `#MustFinish(m1, m2, on_fail: m)` on a type lists the methods that finish it and, optionally, the one that runs on error exits. `#SingleUse` is replaced; task handles declare `#MustFinish(join, detach)`.
options.technical: Same exactly-once checker as D-LIN1, in the self-hosted ownership checker (Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Ownership), with a per-type list of finishing methods. Existing E0140-E0143 snapshots must stay at least as strict.
options.code:

struct Txn { conn: DBLease }

options.name: Keep #SingleUse
options.detail: No change. Any consuming call finishes the value, and every error exit needs a hand-written rollback.
options.technical: No change.

options.name: Automatic rollback at scope end
options.detail: No new marker. `Txn` is an ordinary resource: the existing scope-end cleanup (S63) rolls it back if `commit` never ran, as Rust's sqlx does.
options.technical: Library change only: Txn's close rolls back.
options.code: struct Txn { conn: DBLease }  // close() rolls back

comparisons.note: Every resource is linear; operations thread new handles. Strong guarantee, heavy ergonomics.
A type can forbid implicit destruction and name the fix; a `deinit self` method ends the value.
comparisons.code:
struct Example(Deinitable where (False, "call 'cleanup()'")):
    def cleanup(deinit self): ...

comparisons.note: A dropped Transaction rolls back automatically; forgetting commit is not a compile error.

recommendation.why: A turns a forgotten commit or rollback into a compile error that names the fix. It also removes the hand-written rollback at every error exit.

whyNot.reason: B's errors say "consume" instead of naming the job, and every `?` before commit needs its own rollback branch.
C compiles a forgotten commit, so every payment can silently roll back.

recommendation.tradeoff: Types that opt in must be finished on purpose; everything else keeps automatic cleanup.

decisions.title: One lane type: exact widths plus a native, scalable width
decisions.gist: Should Jet's twenty named SIMD lane types become one generic type, plus a native type whose width the machine decides?
decisions.lesson: A SIMD lane type holds several numbers that one instruction processes together. Jet has twenty fixed names, like `F32x8`. Code cannot ask for "the widest width here". Arm SVE and RISC-V vector machines choose their width while the program runs. Automatic vectorization of plain loops stays the default whatever wins.
decisions.story: Ines writes an audio filter. On her laptop the best width is eight floats, on the build server sixteen, and on her Graviton host the CPU decides at run time. Today she writes the kernel twice and cannot use the third machine's width at all.
decisions.detail:
Conflicts: D-SIMD1, D-SIMD2, and D-SIMD3=B ratified the twenty named lanes (Docs/spec/reference/core-library.md:1792-1798). A, C, and D supersede that list. They keep auto-vectorization and the `#Scalar` opt-out. Number parameters (#3505, D-CONSTGEN1=A) are required by A and C; today `Packet<4>` is rejected (probe J5).

One meaning across tiers (I9) and D-DEVMODE1: a native width differs between AOT, the Cranelift JIT, and web. `reduce(.Add)` on `Lanes<T>` therefore folds in one fixed logical order, so every tier prints the same bits. An explicit `reduce_unordered(.Add)` trades that guarantee for speed and is visible in review.

Sizeless values: like Arm's `svfloat32_t`, `Lanes<T>` may live in locals, parameters, and returns, but not in struct fields, lists, or `[T#N]`. On fixed-width targets, the build profile's CPU sets its width; D-CPU-DISPATCH1 decides how one binary uses wider units.

Performance gate: ratification needs a paired cell comparing `sum_sq` written with `Lanes<F32>` and the plain auto-vectorized loop, on AVX2, AVX-512, and an SVE host.

Related ratified law (found 2026-10-02): D-FRED1=A already fixes Float reductions to one eight-way pairwise order in every run mode, which settles the I9 reduction concern for lane sums.

options.name: Exact plus native lanes
options.detail: `Lanes<T, N>` takes a fixed-width element type and an exact lane count. `Lanes<T>` is the native vector for the target, with `.count()` known at run time. Lists gain `.lanes()` and `.lanes<N>()` chunk iteration with a masked tail. The ratified operations stay, plus `shuffle` on exact widths.
options.technical: Defined in Core over compiler lane intrinsics (card #4179). `Lanes<T>` lowers to SVE or RVV registers, or to the profile's widest fixed register. Fixed reduction order is part of the Core definition.
options.code: acc := Lanes<F32>.splat(0.0)

options.name: Keep the named family
options.detail: Keep the twenty ratified names and add more, such as F32x16, as hardware needs them.
options.technical: No change.
options.code: acc := F32x8.splat(0.0)

options.detail: Every fixed-width numeric type is defined in Core as a one-lane `Lanes` value, as in Mojo.
options.technical: Fixed-width scalars become library aliases; diagnostics, layout, and FFI mapping must hide the lane form.
options.code: type F32 = Lanes<F32Bits, 1>

options.name: Native width only
options.detail: Only `Lanes<T>`; no exact-width lane types in source.
options.technical: Like Highway with only ScalableTag.
options.code: acc := Lanes<F32>.splat(0.0)

comparisons.note: `Int = Scalar[DType.int]`; all arithmetic is SIMD methods over pop operations.
Sizeless vector types cannot be struct members or array elements.

`#simd[N]T` plus array programming; probe O2 found no SIMD instructions for array math at the tested setting.

whyNot.reason: B needs a new name and a new kernel for every width, and cannot use SVE fully.
C changes every fixed-width type's identity for a SIMD convenience.
D alone cannot pin a width; A keeps D's native type and adds exact widths.

recommendation.tradeoff: Jet migrates twenty names once, so lane code follows new hardware with no new syntax.

decisions.title: Using newer CPU instructions safely in one binary
decisions.gist: How should one Jet binary use newer CPU instructions where they exist and still run everywhere?
decisions.lesson: CPUs add instructions over time, such as AVX-512 on x86. Ratified law builds for a baseline CPU, and an advanced build refuses to start on older machines (D-FFI-ASM-CPU1=B). Today's release builds instead target the build machine's own CPU (card #4192). Experts reach new instructions only through audited assembly. Auto-vectorization stays.
decisions.story: Kai ships a search engine to thousands of customer machines, from old laptops to new servers. He cannot ask customers which CPU they have. He wants one binary that uses AVX-512 where it exists and never fails where it does not.
decisions.detail:
Conflicts: D-FFI-ASM-CPU1=B (baseline by default, explicit flags) stays the default for unmarked code. `Compiler/JetCli/Source/Cli/Host.jet:141` passes `-C target-cpu=native` to release builds against that law; card #4192 fixes it whatever wins. D-OSTARGET2=B made `comptime if $build.os` (then spelled `prep if`) the one dispatch primitive for operating systems; A extends the same primitive to CPU levels inside each copy. D-CORE-CALL1 keeps `__core_intrinsic` compiler-only; A and B add a public, typed `core.arch` instead.

Same bits everywhere: D-DET1 says pure code is reproducible, and I9 requires one meaning across tiers. Copies of a multiversioned function must produce identical bits. Intrinsics that round differently, such as fused multiply-add, are allowed only when the function's effect row admits non-reproducible results. The interpreter and JIT run the baseline copy, so they match it exactly.

AVX-512 and SVE intrinsics need D-LANES1's lane types; 512-bit lanes do not exist today. The start-up probe runs once in the Prelude on every tier.

Related ratified law (found 2026-10-02): D-ACCEL1=A covers measured automatic acceleration of proven kernels; per-CPU copies must compose with it rather than add a second selection mechanism.

options.name: Multiversioned functions
options.detail: `#Multiversion(levels...)` marks a function. The compiler builds one copy per listed CPU level. Inside each copy, `$build.cpu` describes that level, so `comptime if $build.cpu.has(.AVX2)` selects typed `core.arch` intrinsics at build time. At start, the Prelude probes the CPU once and binds the best copy.
options.technical: Typed intrinsics are generated from vendor tables per ISA. Calls from inside a copy go to callees compiled for the same level when they are also marked, else to the baseline. The interpreter and JIT use the baseline copy (I9).

options.name: Run-time feature blocks
options.detail: `cpu.has(...)` returns a Bool and records a flow fact. A `#Target(CPU...)` block is legal only where that fact holds; inside it, intrinsics are callable and codegen enables the features.
options.technical: Blocks lower to outlined functions with target attributes. Callees inlined into a block are cloned so features never leak into baseline callers.
options.code: if cpu.has(.AVX2) { #Target(CPU.AVX2) { ... } }

options.name: Baseline plus build flags
options.detail: Keep D-FFI-ASM-CPU1=B: one CPU level per binary, chosen by build flags. Assembly reaches instructions Jet does not expose.
options.technical: No change beyond fixing #4192.
options.code: jet build --cpu=znver4 --features=+avx2

options.name: Compiler clones hot code
options.detail: A build option compiles hot loops for several CPU levels and dispatches once at start, with no source markers or intrinsics.
options.technical: Function multiversioning chosen by profile or loop heuristics.

decisions.title: Co-editing one program from text and Canvas
decisions.gist: When text and Canvas edit the same file at once, should both edits land, and how?
decisions.lesson: Canvas is Jet's visual editor. Its edits are meaningful operations, such as "rename greet to welcome", each tagged with the file revision it saw. If the file changed meanwhile, Jet refuses the edit. EYG instead treats the syntax tree as the program and shares it over the wire, so many editors can work on it.
decisions.story: Leo moves a call in Canvas while his teammate renames another function in a text editor. The teammate saves first, so Canvas refuses Leo's edit as stale and he redoes it. He wants both edits to land when they do not touch the same thing.
decisions.detail:
Existing law: D-CANVAS-RAD1=A sends every Canvas change through one source-transaction engine. Today that engine checks the file revision and refuses stale edits (Docs/spec/reference/canvas-protocol.md:93-121). A keeps the engine and changes only the stale case: resolve the edit's anchors (names, source ids, resolved references) in the newest revision, replay, format, re-check, and publish atomically. If anchors fail or the check fails, nothing is written, as today.

B conflicts with the Canvas rule that transactions create no graph-side sidecar (canvas-protocol.md:157-158). Text editors keep standard LSP text edits under every option; Canvas keeps its HTTP transport.

Mojo's "no AST" lesson is a separate, internal question about the self-hosted front end. It needs no owner choice and is not on this ballot; the report records it. Content addressing: Jet already hashes build records, and D adds per-definition hashes, which co-editing does not need.

options.name: Replay stale edits
options.detail: When a Canvas edit arrives with an old revision, the server tries to replay it on the current text. It resolves each anchor by name and reference, applies the same semantic operation, formats, and re-checks. Success publishes a new revision. Failure returns a conflict naming the anchor that no longer resolves or the diagnostic that the merged program fails.
options.technical: Reuses the existing check-before-publish seam. Conflict rules: delete versus edit of the same anchor conflicts; edits to different declarations always replay; an edit whose result fails the front-end check is refused with diagnostics.
options.code: {"ok": true, "revision": "sha256-7c…"}

options.name: Shared tree with node IDs
options.detail: The server assigns stable IDs to nodes and stores them beside each file. Editors send tree operations by ID, merged by operational transformation.
options.technical: Red-green tree with an ID map; plain text saves and checkouts force reassignment.
options.code: {"op": "move", "node": "call-91ab", "after": "stmt-22e0", "base": 41}

options.name: Refuse stale edits
options.detail: Keep the current protocol.
options.technical: No change.
options.code: {"ok": false, "conflict": "stale revision"}

options.name: Tree is the program
options.detail: Store definitions as content-addressed trees in the store; text files become generated views and edit buffers.
options.technical: New project storage, version-control adapter, and review tooling.
options.code: welcome = #sha256:4f1c…

comparisons.note: Structural editor targets the IR; text-position mapping is a stated non-goal.
Definitions stored by hash; renames are metadata.
Replay concurrent operations against the newest version and surface true conflicts.

recommendation.why: A lets text and Canvas edits both land when they do not collide, using the semantic edits Canvas already sends.

whyNot.reason: B's stored IDs break on the very edits co-editing must survive, such as a plain save.
C makes the second of two simultaneous edits fail and be redone.
D breaks git, grep, and every text tool for identity Jet does not need here.

recommendation.tradeoff: Jet replays meaningful edits against the newest text instead of storing node identity.

decisions.title: Jet's own sandbox: one portable, confined way to run programs, replacing Docker and WebAssembly
decisions.gist: How should Jet's own sandbox run programs safely on any machine, so it replaces Docker and WebAssembly?
decisions.lesson: Docker confines a program with operating-system walls and ships its Linux files as an image. WebAssembly runs anywhere and grants typed imports, but Jet's ownership and rights words do not survive into it. Unison and EYG show another way: the program is checked code, and the host grants each power. Jet wants its own sandbox like that. This ballot picks what it runs and where its walls come from.
decisions.story: Tomas built a notes tool. Linux users want a binary, his company wants a container, and a partner wants WebAssembly. He maintains three pipelines, and none tells a user what the tool may touch. He wants to ship one file that runs on any machine, asks before it writes anywhere, and cannot do more than it asked.
decisions.detail:
Owner direction (2026-10-02): Jet should build a new, fundamental sandbox for running programs that replaces Docker and WebAssembly. It should follow the spirit of Unison and EYG. Jet must still be able to produce WebAssembly. The earlier draft shipped native builds plus a WebAssembly fallback inside one file. It misread that goal and is withdrawn.

What stays the same under every option:

- WebAssembly stays an export: `jet build --target=wasm32-wasip2` (D-WASISRV1=A) for WASI hosts such as Wasmtime. Running in a browser needs a separate adapter, as today. WebAssembly is no longer how Jet sandboxes its own programs.

- Rights use Jet's existing words: effect rows such as `-[FS.Write, IO]>`, `--allow=`/`--deny=` (D-RIGHTS-CLI1=B), the run prompt (D-SCRIPT-CONFIRM1), and Authority lending (D-PLUGIN1=A).

- The file is `Output.Bundle{..., form: .Portable}` producing `notes.jetapp`, an app form inside `Bundle` (D-ECO-OUTPUT-KINDS1=A). `.jetapp` is a new `.jet*` artifact kind, which D-ARTIFACT-EXT1 says needs a ballot; this is that ballot.

- Grants live in the host's trust store, never in the shipped file. This amends D-SCRIPT-CONFIRM1 for app files. Today `always` writes the grant into the script or package.jet. A shipped app file cannot change, so `always` saves the grant in the trust store, keyed by the file's hash. The prompt words stay the same. An app grants a dependency only rights it holds itself.

The Jet sandbox under A and B (new). The shipped file holds checked Jet code in a versioned portable format. It is built from Jet's shared program form (D-TIER-FORM1=A MIR) with a stable encoding. Every library inside is named by the hash of its content, as Unison names definitions. So a host verifies and stores each library once, and two apps share it. Before anything runs, the host:

1. Checks the format version. An unknown version stops with a message naming the Jet runtime that can run it.

2. Verifies the code itself: structure, types, memory safety, control flow, and the list of host calls. It never trusts types or rights written by whoever built the file. A file that fails verification never runs. A changed file that still verifies is a different program: it has a new hash, and its grants are asked again. When the user requires a signature, a signature mismatch stops it too.

3. Compares the rights the code needs with the grants given. Missing grants stop the program before it starts, or prompt.

Then the program runs with no ambient authority. Files, network, clock, and processes are reached only through handles the host hands in, and a handle cannot be forged. Effect rows erase after compiling today (spec.md:1335-1339). In the sandbox, host calls are real gates checked again on every call, not erased facts.

- Narrow grants: a handle can be narrowed, for example to one directory. A narrowed handle cannot reach outside it, even through `..` or symbolic links. The command-line spelling for narrow grants is the open D-AUTH-NARROW1. Until it lands, the examples grant whole effects such as `FS.Write`, which means all files the user can write.

- Speed: the first run starts in Jet's interpreter while native code is compiled on that machine; later runs use the cached native code. Interpreter, JIT, and native code enforce the same walls. The native cache and the record of verified libraries have a combined key. It covers file hash, host, compiler version, verifier version, and security policy. Native code inside a shipped file is never trusted.

- Limits: memory, CPU time, stack, task count, open handles, disk, and output are capped per run. Defaults are safe; the user raises them with flags.

- A pure Jet app runs on any CPU and OS that has the Jet runtime, with the same behavior, as every Docker machine needs Docker.

- `jet build --target=sandbox` (D-ONCE-SANDBOX1) produces this file instead of a WebAssembly component. This reverses D-DEP-WASM1's choice of WebAssembly over a Jet virtual machine for sandboxing.

- Trusted base: the verifier, the runtime and its host-call broker, the native compiler and its cache. For helpers under A, it also includes the OS kernel and its isolation features. Not promised: protection from bugs in these, or from hardware side channels such as Spectre. They need their own security review.

The one difference between A and B: foreign code. Many Docker images exist to run C libraries and other programs. Foreign code (`FFI`) cannot be verified, so it cannot run inside the sandbox.

- A: foreign code runs in a separate helper process walled off by the operating system. The walls are Linux namespaces with seccomp and Landlock, macOS App Sandbox, or Windows AppContainer. The app talks to the helper only through a typed interface: values are copied across, and resources cross as handles. The helper gets only rights the app lends it.

- A, what cannot cross: C pointers, callbacks, and borrowed buffers cannot cross a process boundary. A foreign API that needs them must be wrapped by Jet code inside the helper that offers a typed interface. Otherwise the build rejects it.

- A, where helpers run: helpers are native code, so they are built per CPU and OS. An app with helpers runs only where a helper build exists. Elsewhere it stops with a message naming the missing build. If the host cannot provide the OS walls, the helper does not start and the app stops. Under A there is no unconfined fallback.

- B: a portable app cannot contain foreign code. Apps that need it ship as ordinary native programs, which the host labels TRUSTED (as D-MEM-GUARANTEE1 labels memory facts).

C (new) uses operating-system walls only. The file holds a native build per CPU and OS. The host runs it inside the same OS walls A uses for helpers, with a broker for every request. Foreign code works as in Docker. An unlisted CPU or OS cannot run the app. The walls differ by OS, and a native program's rights are only as strong as those walls.

Acceptance for whichever option wins. A denied write stops before running, and a granted write succeeds. A narrowed handle cannot write outside its directory. A file that fails verification is rejected before running. A missing OS wall stops a helper. The same pure Jet file gives the same output on two CPU types. These are criteria, not results.

Performance gate: a paired cell compares startup, size, and throughput with an OCI container and with plain wasmtime on the same app.

Removed from the earlier draft: native builds plus a WebAssembly fallback, because the owner rejected WebAssembly as the sandbox. Also removed: source rebuild, which needs a compiler on every host and adds no walls, and "no change".

The unratified proposal Docs/proposals/jetpack/portable-platform-specification.md (JPM/1, JPH/1) is A and B's ancestor; this ballot replaces it as the decision point. JetOS's capability-first install (D-JOS-INSTALLTRUST1) should install the same file. A amends the embedding rules (spec.md:4029-4043) so that foreign calls cross a process boundary.

options.technical: Versioned portable encoding of D-TIER-FORM1 MIR; host verifier; brokered unforgeable handles; interpreter then local native cache; per-OS helper isolation.
options.code: SHIP :: Output.Bundle{name: "notes", of: APP, form: .Portable}

options.name: Jet sandbox, no foreign code inside
options.detail: Everything in A, but a portable app cannot contain foreign code; apps that need it ship as trusted native programs.
options.technical: As A, without the helper layer.
options.code: SHIP :: Output.Bundle{name: "notes", of: APP, form: .Portable}

options.name: Native builds behind OS walls
options.detail: The file holds a native build per CPU and OS. The host runs it inside OS walls with a broker for every request, like a typed Docker.
options.technical: Per-target native builds; per-OS isolation; brokered requests.
options.code:
SHIP :: Output.Bundle{name: "notes", of: APP, form: .Native,
    targets: ["x86_64-linux", "aarch64-macos"]}

comparisons.note: OS walls around a whole Linux userland; rights are mounts and flags, not typed.
Bounds-checked memory; outside access only through granted imports; Jet types and ownership are flattened away.
Abilities declare effects and handlers supply them; code is named by content hash.
comparisons.code:
structural ability Abort where
  abort : {Abort} a

comparisons.note: Every effect is performed through the host, and a program's effects are known before it runs.

recommendation.why: A is Jet's own sandbox: verified code, host-granted powers, and pure Jet apps that run alike everywhere. It still runs foreign code, as Docker does.

whyNot.reason: B leaves every app that uses a C library outside the sandbox, still needing Docker.
C is a typed Docker: walls differ by OS, and an unlisted CPU cannot run the app.

recommendation.tradeoff: Jet must make its verifier and runtime trustworthy, and foreign code needs per-system helper builds. In return, every app runs confined, and pure Jet apps run anywhere.

decisions.title: One protection duty follows every sensitive copy
decisions.gist: Should sensitive data stay protected across memory, CPU registers, swap, crash reports, and outgoing copies?
decisions.lesson: Mark sensitive data at input: #Credential for tokens, #Secret for keys, and #PII for private personal information. Wiping overwrites old bytes. Registers are the CPU's temporary storage; swap and crash dumps save memory to disk. Today, crypto buffers get some cleanup, but labels alone do not promise it. This choice covers sensitive copies throughout the program. Plain memory is never wiped.
decisions.story: Nora verifies a login token with a private key. She wants every temporary copy protected, including copies inside the verifier or a crash report. A later deliberate send must name an authorized receiver; it must not silently weaken local cleanup.
decisions.detail:
Owner refinement: A must cover controlled heap and stack copies, CPU registers, swap, core dumps, crash reports and outgoing copies. The previous exclusions are removed. The sole disclosure boundary is an explicitly authorized send after which kernel or recipient copies belong to that destination. No automatic weakening is allowed when a required primitive is absent.

The displayed Jet verification program passed night12 source checking through laneS on 2026-10-02. Scratch: ~/.cache/jet-test-scratch/sol/BallotRev4/memory.jet. This establishes accepted ordinary code, not implemented protection or runtime login success. No security, page-lock, register-erasure or memory-recovery experiment was run.

Docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:2789-2799 records D-TAINT1 and ratified D-TAINT2=A. #Credential expr is the direct expression spelling used in Examples/features/crypto/auth_tokens.jet:6-9 and tests/taint.rs:459-461. Docs/spec/spec.md:542-548 permits direct tags on values. Core/sys/sys.jet:14 does not classify every environment variable as secret; the example marks its acquisition result immediately.

Core/auth/auth.jet:51-74 copies token bytes, splits and decodes components, makes strings and parses them before signature verification. Those internal copies must share A's protection duty. Core/crypto/crypto.jet:95-112 already provides Secret.Close through core.crypto.__zeroize. crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/CoreLib/Top/CryptoEntropy.rs:143-148,515-520 provides volatile erasure and a compiler fence. Existing tagged-expression lowering in Codegen/TIR/lower/expressions.rs:8413-8416 currently adds no storage protection.

A uses one sensitivity duty, independent of permission to disclose. Canonical Secret, Credential and PII labels and Core crypto secret types seed it. Input and ordinary origin labels do not. The duty follows actual sensitive contents through acquisition, conversion, copies, interpolation, collections, captures, Core helpers and foreign staging. Scrub and token validation cannot remove cleanup from surviving sensitive bytes. Unrelated plain fields remain ordinary and are never wiped.

Heap contents, sensitive stack slots and compiler spills live in dedicated protected storage. Do not put secret spills on an unlocked ordinary stack. Reserve and protect storage before populating it. Wipe abandoned bytes on growth, shrinking, overwrite, physical move-out and final release. A pointer transfer makes no new content copy. Retain live aliases and wipe only after their last use. Track sensitive extents; do not erase unrelated plain fields or already-clean space.

Select cleanup during compilation when contents are known. Input-dependent mixed containers retain minimal sensitivity state. There is no global ordinary-memory scan and no allocator-wide wiping. Group small sensitive allocations into bounded protected pools rather than one costly page allocation per string. Preserve these properties across inlining, optimization, register allocation and every execution backend.

Only functions touching sensitive contents receive register cleanup. Clear every physical integer, floating-point or vector register that held secret bits when the sensitive operation returns. Track callee-saved registers, temporary lanes and exceptional exits, not just argument registers. Return sensitive results through protected storage so clearing registers cannot erase a live return value. Restore unrelated caller state correctly. A compiler backend unable to prove its spill and register cleanup refuses sensitive code.

Real precedent: GCC's -fzero-call-used-regs and Clang's zero_call_used_regs attribute clear selected caller-used registers at function return. Sources: https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc/Optimize-Options.html and https://clang.llvm.org/docs/AttributeReference.html#zero-call-used-regs. These are useful mechanisms, not complete guarantees. They do not alone cover every callee-saved secret, sensitive return register, stack copy or asynchronous crash. A requires the stronger tracked cleanup described above.

Swap protection is mandatory. Use mlock on Linux/POSIX and VirtualLock on Windows for controlled sensitive pages, checking every result. Reserve the bounded sensitive pool before input acquisition. Insufficient lock allowance produces a clear startup error naming required and available bytes and the missing permission or limit. Never populate an unlocked fallback. Later growth either secures new storage before copying or fails without exposing old contents. Ordinary-only programs do not reserve this pool.

Sources: https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/mlock.2.html and https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/memoryapi/nf-memoryapi-virtuallock. Locks operate on whole pages and can fail under host limits. Linux locks do not automatically protect forked children. Use protected stack/spill storage, suppress uncontrolled copying during fork, and require a protected child startup for declared secret ownership. On Linux, MADV_DONTFORK prevents accidental inheritance of the protected pool.

Crash protection is mandatory too. Exclude protected pages using MADV_DONTDUMP or a verified platform equivalent. Runtime panic, error, logging and crash-report paths never render secret values. Page omission is insufficient when a crash catches a live secret in a CPU register. Therefore disable ordinary raw process dumps while sensitive code can execute, and produce secret-free Jet reports instead. On Linux use verified PR_SET_DUMPABLE=0, not merely RLIMIT_CORE=0, which piped dump collectors can ignore.

Sources: https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/madvise.2.html, https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/core.5.html and https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/PR_SET_DUMPABLE.2const.html. Windows WerRegisterExcludedMemoryBlock supplies report-memory exclusions, but not by itself complete register-context protection. Its documentation is https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/werapi/nf-werapi-werregisterexcludedmemoryblock. A Windows provider must also prove register-context and crash-channel suppression. VirtualLock plus this page API alone is not advertised as full support.

Ordinary mlock does not prevent hibernation from saving RAM. Do not conceal that gap. Linux memfd_secret inhibits hibernation while its protected mappings exist, locks their memory, marks them non-dumpable and isolates them from ordinary kernel access. Use it for protected sensitive storage where available, alongside register and crash controls. Its kernel free path zeros pages, covering abrupt process death without depending on user cleanup. The descriptor is private, close-on-exec and not inherited into unapproved children.

Sources: https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/memfd_secret.2.html and https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/master/mm/secretmem.c. The kernel source explicitly sets VMA_DONTDUMP and zeroes pages in secretmem_free_folio. Some kernels or architectures lack this primitive. Other hosts need a verified equivalent for protected residency, crash exclusion and zero-on-final-release, including abrupt termination. Otherwise A refuses sensitive execution; it does not substitute best effort or assume a plain lock solves hibernation.

Input adapters also protect process-owned source copies. Environment input must protect the original live environment value and controlled loader temporaries, not merely the returned String. If that adapter cannot take protected ownership of its source copy, refuse it and require a protected input channel. The same duty covers input decoding and any late classification still capable of leaving old controlled copies. Reject classifications too late to cover abandoned copies; never claim retroactive recovery.

Every Jet-controlled external boundary carries the duty or refuses the operation. This includes FFI arguments and results, I/O staging, serialization, logging, subprocess environments and crash collectors. A declared receiving owner must accept sensitive ownership, protect its copies and clear them; an unannotated foreign routine is not trusted because it borrowed a pointer. Use existing ownership signatures and audited authority/taint exits, not an implicit plain-string escape. Scrub removes a disclosure restriction, never the protection duty.

An explicit authorized send identifies the destination and deliberately transfers responsibility for bytes it keeps. Kernel send buffers and remote receiver copies after that handoff are the one boundary; Jet cannot erase another owner's live data. Jet still protects and wipes its own marshalling, retry, serialization and I/O buffers. Sending or saving secret bytes without that declared handoff is refused. No new send syntax is invented here; existing audited authority and owning-receiver declarations carry the approval.

memfd_secret pages cannot be passed directly to system calls. Approved sends therefore use narrowly scoped locked, non-dumpable staging, cleared after the kernel accepts the authorized transfer. Isolate any such staging from unrelated plain buffers. Likewise a foreign library must provide an audited protected adapter rather than secretly copying into ordinary heap memory. Controlled local copies never become exempt merely because the API belongs to another language.

Exact unsupported-platform policy: compilation refuses a target/backend without the complete protection contract. Kernel availability, locked-memory allowance and enforced crash controls are checked before the first sensitive input. Failure is a named startup error, not a warning followed by execution. Browser JavaScript and WASI hosts without enforceable register, residency and dump controls are refused for sensitive code. Managed-runtime immutable strings are not a fallback. Plain code remains available and unchanged.

B is the credible portable alternative: perform available cleanup and protections, but continue when a host primitive is missing. It publishes missing protections in build facts and startup warnings. libsodium documents a similar best-effort allocation policy: sodium_malloc may return unlocked memory if locking fails. Source: https://libsodium.gitbook.io/doc/memory_management. A borrows its erasure and locking mechanisms but removes that silent weakening. The Rust peer shows the same login workload with final-string cleanup, not A's full guarantee.

Design-away pass: A protects one sensitivity duty rather than requiring several user wrappers. Compilation avoids overhead for plain-only paths and redundant wipes. Protected pooling avoids needless page allocations. Page protections, register clearing, protected external ownership and secret-free reports close the old recommendation's gaps. Required overwriting and locked residency cannot be eliminated while promising erasure and no swap. Unsupported hosts refuse rather than manufacture trust.

Self comprehension pass, BallotRev4 using RLI5: explain finds registers, swap, dumps and wiping defined before the code. Predict distinguishes protected local copies from a later authorized receiver. Modify marks newly acquired private personal data with #PII. Derive finds the unsupported-host refusal and startup lock error stated on the surface. The pass removes the old exclusions and explains why raw crash dumps need replacement. This is an author self-pass, not independent review or security verification.

options.name: Guaranteed protection, or refuse
options.detail: One duty follows every sensitive copy. Wipe dead heap and stack copies, clear secret registers, prevent swap and secret crash output, and check external handoffs. Refuse missing protections before reading secrets. Plain memory is never wiped.
options.technical: Compiler-directed protected storage and register cleanup combine with mandatory page locking, dump exclusion, crash-context suppression and audited owning receivers. Unsupported platforms are refused; insufficient locked-memory allowance is a startup error. All controlled marshalling and source copies remain covered. Only explicitly authorized kernel/recipient ownership crosses the guarantee boundary.

options.name: Best effort, with visible gaps
options.detail: Use the same labels and ordinary calls, but continue if required host protections are unavailable. State missing protections in build facts and startup warnings. Local wiping still runs; swap, registers or crash copies may remain.
options.technical: Attempt available page locking, crash exclusions and register cleanup. Record which protections are absent, but allow execution to continue. This preserves portability by explicitly weakening the guarantee. Plain memory remains unwiped; disclosure restrictions remain.

comparisons.note: Zeroizing automatically erases final owned buffers on drop. Its documentation explicitly warns about earlier reallocations, moves and temporaries, and excludes register clearing and operating-system protection. Source: https://docs.rs/zeroize/latest/zeroize/.

SecretBox provides explicit secret access, prevents accidental logging and wipes on drop. Loading from deserialized input still requires care with intermediate secret input. Source: https://docs.rs/secrecy/latest/secrecy/.

Both provide selective function-return register clearing. This does not independently prove secure spills, live return values, callee-saved secrets or crash contexts. Sources: https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc/Optimize-Options.html and https://clang.llvm.org/docs/AttributeReference.html#zero-call-used-regs.

sodium_mlock checks host locking; sodium_malloc can continue with unlocked memory if locking fails. sodium_free overwrites before release. Source: https://libsodium.gitbook.io/doc/memory_management. A adopts the mechanisms but refuses the fallback.

recommendation.why: A combines compiler-placed erasure with protected storage and checked handoffs. Ordinary data stays unchanged. Missing protections fail before secrets are read, rather than creating false trust.

whyNot.reason: B reports missing protections but still permits secrets to reach registers, swap or crash files.

recommendation.tradeoff: After an explicitly authorized send, copies kept by the kernel or recipient belong to that destination. Jet still wipes its own buffers.

surface.gist: Should sensitive data stay protected across memory, CPU registers, swap, crash reports, and outgoing copies?
surface.lesson: Mark sensitive data at input: #Credential for tokens, #Secret for keys, and #PII for private personal information. Wiping overwrites old bytes. Registers are the CPU's temporary storage; swap and crash dumps save memory to disk. Today, crypto buffers get some cleanup, but labels alone do not promise it. This choice covers sensitive copies throughout the program. Plain memory is never wiped.

current.note: Jet accepts this real login check. Labels restrict disclosure, but do not yet promise erasure of its temporary copies.

wild.note: Rust's Zeroizing wipes final strings, not every earlier copy. Sources: https://docs.rs/zeroize/latest/zeroize/ and https://docs.rs/jsonwebtoken/latest/jsonwebtoken/fn.decode.html.

options.name: Guaranteed protection, or refuse
options.gist: One duty protects every sensitive copy; missing protections stop execution.
gains: Copies and CPU registers are cleared; locked pages cannot enter swap.
Secret pages and registers never enter crash dumps or diagnostic output.
Outgoing copies stay protected unless you explicitly authorize their destination.
losses: Sensitive storage needs erasure and locked memory.
Unsupported platforms or insufficient lock allowances cannot run sensitive code.
Raw crash dumps are replaced by secret-free reports.

options.name: Best effort, with visible gaps
options.gist: Continue with a warning when the host cannot supply every protection.
gains: Sensitive programs can run on more platforms.
losses: Registers, swap or crash files can retain sensitive bytes.
Warnings do not make missing protection safe.

recommendation.why: A combines compiler-placed erasure with protected storage and checked handoffs. Ordinary data stays unchanged. Missing protections fail before secrets are read, rather than creating false trust.
gains: Plain memory is never wiped; existing string operations remain.

losses.loss: Sensitive storage needs erasure and locked memory.
losses.mitigation: Erasure overwrites bytes; preventing swap requires keeping their pages in memory. Ordinary data pays neither cost.

losses.loss: Unsupported platforms or insufficient lock allowances cannot run sensitive code.
losses.mitigation: A host without the required protections cannot supply this guarantee. Jet reports missing support or insufficient allowance before reading secrets.

losses.loss: Raw crash dumps are replaced by secret-free reports.
losses.mitigation: A crash can catch a secret in a CPU register. Omitting secret pages alone cannot remove that register from a dump.

whyNot.reason: B reports missing protections but still permits secrets to reach registers, swap or crash files.

recommendation.tradeoff: After an explicitly authorized send, copies kept by the kernel or recipient belong to that destination. Jet still wipes its own buffers.

decisions.title: Check through verified MIR, with a quick escape
decisions.gist: Should jet check verify lowered code by default, with a quick mode and reuse for unchanged builds?
decisions.lesson: Semantic checking checks source rules. Lowering turns checked source into MIR, the compiler's typed middle representation. Its verifier catches broken compiler output. Today, the Rust CLI stops before lowering; the Jet CLI goes farther. Neither behavior promises emission or linking success. This choice makes both compilers share one checking path. Reuse depends on D-EFF-BUILD-REUSE1 passing.
decisions.story: Iris checks a report program before committing it. Check says it has no problems, but build finds a missing compiler route for core.math.copy. She wants check to find that compiler defect before she asks for an executable.
decisions.detail:
Source/CmdCompile.rs:3473-3645 handles the Rust CLI check path and returns before runtime compilation. Driver/mod.rs:6579-6607 lowers build input and validates MIR. Lowering failure is an internal compiler error under I2, not bad user source. Existing build verification stays mandatory under every option.

The Jet CLI has drifted: Host.jet:49-58 calls jet_cli_compile_file, as does build. Request.jet:226 calls jet_driver_compile. Pipeline.jet:2467-2680 lowers, optimizes, validates, and emits Rust into memory. Whichever option wins, both compilers move to the same stage-controlled path. No check option emits source, machine code, or calls rustc.

Shared deep path: finish semantic checking, lower the same selected source closure that build uses, and verify the resulting MIR. Include the selected MIR transformations and final legality check before saving a reusable artifact. Add the copy-fact rule from #4318 and ownership verification from #4309 as those checks land. Check and build use identical target, profile, facts, and verifier versions. Do not suppress a failure or report an internal defect as a source mistake.

Scope remains read-only. Project checks retain their existing inspect-only programmable-build behavior, without running build actions or granting new authority. Deep checking does not invoke the program. A verified-MIR success means lowering and the available MIR checks passed for these exact inputs. It cannot promise future backend, emitter, linker, toolchain, resource, or runtime success. I2 still requires fixing those defects rather than blaming user code.

A uses the owner's proposed --quick spelling for sema-only checks. B uses --deep for explicit deep checking. These are new CLI flags, not existing spellings. Alternatives considered were a new jet verify command and existing jet build --verify <receipt-id>. The former duplicates check; the latter rebuilds a recorded artifact, not an arbitrary source-only check. The ballot chooses the two flag spellings directly and adds no second command.

A's reuse is the check-to-build case of D-EFF-BUILD-REUSE1 on #4308, the default bounded local reuse proposal. Store verified MIR and checked facts, not a boolean success. Key them by a content hash covering every input. Include sources, dependency and generated-source closure, Core, compiler/schema identity, target, profile, options, and checked settings. Include positive and negative dependencies, authority-sensitive facts, and build-input facts.

Check and build normalize to the same compilation key; command presentation is separate. No matching key means recompute the full path. No partial invalidation is introduced. An unchanged build starts from that exact verified artifact and facts, then performs its remaining emission and linking work. Quick check cannot publish a verified-MIR record. Failed or incomplete checking cannot publish one either.

Cache trust, integrity, identical diagnostics, limits, eviction, leases, and bypass follow D-EFF-BUILD-REUSE1. If its A loses, this ballot's cache portion falls away; default depth and --quick remain independently usable. B does not introduce a new cache policy. Full-build measurements retain the separate no-user-reuse lane.

Measured once through laneS with the prebuilt night12 compiler. The scratch fixture copies the 68 non-comment lines of Examples/features/math/math_audit.jet. Check took 7.564 seconds, exit 0. Build took 12.744 seconds, exit 101, before emission. Its error says checked Core call core.math.copy has no canonical TIR record. The surface shows that workload's small excerpt; the excerpt was not separately executed. No timing rerun or attempted fix was made.

The observed gap is 5.180 seconds, about 40.6% of the aborted build's elapsed time. It includes build preparation and repeated front-end work, not an isolated lowering-plus-verifier measurement. There is no successful-build timing or measured deep-check overhead here. A's exact overhead and reuse savings remain unmeasured. Lowering and verification add work on misses; emission and rustc are deliberately excluded. Store and reuse only complete verified results, so this failing fixture cannot become a cache hit.

options.name: Deep by default, quick on request
options.detail: Plain check lowers and verifies MIR. --quick stops after semantic checking. With D-EFF-BUILD-REUSE1=A, unchanged build reuses the complete verified MIR and checked facts. Any changed input recomputes everything. Check still makes no emission or linking promise.
options.technical: One shared stop-after-verified-MIR pipeline serves both compilers and builds. Retain copy and ownership facts for their validators. --quick is an explicit weaker result. Conditional bounded local storage uses complete content-key equality, not partial invalidation.

options.name: Deep only with a flag
options.detail: Plain check remains sema-only. The new --deep flag uses the shared lowering and MIR verification path without emission. Iris must remember it to find this compiler defect. Build always verifies independently.
options.technical: Use the same stage-controlled pipeline as A, but default to the semantic stop point. --deep selects verified MIR. Neither --deep nor this option claims a successful emitter or linker. Existing bounded reuse decisions remain separate.

options.name: Deep checking only during build
options.detail: Keep check sema-only with no new flag. Build lowers and verifies before emission, as the Rust CLI does today. Iris discovers the defect only when requesting an executable. Align the Jet CLI with that split.
options.technical: The shared pipeline has semantic and verified-MIR stop points, but only build selects the latter publicly. Remove unnecessary lowering and in-memory emission from JetCli check. Both compilers retain the same source, authority, and diagnostic rules.

comparisons.note: Cargo omits final code generation. Rust checks MIR ownership first, but emission-only errors can still remain. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-check.html and https://rustc-dev-guide.rust-lang.org/overview.html

recommendation.why: A makes ordinary check find lowering defects. Quick remains available, and conditional reuse avoids repeating verified work in an unchanged build.

whyNot.reason: B makes the useful check depend on remembering a new deep flag.
C leaves lowering defects hidden until users ask for an executable.

recommendation.tradeoff: Changed-input checks do more work. Quick opts out, and unchanged builds can reuse verified results if the reuse proposal wins.

gains: Ordinary check catches lowering, copy-fact, and ownership-verifier failures as checks land.
Unchanged builds reuse verified work if D-EFF-BUILD-REUSE1 passes.

options.gist: Plain check stays sema-only; new --deep requests lowering and verification.

options.gist: Keep sema-only check; build remains the first lowering and verification step.
gains: No new check flag.
losses: Users must request a build to discover lowering defects.

gains: One shared verified-MIR path defines what ordinary check actually proves.

losses.loss: Changed-input checks pay additional lowering and verification work.
losses.mitigation: Source checks alone cannot prove that lowering produced legal MIR. The extra pass must run on changed inputs.

losses.loss: Conditional reuse stores bounded local compiler artifacts.
losses.mitigation: Reusing complete verified work requires keeping MIR and facts. Storage limits follow D-EFF-BUILD-REUSE1; if reuse loses, this loss disappears.

decisions.comment: Owner chose C in chat 2026-10-02: jet check stays sema-only; build is the first lowering and verification step. Follow-up: both compilers move to one shared check path that stops after sema (the JetCli drift where check runs the whole pipeline is a defect).

decisions.title: User-defined equality for Map and Set keys
decisions.gist: How should a type tell Map and Set when two of its values count as the same key?
decisions.lesson: A Map finds values by key; a Set keeps one copy of each value. Today both compare raw fields, so values a type calls equal can become separate entries. Every option lets a type define key sameness. They differ in how much the author writes, and whether ==, sorting and lookup can ever disagree.
decisions.explainer:
Words first. A Map stores values under keys, like a dictionary stores definitions under words. A Set stores each value once, like a guest list. Equality decides whether two keys are the same. Ordering decides which key sorts first, and Jet keeps Map keys sorted. Hashing turns a value into a number that picks a storage bucket quickly. It never decides sameness on its own.

Today Jet checks a key by looking at its fields. A struct whose fields are numbers, text or other such structs is accepted, and Map compares those fields exactly. A hand-written equal function on the type is ignored by Map. So == can say two emails match while the Map stores both.

Option A adds one small trait, KeyBy. A type writes one function, key, that returns an ordinary value such as lowercase text. Jet builds ==, ordering, sorting, Map lookup and Set hashing from that one value. Because everything comes from one value, the rules cannot contradict each other. The author proves no comparison laws and writes no hashing code. Choosing the right key is still the author's job, checked by ordinary tests.

Option B keeps today's field rules and adds a wrapper, Key<T>. The author writes equal, compare and hash by hand, then wraps every key with Key.new. Option C honours the same three hand-written functions directly, with no wrapper. B and C both need a new public hashing API. Both trust the author to keep three functions consistent.

Reading the code: x := ... creates a changeable variable. [Email:Int]{} creates an empty Map from Email to Int. m[k] = 1 stores 1 under k. m.get(k) ?? 0 looks k up and gives 0 when it is missing. impl Email.KeyBy { ... } attaches the KeyBy trait to Email.

Edge cases. Under A a lookup cannot miss a stored key, because the key value uses Jet's own lawful comparisons. Under B and C a wrong hand-written rule can make a lookup miss, though it never corrupts memory. Re-inserting an equal key replaces the value and keeps the first stored key, under every option.
decisions.story: Ana is porting the Jet command-line tool from Rust. It keeps tables keyed by file paths, and a//b and a/b must land in one entry, exactly as in Rust. Her sign-up demo has the same problem with emails that differ only in capital letters.
decisions.detail:
Current code. Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Comparability.jet:367-375 and 422-465 accept a Map key by walking its fields; a hand-written equal is not consulted. Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Expressions/Literals.jet:552-553 holds the E0502 refusal text, which also refuses lists as keys.

crates/jet-foundation/src/Collections.rs:75-100 keeps separate Map-key and Set-element checks. crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Core.rs:2681 stores Map in a sorted BTreeMap. No public Hash or KeyHasher declaration exists today.

Scope. Card #4499 needs path keys for the command-line port. The OSPath type and its component rules belong to D-OSPATH-NATIVE1 (#4378), which uses whichever mechanism this vote picks. Under A this ballot amends D-MAP-KEY1=A twice: KeyBy types become keys, and lists of eligible keys become keys. Sorted Map iteration stays. Examples are proposed, not run.

options.name: One comparison key (KeyBy)
options.detail:
A type writes one function that returns its comparison key. Jet derives ==, ordering, sorting, Map lookup and Set hashing from that key, so they always agree. Ordinary structs keep today's automatic field rules unchanged.

Beginner: write fn key(self) returning the value that should decide sameness, often one field. Expert: return a tuple for a multi-part key, or a list for a path-like key. No separate equality, ordering or hash laws need proving, because all three come from one value.

Whether that value matches the program's idea of identity is still the author's choice, and ordinary tests check it. For example, key returning text.lower(self.address) makes Ana@Example.com and ana@example.com one entry. Returning self.address unchanged makes them two entries again.

Types that already hand-write equal or compare and are used as keys are migrated by jet fix, so no existing behavior changes. OSPath from D-OSPATH-NATIVE1 uses this mechanism. Its key is its list of path components, so a//b and a/b are one entry.
options.technical:
Core adds trait KeyBy with one method, fn key(self) -> K, where K is the trait's associated key type (D-LIB2). key must be pure and infallible: no effect row and no error suffix. Otherwise E0502 names the effect or error.

K must be Map-eligible for Map use and Set-eligible for Set use. Eligible now includes [T] for eligible T, ordered item by item with a shorter prefix first. K may be another KeyBy type; a cycle is E0502. Float stays ineligible.

A KeyBy type gets Equatable, Comparable and internal hashing derived from key. A hand-written equal or compare, or a signed marker for those traits, on the same type is a new error naming both declarations. A type with hand-written equal or compare and no KeyBy stops being a key; E0502 suggests KeyBy.

Migration for those types, which are keys today through the field walk (Comparability.jet:446-453). jet fix finds each one used as a Map key or Set element. If its equal compares one derived value, f(self.x) == f(other.x), KeyBy returns f(self.x) and the hand-written equal and compare are deleted. Otherwise KeyBy returns the tuple of all fields, exactly today's Map identity. The old equal becomes the named method equal_by_rule, and existing == calls on that type are rewritten to it, so both behaviors stay.

In the second case, equality reached through generic code, such as list contains or assert_eq, cannot be rewritten at its site. jet fix lists those uses for review.

The implementing type may not hold Shared, Cell, Atomic, weak or native-handle fields at any depth, so its key cannot change while stored. Such fields are not key-eligible today either, so no current key type is excluded. Each insert, get or remove calls key once on its argument. A computed key is stored beside its entry; a key that only reads fields is read in place.

Re-inserting an equal key replaces the value and keeps the first stored key. Set union and intersection keep left-side values; difference keeps left-only values. Iteration follows key order. Every tier uses the same derived code, and no public hasher or seed is exposed.

options.name: Explicit Key wrapper
options.detail:
Keep today's field rules for ordinary keys. Add one Core wrapper, Key<T>, whose Map and Set behaviour calls the type's hand-written equal, compare and hash.

Beginner: learn the wrapper and three trait functions for any custom key. Expert: write all three and keep them consistent; wrap at every insert and lookup. A wrong rule can make lookups miss but cannot corrupt memory.
options.technical:
Key.new(^T) owns its value; T needs Equatable, Comparable for Map and Hash for Set. Missing traits are front-end errors. The new public trait is Hash.hash(self, state: &KeyHasher). KeyHasher.write(value) accepts any Set-eligible value; its seed is runtime-owned and never exposed.

Laws are the author's duty: compare says Equal exactly when equal is true, ordering is consistent, and equal values hash alike. The compiler checks signatures, purity and immutability only. Replacement, removal and Set representative rules match A.

options.name: Honour hand-written traits directly
options.detail:
Map and Set call the type's hand-written equal, compare and hash with no wrapper. Ordinary structs keep today's field rules.

Beginner: ordinary Map syntax, but three trait functions to write. Expert: full control over each rule, with the duty to keep all three consistent. A wrong rule can make lookups miss but cannot corrupt memory.
options.technical: Uses the same new public Hash and KeyHasher API, laws and immutability checks as B. Map uses compare; Set uses hash then equal. The compiler checks signatures, purity and immutability, not mathematical laws.

comparisons.note: Rust Path compares components, while BTreeMap and HashSet use key traits.

recommendation.why: One key value makes equality, sorting, Map and Set agree by construction. Authors write one short function, prove no comparison laws and never write hashing code.
gains: ==, sorting, Map and Set can never disagree.
A custom key needs one short function and no hash code.
No new public hashing API is needed.

losses.loss: A computed key is stored once beside each entry.
losses.mitigation: computing and storing are separate costs. key runs once per insert, get or remove, never during the search. Only computed keys are stored, about the key's own size per entry; keys that only read fields are read in place and add nothing.

losses.loss: Existing key types with a hand-written equal or compare stop being keys until migrated.
losses.mitigation: jet fix migrates each one. A simple equal becomes the key; otherwise the key is all fields, as Map uses today, and == calls move to the old equal, now equal_by_rule.

whyNot.reason: Wrapping every key adds ceremony, and authors must still keep three hand-written functions consistent.
Three hand-written functions can quietly disagree and make lookups miss. It also needs a new public hashing API.

recommendation.tradeoff: A asks for one key function instead of three. Its costs are one stored copy of a computed key and a jet fix migration for key types that already hand-write equal or compare.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Run the Email and path examples on every tier: both spellings find one entry and == agrees. Check refusals for an effectful or fallible key, hand-written equal beside KeyBy, a Shared field, a key cycle and a Float key.

Check list keys order item by item, re-insert keeps the first key, Set union keeps left values and sorted iteration stays.

Migration: an Email with hand-written equal comparing lower(address) becomes KeyBy with that key. A type with an unrecognized equal gets the all-fields key and equal_by_rule, and its Map results and == results match before and after jet fix.
