recommendation.tradeoff: A asks for one key function instead of three; it costs one stored computed key and a jet fix migration.

decisions.situation: Jet's Map is a lookup table from keys to values, and its Set is a collection that keeps each value once. Today both decide whether two keys are the same by comparing their raw stored fields, even when the type has its own idea of equality. So Ana@Example.com and ana@example.com, or the file paths a//b and a/b, become two separate entries. That is why the Jet command-line port cannot keep its path-keyed tables faithful to the Rust original. Beginners meet it as == saying true while the Map disagrees, and experts porting code meet it as quiet duplicate entries. You are deciding how a type tells Map and Set what the same key means. We recommend that a type name one plain comparison key, from which Jet derives equality, sorting, hashing and Map and Set behaviour, so they can never disagree.

decisions.title: Lossless native paths with target-native separators
decisions.gist: Should Jet paths keep the exact name the operating system uses, or refuse names that are not text?
decisions.lesson: Operating systems allow file names that are not valid text. Two such names can print identically. Every option uses each system's own folder separator and keeps plain text paths easy. They differ in whether unusual names stay reachable, and whether a//b and a/b count as one path.
decisions.explainer:
Words first. A file name is stored as numbers. UTF-8 and UTF-16 are two ways to store text as numbers. Linux lets a name use any byte except zero, even bytes that are not text. Windows lets a name use 16-bit units, even broken ones. NUL is the number zero; it ends a name, so no name may contain it.

A component is one folder or file name between separators, like a, b and c in a/b/c. The separator is / on Linux and macOS. On Windows both / and \ separate. A label is text made for people to read; here it means display(), which swaps unreadable parts for the mark �.

Option A keeps the exact system name inside a new OSPath type. Text paths still work: a quoted path such as "notes.txt" written where a path is expected becomes an OSPath automatically, and OSPath.from(text) converts a text variable. Unusual names come from folder listings, from native command-line arguments, or from OSPath.from_native_bytes. Printing uses display(); getting real text uses to_text(), which reports NotText when the name is not text.

Option B keeps paths as text and refuses any name that is not text, before opening anything. Option C keeps exact names like A, but compares paths by exact spelling, so a//b and a/b are different. A and B both compare by components, so a//b and a/b are the same path. Comparing by components looks only at the written names, not at the disk, and does not follow links. a and a/ also compare equal, though only a folder can be opened as a/.

Reading the code: p :: value names a value. [U8]{97, 255} is a list of two bytes: 97 is the letter a, and 255 alone is not text. ?? panic("NUL") stops the program if the call fails. Replacing 255 with 98 gives the name ab, which every option accepts; replacing it with 0 fails with ContainsNUL.

Saving paths. Under A, a path that is text is saved as plain text, exactly as today. A path that is not text is saved as its exact bytes or units, so nothing is lost. Reading a Windows-only form on Linux fails with WrongTarget instead of guessing.
decisions.story: Ana's backup tool lists a Linux folder holding two files whose names contain bytes that are not text. Both print as a�. Her tool must copy each one, and must never open one when it meant the other.
decisions.detail:
Current code. Core/files/path.jet:24-29 declares Path with raw: String, so bytes that are not text cannot be stored. Core/files/files.jet:232-242 treats backslash and drive letters as separators and roots on every system. Core/files/files.jet:139-141 and 347 take String paths.

Naming follows the acronym rule S66: OS is all capitals, so the type is OSPath, its error OSPathError. The existing Path type is renamed to OSPath with no alias. OSPath.from follows D-ONCE-VERB1, where bare from is the conversion constructor.

OSPath equality uses components through the key mechanism chosen in D-KEY-TRAITS1 (#4499). Under that ballot's A, OSPath's key is its component list. Target facts come from the selected build target (#4483). Examples are proposed, not run.

options.name: Lossless OSPath
options.detail:
OSPath stores the exact system name, so every file the system can list or open stays reachable. Paths compare by their components, the names between separators. a//b and a/b are equal, while names with different components, like the two a� files, never are.

Equality is about the written names, not the disk; it does not follow links. a and a/ are equal, but the system still receives the exact spelling, so a/ only opens a folder.

Beginner: write "notes.txt" where a path is expected, or OSPath.from(text) for a text variable; it fails only if the text holds NUL. Use display() to print. Expert: native bytes or units are available as read-only views, and to_text() checks for real text.

Saving keeps text paths as text, and stores other names exactly. A lint warns about a backslash in a path literal on Linux or macOS, where it is a normal letter. Existing code moves over once with jet fix.
options.technical:
Representation: Unix holds owned bytes [U8] without NUL. Windows holds owned 16-bit units [U16] without NUL, lone surrogates included. System calls receive these units directly, with a terminating zero added at the call. Nothing decodes and re-encodes a name.

Construction: OSPath.from(text: String) -> OSPath OSPathError! fails only on NUL. A string literal in an OSPath position is adopted at compile time, like numeric literals under D-LITCARRIER1; a literal NUL is a compile error. OSPath.from_native_bytes([U8]) exists only on Unix targets, and OSPath.from_native_units([U16]) only on Windows targets.

A wrong-target constructor is a compile error even when the host has it. Web and other targets without a native filesystem get no native constructors. Generic file APIs there keep their virtual-path contract.

Projections: native_bytes() or native_units() return read-only views that cannot outlive the path. to_text() -> String OSPathError! returns NotText for non-text names. display() -> String never fails and uses U+FFFD for invalid parts. has_trailing_separator() -> Bool reports a final separator. OSPathError is ContainsNUL, NotText or WrongTarget.

Components, Unix: only / separates. a//b and a/./b have components a, b. A trailing / is ignored for equality but kept in the spelling sent to the system. A leading ./ stays a component. Root / is its own component, and .. is never resolved without IO.

Components, Windows: C:foo (drive-relative), C:\foo, \foo, UNC \\server\share and verbatim \\?\ prefixes are distinct. / and \ both separate, except inside verbatim paths. No case folding, Unicode normalization or filesystem identity is applied.

Three meanings stay separate. The native spelling is the exact bytes or units the system receives. Equality, ordering and Map keys use lexical components only. Filesystem identity, such as symlinks, hard links, case-insensitive volumes or .., is never judged without IO.

Trailing separator: for a regular file a, a == a/ is true, matching Rust. files.read on a succeeds, while on a/ it fails with the system's not-a-directory error, because the spelling is kept. Code that must tell them apart checks has_trailing_separator().

Ingress: list_dir entries and the current directory produce OSPath. Command-line arguments are not all paths, so process.args() keeps returning [String]. process.native_arg_bytes() -[Exec.Args]> [[U8]] on Unix and native_arg_units() -[Exec.Args]> [[U16]] on Windows return each argument exactly, under the constructors' target rule. A program converts only its path arguments; flags, URLs and expressions stay raw or text. Environment variables keep their String API in this decision.

API: files, process program and current_dir, and store roots take OSPath. name, stem, suffix and parent return OSPath.

Migration by jet fix, once. Path becomes OSPath, with no alias. String literal arguments need no change. A String variable argument becomes OSPath.from(x)? where the enclosing function can return the error, adding OSPathError to its error set. Elsewhere jet fix lists the call, so the author decides how to handle ContainsNUL.

Where the old String result of name, stem or suffix is printed or interpolated, jet fix appends .display(). Where it is used as other text, it appends .to_text()? under the same rule, or lists the site.

Saving: Codable writes a text path as a plain string, otherwise {unix_bytes: [...]} or {windows_units: [...]}. Decoding accepts all three. A native form from the other system family returns WrongTarget. Caches that stored text paths decode unchanged.
options.code:
use core.files as files
use core.files.path.[OSPath]

// Unix folder holding two files named by raw bytes:
// a,0xFF contains X and a,0xFE contains Y. 97 is "a"; 0xFF and 0xFE are not text.
p :: OSPath.from_native_bytes([U8]{97, 255}) ?? panic("NUL")
q :: OSPath.from_native_bytes([U8]{97, 254}) ?? panic("NUL")
print(p.display())                    // a�  (a label for people only)
print(q.display())                    // a�
print(p == q)                         // false: two different names
print(files.read(p) ?? panic("read")) // X
print(files.read(q) ?? panic("read")) // Y
print(files.read("notes.txt") ?? panic("read"))   // written-out text paths just work
x :: OSPath.from("a//b") ?? panic("NUL")
y :: OSPath.from("a/b") ?? panic("NUL")
print(x == y)                         // true: same components
// Converting p.display() back with OSPath.from would name a different file.

options.name: Text-only OSPath
options.detail:
OSPath stays text. Any system name that is not text is refused with NotText before lookup, joining or hashing. Separators, components and text literals work exactly as in A.

Beginner: nothing new to learn. Expert: catch NotText and ask the user to rename the file, because Jet cannot open it.
options.technical: Every native ingress decodes once and refuses invalid UTF-8 or broken UTF-16 with OSPathError.NotText. Valid Windows surrogate pairs decode losslessly. Lossy text is never used to accept a path. Saving is always plain text.
options.code:
use core.files as files
use core.files.path.[OSPath]

// Unix folder holding two files named by raw bytes:
// a,0xFF contains X and a,0xFE contains Y. 97 is "a"; 0xFF and 0xFE are not text.
print(OSPath.from_native_bytes([U8]{97, 255}))   // Err(NotText), refused before lookup
print(OSPath.from_native_bytes([U8]{97, 254}))   // Err(NotText)
// files.list_dir(".") reports both names as Err(NotText); neither file can be opened
print(files.read("notes.txt") ?? panic("read"))   // written-out text paths just work
x :: OSPath.from("a//b") ?? panic("NUL")
y :: OSPath.from("a/b") ?? panic("NUL")
print(x == y)                         // true: same components

options.name: Lossless OSPath, exact-spelling equality
options.detail:
Same lossless storage, construction and saving as A. Equality, ordering and Map keys compare the exact native spelling instead of components.

Beginner: a//b and a/b are different keys even though they open the same file. Expert: normalize paths yourself before comparing or using them as keys.
options.technical: Identical to A except that the key is the raw native unit list. Repeated separators, ./ segments and trailing separators all make paths unequal.
options.code:

use core.files.path.[OSPath]

// Unix folder holding two files named by raw bytes:
// a,0xFF contains X and a,0xFE contains Y. 97 is "a"; 0xFF and 0xFE are not text.
p :: OSPath.from_native_bytes([U8]{97, 255}) ?? panic("NUL")
q :: OSPath.from_native_bytes([U8]{97, 254}) ?? panic("NUL")
print(p == q)                         // false: two different names
print(files.read(p) ?? panic("read")) // X
print(files.read(q) ?? panic("read")) // Y
print(files.read("notes.txt") ?? panic("read"))   // written-out text paths just work
x :: OSPath.from("a//b") ?? panic("NUL")
y :: OSPath.from("a/b") ?? panic("NUL")
print(x == y)                         // false: compared by exact spelling

comparisons.note: Rust keeps native path units separately from lossy display.

recommendation.why: Keep the exact system name so every file stays reachable and is never confused with another. Written-out text paths, printing and saving keep working with no extra code, and jet fix moves existing code over once.
gains: Every file the system can name stays reachable.
Written-out text paths need no extra code.
a//b and a/b are one path, matching Rust.

losses.loss: Existing path code needs a one-time migration: Path is renamed, String variables need OSPath.from, and name, stem and suffix return OSPath.
losses.mitigation: jet fix does the rename and inserts the conversions and text views. It lists only calls where the author must choose how to handle a NUL or a non-text name. Written-out text paths need no change.

whyNot.reason: Refusing names that are not text leaves real files unreachable, so faithful ports and file tools fail.
Exact-spelling equality makes a//b and a/b separate keys, unlike Rust and unlike how the system finds files.

recommendation.tradeoff: A changes the path type and its API once, through jet fix. Afterwards the visible differences are display marks for non-text names and an explicit, fallible conversion for text held in variables.

decisions.checkInstructions:
On Unix, test the two non-text names: distinct, both readable, same label. On Windows, test lone surrogates. Test NUL refusal, literal adoption, wrong-target constructor errors and the backslash lint.

Test components for drives, UNC, verbatim, leading ./, repeated and trailing separators and .. on each target. For a regular file a, assert a == a/, files.read(a) succeeds, files.read(a/) fails with not-a-directory, and has_trailing_separator() differs. Round-trip saved paths, including WrongTarget.

Prove list_dir, native_arg_bytes or native_arg_units, process spawn, rename and store roots reach the exact name, and that process.args() is unchanged. Run jet fix on String-variable call sites: functions that can return the error get OSPath.from(x)?, others are listed, and name, stem and suffix uses get display() or to_text().

decisions.situation: A file path is the name a program uses to find a file, such as notes/today.txt. Jet stores paths as text, but Linux allows names made of any bytes and Windows allows broken UTF-16, so some real names are not text. Two such files can both print as a�, so a text-only path can open the wrong file or never reach it, and Jet also wrongly splits Linux names at backslashes. This matters to file tools, backup scripts and the Jet command-line port, which must reach every file the system can name. You are deciding whether Jet's path type keeps the exact system name or refuses names that are not text. We recommend a new OSPath type that keeps the exact name, accepts written-out text paths with no extra code, and moves existing code over with jet fix. Two effects remain: an unusual name prints with a replacement mark while still opening the right file, and text held in a variable needs one explicit conversion that can fail.

decisions.title: Keep only some items of a list, in place
decisions.gist: Should List get an in-place retain that keeps matching items in order, or should code keep rebuilding lists?
decisions.lesson: Keeping some items of a list should not scramble their order. Today you build a second list, which allocates memory each time. An in-place retain reuses the same storage. It must stay safe when the test itself fails: the list should then be left exactly as it was.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A test, or predicate, is a small function that answers yes or no for one item. Stable means the kept items stay in their original order. Allocation means asking for new memory. Capacity is the spare room a list has already reserved. Dropping an item means releasing whatever it owns, exactly once.

Copy-on-write: when you write other := values, Jet does not copy the list right away. Both names share one storage until one of them changes; the changing side then takes its own copy. So a trim on a shared list makes that one copy, like any other change, and the other name keeps the old items.

In the code, |n| n % 2 == 0 is a test for one item n. The % sign gives the remainder after division, so == 0 picks even numbers and != 0 picks odd ones. := creates a list you may change, and & in front of a call marks that the call changes it. Both options print [2, 4]. Changing the test to != 0 prints [1, 3].

What if the test can fail? Suppose it checks [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] and reports an error on 4. Under option A, the list is still [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] and the error comes back to you. Option B gives the same result, because the old list is only replaced after every test succeeds.

Option A changes the list in place. Option B keeps today's way: build a new list with filter and assign it back.
decisions.story: Mina removes expired entries from a notebook trust list. The surviving entries must stay in their original order, and the list is trimmed often.
decisions.detail:
Card #4412 reports that ports of Rust Vec::retain must either drain into a new list or do repeated removes, which is quadratic. List has filter (crates/jet-sema/src/Sema/CheckerInfer/calls/builtin_methods.rs:60-83 returns a new List) but no in-place retain.

Callback failure and effects follow D-CALLBACK-ERR1=A (ratified). This surface is added for performance. Under AGENTS.md:165-168, ratification waits until a paired two-program cell (retain against the filter rebuild) strictly wins. No cell or measurement exists yet, and no speed number is claimed here. Examples are not executed.

options.name: List.retain, safe on failure
options.detail:
Write &values.retain(test). Each item is tested once, in order. Kept items slide forward and the rest are dropped. A list that no other name shares keeps its storage, so no new list is made. A shared list takes its own copy only once an item is actually dropped.

If the test can never fail, retain does all of this in one pass. If the test can fail, retain first asks the test about every item and only then changes the list. A failure therefore leaves the list exactly as it was. Remembering the answers costs one bit per item, kept on the stack for lists up to 4096 items.

If you write values = values.filter(test) on the same list, the compiler suggests retain with a fix, but only when the test also works inside retain. A test that looks at values itself, such as |n| n < values.len(), stays on filter.
options.technical:
Signature: List<T>.retain<E>(&self, keep: fn(&T) -> Bool E!) -> Unit E!. Callback failure and effects forward per D-CALLBACK-ERR1=A. The callback receives a read loan &T, never an owning value or a mutable element.

Never-failing callback (E = Never): one pass in ascending index order. Kept items move forward and rejected items drop exactly once. No allocation for uniquely owned storage. A panic stops the task, and every item is still dropped exactly once.

Fallible callback: decide, then commit. Pass 1 calls keep on every item in index order and records each answer as one bit. The bits live on the stack up to 4096 items, then on the heap at 125 bytes per 1000 items. On the first failure, retain returns that original error and the list is untouched. Pass 2 compacts using the bits and cannot fail.

Shared storage: nothing detaches until the commit finds the first item to drop. Keep-all never allocates, even for shared storage. A copy made earlier (other := values) keeps its original contents under the existing copy-on-write rule.

Cost bound: the worst cases are a shared list that drops an item, which copies once, and a fallible callback over more than 4096 items, which adds the bit scratch. Rebuilding with filter always allocates a survivor list of up to n elements, so retain never allocates more than B.

Aliasing: the list is on exclusive loan for the whole call. A callback that captures the same list to read, push, remove or retain is rejected at compile time by the existing exclusive-loan rule. Owning elements such as secrets cannot be moved or kept by the callback; rejected ones close once after their loan ends.

Edge cases: an empty list makes no calls. All kept leaves the list unchanged. None kept leaves an empty list with its capacity. Capacity never shrinks. Truncate and swap are not part of this decision.

Lint: values = values.filter(keep) on the same variable suggests &values.retain(keep) only when keep, unchanged, type-checks as a retain callback. It must accept a read loan &T and capture no alias of values. Answers and the failure result are then identical, because both leave the list unchanged on failure. Counterexample, left on filter with no lint: values = values.filter(|n| n < values.len()), since the callback reads values while retain holds the exclusive loan.

options.name: Keep rebuilding with filter
options.detail: Add nothing. Code keeps writing values = values.filter(test). filter builds a new list of the survivors, in order, and then the old one is replaced. On failure the old list is untouched. Until the swap, memory holds the old list plus the survivor list, on every trim.
options.technical: No retention API is authorized. Ports use the existing List.filter, which returns a new List (builtin_methods.rs:60-83) and lifts callback failure around the result. Where the element cannot be copied, they use an ordered ownership drain. The original list is replaced only after every callback succeeds. Repeated remove calls are not accepted as parity because they are quadratic. Peak memory is the old list plus the survivor list. Exact allocation counts, such as for an empty result, are not measured.

comparisons.note: Vec.retain keeps order and tests each item once, in place.

recommendation.why: Trim a list in place, with no new list unless storage is shared, while failure still leaves it untouched. Ratify only once the paired speed test strictly beats rebuilding.
gains: Unshared lists reuse their storage; shared lists copy only when an item is dropped.
A failing test leaves the list exactly as it was.
Kept items stay in their original order.

losses.loss: A fallible test over more than 4096 items needs heap scratch, and a shared list still copies once when it drops an item.
losses.mitigation: scratch is one bit per item, 125 bytes per 1000, and the shared copy is the same one any change makes; both stay at or below what filter always allocates.

whyNot.reason: Rebuilding gives the same answers but builds a new survivor list on every trim.

recommendation.tradeoff: One new list method; rebuilding with filter still works, and a lint points to retain.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Add the paired retain-versus-filter cell to the canonical manifest. Apply the strict comparator before ratification.

Test stable order, empty, keep-all and keep-none. Test failure on the fourth of five items: the list is unchanged and the original error returns. Test one drop per rejected item, no allocation for unique storage, no detach on keep-all for shared storage, and one detach when a shared list drops an item. Test captured-alias rejection on every execution level. Test that the filter-to-retain lint fires for |n| n % 2 == 0 and stays silent for |n| n < values.len().

current.note: Lists can filter into a new list, but cannot trim in place.

wild.note: Vec.retain keeps order and tests each item once, in place.

options.gist: Trim the same list in place; a failing test changes nothing.
gains: Unshared lists reuse storage; shared lists copy only when dropping.
A failing test leaves the list exactly as it was.
Kept items stay in their original order.
losses: Long fallible tests need bit scratch; shared lists copy once.

options.name: Keep rebuilding with filter
options.gist: Add nothing; code keeps building a new list with filter.
gains: No new list method to learn.
losses: Every trim builds a new survivor list in new memory.

recommendation.why: Trim a list in place, with no new list unless storage is shared, while failure still leaves it untouched. Ratify only once the paired speed test strictly beats rebuilding.
gains: Unshared lists reuse storage; shared lists copy only when dropping.
A failing test leaves the list exactly as it was.
Kept items stay in their original order.

losses.loss: Long fallible tests need bit scratch; shared lists copy once.
losses.mitigation: one bit per item, and the copy any change makes; never more than filter allocates.

whyNot.reason: Rebuilding gives the same answers but builds a new survivor list on every trim.

recommendation.tradeoff: One new list method; rebuilding with filter still works, and a lint points to retain.

decisions.situation: Programs often trim a list: keep the items that pass a test, drop the rest, and leave the survivors in their original order. Jet's List cannot do that in place today, so code builds a second list of survivors with filter, which needs new memory every time. Ported tools such as the notebook trust store do this on busy paths, where the extra copy costs speed and memory. You are deciding whether List gets an in-place keep-only-these operation called retain, or whether people keep rebuilding lists. We recommend adding retain, designed so a failing test leaves the list untouched, and ratifying it only after a paired speed test shows it beats rebuilding.

decisions.title: One lossless way to read keys from the terminal
decisions.gist: How should Jet programs receive keys: as a stream, in batches, or from a one-key function?
decisions.lesson: The terminal sends bytes, not keys. One read can hold half a key or several keys, so a decoder must remember leftovers. Today Jet keeps only the first key of each read and loses the rest. Every option below uses one shared decoder that loses nothing. Only a lone Escape press may wait, 10 ms at most, and newer terminals skip even that. The choice is how programs receive its keys.
decisions.explainer:
Think of the terminal as a mail slot that drops in bytes. The key "a" is one byte. The key "é" is two bytes, and F1 is three bytes: Escape, then O, then P. A paste pushes several keys through the slot at once, and a slow connection can split one key across two drops. A decoder is the helper that collects the bytes and hands out whole keys.

Escape is tricky on older terminals. The Escape key sends the same byte that starts F1 and the arrow keys. When a whole key arrives in one drop, which is the normal case, the decoder reads it at once. Only a lone Escape byte with nothing after it makes the decoder wait, at most 10 milliseconds, to see whether more bytes follow. That is shorter than one screen refresh; the REPL waits 100 ms today.

Newer terminals, such as kitty, foot, WezTerm, Ghostty, Alacritty and iTerm2, can send Escape as its own code that nothing else starts with. Jet asks the terminal once whether it can. If it can, Escape never waits. Jet turns that mode on only while the program waits for a key, so Ctrl-C still stops a busy program.

If a very slow connection to an older terminal delivers the bytes of F1 more than 10 ms apart, they read as Escape, O and P. A program can raise the wait with term.set_escape_wait, or lower it to 0 ms.

Keys and lines share one input tray. One drop can bring a key and the start of a typed line together. Taking a key removes only that key's bytes, so a later readline() still finds the rest.

End of input is not a key. It means the input stream closed, for example when keys come from a file that ran out. Ctrl-D is just a key, Ctrl("d"), and the program decides what it means.

A channel in Jet is a pipe between tasks: one end sends values, the other end receives them in order. Programs already drain a channel with `loop item in receiver`, wait with a timeout using an `if { ... after 250ms -> ... }` table, and poll with `try_receive()`. Option A makes the keyboard one more such pipe.
decisions.story: Sam is writing a small menu program. He pastes "ab" and then presses F1. He expects three keys: a, b and F1. Today he gets only a, and his F1 often arrives as a stray Escape character.
decisions.detail:
Code facts, checked 2026-10-04. crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Core/TermKey.rs:104-131 reads up to six bytes once per call. A multi-byte read returns only its first scalar, so pasted "ab" yields Char(a) and loses b. ESC O P (the SS3 form of F1) is valid UTF-8, so it comes back as Char(ESC). A zero-byte read, meaning end of input, returns Unknown.

Core/term/term.jet:39-49 and Compiler/JetFoundation/Source/Registry/CoreEnumRows.jet:111 declare Key with only Char, Escape, Backspace, Tab, the four arrows and Unknown. The Rust JetKey (TermKey.rs:32-58) also has Enter, Delete, F and Ctrl, and crates/jet-jit/src/IO.rs:1383-1396 forwards them. The two views disagree.

Other decoders exist. crates/jet-repl/src/Term.rs:292-351 decodes byte by byte with a 100 ms Escape wait, adds Home, End and EscapeEnter, and maps Ctrl-D to end of input. Jetpack/CLI/Source/Dashboard/DashboardSnapshot.jet:100 calls term.read_key_timeout, which does not exist in Core, and treats byte 4 as end of input. crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Core/ArgsProjection.rs:274-277 treats Unknown as end of input.

Escape timing today. TermKey.rs:114 calls a one-byte ESC read Escape with no wait, so an F1 split across reads misreads. The REPL waits 100 ms through stty min 0 time 1 (crates/jet-repl/src/Term.rs:32-38 and 313-318). Live blocks clear echo and line mode but keep signal keys on, so Ctrl-C raises SIGINT there (crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Term.rs:717-736, TermKey.rs:213-217). The REPL editor turns signal keys off (crates/jet-repl/src/Term.rs:37-38).

Outside sources, checked 2026-10-04. tmux 3.5 lowered its default escape-time to 10 ms (tmux CHANGES, section 3.4 to 3.5). Neovim's ttimeoutlen defaults to 50 ms (runtime/doc/options.txt), and Vim's defaults.vim sets 100 ms. crossterm calls a lone ESC Escape at once when no more input is ready (src/event/sys/unix/parse.rs:35-42).

The kitty keyboard protocol (sw.kovidgoyal.net/kitty/keyboard-protocol) defines CSI > 1 u to push disambiguation, CSI < u to pop it and CSI ? u to query it. With it, Escape is CSI 27 u, and Ctrl keys become CSI u codes, so Ctrl-C no longer raises SIGINT. Enter, Tab and Backspace keep their old bytes, so typing reset still works after a crash.

The spec detects support by following the query with a device-attributes request, CSI c. Neovim sends exactly CSI ? u CSI c and enables the mode when the first reply comes back (runtime/doc/tui.txt). Neovim's fallback, xterm modifyOtherKeys, changes only modified keys such as Ctrl-[, so a plain Escape stays the lone byte and still needs the wait. Jet therefore does not use it.

Precedent for host-fed receivers: Core/tasks/tasks.jet:107-113 returns timer and interval sources as Receiver<Int>. None of the proposed examples or timings were run.

options.name: Keys arrive on an ordinary channel
options.detail:
`term.keys()` returns the terminal's key stream as a `Receiver<Key>`, the same receiving end any channel has. Each receive gives exactly one whole key. A paste simply makes several keys ready at once, and a `loop` drains them with no list to build.

Everything Jet already teaches about channels works unchanged. `loop key in term.keys()` ends when input ends. The `if` table waits for a key or a timeout, and the same table can also wait on timers or messages. `try_receive()` checks for a key without waiting.

Keys and `readline()` take bytes from one shared input buffer. Receiving a key removes only that key's bytes, so switching to `readline()` after a key still gets the rest of a paste.

Only a lone Escape press can wait, at most 10 ms by default; every other key and every whole key arrives at once. On terminals that can send Escape as its own code, Jet asks once and turns that mode on only while a receive waits, so Escape never waits. `term.set_escape_wait` adjusts the wait from 0 ms to 1 s.

Experts and tests use `term.KeyDecoder` directly: feed it bytes with a timestamp and take keys out. The receiver uses that same decoder inside, so every tier, the REPL and the CLI share one decoder.
options.technical:
Final enum: Key has Char(String) holding exactly one Unicode scalar, Ctrl(String) holding one lowercase ASCII letter, and F(Int) for 1..12. Its other cases are Enter, Escape, EscapeEnter, Backspace, Tab, Delete, Up, Down, Left, Right, Home, End and Unknown. code() is the scalar for Char, the letter for Ctrl, f1..f12 for F, and lowercase names otherwise, with escape-enter for EscapeEnter. modifier_bits() is 1 for Ctrl and 0 otherwise.

term.keys() -[IO]> Receiver<Key> Never! returns an alias of the one process-wide key source. All aliases share one decoder. The source has no queue of decoded keys: a key is decoded only when a receive, try_receive or if arm asks for one. receive() -> Key !Closed reports Closed after stdin ends and pending bytes have flushed.

Shared stdin: the runtime owns one process stdin buffer. The key source, readline(), read_until() and every other Core stdin reader take bytes only from it. One OS read may bring several keys, or a key plus a line; extra bytes stay in the buffer. The key source removes only the bytes of each key it returns. Bytes of an unfinished key stay at the front, so a later readline() reads them as text. A timed-out if arm removes nothing.

Exact case: one read delivers x, h, i, newline. keys.receive() gives Char("x"); then readline() gives "hi".

Timing uses the monotonic core.time.instant(). The Escape wait applies only to a lone ESC that is the last byte in the shared buffer. Bytes already buffered, such as ESC O P from one read, decode at once. If bytes arrive during the wait, decoding resumes the moment they arrive. The wait defaults to 10 ms, tmux's default since 3.5.

ESC then Enter within the wait is EscapeEnter. ESC alone becomes Escape when the wait ends. ESC at 0 ms then O,P at 5 ms is F(1); O,P at 15 ms gives Escape, Char(O), Char(P). No byte is dropped, but a key split by more than the wait reads as separate keys. At exactly the wait the ESC expires before new bytes are read. At end of input a lone ESC is Escape at once.

A pending ESC never blocks the program: an if table still serves its timers and messages during the wait.

term.set_escape_wait(wait: Duration) -[IO]> Unit IOError! sets the process-wide wait from 0 ms to 1 s. 0 ms is crossterm's rule: a lone ESC at the end of the buffer is Escape at once. Outside that range it returns InvalidInput and changes nothing.

Terminal key mode, on Unix when stdin and stdout are both terminals: the first receive that must wait writes CSI ? u then CSI c. A CSI ? flags u reply before the device-attributes reply CSI ? … c means support; the device-attributes reply alone means none. The answer is kept for the process, and until it arrives the 10 ms rule applies. Windows keeps the 10 ms rule; this decision does not request the mode there.

The shared stdin buffer removes the replies to Jet's own query, so they never reach a key or readline(). If raw mode ends while an answer is outstanding, Jet waits for it, at most 100 ms, before echo returns, so a reply never prints on screen.

With support, Jet writes CSI > 1 u when a receive or if arm starts to wait and CSI < u when that wait ends, before the program runs again. A receive that finds a key ready, and try_receive, write nothing. In the mode Escape arrives as CSI 27 u, so no key press waits. A lone ESC from a press made while the mode was off still decodes by the 10 ms rule.

The decoder always reads both forms, and one press gives the same Key in both. CSI 27 u is Escape. Ctrl+i, Ctrl+m, Ctrl+j, Ctrl+h and Ctrl+[ give Tab, Enter, Enter, Backspace and Escape, as their old bytes do. Alt+Enter, CSI 13;3 u, is EscapeEnter, matching the old ESC CR. Other Alt combinations are Unknown in both forms, as in the REPL today (crates/jet-repl/src/Term.rs:322-324).

Signal keys: when the terminal's signal keys are on, as in live blocks (crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Term.rs:724-729), its interrupt, quit and suspend characters are never keys. If one arrives as a CSI u code, Jet writes CSI < u, then raises SIGINT, SIGQUIT or SIGTSTP, as the terminal would have. Between waits the mode is off, so Ctrl-C stops a busy program exactly as today.

A crash or SIGKILL during a wait can leave the mode on, as raw mode itself can today. Enter, Tab and Backspace keep their old bytes in the mode, so typing reset repairs the terminal.

term.KeyDecoder.new(escape_wait: Duration = 10ms) -> KeyDecoder IOError!, with the same 0 ms to 1 s range. It writes nothing to the terminal and reads both key forms. feed(&self, bytes: ^[U8], now: Instant) -> Unit KeyFeedError! takes one chunk of at most 65536 bytes. KeyFeedError is Busy(bytes) when the previous chunk is not drained, or TooLarge(bytes); both return the identical untouched bytes. next(&self, now: Instant) -> Key? gives one key or None. end(&self) marks end of input so next() flushes pending bytes.

At most 64 bytes of an incomplete sequence are kept; an over-long escape becomes one Unknown and decoding resumes after it. Invalid UTF-8 consumes the maximal invalid prefix only: FF,61 gives Unknown then Char(a); C2,61 likewise; C0,AF gives two Unknowns. E2,82 waits on timeout and becomes one Unknown at end of input. Unknown CSI or SS3 sequences consume through their final byte.

Migration: term.read_key() is retired. jet fix rewrites it to `term.keys().receive() ?? Key.Unknown`, which keeps today's end-of-input result. The REPL decoder, the dashboard byte mapping and ArgsProjection move to the shared source. CoreEnumRows, term.jet, Show, key-code and modifier dispatch and every host carry the final enum. Exhaustive matches on Key get the ordinary missing-case diagnostic.

options.name: Keys arrive in batches
options.detail:
`term.read_keys(max: 64)` waits for input, then returns a list of every whole key ready right now, up to `max`. A paste usually comes back as one list. The same shared decoder sits underneath, so nothing is lost; keys that do not fit wait for the next call.

Every program needs two loops: one to keep reading and one to walk each list. Each call builds a new list. Timeouts need their own `timeout:` parameter, separate from the channel `after` arm, so a key read cannot share one wait with timers or messages.
options.technical:
term.read_keys(max: Int = 64, timeout: Duration? = None) -[IO, Time.Wait]> [Key] KeyReadError!, with max in 1..4096 and KeyReadError = Timeout | EndOfInput | IO(IOError). It waits for at least one key, then returns every whole key ready, up to max; the rest stay undecoded in the shared stdin buffer. EndOfInput is returned once stdin ends and pending bytes have flushed. Same decoder, shared stdin buffer, Key enum, timing, terminal key mode, set_escape_wait, invalid-byte rules and KeyDecoder as A.

Migration: term.read_key() is retired. jet fix rewrites it to `(term.read_keys(max: 1) ?? [Key]{Key.Unknown})[0]`, so end of input and read errors still give Unknown as today. The REPL, dashboard and ArgsProjection call read_keys.

options.name: A one-key function with its own timeout and end markers
options.detail:
`term.read_key()` returns one result per call: a key, a timeout, or end of input. The same shared decoder sits underneath, so a paste is not lost; the other keys wait for the next call.

This is easy for a single key press. But timeout and end of input become a separate vocabulary from channels. A program cannot wait for a key and a timer or message in one `if` table, so a dashboard has to poll in a loop instead.
options.technical:
term.read_key(timeout: Duration? = None) -[IO, Time.Wait]> KeyRead IOError!, with KeyRead = Key(Key) | Timeout | EndOfInput. Timeout is returned only when a timeout was given. EndOfInput is returned once stdin ends and pending bytes have flushed. Same decoder, shared stdin buffer, Key enum, timing, terminal key mode, set_escape_wait, invalid-byte rules and KeyDecoder as A.

Migration: read_key keeps its name but changes its result type. jet fix rewrites each old call that expects a Key to `if (term.read_key() ?? term.KeyRead.EndOfInput) == { .Key(key) -> key  else -> Key.Unknown }`, so end of input and read errors still give Unknown as today. The REPL, dashboard and ArgsProjection call read_key.

comparisons.note: tcell can deliver terminal events on an ordinary Go channel, so programs reuse select and range.
A raw read returns any available chunk, not one key, so the caller must keep leftover bytes.

recommendation.why: A keeps every key and reuses what programs already know about channels. Loops, timeouts, polling and waiting on several sources need no new rules. One decoder replaces the three that exist today.
gains: Pastes and split keys arrive whole and in order; no byte is dropped, even when switching to readline().
Timeouts and multi-source waits reuse the existing channel if table.
One decoder replaces the REPL, dashboard and runtime copies.

losses.loss: On terminals without their own Escape code, a lone Escape press arrives up to 10 ms late. A key whose bytes arrive more than 10 ms apart reads as Escape plus letters.
losses.mitigation: Only a lone Escape waits; whole keys and every other key arrive at once. 10 ms is tmux's default since 3.5 and shorter than one 60 Hz frame; the REPL waits 100 ms today. Newer terminals wait 0 ms, and term.set_escape_wait tunes the wait from 0 ms to 1 s.

losses.loss: On newer terminals Jet writes two short codes around each key wait, and a process killed during a wait can leave that key mode on.
losses.mitigation: The mode is on only while Jet waits, so busy programs, Ctrl-C and child programs see today's terminal. Enter still works in the mode, so typing reset repairs it, as Neovim advises; raw mode carries the same risk today.

whyNot.reason: Batches add a list and a second loop to every program, and timeouts get their own separate rule.
A one-key function invents its own timeout and end markers, so keys cannot share one wait with timers or messages.

recommendation.tradeoff: A lone-Escape wait of at most 10 ms on older terminals, and none on newer ones, buys keys with no dropped bytes through channel tools Jet already has.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Feed every byte split of UTF-8, CSI, SS3 and CSI u sequences through KeyDecoder and term.keys(). Assert pasted ab gives two keys, Ctrl-D stays Ctrl(d), and end of input closes the receiver. Deliver x, h, i, newline in one read: keys.receive() gives Char(x), then readline() gives hi. A timed-out if arm consumes no byte.

Check the Escape table at the default 10 ms and after set_escape_wait, including 0 ms, 1 s and InvalidInput outside them. ESC O P in one read gives F(1) with no wait. ESC then O,P 5 ms later gives F(1) when they arrive, not at 10 ms. A pending ESC still lets an if table's timer arm fire.

With a scripted terminal that answers CSI ? 0 u, assert one query, no reply bytes in keys or readline(), and CSI > 1 u and CSI < u around each blocking wait only. CSI 27 u gives Escape at once, and every key gives the same Key as its old bytes. With signal keys on, CSI 99;5 u writes CSI < u, then raises SIGINT. A terminal that answers only CSI c gets the 10 ms rule and no mode writes.

Check the invalid-byte suffix rules, the 64-byte cap and the returned fed chunk. Prove one decoder and one stdin buffer serve AOT, JIT, evaluator, Web, headless, the REPL and the CLI dashboard.

surface.gist: How should Jet programs receive keys: as a stream, in batches, or from a one-key function?
surface.lesson: The terminal sends bytes, not keys. One read can hold half a key or several keys, so a decoder must remember leftovers. Today Jet keeps only the first key of each read and loses the rest. Every option uses one shared decoder that loses nothing. Only a lone Escape press may wait, at most 10 ms. The choice is how programs receive its keys.

current.note: Today's reader keeps only the first character of each read.

Timeouts and multi-source waits use the existing if table.

losses: Its own timeout and end markers, separate from channels.
Cannot wait for a key and a message together.

gains: No byte dropped: pastes arrive whole, and readline() gets the rest.
No new timeout or polling rules to learn.
One decoder for every tier, the REPL and the CLI.

losses.mitigation: whole keys never wait; newer terminals never wait; 10 ms is tmux's default; set_escape_wait tunes 0 ms to 1 s.

Its own timeout and end markers cannot share one wait with timers or messages.

decisions.situation: When a program reads the keyboard, the terminal hands it bytes, and one read can hold half a key or several keys at once. Today Jet's key reader keeps only the first character of each read, so pasted "ab" loses its "b" and F1 often arrives as a stray Escape character. This hurts anyone writing a menu, game, editor or REPL, and it is why the REPL and the CLI dashboard each grew their own separate key decoder. You are deciding how programs receive decoded keys: one at a time from a stream, in batches, or from a one-key function with its own timeout rules. We recommend one shared decoder that delivers keys on an ordinary channel and shares one input buffer with readline, so no byte is dropped. Older terminals reuse the Escape byte to start other keys, so there a lone Escape press arrives up to 10 milliseconds late; every other key is instant. Newer terminals such as kitty, WezTerm and Ghostty can send Escape as its own code, and Jet uses that so Escape never waits there.

decisions.title: One checked binary pack and unpack contract
decisions.gist: Should packing numbers into bytes refuse values that do not fit, or silently wrap them, on every route?
decisions.lesson: Packing 300 into one byte can fail or silently become 44. Today the answer depends on which internal route runs. The choice is one rule for all routes: refuse out-of-range values and wrong-sized buffers, or wrap values and allow extra bytes.
decisions.explainer:
Packing turns numbers into bytes; unpacking turns bytes back into numbers. A byte holds a whole number from 0 to 255. A field is one value inside a record; its width is how many bytes it uses.

A format string describes a record. Each letter is one field. B is an unsigned 1-byte field (0 to 255) and b is a signed one (-128 to 127). H is unsigned 2 bytes and h signed 2 bytes. I and L are unsigned 4 bytes; i and l are signed 4 bytes. Q is unsigned 8 bytes and q signed 8 bytes. c is one raw byte, and x is a padding byte with no value. A number before a letter repeats it, so 3B means three B fields.

Byte order says which end of a number comes first. Little-endian puts the lowest byte first, so 1 as two bytes is [1, 0]. Big-endian puts the highest byte first: [0, 1]. A format may start with < for little-endian, > or ! for big-endian, or = for the target machine's own order. With no prefix, Jet uses little-endian.

Wrapping keeps only the low bits that fit. 300 is 256 + 44, so wrapped into one byte it becomes 44. A signed field stores negative numbers in two's complement: in one byte, -1 is stored as 255.

BinaryError has four kinds. Format means the format string is invalid. Values means the wrong number of values was given. Range means a value does not fit its field. Buffer means the byte list has the wrong length.

In the examples, print shows a result. Ok(...) is a success and Err(...) a failure; none of these programs was run.
decisions.story: Ana parses a binary record from a sensor, changes one field, and writes it back. A too-large value or an extra trailing byte must be caught the same way whether her program runs in the interpreter, the JIT or a compiled build.
decisions.inWild:
# Python struct: checks ranges and exact buffer sizes.
# https://docs.python.org/3/library/struct.html
import struct
struct.pack("B", 300)              # struct.error: out of range
struct.pack("<H", 1)               # b'\x01\x00'
struct.unpack("<H", b"\x01\x00\x09")  # struct.error: needs exactly 2 bytes
struct.unpack_from("<H", b"\x01\x00\x09", 0)  # (1,): reads from the front
decisions.detail:
## What the code does today

The Jet source module checks ranges and sizes. pack_u8 refuses values outside 0 to 255 with Range (Core/encoding/binary.jet:32-35). Generic pack and unpack take and return [Int], check the value count, and require an exact buffer length (binary.jet:167-212). iter_unpack requires a positive record size and a whole number of records (binary.jet:214-219).

The source format parser rejects @ and zero repeats, and treats = as little-endian (binary.jet:248-300). Field codes are x c b B h H i I l L q Q (binary.jet:302-310).

The native routes behave differently. Fixed packs take a 64-bit machine integer and cast it, so 300 becomes 44 (crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Core/EncodingBase.rs:239-269). The 64-bit unpack returns its bytes as a signed machine integer, so all-255 bytes read back as -1 (EncodingBase.rs:301-311).

Generic native unpack accepts extra trailing bytes and does not sign-extend b, h, i or q (EncodingBase.rs:407-504). Native parsing accepts @ as little-endian and treats a repeat of 0 as 1 (EncodingBase.rs:347-364). Native errors are free text, not BinaryError (EncodingBase.rs:446-520).

The compiler routes every one of these calls to the native functions (Compiler/JetFoundation/Source/Registry/CoreCallRows.jet:739-762). Jet source signatures already return BinaryError!, so Jet callers already handle failures.

## Same program in every option

Both options run Ana's checks on the same inputs. Only the results differ. Floating-point fields use the separate pack_f64le, pack_f64be, unpack_f64le and unpack_f64be functions in both options. The separate D-BINARY-SIGNEXT1 decision owns sign_extend with an invalid width.

options.name: One checked contract on every route
options.detail:
Every route follows today's Jet source rules. Values that do not fit their field return Range. A generic unpack needs exactly the record's byte count. Numbers stay exact, so an all-255 Q field reads as 18446744073709551615, never -1.

A new helper, unpack_from, reads one record starting at a given position and leaves the rest of the buffer alone. That keeps reading a header from a bigger buffer easy.

Beginner: handle the BinaryError you already see in the signature. Expert: when wrapping is really wanted, keep the low bits first, for example pack_u8(n & 255).
options.technical:
Signatures, unchanged except one addition: pack_u8, pack_i8, pack_u16le/be, pack_u32le/be and pack_u64le/be take Int and return [U8] BinaryError!. unpack_u8 through unpack_u64be take ([U8], offset: Int) and return Int? Never!. calcsize(fmt) returns Int BinaryError!. pack(fmt, [Int]) returns [U8] BinaryError!. unpack(fmt, [U8]) returns [Int] BinaryError!. iter_unpack returns [[Int]] BinaryError!.

New: unpack_from(fmt: String, data: [U8], offset: Int) -> [Int] BinaryError!. It reads exactly calcsize(fmt) bytes starting at offset. Bytes after the record are allowed. A negative offset or too few bytes returns Buffer.

Records: unpack reads exactly one record and needs exactly its byte count. iter_unpack reads every record in order and needs a whole number of records. An empty buffer gives Ok([]). A zero record size gives Format. Any leftover partial record gives Buffer, so two 2-byte records plus one byte fail.

Format grammar: an optional first character < (little), > or ! (big), or = (the selected target's byte order, never the compiling machine's). Every currently supported target is little-endian. No prefix means little-endian. There is never alignment padding. @ is Format, with the hint "Jet has no C-alignment mode; use < and explicit x padding". Codes are x c b B h H i I l L q Q. A decimal repeat must be at least 1. Anything else is Format.

Size limit: a format whose total size is above EncodingLimits.max_item_bytes (16 MiB by default) returns Format before anything is allocated. That stops a format such as 999999999x from filling memory.

Error order, first match wins: Format, then Values (wrong count), then Range (the first value that does not fit, in order), then Buffer. unpack checks Format before Buffer. iter_unpack rejects a zero record size and a buffer that is not a whole number of records before returning any record.

Numbers: inputs and results are Jet's exact Int. Unsigned fields hold 0 to 2^w - 1 and signed fields hold -2^(w-1) to 2^(w-1) - 1, where w is the width in bits. Signed codes b, h, i, l and q are sign-extended on unpack.

Routes: the native and JIT functions are cut over to this exact meaning. They pass Jet's Int carrier, which is already one machine word (crates/jet-foundation/src/Numeric.rs:2800-2809). They return BinaryError, not free text. The cast-based, prefix-accepting and @-accepting code paths are deleted. Values up to 2^62 - 1 stay on the one-word fast path; only larger Q and q values use Jet's big-number path.
options.code:
use core.encoding.binary as binary
print(binary.pack_u8(300))                      // Err(Range): 300 does not fit in one byte
print(binary.pack("<H", [1]))                   // Ok([1, 0]): low byte first
print(binary.pack(">H", [1]))                   // Ok([0, 1]): high byte first
print(binary.unpack("<H", [U8]{1, 0, 9}))       // Err(Buffer): 3 bytes for a 2-byte record
print(binary.unpack_from("<H", [U8]{1, 0, 9}, 0))  // Ok([1]): header read; ignores the rest
print(binary.iter_unpack("<H", [U8]{1, 0, 2, 0, 9}))
// Err(Buffer): two whole records plus one stray byte
print(binary.unpack("<Q", [U8]{255, 255, 255, 255, 255, 255, 255, 255}))
// Ok([18446744073709551615]): exact, never -1
print(binary.unpack("<q", [U8]{255, 255, 255, 255, 255, 255, 255, 255}))
// Ok([-1]): q is the signed code
print(binary.pack("@H", [1]))                   // Err(Format): no C-alignment mode

options.name: Wrap values to fit; allow extra bytes
options.detail:
Every route wraps integer values to their field width, as today's native code does, but keeps exact Int inputs and results. 300 packs as 44. A generic unpack reads the record from the front of the buffer and ignores extra bytes.

Format and count errors stay typed. Beginners must learn that a too-large value is silently changed. Experts must check ranges themselves when wrapping is wrong for their protocol.
options.technical:
Same signatures, grammar, size limit, error kinds and exact-Int routes as A, without unpack_from. pack reduces each integer modulo 2^w; signed fields store the low w bits of the two's-complement value. Range is still returned for non-integer problems, such as an impossible float conversion in pack_f64le.

unpack is a prefix reader: it needs at least one record's bytes, reads that one record from the front, and ignores everything after it. That same call is B's header read. An unpack buffer shorter than one record is still Buffer.

iter_unpack reads every complete record in order and drops an incomplete tail shorter than one record. So two 2-byte records plus one byte give both records, and the stray byte is lost silently. An empty buffer gives Ok([]). A zero record size is still Format. Unsigned Q still reads exact 0 to 2^64 - 1; signed codes are sign-extended.

print(binary.pack(">H", [1]))                   // Ok([0, 1]): high byte first
print(binary.unpack("<H", [U8]{1, 0, 9}))       // Ok([1]): no size check; the extra 9 is ignored
print(binary.unpack("<H", [U8]{1, 0, 9}))       // Ok([1]): header read; unpack already reads the front
print(binary.iter_unpack("<H", [U8]{1, 0, 2, 0, 9}))
// Ok([[1], [2]]): both whole records; the stray 9 is dropped
print(binary.unpack("<Q", [U8]{255, 255, 255, 255, 255, 255, 255, 255}))
// Ok([18446744073709551615]): exact, never -1
print(binary.unpack("<q", [U8]{255, 255, 255, 255, 255, 255, 255, 255}))
// Ok([-1]): q is the signed code

decisions.situation: Jet's binary module turns numbers into raw bytes and back, the way network protocols and file headers store them; this is called packing and unpacking. Today the same call can give two different answers. The Jet source version refuses to pack 300 into one byte, while the faster native version silently stores 44. The native version also reads very large 64-bit values back as negative numbers. A protocol record can therefore change meaning depending on how the program happens to run. This matters to anyone reading or writing file formats, network messages or hardware registers, where one wrong byte corrupts data quietly. You are deciding whether every route refuses out-of-range values and wrong-sized buffers, or wraps values to fit. We recommend one checked contract on every route, with exact numbers, typed errors, and a new unpack_from helper for reading a record from the front of a larger buffer.

decisions.title: Raw HTTP request bodies and one form decoder
decisions.situation: When a browser submits a web form, it sends text such as name=Ann+Lee&city=Oslo, where + means a space and %41 is a coded character (here the letter A). Jet's form reader turns that back into names and values. Today it gets bad input wrong: for name=%FF+ it gives back the raw text %FF+ unchanged, instead of a readable value or a clear error. Also, Jet's request reader refuses an uploaded body whose bytes are not text, so a small binary upload is lost. You decide what the form and query readers do with bad codes: follow the browser standard and show a replacement mark, or refuse with an error. We recommend the browser standard by default, plus strict siblings that code picking files or accounts must use. The binary-upload fix happens either way and is not part of this vote.
decisions.gist: Should form and query decoding use standard tolerant decoding with a strict companion, or strict decoding only?
decisions.lesson: Form text uses + for space and %HH for one coded byte. A follows the browser standard: a broken code such as %QZ stays as written, and bytes that are not valid text become the replacement mark �. Strict siblings refuse both, and code that picks files or accounts must use them. B refuses every bad code with an error. Both keep binary uploads intact; that fix is not part of the vote.
decisions.explainer:
Plain words first. A byte is a number from 0 to 255. Code writes one as U8{255}. FF is 255 written in hexadecimal (base 16), and 00 is 0. Text in Jet is UTF-8, a rule for spelling letters as bytes. The byte hexadecimal 0x41 (65) is the letter A, while a lone 0xFF byte is not valid text. An HTTP request is a header, a blank line, then the body bytes.

Form codes. In form text, + means a space and %HH means one byte written as two hex digits. So %41+ means "A ", and %FF+ means byte 0xFF followed by a space. Each code is decoded exactly once: %252F becomes %2F, never /.

Two jobs, one scanner. form_decode("name=%FF+&x=1") splits the text at & and = into a Query, a list of name and value pairs. query_decode does the same for the part of a web address after ?; today form_decode simply calls query_decode. Both options keep that split, and both use one shared scanner for + and %HH.

What A does with bad input. Like every browser, it keeps a broken code such as %QZ as plain text. It turns bytes that are not valid text into �, the replacement mark. That display text cannot tell %FF from %FE; both show �.

When that matters, as when a value picks a file or an account, the code must call a strict sibling instead. It refuses before any replacement happens. The original form text stays available only if your code kept it, because a request body can be read once.

In a real server, a refusal becomes the existing 400 Bad Request answer, not a crash. The handler keeps text, so it could log the exact input:

```jet
fn open_file(req: HTTPRequest) -> HTTPResponse HTTPError! {
    text :: req.body().text(4096) ?? return Ok(http_server.response(400, "bad body"))
    form :: http.form_decode_strict(text) ?? return Ok(http_server.response(400, "bad form"))
    name :: http.query_get(form, "file") ?? return Ok(http_server.response(400, "no file"))
    return Ok(http_server.response(200, "opening {name}"))
}
// body file=report.txt → 200 "opening report.txt"
// body file=%FF+       → 400 "bad form" (tolerant form_decode would give "� ")
```

The ?? panic(...) in the short examples only keeps them short; servers use the 400 route above.
decisions.story: Mina's server receives a two-byte binary upload and a form field written name=%FF+. She wants the upload kept byte for byte. She wants the form field handled the way browsers handle it, and she wants a clear refusal when a field is used to pick a file.
decisions.detail:
Code facts checked. Core/http/http.jet:87-90 already has Body.Empty, Body.Text and Body.Bytes. body_as_text (:291-298) turns bytes that are not valid text into an empty string. with_body (:832-834) and request_with (:856-859) route every body through it, so a Body.Bytes upload is lost. parse_request (:557-559) refuses a body that is not valid text with UnsupportedEncoding.

query_decode (:734-766) is the public, infallible pair splitter, and form_decode (:769) is a one-line call to it. query_decode strips one leading ?, skips empty segments, and treats a field without = as an empty value. Above C_MAX_BODY_BYTES (1 MiB) it silently returns an empty Query. It decodes keys and values with the private percent_decode (:1114-1136).

percent_decode falls back to the original text when the result is not valid text. query_get (:682) returns the first pair with a matching name. The devserver's own decoder (crates/jet-devserver/src/lib.rs:243-266) already uses browser-style replacement. Core/net/url.jet:274-291 is a separate strict URL decoder that keeps + as +; it is unchanged. tests/conformance/corpus/core/http has form_decode.jet and query_decode.jet.

Common repair, not voted. parse_request keeps a non-text body as bytes. with_body, request_with and response_ok pass Body.Bytes through the existing byte body source. Reading uses the existing one-shot body API: req.body().bytes(limit) or req.body().text(limit). A body can be read once; a second read reports BodyConsumed, as today. Streaming bodies, size limits and backpressure (slowing a fast sender) are unchanged.

No new body accessor or ownership rule is added.

The vote. It covers what query_decode, form_decode and the component decoder do with broken codes, bytes that are not valid text and oversize input. Both options share one splitter, one percent scanner and one text decoder, selected by a named policy. The devserver drops its private copy and calls the shared one.

Splitting rules shared by every entry point and both options: one leading ? is stripped; empty segments such as a&&b are skipped; a field without = has an empty value; an empty name is kept. Duplicate names are all kept in order, and query_get returns the first.

options.name: Standard tolerant helper with strict companion
options.detail:
query_decode, form_decode and form_component_decode follow the browser standard. + becomes a space, valid %HH codes become bytes, and broken codes such as %QZ stay as written. Bytes that are not valid text become �. Existing calls are signature-compatible, so ordinary HTML forms and query strings never need error handling. Input above 1 MiB still gives an empty Query, as today.

Strict siblings use the same scanner but refuse instead of replacing. query_decode_strict and form_decode_strict split a whole query or form; form_component_decode_strict handles one value. They return FormDecodeError: Escape for a broken code, UTF8 for invalid text, TooLarge above 1 MiB.

Compiling unchanged is not the same as staying correct. Under A, %FF and %FE both decode to �, so two different inputs can name the same thing. Code that uses a decoded value to pick a file, path or account must therefore switch to a strict sibling before decoding. The replacement mark cannot be undone afterwards.

The cutover does that for every such caller in this repository. jet fix lists each remaining query_decode and form_decode call in user code for review, and the release note names the change.
options.technical:
One splitter split_pairs(text, policy: FormPolicy) with FormPolicy.Tolerant and FormPolicy.Strict, one byte scanner and one UTF-8 decoder serve every entry point. form_component_decode(text: String) -> String Never! follows the WHATWG application/x-www-form-urlencoded percent-decode and UTF-8 decode with replacement, as consulted 2026-10-03.

form_component_decode_strict(text: String) -> String FormDecodeError! fails with FormDecodeError.Escape on an incomplete or non-hex escape. It fails with FormDecodeError.UTF8 on invalid decoded UTF-8.

query_decode(text) -> Query Never! and form_decode(text) -> Query Never! keep their signatures and use Tolerant. Above C_MAX_BODY_BYTES they return an empty Query, unchanged. query_decode_strict(text) -> Query FormDecodeError! and form_decode_strict(text) -> Query FormDecodeError! use Strict and fail with FormDecodeError.TooLarge above C_MAX_BODY_BYTES. form_decode and form_decode_strict stay one-line calls to the query pair, as form_decode is today.

Frozen vectors: FF gives one U+FFFD; C0 AF gives two; ED A0 80 gives three; E2 28 A1 gives U+FFFD, (, U+FFFD; truncated E2 82 gives one. The devserver calls the shared codec. Core/net/url.jet percent_decode is unchanged.

Cutover: every in-repo caller whose decoded value selects a file, path, account or other identity moves to a strict entry point. jet fix reports every remaining query_decode/form_decode call site for author review; it does not rewrite them.

use core.http as http

upload := "POST / HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: example\r\nContent-Length: 2\r\n\r\n".bytes()
&upload.push(U8{255}) // byte 0xFF: not valid text
&upload.push(U8{0})   // byte 0x00
req :: http.parse_request(upload) ?? panic("framing") // today: refused
print(req.body().bytes(1024) ?? panic("read")) // the two bytes 255 and 0, unchanged

q :: http.form_decode("name=%FF+&x=%41&path=%252F")
print(http.query_get(q, "name") ?? "missing") // "� " (today: "%FF+")
print(http.query_get(q, "x") ?? "missing")    // "A"
print(http.query_get(q, "path") ?? "missing") // "%2F", decoded once
print(http.form_component_decode("%QZ"))       // "%QZ", kept as written
link :: http.query_decode("?x=%41&&x=2")
print(http.query_get(link, "x") ?? "missing") // "A" (? stripped, empty segment skipped, first x)
strict :: http.form_decode_strict("name=%FF+&x=%41") // Err(FormDecodeError.UTF8)
bad :: http.form_component_decode_strict("%QZ")    // Err(FormDecodeError.Escape)

options.name: Strict helper only
options.detail:
There is only one, strict, behavior. query_decode, form_decode and form_component_decode refuse broken codes and bytes that are not valid text with FormDecodeError. Oversize input fails with TooLarge instead of giving an empty Query. Valid forms and query strings decode exactly as in A.

query_decode and form_decode change from never failing to possibly failing. Every existing caller must handle the error, usually with a 400 answer. Forms that browsers accept with a replacement mark are refused by Jet servers and the devserver.
options.technical:
form_component_decode(text: String) -> String FormDecodeError! with Escape and UTF8 cases. query_decode(text: String) -> Query FormDecodeError! and form_decode(text: String) -> Query FormDecodeError! add TooLarge above C_MAX_BODY_BYTES. form_decode stays a one-line call to query_decode.

Same splitting rules as A. All callers, including the conformance corpus, migrate in one cutover with no infallible alias. The devserver's tolerant query_param changes to the strict contract. Same shared scanner, same once-only decoding and same common body repair as A.
