decisions.title: Remove the unused #wire field marker instead of renaming it
decisions.situation: Jet accepts a marker spelled #wire on struct fields, but nothing in the compiler reads it, so writing it changes nothing. It is one of two lowercase markers left, and the owner directed that markers be capitalized. Renaming it would keep a marker that silently does nothing. This vote decides whether #wire is removed, or kept as #Wire with or without a job.
decisions.gist: Should the do-nothing #wire field marker be removed, or kept as #Wire?
decisions.lesson: A marker is a # tag on code, such as #Skip on a field. Jet's registry lists every marker. The data-format markers already exist: #Rename sets a field's outside name per format, and #Skip leaves a field out.
decisions.explainer:
Today #wire is accepted on any field and ignored. No decision defines it and no program uses it. Its only other mention is a zero-use triage entry in a test.

The jobs a wire marker might do already have markers. #Rename("user_id", json: "userId") names a field for each format. #Skip leaves a field out. #Encode, #Decode and #Codable request the codecs. The open casing ballot for outside names builds on #Rename.

Under A, #wire is deleted. Writing it gets the normal unknown-marker error with a did-you-mean, which suggests #Rename or #Skip.

Beginner path: no change, since nobody writes it. Expert path: the existing format markers.
decisions.story: Ana sees #wire in the marker list and puts it on a field she wants sent as JSON. Nothing changes in her output, and nothing tells her why.
decisions.detail:
Code facts, checked 2026-10-05 on the dev worktree.

crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Markers.jet:213 declares marker wire($sites: [.Field]). The same file declares Rename at :126, with per-format names for json, cbor, csv, toml, yaml, xml, args, env, db and layout. It declares Skip at :128, and Encode, Decode and Codable at :79-86.

tests/truthfulness.rs:609 lists wire in the zero-use triage, citing card #1830, which is done. The Core-foundations catalogue (Docs/research/core-foundations-2026-10-04.md, row 31) found no source use, no defining decision and no arguments. The row entered in commit 413ac90b6 without a ruling.

D-MARKER-CASE1=A (2026-10-05) says #allow and the unused #wire get capitals. Owner question q00mjarf (2), from 2026-10-01, asks whether #wire is renamed, given a meaning, or something else. The owner rule of 2026-10-01 says only the owner removes features, hence this ballot.

Open ballot D-WIRE-CASE1 maps Jet names to outside names through #Rename and a package naming key. A second field marker for the same job would give two spellings for one meaning, which I8 forbids.

Research. serde (Rust), System.Text.Json (.NET) and Go's encoding/json each have one per-field rename and one skip mechanism. None ships a marker that is accepted and ignored. Silent acceptance of a no-op tag is the wrong way: users believe it works.

options.name: Remove #wire
options.detail: Delete the marker row, its test entries and its triage line. Writing #wire gets the unknown-marker error, whose did-you-mean suggests #Rename or #Skip.
options.technical: Remove marker wire from Prelude/Markers.jet and the truthfulness zero-use entry. Add wire to the retired-marker teaching table, pointing to #Rename and #Skip. Both compiler halves read the one registry (I9). The #allow to #Allow rename under D-MARKER-CASE1 is unaffected.

options.name: Rename to #Wire, no job
options.detail: Capitalize it as directed and keep it accepted on fields. It still does nothing.
options.technical: Rename the row to Wire. Keep the zero-use triage entry. Writing it compiles and has no effect.

options.name: Give #Wire the outside-name job
options.detail: Make #Wire("userId") set a field's outside name, beside or instead of #Rename.
options.technical: Either a second spelling of #Rename, or a migration of every #Rename use and of the open D-WIRE-CASE1 design to the new word.

comparisons.note: One struct tag per format sets the outside name; a dash skips the field (pkg.go.dev/encoding/json).

recommendation.why: A marker that compiles and does nothing misleads people. Its possible jobs already belong to #Rename and #Skip, so removing it loses nothing and completes the PascalCase cleanup.
gains: No marker silently does nothing.
One way to name and skip fields.
The marker list is fully capitalized.

whyNot.reason: It keeps a marker that compiles and does nothing, which misleads anyone who writes it.
It duplicates #Rename, giving two spellings for one job.

recommendation.tradeoff: Removing an unused name rather than renaming a no-op.

decisions.title: Creating and removing game entities: checked handles, changes queued during systems
decisions.situation: Jet games already have a ratified way to declare components and query them, and a ratified scheduler that runs game systems in parallel. Nothing yet says how a game creates a new thing, such as a bullet, or removes one, such as a destroyed enemy. Without that rule the entity system cannot be built, and today's query returns one built-in placeholder row. This vote picks how entities are created, referred to and removed, including while systems run in parallel.
decisions.gist: How does a Jet game create, refer to and remove entities, including while systems run in parallel?
decisions.lesson: An entity is one thing in a game world, such as a bullet. A component is a data struct attached to it, such as Position. A system is a function run every frame over matching entities. A handle is a small value that refers to one entity.
decisions.explainer:
Ratified so far: components are plain structs (D-GAME-ECS1=B), registered with scene.component<T>() and read with scene.query<Position, Velocity>(). Systems are listed with scene.systems([...]) and run in parallel when their data does not conflict (D-SYSSCHED1=A). That scheduler already merges commands at each stage end, in declaration order, so output repeats exactly.

Under A, scene.spawn(...) returns an Entity handle. A handle holds a slot number and a generation count, the same idea as Jet's Pool and Id. When an entity is removed, its slot's generation goes up, so an old handle can never reach the slot's next occupant. scene.get<Position>(e) returns Position?, which is None once e is gone.

The same calls work everywhere. In setup code they apply at once. Inside a system they are queued and applied at the stage end, so parallel systems never see a half-changed world.

Beginner path: spawn, despawn, insert and get, with no new concepts. Expert path: .after() orders a reader after a spawner, and jet inspect choices --frame shows when each queued change applied.

Shared work in every option: build columnar component storage and real queries, replacing the placeholder row.
decisions.story: Kai is writing a space shooter. A gun system creates bullets every frame, and a collision system removes bullets and enemies. He needs both to run each frame without crashes or one system seeing half of another's changes.
decisions.detail:
Code facts, checked 2026-10-05.

Core/game/game.jet has Scene, Replay and Backend only; there is no entity type. The 2026-10-05 systems-perf mine reports that jet_game_scene_query returns one hard-coded Position and Velocity row. That gap is #238 criterion 10, absorbed from #820.

Card #820's plan said ballot first: draft D-GAME-ENTITY1 with same-program alternatives. Its recommended shape was scene.spawn, scene.despawn, &scene.insert and a generation-checked Entity. The ballot was never drafted. The 2026-10-05 mine flagged it again.

Ratified law this builds on. D-GAME-ECS1=B: struct components, scene.component<T>(), scene.query<...>(). D-SYSSCHED1=A: parallel systems from checked data access; commands, events and logs merge in declaration order at each stage end. D-GAME-LOOP1=A: the backend runs on_frame until the window closes. D-PIN1=A: Pool<T> hands out Id<T> links instead of addresses; Core/mem/mem.jet:29 declares Pool<T>.

Research. Bevy's Entity packs an index and a generation, and Commands defer spawn, despawn and insert to sync points. EnTT keeps a version in each entity identifier and refuses stale ones. flecs gives entity ids a generation and defers structural changes while systems iterate. Unity DOTS records structural changes from jobs in an EntityCommandBuffer, played back later. Rust's slotmap crate popularized the same generational handle for plain collections.

The common failures these designs avoid. Raw index reuse lets an old reference silently read a new entity, a version of the ABA problem. Changing structure while iterating invalidates iterators or races between threads. Unity's older GameObject model shows a third trap: a destroyed object compares equal to null through operator overloading, which surprises users.

Best-of-all-worlds: generational handles from Bevy, EnTT and flecs. Deferred structural change only where parallelism needs it, as Bevy and Unity do. Immediate change in setup code, so beginners see one spelling. Optional get instead of a fake-null object.

options.name: Checked handles; changes queued inside systems
options.detail: spawn returns an Entity handle with a generation check. despawn, insert and remove use it, and get returns an optional. In setup code changes apply at once. Inside systems they queue and apply at the stage end in declaration order, reusing the scheduler's merge.
options.technical:
Entity is a value type holding a slot index and a generation, the same scheme as Pool<T>/Id<T>. The scene keeps a free list and per-component columnar storage. scene.spawn(c1, c2, ...) -> Entity; scene.despawn(e); &scene.insert(e, c); scene.remove<C>(e); scene.get<C>(e) -> C?.

Inside a system body these record into the stage's command list, which D-SYSSCHED1 already merges in declaration order at stage end. A queued spawn returns its Entity at once, so it can be stored and linked. Queries iterate storage directly with no per-row handle check. Replays record commands, keeping runs repeatable. One meaning on every tier (I9).

options.name: Changes apply at once; such systems run alone
options.detail: Every spawn and despawn applies immediately, even inside systems. Any system that changes structure runs by itself, never in parallel with others.
options.technical: Same handle type. The scheduler marks structure-changing systems as conflicting with every other system and serializes them. Queries must snapshot or guard against changes during iteration.

options.name: One pool per kind of thing
options.detail: No scene-wide entity. Each kind of thing lives in its own Pool<T>, referred to by Id<T>. Queries read one pool at a time.
options.technical: Reuse Pool<T>/Id<T> from D-PIN1. A game declares pools such as Pool<Bullet>. Adding a component to an existing thing means changing its struct. Cross-kind queries need hand-written joins.
options.code:
bullets :: Pool<Bullet>.new()
id :: bullets.add(Bullet{x: 0})
bullets.remove(id)

comparisons.note: Jobs record structural changes in an EntityCommandBuffer that plays back later (docs.unity3d.com/Packages/com.unity.entities).
Entity identifiers carry a version; a destroyed entity's old id is no longer valid (github.com/skypjack/entt/wiki).

recommendation.why: It combines what every mature entity system converged on: handles that cannot reach the wrong entity, and queued changes so parallel systems stay safe and repeatable. Setup code still changes at once, so beginners learn one spelling.
gains: A stale handle can never read a different entity.
Systems that spawn still run in parallel.
Runs and replays repeat exactly.

losses.loss: A spawn inside a system is invisible to other systems until the stage ends.
losses.mitigation: Use .after() to order a reader; jet inspect choices --frame shows when each change applied.

whyNot.reason: Every system that spawns or removes loses parallelism, and iteration needs extra guards.
It cannot attach components to existing things, which the ratified component queries need.

recommendation.tradeoff: Changes made inside systems land at the stage end in exchange for safe parallel systems.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Drafted by BallotInventory 2026-10-05, from card #820's planned ballot, now #238 criterion 10. Only the ballot validator ran; no programs ran.

After ratification under A, build Entity, the free list and columnar storage in Core/game. Route spawn, despawn, insert and remove through the stage command list inside systems. Replace the placeholder query row.

Prove: a despawned handle's get returns None after its slot is reused. Spawns from two parallel systems land in declaration order. A replay reproduces the same entity handles. The game goldens match on every tier.

surface.gist: How does a Jet game create, refer to and remove entities, including while systems run in parallel?
surface.lesson: An entity is one thing in a game, such as a bullet. A component is data on it. A system runs every frame. A handle refers to one entity.

current.note: Today: components and queries are ratified; creating or removing is undefined.

wild.note: Index plus generation; changes queued to sync points (docs.rs/bevy).
wild.code:
let e = commands.spawn((Position { x: 0.0 },)).id();
commands.entity(e).despawn();

options.name: Checked handles; changes queued inside systems
options.gist: Immediate in setup, queued inside systems.
gains: Stale handles never reach the wrong entity.
Spawning systems stay parallel.
losses: A spawn shows up at the stage end.

e :: scene.spawn(Bullet{}, Position{x: 0})
scene.get<Position>(e)   // Position?
scene.despawn(e)
// inside a system: applied at stage end

options.name: Changes apply at once; such systems run alone
options.gist: Immediate everywhere; changers run serially.
gains: Changes are visible at once.
losses: Spawning systems lose parallelism.

options.name: One pool per kind of thing
options.gist: No entity; a Pool<T> per kind.
gains: Reuses existing Pool and Id.
losses: No components added to existing things.

proposed.code:

id :: bullets.add(Bullet{x: 0})
bullets.remove(id)

recommendation.why: Safe handles plus queued changes, as mature entity systems converged on; setup code still changes at once.
gains: No stale-handle bugs; parallel and repeatable.

losses.mitigation: Use .after() to order a reader; jet inspect choices --frame shows when it applied.

whyNot.reason: Spawning systems lose parallelism and iteration needs guards.
It cannot add components to existing things, which ratified queries need.

recommendation.tradeoff: Changes inside systems land at the stage end, for safe parallel systems.

designAway.loss: Two rules, immediate in setup and queued in systems, could confuse beginners.
attempts: One spelling everywhere; the queue is invisible except for timing, and inspect shows it.
designAway.result: Negligible: beginners write the same calls in both places.

designAway.loss: A handle check on every access could cost speed.
attempts: Queries iterate storage directly; only get by handle compares one generation number.
designAway.result: Removed from hot loops.

decisions.title: Which characters can a name use, and how Jet warns about look-alike names
decisions.situation: Jet already lets you name things in many languages, but the rule has holes. A Hindi name fails with a confusing error, and so does an accent typed as a separate mark. A Latin a and a Cyrillic a quietly become two different names, and an invisible filler letter is a valid name. You are deciding which characters names may use and how Jet handles look-alikes; we recommend Unicode's standard name rule plus a look-alike warning.
decisions.gist: Which characters may names use, and how should Jet handle names that look identical?
decisions.lesson: A name is the word you give a value, like `total`. Unicode can store one letter as one piece or as a letter plus an accent mark. Today Jet accepts letters and digits, even an invisible filler letter, and keeps no single stored form. Hidden direction marks are blocked by separate work, whichever option wins. Every Jet compiler must read one shared character table.
decisions.story: Asha teaches programming in Pune. Her students name variables in Hindi, the way they think about the problem, and Jet stops partway through नमस्ते with 'doesn't mean anything here'. Her colleague Lukas reviews a pull request where a Cyrillic а sits beside a Latin a; the two names look identical, and Jet says nothing.
decisions.detail:
Exercised 2026-10-05 with release jet $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/candidates/dev-05ea86f65/jet. Probes and outputs are in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/mine/legwork/languages-b/probes/.

Probe A: NFD café gives E0001 'The character U+0301 doesn't mean anything here (yet)'. Its Why text wrongly calls the mark unprintable. Probe C: नमस्ते gives E0001 on U+094D, the virama; vowel signs such as U+0947 are already accepted as alphabetic. Probe D: Latin a and Cyrillic а bind two names and print 1 then 2, with no warning. Probe E: U+202E in a comment and U+2066 in a string literal compile and run.

Source reading: both lexers accept alphabetic or numeric scalars only (Compiler/JetLexer/Source/Lexer/Scan.jet:47-55; crates/jet-lexer/src/Lexer/Scan.rs:772). The self-hosted lexer uses Core's approximate classifier (#4426). So the two compilers can disagree on which names are valid.

Batch witnesses: in CURSED (BiFt4vw1-uM 13:29-24:08) an agent added emoji names by changing only the start and continue tables. The Bun copy then emitted JavaScript that could not run, and the compiler copy segfaulted. A name rule is end-to-end law. DreamBerd (_oiBWfuf0Oo 03:52-04:31) shows the demand for emoji names. D-EXT-EMOJI1=A already rejected an emoji file extension, partly over invisible variation selectors.

Rule-9 research, legwork resources 01-10. Rust RFC 2457: UAX #31, NFC, confusable warning, and the NFC over NFKC rationale. Rust CVE-2021-42574 advisory: deny lints for the nine direction marks in literals and comments. It suggests escapes and found 5 affected crates, none malicious.

Trojan Source paper (Boucher and Anderson, arXiv 2111.00169, section 7.6): ban direction controls in specs and compilers. Use escapes for legitimate text, and keep defenses on by default. PEP 3131: XID with combining marks, normalized to NFKC. C++ P1949R7: UAX #31 and NFC, emoji ill-formed, homoglyphs left to tools.

Go spec: no canonicalization, so accented forms differ. Swift: broad hand-written ranges that include U+200B to U+200D and U+202A to U+202E. Zig #4151: closed for ASCII names plus @"..." quoted names. UAX #31 and UTS #39 introductions.

What worked: UAX #31 with NFC is the converged rule in Rust and C++, and Python uses the NFKC variant. Direction-mark bans shipped in Rust 1.56.1 with negligible ecosystem impact. What failed: hand-made ranges in Swift and pre-23 C++ admitted invisible or accidental characters. No normalization, as in Go and Jet today, makes same-looking names differ.

Evidence gap: no friction data for confusable warnings beyond Rust's note that they stay warnings for forward compatibility. Shared work for any option: one generated character table read by both compilers, the spec.md:47-48 rewrite, registry, grammars and goldens.

Scope change at distill on 2026-10-05. Hidden direction marks in source (probe E, CVE-2021-42574) already have an owner: #3881 criterion [#4204]. That work needs no owner vote, because it follows the ratified UTF-8 source rules. So this ballot drops direction marks, and every option inherits that fix.

Adversarial pass, 2026-10-05, same release; probes in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/mine/legwork/adversary2/. hangul.jet: the invisible Hangul filler U+3164 binds and prints a name today, the trick behind the 2021 'invisible JavaScript backdoor' write-up by Certitude. vs16.jet: U+FE0F after a is E0001 today, yet plain XID_Continue admits it.

subscript.jet: v₀, x² and ⓐ are valid names today and print 13; plain XID rejects all three. So plain UAX #31 would both reopen a hole and break working names.

A therefore adopts two UAX #31 standard profiles added in Unicode 15.1: the Default-Ignorable Exclusion Profile (section 7.3) and the Mathematical Compatibility Notation Profile (section 7.1). UAX #31, fetched from unicode.org/reports/tr31 on 2026-10-05, points to UTS #55, Unicode Source Code Handling, for their use in programming languages. Swift and Julia already accept subscript names.

Only circled letters such as ⓐ remain lost; a repository search found no .jet file using circled, subscript or superscript names. Rust additionally warns on Restricted characters (uncommon_codepoints); A removes the invisible ones at the rule instead.

options.name: Every script, one stored form, look-alike warning
options.detail:
Names follow Unicode's default identifier rule. A name starts with a letter or underscore, then letters, combining marks and digits. So Hindi, Arabic, Thai and accented names all work. Unicode's standard math add-on keeps names Jet accepts today, such as v₀ and x², and adds ∂, ∇ and ∞.

Invisible characters are never part of a name. That closes today's hole where the invisible Hangul filler ㅤ is a valid name, and it keeps out invisible variation selectors. Circled letters such as ⓐ, which Jet accepts today, are not letters under the rule, so they stop being names.

Each name is stored in one normal form. An é typed as one piece and an e plus an accent are the same name. The formatter rewrites names, never text inside quotes, to that one form once.

Different letters that only look alike, such as Latin a and Cyrillic а, stay two names. Two such names in one package get a warning naming both, and so does a single name that mixes scripts to look like another word. Emoji are not names, as in Rust and C++. Invisible direction marks are rejected by separate, already-approved security work in every option.
options.technical:
Identifier = (XID_Start | '_') XID_Continue*, the UAX #31 default identifier, with two UAX #31 standard profiles. The Default-Ignorable Exclusion Profile (section 7.3) removes Default_Ignorable_Code_Point characters such as U+3164, U+115F, U+034F, U+200B-U+200D and U+FE00-U+FE0F.

The Mathematical Compatibility Notation Profile (section 7.1) adds ID_Compat_Math_Start (∂, ∇, ∞ and their styled variants) and ID_Compat_Math_Continue (subscript and superscript digits and signs). No Jet lexer uses those symbols as operators. The Unicode version is pinned with the Core UCD data of #4426.

Identifiers are NFC-normalized at lex time; string and comment contents are never normalized. ASCII names pass the NFC quick check, so ASCII-only code pays no normalization cost. RFC 2457 explains NFC over NFKC: math letters stay distinct, and search tools find NFC text. Field names used as wire keys use the NFC spelling.

The confusable check uses the UTS #39 skeleton per package, also against keywords, plus the UTS #39 mixed-script confusable check for a single name (Rust's mixed_script_confusables). It is a warning only (D-LINTPOLICY1).

One generated table is read by the Rust and self-hosted lexers and by the casing check (D-CASE-LAW1, Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Casing.jet). That check already accepts an uncased first letter for both PascalCase and snake_case (Casing.jet:138-160). It must also count combining marks and math-profile characters as word characters, or Hindi type names and ∂f would fail E0357. Route, registry and file names keep their own rules.

Backends must spell every accepted name in their output. Rust and JavaScript reject math-profile characters, and the Rust emitter only prefixes names with __jet_ (Compiler/JetCodegen/Source/Emit/Context.jet:432-436). So emitted names encode any character outside the target's identifier set; the CURSED witness in detail shows why.
options.code:
café :: 1        // either typing of é is one name
नमस्ते :: 3       // works
v₀ :: 0          // math subscripts keep working
a :: 4
а :: 5           // warning: looks like `a` on line 4

options.name: English letters only
options.detail: Names use A to Z, digits and underscore, as in Zig and early Rust. Text and comments still hold any language. Look-alike names cannot exist, but students and teams who name things in their own language lose that, and existing accented names must be renamed.
options.technical: Identifier = [A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*. No normalization or confusable table needed for names.
options.code:
cafe :: 1        // café as a name: error, use ASCII
naam :: 3        // the Hindi spelling is an error; write naam
print("नमस्ते")   // fine inside text

options.name: Keep today's letters
options.detail: Keep the current rule: letters and digits as Unicode classifies them, with no combining marks, no single stored form and no look-alike check. Scripts that need marks stay broken, and look-alike names stay silent.
options.technical: Status quo: Compiler/JetLexer/Source/Lexer/Scan.jet:47-55 (unicode.is_alphabetic / is_numeric, approximate per #4426) and crates/jet-lexer/src/Lexer/Scan.rs:772 (char::is_alphabetic).
options.code:
café :: 2        // e + accent mark: E0001
नमस्ते :: 3       // E0001
а :: 5           // silent second name

comparisons.note: UAX #31 identifiers with NFC normalization; confusable_idents warns (warn, not deny, so new confusables never break builds); 1.56.1 added deny-by-default lints for direction marks in literals and comments. A crates.io scan found 5 crates with those marks, none malicious. RFC 2457; blog 2021-11-01.
comparisons.code:
let café = 1;
let а = 5;   // warning: confusable_idents

comparisons.note: PEP 3131: XID_Start XID_Continue*, which includes combining marks (Mn, Mc); NFKC normalization (folds more than NFC; Rust rejected NFKC because it merges math letters).
P1949R7 adopted UAX #31 and NFC, and made emoji names ill-formed because emoji support was an accident and incomplete. It left homoglyph defense to tools.
comparisons.code:
int café = 1;   // OK
class 💩 {};      // ill-formed since C++23

comparisons.note: Letters (Lu, Ll, Lt, Lm, Lo) and Nd only, no normalization: 'a single accented code point is distinct from the same character constructed from combining an accent'. Same holes as Jet today.
Broad hand-written ranges that admit emoji, and its identifier-head list even includes U+200B-U+200D and U+202A-U+202E, the invisible and direction characters A rejects.
ASCII names only; the non-ASCII proposal (#4151) was closed for status quo, with @"..." quoted names as the escape hatch.

recommendation.why: A lets every learner use their own language, makes one letter typed two ways one name, and bans invisible names. It follows the Unicode rules Rust, Python and C++ converged on, and flags look-alikes in review.
gains: One rule works for every script.
Invisible or look-alike names cannot hide in review.

losses.loss: Rare circled letters such as ⓐ stop being names.
losses.mitigation: The error names the character and suggests a plain letter; no Jet file in the repository uses one. Names typed in split accent form are respelled by jet fmt, names only, with no change in meaning.

losses.loss: Look-alike names across scripts get a warning.
losses.mitigation: It is a warning that never blocks, and it names both places, so one rename fixes it.

whyNot.reason: B shuts out learners who think in other languages, which Jet's beginner promise rejects.
C keeps Hindi broken, look-alike names silent and invisible names valid.

recommendation.tradeoff: Jet adopts Unicode's name rule plus one look-alike warning; only rare circled-letter names are lost.

decisions.title: Carriage return and Unicode escapes in plain strings
decisions.situation: Web, mail and CSV formats end lines with carriage return then newline, but Jet text cannot spell the carriage return, so programs build it from raw byte numbers. Jet's own debug printing already shows text as "a\r\u{1b}", which Jet then refuses to read back. You asked for named terminal codes, easy helpers and a checked terminal-text form instead of raw codes in plain strings, and a companion vote, now ratified, provides exactly that. This vote decides only the plain-text floor beneath it: whether quoted text gains a carriage-return escape and one escape for any Unicode character.
decisions.gist: Add \r and \u{…} to quoted text, add \r only, or keep four escapes and use byte literals?
decisions.lesson: An escape is a backslash code inside quotes that stands for a character you cannot type or see. Jet strings know four: \n newline, \t tab, \" quote and \\ backslash. A carriage return is character 13; web headers end every line with carriage return plus newline. A Unicode escape \u{1F600} names any character by its hexadecimal number.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: write "GET / HTTP/1.1\r\n" exactly as in RFCs, tutorials and other languages. Terminal colors and cursor moves do not use raw codes in plain text: the companion terminal vote gives checked ANSI{"[bold red]error:[/] {name}"} text and helpers such as tui.clearLine(). Expert path: write invisible or confusable characters by number, such as "\u{200B}" for a zero-width space, so a reviewer can see them. Byte literals keep their own \x0D form because bytes are not text.

Shared work under every option: E0001 lists the full escape set, the Rust and Jet lexers stay identical, and Debug output prints only escapes that the lexer reads back.
decisions.story: Ana writes a tiny HTTP client over a TCP socket. Every tutorial writes the request as "GET / HTTP/1.1\r\n...", and Jet answers E0001. She copies a workaround that builds the two characters from byte numbers, then prints the request with Debug and sees \r again.
decisions.detail:
Suite revision by BallotSuite1, 2026-10-07. Wording only: the companion terminal vote D-TUI-ANSI1 was ratified as A on 2026-10-06, so the situation no longer calls it a proposal. Options and claims are unchanged.

YOUR QUESTION (q4p8lzbr, 2026-10-05)

You asked for three things. First, ANSI escape constants in the TUI Core library, so every terminal code lives in one place. Second, helpers that color text, clear lines, move or reset the cursor and switch to the alternate screen. Third, a strongly typed string literal for terminal codes, so they never mix with plain "" text.

Answer: yes, through the companion ballot D-TUI-ANSI1 on this card. It recommends core.tui constants (tui.ESC, tui.CSI), helpers (tui.moveCursor(row:, col:), tui.clearLine(), tui.altScreen(on:), tui.mouse(on:)) and a checked ANSI{"[bold red]error:[/] {name}"} literal. That literal makes a terminal-text value, not a String. A misspelled style fails the build, inserted user text prints as text, and styles always close. It reuses Jet's existing checked literal heads, such as SQL{…} and HTML{…}, so it adds no new syntax.

What changes in this ballot: it stays the plain-text floor, and it no longer teaches terminal styling through raw codes. Protocol text still needs \r. Debug output, review of invisible characters and core.tui's own source still need \u{…}. Option A's example now shows a zero-width space instead of a hand-written color code, and the beginner path for colors points to the companion. The two votes are independent: D-TUI-ANSI1's checked literal works under every option here.

CODE FACTS

These code facts were checked on 2026-10-05 against dev 91a438ce4 and release jet dev-05ea86f65.

Law: spec.md:62-63 and S20 allow four escapes. Any other escape is E0001. D-BOUND-RAW1 and D-RAWSTR1 reaffirm the four-entry table. Byte-head literals already accept \xNN (Compiler/JetLexer/Source/Lexer/Payload.jet:551-572): [U8]{"GET / HTTP/1.1\x0D\x0A..."} produced 27 bytes with byte 14 = 13 in a probe.

Exercised: "{head}\r\n..." fails E0001 three times (probe status_line.jet, first version).

Workarounds in the tree: Examples/features/net/http_parse_body_limits.jet:32 `crlf :: String.from_bytes([U8]{13, 10}) ?? panic("CRLF")`; Compiler/JetDriver/Source/Driver/Loader.jet:211,263,571 and Pipeline.jet:2503 `String.from_bytes([U8]{U8{13}}) ?? ""`; Examples/features/net/http_server_trailers.jet:26-29 pushes bytes 13 and 10 per line. 105 tracked .jet files compare or push byte 13.

Debug round trip: the evaluator renderer (Compiler/JetEval/Source/Formatting/Values.jet:157-181) and the default-run runtime both follow Rust's {:?}. A probe ($JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/mine/legwork/adversary2/debug_rt.jet) printed the text a, CR, NUL, ESC, {b}, ', e plus U+0301 as "a\r\0\u{1b}{b}'e\u{301}". None of \r, \0 or \u{…} lex today. Compiler/JetCodegen/Source/Emit/Context.jet:476-520 only spells Rust source literals, so it is not a Debug renderer.

Ratified example drift: D-HTTP-BYTES-FORM1's code writes "POST / HTTP/1.1\r\n...", which does not compile today (handled on card #4428 independently of this vote).

No decision was found that rejected \r or \u{...} on purpose; S20 is the original four-entry choice.

Fresh review reconciliation, 2026-10-05. D-BOUND-RAW1's line that plain strings keep the four-entry table only states its own scope, so A amends it together with S20. Once #3881 [#4204] rejects raw direction marks inside literals, \u{202E} becomes their legitimate visible spelling, as rustc's lint already suggests.

Java decodes \u escapes before lexing, so a comment containing \u000a ends early; that design is a known failure. A avoids it because Jet decodes escapes only inside quoted text. In interpolated text the lexer reads \u{ as an escape before a brace can open a hole, so "\u{1b}" never names a binding 1b.

Adversarial pass, 2026-10-05, same release; probes in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/mine/legwork/adversary2/. Braces: the probe above prints {b} unchanged, and pasting "a{b}" back would interpolate b. So the round-trip promise covers escapes only. Doubling braces in Debug was rejected because it would make every JSON value in Debug output harder to read, and Rust prints them plainly too.

char_quote.jet: '\'' is E0001 today, although the char-literal E0001 text lists \' as an escape. So no apostrophe Char can be written, yet the evaluator's Debug prints one as '\''. A adds \' to character literals so that Char Debug output reads back too.

One table, Syntax::ESCAPES (crates/jet-foundation/src/Syntax/math_layout.rs:456), feeds plain strings, character literals, [U8] byte-head bodies and the module evaluator (crates/jet-env-model/src/ModuleEval/Eval.rs:2608). Adding r there gives byte literals \r as well, as in Rust's b"\r"; \u{…} is handled outside that table and stays text-only.

options.name: Add \r and \u{…}
options.detail:
Quoted text and character literals gain \r (character 13) and \u{H}. H is one to six hexadecimal digits naming any Unicode scalar. Surrogates (D800-DFFF), values above 10FFFF, empty braces and seven digits are E0001 at the exact span. Character literals also accept \', which today's error text already lists but the lexer rejects. Byte literals gain \r through the shared table, keep \xNN for other bytes, and do not gain \u.

Debug prints only \n \t \r \" \' \\ and \u{…}, so every escape it prints reads back as the same text. Braces still print as themselves, as in Rust, so pasted Debug text containing { needs {{. jet fmt rewrites \u{a}, \u{9} and \u{d} to \n, \t and \r, and writes other hex in lowercase without leading zeros. Each character keeps one spelling in formatted code.
options.technical:
Both lexers change. Rust paths: crates/jet-lexer/src/Lexer/Strings.rs:195-210,550-561 and Scan.rs:1014-1030. Self-hosted path: Compiler/JetLexer/Source/Lexer/Payload.jet:574-590. Syntax::ESCAPES gains r=13, the char-literal path gains \', and a braced scalar escape is added for text and Char only. Validation uses the scalar rule of D-CHAR-SCALAR1 Char.from_u32: 0..=0x10FFFF minus 0xD800..=0xDFFF.

Triple-quoted strings follow automatically, since spec.md:73-74 gives them the ordinary escape rules. Raw backtick strings and typed text heads are unchanged (D-RAWSTR1, D-BOUND-RAW1). The module evaluator's literal decoder (crates/jet-env-model/src/ModuleEval/Eval.rs:2608) learns \u{…} too.

The evaluator renderer (JetEval Values.jet:157-181) and the runtime Debug formatter for default run and AOT print NUL as \u{0} instead of \0. Everything else they print already lexes under A. E0001 why-text lists the six text escapes, and the char-literal text matches its real set. jet fmt canonicalization is a formatter rule, not a new diagnostic.

head :: "GET / HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: example\r\n\r\n"
zwsp :: "\u{200b}"          // zero-width space, now visible in review
print("{"a\rb":Debug}")   // "a\rb" — paste it back and it is the same text
quote :: '\''              // apostrophe as a Char
bad :: "\u{D800}"          // E0001: D800 is a surrogate, not a character

options.name: Add \r only
options.detail: Quoted text and character literals gain \r. Everything else stays: NUL, escape and other invisible characters still have no spelling, so Debug output for them cannot be read back and must keep printing an unreadable form.
options.technical: Same two-lexer change limited to r=13. Debug renderers keep \0 and \u{hex} for other controls, which remain unlexable; or they print those characters raw, which hides them.
options.code:
head :: "GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: example

"
esc :: String.from_bytes([U8]{27}) ?? ""
bold :: "{esc}[1mready{esc}[0m"

options.name: Keep four escapes; teach byte literals
options.detail: No lexer change. Wire fixtures use byte literals such as [U8]{"...\x0D\x0A"}; text that needs a carriage return interpolates a value built from bytes. E0001 for \r gains a fix line pointing to the byte literal. Debug output still prints \r and \0 that Jet cannot read.
options.technical: Only the E0001 fix text changes. Byte literals are [U8], so any text processing first needs String.from_bytes with a failure path.

comparisons.note: Reference, tokens chapter, consulted 2026-10-05: \n \r \t \\ \0, \x up to 7F, \u{…} up to six digits, must be a scalar.
From the language guide (not fetched in this run): \0 \\ \t \n \r \" \' and \u{n} with one to eight hex digits.

recommendation.why: A lets protocol text read exactly like the specifications, gives every invisible character a visible spelling, and makes every escape Debug prints something Jet can read back. Terminal colors and cursor moves get named, checked forms in the companion terminal vote, which builds on this floor.
gains: Every RFC and tutorial line pastes in unchanged.
Hidden or confusable characters get a visible spelling.
Every escape Debug prints is valid Jet.

losses.loss: Two spellings exist for newline, tab and carriage return (\n or \u{a}).
losses.mitigation: jet fmt rewrites the numeric form of those three to the short form, so formatted code has one spelling.

losses.loss: Learners meet two more escapes, plus \' in character literals.
losses.mitigation: E0001 lists the full set with one example each, and the HTTP and CSV lessons introduce \r where it is needed. \' is the spelling C, Java and Rust programmers already type.

whyNot.reason: Fixes line endings but leaves escape, NUL and zero-width characters unwritable, and Debug still prints escapes Jet cannot read.
Keeps the language smallest, but text code still builds characters from bytes with a failure path, and Debug still prints escapes Jet cannot read.

recommendation.tradeoff: Two short escapes, normalized by the formatter, instead of byte-building workarounds.

reviewPasses.beginner: Fresh agent: MineReview. Skill: rli5. Predict tasks failed on hex, on \u{1b} and on option B calling a control character 'Escape'; all three are now explained in the surface. Explain, modify and derive tasks passed, and Debug and byte literals are not needed to choose.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Validate the payload without Tower writes. After ratification of A, both lexers accept \r and \u{1..6 hex} in quoted, triple-quoted and character literals, and \' in character literals. They reject surrogates, values above 10FFFF, empty braces and seven digits with E0001 at the exact span. Byte literals accept \r and \xNN and reject \u{…}.

Debug of "a\r\u{0}\u{1b}" prints that same spelling. The printed text lexes back to equal text on default run, AOT and the evaluator. Debug of text with braces prints them unchanged. jet fmt rewrites \u{a}, \u{9} and \u{d} to \n, \t and \r, and \u{001B} to \u{1b}.

Migrate the workarounds named in detail in the same cutover. They are http_parse_body_limits.jet:32, Loader.jet:211, 263 and 571, Pipeline.jet:2503 and http_server_trailers.jet:26-29. Update spec.md:62-63, S20, S41 and both E0001 registry texts together.

decisions.title: Should unused-name warnings reach fields never read and cases never built?
decisions.situation: Jet already warns about unused imports, unused variables, private functions nobody calls, and exports nobody imports. It says nothing about a struct field that is written but never read, or an enum case that is matched but never created. In a growing app these leftovers mislead new readers about which data matters and can keep costly data moving. You are deciding whether the existing unused-name warnings reach inside types; we recommend yes, with encoding and foreign code counted as real use.
decisions.gist: Should Jet warn about struct fields no code reads and enum cases no code creates?
decisions.lesson: A field is one named part of a struct. A case is one choice in an enum. Today Jet's unused warnings stop at whole names, so a dead field or case stays silent. Whichever option wins, library `pub` items stay exempt and warnings never block a build.
decisions.story: Ravi joins a team whose `User` type has a `nickname` field and whose `Plan` enum has a `Legacy` case. He spends an afternoon preserving both in a refactor before learning that no code reads `nickname` and nothing ever creates `Legacy`.
decisions.detail:
Exercised 2026-10-05 with release jet $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/candidates/dev-05ea86f65/jet on probe $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/mine/legwork/languages-b/probes/F-member-liveness.jet. `jet check` exits 0 with exactly one Warning [L0104] (unused_private_fn) for `unused_helper`. No warning names `nickname` or `Legacy`. `jet run` prints a, 3, free, pro.

Current law: D-STRUCT-LIVE1=A (Docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:7596-7601) warns on unused imports, bindings, private functions and unreachable package or application exports. Warnings follow D-LINTPOLICY1, the repair is delete or `_name`, and library `pub` is exempt. Its recommendation called this one law: every declared name is reachable or carries the `_` mark. Fields and cases are declared names it does not yet reach.

Source witness: the ReScript interview (yKl2fSdnw7w 52:39-60:06). reanalyze finds 'you're never actually reading the name field' and 'this variant you're never constructing'. Teams switch it on, get thousands of findings, and remove old experiments. ReScript-Relay reuses the facts in CI to drop over-fetched GraphQL selections.

Rule-9 research, legwork resources 11-15. Rust 1.57 release notes and PR 85200: derived Clone and Debug no longer count as reads, a compatibility break for deny(dead_code). reanalyze README: the use rules above, @dead and @live annotations, and automatic annotation writing.

Periphery README: index-store analysis misses synthesized Codable, Equatable and Hashable reads, so it needs retain flags. Objective-C dynamic dispatch is unanalyzable. staticcheck U1000: field accesses use fields, and unnamed structs are assumed fully used.

What worked: in-compiler analysis (Rust) sees derives and runs in normal checks. ReScript users report large cleanups. What failed: external tools such as Periphery raise false alarms where they cannot see synthesized code. Counting trivial derived reads hid real dead fields until Rust changed the rule. Evidence gap: no measured false-positive rates; adoption claims are speaker and README testimony.

Design-away in A: Jet's compiler sees its own derives, encoding and reflection, so A counts them precisely instead of offering retain flags. FFI-exported layouts and foreign returns count as use, replacing reanalyze's @live. The existing `_` rename replaces @dead.

options.name: Fields and cases join the unused warnings
options.detail:
Jet's unused-name warnings also cover struct fields that no code reads and enum cases that no code creates. Writing a field does not count as reading it. Matching a case does not count as creating it.

Encoding or decoding, derived equality, hashing or ordering, reflection, and foreign code all count as real use. So data that leaves the program never warns. Derived printing and cloning do not count, because they touch every field by construction.

The fix is the one Jet already teaches: delete it, or rename it with a leading underscore.
options.technical:
Extends the D-STRUCT-LIVE1 liveness pass to members over the closed package or application graph.

A field is live if a field access, a destructuring pattern, encode or decode derivation (Dyn.from, decode<T>), derived Eq, Hash or Ord, reflection (D-METADEPTH1), or an FFI-exported layout reads it. A case is live if an expression, decode, or a foreign return constructs it.

Derived printing and Clone do not make members live, the Rust PR 85200 lesson. Library `pub` members are exempt. The warning class follows D-LINTPOLICY1, the machine fix is delete or `_` rename (D-NAME-SIGIL1), and both compilers give the same verdicts.

options.name: Report only when asked
options.detail: Normal checks stay as they are. A separate check option lists dead fields and cases for cleanup sessions. This is how ReScript's reanalyze and Swift's Periphery work, as tools users run on purpose.
options.technical: Same member analysis as A behind an opt-in `jet check --members` report; no default warnings.

options.name: Whole names only
options.detail: Keep D-STRUCT-LIVE1's four warnings: imports, bindings, private functions and unreachable exports. Fields and cases stay unchecked.
options.technical: Status quo; exercised by probe F (only L0104 fires).

comparisons.note: Built-in dead_code warns 'field is never read' and 'variant is never constructed'. Rust 1.57 (PR 85200) stopped derived Clone and Debug from counting as reads; the release notes warn this broke builds that deny dead_code.
reanalyze is a separate analyzer. A case is dead if never constructed, and matching does not count. A field is dead if never read, and creating does not count. @live marks FFI uses it cannot see.
comparisons.code:
reanalyze.exe -dce-cmt root/containing/cmt/files
// reports dead record labels and variant cases (README rules; output text not captured)

comparisons.note: External indexer finds assign-only properties, but synthesized Codable, Equatable and Hashable code is invisible to it, so it needs retain flags to avoid false alarms.
Field accesses mark fields used; unnamed struct types are assumed to use all fields to avoid false positives.
comparisons.code:
staticcheck -checks U1000 ./...
// reports unused fields of named structs (output text not captured)

recommendation.why: A finishes the rule Jet already teaches: every declared name is used or marked with `_`. Counting encoding and foreign code as use avoids the false alarms external tools suffer.
gains: Dead fields and cases appear where people already look.
No new marker or command.

losses.loss: An older app may see many new warnings.
losses.mitigation: Warnings never block, and each carries a one-step delete or rename fix.

losses.loss: A field kept for later warns until renamed.
losses.mitigation: Renaming it with a leading `_` records the intent and silences it.

whyNot.reason: B hides the finding behind a command most people never run, as ReScript's separate analyzer shows.
C leaves the longest-lived dead code invisible while smaller dead names warn.

recommendation.tradeoff: Jet accepts a one-time burst of warnings in older apps to keep dead data visible from then on.

decisions.title: What a map literal does when two of its keys are equal
decisions.situation: When one map literal writes the same key twice, Jet today keeps the later value and silently drops the earlier one. A beginner course shows the trap: a pasted second level entry quietly replaced the real level. Jet's own JSON reader already refuses a repeated name. You decide what a repeated key in a literal does; we recommend refusing it, at check time for written keys and at run time when computed keys collide.
decisions.gist: When one map literal contains the same key twice, should Jet refuse it or keep one of the values?
decisions.lesson: A map stores values under keys. A map literal writes all its pairs at once, so each key is meant to appear once. Today a repeated key keeps the later value and silently loses the earlier one. A refuses repeated keys: at check time when they are written out, and with a stop naming both entries when computed keys collide. B refuses only written-out repeats. C keeps today's rule and adds a warning.
decisions.explainer:
A map is a collection that stores each value under a key, like a word and its meaning. A map literal is the written form that builds one in a single expression. Each pair in it is an entry.

Today Jet builds the literal one entry at a time. When a later entry has a key that an earlier entry already used, the later value replaces the earlier one. Nothing reports it. The map simply has fewer entries than the literal shows.

Keys can be written out, such as the text "level", or computed, such as a variable. Written-out repeats can be found before the program runs. Computed keys are only known while it runs.

A treats any repeat as a mistake. Written-out repeats are an error when you check the program. Computed keys that turn out equal stop the program with a report naming the key and both entries. When you really mean to replace a value, you write a separate assignment after the literal.

B refuses written-out repeats but keeps the later value for computed keys, as Go does. C keeps today's rule and adds a warning for written-out repeats.
decisions.story: Ana builds a player record whose level comes from a parameter. She pastes an old line that also sets level to 99. Every new player now starts at level 99, the program runs without complaint, and nothing points at the pasted line.
decisions.detail:
Observed 2026-10-05 on the dev candidate jet (built 14:16 from dev 05ea86f65) and on the main checkout's debug jet. A literal with "level" twice prints the later value 99 and checks clean. A literal whose two variable keys are equal prints length 1 and keeps the later value. Probes: p02_dup_map_key.jet and p12_dynamic_dup_key.jet in the batch report.

Jet already refuses repeated names elsewhere. The JSON parse, decode and reader reject a repeated object name with its path and position; the allow_duplicates siblings are the explicit opt-in (Docs/spec/reference/core-library.md:2170-2174). The owner's 2026-10-05 DataTree ruling makes duplicate object keys a parse error with an explicit opt-in (card #4602, D-DATATREE-RULES1).

Source evidence: a beginner Python course demonstrates repeated level keys in one dictionary literal silently keeping the last value (youtube 4M87qBgpafk, 05:54-05:56). Python's reference states clashes between duplicate keys are not detected and the rightmost value prevails.

options.name: Repeated keys are an error
options.detail: Written-out keys that are equal are a check error. The report points at both entries and offers to delete one. Computed keys that turn out equal while running stop the program with a report naming the key and both entry positions. Intended replacement is written as an assignment after the literal, such as stats["level"] = 99.
options.technical: Sema compares literal, enum-case and constant-folded keys with the key type's equality and reports a registered error at the second entry with a note at the first. Runtime literal construction already locates each key's slot before inserting; a found slot raises a registered stop instead of overwriting. No extra hashing, no extra pass and no allocation are added. The same rule covers every tier and the comptime evaluator. Corpus migration: rewrite any intentional overwrite to an explicit assignment.

options.name: Refuse written-out repeats only
options.detail: Written-out keys that are equal are a check error, as in A. Computed keys that turn out equal keep the later value, as today. This matches Go.
options.technical: Same check-time rule as A. Runtime construction keeps its current overwrite. A computed-key collision still loses an entry silently.

options.name: Keep the later value, warn on written-out repeats
options.detail: Today's rule stays: the later entry wins everywhere. A new warning marks written-out repeats. Warnings show in check and in the editor, not on jet run.
options.technical: Adds one advisory lint. Runtime behavior is unchanged.

comparisons.note: A constant key written twice in a map literal is a compile error. Computed keys overwrite.
The compiler warns on repeated literal keys, and any repeated key in a dictionary literal stops the program.
Duplicate keys are not detected; the rightmost value prevails.

recommendation.why: A literal states one value per key. Losing an entry silently is the kind of quiet data loss Jet's JSON reader already refuses. A catches written repeats before running and computed collisions at the exact literal, at no extra cost.
recommendation.tradeoff: A few programs that relied on a silent overwrite must write the replacement as its own line.
gains: A written repeat is caught before the program runs.
A computed collision stops at the literal instead of losing data.
Map literals follow the same rule as Jet's JSON reader.

losses.loss: A literal with colliding computed keys now stops the program instead of continuing.
losses.mitigation: The stop names the key and both entries. Code that means to replace writes the replacement as an assignment after the literal, which never stops.

whyNot.reason: B still loses an entry silently when computed keys collide, which is the harder case to notice.
C keeps the silent loss. Its warning is hidden on jet run, where beginners spend most of their time.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Check that a literal with two written-out equal keys is a check error with a note at the first entry, on text, integer and enum-case keys. Check that two equal computed keys stop with the registered report naming both entry positions, on every tier and in the compile-time evaluator.

Check that an explicit assignment after the literal still replaces the value. Scan the example corpus and Core for literals whose computed keys can collide and rewrite any intentional overwrite.

surface.gist: When one map literal contains the same key twice, should Jet refuse it or keep one of the values?
surface.lesson: A map literal writes all its pairs at once, so each key is meant to appear once. Today a repeated key silently keeps the later value. A refuses repeats: at check time when written out, and with a stop when computed keys collide. B refuses only written-out repeats. C keeps today's rule with a warning.

current.note: The earlier level is lost and nothing reports it.
current.code:
stats :: [String:Int]{"level": level, "rank": 2, "level": 99}
print(stats["level"])   // 99, no message

wild.note: A key written twice in a map literal is a compile error.
wild.code:
m := map[string]int{"level": 7, "level": 99}
// compile error (Go spec: same constant key value)

options.name: Repeated keys are an error
options.gist: Written repeats fail the check; computed collisions stop at the literal.
gains: A written repeat is caught before running.
No entry is ever lost silently.
losses: Colliding computed keys stop the program.

options.name: Written repeats only
options.gist: Written repeats fail the check; computed collisions keep the later value.
gains: A written repeat is caught before running.
losses: Computed collisions still lose an entry silently.

options.name: Later wins, with a warning
options.gist: Today's rule stays; written repeats get a warning.
gains: No program changes behavior.
losses: The silent loss remains.
The warning is hidden on jet run.

recommendation.why: Each key in a literal means one value. A catches written repeats before running and computed collisions at the literal, matching how Jet's JSON reader treats repeated names.
gains: No silent data loss in map literals.
One rule for literals and JSON.

losses.loss: Colliding computed keys stop the program.
losses.mitigation: The stop names the key and both entries; intended replacement is a separate assignment.

whyNot.reason: B still loses data when computed keys collide.
C keeps the silent loss, and its warning is hidden on jet run.

recommendation.tradeoff: Rare intentional overwrites move to their own line.

designAway.loss: A literal with colliding computed keys now stops the program instead of continuing.
attempts: Return a failure result from every map literal instead of stopping. Rejected: every ordinary literal would need failure handling for a case that only computed keys can reach.
Prove distinct keys at check time. Kept for every written-out, enum-case and constant key, so the stop can only arise from keys computed while running.

decisions.title: Show how many bytes each type uses in this build
decisions.situation: Every Jet value takes memory, and a list of a million values multiplies it, but Jet shows byte sizes only for types pinned to a C-compatible layout. So a programmer cannot discover that one rare, large enum case makes every list element heavy. You decide whether the tools show the sizes this build actually uses, while the language still promises nothing about them. We recommend showing them in the inspect command and editor hover, labeled as this build only.
decisions.gist: Should Jet's tools show how many bytes each type uses in this build?
decisions.lesson: A type's layout is how a value sits in memory: its size in bytes, where each field starts, and unused padding between fields. An enum stores a small tag naming its current case, plus room for its largest case. Jet chooses the layout of ordinary types itself and may improve it between versions or targets. A type marked with a C layout keeps a fixed, promised layout instead.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: run the inspect command on a file, or hover a type in the editor, and read one size line. Expert path: read field positions, padding holes, the enum tag and the largest case, then decide whether to move a rare large payload into a pool and keep a small id.

Shared work in every option: the compiler already computes these facts for the target it builds. The vote is only about who may see them, and whether programs may read them.
decisions.story: Priya keeps a million input events in a list, and memory use is far higher than she expected. She suspects the rare Resize event, which carries a 4x4 matrix. Nothing in Jet will tell her how large one event is.
decisions.detail:
Current law and code. D-LAYOUT-FACTS1=B makes T.$layout the focused projection of reflection. Byte facts are computed for Jet-owned physical layouts and stay optional when physical layout is not guaranteed. The example Examples/features/comptime/layout_facts.jet prints null size and offset for a default-layout struct. Source/CmdInspect.rs on dev projects only layout kind and alignment in the shapes plane. Card #1690 made unguaranteed byte facts refuse honestly. #Layout(c) rejects growable fields with E1104.

Tool precedents, fetched 2026-10-05. rust-analyzer shows memory layout on hover by default, with size, alignment, offsets, padding and niche settings. Java has no size operator; the JOL tool prints field offsets, alignment gaps and space losses for the running VM. The pahole manual shows struct layouts from debug data and can reorganize members to remove holes.

Warnings about advice, fetched 2026-10-05. Clippy's large_enum_variant warns above 200 bytes but documents that it cannot see how often each variant occurs. Clippy suggests an arena or ECS as an alternative to boxing, and says to always measure. Go's fieldalignment analyzer is left out of vet and gopls because its findings rarely indicate a significant problem. So the recommended report states facts and offers its note as information, never as a warning.

Why not a language value. Rust exposes size_of for types whose default layout is unspecified. Its unstable randomize-layout flag exists to find unsafe code that accidentally relies on that unspecified layout. Rust's unstable book states that randomization is not a safety oracle. No adoption or friction measurements were found; these are mechanism precedents, not user studies.

Source witnesses. A 39-minute Rust memory-layout explainer teaches enum size as tag plus largest variant, padding, niches and boxing large variants. Jonathan Blow argues that visibility into what a program does is what makes systems bugs tractable. Jet card #3142 needs the same facts to measure flat enum layout and niches.

options.name: Show this build's sizes in the tools, labeled
options.detail: The inspect command and editor hover print size, field positions, padding and the enum tag for the selected target. Every line says it describes this build and is not promised. T.$layout stays empty for ordinary types, so programs cannot depend on these numbers.
options.technical:
Add an observed-representation record to the shapes plane, its JSON and hover, separate from T.$layout. Fields: target triple, compiler identity, guarantee none, size, alignment, stride, field offsets and widths, padding holes, enum tag width, per-case payload sizes and niche use. 

Compute it from the canonical target layout engine for the selected target without building or running. Never feed it into reflection, comptime or code generation. When one case sets the size and exceeds the others by a stated ratio, add an informational note naming the pool-and-id rewrite and saying to measure first; it is never a warning.

options.name: Make every size a language value
options.detail: Event.$layout.size returns this target's number for every type, as in Rust, Go and Swift. Programs may branch on it at compile time. Code can then silently depend on sizes Jet later improves.
options.technical: Fill size, alignment and offsets in T.$layout and reflection for default layouts with guarantee none. Comptime and derives can read them. Any later layout improvement becomes a visible change for code that read the numbers.

options.name: Keep sizes for pinned layouts only
options.detail: Today's rule stays. A programmer sees bytes only after marking a type with C layout. C layout rejects lists and text fields, so many ordinary types can never be inspected.
options.technical: No change. T.$layout and the shapes plane keep refusing byte facts for default layouts; allocation profiles remain the only indirect evidence.

comparisons.note: Every type answers size_of, and hover shows layout; illustration, not executed.
No language size operator; the JOL tool prints layout for the running VM only.

recommendation.why: Programmers see the real memory cost of their data, while Jet keeps the freedom to improve layouts without breaking code.
gains: Learners see padding, tags and the largest enum case.
Experts find heavy types before profiling.
Jet keeps freedom to improve layouts.

losses.loss: People may treat shown numbers as promises.
losses.mitigation: Every line names the build and says not promised; the same report shows how to pin a C layout when bytes matter.

whyNot.reason: Programs could quietly depend on sizes Jet may change, the problem Rust built a randomizing flag to expose.
Most real types stay invisible, because C layout rejects lists and text fields.

recommendation.tradeoff: Visible costs in the tools, with no new promise in the language.

decisions.checkInstructions: Validator dry run only; no compiler program was run. The 136-byte figures are illustrative for a tag plus a 128-byte payload at 8-byte alignment. After ratification, prove the shapes JSON against hand-derived fixtures for a struct with padding, a three-case enum and a niche case, then confirm T.$layout stays empty for default layouts.

gains: Learners and experts see real costs.

decisions.title: A busy task still stops on time and lets others run
decisions.situation: Jet runs many small tasks on a few processor threads, and a task stops or gives way only when it waits, such as on a timer or the network. A loop that never waits keeps its thread, so a deadline cannot stop a runaway handler, a cancelled race loser holds up the winner, and busy tasks can starve the server. You decide whether each loop turn also becomes a place where cancellation, deadlines and fair turns can land. We recommend one cheap check per loop turn, switched on only after a speed gate shows no slowdown.
decisions.gist: Should cancellation, deadlines and fair turns reach a task that is busy in a loop and never waits?
decisions.lesson: A task is a small piece of work that runs alongside others; Jet runs many tasks on a few processor threads. A wait point is where a task already pauses, such as sleep, a channel receive or network input. Today cancellation, deadlines and turn-taking happen only at wait points, so a loop that never waits runs to its end no matter what. The choice is whether a loop's turn back to its top also becomes a safe stopping place.
decisions.explainer:
Plain words first. A task is a small job, such as handling one web request. Jet runs thousands of tasks on a few processor threads, one per processor core, and switches between tasks when one of them waits.

A wait point is a place where a task already stops for a moment: a sleep, a channel receive, a network read, or waiting for another task. Today those are the only places where Jet can cancel a task, report a missed deadline, or let another task have the thread.

A busy loop is a loop that computes without waiting, such as adding up a billion numbers. Under today's rule it keeps its thread until it finishes. If a deadline passes, nothing notices. If the task lost a race, the race still waits for it.

A time slice is a short turn, such as ten milliseconds. Fair sharing means a task that used its whole slice gives the thread to waiting tasks and then continues later.

The check proposed in A is one memory read and one branch at the bottom of a loop. Loops that count over a known range check once per block of iterations, not every time, the way Java's optimizing compiler has done since Java 10.
decisions.story: Ravi runs a Jet API with a one-second request deadline. One customer uploads a pathological input, and a parsing loop in his handler runs for twenty minutes. The deadline never fires, the request never ends, and on deploy the server cannot drain, so it is killed without cleanup. A second such request leaves only the other cores for every other customer.
decisions.detail:
Code facts come from source reading of the checkout at the time of drafting. Nothing here was executed.

Law today. core.tasks is cooperative: "the scheduler does not turn a blocking computation into preemptive parallelism" (Docs/spec/reference/core-library.md:2609-2611). The scheduler is M:N with no async coloring (Docs/spec/spec.md:2302-2306, D-ASYNCRT1=A, which chose Go's goroutine model). Cancellation unwinds only at wait points (spec.md:2107-2111, D-CANCELMODEL1=C).

D-FOUND-LIFECYCLE1=A states the consequence as its tradeoff: "a CPU-bound handler notices its deadline at its next wait point". D-TASK-PAUSE-TIER1=E kept pause at wait points by default. It also ratified an optional strong mode, mode: .CheckLoops, with portable back-edge checks on every engine.

Runtime today. The shared scheduler runs one work-stealing worker per core and has no time-slice preemption (crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Scheduler.rs:3669-3805). task.all, task.race and task.any cancel losers and then drain them (crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/TaskGroup.rs:485-498). A drain blocks on the child's result (Scheduler.rs:3956-3959).

So a cancelled child that never reaches a wait point is joined only when it ends by itself. The race result, a parent deadline and E3003 all wait for it (Scheduler.rs:4032-4056).

Inside Jet already. Sandbox plugins, build plugins and compiler extensions enable Wasmtime epoch interruption (Prelude/Plugin.rs:240-243 and 1372-1406, BuildPlugin.rs:26-28, CompilerExtension.rs:90-93). They stop a guest that passes its time limit, two seconds per call by default (D-CORE-PLUGINLIMITS1=A). Epoch interruption is a counter check at loop back-edges and function entries.

The REPL interpreter already polls before each instruction, so Ctrl-C returns within 100 ms (spec.md:3363-3366, D-FE-REPL-INTERRUPT1=A). The only Jet code a runaway loop can hold forever is ordinary compiled Jet code.

What this does not cover. Foreign C and C++ calls already run on worker threads (Docs/spec/reference/mixed-repo.md:101-102). A deadline that passes during one is delivered when it returns, in every option. Memory per request is a separate question.
Prior owner ruling. D-TASK-PAUSE-TIER1 rejected its option C because forced checks on every pause tax the default fast path. This ballot keeps that ruling for pause.

This ballot asks a different question. Should cancellation, deadlines and fair turns use the back-edge sites that the ratified strong pause (.CheckLoops) already requires on every engine? Option A turns its default on only after the hot-loop speed gate shows no measurable slowdown. Counted loops check once per block. Loops that already wait need no check. If the gate fails, the sites stay opt-in and the D-FOUND-LIFECYCLE1=A tradeoff stands.

Independent of the vote, strong pause is ratified but unbuilt. pause(mode: .CheckLoops) is rejected with E0764, and no engine calls the Prelude loop pause hook. Building that shared back-edge check is repair work on the owning card whichever option wins.

Merged sources (2026-10-05 mining). RntfkL8lUY4: BEAM promises a greedy green thread never blocks the scheduler, and a bad regex must not either. IxQ586TS8Gw 45:46-48:32: in Riot, a while-true actor bricks a cooperative scheduler, so the speaker wants compiler-inserted yields. The same talk records the dissent that preemptive scheduling beats polite yields.

options.name: Loops are stop points
options.detail:
Every engine checks one per-thread attention flag where a loop returns to its top and on entry to a function that can call itself. The check is one load and one branch. A loop over a known range checks once per block of iterations instead of every time.

When the flag is set, the task does what it would do at a wait point. A pending cancellation or blown deadline unwinds with Drop cleanup, a strong pause stops, and a task past its time slice gives its thread to waiting tasks and continues later. #Shield keeps deferring cancellation and deadlines exactly as today.

Beginners write nothing new: deadlines and races just work for busy code. The default is switched on only after the hot-loop speed gate shows no measurable slowdown; until then today's rule stays, so no program gets slower.
options.technical:
Amends D-CANCELMODEL1=C: delivery points become wait points plus loop back-edges and recursive entries. Amends the stated tradeoff of D-FOUND-LIFECYCLE1=A. Under D-TASK-PAUSE-TIER1=E the .CheckLoops sites become the default sites for cancel, deadline and fairness; pause may keep its wait-point default.

The mechanism follows Wasmtime epoch interruption, which Jet already uses for plugins. A timer thread raises a worker's attention word when its task has run past the slice while runnable work waits. cancel() and an expired #Context deadline raise the target task's word directly.

Counted loops are strip-mined as in HotSpot C2 loop strip mining (JDK-8186027, Java 10): the inner block runs check-free and the outer loop checks. Checks are elided in loops whose body already reaches a wait point or a checked call on every iteration. One Prelude delivery function serves every engine, and the interpreter keeps its per-instruction poll.

Safety argument: the unwind lands only between iterations. That is a statement boundary where an index or arithmetic panic can already unwind today. Shared-state critical sections keep #Shield.

options.name: Fair turns only
options.detail:
The runtime interrupts a task that used its whole time slice with an operating-system signal and runs other tasks, then resumes it later. Loops get no added check, so tight loops run at full speed. This is how Go solved starvation in Go 1.14.

Cancellation and deadlines still land only at wait points. A busy race loser still keeps the race waiting, and a runaway handler still ignores its deadline and blocks a clean shutdown.
options.technical: Signal-driven preemption needs the runtime to suspend a task at an arbitrary instruction and switch stacks from a signal handler. Runtime locks and allocation need no-preempt regions. Go's design (proposal 24543) also needed safe-point metadata for its garbage collector. Jet's ownership model needs less of that, but each engine still needs its own signal and context-switch path, and Windows needs SuspendThread. Unwinding at an arbitrary instruction is not safe, so this cannot deliver cancellation.

options.name: Keep waits as the only stop points, and warn
options.detail:
The rule stays as today. The compiler adds a warning for a loop that never waits inside task or request-handler code, and the docs teach calling tasks.yield_now() in long loops.

There is no runtime cost. Every author and every library must remember the call, including text parsing, sorting and decoding loops the author never wrote.
options.technical: A lint over loop bodies with no reachable wait point, scoped to task bodies and handlers. Library loops are reached through calls, so the lint either floods or misses them. Tokio documents the same rule and states it will not detect blocking tasks (tokio.rs/blog/2020-04-preemption).

comparisons.note: Go first used cooperative turns, and tight loops could hang the scheduler for five years. A loop check cost a 7.8% geomean slowdown in 2017 tests. Go 1.14 then switched to signal preemption, but cancellation by context stayed cooperative.

The BEAM preempts every process on a reduction budget, so a hot loop or a slow regular expression cannot block a scheduler. Native code must return within about a millisecond or run on dirty schedulers.
comparisons.code:
%% https://www.erlang.org/doc/apps/erts/erl_nif.html#long-running-nifs
loop(N) -> loop(N + 1).   % other processes keep running; exit(Pid, kill) stops it

comparisons.note: Epoch interruption loads one counter and compares it at loop back-edges and function entries. It measured about twice as fast as fuel counting, and one mechanism can yield, trap or call back. Jet's plugin host already uses it.

recommendation.why: A makes deadlines, races, cancellation and fair sharing work for busy code with no new syntax. It uses the check Jet already runs for plugins and already ratified for strong pause. The speed gate means no program gets slower to get it.
gains: A request deadline stops a runaway handler and a clean shutdown can drain it.
task.race returns when the winner finishes, not when the slowest loser does.
Busy requests share the processor, so one heavy input cannot stall the server.

losses.loss: Loops that never wait run one extra check, which the Go team measured as costly in its tightest loops.
losses.mitigation: Counted loops check once per block and loops that already wait need no check. The default turns on only after the hot-loop speed gate shows no measurable slowdown.

losses.loss: Cancellation can now land between two loop turns, not only at a wait.
losses.mitigation: It lands only at a whole-turn boundary where a panic can already unwind today, Drop cleanup still runs, and #Shield still keeps critical sections whole.

whyNot.reason: B stops starvation but leaves deadlines, races and shutdown waiting on busy code, and it needs a separate signal and stack-switch path on every engine.
C makes every author and library remember a manual call, and the warning cannot see loops inside library code.

recommendation.tradeoff: A asks Jet to build a strip-mined loop check that passes the hot-loop speed gate. In return, every Jet task honours its deadline, cancellation and fair share whether or not it waits.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Build the gate first. Take the hot-loop gauntlet cells from card #2254 plus a counted sum, a while loop over a linked structure, recursive Fibonacci, a regex scan and a JSON decode of a large input. Run each as a paired program with the check on and off in the same release profile, and compare against Rust. The default turns on only where every cell stays within the strict performance gate.

Then check behaviour on every engine. A task.race between an immediate value and a busy loop returns the value within one slice. A #Context deadline of 20 ms around a busy loop reports E3003 within one slice and runs Drop cleanup. A cancelled busy task inside #Shield finishes the shielded block first.

Eight busy tasks plus one sleeping task on a two-core machine still wake the sleeper within a few slices. SIGTERM during a busy handler drains within the serve deadline. Strong pause keeps working. A loop that already waits on every turn shows no added check in the generated code.

surface.gist: Should deadlines, cancellation and fair turns reach a task that is busy in a loop and never waits?
surface.lesson: Jet runs many small tasks on a few processor threads. Today a task stops or gives way only when it waits, such as sleeping or reading the network. A loop that never waits keeps its thread until it ends, so deadlines, races and shutdown wait for it. A makes each loop turn a safe stopping place.

current.note: Today the race waits for the busy loser to finish by itself.

wild.note: Since Go 1.14 a busy loop no longer blocks other goroutines.

options.name: Loops are stop points
options.gist: Each loop turn checks one cheap flag for cancellation, deadlines and fair turns.
gains: Deadlines and races work for busy code.
Busy requests share the processor fairly.
No new syntax; plugins already work this way.
losses: One cheap check in loops that never wait.
Cancellation may land between loop turns.

proposed.code:
answer :: (task.race { cached(), slow_count(50_000_000_000) }) ?? 0
print(answer)   // 42 at once; the loser stops at its next loop turn

options.name: Fair turns only
options.gist: The runtime interrupts long turns so others run, but stopping still waits for a wait point.
gains: No added check in any loop.
Busy tasks no longer starve others.
losses: Deadlines and races still wait for busy code.
Needs a separate interrupt path on every engine.

proposed.code:
