let _g = info_span!("frame").entered();
if paused { return; }   // span exits here

options.name: Closes at block end
options.gist: Opening a span enters it; the block's end closes it.
gains: No span stays open by mistake.
Same rule as files and locks.
losses: A long span must be returned or stored.

proposed.code:
s :: log.span("frame")
if paused -> return   // closes here
step(&world)
// closes at block end

options.name: Warn on a missing close
options.gist: Manual calls stay; the check warns.
gains: No API change.
losses: Bookkeeping stays manual.
Silent on jet run.

proposed.code:
s :: log.span("frame")
log.enter(s)
defer log.close(s)

options.name: Block form
options.gist: A function runs the work inside the span.
gains: Wrapped work closes correctly.
losses: Two ways to make spans.
Manual way stays silent.

recommendation.why: A removes the forgotten close instead of warning about it. It reuses the scope rule Jet's files and locks already follow.
gains: Balanced spans on every path.
One rule for owned resources.

losses.loss: A long span must be returned or stored.
losses.mitigation: That moves ownership like a file; one line.

whyNot.reason: B keeps manual bookkeeping.
C adds a second way and keeps the first risk.

recommendation.tradeoff: Long spans move with their owner.

designAway.loss: A span that should outlive its block must be returned or stored, as an open file must.
attempts: Keep log.enter for long spans. Rejected: it keeps two ways and the forget risk.
Use the owned-resource move rule. Kept: a returned or stored handle stays open, and its new owner's scope closes it.

decisions.title: Choosing the order of a priority queue or ordered set when you create it
decisions.situation: A priority queue hands back items in order, and an ordered set keeps its items sorted. In Jet both always use the item type's own order today. So a queue that should serve the highest score first, or jobs by deadline, needs a new wrapper type just to flip or change the order. You decide whether these containers accept an order when they are made; we recommend the same by and by_desc spelling lists already use for sorting.
decisions.gist: Should a priority queue or ordered set take its sorting order when you create it, instead of needing a wrapper type?
decisions.lesson: A priority queue always gives back the smallest item first. An ordered set, called Rank in Jet, keeps items sorted. Both use the type's own order today. A lets you pass an order when you create one, with the by and by_desc words lists already use for sort_by. B adds one Core wrapper that reverses any order. C makes the order part of the container's type.
decisions.explainer:
A priority queue is a container whose pop always returns the item that comes first in some order. An ordered set keeps its items sorted and unique. Jet's PriorityQueue and Rank both take the order from the item type. Numbers and text sort ascending, and a struct uses the order its type declares (D-KEY-TRAITS1).

That is fine until one program needs two orders for the same type. Popping the largest score, serving jobs by deadline, or keeping names sorted by length all need a new wrapper type today. Lists already avoid this, because sort_by and sort_by_desc take a key function.

Option A brings the list spelling to these containers. PriorityQueue.by(key) and PriorityQueue.by_desc(key) make a queue ordered by that key. Rank.by and Rank.by_desc make an ordered set the same way. new() and from(xs) keep the type's own order. When two containers with different orders combine, the result keeps the receiver's order.

Option B adds one Core wrapper, Desc<T>, that reverses any order, and keeps everything else. Option C writes the order into the container type, as C++ and Gren do.
decisions.story: Priya builds a leaderboard that should always pop the highest score. Jet's priority queue pops the lowest. She writes a HighScore wrapper type with its own comparison, converts every score into it and back, and her teammate asks why a number needed a new type.
decisions.detail:
Current state: PriorityQueue.new() and PriorityQueue.from(xs) take no order or key, and Rank.new() and Rank.from(xs) likewise (core-library.md:282, 284). Order and equality come from the type through D-KEY-TRAITS1=A (KeyBy per type). Lists already have sort_by((item) -> key or (a, b) -> Ordering) and sort_by_desc((item) -> key) (core-library.md:558-559). The v3 A2-langs re-read confirmed the gap (note 1).

Sources: Gren talk (DuGy1tmKP-w 32:06-33:53), where a reverse-sorted dictionary is made by passing a different compare module, and type classes allow only one instance per type. Roc (DzhIprQan68, about 27:00) makes the same point. Claim languages-a:Q28, attached to #4499.

Proven approaches. Java's PriorityQueue and TreeMap and Kotlin's PriorityQueue take a comparator at construction, and this is the most used form in practice. Rust's BinaryHeap takes order from Ord, so a max-heap of a custom key needs Reverse<T> or a newtype. That wrapper friction is a frequent Rust forum topic.

C++ std::priority_queue and Gren's Dict take the comparator as a type or module parameter. That is precise but makes the order part of every signature. Python's heapq takes no key, so programs push (key, item) tuples by hand.

Option A reuses Jet's existing sort_by vocabulary. The key function must be pure, which sema already checks for callbacks. Combining two containers with different orders uses the receiver's order, as Java's addAll does.

options.name: Pass the order when you create the container
options.detail: PriorityQueue.by(key) and PriorityQueue.by_desc(key) make a queue ordered by a key function. Rank.by and Rank.by_desc do the same for ordered sets. new() and from(xs) keep the type's own order. Combining two containers keeps the receiver's order.
options.technical: The container stores one pure key function and compares keys with the key type's order. by_desc reverses that comparison. The key function must have an empty effect row, the rule callbacks already follow. from(xs) gains by and by_desc variants. Equality between two containers compares items and ignores order functions.
options.code:
scores := PriorityQueue.by_desc((s: Score) -> s.points)
&scores.push(Score{name: "Ana", points: 90})
best :: &scores.pop()   // highest points first

by_len :: Rank.by((w: String) -> w.len())

options.name: One Core wrapper that reverses order
options.detail: Core gains Desc<T>, a wrapper whose order is the reverse of T's. Containers keep using the type's order. Any other order still needs a custom wrapper type.
options.technical: One generic struct with a reversed KeyBy implementation. Items are wrapped on the way in and unwrapped on the way out. Orders other than reversal, such as by deadline, still need a new type.
options.code:
scores := PriorityQueue.new()
&scores.push(Desc{Score{name: "Ana", points: 90}})
best :: (&scores.pop()).value

options.name: The order is part of the container's type
options.detail: An ordered container's type names its order, such as PriorityQueue(Score, ByPointsDesc). Two queues with different orders are different types.
options.technical: The order becomes a build-time parameter of the container type (D-GENERIC-TYPEFN1). Every signature that holds such a container must name the order.
options.code:
ByPointsDesc :: order((s: Score) -> s.points, .Desc)
scores := PriorityQueue(Score, ByPointsDesc).new()

comparisons.note: PriorityQueue and TreeSet take a comparator when they are created.
comparisons.code:
var q = new PriorityQueue<Job>(Comparator.comparing(Job::deadline));
var s = new TreeSet<String>(Comparator.comparingInt(String::length));

comparisons.note: Order comes from Ord; a max-heap or custom key needs a wrapper.
The comparator is a template parameter of the queue type.

recommendation.why: A lets one program use several orders for one type without inventing wrapper types, and it reuses the by and by_desc words Jet already teaches for sorting lists. Java and Kotlin show this is the form people use most.
recommendation.tradeoff: An ordered container now carries one small key function.
gains: Max-heaps and custom orders need no wrapper type.
Sorting lists and ordering containers use the same words.
The type's own order stays the default.

losses.loss: Two containers built with different orders can be combined, and the result silently follows one of them.
losses.mitigation: The rule is fixed and documented: the receiver's order wins, as in Java. The editor shows each container's order in its hover, so the choice is visible.

whyNot.reason: B only covers reversal; ordering by a field still needs a hand-written wrapper type.
C makes every signature spell the order, which is heavy for a beginner and rarely needed.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Check that PriorityQueue.by and by_desc pop in key order and reverse key order, with ties stable by insertion. Check the same for Rank.by and Rank.by_desc on first, last and to_list.

Check that a key function with effects is rejected with the callback diagnostic. Check that union and merge keep the receiver's order. Check that new() and from(xs) behavior is unchanged on every tier.

surface.gist: Should a priority queue or ordered set take its sorting order when you create it, instead of needing a wrapper type?
surface.lesson: Jet's priority queue and ordered set always use the item type's own order. A lets you pass an order when you make one, with the by and by_desc words lists use. B adds one reversing wrapper. C writes the order into the type.

current.note: A highest-first queue needs a hand-written wrapper type.
current.code:
scores := PriorityQueue.new()   // lowest first only
&scores.push(HighScore{s})       // custom wrapper
best :: (&scores.pop()).inner

wild.note: The order is passed when the queue is made.
wild.code: val q = PriorityQueue(compareByDescending<Score> { it.points })

options.name: Order passed at creation
options.gist: by and by_desc pick the order when you make it.
gains: No wrapper types.
Same words as sort_by.
losses: Combining two orders keeps the receiver's.

proposed.code:
scores := PriorityQueue.by_desc((s: Score) -> s.points)
best :: &scores.pop()   // highest first

options.name: A reversing wrapper
options.gist: Core adds Desc<T> to flip any order.
gains: Max-heaps without a custom type.
losses: Ordering by a field still needs a wrapper.

proposed.code:
&scores.push(Desc{s})
best :: (&scores.pop()).value

options.name: Order in the type
options.gist: The container's type names its order.
gains: Different orders never mix.
losses: Every signature spells the order.

proposed.code: scores := PriorityQueue(Score, ByPointsDesc).new()

recommendation.why: A gives several orders per type with no wrapper types, using words Jet already teaches for sorting.
gains: Custom orders in one line.
One vocabulary for ordering.

losses.loss: Combining two orders keeps the receiver's.
losses.mitigation: A fixed, documented rule shown in hover.

whyNot.reason: B covers only reversal.
C puts the order in every signature.

recommendation.tradeoff: Containers carry a key function.

designAway.loss: Two containers built with different orders can be combined, and the result silently follows one of them.
attempts: Reject combining containers with different orders. Rejected: key functions cannot be compared for equality, so the check would be guesswork.
Fix the receiver's order as the rule and show each container's order in hover. Kept.

decisions.title: What happens when code sets an invalid web header
decisions.situation: Web messages carry headers, named lines such as Content-Type. Jet's header functions quietly ignore a header whose name has a space or whose value has a control character, so a typo like "Content Type" simply vanishes. A course and a probe both show this. You decide what an invalid header does; we recommend checking written header names when the program is checked, and returning a failure for names built while running.
decisions.gist: When code sets a web header with an invalid name or value, should Jet refuse it or keep ignoring it?
decisions.lesson: A header is a named line in a web message. Its name may not contain spaces, and its value may not contain control characters such as a line break. Today Jet drops an invalid header without a word. A checks written names and values at check time and makes runtime ones report a failure. B makes every header call report a failure. C stops the program on an invalid header.
decisions.explainer:
Every web request and response carries headers: a name, a colon, and a value. The web standard limits names to a set of token characters, so spaces are not allowed. Values may not contain control characters, because a line break inside a value can smuggle in a fake header.

Today headers_set, headers_append and with_header check both rules and, when one fails, return the headers unchanged. The HTTP client builder does the same, and its retry setter quietly clamps bad numbers. The program keeps running with a header missing.

Option A uses a pattern Jet already has for checked text. A header name and a header value become checked text types. A written string such as "Content-Type" is checked when the program is checked, so ordinary code needs no failure handling and a typo is a check error. A name or value built while running is converted with a parse call that returns a failure the caller must handle.

Option B makes every header call return a failure, written or not. Option C keeps the calls as they are but stops the program on an invalid header.
decisions.story: Sam adds http.with_header("Content Type", "application/json") to an API response. The browser keeps treating the reply as text. Nothing in the check or the run mentions the header, and the space in the name takes him an afternoon to spot.
decisions.detail:
Suite revision by BallotSuite1, 2026-10-07. D-DEADLINE-ONE1=A (ratified 2026-10-06) retires session_timeout with the other per-call timeout setters in favor of deadline blocks, so this ballot no longer covers timeouts. Nothing else changed.

Current state: headers_set, headers_append and with_header return the input unchanged when the name is invalid or the value has a control byte (claims v3-H2:FknTw9bJsXM-B30; web-data-net:C59). The HTTP client builder repeats the silent ignore (`header_name(line) ?? return ~client`), and session_retries clamps out-of-range values (client.jet:58-61, 117-127; APICompWeb). core-library.md:937 documents the setters as plain replace and append.

D-BOUND-SINK1=A lets libraries declare checked text types. D-BOUND-HEAD1=A gives typed literal heads for URL, Path and DateTime with check-time validation. Stdlib law 2 asks that failures carry enough context (stdlib-api-laws.md:74-83).

Source: ThePrimeagen's From TCP to HTTP (FknTw9bJsXM), where set versus append matters for Content-Length and header names must be RFC tokens (web-data-net:C40, C58).

Proven approaches. Rust's http crate makes HeaderName and HeaderValue checked types: from_static is checked in constant evaluation, and from_bytes and from_str return Result. Node's setHeader throws ERR_INVALID_HTTP_TOKEN and ERR_INVALID_CHAR. Python requests raises InvalidHeader.

The failure pattern to avoid is silent dropping, which hides the bug and, for values, can mask header injection attempts. Option A follows Rust's split, so literals cost nothing and runtime text must be handled.

options.name: Check written headers; runtime ones return a failure
options.detail: Header names and values become checked text types. A written string is checked when the program is checked; an invalid one is a check error naming the bad character. Text built while running converts with HeaderName.parse or HeaderValue.parse, which return HTTPError.InvalidHeader for the caller to handle. The client retry setter rejects out-of-range values the same way; the timeout setter is already retired by the deadline-block vote.
options.technical: Declare HeaderName and HeaderValue under D-BOUND-SINK1 with the token and field-value rules as their literal validators, as D-BOUND-HEAD1 does for URLs. headers_set, headers_append, with_header and the client builder take the checked types. String literals convert at check time; runtime String converts only through parse. No validation runs twice at run time.
options.code:
res :: http.response(200, body)
    |> http.with_header("Content Type", "application/json")
// error: header name has a space at column 8

name :: http.HeaderName.parse(user_key) ?? return

options.name: Every header call can fail
options.detail: headers_set, headers_append, with_header and the client setters return a failure for an invalid name or value, whether written or built while running. Every call needs ? or ?? even for a fixed, correct name.
options.technical: Signatures gain !HTTPError. No check-time validation. Each call validates at run time.

options.name: Stop the program on an invalid header
options.detail: The calls keep their shape. An invalid name or value stops the program with a located report. Text from outside the program, such as a user-supplied key, can therefore stop a server.
options.technical: The silent return becomes a registered stop. No signature change.

comparisons.note: Checked name and value types; literals are checked early, runtime text returns Result.
setHeader throws on an invalid name or value.
An invalid header value raises InvalidHeader before sending.

recommendation.why: A turns the silent typo into a check error, costs nothing for the fixed header names nearly all code writes, and makes runtime text prove itself before it reaches the wire. It follows Rust's proven split and Jet's existing checked text types.
recommendation.tradeoff: Code that builds header names from runtime text must handle one parse failure.
gains: A misspelled header name is caught before running.
Written headers need no failure handling.
Injected line breaks can never reach the wire.

losses.loss: Header names or values built from runtime text need a parse call and a failure route.
losses.mitigation: This is exactly the case where a bad character is possible; the parse failure names the character and position, and ?? keeps the route to one line.

whyNot.reason: B makes every fixed, correct header line carry failure handling it can never need.
C lets text from outside the program stop a server.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Check that a written header name with a space or a written value with a line break is a check error naming the character. Check that HeaderName.parse and HeaderValue.parse return HTTPError.InvalidHeader for runtime text.

Check that headers_set, headers_append, with_header and the client builder accept only the checked types. Check that session_retries rejects out-of-range values. Update core-library.md:937.

surface.gist: When code sets a web header with an invalid name or value, should Jet refuse it or keep ignoring it?
surface.lesson: Header names may not contain spaces, and values may not contain line breaks. Today an invalid header silently vanishes. A checks written headers at check time and makes runtime text return a failure. B makes every call fallible. C stops the program.

current.note: The misspelled header silently disappears.

wild.note: An invalid header name throws.
wild.code:
res.setHeader("Content Type", "x");
// TypeError [ERR_INVALID_HTTP_TOKEN]

options.name: Check written, fail runtime
options.gist: Written headers are checked early; runtime text must parse.
gains: Typos caught before running.
No handling for fixed names.
losses: Runtime header text needs a parse.

options.name: Every call can fail
options.gist: All header calls return a failure.
gains: One rule for all headers.

decisions.title: Whether Jet Learn can run in a web browser with nothing installed
decisions.situation: Jet Learn is Jet's built-in exercise track, and today it runs only inside the installed toolchain. Many beginners meet a language in a browser first: the Python course in the mining run runs Python itself in the page, so learners install nothing. Jet already compiles to WebAssembly, the format browsers run. You decide whether Learn gets a zero-install browser lane; we recommend the same exercises running in the page, with the compiler itself in WebAssembly.
decisions.gist: Should Jet Learn also run in a web browser with nothing installed, and if so, where does the compiler run?
decisions.lesson: WebAssembly is a code format every modern browser runs. A compiles Jet's checker and runner to WebAssembly, so the same Learn exercises run inside the page with no install and no server. B compiles exercises on a hosted server, as the Go and Rust playgrounds do. C keeps Learn install-only.
decisions.explainer:
Jet Learn opens an exercise, asks for a prediction, runs the learner's code and reveals what happened. Jet chose to keep it inside the toolchain and offline, so learning and real work use the same compiler. That choice stays.

The missing piece is the first ten minutes for someone who cannot or will not install a toolchain. Browser-first learning is now common. The course mined on 2026-10-05 runs Python inside the page with Pyodide. The TypeScript playground runs the real compiler in the browser, and Roc ships its whole compiler as about 6 MB of WebAssembly.

Option A adds a browser lane over the same exercises. Jet's checker and runner compile to WebAssembly and load in the page, so nothing runs on a server and the page works offline after its first load. Exercises that touch files or the network get in-memory test doubles, which Jet already uses in tests. Progress can be exported to the installed jet learn.

Option B compiles on a hosted server, as the Go and Rust playgrounds do. Option C keeps Learn install-only.
decisions.story: Nia, a school student on a locked-down laptop, wants to try Jet after a friend's demo. She cannot install anything. The Python course her class uses runs in the browser, so she stays with Python.
decisions.detail:
Current state: D-LEARN1 ships jet learn as an in-toolchain, offline exercise runner, and D-LEARN-FEEDBACK1 fixes predict-then-reveal. Jet has a web target (D-WASM1, D-FREESTAND-WASM1) and source-defined playgrounds (#2464). No record covers a browser lane for Learn (claim v3-P1:PYA-068). Card #4630 owns the zero-experience beginner arc.

Sources: the Boot.dev Python course (4M87qBgpafk), which runs CPython compiled to WebAssembly in the browser (claim v3-P1:PYA-068). Also Roc's in-browser REPL, built as a traffic-proof static page with the whole compiler as about 6 MB of WebAssembly (DzhIprQan68, claim languages-a:R43). And TypeScript's browser-hosted compiler (learning-compilers:AH2).

Proven approaches. Pyodide, the TypeScript playground and Roc run the real toolchain in the page with no server cost and no remote sandbox. The Go Playground, Rust Playground and Kotlin Playground compile on servers. That needs sandboxing, rate limits and uptime, and the Rust playground limits which crates and how much run time a program gets.

The known failure of in-browser toolchains is a large first download. Option A loads lazily, caches across visits and keeps a written payload budget.

decisions.title: Terminal colors, cursor moves and screen clearing in core.tui
decisions.situation: Terminal programs color words and move the cursor by printing hidden control codes. Jet has no named list of these codes, and its one styling call silently prints plain text when a color is misspelled. Text from users can also carry its own codes, which rewrite the screen when printed. This vote decides how Core spells colors, cursor moves and clearing; I recommend a checked terminal-text form that refuses typos and makes user text harmless.
decisions.gist: How should Jet programs color terminal text and move the cursor?
decisions.lesson: A terminal reads hidden codes inside printed text: one code turns words red, another clears a line. Jet already has checked text forms, such as `SQL{"…"}` and `HTML{"…"}`, which check their contents when the program is built and make inserted values safe. Terminal codes have no such form today, so they are unchecked plain text.
decisions.explainer: Beginner path: write `ANSI{"[bold red]error:[/] {name}"}` and print it; a misspelled style fails the build, and `name` prints as text even if it hides codes. Expert path: `tui.moveCursor(row:, col:)`, `tui.clearLine()`, `tui.altScreen(on:)` and `tui.mouse(on:)` return the same checked value, and `tui.ESC` and `tui.CSI` reach codes the table lacks. Shared work under every option: plain strings keep whatever escapes the carriage-return ballot grants, and full-screen apps keep `tui.run` with `TUIStyle`.
decisions.story: Omar writes a deploy tool that prints red errors next to server names typed by users. A misspelled color printed plain text for a week. A server name holding hidden codes once cleared his whole screen.
decisions.inWild:
# Python rich (rich.readthedocs.io/en/stable/markup.html)
from rich.markup import escape
console.print(f"[bold red]error:[/] no user {escape(name)}")
# forget escape() and `name` can inject its own markup
decisions.detail:
Origin. Owner question q4p8lzbr on D-STR-ESCAPE1 asked for terminal escape constants and helpers in the TUI library, controlled by a strongly typed string literal. D-STR-ESCAPE1 stays the lexer floor (`\r`, `\u{…}` in plain strings). This companion ballot owns the terminal vocabulary. Both outcomes of D-STR-ESCAPE1 work with every option here.

Jet today. Core/tui/tui.jet:30-41 has `TUIColorProfile` and `TUIColor` (`ANSI16`, `ANSI256`, `RGB`), and `TUIStyle` with `style_text`. Core/term/term.jet:101 `term.style(style, text)` calls the host. crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Term.rs:273-288 accepts one of ten single words and returns the text unstyled for anything else, so `"bold red"` and `"redd"` both print plain.

More of today. Core/term/term.jet:103-178 `style_force` parses a different multi-word table, so the two tiers disagree. Term.rs:245-262 already applies NO_COLOR, FORCE_COLOR and the is-a-terminal test. No cursor, erase, alternate-screen or mouse codes exist. Eight `term.style` calls sit in six tracked .jet files. Two files build the escape byte with `String.from_bytes([U8]{27})`.

Rust. crossterm (docs.rs/crossterm 0.29) exposes typed commands: `cursor::MoveTo`, `terminal::Clear`, `EnterAlternateScreen`, `EnableMouseCapture`, queued onto a writer. owo-colors adds zero-allocation methods such as `"x".red()`. It honors NO_COLOR, FORCE_COLOR and terminal detection only through `if_supports_color` and an optional feature.

Go. lipgloss builds style values (`NewStyle().Bold(true).Foreground(Color("205"))`) and renders text through them. It downsamples true color to 256, 16 or no color for the detected terminal. Styles are values, but each colored word needs its own render call.

Python. rich uses bracket markup, `[bold red]alert![/]`, inside strings, and raises MarkupError on mismatched tags. Its own docs warn that interpolated text can inject tags and require `rich.markup.escape`. That check runs at run time, and forgetting `escape` is silent.

Node. chalk chains styles (`chalk.red.bold("x")`) and drops codes when color is unsupported. chalk-template is a tagged template, `` chalkTemplate`{red ${x}}` ``. It escapes braces in inserted values but not control codes, and its docs say raw template input must be escaped by the caller.

Known failure. Terminal escape injection is a recorded bug class: CVE-2021-25743 says kubectl did not neutralize escape and control sequences in data printed to a terminal (CWE-150). The code table follows the common reference, fnky's ANSI Escape Sequences gist (gist.github.com/fnky/458719343aabd01cfb17a3a4f7296797).

What the evidence says. Typed values with automatic terminal detection (lipgloss, chalk) prevent codes leaking into files. Markup (rich, chalk-template) reads best for mixed inline styles. Every surveyed library leaves inserted text unescaped by default or behind an extra call. Option A combines the readable markup, build-time checking, terminal detection, and inserted text that is made harmless by default.

How A fits Jet. D-TEXTHEAD-TYPE1=A lets a library declare checked text as a String-backed type with a `CheckedText` impl, so `ANSI` needs no compiler change. D-UNIFYLIT1=A and D-REGEX-LIT1=D fix the `Type{"…"}` head form. D-TEXT-CONTROL1=A supplies the control-character test used for inserted text.

Names. The helpers use the camelCase spelling from the owner's question. Under the ratified D-CASE-LAW1=A they would read `move_cursor` and `clear_line`; D-CASE-LAW2 is open and decides which spelling ships.

bad :: ANSI{"[redd]x"}  // error: unknown style `redd`; did you mean `red`?

println!("{} no user {}", "error:".red().bold(), name);

comparisons.note: Style values with automatic color downsampling. Source: lipgloss README.
Chained styles, plus a tagged template that escapes braces but not control codes. Source: chalk and chalk-template READMEs.
comparisons.code:

console.log(chalkTemplate`{red.bold error:} no user ${name}`);

recommendation.why: Misspelled styles fail the build, inserted user text can never run terminal codes, styles always close, and piped output stays clean. It reuses the checked text form Jet already has for SQL and HTML.

No new syntax: the same `Type{"…"}` form as SQL and HTML.

decisions.title: Does Jet need const or frozen parameters beyond read access?
decisions.situation: In C++ a programmer writes const on a parameter to promise the function will not change it. In Jet every parameter without a mark is already read-only, and the compiler also stops anyone else from changing that value while the call runs. The caller's variable may still be changeable before and after the call. You are deciding whether Jet adds anything on top: a C++ style const keyword, or a frozen parameter that demands a value nobody can ever change. We recommend neither, because read access already gives a stronger promise at no cost.
decisions.gist: Should Jet add a const or frozen parameter kind, or is today's read parameter enough?
decisions.lesson: A read parameter is one with no mark: the function may look but not change it, and nobody else may change it during the call. Frozen means changed by nobody, ever, made with freeze(x). A keeps read as Jet's const and freeze for lasting immutability. B adds a parameter kind that demands a frozen value. C adds a C++ style const keyword.
decisions.explainer:
Jet has three ways to pass a value. No mark means read. &T means exclusive write, and the caller writes & too. ^T means the function takes ownership, and the caller writes ^.

A read parameter is passed as a plain pointer to the caller's value. Nothing is copied, even when the caller's variable is mutable. During the call, no one may change it: passing the same list as read and as write in one call is a compile error, and links that might alias are checked.

That is stronger than C++ const in three ways. It is deep, so fields inside cannot change either. It cannot be cast away. And it also binds every other writer, which is what lets a compiler keep values in registers.

freeze(x) makes a deeply immutable value that stays that way forever. Tasks may share frozen values without locks, and any write through them is a compile error.
decisions.story: Omar comes from C++ and asks whether Jet passes his large mutable list by copy when a function only reads it, and whether he should mark it const for speed. He also wonders whether the function could see the list change halfway through.
decisions.detail:
Owner question 2026-10-05: how does Jet handle const params; what if the values are mutable; do we lose performance?

Current law: D-MEM1 makes an unmarked parameter read, enforced, never elevated. D-MEMREF-EXCL1=A stops any write while a read is live: proven at compile time where possible, checked at run time for aliasing links. D-CONC-FREEZE1=A gives freeze(x) for lasting deep immutability. The memory proposal (Docs/proposals/memory-model-2026-10-05.md sections 4.3 and 4.6) puts read parameters in zero-copy class Z0. It calls their no-alias facts the main speed prize, emitted only after an independent re-proof (card #4619).

Exercised on dev-05ea86f65 (probes in $JET_STATE_ROOT/scratch/OwnerFeedback/sem-probes). p01: a mutable list passed to a read parameter lowers to Rust &Vec<JetInt>, a shared reference with no copy. Rust gives such references LLVM noalias readonly facts. p02: nums passed as read and &nums in one call is E0204. p03: a write through a read parameter is E0202.

p05: a write through a frozen value is E1113. p04: storing a read parameter in a struct field copies it automatically. Returning it as-is is E0120, an inconsistency filed in the report.

Corpus: 34,680 named parameters in Examples, Core and Compiler. 81.7% are read, 17.6% write and 0.7% take. Receivers: 248 read, 89 write, 30 take. Five freeze calls exist, all in Examples.

Other languages: Mojo's default argument convention is an immutable read-only reference, with mut and owned as the marked forms, the same shape as Jet. Swift's default is borrowing with exclusivity enforcement. D has transitive const and immutable. Pony's val means nobody can write. C++ const is shallow and removable with const_cast.

options.name: Read is Jet's const
options.detail: No new keyword. An unmarked parameter keeps meaning deep, call-long, no-copy read access. freeze(x) stays the way to make a value immutable forever. Hover and jet inspect show each parameter's promise in words.
options.technical: No grammar change. Hover and the honest-signature view (D-HONEST-SIG2) print read as "read: nobody changes this during the call". The native backend emits no-alias read facts for read parameters once MIR Lint re-proves them (memory proposal 5.8).
options.code:
fn total(xs: [Int]) -> Int { ... }   // read: no copy, nobody changes xs during the call

nums := [1, 2, 3]
print(total(nums))      // nums is mutable; still no copy
&nums.push(4)

options.name: Add a frozen parameter kind
options.detail: A parameter can demand a value that can never change, written with a new mark. Callers pass freeze(x) or a value already frozen.
options.technical: A fourth access kind beside read, write and take. Sema checks the argument's frozen fact. Useful for long-lived caches and cross-task sharing, which freeze already covers.

options.name: C++ style const keyword
options.detail: Parameters become changeable by default, and const marks the read-only ones, as in C++.
options.technical: Reverses D-MEM1's default. Every read parameter in the corpus gains a keyword.
options.code: fn total(xs: const [Int]) -> Int { ... }

comparisons.note: The default argument convention is an immutable read-only reference; mut and owned are marked.
comparisons.code:
fn total(xs: List[Int]) -> Int: ...     # read by default
fn fill(mut xs: List[Int]): ...

comparisons.note: const is shallow and can be cast away, so it gives no aliasing guarantee.

recommendation.why: Jet's read parameter already does what const promises, and more: it is deep, cannot be cast away, and stops other writers during the call. That costs nothing and copies nothing, even for a mutable caller value.
recommendation.tradeoff: C++ programmers do not see the word const; the hover and the docs say read.
gains: No copy for read parameters, mutable caller or not.
A deeper promise than C++ const, with no keyword.
freeze stays the one lasting immutability tool.

losses.loss: Newcomers may not realize read is enforced.
losses.mitigation: Hover prints the promise in words, and E0202 names the read mark when a write is tried.

whyNot.reason: B forces callers to freeze copies for functions that only read during the call, and adds no speed.

decisions.title: How much of a program's types Jet works out for you
decisions.situation: Type inference means the compiler works out a type you did not write. Jet asks for written types on every function's inputs and result, and works out most types inside function bodies. Two local cases still need a written type: an empty list or map filled later, and a None that gets a value later. Today the error for names := [] even suggests [Int]{} when the next line pushes text. You are deciding Jet's inference level. We recommend keeping each value's type where it starts, and making the error read the next line, name the right type and let jet fix write it.
decisions.gist: Should Jet keep written types where values start, with an error that writes the right one, or infer more?
decisions.lesson: A signature is a function's written inputs and result. A keeps signatures written and keeps the type where an empty list, map or None starts; its error now reads the next line, names the right type, and jet fix writes it. B lets later lines in the same function settle that type, as Rust does. C makes signature types optional too, as OCaml and Gleam do.
decisions.explainer:
Jet already infers most local types. x :: 5 is an Int, a lambda passed to map takes its parameter type from the list, and a generic call works out its type arguments. names :: people.map((p: Person) -> p.name) needs no written type either. Effects and failure kinds are inferred and shown in tools.

What Jet does not do is look ahead. names := [] alone does not say what the list holds, so Jet asks for the type. Today's message is generic and even suggests [Int]{} when the next line pushes text. That wrong hint is the real beginner stop.

Under A, the message reads the first later line that uses the name and names the type it implies: line 3 puts text in names, so write [String]{}. The same edit is attached as a safe fix, so jet fix or the editor's quick fix writes it in one step. With no such line, the message stays general.

What A keeps. The type shows where the value starts, even in a code review with no editor. A wrong first push is reported on that push. Every typed value starts with its type, which is one rule. Safety and program speed are the same under every option.

B saves writing the type. In exchange, the line no longer says what the list holds, and a mistaken first push makes Jet blame the next, correct line. C goes further and works out signatures from bodies and callers, as OCaml, Haskell and Gleam do.
decisions.story: Lena writes her first Jet script. She types names := [] and then pushes text into it. Jet stops her and suggests [Int]{}, which is wrong for her list. She wants the error to tell her what to write, or to write it for her.
decisions.detail:
Owner question q53w5bht, 2026-10-07: "Im not sold on why this is a good or useful idea, you just say that python habits work. Are those habits good? What is the CBA?" The answer concluded that both sides are small and the costs of look-ahead fall on readers. It recommended keeping today's rule with a better error that names the type and that jet fix writes in. This revision offers exactly that as A. The former A, look-ahead within a function, is now B.

Cost-benefit, A against B. B saves typing the type. The owner answer counted at most about 6,300 written types in Jet's own code: 5,363 empty lists or maps and 927 None starts. The first census, with a narrower match, counted 4,258 and 825. Some would stay under B, where no later line settles them.

B's costs. Reading: names := [] stops saying what it holds, and a GitHub review shows no editor hint. Error placement: if the first push is the mistake, Jet blames the next, correct line, a known problem with inference that flows backward (Wand 1986; Heeren's Helium; Seidel et al., OOPSLA 2017). One rule: a typed value in Jet starts with its type, the rule D-ANGLE-CAST2's recommendation keeps, and B makes empty literals an exception. Work: new solving machinery in the checker during the Rust exit.

A's cost. A newcomer still meets one error the first time. It cannot reach zero without B's trade, because a type that shows on its line has to be written by someone. A makes the tool write it: the message names the type, and the attached safe edit is applied by jet fix or the editor.

Corpus census (Examples, Core, Compiler; semantics-metrics.mjs). Every one of 34,680 named parameters, receivers aside, has a written type. About 41,500 local bindings exist, and about 85% carry no written type head. Lambdas in the compiler are 133 untyped and 1 typed.

Other languages. Kotlin, Swift, Go and C# require a type on an empty collection, and their tools offer to write it: IntelliJ's specify-type action, Swift fix-its, gopls quick fixes. Java's diamond takes the type from the declared variable. Rust settles an empty Vec from later uses, which is option B. TypeScript lets an empty array widen as it is filled, a known source of loose types under noImplicitAny.

Evidence for written signatures. Rust requires them by design. TypeScript 5.5 added isolatedDeclarations for fast parallel builds. Kotlin explicit API mode requires them for public library code. GHC warns on missing top-level signatures. Crystal's whole-program inference prevents separate compilation of modules. ML-style inference is exponential in the worst case (Mairson, POPL 1990), though linear in practice.

Jet today, exercised on dev-595e0dca3 (probes in $JET_STATE_ROOT/scratch/BallotPolish/probesA). i1: names := [] then a text push gives E0501 with "Fix: Name the element type on the literal, such as `[Int]{}`". i2: best := None then best = Val(3) gives E0308 "Add a type annotation". i3: [String]{}, [String:Int]{} with counts["a"] = 1, and Int?{ None } all compile and print 1 1 3. i5: people.map((p: Person) -> p.name) needs no written type and prints 2.

Earlier probes (OwnerFeedback/sem-probes): p20 E0433, p21 an E0305 cascade, p23 E0801, and p25 generic inference with E0904 on conflicts.

D-BODY-LAST1 relies on written return types and is unchanged by A. A changes only diagnostics: no accepted program and no type rule changes.

options.name: Written where it starts, with an error that writes it
options.detail: Signatures stay written, and an empty list, map or None still starts with its type. The error now reads the first later line that uses the name and names the type it implies. jet fix and the editor's quick fix write it in. Lambdas and generic calls keep taking types from context.
options.technical:
Diagnostic-only change. When E0501 or E0308 fires at a binding, the checker scans forward in the same function for the first use of that name that implies a type. Implying uses are a push or insert argument, a map add or index assignment, an assignment, a return, and a typed call argument. The message names that line and type.

A Safe machine-applicable edit writes [String]{}, [String:Int]{} or Int?{ None }. With no implying use, the current advice stays, without the misleading [Int]{} example. The accepted language, type rules and per-function checking are unchanged. Every tier sees the same types.

options.name: Look ahead within a function
options.detail: Signatures stay written. Inside one function, the first later use that fixes an empty list, map or None settles its type. The line that starts the value no longer shows its type, and a mistaken first push makes the error land on the next, correct line.
options.technical: Adds function-local type variables for empty collection literals and bare None at binding sites, solved by unification over the function body in source order. The first constraining use is recorded and cited in any mismatch. Unsolved variables at function end report E0501 or E0308 as today. Signatures, struct fields and module globals are unchanged. Checking stays per function.

options.name: Optional signature types
options.detail: Parameter and result types may be left out anywhere. The compiler works them out from bodies and callers.
options.technical: Hindley-Milner style inference with generalization across functions. Public API snapshots record the inferred types.

comparisons.note: An empty collection names its type; the editor offers to write it. This is option A.

comparisons.note: Written signatures; bodies infer from later uses. This is option B.
Signatures optional; whole functions are inferred. This is option C.

recommendation.why: Types written where values start keep code readable in review, keep errors on the line that is wrong, and keep one rule for typed values. The real beginner stop was a wrong hint, so A makes the error name the right type and lets jet fix write it.
recommendation.tradeoff: One fix step the first time, for types that show where values start and errors that point at the mistake.
gains: Every value's type shows where it starts, even in a code review.
A mistaken first push is reported on that line.
The error names the right type, and jet fix writes it.

losses.loss: A newcomer still meets one error the first time an empty list has no type.
losses.mitigation: The error names the exact type from the next line, and jet fix or the editor's quick fix writes it in one step.

whyNot.reason: B saves writing about 6,300 types, but each such line stops saying what it holds, and a mistaken first push blames the next, correct line.
C hides function contracts, slows separate builds and moves errors away from their cause.

Check the same for a map add or index assignment, writing [String:Int]{}, and for best := None then best = Val(3), writing Int?{ None }. Check that an empty list with no implying later use keeps the general advice without the [Int]{} example. Check that no accepted program or type rule changes, on every tier.

surface.lesson: A signature is a function's written inputs and result. A keeps the type written where an empty list or None starts, and its error now names and writes the right type. B lets later lines settle that type. C makes signature types optional.

decisions.title: Fold six variant commands into their parent commands
decisions.situation: Jet's command line has 61 top-level commands, more than twice what Go or Deno show. Several are modes of another command: fuzz and test-compare run tests, and budget checks what perf measures. Likewise gc and emit show facts that inspect explores, and eval runs code like run does. This vote decides whether those six become options of their parent, so the help screen is easier to scan.
decisions.gist: Should fuzz, test-compare, budget, gc, emit and eval become options of test, perf, inspect and run?
decisions.lesson: A top-level command is a word after `jet`, such as `jet test`. Some commands are really a mode of another one. Folding them keeps every feature and shortens the list a learner scans. Whichever option wins, the old words get errors that print the new spelling.
decisions.explainer:
Jet's command registry drives help, completion and the man page, so folding is one table change. Under A:
- `jet fuzz` becomes `jet test --fuzz` (Go 1.18 made the same move).
- `jet test-compare` becomes `jet test --compare`.
- `jet budget` becomes `jet perf budget`, beside perf run, test, compare and export.
- `jet gc` becomes `jet inspect gc`, one more inspect view.
- `jet emit` becomes `jet inspect emitted`.
- `jet eval <expr>` becomes `jet run --eval <expr>`, like `lua -e` and `node -e`.

The list drops from 61 to 55. The retired words print the new spelling (the registry already has 17 retired rows with this behaviour).

Beginner path: fewer words on the help screen; daily commands (run, test, build, check, fmt) are untouched. Expert path: the same features under the command they belong to.
decisions.story: Lena wants to find slow code. She sees perf, budget, audit and inspect in the help list and cannot tell which one measures speed.
decisions.inWild:
# Go 1.18 folded fuzzing into the test runner (go.dev/doc/fuzz)
go test -fuzz=FuzzParse
# Lua runs a snippet with a flag, not a separate command
lua -e "print(1 + 2)"
decisions.detail:
Code facts, checked 2026-10-05: crates/jet-cli/src/CLI.rs COMMANDS has 61 top-level rows, 57 literal nested actions plus 9 inspect planes, and 17 RetiredCommandSpec rows. Summaries: fuzz "Find failing inputs for property tests". test-compare "Compare one recorded observation corpus against its relation". Budget "Check performance limits or update baselines". Perf "Collect and inspect performance traces". Gc "Show values moved into automatic memory management". Emit "Print generated build output". Eval "Evaluate pure Jet and print the value".

Docs/spec/reference/cli.md:116-117 lists `gc report` and `perf run|test|attach|view|compare|export`.

Other findings recorded for cards, not this vote: the registry spells one command `Fold` with a capital letter; `search` (package catalog) and `find` (code) are easy to confuse.

Comparison counts [approximate, from each tool's help output as documented]. Go about 19 commands (go help), Deno about 28 subcommands, Cargo about 30 built-in commands, Zig about 25, Lua 2 executables (lua, luac) with flags.

Research: Go folded fuzzing into `go test -fuzz` (Go 1.18, 2022) rather than ship a fuzz command. Deno groups test, bench and coverage but keeps fmt, lint and check separate, matching daily jobs. The lesson: fold modes into the command that owns the job; keep distinct daily jobs as words.

decisions.title: A counted surface budget: new words must pay for themselves
decisions.situation: Lua stays small because its authors make each new feature replace several old ones. Jet already requires one mechanism per meaning, but nothing counts how many words, marks, markers and commands a learner faces. The official keyword list has even drifted: it names nine markers and misses five real words. This vote decides whether a test counts Jet's language surface on every change and stops growth that no owner decision approved. Library functions are counted and shown, never gated.
decisions.gist: Should a test count Jet's keywords, marks, markers and commands, failing growth no owner decision approved?
decisions.lesson: The language surface is what a user types or runs that the language itself defines: keywords, marks like # and $, markers, commands. Jet registers each in one place, so counting is cheap. A ceiling that only an owner decision can raise makes growth visible. Library functions are counted but never gated. Whichever option wins, the stale keyword list gets fixed.
decisions.explainer:
Under A, the syntax registry computes counts: live keywords, marks, live markers, fact rows and top-level commands. A checked-in ceiling file records the current numbers. A guard test fails when one of these counts rises, unless the change names the owner decision that raised that ceiling. Retiring something lowers the ceiling automatically, so the budget only tightens by default.

Public Core functions per module are counted and shown with their trend, but never gated. Adding a library function under an approved library contract is routine work, not an owner choice, and gating it would turn every new function into a ballot. `jet self devtools surface` prints every count, and every ballot that adds language surface shows the before and after numbers.

Today's numbers: 49 live keywords after D-MARKER-DECL1 retired two, 43 lexical-ledger rows, 83 live markers (110 rows, 27 retired), 49 fact rows, 61 top-level commands (counted 2026-10-05). For scale: Lua 22 keywords, Go 25, Python 35 plus 4 soft, Rust 38 strict, Zig 49 plus about 120 builtins.

Beginner path: unaffected; they see a smaller, stable surface. Expert path: a ballot that adds a word must say what it costs and, where possible, what it retires.
decisions.story: Three teams each add a marker in the same month for nearly the same job. Nobody notices until a learner asks why #Track, #Persist and #Reactive all seem to watch values.
decisions.inWild:
-- Lua 5.4: 22 reserved words (lua.org/manual/5.4/manual.html, section 3.1)
and break do else elseif end false for function goto if in
local nil not or repeat return then true until while
decisions.detail:
Revision by OptionQuality1, 2026-10-07. The posted A also put public Core functions under the owner-raised ceiling. Every new library function would then have needed an owner decision, although the ballot rules say routine work under an approved contract is not a ballot. A now gates the language surface only and reports library counts.

Counts are refreshed: D-MARKER-DECL1=A retired two keywords (51 to 49), and owner directive 21 removed `pub`, so the old count of 2,419 `pub fn` no longer measures anything. The guard's example no longer names a Rust test runner (directive 19). Options, letters and the recommendation are otherwise unchanged.

Code facts, checked 2026-10-05. Keyword list drift: crates/jet-foundation/src/Syntax/package_files.rs:464-551 JET_KEYWORD_LIST (55 entries) is documented as the single source for LSP, formatter and grammar. It includes nine marker names (Unsafe, Impure, Context, Transact, Job, Test, Todo, State, Transition) and the literal None. It omits five live words: prep (Syntax.rs:67), next (math_layout.rs:408), fact (effects_surface.rs:143), yield (core_surface.rs:514) and rust (math_layout.rs:571). Card c0bs5inj already tracks keyword-table consistency.

Registry location. AGENTS.md I7 names crates/jet-foundation/src/Syntax.rs as the registry of every keyword and sigil today. Under owner directive 19 that registry moves into Jet with the rest of the toolchain; the guard reads whichever registry is canonical, so the choice here does not depend on the move.

Counts: LEXICAL_LEDGER 43 rows (Syntax.rs:20-64). Prelude/Markers.jet 110 marker rows, 27 carry $retired. Prelude/Facts.jet 49 fact rows. CLI COMMANDS 61 top-level. Corpus marker usage: 1,854 #Name uses, 113 distinct names, 56.4 per 10k lines.

Peers: Lua 5.4 manual 3.1 (22). Go spec Keywords (25). Python 3.12 keyword.kwlist 35 and softkwlist 4. Rust Reference Keywords (38 strict, 14 reserved). Zig language reference (49 keywords, builtins listed separately). Swift Lexical Structure about 95-100 counting context-sensitive and # keywords [approximate].

Research. Ierusalimschy et al., "The Evolution of Lua" (HOPL III, 2007) and "Passing a Language through the Eye of a Needle" (ACM Queue, 2011). Lua adds a feature only when it is a general mechanism and removes features in major versions (module() deprecated in 5.2). Go's Go 1 compatibility promise plus a high bar for keywords kept it at 25 for over a decade; generics (1.18) added zero keywords.

Why library functions are reported, not gated. Lua and Go keep their languages small while their libraries grow freely. A library function adds no grammar and is found through completion and docs. Jet's one-mechanism rule (I8) and the library laws already review library growth.

Jet precedent: D-ONCE-LAW1 (say it once, with a guard) and the existing copy and unsafe count guards in Tools/agent (copy-ratchet.mjs, check-unsafe-ratchet.mjs) show count guards work here.

Retired rows lower counts. JET_KEYWORD_LIST is regenerated from the registry so it cannot drift. Public Core functions per module are printed with their trend and never fail the guard.

decisions.title: One trusted rail for code that runs at project lifecycle moments
decisions.situation: Projects run small jobs at set moments: entering the dev shell, before a git commit, while installing a package, or before a deploy. Jet has six separate ways to declare these today, each with its own approval step or none. Some run unchecked shell commands. This vote decides whether every lifecycle moment becomes a hook point that runs a named, checked job function, approved through one trust grant that lists exactly what it may touch.
decisions.gist: Should every project lifecycle moment run checked job functions through one trust grant, replacing six separate hook styles?
decisions.lesson: A job is a Jet function marked #Job that the tools can run. Lifecycle moments include shell entry, git commit, package install and deploy. A trust grant records approval of exact code and its rights. Whichever option wins, unreviewed third-party code never runs.
decisions.explainer:
Today: env on_enter lists jobs. Env checks lists jobs. Env hook is a Jet function given a shell (expert, trust-gated). Explicit hook records carry a command, a folder and trusted: true. git_hooks_path points git at a folder of scripts. Package build and install hooks have their own digest-bound approval.

Under A, each moment is a hook point: env.entered, env.checked, git.pre_commit, git.pre_push, package.installing, deploy.before and deploy.after. A #Job function attaches with #On. The short list fields stay as the beginner spelling: `on_enter: [seed_config]` means exactly `#On(env.entered)` on seed_config, shown by `jet inspect hooks`. Jet writes small git hook shims that call the jobs, so hooks work the same on Windows, macOS and Linux without shell scripts.

Every job that touches the outside world runs under one trust grant shape: job identity, code digest and requested rights. A change re-prompts with a diff. CI fails with the exact grant command. Raw command records and the shell-function hook retire into jobs.

Beginner path: list job names, as today. Expert path: one grant law and one audit list for everything that runs automatically.
decisions.story: Jo clones a repo and enters its dev shell. A git hook script, an env hook and a package install step each run, each approved differently, and one is a shell script she cannot read on Windows.
decisions.inWild:

  commands:
    lint:
      run: npm run lint
decisions.detail:
Code facts, checked 2026-10-05.

Six shapes: env fields on_enter, checks, git_hooks_path, formatter (crates/jet-foundation/src/Syntax/jetpack_config.rs:619-630; D-ENV-LIFECYCLE1/2, D-ECO6). Env `hook:` fn(sh: Shell) (D-ECO7=A, D-ENV-LIFECYCLE2=A). Explicit hook records needing command, working directory and `trusted: true`, rejected with E1329 when untrusted (Docs/spec/reference/jetpack-epoch5.md:196-205). Package build and install hooks held until a digest-bound policy.trust grant (D-JPK-BUILDSCRIPT1=D). #Job lifecycle names (D-TASK-META1, D-DX-GENERATE1).

D-ENV-LIFECYCLE2=A already says one task and grant planner; this ballot makes that planner the public model and retires the raw command and shell-function shapes.

Research. Husky and lefthook exist because raw .git/hooks scripts are not versioned, not portable and not reviewed; both are widely used [download counts approximate]. pre-commit (Python) pins hook sources by revision, the digest idea A keeps. npm install scripts are a long-running supply-chain vector (event-stream 2018, ua-parser-js 2021). Pnpm 10 and Bun now block dependency lifecycle scripts by default and require an allowlist, the same deny-unless-granted rule as D-JPK-BUILDSCRIPT1.

options.technical: Points live in core.jobs. on_enter/checks lists desugar to hook attachments in the env planner (no second runner). git_hooks_path retires: jet env sync writes shims that call `jet jobs run <job>`. D-ECO7 hook and explicit command records retire with teaching errors pointing to #Job. Grant shape reuses D-JPK-BUILDSCRIPT1: identity, digest, rights.

fn quick_checks() -[Exec]> Unit Never! {
    run_lints()
}

decisions.title: Framework and runtime hooks: free when unused, watch-only for the scheduler and memory
decisions.situation: Web servers, games and apps run code at moments such as each request, each frame or shutdown. Jet's web, game, transaction and process libraries each expose these moments differently, through handler wrappers, frame callbacks, commit methods and signal callbacks. Hooks on the busiest paths must cost nothing when nobody listens. This vote decides whether these moments become typed hook points, narrowed to part of a site where needed, and whether hooks may only watch, never change, the task scheduler and memory allocator.
decisions.gist: Should framework moments be typed hook points that cost nothing unused, with scheduler and allocator hooks watch-only?
decisions.lesson: A framework moment is a point like "request arrived" or "frame starting". A decision hook can let a request continue, change it, or answer it early, which is what web middleware does. A request point can be narrowed to one part of a site, such as pages under /admin. Whichever option wins, the allocator is still chosen by its existing setting, not by hooks.
decisions.explainer:
Under A, libraries publish these points. app.started, app.stopping, process.signal(Signal), web.request (a decision hook: continue, transform, or cancel with a response, replacing middleware wrappers). web.responded, web.failed, game.frame(Frame), game.fixed_step, game.scene_entered and game.scene_left, test.before_each and test.after_each. Per-value moments stay scoped subscriptions: tx.on_commit becomes `tx.committed.on(tx.scope, f)`.

The request point can be narrowed to a path prefix: `web.request.under("/admin")` is the same decision hook, run only for requests under that prefix. This keeps what per-route middleware does in Express (`app.use("/admin", mw)`) and ASP.NET (`UseWhen`). It is an ordinary library method on the point value, so it adds no syntax. The narrowing is static, so the hook table still lowers to direct calls per route.

Scheduler and allocator moments (task.spawned, task.finished, allocation statistics) are watch-only Event points fed by the existing observation stream; no hook can delay a task or change an allocation. The allocator stays a package setting, as ratified.

Cost rule: a point with no static attachment compiles to nothing; static attachments compile to direct calls in declaration order; only run-time .on subscriptions pay for a listener list.

Beginner path: #On(web.request.under("/admin")) replaces learning middleware. Expert path: watch the scheduler live without patching it.
decisions.story: Ravi adds login checks for his admin pages with one middleware wrapper, metrics with another, and a shutdown flush with a signal callback. The three use three styles, and the wrapper order silently decides which runs first.
decisions.detail:
Revision by OptionQuality1, 2026-10-07. The posted A ran every login check on every request through a global web.request point. Its own example redirected visitors without a session to /login, and that rule also ran on /login, so the page could never load. Per-route middleware is the common case in Express, ASP.NET Core and Axum, and the posted A hid its loss. A now narrows the point to a path prefix with an ordinary library method on the point value, and its example guards /admin only.

Generic types in examples use parentheses, HookDecision(web.Request, web.Response), following D-GENERIC-TYPEFN1=A, which removes angle brackets. Options, letters and the recommendation are otherwise unchanged.

Code facts, checked 2026-10-05.

Today: transactions on_commit/on_rollback (Docs/spec/spec.md:1162-1166, D-TXN3, D-STM1). Game frame hook through game.run (spec.md:1568-1570). process.on_signal (Core/process). web.on(path, title, handler) (core-library.md:2860) and core.http.middleware.compress(enc, handler) wrappers (checker core_call.rs, noted undocumented by the API mining). WebRouter loader and boundary callbacks (Prelude/CoreLib/Top/WebRouter.rs:597-600). Observation stream: JET_OBSERVE and jet inspect live (spec.md:3086-3093, D-OBSERVE-LIVE1). Allocator setting: D-ALLOC-DEFAULT1=A.

Ratified frame. D-HOOK-ONE1=A: one typed hook mechanism; `#On(point)` attaches statically, `point.on(scope, f)` at run time, and the On marker takes the point as a value. So a narrowed point such as web.request.under("/admin") needs no new marker or syntax.

Cost evidence: Linux static keys and tracepoints patch a disabled hook to a no-op; Rust tracing caches per-callsite interest so disabled spans cost a branch. Neovim's CursorMoved and on_bytes callbacks show the failure mode when every listener runs on every event. Neovim's autocmd patterns, which narrow an event to matching files, are the precedent for narrowing a point.

Go and Rust expose allocator choice as a setting (GODEBUG/runtime knobs, #[global_allocator]), not as per-allocation hooks, because hooks on that path cost too much and can break invariants.

Research. ASP.NET Core, Express and Axum (tower layers) model middleware as an ordered pipeline; ordering bugs are the common failure. All three also scope middleware to part of a site. A decision hook with explicit priority, a path prefix and a listed order (jet inspect hooks) keeps the pipeline power and makes order visible.

options.name: Typed points, zero-cost, watch-only engine
options.detail: Publish the points listed; middleware wrappers retire into web.request, which a hook can narrow to a path prefix; scheduler and allocator points are watch-only Events.
options.technical: Static attachments lower to direct calls; empty points emit no code. web.request.under(prefix) returns the same DecisionHook point restricted to that prefix; the router dispatches it only on matching routes. Order: priority, then package order, then declaration order, listed by jet inspect hooks with each hook's prefix. Watch-only points are Event(T) with no return channel, fed by the observation writer under its existing bounds.

options.name: Keep library callbacks
options.detail: Each library keeps its own callback design.
options.technical: No change.
options.code: handler :: auth(log(app_handler))  // order hidden in nesting

options.name: Allow engine intervention
options.detail: Scheduler and allocator points become decision hooks.
options.technical: Every spawn and allocation consults listeners.
options.code: #On(mem.allocating) fn cap(a: Alloc) -> HookDecision(Alloc, Never) { ... }

comparisons.note: Disabled callsites cost a cached branch (docs.rs/tracing, callsite interest).
comparisons.code:
#[tracing::instrument]
fn handle(req: Request) { /* span only if a subscriber cares */ }

comparisons.note: Middleware can be mounted on one path prefix.

recommendation.why: One decision hook replaces middleware wrappers, keeps per-route checks through a path prefix, and makes order visible, and unused points compile away. Watch-only scheduler and allocator hooks protect the hottest paths and safety while experts can still observe them.
gains: Middleware order is visible.
Zero cost when unused.
Engine stays safe and observable.

losses.loss: Existing middleware wrappers and frame callbacks are rewritten.
losses.mitigation: Teaching errors show the #On form, and jet fix rewrites single-wrapper chains, keeping a mounted wrapper's path as the prefix.

whyNot.reason: Four styles, and wrapper nesting hides which check runs first.
Listeners on every spawn and allocation cost the hottest paths and can break safety.

recommendation.tradeoff: Watch-only engine hooks in exchange for fast, safe scheduling and allocation.

Add the paired cell (request loop with an empty point vs no point; with one attachment vs a direct call) required by the performance gate.

A request point can be narrowed to part of a site. Whichever option wins, the allocator is still chosen by its existing setting.

decisions.title: Automatic WebP images in the Jet web framework
decisions.situation: Photos are usually the heaviest part of a web page, and the WebP format makes them roughly a quarter to a third smaller at the same visual quality. Jet's web framework serves image files exactly as written and has no image pipeline yet. Every major web framework now converts images automatically, but they differ on when they do it. This vote decides whether Jet converts at build time, on first request while running, or never automatically, and which formats are on by default.
decisions.gist: When should the Jet web framework convert page images to WebP: at build, on first request, or never automatically?
decisions.lesson: WebP and AVIF are newer image formats that browsers read; almost every browser supports WebP. Conversion can happen once while building, or on demand while the server runs. Jet's image library is ratified but not built yet. Whichever option wins, original files stay available as a fallback.
decisions.explainer:
Under A, a page writes `web.image("hero.jpg", alt: "Our team")`. At `jet build`, Jet writes WebP versions at up to three widths (640, 1280 and 1920 pixels, never larger than the original), named by content hash so browsers can cache them forever. The page gets a `<picture>` element with a srcset, plus the original file as the fallback. JPEG photos use lossy quality 75, the default of Next.js, Hugo and Squoosh. PNG images use lossless WebP, so graphics never blur.

If a WebP file would be larger than the original, Jet keeps the original. Animated GIFs are left alone.

`jet dev` converts on first request with the same encoder and the same cache, so dev and build output match. AVIF is one setting away (`images: .{ formats: [.AVIF, .WebP] }`) because it encodes several times slower. Images users upload while the app runs are not converted automatically; the image library offers an explicit call for them.

Beginner path: write web.image and get smaller pages. Expert path: set widths, quality, formats, or turn conversion off per image.
decisions.story: Ana builds a portfolio site with twenty phone photos. Each is 4 MB, and the home page takes eight seconds to load on a train.
decisions.detail:
Jet facts, checked 2026-10-05: no image pipeline exists. core.image is ratified (D-CORE-IMAGE1=A) as Jet-owned PNG, JPEG and GIF decode, PNG and JPEG encode, and nearest-neighbour resize under explicit budgets. It has no Core module yet, in Core/ or the CoreLib. Core/net/mime.jet:108 already maps webp. BuildContext lists b.add_asset_bundle in the spec (spec.md:4060, D-BUILDTARGET1) with no implementation. Core/web/web.jet has page and app records but no asset handling.

Framework survey [defaults from current docs; verify at ratification]:
- Next.js next/image. on-demand at request time through /_next/image, Accept-header negotiation, images.formats default ["image/webp"], AVIF opt-in ("AVIF generally takes longer to encode but compresses smaller"). Quality 75, disk cache in .next/cache/images, encoder sharp (Apache-2.0, over LGPL libvips).
- Astro astro:assets: default output WebP; build time for static pages, an on-demand endpoint for server-rendered pages; <Picture formats={["avif","webp"]}> for more; sharp by default.

- Nuxt Image: IPX provider (sharp) on demand in server mode, prerendered for static; NuxtPicture adds WebP with original fallback.
- SvelteKit @sveltejs/enhanced-img: build time; emits AVIF and WebP automatically with the original fallback.
- Gatsby gatsby-plugin-image: build time; formats ["auto","webp"] default, AVIF opt-in.
- Eleventy Image: build time; formats ["webp","jpeg"] by default.
- Hugo: build-time image processing with quality 75 default and WebP output; results cached in resources/_gen.
- Vite: no built-in conversion; plugins (vite-imagetools, vite-plugin-image-optimizer).

Savings. Google's WebP study reports lossy WebP 25-34% smaller than JPEG at equal SSIM, and lossless WebP 26% smaller than PNG (developers.google.com/speed/webp/docs/webp_study, webp_lossless_alpha_study). AVIF typically saves more than WebP versus JPEG (web.dev AVIF article; Netflix tech blog 2020). Browser support: WebP is supported by all current major browsers (Safari since 14/macOS Big Sur), about 95%+ of users; AVIF since Safari 16.4 and Edge 121 (caniuse.com) [approximate shares].

HTTP Archive Web Almanac (Media and Page Weight chapters) reports images as the largest byte share of a median page.

Why build time: Jet's build already knows every referenced image, so there is no server CPU, no writable cache, and static hosting works. Accept-header negotiation needs Vary: Accept, which fragments CDN caches; <picture> lets the browser choose with one cache key per file.

options.name: Convert at build; dev on demand
options.detail: Build-time variants at up to three widths, hashed names, <picture> with fallback. JPEG lossy q75, PNG lossless. Dev converts on first request with the same encoder and cache. AVIF opt-in. Uploads use the explicit image API.
options.technical: web.image registers an asset node in the build graph (b.add_asset_bundle). Variants are cached by (source hash, width, format, quality, encoder version) in the project cache, so only new or changed images encode. Responses send Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable for hashed names. Settings: images: .{ formats, widths, quality, enabled }. Encoder per the companion encoder ballot.
options.code: use core.web as web fn home() -> web.WebPage { web.page("Home", web.image("hero.jpg", alt: "Our team")) } $ jet build // illustrative output; sizes vary by photo images: 20 sources, 60 variants written (cached next time)

options.name: Convert on first request
options.detail: A runtime endpoint converts per request using the Accept header and caches results on disk.
options.technical: Adds a server route, a disk cache with eviction, and Vary: Accept.
options.code:
GET /_jet/image?url=hero.jpg&w=1280
Vary: Accept

options.name: No automatic conversion
options.detail: Only the image library's explicit encode call exists.
options.technical: No pipeline.
options.code: webp :: image.encode_webp(&pixels, quality: 75)?

comparisons.note: On-demand optimizer; formats default WebP, AVIF opt-in, quality 75 (nextjs.org/docs, next/image).
enhanced-img converts at build and emits AVIF and WebP (svelte.dev/docs/kit/images).

recommendation.why: Jet's build already knows every page image, so converting once at build gives the byte savings with no server cost, works on static hosts, caches cleanly, and keeps dev identical to build. AVIF stays one setting away.
gains: Smaller pages by default.
No server CPU or cache.
Dev and build output match.

decisions.title: Where the WebP and AVIF encoders come from
decisions.situation: Converting images needs an encoder, the code that turns pixels into a WebP or AVIF file. Jet's image library is planned to be written in Jet with no outside code, but a full WebP encoder is a large piece of work and an AVIF encoder is far larger. Image code written in C has a long record of serious security bugs. This vote decides whether Jet writes its own WebP encoder, wraps Google's open-source library, or wraps libraries for both formats now.
decisions.gist: Should Jet write its own memory-safe WebP encoder, or wrap Google's libwebp and an AVIF library now?
decisions.lesson: An encoder writes an image format; a decoder reads it. libwebp is Google's permissive-license WebP library. Jet accepts outside libraries only by owner decision through a reviewed bridge. Whichever option wins, the web pipeline's settings and output names stay the same.
decisions.explainer:
Under A, core.image gains a WebP decoder and encoder written in Jet: lossless first (used for PNG sources), then lossy for photos. The web pipeline turns WebP on by default for each source type only once its encoder passes a measured gate. Output size within a stated margin of libwebp at equal quality, and speed inside Jet's performance gate. Until lossy passes, JPEG photos stay JPEG, so nothing gets worse.

AVIF is not built now; it returns as its own owner decision if measured demand appears. Owner directive 19 rules out a Rust encoder such as rav1e, so that decision would weigh a Jet encoder against a C library such as libaom.

Why write it in Jet: the 2023 libwebp heap overflow (CVE-2023-4863) was exploited in the wild through every browser and app that bundled the library. A Jet encoder and decoder cannot have that class of bug, needs no new dependency, and runs the same on every tier and target, including the browser build.

Beginner path: no difference. Expert path: the encoder is ordinary Jet code they can read and tune.
decisions.story: Ben's app accepts profile photos. A crafted WebP file in a C library crashes the server, or worse; he never chose that library, a framework bundled it.
decisions.detail:
Jet facts, checked 2026-10-05. I6 (AGENTS.md): compiler and seam crates use path dependencies only; any new stdlib external dependency needs an owner decision and an approved bridge pattern. D-CORE-IMAGE1=A: core.image is Jet-owned with no ambient filesystem or process image library. D-CORE-ARCHIVE-BOUND1: one shared Core inflater for image work. No core.image module exists yet.

Revision by OptionQuality1, 2026-10-07. Owner directive 19 (2026-10-06) removes Rust from the toolchain: host access goes through Jet's own foreign-function surface inside vetted #Unsafe Core internals. The posted B linked libwebp through a Rust bridge crate, and C named rav1e, a Rust AV1 encoder. B and C now bind the C libraries through Jet's own foreign-function surface, and C uses libaom, the C reference AV1 encoder. Their new shared loss is a C compiler or prebuilt per-platform libraries in the toolchain. Options, letters and the recommendation are otherwise unchanged.

Licences and sizes [approximate line counts]: libwebp BSD-3-Clause (Google; encoder sources on the order of 20k lines of C with SIMD paths). Libavif BSD-2-Clause. Libaom BSD-2-Clause plus the AOM patent licence. rav1e BSD-2-Clause (Rust AV1 encoder, on the order of 100k lines; excluded by directive 19). Libvips LGPL-2.1+ (sharp, used by Next.js, Astro and Nuxt, bundles it). image-webp MIT/Apache-2.0 (pure Rust decoder plus lossless encoder; no lossy encoder; cited as precedent only).

Security: CVE-2023-4863 (heap buffer overflow in libwebp's lossless decoder, exploited in the wild, patched across Chrome, Firefox, Electron apps and many Linux packages, September 2023). Google's security blog reports most high-severity browser bugs are memory-safety bugs and documents moves to memory-safe parsers.

Performance gate (AGENTS.md): Jet must beat matched peers per cell; image encoding inside the build is part of the build-time cell for the web workload. The gate in A makes default-on wait for a passing measurement rather than shipping a slower or larger encoder.

Compression evidence for staging: Google's lossless study puts lossless WebP 26% below PNG, so the lossless stage alone delivers savings on PNG-heavy sites.
