decisions.title: Should every :: value be computed while compiling when it can be, with comptime or prep to require it?
decisions.situation: Jet can run ordinary code while it compiles your program, so the finished program starts with answers already worked out. Today that only happens inside a block marked prep, and even a file constant like CELLS :: area(12, 5) is refused without it. You asked that every fixed value written with :: be computed while compiling whenever it can be, with a keyword only to require it. The ballot says exactly when :: falls back to run time, sets no size limit on early values, and asks you to pick comptime or prep as that keyword.
decisions.gist: Should :: always try to compute a value while compiling, with comptime or prep as the word that requires it?
decisions.lesson: Compile time is when Jet turns your source into a program. Run time is when that program runs, starting at fn run(). A :: binding is a name that is never given a new value. Trying means Jet computes the value while compiling whenever it can. If it cannot, Jet quietly computes it when the line runs. Requiring means it must happen while compiling, or the build stops with an error. Both options share the trying rule and differ only in the keyword.
decisions.explainer:
Your question: yes. Every :: value is computed while compiling whenever it can be, at every optimization level, meaning in debug and release builds alike. The running program does less work. The keyword, comptime under A or prep under B, is only for when early computation must happen.

Today Jet already does this quietly for some simple values inside functions, such as numbers, text and lists of them, with hidden limits and no way to see what happened. This change makes it a promise for every value that can be computed, removes those limits, and shows the outcome.

When :: falls back to run time. Four everyday reasons send a value to run time. First, it uses something that exists only while the program runs, such as a function parameter, what the user types, or the program's arguments.

Second, it has an outside effect, such as printing, reading the clock, a file or the network, or making a random number. Running those while compiling would change what the program does. Building a list or a string is not an outside effect, so it never blocks a try.

Third, the value cannot be stored in the program file. That covers open files, connections, threads, memory addresses and calls into C code. It also covers shared cells and Atomic values, because each run of the line must make a fresh one. Generators and reactive values fall back too, because they change as the program runs.

Fourth, it stops before finishing. It hits an error such as an index out of range, or it uses up the step budget. It may also hit one of the size guards described below, or use code the compile-time engine cannot run yet. If the line would leave the function through ? or ??, it also runs as written.

Deliberate exceptions, which you may strike. A few values could run early but are kept at run time on purpose. Code that asks $phase which stage is running would get a different answer. #Runtime(.NoEager) opts a function out. Memoized functions keep their cache statistics honest. keep() and .measure benchmark blocks stay real work. In development builds, debug() traces print when the line runs.

There is no size cap. A large table computed early is stored in the program file. Hover shows its size, and each build prints one total line, such as early values: 3.2 MB in 4 bindings. The guards that already protect the compiler still apply: at most 1,000,000 list items or text characters, and calls nested at most 1,024 deep.

Inside a function, a fallback is never a warning or an error. The line runs when it is reached, exactly as written, so an error inside it happens only if that line actually runs. To see what happened, hover over the name.

Hover shows either "computed while compiling: 60" or the reason it runs later, such as "runs when reached: uses parameter width". It also shows the steps used and the time taken. The command jet inspect expand --facts=comptime lists every :: binding in a file the same way; under B the lens is named prep.

Checking stays fast. jet check and the editor first sort each line into tries and fallbacks without running anything. They then run tries in the background, and hover says "pending" until the result arrives. Effect checks, including bans such as -[!Mem.Alloc]>, always read the code as written, so a try never changes whether a program passes them.

The step budget. A step is one evaluated expression or statement, counted the same on every machine. It exists because no compiler can tell in advance whether a calculation ever finishes. We recommend one budget for both :: and the keyword: 10,000,000 steps per binding, today's compile-time default.

If a :: value uses up the budget, Jet stops trying and computes it at run time, and hover says "ran out of steps". Write #StepLimit(n) on the line above to give it more; that marker was approved earlier but is not built yet. Or write the keyword to make running out an error.

A smaller budget for :: alone would quietly push the slowest work, which gains most from early computation, back to run time.

A library's tries cost you once. Their results and fallbacks are cached per library version, and a library cannot raise its own budget without your project's permission. In a generic function, each copy made for a different type is tried separately.

The keyword turns trying into a requirement. comptime { … } must succeed, or the build stops with an error. So must a use that needs the value while compiling, such as the 4 in the fixed-size list type [Int#4].

Some built-in helpers exist only while compiling. embed_file copies a file into the program, find lists files matching a pattern, and fetch downloads a file whose hash is pinned. #Impure code may also read things like environment variables, if the build allows it. These always need the keyword.

So motd :: embed_file("motd.txt") is an error even inside a function: there is no run-time version to fall back to. The fix is motd :: comptime { embed_file("motd.txt") }. Your own function named find or fetch is not the built-in, and is tried like any other.

One simple promise follows. When :: computes a value early, adding the keyword changes nothing. When :: falls back, the keyword either does the extra thing it is allowed to, such as reading a file, or stops with an error naming the same reason. One exception: code that reads $phase gets the compile-time answer under the keyword, so its value changes.

At file scope there is no line that runs later, because Jet runs no hidden code before fn run(). So a file constant must be computable while compiling, or the build stops with an error naming the reason. There, debug() prints while compiling, $phase reads the compile phase, and #Runtime(.NoEager) is an error. Zig and Odin draw the same line at file scope.

CELLS :: area(12, 5) just works. Mutable and #Persist globals, which are storage the program changes, keep today's literal-only rule.

A compile-time branch picks its arm while compiling. In comptime if $build.os == { … }, $build.os is the system the program is built for, and only the matching arm is kept. Its print still runs when run() reaches it.

Debugging and coverage. A call computed early runs while compiling, so a breakpoint inside it does not stop the running program. Coverage reports count lines run while compiling as covered.

How other languages draw the line. Each one below computes a value early when you require it, and stops with an error if it cannot. They differ in what happens when you write no word.

```text
             no word, file level      no word, in a function       word that requires it     budget
Zig const    early, or an error       literal math early;          comptime (expression,     1,000 backward branches;
                                      calls run at run time        block, parameter)         @setEvalBranchQuota
Odin ::      early, or an error;      same as file level;          none: :: already          none: no code runs
             constant math only       a procedure call is an error requires it
Jai ::       constant only            constant only                #run, any code,           none documented
                                                                   even file access
Jet :: (A)   early, or an error       tried early; quiet fallback  comptime { … }            10,000,000 steps
```

Odin's :: always means compile time, but Odin cannot run procedures while compiling, so CELLS :: area(12, 5) is an error. In Zig a file-level const is always computed early. Inside a function, though, a call runs at run time unless written comptime.

In Jai, :: needs a constant, and #run runs any code while compiling, even file and network access. Jet under A keeps Zig's file rule and keyword and Odin's :: spelling. It goes further inside functions: every call is tried, and a failed try is quiet.

Beginner path: write :: and never think about it; hover when curious. Expert path: write the keyword when early computation is a promise, #StepLimit(n) for long work once it is built, and #Runtime(.NoEager) to keep a function's values at run time.
decisions.story: Sam writes CELLS :: area(12, 5) at the top of a file, and Jet refuses it until he wraps it in prep. Inside a function the same kind of line is accepted, but he cannot tell whether Jet computed it early, or why not. He wants Jet to do the fast thing on its own and explain only when he asks.
decisions.detail:
Owner question, recorded 2026-10-11 13:34 UTC, verbatim: "Anything that can run at comptime when using :: should be. Comptime keyword is the explicit requirement but :: should always attempt to be done at comptime for performance reasons. Update to clarify accordingly". The earlier question, recorded 2026-10-11 00:16 UTC, asked for :: to be a request rather than a requirement, and for the comptime and prep trade-offs.

Owner question q5t7yzpf, as relayed by Main: "How does zig and odin and any info we can get on jai handle this? In odin I think :: always means comptime, but what about zig? Where do they draw the line, what is required vs fail error etc?" The research paragraphs below and the explainer's table answer it.

What this revision changes. The rule is now phrased as always try, with a closed list of fallback reasons and a separate list of deliberate exceptions the owner may strike. The separate 100,000-step request budget, the 64 KiB result cap, and today's hidden fold limits are deleted. Tries and requirements share one budget and one set of guards.

Deliberate exceptions. These values could run early, but the ballot keeps them at run time: $phase reads, #Runtime(.NoEager), memoized callees, keep() and .measure regions, and debug() in development builds. Each has a reason below. Striking one changes only that line of the rule.

What this revision corrects. The earlier revision said today's automatic folding lives in the backend optimizer and depends on optimization level. It does not: a pure-fold pass runs for every execution tier, described below. Its real problems are that it is hidden and narrowly limited.

Today at file scope, from the Rust-host jet built from 79f81529e on 2026-10-10: SECONDS :: 60 * 60 and LIMIT :: fib(10) are both E0622, a module binding's value must be a literal. Both compilers still carry that rule on 790e861db: crates/jet-sema/src/Sema/Registration/Items.rs:1597 and Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Registration/Checked.jet:3002. The fix text offers NAME :: prep { value }.

No jet binary could be run for this revision, because the jet on PATH reports no debug build. Syntax claims are grounded in crates/jet-foundation/src/Syntax.rs:31, Docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md lines 31-35, and Examples/features/comptime/fact_plane.jet for the branch form.

Today's hidden try. Both compilers already fold some function-local :: values while compiling, for every execution tier. A pure-fold pass runs on the assembled program before the optimizer. It lives in Compiler/JetDriver/Source/Driver/PureFold.jet, called from Pipeline.jet:3183, and in crates/jet-codegen/src/Codegen/MIREval/PureFold.rs. Nothing shows its result, and jet check never sees it.

Its limits are implementation choices. Results must be Int within 64 bits, sized integers, floats, Bool, Char, String, or lists of those. A result weighing over 262,144 units, an input needing more than 256 instructions to rebuild, or a chain deeper than 8 rounds stays a run-time call.

It also skips fallible, memoized, generic, capturing, generator, reactive and foreign callees, even when the call would succeed. The Rust source says folding is an optimization, not a way to force a large value into every tier. Under this ballot the size, type, slice and round limits go, and fallible, generic and capturing callees are tried. Memoized, generator, reactive and foreign callees still fall back, for the reasons below.

The retired E0374 row says Jet folds ordinary foldable expressions automatically, the D-VERDICT-1308-1 beginner default. The trying rule turns that sentence into a precise promise. Its fallback reasons move into the checker, so hover can show them and jet check, jet run and jet build agree.

Known inputs, at the evaluation site. Literals, other early-computed values, $build and $package facts, type facts, and compile-time parameters are known. A called function's parameters are known when the call passes known arguments. A run-time parameter, a := variable, an ordinary loop value, and any :: value computed from one are not known.

Effects. Jet records memory events such as Mem.Alloc and Mem.Rc in effect rows (Docs/spec/spec.md:1394-1400). A try needs no ambient effect: no IO, FS, Net, Time, Rand, Env, Exec, DB, Log, GPU, FFI, Browser or Secret, found by the one call-graph walk behind E3401. Memory events do not block a try.

Phase. Any reachable read of $phase falls back, because D-PREP-SURFACE2=A makes $phase report the evaluation site. #Nondeterministic and #Impure code never qualifies for a try. Calls into foreign code fall back, because the target's library may not exist on the build machine.

Identity and change over time. A shared T{…} cell, an Atomic<T>, or anything holding one has identity: two runs of the line must make two cells, and .same() can tell (Examples/features/memory/shared_same.jet). Such a result is not storable. Generators and reactive values are defined by run-time pulls or signals, so they fall back too.

Control flow in an initializer. Only the value is tried. If an initializer such as n :: parse_int("12") ?? return or x :: f()? would take the ?? or ? path, the line falls back and runs as written.

Memoized callees. name.cache() returns run-time MemoStats (D-MEMO1). A call computed early would never reach the cache, so the hit and miss counts the program reads would change. A memoized callee therefore falls back. The owner may strike this and accept that early calls are not counted.

Benchmarks. keep<T>(value) in Core/prelude/prelude.jet:15 is a pure identity, so a try would fold r :: keep(fib(30)) and the benchmark would measure a constant. Under this ballot keep() is a try barrier, and no :: inside a #Test .measure region is tried. The D-CLAIM-BENCH1 trap list gains this rule.

Runtime barriers. D-PREP-SURFACE2=A ratified #Runtime(.NoEager) and #Runtime(.Only) on functions, methods and blocks. NoEager stops tries but allows an explicit requirement; Only rejects both. Neither is in the Prelude marker registry on 790e861db. This ballot puts both in scope as new work, because the size mitigation relies on NoEager.

Determinism of checks. Effect rows, denials such as -[!Mem.Alloc]> or !Mem.Alloc(above: N) (E0921), and E3401 are checked on the source as written, as if every :: ran at run time. A successful try never makes a program pass a check it would otherwise fail.

Why no size cap. Nothing technical limits the size of plain data stored in a program file. Size caps only guard against a bigger file, and the owner asked for speed first. The cost is visible instead: hover, the comptime lens and a one-line build summary show stored size, and #Runtime(.NoEager) keeps a large table at run time.

What is a hard limit. Values tied to a running process or carrying identity cannot be stored. Lists longer than 1,000,000 items and calls deeper than 1,024 hit the existing evaluator guards in Compiler/JetEval/Source/EvalValues.jet:533. This ballot counts a String or byte buffer against the same 1,000,000 guard by length. [INFERENCE: grep only] The Rust comptime interpreter has no matching depth or collection guard; it must gain them.

Why a step budget at all. Whether a calculation finishes cannot be decided in advance; this is the halting problem. So every compile-time engine needs a stopping point. A step is one evaluated expression or statement in the source-level count, never wall time, so every machine stops at the same place.

One engine is a prerequisite. On 790e861db Jet still has an AST comptime interpreter, the MIR evaluator behind the pure fold, and a Cranelift JIT. The AST interpreter counts one step per node (Interpreter.rs:322-354); MIREval counts one per MIR loop step (MIREval.rs:4838-4842). Until D-EXEC1 lands, tries and requirements must run in the same engine with the same step unit, or the shared-budget promise does not hold.

Which default. Today's default is FUEL_BUDGET = 10,000,000 in crates/jet-comptime/src/Comptime/Interpreter.rs:17 and fuel: 10000000 in the Jet evaluator, which the pure-fold pass already uses. Clang's -fconstexpr-steps defaults to 1,048,576, and GCC's -fconstexpr-ops-limit to 33,554,432.

#StepLimit is ratified but unbuilt. D-PREP-FUEL1=A kept the 10,000,000 default and ratified #StepLimit(n) on prep bindings. No tracked file on 790e861db mentions StepLimit, so the marker, its E0952 fix text and the package ceiling are new work under this ballot, which also extends the marker to plain :: bindings.

Which default, continued. Zig's @setEvalBranchQuota starts at 1,000 backward branches and is often raised. Rust 1.72 removed its fixed const-evaluation cap in favor of a lint for long-running evaluation. 10,000,000 sits between the C++ compilers. A lower budget for tries alone would quietly move the slowest, most valuable work to run time.

What happens when the budget runs out. A try stops at the limit, records ran out of steps after 10,000,000, and the line runs when reached. A requirement stops with E0952; once #StepLimit is built, its fix names the marker and the steps reached. A file-scope constant has no run-time slot, so it also gets E0952.

Compile-time cost in the checker and editor. jet check and the language server first classify every :: without evaluating, which is cheap. They then evaluate tries in the background and cache the outcome; hover shows pending until it arrives. jet build waits for every try. An edit re-runs only tries whose callees changed.

Compile-time cost across packages. Each try costs at most its budget. Results and fallbacks are cached per package version, target and compiler, so a library's tries cost each machine once. D-PREP-FUEL1=A's grant rule covers tries too: a dependency cannot raise a try above the default without the root package's grant. The root may also set a lower try budget for dependencies.

Generic functions. A :: inside a generic function is tried once per instantiation, each with its own budget and cache entry, because the inputs differ per type. No census of how many local bindings read run-time inputs was run, so this ballot makes no claim about the share that fails the known-input test.

Determinism. The outcome depends only on source, target facts, compiler version and limits, never on optimization level, build order or cache state. A warm cache hit charges the same steps as a cold run. Compile-time code runs through O0 under D-EXEC1, and S26's differential check requires bit-for-bit agreement with the running program.

Stops and engine gaps. If evaluation stops, such as an out-of-range index, the try falls back and the line fails at run time exactly as written. There is no warning, so an unreached line never breaks a build. If the engine cannot handle a construct, the reason is compiler gap. Under a requirement, that gap is a compiler defect, today E0956.

The debug() case. D-DBG1=A makes debug(value) effect-free, and it prints while compiling inside compile-time code. Under always try, a helper with a debug() call would print during the build, not when the line runs. Falling back keeps the trace where the reader expects it. E3405 already rejects debug() in shipped builds, so shipped output never differs.

Debuggers and coverage. A call computed early runs while compiling, so an O0 breakpoint inside it does not fire in the running program. jet test --coverage counts lines run while compiling as covered, so a helper used only by early bindings is not reported as dead.

Requirements keep their power. The fallback list applies only to tries. comptime { … } keeps today's tiers: Tier 1 embed_file, embed_bytes, find and pinned fetch recorded in .jet/lock, and Tier 2 ambient reads under #Impure with --gate impure=allow. Errors stay E0952 steps, E0953 authored stop, E0955 missing input, and E3410 or E3411 ungated effects.

Tier 1 built-ins never fall back. D-PRELUDE-LAW1=A lists embed_file, embed_bytes, find and fetch as comptime-gated ambient names, so the built-ins have no run-time version. A plain :: that calls the built-in is an error in any scope, with the fix motd :: comptime { embed_file(path) }. [INFERENCE: today's diagnostic code for this was not probed.]

Shadowing. D-PRELUDE-LAW1=A also says user shadowing wins. A user's own find or fetch, such as idx :: find(xs, 3), is not the built-in and is tried like any other call.

File scope. An immutable NAME :: value must be computable while compiling, and failure is an error naming the reason. Jet runs no hidden code before fn run(), so a lazy run-time fallback would need startup code and an initialization order; C++ calls that the static initialization order problem. Mutable and #Persist globals keep E0622.

File scope, exceptions. There is no run-time slot, so the deliberate exceptions resolve differently. debug() prints while compiling, $phase reads the compile phase, and #Runtime(.NoEager) on a file constant is an error. A memoized callee runs while compiling and is not counted in run-time cache statistics.

File scope, continued. Initializers may read other module constants, evaluated in dependency order. A cycle gets one new registered diagnostic naming the loop. This amends the module-value rule recorded in the E0622 registry row as D-MODULE-VALUE1, which has no Tower record.

Research: Zig, checked with zig 0.15.2 on 2026-10-11 and the official 0.14.0 language reference. The reference says a container-level initializer is implicitly comptime, and a local const is comptime-known only when its initializer is. Probe: const cells = area(12, 5) at file level compiles and prints 60.

Zig, continued. A file-level const that reads the clock fails with unable to evaluate comptime expression. A file-level loop of 5,000 iterations fails with evaluation exceeded 1000 backwards branches, and the note suggests @setEvalBranchQuota. So Zig's file level is early or an error, never a quiet fallback, which matches Jet's file rule.

Zig, continued. Inside a function, const local = area(12, 5) is a run-time call: using it as an array length fails with unable to resolve comptime value. const n = 5 * 12 is comptime-known. comptime area(12, 5) is required early. An out-of-range index inside an ordinary call panics only when the line runs. Release builds may still fold calls through LLVM, invisibly.

Zig, continued. Inside a comptime expression, the reference says every call is interpreted while compiling, and code with run-time side effects is a compile error; calling an extern function is its example. @embedFile works without comptime because it is a built-in that always runs while compiling.

Research: Odin, checked with odin dev-2026-05 on 2026-10-11 and the official overview and FAQ. The FAQ says :: declares a compile-time-known constant, and := a run-time variable. :: means the same inside a procedure. SECONDS :: 60 * 60, MOTD :: #load(path, string), ODIN_OS_STRING and when ODIN_OS == .Linux all compile and run.

Odin, continued. CELLS :: area(12, 5) fails with 'area(12, 5)' is not a compile-time known constant, both at file level and inside a procedure. Odin runs no user procedures while compiling, so it has no budget and no fallback. Compile-time file access goes only through directives such as #load, #load_directory and #exists.

Research: Jai. There is no public compiler or official reference, so these facts come from the Jai-Community wiki pages Getting-Started and Metaprogramming, fetched 2026-10-11. :: declares a constant. #run runs any code while compiling in a bytecode interpreter, including file and network access, as in PI :: #run compute_pi().

Jai, continued. The wiki says circular #run dependencies are a compile error, and that returning structs holding pointers is complicated. No step budget is documented. [INFERENCE: no public compiler to probe] A plain X :: compute_pi() without #run is assumed to be an error, because :: needs a constant value.

Research: the explicit requirement word. A C++ constexpr variable is always computed early; a constexpr function called elsewhere is the optimizer's choice. C++20 added consteval and constinit because people could not rely on early evaluation. D evaluates early only where a constant is required.

Research: what Jet does differently. Zig, Odin, Jai, C++ and D all need a word or a constant context before a call runs early, and all make a failed requirement an error. None tries every call inside a function at every optimization level, with a visible reason. Jet takes Zig's file rule and word, Odin's :: spelling, and adds a deterministic, cached, budgeted try.

Census on 790e861db, tracked .jet files in Examples, Core, Compiler and Jetpack: 2,316 files, 517,778 lines. Core has no prep. 1,846 lines contain prep; 63 are comments. 1,675 are NAME :: prep { … } heads: 1,566 one line, 109 opening multi-line tables, and 14 of all heads inside functions. FreshAdversaryD's recount found about 1,672 heads.

Census, continued. Of those heads, 30 wrap embed_file, find or fetch and keep the word. None read $phase. 43 read compiler facts such as $build or Type.$range and unwrap. 58 one-line heads wrap calls, which the checker decides one by one. The rest wrap literal data and always unwrap.

Census, continued. 54 lines are other compile-time forms that always keep the word: prep if 31, prep loop 12, prep fn 6, <prep N> 3, and prep { } blocks 2. About 54 more mention prep in strings, diagnostics or an ordinary variable named prep. tests/ adds 138 prep lines.

Census, result. Between about 84 and 250 lines keep the word, so roughly 1,425 to 1,590 wrappers disappear. That is one keyword per 2,000 to 6,000 lines. The earlier count of 3,056 lines on 2f2a18628 covered a larger tracked tree. Counts came from git grep patterns over git ls-files output.

Migration. jet fix unwraps a wrapper only when the checker proves the plain constant is computed early with the same value, phase, effects and failure. Every other wrapper stays and is renamed under A. Local wrappers follow the same rule.

Side by side: meaning. comptime says when the code runs. prep says something gets ready, not when. D-PREP-SURFACE2=A chose prep when one preparation step had to mean the same in the interpreter, the Cranelift JIT and AOT builds. D-EXEC1 decided to merge those engines into one; once merged, preparation simply means compile time.

Side by side: length and messages. comptime has eight letters and prep four, a small difference at one use per several thousand lines. Diagnostics already say comptime: E0952 Comptime budget exhausted, E0955 Comptime file input missing, E3410 a comptime effect. Under B they can say this prep block runs at compile time instead.

Side by side: names and precedent. prep is a contextual word today, so a value named prep still works, as in Examples/features/comptime/prep_block.jet. comptime is already reserved by the lexer (KwComptime, crates/jet-lexer/src/Lexer/mod.rs:76) for the retired-keyword error. So neither option blocks a new name. Zig uses comptime for this meaning; no surveyed language uses prep.

Side by side: migration and history. A renames the remaining few hundred lines with jet fix; B renames none. The word has moved from comptime to #Known, $, @ and prep since July. comptime was retired for implicit folding plus a separate mark; the trying rule makes that folding reliable, so comptime returns only as the requirement word.

Why not a marker. On 2026-07-28 the owner preferred a marker, #Known, as the more coherent system. A marker cannot spell the block forms comptime if, comptime loop, comptime fn and compile-time parameters, so the requirement needs a keyword under either option.

The forms under A. comptime { … }, name :: comptime { … }, comptime if, comptime loop and comptime fn literal hooks are built today as prep forms. Ratified but unbuilt: type-making functions, comptime fn Pair(T: Type) -> Type, and compile-time parameters, fn larger(comptime T: Comparable, a: T, b: T).

Shared model with D-META-HASH1. :: tries compile time, the keyword requires it, and # markers attach to a declaration. $ reads compiler facts today, as in $build.os; D-META-HASH1 may respell those reads as ##, which would change only that spelling in this ballot's examples.

options.name: Always try on ::, comptime to require
options.detail: Every :: value is computed while compiling whenever it can be. It falls back to run time for run-time inputs, outside effects, values that cannot be stored, or a stop, including running out of steps. A short list of deliberate exceptions, which you may strike, also stays at run time. The fallback is quiet; hover and jet inspect show the reason. File constants must be computable early and need no word. comptime marks code that must run early, keeps today's full compile-time power, and shares the same budget.
options.technical:
Front end: sema classifies every immutable :: initializer before evaluation, using checked facts. It falls back without evaluating when an input is run-time after argument substitution. It also falls back when the call graph reaches an ambient effect: IO, FS, Net, Time, Rand, Env, Exec, DB, Log, GPU, FFI, Browser or Secret. Mem.Alloc and Mem.Rc events do not block a try.

It also falls back when a $phase read is reachable, inside a #Runtime(.NoEager) or .Only barrier, or when it reaches keep() or sits in a .measure region. The same goes for memoized, generator, reactive or foreign callees, a non-storable result type, and a reachable debug() call in a development compile.

Everything else runs in the compile-time engine. A stop, an exhausted budget, a guard hit or an engine gap also falls back, as does a value whose initializer would take a ? or ?? exit. Each binding records its outcome, step cost, time, stored size and reason. Hover and a new comptime lens, jet inspect expand --facts=comptime, read that one record.

Engine prerequisite: until D-EXEC1 merges the AST comptime interpreter and MIREval, tries and requirements must run in one engine with one step unit. Otherwise the shared budget and the keyword promise do not hold.

Checker and editor: classify synchronously, evaluate tries in the background with a pending hover, re-run only tries whose callees changed, and share the build cache. jet build waits for all tries.

Tier 1 built-ins stay comptime-gated under D-PRELUDE-LAW1=A. A plain :: that calls the built-in embed_file, embed_bytes, find or fetch is an error in every scope, never a fallback. The fix wraps it in the keyword. A user-defined function with one of those names shadows the built-in and is tried normally.

This replaces the private eligibility test of the pure-fold pass in Compiler/JetDriver/Source/Driver/PureFold.jet and crates/jet-codegen/src/Codegen/MIREval/PureFold.rs. Its result-type list, 262,144-unit output budget, 256-instruction slice and 8-round chain limit are deleted, and fallible, generic and capturing callees are tried. Lowering emits whatever constant the checker recorded.

Storable means no tie to a running process and no identity. Handles, resources, borrowed views, live links, raw addresses, shared cells, Atomic<T> and anything holding them are not storable. Functions are storable because they name code in the program; closures are storable when everything they capture is.

Checks on the source as written: effect rows, denials such as -[!Mem.Alloc]> and E0921, and E3401 ignore try outcomes, as if every :: ran at run time.

Budget: one per-binding budget for tries and requirements, D-PREP-FUEL1=A's 10,000,000 steps, with call depth 1,024 and collection length 1,000,000. A String or byte buffer counts by length. The Rust host must enforce the same guards. The previous revision's 100,000-step request budget and 64 KiB result cap are deleted.

Dependencies and generics: outcomes are cached per package version, target and compiler. D-PREP-FUEL1=A's grant rule covers tries, and the root package may set a lower try budget for dependencies. A try inside a generic function runs per instantiation. Each build prints one line with the total bytes of early values.

New work, ratified but unbuilt on 790e861db: #StepLimit(n) from D-PREP-FUEL1=A, with its E0952 fix text and package ceiling, extended to plain :: bindings. #Runtime(.NoEager) and #Runtime(.Only) from D-PREP-SURFACE2=A on functions, methods and blocks.

Cache: the key covers source, compiler version, target facts and every limit. Fallback outcomes are cached with their step cost too, so a warm build neither re-runs a failed try nor changes its outcome. The outcome never depends on optimization level, build order or cache state.

File scope: lift E0622 for immutable initializers that can be computed early; a failure reports the fallback reason as an error, and an exhausted budget is E0952. debug() prints while compiling, $phase reads the compile phase, and #Runtime(.NoEager) on a file constant is an error. Add one registered cycle diagnostic. Mutable and #Persist globals keep E0622.

Benchmarks and tooling: keep() is a try barrier, and the D-CLAIM-BENCH1 trap list gains early computation. jet test --coverage counts lines run while compiling as covered.

Spelling: KW_PREP becomes comptime in Syntax, both parsers, the formatter, highlighting and diagnostics. Phase.Preparation becomes Phase.Comptime, and the stage value Prepared moves with it. The stale E0374 row is deleted, and prep gets a retirement row whose safe fix writes comptime.

jet fix unwraps only wrappers the checker proves equal, then renames the rest. This amends D-PREP-SURFACE2=A, D-PREP-BRANCH1=A, D-PREP-FN1=A, D-CONSTGEN2=A, D-GENERIC-TYPEFN1=A and D-PREP-FUEL1=A in spelling. It extends D-PREP-FUEL1=A's #StepLimit to plain :: bindings and amends the module-value rule.

options.name: Always try on ::, prep to require
options.detail: The same always-try rule, fallback list, exceptions, budget, hover, file-scope change and requirement power. The requirement word stays prep. jet fix removes a NAME :: prep { … } wrapper only when the checker proves the plain line gives the same value, and nothing is renamed. The inspect lens is jet inspect expand --facts=prep. Messages explain prep as code that runs at compile time, because the word itself does not say so.
options.technical: The same front-end, budget, cache and file-scope work as A. No keyword rename; Phase.Preparation and the stage value Prepared stay. Diagnostics may keep the word comptime in explanations or say this prep block runs at compile time.

comparisons.note: A file-level const is computed early or the build fails. Inside a function only literal math is early, and a call needs comptime. Checked with zig 0.15.2.
comparisons.code:
const cells = area(12, 5);           // file level: early, or a compile error
const started = now();               // error: unable to evaluate comptime expression
pub fn main() void {
    const local = area(12, 5);       // run-time call
    var buf: [local]u8 = undefined;  // error: unable to resolve comptime value
    const sure = comptime area(12, 5);  // early, or a compile error
}

comparisons.note: The :: form always means compile time, in a file or a procedure. Only constant math and built-ins such as #load are allowed, and Odin never runs procedures early. Checked with odin dev-2026-05.
comparisons.code:
SECONDS :: 60 * 60                  // constant math: fine
MOTD :: #load("motd.txt", string)   // built-in file read while compiling
CELLS :: area(12, 5)                // error: 'area(12, 5)' is not a compile-time known constant
main :: proc() {
    cells := area(12, 5)            // := is a run-time variable
    when ODIN_OS == .Linux { fmt.println("linux") }  // compile-time branch
}

comparisons.note: No public compiler or official reference; this comes from the community wiki. The :: form declares a constant, and #run runs any code while compiling, even file and network access, with no documented budget.
A constexpr variable must be computed early; a constexpr call elsewhere is the optimizer's choice. C++20 added consteval and constinit so early evaluation could be required.
comparisons.code:
constexpr int cells = area(12, 5);   // required: computed while compiling
int later = area(12, 5);             // optimizer may or may not fold it
consteval int table_size() { return 64; }  // every call must run early

recommendation.why: Always trying puts early computation into the plain :: you already write, for every value that can be computed early, at every optimization level. The keyword then becomes rare and means one thing: this must run while compiling. A rare word should say what it means, and comptime does.
gains: Every fixed value that can be computed early is, with no word and no warnings.
File constants like area(12, 5) just work, and about 1,500 wrappers disappear.
One shared budget, so leaving out the keyword never costs speed in effect-free code.
The remaining word says when its code runs, and requirements keep their full power.

losses.loss: One more respelling of a mark that has moved several times.
losses.mitigation: jet fix renames the 84 to 250 lines left after unwrapping. Jet is merging its three ways to run code into one, after which prep would only mean while compiling.

losses.loss: comptime is four letters longer than prep.
losses.mitigation: After the change the word appears about once per several thousand lines, where clarity matters more than length.

whyNot.reason: prep was chosen when Jet had three different ways to run code. Jet is merging them into one, so prep will only ever mean while compiling, and comptime says that directly.

recommendation.tradeoff: A last mechanical respelling of a now-rare word, for a word that says when its code runs.

reviewPasses.beginner: Fresh agent: FreshBeginnerD. Skill: rli5. The reader predicted the full example but stumbled on a growing reason list, an unscoped no-error rule, embed_file in a function, a do-nothing surface keyword and unbuilt #StepLimit. The repair counts the reasons honestly, scopes the rule to functions, shows embed_file needing the word everywhere, labels #StepLimit unbuilt, and applies the wording fixes.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: claude. Adversarial model family: claude. Fresh agent: FreshAdversaryD. The review confirmed every code citation and the census, and found gaps in effect rows, shared values, cost, checks, memo, benchmarks, $phase, engines, shadowing, naming and #Runtime. The repair lists blocking effects, keeps identity, memo, keep() and .measure at run time, bounds checker and dependency cost, checks effects on source, and scopes new work.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Reworked by BallotComptime on 2026-10-11 for owner questions q3ma97v4 and q5t7yzpf, on top of the BallotRework revision of 2026-10-10. FreshBeginnerD and FreshAdversaryD reviewed this revision; their required edits are applied. No Tower write was made by BallotComptime.

Owner acceptance: every immutable :: value that can be computed while compiling is, at every optimization level. It falls back for run-time inputs, ambient effects, non-storable or identity-bearing values, stops, exhausted budget, guards and engine gaps. Deliberate exceptions, which the owner may strike: $phase reads, #Runtime barriers, memoized callees, keep() and .measure regions, and development debug() calls.

Owner acceptance, continued: inside a function the fallback has no diagnostic, and hover shows the reason, steps and time. Tries and requirements share one 10,000,000-step budget and the same guards. There is no result size cap, and each build prints the total bytes of early values. A plain :: calling a built-in embed_file, embed_bytes, find or fetch is an error in every scope.

Prerequisite: tries and requirements run in one engine with one step unit; until D-EXEC1 lands, that means choosing one of the AST interpreter or MIREval.

New work: #StepLimit(n) from D-PREP-FUEL1=A on prep and plain :: bindings, its E0952 fix text and package ceiling. #Runtime(.NoEager) and #Runtime(.Only) from D-PREP-SURFACE2=A on functions, methods and blocks. Matching depth and collection guards in the Rust comptime interpreter.

Acceptance matrix, part 1: a pure call with literal arguments, the same call with a run-time parameter, and a :: value derived from a run-time value. Add a $phase read in a helper, #Runtime(.NoEager) with a try and with a requirement, #Runtime(.Only) with a requirement, and a helper containing debug().

Acceptance matrix, part 2: a try that exhausts 10,000,000 steps falls back, the same line with #StepLimit is computed early, and the same body under the keyword fails with E0952. A non-storable handle falls back. An out-of-range stop, an engine gap and a ?? return exit fall back. A plain built-in embed_file in a function is an error; a user-defined find is tried.

Acceptance matrix, part 3: a struct, a map, an enum and a big Int result, a list weighing over 262,144 units, and a chain of nine dependent :: values are computed early. Successful calls to fallible, generic and capturing helpers are computed early. Memoized, generator and reactive callees fall back.

Acceptance matrix, part 4: two shared bindings in a function called twice stay distinct, and .same() returns false. An interpolated string is tried despite Mem.Alloc. A -[!Mem.Alloc]> function fails the same with and without a successful try. r :: keep(fib(30)) and :: inside .measure are not tried, and name.cache() counts match run time.

Acceptance matrix, part 5: cold, warm and reordered builds near the budget give the same outcome and hover text. O0, O1 and O2 give the same output and hover reasons. A generic function tries per instantiation. A dependency's tries are cached per version and need a grant to raise their budget. jet check shows pending, then the result.

Acceptance matrix, part 6: a file-scope cycle gets its diagnostic, and mutable globals keep E0622. File-scope debug() prints while compiling and #Runtime(.NoEager) on a file constant is an error. comptime { embed_file } and #Impure requirements still work with their grants. Coverage counts lines run while compiling.

Migration proof: jet fix unwraps only proven-equal wrappers, keeps effectful and phase-reading ones, and produces identical goldens across the corpus. Add UI snapshots for every new or changed diagnostic and for the hover reasons.

surface.gist: Should :: always try to compute a value while compiling, with comptime or prep as the word that requires it?
surface.lesson: A :: name is never given a new value. Jet tries to compute every one while compiling, so the program does less work. It quietly waits until run time only when it cannot. The keyword requires it: early, or an error.

current.note: Today a computed file constant needs the word.

wild.note: A file-level const is early or an error. Inside a function a call runs at run time unless written comptime.

gains: The word says when code runs.
Matches messages that already say comptime.
losses: Another respelling, a few hundred lines.

options.name: Always try on ::, prep to require
options.gist: The same always-try rule; the word stays prep.
gains: No keyword rename.
Four letters shorter.
losses: The word does not say compile time.

recommendation.why: Always trying makes the word rare. A rare word should say what it means, and comptime says when its code runs.
gains: Fixed values are computed early with no word.
Inside functions, a fallback never breaks a build.
The remaining word explains itself.

losses.loss: One more respelling.
losses.mitigation: jet fix renames the few remaining uses.

losses.loss: Four more letters.
losses.mitigation: The word appears about once per several thousand lines.

recommendation.tradeoff: A last respelling of a rare word, for a word that explains itself.

designAway.loss: Computing early could change what a program does.
attempts: Compute any code without outside effects early; rejected because a $phase read would answer differently, a #Runtime barrier would be ignored, shared cells would merge across calls, and memo statistics and benchmarks would change.
Fall back for run-time inputs, ambient effects, non-storable or identity-bearing values and stops, and list $phase, #Runtime, memo, keep(), .measure and debug() as deliberate exceptions; kept.
Check effect rows and denials on the source as written, never on try outcomes; kept.
designAway.result: Removed: an early value is always the value the line would give at run time, and no check depends on a try.

designAway.loss: Arbitrary limits could send computable values to run time.
attempts: Keep today's hidden fold limits, or give tries a 100,000-step budget and a 64 KiB cap; rejected because the owner asked for every computable value, and none of these limits is technical.
Share the 10,000,000-step budget and the existing guards with comptime, allow any storable result, and drop size, round and slice caps; kept.
designAway.result: Removed: only the halting guard, the existing memory and depth guards, and the storable rule remain.

designAway.loss: Trying every :: value could slow compiling.
attempts: Add a whole-build budget; rejected because which binding ran out first would depend on build order.
Evaluate every try synchronously in jet check and the editor; rejected because a 10,000,000-step try on each edit would stall typing.

Classify first and evaluate tries in the background with a pending hover; cache results and fallbacks per package version; extend the dependency grant rule to tries; try generics per instantiation; kept.
designAway.result: Bounded per binding, paid once per machine for libraries, and never blocking the editor; #StepLimit and #Runtime(.NoEager) adjust it where wanted.

designAway.loss: Dropping the size cap could make program files bigger.
attempts: Keep a size cap; rejected because no technical limit exists and it would move fast lookups to run time.

Show stored size on hover, in the comptime lens and in a one-line build total, count text length against the existing guard, and build #Runtime(.NoEager) as part of this work so a big table can stay at run time; kept.
designAway.result: Retained with mitigation: the size is visible every build, and one marker, built here, opts out.

designAway.loss: A quiet fallback hides why a value was not computed early.
attempts: Warn when a try falls back; rejected because a deny-able warning could fail a build for a line never reached.
Print a note in jet check that can never fail a build; rejected because notes on every unreached line add noise to each check, and the owner asked for none.
Show the reason, steps and time in editor hover and the inspect lens, and let the keyword turn a fallback into an error; kept.
designAway.result: Removed.

designAway.loss: One shared test could take power away from explicit requirements.
attempts: Apply the fallback list to requirements too; rejected because embed_file and approved #Impure reads would stop working.
Keep the fallback list for tries only, and keep today's tiers and grants for requirements; kept.
designAway.result: Removed.

designAway.loss: A debug() trace could print while compiling instead of when the line runs.
attempts: Treat debug() as an effect everywhere; rejected because explicit compile-time code relies on debug() printing while compiling.
Fall back only for tries in development compiles, which are the only compiles that accept debug(); kept.
designAway.result: Removed.

designAway.loss: Respelling churn after several earlier spellings.
attempts: Keep prep; kept as option B, but its reason, several separate engines, is going away.
Shrink the word's use first with the always-try rule, then rename the remaining uses with jet fix; kept.
designAway.result: Retained with mitigation.

decisions.title: Unary minus and modulo for number-like types you define
decisions.situation: Jet lets your own types use +, -, * and / by implementing a matching trait, and comparisons through one compare function. Two everyday arithmetic symbols are missing: a leading minus, as in -velocity, and the wrap-around symbol %, as in an angle past 360 degrees. A game vector or a money type must write v.negate() instead of -v. You are deciding whether Jet adds these two hooks with the same rules as the others, and we recommend adding both.
decisions.gist: Should your own number-like types support a leading minus and the wrap-around symbol %, like built-in numbers?
decisions.lesson: A trait is a named set of methods that a type promises to have. An operator hook is a trait whose method the compiler calls for a symbol: Add for +. Jet has hooks for + - * / and comparisons. A adds Neg for a leading minus and Mod for %. B adds Neg only. C adds neither, so these types use named methods.
decisions.explainer:
Jet's operator rule: only existing symbols can be given meaning, precedence never changes, and arithmetic symbols must mean arithmetic. Each symbol family is one trait.

Today the families are Add, Sub, Mul and Div, plus Equatable for == and != and Comparable for <, <=, >, >= and <=>. Index gives [ ] reads and IndexMut gives [ ] writes.

A leading minus has no hook, so only Int and Float can be negated. The symbol % works on Int only. On Int it is modulo: it wraps around, and its answer takes the sign of the right side, so -7 % 2 is 1. Its partner /% divides and rounds down. A second symbol, %%, is the plain remainder, which keeps the sign of the left side: -7 %% 2 is -1.

A adds two traits in the same style. Neg has one method, neg(self). Mod has mod(self, rhs), and the type of rhs picks the right side, as with Mul. The name Mod matches what % means in Jet; Rust's name Rem would suggest the other one, %%. Mirroring means Jet also accepts 2 * v when only v * 2 is defined. It applies only to + and *, so Mod never mirrors: 360 % angle stays an error. %%, /% and bit operations stay as they are.

A minus written straight before a number, such as -5, stays part of that number under every option. A type that is built from number literals therefore accepts -5 without Neg; Neg is for negating a value.
decisions.story: Kai writes a 2D game. His Vec2 type adds and scales with + and *, but bouncing off a wall needs -velocity. Jet says only Int and Float can be negated, so he writes velocity.negate() in a formula that otherwise reads like math.
decisions.detail:
Owner question 2026-10-05: how far does Jet go compared with C++ operator overloading? Current law: D-OPDEF1=A fixes the symbol set, precedence and arithmetic meaning. D-OPMIX1=D and D-FOUND-OPMIX1=A add typed right sides and the number mirror. D-CMP3WAY1=B adds <=>. D-INDEX-HOOK gives Index and IndexMut. D-SIGIL-ALGEBRA1=B moves bit arithmetic and power to named methods. D-TRAIT-OVERLOAD1=A defines Numeric over Add, Sub, Mul and Comparable. D-MODSEM1=A and D-FLOORDIV1=A make % the floored modulo partnered with /%, and %% the truncated remainder partnered with /.

Exercised on dev-05ea86f65 (probes in $JET_STATE_ROOT/scratch/OwnerFeedback/sem-probes). p10: -v on a type with Sub gives E0109, Only Int and Float values can be negated. p11: % on a user type gives E0109, Int only. p15: <=> and chained comparison on a user Comparable work. Re-checked 2026-10-05 on dev-595e0dca3 with jet check: -velocity on Vec2 gives the same E0109. There, angle % Angle{deg: 360} gives E0109, "% works on Int (a whole number) only, but this has Angle and Angle".

Negative literals, probed 2026-10-05 on dev-595e0dca3. Money implements Literal.Int (D-FOUND-LITERAL1=A), so show(5) builds a Money. show(-5) fails with E0109, "- needs a number, but this is Money". The minus is read as negating a Money, not as part of the literal. A fixes this by folding a minus straight before a number literal into the literal, so from_literal receives -5. A prep from_literal that rejects negatives still refuses it while compiling, and Swift treats negative literals the same way.

Naming. Rust and Kotlin name the % hook rem because their % keeps the sign of the left side. Jet's % is floored, so its hook takes the floored name, as Kotlin's mod() and Python's __mod__ do. %% gets no hook, so a type has one modulo meaning.

Hook registry today (crates/jet-foundation/src/Syntax/effects_surface.rs:243-262): Index, IndexMut, Add, Sub, Mul, Div, Equatable, Comparable, Numeric. Corpus: 33 Add/Sub/Mul/Div impls in Examples; none for negation, because none is possible.

Other languages: Rust has Neg and Rem traits. C++, C#, Swift, Kotlin (unaryMinus, rem) and Python (__neg__, __mod__) all allow both. Unary minus is needed for vectors, complex numbers, money and intervals.

options.name: Add Neg and Mod hooks
options.detail: A type implements Neg to support -x and Mod to support x % y. Both follow the existing hook rules: fixed precedence, typed right side for Mod, number mirroring off for Mod. A minus straight before a number literal stays part of the literal.
options.technical:
Two traits in Core with builtin roles (D-CORE-ROLE1): Neg { fn neg(self) -> Self } and Mod(R) { fn mod(self, rhs: R) -> Self }, same coherence (E0902) as Mul. Mod never mirrors, like - and /. Sema resolves unary - and % on non-numeric operands to the hooks; numeric operands keep the built-in path. Built-in signed numbers implement Neg and whole numbers implement Mod, so a generic bound such as T: Neg can write -x.

Numeric is unchanged, so unsigned types are not forced to negate. A unary minus applied directly to an integer or float literal folds into the literal before Literal.Int or Literal.Float runs, which removes today's E0109 on show(-5). Every tier lowers to the same call.

options.name: Neg only
options.detail: Add the leading-minus hook. % stays whole-number only.
options.technical: Neg and the literal fold as in A; no Mod trait.

options.name: Neither
options.detail: Keep today's set. Your types use named methods for negation and modulo.
options.technical: No change. show(-5) on a literal-built type keeps failing with E0109.

comparisons.note: Neg and Rem are ordinary traits in std::ops; Rust's % keeps the left side's sign.
comparisons.code: impl Rem for Angle { type Output = Angle; fn rem(self, r: Angle) -> Angle { ... } }

comparisons.note: operator fun unaryMinus; % calls rem, and a separate mod() wraps around.
__mod__ is the hook for a floored %, the same meaning as Jet's %.

recommendation.why: A number-like type you define should read like a built-in number. Minus and modulo are the two arithmetic symbols still missing. A adds them under the same rules, so no new kind of rule is learned.
recommendation.tradeoff: Two more traits in the operator list.
gains: Formulas with vectors, angles and money read like math.
Generic code with a Neg bound can write -x.
Your number types become full peers of Int and Float.

losses.loss: Two more traits in the operator list.
losses.mitigation: Each has one method and follows the rules of Add and Mul exactly.

whyNot.reason: B leaves % out for angles, clock times and modular numbers, where it is the natural spelling.
C keeps -v as a named call in formulas that otherwise read like math.

The repair defines each term with -7 examples, removes the contradiction, and gives every option the same values with results and A's refusals.

The review found that the % hook was named Rem although Jet's % is floored modulo and %% is the remainder, and a probe showed show(-5) on a literal-built Money fails with E0109 today. The repair renames the hook Mod, uses a negative angle to show wrap-around, and folds a minus on a number literal into the literal.

Check that -5 passed where a Literal.Int type is expected calls from_literal(-5) with no Neg, and that a from_literal rejecting negatives refuses it while compiling. Run on every tier.

surface.lesson: A trait is a named set of methods a type promises to have. An operator hook is a trait the compiler calls for a symbol, such as Add for +. A adds Neg for -x and Mod for %. B adds Neg only. C adds neither.

options.name: Neither
options.gist: Use named methods for these two.
gains: No new traits.
losses: Formulas mix symbols and method calls.

recommendation.why: Number-like types should read like numbers. Minus and modulo are the two missing symbols, added under the existing rules.
gains: Full arithmetic for your number types.
No new kind of rule.

losses.loss: Two more traits in the list.
losses.mitigation: Each has one method and follows Add's rules.

whyNot.reason: Angles and modular numbers lack their natural %.
Formulas keep -v as a method call.

recommendation.tradeoff: Two one-method traits join the operator list.

designAway.loss: Two more traits in the operator list.
attempts: Derive negation from Sub and a zero value. Rejected: some types have no zero, and the derived code would be slower.
Keep each hook a one-method trait under the existing rules. Kept.

designAway.loss: A hook named after another language's % could teach the wrong sign rule.
attempts: Name it Rem, as Rust does. Rejected: in Jet the remainder is %%, so Rem would point readers at the wrong symbol.
Name it Mod, after what % means in Jet, as Kotlin's mod() and Python's __mod__ do. Kept.

decisions.title: Calling a value of your own type with parentheses
decisions.situation: In C++ a struct can define operator() so that a value is called like a function. Jet already calls functions and lambdas this way, and a returned function can be called directly. A value of your own struct type cannot be called with parentheses; you call one of its methods by name. Today the error for trying it wrongly says nothing with that name exists. You are deciding whether Jet adds a call hook for your own types, and we recommend not adding it and fixing the error instead.
decisions.gist: Should a value of your own struct type be callable with parentheses, like C++ operator()?
decisions.lesson: A struct is a type you define with named fields, such as Scale{factor: 3}. A method is a function attached to it, called with a dot: triple.apply(4). A lambda is a small unnamed function that can be stored and called. A keeps calls for functions and lambdas only; a struct offers named methods, and the error explains that. B adds a Call trait, so triple(4) runs a method on the value triple.
decisions.explainer:
C++ added operator() before it had lambdas, so function objects were the way to carry state into algorithms. Jet has lambdas that capture their surroundings, so a stateful function is written as a lambda or a struct with a named method.

A keeps parentheses for functions and lambdas. Calling a struct value gives a clear error that names the value's type and its methods. A struct that should act as a function can hand out a lambda through a method you write, such as as_fn() in A's example. The lambda keeps the factor, so times3(4) is an ordinary call.

B adds a Call trait. Any value whose type implements it can be called with parentheses. Readers then cannot tell from triple(4) whether triple is a function or a struct running a method.
decisions.story: Mia ports a C++ image filter. Her Blur struct used operator() to apply itself to a pixel. In Jet she writes blur(pixel) and is told nothing named blur exists, which is wrong: blur exists, it just is not a function.
decisions.detail:
Owner question 2026-10-05: C++ operator overloading includes () and the comma; how far does Jet go? Current law: D-OPDEF1=A keeps a fixed symbol set and never allows new or repurposed symbols. D-CALLVALUE2=A lets any expression of function type be called, as in make_adder(40)(2). Jet rejects overloading by arity (E0105).

Exercised on dev-05ea86f65 (probes in $JET_STATE_ROOT/scratch/OwnerFeedback/sem-probes). p12: triple(4) on a struct value gives E0102 Nothing named triple exists here, which is false. triple.call(4) works as an ordinary method. Re-checked 2026-10-05 on dev-595e0dca3 with jet check: option A's Scale with apply and as_fn checks clean, and only triple(4) fails. Its E0102 says "Only functions that have been defined (or built in, like print / input) can be called".

No C++ source importer exists: Docs/reference/migration-tier-map.md lists C++ as binder-only, with no source importer by deliberate verdict. An earlier draft's mitigation that jet import maps operator() to a method was removed.

Other languages: Swift added callAsFunction in SE-0253 (2019), motivated by Swift for TensorFlow, which was archived in 2021. Rust's Fn traits for user types have been unstable since 2015 (tracking issue rust-lang/rust#29625). Kotlin has operator fun invoke and Python has __call__.

Jet keeps several C++ forms out by design. The comma operator, &&, || and unary & are out; the Google C++ Style Guide also forbids overloading them. operator-> and new/delete are out, because safe Jet has no raw pointers or manual allocation. Implicit conversion operators are out, because Jet's prelude law forbids implicit conversions. Target.from(x) is the one conversion spelling.

options.name: No call hook; a clear error
options.detail: Parentheses call functions and lambdas only. Calling a struct value gives an error that names its type, lists its methods, and suggests a lambda when the value should act as a function.
options.technical: Replace E0102 for a callee that resolves to a non-callable value with a registered error naming the value, its type and its callable members. No language change.

options.name: A Call trait
options.detail: A type that implements Call can be called with parentheses. The call runs its call method.
options.technical: Core trait Call(Args) -> R with a builtin role. Sema resolves a call on a value of such a type to the method. Effects and failures come from the method. Coherence as other hooks.

comparisons.note: operator() predates lambdas and powered function objects.
comparisons.code: struct Scale { int f; int operator()(int n) const { return n * f; } };

comparisons.note: Implementing Fn for your own type has been unstable since 2015.
comparisons.code:
// #![feature(unboxed_closures, fn_traits)] needed
impl FnOnce<(i32,)> for Scale { ... }

recommendation.why: Jet's lambdas already carry state, so a call hook adds a second way to write a function. Readers keep one rule: parentheses after a value run a function or lambda, and the only other use is building an enum case such as Ok(5).
recommendation.tradeoff: Porters of C++ function objects write a method call or a lambda.
gains: f(x) runs a function or lambda, never a hidden struct method.
The misleading error becomes a helpful one.

losses.loss: C++ function objects need a method name or a lambda.
losses.mitigation: The error names the type, lists its methods, and shows the method or lambda form, so each call site becomes triple.apply(4).

whyNot.reason: B makes every call site ambiguous between a function and a struct method, for a need lambdas already meet.

reviewPasses.beginner: Fresh agent: ReadB2. Skill: rli5. Author and beginner model family: claude-opus; the reader could not predict A's fix, because apply and as_fn were never shown, and struct and method were untaught. The repair defines both, shows a checked Scale with apply, as_fn and outputs, completes B's example, and drops a jet import claim, since Jet has no C++ source importer.

The review attacked the one-meaning claim and found it overstated, because parentheses also build enum cases such as Ok(5) and Val(x), which Core uses widely. The repair narrows the claim to never running a hidden struct method, which still separates A from B, and asks the new error to cover every non-callable value.

Check the same error for other non-callable values, such as an Int or a String. Check that calling a function value, a lambda, a returned function and an enum case such as Ok(5) still works on every tier.

A keeps parentheses for functions and lambdas and fixes the error. B adds a Call trait so a struct value can be called.

decisions.title: Spelling a deliberate copy now that copies are rare
decisions.situation: Today a Jet programmer writes ~x to make an independent copy of a value. The tilde was picked when Jet demanded a written copy almost everywhere, but Jet now moves or shares values by itself. In Jet's own code about 87 of every 100 tildes would then be unnecessary, and the rest keep a snapshot of something that later changes. This vote decides how that rare, deliberate copy is spelled; we recommend the plain method x.copy().
decisions.gist: Should a deliberate copy be written x.copy() instead of ~x?
decisions.lesson: A copy is a second, independent value: changing one never changes the other. Jet moves a value at its last use, and values stored in two places share data until one changes. A local name made with saved :: board is only a live view, so Jet stops board from changing while saved is still used. That snapshot case is the only place you write a copy.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: you almost never write a copy. When Jet stops you because a saved name is still looking at something you change, the error offers one fix: add .copy().

Expert path: under a policy that forbids hidden copies, every copy is spelled .copy(), so a reviewer can search one word. The memory model's cost classes and denials are unchanged.

Shared by every option: the compiler still decides move or share when nothing is written, and an explicit copy still costs nothing until someone writes.
decisions.story: Mia keeps a saved game board while play keeps changing the live one. She writes saved :: board, and Jet says the board cannot change while saved is still looking into it. She wants one obvious way to say make my own copy.
decisions.detail:
Owner feedback, 2026-10-05: the memory proposal suggests ~ is no longer needed as a copy sigil. Consider MyVar.Copy() if copies are rare, freeing ~. Methods are snake_case under the casing law (D-SHAPE-CASE1=C), so the spelling is .copy().

History. D-CAP2/S4 shipped the word copy x on 2026-07-04. At that time D-MEM1 made every copy of a reused value a hard error (E0209). D-SHAPE-COPY1=A replaced the word with ~x on 2026-07-15, by the owner's rule that the rarest marked ownership act gets the last leftover mark. That ballot records that the owner declined a method x.copy() on 2026-07-15, when copies were still written everywhere. This ballot exists because the owner now proposes the method himself, after the premise changed.

D-COPY-DEFAULT1=A later moved the choice to the compiler: last use moves, reuse shares, and the first write copies. The memory-model proposal (section 4.4) says ~x is never needed for speed or for the checker. It only means an independent snapshot. D-SIGIL-ALGEBRA1=B retires ~| exclusive-or, so after both changes ~ has no meaning.

Jet already has the method for some types. Lists, maps, sets, Bits, text and byte buffers have a built-in .copy() today (Collections.rs method tables; Examples/features/collections/set.jet:38 and text/strings.jet:38). A probe on the dev candidate accepts xs.copy() and "jet".copy(), and rejects p.copy() on a plain struct with E0102. So today those types have two copy spellings, ~xs and xs.copy(). Option A makes the method the only one and extends it to every copyable type.

The word copy is still teaching-reserved: copy xs gives E0991, and fn copy(self) gives E0003, so no type can declare a copy method today. Module functions such as files.copy(from, to) and math.copy are not methods. Jet has no uniform call syntax (D-UFCS1 declined), so they keep their names under every option.

Metrics, 2026-10-05. A comment- and string-stripped census covered every .jet file in Examples/, Core/ and Compiler/: 287,354 code lines. The script is $JET_STATE_ROOT/scratch/OwnerFeedback/tilde-classify.mjs. It found 1,927 prefix-~ sites with a name operand: Examples 357, Core 969, Compiler 601. Compiler has 48 more on parenthesized expressions.

Each site was classified by what follows in its function. The copied name is never used again at 790 sites (41%), so a move is identical. It is only read again at 893 (46%), so sharing is identical. It is written again at 236 (12%), where a snapshot may be meant.

That is at most one meaningful copy per about 1,200 code lines, and 8 in the 33,506 lines of Examples. The classifier treats any later write to the root name as meaningful, so 236 is an upper bound.

Live probe on the dev candidate (jet check, 2026-10-05). saved :: board followed by &board.push(4) is E0212, and its fix text already says make an owned copy. Sharing into a struct field without ~ is accepted today.

Other languages. Swift SE-0377 added copy x as a contextual keyword, and the compiler may still remove the copy. Hylo's specification writes a.copy(). Rust writes .clone(). Mojo uses the ^ transfer mark and copies copyable types implicitly. No mainstream language spells copy with a one-character mark.

options.name: The method x.copy()
options.detail: Every copyable value has a built-in copy() method that returns an independent value. Lists, maps, sets and text already have this method today, so A extends it to every type and removes the second spelling. It is owned by the compiler: a type cannot redefine it, and it lowers to the same share-until-write copy as today's ~x. It chains like any method. ~x becomes a teaching error whose fix rewrites it, and the E0212 fix text offers .copy().
options.technical:
Expr::Copy keeps its node; only the surface changes from prefix ~ to a reserved method name resolved before ordinary method lookup. The existing collection, text and buffer copy() rows fold into that one built-in. copy stays teaching-reserved, so fn copy on any type stays rejected; the message changes from E0003 to one naming the built-in, and E0991 (copy x) now points at x.copy(). Module functions such as files.copy(from, to) are not methods and keep their names.

#Policy(copies: .Explicit), !Mem.Copy diagnostics, editor ghost hints and jet fmt --explicit-copies print .copy(). Amends D-SHAPE-COPY1=A, D-ITER-COPY1=A and D-MEM-COPYSEM1=A's spelling only; semantics of D-COPY-DEFAULT1=A and D-MEM-COPYSEM1=A unchanged. One cutover rewrites the 1,975 existing sites with jet fix, and deletes the 87% that the classifier marks as move or share once the share-on-reuse build lands.
options.code:
board := [1, 2, 3]
saved :: board.copy()      // my own snapshot
&board.push(4)
print(saved.len())          // 3

grid := input.copy().rotate()

options.name: Keep ~x
options.detail: The tilde stays the copy mark. It is one keystroke, it is already in every example, and the compiler still decides move or share when nothing is written. Chaining a method needs parentheses. Lists, maps, sets and text keep their existing .copy() method too, so those types keep two spellings unless a later change removes the method.
options.technical: No change. D-SHAPE-COPY1=A stands; the share-on-reuse build still removes most existing tildes. The built-in collection and text copy() rows remain beside ~x.
options.code:
board := [1, 2, 3]
saved :: ~board
&board.push(4)
print(saved.len())          // 3

grid := (~input).rotate()

options.name: The prefix word copy x
options.detail: Bring back the word Jet used before the tilde, as Swift does. It reads as English, but chaining a method still needs parentheses. Lists, maps, sets and text would keep their .copy() method beside the word, or lose it in the same change.
options.technical: Reverses D-SHAPE-COPY1=A to D-CAP2/S4's spelling. copy changes from a teaching-reserved word (E0991) to a live prefix keyword, and E0991 retires.
options.code:
board := [1, 2, 3]
saved :: copy board
&board.push(4)
print(saved.len())          // 3

grid := (copy input).rotate()

comparisons.note: A contextual keyword; the compiler may still remove an unneeded copy.
An ordinary method from the language specification.

recommendation.why: A copy is now a rare, deliberate act, so it gets a readable word that chains like any method and frees the tilde for later use.
gains: Reads as what it does, with no symbol to learn.
Chains without parentheses.
Frees ~ entirely; its only other use, the bit-math mark ~|, is retired by a separate vote.

losses.loss: Seven characters instead of one at each deliberate copy.
losses.mitigation: After the cutover a copy appears about once per 1,200 lines, and the fix rewrites old ones.

losses.loss: A method looks like something a type could redefine.
losses.mitigation: copy is already a reserved word, so no type can declare it today; the cutover keeps that and its error names the built-in.

whyNot.reason: B spends a one-key mark on an act that is now rare, keeps .copy() on lists and text as a second spelling, and chains need parentheses.
C turns a teaching-reserved word back into a live keyword, still needs parentheses in chains, and sits beside the existing .copy() method.

recommendation.tradeoff: A few more keystrokes on a rare act, for a self-explaining copy and a free symbol.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Drafted by FeedbackSigils for the owner-feedback report. Ran validate.mjs offline only; no Tower write. The change touches Syntax.rs, so it carries the full two-reader profile.

Owner acceptance: a deliberate copy is spelled .copy(); ~x is a teaching error with an automatic fix.

After ratification: one greenfield cutover replaces SIGIL_COPY with the reserved method in Syntax, both parsers, formatter, fix-its, docs and every example. jet fix rewrites ~x to x.copy(). Proof: the copy-site policy UI snapshots, the E0212 fix text, and identical goldens after jet fix. D-INTENT-ROOT1 decides what ~ means afterwards.
