decisions.title: Writing web markup inside Jet code
decisions.situation:
Web programmers often write page markup, such as

Hello

, right inside their code, the way React does. Jet already has a value for this: the HTML type and its literal, HTML{"

Hello {name}

"}, which encodes every hole. What it lacks is checking, so a misspelled attribute or a wrong closing tag passes silently, and a link or a checkbox hole has no safe rule. This vote picks one way to write markup in code. We recommend keeping the HTML literal as the only spelling, with the compiler checking its tags, links and holes, and editors coloring it as HTML.
decisions.gist: Should markup in code stay the HTML{"…"} literal, now checked, or become bare <tags> or a #HTML block?
decisions.lesson:
Markup is the tag language of web pages, such as

Hello

. A hole inserts a value: if name is the text Ann, {name} writes <b>Ann</b>, so the browser shows those characters rather than bold markup. A hole in a link is encoded as part of the address. All three options build HTML and share these checks and hole rules; only the source delimiters differ. Exactly one markup spelling survives.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path under A: fn declares a function, name: String accepts text, and -> HTML says it returns markup. Calling greeting("Ann").text() gives

Hello Ann

. The .text() method reads the value, not displays it in a browser. In menu, map produces one HTML list item per input string. In profile, id becomes part of the link address, and done adds or leaves out checked. Three-quote bodies allow plain attribute quotes on interior lines. Opening and closing quote lines contain only indentation. Common contract for A, B and C: every form yields HTML. Structure and supported element/attribute names are checked at compile time. E0155 identifies the source line and repair. Text holes in element text and quoted ordinary attributes are encoded for that position. HTML and [HTML] holes are allowed only in element-content positions. Lists join in order; empty lists insert nothing. Holes by position, for every option. In a link attribute such as href or src, a hole after fixed text, as in href='/users/{id}', is percent-encoded as one part of the address. A hole that is the whole address takes a URL value; Jet writes it only when its scheme is http, https or mailto, and otherwise writes the harmless link about:invalid. A Bool hole in a yes-no attribute such as checked or disabled writes the attribute when true and leaves it out when false. Holes cannot supply tag or attribute names, unquoted attributes, event-handler attributes, script or style bodies. Jet code reacts to clicks through its own handlers, not onclick text, and data reaches scripts through data-* attributes, which take ordinary holes. Checking is not a sanitizer for programmer-written fixed scripts or URLs. Expert path: components are ordinary HTML-returning functions called in holes, such as {card(user)}. Static fragments are checked once; execution copies fixed text and processes holes. HTML.raw("…") bypasses structure checking and encoding, not substitutes for customer-text holes. Its existing origin gate refuses external origin-marked text with E0721 (D-BOUND-TAINT1). Audited #Scrub/gate inspection retain that contract, not a new permission here. Core's web schema covers the standard HTML, SVG and MathML elements, their attributes, global attributes and data-* / aria-* families. Void elements such as br need no closing tag. Hyphenated custom elements are accepted; unknown ordinary tags and attributes error. The schema is Core data, not compiler keywords. Unknown gives E0155 with supported-name suggestions, such as h1, and the schema reference. Other foreign vocabularies need schema entries; they never bypass checking. Reading the literal. Under A, Jet's editor grammars color the inside of HTML{"…"} as HTML, tags and attributes included, as the editor plugins for Lit's html`…` templates do. The three-quote form takes ordinary double-quoted attributes; a one-line literal uses single-quoted attributes, which HTML accepts. File pairing is separate: #HTML(page) associates a Jet file with its host HTML page, the outer browser document. It constructs no inline value and survives all options. Ordinary < and > comparisons survive.
decisions.story:
Lena builds a small dashboard. Her function returns HTML{"

Hello {name}

"}. It compiles today, and the broken page ships. She wants Jet to catch both mistakes at the line, without learning a second way to write markup.
decisions.detail: Revision, 2026-10-10, by BallotPolishA. The posted A carried three losses. Two were not A's: calling a component in a hole and the restricted hole positions apply to every option, so they are now stated once as shared contract. The restriction itself was redesigned. Link holes were simply refused, which would block the most common dynamic markup, . They are now encoded by position, as the proven template systems do. Bool holes in yes-no attributes gained a rule, and SVG and MathML joined the schema. The third loss, quotes, is reduced to single-quoted attributes in one-line markup. Editor coloring inside the literal is part of A's delivery in Jet's own grammars. It is no longer a separate acceptance item. Proven designs used here. Go's html/template escapes each hole for its position, percent-encodes URL parts and replaces an unsafe scheme with #ZgotmplZ. Google's Closure Templates do the same under strict autoescaping, with about:invalid#zSoyz. React warns on javascript: URLs and plans to block them. Lit's html`…` tagged templates keep markup in ordinary template text, with no grammar change. Its editor plugin, lit-plugin, colors and checks the markup inside. Lit writes ?disabled=${x} for yes-no attributes; React writes disabled={x}. Jet facts. D-URL1=A gives Jet a typed URL with component percent-encoding, which core.web consumes. D-UI-EVT-DISP1=E and D-WEB-CLICK-PORT1=D route browser clicks to Jet handlers by node identity, so markup never needs onclick text. Jet ships tree-sitter, Zed and TextMate grammars under Tools/editors; tree-sitter injections and TextMate embedded grammars are the standard ways to color one language inside another. Why A, against C. C's block removes the quotes, but HTML would become the only checked text not written as Type{"…"}, beside SQL{"…"} and Sh{"…"}. Every existing literal would be rewritten for two quote characters per piece. Each piece of markup carries a head under A and C alike: HTML{ or #HTML {. Owner question q0j9las3 correctly identified duplicate spellings for one HTML value. A keeps the checked literal, B replaces it with bare tags, and C replaces it with a labeled block. HTML.raw is an audited construction boundary, not a second ordinary markup spelling. #HTML(page) remains file pairing rather than value construction. Letters: A is new checked literal; B remains bare markup so D-ANGLE-CAST2's guard is unchanged; C is the former labeled-block option. Builders are withdrawn. Both occurrences of the stale A/C phrase in D-ANGLE-CAST2 are updated in the questions copy, without changing its guard or recommendation. Recorded current evidence in ANSWERS.md: the three-quote literal accepts plain attribute quotes; a text hole Ann is encoded; malformed tags and clas pass unchanged; [HTML] holes fail E0112. These are supplied probes, not rerun by this review. D-TYPEDTEXT1, D-UNIFYLIT1 and D-TEXTHEAD-TYPE1 own the existing HTML head/CheckedText mechanism. The registered block site of #HTML is unbuilt; file pairing is separate. The proposed shared contract in the explainer replaces the vague 'HTML inserted' promise with explicit positions and defines vocabulary extensions, void elements and unknown-name repair. The schema is Core data for every option, even though B's element production adds web-aware grammar. Static programmer source is checked for structure, not sanitized into harmless browser content. A adds structure/list checking through the existing type; B adds grammar and retires the head; C uses D-META-DSL1's library block and retires the head. Clean cutover includes all callers/examples/tools. Retired syntax gets ordinary errors under D-S14-PAUSE; no new teaching system is smuggled in. Attack on A: quotes cost readability, components are function calls rather than tags, and a closed vocabulary without custom/data/aria rules would obstruct modern web code. The repaired shared schema addresses that last problem; B and C retain their real quote-free advantages. A remains recommended because it answers the duplicate concern while preserving the existing literal, not because grammar checking is intrinsically unsafe or impossible. Foreign-language history is motivation, not executable Jet evidence.

options.name: Checked HTML literal, the one spelling
options.detail: Markup in code stays the HTML{"…"} literal Jet already has, including the three-quote form for several lines. The compiler now checks it: tags must be well formed and closed in order, elements and attributes must be known, and every hole follows the position rules shared by all options. Jet's editors color the inside as HTML. Nothing new is added to the grammar, and the unbuilt #HTML block row retires, so there is one way to write markup.
options.technical:
The HTML type's CheckedText check (D-TEXTHEAD-TYPE1=A) validates against Core's web schema at compile time; invalid source is E0155 naming the tag, line and repair. The common position rules, list joining and schema vocabulary in the explainer apply to all alternatives. Lifts E0112 for [HTML] content holes.

Amends D-HTML-NAME1=B: removes the #HTML block row; retired block syntax receives an ordinary syntax error under D-S14-PAUSE, with the canonical literal documented here. #HTML(page) file pairing stays. No grammar, type or marker is added.

Hole positions: link holes are percent-encoded by position through Core's URL encoder. A whole-address hole requires URL and writes about:invalid for a scheme other than http, https or mailto. A Bool hole in a schema yes-no attribute toggles the attribute.

Editor delivery: the tree-sitter and Zed queries inject the HTML grammar into HTML-headed literals, holes excluded. The TextMate grammar embeds text.html.basic the same way.

options.name: Bare markup in expressions
options.detail: A tag may start any expression, as in JSX, and Jet's core grammar owns HTML. It is the shortest form. The HTML literal retires for markup written in code, and jet fix rewrites existing literals, so there is still one spelling. Every Jet program, including embedded and game code, carries web rules in its grammar.
options.technical: Adds an element production at expression start to both parsers, formatter and highlighter. HTML vocabulary lives in Core schema data consumed by that production, not a compiler keyword per tag. Uses the same HTML result, compile-time E0155 checks and position-safe hole/list rules as A. Amends D-UNIFYLIT1=A and D-HTML-NAME1=B: HTML head and #HTML block retire for markup in code; HTML.raw and #HTML(page) stay. D-ANGLE-CAST2's B is withdrawn under its guard.

options.name: Labeled markup block
options.detail: #HTML { … } becomes legal wherever a value goes, and holds raw tags checked by the HTML library. It yields the same HTML type. The HTML literal retires for markup written in code, and jet fix rewrites existing literals into blocks, so there is still one spelling. Each separate piece of markup needs the #HTML label, including one nested in a hole.
options.technical: Adds the Expression site to #HTML; its inside is read by the HTML library under D-META-DSL1=A and yields HTML with the common compile-time E0155 checks and hole/list rules. Amends D-UNIFYLIT1=A: the HTML head retires for markup in code; HTML.raw and #HTML(page) stay. Literal braces in content use a text hole, {"{"}. The implementation uses the ratified marker/library route, not a second result type.

comparisons.note: Markup stays in ordinary template text with no grammar change; an editor plugin colors and checks it. This is the shape of option A.
XML literals in the grammar are marked dropped, replaced by a string interpolator, which is the shape of option A.
Bare tags in code, turned into function calls by a toolchain outside the core language.

recommendation.why: A keeps the one markup spelling Jet already has and makes the compiler check it, links and yes-no attributes included. There is nothing new to learn, no second way to write the same page, no web rules in Jet's grammar, and the same quoted form as every other checked text.
gains: No new syntax: the HTML literal people already use.
Tags, closing order, attributes and link holes checked at compile time.
Editors color the markup inside as HTML.

losses.loss: One-line markup sits inside quotes, so its attributes use single quotes.
losses.mitigation: The three-quote form takes ordinary double-quoted attributes, and Jet's editor grammars color the inside as HTML.

whyNot.reason: B puts one web language into the core grammar of every program, the path Scala and E4X later reversed, and rewrites every existing HTML literal.
C rewrites every working literal to drop two quote characters, and makes HTML the only checked text not written like SQL{"…"}.

recommendation.tradeoff: Quotes around one-line markup, for one checked spelling, no new grammar and one form for all checked text.

reviewPasses.beginner: Fresh agent: QsBeginner. Skill: rli5. The beginner pass tested the complete ballot. Repaired: shared option semantics, concrete encoding, vocabulary lookup, first call, raw boundary and file-pairing definition.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: claude-opus. Adversarial model family: gpt. Fresh agent: QsAdversary. The adversarial review attacked the recommendation. Repaired: contextual hole safety, schema/custom-element rules, ordinary retired-syntax errors and honest editor/performance acceptance; A retained.

decisions.checkInstructions: Fresh complete-ballot reviews are in review/D-MARKUP1-QsBeginner.md and review/D-MARKUP1-QsAdversary.md; disposition is in review/D-MARKUP1-repairs.md. Nothing was written to Tower. Owner acceptance for A: the one HTML literal rejects clas and a mismatched closing tag with E0155; valid void elements, data-/aria- attributes and custom elements follow the schema contract. Text Ann is encoded; HTML and HTML-list content holes insert in order, including empty lists. Hole and editor acceptance for A: href='/users/{id}' percent-encodes the hole; a whole-address hole needs a URL and writes about:invalid for javascript:; checked="{done}" toggles the attribute. HTML holes in attributes and holes in handler, script, style or name positions are rejected. The tree-sitter, Zed and TextMate grammars color HTML inside the literal. Retired #HTML blocks get ordinary syntax errors, and #HTML(page) still pairs files. No new teaching-error mechanism is introduced. After ratification: add checking, list holes and retire the block row in one cutover. Exercise UI snapshots for bad tags and unsafe hole positions, web examples for all content categories, and file pairing. Inspect lowered code to establish no runtime markup parser; a run alone cannot prove that absence. Grammar goldens prove the HTML coloring. B/C have the same semantic checks and migrate every existing markup literal to their sole spelling. Revision note: BallotPolishA redesigned the shared hole rules and A's editor delivery on 2026-10-10. The reader passes above reviewed the earlier draft; run fresh beginner and adversarial passes on this revision before posting.

decisions.title: Match a map or a JSON object by its keys
decisions.situation: Jet can match a value against a shape in an if table, but only for enum cases, options, literals and ranges. A map, or a JSON object read without a struct, cannot be matched by its keys. Code that routes a webhook on its type field today needs three nested if statements and two lookups. ReScript recently added dictionary patterns for exactly this job. You are deciding whether a map pattern joins Jet's patterns, and we recommend it: written like a map literal, with optional keys marked by a question mark.
decisions.gist: Should Jet let an if table match a map or JSON object by its keys?
decisions.lesson: A pattern is a shape that a value is tested against; it can also pull parts out into names. A map pattern is written like a map literal: ["type": kind, ..]. It matches when each listed key is present and its value matches. The closing .. allows other keys; without it the keys must be exactly those listed. A key marked with ? may be missing, and its name then holds an optional value. Arms run top to bottom. A adds this. B adds only required keys. C keeps lookups and nested ifs.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. JSON read without a struct is one of a few cases: .Object holds a map from keys to JSON values, .Text holds text and .Int a whole number. Looking up a key with .get gives an optional: .Val(x) when the key is there, None when it is not. x ?? y means x's value if it is present, otherwise y.

Jet's if table compares one value against a list of arms, tried top to bottom; the first arm that matches runs. Each arm head can be a value, a range, an enum case such as .Ok(v), or a guard. Today there is no head for a map.

A map pattern mirrors the map literal Jet already has. ["type": .Text(kind), ..] matches a map whose "type" key exists and holds a text value; kind then names that text. The closing .. means other keys may be present, which real JSON objects usually have.

Without .., the listed keys must be all the keys. That is exactly what m == ["a": 1] means today, so existing code keeps its meaning. It is also how struct patterns already work: leaving fields out needs a closing ... An exact pattern is the way to reject unknown keys, and [:] matches only an empty map.

A key written as "nick"?: means the key may be absent. Its sub-pattern then sees the optional result of looking the key up, so nick holds a text or nothing, and "nick"?: None tests that the key is missing.

Keys must be written-out values or ALL_CAPS constants, so the compiler sees every key. A key repeated in one pattern is an error. Because a map can always hold other keys, a table of map patterns needs an else arm unless one arm can never fail.

Typed decoding into a struct stays the way to read a whole known schema. A map pattern is for routing on one field, partial reads, and objects whose shape varies.
decisions.story: Ana writes a small server that receives JSON events from a code host. Each event is an object with a type field and different other fields per type. She has no struct for every event kind. Her handler is a staircase of nested ifs and lookups, and a push without a ref field quietly lands in the branch meant for events she ignores.
decisions.detail:
Owner request 2026-10-05: look into ReScript dictionary pattern matching. Sources: the ReScript talk (youtube yKl2fSdnw7w 87:05-88:52). Also the ReScript 12 manual, Dictionary and Pattern Matching pages (rescript-lang.org/docs/manual/dict, read 2026-10-05). ReScript matches present keys by default. It uses ?b to bind an optional value for a key that may be missing.

The 2026-10-05 mining distillation (languages-b R14) rejected dictionary patterns as a second decode path beside decode<T>(). This ballot answers that objection. A pattern tests a value already in hand, as enum patterns do beside enum constructors. Decode converts a whole tree to a declared type. Today's equivalent is nested if statements over entries.get(...), the same test written by hand.

Exercised on dev-05ea86f65 (probes in $JET_STATE_ROOT/scratch/OwnerFeedback/sem-probes). p30: the map head ["a": x] gives E0107 on x. p35: .Object(["name": .Text(name)]) gives E0003. p33 shows today's working form with two .get lookups and a guard. Re-checked 2026-10-05 on dev-595e0dca3: option C's event and user code checks clean, and a push without ref reaches its else branch. Corpus counts across Examples, Core and Compiler: 90 .Object( case patterns, 98 string-key indexes, 139 .get("...") lookups. json_coerce.jet and no_any_alternatives.jet use the nested form.

Why the closing .. (adversarial review, 2026-10-05). On dev-595e0dca3, if m == ["a": 1] and an arm ["a": 1, "b": 2] both check clean today and compare whole maps exactly. If map patterns were open by default, that text would silently start matching any map holding "a": 1. The same words would then mean exact equality outside an if and an open match inside one.

Open-by-default would also break Jet's own pattern rule. D-DESTRUCT1 makes a partial struct pattern without a closing .. an error (E0326), and D-PAT-RECORD1 uses .. for the rest of a list. Rust struct patterns also need ... Under open matching, Python's empty mapping pattern {} matches every mapping, a case the closed form avoids.

Other languages: Python 3.10 mapping patterns {"k": v, **rest} ignore extra keys (PEP 634). Elixir %{"k" => v} matches any map holding the key. C# 8 property patterns test named members. Rust, Swift and Go have no map patterns. TC39 pattern matching for JavaScript is a stage 1 proposal with object patterns. D-DATATREE-PATH1 (tree["user"]["name"]) is ratified but unbuilt; p36 gives E0505. D-INFER-PRIVATE1 renames DataTree to Dyn; the pattern works on either name.

options.name: Map patterns with optional keys
options.detail: A head written like a map literal matches when every plain key is present and its value matches. A closing .. allows other keys; without it the keys must be exactly those listed, as == on maps means today. Keys with ?: may be missing; their sub-pattern sees the optional lookup result. Works for any [K:V] with written-out or constant keys, and nested inside a JSON object case.
options.technical:
Parser: a map-literal-shaped pattern in arm heads, after == in pattern tests, and nested in case payloads, sharing the literal grammar plus one optional trailing .. entry, as in D-PAT-RECORD1 list patterns. Sema: keys must be literals, enum cases or ALL_CAPS constants of K; duplicate keys reuse the D-MAPLIT-DUP1 check. A pattern without .. also checks the map's length, so with no bindings it equals today's map equality.

Lowering: one lookup per distinct key per table, shared across arms; bound values are read windows into the map, so nothing is copied or allocated. Exhaustiveness: else is required unless an arm has .. and only ?: entries with irrefutable sub-patterns. Every tier lowers to the same lookups.

options.name: Required keys only
options.detail: The same map pattern, including the closing .., but every written key must be present. A possibly missing key is read with a lookup inside the arm.
options.technical: Same parser and lowering as A without the ?: entry form. A missing-or-present field needs a second arm or a .get call in the body.

options.name: Keep lookups and nested ifs
options.detail: No map patterns. Code reads keys with .get and tests each result, or decodes into a struct.
options.technical: No change. JSON objects are matched with .Object(entries) and then entries.get(key) per field.

comparisons.note: Dictionary patterns match present keys; ?b binds an option for a key that may be missing.
PEP 634 mapping patterns ignore extra keys; **rest captures them.
comparisons.code:
match event:
    case {"type": "push", "ref": ref}: deploy(ref)
    case {"type": kind}: print("ignored", kind)

comparisons.note: Struct patterns that leave fields out must say .., the rule A follows for maps.
comparisons.code: match p { Point { x: 0, .. } => on_axis(), _ => off_axis() }

recommendation.why: Maps and JSON objects are some of the most common data a web or script program touches. A reuses the map literal shape, so the pattern reads like the data. It covers present, missing and varying keys in one arm table, with the same lookups a hand-written version makes.
recommendation.tradeoff: One more pattern form to learn, written exactly like a map literal.
gains: A webhook or config router is one flat table instead of nested ifs.
Missing and present keys are both expressed in the pattern.
No extra cost: one lookup per key, no copies.

losses.loss: A table of map patterns usually needs an else arm.
losses.mitigation: Maps can always hold other keys, so else states that case. The error names the missing else and offers it as a fix.

losses.loss: An arm that forgets the closing .. matches only maps with exactly its keys.
losses.mitigation: That arm then falls to else on the first test input, and every example of JSON routing shows the closing ..

whyNot.reason: B needs a second arm or a lookup for every optional field, which is the most common JSON case.
C keeps the nested staircase, where each missing-key case hides inside an else instead of standing as its own arm.

reviewPasses.beginner: Fresh agent: ReadB2. Skill: rli5. Author and beginner model family: claude-opus; the reader lacked .Object, .Text, .Val and ??, met unrelated A and B programs, and saw A and C agree on a ref-less push. The repair teaches those terms, adds sample inputs and outputs, puts the same program in every option, and shows the missing-ref case as its own arm.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: claude-opus. Adversarial model family: claude-opus. Fresh agent: ReadA2. A probe showed if m == ["a": 1] is whole-map equality today, so open matching by default would silently change it and break the struct rest-mark rule. The repair makes map patterns exact unless they end with the rest mark, updates every example, and records forgetting that mark as a mitigated loss.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Check that a map pattern matches when listed keys are present, binds ?: entries as optional values, and fails cleanly when a required key is missing. decisions.title: Match a struct or a list by its shape in an if table
decisions.situation: A pattern is a shape that a value is tested against in an if table, Jet's list of cases where the first case that fits runs. Today a struct, a value with named fields such as a point, matches only at the top of a table and only without its type name, as {x: 0, y}. A list cannot be a pattern at all, so programs that route a command by its first word read items by position and can read past the end. You are deciding whether lists and named struct shapes become patterns everywhere, and we recommend both, written exactly like the values they match.
decisions.gist: Should Jet's if tables match a struct by its fields and a list by its items?
decisions.lesson: A pattern is a shape a value is tested against; it can also pull parts out into names. A struct is a value with named fields, like a Point with x and y. An if table runs the first arm that fits. Today a struct pattern works only at the top of a table, without its type name: {x: 0, y}. A adds list patterns such as [] and [first, ..rest], and lets struct patterns name their type and nest. B adds only the struct part; C keeps guards.
decisions.explainer:
Jet's if table compares one value against a list of arms, tried top to bottom; the first that fits runs. Today an arm head can be a value, a range, an enum case, a guard (any true-or-false test), or an unnamed struct pattern such as {x: 0, y}.

A struct pattern lists some fields in braces, exactly as the value is built. {x: 0, y}, or under A and B also Point{x: 0, y}, matches a point whose x is 0 and puts its y in a new name y. Fields left out need .. at the end, the rule enum field patterns already follow. The named head matters on a one-line if, where a bare { after == would open a table.

A list pattern writes items in brackets. [] matches an empty list. [only] matches exactly one item. [first, ..] matches one or more items. ["add", name, ..] matches two or more items whose first is "add". [first, ..rest] also names the remaining items as a read-only window, so nothing is copied.

One rule covers every brace and bracket pattern: it is exact unless its last entry is the two dots. A struct pattern names every field or ends with the dots, and [a, b] matches exactly two items. The companion map pattern ["k": v] works the same way, and [:] matches only an empty map.

A bare name inside a pattern always makes a new name; it never compares with a name you already have. To compare, add a guard: [c, ..] && c == wanted -> …. Reusing a name already in scope is the existing E0118 error, so a pattern can never silently capture a value you meant to compare.

Coverage works as for enums: [] plus [first, ..rest] covers every list, so no else is needed. Leave out [] and the compiler refuses the table with E0307, naming the empty list as the missing case.
decisions.story: Sam writes a command-line tool that reads words typed by a user. He wants one table: no words, "help", "add" with a name, anything else. Today he checks the length, reads words[0] and words[1], and once read past the end of a one-word list.
decisions.detail:
Owner request 2026-10-05: Jet's focus on pattern matching, and ReScript's record and dictionary patterns. Companion ballot D-PAT-MAP1 covers maps and JSON objects.

Current law: S31 pattern tests cover enums and options. D-PAT-NAMED-NEST1=A adds named fields for enum cases and its if-condition brace rule. D-LIT-DOT1=B dropped the dot from literal heads, so the unnamed record shape is {…}; .{…} is E0320.

Exercised on dev-05ea86f65 (probes in $JET_STATE_ROOT/scratch/OwnerFeedback/sem-probes). p31: Point{x: 0, y} as an arm head gives E0003 at the brace. p32: [first, ..] gives E0003 at the dots. Corpus: 5,261 subject if tables and 3,105 enum pattern tests across Examples, Core and Compiler, so tables are the main control form.

Re-probed on dev-595e0dca3 with jet check ($JET_STATE_ROOT/scratch/ReadB3). Arm heads {x: 0, y: 0}, {x: 0, y} and {x, ..} in a subject table already pass, with no else needed (p5). Nested .Val(Point{x: 0, y}) and .Val({x, ..}) give E0003 (p6). The one-line if q == {x: 0, y} -> … gives E0003 because { opens a table.

Adversarial probes on dev-595e0dca3 with jet check ($JET_STATE_ROOT/scratch/ReadA3). a1: today a list arm head is a value, so [cmd] -> … compares the subject with a one-item list built from the in-scope cmd, and passes. a3: a pattern name that reuses an in-scope name, Val(n) with parameter n, is E0118. So under A the old [cmd] head becomes E0118 with a guard fix, never a silent capture. A corpus search of Examples, Core and Compiler finds no list arm head that holds a name.

a1 also shows [] as an arm head is E0501 today (no element type), which A gives a meaning. a7: if p == Point{x: 0, y: 4} -> … is E0003 today because { opens the body. So the one-line named head needs the D-PAT-NAMED-NEST1 lookahead: first entry `..`, `field:`, `field,` or a lone `field}` before the body.

Python 3.10 lesson: case NOT_FOUND: silently captures instead of comparing, a well-known trap, and PEP 634 makes an irrefutable capture before other cases a syntax error to limit it. Jet avoids the trap by refusing reuse of an in-scope name (E0118) and teaching the guard.

The self-hosted parser, Compiler/JetParser/Source/Parser/Patterns.jet:462 and :505-506, already parses both {…} and Name{…} struct patterns. So the two parsers disagree on the named head.

Other languages: Rust has struct and slice patterns with .. rests. Python 3.10 has class and sequence patterns (PEP 634). C# 8 added property patterns and C# 11 list patterns. ReScript matches records by field and lists with list{head, ...tail}. Swift has neither for structs or arrays.

options.name: Struct and list patterns
options.detail: Struct patterns may write the type name, Point{x: 0, y}, or leave it off as today, {x: 0, y}, and may sit inside other patterns. List patterns use brackets with .. for any rest. Both nest inside each other and inside enum cases.
options.technical:
Rust parser: the D-PAT-NAMED-NEST1 brace form with a type head, struct patterns in nested positions, and a bracket form with at most one .. entry, which must come last. In an if condition the named head uses the same lookahead as D-PAT-NAMED-NEST1, so { still opens the body otherwise. A bracket head whose first entry is followed by : is a D-PAT-MAP1 map pattern, exact unless it ends with .., and [:] matches only an empty map. The self-hosted parser already accepts both struct heads.

Sema: one exactness rule for struct, list and map patterns: exact unless a trailing .. (or ..rest for lists) opens the rest, matching D-DESTRUCT1 and E0326/E0327. Field names follow E0302/E0303. List patterns check item patterns against T for [T] and fixed-size [T#N], where a length the type rules out is a compile error. A bare name in any pattern binds, and E0118 refuses reuse of an in-scope name. Literals inside a pattern compare with ==, so a literal-only list head keeps today's meaning.

Lowering: field reads and one length test per table. A ..rest name is a read-only view of the remaining items, copied only when stored in an owning slot (the existing view rule). Exhaustiveness: lists split by length, with E0307 for a hole; structs by field patterns. Every tier lowers to the same tests.

options.name: Struct patterns only
options.detail: Struct patterns as in A, with or without the type name and at any depth. Lists are still tested by length and index reads.

decisions.title: Everything applied with # is declared with marker
decisions.situation: Jet code attaches rules to code with a # tag, such as #PII on a field or #Policy(audit("users")) on a function. Three different words declare those tags today: marker, tag, and policy with a wrap block. A test run also found that a policy wrapper is skipped when its function is called directly; that bug gets fixed whichever option wins. This vote decides whether tag and policy fold into marker, so one word declares everything you apply with #.
decisions.gist: Should tag and policy declarations fold into marker, so one word declares everything applied with #?
decisions.lesson: A marker is a # tag on code; its declaration says where it attaches and what it does. Labels on data (tags, such as #PII for private data) and call wrappers (policies) are applied with # but declared with their own words. Whichever option wins, #Policy keeps its scoped compiler settings such as #Policy(gc).
decisions.explainer:
A tag is a label on data. #PII marks private data, and a declaration such as deny: [Log, Net] stops a labeled value from reaching logs or the network. PII is built in; you declare your own labels, such as CardNumber. A policy wraps a function: inside wrap(call) { ... }, call() runs the original function and returns its result.

Jet already ruled that a user-written marker has the same power as a compiler marker: no body records a fact, a body adds code. So tags, policies and markers are one mechanism with three declaration words.

Under A, `tag CardNumber { deny: [Log, Net] }` becomes `marker CardNumber { deny: [Log, Net] }`. `pub policy audit(topic: String) { wrap(call) { ... } }` becomes `pub marker Audit(topic: String) { wrap(call) { ... } }`, applied as `#Audit("users")`; marker names are PascalCase, so audit becomes Audit. The body tells the compiler where the marker may go: deny/from means values and types, wrap means functions and methods. An explicit sites list still overrides.

The skipped-wrapper bug is fixed under A and B alike: the wrapper becomes part of the function's definition, so direct calls and method values run it. Under A, apply() itself retires. A call site can then no longer swap or drop a function's wrappers. Code that needs the bare body keeps it in an unmarked function and marks a one-line front.

The built-in retry and trace policies become built-in markers, #Retry and #Trace. Stacked markers wrap outermost first: in `#[Retry(3), Audit("users")]`, Retry runs around Audit. Under A, #Policy keeps exactly one meaning: scoped compiler settings (gc, copies, sentries, the escape ladder).

Beginner path: nothing changes until they declare their own label; then there is one word to learn. Expert path: one declaration form, one reflection table, one audit grep (`marker`).
decisions.story: Priya writes a billing audit wrapper as a policy, marks charge() with it, and ships. In production nothing is logged, because direct calls skip the wrapper and only apply() runs it.
decisions.detail:
Code facts, checked 2026-10-05 on the main checkout and dev release dev-05ea86f65.

Declaration words: crates/jet-foundation/src/Syntax/math_layout.rs:707 KW_TAG (D-QUAL2), Syntax/core_surface.rs:481-483 KW_POLICY and KW_WRAP (D-STRUCT-POLICY1), Syntax/effects_surface.rs:138 KW_MARKER (D-META-NAME1). D-QUAL2 text: "A tag is a marker that erases at runtime and carries no methods." D-META-USER1=A: "A rule with no body records a fact. A rule with a body adds code.

This is the same power the compiler has." D-STRUCT-POLICY1=A says a package declares a policy setting the way it declares a marker, reusing the D-META-USER1 machinery.

Probe (dev-05ea86f65, $JET_STATE_ROOT/scratch/OwnerFeedback/mech-probes/policy_apply.jet): `#Policy(audit("users.load")) fn load_user()` called directly prints 7 with no audit line. `apply(audit("users.load"), load_user)()` prints the audit line. The shipped examples (Examples/features/callable/user_policies.jet, callable_policies.jet) only exercise apply(), so no golden catches this.

#Policy double meaning. D-CALLPOLICY2=C said #Policy means wrappers only, yet #Policy(gc), #Policy(copies: .Explicit) and #Policy(sentries: .Off) are live scoped settings (Compiler/JetParser/Source/Parser/Declarations/Policies.jet:1-5, D-MARK-SCOPE1, D-AUTHORITY-MEM1, D-ONCE-GATE1). Under A the wrapper half moves to user markers and #Policy keeps settings only.

Corpus impact (Examples + Core + Compiler, 1,660 files, 328,724 lines). 7 `tag` declarations (Examples/features/types/*, reflection/fact_reads.jet, suites/finite_state.jet), 2 `policy` declarations (both callable examples). 4 apply() calls: callable_policies.jet:14-16 and user_policies.jet:11. Prelude: 0 tag or policy declarations. Keyword list: 51 live words drop to 49.

Adversarial findings. D-CALLPOLICY1=E gives apply() two powers: apply(chain, f) replaces a function's wrapper chain at one call site, and apply(f) selects the bare function. Under A both go, which the recommendation now lists as a loss. retry(3) and trace(...) in callable_policies.jet are built-in callable policies, so A must give them marker spellings. PII is a built-in tag (Syntax/effects_surface.rs:87 BUILTIN_TAGS), so the examples declare CardNumber instead.

Research. Python decorators (PEP 318) and C# attributes use one application syntax with one declaration form. Python keeps the bare function reachable through functools.wraps and __wrapped__. Rust has one attribute syntax but four declaration kinds (derive, attribute, function-like proc macros, built-in attributes), a common learner complaint. TypeScript decorators went through two incompatible designs (experimentalDecorators, then TC39 stage 3 in TS 5.0) because wrapping and metadata were specified separately. Lesson: one declaration form for everything applied with one glyph.

options.name: One word: marker
options.detail: tag and policy retire as declaration words. A deny/from body declares a value label; a wrap(call) body declares a call wrapper. Applying the marker to a function wraps its definition, so direct calls and method values run it. apply() retires. #Policy keeps only scoped settings.
options.technical:
Remove KW_TAG and KW_POLICY from JET_KEYWORD_LIST; keep `wrap(call)` as a marker-body statement beside `add`. Sites are inferred from the body kind unless `$sites:` is written. Retired-word teaching errors (E0003 family) rewrite `tag X {` to `marker X {` and `policy x(` to `marker X(`.

The built-in callable policies retry and trace become Prelude markers Retry and Trace. apply() retires with a teaching error pointing at the marker, an unmarked inner function, or ordinary function composition. E0731 becomes "a label marker is used where a trait is needed". Wrapper lowering moves to the definition site, fixing the direct-call defect on every tier (I9).

options.name: Keep three words, fix the wrapper
options.detail: Keep tag, policy and marker. Fix lowering so #Policy(audit(...)) wraps the definition.
options.technical: Bug fix only; registry unchanged. #Policy keeps wrapper chains and scoped settings in one argument list.

options.name: Also fold fact into marker
options.detail: Everything in A, and the fact declaration word also retires. fact is written only in the Prelude, Jet's built-in library file, to declare compiler-owned labels such as planes, rights and build facts; they become bodiless markers with a $holds column.
options.technical: Amends D-FACTDECL1. 49 rows in Prelude/Facts.jet change spelling; no user corpus writes `fact`.

marker Rights($holds: .Scope, $safe: .Shrink)

comparisons.note: Every attribute is a class deriving from Attribute; one declaration form (learn.microsoft.com, Attributes).
One #[...] application syntax, but four declaration kinds; a frequent learner complaint.

gains: One word declares every # tag.

losses.loss: apply() retires, so a call site can no longer swap or drop a function's wrappers; its four example calls are rewritten.
losses.mitigation: Only two teaching examples use it. Code that needs the bare body keeps it in an unmarked function and marks a one-line front, as Python code reaches __wrapped__.

whyNot.reason: It keeps three words and a two-meaning #Policy for one mechanism.
fact is written only in the Prelude, so folding it helps no learner and blurs build facts.

recommendation.tradeoff: A familiar short word (tag) gives way to one word for every # tag.

decisions.title: One way to bound waiting: deadline blocks replace per-call timeout setters
decisions.situation: Network code needs time limits so a stuck server cannot hang a program. Jet has a deadline block that every wait inside it obeys, and separately six setter functions plus a timeout argument on ten lookup and connect calls. Two ways to say one thing means two sets of rules to learn, test and audit. This vote decides whether a deadline block with a plain duration becomes the one way to bound waiting.
decisions.gist: Should a deadline block be the one way to time-limit waiting, replacing per-call timeout setters and arguments?
decisions.lesson: A deadline is a time limit on waiting. Jet's expert #Context(deadline:) block already makes every wait inside it, including network reads, stop when time runs out. Network and HTTP also have their own timeout setters. Whichever option wins, the runtime keeps one timer per innermost deadline.
decisions.explainer:
Today a time limit can be set two ways. #Context(deadline: <epoch ms>) { ... } is an expert-only block; epoch ms is a clock time counted in milliseconds since 1970. Every wait inside it inherits the deadline: joins, channel receive, sleep, and network reads and writes.

Separately, core.net has five timeout setters (tcp_connect_timeout, set_timeout, set_read_timeout, set_write_timeout, udp_set_timeout) and core.http.client has session_timeout. Nine DNS lookups and tcp_connect_happy also take their own timeout argument. core.tasks.timeout(delay) is named like a limit but only sleeps.

Under A, a beginner marker #Deadline(5s) { ... } takes a relative duration, written with Jet's duration literal. It replaces the #Context deadline field and the six setters, and the ten timeout arguments go. A lookup with no deadline around it keeps today's 5-second default. tasks.timeout is renamed or retired. A block inside another can only shorten the time left, never extend it, because nested blocks take the earliest deadline. So a per-read idle limit is a block inside the loop, and a separate connect limit goes on the connecting function.

When time runs out, the waiting call fails with its ordinary typed error, a NetError for a socket. That error passes up like any other, so retry code handles one kind, and only an uncaught one ends the program with the E3003 report. The runtime maps the innermost deadline onto the socket poller, so there is no extra timer per call.

Two things keep their own time argument because they are not limits on a blocking call. tcp_ready is a readiness check where 0 means look without waiting, and browser automation timeouts are sent to the browser, which enforces them.

Beginner path: one block around the slow part. Expert path: the same block with an absolute instant, and `jet inspect live` already shows deadlines.
decisions.story: Omar sets a 30-second read timeout on a socket. A struggling server sends one line every 20 seconds, so no single read ever times out, and his request runs for an hour. A deadline around the whole request would have stopped it at 5 seconds, but only experts see that block today.
decisions.inWild:
# Trio (Python): one cancel-scope mechanism; no per-socket timeouts
# vorpus.org/blog/timeouts-and-cancellation-for-humans (N. J. Smith, 2018)
with trio.fail_after(5):
    conn = await trio.open_tcp_stream(host, 443)
    data = await conn.receive_some()
decisions.detail:
Code facts, checked 2026-10-05.

Deadline mechanism: Docs/spec/spec.md:2231-2234 and D-DEADLINE1 define #Context(deadline: <Int epoch_ms>). Task joins, channel receive, time.sleep and network reads and writes inherit it, and expiry reports E3003. crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Markers.jet:177 declares Context(allocator, logger, deadline). Syntax/math_layout.rs:946 marks Context expert-tier only.

Expiry today is ambiguous. spec.md:2233 says exceeding the budget emits E3003 and exits. spec.md:848 treats E3003 as the report of an unhandled error returned by the entry function, and D-DEADLINE1's example handles a cancelled join. A pins the catchable reading.

The runtime already takes the catchable reading for sockets. crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/CoreLib/Top/NetHTTP.rs:918-938 turns an expired deadline at every socket wait into NetError.Timeout. The setters feed the same per-operation deadline (jet_net_operation_deadline, NetHTTP.rs:1682), so a setter and a deadline already give the same error. The real gap is reach, not error kinds: a per-read limit never caps a whole request.

Per-call setters: Core/net/net.jet:131 tcp_connect_timeout, :228 set_timeout, :234 set_read_timeout, :240 set_write_timeout, :283 udp_set_timeout; Core/http/client.jet:117 session_timeout. Core/tasks/tasks.jet:154 `timeout(delay)` only sleeps (recv on tasks.after), a misleading name the mining also flagged for core.tasks.

Timeout arguments: Core/net/net.jet:357-411 gives nine dns_* lookups an ms argument, and :136 gives tcp_connect_happy a timeout_ms. gethostbyname (:415) passes 5000, the default A keeps. tcp_ready (:194) is a readiness check, and Core/web/browser.jet:136 timeout(ms) is enforced by the browser; both stay.

Examples follow today's rules, checked with jet check on dev-595e0dca3 ($JET_STATE_ROOT/scratch/ReadB3/d1.jet, d2.jet, with #Deadline removed). Bare ? is retired (E-ERR-PROPAGATE), a SocketAddr connects through tcp_connect_addr, and the error type is written NetError. The duration literal is 5s, not 5.seconds (ReadA3/a6.jet, a8.jet, with #Context standing in for #Deadline).

Research. Nathaniel J. Smith, "Timeouts and cancellation for humans" (2018): per-operation timeouts do not compose; cancel scopes (Trio, then AnyIO, Python 3.11 asyncio.timeout) do. His example is a server that sends a little data just before each read timeout, so the request never ends. Go kept both net.Conn.SetDeadline (absolute, per connection) and context.Context deadlines; the dual model is a known source of bugs where one is set and the other ignored.

Kotlin coroutines use withTimeout scopes; Swift structured concurrency uses Task cancellation with timeouts as scopes. Java's per-socket SO_TIMEOUT plus separate executor timeouts is the pattern A avoids.

Performance: a deadline scope lowers to the same poller timer the setters use (one timer per innermost scope). The paired two-program cell compares a timed read loop under #Deadline with the set_read_timeout spelling before ratification, per the AGENTS.md performance gate.

options.name: One deadline block

options.technical:
Marker Deadline(limit: Duration | Instant, $sites: [.Block, .Function]). Innermost deadline wins; nested blocks take min(). The runtime binds the active deadline to the socket poller; no per-call timer allocation. An expired wait returns the call's typed error (NetError for sockets); E3003 is the report when that error is unhandled at the entry function. Joins report .DeadlineBlown.

The nine dns_* lookups and tcp_connect_happy drop their ms argument and read the active deadline, defaulting to 5000 ms with none, as gethostbyname does today. tcp_ready keeps its readiness argument. tasks.timeout(delay) renames to tasks.sleep_for or retires in favour of time.sleep.

decisions.title: One hook mechanism for every part of Jet
decisions.situation: A hook lets your code run when something happens, like Neovim running a formatter just before a file is saved. Jet has many such places, from test setup to transaction commit to compiler plugins, registered in fourteen different ways. Jet's event library already has typed events and hooks with scopes, priority and run-once rules. This vote decides whether every part of Jet offers its hook points as those same typed values, attached with one marker.
decisions.gist: Should every Jet subsystem offer typed hook points from the event library, attached with one #On marker?
decisions.lesson: A hook point is a named moment, such as "a request arrived" or "the program type-checked". The event library already defines typed events, hooks that return a value, and decision hooks that can continue, change, cancel or fail. Whichever option wins, untrusted code still runs sandboxed, walled off from anything it was not granted.
decisions.explainer:
Today each subsystem invents its registration. #Test and #Job markers, #Every schedules, #DevPanel, on_commit and on_rollback methods, process.on_signal, web.on and HTTP middleware wrappers. The game frame callback, env on_enter jobs, git hook paths, package build hooks, and a compiler extension chosen by an environment variable.

Under A, each subsystem publishes its moments as typed values from core.event. Event<T> is a plain notification. Hook<T, R> asks handlers for a value R. DecisionHook<T, E> lets each handler answer Continue, Transform(new value), Cancel, or Fail(e), where E is what Fail carries. For web.request, E is the reply, so .Fail(reply) answers early instead of running the page.

Code attaches in one of two ways: `#On(point)` on a function for a fixed attachment, or `point.on(scope, handler)` for one made while running. A scope is a group of attachments removed together. The handler's signature must match the point, or the compiler names the expected signature.

When several handlers share a point, they run by priority, then package order, then declaration order. #On(point, priority: 10) sets a priority, as event.on_priority already does. `jet inspect hooks` prints that exact order, so nothing depends on which file the compiler read first.

#Test, #Job, #Every and #DevPanel keep their spellings and register on the same points from the Prelude, the built-in library every program sees, so nobody rewrites tests. Which older calls, such as tx.on_commit or process.on_signal, retire is set per subsystem by the companion ballots; until then they keep working. `jet inspect hooks` lists every attachment with its package, so an enterprise can audit what runs where.

Beginner path: the familiar markers keep working. Expert path: one way to extend any subsystem, and one way to publish hook points from your own library.
decisions.story: Sam wants to run a check before each deploy, add a header to each web response, and lint for a banned function. Today he learns three registration styles and three error vocabularies.
decisions.detail:
Code facts, checked 2026-10-05.

Existing mechanism: Docs/spec/spec.md:3031-3093 and Core/event/event.jet:20-46. event.scope(), event.new<T>(), on/once/on_priority with scope, priority ordering, snapshot dispatch, async events with bounded queues, event.hook<T, R>(fallback). event.decision_hook<T, E>(HookPolicy) with HookDecision Continue, Transform, Cancel, Fail (D-EVENT1, D-EVENT2, D-EVENT-CONTINUE1=C "one typed hook mechanism for transform/cancel/fail"). Probe (dev-05ea86f65, mech-probes/hooks.jet): priority and once behave as specified.

Two defects found: `EventTrace.summary()` prints `<invalid>`, and the spec example at spec.md:3081 writes `print(&clicked.emit(1).summary())`, which now fails E0225.

Registration shapes today (14): #Test, #Job, #Every, #DevPanel, #Interrupt markers. tx.on_commit/on_rollback. process.on_signal. web.on(path, title, handler) and core.http.middleware wrappers. game.run frame callback. Env on_enter/checks. Env hook fn(sh: Shell) (D-ECO7) and explicit hook records. git_hooks_path. Package build/install hooks (D-JPK-BUILDSCRIPT1). JET_COMPILER_EXTENSION (D-DX5-HOOK1). compiler.advanced.register* (D-META-CONTROL2). Corpus use of event.hook: 4 sites in 2 files.

Research. Neovim: one autocmd mechanism (over 100 events, :help autocmd-events) with groups for bulk removal, once, pattern filters, and the same event set for Vimscript and Lua since 0.7 (2022). Its known failure: heavy handlers on hot events (CursorMoved, on_bytes buffer callbacks) cause lag, which led to lazy-loading managers and --startuptime profiling. Emacs hooks (add-hook/run-hooks) are one mechanism for the whole editor.

webpack's tapable offers nine hook kinds (sync, bail, waterfall, loop, async series and parallel); Jet's Event, Hook, DecisionHook and AsyncEvent cover the same space with four. Rollup and Vite use one plugin hook interface for dev and build. Lesson: one registration mechanism with typed points, scoped removal, and visible cost.

options.name: Typed hook points, one #On marker
options.detail: Every subsystem exposes its moments as Event, Hook or DecisionHook values. #On(point) attaches a function statically; point.on(scope, f) attaches at run time. #Test, #Job, #Every and #DevPanel keep their spellings and register on the same points from the Prelude.
options.technical:
Marker On(point: Value, priority: Int{0}, $sites: [.Function]); the compiler checks the handler type against the point type. Order on one point is priority, then package order, then declaration order, for static and dynamic attachments alike; a dynamic .on registers after every static attachment of the same priority. Friendly markers keep their own sites (#Test("name") { ... } stays a top-level block claim) and register on the same points.

Static attachments are listed in a per-package hook table read by `jet inspect hooks` and lowered to direct calls; a point with no attachment emits no dispatch code. Dynamic .on keeps D-EVENT1 scope rules. Trust and sandbox rules come from the subsystem (see the companion ballots on compiler stages, lifecycle and runtime hooks).

options.detail: Each library designs its own callbacks; new subsystems add new styles.

options.technical: Dynamic dispatch on every point; no static list for audit, caching or dead-code removal.

comparisons.note: One hooks object per compiler; nine hook kinds (github.com/webpack/tapable).
add-hook and run-hooks are the one hook mechanism for the editor (GNU Emacs manual, Hooks).

recommendation.why: Jet already ships the right primitive: typed events and decision hooks with scopes, priority and once. Making every subsystem publish points through it, with one static marker, gives one lesson, compile-time signature checks, a full audit list and zero cost for unused points.
gains: One extension lesson for every subsystem.
Wrong handler signatures fail at compile time.
Unused hook points cost nothing.

decisions.title: Which compiler and tool moments packages may hook, as ordinary Jet metaprogramming
decisions.situation: Packages want to add their own checks, generated code and editor actions at moments such as after a file is parsed or a program is checked. Jet's metaprogramming already lets a marker body read checked facts, reject code and add items while a program builds. A compiler hook is the same compile-time Jet, attached to a compiler moment instead of a written #Name. Today's only compiler hook is a separate plugin outside Jet, chosen by an environment variable, and both options delete it. This vote decides how many moments to publish now. We recommend the full stage table, with every hook following the rules marker bodies already follow.
decisions.gist: Which compiler and tool moments may packages hook with compile-time Jet, and how many should Jet publish now?
decisions.lesson: A hook is package code Jet runs at a named moment, such as after checking a program. Both options use ordinary compile-time Jet and the same runner as marker bodies. A stage determines the read-only input and allowed results: B can return findings and proposed edits only; A also has an additive generation point. Neither silently rewrites source, and the compiler alone decides validity.
decisions.explainer:
Words: the root package is the one being built. Findings are located lint warnings; editor actions are fixes offered for acceptance. Digests/fingerprints are content-derived change identities, not timings.

Markers run where #Name is written; hooks run on each item at a moment. Both use the ordinary compile-time runner, fact views and Meta policy. Powers depend on stages. A's declared point adds items through compiler.generate's checking/provenance path. B's checked point supplies findings and proposed edits only.

Edits apply through jet fix/editor acceptance. Advanced root-opted-in change sets remain D-META-RECONCILE1's contract; vote that first.

A lifecycle: parse -> resolve declarations/signatures/direct named calls -> declared hooks -> check original/added items -> checked -> emitted. Parsed knows syntax, not types; declared knows resolved names, not validated bodies. Checked includes validated added items, which never re-enter declared hooks. Build points view the single fn build graph; fmt/lsp/test/doc are tool views. B begins at checked.

Layout: lint_rules/package.jet identifies the package; lint_rules/no_print.jet is a source module. Included modules supply discovered #On functions without another registration list. Hook modules/imports compile first. Hooks cannot inspect themselves or their support dependency closure; cycles error.

The import use core.compiler supplies payload/result types. Attachment #On selects a typed point. A function returning [compiler.Finding] returns warnings; return [] means none. B's filter selects declarations and map produces one finding per match.

Level 0 is pure computation; level 1 is declared deterministic inputs recorded in .jet/lock. Existing embed_file/embed_bytes/find snapshot inputs. The expression rules :: embed_file("rules.txt") reads a declared package-relative input, not arbitrary fs.read. Hook level 1 excludes network, including pinned fetch. This is explicitly narrower than general metaprogramming.

Steps are deterministic metaprogram evaluator operations under D-PREP-FUEL1. Package maximum and #StepLimit raises retain that contract; no new limit spelling is added. Ambient clock/random/files/network and #Impure are forbidden. Meta.Generate denial blocks additive output.

Jet's own sandbox uses the shared runner. Powers require granted handles; native compile-time machine code is checked before execution. No separate engine/carrier/protocol remains.

Dependencies hold until the root grants their printed jet trust identity. Source/dependency/stage/power/input-authority changes re-prompt with a diff. Compiler-only upgrades rebuild code/cache, not approval. Root hooks run directly within identical ceilings. CI fails with the exact missing grant, not omits checks.

Cache identity includes code, read inputs, full bodies/spans, payload/compiler identity and grants. Trust precedes reuse; revoked/stale grants cannot replay results. Per-item reuse requires unchanged inputs; whole-program hooks rerun when snapshots change. Actual cost appears in jet build --timings; sample figures are illustrative.

Stage-local identities govern merging, not priority. Identical values deduplicate; contradictions/overlapping edits error naming contributors. Presentation follows priority/package/declaration order. Authors still learn stage types, results and trust, but no separate plugin system.
decisions.story: Mia's team bans print in library code. Today she must build a separate compiled plugin outside Jet and set an environment variable on every developer machine and CI job. She wants to write the rule in Jet, next to her other metaprograms.
decisions.detail:
Owner question q47892zx asks for hooks integrated with metaprogramming and Jet's own sandbox. Both alternatives answer unconditionally: ordinary #On Jet functions use the same compile-time runner as markers/prep, with no external plugin engine. The old post-check plugin and JET_COMPILER_EXTENSION retire. Execution architecture independently supplies the baseline runner and native-code isolation check; hooks do not retain a fallback engine while that cutover is voted.

The choice is breadth, not execution technology: A publishes the whole typed table; B publishes only compiler.checked. D-HOOK-ONE1/A already chooses typed #On attachments. This ballot changes the old D-DX5-HOOK1 carrier, not its read-only/checker-authority intent. D-META-USER1, D-MARKER-LAW1, D-META-PUBLISH2 and D-META-GATE1 govern fact reads, additive publication, provenance and denied powers. D-META-CONTROL2/OPTIN2 change-set reconciliation remains D-META-RECONCILE1; directive 23 allows that reconciliation and forbids new AST-report proposals. None are adopted here.

A's CompilerStage mapping is explicit: compiler.parsed -> Parsed; compiler.declared -> Resolved; added-item checking/ordinary preparation passes through Typed/Prepared; compiler.checked is the validated post-Prepared snapshot; compiler.emitted -> Emitted. Hook modules are compiled first without self/closure inspection; cycles error rather than using an incomplete hook. The stage table determines which facts are available, and no stage promises future facts.

Merge rules in the technical table specify all public results. Step exhaustion is E0952, assertion failure E0953, malformed or cap-exceeding output E1402 naming the hook, package, cap and actual count. Per invocation at most 256 findings and 64 proposed edits; the 257th finding or 65th edit rejects the invocation, not truncates it. Failed invocations produce no accepted partial results and are never cached. Findings are L1401 under the package-qualified hook/lint identity; policy deny converts them to E1293.

Grant identity includes source/dependency closure, stage, result powers and declared-input authority; compiler versions invalidate compiled code, not human approval. Cache identity separately includes compiler/payload schema identity and actual granted scope. Revocation disables both execution and cached results. Declared file contents invalidate results without silently adding file-read authority. Package-owned hooks obey effect/sandbox rules even when no dependency prompt applies.

Asset requests enter the one BuildPlan graph and use its dependency/cycle validation. Asset hooks inspect original graph assets once; returned replacements/additions are not recursively fed to the same hook pipeline. Formatter output is for declared non-Jet kinds; it cannot rewrite Jet source through a formatting side door. Editor edits require selection. Added docs and hovers remain presentation outputs, not compiler validity powers.

Attack on A: one runner does not make a broad public stage surface free. B is genuinely easier to stabilize, and evidence from Kotlin KSP supports stable APIs, not publishing every moment. A remains recommended because the owner wants compiler/tool integration and the typed table supplies per-item checks, additive generation and tool moments without a second mechanism. Payloads can evolve independently only when their dependencies permit; there is no promise of version immunity. Publishing all of A commits to every named point now, not a deferred subset.

options.name: Named stages, run as compile-time Jet
options.detail: Publish every typed point in the table, attached with #On and run by the marker/prep runner. Hook modules are discovered in package sources and listed by jet inspect hooks; self/support-closure inspection and cycles are forbidden. Root hooks run directly within the common ceilings; dependency hooks need grants. A commits to more payloads, cache invalidation sites and debugging surfaces. Separate typed payloads localize changes only where dependencies permit, not guarantee isolation from every future API change.
options.technical:
Compiler stage table, payload -> output. compiler.parsed(File): syntax -> findings. compiler.declared(Declaration): resolved signature/body/direct named calls/spans -> findings and added items. compiler.checked(CheckedProgram): validated program -> findings and proposed edits. compiler.emitted(Artifact): read-only artifact -> findings.

Build/tool table. build.planned(BuildPlan): graph -> findings and asset requests. build.asset(Asset): original asset -> replacement or added assets. fmt.file(File): declared non-Jet kind -> formatted text. lsp.code_actions(ActionRequest) -> editor actions; lsp.hover(HoverRequest) -> notes. test.finished(TestReport) -> findings; doc.page(DocPage) -> sections. Types belong to core.compiler. Formatter-kind ownership is declared with attachment; different results conflict.

Merge identity: items by module/name, assets by normalized path, findings by package-qualified lint/span, edits by source revision/span. Overlapping edits conflict. Docs key by page/section ID, hovers by request/location/note ID, actions by request/action ID, formatted text by file/revision/kind.

Distinct IDs coexist in deterministic order. Identical values deduplicate; different values at one identity error naming contributors. Invalid combined generated code reports publication provenance, not selects one hook.

Stages run once. Added items pass ordinary checking/publication, appear in checked, and never return to declared. Edits never apply during builds. Graph outputs use existing cycle/provenance rules. Advanced changes stay outside this contract awaiting D-META-RECONCILE1.

Runner: marker/prep runner, levels 0/file-only 1, existing prep limits and Meta policy. Deterministic-input APIs snapshot declared files and record locks. No external engine/carrier. Atomic caps are in detail. Code caches include compiler version. Result caches include payload/compiler identity, code, bodies/spans/files and grants. Trust precedes replay.

options.name: One checked stage now, more by later votes
options.detail:
Only the shared work: the existing post-check moment becomes the typed point compiler.checked, attached with #On and run as compile-time Jet like any marker body. The environment variable and the plugin protocol retire, as under A. Grants, inputs, limits, merging and caching follow the same rules as A for this one stage. Every further stage needs its own ballot.

B's case: the smallest payload surface to keep stable, the lesson of Kotlin's move from compiler plugins to KSP, with fewer invalidation sites and one place to debug. Its cost: the only moment is the whole checked program, so a per-declaration rule reruns on every program edit, and generators, asset hooks and editor hooks wait.
options.technical: Publishes one point, compiler.checked(CheckedProgram), with findings and proposed edits, carrying D-DX5-HOOK1's read capabilities as its payload. Registration is #On in source. Runner, limits, grants, declared inputs, failure handling, merge identity and the whole-snapshot cache key follow A's technical note. JET_COMPILER_EXTENSION becomes an error whose fix names the #On form. Any other compiler stage name is an error naming the ballot that would add it.
options.code:
// lint_rules/no_print.jet: the same rule over the whole checked program
use core.compiler

#On(compiler.checked)
fn no_print_in_lib(p: compiler.CheckedProgram) -> [compiler.Finding] {
    p.declarations
        .filter(d -> (d.module == "lib" || d.module.starts_with("lib.")) && d.calls.contains("print"))
        .map(d -> compiler.finding(d, "print in library code"))
}

// grant as under A: jet check names the jet trust grant
$ jet check
Warning [L1401] (no_print_in_lib): print in library code
  --> lib/report.jet:12:5
$ jet build --timings
hooks: no_print_in_lib 41 ms (whole program; reruns on any edit)   // illustrative figures

comparisons.note: A stable symbol API replaced internal compiler plugins (kotlinlang.org/docs/ksp-overview.html).
A compile-time program in the same language receives compiler messages for each phase. [INFERENCE: recalled from the Jai beta material, not re-read this session.]

recommendation.why: A publishes the requested compiler and tool moments as one typed metaprogramming surface, allowing per-item checks and additive generation without a second plugin system. Authors still learn stage types and trust; B's smaller stability commitment remains a real alternative.
gains: Lint rules and generators in plain Jet, at the moment they need.
One metaprogramming system: hooks follow the rules marker bodies follow.
No dependency hook runs unasked.

losses.loss: A whole-program hook reruns on any program edit.
losses.mitigation: Per-file and per-declaration points cache per item, and --timings shows each hook's cost.

losses.loss: More hook stages to keep stable across releases.
losses.mitigation: Separate typed payloads localize change where dependencies permit; they do not guarantee that another stage or its consumers can never be affected.

whyNot.reason: B is the smaller, easier-to-stabilize surface, with the same runner and rules for one stage. But per-declaration caching, generators and tool hooks each wait for another vote, and whole-program reruns are the only choice meanwhile.

recommendation.tradeoff: A larger hook surface in exchange for rules that run at the right moment and cache per item.

reviewPasses.beginner: Fresh agent: QsBeginner. Skill: rli5. The beginner pass tested the complete ballot. Repaired: stage-dependent generation, lib/liberty parity, lifecycle/discovery, trust glossary, all merge identities and cap errors; B's stability case retained.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: claude-opus. Adversarial model family: gpt. Fresh agent: QsAdversary. The adversarial review attacked the recommendation. Repaired: no retired-engine references, revocation-safe schema/grant cache keys, hook dependency cycles, asset feedback ceiling and atomic caps; A retained.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Reader evidence and disposition are in D-HOOK-STAGES1's three review files: QsBeginner, QsAdversary and repairs. Docs only; no Tower writes. Vote D-META-RECONCILE1 first.

Shared acceptance: #On uses the marker/prep runner and Jet's own sandbox. Pure/declared-file work obeys step limits/Meta policy. Retire carrier/protocol/variable; JET_COMPILER_EXTENSION errors naming #On. Dependencies hold pending trust. Source/dependency/stage/power/input-authority changes re-prompt; compiler-only upgrades do not. Revocation blocks replay. E0952/E0953 stops are uncached. Malformed/257-findings/65-edits produce atomic E1402, not partial output.

A publishes every table point. No-print matches lib/lib.* but not liberty, through direct resolved calls only; function-value calls are outside this detector. Deny gives E1293. Isolated body edits rerun their declaration when no other read fingerprint changes. Any whole-snapshot change reruns checked hooks. Cached/uncached results agree per tier; backend bytes may differ.

Test support cycles, generation visibility/no feedback, asset graph cycles/no repeated processing and every merge identity. Include identical dedup, contradictory doc/hover IDs, overlapping edits, atomic caps, denied powers and revoked-cache replay. Edits never apply at build. B accepts only checked results and rejects generation/absent stages. Implement the entire option, not a subset.

decisions.title: Where the row policy check and display live
decisions.situation: A row policy is a database rule such as "a user may only see tickets they own". Jet builds that rule with the database library. The only way to test one rule against a user, or to print it, sits in the sync library. That copy shares a type name with an unrelated permission list and is being removed, so programs lose both abilities. The vote picks their new home; we recommend two small functions beside the existing database policy function.
decisions.gist: Where should code check a database row policy against a user and print it?
decisions.lesson: A row policy is a database rule that hides rows a user may not see. The database library already builds one with db.policy. Checking a single row by hand and printing the rule are only possible through a sync library copy that is being removed. Whichever option wins, queries keep enforcing the policy automatically.
decisions.story: Priya writes a help-desk app where each user sees only their own tickets. She builds the rule with db.policy and wants a quick test that alice cannot read bob's ticket, plus a readable print of the rule in her logs.
decisions.inWild:
CREATE POLICY own ON tickets USING (owner = current_user);
-- https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/ddl-rowsecurity.html
decisions.detail:
D-DBPOLICY1=A puts per-row access rules in core.db. There, db.policy compiles a checked RowPolicy, and every query, mutation and live path satisfies it or gets a generated filter.

The core library reference documents the core.sync RowPolicy as a closed allow/deny action policy. The runtime leaves (Prelude/Sync.rs) and the tooling/sync_crdt example instead use an owner == user row policy through core.sync.

Restoring the documented core.sync surface removes that row-policy copy. Then core.db has only policy and policy_audit. GoldenW2b and GoldenFix13 found this on 2026-10-07.

options.name: Two database functions
options.detail: Add core.db.policy_allows(policy, user:, owner:) -> Bool and core.db.policy_show(policy) -> String with the same meaning and output as the current runtime leaves. core.sync keeps only its documented action policy.
options.technical: Move the existing Prelude leaves from core.sync rows to core.db rows; the sync_crdt example imports core.db for the policy lines.
options.code:
print(db.policy_show(policy))
print(db.policy_allows(policy, user: "alice", owner: "bob"))

options.name: Methods on the policy
options.detail: RowPolicy gains a Display form and an allows method.
options.technical: Display impl plus a method row on RowPolicy in both compiler halves.
options.code:

print(policy.allows(user: "alice", owner: "bob"))

options.name: Queries only
options.detail: No direct check or display; examples observe policies through scoped queries and policy_audit, and the sync example's expected output changes.
options.technical: Delete the runtime leaves; migrate the example.
options.code: print(db.policy_audit(scope))

comparisons.note: Row policies live with the database; their text is readable from the catalog. https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/ddl-rowsecurity.html

recommendation.why: It keeps every row policy ability in the database library, matches its existing function style, and preserves today's behavior and output exactly.
gains: One library owns building, checking and printing a row policy.

losses.loss: Two new public function names.
losses.mitigation: They replace the removed sync copies one for one, so the total surface does not grow.

whyNot.reason: B mixes method and free-function styles in one library and hides printing inside interpolation.
C removes a simple check people use in tests and forces a database scope for every rule test.

recommendation.tradeoff: Two new names in the database library; the same two names leave the sync library.
