decisions.title: Whether the portable sandbox's walls depend on the compiler being bug-free
decisions.situation: A Jet app file is one portable program that any machine checks, compiles and runs inside sealed walls, the way WebAssembly runs code. Today the plan trusts the machine's own compiler to build those walls correctly, so a compiler bug could let an app escape. Another engine's compiler had exactly such a bug, rated 9.9 out of 10. The vote decides whether a small checker inspects the final machine code before it runs; we recommend yes, so the walls hold even when the compiler is wrong.
decisions.gist: Should the host check an app's final machine code before running it, so compiler bugs cannot break the walls?
decisions.lesson: The walls, or isolation, keep an app inside its own memory and away from anything the host did not grant. The host already verifies the app file and grants each power. Whichever option wins, safety inside the app and the same answers as a native build still rest on Jet's compiler and its tests.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. An app file (`.jetapp`) holds checked portable Jet code. The host is the machine that runs it. The walls, or isolation, mean the app can touch only its own memory and the handles the host gave it. Machine code is what the host's compiler produces from the app file. A side channel is a way to leak secrets through chip timing, such as Spectre.

Beginner path: nothing changes. `jet run notes.jetapp` asks for powers and runs the app.

Expert path: hosts that run several untrusted apps in one process turn on side-channel hardening with one host setting; one app per process relies on the operating system's process walls.
decisions.story: Omar runs other people's plugins inside his note app. One plugin triggers a rare bug in the host's compiler. Under today's plan that bug can let the plugin read his notes; with a final-code check, the plugin is refused before it runs.
decisions.detail:
Source: RESEARCH.md revision 2 ($JET_STATE_ROOT/scratch/ExecArch1), section 4.7, and owner decisions 7 to 9. The adversarial audit's blocking finding 10 showed that 'validation removes the optimizer from the trusted base' is true only for the walls. It does not hold for safety inside the app or for keeping the same answers.

Jet today. D-PORTABLE1=A ratified the Jet sandbox. The app file holds a versioned portable encoding of MIR. The host verifies structure, types, memory safety, control flow and host calls, and grants powers through unforgeable handles held in its own trust store.

D-PORTABLE1's trusted base names the verifier, the runtime and its broker, the native compiler and its cache. It explicitly does not promise protection from bugs in them, or from side channels such as Spectre. It starts a first run in an interpreter while native code compiles.

D-EXEC2=A later retired the interpreter once native in-memory O0 lands. So under both options here, the first run uses quick native code compiled on arrival. D-HOST-CAPS1 (open, proposed A) makes hardware such as tensor cores visible as build facts. A hardware fact never grants a power; only host handles do.

Evidence. Crocus (ASPLOS 2024) reproduced a 9.9 of 10 CVE in Cranelift's lowering rules, a real compiler bug that broke WebAssembly isolation. Native Client (2009) validated x86 code before running it, at under 5% (ARM) and 7% (x86-64) run-time cost for its fault-isolation scheme (Sehr et al. 2010).

VeriWasm (NDSS 2021) checks the native code Lucet produced, so the compiler leaves the isolation trusted base. Its disassembler and control-flow builder stay trusted. It does not check indirect-call types and allows some reads Wasm would not.

Swivel (USENIX Security 2021) shows that side-channel hardening costs depend strongly on the threat model. Process isolation is the common alternative.

What A requires. The compiler emits code in a checkable shape: memory accesses within the app's region or through checked handles, jumps only to known targets, and host calls only through the broker. A published checker validates each compiled function and refuses the app on any failure.

Checked code is cached by app hash, host, compiler, checker version and policy, as D-PORTABLE1 already keys its cache. Checker cost is unmeasured for Jet. A gauntlet cell for bundle start-up and steady speed measures it before ratification of the checker design.

Edge cases under both options. Hosts that forbid making code at run time, such as iOS apps, get a native copy built and signed ahead of time by the host's operator. Under A, the checker runs on that copy too. In browsers, apps still export to WebAssembly and WebGPU (D-WASISRV1, D-PORTABLE1) and inherit their limits.

options.name: Check the final machine code
options.detail: Before an app runs, the host checks the compiled machine code against the wall rules. Memory accesses stay in the app's region or go through handles, jumps go only to known places, and host calls go only through the broker. A compiler bug can then make the app wrong, but cannot let it out. Hosts that run several untrusted apps in one process turn on side-channel hardening.
options.technical:
Amends D-PORTABLE1's trusted base. For isolation, the trusted parts become the verifier, the machine-code checker, the runtime and broker, and the loader; the native compiler is untrusted. For memory safety inside the app and for same-answer behaviour, the compiler stays trusted and is covered by D-EXEC3's rule proofs, checkers and example runs.

Adds a host policy for side channels: `isolate: process` (default; one app per process) or `isolate: shared` with side-channel hardening. The checker spec, its admissible machine-code shape and its cost cells land before the checker is built.

decisions.title: How Jet's build levels share speed-ups, check them, and choose which examples rerun
decisions.situation: Jet builds a program at three levels: quick runs while you work, everyday builds, and the fastest release builds. They share one runtime and one checked program, but nothing says which speed-ups each level shares or how a level-only speed-up shows it keeps the meaning. Nothing says which examples a change must rerun either, so some changes merge without running a level at all. The vote sets those rules; we recommend shared speed-ups, proved or checked level-only ones, and rerunning exactly the examples whose build changed.
decisions.gist: How should Jet's build levels share speed-ups, check level-only ones, and choose which examples a change reruns?
decisions.lesson: A level is how hard the compiler works: O0 for quick runs, O1 for everyday builds, O2 for release. A golden example is a saved program with its expected output. Whichever option wins, every example still runs on every level before each milestone, and running out of stack or memory is a separate vote.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A level, or tier, is one way of building. O0 serves `jet run`, `jet dev` and compile-time code, O1 serves `jet build`, and O2 serves `jet build --release`. Compile-time code runs while the program is being built. The web is a level too, where a feature applies.

The runtime is the built-in library every program calls, such as `print` and lists. A speed-up, or optimization, rewrites the checked program so it does less work. A shared speed-up is one piece of compiler code that every level runs; a level-only speed-up runs on some levels.

A rewrite rule replaces one small pattern with an equal one, such as `x * 2` with `x + x`. A proof of a rule is a machine-checked argument that the rule never changes the answer. A checker is a small program that inspects one compiler result and refuses it when it is wrong. A golden example is a saved program with its expected output; passing examples is regression evidence, not proof.

A milestone is the point where finished work joins the released line, after one full test run of everything. In the example, `sum(1..=10)` adds the whole numbers 1 through 10, giving 55. `jet build --release sum.jet` makes a program file and `./sum` runs it.

Beginner path: nothing to write. With enough stack and memory, `jet run`, `jet build` and `jet build --release` print the same output.

Expert path: `-O0`, `-O1` and `-O2` still pick a level. `jet inspect passes` lists every speed-up with its levels and its evidence: proved, checked or tested. It also lists what each proof or checker covers and what it does not.
decisions.story: Priya adds a speed-up that only release builds use. She wants to know before merging whether it can change any program's output. She also wants her change to rerun only the examples it can affect, not every example at every level.
decisions.detail:
Source: the owner's execution requirements (a) to (f), relayed by Main on 2026-10-07. Tiers must not be able to differ, without running every test on every tier. Every tier must be as fast as possible. A hardware-agnostic optimizer is shared by all tiers, and release adds hardware-specific work.

Research: $JET_STATE_ROOT/scratch/ExecArch1/RESEARCH.md revision 2, after two audits (AUDIT-adversary.md, AUDIT-Verifier.md). Fresh reviews of this ballot: review/D-EXEC3-ExecReaderBeginner.md and review/D-EXEC3-ExecReaderAdversary.md, repaired as listed in review/D-EXEC3-repairs.md. Section numbers below refer to RESEARCH.md.

Jet today. D-EXEC1=A ratified one runtime and one Jet code generator with O0, O1 and O2, with LLVM first for O2. D-EXEC2=A retired the Cranelift JIT; until native O0 lands, `jet run` and `jet dev` build and then run. D-TIER-FORM1=A and D-TIER-ONEIR1=A give every back end one checked MIR from one semantic lowering.

I5 requires every feature example to prove the same meaning on every applicable tier. I9 requires one executable meaning, compiled once into one runtime that code generators only call. AGENTS.md runs each card's narrow proof after integration and one composed sweep per milestone. No rule says which examples a change must rerun.

Already settled, so not on this ballot. D-ADAPTIVE-TIER1=B covers run-time re-optimization. D-SIMD3=B, D-CPU-DISPATCH1=A and D-COMPUTE-BACKEND1=D keep floating point bit-identical except under named recorded profiles. D-RTFAIL1=A and D-FAIL-BREACH1=A fix one report text and trace shape per failure on every tier. D-PORTABLE1=A fixes the portable form as MIR. D-BACKEND-OWN1 (open) decides whether Jet O2 replaces LLVM.

Not voted here. Which technology builds O0 (the Jet selector, a template baseline or copy-and-patch) is an implementation choice under D-EXEC1, measured on a real corpus. Copy-and-patch would need build-time clang or LLVM, which then needs its own ballot under the no-Rust directive. Running out of stack or memory is D-RESOURCE-LIMIT1; its I9 text starts with the same parity sentence as this one.

Finding 1, sharing (3.1). Sharing removes the duplication class of tier bugs: copied runtimes and per-engine lowering. CPython reports its JIT-only bugs were in the shared micro-op optimizer, not the copy-and-patch step (PEP 744). A shared bug agrees on every level, so differential runs cannot see it; golden outputs, as an independent oracle, can.

Finding 2, proof tools are bounded (3.1, 4.4). Alive2 (PLDI 2021) caught 29 of 36 known LLVM miscompilations. It checks one function at a time, had no function pointers and supported 21% of intrinsics. Crocus verified Cranelift AArch64 integer lowering rules and reproduced a 9.9 of 10 CVE, but trusts other passes and the runtime. regalloc2's checker validates register moves, not scheduling or calling conventions.

So proofs and checkers reduce risk without replacing whole-program runs. Every stage is therefore labelled proved, checked or tested, with its covered properties.

Finding 3, rerunning exactly what changed. A level's output for an example depends only on the example's checked program after shared speed-ups, that level's compiler, the runtime, the target and the build settings. If none of these changed and the build is reproducible, the result is the same program, so its earlier pass still stands. Reproducibility is already required for trusted cache outputs (D-JPK-REPROCACHE1=D); a rerun skip uses only such outputs.

A shared change that alters an example's checked program reruns that example on every level, which closes the gap a touched-files rule would leave (adversary 2). Milestone sweeps rebuild and rerun everything from scratch, which catches cache or reproducibility defects.

Finding 4, budgets (5.1). One optimizer output at every level would make the first quick run pay release cost, or cap release at quick-run cost. So levels share pass code and differ in budget. Running a shared pass longer at O2 is not a level-only speed-up.

Finding 5, the runtime boundary (4.1). Opaque runtime calls hide work from the optimizer. A adds an I9 clause letting levels inline runtime functions, but only from the runtime's own source and version. They must keep its allocation, traps, cleanup, captures and termination, and never rewrite its policy.

Finding 6, heavy search (4.5). Cranelift's e-graph pipeline gained about 2% run time for 7 to 8% more compile time, and keeping alternative forms gained about 0.1%. Superoptimizers search for seconds to hours per fragment. Under A they run offline to find rules, or at release within budgets counted in deterministic fuel, after a paired measurement shows a win.

Finding 7, optimality (3.2, 3.3). The claim that no faster organization exists cannot be computed (Rice) and is undefined without a hardware cost model. A promises a monotone reduction in named work counters. Each result is labelled completed or stopped by fuel. Removed drops are dead or redundant only; observable cleanup is preserved. Each gauntlet cell reports its measured fraction of a stated hardware bound, and matched peer cells stay the gate.

Scope of parity. It covers every applicable tier: O0, O1 and O2, and compile-time code, which uses the target's layout, not the host's. It also covers the web adapter where a feature applies, and portable apps compiled on arrival. Programs whose `#Unsafe` blocks break their stated obligations are not compared; sentries and hardened profiles report them under their own law.

Concurrent examples compare the output their contract fixes, not one interleaving. Foreign callbacks, task ordering, ownership and drop paths, and failures during cleanup each get named example families.

Costs of A. A level-only speed-up waits until its proof or checker exists. Proofs, models and checkers need upkeep when rules or targets change. The runtime keeps an inlining interface. The pass registry and the input-hash record must be maintained. Optimizing O0 can hide variables in the debugger, so O0 shared speed-ups must keep source stepping and variable visibility.

Right ways elsewhere. One instruction definition generates both interpreter and JIT (CPython, Deegen). Lowering rules are checked (ISLE with Crocus), and a checker runs after register allocation (regalloc2; CompCert validates allocation). Bazel reruns only actions whose inputs changed. Wrong ways: per-engine runtimes (Jet's old Cranelift engine, about 130,000 duplicated lines per D-EXEC1's text). Unchecked compiler facts: Rust disabled mutable-reference noalias from 2018 to 2021 after LLVM miscompilations.

options.name: Shared speed-ups, checked extras, rerun what changed
options.detail: Every level runs the same shared speed-ups, written once. A speed-up that only some levels run needs a proved rule or a checker on each result; an unproved rule never ships. A change reruns an example on a level exactly when that level's build of it changed, and keeps the earlier pass otherwise. Every milestone rebuilds and reruns every example on every level. Release picks hardware-specific code only among choices proved equal.
options.technical:
Amends I5: "Every feature has an example with golden-tested output. Each change reruns an example on each applicable tier whose build inputs for it changed. Those inputs are the checked program after shared passes, the tier's compiler, the runtime, the target and the settings. Every milestone and cutover rebuilds and reruns every example on every applicable tier."

Amends I9 by adding: "Programs run with enough stack and memory print identical output, exit status and reports on every applicable tier. Tiers share one checked MIR, one runtime and one implementation of each shared pass. A transform only some tiers run is a proved rule or passes a recorded checker. Any other stage is tested and labelled so."

"An unknown or timed-out proof keeps a rule out. A checker that cannot handle its input is a Jet defect, never a pass. Tiers may inline runtime functions only from the runtime's source and version, keeping its allocation, traps, cleanup, captures and termination." This replaces I9's call-only wording.

Jet-generated selectors (O0, O1 and any future Jet O2) come from shared lowering rules. Today's O2 emits LLVM IR from Jet rules; LLVM's own passes stay an external stage, tested by examples and by Alive2 runs in CI that are known to be bounded.

Adds one inspect view, `jet inspect passes`, beside the existing `jet inspect` views. Performance claims follow detail finding 7. Unchanged: D-EXEC2, D-ADAPTIVE-TIER1, D-SIMD3, D-RTFAIL1, D-PORTABLE1, D-BACKEND-OWN1, and the O0 technology choice.
options.code:
fn run() { print(sum(1..=10)) }   // adds 1 through 10
$ jet run sum.jet                       # O0: shared speed-ups
55
$ jet build --release sum.jet && ./sum  # O2: shared + proved extras
55
// a change reruns this example only where its build changed

options.name: Keep the current plan
options.detail: Add no rule. I5 and I9 stay as written. Each card's proof picks its own examples, and the milestone sweep runs every example on every level. A level may add a speed-up that only examples check.
options.technical: No amendment to I5, I9 or D-EXEC1. Current cadence per AGENTS.md: a narrow proof per card after integration and one composed sweep per milestone. The O0 technology choice stays an implementation choice, as under A.
options.code:
fn run() { print(sum(1..=10)) }   // adds 1 through 10
$ jet run sum.jet                       # O0
55
$ jet build --release sum.jet && ./sum  # O2

// which examples a change reruns is chosen per card

options.name: Check every compile instead of rerunning examples
options.detail: Every build checks each compiled function against its checked program with a sound checker. Anything the checker cannot handle fails the build. Examples run on every level only at milestones. How hard each level searches for speed-ups is a separate question, left as under A.
options.technical: Amends I5 to replace per-change example runs with per-build translation validation of every function, failing closed. Examples run on every applicable tier at milestones. Needs validators covering all of Jet's MIR, the runtime boundary, ABI, concurrency and the LLVM path before it can be switched on; until then builds of unsupported programs fail.
options.code:
fn run() { print(sum(1..=10)) }   // adds 1 through 10
$ jet build --release sum.jet
  check   every function shown equal to its checked program
$ ./sum

decisions.title: How deep recursion and running out of memory behave on each build level
decisions.situation: When a function calls itself, each waiting call holds a little memory called stack, and too many at once runs it out. Quick runs keep more in each call than release builds, which can even turn the calls into a loop. So one program can stop with a stack-overflow report in a quick run yet finish in a release build. Jet's rule that every level means the same thing says nothing about this. The vote decides how deep recursion behaves on each level; we recommend that a declared depth is exact everywhere and an undeclared one depends on the machine.
decisions.gist: How should deep recursion and running out of memory behave across quick runs and release builds?
decisions.lesson: The stack is the memory running function calls use; deep recursion fills it. Jet stops an overflow with a registered report. A ratified mark, `#MaxDepth(n)`, states how deep a function may recurse, but nothing yet says whether that limit is enforced. Whichever option wins, programs with enough memory give the same output on every level.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A call frame is the slice of stack one waiting call needs. Recursion means a function calls itself. In the example, `depth(n)` calls `depth(n - 1)` until n reaches 0, so `depth(2)` has three calls waiting at its deepest point: for 2, 1 and 0. A quick run (O0, used by `jet run`) keeps every value in its frame. A release build (O2, `jet build --release`) keeps values in registers, which are the processor's own small storage, and can turn recursion into a loop.

The heap is where lists and text live. Ambient memory is whatever the machine gives the program; a budget is a fixed amount the program sets itself, such as a fixed-size arena. A plain allocation that fails stops the program, as today. A `try_` allocation, such as `list.try_push(x)`, returns an error value the program can handle.

Beginner path: nothing to write. A program with enough stack and memory prints the same output on every level. When a quick run or everyday build runs out of stack, it stops with the stack-overflow report.

Expert path: write `#MaxDepth(n)` on a deep recursive function. It means at most n calls of that function wait at once, counting the first call. Under A, every level then reserves room for n calls and stops the call after n with the same report. `jet inspect memory app.jet` shows, per entry point and level, the stack needed, the stack requested and the stack actually granted.
decisions.story: Sam writes a recursive JSON walker. His tests pass in a release build, but `jet run` on a deeply nested file stops with a stack overflow. He cannot tell whether his program is wrong, or how deep it may safely go on every level.
decisions.inWild:
# Python: a configured recursion limit
import sys
sys.getrecursionlimit()   # 1000 by default
# deeper calls raise RecursionError
# docs: the safe maximum is platform-dependent
decisions.detail:
Source: RESEARCH.md revision 2 ($JET_STATE_ROOT/scratch/ExecArch1), sections 3.1 and 6.3, and its owner decision 2. Fresh reviews: review/D-RESOURCE-LIMIT1-ExecReaderBeginner.md and review/D-RESOURCE-LIMIT1-ExecReaderAdversary.md, with repairs listed in review/D-RESOURCE-LIMIT1-repairs.md. This ballot and D-EXEC3 share one parity rule, quoted in both.

Probe. A C program with fully defined behavior was built with clang 21.1.8 and an 8 MiB stack. It overflowed at depth 74,446 at -O0. At -O2 it finished 50,000,000 levels with the correct value, because the compiler turned the recursion into a loop. A sanitizer build overflowed at 130,283. This shows that levels can differ; it is not a Jet limit or ratio. Receipts: ExecArch1/tierdiff.log.

Jet today, as implemented. E3012 is the registered runtime report `Stack overflow in {fn}` (Compiler/JetFoundation/Source/Registry/DiagnosticRows.jet). `jet run` builds and then runs the program, until native in-memory O0 lands (D-EXEC2=A).

Jet today, ratified but not yet built. D-STACKBOUND1=A computes worst-case stack per entry point from each target's frame sizes and the sealed call graph. It enforces `!Mem.Stack(above: N)` and needs `#MaxDepth(n)` on recursion to compute that bound. It does not say how depth is counted or what happens past n; this ballot settles that. `#MaxDepth` is not yet registered in Syntax.rs, and this ballot adds no new spelling.

Other law this ballot keeps. D-RTFAIL1=A and D-REPORT-LAW1=A require one registered report with the same text and trace shape on every tier. S36 sends program stops through one report and cleanup boundary. D-ALLOCFAIL1=A keeps the hosted abort for plain allocation and makes `try_` allocation return an ordinary AllocError. D-FIXED-BACKING1 makes fixed-backing allocation fail atomically at its capacity, with no heap fallback.

The shared parity rule, quoted in D-EXEC3 and in A here. Programs run with enough stack and memory must print identical output, exit status and reports on every applicable level. A run that exhausts ambient stack or memory may stop at a different point on different levels. Its report code is the same, and everything it printed before stopping is a prefix of what the complete run prints.

The rule never excuses a wrong value, a different non-resource error, different output before the stop, or a changed budget failure. Goldens run with granted resources; exhaustion has its own fixtures, compared by report code and the prefix rule.

Runaway recursion. A release build may turn recursion into a loop, as clang did in the probe. Then a recursion that never ends does not overflow; it runs like an endless loop. Under A, only O2 may remove recursive calls, so `jet run`, `jet dev` and `jet build` always stop it with E3012. A marked function stops at n+1 on every level. Under B, the counter stops it at the limit on every level.

Stack sizing under A. Each level sizes stacks from its own frames, as it compiles, so a quick run never waits for a release build. A marked function's need is D-STACKBOUND1's worst case on that level's actual call graph, plus call, runtime and cleanup overhead. An unmarked program's quick run gets a larger default stack. That is a risk reduction, not a guarantee.

Where the room comes from. On hosted Linux, macOS and Windows, the runtime switches the entry point onto a larger stack on the same operating-system thread. Thread identity, thread-local data and main-thread-only APIs are unaffected; Windows also updates the thread's recorded stack bounds. Signals use their own alternate stack. Embedded and interrupt entries keep D-STACKBOUND1's static `!Mem.Stack` check and never grow.

Browsers and wasm engines own the stack: a marked depth beyond the engine's published minimum is refused at build time. Tasks get a stack sized from their own entry point. Room is reserved address space committed on use, so many tasks cost address space before memory.

Outcomes when room is short. If the platform cannot ever give the declared room, the build fails with a registered error naming the depth, the need and the limit. If the room cannot be reserved when the entry or task starts, a registered start-up stop fires before any of its code runs. If an admitted guarantee is still broken, that is a Jet defect, exit 101.

Foreign code. A marked recursion whose cycle passes through foreign code is refused at build time, because foreign frames are outside the sealed call graph. A marked function called from a foreign thread's callback keeps its limit check but has no room guarantee, and a lint says so. Raw C callback restrictions are unchanged. `#Unsafe` sentries and hardened profiles add their own frame needs, which are included when that profile is built. A memory-safety fault is never treated as exhaustion.

Heap under A. Ambient memory is the machine's. A plain allocation that fails keeps today's hosted abort. A `try_` allocation against ambient memory may fail on one level and not another, but only under real memory pressure; goldens never run under pressure. A level may remove an ambient allocation it proves unused, which removes its chance to fail.

Budgets are part of meaning on every level: arenas, `mem.Fixed` backings and allocator limits. Allocations against a budget are never removed or merged in a way that changes what the budget counts, so a budget failure happens at the same call everywhere.

Reports and cleanup. The overflow report renders from reserved emergency room without allocating. Its trace collapses repeated recursive frames into one line without a count, so the trace shape matches across levels. It never prints a reached depth, because optimized levels cannot know it.

S36's cleanup boundary then runs on that reserved room. If cleanup itself runs out of room or memory, the program ends with the first report; the first fault wins. Under A, the marked-depth stop is identical on every level, including function name and source location.

Right ways elsewhere. Python fixes a configured recursion limit, raising RecursionError when it is reached. Its docs warn that the safe maximum is platform-dependent and too high a limit can crash (docs.python.org/3/library/sys.html). Java and Go never turn recursion into loops, so runaway recursion always overflows. Rust and C release builds may turn it into a loop.

Costs, unmeasured. A adds a counter only inside marked functions, and per-level frame sizing during compiles. B adds an increment, check and decrement on every call inside a recursive cycle, and reserves room for the default depth in every program. Neither cost is measured; a gauntlet pair cell measures B's counter before ratification of an implementation.

options.name: Declared depth exact, undeclared depth depends on the machine
options.detail: A program with enough room prints the same output on every level. Without a mark, the point where it runs out of stack may differ, and only release builds may turn recursion into a loop. So quick runs and everyday builds always stop runaway recursion with the report. With `#MaxDepth(n)`, every level reserves room for n waiting calls and stops the call after n with the same report, or refuses the build and says why. Budgets fail at the same call everywhere.
options.technical:
Adds to I9: "Programs run with enough stack and memory print identical output, exit status and reports on every applicable tier. A run that exhausts ambient stack or memory may stop at a different point on different tiers. Its report code is the same, and everything it printed before the stop is a prefix of the complete run's output. Allocator budgets are part of meaning. Only O2 may remove recursive calls."

Defines D-STACKBOUND1's `#MaxDepth(n)`. At most n activations of the marked function are live at once on one thread, counting the outermost. Depth 0 is invalid. Mutual recursion counts activations of the marked function only. The (n+1)th activation stops with a new registered depth-limit report, identical on every tier. Room for n activations is computed per tier from that tier's frames and reserved at entry or task start.

Refusals: a build error when the platform can never supply the room; a registered start-up stop when reservation fails at launch. A marked cycle through foreign code is a build error. Stacks grow by switching stacks on the same OS thread; embedded and web entries do not grow. The details are in the long-form detail.
options.code:
#MaxDepth(1000001)
fn depth(n: Int) -> Int { if n == 0 -> 0 else -> 1 + depth(n - 1) }
fn run() { print(depth(1000000)) }
$ jet run deep.jet
1000000
$ jet build --release deep.jet && ./deep
1000000

options.name: One depth limit for every recursive call
options.detail: Every call inside a recursive cycle counts against one limit of 100,000 waiting calls per thread, on every level, even where a release build turns the calls into a loop. A runaway recursion stops at exactly the same call everywhere. `#MaxDepth(n)` raises or lowers the limit for one function. Every program reserves room for its limit. Heap behaves as in A.
options.technical:
Adds the same I9 text as A, except that the depth stop is part of meaning: "every tier stops at the same activation".

A per-thread logical counter is incremented on entry to, and decremented on return from, functions in recursive cycles and dynamic calls that may recurse. Non-recursive calls are not counted, and removed recursion keeps the counter in a register. Default limit 100,000; `#MaxDepth(n)` overrides it per function.

Each tier reserves physical room for the limit from its own frames at entry or task start, with the same refusals as A. A program whose room cannot be reserved is refused before running, so the logical stop is never pre-empted by a physical one. Raw C callbacks on foreign threads cannot update the counter; Jet code reached from them is refused unless it is non-recursive.

options.name: Keep the current plan
options.detail: No rule is added. `#MaxDepth(n)` stays an input to stack reports only. Where a program runs out of stack or memory, and whether that breaks the one-meaning rule, stays unstated. Golden examples must avoid running out.
options.technical: No amendment to I9, D-STACKBOUND1 or D-ALLOCFAIL1. D-EXEC3's parity rule still says resource-adequate runs must match; exhaustion has no comparison rule.

comparisons.note: A configured recursion limit; docs warn the safe maximum is platform-dependent and too high a limit can crash. Source: docs.python.org/3/library/sys.html.
One defined program overflowed at depth 74,446 unoptimized and finished 50,000,000 levels optimized, because the optimizer made it a loop (RESEARCH.md 6.3).
comparisons.code:
$ clang -O0 t.c && ./a.out   # stack overflow at depth 74446
$ clang -O2 t.c && ./a.out   # finishes

recommendation.why: Ordinary calls stay free and quick runs still catch runaway recursion. A program that needs depth declares it once and gets the same result on every level.
gains: A declared depth is exact on every level, or refused before running.

losses.loss: Undeclared deep recursion can stop earlier in a quick run than in a release build.
losses.mitigation: Quick runs get a larger stack, and the overflow report explains `#MaxDepth(n)` for code that needs depth.

losses.loss: In a release build, runaway recursion may run forever instead of stopping.
losses.mitigation: `jet run`, `jet dev` and `jet build` always stop it, and a marked function stops on every level.

whyNot.reason: B counts recursive calls in every program and reserves room for a depth most programs never use.
C leaves the one-meaning rule silent exactly where levels differ.

recommendation.tradeoff: Undeclared depth depends on the machine; declared depth is exact everywhere.

Repairs: one parity rule shared with D-EXEC3, O2-only recursion removal, exact #MaxDepth counting, same-thread per-level stack sizing, refusals, budget and first-fault rules, and option C.

decisions.title: Web-style names: camelCase for functions, fields and variables
decisions.situation: Today Jet writes function, field and variable names in lowercase with underscores, such as fetch_user_profile and user_id. You asked for the most practical defaults across fields of work, leaning toward web development, where JavaScript, TypeScript, Kotlin, Swift and Go write these names in camelCase. You already decided that type names keep capital acronyms, such as TaskID, and that camelCase JSON keys write acronyms as words, such as userId. This vote decides how values are spelled in code. We recommend camelCase with acronyms in capitals, userID, so every Jet name follows one acronym rule while web data still reads userId.
decisions.gist: Should Jet values use camelCase, and should acronyms inside them read userID or userId?
decisions.lesson: camelCase capitalizes each word after the first: fetchUserProfile. snake_case joins lowercase words with underscores: fetch_user_profile. An acronym is a word of initials, such as ID or URL. Types keep capital acronyms under every option: HTTPClient, TaskID. camelCase JSON keys write acronyms as words, userId, as you already decided. The choice is how values look in code.
decisions.explainer:
Every option shows the same small program: one record type, one choice type, one constant and two functions. Types, markers, effects and enum cases stay PascalCase with capital acronyms in every option, as already ratified. Constants stay in full capitals. Shared work for A or B: one casing section in the spec, compiler checks with automatic fixes, and one rename of Jet's own code.

Under A, an acronym looks the same in every Jet name: TaskID the type, taskID the field, parseURL the function. Only a leading acronym is lowercase, as in urlText and httpClient, the Swift and Go rule. Two touching acronyms take the underscore type names already use: parseHTTP_URL, like HTTP_API.

JSON keys are computed, not copied. Under A, the field userID sends and reads the key userId, the web's usual spelling, because you ratified word-cased acronyms in data keys. A key spelled userID gets an error naming userId, and jet inspect shapes prints every outside name.

Under B, acronyms in values are written as words: userId, avatarUrl, parseHttpUrl. A field then matches its JSON key letter for letter. But a value and its type spell the acronym differently, taskId: TaskID, which is a second acronym rule. It also reverses your ratified note that Jet code keeps userID.

Under C, values keep underscores, and JSON keys default to snake_case unless a package asks for camelCase.
decisions.story: Kai builds a web service in Jet and its browser front end in TypeScript. The same record travels between them as JSON. He wants Jet names that read like the rest of his web code, one acronym rule to learn, and JSON keys his front end already expects.
decisions.detail:
Revision, 2026-10-10, by BallotPolishA. The owner ratified D-WIRE-CASE1=A and D-WIRE-ACRONYM1=A at 2026-10-07T20:23, about two hours after this ballot was posted. D-WIRE-ACRONYM1=A recommends "writing userId in data keys while Jet code keeps userID". Its option text says "Inside Jet code, acronyms stay fully capitalized." D-WIRE-CASE1=A's examples use camelCase fields with capital acronyms.

The posted A word-cased value acronyms and withdrew D-WIRE-ACRONYM1. That contradicts law ratified since, so the capital-acronym option now leads. Mapping: new A is the posted B; new B is the posted A; C is unchanged. Its detail now states that companion keys are computed under A, so A no longer carries the posted B's loss that a field "differs from common JSON keys" without a remedy.

Replaces D-CASE-LAW2 (OptionQuality1, 2026-10-07). D-CASE-LAW2's C, which also word-cased acronyms in types (HttpClient, Url), stays withdrawn: it reverses the owner's type rule.

Why A leads. D-ACRO-CASE1=A and the owner rule of 2026-09-30 (spec S66) put capital acronyms in every word of every type-like name. D-WIRE-ACRONYM1=A then decided camelCase data keys word-case acronyms while Jet code keeps userID. A completes that pair: one acronym rule for every Jet name, and computed keys for web data. B would give values a second acronym rule and reverse the ratified note.

Irreducible part. Given the owner's type rule and the web's word-cased keys, some pair must differ: either field and key (A) or field and type (B). A keeps Jet code on one rule and lets the ratified projection convert the 1.9% of fields that hold an acronym. The projection is exact in both directions, and a near-miss key names the expected one.

DECISION BOUNDARY

Owner direction, 2026-10-05, given after D-CASE-LAW1=A was ratified the same day. The owner has personal style preferences but ranks pragmatism higher: the best defaults and rules for the most domains at the greatest criticality. The owner added that naming seems most important in web development, so Jet should likely lean toward web conventions. D-CASE-LAW1 is ratified and immutable, so the re-vote is a new decision. Choosing C re-affirms D-CASE-LAW1=A unchanged.

This ballot changes only the case of value-like names. PascalCase stays for types, traits, enum variants, markers including their library part (#Server.Get), effects, unit families and generic type parameters. SCREAMING_SNAKE stays for module-level immutable bindings and compile-time number parameters. The closed acronym lexicon (D-ACRO-LEX1=A) and full-capital acronyms in type-like names (D-ACRO-CASE1=A) stand under every option. Foreign names stay verbatim inside binding modules (D-SHAPE-CASE2=A), so browser names such as innerHTML keep their spelling.

COMPANIONS

D-PATH-CASE2=A, D-WIRE-CASE1=A and D-WIRE-ACRONYM1=A are ratified and work unchanged under A. The path word key already reads userID, user_id and userId alike. Under B, D-WIRE-ACRONYM1's note that Jet code keeps userID would need an amendment. Under C, keys default to snake_case words per D-WIRE-CASE1's detail.

WHAT OPTION A SPELLS

camelCase covers functions, methods, fields, parameters, locals, labels, lint names, import aliases and module path segments. Most module segments are one lowercase word, so core.text.fmt is unchanged. Manifest keys in package.jet are fields, so they become camelCase, as in npm's package.json (devDependencies). Acronyms follow the Swift and Go rule. Inside a name they are fully capitalized: userID, avatarURL, parseURL. At the start they are fully lowercase: urlText, httpClient. Two touching acronyms keep D-ACRO-CASE1's underscore: parseHTTP_URL. Jet's own code has 43 such functions.

WHAT OPTION B SPELLS

Every word of a value, an acronym included, is capitalized like a word: userId, avatarUrl, parseHttpUrl, httpClient, utf8Bytes. No acronym list is consulted for values, and touching acronyms need no underscore. A value and its type then differ: taskId: TaskID.

RESEARCH: WHAT EACH ECOSYSTEM WRITES

TypeScript and JavaScript use camelCase functions, variables, properties and parameters, and PascalCase classes, types and components. Acronyms are split. The browser platform writes innerHTML, URLSearchParams and toISOString, but also getElementById and XMLHttpRequest. Airbnb 23.9 says acronyms are all upper or all lower case. Google's TypeScript guide word-cases them (loadHttpUrl) unless a platform name says otherwise.

JSON keys are camelCase in Google's JSON style guide, JSON:API's recommendation, Microsoft Graph and protobuf's JSON mapping, and those sources write acronyms as words: userId, webUrl. GitHub's GraphQL API sends avatarUrl and databaseId. Stripe, GitHub REST and Slack use snake_case.

Swift and Go write capital acronyms in values: userSMTPServer, appID. Kotlin and Google Java style word-case them: newCustomerId. C# and .NET write Id and Url. Dart word-cases acronyms longer than two letters.

snake_case values: Python (PEP 8), Rust (RFC 430), Ruby, Elixir, the C standard library, SQL by habit, Odin and Jai. Python keeps capital acronyms in class names and lowercase words in values, the same split option A keeps.

Swift's API Design Guidelines say acronyms that are all capitals in English are "uniformly up- or down-cased according to case conventions": utf8Bytes, isRepresentableAsASCII, userSMTPServer. Go's code review comments ask for capital initialisms such as appID and ServeHTTP, and its linters (golint, staticcheck ST1003) report userId.

POPULATION

Stack Overflow Developer Survey 2024: JavaScript has been the most used language every year except 2013 and 2014. [INFERENCE: chart values recalled, not re-read] All respondents: JavaScript about 62%, Python 51%, SQL 51%, TypeScript 38%, Java 30%, C# 27%. Go and Rust are about 13% each, Kotlin 9%, Dart 6% and Swift 5%.

READING STUDIES

Binkley et al., ICPC 2009, 135 subjects: camelCase had 51.5% higher odds of a correct answer and took 13.5% longer. Sharif and Maletic, ICPC 2010, eye tracking, 15 subjects: no accuracy difference, and underscores about 20% faster. Binkley et al., Empirical Software Engineering 2013, 150 subjects: experience shrinks the effect. No study shows a large stable winner; practice dominates.

CENSUS, 7,409 tracked .jet files at 1e300d0af

22,276 function declarations have multi-word names. About 302,000 occurrences of 43,051 distinct snake_case spellings exist, counting call sites, fields, locals and comments. Fields: 13,571 declarations averaging 1.55 words, so most fields are one word and do not change. About 1.9% of fields contain an acronym. Type declarations: 5,396, unchanged under every option.

MIGRATION

Under A or B, one jet fix pass renames multi-word values and every use in one atomic commit between merge waves. A's rename reads each name's words with the shared splitter and lexicon that D-PATH-CASE2 and D-WIRE-CASE1 already use, so it is deterministic. An in-flight branch rebases and re-runs the same pass. The rename commit goes in a .git-blame-ignore-revs file, which git blame and GitHub both honor, so line history skips it.

decisions.title: Which ratified ceiling governs metaprogramming: the opt-in advanced mode or the older refusal lists
decisions.situation: Metaprogramming is code that writes or changes code while Jet compiles your program. Jet's ratified rules disagree about how far it may go. Rulings from July to mid-September refuse rewriting written code and splicing code into callers during compilation. Two rulings of September 21 allow those powers behind an approved opt-in, as you asked that day. This vote proposes no new powers and only decides which ratified texts govern; we recommend keeping the September 21 contract, with the older refusals binding projects that do not opt in.
decisions.gist: Which ratified metaprogramming ceiling governs: the September 21 opt-in advanced mode, or the older refusal lists?
decisions.lesson: Standard mode is what every program gets: reading compiler facts, adding new generated code, and type recipes such as prep fn Pair(T: Type). A recipe takes a type and returns a new type. Advanced mode is what an approved root package unlocks with metaprogramming: unrestricted. Today's ratified texts both grant and refuse advanced powers. This vote proposes no new powers, and every change is checked like hand-written code.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A ceiling is the most a metaprogram may do. Standard mode needs no setting. Advanced mode needs metaprogramming: unrestricted in the root package, the package being built, and project trust must approve that root and each provider. A provider is a function the root registers to run in advanced mode for chosen targets. A change set is a checked list of edits that the compiler rechecks as a whole before accepting any of them. A receipt records what changed and the recheck result.

This vote proposes no new metaprogramming powers. Programs still generate new code under the powers already ratified; the vote only decides which ratified texts govern the advanced ones.

The conflict. Older rulings refuse rewriting written code and splicing into callers during compilation. The September 21 rulings allow them behind the approved opt-in. Both are ratified, and the spec prints both. The newer ruling governs today; this vote keeps it (A), withdraws it (B), or withdraws part of it (C).

What every option keeps. No mutable handle into the compiler's internal syntax trees. No forged facts about the program. Every change rechecked by ordinary checking. Generated code keeps a record of where it came from. Host permissions stay separate from metaprogramming.

The grammar stays closed: no token macros and no custom syntax. Advanced parsing reads ordinary Jet with the real parser into checked pieces; it never adds syntax. Type recipes stay in standard mode under every option.

Beginner path: unaffected under every option; standard mode is the same. Expert path: A gives the full checked toolkit behind an approved root and provider; B gives standard mode only; C gives the toolkit without edits to written code. Nothing here proves the advanced API runs; it is unbuilt (card #3520).
decisions.story: Mara's team builds a tracing library that wraps every function in a package with timing code. The spec's advanced API section says a root package can opt in and rewrite those bodies in a checked change set. Three other spec sections say rewriting existing code is rejected forever. She cannot tell whether her design is legal.
decisions.detail:
Suite revision, repaired by SuiteRepair1 after the SuiteBeginner2 and SuiteAdversary2 passes, 2026-10-07. Quotations below are verbatim, with line breaks and bold flattened; each names whether it is spec text or Tower option text.

Source. Owner directive 23 (2026-10-07) allows reconciliation ballots that resolve a conflict between existing ratified decisions, naming this conflict: S26, D-METAMUTATE1 and D-META-GATE1 against D-META-CONTROL2, D-META-OPTIN2 and D-GENERIC-TYPEFN1. It forbids acting on new proposals from the AST research report. So every option is a precedence or a withdrawal among ratified texts, and none adds an API, operation, mode or capability name.

AstResearch1's draft question also asked to name new deniable capabilities (Meta.Rewrite, Meta.Expand, Meta.Types); that is a new proposal and is not offered.

Why the owner decides. Under the project rule, a newer ratified ruling wins, so the September 21 contract governs today; A records that and aligns the older prose. B withdraws that contract and C withdraws part of it, which only the owner can do. None of this shows the advanced API runs: its contract is unbuilt, on card #3520.

THE REFUSING TEXTS

S26 (spec text, syntax-decisions.md:2913-2920). It says: "comptime never creates, parameterizes, or selects a type, and never affects dispatch — polymorphism is traits-only." Also: "Rejected forever: token/AST/attribute macros, custom syntax, comptime types, const generics in v1."

D-FRONTENDAPI1=A (2026-07-06; spec text, syntax-decisions.md:5216-5219). core.compiler exposes read-only lexer and parser APIs for tools, and "no AST mutation enters compilation." It refuses mutation within compilation, not parsing as such.

D-METAMUTATE1=A (2026-07-06; spec summary, syntax-decisions.md:5222-5225). It says: "Jai-style AST mutation/message loop/user macros are rejected." It also grants a non-mutating power surface: additive generated modules, registered targets and actions, read-only enforcement, DSL blocks and front-end APIs.

D-METADEPTH1/2 (spec text, syntax-decisions.md:2998-3003): read-only reflection plus derives; "No mutation, no AST injection, no macros"; "libraries can never mutate grammar". Tower records a later August amendment letting user rules record facts and add code, without mutating existing code.

D-META-GATE1=A (2026-09-19; Tower option text): "Refused: splice into existing code, token or tree macros, use-site type factories, in-place rewrite, a type with no file, running the program inside the compiler. Rewrite and Tokens are never named." Its example adds: "refused, not one flag away."

Docs/spec/reference/metaprogramming.md:304-307, an explanatory page rather than a ratification, rejects "arbitrary message-loop mutation" and says to "generate checked items additively".

THE GRANTING TEXTS

D-META-CONTROL2=A (2026-09-21; spec text, syntax-decisions.md:3093-3098). It says: "type construction, code parsing/capture/insertion, specialization, workspace/build control, and existing-program rewrites use an authorized compiler.advanced session". Its Tower text adds that changes are atomic, checked against affected callers and receipted, and never expose compiler nodes. It also says: "This does not promise equivalence with the original application."

D-META-OPTIN2=A (2026-09-21; spec text, syntax-decisions.md:3100-3105): advanced providers require "metaprogramming: unrestricted" in the approved root package and explicit target registration from root preparation. Its Tower text records the owner's request: "full Jai-level capabilities with powers above level 5 gated by metaprogramming opt-in."

OPTIN2's Tower text also requires project trust and enterprise policy to approve the root and provider. "A previously unapproved or changed privileged provider cannot silently run". Noninteractive runs fail closed, and "Revoking authorization invalidates affected preparation artifacts". Registration "uses compiler-issued DeclarationHandles, not unqualified strings", and dependency targets need exact metaprogramming_targets grants.

D-GENERIC-TYPEFN1=A (2026-10-02): types are made by prep fn recipes in standard mode, amending S26 and D-META-GATE1's use-site type-factory refusal. Its Tower text: "Building types from reflection or editing other declarations stays behind D-META-OPTIN2=A." D-CONSTGEN1=A already replaced S26's const-generics refusal. Both stay under every option.

UNIVERSAL LIMITS, KEPT IN BOTH MODES UNDER EVERY OPTION

These come from specific clauses and never become standard-only. No token, tree or attribute macros and no custom syntax (S26, D-META-GATE1, D-METADEPTH2). No message loop and no user macros (D-METAMUTATE1). No mutable compiler nodes and no forged facts (D-META-CONTROL2). Host permissions stay separate (D-META-OPTIN2), and no AST mutation enters compilation (D-FRONTENDAPI1).

Advanced parsing runs the real Jet lexer and parser into checked fragments; it is not a token or tree macro, so the closed grammar holds in both modes.

OPTION A: CLAUSE MAP

A keeps D-META-CONTROL2 and D-META-OPTIN2 in full: approval, changed-provider refusal, revocation, handles, dependency grants and the non-equivalence rule included. The older texts are amended clause by clause, not whole paragraphs. S26: the type clause points to D-GENERIC-TYPEFN1, and the dispatch clause binds standard mode, while advanced specialization follows D-META-CONTROL2. Its macro and syntax ban stays universal.

D-METAMUTATE1: the message-loop and user-macro ban stays universal; its refusal of rewriting written code binds standard mode, with advanced rewrites only as D-META-CONTROL2 change sets. D-METADEPTH1/2: "no macros" and the grammar ban stay universal; "No mutation, no AST injection" binds standard mode.

D-META-GATE1: token or tree macros stay refused everywhere. Splice into existing code, in-place rewrite, a type with no file and running the program inside the compiler bind standard mode; advanced mode has them only through D-META-CONTROL2. "Rewrite and Tokens are never named" stays, since there is no capability name. The example's "not one flag away" is amended: the approved root opt-in is that gate.

OPTION B: CLAUSE MAP

The older refusals govern. D-META-CONTROL2's compiler.advanced operations are withdrawn, and the compiler.advanced rows leave the syntax table. D-META-OPTIN2 keeps its manifest member with one value: omitted or metaprogramming: standard. The unrestricted value and metaprogramming_targets are withdrawn, so writing them is an unknown-value error.

Standard mode keeps D-META-REFLECT2 facts, D-META-PUBLISH2 additive generation, type recipes and const generics. In D-GENERIC-TYPEFN1, "stays behind D-META-OPTIN2=A" becomes stays refused.

OPTION C: CLAUSE MAP

C keeps D-META-OPTIN2 in full and keeps every D-META-CONTROL2 clause that only adds. Kept: the ChangeSet add operation, the types service, parsing into new items, specialization, and workspaces with build control and run_prepared. For those, D-META-GATE1's "a type with no file" and "running the program inside the compiler", and S26's dispatch clause, are amended for advanced mode.

C withdraws every D-META-CONTROL2 clause that edits written code: the ChangeSet operations remove, replace_body, replace_signature, replace_type and insert, and register_expansion's caller expansion. For those, D-METAMUTATE1 and D-META-GATE1's "splice into existing code" and "in-place rewrite" prevail in every mode. C only withdraws named existing clauses; it adds no operation or gate.

THE STORY UNDER EACH OPTION

Mara's tracing library needs to change existing function bodies. Under A, an approved root and approved provider can replace them in a checked change set. Under B and C it cannot; the library can only generate new wrapper functions that callers call explicitly. Those wrappers are not transparent rewrites.

WHAT B AND C OFFER

B keeps the meaning of written code in the file itself. A reader and the editor never apply a transformation to know what code does, the benefit D-METADEPTH2 and D-METAMUTATE1 argued for. B also has the smallest authority surface. C keeps the advanced additions while written bodies never change, the clearest audit story of the three.

Precedent, as illustration only. Swift macros add declarations and expand marked uses but never edit other written code; C also refuses call expansion. Rust procedural macros rewrite only the item they are attached to. Jai's message loop may rewrite code. Zig builds types at compile time with no syntax access, which matches Jet's standard mode.

INTERPLAY

Vote this ballot before D-HOOK-STAGES1. That open ballot's change-set rule defers to D-META-CONTROL2 and D-META-OPTIN2 as this vote leaves them. Under A, approved providers may return change sets; under C, only additions; under B, findings and Generated items only. This ballot adds no hook API. Card #3520 holds the advanced contract.

Suite pass repairs (SuiteBeginner2 and SuiteAdversary2, 2026-10-07). Examples now copy the ratified handle-based registration. A keeps OPTIN2's approval, revocation and dependency rules in full. Every option has a clause-level map, with universal limits kept in both modes, and C is defined only by withdrawing named clauses.

B's manifest change is exact. The non-equivalence of rewrites, provider granularity, the tracing story under each option and the strengths of B and C are stated. Quotation sources are labeled.

options.name: The September 21 opt-in rulings govern
options.detail: The current advanced contract stays in force: D-META-CONTROL2 and D-META-OPTIN2 in full. An approved root package that sets metaprogramming: unrestricted may register an approved provider for exact targets. That provider may build types from facts, parse code, expand marked calls and rewrite written code, all in checked change sets. Rewrites may change what code does; receipts show that, without promising equivalence. The older refusals bind projects that do not opt in, and the universal limits bind everyone.
options.technical: Apply the A clause map in the detail to the spec text of S26, D-METAMUTATE1, D-FRONTENDAPI1, D-METADEPTH1/2 and D-META-GATE1, each with an amendment link to D-META-CONTROL2 and D-META-OPTIN2. Universal limits stay in both modes. Update metaprogramming.md's design boundary the same way. S26's comptime-type clause points at D-GENERIC-TYPEFN1. No new names, capabilities or syntax.

options.detail: The September 21 advanced contract is withdrawn. Metaprograms read facts, publish new generated code, and use type recipes and const generics. options.name: Opt-in mode adds code but never edits written code
options.detail: Advanced mode stays behind the same approved root and provider, but only for clauses that add: building types from facts, specialization, parsing code into new items, and workspaces with build control. Every clause that edits written code is withdrawn: replacing bodies, signatures or types, removing code, inserting into existing code and expanding calls. Written bodies never change, which gives the clearest audit story.

Keep D-META-CONTROL2's ChangeSet add, the types service, parse-into-new-item, specialization and workspace operations. decisions.title: What a REPL step that fails while running does to earlier variables
decisions.situation: A REPL is the prompt where you type Jet one line at a time and keep variables between lines; notebooks work the same way. Sometimes a line fails while it runs, after it already changed a variable. Today the Jet-written REPL then forgets every variable, while the older Rust REPL keeps them. The vote decides what survives a failed line; we recommend keeping everything that already ran, as Python and Jupyter do.
decisions.gist: When a REPL or notebook step fails while running, what happens to variables from earlier steps?
decisions.lesson: A REPL runs one step at a time and keeps variables between steps. A step can fail while it runs, after it already changed some of them. Jet's Rust REPL keeps earlier variables. The Jet-written REPL currently drops them all. Whichever option wins, a crash of the running program still loses everything.
decisions.story: Mia loads a large data set in a notebook, then spends an hour cleaning it. One cell indexes past the end of a list. She needs to know whether her cleaned data is still there.
decisions.inWild:
>>> items = [1, 2, 3]
>>> items.append(4); items[10]
IndexError: list index out of range
>>> items
[1, 2, 3, 4]
# https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/errors.html
decisions.detail:
Suite revision by BallotSuite1, 2026-10-07. Drafted by ExecHost4 and folded into the suite by BallotSuite1. Checked against the ratified execution and session decisions. D-EXEC3=A runs every level with one meaning, so a REPL turn runs at the quick level and fails with the same report as jet run. D-RESOURCE-LIMIT1=A makes stack and memory exhaustion a stop; option A now says that such a stop restarts the session.

Notebooks. D-DX-CELLS1=A makes Jet notebooks reactive: pure descendants rerun and effectful cells wait for confirmation. Under option A a failed cell publishes no new names, its descendants are marked stale rather than rerun, and earlier cells keep their values. Under C every cell would need rerunning after any failure, which D-DX-CELLS1's bounded live state was meant to avoid. No other open ballot touches the REPL.

Card #4719. Rust REPL (crates/jet-repl) clones pure comptime values per trial step, so a failed step keeps all prior bindings. The Jet REPL port (port/solseams2 a5be604c4, Main-approved 2026-10-06) retires the evaluator machine on a run-time failure and reports that runtime bindings were reset. It does so because owned host handles and shared cells cannot be copied.

Under D-EXEC1/D-EXEC2 the REPL moves to the native session host (#4720): bindings live in typed session slots in one persistent child. A recoverable failure (an error value, cancellation, deadline) returns through MIR cleanup; published slots survive. A panic or trap invalidates the child; the host restarts it with a fresh session and never replays earlier steps.

Static check failures already roll back exactly and are not part of this choice. External side effects are never rolled back under any option.

options.name: Keep what ran
options.detail: Earlier bindings stay after a run-time failure, and changes the failed step made before failing stay. A panic or trap still restarts the session and says which bindings were lost.
options.technical:
Session slots published by earlier turns are untouched; the failed turn's unpublished slots are released without glue (CAbiSession end). Fatal invalidation restarts the child with a fresh session.

Resource stops follow D-RESOURCE-LIMIT1=A. A stack overflow (E3012), a #MaxDepth limit or running out of memory is a stop, so it counts as a fatal invalidation: the session restarts and says which bindings were lost. Output printed before the stop stays on screen, as the prefix rule requires. A failed turn prints the same registered report as jet run, per D-RTFAIL1 and D-EXEC3.
options.code:
>> items.push(4); items[10]
error: index 10 is out of range (length 4)
>> items
[1, 2, 3, 4]

options.name: Undo the step
options.detail: Before each step, copy every binding the step may change; restore the copies if it fails. A step that may change an uncopyable binding (file, socket, shared cell) cannot be undone.
options.technical: Per-turn snapshot of written slots via Clone glue; uncopyable slot types either refuse the turn or are excluded from rollback.
options.code:

options.name: Start over
options.detail: Any run-time failure resets every binding, as the Jet REPL port does today.
options.technical: The failed turn retires the whole session; the next step starts empty.
options.code:

error: unknown name `items`

comparisons.note: Interactive mode keeps all variables after an exception; partial changes stay. https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/errors.html

In [3]: items
Out[3]: [1, 2, 3, 4]

recommendation.why: Keeping what ran costs nothing per step, keeps files and connections usable, and matches what people expect from Python and notebooks.
gains: A mistake never costs the session's earlier work.

losses.loss: A half-finished step can leave a variable partly changed.
losses.mitigation: The error names the step that failed; printing the variable shows its current value.

whyNot.reason: Undo copies data every step and still cannot undo files, sockets or printed output.
Starting over throws away a whole session for one mistake.

recommendation.tradeoff: A failed step may leave partial changes, which the user can see and fix.

decisions.title: A field and a method with the same name
decisions.situation: An error object can store its cause in a field and offer a method that returns that cause. Jet currently rejects the shared name in its own encoding library, which prevents the compiler's JSON reader from loading before a user's program runs. The choice is whether fields and methods may share a name, or whether the error must lose its public field or its method. We recommend keeping both operations and letting field access and method calls select the requested operation.
decisions.gist: Can a field and a method share a name, or must the error API choose one?
decisions.lesson: The choice is member declaration and resolution, not error propagation or read-only storage. Shared cause data remains handle-free and typed.
decisions.explainer: Choose whether fields and methods have separate namespaces or share one member namespace. Separate namespaces keep the same name for both operations; access syntax chooses the operation.
decisions.story: Mira checks an encoding error's stored cause and sometimes asks its accessor for an owned cause. Core declares both, so loading the compiler's JSON reader currently rejects Core itself. She needs an ordinary rule, not a special-case exemption for this error.
decisions.inWild: Physically read https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch05-03-method-syntax.html: its Rectangle.width example declares a field and method with the same name. The text says parentheses mean the method; without parentheses Rust means the field. Supplementary exact sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/expressions/method-call-expr.html and https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/expressions/field-expr.html. No external executable was run.
decisions.detail:
No D-MEMBER-NAMESPACE1 decision existed in canonical live Tower revision75711 or its history. STREAMS431/446 records an undecided question;450 shows this collision already existed on497. Main has now created card4905, c00hgc5h. Current Core/encoding/encoding.jet145 and160 declare public cause storage and a pure cause() accessor. Registration.rs1747-1756 emits E0105 with the message shown here; this implementation is not ratified law.

D-CALLVALUE1=B governs callable values and literal call-member shadowing. Source method_calls.rs7951-7978 currently tries callable fields before resolve_method_sig7989. Choosing A requires paired method-primary resolution, not just deleting a diagnostic. An inaccessible or ill-typed method must report its normal error, never fall through to a field. Existing computed, inherited, trait, generic and operator resolution remains.

Official Rust Book https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch05-03-method-syntax.html was physically read. Its same-named Rectangle.width field/method example distinguishes calls with parentheses from field access. Exact Reference URLs are https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/expressions/field-expr.html and https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/expressions/method-call-expr.html. No Rust example or proposed Jet program was executed. This short choice changes no Syntax.rs keyword or sigil, invariant, error propagation, read-only-field rule or private Core permission.

options.name: Separate fields and methods
options.detail:
Reject duplicates within fields or within methods, not a field-versus-method pair. A value-position field read keeps its meaning. An ordinary member call chooses the existing method; only absence of a method permits the existing callable-field route. An inaccessible method or wrong arguments report the normal method error, never fall through to a field.

Invoke a callable field explicitly through value.field.call(args). Preserve existing member references, computed fields, inherited and trait methods, operator hooks, visibility, receiver access, effects and provenance. Preserve literal call-member shadowing. EncodingError keeps its public cause field and pure Never accessor. Both compiler paths must migrate their current callable-field-first lookup.

The separate Worker example stores a function that adds one and defines a method that adds ten. Input two produces twelve through the method, or three through step.call. EncodingError.cause is not callable. This example is authored, not executed; its function field and lambda spelling come from existing tests/closures.rs255-259. Same-name coexistence is proposed A.

options.name: Keep the field only
options.detail: One namespace keeps duplicate field/method declarations illegal. Remove EncodingError.cause() and migrate every method caller to its public cause field. The method currently returns a copied value that its caller owns separately. A field read can borrow the stored value instead; use ~err.cause when that separate copy is needed. Preserve cause field name/order/type, constructor literals and handle-free data. No replacement getter or hidden allocation is introduced.

options.name: Keep the method only
options.detail: One namespace remains. Move cause storage to a private differently named field and retain cause()/new()/with_cause(). A public field lets callers read err.cause and construct EncodingError{..., cause: None}. Those operations must change to cause() and the existing constructors when storage becomes private. Compiler records that describe and carry the stored fields must change together, not keep a stale cause field. Migrate every public field read/write/literal constructor and every checked native/Source carrier projection. No alias or field-name-based reporting inference is allowed.
options.code:
print(err.cause() == None)
// Use new()/with_cause(), not EncodingError{..., cause: None}.

comparisons.note: Official Book, physically read: https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch05-03-method-syntax.html; its same-named width field/method example explains parentheses. Exact Reference URLs: https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/expressions/field-expr.html and https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/expressions/method-call-expr.html.
comparisons.code:
let field = e.cause;
let owned = e.cause();

recommendation.why: Preserve both existing operations with ordinary resolution rather than changing public error data.
gains: Existing cause access remains
No public field/constructor migration

losses.loss: Callable field overlaps a method name
losses.mitigation: Use value.field.call(args) for the field explicitly.

whyNot.reason: Retires the existing method and changes owned-reader callers.
Changes public data construction and all stored-shape projections.

recommendation.tradeoff: Explicit callable-field invocation makes the overlap teachable without removing data.

One shared namespace retires either field access or the method. Every option still needs checked compiler behavior and matching tests.

decisions.title: Restoring database developer commands
decisions.situation: Database developer commands let people inspect and query data from the terminal, but their original implementation never compiled and was removed during the self-host repair. Restoring them needs CSV and JSON readers with real input limits, plus a quiet output mode for scripted use. Without those limits, inspecting a large file could use excessive memory instead of failing clearly. You choose to restore the feature through those APIs, defer it, or remove it permanently; we recommend designing the safe APIs and restoring it.
decisions.gist: Should Jet restore its database developer commands with bounded input?
decisions.lesson: These terminal commands depend on safe CSV and JSON input and a quiet output mode. Those APIs must be designed before restoration. A does that work and restores the feature, B keeps it planned but unavailable, and C removes it permanently. A does not authorize unbounded readers.
decisions.explainer: The feature is not restored merely by retaining its files. Input size and nesting limits must be enforced before the commands become available. Quiet output is part of their usable scripting behavior.
decisions.story: Bea inspects a table from the terminal. She needs a large or deeply nested input to fail at a known limit rather than fill memory or overwhelm her script's output.
decisions.inWild:
# SQLite ships a developer CLI for queries and importing CSV data.
# https://www.sqlite.org/cli.html
sqlite3 data.db 'SELECT * FROM items LIMIT 10;'
# SQLite also exposes resource limits, including expression depth and length.
# https://www.sqlite.org/limits.html
# These precedents do not supply Jet's proposed CSV/JSON reader limits.
decisions.detail: The source ballot links restoration to the ratified SQL safety plan. Its proposed CLI input defaults are 32 MiB and 64 nesting levels. The exact bounded-reader and quiet-mode APIs remain subject to design and ratification; the example below specifies behavior without inventing a current Core function.

options.name: Design safe APIs and restore commands
options.detail: Design bounded CSV and JSON readers and a quiet output mode, then restore the commands using them. Enforce the agreed limits rather than reviving code that never compiled.
options.technical: Bounded readers use size limits and JSON nesting limits. Proposed CLI defaults are 33,554,432 bytes and depth 64; the output-mode type includes quiet.
options.code:
# After API design and command restoration:
jet db --help
# Database commands documented with bounded CSV/JSON input
# and a quiet output mode; exact flags come from that design.

options.name: Keep the feature planned for later
options.detail: Retain the feature as future work but keep it outside this CLI release. Restore nothing until the dependencies are designed and ratified later.
options.technical: No database developer commands are exposed in this release.
options.code:
# This release has no database developer commands.
# Restoration remains planned.

options.name: Drop the feature permanently
options.detail: Remove the developer command implementation and its feature-specific tests. The CLI no longer promises this feature.
options.technical: Delete the feature's command files and tests from the current tree, without deleting unrelated database APIs.
options.code:
# Database developer commands are removed from the product.
# No restoration is promised.

decisions.title: Whether Jet adds 128-bit integer types
decisions.situation: Integer types set the sizes of whole numbers a program can represent, and Jet's specified fixed-width list currently stops at 64 bits. Compiler code introduced 128-bit names without making them part of that language contract, leaving users unable to rely on consistent support. Adding them would require overflow and conversion rules rather than just keeping two names in one file. You choose the existing list or complete 128-bit support; we recommend the existing list until a real program needs the larger types.
decisions.gist: Should Jet add signed and unsigned 128-bit integer types?
decisions.lesson: Fixed-width integers have a maximum range and rules for overflow. Jet's current list stops at 64 bits. A removes unapproved 128-bit names; B adds both types with full conversion and overflow rules. A leaves larger-number needs to a library or a later language decision.
decisions.explainer: A compiler's internal name is not automatically a supported language type. Adding I128 and U128 requires a consistent contract across checking, execution and conversions.
decisions.story: Hank sees a 128-bit name in compiler code while writing a large-number hash. He needs to know whether that type is truly supported or merely an unapproved implementation detail.
decisions.detail: The source ballot says the integer-kinds module introduced I128 and U128 outside the spec, and its one 128-bit use had already moved to Int. Option B is a proposed language addition, not a claim that these types work today.

options.name: Keep the specified integer list
options.detail: Remove the unapproved I128 and U128 names. Retain the specified types at 64 bits or less rather than creating a language addition without a demonstrated caller.
options.technical: Integer kinds and exposed numeric names must agree with the current specification; the one reported use remains Int.
options.code:
count := Int{0}
// The supported list remains at 64 bits or less.

options.name: Add complete 128-bit support
options.detail: Make I128 and U128 supported fixed-width language types. Specify overflow traps and conversions, and implement them consistently rather than preserving unsupported names.
options.technical: Add signed and unsigned 128-bit types to the numeric menu with overflow trapping consistent with other fixed-width integers.
options.code:
// Proposed type, available only if B is implemented:
count := I128{0}

recommendation.why: A keeps the implementation aligned with the current spec and avoids adding types without a demonstrated program need.
gains: One consistent, specified list of integer types.

losses.loss: Programs needing more than 64 bits cannot use these built-in types.
losses.mitigation: State the limit clearly and revisit complete wider-type support when a real program demonstrates the need.

whyNot.reason: B is a full language addition with overflow and conversion rules, while the source ballot identifies no current program requiring it.

recommendation.tradeoff: Keep the specified type list now while acknowledging that wider built-in arithmetic requires a later explicit decision.

decisions.checkInstructions: Under A, check numeric names and integer kinds contain no unapproved 128-bit types and the reported caller uses Int. Under B, require consistent overflow, conversion and execution tests before claiming support.

surface.gist: Should Jet add 128-bit integer types?
