decisions.title: Replacing a borrowed field while returning its old value
decisions.situation: A reusable reader stores the current row in a field, then needs to hand that row to its caller and begin the next one. Jet forbids moving a value out of a borrowed field, so today's workaround copies the row and resets the field, adding an allocation each time. A replace operation would put a new value in immediately while returning the old one without that copy. You choose standard replacement, continued copying, or consuming the whole reader; we recommend one standard replacement operation.
decisions.gist: Should Jet add a standard operation to replace a field and return its old value?
decisions.lesson: Borrowing permits access without taking ownership. Moving a field out would leave a borrowed object incomplete. Replacement fills the field while returning its old value. A adds that operation, B copies and resets, and C consumes the whole object. A lets a reader continue without a row copy.
decisions.explainer: The desired operation does not weaken the rule against leaving a borrowed field empty. The replacement is already present before the old value is returned. Consuming an entire object works for final results but not for a reader that must produce another row.
decisions.story: Priya's file reader emits thousands of rows. She wants each finished row handed to its caller without copying its values or giving up the reader she needs for the next row.
decisions.detail: The source ballot identifies an extra allocation per emitted row from copying before reset. mem.replace is proposed Jet API, not an existing function in core.mem. The syntax below uses current Jet borrowing and collection construction; A requires adding the operation's checked move semantics.

options.name: Add standard replacement
options.detail: Add one operation that installs a new value in a writable place and returns the old one. Use it for row handoff instead of copying, without ever leaving the borrowed object incomplete.
options.technical: Proposed mem.replace(&place, new) returns the old value. The write borrow ends before the following statement, and the old value is moved rather than copied.

options.name: Keep copying and resetting
options.detail: Keep the current borrowed-field move rule and add no replacement operation. Reusable readers copy the finished row and reset their field, retaining an allocation for every row.
options.technical: No new Core operation or special field extraction. The copy remains an ordinary allocation.

options.name: Consume the object for its final result
options.detail: Give types a finishing method that consumes the whole object and returns its result. Avoid a general replacement operation, but the object cannot continue producing rows afterward.
options.technical: A consuming finish method moves its payload out and ends the object's use. This fits terminal results such as a hash digest, not repeated handoff from a reusable reader.

recommendation.why: A preserves the borrowed-field rule while giving reusable readers an allocation-free handoff instead of copying each row.
gains: Reusable readers hand off old values without an extra copy allocation.

losses.loss: Users must learn one additional operation and its ownership rule.
losses.mitigation: Document replacement next to existing cell swapping, with one reader example showing the new value remains installed.

whyNot.reason: B keeps a copy allocation on every row even though replacement can preserve the ownership rule.
C fits a final result but consumes the reader needed to produce the next row.

recommendation.tradeoff: Add one explicit ownership-preserving operation rather than pay per-row copies or restrict handoff to final results.

decisions.checkInstructions: Test that replacement returns the old value, leaves the new value installed and ends its write borrow before the next statement. Exercise repeated reader handoff without a copy allocation and verify consuming finish still forbids reuse.

surface.gist: Should a standard replacement operation return a field's old value without copying?
surface.lesson: Moving out of a borrowed field is forbidden. Today the reader copies its row and resets the field. A replaces the field and returns its old value, B keeps copying, and C consumes the whole object. Only A avoids copies while letting the same reader continue.

current.note: Each row is copied before the reader resets its field.
current.code:
row := ~self.fields
self.fields = [String]{}

wild.note: Replacement preserves a complete object without cloning the payload; source is in the long form.
wild.code: let row = std::mem::replace(&mut reader.fields, Vec::new());

options.name: Standard replacement
options.gist: Install a new field value and return the old one.
gains: No row-copy allocation.
Reader can keep producing rows.
losses: One operation and ownership rule to learn.

proposed.code:
// Proposed Jet operation:
row :: mem.replace(&self.fields, [String]{})

options.name: Copy and reset
options.gist: Keep the current workaround and ownership rules.
gains: No new operation.
losses: An extra copy allocation per row.

proposed.code:
row := ~self.fields
self.fields = [String]{}

options.name: Consume at the end
options.gist: A finishing method returns the payload and consumes its object.
gains: No general replacement operation.
No copy for terminal results.
losses: The consumed reader cannot produce another row.

// Reader is consumed.

recommendation.why: A avoids the row copy while preserving a complete borrowed object and allowing the reader to continue.
gains: Allocation-free row handoff.

losses.loss: One more ownership operation.
losses.mitigation: Document it beside cell swapping with an example showing the installed replacement.

whyNot.reason: B pays a copy allocation on every row.
C ends the reader instead of letting it produce more rows.

recommendation.tradeoff: Learn one replacement operation to avoid repeated copies without weakening ownership rules.

decisions.title: User Rust libraries in native Jet programs
decisions.situation: A Jet program can call a Rust library supplied by its author, with Cargo building a helper outside Jet's own runtime. Native support is already ported, but the owner must choose whether helpers use a static musl build, disappear, or link dynamically against glibc. Static musl avoids a target glibc dependency but currently needs an opt-in toolchain limited to x86_64 Linux. We recommend retaining user Rust support through that static helper, with the platform limit stated clearly.
decisions.gist: Should native Jet retain user Rust libraries through a static musl helper?
decisions.lesson: User-written Rust is separate from Jet's runtime. Cargo can remain the user's external build tool. A keeps static helpers on x86_64 Linux with an opt-in musl toolchain, B removes Rust support, and C uses dynamic glibc helpers. Dynamic output needs compatible libraries on the target machine.
decisions.explainer: Removing Rust from Jet itself does not necessarily remove a user's choice to call Rust. This vote concerns authorized user helpers, not permission to run Cargo or LLVM by default. Static libraries still need their native dependencies accounted for.
decisions.story: Hank calls his team's Rust hashing library from Jet. He wants to build the helper once and run the result without installing Rust or depending on a target glibc version.
decisions.inWild:
# Rust supports staticlib for linking Rust into a non-Rust application.
# https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/linkage.html
rustc --crate-type=staticlib helper.rs
# The x86_64 Linux musl target defaults to a static C runtime.
# https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/linkage.html#static-and-dynamic-c-runtimes
cargo build --target x86_64-unknown-linux-musl
# A cdylib is a dynamic library for loading from another language.
rustc --crate-type=cdylib helper.rs
decisions.detail: The source ballot reports native RustForeign.jet support in 00f3b5bb5 and an opt-in musl toolchain in ce42a475a. JET_RUST_MUSL_TOOLCHAIN selects it; normal compiles retain the default nixpkgs toolchain. Docs/spec/reference/jetpack-epoch5.md permits only committed, source-proved foreign crate cases and denies Rust/LLVM execution by default. Card #4948 separately decides the cargo-metadata environment-forwarding gap. The static option currently covers x86_64 Linux only.

options.name: Retain static musl Rust helpers
options.detail: Keep Cargo as the user's external tool. Build authorized user helpers as musl static libraries with the opt-in toolchain. Avoid a glibc dependency while clearly limiting this path to supported x86_64 Linux builds.
options.technical: Use JET_RUST_MUSL_TOOLCHAIN, JET_RUST_MUSL_LINKER and JET_RUST_MUSL_AR. Preserve source-proof authorization. Cargo environment forwarding is decided separately.
options.code:
# Generated helper crate uses crate-type = ["staticlib"].
cargo build --target x86_64-unknown-linux-musl
# Jet links the resulting authorized helper archive.

options.name: Remove user Rust support
options.detail: Remove native user Rust helpers and their toolchain integration. Users must expose their library through the C interface or rewrite it; direct Rust support no longer exists.
options.technical: Remove RustForeign.jet, its fixtures and ABI test, the musl toolchain exposure and the spec permission for foreign crate builds.
options.code:
# Native Jet no longer builds a user Rust helper.
# Use an explicitly supplied C interface instead.

options.name: Use dynamic glibc helpers
options.detail: Build helpers with the default Rust toolchain as dynamic libraries against glibc. Avoid the special musl toolchain, but require compatible glibc and the helper library on the target machine.
options.technical: Use the default nixpkgs Rust target for helpers. Remove musl toolchain exposure and document dynamic linking for these FFI programs.
options.code:
# Generated helper crate uses crate-type = ["cdylib"].
cargo build --target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# Target deployment includes the helper and compatible glibc.

recommendation.why: A keeps authorized user Rust libraries working without making the resulting program depend on the target's glibc version.
gains: User Rust support remains available without a target glibc dependency.

losses.loss: The opt-in static helper path currently supports only x86_64 Linux.
losses.mitigation: Document the supported target and required toolchain, refuse unsupported builds clearly, and keep the environment-forwarding gap separately tracked.

whyNot.reason: B removes a working user feature already admitted under the source-proof authorization rule.
C introduces target glibc and dynamic-helper deployment dependencies that the static option avoids.

recommendation.tradeoff: Keep static user Rust helpers on the explicitly supported target, with an opt-in toolchain rather than dynamic deployment dependencies.

decisions.checkInstructions: Use the committed foreign-helper fixtures and ABI test on x86_64 Linux. Verify static native linkage and the absence of a glibc dependency. Confirm unsupported targets are refused clearly and default builds do not execute unauthorized Rust tools.

surface.gist: Should native Jet keep static user Rust helpers?
surface.lesson: A user's Rust library is separate from Jet's runtime. A builds static musl helpers with an opt-in x86_64 Linux toolchain. B removes direct Rust support. C uses ordinary dynamic glibc helpers and requires compatible libraries at deployment. Authorization remains unchanged.

options.gist: Users expose a C interface or rewrite their library.

losses: Existing direct Rust use stops working.

losses: Target needs compatible glibc and the helper library.

recommendation.why: A preserves authorized user Rust support without adding a target glibc dependency.
gains: Static user Rust integration.

losses.loss: Opt-in toolchain; x86_64 Linux only.
losses.mitigation: Document the exact target and toolchain, and refuse unsupported builds clearly.

whyNot.reason: B removes user functionality already allowed under the authorization rule.
C requires compatible dynamic libraries on the target.

recommendation.tradeoff: Accept an explicit toolchain and platform limit instead of dynamic deployment dependencies.

decisions.title: What happens when a native runtime feature is missing
decisions.situation: A native build uses Jet's replacement runtime, but some existing features still have no native implementation. Today a UDP program can reach the linker before a missing-provider error names an internal symbol instead of explaining the unavailable feature. This leaves application authors unsure whether their code is wrong or the runtime is incomplete. You choose clear compiler refusals, today's linker errors, or delaying the entire cutover; we recommend clear refusals for each missing feature.
decisions.gist: Should missing native features be rejected clearly before linking?
decisions.lesson: A compiler checks code before the linker assembles the executable. Some native runtime features are still missing. A explains each missing feature at compile time, B keeps the generic linker error, and C waits for every feature before cutover. No option may pretend missing features work.
decisions.explainer: This vote chooses how unavailable features are reported and whether they block the whole cutover. It does not authorize reducing any feature's behavior or decide which implementation to port first.
decisions.story: Nora receives a UDP packet in her program. Today her native build fails with a missing symbol; she needs an error that explains the unavailable feature and her next step.
decisions.detail: The source ballot lists service authority, workflows, HTTP server, WebSocket, UI host, browser, Raylib, devtools, process pipelines, sandboxed launches and UDP as incomplete. TLS is decided separately in D-NATIVE-TLS1. Today's missing-provider linker diagnostic is E2104. New per-family codes must enter the diagnostic catalog and documentation.

options.name: Clear compiler refusal for each feature
options.detail: Reject each unavailable runtime family at compile time. Name the family, explain why this build lacks it, and give the fallback or next step. Register and document every new diagnostic code.
options.technical: One availability list drives both the native checker and runtime pack. Each excluded family has one canonical diagnostic.

options.name: Keep the generic linker error
options.detail: Keep today's behavior. Linking fails with the generic missing-provider error and an internal symbol name. No new compiler refusal is added.
options.technical: The existing native link path reports E2104. No fake provider is introduced.

options.name: Wait for every native feature
options.detail: Block the cutover until every listed runtime family is implemented natively. Programs retain the full feature set at cutover, but complete features cannot ship ahead of unfinished ones.
options.technical: The native runtime pack's exclusion list must be empty before cutover.

recommendation.why: A explains missing features before linking and lets completed native work ship without pretending the rest works.
gains: Users learn which feature is missing and what to do next.

losses.loss: New diagnostic codes must remain correct and documented.
losses.mitigation: Drive compiler refusals and the runtime pack from one availability list, and register each code in the catalog.

whyNot.reason: B gives users an internal symbol name late in the build instead of an actionable explanation.
C holds the entire cutover behind every remaining feature even when unrelated native programs already work.

recommendation.tradeoff: Keep a small set of documented refusals rather than delay all completed native functionality.

decisions.checkInstructions: For each excluded family, verify one canonical compiler diagnostic and its documented next step. Confirm the checker and runtime pack read the same availability list and that implemented families are not refused.

surface.gist: How should a native build report an unavailable feature?
surface.lesson: Some runtime features are not native yet. Today the linker names a missing symbol. A gives a clear compiler refusal, B keeps that error, and C delays cutover until every feature works. Missing behavior must never be faked.

// Linker: E2104, missing provider.

compile_error!("enable foo or bar");

options.gist: Explain the unavailable feature before linking.
gains: Early, actionable explanation.
losses: Diagnostic codes need documentation.

// Compiler names UDP and the next step.

options.name: Generic linker error
options.gist: Keep today's missing-symbol report.
gains: No new diagnostic codes.
losses: Late error with an internal symbol.

proposed.code:

// Linker: E2104, missing provider.

options.name: Wait for all features
options.gist: Do not cut over with any missing family.
gains: Full feature set at cutover.
losses: Every unfinished family delays cutover.

// Cutover waits until all families work.

recommendation.why: A tells users what is missing without holding completed native programs behind unrelated ports.
gains: Clear errors without fake behavior.

losses.loss: More diagnostic codes to maintain.
losses.mitigation: Use one availability list for compiler refusals and the runtime pack.

whyNot.reason: B reports an internal symbol too late to explain the missing feature well.
C delays every native program behind every unfinished family.

recommendation.tradeoff: Maintain documented refusals while completed native features ship.

decisions.title: Process pipelines and sandboxed launches on the native runtime
decisions.situation: A process pipeline connects commands while sharing time and output limits, and a sandbox restricts what a launched command can access. Both still depend on Rust, so native build scripts using pipelines fail before their commands start and sandboxed launches remain refused. Running commands one by one or silently removing a sandbox would change promised behavior. You choose a complete port, continued exclusion, or pipelines first; we recommend faithful pipelines first and a separate security-reviewed sandbox port.
decisions.gist: Should native Jet restore process pipelines before sandboxed launches?
decisions.lesson: Pipelines connect running commands and share limits, cleanup and cancellation. A sandbox is a security boundary. A ports both, B leaves both unavailable, and C restores pipelines first. A missing sandbox must always refuse the launch, never run the command without protection.
decisions.explainer: Plain run, spawn and capture are separate from this vote. The pipeline port must preserve direct pipes, bounded relays, shared budgets and process-group cleanup. Serial execution is not equivalent.
decisions.story: Sam's build script pipes generated source through two tools with a timeout. Native linking currently fails before any stage runs, and he needs the same cancellation and cleanup guarantees back.
decisions.inWild:
# POSIX shells connect concurrently running commands with pipelines.
# https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9799919799/utilities/V3_chap02.html#tag_19_09_02
printf 'hello\n' | wc -c
# Bubblewrap provides Linux sandboxing as a separate process tool.
# https://github.com/containers/bubblewrap
bwrap --ro-bind / / --unshare-net /bin/true
decisions.detail: The source ballot identifies Process.rs around lines 2051-2455, about 405 lines, and ProcessSandbox.rs at about 1,059 lines. Plain run, spawn and capture were being ported separately for the native CLI. Restore pipeline lifecycle and timeout cases. These sizes describe reference Rust code, not a measured Jet implementation.

options.name: Port pipelines and sandboxes together
options.detail: Restore both implementations with the same shared limits, cleanup, cancellation and sandbox restrictions. Completion waits for pipeline behavior and the security-reviewed sandbox profiles.
options.technical: Port direct-pipe versus bounded-relay behavior, per-stage process groups, bubblewrap probing, profiles and secure output directories. Preserve existing error codes.

options.name: Keep both unavailable
options.detail: Keep pipeline and sandbox-bound launches outside the native pack. Plain run, spawn and capture are unaffected. Refuse missing behavior rather than substituting serial execution or an unsandboxed launch.
options.technical: Private pipeline launch and sandbox-bound ProcessSpec remain unbound. The source wrapper remains in Jet; missing pipeline providers report E2104.

options.name: Port pipelines first
options.detail: Restore faithful pipelines with their limits, cleanup and cancellation. Keep sandbox-bound launches refused until a separate port and security review are complete.
options.technical: Port the pipeline engine and lifecycle/timeout tests. Sandbox-bound requests remain refused and never execute without the requested sandbox.

recommendation.why: C restores pipelines without tying them to the separate security review required for sandboxed launches.
gains: Native pipelines retain shared limits, cancellation and cleanup.

losses.loss: Sandbox-bound launches remain unavailable natively.
losses.mitigation: Refuse every sandbox-bound request and track its separate port with the security review, never running it unsandboxed.

whyNot.reason: A makes pipeline availability wait for sandbox profiles and their security review.
B leaves the pipeline path unavailable even though it can be ported independently.

recommendation.tradeoff: Restore pipelines separately while retaining a strict refusal for every unavailable sandboxed launch.

decisions.checkInstructions: Restore shared time/output budgets, direct pipes, bounded relays, cancellation and per-stage process-group cleanup tests. Verify that sandbox-bound requests never execute unsandboxed. Missing-feature error timing follows D-NATIVE-GAPS1.

surface.gist: Should native Jet restore pipelines before sandboxed launches?
surface.lesson: Pipelines connect commands and share limits and cleanup. Sandboxes restrict command access. Both are missing natively. A ports both, B leaves both out, and C ports pipelines first. An unavailable sandbox must refuse the launch rather than weaken protection.

options.gist: Restore pipelines and reviewed sandboxed launches together.
gains: Both forms of launch work natively.
losses: Pipelines wait for sandbox security review.

// Pipeline and sandbox support restored.

options.name: Leave both unavailable
options.gist: Keep plain launches but refuse pipelines and sandboxed launches.
gains: Neither port holds up cutover.
losses: Pipelines and sandboxed launches remain unavailable.

proposed.code:

// Missing-provider refusal remains.

options.name: Pipelines first
options.gist: Restore pipelines with unchanged limits and cleanup.
gains: Pipelines return independently.
losses: Sandbox-bound launches remain unavailable.

// Works unless a step requires the unavailable sandbox.

recommendation.why: C restores pipelines without rushing a separate security boundary.
gains: Faithful native pipelines.

losses.loss: Sandbox-bound launches remain unavailable.
losses.mitigation: Refuse them explicitly and track a separate security-reviewed port; never execute them unsandboxed.

whyNot.reason: A makes pipelines wait for the sandbox's security review.
B leaves an independently portable pipeline engine unavailable.

recommendation.tradeoff: Pipelines return first; sandbox protection is never silently removed.

decisions.title: The native layout for received UDP packets
decisions.situation: UDP sends separate network messages, and Jet represents a received message with its bytes, sender, original length and truncation flag. Six native socket routines are already ported, but native programs cannot use UDP until a bridge returns that packet record to Jet. This blocks packet-reading programs and the tests that check their data and sender information. decisions.title: Unwired CLI files outside the self-hosted compiler build
decisions.situation: The self-hosted compiler is built from Jet source, but some command files and their package-publication dependencies are left outside its assembly. Today package commands such as add are recognized but have empty actions, so users do not get the feature those names suggest. Wiring them would bring roughly 170 additional files into the build and deliberately expand its agreed boundary. You choose continued exclusion, wiring now, or deletion; we recommend keeping the files outside the build until their command wiring is designed.
decisions.gist: Should unwired CLI files stay outside the self-hosted build until their commands are connected?
decisions.lesson: Files can remain in the repository without being built. These package commands have no action today. A retains the files outside the build, B connects the commands and includes their dependencies, and C deletes the callers. A preserves the work but does not make the commands functional.
decisions.explainer: Recognizing a command name is not evidence that the command works. The build boundary and the command wiring are separate obligations; retaining excluded source does not authorize calling unfinished package operations complete.
decisions.story: Priya runs jet add to add a dependency. Today the name is recognized but nothing happens, and she needs the release to state that limitation plainly.
decisions.inWild:
# Cargo supports source retained behind disabled features and optional dependencies.
# https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/features.html
cargo build --no-default-features
# Go build constraints likewise control which source files enter a build.
# https://pkg.go.dev/cmd/go#hdr-Build_constraints
//go:build linux
# These are build-scope precedents, not precedents for silent no-op commands.
decisions.detail: The eight excluded CLI files are Jobs, Package/Bundle, Package/FlashAudit, Package/FlashPlan, Package/NativeBundle, Package/NativeFlash, Supply and ToolchainPin. Dependency.jet also stays outside assembly, with a 162-file fetch closure covering publication, providers, trust, registries and storage. Commands.jet has empty add/remove/fetch/update actions. The sandbox path remains wired through Host.jet:1528 to jet_cli_compile_sandbox. Closure receipt: $JET_STATE_ROOT/scratch/CliR12Fix/fetch-closure.json.

options.name: Keep excluded files until wiring is designed
options.detail: Keep the eight CLI files, Dependency.jet and its publication closure outside assembly while preserving them in the repository. Keep package actions unfinished until separately designed wiring is ready. Explicitly label those commands unavailable.
options.technical: Preserve the pre-merge assembly boundary. Commands.jet actions remain empty and Front.jet recognizes the names; the source files are retained, not deleted.
options.code:

options.name: Wire commands and include the closure now
options.detail: Connect add, remove, fetch and update and the eight CLI files, then include the exact fetch closure. Expand the self-hosted build by roughly 170 files and cross the publication boundary deliberately.
options.technical: Dispatch package dependency commands to jet_cli_package_dependency. Assemble the closure recorded in fetch-closure.json and check the expanded self-host assembly boundary.
options.code:

# Resolves the package and writes its lock entry.

options.name: Delete excluded callers and commands
options.detail: Delete the eight CLI files and Dependency.jet, remove their command rows and front-end names, and remove caller-specific tests. Do not delete shared Jetpack dependency files that other code may use.
options.technical: Remove package/flash catalog rows depending on these callers. The Jetpack closure itself is not deleted.

losses.loss: Add, remove, fetch and update remain non-functional.

recommendation.tradeoff: Keep the smaller build and retained source while explicitly acknowledging that these package commands remain unfinished.

decisions.title: Expert metaprogramming as nested effects you can block as a family or one at a time
decisions.situation: Jai, the game language Jet is matching, trusts the programmer completely: build code can rewrite your program, run any tool while compiling, and switch off array checks for a whole build. Jet already has one way to say what code may do: effects such as Net or FS.Read, which nest, so denying FS also denies FS.Read. The earlier draft of this ballot added a separate list of powers beside effects, a second way to give permission. The vote decides how Jet's strong metaprogramming becomes a family of nested effects that a team can block whole or one at a time, and where whole-build check removal belongs. We recommend a Meta effect family, with check removal kept on the existing safety-gate rules.
decisions.gist: Should Jet's strong metaprogramming be nested effects a team can block whole or one at a time, and where does check removal go?
decisions.lesson: An effect names something code may do, such as Net. Effects nest: denying FS also denies FS.Read. A package's authority block lists effects it holds (may use) and denies. Expert effects are strong ones, such as rewriting code while compiling; nobody holds them until the main package names them. A safety gate, such as `#Unsafe`, is a written, audited place where a safety check is waived. A bounds check stops a read past the end of a list; without it, a bad index can corrupt memory.
decisions.story: Ravi ports a Jai game to Jet. His build runs the level editor while compiling, one library rewrites functions marked as game systems into faster code, and release builds run without array checks. His security lead wants one line for a sister project: generated code and macros yes, anything stronger no. Both want to use the effects and safety rules they already know, not a second list of switches.
decisions.detail:
Owner question q2d1w7aw: the earlier powers list deviated from effects. Powers should be nested effects, so a team can block all stronger metaprogramming or one thing. The old syntax was not idiomatic. Jet is the language being designed; Jai is Jonathan Blow's game language that Jet is reaching parity with (Docs/audits/jai-parity-2026-10-16.md). Spellings use `comptime` (D-COMPTIME-WORD1=A) and the arrow form `-[ ]>` (D-EFFECT-ROW2).

Ratified ground for effects: D-AUTHORITY-MODEL1=A (one rights tree), D-AUTHORITY-ROOTS1=A (nested roots; `!FFI` denies every leaf), D-EFFTREE1 (holding a parent covers its children). Also D-AUTHORITY-MANIFEST1=A (the `authority` block; `policy:` keeps floors and unsafe mode). Also D-EFFECT-DECL1=A (`effect` declarations) and D-META-EFFECT1=A (one effect model at both stages).

For metaprogramming: D-META-GATE1=A (`Meta.Generate`, `Meta.Include`), D-META-OPTIN2=A, D-META-CONTROL2=A and D-META-RECONCILE1=A (the opt-in advanced mode governs; older refusals bind projects that do not opt in). Also D-JAI-CODE1=A (everyone gets code values, pasting and macros; text-to-code is expert). For safety gates: D-ONCE-GATE1=A and D-GATE-LAW1=A.

THE META FAMILY UNDER A. Effects.jet gains these declarations. `$expert` is a new value in the attribute slot that already holds `$irreversible`.

```jet
effect Meta                        // compile-time code acting on the program
effect Meta.Generate               // add generated files: b.generate, derives
effect Meta.Include                // run a dependency's build inside yours
effect Meta.Paste                  // code values and #Expand macros pasted at a call
effect Meta.Code $expert           // change the program beyond adding and pasting
effect Meta.Code.Raw $expert       //   parse(text) to code, and macros with uses: *
effect Meta.Code.Types $expert     //   build types from facts, with no source file
effect Meta.Code.Rewrite $expert   //   change written code through checked change sets
effect Meta.Host $expert           // reach the build machine while compiling
```

HOLDING. Every Meta leaf is checked against the package's authority block, as Net is. Deny always wins, and denying a parent denies every child: `deny: [Meta]` blocks the whole family. Held means the package may use it. Non-expert leaves are held unless denied, so beginners write nothing. An `$expert` leaf is never held by default, and holding a parent never covers it: it must be named.

`allow: [Meta]` holds Generate, Include and Paste only; a note names the expert leaves it left out. `allow: [Meta.Code]` names an expert node, so it holds all three of its children. Only the main package, the one you build, may hold an expert leaf. It may pass one to a named dependency with `grants:`; a dependency cannot hold one by itself.

This follows existing precedent: effect declarations already carry an attribute, and the Mem and Panic roots already have their own holding rule (deny-only, E0751). There is one rights tree and one attribute table.

APPROVAL. Adding an expert leaf to the main package is a project-policy edit. The trust prompt's Update project policy choice shows the diff (D-TRUST-LAUNCH1=A). Expert leaves are never approved by Trust once, `--trust`, `-T` or `--allow`. CI never prompts; it fails with the exact `authority` line to add. Removing a leaf needs no approval. An organization file may deny any Meta leaf, and the outermost refusal wins.

WHERE META LEAVES APPEAR. Meta leaves describe compile-time work, so they appear only in rows of compile-time code: `fn build`, providers, hooks and `comptime fn`. A run-time function that calls a macro keeps its own row; the package's hold of `Meta.Paste` governs the paste. So `fn build(b: BuildContext) -[!Meta.Generate]> BuildPlan` makes `b.generate` an error there. Holding is the package's permission; a build entry's row still lists the Meta leaves it uses, as D-META-GATE1=A requires.

WHAT EACH OLD POWER BECOMES. `metaprogramming: unrestricted` (D-META-OPTIN2) becomes holding `Meta.Code`; its registration, target and approval rules stay. raw_code (D-JAI-CODE1) becomes `Meta.Code.Raw`. comptime_host becomes `Meta.Host`: compile-time code that runs programs, uses unpinned network, loads foreign libraries or opens windows needs `Meta.Host` held.

The site still writes `#Impure("reason")`, and the function row still lists the ordinary effect, such as Exec. That is the same shape as run-time code. unlimited_steps is dropped: the step limit is a budget, not an effect, and `#StepLimit(n)` (D-PREP-FUEL1=A, ratified, not yet built) covers long work. open_generics is dropped with the D-JAI-GENERIC1 revision.

CHECK REMOVAL UNDER A. Removing run-time checks is not something code does, so it is not an effect. It is an audited safety waiver, like `#Unsafe`, and uses the existing gate rules. A new gate kind, `check_removal`, joins the D-GATE-LAW1 list. Its written gate is a check field set to `off` in the main package's build settings (D-JAI-BUILDOPT1), such as `bounds: off`, or `#Unchecked(bounds)` inside `#Unsafe("reason")`.

The default `.GateOnly` allows it and lists it in `jet inspect gates` and the build receipt. A package whose policy says `check_removal: .Forbid` is always compiled with its checks, even in an unchecked build, and the receipt says so. An organization `.Forbid` refuses the build. Generic and inlined code takes the setting of the package that wrote it.

I1 AMENDMENT. Today I1 reads: 'The expert escape hatch is a user-written, audited `#Unsafe("reason") { … }` block or `#Unsafe("reason") fn`. Generated Rust `unsafe` appears only there or in vetted standard-library and memory internals.'

Under A and B, the code generator leaves out the named check at each site in packages built with the gate. On the Rust tier that site becomes an unchecked access inside a generated `unsafe` block. The receipt lists the gate and every package built without the check. I1 adds this text: 'or a check field set to off in the main package's build settings, an audited gate listed in every receipt.'

Under C, I1 is unchanged.

AMENDS. D-AUTHORITY-ROOTS1 (root list gains Meta). D-META-GATE1: the Meta family replaces its names. Its refusals ('in-place rewrite, a type with no file, running the program inside the compiler') were already lifted for opted-in projects by D-META-RECONCILE1=A.

Under A, opted in means holding `Meta.Code` or `Meta.Host`. Also `Meta.Reflect` and `Meta.Const` are not declared, since reflection is pure and compile-time parameters are ordinary generics. D-META-OPTIN2: the manifest member becomes holding `Meta.Code`. Its standard mode 'forbids … caller-code insertion'; pasting is now allowed there, as D-JAI-CODE1=A already ruled.

Also D-CTEFFECT1 and D-ONCE-GATE1: at compile time `Meta.Host` replaces the per-run `--gate impure=allow`, and E3410, E3411 and E1343 change their fix text. Run-time `#Impure` keeps its gate. D-TRUST-LAUNCH1: expert leaves are excluded from one-run approval. D-JAI-BUILDOPT1: `off` needs the `check_removal` gate instead of a power. D-GATE-LAW1: the gate list gains `check_removal`.

MIGRATION. One cutover with machine-applicable `jet fix` rewrites: `metaprogramming: unrestricted` becomes `authority: { holds: { allow: [Meta.Code] } }`, and a compile-time `--gate impure=allow` becomes an `allow: [Meta.Host]` line. No aliases remain. New names get Syntax.rs and Effects.jet rows (I7); every refusal has a registered code and UI snapshot (I4).

BEGINNER AND EXPERT PATHS. A beginner writes nothing: generated code, includes and macros work, and every expert effect and every check stays on. An expert names expert leaves in the main package's allow list, or sets `bounds: off` in a release profile. A careful team writes `deny: [Meta.Code, Meta.Host]` and `check_removal: .Forbid`.

WHY NOT B. B makes check removal an `Unchecked` effect family too. A held effect does nothing by itself, and an effect row cannot see how another package was compiled, so `-[!Unchecked]>` could not be checked by the call graph. WHY NOT C. C keeps every Meta effect but offers no whole-build check removal; experts waive checks only per scope.

OPEN DEPENDENCIES. D-META-HASH1 (open) may respell `$` attributes mechanically. D-LSP-BUILDSAVE1 (open) says a check never uses `Meta.Host`.

EVIDENCE. Jai: #run opens windows and calls DLLs while compiling (Blow UTqZNujQOlA 00:44:04-00:53:31). Jai build options turn checks off (The Way to Jai examples/30/30.4_build_options.jai:50-123). Rust: `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]` lets a crate refuse a power at its root. Zig: build-wide safety modes plus per-scope `@setRuntimeSafety`.

options.name: Meta effect family; check removal as a safety gate
options.detail: Strong metaprogramming becomes the Meta family on the one effect tree, with expert leaves that must be named by the main package. Deny a family or one leaf, exactly as with Net. Whole-build check removal is an audited safety gate under the existing gate rules, which any package or organization may forbid.
options.technical: Effects.jet rows above with the `$expert` attribute: excluded from default holding and from ancestor holding, root-only, grantable per dependency through `authority.grants`, approved only through a project-policy edit. New gate kind `check_removal` on the D-GATE-LAW1 list; written gate is a D-JAI-BUILDOPT1 check field set to `off` or `#Unchecked` inside `#Unsafe`.

options.name: Meta and Unchecked effect families
options.detail: The Meta family of A, plus a second expert family, Unchecked, with leaves Bounds, Null and Casts. Holding a leaf lets the main package turn that check off; a library denies Unchecked to keep its checks.
options.technical: As A, plus `effect Unchecked $expert` and three leaves. `bounds: off` needs `Unchecked.Bounds` held. A package denying Unchecked is compiled with checks.

options.name: Meta effect family; checks removed only per scope
options.detail: The Meta family of A. There is no whole-build check removal: an expert waives checks only in a written `#Unchecked(bounds)` scope inside `#Unsafe("reason")`.
options.technical: As A for Meta. D-JAI-BUILDOPT1 check fields lose the `off` value; `fatal` and `report` remain. I1 unchanged.

comparisons.note: Build options turn checks off for a whole build, and #run code has no limits at all.
A crate may refuse a power for all of its own code at its root.
Build-wide safety off with ReleaseFast; per scope with @setRuntimeSafety.

recommendation.why: A puts Jai's metaprogramming power under the effects Jet users already know: one deny blocks the family, one leaf blocks one power. Check removal stays where Jet already audits waived safety checks.
gains: One effect system for every metaprogramming power.
Block the whole family or one power.
Any library can keep its own checks.

losses.loss: An expert grant carries no written reason.
losses.mitigation: Each use site keeps its reason marker, and the build receipt lists every expert grant and site.

losses.loss: Unchecked builds can hide memory bugs.
losses.mitigation: It is an audited gate in every receipt, and any package or organization may forbid it.

whyNot.reason: B calls check removal an effect, but removing a check is not something code does, and rows cannot check it.
C is safer but leaves Jai's whole-build check removal with no Jet form.

recommendation.tradeoff: One effect family and one gate kind, for all of Jai's power under rules Jet already has.

decisions.title: Code values and macros that paste code at the call site
decisions.situation: A macro is a function whose body is pasted where it is called, so it can wrap your code, time it or loop around it. Jai has macros and lets build code pass pieces of code around as values. Jet has neither in everyday code, and its rules still forbid macros forever, so ported Jai code needs awkward rewrites. The vote decides whether Jet adds checked macros and code values; we recommend adding them for everyone, with text-to-code only for experts.
decisions.gist: Should Jet add Jai-style macros and code values, and who may use them?
decisions.lesson: A code value is a piece of source held before it runs. Pasting puts it somewhere. A macro is a function whose body is pasted at each call. Jai is a game language that uses macros widely. Whichever option wins, pasted code is checked like code you typed, and errors point at your line.
decisions.story: Mei ports a Jai profiler that wraps any block in timing code, and a renderer that loops over visible entities with custom loop logic. Both use macros that paste code into the caller and change the caller's variables. Jet gives her closures, which can do neither.
decisions.detail:
Audit rows refer to Docs/audits/jai-parity-2026-10-16.md. Spellings use today's `prep` keyword and `$` fact mark (D-COMPILER-NS1=A, shipped 2026-09-30). The open ballots D-COMPTIME-WORD1 (prep to comptime) and D-META-HASH1 ($ reads to ##) would respell them mechanically. No choice here changes with those outcomes. Words used here. Jai is a systems programming language by Jonathan Blow, built for games, with no guardrails by default. `prep { }` runs Jet code while compiling.

A `$` word such as `T.$fields` reads a fact the compiler knows. A `#Name` marker attaches a rule to the code below it. `package.jet` is a package's settings file. The main package is the one you build directly.

DESIGN UNDER A. (1) Code values: `code { ... }` and `code(expr)` hold parsed, not yet checked, source. D-META-CODE1 is recorded as A, with the owner's ratification comment 'Both option A and b. A is the simple case, b is the expert case'. This ballot builds option B on that comment and asks the owner to confirm it. Code values are unbuilt, and `Syntax.rs:119-122` still says no code values exist.

Template bodies in derive and b.generate are code values written in place, so there is one concept. (2) `paste c` pastes a code value at a statement, item or expression position (Jai #insert). The word is `paste` because D-API-STORE1 retired `insert`. Names in a code value resolve where it was written (hygiene). `paste c with [i]` lets the pasted code see listed macro names (Jai #insert,scope()). (3) `#Expand fn` is a macro (Jai #expand).

Parameters of type Code receive caller code unevaluated, written `code { }` at the call. No trailing-block syntax is added, so D-TRAILBLOCK2 stands. Other parameters are evaluated once, in order. Macro-local names never clash with the caller's. (4) Caller variables (Jai backtick): `#Expand(uses: [total])` lists caller variables the macro may read or write. The pasted code is checked at the call as if written there, so moves and borrows of those variables follow the caller's ordinary rules.

`defines: [name]` declares new caller names, and an existing name of that spelling is a registered error. `exits` allows return, break and next to leave the caller (Jai's backtick return). Such a macro is called as `timed!(...)`, so control flow stays visible. Inside a macro, `$caller.code` is the call as a Code value (Jai #caller_code). D-JAI-SITE1 defines `$caller`, and if SITE1 loses, this ballot adds `$caller.code` alone.

(5) `c.nodes()` gives a typed, read-only tree with kinds, children, locations and, after checking, types (Jai compiler_get_nodes). `c.map(f)` builds new code from a transform. Compiler nodes are never mutable. (6) Jai for_expansion maps to `Iterable` (D-ITER-HOOK), which stays the one loop protocol. A macro pastes code and defines no loop protocol. Inside pasted code, `?` and `defer` behave as if written at the call.

(7) Limits and tools: 100 nested expansions by default, raised by `#ExpandLimit(n)`. Errors name the call, the macro line and the pasted line. `jet inspect expand` prints any expansion. The debugger steps through macro lines unless the macro carries `#NoDebug` (Jai #no_debug). (8) The raw_code power (D-JAI-EXPERT1) adds two things. `parse(text)` turns text into a Code value in prep and macros (Jai #insert of a string).

`uses: *` lets a macro touch any caller name (Jai backtick). Every new word is registered in Syntax.rs under this decision (I7).

LAWS AMENDED. S26 'Rejected forever: token/AST/attribute macros'. D-METAMUTATE1 'user macros are rejected'. D-METADEPTH2 'no macros'. D-META-GATE1 'token or tree macros'. The D-META-RECONCILE1 universal limit on user macros. D-METHODMACRO1's decline of call-site expansion. D-META-CONTROL2 and D-META-OPTIN2, which place code capture and insertion in advanced sessions (pasting moves to standard mode). And, for raw_code only, the D-META-CODE1 and D-METADERIVE1 rule that generated code never re-lexes text.

KEPT. The closed grammar (macros add no syntax), checking of every expansion (I3), no mutable compiler nodes, and D-META-CONTROL2 change sets for rewriting written code.

REGRETS DESIGNED OUT. Backtick clumsiness (OAIqCpqszVw 00:34:34) becomes a checked list. Macro errors without the call site (6qkL_DmHOuo 00:35:04) get three locations. Missing macro debug info (QX46eLqq1ps 00:59:00) is fixed. Blow's Lisp-list versus typed-tree question (pg_Wk2GBZDw 00:22:00) is answered with typed trees.

EVIDENCE. Jai #expand, #insert, #code, backtick and for_expansion (Blow QX46eLqq1ps 00:13:12-01:24:24, 6qkL_DmHOuo. The Way to Jai Appendix C and book/26C:139-268). Nim templates and Racket hygiene show hygiene-by-default with explicit escapes works. Rust's `!` shows a visible call mark. C text macros show the failure mode.

options.name: Checked macros for all
options.detail: Everyone gets code values, pasting and macros. Pasted code is checked at the paste site like hand-written code. A macro lists the caller variables it reads or writes, and a macro that can return or break out of the caller is called with a visible `!`. Turning text into code needs the raw_code expert power.
options.technical:
Type `Code`. Literal `code { ... }` (D-META-CODE1's option B, per the owner's comment) and `code(expr)`. Statement `paste c` at statement, item and expression positions. `paste c with [names]` exposes listed macro-local names. Marker `#Expand` with `uses: [names]`, `defines: [names]` and `exits`. A macro declaring `exits` is called as `name!(...)`, checked by sema. Read-only typed tree `c.nodes()`. Transform `c.map(f) -> Code`. Depth limit 100, raised by `#ExpandLimit(n)`. `#NoDebug` skips macro lines in the debugger.

Expert: `parse(text) -> Code` and `uses: *` under the raw_code power.

options.name: Experts only
options.detail: The design of A, but every macro, code value and paste needs a `macros` power in the main package, including macros from libraries.
options.technical: As A, gated by a D-JAI-EXPERT1 power `macros`. A dependency declaring a macro builds only if the main package lists that power.

options.name: No macros
options.detail: Keep today's universal macro ban. Jai macros map to closures, `#Inline` hints, `Iterable`, derive templates and the advanced change-set API. A closure cannot change the caller's variables or leave the caller.
options.technical: No change. S26, D-METAMUTATE1, D-METHODMACRO1 and the D-META-RECONCILE1 universal limit stay.

comparisons.note: Templates are hygienic by default; {.inject.} deliberately exposes a name to the caller, like `uses:`.

template withLock(l, body) =
  acquire(l)
  body
  release(l)

comparisons.note: Macros are called with `!`, so a reader knows the call may expand to anything.
comparisons.code: macro_rules! timed { ($l:expr, $b:block) => {{ let s = Instant::now(); $b; println!("{}: {:?}", $l, s.elapsed()) }} }

comparisons.note: Backtick reaches caller names; Blow calls it clumsy and plans a version 2 (Q&A, December 2022, 00:34:34).

recommendation.why: Macros are a core Jai tool. Checking every expansion and listing the caller variables it touches makes them safe enough for everyone.
gains: Jai macro power, with text-to-code for experts.
Errors point at both the call and the macro.

losses.loss: A macro call can hide pasted control flow.
losses.mitigation: A macro that can leave the caller must be called with `!`, so the call site shows it.

losses.loss: Functions and macros overlap for simple cases.
losses.mitigation: A lint suggests a plain function when a macro takes no code and touches no caller variables.

whyNot.reason: B keeps beginners away from macros but makes every user of a macro library opt in, unlike Jai.
C is simplest but cannot paste code, so many Jai designs have no direct Jet form.

recommendation.tradeoff: One new concept, macros, in exchange for Jai's code-as-data toolkit with checked expansions.

decisions.title: Compiler moments Jet's hooks still lack, compared with Jai's message loop
decisions.situation: In Jai a build program watches the compiler work: it hears each module import, adds code after everything is checked, takes over linking, and processes the finished program file. Jet's ratified hook table covers parsing, declarations, checking and output, but not these moments. Without them, Jai build programs such as custom linkers and whole-program code generators cannot be ported. The vote decides which moments Jet adds; we recommend all of them, plus an ordered read-only event view for experts.
decisions.gist: Which compiler moments should Jet hooks gain so they can do everything Jai's message loop does?
decisions.lesson: A hook is a Jet function the compiler calls at a set moment, attached with `#On(stage)`. Jai, a game language, instead gives build code a loop of compiler messages. Jet's ratified stages are parsed, declared, checked and emitted, plus build moments. This vote adds imported, settled, link, before_write, after_write and finished.
decisions.story: Ken maintains a Jai editor whose build program links with a hand-tuned linker command, generates a settings table from every checked struct, and sets the program icon after linking. Jet's hooks can report problems but cannot do any of those three jobs.
decisions.detail:
Audit rows refer to Docs/audits/jai-parity-2026-10-16.md. Spellings use today's `prep` keyword and `$` fact mark (D-COMPILER-NS1=A, shipped 2026-09-30). The open ballots D-COMPTIME-WORD1 (prep to comptime) and D-META-HASH1 ($ reads to ##) would respell them mechanically. No choice here changes with those outcomes. Words used here. Jai is a systems programming language by Jonathan Blow, built for games, with no guardrails by default. `prep { }` runs Jet code while compiling.

A `$` word such as `T.$fields` reads a fact the compiler knows. A `#Name` marker attaches a rule to the code below it. `package.jet` is a package's settings file. The main package is the one you build directly.

BASELINE. D-HOOK-STAGES1=A was ratified on 2026-10-07 (Tower card #3520). Its stages have no code yet (#4760).

MAPPING UNDER A. Jai .FILE maps to compiler.parsed (ratified). .IMPORT maps to compiler.imported, once per resolved module. .TYPECHECKED maps to compiler.declared (ratified). ALL_SOURCE_CODE_PARSED has no separate stage: compiler.declared runs after all files parse, and code a Jai program adds there is added in settled instead. The TYPECHECKED_ALL_WE_CAN phase maps to compiler.settled, which runs after compiler.checked.

Its Round payload has the program and the items new since the last round. A hook returns findings and items. Added items are checked and published through compiler.generate (D-META-PUBLISH2), so a re-run that publishes an identical item is a no-op. More than 16 rounds is an error naming the hooks. This covers Jai's collect-then-generate pattern (The Way to Jai examples/30/30.11).

Jai #placeholder needs no new marker: names published by compiler.generate exist before user code is checked, and an unpublished name is an ordinary error. ALL_TARGET_CODE_BUILT maps to compiler.emitted (ratified, read-only). READY_FOR_CUSTOM_LINK_COMMAND maps to build.link. One hook per target may replace linking. It receives object files, libraries, linker arguments and the default command, and returns the artifact (focus first.jai:75,153-155,357-391).

PRE_WRITE_EXECUTABLE maps to build.before_write, which may replace the file, and POST_WRITE_EXECUTABLE to build.after_write, which may sign or add an icon. Link and write hooks run as declared build actions with Exec and FS capabilities, so they keep D-BUILDACTION1's grants and cache keys. Only the main package may attach them, and two link hooks for one target are a registered error naming both. COMPLETE and ERROR map to compiler.finished.

DEBUG_DUMP (a compiler crash) stays an internal error with exit 101 under I2. Link and write hooks are build actions with declared capabilities, so they are an amendment to D-HOOK-STAGES1's Tier 0/1 rule for those two stages only. Jai's wild example ports as one settled hook adding code and one build.link hook running the linker command and returning the artifact. Hooks are compiler stages, not `core.event` events (D-EVENT1).

The ordered view is named `stages()` to avoid that word. D-JAI-BUILDOPT1 relies on build.link for Jai's custom link command. If this ballot picks C, that row stays open. Jai -plug and +Plugin map to hook packages listed in the main package.jet with D-JPK-BUILDSCRIPT1 grants. First-party hook packages cover Jai's bundled Check, Polymorph_Report, Program_Print, IProf, Autorun and Icon. Jai intercept flags only filter which messages a metaprogram receives.

A Jet hook receives its stage's payload and ignores what it does not need. Jai's loop maps to `Session.stages()` under the metaprogramming power: the same payloads, read-only, in a fixed order (module path, then declaration order). It cannot add or change code. Additions go through stage returns. This amends D-METAMUTATE1's 'message loop' rejection for a read-only view only.

REGRETS DESIGNED OUT. Nondeterministic order (Blow KHIeP_-Kp00 01:28:00. KHmbabcL-is 01:17:51) gets a fixed order and order-free merges. Silently filtered declarations (KHIeP_-Kp00 00:33:00) become payloads with a `complete` flag. Polymorphs sent only when used (jjCfAg_gtDw 01:18:09) become generic declarations delivered once, with instances listed in settled's program. Late generated code hiding real errors (SSVHWrYG974 00:44:00) gets provenance on every added item.

Message release rules (KHIeP_-Kp00 00:50:49) become immutable payloads.

AMENDS D-HOOK-STAGES1: adds rows. 'stages run once' gains the settled exception. New stage names, payload types and errors are registered (I4, I7).

EVIDENCE. Jai message kinds and phases (The Way to Jai book/30B:113-206. Focus first.jai:98-169. Tsoding jai-wasm first.jai:31-77). KSP rounds and Roslyn incremental generators are the proven precedents for repeated generation and deterministic stages.

options.name: All Jai moments
options.detail: New stages: imported runs for each module, and settled adds code after the whole program is checked, repeating with only new items until none are added. link replaces linking for one target, before_write and after_write process the program file, and finished reports success or failure. Experts with the metaprogramming power get a read-only, ordered view of every stage payload.
options.technical:
Rows added to the D-HOOK-STAGES1 table: compiler.imported(Module) -> findings. Compiler.settled(Round{program, new_items}) -> Output{findings, items}, repeated until no items are added, at most 16 rounds (registered error beyond). Build.link(LinkInputs) -> Artifact, one hook per target, root-listed only. Build.before_write(Artifact) -> replacement Artifact. Build.after_write(Artifact) -> findings. Compiler.finished(Outcome) -> findings.

Link and write hooks run as build actions (D-BUILDACTION1) with declared Exec and FS capabilities, and their outputs enter the action cache key. `compiler.advanced.Session.stages()` yields stage payloads read-only in a fixed order.

options.detail: imported, settled and finished as in A. Custom linking and before or after write steps are steps of the fn build plan (D-BUILDPLUGIN1), not hooks. No ordered view.
options.technical: Compiler stages as A. `link:` and plan steps on BuildContext instead of build.link and the write stages. No `Session.stages()`.

options.name: Keep today's table
options.detail: D-HOOK-STAGES1 as ratified. Jai custom linkers, settled-phase generators and post-write steps have no Jet form.
options.technical: No change.

comparisons.note: Processors run in rounds until no new files appear, the same idea as the settled stage.
Incremental generators are staged, cached and deterministic, the model Jet's stages follow.
One pull loop over messages and phases.

recommendation.why: Jai build programs depend on these moments. Typed stages give each one with deterministic, cacheable results, and the event view keeps Jai's loop style read-only.
gains: Every Jai phase maps to a stage.
Stage results are cached and keyed.

losses.loss: More stages to keep stable across releases.
losses.mitigation: Each stage has its own versioned payload type, so one stage can change without touching the others.

whyNot.reason: B keeps linking in the plan, but hook packages cannot offer link or signing steps, and there is no ordered view.
C keeps today's table, so custom linkers and whole-program generators cannot be ported.

recommendation.tradeoff: A larger stage table, for every Jai message-loop capability.

decisions.title: Facts about where code is: caller location, current location, constness and the called function
decisions.situation: A logging or checking function is most useful when it reports the file and line of the code that called it. Jai provides this and related facts, such as the current function's name and which function a call will pick. Jet has none of them, and its rules mention a caller-location value that was never built. The vote decides which of these facts Jet adds; we recommend all of them, read with Jet's existing fact mark.
decisions.gist: Which facts about the code's own location should Jet provide, like Jai's #caller_location?
decisions.lesson: A fact is a value the compiler already knows, read with `$`, such as `T.$fields`. A source location is a file, line, column and enclosing function. The caller location is where the current function was called from. A default is the value a parameter takes when the call omits it, written `name: Type{value}`.
decisions.story: Lena writes a check helper used in two hundred places. When a check fails, the log points inside the helper, not at the failing call, so she has to search by message text. Jai's version reports the caller's file and line.
decisions.detail:
Audit rows refer to Docs/audits/jai-parity-2026-10-16.md. Spellings use today's `prep` keyword and `$` fact mark (D-COMPILER-NS1=A, shipped 2026-09-30). The open ballots D-COMPTIME-WORD1 (prep to comptime) and D-META-HASH1 ($ reads to ##) would respell them mechanically. No choice here changes with those outcomes. Words used here. Jai is a systems programming language by Jonathan Blow, built for games, with no guardrails by default. `prep { }` runs Jet code while compiling.

A `$` word such as `T.$fields` reads a fact the compiler knows. A `#Name` marker attaches a rule to the code below it. `package.jet` is a package's settings file. The main package is the one you build directly.

FACTS UNDER A. `$here`: SourceLocation for the expression where it is written (Jai #file, #line, #filepath, #location and, through `$here.function`, #procedure_name). SourceLocation is new: SourceSpan holds byte offsets and SourceInfo describes generated source identity (D-META-REFLECT2), so neither carries line and column. Unlike D-META-REFLECT2's fallible queries, these roots never fail. Inside a closure, `function` is the enclosing named function.

`$caller`: SourceLocation of the call, legal only as a parameter default and inside an #Expand macro (D-JAI-CODE1), where `$caller.code` is the call as Code. Anywhere else, `$caller` is a registered error naming those two places. A wrapper forwards its own location by declaring `at: SourceLocation{$caller}` and passing `at`. Nothing is implicit. Function values carry no defaults, so a call through one passes the location explicitly. SourceLocation prints as `path:line:column`.

`x.$known` is true when x is a constant expression or a prep value. GENERIC1's `prep?` uses the same front-end definition, identical on every tier. It differs from `$phase`, which says where code runs. For `LIMIT :: 5` and `LIMIT :: prep { 5 }` it is true. For a run-time variable it is false (Jai is_constant). `call.$callee`: FunctionInfo of the function a call resolves to, without running it (Jai #procedure_of_call).

Jai #this maps to `Self` in a type and to the function's own name in a procedure. No new fact is needed. Jai #compile_time maps to the ratified `$phase`. Jai #location(code) maps to `c.$location` on Code values in D-JAI-CODE1.

AMENDS. D-COMPILER-NS1 gains two subjectless roots. E2414 (defaults must be compile-time constants) treats `$caller` as a per-call constant. D-SHAPE2's `#Caller()` mention is replaced under A and B and built as a marker under C.

STATUS. None of these exist in code today. Each needs a registry row, an example with golden output on every tier (I5), and diagnostics. The example's `print` inside prep follows the compile-time output rules of D-CTIO1. The stale `@` fact text at D-ONCE-AT1 is cleaned up in the same cutover.

REGRETS. In 2015 Blow had no call-site file and line for asserts (0KkW_Zo_pDc 00:05:15). #caller_location was not constant inside #run (pgiVrhsGkKY 00:40:09). `$caller` is a constant wherever it is legal. These citations come from the mining notes.

EVIDENCE. Jai Appendix C rows for #file, #line, #filepath, #location, #caller_location, #procedure_name, #procedure_of_call and #this. Blow yJukJS81o-k 00:19:28-00:21:38. Rust, Swift and C++20 prove the caller-location default works with no run-time lookup.

decisions.title: Every Jai build option as a Jet build option, and pinning options in fn build
decisions.situation: Jai lets a project control dozens of build settings from code, from the target processor to linker arguments and which runtime checks stay on. Jet's build profile has a handful of settings, and its rules say the command line always wins, so a project cannot fix a setting it depends on. Games, embedded programs and plugins therefore cannot be built the way their authors intend. The vote decides which settings Jet adds and whether build code may pin them; we recommend all of them, and pinning.
decisions.gist: Should Jet offer every Jai build setting, and may build code pin a setting the command line cannot change?
decisions.lesson: A build profile is a named group of settings, such as release, written in package.jet. `fn build` is Jet code that registers what to build. Pinning means build code fixes a setting so a command-line flag cannot change it. Today the command line always wins; option A reverses that where a project pins.
decisions.story: Sam ships a game to the web, a desktop build with a custom linker script, and a plugin library. He needs CPU features, linker arguments, a dynamic-library output and dead-code removal set from code, and he needs CI flags never to undo them.
decisions.detail:
Audit rows refer to Docs/audits/jai-parity-2026-10-16.md. Spellings use today's `prep` keyword and `$` fact mark (D-COMPILER-NS1=A, shipped 2026-09-30). The open ballots D-COMPTIME-WORD1 (prep to comptime) and D-META-HASH1 ($ reads to ##) would respell them mechanically. No choice here changes with those outcomes. Words used here. Jai is a systems programming language by Jonathan Blow, built for games, with no guardrails by default. `prep { }` runs Jet code while compiling.

A `$` word such as `T.$fields` reads a fact the compiler knows. A `#Name` marker attaches a rule to the code below it. `package.jet` is a package's settings file. The main package is the one you build directly.

TODAY. The rules list five profile fields: optimize, debug_info, small, panic and settings (D-BUILDPROFILE1). THE CATALOG UNDER A AND B, with Jai names in brackets. Output: the output kind is chosen where it is today, by the package kind and by registration (`b.add_executable`, `b.add_library`). `b.add_library` gains `link: .Static` or `.Dynamic`, `b.add_object` is new, and check-only is `jet check` [output_type]. output_dir and work_dir [output_path, intermediate_path].

Entry name for freestanding targets is the target profile's entry fact [entry_point_name]. Target: os, arch, cpu (native or a name. The existing `--cpu` flag), cpu_features, min_os [os_target, cpu_target, machine_type, target_system_cpu, target_system_features, minimum_os_version]. Code generation: optimize keeps none, basic, full and size, and adds min_size [Optimization_Type]. Inline auto or never. Lto. Split_units. Function_sections. Frame_pointers. Red_zone.

Vectorize, unroll, tail_calls, merge_functions [llvm_options]. Emit ir, bitcode, asm or object [output_llvm_ir, output_bitcode]. Backend_args raw passthrough [llvm_options.command_line]. Fields apply per backend (Jet-native, Cranelift, rustc). A field a backend cannot honour is a registered error naming the backend, never silently ignored. Raw backend_args that make the backend reject the program remain an internal error under I2, and the receipt marks such builds.

Runtime checks: bounds, null and casts take fatal, report or off [array_bounds_check, null_pointer_check, cast_bounds_check]. `off` needs the unchecked_bounds, unchecked_null or unchecked_casts power. overflow sets the build default for `#Arithmetic` (D-WRAP-SCOPE1) and needs no power [math and arithmetic checks]. Per scope, `#Unchecked(bounds, casts, null)` removes named checks on one block or function (Jai #no_abc).

It is legal only inside an `#Unsafe("reason")` scope, the existing I1 gate, so it needs no power. The written reason is the audit record, `policy.unsafe` can deny or confine such scopes, and the build receipt lists each `#Unchecked` site. Today `#Unsafe` keeps bounds checks, and D-OOBPROOF1 elides only proven ones. Debug: debug_info none, lines or full (a Bool today). Debug_format. Stack_traces. Crash_backtrace. Debugger_names.

Step_into_expansions [emit_debug_info, stack_trace, backtrace_on_crash, use_natvis_compatible_types, -debug_for]. Size: dead_code all, packages or none [dead_code_elimination, -no_dce]. Type_info full, reachable or none [runtime_storageless_type_info, #type_info_none]. Max_instance_depth [maximum_polymorph_depth]. Link: link_args, libs, lib_paths [additional_linker_arguments]. Lazy_foreign [lazy_foreign_function_lookups]. A custom link step is D-JAI-EVENTS1's build.link.

Runtime: scratch_size [temporary_storage_size], only if D-JAI-CONTEXT1 adds scratch memory. Diagnostics: diagnostics human, msvc or json. Color. Short_paths. Timings. Quiet [use_visual_studio_message_format, shorten_filenames_in_error_messages, text_output_flags]. Data for build code: typed settings exist [user_data_*]. `jet build -- args` passes strings to fn build as `b.args` [compile_time_command_line].

COMMAND-LINE JAI FLAGS. -run maps to the existing `jet eval`. -add maps to `jet build --add 'decl'` under the raw_code power, if D-JAI-CODE1 passes. -debugger maps to card #5008, which debugs compile-time code. -very_debug maps to the existing hardened profile (D-HARDENED1) with full debug info. -no_jobs is the existing `--threads 1`. -randomize, -seed and -chaos map to `jet build --shuffle[=seed]`, the spelling `jet test` already uses. -report_poly maps to `--report instances` (#5000).

-no_cwd needs nothing. -import_dir maps to path and vendored dependencies, since Jet resolves packages by identity. PINNING (A only). `b.pin(setting, value)` in fn build makes a flag for that setting a registered error naming the pin. This reverses D-BUILDCTX-FLAGS1 ('command line always wins'), which the owner's 2026-10-07 notes digest restates, for pinned settings only, and adopts Blow's rule that program-set options win for reproducibility (OAIqCpqszVw 01:06:25).

INTERPLAY. D-JAI-EXPERT1 names the check powers. D-JAI-CONFIG1 reuses these fields for each profile, so if C wins, CONFIG1's os field comes from `--target` instead.

EVIDENCE. The Way to Jai book/30A, 30B and examples/30/30.4_build_options.jai:50-123. Focus first.jai:23-90. Infinite-pong first.jai:7-33. Cargo's typed profiles succeeded while RUSTFLAGS raw text is a long-standing pain. Zig's typed target query is the closest precedent.
