decisions.title: One list of what a project makes, written as data or code
decisions.situation: An output is one thing a project makes, such as a program, a server program, a library or a set of checks. Today Jet keeps two separate lists, one in the package file and one made by build code, so `jet run` and `jet build` see different outputs. Game teams porting from Jai, where build code makes each separate build with its own settings, cannot tell which list to use. The vote decides where outputs live, and we recommend one list that the package file and build code both add to, with every output picked by name.
decisions.gist: Where does a project declare what it makes, including Jai-style builds with their own settings?
decisions.lesson: An output is one thing a project makes: a program, server program, library or set of checks. Today the package file and build code keep two separate lists. A root `fn run` still runs first for bare `jet run` and `jet dev`; the default picks only when no root `fn run` exists. Each output can carry its own build settings, like a Jai workspace. A separate Jai-workspaces vote, shown after the settings-order and naming votes, decides how build code copies these settings and changes an output.
decisions.story: Mia keeps a small API and a command-line tool in one package. She lists both in the package file and types `jet dev api`. Her teammate Tomi adds a web build of their game from build code, with its own settings. Mia wants `jet dev game_web` to find it the same way. She also wants `jet run`, `jet dev` and `jet build` to see the same list.
decisions.detail:
Scope. This ballot decides where outputs are declared and how commands pick one. Sibling ballots on card c07glrub decide the rest. D-ENTRY-SHAPE1 decides entry shape, including `fn build(b: Build)` with no return value and `b.default(app)`. D-SETTING-ORDER1 decides the one settings order. D-ENTRY-NAMES1 decides type names. D-DEV-STATE1 and D-DEV-SERVICES1 decide dev state and services.

Words. Output means a thing the project makes: a program, a server program, a library or a set of checks. Target means only the platform, as in `#Target(Web)` and `--target=web`. Code uses the slate spellings `fn build(b: Build)` and `b.default(app)`. If those sibling ballots lose, only the spellings revert to `BuildContext`, `-> BuildPlan` and `b.plan(default: app)`.

Today, from the code. `jet build` names its artifact after the build plan's default entry, in `programmable_build_target_name` at Source/CmdCompile.rs:10295. `jet run` picks its entry from package `outputs:` through `select_output("run")` at crates/jet-pkg-model/src/Package/mod.rs:1089 and :1228. Neither reads the other. The Jet twin is `select_output` in Jetpack/PackageModel/Source/Manifest/Compose.jet:30.

The spec documents both lists. `Output` values are at Docs/spec/spec.md:4063-4086, and `b.add_*` calls at :4369-4375. The default has two homes: `defaults:` checked by `validate_defaults` (mod.rs:1062), and `b.plan(default)` read by `default_target()`. The canvas fixture at tests/canvas_scenarios.rs:1308 lists seven outputs with `defaults: { run: cli }`. A grep on 2026-10-19 found 61 `.jet` files calling `b.add_executable(`.

Ratified law involved. D-ECO-OUTPUT1=A: one typed output collection that commands select from. D-ECO-OUTPUT-KINDS1=A: nine closed kinds. D-ECO-OUTPUT-DEFAULT1=A: an ordered selection rule, and adding a candidate never silently retargets automation. D-ECO-OUTPUT-PAYLOAD1=A: thin outputs. D-SHAPE-OUTPUT-CALLABLE1=A: `entry` is a checked function reference. D-DX-ENTRY1=C: bare command order, with a root `fn <cmd>` first.

More ratified law. D-BUILDTARGET1=A: `b.add_*` returns handles, and `b.plan(default: app)` names the default. D-BUILDENTRY1=B and D-CONF-ENTRY1=A: one `fn build` per package. D-ECO19=A: `pkgs.dep.name` accessors. D-BUILD-INCLUDE1=A: `b.include(pkg)` runs a dependency build in a sandbox. D-JPK-DEVCOMPOSE1=D: `jet env` never runs project functions. D-CLAIM-BENCH1=A: no bench output. D-JAI-CONFIG1 (open, rewritten 2026-10-19 to this slate's terms) decides how build code copies settings, changes an output and reads the build machine; per-output `options:` is decided here.

Option A design, one list. Each entry is an `Output` value. `outputs:` adds data entries, and each `b.add_*` call adds a code entry and returns it as an `Output`. Names are unique across both sources. A duplicate is a registered error naming both lines.

Option A kinds from code. `b.add_executable` makes an Executable, and the new `b.add_service` a Service. `b.add_library` makes a Library, and `b.add_test` a Check. `b.add_asset_bundle`, `b.add_doc` and `b.add_package` make a Bundle. `b.add_install` and `b.add_publish` stay steps on an output. No new kind is added. Environment, Image, System and Fleet stay data only, because `jet env` and deploy must read them without running project code.

Option A fields. A code-made output may pass `entry:`. Without it, the entry is `fn run` in its first source file, as today. Both forms accept `options:`, the output's own build settings, which is where Jai workspaces live. The data form writes `options: .{ os: web, optimize: size }`, the profile spelling of D-JAI-BUILDOPT1=A with the type name elided. `b.output(name)` lets build code change a data-made output before the plan is sealed.

Option A zero setup and the default. With no runnable output, the root `fn run` is one implicit Executable named after the package. A root `fn run` still runs first for bare `jet run` and `jet dev`; the default picks only when no root `fn run` exists. So adding an output never retargets a bare command. The default row is `defaults: { run: cli }` in data, `b.default(cli)` in code, and `jet run cli` for one run, in the D-SETTING-ORDER1 order.

Option A default, continued. `jet dev` uses the `run` default, because dev always runs the program. Other command defaults, such as publish, keep their `defaults:` keys and take `b.default(t, command: .Publish)` in code. `jet inspect build` marks which output a bare command starts.

Option A names on the command line. A word naming a listed output selects it. A path with `/` or ending in `.jet` selects a file. A word naming both a file and an output whose entry is in that file selects that output. So in package `game` with `game.jet`, `jet run game` works. Only a word naming two different things is an error listing both.

Option A listing cost. Editors list code-made outputs from the last `jet inspect build`; data outputs need no build run. Option B pays that cost for every output, including the simplest two-program project.

Research, proven right ways. Cargo shows that one program needs no setup and that the default is one data line, `default-run`. SwiftPM evaluates Package.swift code into a plain manifest that tools read with `swift package dump-package`. Bazel macros make many targets, and `bazel query` lists them without building. Nix flakes keep programs, checks and dev shells in one typed `outputs` set, the model Jet's Output kinds already follow.

Research, known failures. Cargo's build.rs cannot add a program, so projects add helper crates such as the cargo-xtask pattern (github.com/matklad/cargo-xtask). Zig and Gradle make programs only in code, so editors must run build code to learn them. ZLS ships a build runner for this, and Gradle added a configuration cache to cut that cost (docs.gradle.org, configuration cache). No adoption numbers were gathered; these are documented designs, not measurements.

Design away, loss one: two ways to write one output. Attempt one was data only, option C. It was rejected because build code could no longer make builds in a loop. Attempt two was code only, option B. It was rejected because two programs would need build code and tools would have to run it. Result: one value type, one name space, a duplicate-name error, and the rule of data for fixed outputs and code for loops. Negligible.

Design away, loss two: other packages see only data outputs. The attempt to run every dependency build to list outputs was rejected, because it reverses the ratified rule that dependency builds are checked but not run. Result: `b.include(dep)` already reaches code-made outputs, and the error names both fixes. Reduced to one visible fix.

Amendments if A wins. Amends D-BUILDTARGET1=A: `b.add_*` calls add entries to the one output list and return `Output` instead of `BuildTarget`. `b.add_service`, `b.output(name)` and `b.profile(name)`, which returns a fresh copy of a package.jet profile, are new. The default's code spelling, `b.default(app)` or `b.plan(default: app)`, is decided by D-ENTRY-SHAPE1. Amends D-ECO-OUTPUT1=A: build code may add outputs of the compiled kinds, while Environment, Image, System and Fleet stay data.

Amends D-ECO-OUTPUT-DEFAULT1=A: `b.default(t)` is the code form of the `defaults:` row, ordered by D-SETTING-ORDER1, and `jet dev` uses the `run` default. Its root `fn run` first rule is kept. Amends D-ECO-OUTPUT-PAYLOAD1=A: an output may carry `options:`, its own build settings; every other graph fact stays single-copy on the graph.

Amends D-SHAPE-OUTPUT-CALLABLE1=A only in wording: code-made outputs may pass `entry:`, and the spec drops the word legacy for `fn run`. Amends D-DX-ENTRY1=C: bare `jet dev` reads `defaults.run`; `defaults.dev` naming an Environment becomes an error pointing to `--env`.

D-JAI-CONFIG1 (open) was rewritten on 2026-10-19 to these terms (outputs, `BuildOptions`, `b.default`, seal at return, no exact-options rule) and takes per-output `options:` and `b.output(name)` from this ballot. Unchanged by this ballot: D-ECO-OUTPUT-KINDS1=A, D-ECO19=A, D-BUILD-INCLUDE1=A and D-CONF-ENTRY1=A. D-BUILDENTRY1=B keeps one `fn build` per package here; D-ENTRY-SHAPE1 changes its signature.

Cutover. Join `programmable_build_target_name` and `select_output` over one list, in Rust and in the Jet twins. Rename the `BuildTarget` handle in Core/build/declarations.jet:175 and its Rust twin. Add `b.add_service` and `b.output`. Change the `dev` intent in `intent_accepts_kind` (mod.rs:1883), which selects an Environment today, to select like `run`. Environments stay selected by `--env` (D-ENVFLAG1=A).

Cutover, continued. Update spec sections Program commands and Output and Programmable builds. Register `b.add_service`, `b.output`, `b.profile`, the `command:` argument of `b.default` and `options:` on outputs (I7). Also register the output list in the existing `jet inspect build` (D-CLI-ONE1=A), the duplicate-name error and the name-clash error. The 61 existing `b.add_executable(` callers keep working unchanged.

Review: one fresh combined pass (beginner + adversarial), agent SlateReview, Claude family, 2026-10-19, per owner directive for one review. Repaired: root `fn run` rule, story, name-or-file rule, D-DX-ENTRY1 amendment, listing cost, `b.add_object`, code comments, output wording, mitigations, D-JAI-CONFIG1 note, length. Cohesion pass CohesionReview 2026-10-19 repaired: D-JAI-CONFIG1 references, inspect build, b.profile ownership, amendment lists, output wording.

options.name: One list, data or code
options.detail: The package has one output list. The package file adds plain entries, and `fn build` adds entries with `b.add_*`. Both make the same value with the same fields, so a command cannot tell them apart. `jet run name`, `jet dev name` and `jet build name` pick any output by name. Each output may carry its own build settings in data or in code, which is where Jai workspaces live.

options.name: Build code only
options.detail: Only `fn build` makes the outputs Jet compiles. The package file keeps no `outputs:` or `defaults:`, only machine setups such as environments, which `jet env` reads without running code. `b.default(cli)` is the only default. This is the Zig and Jai model.
options.technical: Retire `outputs:` entries of kinds Executable, Service, Library, Check and Bundle, and the `defaults:` block. Add `b.add_service`. With no `fn build`, the root `fn run` is still one implicit Executable. Editors, package tools and `pkgs.dep.name` accessors must run each package's `fn build` to learn any output. So dependency builds run whenever a consumer reads them, which reverses the ratified rule that they are checked but not run.
options.code:

    cli :: b.add_executable("cli", ["cli.jet"], [])
    b.add_service("api", ["api.jet"], [])
    b.default(cli)
}
$ jet dev api

options.name: Package file only
options.detail: Only the package file lists outputs, and each entry may carry its own `options:`. `fn build` may change a listed output by adding sources, generated code or settings, but it cannot add one. This is the Cargo model with per-output settings added.
options.technical: Retire `b.add_executable` and the other `b.add_*` output calls, and `b.plan(default:)`. `b.output(name)` returns a listed output for the change calls of D-JAI-CONFIG1. The default is `defaults:` only. Settings in data can set fields but cannot be computed. Jai's `compiler_create_workspace` in a loop has no Jet form.

comparisons.note: Build code is the only way to make a workspace, and each workspace has its own options and files (The Way to Jai, chapter 30).
build.zig is code only. The Zig editor server ships a build runner so it can run build.zig and learn the modules.

b.installArtifact(exe);

comparisons.note: One src/main.rs needs no setup, `[[bin]]` lists more programs, and `default-run` picks the default. build.rs cannot add a program, so teams use helper crates such as cargo-xtask.

[[bin]]
name = "server"
path = "src/server.rs"

One `outputs` set holds packages, apps, checks and dev shells, and `nix run .#name` picks one by name.
BUILD files declare targets, and macros can make many. `bazel query` lists them without building.

recommendation.why: One list gives one set of names and one way to pick. Data stays readable without running code, and code keeps Jai builds made in loops.
gains: `jet run name`, `jet dev name` and `jet build name` find every output.
Plain data for fixed outputs, and code for Jai-style loops.
Tools read data outputs without running code.
Jai-style builds keep their own settings, in data or code.

losses.loss: Two ways to write one output.
losses.mitigation: Use data for fixed outputs and code only for loops; `jet inspect build` lists both with their lines.

losses.loss: Other packages see only a dependency's data outputs.
losses.mitigation: The error names both fixes: list the output as data, or call `b.include(dep)` in build code.

whyNot.reason: Even two plain programs would need build code, and every output would need a build run before tools could list it.
Build code cannot make builds in a loop, which is the heart of Jai's workspaces.

recommendation.tradeoff: Two spellings of one value, for zero setup and the Jai model.

decisions.title: One table and one order for every setting
decisions.situation: A setting is one value that changes how a command works, such as the port `jet dev` serves on. Today one setting can be written in several places, and the commands rank those places in different ways. The `--port` flag works for a plain web app but is silently ignored once the project has a `fn dev`, so people cannot predict the value. The vote decides one table and one order for every setting, and we recommend that a flag wins for one run unless project code pins the value.
decisions.gist: When one setting is written in several places, which place wins, and is that order the same for every command?
decisions.lesson: A setting is one value, such as the dev port. Jet's built-in value is the stock default. A flag such as `--port=8080` changes one run. A package.jet field such as `dev: { port: 8080 }` records project data. A method on an entry handle such as `d.port(8080)` records it in code. A few settings also have a source marker, such as `#Target(Web)`. A pin is a code line that refuses a different flag. `jet explain dev` shows which place set each value.
decisions.story: Mia keeps her dev port in code as `d.port(8080)`. One afternoon another app holds port 8080, so she types `jet dev --port=3000` for one run. She expects it to work the way a flag works for `jet build`. Her teammate Omar ships a web build that must stay small. A stray CI flag must never change that one setting, and Omar wants the CI run to fail with a clear reason instead.
decisions.detail:
Scope. This ballot decides the setting table, the one precedence order, pins, the port rule and the dev rows. Sibling ballots on card c07glrub decide the rest. D-ENTRY-SHAPE1 decides the entry shape, `d.run()` and the process model. D-TARGET-ONE1 decides where outputs are declared. D-ENTRY-NAMES1 decides type names, D-DEV-STATE1 decides state across restarts, and D-DEV-SERVICES1 decides where local services are defined.

Words. An output is a thing a project makes: a program, a server program, a library or a set of checks. A target is only the platform, as in `#Target(Web)` and `--target=web`. This follows D-TARGET-ONE1.

Owner rules relied on. Card #4913 records owner directive #51 of 2026-10-09: no CLI-only or config-only options, all from one option definition. The owner direction of 2026-10-19 asks for `jet dev --watch --port=8080` for one run. It also asks for `fn dev(d: Dev) { d.port(8080); d.watch(true) }` in the project. Both forms exist in every option; the options differ in which wins.

The order under A. Stock default, then source marker, then package.jet, then entry code, then flag. Each later place replaces an earlier one for that row. The stock value may differ by command, as D-BUILD-DEFAULT1=B gives `jet dev` the fast profile and `jet build` the optimized one. The order itself is the same for build, run, dev, test and check.

Commands with no entry function. `jet run` and `jet check` have no entry function, so their rows have two layers: package.jet and flag. That still meets #4913, because no row is CLI-only or config-only. For example, `jet run --watch` has the package form `run: { watch: true }`. The `Dev` handle is the code form of the dev session's rows.

What each layer is. Source markers are file-level markers; today only the web platform has one, `#Target(Web)`. Package.jet covers profile fields, typed `settings:`, the `dev:` block, new `run:` and `test:` blocks and data-written output options. Entry code is a method call on `Build`, `Dev` or `Test`. Flags are the command line for this run.

The platform row. The platform is one row: flag `--target=web`, package `target: web` and marker `#Target(Web)`. Its other form is the `os` field of a `BuildOptions` value (`os: web`, `web.os = .Web`) in a profile or an output's `options:`.

Profiles. Choosing a profile is its own row: `--profile=NAME` as a flag and `b.default_profile(...)` in code. The chosen profile's values stay in the package.jet layer. So entry code and other flags still beat them. For example, `b.optimize(.Size)` with `--profile=release` builds at size, and `--optimize=full` beats both.

Outputs. D-TARGET-ONE1 lets an output be written as package.jet data or by `b.add_*` in code. Its `options:` sit in the layer where they are written: data in the package.jet layer, code in the entry-code layer. A flag reaches every output the command selects. `jet build` selects all outputs, and `jet build web` selects one.

The default output is a row too. Its package form is `defaults: { run: app }`. Its code form is `b.default(app)`, and its one-run form is the name on the command line, as in `jet run app`. The name wins, as for any flag.

Root `fn run` first. A root `fn run` still runs first for bare `jet run` and `jet dev`; the default picks only when no root `fn run` exists. This is the ratified order of D-ECO-OUTPUT-DEFAULT1=A and D-DX-ENTRY1=C, and this ballot keeps it.

Naming rule. One row yields every spelling. The package field `cpu_features` is the flag `--cpu-features` and the method `b.cpu_features(...)`. A Bool row takes a bare flag for true and `=off` for false, so `--open` and `--open=off`. Enum values read `size` in package.jet, `--optimize=size` as a flag and `.Size` in code. Optimize values are `none`, `basic`, `full`, `size` and `min_size` (D-JAI-BUILDOPT1=A).

Dev rows, part one. Each row lists flag, package field, then code. Port: `--port=8080`, `dev: { port: 8080 }`, `d.port(8080)`. Open the browser: `--open` or `--open=off`, `open: true`, `d.open(true)`; stock off. Watch: `--watch` or `--watch=off`, `watch: true`, `d.watch(true)`; stock on for dev. In `jet dev`, watch off serves once and does not rebuild on save.

Dev rows, part two: local services. A local service's definition is structure, written as data only. Each listed local service's on or off state is one setting row. Its package form is the record's `enable` field. Its code form is `d.service("redis")` or `d.service("redis", on: false)`, and `t.service` in tests. Its flag is `--service=redis` or `--service=redis=off`. Pins work as for any row.

When local services start. Every selected local service starts when the session starts. That is when the entry returns or calls `run()`, or at once when there is no entry. Then the `d.before` jobs run, and then the program starts. D-DEV-SERVICES1 decides where local services are declared.

Dev rows, part three. Before: `--before=seed_demo`, `before: ["seed_demo"]`, `d.before(seed_demo)`. It runs a named dev `#Job` once, after local services are ready (D-JOB-SUBCMD1=C). Record: `--record=NAME`, `record: "NAME"`, `d.record("NAME")`. The existing `records: { capture, budget }` fields join the table under the naming rule. Fresh, if D-DEV-STATE1 A wins: `--fresh` or `--fresh=off`, `fresh: true`, `d.fresh(true)`, stock off. It starts the session without kept `#Persist` values.

Dev rows, part four. Share: `--share=lan`, `share: lan`, `d.share(.Lan)`. Args: `-- <args>`, `args: [...]`, `d.args([...])`. An `-- <args>` list replaces the code list for that run; it is not appended.

Several outputs. One `fn dev` configures the whole dev session for whichever output was picked. Code can branch on `d.output()`, as in `if d.output() == "game_web" { d.port(8081) }`. This follows D-ENTRY-SHAPE1.

Test rows, for example. Measure: `--measure`, `test: { measure: true }`, `t.measure(true)` (D-CLAIM-BENCH1=A). Filter: `--filter=parse`, `filter: "parse"`, `t.filter("parse")`. Before: `--before=seed_test`, `test: { before: ["seed_test"] }`, `t.before(seed_test)`. It runs a named dev `#Job` once, after the test environment's local services are ready and before the checks.

Build rows, for example. Build rows are the D-JAI-BUILDOPT1=A fields, such as `--optimize=size`, `build: { web: .{ optimize: size, os: web } }` and `b.optimize(.Size)`. Typed program settings keep `--set k=v` (D-CONF-KEY1=A).

Port rule. `d.port` is the port of the dev server Jet runs, used when Jet serves an `App` or a web build. An explicit port from any layer binds exactly. If it is busy, the error names the process that holds it when the system reports one. With no explicit port, Jet scans 8080 to 8089, as today.

Port rule, when Jet serves no page. If Jet serves no page, `--port` and `d.port` are an error, so the value is never silently ignored. The error reads: `jet dev serves no page here; pass your program's port after --, as in jet dev -- --port=8080`. It is registered under I7.

Port rule, continued. `d.port` never sets a server program's own listening port. A program that binds its own socket reads its port from its own flags or settings, passed with `--` or `--set`. This keeps D-CLIFLAG1=A unchanged: no name matching fills a `#Env("PORT")` field behind the program's back.

Arguments after `--`. For run, dev and test, text after `--` always goes to the program. For build it stays `b.args`, as D-JAI-BUILDOPT1=A says, because build runs no program. There is no `DevArgs` type.

Sharing on the network. `share` is the one row that opens the developer's machine to other computers. It keeps its place in the order, but a package.jet or code value is only a request. It takes effect with the flag or with a recorded `jet trust` grant. The `jet env` trust summary lists the request. A cloned project cannot approve itself.

Pins. `b.pin(.optimize, .Size)`, `d.pin(.port, 8080)` and `t.pin(.measure, true)` fix a row in entry code. A flag with the same value is accepted. A flag with another value is an error that names the pin's file, line and value and says how to remove it, as D-JAI-BUILDOPT1=A already promises.

Pins for one output. `b.pin(.optimize, .Size, output: game_web)` pins one output only. Its error reads `optimize is pinned to size for output game_web`, with the file and line.

Why pins live only in entry code. One place answers the question of why a flag was refused. Package.jet values stay plain data that code or a flag may replace. `jet run` and `jet check` have no pins, because they have no entry code. This follows D-AUTOPIN1=A: every automatic choice can be seen and locked, with no second mechanism.

Structure is not a setting row. Outputs, proxies, hooks and local service definitions are structure. Structure is written as code or data only. The command line picks an output by name, as in `jet dev api`. Turning a listed local service on or off (`--service=postgres`) and choosing `before` jobs (`--before=seed_demo`) are setting rows above; the definitions they name are structure. This is the scope of #4913 parity: it covers setting rows, not structure.

One more flag outside the table. `--show-default` keeps its meaning: use and report the stock default and ignore the entry. It skips the entry-code layer and its pins, so an entry can never mint a CI pass. It has no code or package form by design, because its job is to ignore project code.

Ladder bridge. The first time a flag sets a row in a project, Jet prints its lasting form once, such as `tip: to keep it, write d.port(4000) in fn dev`. Rows of `jet run` and `jet check` name the package.jet field instead. If no `fn dev` exists yet, the tip names `@dev.jet`. Which tips were shown is remembered under `.jet/`. Tips print only on a terminal, never in `--json` output.

Which value won. When a flag replaces a value from package.jet or code, Jet prints one line each run. An example is `note: --port=4000 replaces d.port(3000) at @dev.jet:1 for this run`. `jet explain dev` prints the effective `fn dev` as Jet source, with a comment naming each value's layer. `jet explain build` already lists each build setting's value and source (D-JAI-BUILDOPT1=A).

Removed with D-EXEC2=A. Dev rebuilds and restarts; hot swap is retired. So `jet dev --swap`, `jet dev --restart` and the package field `dev: { swap }` are removed. `jet run --watch` stays, because D-RUN-WATCH1=A keeps `--watch` as a modifier on run, test and check.

Today in code. Source/main.rs:4205-4213 runs a top-level `fn dev()` through run_dev_entry without the parsed `dev_port`. So `jet dev --port=3000` is silently ignored in a project with `fn dev()`. The App, web and native restart paths at Source/main.rs:4216-4265 do receive it. `--port` is parsed at Source/main.rs:2909-2923.

Today in code, continued. crates/jet-devserver/src/WebHost.rs:55 sets the scan range 8080..=8089. WebHost.rs:3461-3506 binds an explicit port exactly and fails when it is taken; its fix text names no holder. Source/main.rs:5005-5024 resolves the web platform as flag, then package `target:`, then `#Target(Web)`. That is D-WEBDEFAULT1=A, and it is already this order.

Today in code, more. crates/jet-pkg-model/src/Package/Blocks.rs:1135-1233 parses `dev: .{ swap, records }`, with swap on by default. Blocks.rs:1375 lists today's optimize values `none`, `basic` and `full`. The package parser at crates/jet-pkg-model/src/Package/mod.rs:2566-2727 has no `run:` or `test:` block. crates/jet-cli/src/CLI.rs:781-782 lists `--restart` and `--swap`.

Today in code, last. CLI.rs:790 scopes `--share` to the local-app mode of `jet dev --app`. No `--open` or `--service` flag exists. Core/build/declarations.jet:134 makes `b.add_*` take at least three arguments, so every example passes `[]` for no extra steps.

D-JAI-CONFIG1 (open) was rewritten on 2026-10-19 and no longer proposes that an output with its own `options:` is built exactly as its code says; D-TARGET-ONE1 moved that question here. Under A, code-written options are the entry-code layer, flags reach every selected output, and `b.pin(..., output:)` gives the exact build. Option B names the exact rule only as the rule proposed for Jai workspaces, not as law.

Amends D-JAI-BUILDOPT1=A: the one option table now also drives dev, run and test rows, the package `dev:` block and new `run:` and `test:` blocks. Its generated methods live on the `Build`, `Dev` and `Test` handles instead of `BuildContext`. `b.pin` gains an optional `output:`, and `d.pin` and `t.pin` join it with the same error text.

Amends D-BUILDCTX-FLAGS1=A: its merge order of command defaults, then `fn build` defaults, then explicit flags becomes one case of the one order. The marker and package.jet layers sit between. `b.default_profile` and `b.default_allow` keep their spellings and sit in the entry-code layer. Its rule that the command line wins stays, except where code pins.

Amends D-LIVE1=A: `jet dev --restart` and the package field `dev: .{ swap: false }` are removed, as is `--swap`. D-EXEC2=A already retired hot swap in practice. Amends D-JPK-GRANTCMD1=A: `jet trust` gains a grant for a dev session to listen on the local network.

Unchanged and relied on. D-WEBDEFAULT1=A is the marker, package and flag part of this order. D-CONF-KEY1=A keeps flag, then profile, then default for typed settings. D-BUILD-DEFAULT1=B keeps the stock profile per command. D-ECO-OUTPUT-DEFAULT1=A and D-DX-ENTRY1=C keep root `fn run` first, as amended by D-TARGET-ONE1 for `defaults.dev`.

Also unchanged. D-CLIFLAG1=A and D-CLI-GLOBAL1=E keep program flags after `--`. D-RUN-WATCH1=A, D-EXEC2=A and D-AUTOPIN1=A stand.

Research, right ways. Git reads its config files in one fixed order, lets `-c` beat them for one run, and shows the source with `--show-origin` (https://git-scm.com/docs/git-config). Cargo documents one order: command line, then environment, then files (https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/config.html). Both use one order for every command, and option A follows them.

Research, more right ways. Vite reads the dev port from its config file, and `vite --port` replaces it for one run. Its `strictPort` option fails when the port is taken instead of moving on (https://vite.dev/config/server-options). Option A makes an explicit port strict and the stock port a scan, which is today's Jet behavior.

Research, wrong ways. In Jai, options set by the build program win over the command line (cited in D-JAI-CONFIG1). A one-run change must go through arguments that the build program itself parses. That is option C's cost. Jet today has the per-command problem of option B: `--port` reaches the web paths but not a project with `fn dev()`.

Research limits. No adoption or friction data was found for precedence rules in any of these tools. The evidence is their documentation and Jet's own code. The Git, Cargo, Vite and Jai sources were cited from their documentation, not re-read for this ballot. No repository census was run.

Cutover. Extend the package parser: `dev:` gains the dev rows and loses `swap`, and new `run:` and `test:` blocks hold their rows. Add `--open`, `--service` and dev `--before`, widen `--share` to every dev session, and remove `--swap` and `--restart`. Pass every parsed dev flag to the entry path. Register the pin error, the busy-port and no-page port errors, and the tip and note lines under I7.

Cutover, continued. Build the #4913 table so one row generates the flag, the package field and the handle method. Teach `jet explain dev` to print each value's layer. Update the spec's command and package sections.

Review: one fresh combined pass (beginner + adversarial), agent SlateReview, Claude family, 2026-10-19, per owner directive for one review. Repaired: run and check rows, profile row, no-page port error, local-service row, output wording, root fn run first, optimize values, add_executable arguments, watch off, terms, tip state. Cohesion pass CohesionReview 2026-10-19 repaired: D-JAI-CONFIG1 references, port example, platform row, min_size, t.before row, structure wording, output options vs command-wide calls.

options.name: One order, flag wins unless pinned
options.detail:
Every setting is one row of one table. A row has a flag for one run and a package.jet field for project data. Where the command has an entry function, the row also has a method on its handle, such as `d.port(8080)`. A few rows also have a source marker, such as `#Target(Web)`.

One order holds in every command: stock default, then source marker, then package.jet, then entry code, then flag. A later place replaces an earlier one. A pin in entry code, such as `d.pin(.port, 3000)`, makes a conflicting flag an error that names the pin.

When a flag replaces a value from package.jet or code, Jet prints one line naming what it replaced. The first time a flag sets a row in a project, Jet also prints its code or package form once.

Gains: one order to learn, a flag always means this run only, and each flag teaches its lasting form. Losses: a flag can replace a code value for one run, and Jai ports add pins where they need Jai's rule.
options.technical:
The option table generates the flag, the package field and the handle method from one row, by one naming rule. The field `cpu_features` is the flag `--cpu-features` and the method `b.cpu_features`. A Bool row takes a bare flag for true and `=off` for false, as `--watch=off` does today.

The stock layer may differ by command, such as the fast profile for `jet dev`, but the order never does. Inside entry code, the last call wins, as in ordinary code, and an output's own `options:` beat command-wide calls such as `b.optimize(.Size)` for that output, whatever their order. A flag reaches every output the command selects. `b.pin` takes an optional `output:` to pin one output only.

Rows that open the machine to other computers, such as `share`, follow the same order. But a package.jet or code value for them is only a request, approved by the flag or a recorded `jet trust` grant.

options.name: Each command keeps its own order
options.detail:
Each command keeps its own order, and one table still gives every row its spellings. Dev and test use stock default, then package.jet, then entry code, then flag. Build keeps the rule proposed for Jai workspaces. Defaults set in `fn build` lose to flags, but an output with its own settings is built exactly as its code says, as in Jai. `b.pin` still locks a setting.

Gains: Jai ports behave as they do in Jai. Losses: the same flag changes a dev value but is ignored by some build outputs. Users learn one order per command and must check `jet explain` to know which one applies.
options.technical: The table and spellings are as in A. The merge has one path per command. Dev and test merge flags last. Build merges flags into the command's settings only. An output with its own `options:` skips them, and Jet prints a note naming the outputs that ignored the flag. `d.pin` and `t.pin` exist as in A.

options.name: Code always wins
options.detail:
Code always wins, as in Jai. The order is stock default, then source marker, then package.jet, then flag, then entry code. A flag only fills a value that entry code leaves unset. A flag that disagrees with entry code is an error naming the code line, so a flag never silently does nothing. No pin is needed, because every value in code acts as a pin.

Gains: reading the code shows the value in use, and the rule matches Jai. Losses: a one-run change to a value that code sets needs an edit. The owner's one-run `jet dev --port=8080` stops working once `fn dev` sets a port, and CI flags cannot adjust a code value.
options.technical: Same table and spellings as A. The merge puts entry code last. The conflict error reuses the pin error text, which names the file, line and value. `b.pin`, `d.pin` and `t.pin` are removed because every code value already acts as one.

comparisons.note: Git reads system, user and project config files in a fixed order, and a later file wins. `git -c name=value` beats every file for one run. `git config --show-origin` names the file behind a value. This is option A without pins. Source: https://git-scm.com/docs/git-config.
comparisons.code:
$ git -c core.editor=nano commit
$ git config --show-origin core.editor
file:.git/config    vim

comparisons.note: Cargo merges config in one order: `--config` on the command line, then environment variables, then config files. The command line always wins. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/config.html.

The config file sets the dev server port, and `vite --port` replaces it for one run. `strictPort: true` exits when the port is taken instead of trying the next one. That is the explicit-port rule in option A. Sources: https://vite.dev/config/server-options and https://vite.dev/guide/cli.
Options set by the build program win over the command line. A one-run change goes through arguments that the build program itself must read. This is option C.

recommendation.why: One order works in every command. A flag means this run only, and code means this project. A pin keeps Jai's rule where a project needs it.
gains: One order to learn, in every command.
Every flag has a lasting form, and Jet shows it.
The owner's two forms both work: `jet dev --port=8080` and `d.port(8080)`.

losses.loss: A flag can replace a value written in code.
losses.mitigation: Jet prints one line naming the code line the flag replaced.

losses.loss: Jai ports must add pins to keep Jai's rule.
losses.mitigation: One pin call per setting restores it, and the refusal names the pin's line.

whyNot.reason: Users learn an order per command, and a flag works in dev but not on some outputs.
A one-run change, such as another port, needs a code edit.

recommendation.tradeoff: A flag may replace code for one run. Jet names what it replaced, and a pin stops it.

surface.gist: When one setting is written in several places, which place wins, and is that order the same for every command?
surface.lesson: A setting is one value, such as the dev port. Jet's built-in value is the stock default. A flag, a package.jet field or a line in `fn dev` can also set it. A few settings have a source marker, such as `#Target(Web)`. A pin is a code line that refuses a different flag. `jet explain dev` shows which place set each value.

current.note: A project with `fn dev` silently ignores `--port`. Each command ranks the places its own way.
current.code:
fn dev() {                        // replaces the program
    server :: devserver.app()
    server.port(8080); server.serve()
}
$ jet dev --port=3000             // ignored: still 8080

wild.note: Git reads config files in one fixed order. `-c` beats them all for one run (git-scm.com/docs/git).

# .git/config (this project) beats ~/.gitconfig (this user)
$ git -c core.editor=nano commit      # this run only

decisions.title: A new name for the build settings value, now that Build is the build handle
decisions.situation: A build's settings, such as how hard to optimize and which machine to build for, form one typed value. Today a project writes that value as `Build{ optimize: full }` in its package file, and build code gets a separate handle called `BuildContext`. The owner has now given the name `Build` to that handle, so the settings value needs a new name. We recommend `BuildOptions`, which most projects never type because package files may leave the name out.
decisions.gist: Now that `Build` names the build function's handle, what should the value holding a build's settings be called?
decisions.lesson: A build's settings, such as `optimize`, `os` and `debug_info`, form one typed value. A profile is a named copy of it in the package file, picked with `--profile=web`. Build code can copy a profile, change a field, and give the copy to one output as its `options:`. The owner gave the name `Build` to the handle of `fn build`, so this value needs its own name. Package files and `options:` may leave the name out, so most people meet it only on hover and in errors.
decisions.story: Tomi ports a game build from Jai, where each build's settings are a `Build_Options` value. In Jet he writes `fn build(b: Build)`, copies the release profile, sets the platform to web, and gives the copy to one output as `options:`. When he hovers over the copy, the type name should tell him at once that it holds build settings, not the build itself.
decisions.detail:
Scope. This ballot names the typed build settings value. It also records the entry type names the owner settled. Sibling ballots on card c07glrub decide the rest. D-ENTRY-SHAPE1 decides entry shape, including `fn build(b: Build)` with no return value and `b.default(app)`. D-TARGET-ONE1 decides where outputs are declared, including `options:` on outputs. D-SETTING-ORDER1 decides setting rows and the one settings order. D-DEV-STATE1 and D-DEV-SERVICES1 decide dev state and services.

Presentation order. Show this ballot after D-ENTRY-SHAPE1, D-TARGET-ONE1 and D-SETTING-ORDER1, and before D-JAI-CONFIG1. The gain that the name matches `options:` and `b.options()` holds only if outputs carry their own settings, as D-TARGET-ONE1 option A proposes. The name stands on its own if that ballot loses: a profile is still a `BuildOptions` value.

Words. Output means a thing the project makes, as in D-TARGET-ONE1. Target means only the platform, as in `#Target(Web)` and `--target=web`.

Settled by the owner on 2026-10-19, not voted. `BuildContext` becomes `Build`, the handle of `fn build(b: Build)`. `TestSuite` becomes `Test`, the handle of `fn test(t: Test)`. `Dev` is new, the handle of `fn dev(d: Dev)`. There is no `Bench` type: `BenchSuite` also becomes `Test`, and measurement is a test setting, `t.measure(true)` or `jet test --measure`, as D-CLAIM-BENCH1=A already ratified.

Also settled. The `#Test` marker stays and lives beside the `Test` type, as the `#Target(Web)` marker lives beside the `Target` enum in Core/compiler/lang.jet:161. `#Test fn f(t: Test)` becomes a registered error. Today it reads as a property test that generates `Test` values (D-TEST1) and fails with the general E0613 text. The new error says that a test handle belongs in `fn test(t: Test)`. The editor grammar stops treating `Test` as a keyword, so `t: Test` highlights as a type.

Why a new name is needed. The package file names its settings constructor `Build` today. That is BUILD_CTOR at crates/jet-foundation/src/Syntax/package_files.rs:614. Its twins are Compiler/JetFoundation/Data/Syntax/package_files.jet:647 and Jetpack/Foundation/Source/Syntax.jet:501. D-JAI-BUILDOPT1=A ratified `Build` as the name of the typed profile value. Once `Build` is the handle, one name cannot mean both.

Today in code. The parser accepts `Build{ … }`, `Build.{ … }` and a bare `{ … }` for a profile (crates/jet-pkg-model/src/Package/Blocks.rs:1366-1377; Jetpack/PackageModel/Source/Manifest/Blocks/BuildProfiles.jet:202-210). So leaving the name out already works with braces. The slate writes the elided form as `build: { web: .{ … } }`, and the parser must also accept `.{ … }`. `b.profile` and per-output `options:` are new in D-TARGET-ONE1, and `b.options` is in the open D-JAI-CONFIG1; Core/build has no such method yet.

Collision search, 2026-10-19, over crates/, Core/, Compiler/, Source/ and Jetpack/. `BuildOptions`: no match anywhere. `Options`: no Jet type of that name. Rust-only host structs named `Options` exist, which shows the name is common for local settings. Examples are crates/jet-foundation/src/CborKernel.rs:54, Source/Doctor.rs:90 and Source/CmdBudget.rs:35. Core/http/http.jet:60 has the HTTP case `Method.Options`.

`Profile` collisions. `Profile` is a registered env type for `profile.<name>` package sets (D-JPK-PROFILE1=D). It is defined at jetpack_config.rs:254 with Jet twins, and checked in Jetpack/EnvModel/Source/ModuleEval/ProfileEval.jet:25. The fact `Build.Profile` (crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Facts.jet:28) is the selected profile name. `BuildProfile` is a Rust-only enum at Source/main.rs:569.

`Build.*` fact names. The build facts are named `Build.Package.Name`, `Build.OS`, `Build.Profile`, `Build.Settings` and `Build.Stamp.*` (Facts.jet:25-33). They share their first word with the new handle type, but they are fact names, not types. Users read them as `$build.os`, `$build.profile` and `$build.settings.tls` (D-CONF-READ1=A). They also appear as contribution keys such as `Build.Settings.cache_slots` in build receipts. [INFERENCE] No source position can name both a fact and a type, so they do not clash and stay unchanged.

No `Settings` option. A `Settings` name was not offered. `settings:` is already the typed user settings field inside a profile (D-CONF-KEY1=A), and `Build.Settings` is its fact (Facts.jet:29).

Entry names in code. `BuildContext` and `BuildPlan` are TYPE_BUILD_CONTEXT and TYPE_BUILD_PLAN at crates/jet-foundation/src/Syntax/core_surface.rs:1122-1123. `TestSuite` is a Core and prelude type. It appears at Core/testing/testing.jet:302, crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/CommandSuite.rs, TIR/subset/handles.rs:190, core_types.rs:298 and CoreModuleExports.rs:521.

More entry names. `BenchSuite` has no match in code; it exists only in the text of D-CMD-OVERRIDE1. `Test` is KW_TEST (math_layout.rs:795) and a Zed anonymous token (highlights.rs:1207), generated into Tools/editors/tree-sitter/grammar.js:17.

`Dev` checks. `JobScope.Dev` is an enum case in core.compiler (CoreModuleExports.rs:225-226) and agrees in meaning: dev only, stripped from release (D-JOB-SUBCMD1=C). The perf budget profile word `Dev` (jetpack_config.rs:218) is a string. Neither is a type, so neither clashes. One test fixture declares its own `struct Build` (tests/cases/prove/moving_method_results_can_reinitialize_their_receiver_place.fixture/run.jet:1). User names win over prelude names (Docs/spec/spec.md:318), and the cutover checks that this fixture still passes.

Option C shadowing. Docs/spec/spec.md:318 says a user declaration shadows a readable prelude alias. [INFERENCE] The settings type is such a prelude name, not a reserved built-in, so a project's own `Options` type would hide C's name inside that package.

Code spellings. `b.add_executable(name, [sources], [])` takes three arguments, because Core requires at least three (Core/build/declarations.jet:134). `:=` makes a binding you can change, so `web := b.profile("web")` is an editable copy; `::` would make it fixed. A root `fn run` still runs first for bare `jet run` and `jet dev`; the default picks only when no root `fn run` exists.

Research, right ways. Jai names the settings value `Build_Options` and edits one per workspace (Docs/audits/jai-parity-2026-10-16.md section 1.5; Default_Metaprogram turns flags into `Build_Options`). Zig names its build handle `std.Build` and gives each artifact an options value such as `ExecutableOptions` (lib/std/Build.zig in 0.13.0, lines 638 and 669). Option A copies both: the handle is `Build`, and its settings value is `BuildOptions`.

Research, wrong ways. One word for two things already cost Jet a rename. D-CONF-WORD1=A moved environment profiles to the word preset, because profile answered two questions (E1300 text). Option B would bring that problem back with the `Profile` env type. Cargo uses profile safely only because it has no settings value in build code. No adoption numbers were gathered; these are documented designs, not measurements.

Design away, loss one: a longer name. Attempt one kept `Build` for the value and named the handle something else; rejected because the owner settled `Build` as the handle. Attempt two was the short `Options`; rejected for the clash and vagueness in option C. Result: the name may be left out in package files and in `options:`, and hover and `jet explain build` show the full name. Negligible.

Shared work, not a loss of any option. Every option must change today's `Build{ … }` profile spelling, because `Build` becomes the handle. A repository search on 2026-10-19 found about 15 files that write `Build{` in a profile: 12 package.jet files, one package.template and two .jet modules. Deleting the word `Build` already parses today, and the cutover error names both fixes.

Amends D-JAI-BUILDOPT1=A: the typed profile value is renamed from `Build` to `BuildOptions`, and its "BuildContext method" wording becomes "Build method". The catalog, `b.pin` and `b.args` as strings are unchanged. Amends D-BUILDPROFILE1: the profile constructor `Build{ … }`/`Build.{ … }` becomes `BuildOptions{ … }` or the elided `.{ … }`, and E1219 text changes to match.

Amends D-CMD-OVERRIDE1=C: the handed-in values `TestSuite` and `BenchSuite` become one `Test`. The override shape is decided in D-ENTRY-SHAPE1. Amends D-BUILDENTRY1=B, D-BUILDTARGET1=A and D-BUILDCTX-FLAGS1=A in wording only: `BuildContext` becomes `Build`. Their signature, default and order changes belong to D-ENTRY-SHAPE1 and D-SETTING-ORDER1.

D-JAI-CONFIG1 (open, rewritten 2026-10-19) already writes the value as `BuildOptions` and names this ballot as owner of the name. If B or C wins here, its `BuildOptions` reads `Profile` or `Options`.

Unchanged and relied on: D-CLAIM-BENCH1=A (no bench type) and D-CONF-WORD1=A (`--profile=name` still picks a named profile). Also unchanged: D-CONF-KEY1=A (`settings:` field), D-CONF-READ1=A (`$build.profile` stays a name), D-TEST1 (property tests) and D-JOB-SUBCMD1=C (`JobScope.Dev`).

Cutover. Rename TYPE_BUILD_CONTEXT to `Build` and every `fn build(b: BuildContext…)` site. Rename `TestSuite` to `Test` across Core, the prelude, TIR handles, sema and Core exports. Add the prelude `Dev` handle. Re-register BUILD_CTOR as `BuildOptions` in the Rust and Jet twins, and accept `.{ … }`. Update the parser errors at Blocks.rs:1375 and BuildProfiles.jet:209, E1219 text, and the about 15 profile files.

Cutover, continued. Add the registered errors for the old `Build{` profile spelling and for `#Test fn f(t: Test)` (I7). Drop `Test` from the keyword and Zed anonymous-token lists in highlights.rs and regenerate grammar.js. Update the spec sections on build profiles and programmable builds.

Review: one fresh combined pass (beginner + adversarial), agent SlateReview, Claude family, 2026-10-19, per owner directive for one review. Repaired: `build: { … }` profile blocks, three-argument `b.add_executable`, `options:` gain made conditional with presentation order, `Build.*` fact names addressed, `:=` explained, output/target wording, surface trimmed. Cohesion pass CohesionReview 2026-10-19 repaired: D-JAI-CONFIG1 reference, presentation order, root fn run sentence, today snippet.

options.name: `BuildOptions`
options.detail:
The settings value is named `BuildOptions`. A profile in the package file is a `BuildOptions` value, written in full or with the name left out. In build code, `b.profile("web")` returns a copy of a profile and `b.options()` returns the settings of the current command, both as `BuildOptions`. An output takes one through its `options:` field, if outputs carry settings as the output-list ballot proposes.

Gains: the name says what the value holds, and the value, its field and its getter share one word. Jai calls the same value `Build_Options`, and Zig pairs its `Build` handle with option values such as `ExecutableOptions`. No Jet type uses the name today. Loss: the name is longer than today's `Build`, but most projects leave it out.
options.technical: `BuildOptions` is a prelude-owned struct whose fields are the rows of the #4913 option table (D-JAI-BUILDOPT1=A). Signatures: `b.profile(name: String) -> BuildOptions`, `b.options() -> BuildOptions`, `options: BuildOptions?` on `b.add_*` and on package outputs. The package parser accepts `BuildOptions{ … }`, `BuildOptions.{ … }`, `.{ … }` and `{ … }` for a profile, and the checker fills the type where the name is left out. `$build.profile` keeps naming the selected profile as a string (D-CONF-READ1).

options.name: `Profile`
options.detail:
The settings value is named `Profile`. A profile in the package file is a `Profile` value, and `b.profile("web")` and `b.options()` return `Profile` values. An output still takes one through its `options:` field.

Gains: the name matches `--profile=web`, the list of named profiles in the package file, and Cargo's `[profile.release]`. Losses: `Profile` is already the type of a package set in env files, so one word names two types. A value made by editing a copy in code, or the current command's settings, is not a named profile, yet its type says it is.
options.technical: Same signatures as A with `Profile` in place of `BuildOptions`. `Profile` is already the registered type of a `profile.<name>` package set in env files (D-JPK-PROFILE1=D). See crates/jet-foundation/src/Syntax/jetpack_config.rs:254 and Jetpack/EnvModel/Source/ModuleEval/ProfileEval.jet:25. Choosing B means renaming that type or living with two types of one name.

options.name: `Options`
options.detail:
The settings value is named `Options`. A profile in the package file is an `Options` value, and `b.profile("web")` and `b.options()` return `Options` values.

Gains: the name is short and matches the `options:` field exactly. Losses: the name does not say which options, so hover text and error messages read `Options` with no subject. A project that declares its own `Options` type, a common name for command-line settings, hides the build type inside that package, because a user's own name wins over a prelude name.
options.technical: Same signatures as A with `Options` in place of `BuildOptions`. Spec.md:318: a user declaration shadows a readable prelude alias. Core/http/http.jet:60 has an `Options` case of the HTTP `Method` enum. It is a case, not a type, so it does not clash, but it reads alike in search results.

comparisons.note: The build program edits a `Build_Options` value for each workspace. The value's name says it holds options for a build. Source: Docs/audits/jai-parity-2026-10-16.md section 1.5 and The Way to Jai, chapter 30.

The build handle is `std.Build`, and each artifact takes a separate options value such as `ExecutableOptions`. This is the pairing option A copies. Source: lib/std/Build.zig in Zig 0.13.0, lines 638 and 669.
comparisons.code:
pub const ExecutableOptions = struct { name: []const u8, ... };
pub fn addExecutable(b: *Build, options: ExecutableOptions) *Step.Compile

comparisons.note: Settings live in named profiles in Cargo.toml. Cargo has no settings value in build code, so the word profile never has to name an edited copy. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/profiles.html.

recommendation.why: `BuildOptions` says what the value holds, matches Jai, and clashes with no Jet name. Package files leave it out, so most projects never type it.
gains: The name says what the value holds.
No clash with any existing Jet name.

losses.loss: Longer than today's `Build`.
losses.mitigation: Package files may leave the name out, and hover shows the full name.

whyNot.reason: `Profile` already names package sets in env files, so one word would mean two things.
`Options` says nothing about builds, and a project's own `Options` type would hide it.

recommendation.tradeoff: A longer name that most people never type, for a name that says what the value is.

decisions.title: Where local services are written, and how dev and test switch them
decisions.situation: A local service is a helper program, such as a database, that Jet starts and watches while you work. Today a project lists local services in its dev environment, but `jet dev` does not start them, so people start them with a second command. The vote decides where local services are written and how `jet dev` and `jet test` turn one on or off. We recommend listing every local service as data in package.jet and switching one by name from a flag or from entry code.
decisions.gist: Where are local services such as a database written, and how do `jet dev` and `jet test` turn them on?
decisions.lesson: A local service is a helper program, such as postgres or redis, that Jet starts, checks for readiness, and stops while you work. Jet already supervises local services listed in an environment, and the `jet env` trust prompt shows them before any code runs. Whichever option wins, `jet dev` starts the local services that are on and waits until they are ready. The vote decides where they are written and how one is switched.
decisions.story: Priya's web app keeps sessions in redis on every run. Only the billing pages need postgres, which is slow to start, so she wants it on only for billing work. Some days she debugs without the cache and wants redis off for one run. Her CI runs `jet test` against its own postgres. Her teammate Ken clones the repo and wants to see every program it can start before he trusts it.
decisions.detail:
Scope. This ballot decides where local services are written and how `jet dev` and `jet test` switch them. Its sibling ballots on card c07glrub are ratified with A on 2026-10-19. D-ENTRY-SHAPE1=A settled entry shape, `run()` and the process model. D-SETTING-ORDER1=A settled the setting table and the one order, including the service row. D-TARGET-ONE1=A settled outputs, D-ENTRY-NAMES1=A type names, and D-DEV-STATE1=A kept values across restarts.

Two meanings of service. A local service here is a helper program Jet supervises, such as postgres. A Service output in D-TARGET-ONE1=A and D-ECO-OUTPUT-KINDS1=A is a long-running program the project builds, made by `outputs:` or `b.add_service`. Both words stay for now, and the surface says local service throughout. D-SERVICE-WORD1 decides whether the two meanings merge or one is renamed. If its option A wins, the output-name error below is replaced by running the named Service output as a service.

The output-name error. Unless D-SERVICE-WORD1 A wins, a registered error under I7 catches the likely mistake. Its text is "`--service=api`: `api` is an output your project builds; start it with `jet dev api`". `d.service`, `t.service` and `jet services up` give the same error.

The rule under A, part one. Every local service is a record under `environments.<name>.services` in package.jet. `jet dev` uses the dev environment and `jet test` the test environment, as D-JPK-DEVCOMPOSE1=D gives each verb its environment. In project environments a record with no `enable` field is on. This matches the ratified D-JPK-SERVICE1 example, where `redis: Service.{}` starts with `jet dev`. It covers project environment services only; `system.*` services keep `enable` required.

The rule under A, part two. A name switches a listed local service. On: `d.service("postgres")`, `t.service("postgres")`, `--service=postgres` on `jet dev` or `jet test`, and `jet services up postgres`. Off: `d.service("redis", on: false)` and `--service=redis=off`. This follows the `=off` rule for every setting row. Naming a local service changes no field of its record.

One setting row. The on/off value of each local service is one row of the D-SETTING-ORDER1=A table. The one order applies: the record's `enable` field (package.jet layer), then entry code, then the flag. So `--service=redis=off` wins over `d.service("redis")` for one run, and a pin in entry code makes a conflicting flag an error, as for any row. `jet explain dev` names the layer and line that set each local service. This ballot adds the test forms `t.service` and `jet test --service`.

One start time. All local services that end up on start together when the session starts, and Jet waits for readiness. The session starts when the entry returns or calls `run()`, as D-ENTRY-SHAPE1=A says; with no entry it starts at once. Then `d.before` jobs run (D-JOB-SUBCMD1=C), then the program.

Calls and `run()`. A service call after `run()` is the same error as any setting after `run()`; with no `run()`, every call comes first. Setup that needs a running database is a `d.before` or `t.before` job. This ballot fixes the start time of the service row that D-SETTING-ORDER1=A lists.

Process model. Per D-ENTRY-SHAPE1=A, the `jet` tool process holds the local-service supervisor and runs the compiled `fn dev` session. Editing program code restarts only the program. Editing `fn dev` or the environment re-enters the session, and running local services survive; Jet starts newly picked ones and stops dropped ones. Ctrl-C stops everything.

Errors. An unknown name is a registered error under I7 that lists the declared names. A literal name in `fn dev` or `fn test` is checked when the entry compiles, because package.jet is project data the compiler already reads. A computed name is checked when the session starts. A named local service whose `after` list holds a service that is off is an error naming that service and the fix, as jetpack-epoch5.md:386-391 says today.

What data buys, stated plainly. `fn dev` is ordinary runtime code, so it can start any process itself; data is not a sandbox. The gain is review: every supervised local service can be listed by `jet env`, images and `jet services` without running code. D-JPK-DEVCOMPOSE1=D made `jet env` never run project code and show hooks and services in a trust summary first. Under B that summary would be empty. Local services are arbitrary commands; tests/canvas_scenarios.rs:1313 runs `node` with inline script text.

I8, one mechanism. A keeps one place where local services are written: the environment data, which image projection and the Canvas already read. The flag, the method and `jet services up` are selections, not definitions. B would need a second source for images, and C leaves the service row without its flag and code forms, against owner rule #4913: no CLI-only or config-only options.

Today in code. crates/jetpack/src/CLI/services_secrets_config.rs:161-210 defines `wait_for_services_ready`, which starts enabled services and waits for E1261 readiness. It is `#[allow(dead_code)]`, and so is the project `cmd_dev` at crates/jetpack/src/CLI/run_enter_dev.rs:4112-4216 that calls it. The compiler's `jet dev` path in Source/main.rs never starts services. So today people run `jet services up` first (Source/main.rs:3969-3978 dispatches it).

Today in code, continued. services_secrets_config.rs:521-532 refuses `jet services up NAME` for a service marked off, with the text "service `NAME` is disabled". crates/jet-pkg-model/src/Package/mod.rs:3506-3608 already parses `environments: { dev: Environment{ services: ... } }` in package.jet; an absent `enable` reads as false there. crates/jet-env-model/src/ModuleEval/Types.rs:310-320 calls `enable` required, for env services and `system.*` services alike.

Today in code, more. ModuleEval/Source.rs:610-665 selects exactly one environment and takes services only from it, picking `dev` when none is requested (Source.rs:1019-1042). Trust.rs:401-405 puts every service record in the trust fingerprint. Image projection picks environment services by name, as in tests/cases/image/environment_image_projects_supervised_services.fixture/env.jet. Canvas reads them at crates/jet-devserver/src/Canvas/project_scan.rs:1184-1188.

Amends D-JPK-SERVICE1=A: adds switching by name. `d.service`, `t.service` and `--service` turn a listed local service on or off, and `jet services up NAME` now starts a service marked off instead of refusing it. In project environments a record with no `enable` field is on. The typed fields, presets, supervisor, readiness and logs are unchanged.

Amends D-JPK-DEVCOMPOSE1=D: its order "services ready, then fn dev()" becomes: entry settings, then local services ready, then `d.before` jobs, then the program. `jet test` selects the test environment by default. The trust summary lists local services that are off as well, because a name can start them. Ratified D-ENTRY-SHAPE1=A already amended the same decision's `fn dev()` shape.

Unchanged and relied on. D-NAME-ROLEMOD1=A moves env.jet into package.jet; code here uses the parser's `environments:` and `Environment` spelling, which prose calls the dev environment. D-ECO-DECL1=A, D-ECO-ENV1=A, D-ECO-OUTPUT-KINDS1=A and D-JOB-SUBCMD1=C stand. D-EXEC2=A, D-CLAIM-BENCH1=A, D-RUN-WATCH1=A and the ratified siblings D-ENTRY-SHAPE1=A, D-SETTING-ORDER1=A and D-DEV-STATE1=A stand.

Research, right ways. devenv keeps services as data, `services.postgres.enable = true`, and `devenv up` starts them (https://devenv.sh/services/). D-JPK-SERVICE1 cites devenv as the reason services belong in Jet. Docker Compose keeps services as data and keeps a service with a profile off until the profile is on. Naming such a service on the command line turns its profile on (https://docs.docker.com/compose/how-tos/profiles/). Option A takes both ideas.

Research, wrong ways. Testcontainers defines services in test code (https://testcontainers.com/). It is flexible, but each suite repeats its definitions and no tool can list them without running the tests. A Tiltfile is a Starlark program that Tilt must run to learn its resources (https://docs.tilt.dev/). Both are the shape of option B. Before Compose profiles, teams kept extra override files to switch services, a second place that option A avoids.

Research limits. No adoption or friction data was found that compares data-defined and code-defined dev services. The evidence is the tools' documentation and Jet's own code. Repository count, by search for `services:\s*\{` in `*.jet` under tests and Examples on 2026-10-19: 65 files. That count includes trust maps and JetOS system services, so it overstates dev services; it measures repository sites, not users.

Make an absent `enable` mean on for project environment services only. Let `jet services up NAME` start a service marked off.

options.name: Data lists them, a name switches one
options.detail:
Every local service is written as data in the environments of package.jet. The dev environment serves `jet dev`, and the test environment serves `jet test`. A listed local service is on unless it says `enable: false`.

A name switches a listed local service on or off. `d.service("postgres")` in `fn dev` and `t.service("postgres")` in `fn test` turn it on for the project. `d.service("redis", on: false)` turns it off. `jet dev --service=postgres` and `jet dev --service=redis=off` do the same for one run, and `jet test` takes the same flag. Naming a local service changes nothing else: not its command, ports or data.

All local services that end up on start together when the session starts, and Jet waits until each is ready. Then `d.before` jobs run, then the program. Gains: `jet env` shows every local service without running code, and each one has the flag, data and code forms every setting has. Loss: code cannot add a local service or change its command. Each variant is listed as its own local service instead.
options.technical:
Local services stay the typed records of D-JPK-SERVICE1 with their existing fields (`enable`, `run`, `ports`, `ready`, `restart`, `after`, `before_start` and the rest) and the built-in postgres and redis presets. They sit under `environments.<name>.services` in package.jet. Jetpack reads them without running project code, so the trust fingerprint, `jet env info`, the Canvas, image projection and `jet services` keep one source.

`d.service(name, on: Bool = true)` and `t.service(...)` are setting calls on the handle. The on/off value of each local service is one setting row, ranked by the one settings order: the `enable` field, then entry code, then the flag. `--service=NAME` and `--service=NAME=off` may repeat. A literal name is checked when the entry compiles, and a computed name when the session starts.

The session starts when the entry returns or calls `run()`, as ratified D-ENTRY-SHAPE1=A says; with no entry it starts at once. Every selected local service starts then, so code and flags start them at the same time.

A service call after `run()` is the same error as any setting after `run()`; with no `run()`, every call comes first. The supervisor lives in the `jet` process, per the D-ENTRY-SHAPE1=A process model. Editing `fn dev` re-enters the session without stopping running local services; Jet starts newly picked ones and stops dropped ones.

options.name: Entry code defines local services
options.detail:
Local services exist only in entry code. `d.service("postgres", .{ ports: [5432] })` in `fn dev` defines a local service and starts it, and `t.service(...)` does the same in `fn test`. Code may compute any field, such as a port from a setting. package.jet environments no longer hold `services:`.

Gain: code can compute a command and ports. Losses: `jet env` cannot list local services without running project code. Images, `jet services logs` and the Canvas lose their list. Dev and test each write their own copy unless they share a helper function.
options.technical: `Dev` and `Test` gain `service(name, Service)` methods that hand a typed record to the supervisor at run time. The `services:` field leaves the environment entry. The trust summary can no longer fingerprint local services, because they are known only after `fn dev` runs. Image projection, which today picks environment services by name, needs a new source. `jet services up|logs|down` work only on local services a running session started.

options.name: Data only, `enable` is the one switch
options.detail:
Local services are data in package.jet, as in A. The `enable` field is the only switch: `jet dev` and `jet test` start every local service that is on. There is no `d.service`, no `t.service` and no `--service` flag. To switch a local service for a while, you edit its `enable` field.

Gain: nothing new to learn, and there is never a second switch. Losses: a one-run change needs a file edit, and this setting has no flag or code form, which breaks the rule that every setting has them.
options.technical: This is D-JPK-SERVICE1 and D-JPK-DEVCOMPOSE1 as ratified, with the dev start built and the env.jet form moved into package.jet. `jet services up NAME` keeps refusing a service marked off. The setting table has no service row.

comparisons.note: Services are data in `devenv.nix`, and `devenv up` starts the ones that are on. This is the data half of option A and all of option C. D-JPK-SERVICE1 names devenv as the demand Jet absorbs. Source: https://devenv.sh/services/.

Services are data. A service with a profile stays off until the profile is on or the service is named on the command line. That is option A's `enable: false` plus a name. Source: https://docs.docker.com/compose/how-tos/profiles/.
comparisons.code:
services:
  billing:
    image: postgres:16
    profiles: [billing]
# docker compose --profile billing up

comparisons.note: Test code defines and starts each service. Setup is flexible, but each suite repeats its definitions, and nothing lists the services without running the tests. That is option B. Source: https://testcontainers.com/.

A Tiltfile is a Starlark program, and Tilt runs it to learn what to start. `tilt up api` starts only named resources. Code-defined services need the program to run before anyone can list them. Source: https://docs.tilt.dev/.

recommendation.why: Data keeps every local service listable by `jet env`, images and `jet services` without running code. Code and flags pick listed local services by name.
gains: Dev and test switch local services the same way.
One run can turn a local service on or off without a file edit.

losses.loss: Code cannot add a local service or change its command.
losses.mitigation: List each variant as its own local service, such as `postgres_big`, and pick it by name.

whyNot.reason: Local services written in code cannot be listed, reviewed or used by images without running project code.
A one-run change needs a file edit, and the flag and code forms every setting has are missing.

recommendation.tradeoff: Commands live only in data or are your own Service outputs. Flags and code only pick among them.
