decisions.title: Keep #Persist values when jet dev restarts the program
decisions.situation: `#Persist` marks a module value, such as a game score, that should survive your edits while `jet dev` runs. It was made for live code swap, which is retired, so `jet dev` now restarts the program on every save and the marked value starts over each time. This vote decides whether Jet saves marked values when it stops the program and restores them at the next start, or leaves the mark idle until a code swap engine returns. We recommend saving and restoring, with `jet dev --fresh` or `d.fresh(true)` to start over.
decisions.gist: Should `jet dev` keep values marked `#Persist` when it restarts your program after a save?
decisions.lesson: `#Persist` marks a module value, such as a score, that should survive your edits while `jet dev` runs. It was made for live code swap, which is retired. Now `jet dev` restarts the program on every save, and the marked value starts over. Today a marked value must start as a simple value such as a number. `jet run` always starts fresh, and release builds ignore the mark.
decisions.story: Ken is building a small game. A bug shows up three minutes into a boss fight. He marks the level number, the score and the boss's health with `#Persist`, so he can tune the enemy logic without replaying. Since live swap was retired, every save restarts the game and the fight is gone. He needs each restart to bring those values back.
decisions.detail:
Scope. This ballot decides what happens to `#Persist` values when `jet dev` restarts the program. Sibling ballots on card c07glrub decide the rest. D-ENTRY-SHAPE1 decides entry shape, the reload boundary and the one process model. D-SETTING-ORDER1 decides setting rows and removes `--swap`, `--restart` and the package `dev: { swap }` field; option A adds one `fresh` row to its table. D-TARGET-ONE1, D-ENTRY-NAMES1 and D-DEV-SERVICES1 decide outputs, names and local services.

Why the owner must decide. D-EXEC2=A retired hot swap: `jet dev` rebuilds and restarts on every save. D-PERSIST1, D-PERSIST-DEVSTATE1, D-LIVE-PERSIST1 and D-HOTSTATE1 all describe values that survive a live swap. No ratified text says what the mark does under restarts. The adversarial review of the slate proposal flagged this gap and named the two options here.

Today in code. The default `jet dev` engine is run_dev_restart at Source/CmdDevTools.rs:912-970. Each save kills the child with `running.kill()` at line 957 and starts a fresh `jet run`. A `#Persist` binding lowers to the Prelude `JetPersistCell` (crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Core.rs:11-50), which starts from the literal. Nothing restores it, so the mark has no effect in default `jet dev`.

Today in code, continued. The value store is jet_foundation::Persist (crates/jet-foundation/src/Persist.rs). It is a process-wide static (line 19) with typed outcomes Kept, Migrated, Reset and Rejected (lines 112-120) and a preflight `plan_migrate` (line 256). Only the Canvas in-process loop still uses it (Source/CmdDevTools.rs:1696, 1759-1767 and 1952-1966). The dev session records those outcomes as live-value facts (crates/jet-devserver/src/Session.rs:2319).

Today in code, more. E0622 (crates/jet-sema/src/Sema/Registration/Items.rs:1587-1603) limits a `#Persist` starting value to a scalar literal, such as an integer, float or bool. So D-PERSIST1's own `World.load(...)` example does not compile today, and the story uses only simple values. The test persist_example_survives_hot_reload (tests/dev_parts/routine.rs:835-892) runs `jet dev --swap` and waits for `count=2`. By reading the code, dev_restart_argv drops `--swap` (Source/CmdDevTools.rs:887-889), so the restart engine prints `count=1` there.

Process model, from D-ENTRY-SHAPE1 option A technical. `fn dev` and the program compile into one O0 binary. The `jet` tool process holds the `#Persist` store and the local-service supervisor. It runs the compiled `fn dev` session, which runs the program as its child. Editing program code restarts only the child. Editing `fn dev` or the env definition ends the session and starts it again; the `jet` process stays, so kept values and running services survive. Ctrl-C ends everything.

Option A, mechanism. The `jet` process gives each program child a private pipe, passed down through the session and named in an environment variable that only `jet dev` sets. A runtime thread in the child waits on it. On a stop request, or when `fn run` returns, the thread copies each `#Persist` cell and sends it to the `jet` process. Then the program ends as it does today. The next child reads the values before `fn run` starts.

Option A, why the copy is safe. Each cell is guarded by a lock, and E0222 and E0223 forbid partial moves and mutable borrows of persistent state. So every write replaces the whole value, and the thread copies each value whole without pausing the program. Two bindings may be copied at slightly different moments. Values that must agree belong in one binding.

Option A, one store. The wire format is the existing PersistEntry: module path, binding name, shape fingerprint and payload. Restore runs `plan_migrate` and reports the same outcomes the dev session already records. The store moves from a process-wide static into the `jet` process's session state; only the transport is new. One store exists per program the session runs, keyed by output name (D-TARGET-ONE1).

Option A, type changes. A value of the same shape is kept. Otherwise the ratified live-value rules apply at restore: D-LIVE-PERSIST1=A migration blocks, as widened by D-HOTSTATE1=A, where added fields take their defaults and removed fields are dropped. When no rule applies, the value starts over from its starting value. The line names the change and the migration block to write, as D-PERSIST1 and D-LIVE-PERSIST1 require.

Option A, edges. A renamed or removed binding starts over, and the line says so (D-LIVE-PERSIST1). An edited starting value does not replace a kept value; the line says so and names `--fresh`. After a crash, or if the program does not answer in two seconds, nothing is saved and the next start is fresh. A crash may come from the state itself, so Jet never replays it. A program paused in a debugger is killed after two seconds and starts fresh.

Option A, the fresh row. `fresh` is one row of the D-SETTING-ORDER1 table: `--fresh` or `--fresh=off`, `dev: { fresh: true }`, and `d.fresh(true)`; stock off. When on, no kept value is restored at any start of the session, so every binding begins at its starting value. Writing `d.fresh(true)` in `fn dev` and saving restarts the session with fresh values while the `jet` process and its local services stay. Removing it turns keeping back on.

The fresh row, continued. It follows the one order: a flag beats entry code, which beats package.jet. `jet test --fresh` already bypasses the persisted test-result cache (Source/CmdCompile.rs:6836). Both rows mean start without saved results for their own command, so the word keeps one meaning.

Option A, lifetime. Values live in the memory of the `jet` process, never on disk. Ctrl-C ends them, and the next `jet dev` starts fresh. They survive a re-entered `fn dev` (D-ENTRY-SHAPE1), because the `jet` process stays. `jet run`, `jet build`, `jet test` and `jet run --watch` always start fresh, and release builds ignore the mark, as D-PERSIST1 says.

Option A, other hosts. A web build already sends a `persist_live_value` row for each binding to the dev server for display (crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/DomRuntime.js:332, crates/jet-devserver/src/BrowserWebAdapter.rs:381). Option A widens that row to the typed payload and restores it after the live reload. The Canvas loop keeps its in-memory store and reports the same outcomes, so every host follows one rule.

Option A, plain data. Values cross a process boundary, so only plain data can be kept. The store already rejects closures and native handles (crates/jet-foundation/src/Persist.rs:390-392). Today E0622 allows only scalar starting values, so every legal binding qualifies. If struct starting values arrive later, a marked type that holds a handle or closure becomes a registered compile error at the declaration (I7).

Option B, mechanism. The mark keeps values only while the program stays in memory. Default `jet dev` restarts, so every start is fresh, and Jet prints one registered note at start when the program has marked values. The Canvas loop keeps them until the evaluator retires. The mark wakes when an engine that swaps code in memory returns. D-EXEC2=A plans native in-memory O0 to replace build-and-execute, but no ratified plan restores code swap.

Byte identity. D-DEVMODE1 requires dev output to be byte-identical to the release build. Under A, a restored value is a program input from the session. With no restored values, such as the first start or a `--fresh` session, dev output stays byte-identical. This ballot is where D-DEVMODE1 is amended; sibling ballots point here.

Amends D-PERSIST1=A: a marked value survives a `jet dev` restart, saved at stop and restored at start, instead of a hot reload. Opt-in, module-level only, identity by module path and binding name, and no release meaning all stay. Amends D-PERSIST-DEVSTATE1=A: the purpose reads across a dev restart instead of a hot reload. The rule that a marked binding is writable stays.

Amends D-LIVE-PERSIST1=A: migration runs at restore instead of in place, and its announced-restart fallback becomes a start-over for that value, with the same line. Amends D-HOTSTATE1=A: its rules apply at restore to `#Persist` values only, because nothing else survives a restart. Its restart fallback also becomes a start-over.

Amends D-LIVE1=A and D-HOTSWAP1: the per-save line `saved game.jet  swapped chase  kept world` becomes `saved game.jet  restarted  kept score = 40`. A layout change starts that value over instead of restarting the program. Amends D-DEVMODE1: a restored value counts as a program input for the byte-identity rule. D-SETTING-ORDER1 removes the swap flags and field and gains the `fresh` row.

If B wins, it amends D-PERSIST1=A and D-PERSIST-DEVSTATE1=A: the mark keeps values only while the program stays in memory. D-LIVE-PERSIST1=A and D-HOTSTATE1=A stay law but apply only in the Canvas loop. Unchanged under both: D-EXEC2=A, D-RUN-WATCH1=A, the D-VERDICT-1231-2 spelling, and E0145.

Research, right ways. Vite's `import.meta.hot.data` keeps one object per module across replacements, and `hot.dispose` fills it before the old module goes (https://vite.dev/guide/api-hmr). That is save at stop, restore at start. React Native Fast Refresh keeps state only when safe, resets it otherwise, and remounts after a runtime error (https://reactnative.dev/docs/fast-refresh). Option A follows both.

Research, wrong ways. With domain reload off, Unity keeps every static field between play sessions, and its manual says you must reset static state yourself (https://docs.unity3d.com/Manual/domain-reloading.html). That is the keep-everything default D-PERSIST1 rejected. Flutter keeps globals on hot reload, and a changed initializer needs a hot restart (https://docs.flutter.dev/tools/hot-reload). Option A keeps that rule, names the kept value, and adds `--fresh`.

Research limits. The sources are official documentation read on 2026-10-19. No adoption or friction data was found for any of these features. No repository census was run for this ballot.

Cutover for A. In run_dev_restart, replace the kill with a stop request, then a kill after two seconds. Add the pipe, the runtime copy thread and the restore before `fn run`. Move the store into the `jet` process's session state. Widen the web row. Add the `fresh` row. Register the kept, start-over, crash and starting-value lines under I7. Update persist.jet, its test without `--swap`, Docs/spec/spec.md:452-453 and the E0146 fix text that says hot-reload state.

Review: one fresh combined pass (beginner + adversarial), agent SlateReview, Claude family, 2026-10-19, per owner directive for one review. Repaired: process model (the `jet` process holds the store; editing `fn dev` keeps values), story limited to simple values, `--fresh`/`d.fresh(true)` row, output wording, debugger timeout, situation and surface trim. Cohesion pass CohesionReview 2026-10-19 repaired: canonical process model.

options.name: Save on stop, restore on start
options.detail:
When a save makes `jet dev` restart the program, Jet first asks the program to stop. The program sends each `#Persist` value to the `jet` process and ends. The new program takes back each value whose name and type still fit, and then `fn run` starts. One line per save names every kept value.

Values are saved when Jet stops the program and when `fn run` returns. After a crash, the next start is fresh, because the saved state may have caused the crash. A changed type uses the existing keep, migrate or start-over rules. A renamed value starts over. An edited starting value does not replace a kept value, and the line says so.

To start over, run `jet dev --fresh` for one session or write `d.fresh(true)` in `fn dev`. Values live only while `jet dev` runs, and Ctrl-C ends them. Gains: the mark keeps its promise with restarts. Loss: an edited starting value applies only when you start fresh.
options.technical: The `jet` process holds the store, as in the process model of D-ENTRY-SHAPE1. It gives each program child a private pipe through the session. A runtime thread in the child copies every `JetPersistCell` whole on a stop request or when `fn run` returns. E0222 and E0223 make each write a whole-value replacement, so no pause is needed. The payload is the existing PersistEntry, and restore runs `plan_migrate` with the existing outcome types. A program that does not answer in two seconds is killed and the next start is fresh.
options.code:
#Persist score := 0
$ jet dev game.jet       // play until score is 40, edit tick, save
saved game.jet  restarted  kept score = 40
saved game.jet  restarted  kept score = 40 (new start value 5 applies with --fresh)
saved game.jet  restarted  score is now Float: started over at 0.0
game.jet crashed  restarted fresh: values are not kept after a crash

options.name: Keep values only in memory
options.detail:
The mark keeps values only while the program stays in memory. Default `jet dev` restarts the program, so every start is fresh. When a program has marked values, `jet dev` prints one note at start. The Canvas view, which runs the program inside Jet, keeps values until that engine retires. The mark wakes if an engine that swaps code in memory returns.

Gains: every start is clean, and nothing new is built now. Losses: the mark does nothing in default `jet dev`. No plan brings code swap back, and game developers replay to reach a bug after each save.
options.technical: No transport and no `fresh` row are added. The start note is registered under I7. The Canvas loop keeps the process-wide store and HotReplaceTxn, so D-LIVE-PERSIST1 and D-HOTSTATE1 apply only there. The test persist_example_survives_hot_reload moves to Canvas or expects `count=1`. The example persist.jet says the mark is idle in default `jet dev`.
options.code:
#Persist score := 0
$ jet dev game.jet
note: #Persist is idle while jet dev restarts; score starts at 0
— game.jet changed, re-running —      // score is 0 again
$ jet dev game.jet --canvas           // keeps score until that engine retires

comparisons.note: `import.meta.hot.data` is one object per module path that survives each replacement. `hot.dispose` fills it before the old module goes. This is save on stop, restore on start. Source: https://vite.dev/guide/api-hmr.

decisions.title: One meaning for the word service
decisions.situation: Jet uses the word service for two things: a server program your project builds, and a helper such as a database that Jet starts and watches while you work. Both are even spelled with the same type name, so a newcomer who asks Jet to start their own server as a service gets an error. The vote decides whether the two become one idea, one is renamed, or both stay apart. We recommend one idea: a service is a long-running program Jet supervises, from a package or from your own code.
decisions.gist: Should "service" mean one thing, a long-running program Jet supervises, whether it comes from a package or your own code?
decisions.lesson: Jet uses "service" twice. A Service output is a server program your project builds; it takes no flags and runs until stopped. A dev-environment service is a helper, such as postgres, that Jet starts, checks for readiness, and restarts while you work. Both are long-running programs, and both appear in images. The vote decides whether they become one idea, or whether one is renamed or kept apart with an error.
decisions.story: Mia builds a game and a small API server in one project. She wants `jet dev game` to start postgres and her own API, wait until both are ready, and rebuild the API when she edits it. Today postgres can be a helper, but her API cannot, because "service" means something else for it. Her teammate Omar writes integration tests that need the same API running.
decisions.detail:
Scope. This ballot answers the open card question q01laxht on card c07glrub: "service" means two things. It decides the word and whether your own Service output can run as a service. D-DEV-SERVICES1 (open) decides where services are written and how dev and test switch them. Its rules apply to output-backed services unchanged.

A holds against ratified law, part one. D-ECO-DECL1=A already writes a service as `Service{ run: packages.api }` and an image as `Image{ services: [services.web] }`. So the ecosystem ruling already treats a service as a supervised run of the project's own program. D-ECO-OUTPUT-CALLCONTRACT1=A says services run unattended, take no parameters, and live while their call lives. That is a supervised long-running program.

A holds against ratified law, part two. D-JPK-SERVICE1=A says `system.*` services are the same Service type with a different lifecycle owner. D-JPK-SERVICEDEPTH1=A gives one Service record from a bare `run` to full readiness. D-ECO-OUTPUT-KINDS1=A keeps its nine kinds under A, including Service. D-TARGET-ONE1=A keeps one output list and `b.add_service`.

A holds against code. Output.Service entries take no parameters: E1321 says "A Service or Check takes no parameters" (tests/ui/output_entry_contract.stderr). The `run` intent already accepts Executable or Service (crates/jet-pkg-model/src/Package/mod.rs:1876-1881). The package parser's service field list already allows `from` and `run` (mod.rs:3655-3674). Readiness, restart and logs live in the supervisor (crates/jetpack/src/Services.rs:4422-4585).

What A must add. The `run` field of a service record accepts an output reference, such as `outputs.api`, beside an argument list. The `outputs.` prefix follows the D-ECO-DECL1 section-qualified form. Today the env.jet reader rejects unknown fields with E1262 and does not know `from`. The package.jet parser accepts `from` without meaning, so A uses `run` and leaves `from` unused.

The implicit entry. Every Service output appears in the dev and test environments as a service of the same name, off until named. This gives the magic default: `jet dev game --service=api` works with no extra data. An explicit entry adds ports, readiness, `after` or `enable`, and is on unless it says `enable: false`. A clash between an output name and a package service name is a registered error naming both.

Roles. `jet dev api` makes `api` the program of the dev session, as D-TARGET-ONE1=A and D-ENTRY-SHAPE1=A say. When the session's program is a Service output, its own service is not started, even if an entry, `d.service` or `--service` turns it on. The first line then says `api: running as the program`.

Roles, continued. `--service=api` keeps another output as the program and runs `api` beside it under the supervisor. The supervisor gates the program on readiness. The first `jet dev` line names each role, for example `services: postgres ready · api ready on :8080 · running game`.

Build and restart. An output-backed service is its own binary on the normal build path, with the dev command's settings, its own `options:`, and flags that reach selected outputs (D-SETTING-ORDER1=A). The dev session builds it with the program. Per the D-ENTRY-SHAPE1=A process model, the `jet` process holds the supervisor, so the service survives a re-entry of `fn dev`.

Build and restart, continued. Saving its sources rebuilds and restarts it only, as D-EXEC2=A requires. An output-backed service keeps `#Persist` values across its restarts as the program does (D-DEV-STATE1=A). `jet services up api` builds it with the dev command's settings; outside a dev session nothing rebuilds it on save.

Trust. D-DEV-SERVICES1 keeps service commands as data so `jet env` lists them without running code. An output-backed service runs a program compiled from the project's own sources, which `jet dev` already runs as explicit intent (D-JPK-DEVCOMPOSE1=D). It adds no arbitrary command. Outputs written in package.jet are listed by `jet env`; outputs made by `fn build` are known after compiling, like the dev program itself.

Images and the trust fingerprint. Implicit entries do not join image projection or the trust fingerprint (Trust.rs:401-405). crates/jetpack/src/CLI/add_remove_push_image.rs:640-664 raises E1336 when an environment has services that an image does not select. That check counts written entries only, so an existing `from: env.dev` image keeps working when the project gains a Service output.

A third use, unchanged. D-SERVICE1=D's `core.service` tree organizes supervised workers inside one program. Under A it reads as the same idea at a smaller scale: workers inside one Service output. D-SERVICE1 says Jetpack owns supervised external development processes, which A keeps. JetOS system services stay the same record with JetOS as owner.

Why not B. It amends D-ECO-OUTPUT-KINDS1=A (Service becomes Server), D-ECO-OUTPUT1=A and D-CONF-NAME1=A examples, D-ECO-OUTPUT-CALLCONTRACT1=A wording, D-ECO-DECL1=A examples, D-TARGET-ONE1=A (`b.add_server`) and E1321 text. A worker that consumes a queue serves no requests, so `Server` misnames it. Running a server beside your program would need A's `run: outputs.api` rule too, under a second word.

Why not C. C is today's D-DEV-SERVICES1 text. It keeps two types named `Service` and relies on a registered error to teach the split. Running your own server beside your program needs `run: ["jet", "run", "api"]`. That nested `jet` is not rebuilt or restarted by the dev session.

Today in code. Output.Service appears in 18 files under tests, Examples and the spec, by search for `Service\{ ?name:|\.Service\.?\{` on 2026-10-19. `jet services up api` with no environment entry fails with "no dev service named `api`" (crates/jetpack/src/CLI/services_secrets_config.rs:607-621). These counts measure repository sites, not users.

Name-clash migration. The name-clash error affects projects that already have an environment service and a Service output with the same name; none found beyond the Canvas `service` output. Search of 2026-10-19: every file with a Service output (tests, Examples, spec) was checked for a `services:` map. Only tests/canvas_scenarios.rs:1308-1313 has both, with output `service` and environment services `custom_server` and `canvas_service`, so no name clashes.

Research, right ways. Docker Compose runs published images and your own `build:` code in one `services:` list, with one health and start-order model (https://docs.docker.com/reference/compose-file/services/). .NET Aspire models a packaged database and your own project as the same resource kind (https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/aspire/). systemd's `.service` unit runs any long-running program under one supervisor. All three tie the word to supervision, not origin.

Research, wrong ways. devenv uses two words, `services` for packaged helpers and `processes` for your own programs (https://devenv.sh/processes/). Users must learn which list a program belongs in, and only processes can run their own code. That is the split of options B and C. No adoption or friction data was found that measures either model; the evidence is documentation and Jet's code.

Amends under A. D-JPK-SERVICE1=A: a service's `run` may name a Service output, and every Service output is a service of its own name, off until named. D-JPK-SERVICEDEPTH1=A: the record's `run` field takes an output reference beside an argument list.

Amends under A, continued. D-DEV-SERVICES1 (open): the output-name error is removed, `--service=api` runs the output as a service, and its "local service" wording becomes "service". D-TARGET-ONE1=A wording: a Service output is "a long-running program", not only "a server program", and it can run as a service beside the dev program.

Amends D-SETTING-ORDER1=A (if A wins): a local service's definition is written as data only, or implied by a Service output. In its "Words." paragraph, "a server program" becomes "a long-running program". Its service on/off row covers output-backed services with no new row.

Unchanged under A. D-ECO-OUTPUT-KINDS1=A, D-ECO-DECL1=A (A follows its example), D-ECO-OUTPUT-CALLCONTRACT1=A, D-SERVICE1=D, D-EXEC2=A, D-ENTRY-SHAPE1=A and D-DEV-STATE1=A.

Cutover under A. Teach both environment readers that `run` may hold an output reference, and add the implicit entry for each Service output. Build output-backed services with the dev and test session, and restart them on source change. Register the wrong-kind and name-clash errors under I7, and print roles on the first `jet dev` line. Update D-DEV-SERVICES1 and the spec's Services sections.

Review: one fresh combined pass (beginner + adversarial), agent Round3Review, Claude family, 2026-10-19, per owner directive for one review. Repaired: example `enable: false`, program's own service, image and trust scope, `jet services up`, build settings, B loss, late name check, `#Persist`, settings-order amendment, clash search.

options.name: One idea: a supervised long-running program
options.detail:
A service is a long-running program Jet supervises: it starts it, waits until it is ready, restarts it on failure, and keeps its logs. The program comes from a package, such as postgres, or from one of your own Service outputs. A Service output keeps its name because it is the shipped form of the same idea.

Every Service output is available as a service under its own name, off until named. `--service=api`, `d.service("api")` and `t.service("api")` run it beside the program you work on. A service entry such as `api: .{ run: outputs.api, ports: [8080], enable: false }` adds readiness, ports or order. Like any listed service, an entry without `enable: false` is on for every session.

`jet dev api` still makes `api` the program you work on, and then its own service is not started. `jet dev game --service=api` runs your game and your API together under one supervisor. Jet rebuilds and restarts the API when its code changes, as it does for the program. Gains: one word and one type, and a path for several of your programs at once. Loss: a name can play two roles, which Jet names on the first line.
options.technical:
One record type, the D-JPK-SERVICEDEPTH1 `Service` record. Its `run` field takes an argument list, as today, or an output reference such as `outputs.api`. This follows the ratified D-ECO-DECL1 form `Service{ run: packages.api }`. The reference must name an output of kind Service; another kind is a registered error naming the kind.

Each Service output adds an implicit service entry `{ run: outputs.<name>, enable: false }` to the dev and test environments. An explicit entry with the same name and that `run` replaces it and, like any listed service, is on unless it says `enable: false` (D-DEV-SERVICES1). An explicit entry with the same name and a different `run` is a registered error naming both. A name that matches only an output made by `fn build` is checked after `fn build` runs.

When the session's program is a Service output, its own service is not started, even if an entry, `d.service` or `--service` turns it on. The first line then says `api: running as the program`.

An output-backed service is built on the normal build path with the session. It is its own binary, with the dev command's settings, its own `options:`, and flags that reach selected outputs (D-SETTING-ORDER1). Per the D-ENTRY-SHAPE1 process model, the supervisor in the `jet` process runs it. Saving its sources rebuilds and restarts it (D-EXEC2=A). An output-backed service keeps `#Persist` values across its restarts as the program does (D-DEV-STATE1=A).

Readiness defaults to process start, as D-JPK-SERVICEDEPTH1 gives a bare `run`; listed `ports` add a port probe. Its entry takes no parameters (E1321), so the supervisor passes no flags. `jet services up api` builds `api` with the dev command's settings and starts it under the supervisor. Outside a dev session nothing rebuilds it on save.

Trust. An output-backed service runs your own compiled program, which `jet dev` already runs; it adds no arbitrary command. The `jet env` summary lists the Service outputs written in package.jet.

Images. Implicit entries count as listed for `--service` and `jet env`, but not for image projection or the trust fingerprint. An image selects one only by name, and E1336's 'declares services but the image does not select them' check counts written entries only. A selected output-backed service needs a verified package build; until then E1336 refuses it and names the fix.

options.name: Rename the output kind to Server
options.detail:
The output kind `Service` becomes `Server`: `.Server{ name, entry }` in package.jet and `b.add_server` in build code. "Service" means only a helper in the environment that Jet supervises.

Gain: each word has one meaning. Losses: it changes the ratified closed list of output kinds and every example that uses `Service`. A queue worker or a scheduler is not a server, but must be called one. Running your server beside your program needs A's `run: outputs.api` rule too, under a second word.
options.technical: Rename `PackageOutputKind::Service` and `Output.Service`, and the new `b.add_service` from D-TARGET-ONE1 becomes `b.add_server`. The D-ECO-DECL1 example `Service{ run: packages.api }` and image `services: [services.web]` lose their meaning as written and need restating. E1321 text changes from "A Service or Check" to "A Server or Check". The environment `Service` record is unchanged.

options.name: Keep both meanings, with a mix-up error
options.detail:
Both meanings stay, and both types keep the name `Service`. Naming an output where a helper is expected is a registered error that points to `jet dev api`. This is the current text of the local-services ballot.

Gain: no rename and no new rule. Losses: one word keeps two types, and newcomers learn the split from an error. Your own server cannot run beside your program, except through a command such as `run: ["jet", "run", "api"]`, which the dev session does not rebuild.
options.technical: No change to the output kinds or the environment record. The error "`--service=api`: `api` is an output your project builds; start it with `jet dev api`" is registered under I7 for `--service`, `d.service`, `t.service` and `jet services up`.

comparisons.note: One `services:` list. Each entry runs a published image or builds your own code with `build:`. Both get the same start order, health checks and logs. This is option A. Source: https://docs.docker.com/reference/compose-file/services/.
The app host treats a packaged database and your own project as the same kind of resource, with references between them. This is option A. Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/aspire/.

Two words: `services` for packaged helpers and `processes` for your own programs. Users learn both, and only processes run your code. This is the split of options B and C. Sources: https://devenv.sh/services/ and https://devenv.sh/processes/.
A `.service` unit runs any long-running program, packaged or your own, under one supervisor. The word means supervision, not origin. Source: man systemd.service.

recommendation.why: Both meanings already describe one thing: a long-running program Jet supervises. Making them one idea removes the mix-up, and lets the same supervisor run your own server beside your program.
gains: One word, one type, one supervisor for helpers and your own servers.
Several of your own programs run together in one `jet dev`.

losses.loss: `jet dev api` and `--service=api` both run `api`, in different roles.
losses.mitigation: `jet dev api` makes `api` the program you work on. `--service=api` runs it beside that program. The first-run line says which.

whyNot.reason: It renames a ratified kind and misnames workers; running a server beside your program would need A's rule under a second word.
It keeps two types under one name and only teaches the split through an error.

recommendation.tradeoff: One name now runs in two roles. Jet says which role it picked.

decisions.title: Compiler pipeline: one non-SSA slot IR between the AST and machine code
decisions.situation: The compiler copies every program through five forms on the way to machine code: the syntax tree, a typed tree, two SSA graphs, and a machine instruction list. Each copy costs allocation, lookups and a separate validation walk, and together they hold most of the 105 second self-compile. The vote picks the shape we build next; we recommend one flat, slot-based IR that keeps loops and branches structured, with SSA built only where a pass proves it needs it.
decisions.gist: Which intermediate form should sit between the syntax tree and machine code?
decisions.lesson: An intermediate representation is the program as the compiler works on it after parsing. Fewer forms means fewer full copies of the program, which is where much of compile time goes.
decisions.story: Jet compiles itself in 105 seconds today; the goal is 30 seconds now and a million lines per second later. Parsing to machine code passes through AST, TIR, MIR, LIR and an x64 list.
decisions.inWild:
Jai: one linear bytecode, interpreted at compile time and translated to machine code.
Wasm: structured blocks and local slots, no SSA.
decisions.detail:
Measured phases on a quiet run: front end about 45 s, MIR lowering 8 s, optimizer 7 s, native lowering 14 s, object emission 23 s. Half of all LIR instructions were back-edge copies created by SSA block parameters. Option A with a data-oriented front end is the route to 30 s; the IR change alone reaches about 60 to 70 s.

Card #5073 maps every current consumer and the migration. Consumers include the comptime evaluator, web emit, O1 and O2 passes, debug info, hot reload, LSP and the package store. Each cutover is proven by identical program behavior on the old and new paths.

options.name: One slot IR
options.detail: AST plus sema facts in node-id tables, then one linear slot-based IR per function with structured blocks, loops and branches, then machine code. Ownership is explicit move/copy/drop instructions. A pass that needs SSA builds a per-function SSA view and discards it, so debug builds never pay for SSA.
options.technical: IR: flat arena per function, integer ids, content-hashable. Machine layer: linear-scan allocation over slot live ranges. Migration: spike on Core plus examples first (go/no-go on speed and identical output), then front end, then IR, each cutover proven by identical program behavior on old and new paths.
options.code: source -> AST (+ facts by node id) -> IR (slots, structured control) -> machine code

options.name: Keep SSA, flatten
options.detail: Keep AST, TIR, MIR and LIR, but store each in flat arrays with integer ids and interned names.
options.technical: Data-oriented internals only; structure unchanged.
options.code: source -> AST -> TIR -> MIR (SSA) -> LIR (SSA) -> machine code, all flat

options.name: One SSA IR
options.detail: Drop TIR for facts tables and lower one SSA graph in place from semantic to layout level.
options.technical: MLIR-style progressive lowering inside one SSA form.
options.code: source -> AST (+ facts) -> IR (SSA, lowered in place) -> machine code

recommendation.why: Jet owns both ends, so SSA is not needed as an exchange format; one slot IR removes the most copies.
gains: Fewest full program copies; debug builds skip SSA entirely.

losses.loss: SSA-based optimizer passes must be rewritten.
losses.mitigation: Passes that truly need SSA build a per-function SSA view on demand; the spike measures this before any cutover.

whyNot.reason: B keeps every copy and the SSA overhead, so it cannot reach the speed goals.
C still pays SSA construction on every build and does not map onto Wasm structured control.

recommendation.tradeoff: More rewrite now in exchange for the fewest copies and one meaning across comptime, native and web.

fn run() -> Unit<>

  local l1 n: Int [copy] at p1
  place p0 = l0: Int
  place p1 = l1: Int

  b1:

    jump b3
  b2:

    write p0 <- v1
    jump b0
  b3:
    v6: Bool [copy] = loop-range-has-next v7
    branch v6, b6, b2
  b4:
    v12: String [owned] = string ["liftoff"]
    v15: Unit<> [copy] = semantic Print [v12]
    return
  b5:
    v4: Int [copy] = read p0
    v10: String [owned] = string ["t-minus ", v4]
    v14: Unit<> [copy] = semantic Print [v10]
    v3: Int [copy] = const 1
    v8: Int [copy] = read p0
    v9: Int [copy] = sub v8, v3
    write p0 <- v9
    jump b0
  b6:
    v5: Int [copy] = loop-range-value v7
    write p1 <- v5

Wasm and JS emit map directly from structured blocks.
losses: The optimizer passes written for SSA are rewritten.

options.name: Keep SSA, flatten

options.name: One SSA IR

proposed.code: source -> AST (+ facts) -> IR (SSA, lowered in place) -> machine code

recommendation.tradeoff: More rewrite now in exchange for the fewest copies and one meaning across comptime, native and web.

decisions.title: Jetpack: delete the two legacy migrations
decisions.situation: Jetpack still carries two migrations from older layouts. One command folds old role files such as pkg.jet and config.jet into package.jet, and every write command first converts an old on-disk store layout. Both keep retired file names alive in the code after everything else moved to package.jet. The vote decides whether they go now; we recommend deleting both, with env.jet and workspace.jet staying canonical.
decisions.gist: Should Jetpack keep its migrations from retired file layouts?
decisions.lesson: A migration rewrites old files or stores into the current layout. Keeping one means the old names stay understood forever; deleting it means old layouts become plain errors.
decisions.story: Every other retired spelling was removed on 2026-10-20. These two migrations are the last code that still reads pkg.jet and the old store layout.
decisions.inWild: Cargo reads only Cargo.toml; a directory without it is an error, not a migration.
decisions.detail:
TransitionPlan.jet holds env_transition_legacy_plan. It reads pkg.jet, env.jet, workspace.jet and config.jet, then writes package.jet. Jetpack Foundation still defines PAYLOAD_FILE (pkg.jet) only for it and marks CONFIG_FILE retired.

store_migrate_legacy_hangar runs before every jetpack command that writes. env.jet and workspace.jet are still current files that the devserver and env model read.

options.detail: Delete env_transition_legacy_plan, PAYLOAD_FILE, the retired CONFIG_FILE handling and store_migrate_legacy_hangar in one cutover. env.jet and workspace.jet stay canonical.

decisions.title: Command entry functions take one context named after the command
decisions.situation: A Jet package can replace what a command does by writing a function named after it, such as fn build or fn test. Today each one takes a differently named context: BuildContext for build, TestSuite for test, and nothing at all for dev. The compiler build is about to become the first large fn build, so the shape should be settled first. We recommend one rule where every entry takes a context named after its command.
decisions.gist: What parameter should each command entry function take?
decisions.lesson: A command entry is a function the toolchain calls for a command, like fn build for jet build. Its parameter is the handle it uses to do the work.
decisions.story: The Jet compiler will build itself with jet build Compiler/, which runs fn build in the compiler workspace instead of a separate script.
decisions.inWild: Zig: `pub fn build(b: *std.Build) void` takes a handle named after the command.
decisions.detail: Ratified today: D-CONF-ENTRY1 (one fn build(b: BuildContext) -> BuildPlan per package), D-CMD-OVERRIDE1 (fn test(suite: TestSuite), fn bench(suite: BenchSuite)), D-ENTRY-VALUE1 (fn run() -> App; fn dev() replaces the dev default). This ballot only renames the parameter types and gives dev and run a context.

options.name: Named after the command
options.detail: Every command entry has the same shape: the function is named after the command and takes one context value named after it. Build returns its plan; the others return nothing or their result. A no-parameter override still replaces the default, as ratified.
options.technical: Rename BuildContext to Build, TestSuite to Test, BenchSuite to Bench; add Dev and Run contexts carrying the watch, reload and argument surfaces. One cutover migrates every in-repo caller.

options.name: Keep current names
options.detail: Keep the ratified signatures: `fn build(b: BuildContext) -> BuildPlan`, `fn test(suite: TestSuite)`, `fn bench(suite: BenchSuite)`, and a parameterless `fn dev()` override.
options.technical: No change.

recommendation.why: One shape for every command entry is easier to learn and lets dev receive a context like the others.
gains: A beginner learns one rule that covers build, dev, test, bench and run.

losses.loss: Existing build and test entries are renamed.
losses.mitigation: One cutover migrates every in-repo caller; the compiler build is the first user.

whyNot.reason: B keeps three naming styles for one idea and leaves dev without a context.

recommendation.tradeoff: A one-time rename in exchange for one uniform entry rule.

decisions.title: fn run() has no return type; apps serve themselves

decisions.lesson: A long-running app keeps the program alive by serving requests; a script finishes and exits. Either can be told apart by what run does, not by its return type.

decisions.title: May a function borrow a #Persist binding for writing?
decisions.situation: A #Persist binding keeps game or app state across a hot reload, and functions may already write to it with total += 1. Passing it to a helper with bump(&total) is rejected today, and the two compilers even give different wrong errors. The vote decides whether a write borrow of a pinned binding is allowed. We recommend allowing it, because it is the same write the function could already do directly.
decisions.gist: Can `bump(&total)` write to a `#Persist` module binding through a write parameter?
decisions.lesson: A `#Persist` module binding keeps its value when `jet dev` reloads changed code, and a function may write to it directly. A write parameter (`value: &Int`) lets a function change the caller's variable. The question is whether the two combine.
decisions.story: Mia is building a game with jet dev. Her score is `#Persist score := 0`. She moves the scoring code into a helper `add_points(points: &Int, n: Int)` and calls `add_points(&score, 10)`. Today that fails to compile, although `score += 10` in the same place works.
decisions.detail: Fixture tests/ui/static_mutable_borrow.jet. Today the Rust oracle reports E0355 (a policy at a prohibited scope) and the Jet compiler reports E0145 (#Persist on a binding that is not module-level). Both are wrong for this program: the binding is module-level, and D-PERSIST-DEVSTATE1=A makes a #Persist binding writable from a function. No decision says whether a write borrow counts as such a write. Edge cases: a hot reload happens between calls, never while a borrow is live; a borrow of an ordinary module binding stays E0111.

options.name: Allow the write borrow
options.detail: A #Persist binding may be passed to a write parameter. The program prints 1. Ordinary module bindings stay read-only from functions (E0111).
options.technical: Sema treats &persist_binding as a write place like a direct assignment; the borrow ends at the call. The fixture becomes a run example with golden output 1.

options.name: Direct writes only
options.detail: Passing a #Persist binding to a write parameter is rejected with a dedicated error that teaches a direct write or returning the new value.
options.technical: Sema reports one registered diagnostic at the &total argument; the fixture snapshot records it.

comparisons.note: Swift lets a global variable be passed to an inout parameter with &. See https://docs.swift.org/swift-book/documentation/the-swift-programming-language/functions/#In-Out-Parameters

recommendation.why: D-PERSIST-DEVSTATE1 already makes a pinned binding writable from a function; a write parameter is the same write, done by a helper.
gains: Helpers work on pinned state with no special rule.

losses.loss: Module state can change inside a helper call.
losses.mitigation: The & at the call site shows the write, and only #Persist bindings allow it.

whyNot.reason: It adds a second rule for the same write and forces game code to be restructured.

recommendation.tradeoff: A little more reach for pinned state, marked by & at every call.

decisions.title: How diagnostics name Core library types
decisions.situation: When an error mentions a Core library type, Jet prints an internal path such as module:14:source-root:0 followed by the name. Nobody can read that, and it differs between the two compilers. The vote picks one readable naming rule for every message. We recommend the plain name, with the module path added only when two different types in one message share that name.
decisions.gist: When an error message mentions a Core type such as `Secret`, how should it be named?
decisions.lesson: Error messages name the types involved. User types already print as their plain name. Core library types currently leak an internal path such as `module:14:source-root:0::…::Secret` or `<corelib>/core.crypto::Secret`.
decisions.story: Leo reads the raw bytes of a `crypto.Secret` by mistake. The error says the problem is with `module:14:source-root:0::core::crypto::Secret`. He wanted to see `Secret`.
decisions.inWild: expected `HashMap<String, u32>`, found `Vec<u8>`
decisions.detail: Fixtures: tests/ui/crypto_secret_bytes_exposure.jet (E0510), tests/ui/path_builtin_not_core_record.jet (E0112/E0108), tests/ui/ui_facade_single_uinode_identity.jet. The registry templates print `{Type}`, and user types print their leaf name. No decision fixes Core type naming. Edge case: a user type named like a Core type in the same message.

options.name: Plain name, path on a clash
options.detail: Core types print as their plain name. When two different types in one message share that name, each prints as module path plus name, as the user would write it (crypto.Secret).
options.technical: One shared type-display function strips internal module identities and qualifies only names that collide within the message; every diagnostic uses it.
options.code: error[E0510]: reading the bytes of `Secret` needs #Unsafe

options.name: Always the plain name
options.detail: Every type prints as its plain name, with no qualification.
options.technical: The shared type-display function keeps the last path segment.
options.code: error[E0510]: reading the bytes of `Secret` needs #Unsafe

options.name: Always the module path
options.detail: Core types always print with their full dotted module path.
options.technical: The shared type-display function prints the dotted Core module path.
options.code: error[E0510]: reading the bytes of `core.crypto.Secret` needs #Unsafe

comparisons.note: rustc prints the shortest name that is unique in the crate graph ("trimmed paths"), and the full path only when names clash. See https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/73996

recommendation.why: Messages stay as short as user-type messages, and the rare clash still reads unambiguously.
gains: Readable messages with no internal paths, and no ambiguity.

losses.loss: The same type can print two ways in different messages.
losses.mitigation: The longer form appears only when the short one would be ambiguous.

whyNot.reason: It prints two different types the same way when names clash.
It makes every Core message longer for a clash that rarely happens.

recommendation.tradeoff: Rare longer names, in exchange for short messages everywhere else.

decisions.title: A prep value inside a function
decisions.situation: A prep block computes a value while the program is built. A test expects such a block inside a function to be refused with an error saying it is not supported yet, while D-PREP-SURFACE2 says prepared values use ordinary names. Neither compiler gives that error today. The vote decides whether a local prep value is part of the language; we recommend yes, built once and baked in.
decisions.gist: Does `lanes :: prep { calculate_lanes() + 0 }` inside a function compute its value at build time?
decisions.lesson: A `prep { … }` block runs while the program is built, and its last expression is its value. At module level `NAME :: prep { value }` is ratified. A fixture expects a local `lanes :: prep { … }` inside a function to be rejected with E0391, which says the form is not supported yet.
decisions.story: Kai's renderer needs the number of lanes. He writes `lanes :: prep { calculate_lanes() }` inside `run` so the work happens once at build time instead of every run.
decisions.detail: Fixture tests/ui/prep_block_value_unsupported.jet; its comment cites D-PREP-SURFACE2=A and expects E0391. D-PREP-SURFACE2=A: prep is always an expression whose final expression is its value, and prepared values use ordinary names. A 'not supported yet' diagnostic conflicts with the greenfield rule of one canonical current form. Edge cases: the prep body may not read run-time locals; it runs once per build, not per call.

options.name: Supported
options.detail: A local prep binding is computed at build time. The fixture becomes a run example with golden output 8, and E0391 is removed.
options.technical: Comptime evaluates the block once per build; codegen emits the constant. The prep body may not reference run-time locals (existing prep rules).

options.name: Module level only
options.detail: A prep value inside a function is rejected with a permanent error that teaches moving it to a module-level `NAME :: prep { … }`.
options.technical: E0391 is reworded as a permanent rule with a fix; the fixture keeps its snapshot.
options.code:
LANES :: prep { calculate_lanes() + 0 }
fn run() { print(LANES) }

comparisons.note: Zig evaluates a comptime expression inside a function and bakes the value in. See https://ziglang.org/documentation/master/#comptime

recommendation.why: D-PREP-SURFACE2 already says prepared values use ordinary names, and a local value keeps build-time work next to the code that needs it.
gains: One rule for prep values everywhere, with no 'not yet' error.

losses.loss: The compiler must fold local prep values.
losses.mitigation: The same evaluator already folds module-level prep values.

whyNot.reason: It splits one feature by location and turns a 'not yet' into a permanent restriction.

recommendation.tradeoff: A little more compiler work for a uniform rule.
