options.gist: The value is computed once at build time and the program prints 8.
gains: Matches D-PREP-SURFACE2: prepared values use ordinary names anywhere.
Removes a 'not yet' diagnostic.
losses: The build-time fold must be implemented for locals.

options.name: Module level only
options.gist: Only `NAME :: prep { … }` at module level; inside a function the error says to move it there.
gains: One place for build-time values.
losses: Values only one function uses must move to module scope.

proposed.code:
LANES :: prep { calculate_lanes() + 0 }
fn run() { print(LANES) }

recommendation.why: D-PREP-SURFACE2 already says prepared values use ordinary names, and a local value keeps build-time work next to the code that needs it.
gains: One rule for prep values everywhere, with no 'not yet' error.

losses.loss: The compiler must fold local prep values.
losses.mitigation: The same evaluator already folds module-level prep values.

whyNot.reason: It splits one feature by location and turns a 'not yet' into a permanent restriction.

recommendation.tradeoff: A little more compiler work for a uniform rule.

decisions.title: Do method calls into Core count toward the rights a program needs?
decisions.situation: Before a program runs, Jet works out which rights it needs (reading the environment, reading files and so on) and stops with E1803 when the application has not decided them. The self-hosted compiler follows method calls such as `Path.home()` into Core and finds the Env and FS.Read rights they use. The Rust compiler only follows plain function calls, so it never sees those rights. Eleven run goldens (io/path, io/args_spec, dyn/bytes_datetime, io/system_projection and others) expect the program to run with no grants, which matches the Rust result. The vote decides which result is the rule.
decisions.gist: Does `Path.home()` in a program make it need the Env right before it runs?
decisions.lesson: A program's rights are the effects it can reach. Rust's check skips method calls, so a program that reads the home directory through `Path.home()` is treated as needing only IO.
decisions.story: Mia writes a small tool that prints her home directory with `Path.home()`. Under one rule it runs straight away; under the other Jet first asks her to grant Env, because that is what the tool reads.
decisions.inWild: deno run --allow-env main.ts   # Deno asks for the env right whenever Deno.env is reached, however it is called
decisions.detail: Jet: Compiler/JetCli/Source/Cli/Authority.jet:153 walks call edges, method calls included. Rust: crates/jet-pkg-model/src/EffectBudget.rs:638 entry_effects over an effect call graph that records only bare-name calls (crates/jet-sema/src/Sema/OSTarget.rs:503-506). Edge cases: trait method calls through a box, closures passed to Core, generic Core functions. Under A the eleven goldens gain the grant they need in their package.jet (authority.holds) and keep their output.

options.name: Every call counts
options.detail: Method calls into Core count like plain calls. The eleven goldens declare the rights they really use and keep their output.
options.technical: Keep the Jet walk; add authority.holds rows to the eleven golden packages; Rust stays the old route and is not changed.

options.name: Match the Rust compiler
options.detail: Only plain function calls count. The goldens run unchanged with no grants.
options.technical: The Jet walk skips method-call edges into Core, as Rust does.
options.code: fn main() { print(Path.home()) }   // runs with no grant

comparisons.note: Deno checks the env right at the point of use, however the code reaches it. See https://docs.deno.com/runtime/fundamentals/security/

recommendation.why: A right that a method call reaches without being counted is a hole in the check. Any program could read files or the environment through a method.
gains: The rights check sees everything the program can do.

losses.loss: Eleven goldens need a one-line grant in their package.
losses.mitigation: Their printed output does not change.

whyNot.reason: It keeps a known gap in a safety check to match an old compiler's omission.

recommendation.tradeoff: A grant line in a few examples for a rights check with no gap.

surface.gist: Does `Path.home()` in a program make it need the Env right before it runs?
surface.lesson: Jet works out a program's rights before it runs. The Rust compiler skips method calls when it does this; the self-hosted compiler follows them.

current.note: Today the golden expects this to run with no grant; the self-hosted compiler stops with E1803 for Env and FS.Read.

wild.note: Deno needs --allow-env however the env is reached.
wild.code: deno run --allow-env main.ts

options.name: Every call counts
options.gist: Method calls count; the example declares Env.
gains: No gap in the rights check.
losses: Examples that use these methods declare the right.

options.name: Match the Rust compiler
options.gist: Only plain function calls count.
gains: The goldens run unchanged.
losses: A method call can use a right the check never saw.

proposed.code: fn main() { print(Path.home()) }   // no grant needed

recommendation.why: A safety check that misses method calls can be bypassed by accident or on purpose.
gains: Rights match what the program can really do.

losses.loss: Eleven examples gain a grant line.
losses.mitigation: Their output is unchanged.

whyNot.reason: It keeps the gap.

recommendation.tradeoff: A grant line for a sound check.

decisions.title: Build, Dev and Test are ordinary Core types
decisions.gist: Should the build, dev and test handles be ordinary Core types with labeled settings, instead of names only the compiler knows?
decisions.lesson: A build file starts with `fn build(b: Build)`. The value `b` is a handle: you call its methods to add programs, steps and settings. Today `Build`, `Dev` and `Test` live in private compiler tables, so nothing can show their methods and arguments work only by position. The names, the empty return and `b.default(app)` are already decided and do not change here.
decisions.story: Mara keeps a small game package. She wants a helper library that adds a shader step to any build, and she wants hover to tell her what `b.action` takes. Today neither works. Her library cannot name the `Build` type, and hover finds no declaration. When she writes `toolchain: native` to make a long call readable, the compiler rejects the label. With option A she reads the method in the editor, passes `b` to her helper, and labels each setting.
decisions.inWild:
Zig: the build handle is the ordinary standard-library type `std.Build`, and its methods take named option fields. Source: https://ziglang.org/learn/build-system/

Bazel: rule code calls `ctx.actions.run(executable = ..., inputs = ..., outputs = ...)`, a documented API with named arguments. Source: https://bazel.build/rules/lib/builtins/actions#run
decisions.detail:
Provenance: the owner approved the proposal on build programs and compiler events (Docs/proposals/build-programs-and-compiler-events-2026-10-22.md) and set the direction for this question to option A. The losing option keeps the compiler-private names and the string router.

Already settled, not re-decided here: D-ENTRY-CTX1=A names the handles `Build`, `Dev`, `Test`, `Run` and `Bench` and retires `BuildPlan`. D-ENTRY-SHAPE1=A settles `b.default(app)`, the empty return with `!BuildError`, sealing at return, and `d.run()` and `t.run()`. This ballot decides only where the handles are declared and how their methods take arguments.

Amends D-ENTRY-SHAPE1=A in one point: it calls `Dev` and `Test` prelude-owned handles. Under A they are ordinary Core declarations, not compiler-owned names. D-ENTRY-SHAPE1 also names `core.build.graph` as the reader of the sealed plan. A replaces it with `b.graph()`, so build code and tools read one value. Nothing else in that ruling changes.

Method-set question folded in: the proposal listed the exact methods and spellings as a possible fifth ballot. It is not a real choice with at most three options. Most rows are already law: D-TARGET-ONE1, D-SETTING-ORDER1, D-JAI-BUILDOPT1, D-BUILDCTX-FLAGS1, D-BUILD-IO1, D-BUILD-INCLUDE1, D-BUILD-GENVALUE1 and D-ENTRY-NAMES1. The rest follows from Jet's ordinary call rule, positional values first and then labels. Option A's technical text lists the full set.

Corrections to the proposal, checked against the code on 2026-10-22: today's dev table holds `watch(String)`, `serve(port:)` and `reload(mode)`, not `reload(target:)`. Test has no method table, but test entries already use `run()`, `iteration` and `result`. The proposal's new test methods, such as a suite or golden helper, are out of scope here.

Code facts: the build call checker rejects any label with E0764 and reports argument counts with E0104. The reserved type list still holds `Build`, `Dev`, `BuildPlan` and the other build names. `FileReader` in Core is the host-backed type pattern A follows. The spec's programmable-builds section still shows a `BuildPlan` return and must be updated in the cutover.

Profile: short. This is one mechanism with two options. Removing `BuildPlan` from the Core surface registry is a removal D-ENTRY-CTX1 already ratified, not new grammar, and labels use the existing call grammar.

options.name: Ordinary Core types
options.detail:
Core declares `Build`, `Dev` and `Test` the way it declares `FileReader`: a type with documented methods whose work is done by the build host. Required values come first. Every optional setting has a default and is written with a label. Hover, completion, go to definition and generated docs read these declarations, so they work with no extra code.

A library may take `b: Build` as a parameter and add outputs or steps to it. `b.graph()` returns the checked build graph registered so far. Build errors are cases of one Core `BuildError` enum, so a caller can match them.
options.technical:
Method set (this folds in the separate method-set question). Build outputs, per the one-output ruling: `add_executable`, `add_library`, `add_test`, `add_asset_bundle`, `add_doc`, `add_package`, `add_service`, `add_install`, `add_publish`. Each takes `name` and `sources`, then labeled `actions:`, `deps:`, `probes:`, `toolchain:`, `signing:` and `options:`, and returns `Output`.

Build steps: `action(name, run:, inputs:, outputs:, allow:, toolchain:, probes:, signing:, kind:, pools:, env:, env_allowlist:, helpers:, labels:, cache:)` returns `BuildAction`. The labels are the fields of today's session action record; `allow:` holds the effect list now passed as strings. `legacy` takes the same labels plus `wrapper:`.

Tools: `toolchain(name, target_triple:, role:, host_triple:, sdk:, linker:, sysroot:)`, `probe(name, kind:, value:)` with `kind` one of program, pkg-config or header, and `signing(name, label:)`. Code and checks: `generate(name) { ... }`, `include`, `error(at:, what:, why:, fix:)`, `plugin` and `contribute`, each written with labels.

Whole build: `default(output)`, `output(name)`, `profile(name)`, `options()`, `pin(..., output:)`, `graph()`. Setting methods such as `optimize`, `default_profile` and `default_allow` are generated from the one option table, as the setting-order ruling requires. The generator writes them into the Core declaration, so they are documented like hand-written methods.

Dev: `run()`, `output()`, `pin(...)` and the generated setting rows `port`, `open`, `watch`, `service`, `before`, `record`, `fresh`, `share` and `args`. Test: `run()` returning the results, `pin(...)` and the generated rows `measure`, `filter`, `before` and `service`. Run and Bench, the other entry handles, follow the same rule, so there is one convention.

Removed: `find`, `embed` and `fetch` leave `Build`; they are ordinary functions under the build-input ruling. `plan()` is gone under the entry-shape ruling. Today's dev methods `watch(glob)`, `serve(port:)` and `reload(mode)` give way to the generated setting rows.

Cutover, in one change. Delete the sema method tables in the build and dev call checkers and the codegen route for build calls. Delete the string router in the build session host and the arity text. Remove `BuildPlan` from the reserved type list and the Core surface registry, which the entry-context ruling already retired. Migrate every in-repo caller to labels in the same change. Update the programmable-builds section of the spec, which still shows a `BuildPlan` return.

options.name: Keep the compiler tables
options.detail: The handles keep their already-decided names and shapes, but the compiler still defines them. Private tables list each method and how many arguments it takes. The build host picks the work by matching the method name as text. Arguments keep their positions, and labels stay an error. Libraries cannot name the handle types.
options.technical: Keeps the build and dev method tables in sema, the codegen route for build calls, the string router in the build session host and the arity text, all in step by hand. The ratified renames still apply. Editor features need separate hand-written entries for each method.

comparisons.note: The build function receives the ordinary standard-library type `std.Build`. Its methods take a struct of named fields. Source: https://ziglang.org/learn/build-system/
Rule code calls documented API methods with named arguments, so each input and output is labeled. Source: https://bazel.build/rules/lib/builtins/actions#run
comparisons.code:
ctx.actions.run(
    executable = ctx.executable._tool,
    inputs = [src],
    outputs = [out],
    arguments = [src.path, out.path],
)

comparisons.note: `Project` and task types are declared API classes, so the IDE completes and documents them. Source: https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/kotlin_dsl.html

recommendation.why: Build handles then work like every other Core type. People and editors can read the methods, labels make long calls clear, and libraries can extend a build.
gains: One way to declare, check and document every Core API.
One edit adds a build method, not three.

losses.loss: Build methods become a public API that must stay stable.
losses.mitigation: Methods change only with a Core release, and an old call fails with a checked error naming the new label.

whyNot.reason: B keeps private tables that nobody can read, and every method change must edit three compiler places in step.

recommendation.tradeoff: Build, Dev and Test become versioned public API in exchange for being readable and checked like any other type.

surface.gist: Should the build, dev and test handles be ordinary Core types with labeled settings?
surface.lesson: A build file starts with `fn build(b: Build)`. You call methods on `b` to add programs and steps. Today the compiler invents `Build`, `Dev` and `Test` from private tables. Nothing can show their methods, and arguments work only by position. Their names and the empty return are already decided.

current.note: Hover finds no declaration for `b`. Each argument means something only by its position, and a label is an error.
current.code:
stamp :: b.action("stamp", ["in.txt"], ["out.txt"],
    ["cp", "in.txt", "out.txt"], ["FS"], native)

b.action("stamp", ["in.txt"], ["out.txt"], ["cp"], ["FS"], toolchain: native)
// error[E0764]: `Build.action` takes positional arguments

wild.note: Zig's build handle is an ordinary library type with named fields. Source: ziglang.org/learn/build-system.

options.name: Ordinary Core types
options.gist: Core declares the handles like any type; optional settings take labels.
gains: Hover, completion and docs show every method.
Labels name each setting; unused ones take defaults.
A library can take `b: Build` and add steps.
losses: Each build method becomes public API to keep stable.

options.name: Keep the compiler tables
options.gist: The compiler keeps private method tables and matches calls by name.
gains: No change to today's build files.
losses: Editors cannot show or document build methods.
Long calls stay readable only with the table open.
Libraries cannot name the handle types.

recommendation.why: Build handles then work like every other Core type. People and editors can read the methods, labels make long calls clear, and libraries can extend a build.
gains: One way to declare, check and document every Core API.

losses.loss: Build methods become public API that must stay stable.
losses.mitigation: Methods change only with a Core release, and an old call fails with an error naming the new label.

whyNot.reason: B keeps tables nobody can read, and each method change edits three compiler places in step.

recommendation.tradeoff: The handles become versioned public API, and in return they are readable and checked.

decisions.title: One Compiler value and one event stream for compile-time control
decisions.situation: Ratified Jet rules let an opted-in build provider rewrite function bodies through checked change sets, but none of that is built. Today no build can change a written function or watch the compiler work, so a team that wants tracing on every marked function copies the same lines into each one. This ballot replaces that unbuilt design and decides who may hold compiler control and how it runs. Under every option macros stay removed, code is quoted with #code and values are spliced in with $. The recommendation is one value that only the application's own source can create and must pass on by hand, which watches compiler events and can add code or rewrite checked function bodies.
decisions.gist: How should a build program control the compiler: one passed value with event handlers, hooks only, or a package-wide grant?
decisions.lesson: A compile-time program is Jet code the compiler runs while it builds. A function is checked once the compiler has confirmed its names, types and effects. Jai lets compile-time code watch every checked function and replace its body. Jet's hooks, functions the compiler calls at fixed stages, can only read, report and add code. A marker such as `#Traced` only tags a declaration. Under every option macros stay removed and code is quoted as `#code { }`.
decisions.story: Ines runs a web service with forty route functions marked `#Traced`. Each starts with the same two tracing lines, written by hand, and new routes keep forgetting them. Her package file names compiler control with `authority: { holds: { allow: [Meta.Code] } }`. Under option A her build creates one compiler value and hands it to the tracing library, which wraps every marked function. She deletes the hand-written lines. `jet inspect expand --facts meta` prints each function's final code. Libraries she never handed the value to cannot touch her code.
decisions.inWild:
Jai: the build program loops on `compiler_wait_for_message()` and may replace a checked procedure with `compiler_modify_procedure`. Source: The Way to Jai, chapter 30, https://github.com/Ivo-Balbaert/The_Way_to_Jai

Rust: procedural macros rewrite token streams before type checking, and any dependency may define one. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/procedural-macros.html

Zig: compile-time code computes values and types but cannot change another function's body. Source: https://ziglang.org/documentation/master/#comptime
decisions.detail:
For maintainers. Provenance: the owner approved the proposal on build programs and compiler events (Docs/proposals/build-programs-and-compiler-events-2026-10-22.md) and set this question's direction to A. The owner ruled out macros: markers plus compile-time functions cover them, and the goal is full Jai power. The owner named the losing directions: hooks only, and a Jai-style loop with no value to hold.

Shared by every option. Macros stay removed, by owner ruling, and code values are quoted `#code { }` with `$` splices. This answers the owner's comment on D-JAI-CODE1=A, which asked for idiomatic, cohesive syntax. `paste`, `#Expand`, `name!()` calls, the `uses:`, `defines:` and `exits` clauses, `#ExpandLimit` and `#NoDebug` are removed. The `Code` type, `c.nodes()` and `c.map` survive; `code(expr)` becomes `#code { expr }`.

What replaces each macro use. Wrapping a declaration becomes a marker plus `rewrite_body`. Timing a block, D-JAI-CODE1's own example, becomes a closure plus `defer`: `timed("load", () -> assets.load_all())`. Generating declarations becomes `b.generate` or `meta.add`. Changing the caller's own variables has no replacement; that is an accepted loss under the owner's ruling.

Splicing. D-NAME-SPLICE1=B is extended: `$name` splices a compile-time binding inside `#code` as it does in templates, so Jet keeps one splice sigil. The retired `#( )` spelling stays retired. D-META-HASH1, still open, proposes `#` for values Jet supplies while `$` keeps splicing; `#code` fits it, and another outcome is a mechanical respelling.

Replaces D-META-CONTROL2=A's API: the advanced session, change sets, `commit` and the `register`, `register_expansion` and `register_specialization` providers. Call-site expansion leaves with macros. Specialization control is left to D-JAI-GENERIC1, which is open. Signature replacement is not carried over. Compared with change sets, A gives up order-free merges and per-item caching of a stateless provider. A keeps CONTROL2's atomic re-check of affected callers.

Replaces the read-only `stages()` view of D-COMPILER-EVENT1=A and D-JAI-EVENTS1=A with `meta.events(watch:)`. The one `compiler.Event` type stays and gains the loop kinds `Checked`, `Stuck`, `Error` and `Done`. Settled becomes `Stuck` and finished becomes `Done`. Parsed, imported and declared stay hook stages and are not loop events. The session wire uses the same four kind names.

Amends D-HOOK-STAGES1=A. Its rejection of a full message loop with in-place rewriting is reversed for `Compiler` holders. Its rule that stages run once and never return to declared is kept, and extended: a rewrite produces no new event. Its rule that overlapping edits are an error still binds hooks; `Compiler` holders instead stack in registration order. Hooks still only read, report and add.

Keeps D-HOOK-ONE1 and D-JAI-CONFIG1. Keeps D-EXPANDCLI1: final code lives in `jet inspect expand --facts meta`, a new lens, not in a new `jet expand` command as the proposal wrote. Keeps D-FRONTENDAPI1: the shipped `core.compiler.parse` makes code from text, so there is no second parser; inserting that code is what `Meta.Code.Raw` gates.

Amends D-MARKER-LAW1=A: built-in derives move from compiler code to Core library code over the read-and-add view, as the owner directed. The user derive form of D-METADERIVE1 is unchanged.

Amends D-JAI-EXPERT1=A. The `Meta.Paste` leaf is removed with macros. `Meta.Code` gates creating a value; `Rewrite`, `Raw` and `Types` gate `rewrite_body`, adding code made from text, and adding type declarations. Passing the value is the grant to a library, so `grants:` no longer applies to `Meta.Code` leaves under A. Default holding is D-META-HOLD1.

Interplay. Until D-META-CROSSPKG1 rules, rewrites may touch only the application's own package. D-META-OPTIN2's target records stand until then. The story assumes D-META-HOLD1=A, so Ines's package file names `Meta.Code`; without that line `b.compiler` stops with an error printing it.

Amends D-META-OPTIN2=A and D-META-RECONCILE1=A. Under RECONCILE1 the older refusals already yielded for opted-in projects. Opted in now means a build that created a `Compiler` value. That covers D-METAMUTATE1, S26's value-only rule, D-METADEPTH1 and D-META-GATE1. The ban on user macros in D-METAMUTATE1 and S26 returns to full force for everyone.

Effects. D-EFFECT-OMIT1=A infers effects for functions with no written bound, so a rewrite can change a function's effects. A therefore checks affected callers again at round end, and a rewrite past an explicit bound is an error. The step budget is D-PREP-FUEL1's.

Research: Docs/audits/2026-10-07-ast-metaprogramming-report.md recommends a typed code model with quotes and checked insertion, not exposing the compiler's internal trees. A follows it. Docs/audits/jai-parity-2026-10-16.md lists the message loop and procedure rewrite as the main Jai gap.

Profile: full, because A changes quote syntax and removes ratified macro syntax. Two fresh readers reviewed this ballot, and their findings are repaired here.

options.name: One passed Compiler value
options.detail:
Only the application's own source can create a `Compiler` value, with `b.compiler(app)`, one value per program being built. A library gets compiler control only when the application passes it the value. The first hand-off is one visible line, and the `meta` lens lists every later hand-off and every function touched.

A holder registers handlers with `meta.events(watch:)`. The call returns at once, and the handlers run while the program compiles, after `fn build` returns. A handler can add code or rewrite the body of a checked function. Several holders stack in the order they were registered.

The compiler checks every added or rewritten piece of code again, like written code. If a rewrite changes a function's effects, every caller affected is checked again too. The editor marks rewritten functions, and `jet inspect expand --facts meta` prints final code and who changed it.
options.technical:
Creation. `Compiler` is a Core type. `b.compiler(output)` must be written in the root package's own source. A call written in any dependency is an error, even when that dependency's function holds the root's `b`. Creating the value performs `Meta.Code`. Whether the application holds `Meta.Code` by default is D-META-HOLD1.

Events. `meta.events(watch:, handler)` registers a handler and returns at once. Compiling starts after `fn build` returns. `watch:` filters by declaration kind and marker, and only watched declarations wait for handlers. Each declaration's event goes once to each handler, in registration order. A rewrite never produces a new event, so a rewritten function is never delivered to any holder again.

Kinds. `compiler.Event` gains four loop kinds. `Checked` means one declaration passed checking. `Stuck` means the compiler cannot continue until someone adds names it is waiting for. `Error` carries a diagnostic, and `Done` ends compilation. A round is one pass of adding code and checking it again. Round 17 is a registered error naming what still waits, as the ratified event rules already say.

Actions. `meta.add(code)` adds declarations; adding a type declaration needs `Meta.Code.Types`. `meta.rewrite_body(f, code)` replaces a checked body and needs `Meta.Code.Rewrite`. Text becomes code through the shipped `core.compiler.parse`; adding code that came from text needs `Meta.Code.Raw`. Until D-META-CROSSPKG1 rules, rewrites may touch only the application's own package.

Re-checking. A rewrite goes through parse and check like written code. Its effect facts are inferred again. Every caller whose facts change is checked again, all at once at the end of the round, and the public API snapshot records the new facts. A rewrite that widens effects past an explicit bound is an error at the `rewrite_body` call that names the bound.

Composition. Holders stack in registration order. In a handler, `f.body` is the current body, including earlier holders' rewrites in this round. Read-only consumers such as `#On` hooks, `b.program()` queries and derives see a watched function only after the round's rewrites.

Quotes. `#code { ... }` is a value of type `Code`. Inside it, `$name` splices a compile-time binding, as `$` already does in templates. Names in a quote resolve where the quote is written, and spliced code keeps its own scope. A local named `trace` in `load_user` cannot capture the quote's `trace`.

Everywhere. Rewrites apply to every compilation of the output's modules: build, run, test, dev, check and the language server, which runs the same handlers. Handlers record what they read, so an unchanged function replays its recorded rewrite. The compile-time step budget stops a runaway handler.

Provenance. Each added or rewritten item records the build line and library function that changed it. `jet inspect expand --facts meta` prints final code with that record, and lists each value created and every hand-off. This uses a lens, not a new command, as the transparency-command ruling requires.

options.name: Hooks only
options.detail: Compile-time code matches what is built today. Hooks and markers see each declaration and may report problems or add new code. Nothing may change a function that is already written, so the ratified but unbuilt change-set rewrites are dropped. Tracing can be checked but not added; a hook can only ask the author to write the lines.
options.technical: Keeps the hook stages and the read-only stage view. Drops the change-set session of the compiler-control ruling and its body rewrites. Macros stay removed and code values use the same `#code { }` quote with `$` splices as A, for code that hooks add.

options.name: Package-wide grant, no value
options.detail: The application's package file grants rewriting to a whole dependency. That package's compile-time code opens the event loop itself, as in Jai, with no value to create or pass. The grant is visible in the package file, but the build cannot say which call or which functions it covers.
options.technical: Uses the ratified expert-power grants: the main package names `Meta.Code.Rewrite` for a dependency with `grants:`. Event registration and rewrite are free functions in `core.compiler`. Stacking, re-checking, quotes and provenance follow the same rules as A. Macros stay removed.

comparisons.note: The build program intercepts a workspace, waits on messages and may modify a checked procedure. Any metaprogram that runs can do this. Source: The Way to Jai, chapter 30, https://github.com/Ivo-Balbaert/The_Way_to_Jai
An attribute macro rewrites tokens before type checking, so it sees no types. Any dependency can ship one. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/procedural-macros.html
Compile-time code computes values and types, but it cannot change a body written elsewhere. Source: https://ziglang.org/documentation/master/#comptime

recommendation.why: A gives Jai's full control and keeps the first grant visible: one value, created only in the application's source and passed by hand. Every change is checked again, including affected callers.
gains: Full control without hidden power in dependencies.
One event stream serves hooks, tools and build programs.

losses.loss: A rewritten body differs from the source on screen.
losses.mitigation: The editor marks rewritten functions, and the expand meta lens prints final code and who changed it.

decisions.title: Rewriting another package's code needs one line naming that package
decisions.gist: Should a build need one line naming a dependency before compile-time code may rewrite that dependency's functions?
decisions.lesson: A rewrite replaces the body of a function that is already written. An application's build may let a library rewrite the application's own code. A rewrite could also reach into a dependency, such as a database library: code you did not write and may never have read. The lock file already pins each dependency's exact contents, so a permission can name a package without copying hashes.
decisions.story: Ines hands her compiler value to a tracing library so it can wrap her route functions. The library also wants to wrap every query function inside her database package. Under option A the build stops with an error that names the database package and prints the one line to add. She reads it, decides she wants traced queries, and adds the line. Her teammate sees that line in review.
decisions.inWild:
Jai: any metaprogram may modify any procedure it sees, including ones from imported modules; there is no per-module consent. Source: The Way to Jai, chapter 30, https://github.com/Ivo-Balbaert/The_Way_to_Jai

Rust: a crate can refuse a power at its root with `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`, and the refusal is visible in source. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/attributes/diagnostics.html#lint-check-attributes
decisions.detail:
Provenance: the owner approved the proposal on build programs and compiler events (Docs/proposals/build-programs-and-compiler-events-2026-10-22.md). The owner named A, an explicit `meta.allow_rewrite(package:)` call in the application's build, and B, allowed by default as in Jai. C is today's ratified rule, included as the honest third option.

Depends on D-META-COMPILER1. This ballot applies only if that ballot ratifies the `Compiler` value. If it does not, this ballot is moot. Until this ballot rules, D-META-COMPILER1 limits rewrites to the application's own package, and D-META-OPTIN2's target records stand.

Amends D-META-OPTIN2=A. Under A, its `metaprogramming_targets` records (package identity, source digest, exact declarations list) are removed. The per-package call replaces them, and the lock file supplies the digest. OPTIN2's rule that a rewrite never changes the dependency's cached source stays. D-META-RECONCILE1=A quoted the same records as the dependency-target rule; that reference now points here.

Keeps D-JAI-EXPERT1=A: `Meta.Code.Rewrite` stays an effect leaf that must be held, and a deny from a team or organization file still wins over this call. Default holding is D-META-HOLD1.

Why per package and not per function: rewrites usually follow markers across a package, and a per-function list goes stale on every update. The `meta` lens shows the exact functions changed, so review keeps per-function detail without a hand-kept list.

Profile: short. One mechanism, three options, no new syntax; `allow_rewrite` is an ordinary method on the Core `Compiler` type.

options.name: Name the package in the build
options.detail:
The application's build may rewrite its own code once it has a compiler value. To rewrite another package's functions, the same build must first call `meta.allow_rewrite(package: "orm")`. Without that line, the rewrite stops with an error naming the package and the line to add.

The rewrite applies only to this build's copy of the locked version. The dependency's cached source never changes, and other projects using the same package are not affected.
options.technical:
`Compiler.allow_rewrite(package: String)` records consent for one package, by its locked identity. The lock already pins the package contents, so the consent covers exactly the locked version; an update shows as a lock change in review. A rewrite of a declaration from a package with no consent fails with a registered error at the `rewrite_body` call, naming the package, the function and the fix line.

A consented rewrite follows the same checks as any rewrite. Its effect facts are inferred again, and every affected caller, in the dependency's copy or in the application, is checked again at the end of the round.

Adding new declarations is not a rewrite and needs no consent. Core and the standard library are packages like any other under this rule. The `meta` lens of `jet inspect expand` groups every rewrite by target package. Effect rules still apply: `Meta.Code.Rewrite` must be held, and an organization or team deny still wins.

options.name: Allowed by default
options.detail: Once the application passes its compiler value to a library, that library may rewrite functions in any package the build uses, as in Jai. Nothing in the source names the packages it touches.
options.technical: No consent record exists. The `meta` lens still lists rewrites after the fact, and a team can deny `Meta.Code.Rewrite` entirely.

options.name: Keep exact records
options.detail: Keep today's written rule. The application's package file lists each dependency it may rewrite, with that package's source hash and the exact functions allowed.
options.technical: The ratified records name package identity, source digest and an exact declarations list. No globs and no transitive grants. An update changes the digest and invalidates the record.

comparisons.note: A metaprogram that intercepts the workspace sees every procedure, from any module, and may modify it. Source: The Way to Jai, chapter 30, https://github.com/Ivo-Balbaert/The_Way_to_Jai
A crate root can forbid a power, and the line is visible in source and review. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/attributes/diagnostics.html#lint-check-attributes

recommendation.why: A keeps full rewrite power but makes changing someone else's code a choice you can see. One line per package is cheap, and the lock already pins what it covers.
gains: No silent changes to code you did not write.

losses.loss: A dependency update can change what a rewrite touches.
losses.mitigation: The lock change shows in review, and the meta lens lists every rewritten function by package.

whyNot.reason: B lets any library you hand the value to change any dependency, with no line saying so.
C makes you copy hashes and function lists by hand, and every update breaks them.

recommendation.tradeoff: One line per rewritten package, in exchange for no silent changes to other people's code.

decisions.title: The power to create a Compiler value is named once in the package file
decisions.gist: Must a project name compiler control in its package file before its build can create a Compiler value, or is it on by default?
decisions.lesson: Every package file has one `authority` block that lists the powers the package holds, such as network access. Ordinary powers are on unless denied. Expert powers are off until the project names them, and the trust prompt shows that change when you open a cloned project. The question is which kind the power to control the compiler should be.
decisions.story: Theo clones a game project and opens it. Its build creates a compiler value and rewrites hundreds of functions. Under option A, the clone's package file names that power, so the trust prompt shows it before anything runs, and CI fails with the exact line if it is missing. Under option B, nothing outside the build file says so, and Theo learns about it only if he reads that file.
decisions.inWild:
Rust: a crate can refuse a power at its root with `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`, one visible line. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/attributes/diagnostics.html#lint-check-attributes

Deno: programs get no file, network or subprocess access unless a flag or config names it. Source: https://docs.deno.com/runtime/fundamentals/security/

Jai: every metaprogram may drive the compiler, with no grant at all. Source: The Way to Jai, chapter 30, https://github.com/Ivo-Balbaert/The_Way_to_Jai
decisions.detail:
Provenance: the owner approved the proposal on build programs and compiler events (Docs/proposals/build-programs-and-compiler-events-2026-10-22.md) and asked the author to pick the default from Jet's goals: beginner safety, auditability and pragmatism. The proposal leaned toward on-for-the-application. This ballot recommends the opposite, for the reasons below.

Spelling: the proposal wrote a TOML-style `[meta]` table with `compiler = "none" | "root" | "any"`. Jet's package file is Jet record syntax, and D-AUTHORITY-MANIFEST1=A puts every power in one `authority` block. So option A is the proposal's `none` and option B is its `root`. The proposal's `any` is not offered: D-META-COMPILER1 lets only the application's build create the value.

Why A. Beginner safety: a beginner never sees compiler control unless a tutorial asks for it, and then the error prints the one line. Auditability: the trust prompt, CI and an organization file all read the package file, not build code. Pragmatism: the cost is one line, once per project, which the error prints and `jet fix` can add.

Why not double gating: `b.compiler(app)` is the use, not a second gate. The package line is the only permission. That matches D-META-OPTIN2=A, where the owner chose a package-level opt-in over a package-plus-every-run opt-in.

Under A no ruling is replaced: it confirms D-JAI-EXPERT1=A for `Meta.Code` as D-META-COMPILER1 redefines it. Under B, D-JAI-EXPERT1's expert flag is removed from `Meta.Code` for the main package, and D-META-OPTIN2's rule that omission means standard mode is reversed.

Related: D-META-CROSSPKG1 decides whether rewriting a dependency needs a further line in the build. D-TRUST-LAUNCH1=A already excludes expert leaves from one-run approval, so `--trust` never turns this on.

Profile: short. One mechanism, two options, no new syntax; the `authority` block and `Meta.Code` already exist in ratified law.

options.name: Named once in the package file
options.detail:
Compiler control stays an expert power. A project turns it on with one line in its package file: `authority: { holds: { allow: [Meta.Code] } }`. Without that line, `b.compiler(app)` stops with an error that prints the line to add.

Adding the line is a project-policy change, so the trust prompt shows it when someone opens a cloned project, and CI fails with the line instead of prompting. A beginner who never asks for compiler control never sees any of this.
options.technical:
Confirms D-JAI-EXPERT1=A for the `Meta.Code` node under D-META-COMPILER1: `$expert`, never held by default, only the main package may hold it, approved only through a project-policy edit. Holding `Meta.Code` holds its children `Rewrite`, `Raw` and `Types`; naming only `Meta.Code.Rewrite` is not enough to create the value.

`b.compiler(output)` performs `Meta.Code` and must be written in the main package's own source, so this one line governs every value. If the main package does not hold it, the call fails with a registered error whose fix is the exact `authority` line, machine-applicable through `jet fix` in an interactive edit. Organization and team files may still deny any Meta leaf, and the outermost refusal wins.

options.name: On for the application
options.detail: The application's own build may create a compiler value with no package-file line. Dependencies still never can. A team that does not want it writes `authority: { holds: { deny: [Meta.Code] } }`.
options.technical: Removes `$expert` from the `Meta.Code` node and its children for the main package only, so the main package holds them unless denied. Dependencies still cannot hold them. This amends D-JAI-EXPERT1=A for that node, and the meaning of omission in D-META-OPTIN2=A.

comparisons.note: One line at the crate root changes what the whole crate may do, and review sees it. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/attributes/diagnostics.html#lint-check-attributes
Powers are off until a flag or config names them, and the error names the missing permission. Source: https://docs.deno.com/runtime/fundamentals/security/
comparisons.code:
$ deno run main.ts
error: Uncaught (in promise) NotCapable: Requires net access to "example.com:443", run again with the --allow-net flag
$ deno run --allow-net=example.com main.ts

comparisons.note: Any metaprogram may drive the compiler; there is no grant to write or review. Source: The Way to Jai, chapter 30, https://github.com/Ivo-Balbaert/The_Way_to_Jai
comparisons.code: #run build();   // build() may intercept and modify the whole program

recommendation.why: Rewriting a whole program is the strongest power Jet offers. One package-file line makes it visible to the trust prompt, CI and reviewers, and costs an expert one line, printed by the error.
gains: A cloned project cannot rewrite code without the trust prompt showing it.
One rule for every expert power.

losses.loss: An expert writes one more line before the first use.
losses.mitigation: The error prints the exact line, and `jet fix` can add it.

whyNot.reason: B lets a cloned project rewrite its code with nothing outside the build file saying so.

recommendation.tradeoff: One line per project, in exchange for compiler control that is always visible and approved.

options.gist: Compiler control stays an expert power; one package-file line turns it on.
gains: The trust prompt and CI show it in cloned projects.
The same rule as every other expert power.
losses: One line before first use.

options.gist: The application's build may use it unless the package file denies it.
gains: Nothing to write before first use.

decisions.title: In a cross build, which machine do build-time Core calls act on?
decisions.situation: Build code runs on the build machine, but the program it builds may run somewhere else. Today build code can only read the target, through $build.os, and nothing names the build machine. Core is also inconsistent. Most per-OS Core code asks the running machine, but one Core helper folds $build.os, so during a Windows build on Linux it would use Windows path rules on a Linux disk. We recommend one rule: Core calls act on the machine running them, $build always names the target, and $build.host names the build machine.
decisions.gist: When build code cross-compiles, do its Core calls act on the build machine or the target?
decisions.lesson: Build code runs on your machine, while the program it builds may run on another. A file read in build code can only read your disk. The question is whether Core calls in build code follow your machine, and how build code names each machine. Reading a fact never changes its meaning: $build.os always names the target.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: a normal build on one machine changes nothing. The question matters only when you build a program for another operating system.

If you build a Windows program on Linux, a preparation step that lists a directory must answer for one machine. Jet must say which one, every time, so the build is repeatable.
decisions.story: Theo builds a Windows installer on a Linux laptop. His build code lists the assets folder and checks that every file exists. The listing must use Linux path rules, because it reads his Linux disk. The installer itself still uses Windows rules.
decisions.inWild:
Cargo build scripts: cfg!(target_os) inside build.rs describes the build machine, and the target comes from CARGO_CFG_TARGET_OS. Cargo's docs warn about mixing them up. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-build-scripts

Zig: build.zig is compiled for the build machine; b.graph.host names it, and the target is a separate value. Source: https://ziglang.org/learn/build-system/
decisions.detail:
WHAT EXISTS TODAY

Facts are served by Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Expressions/FactReads.jet:641-649. They are $package.name and version, $build.os and profile, the stamps and $build.cpu.cache_line. There is no host fact. Docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:5268 says $build.os is the --target OS, or the host OS when no target is given.

Build code: Docs/spec/spec.md:4888-4935. jet build runs fn build(b: Build) natively at O0 on the build machine, and the spec example uses the FS and Exec effects directly.

Core already asks the running machine in most places. Core/Sys/Sys.jet:897 and Core/Ui/Host.jet:205 pick PathPlatform from core.files.__path_windows(). Core/Files/Files.jet:1105-1109 list_dir calls the runtime's __list_dir_raw, which can only read the disk it runs on.

The one outlier: Core/Service/Service.jet:1455-1465 StatePathPlatform.windows() folds $build.os. In a Linux-to-Windows cross build, a Service state path computed during build code would use Windows rules on the Linux disk.

CARD

Tower card c0rc40yf (Host facts for prep and build-time code) asks for host OS and architecture facts beside $build. It also asks for one stated rule for per-OS Core calls during preparation. Host reads must enter the cache key, and a policy must be able to reject them.

Related rulings: D-BUILD-FACT3=A puts build facts under $build. D-JAI-CONFIG1=A records every host read in the build record and cache key. D-HOST-CAPS1=A says target hardware facts follow the selected target, never the build machine.

HOW A'S DOWNSIDES ARE DESIGNED AWAY

1. A Core call in build code answers for the build machine. Nothing that ships depends on that answer. Shipped names and paths come from b.add_executable, b.add_install and b.action outputs, which apply $build.os rules themselves. Build code that prints or branches on a target fact reads $build.os.

2. Builds reading the build machine. Every option has this, because build actions run on the build machine under all three. A records each $build.host read and host-touching Core call in the build record and cache key (D-JAI-CONFIG1=A). Equal inputs give equal outputs, and a package policy can deny host reads with a registered diagnostic.

No loss remains. Any output call that lacks a target rule today gains one as work owed under A.

WORK OWED UNDER A

Add $build.host.os and $build.host.arch to FactReads.jet and the syntax registry. Change Service.jet:1459 to ask the running machine, like Sys.jet:897. Add a cross-build golden example that prints both facts.

WHY NOT B OR C

B makes build code describe a machine it is not running on. A file listing cannot read the target's disk, so B must ban direct file and process calls in build code. Every read then becomes a declared action. C makes common calls in every cross build carry a side argument, which is noise when only one answer is possible.

options.name: Core calls act on the machine running them
options.detail: A Core call in build code acts on the build machine, the only one it can touch. $build.os always names the target. Build code reads the build machine through $build.host.os and $build.host.arch, and each read goes into the cache key. Everything that ships goes through Build calls such as b.add_executable and b.add_install, which apply the target's rules themselves.
options.technical: Add $build.host.os and $build.host.arch fact reads. Core per-OS code asks the running machine, as Sys.jet:897 already does; Service.jet:1459 moves to that form. Host reads join the build record, and a package policy can deny them. Build outputs (b.add_executable, b.add_install and b.action outputs) take target-relative paths and apply $build.os rules, such as the .exe suffix, with no host call.

options.name: Everything in build code answers for the target
options.detail: Pure Core calls in build code answer as the target would. Because build code cannot touch the target's disk, direct file and process calls in build code are refused, and each such step becomes a declared action.
options.technical: Build code loses the FS and Exec effects. Reads move to b.action steps, which run on the build machine. No host fact is added.

options.name: Refuse calls that do not name a side
options.detail: In a cross build, a per-OS Core call in build code is a compile error unless it names the machine it means.
options.technical: The checker rejects per-OS Core calls in build code under cross-compilation unless a .Host or .Target argument is given. Adds a side argument to those Core calls.

comparisons.note: In build.rs, cfg!(target_os) describes the build machine. The target comes from CARGO_CFG_TARGET_OS. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html
build.zig runs on the build machine. b.graph.host names it, and the target is chosen separately. Source: https://ziglang.org/learn/build-system/
comparisons.code:
const target = b.standardTargetOptions(.{});
const host = b.graph.host;

recommendation.why: A states one rule: a call acts on the machine running it. It is the only answer a file read can give. $build keeps one meaning, the target, and $build.host names the build machine.
gains: Build code reads its own disk with the right path rules.
$build.os means the target everywhere.
Host reads are recorded, so the cache stays correct.
Shipped files get the target's names and paths from the Build API.

whyNot.reason: B makes build code describe a machine it cannot touch, so every file read must become a declared action.
C adds a side argument to common calls in every cross build, though only one answer is possible.

recommendation.tradeoff: A acts on the running machine, and the Build API applies the target's rules to everything that ships.

const host = b.graph.host;

decisions.title: What the error says when a function can't be a C callback
decisions.situation: Jet lets you pass a function to a C library as a callback, but only a plain one. It must not capture locals, allocate, have effects, be generic, panic or schedule tasks. When a passed function breaks one of these rules, Jet points at the function correctly. The message is wrong, though: it says the callback type is not C-compatible, when the type is fine and the function is at fault. We recommend a dedicated error that names the broken rule.
decisions.gist: When a passed function can't be a C callback, which error should Jet give?
decisions.lesson: A callback type can be fine while the function you pass breaks a callback rule, for example by capturing a local. Those are two different mistakes. The error should name the one you made and the rule it broke, so the fix is obvious.

decisions.title: Report every error by default
decisions.gist: Should check, build, run and test report every error they find, or stop at the first failing phase?
decisions.lesson: A compile can stop after the first phase that finds an error, so users fix errors one round at a time. A full report shows all of them at once. Run naively, later phases would also report errors caused by earlier ones; the recommended design hides those.
decisions.story: Ana runs jet build on a project with a type error in one file and a bad import in another. Under option A she sees both errors in one run and no output file is written. Under option B she sees the type error, fixes it, and only then learns about the import.

decisions.detail:
Owner ruling, 2026-10-09 (card #4914): every phase runs by default for check, build, run and test, with typed traps. No artifact is written when an error occurs. One canonical option is both a CLI flag and a build config setting.

Today the pipeline stops between phases at JetDriver Pipeline.jet:2220 and BodyComptime.jet:221. The full mode exists only behind the compiler-internal JET_KEEP_GOING=1 (Compiler/Bootstrap/Host/Entry.jet:10-128). The card plan keeps JET_KEEP_GOING_SKIP as a developer tool if needed.

No ratified decision found by keyword scan records this default.

Redesign 2026-11-01 (owner: engineer the downsides away). The first version kept two losses: follow-on noise and a longer run. Both are designed away. A failed item is marked failed, and every later phase skips that item and anything whose meaning depends on it. A check that meets a failed type or name stays silent, as rustc does with its error type. So every printed error is a root error, and a later phase does less work, not more.

Follow-on errors are still recorded. The text summary counts them, and --json lists each one with the root it came from. This also settles the owner question about follow-on UI rows: they leave the default output.

Suppressed diagnostics are kept with a caused_by link for --json. The developer-only JET_KEEP_GOING=1 switch is replaced by the canonical option.

decisions.title: How the compiler and Jetpack reach Core operations that user programs must not call
decisions.situation:
Jetpack and the compiler need five Core operations that user programs must never call. Two exist today as `files.compiler_with_process_directory` and `files.compiler_link_held`. They are ordinary public functions, and a user program can call them: we checked one with the tree14 compiler and it passed. The other three are blocked because no rule lets the toolchain reach a private Core module.

We recommend one more qualifier in the existing `priv(…)` family, `priv(toolchain) module`. Only Core, the compiler and Jetpack may use such a module. User programs get E0605, as for any private module.
decisions.gist: Should Core operations meant only for the compiler and Jetpack live in a `priv(toolchain) module`, become public documented functions, or be reached through foreign-call glue?
decisions.lesson: Jet marks privacy on modules, not on functions. A `priv module` is usable only by its enclosing module, and a `priv(package) module` by its own package. Neither lets the compiler or Jetpack, which are separate packages, reach a private part of Core.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. The toolchain is the set of packages the Jet distribution ships: Core, the compiler packages and Jetpack, the package manager. A seam is a Core operation that only the toolchain needs, such as running a child process inside a folder that Jetpack already holds open.

A held folder is a `Directory` value that keeps the folder open. Work done through it cannot be redirected by renaming the folder's path.
decisions.story: Omar's app imports `core.files` and sees `compiler_link_held` in completion. He calls it inside an `#Unsafe` block, and the compiler accepts it, because the function is public. Next release the store changes the function's errno rules and his app breaks. Under A the function lives in `core.files.toolchain`, completion never offers it, and his call is E0605 from the start.
decisions.detail:
Source: card #4896 and its four added cases. Five seams need the same answer.

1. Run a child process inside a held folder. Jetpack's TreeHash.jet:562 calls `files.compiler_with_process_directory`.
2. Link an open file into a held folder. Jetpack's TreeHash.jet:738 calls `files.compiler_link_held`.
3. Pass a held lock to a child process, so a child keeps the same lock. Core has no such operation yet.
4. Lower the compiler's `sort_by` to one private Core kernel, so every tier shares one meaning.
5. Let the compiler's build-receipt producer read Core/build's private session.

Today. The double-underscore names were renamed to legal `compiler_` names, so the CLI source parses. But Sema has no caller check on Core calls (Sema core_call, traced by CoreReview5-2-2). A user file calling `files.compiler_with_process_directory` inside `#Unsafe` passes `jet check` on the tree14 compiler (probe ballot/xb/seam.jet). Seams 3 to 5 cannot be written, because a private module refuses every outside package.

The visibility law. Declarations carry no visibility marker; `priv` marks a module or a field. `priv(package) module` is the one qualified form, and any other qualifier is E0414 (syntax-decisions S18). The draft's `toolchain fn` mark broke that law, so A now uses a module qualifier instead.

What A adds. `priv(toolchain) module` is accepted only in a toolchain package; elsewhere it stays E0414. A use from any other package is E0605, the error every private module already gives. A package counts as toolchain when its source root lies inside the Jet distribution that supplied Core. Package names play no part, so a user package cannot claim the status.

Compiler-generated calls. When the compiler lowers `list.sort_by(f)` in a user program to the Core kernel, the call is the compiler's, so it passes. A call written in the user's source still gets E0605.

Safety. Seams 1 and 2 become typed functions that return `IOError`, with no raw errno tuple and no `#Unsafe` marker. Seam 1 has the same body as the public `Directory.pass_to`, which needs no gate. The `#Unsafe` blocks at Jetpack's two call sites go away.

A side question in the draft, whether diagnostics can read text without copying it, is not a privacy question. Borrowed text is ordinary public Jet, so it needs no seam.

options.name: One `priv(toolchain) module` in Core for all five seams
options.detail:
Core gathers the seams into private modules marked `priv(toolchain)`, such as `core.files.toolchain`. Core, the compiler and Jetpack may use them. Any other package gets E0605, and completion and the reference never list them.

The qualifier joins the existing `priv(…)` family and is accepted only inside a toolchain package. User code can never write it. Calls the compiler generates, such as the `sort_by` kernel, pass. The seams take typed arguments and return `IOError`, so their callers need no `#Unsafe` block.
options.technical:
Parser: `priv(toolchain)` is accepted before `module` when the file's package is a toolchain package, else E0414 as today. Sema: the E0605 check in Calls/Core.jet:354 and Expressions/Places.jet:790 admits a toolchain-private module in two cases. The caller's package root lies inside the distribution root that supplied Core, or the call is compiler-generated.

Core: move the two `compiler_` functions into `priv(toolchain) module toolchain` in Core/Files as `run_in` and `link_into`. Add `pass_lock`, the sort kernel and the build-session readers to toolchain modules beside their owners. Jetpack drops both `#Unsafe` blocks. Syntax-decisions S18 gains one line.

options.name: Make each seam a public, documented Core function
options.detail:
Each seam becomes a public function with documentation, such as `spec.run_in(folder)`, `reader.link_into(folder, name)` and `lock.pass_to(spec, at)`. The sort kernel and the build-session readers become public too.

Anyone may call them, and each becomes a promise Core must keep stable across releases.
options.technical: Rename the two `compiler_` functions to public methods and remove the `#Unsafe` markers. Add `AdvisoryLock.pass_to`. Export the sort kernel from core.collections and the build-session readers from core.build, which turns a read-only query surface into one with mutable session state.

options.name: Reach the runtime directly through foreign-call glue
options.detail:
Jetpack declares the runtime symbols itself with `#Import(c)` and calls them, as C code would. Core adds nothing.

Seams 4 and 5 are Jet functions, not runtime symbols, so glue cannot reach them and they stay blocked.
options.technical: Jetpack adds `#Import(c)` declarations for `jet_process_spec_with_directory_raw` and `jet_files_link_reader_at_raw`, and keeps their argument layouts in step with the runtime by hand. The Core checks in `process_directory` (slot range, closed folder, slot taken) are skipped.

comparisons.note: A module may export a package only to named modules. java.base exports `jdk.internal.misc` to a fixed list of JDK modules, and other code cannot use it. Source: JLS 7.7.2, qualified exports.

A package under `internal/` can be imported only by code rooted at its parent. Since Go 1.23 the linker also refuses new `go:linkname` pulls into the standard library. Source: go.dev/doc/go1.23, Linker.
comparisons.code: import "internal/poll"   // only the standard library may

comparisons.note: The standard library marks internal items unstable with no tracking issue, so stable user code cannot call them. The compiler's own crates opt in with `rustc_private`. Source: rustc-dev-guide, Stability attributes.

recommendation.why: A protects all five operations with the privacy rule Jet already has: one module qualifier and the existing E0605. User programs can no longer reach compiler-only operations, and the three blocked ones can be written.
gains: User programs cannot call compiler-only operations.
One rule for all five operations, with no new declaration marker.
Jetpack's two `#Unsafe` blocks go away.

losses.loss: A third-party package manager cannot use the operations Jetpack uses.
losses.mitigation: An operation useful to everyone moves out of the toolchain module into a public typed API, as `Directory.pass_to` did.

whyNot.reason: Every compiler-only operation becomes a public promise, and the build session gains public mutable state.
Glue skips Core's checks, any user can write it too, and two of the five seams stay blocked.

recommendation.tradeoff: One more `priv(…)` qualifier that only toolchain packages may write. In return, compiler-only operations are closed to user programs and all five seams have a home.

decisions.title: Games and apps share two independent subsystems: ray for visuals and input, audio for sound
decisions.situation: A Doom-style game must show its own pixel buffer, play raw sound samples and read every key press. Jet's game library cannot do these yet. You ruled that Jet talks to the display and sound system itself, with no C library. You also asked that games and desktop apps share one visual subsystem, our raylib, and one audio subsystem, our miniaudio. They should be independent parts, not one big platform. The web stays different. We recommend exactly that: ray and audio, each usable alone and together.
decisions.gist: Should games and apps share two independent subsystems, ray for visuals and audio for sound?
decisions.lesson: A subsystem is a library that owns one kind of hardware. ray owns windows, drawing and the keys and mouse of each window. audio owns speakers and sound mixing. Each works alone, and a program can open several of each. Games, apps and music players combine only the parts they need.
decisions.story: Ana ports a small Doom-style game. Every frame she draws 320 by 200 pixels with a 256-colour palette, queues a footstep sound and reads the arrow keys. Her friend writes a notes app with two windows, and another writes a music player with no window. All three want the same libraries, and tests that check pixels and sound without a screen.
decisions.inWild:
SDL: separate subsystems for video, audio and events, each started on its own with SDL_InitSubSystem. Source: https://wiki.libsdl.org/SDL3/SDL_InitSubSystem

raylib and miniaudio: raylib draws windows and reads input; its sound module is built on miniaudio, which can also be used alone. Source: https://miniaud.io/docs/manual/
decisions.detail:
WHAT CHANGED FROM THE LAST DRAFT

The last draft put window, sound and input into one game.Platform value. You asked for independent, modular systems shared with the app framework, with the web kept apart. Now ray is the visual subsystem and audio is the sound subsystem. Each stands alone; core.game and gui only combine them.

TODAY

Core/Game/Game.jet is a 19-line shell for scenes, input bindings and replays. Core/Game/Raylib.jet (2385 lines, core.game.raylib) opens a window, draws shapes and plays sound files. It cannot show a caller's own pixel buffer, queue raw sound samples, or hand over every input event.

Core/Ui holds app pieces such as dialogs, clipboard and drag and drop, but no window or drawing of its own.

RULINGS IT BUILDS ON

- D-RAYLIB-DRIVER-LOAD1=A: Jet speaks the display and sound protocols itself, and programs stay single static files. GPU drawing is a later opt-in.
- D-RAYLIB-FONT-HOME1=A: ray is Jet's own game library and font its font engine, used by ray and gui. raylib, the binding to C raylib, stays separate.
- D-RAY-API1=A: ray keeps raylib's names but draws through explicit window and frame values, so no state is global.

- Card c0776o2m: the Doom port is as much Jet as possible. The operating-system edge (Wayland or X11, ALSA or PipeWire) stays inside vetted #Unsafe Core code. Acceptance: a window shows a 320x200 indexed buffer at 35 Hz, plays a tone and logs key events on Linux. Headless checksums for pixels and sound match on every build level.

SHAPE UNDER A

ray, the visual subsystem. ray.open(width, height, title) opens a window, and a program may open several. win.frames(fps) yields one frame at a time. frame.events() lists that window's key, mouse and resize events in arrival order.

Each frame offers two levels of control. frame.present(pixels, palette) or frame.present(rgba) shows your own buffer. raylib-style calls such as frame.draw_rect draw for you. ray.gamepads() lists connected controllers, which belong to no window.

audio, the sound subsystem. audio.open(rate) opens an output device, and a program may open several. out.queue(samples) plays raw 16-bit sound at 11025 to 48000 Hz. audio.mixer(out) adds the miniaudio-style level: load sounds, play voices, set volume, and group voices into buses.

Composition. core.game keeps scenes, input bindings and replays. game.run(scene) opens a window and an audio device for you, or takes ones you opened. gui builds its widgets on ray windows and frames, with font for text. Neither holds device code of its own.

Tests. ray.headless(width, height) and audio.headless(rate) return the same types with no device. They record each frame and each block of sound as checksums for golden tests. Their events come from a script or a replay.

Web. core.web stays separate, as you said. Whether ray can also draw on a browser canvas is a later ballot.

HOW A'S DOWNSIDES ARE DESIGNED AWAY

1. Keeping picture and sound in step. They need no shared clock. The screen shows each frame when it is ready. The speakers play from a buffer at their own steady rate. out.queued() says how much sound is waiting, so a game keeps a few frames ahead; game.run does this for you.

2. More to open than one value. A game that uses game.run opens nothing itself. A program that opens its own parts writes one line per part, and only for parts it uses.

3. Tests need two fakes. Each headless call is one line, and game.run takes both, as the example shows.

4. Two ways to draw. present and the raylib-style calls draw into the same frame. A game may mix them, for example a pixel buffer under drawn text.

No loss remains.

EDGE CASES

- Closing one of several windows ends only its frame loop. Its events stop and its frames end.
- No audio device: audio.open returns a typed error, and game.run continues silent with a warning.
- A sound queue that runs dry plays silence and counts the gap, which the headless report shows.

- Two programs, or two outputs in one program, may share one device; the sound system mixes them.
- Keys are read per window, so the focused window gets them. A key press with no focused window reaches nobody.

AFTER A LANDS

core.game.raylib moves into ray, and its sound calls move into audio. The old module is deleted, and every example moves to the new names in the same change.

WHY NOT B OR C

B also splits input from ray. But keys and mouse belong to the focused window, so input has to point back at a window anyway, and a key would be asked about in two places. C keeps one platform value with window, sound and input. An app or music player then takes parts it does not want, and a program cannot have two windows or keep sound running when a window closes.

decisions.title: What an HTTP body value is once the Rust code is gone
decisions.situation: When a Jet program downloads something, the data arrives as an HTTP body. Jet's reader for that body was written in Rust, and that code is now deleted. Jet's own Body is a plain value that cannot hold a download still arriving, so Jet's package manager cannot download anything yet. The vote decides what a body is; we recommend a file-like reader, which keeps the large-download streaming you already approved.
decisions.gist: When a program receives an HTTP body, should it get a file-like reader, or a plain value?
decisions.lesson: A body is the data inside a web request or response, such as a downloaded file. Jet's body() reader used to live in deleted Rust code. Jet's own Body today is a plain value with three cases: empty, text or bytes. A plain value cannot hold a download that is still arriving. Whichever option wins, Jet's HTTP client must then be written in Jet.
decisions.story: Mia's build script downloads a 300 MiB package archive with Jet. She wants it streamed to disk under a size cap, not loaded into memory, and she wants the same body methods on her small server.
decisions.inWild:
resp, err := http.Get(url)
defer resp.Body.Close()
data, err := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 1<<20))
// https://pkg.go.dev/net/http#Response
decisions.detail: Code: Core/http/http.jet:87 defines the Body enum with Empty, Text(String), and Bytes([U8]). A shared, one-shot native body cannot be held there. Option A makes Body opaque with a private shared carrier and constructors and inspection methods. Option B adds a hidden fourth case. Option C reads the whole body on access, which conflicts with the ratified streaming cap. The public carrier for the native body is decided in a separate card, which this ballot depends on.

options.name: A file-like Body
options.detail: Body becomes a closed Core type with private fields. Programs build one with Body.empty(), Body.text(s) or Body.bytes(b). They read one with text(limit), bytes(limit), json(limit), chunks() and copy_to(^writer), each a single pass. The size cap you approved in D-CORE-HTTPBODYLIMIT1 applies to every read. Client and server use the same type.
options.technical: Core/Http/Http.jet: Body becomes a struct with a private shared one-pass reader state (the connection, the remaining framing, a consumed flag) or an in-memory payload. body_as_text and body_as_bytes, the only matches on the cases today, move to the read methods. Calls/Http.jet keeps the same method names and results. No example matches on the cases.
options.code:
text :: resp.body().text(1024 * 1024) ?? panic("body")
resp.body(limit: 2.gib).copy_to(^file)
reply :: Body.text("ok")

options.name: Hidden fourth case
options.detail: Body keeps its Empty, Text and Bytes cases and gains a private Stream case that programs cannot name. Every match on Body then needs an else arm, which runs for streamed bodies.
options.technical: The enum gains a private variant carrying the shared reader state. The checker would need a new rule for a variant that is hidden from user matches.

options.name: Read it all on arrival
options.detail: The client reads the whole body into memory before it returns the response, so Body stays a finished three-case value. Streaming large downloads to disk is no longer possible.
options.technical: send() reads to the end of the framing and stores Body.Bytes. This contradicts D-CORE-HTTPBODYLIMIT1, which ratified a one-pass streamed body with its own cap.
options.code:
resp :: http.get(url) ?? panic("get")
text :: http.body_as_text(resp.body())

comparisons.note: net/http gives Response.Body as an io.ReadCloser that the program reads once: https://pkg.go.dev/net/http#Response.
reqwest reads the body through methods on the response (bytes, text, chunk), not through an enum: https://docs.rs/reqwest/latest/reqwest/struct.Response.html.

recommendation.why: Only a reader can stream a large download under a cap, and Go and Rust clients make the same choice.
gains: Keeps the approved streaming rule and one meaning for Body.

losses.loss: Code can no longer match on .Text or .Bytes cases.
losses.mitigation: Only Core's own helpers do this today, and they move to the read methods.

whyNot.reason: B makes every match carry an else arm that quietly mishandles streams.
C breaks the streaming you already approved and can exhaust memory on big downloads.

recommendation.tradeoff: Body loses pattern matching; reading it uses the same methods everywhere.

decisions.title: How each linked part is spelled, defaulted and reported
decisions.situation: Native Jet programs are fully static today. The GPU driver must load from the user's system, and a static process cannot load it. Each linked part needs its own linkage, because tools and graphics programs differ. We recommend per-part settings in the build function, with defaults that need no annotation in most programs. Tools stay one file.
decisions.gist: How should a program choose static or dynamic linking for each part it uses?
decisions.lesson: A program often mixes parts that must stay static with parts the system must load. One setting per program cannot serve both.
decisions.story: Eli builds a small command-line tool and a game. The tool should stay one file. The game must load the system's graphics driver at run time.
decisions.inWild: go build ./game   // static unless cgo uses a system library
decisions.detail:
Source: card #5088 log, 2026-10-21 owner amendment. Linkage is decided per linked item: Jet runtime and libc, system libraries such as libGL, bundled C libraries, and foreign closures. Defaults: pure Jet and bundled C static; OS driver and system libraries dynamic. CLI --linkage stays a whole-program override. Still open: exact spelling, the full defaults table, and per-item reporting in jet inspect. Ratified D-JPK-VARIANT1 (D) sets the axes.

Redesign 2026-11-01 (owner: engineer the downsides away). The first version listed testing two linkage modes as a loss of A. It is shared work: any design where a graphics program runs needs dynamic loading, and any design where a tool stays one file needs static linking. B and C carry the same test work, so it is not a reason to choose between them.

The test matrix is generated from one list of cells, each run in its required mode. jet inspect shows each part with its linkage and why, so a wrong default is visible at once. A program that names no dynamic part stays one static file, exactly as today.

options.name: Per-part settings in the build function
options.detail: Each linked part has its own linkage. Defaults: pure Jet and bundled C static; OS driver and system libraries dynamic. The build function changes any part. jet inspect lists each part with its linkage and its source.
options.technical: The build function returns a per-item linkage map; the linker resolves each item separately and rejects impossible combinations as diagnostics.

options.name: One setting for the whole program
options.detail: The build command or manifest picks one linkage for everything.
options.technical: One linkage value passes to the linker; no per-item map.
options.code: jet build --linkage=dynamic game.jet

options.name: Separate link file
options.detail: Linked parts are listed in a linking file beside the package.
options.technical: A second input file is parsed and checked against the package's imports.
options.code: link.jet: gpu = dynamic

comparisons.note: Go builds static binaries and links dynamically only when a system library is needed.

recommendation.why: Each part gets the linkage its platform needs, from a default table, so most programs write nothing. Tools stay one static file and graphics programs load the system GPU driver.
gains: Static tools stay single-file.
Graphics programs work out of the box.
jet inspect shows each part’s linkage and its reason.

whyNot.reason: One setting cannot keep tools static and graphics programs working.
A second file adds a place to forget a setting.

recommendation.tradeoff: None remaining: testing both modes is shared work every option needs.
