decisions.title: The language server runs on the one compiler session
decisions.situation: The language server answers your editor: errors as you type, hover text, go to definition. It used to live in the Rust host and checked code on its own path, so the editor could disagree with jet check. On 2026-10-17 you ruled that it is ported one-for-one to Jet and runs on the one compiler session that jet check and jet build use. The port now lives in the compiler tree, and the Rust server is gone. This records your ruling.
decisions.gist: Should the language server be ported to Jet and run on the one compiler session, or stay in the Rust command-line host?
decisions.lesson: A language server is the program an editor talks to for errors, hovers and jumps. If it checks code its own way, the editor and the command line can disagree. Running it on the same compiler session as jet check keeps their answers identical.
decisions.story: Chen edits a file in VS Code. The server is part of Jet and reads the same session as jet check, so the red underline in the editor is exactly the error jet check prints.
decisions.inWild:
Go: gopls is the language server, built on the same analysis packages the go tool uses. Source: https://go.dev/gopls/

Rust: rust-analyzer is the language server, built on the compiler's front-end crates. Source: https://rust-analyzer.github.io/
decisions.detail:
OWNER RULING

Owner ruling, 2026-10-17, recorded in the card #3410 log. It reads: “the LSP is 1:1 Rust-to-Jet parity work and is ported onto the one compiler session (D-LSP1=C)”. It adds: “the plan line keeping the LSP in the Rust host is superseded.” This ballot records it for one-click confirmation. The alternative is kept for the record.

D-LSP1 is not present in decisions.json; its ruling exists only in the card log. The same log records two amendments. D-INCR-PARK1=C (2026-10-17) keeps one compiler service, and editor answers recheck the whole package per edit, with no item-level reuse. D-SESSION-MCP1=A removes the port’s MCP methods and initialize fields, so the LSP speaks only LSP.

Related ratified decisions, all 2026-10-17: D-SESSION-WIRE1=A (NDJSON jet.session.v1), D-SESSION-ENTRY1=C (--listen=- on check, build, test, run and dev) and D-SESSION-OWNER1=A (jet dev --serve and jet self lsp --serve). D-LSP-BUILDSAVE1 is still open on this card.

TODAY

The port lives in Compiler/JetLSP, with 36 source files and 68 test files. The Rust server under Source/LSP is gone from the tree. positionEncoding negotiation is not yet in Compiler/JetLSP/Source, and the LSP 3.18 applicability inventory is still owed. The card is blocked on #3196.

HOW A'S DOWNSIDES ARE DESIGNED AWAY

Parity work is not a cost of A. The Rust server is gone under every option, so any working editor support needs the Jet port to reach parity. A makes parity checkable: the LSP 3.18 inventory lists each item, and positionEncoding is one of them. No loss remains.

options.code: $ jet lsp              # Rust server; separate check path

rust-analyzer runs on the compiler's front-end crates. Source: https://rust-analyzer.github.io/

One session to maintain.

recommendation.tradeoff: A finishes the port, and the editor and the command line share one checker.

decisions.title: Nixpkgs packages come in as native Jet packages, with no Nix
decisions.gist: Should Nixpkgs packages be translated into native Jet packages stored only in Hangar, with no Nix program or store at all?
decisions.lesson: Jetpack can use Nixpkgs packages, but today it can call an installed Nix as a fallback. Jetpack can instead read each Nixpkgs recipe itself and run its build steps inside Hangar, so every package installs with no Nix at all.
decisions.story: Ravi installs a tool that exists only in Nixpkgs. Under option A Jetpack translates its recipe into a native Jet package, and the install needs no Nix on his machine. Under option B Jetpack calls his installed Nix when the translation is missing, so the install depends on a Nix he never chose.
decisions.inWild:
Guix: a package manager with its own store and recipes, separate from Nix. Source: https://guix.gnu.org/manual/en/html_node/Invoking-guix-package.html

Nix: packages are built into /nix/store by the Nix daemon. Source: https://nixos.org/manual/nix/stable/
decisions.detail:
Owner requirement, 2026-09-13 (card #3402): ingest Nixpkgs through an adapter that translates definitions into the native Jet package model. Jetpack owns resolution, builds, installation, updates and removal. Hangar is the only store. No separately installed or bundled Nix package manager, daemon, profile or store is permitted, including hidden or mounted stores. Native Jet packages bypass the adapter. Jet and Jetpack code is MIT; the adapter must not depend on Nix executables, libraries, daemons, services or storage.

The card records that D-NIX-UPSTREAM1 was superseded unratified, so this requirement is not a ratified decision.

Conflict: ratified D-JPK-SNIXREUSE1 (2026-08-25, option A) keeps a local Nix import on a miss, and D-JPK-NIXSTORE1 (2026-07-10, option D) uses a projected Nix store. Both predate the 2026-09-13 requirement and conflict with it. The card's current state: crates/jetpack/src/NixFallbackPolicy.rs and Jetpack/Nix/Source/Fallback/FallbackPolicy.jet still call nix build.

Redesign 2026-11-01 (owner: engineer the downsides away). The first version translated packages one by one, so an untranslated package failed until someone converted it. Now Jetpack translates at the level every package shares. NixEval, Jet’s own Nix-language evaluator, reads the recipe and yields its build plan: sources, dependencies, build script and environment.

Jetpack then fetches the sources by hash and runs that plan in its own sandbox, storing the result in Hangar under Jet’s own paths. That is generic, so any package Nixpkgs can build installs without per-package work, and no Nix program, daemon or store is used.

What can still fail is a recipe that uses a Nix language feature NixEval lacks. That failure names the feature, and one evaluator fix unblocks every package using it.

options.name: Build Nixpkgs recipes natively in Hangar
options.detail: Jetpack reads each Nixpkgs recipe with its own evaluator, fetches the sources by hash, and runs the recipe’s build steps in its sandbox. Hangar stores the result. The installed-Nix fallback is deleted. Native Jet packages skip this path.
options.technical: Delete the fallback files and the JETPACK_NIX_FALLBACK_POLICY variables. NixEval evaluates the attribute to its build plan; the realizer fetches fixed-output sources, runs the builder with the recorded environment in the Hangar sandbox, and rewrites output paths to Hangar paths. Upstream provenance is kept so updates re-evaluate. Unsupported evaluator features become named, tracked diagnostics.
options.code: $ jetpack install ripgrep-nix   # translated; stored in Hangar; no nix on PATH

options.name: Keep an installed-Nix fallback

decisions.title: The optimizer report reads the slot IR optimizer
decisions.situation: The optimization report, jet inspect decisions, tells you what the optimizer did to your program and why it declined some steps. It was first written for the compiler’s old middle layers, which are now deleted. On 2026-10-22 you ruled that the report reads the new IR optimizer’s own records, with no translation layer from the old format. Module totals and declined-loop notes already come from it. This records your ruling.
decisions.gist: When the old middle layers are deleted, should the optimization report describe what the slot IR optimizer did, or be dropped?
decisions.lesson: An optimization report tells you which speed-ups the compiler applied and why it skipped others. It must read the optimizer that actually runs, or it describes code that no longer exists.
decisions.story: Dev wonders why a sum loop stayed scalar. jet inspect decisions prints the loop note from the IR optimizer, with the reason the vectorizing step declined.
decisions.inWild:

Go: the -m flag prints inlining and escape decisions. Source: https://go.dev/wiki/CompilerOptimizations
decisions.detail:
OWNER RULING

Owner ruling, 2026-10-22, architecture cutover card log, quoted: “The optimizer ledger (jet inspect optimization, live report) is retargeted to the IR optimizer report, no shim.” This ballot records it for one-click confirmation. The alternative is kept for the record.

The same ruling ports the web emitter onto the slot IR and drops the old Rust-source emitter. Those parts are covered by the ratified one-IR architecture and the Rust removal scope ballot.

TODAY

The command is jet inspect decisions (Compiler/JetCli/Source/Cli/Inspect.jet:198). It prints the IR optimizer’s report for the checked program at the level jet build uses (InspectDecisions.jet:1-7).

The report is IROptReport (Compiler/JetIR/Source/Opt.jet:123-163). It holds module totals per pass: inlined calls, folds, fused compares, removed dead code and more. It also has one note per loop reduction or stepped index, vectorized or declined with the reason (OptReduce.jet:222-229, OptVersion.jet:194-197). Nothing translates old middle-layer records.

OWED UNDER A

Per-function outcomes for every pass, not only loop notes, so a user can ask about one function.

HOW A'S DOWNSIDES ARE DESIGNED AWAY

1. Recording cost. Per-function notes are recorded only when jet inspect decisions asks for them. A normal jet build passes no recorder, so it does no extra work and its output bytes are unchanged.

2. Per-function outcomes are owed work, not a cost to users. Each pass already decides per function; the note records that decision with its reason, as loop notes do today.

No loss remains.

The old ledger code went with the old layers. Per-function notes are recorded only when jet inspect decisions asks; a normal build passes no recorder and pays nothing.

decisions.title: How a public Core type holds a native value that user code can neither name nor build
decisions.situation:
The ratified HTTP law wants one public `Body` type over a private native stream that reads the body lazily. Today `Body` is a plain enum that holds every byte in memory, so `chunks()` on a large download first buffers the whole body. The stream needs a native value that only Core may create, and Jet has no checked way to hide one.

We recommend that the native value's type live in a `priv module` inside core.http, and that `Body` hold it in a `priv` field. Both forms already exist in the visibility law. The checker then refuses any user code that names the type or builds a `Body` by hand.
decisions.gist: How should Core's `Body` hold a native stream that user code must never name or build?
decisions.lesson: Some Core values wrap a native resource, such as an open socket stream. If user code could build one with any contents, it could read from a resource it never opened. Jet already has `priv` modules and `priv` fields, which keep names and contents inside one module.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A facade is the public type users hold, here `Body`. A carrier is the native value inside it, here the stream that pulls the body's bytes from the connection. Forging means building a value by hand, with a struct literal, instead of getting it from the library.

A `priv module` is usable only by its enclosing module. A `priv` field can be read and written only by code in its type's own module.
decisions.story: Ines downloads a 2 GB file and reads it with `chunks()`. Today her program first holds all 2 GB in memory, because `Body` is a buffered enum. Under A the chunks arrive from the network one at a time. Her test builds a fake body with `http.body_text("…")`, and a typo that builds `Body{…}` by hand is a clear compile error.
decisions.detail:
Source: card #4903, which blocks the HTTP Body cutover and six HTTP goldens. The ratified HTTP law wants one public, source-owned `Body` over a private, lazy native transport.

Today. Core/Http/Http.jet:89 declares `enum Body { Empty, Text(String), Bytes([U8]) }`. `chunks()` (line 216) copies the whole body into a byte list first, so a large download is held in memory. A shared cell gives read-once behavior.

The forging gap, measured on the tree14 compiler (probes ballot/xb/carrier.jet and carrier2.jet). A user program that builds `files.Directory{path: "x", handle: 3}`, `files.FileWriter{path: "x"}` or a struct literal that sets another module's `priv` field passes `jet check`. Reading that `priv` field from another module also passes, and `jet run` prints it. The ui row import_private_field, which expects E0605, fails for the same reason.

So the draft's premise, a public carrier "with no public constructor", is not enforced for any Core carrier today.

The law already has the parts. Syntax-decisions S18 says a `priv` field is readable and writable only by its type's module. It says a `priv module` is usable only by its enclosing module. A only needs these enforced on struct literals and field reads, and the native-carrier registry to accept a carrier declared in a `priv module`.

What the registry holds. FileWriter is a known native carrier whose rows give its clone and drop behavior (core_types). The card notes that these rows are accepted only for public carriers today. A lifts that restriction: the carrier row names its module, and Sema applies ordinary privacy. No new attribute and no new IR kind are needed; the card's joint Core and native review found `Type.Named` sufficient.

Test bodies. User tests still build bodies with the public `http.body_text`, `body_bytes` and `body_empty` (Http.jet:734-741). These return a `Body` whose carrier is an in-memory stream.

Same rule for existing carriers. `Directory.handle` and `AdvisoryLock.handle` become `priv` fields, which closes the measured forging of a folder handle.

options.name: Carrier type in a `priv module`, held in a `priv` field
options.detail:
Core declares the native stream type inside a `priv module` of core.http, and `Body` becomes a struct that holds it in a `priv` field. User code cannot name the stream type and cannot build a `Body` by hand; both give E0605. Bodies come from responses, requests or the public `body_text`, `body_bytes` and `body_empty`.

The checker enforces the existing `priv` rules on struct literals and field reads, which also closes the forging of `Directory` and `FileWriter` measured today.
options.technical:
Sema: report E0605 when a struct literal or field read names a `priv` field outside its type's module. This is the rule S18 states, and it fixes the import_private_field ui row. Registry: a native carrier row may name a carrier declared in a `priv module`; its clone and drop entries match FileWriter's. A known native carrier's native part counts as a `priv` field, so `FileWriter{path: "x"}` outside Core is E0605 too.

Core/Http: `priv module transport { struct BodyStream }` over the runtime body kernel. `struct Body { priv stream: transport.BodyStream }`. `chunks()` pulls from the stream. Core/Files: `Directory.handle` and `AdvisoryLock.handle` become `priv`.

options.name: A new `#Carrier(native)` attribute checked for every wrapper
options.detail:
Core marks the facade with a new attribute that tells the checker it wraps a native value. The checker refuses literals of any marked type outside Core and tracks the native value's lifecycle.

The attribute is a second privacy spelling beside `priv`, and every carrier must adopt it.
options.technical: Add `#Carrier(native)` to the syntax tables, with a Sema rule refusing literals of marked types outside their module. Lifecycle rows key on the attribute rather than on the registry row. `Directory`, `FileWriter` and `AdvisoryLock` are re-marked.

options.name: Drop the facade; the native stream is the public `Body`
options.detail:
The native stream type itself becomes the public `Body`, registered as a known native type like FileWriter. There is no wrapper.

The type must stay literal-free by a special case in the registry, and its methods are native signatures rather than Jet source.
options.technical: Register `Body` as a known native carrier with native method signatures. The facade's Jet-source methods (`text`, `json`, `chunks`) move into the runtime. The forging gap on other carriers is untouched.

comparisons.note: A struct with a private field cannot be built outside its module, so `hyper::body::Incoming` comes only from the library. Source: Rust Reference, Visibility and privacy; hyper docs, body::Incoming.
comparisons.code: let b = Incoming { .. };   // error[E0451]: field is private

comparisons.note: `http.Response.Body` is an `io.ReadCloser` interface; the concrete type is unexported, so user code cannot build the library's body. Source: pkg.go.dev/net/http, Response.
comparisons.code: resp.Body.Read(buf)   // concrete body type is unexported

comparisons.note: `private` and `fileprivate` stored properties block memberwise initializers outside the file. Source: The Swift Programming Language, Access Control.
comparisons.code: struct Body { private let stream: Stream }

recommendation.why: A uses two forms the visibility law already has, a `priv module` and a `priv` field. User code cannot name or forge the stream, and the same rule closes the forging of Core's other carriers.
gains: Large bodies stream; memory stays at one chunk.
No new marker and no new public type.
Directory and FileWriter forging is closed too.

whyNot.reason: A second privacy spelling beside `priv`, which every carrier must adopt.
The body's methods move into the runtime, and a special case must refuse literals.

recommendation.tradeoff: The checker starts enforcing `priv` on struct literals and field reads, so Core code that relied on the gap must use the module's functions. In return no user code can forge a native value.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude. Adversarial model family: Claude. Fresh agent: UiGreen-1 adversarial self-review pass. It found that the draft's 'no public constructor' is not enforced: user code forges Directory, FileWriter and priv-field structs today. A now enforces the existing priv rules and hides the carrier in a priv module, so no public carrier name or new marker remains.

The probes ballot/xb/carrier.jet and carrier2.jet, which pass today, fail with E0605, and the ui row import_private_field passes. Reading a 2 GB body with `chunks(65536)` keeps peak memory near one chunk. `http.body_text("x").text(16)` returns "x" in a user test. The six blocked HTTP goldens pass.

decisions.title: Graphical Jet programs speak the display and sound protocols directly and stay static
decisions.situation: Jet programs are single static files with no dynamic loader. Opening a window today seems to need C driver libraries that a static program cannot load, so games run only headless. But a desktop's display server and sound server are reached over local sockets, and the kernel exposes gamepads as plain files. This vote decides how `ray` reaches the screen, input and sound. We recommend speaking those protocols in Jet, keeping games static, and making GPU drivers a later opt-in.
decisions.gist: Should graphical Jet programs talk to the display and sound servers directly and stay single static files?
decisions.lesson: A window on Linux is a conversation over a local socket with the display server, X11 or Wayland. The program draws pixels into shared memory and tells the server to show them. Sound works the same way with the sound server. Only GPU acceleration needs the vendor's driver library.
decisions.story: Sam builds his Jet game and copies one file to a friend's laptop. It opens a window, reads the gamepad and plays sound with nothing installed. Later he switches on GPU drawing, and that build uses the laptop's own graphics driver.
decisions.detail:
Today. Jet executables are static musl programs, and musl's static dlopen does nothing. The raylib leaves take a no-library path (Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/RouteAGame.jet:1-7), so `window_should_close` is always true natively. The old draft of this ballot recommended dynamic executables for all graphical programs, at the cost of the single-file deploy.

What A does for the screen. On Wayland, `ray` connects to the socket named by WAYLAND_DISPLAY and shares an RGBA buffer through a memfd. It opens the window with xdg-shell. On X11 it connects to the DISPLAY socket and presents with MIT-SHM, falling back to PutImage.

When a Wayland compositor offers no server-side title bar, as GNOME's does not, `ray` uses its X11 path through XWayland. A later stage can draw its own title bar instead.

Input. Keys and mouse arrive as display-server events. Key enums are physical key positions from the kernel key code, which both servers send. Typed-character input reads the XKB keymap the server hands over. Gamepads are read from /dev/input/event files, which logind grants to the seat user.

Sound. `ray` mixes in Jet and streams to the PulseAudio native socket. PipeWire serves that socket on current distros. With no sound server it writes to the kernel ALSA device through ioctl calls, as Android's tinyalsa does.

The operating-system doors. These need sockets with file-descriptor passing, memfd, mmap and ioctl. They sit in the Core platform module from card 5035 as audited calls, not as private runtime powers. Everything above them, including protocol encoding, is ordinary Jet.

GPU, a later stage. Mesa and NVIDIA drivers are glibc shared libraries and cannot load into a static musl process. A program that opts into GPU drawing builds as a dynamic executable that loads libvulkan.so.1 through the system loader. A GPU driver is always an installed shared library, so that build loses nothing a static file could give.

Why not a loader inside the runtime. Loading glibc-built drivers into a musl process mixes two C libraries, two allocators and two thread-local layouts. The glibc linker warns that a static program calling dlopen needs the exact glibc it was built with. Musl ships no static dlopen at all.

Peers. Rust's x11rb and wayland-client both have pure-Rust protocol backends. Go has jezek/xgb for X11 and jfreymuth/pulse for the PulseAudio protocol. Android ships tinyalsa for kernel sound. These show the protocols are stable and small enough to own.

Edge cases. With no DISPLAY or WAYLAND_DISPLAY, `ray.init_window` returns a typed error that names both variables. `ray.headless_window` always works. Programs that never open a window link none of this code.

decisions.title: A built-in exit for expected failures
decisions.situation: Command-line scripts stop with a message when input is wrong. Today each script defines a four-line helper that prints to stderr and exits. The alternative returns an error from the entry function, which prints a framed report. We recommend a built-in fail that takes a message and an exit code. It prints the message, runs scope cleanup, and exits with no frame. Panic stays for program bugs.
decisions.gist: Should scripts get a built-in way to stop with a message and an exit code?

decisions.title: Text search returns a character index
decisions.situation: `find` on text returns a byte offset, and -1 when the text is absent. Slicing takes character positions. On accented text the two disagree, and a slice can cut inside a letter. Ports carry a helper to convert between them. We recommend returning a character index, or nothing when absent. Byte search stays available through the bytes methods. The change is one cutover across every caller.

decisions.lesson: Text search returns a byte offset, but slicing takes characters. Accented text then cuts in the wrong place.

decisions.detail: Source: card #5085, item B3. Today `find` is in Core/Text/String.jet:83, returns a UTF-8 byte offset, and returns -1 when absent. A probe showed `"héllo // c".slice(0, "héllo // c".find("//"))` prints `héllo /`. Ratified D-ITER-REMAINDER1 already reports byte offsets explicitly for char-offset observations. Ratified D-CHAR-SCALAR1 notes no String method decodes a character at a byte position. The card counts 103 lines of byte helpers across ports. The savings figure is an estimate.

options.technical: Signature changes from Int to Int?. Implementation counts scalars up to the byte match. One cutover migrates every caller in Core and the ports.

gains: Found positions compose with slice and len.

losses.loss: Every existing caller of find changes at once.
losses.mitigation: One cutover migrates every caller, and byte search stays available through a bytes method.

whyNot.reason: It keeps two position units, and each port still writes the helper.
It fixes one call shape and leaves the same mismatch in other searches.

decisions.situation: A deployment script checks that a binary is executable before it runs. Today it starts the shell test command and reads the exit code. That needs process authority, for one question about one file. We recommend a file function that reports whether the path names a regular file the process may execute. decisions.title: Named groups on a regex match
decisions.situation: A regex match exposes capture groups only by position. Adding a group to a pattern shifts every later number, and the code reads the wrong text without an error. Named groups already parse, but the source engine offers no way to read one. We recommend a method that returns a named group's text, or nothing when the group did not take part. A literal pattern rejects an unknown name at compile time.

decisions.title: Check fixed regex patterns while building
decisions.situation: Scanner code often compiles a fixed pattern at run time and wraps the result in a panic branch. For a fixed pattern that branch never runs. A typed regex literal is checked when the program compiles, but four ports in the review never used it. We recommend that the compiler check and compile every fixed pattern while building, whichever form it is written in. Users get the literal’s safety and speed with no warning and no rewrite.
decisions.gist: Should Jet warn when a constant regex pattern is compiled at run time?
decisions.lesson: A fixed pattern compiled at run time needs a panic branch for a bug that cannot happen. A literal is checked when the program compiles.
decisions.story: Sam ports a scanner from another language. Every line it compiles a fixed pattern and handles a failure that can never occur, and the code is longer than it needs to be.
decisions.inWild: re.compile("\\d{2}:\\d{2}") ?? panic("bad pattern")
decisions.detail:
Source: card #5085, item B10. Evidence is in the port review: 873 lines of scanners across four ports, with no literal form used. Ratified D-REGEX-LIT1 makes a bare string never a regex, and makes the typed literal Regex{...} the checked form. The lint code is the next free code, to be assigned. The card's speed figures are from the rewritten scanners and are a single measurement set.

Redesign 2026-11-01 (owner: engineer the downsides away). The first version recommended a lint, whose loss was a warning that can be ignored. A lint only asks people to rewrite code. Folding needs nothing from them: a constant string passed to the run-time compile call is compiled while building. A bad pattern then fails the build at the call, and a good one is stored compiled, so the failure branch is provably dead and removed.

This follows the ratified rule for constants: pure work on constant input folds while building. The typed literal stays the one documented form, so no second mechanism is added.

options.name: Check fixed patterns while building
options.detail: A constant string passed to the run-time compile call, or to its flag form, is compiled while building. A bad pattern is a build error at the call, naming the problem. A good pattern is stored compiled, and the dead failure branch is removed. Nothing changes for patterns built at run time.
options.technical: The checker marks a compile call whose pattern argument is a constant with no interpolation. Lowering evaluates it at build time with the same Core regex compiler. An error becomes a diagnostic at the argument span; success becomes a static compiled value, and the Result’s error arm is dropped as unreachable. Same meaning on every tier, because the same Core code runs.
options.code:
rx :: re.compile("\\d{2}:\\d{2}") ?? panic("bad pattern")
// checked while building; the panic branch is removed
re.compile("(\\d") ?? panic("x")
error: this pattern is not valid: unclosed group at 1

options.name: No lint
options.detail: Constant patterns compile at run time with a failure branch, and no warning is shown.
options.technical: No checker change.
options.code: re.compile("\\d{2}:\\d{2}") ?? panic("bad pattern")

comparisons.note: A regex in a constant is built once and checked by the regex crate's macro.

recommendation.why: A fixed pattern cannot fail at run time, so the compiler can prove it while building. Users get the literal’s compile-time check and speed without changing their code or seeing a warning.
gains: Every fixed pattern is checked when the program builds.
Dead failure branches are removed automatically.
Existing code benefits with no rewrite.

whyNot.reason: It keeps unchecked fixed patterns and dead failure branches in every port.

recommendation.tradeoff: None remaining: checked, fast fixed patterns with no user action.

decisions.title: Where the running program and this code live: `$program.dir` and `$here.dir`
decisions.situation: A program that loads files beside it uses the current directory as its root, so running it from another folder reads the wrong files. Any program can need this, not only scripts. Jet already gives code facts about itself through `$` roots: `$here.line` and `$here.function` (ratified D-JAI-SITE1) and `$build.os`. This ballot adds where the code is and where the running program is to that same family, instead of a script-only function.
decisions.gist: How does any program find its own file and directory?
decisions.lesson: Programs that load sibling files assume the current directory. Running them from elsewhere reads the wrong files.
decisions.story: Ana's repository tool reads a config beside its script. Run from a subfolder, it reports missing files, because the working directory is not the repository root.
decisions.inWild: root :: files.cwd()
decisions.detail:
Source: card #5085, item B9. The owner asked on 2026-11-01 for metadata like function, line and build data, not a script-only function. Regular programs also need their own file and directory.

Two questions hide in one. Where is this code written? That is a fact about the source, the same kind as `$here.line`. Where is the program that is running now? That is a fact about the run. Option A gives each its own member in the existing `$` family, so neither one has to stand in for the other.

`$here.file` and `$here.dir` are package-relative (`tools/gen.jet`, `tools`), the same text `$here` already prints in `app.jet:12:5`. So a built binary holds no build-machine path and stays reproducible.

`$program.path` and `$program.dir` are read when the program starts, never stored at build time. Under `jet run`, `jet dev` or a shebang script they name the entry source file, which matches the owner's 2026-10-23 ruling that a script run in memory reports its script path. A built program gets its own executable from the operating system (/proc/self/exe on Linux). In compile-time code, the running program is the file being compiled, so `$program.dir` is that source's directory.

Edge cases: a deleted or moved executable keeps the path the OS reports at start. A program loaded as a library (`jet build --lib`) reports the host executable, as dladdr-free runtimes do. The web target has no file, so `$program.path` is the page URL path.

options.name: Location facts: `$program.dir` and `$here.dir`
options.detail: `$program.path` and `$program.dir` are the file that is running and its directory: the source file under jet run or as a script, the executable when built. `$here.file` and `$here.dir` are where the code is written, package-relative, beside the ratified `$here.line` and `$here.function`. Both are Path values and work in every program.
options.technical: `$program` is an already-registered fact root, and `$here` is ratified (D-JAI-SITE1). The new members are registered in Syntax (I7). `$program.path` is set once by the runtime at start: jet run passes the canonical entry source, as it already passes arguments, and a built image reads /proc/self/exe. Nothing goes in the build record. `$here.file` is a per-site constant relative to the package root. Misuse, such as assigning to a fact, uses the existing fact diagnostics.
options.code:
config :: $program.dir.join("config.toml")
log.info("{$here.file}:{$here.line} in {$here.function}")

options.name: Only `$here.dir`, absolute
options.detail: One fact: the absolute directory of the source file, recorded when the program is compiled.
options.technical: SourceLocation.file becomes absolute, and `$here.dir` folds to a constant string in the binary.
options.code: config :: $here.dir.join("config.toml")

options.name: Keep the working directory
options.detail: The program keeps reading the current directory. Each run needs the caller to start in the right folder.
options.technical: No change.

The source location is a compile-time builtin; the running executable comes from the OS at run time.

recommendation.why: It answers both real questions with the metadata family Jet already has: where this code lives, and where the running program lives. It is not script-only, works from any folder, and stores no build-machine path.
gains: Any program finds its own files from any working directory.
Same `$` family as `$here.line` and `$build.os`, so there is nothing new to learn.
Builds stay reproducible: no absolute build path is stored.
An installed program finds data installed beside its executable.

Every program then depends on the caller's folder.

decisions.title: Compound update of a list slot
decisions.situation: Jet rejects `xs[i] += n` on a list element. The error teaches the total update, which reads the element and stores it again. Maps already have a one-step form: a starting value in the brackets, as in `counts[w, or: 0] += 1`, makes the slot sure to exist. A list element that is in range is just as sure to exist. We recommend one rule for both: a compound update works on any slot that is sure to hold a value.
decisions.gist: Should Jet let `xs[i] += n` update a list element in one step?
decisions.lesson: Updating a list element takes the element twice today. A compound form would write it once, with one bounds check.
decisions.story: Sam tallies rows into buckets. Each update repeats the bucket name twice, and a typo in one copy quietly updates the wrong bucket.
decisions.inWild: loads[lightest] += row.weight
decisions.detail:
Source: card #5085, item B2. Today's rejection is E0164, "Compound assignment can't target an indexed slot". Ratified D-MEM-INDEXMUT1 keeps compound arithmetic rejected on indexed slots, because it hides a default-value question. That reason covers maps only, so this ballot asks whether lists are different. Lists have no default value, and an out-of-range index stops the program. Maps stay on E0164 under either option, as D-MAP-SLOT1 requires.

Redesign 2026-11-01 (owner: engineer the downsides away). The first version listed "maps still need the longer form" as a loss. That is not so: ratified D-MAP-SLOT1 A already gives maps `counts[w, or: 0] += 1`, where the starting value makes the slot exist.

The rule is now stated once for both: a compound update needs a slot that is sure to hold a value. A list element is (an out-of-range index stops before any write); a map slot is when it names a starting value. A bare `m[k] += 1` keeps E0164, whose fix text shows the `or:` form, as D-MAP-SLOT1 requires.

decisions.title: How type names are quoted in error messages
decisions.situation: Jet's error messages quote some type names and not others. A named type gets backticks, as in `WebForm`. A built-in type prints bare with a short explanation, as in String (text). For a generic type, only the head is quoted, as in `Cell`<Int>. Readers cannot tell where the code ends and the prose begins. We recommend one rule: the whole type is quoted as code, and the plain explanation stays outside the backticks.
decisions.gist: Should every type in an error message be quoted whole, with its explanation outside the quotes?
decisions.lesson: In an error message, backticks mark text you could type in your program. A type is something you type, so it gets backticks, all of it. The friendly explanation, such as (text), is prose about the type, so it sits outside them.
decisions.story: Priya passes a string where a web form is expected. The error says the call wants `WebForm`, but this is String (text). A later error mentions `Cell`<Int>. She copies `Cell` into her search box and loses the <Int> part.
decisions.inWild: Rust quotes the whole type in its messages, generics included, for example: expected `HashMap<String, u32>`, found `Vec<u8>`. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/error_codes/E0308.html

TODAY

Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Diagnostics.jet:389-414 sema_type_show builds every type name in type errors. Named types are quoted: .Named gives `WebForm`. Built-in scalars are bare with a gloss: String (text), Int (a whole number), I32 (a 32-bit whole number, ...). Generic types quote only the head: .Apply gives `Cell`<Int>.

The earlier draft said three web snapshots expect bare WebForm and fail. That is stale. I ran the published base compiler on tests/ui/web_suite_forms_type_mismatch, _query_ and _router_. Each prints "`field` wants `WebForm` for argument 1, but this is String (text)", and the committed snapshots match.

Scope of a change: 95 committed test outputs contain a bare built-in with its gloss, and 26 contain a head-only quoted generic (git grep over tests, 2026-11-05).

RULINGS

D-DIAG-CORE-NAME1=A decides how Core type names are spelled, not quoting. D-CASE-PROSE1=A decides case. Docs/spec/proof-replay-decisions.md:602-604 says code is quoted in backticks in every diagnostic. No ruling covers types in particular. The plain gloss after built-ins is kept under every option.

HOW A'S DOWNSIDE IS DESIGNED AWAY

About 120 snapshots change. They come from one function, so one edit to sema_type_show changes them all. The regenerated diff only moves or adds backticks, and a script can check that claim over the whole diff before it lands.

WHY NOT B OR C

B removes all quotes. Multi-word messages then run type names into the prose, as in "wants WebForm for argument 1". C keeps today's mix, so readers keep guessing where code ends.

decisions.title: Zero leaks in the native compiler
decisions.gist: Must the native compiler report zero leaks, double frees and use-after-free across its full test corpus?
decisions.lesson: A leak is memory the compiler never frees. Small leaks grow into large use, so the compiler slows and then fails on big inputs. A zero rule catches each leak, but the current harness still reports some.
decisions.story: Omar compiles a large project and memory keeps climbing. Under option A the leak harness fails on the exact phase that keeps the memory, so it is fixed before the self-build. Under option B the same leak is listed as a known class and shows up again on the next large build.
decisions.inWild:
Zig: the test allocator reports leaked memory at the end of a test, with the allocation site. Source: https://ziglang.org/documentation/master/#Memory

Rust: Miri detects leaks and use-after-free in test runs. Source: https://github.com/rust-lang/miri
decisions.detail:
Owner order (card #5014): the memory-safety release plan requires a zero-leak result.

State recorded in the card: the lircheck harness reports LEAK 0, DOUBLE 0, UAF 0, SHELL 0 as of 2026-10-17. Still open: a mixed probe at 1.89 MB, 89 static LEAK reports, and a full 129-program corpus sweep. Tools live under $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/discovery/memverify/.

No ratified decision found by keyword scan records a zero-leak rule for the compiler. D-MEM-GUARANTEE1 and D-MEM-HARDEN1 concern Jet programs.

options.name: Zero leaks, double frees and use-after-free
options.detail: The native compiler must report zero leaks, zero double frees and zero use-after-free on the lircheck harness and the full 129-program corpus. Static leak reports are cleared or proven false.
options.technical: Keep the lircheck counters at zero in CI. Clear the 89 static LEAK reports and the mixed 1.89 MB probe. Run the 129-program sweep before each cutover.
options.code:
$ tools/memverify lircheck
LEAK 0  DOUBLE 0  UAF 0  SHELL 0

options.name: Zero leaks on the probe set only
options.detail: The rule covers the lircheck probes. Static reports and corpus leaks are tracked as known classes.
options.technical: Keep counters on the probe set. List the static reports as known classes with owners.
options.code:
$ tools/memverify lircheck
LEAK 0  DOUBLE 0  UAF 0  (corpus: 3 known classes)

comparisons.note: The test allocator reports leaked memory with the allocation site. Source: https://ziglang.org/documentation/master/#Memory
Miri detects leaks and use-after-free while tests run. Source: https://github.com/rust-lang/miri

recommendation.why: A compiler that leaks cannot be trusted on large inputs. The owner made zero leaks the release condition.
gains: Each leak is found by the harness, not by a user.
Memory use stays bounded across runs.

losses.loss: Release waits for the 89 static reports and the corpus sweep.
losses.mitigation: Each static report is listed by name, so each has an owner.

whyNot.reason: B leaves corpus leaks known but unfixed, which the release plan does not allow.

recommendation.tradeoff: Slower release, for a compiler that frees all its memory.

decisions.title: Should the `jet run` wait be gated against Lua, LuaJIT, Python and Node?
decisions.situation: Two weeks ago the vote made the wait from typing jet run to seeing the answer a number we show but never gate. The owner now wants Jet to be the fastest scripting language, at least as fast as Lua. Lua answers a tiny script in about 2 ms, which is just the cost of starting any process. We recommend gating the wait on real scripts against Lua, LuaJIT, Python and Node. A tiny hello is gated against that start cost instead, since no program can measurably beat it.
decisions.gist: Should the wait from `jet run` to its answer fail the speed rule when Lua, LuaJIT, Python or Node answer first?
decisions.lesson: The speed rule holds every release while any required benchmark loses. Today the jet run wait is shown but never gated. Lua answers a tiny script at the cost of starting a process, about 2 ms. Gating means Jet must compile and run small scripts with almost no extra time.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. Time to answer is the wall time from pressing Enter on `jet run app.jet` to the program exiting. A gated benchmark cell can fail and hold a release; a reported cell is only shown.

Two states are gated under A and B. After an edit: the script changed since its last run, and Jet's own libraries are as shipped. Repeat: nothing changed. The first run after install is shown only, because no peer rebuilds its standard library on a script run.

Beginner path: nothing to write; `jet run app.jet` just has to answer first.

Expert path: each cell names its exact commands, inputs and cache state, so anyone can rerun the numbers. `jet run -O0` and `-O1` keep their meaning; the cell times plain `jet run`.
decisions.story: Ana keeps a folder of tiny Lua scripts for renaming photos. She tries the same script in Jet. Lua answers instantly; Jet makes her wait a quarter second. Nothing in Jet's rules says that wait must go.
decisions.inWild:
$ time lua -e 'print(1)'      # about 2.2 ms here; /bin/true is 2.0-2.4 ms
$ time luajit -e 'print(1)'   # about 2.2 ms
$ time python3 -c 'print(1)'  # about 14.5 ms
$ time node -e 'console.log(1)'  # about 25.7 ms
decisions.detail:
This reopens D-PERF-RUNCELL1, ratified B on 2026-10-07, which kept the wait reported only. The owner's direction of 2026-10-23 (Jet must be the fastest scripting language, at least Lua-level) conflicts with B, so the question returns to the owner. If A or B wins, it supersedes D-PERF-RUNCELL1=B. It does not touch D-EXEC1/2/3; it gives their in-memory O0 work a gated target.

Main measured these on the reference machine on 2026-10-23, under load, as spawnSync medians. Process floor: /bin/true 2.0-2.4 ms. Peers and Jet: `jet --version` 2.2 ms. Lua and LuaJIT (`-e print`) 2.2 ms each. `python3 -c print` 14.5 ms and `node -e console.log` 25.7 ms. `jet run hello.jet` took 241-311 ms. A shebang script on its repeat path took about 319 ms (ExecBallots probe, same day): the script cache still hashes the toolchain before it starts the kept binary.

Where Jet's time goes today: the Prelude and Core front end about 160 ms, linking about 70 ms, writing the binary, spawning it as a child, and runtime start. The in-memory O0 plan (card #4741) removes link, file and spawn first, then ships a prebuilt Core image. Its hello budget is 5 ms. That budget still loses to Lua's 2.2 ms, so under A and B the hello cell stays red until Jet's own work is near zero.

State of the gauntlet. No `jet run` time-to-answer cell exists yet, reported or gated (no `run_time_to_answer` in Tools/gauntlet). Lua and LuaJIT are not gauntlet peers today (Tools/gauntlet/matrix.json rails: rust, python, node; perf rails add c and zig). A and B add both. `go run` was a peer in the 2026-10-07 A; it compiles before it runs, so it never binds and stays reported.

Noise. Lua sits on the process floor, where three runs vary by about 0.4 ms. A strict comparator there needs many interleaved samples and a confidence bound; an inconclusive cell counts as a loss under the speed rule.

HOW A AVOIDS AN UNWINNABLE CELL

The performance gate in AGENTS.md is strict. Jet/peer and Jet/ceiling must be at most 1.00, an inconclusive result counts as a loss, and every required cell needs an asm-parity ceiling reference. At the process floor that rule cannot be met. Jet, Lua and the best hand-written program each cost one process start, so no measurement can show one strictly faster.

A therefore amends the gate for process-floor cells only. Every other cell keeps the strict rule unchanged.

A process-floor cell is one whose ceiling reference does nothing but start, write its output and exit. Under A that is only the hello cell. Its ceiling reference is a minimal static program that writes the same line and exits, kept in Tools/perf/asm-parity.

On that cell, Jet passes when the 95 percent upper bound of Jet minus the ceiling is at most 0.5 ms. The same band applies against each peer on that cell only. 0.5 ms is about the floor's own spread on the reference machine (/bin/true measured 2.0-2.4 ms).

MEASUREMENT

A round runs Jet, the ceiling and each peer once, in a fresh random order. A cell needs at least 30 rounds. The bound is a one-sided 95 percent bootstrap bound on the median difference, drawn from 10,000 resamples of the paired rounds.

Noise under load: if the ceiling's own spread (90th minus 10th percentile) exceeds 0.5 ms, the machine is too busy to judge. The run is then inconclusive, which counts as a loss, and the harness records the load average with it. A busy machine can therefore never turn a cell green.

The real script cells (cli.app, text.script, files.script, formats.csv-cli) run long enough to separate. They keep the strict comparator against all four peers and need their own asm-parity ceilings. Under the existing rule, a cell without one is uncovered and fails.

WHY NOT B

No peer has a parity band today: AGENTS.md judges Rust like every other peer. B would add a new 5 percent band for lua and luajit on every run cell, which makes it a second rule. A's band covers only the hello cell, where the physics leaves nothing to compare.

options.name: Gate it: beat all four on real scripts
options.detail: Add required cells for jet run time to answer, after an edit and on a repeat run. On real script workloads Jet must beat lua, luajit, python3 and node under the strict rule. The hello cell sits at the process floor, where nothing can be strictly faster. There Jet must come within 0.5 ms of a minimal hand-written program. That amends the gate for this one cell. The first run after install is shown, not gated.
options.technical: Add run_time_to_answer_seconds with cache: edited|repeat; fresh_install is reported only. Script cells use the strict comparator and asm-parity ceilings. The hello cell passes when the 95 percent upper bound of Jet minus its ceiling is at most 0.5 ms. Cells take at least 30 randomly ordered rounds.

options.name: Gate it, Lua counts as a tie
options.detail: Same cells and states as A. Against Lua and LuaJIT, Jet within 5 percent counts as a pass on every run cell. That is a new parity band, since no peer has one today. Against Python and Node, Jet must still be faster.
options.technical: As A, but the manifest gives lua and luajit a new 1.05 parity band on every run cell. This amends the performance gate in AGENTS.md, which judges every peer, Rust included, with no band.

options.name: Keep it shown only
options.detail: Keep the October vote. Show the time to answer next to each script cell, but never fail a gate on it. Only finished programs and build times gate.
options.technical: Adds the same metric and states as reported-only columns, plus the two new peers. Gates and cards ignore them.

comparisons.note: Start an interpreter and run at once; about 2.2 ms here, the cost of starting any process.
comparisons.code:
$ lua rename.lua photos/
$ luajit rename.lua photos/

comparisons.note: Starts the interpreter and compiles to bytecode; about 14.5 ms for a one-line script here.
Starts V8 and its interpreter; about 25.7 ms here.
`go run` compiles, links and runs; since Go 1.24 it caches the linked program, so repeats are faster.
Compiles each method to native code on first call; its first-call wait is a known pain point. Since 1.9, package images cache native code.
`zig run` builds into a cache, then runs. Since 0.15 its own x86 backend is the Debug default, about 5x faster to compile than LLVM.

recommendation.why: The owner asked for the fastest scripting language, and the speed rule only drives work it can fail. A gates every cell Jet can actually win, and holds hello to the process start cost.
gains: The wait users feel first becomes a tracked, gated loss with an owner.
Jet's script speed is measured against the fastest script runners, not only Python.

losses.mitigation: The in-memory O0 and prebuilt Core plan removes link, spawn and Core checking; each red cell carries its gap.

whyNot.reason: B adds a new 5 percent band for two peers on every run cell. A bands only the hello cell, where nothing can be strictly faster.
A number that never fails a gate does not get fixed, and it conflicts with the owner's new direction.

recommendation.tradeoff: Releases wait on script start-up speed until Jet beats Lua on real scripts and reaches the start cost on hello.

decisions.title: What does `jet run` do when the system forbids new machine code in memory?
decisions.situation: With in-memory O0, jet run writes machine code into memory and runs it there. Some hardened Linux systems forbid turning memory into runnable code, while still running program files. Jet can then put the same code in a file and run that, refuse with an error, or interpret the program. You ruled in chat on 2026-10-23 for the file: same code, same output, the real signal on a crash, and only verbose mode mentions it. This records it.
decisions.gist: When the system forbids runnable memory, should `jet run` use a file, refuse, or interpret?
decisions.lesson: Some systems refuse to make memory runnable but still run program files. Jet's in-memory run needs runnable memory. Writing the same code to a file keeps the program's meaning and output identical; only the start is a little slower.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. Runnable memory: memory the processor may execute. Hardened systems can forbid making memory runnable after it was written, to stop attacks that inject code. Program files stay allowed.

Where this happens: systemd services with `MemoryDenyWriteExecute=yes`, SELinux with the `deny_execmem` setting, and PaX kernels. Phones and consoles forbid any new code, but `jet run` does not run there.

Beginner path: nothing changes; the script runs and prints the same thing.

Expert path: `jet run --verbose` prints one line naming the refusal and the fallback. Shipped programs built with `jet build` are never affected.
decisions.story: Omar runs a nightly Jet script from a locked-down systemd service. The first in-memory run is refused by the system. He should not need to know why; the script should just run.

$ go run .                  # always builds a file, then runs it
# LuaJIT on iOS: the JIT is disabled, interpreter only
decisions.detail:
OWNER RULINGS

Owner decision, chat on 2026-10-23 at 05:29, relayed by Main: fall back to writing the same O0 code to a file.

Owner answers, chat on 2026-10-23 at about 05:50, recorded on card c0vsqf8a as binding. They read:

(a) “Relaunch: launching the running program’s own script path (os.executable() under jet run) runs it through the same jet at the same level.”

(b) “Tier-up includes on-stack replacement at loop heads today.”

(c) “A crash under in-memory jet run exits with the real signal, same as the built binary (no conversion to exit 1).”

Answer (c) fixes the fallback’s crash behaviour: every step exits with the real signal, as the built binary does. This ballot records both for one-click confirmation. The alternatives are kept for the record.

What it amends. D-EXEC1=A allows a tiny evaluator only for a platform that forbids creating machine code at run time, and only if Jet must run there. This decision answers hosts that forbid runnable memory but still run files: they get the file fallback, not an evaluator. The evaluator clause stays only for platforms that forbid all new code, where `jet run` is not hosted.

It also narrows D-EXEC2=A: the build-to-file path survives only as this fallback, producing the same image. D-PORTABLE1/2 already keep checked native code in a file cache, so sandboxed apps meet the same rule. D-ADAPTIVE-TIER1 keeps its refusal list for phones, consoles, web and bare metal. I9 holds by construction, because the bytes are the ones the in-memory path maps.

How the fallback works. Main’s plan (o0-plan.md) links the program at a fixed base inside jet, maps it RW, copies, then flips text to RX. If mmap or mprotect with PROT_EXEC fails with EPERM or EACCES, jet writes the same image to a `memfd_create` file. It maps that file read-and-execute at the same base, in the same process.

Both systemd filters allow mapping a file that is never writable and runnable at once. If memfd_create is refused, jet writes the image once to a private 0700 file in the cache directory, named by its hash, checks the hash and maps it the same way. Repeat runs reuse that file. Only if every runnable mapping is refused does jet start the file with execve, so the process is the program. If that is refused too, jet prints a diagnostic naming the policy and suggests `jet build`.

`os.executable()` still returns the script path: jet passes it to the image, which does not trust `/proc/self/exe` (see D-EXEC-RELAUNCH1). With tier-up on by default (D-EXEC-TIERUP1), both in-process steps map each tiered function the same way. The exec step exists only where no runnable mapping is allowed at all. No design can add faster code there, so the program keeps its O0 code with the same output.

Evidence. systemd’s MemoryDenyWriteExecute rejects mmap with PROT_WRITE and PROT_EXEC together, and mprotect adding PROT_EXEC. Its manual says files on non-noexec mounts and `memfd_create` still run code (systemd.exec(5)). V8’s `--jitless` mode (v7.4, 2019) runs without runnable memory; V8 measured 40 percent and 80 percent slower benchmarks. LuaJIT disables its JIT on iOS (luajit.org install notes).

Test. `systemd-run --user --wait --pipe -p MemoryDenyWriteExecute=yes jet run hello.jet` prints the same bytes. Adding `-p SystemCallFilter=~memfd_create` forces the private-file step.

HOW A'S DOWNSIDES ARE DESIGNED AWAY

1. Start cost. The program stays in jet's process: the image is copied to an in-memory file and mapped, which costs one memory copy and no exec. Where memfd_create is refused, the cached file is written once and reused by every later run.

2. Tier-up. Both in-process steps map tiered functions the same way, so tier-up works on every system that allows any runnable mapping. A system that refuses all runnable mappings cannot run new code under any option.

No loss remains.

options.name: Run the same code from a file
options.detail: When the system refuses runnable memory, Jet writes the same machine code to a file and runs it. Output, exit status and signals are the same. Only `--verbose` mentions the fallback. The program stays in the same process, so start-up and tier-up are unchanged.
options.technical: Same linked image. On EPERM or EACCES from mmap/mprotect with PROT_EXEC, jet writes a memfd and maps it PROT_READ|PROT_EXEC at the base, in-process. Else it maps a hash-named private 0700 file in the cache directory the same way, reused across runs. Else it starts that file with execve. Else a registered diagnostic. The script path is passed to the image for `os.executable()`. Tier-up maps tiered code the same way in both in-process steps.
options.code:

hello
$ jet run --verbose hello.jet
note: runnable memory refused (EPERM); running the same code from a file
hello

options.name: Refuse with an error
options.detail: Jet stops with an error that names the system rule and suggests `jet build` and running the binary. Nothing runs until the user acts.
options.technical: On EPERM/EACCES from mmap/mprotect PROT_EXEC, emit a registered diagnostic with the errno, the detected policy, and the `jet build` command. No file is written.

options.detail: Jet keeps a small interpreter and runs the program with it on such systems. No file is written, but the program runs many times slower, and a second way of running code must match the first.
options.technical: Keeps an evaluator for O0 IR as a runtime fallback, the clause D-EXEC1 allowed. It is a second mechanism under I8 and needs its own I9 parity proof for every feature.

comparisons.note: Lua only interprets. LuaJIT turns its JIT off where runnable memory is forbidden, such as iOS, and keeps its interpreter.
CPython interprets; its experimental 3.13 JIT is off by default, so nothing changes.
`--jitless` runs V8 with no runnable memory, interpreter only; V8 measured 40 to 80 percent slower benchmarks.
`go run` always writes a binary file and runs it, so it never needs runnable memory.
Compiles methods into memory with LLVM as they are first called; `--compile=min` mostly interprets instead.
`zig run` writes the binary into its cache and runs it.

One code generator and one runtime; no interpreter to keep in step.
Start-up and tier-up stay in-process on hardened systems.

whyNot.reason: It stops working scripts for a reason the user cannot fix inside the script.
A second way of running code is many times slower and must match the first forever.

recommendation.tradeoff: A runs the same code from an in-memory or cached file, so hardened systems lose nothing.

decisions.title: Does `jet run` speed up hot code on its own while the program runs?
decisions.situation: In-memory jet run compiles quickly with simple code, so long loops run slower than in a built program. Jet can rebuild busy functions with faster code on a background thread while the program runs. That could be on by default for jet run, behind a flag, or replaced by compiling everything slower but better first. You ruled in chat on 2026-10-23: on by default for jet run, entering faster code at loop heads too, with identical output. This records it.
decisions.gist: Should `jet run` rebuild hot functions with faster code by default, only behind a flag, or never?
decisions.lesson: Quick-start code is simple, so long loops are slower than in a built program. Rebuilding only the busy functions in the background keeps start-up fast and lets long scripts catch up. The program's output never changes; only its speed does.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. O0 is Jet's quick-start code level, used by `jet run`. O1 is the level `jet build` uses. Tier-up means rebuilding a busy function at O1 while the program runs, then switching calls to the new code.

Beginner path: nothing to write. Short scripts finish before anything is rebuilt; long ones speed up on their own.

Expert path: `jet run -O0` keeps every function at O0 with no tier-up. `jet run -O1` compiles everything at O1 before starting. Shipped programs from `jet build` never tier up unless their author opts in.
decisions.story: Mia's script sums thirty million numbers. Built with `jet build`, it takes 264 ms. With `jet run` it takes about twice as long, while Node takes 113 ms. Nobody should need a flag to fix that.
decisions.inWild:
$ luajit loop.lua    # interpreter, then a trace JIT after 56 loop iterations
$ node loop.js       # V8 tiers up hot code and loops on its own
$ python3 loop.py    # no JIT unless built with the experimental one
decisions.detail:
OWNER RULINGS

Owner decision, chat on 2026-10-23 at 05:29, relayed by Main: tier-up on by default for jet run.

Owner answers, chat on 2026-10-23 at about 05:50, recorded on card c0vsqf8a as binding. They read:

(a) “Relaunch: launching the running program’s own script path (os.executable() under jet run) runs it through the same jet at the same level.”

(b) “Tier-up includes on-stack replacement at loop heads today.”

(c) “A crash under in-memory jet run exits with the real signal, same as the built binary (no conversion to exit 1).”

Answer (b) makes loop-head entry part of A today, not later. This ballot records both for one-click confirmation. The alternatives are kept for the record.

What it amends. D-ADAPTIVE-TIER1=B made the in-program optimizer opt-in (`--adaptive`) for long-running shipped programs. This decision turns the same mechanism on by default for `jet run` and `jet dev` only. Shipped binaries keep D-ADAPTIVE-TIER1's opt-in. D-EXEC1=A's levels stand: O0 serves `jet run`, and `-O0`, `-O1`, `-O2` pin a level.

Bounds. D-EXEC3=A applies: a speed-up used only at O1 needs a proof or a checker. I9 holds through D-ADAPTIVE-TIER1's forced mode, which tiers up every function at once; every golden must print the same under it. D-RESOURCE-LIMIT1=A covers recursion depth: O1 frames differ in size, so undeclared depth may change, while `#MaxDepth(n)` stays exact.

Mechanism, from Main's plan (o0-plan.md, lane L4). O0 code counts calls at function entry and calls other functions through a per-program table. One compiler thread stays alive after the jump. It rebuilds hot functions at O1 from the same IR with the same code generator. It maps the new code read-and-execute, never writable and runnable at once, then swaps the table entry.

The O1 code calls the program's own runtime copy, not the compiler's. Under the file fallback (D-EXEC-NOEXEC1), tiered code is mapped from a new in-memory file; after an exec step tier-up is off.

Loops. Swapping at function entry never helps a long loop inside `fn run`, which is entered once. That is exactly Main's loop benchmark: jet run 509 ms against node 113 and luajit 160. Tier-up therefore also needs entry into O1 code at loop heads (on-stack replacement). D-ADAPTIVE-TIER1 excluded that for shipped binaries; here it is required.

Precedent. .NET's quick-start level initially skipped methods with loops, because without loop-head entry they stayed slow; .NET 7 enabled on-stack replacement to fix that. LuaJIT records traces after 56 loop iterations by default. V8 tiers up through several compilers, also at loop heads.

Costs. The compiler thread uses one core while it compiles, and its memory stays mapped. Timing changes as code swaps, so benchmarks need warm-up; `-O0` and `-O1` give fixed code.

options.name: On by default for `jet run`
options.detail: `jet run` starts at O0. Busy functions and loops are rebuilt at O1 on one background thread and switched in. Output is identical. `-O0` turns it off; `-O1` compiles everything up front. Shipped programs are unchanged.
options.technical: Entry counters and loop-head counters in O0 code; calls through a per-program function table; one compiler thread kept after the jump. O1 code is mapped RX and bound to the program's runtime symbols. Swap at the next call, plus loop-head entry with the slot frame copied. A forced mode tiers every function for I9 goldens.
options.code:
$ jet run loop.jet
30000000 iterations: 4021
// hot loop rebuilt at O1 while it ran
$ jet run -O0 loop.jet   # no tier-up

options.name: Only behind a flag
options.detail: `jet run` stays at O0 everywhere. Users who want faster loops pass `--adaptive`, the flag shipped programs already use. Speed is predictable, but most users never learn the flag.
options.technical: D-ADAPTIVE-TIER1's opt-in `--adaptive` applies to `jet run` too; without it no compiler thread survives the jump and no counters are emitted.
options.code:
$ jet run loop.jet            # O0 all the way
$ jet run --adaptive loop.jet # rebuilds hot code

options.name: Compile everything at O1 first
options.detail: `jet run` skips O0 and compiles the whole program at O1 before it starts. No background work, but every run waits for the slower compile, including tiny scripts.
options.technical: Changes D-EXEC1's level for `jet run` from O0 to O1. No counters, no table swaps, no compiler thread; start-up pays O1 compile time for every function.
options.code:
$ jet run loop.jet
// every function compiled at O1 before the first line runs

comparisons.note: Lua only interprets. LuaJIT interprets, then compiles hot loops after 56 iterations by default; `-joff` turns that off.
CPython 3.13's JIT is experimental and off unless built with `--enable-experimental-jit`.
V8 starts in an interpreter and tiers hot code up through faster compilers on its own, including at loop heads.
`go run` compiles once with optimizations; nothing changes while the program runs.
Compiles each method with LLVM at its first call, then keeps that code; no later rebuild.
`zig run` compiles once. Its fast Debug backend emits slower code than LLVM, by its own release notes.

recommendation.why: You ruled this in chat on 2026-10-23, loop-head entry included. Fast start and fast long loops without a flag is what LuaJIT and Node users already get.
gains: Short scripts keep the quick start; long scripts approach built speed.
One code generator and runtime, so output cannot differ.

losses.loss: A background thread uses a core while it compiles.
losses.mitigation: Only hot code is rebuilt, once; `-O0` turns it off.

losses.loss: Timings shift during a run, which can confuse quick benchmarks.
losses.mitigation: `-O0` and `-O1` give fixed code; benchmark guides say to use them.

whyNot.reason: Most users never find the flag, so long scripts stay slow for them.
Every tiny script pays the slower compile, losing the quick start.

recommendation.tradeoff: Some background work and shifting timings, for quick start and fast loops together.

decisions.title: What does `os.executable()` name under `jet run`, and how does a script relaunch itself?
decisions.situation: Some programs start a copy of themselves, for example to test crash handling or run workers. They ask for their own executable and run it again. Under in-memory jet run the process file is jet itself, so the program could get jet instead of itself. You ruled in chat on 2026-10-23 that the call returns the script path, and that starting that path runs it through the same jet at the same level. This records it.
decisions.gist: Under `jet run`, should `os.executable()` return the script, the `jet` program, or a built copy?
decisions.lesson: A program that relaunches itself asks for its own executable. Under `jet run` there is no separate program file, only the script and `jet`. Returning the script keeps the call meaning the file that starts this program.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. `os.executable()` returns the path of the file that started the running program. Relaunch means starting a new process of the same program, usually with different arguments.

Beginner path: `process.cmd([os.executable(), "worker"])` starts the same program again, after `jet build` and under `jet run`.

Expert path: after `jet build`, the call names the binary. Under `jet run` it names the absolute script path. A script with `#!/usr/bin/env jet` and the exec bit runs directly when started.
decisions.story: Sam's test program starts itself six times to check that cleanup runs on every kind of exit. Built, it works. Under the old in-memory runner it started `jet` with the wrong arguments and every case failed.
decisions.inWild:
$ python3 -c 'import sys; print(sys.executable)'   # the python program
$ node -p process.execPath                         # the node program
$ go run .   # os.Executable() is the built copy in Go's cache
decisions.detail:
OWNER RULINGS

Owner decision, chat on 2026-10-23 at 05:29, relayed by Main: os.executable() returns the script path under jet run.

Owner answers, chat on 2026-10-23 at about 05:50, recorded on card c0vsqf8a as binding. They read:

(a) “Relaunch: launching the running program’s own script path (os.executable() under jet run) runs it through the same jet at the same level.”

(b) “Tier-up includes on-stack replacement at loop heads today.”

(c) “A crash under in-memory jet run exits with the real signal, same as the built binary (no conversion to exit 1).”

This ballot records both for one-click confirmation. The alternatives are kept for the record. Source card #4346, found on 2026-10-02 under the old in-memory runner, where the call returned jet.

Today. `jet run` builds `.jet/build/<stem>` and starts it as a child, so the call returns that file. A shebang script on its repeat path returns the kept copy in `~/.cache/jet/scripts`. The ExecBallots probe confirmed both on 2026-10-23. So #4346 does not show today; it returns with in-memory O0, where `/proc/self/exe` is `jet`.

What it touches. I9 holds with one stated meaning: the file that starts this program. After `jet build` that is the binary; under `jet run` it is the script. D-SCRIPT-ENTRY1=A makes a script with `#!/usr/bin/env jet` start through `jet run`, so its path starts the same program. No ratified decision is reversed. The contract row in Docs/spec/reference/core-library.md (line 1754, "Return process facts") gains this sentence.

`Examples/features/io/sys_executable.jet` still says the call names `jet` under `jet run`; that comment comes from the old runner and must be rewritten.

Implementation, from Main's plan (o0-plan.md). The runtime reads the path from `/proc/self/exe` today (JetRuntime CompilerHost.jet). Under the in-memory runner that is `jet`, so jet passes the absolute script path to the image on its start stack. The runtime uses it when present. Built binaries keep `/proc/self/exe`, which is absolute, unlike AT_EXECFN.

The file fallback (D-EXEC-NOEXEC1) passes the same path. `process.argv()[0]` becomes the script path as given, which is what the kernel passes for a shebang script.

Edge case, settled by answer (a). cleanup_matrix.jet relaunches process.cmd([os.executable(), path]), and so do the distributed, storage and watcher examples. Their sources have no shebang and no exec bit, so the kernel alone would refuse to start them.

Rule under A, written beside executable() in core-library.md: starting the running program’s own script path runs it through the same jet at the same level. Every existing relaunch keeps working, and #4346’s six identical traces hold under jet run and after jet build.

HOW A'S DOWNSIDES ARE DESIGNED AWAY

1. Starting a script without a shebang. Jet code never needs the kernel to do it: under ruling (a), process.cmd with the program's own script path runs it through the same jet at the same level. Outside programs start a .jet file with jet run, as they do today.

2. Files beside the executable. Under jet run they resolve beside the script, where its files live. A built binary keeps its own folder.

No loss remains.

options.name: Return the script path
options.detail: Under `jet run`, `os.executable()` returns the absolute path of the script. After `jet build` it returns the binary. Starting that path runs the same program again. `process.argv()[0]` is the script path as given.
options.technical: jet passes the absolute script path to the loaded image; the runtime uses it instead of /proc/self/exe. Built binaries are unchanged. The file fallback passes the same path. Starting the own script path reuses the same jet and level.

options.name: Return `jet`, add a relaunch call
options.detail: `os.executable()` always names the process file: `jet` under `jet run`. A new call returns the full command that starts this program again, such as `jet run app.jet`. Existing relaunching programs must switch to it.
options.technical: Keeps `/proc/self/exe` on every tier. Adds a public API, say `process.self_command() -> [String]`, returning `[jet, "run", script]` or `[binary]`. Migrates cleanup_matrix and three other examples. A new public API needs its own surface review.

options.name: Return a built copy
options.detail: On the first call, Jet writes a real program file for this script into its cache and returns that path, as `go run` does. Relaunches start the built copy. The first call costs a full build and link.
