decisions.title: Typed row handles for add-only column tables
decisions.situation: Large programs such as compilers, games and databases keep huge tables of small records and refer to one record by its row number. In Jet that row number is a plain Int, so a node number can be used on the type table by mistake and silently read the wrong record. Jet already stores tables as packed columns and can share frozen data with tasks; only a safe row name is missing. The vote decides that name; we recommend an add-only table that hands out a typed row handle for each record.
decisions.gist: How should a program name one row of a large add-only table of records?
decisions.lesson: A column table keeps each field of a record in its own packed list, so a scan of one field is fast. Jet already has this as Columns<T>, and it already has freeze for sharing data with tasks. What it lacks is a safe name for one row. Today a row is a plain Int, so a node number can index the type table by mistake.
decisions.story: Priya writes a compiler in Jet. Her syntax nodes, types and functions each live in a big table that only grows. She once passed a node number to the type table, and the program printed a wrong type for an hour before she found it. She wants the compiler to catch that mix-up.
decisions.detail:
Already settled, so not on this ballot. Column storage is Columns<T> with field views such as ps.y (D-SOA-SITE1=A). Every tier shares one column store (D-SOA-TIER1=A). Read-only sharing with tasks is freeze(x) (D-CONC-FREEZE1=A). Tables that delete rows use Pool<T> and ID<T>. This ballot decides only the handle for tables that only grow.

Why now: the S3 compiler core (card #5073, D-ARCH-IR1) stores the syntax tree, sema results and flat IR as add-only tables. Those tables are keyed by u32 ids (RustOut-4 s3-design.md, O0Speed-3 flat-ir.md). RustOut-4 proposed a library IdTable<T>, merged here as option A. It is renamed Rows<T> and Row<T> for two reasons. Id<T> next to Pool’s ID<T> differs only in case. The spec also rules out a public Table<T> (D-QUERY-RETAIN1=A).

Measured on the HEAD self-compile (seed a0_017), with one Int-indexed list per IR field. Copies in jet_ir_unique are 13% of ir.opt CPU. Freeing the IR takes about 0.1 s of main-thread time after object writing. The IR merge spends another 0.06 s on duplicate drops. Allocator self time is 9-19% of every phase.

Research. The Rust compiler uses IndexVec with a typed u32 index per table, and push returns the new index. Cranelift uses PrimaryMap, an add-only table with typed u32 keys. Its SecondaryMap side tables reuse the same keys, which is the S3 side-table pattern. Zig’s MultiArrayList stores columns but indexes with a plain usize. The Zig compiler then wraps those indexes in its own enum types, the per-program wrapper that option C leaves to users. No widely used system uses a run-time flag like option B.

options.name: Add-only Rows<T> with Row<T> handles
options.detail: Rows<T> is a Core collection for any struct T, laid out exactly like Columns<T>. It has add, len, index by Row<T>, iteration, field column views and freeze. It has no remove, insert, sort or other reordering, so every handed-out Row<T> stays valid for the table's life. A Row<T> from one table cannot index a table of a different T.
options.technical: Row<T> is a 4-byte copyable u32 index; Row<T>.index() returns it as Int for printing and hashing. add panics past 4,294,967,295 rows. Rows<T> shares the column store and field-view lowering of Columns<T>, so it adds a type and methods, not a second layout. Indexing is bounds-checked like list indexing. freeze(rows) gives tasks lock-free reads. A side table is a [U] indexed by row.index().
options.code:
nodes := Rows<Node>{}
id :: nodes.add(Node{kind: .Call, line: 3})
print(nodes[id].line)
nodes[id].line = 4
kinds :: nodes.kind          // column view
shared :: freeze(nodes)       // tasks may read

options.name: Columns<T> hands out rows itself
options.detail: Columns<T> gains add, which returns a Row<T>. Once any row has been handed out, remove, insert and sort panic at run time because they would move rows under existing handles.
options.technical: Each Columns<T> carries a 'rows handed out' flag set by add and checked by every reordering method. The compiler cannot prove the flag statically, so misuse is a run-time panic.
options.code:
nodes := Columns<Node>{}
id :: nodes.add(Node{kind: .Call, line: 3})
print(nodes[id].line)
nodes.remove(0)   // panics: rows were handed out

options.name: Keep plain Int rows
options.detail: No new API. Programs index Columns<T> with Int. Each program that wants safety writes its own wrapper struct per table.
options.technical: No compiler or Core change.
options.code:
nodes := Columns<Node>{}
nodes.push(Node{kind: .Call, line: 3})
id :: nodes.len() - 1
print(nodes[id].line)

comparisons.note: IndexVec with a typed u32 index per table: https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/nightly-rustc/rustc_index/vec/struct.IndexVec.html.
comparisons.code:
let id: NodeId = nodes.push(node);
let line = nodes[id].line;

comparisons.note: PrimaryMap is add-only with typed keys; SecondaryMap adds side tables: https://docs.rs/cranelift-entity/latest/cranelift_entity/struct.PrimaryMap.html.
comparisons.code:
let block: Block = blocks.push(BlockData::new());
let data = &blocks[block];

comparisons.note: MultiArrayList stores columns but indexes with usize: https://ziglang.org/documentation/master/std/#std.MultiArrayList.

recommendation.why: Most big tables only ever grow. A separate add-only type turns that fact into a compile-time rule, so handles stay valid and cannot cross tables.
gains: Wrong-table and stale-row bugs become compile errors.
Small handles keep large tables compact.

losses.loss: One more collection type next to Columns<T>.
losses.mitigation: Rows<T> is Columns<T> without remove or insert; the docs show it beside Pool<T> and ID<T>.

losses.loss: At most about 4 billion rows per table.
losses.mitigation: add panics with a clear message past the limit; larger tables use Columns<T> with Int indexes.

whyNot.reason: B catches a removal only when it runs, and only after some row was handed out.
C keeps the wrong-table bug and leaves every program to write its own wrapper.

recommendation.tradeoff: Tables that must delete rows keep using Pool<T> or Columns<T>; add-only tables get checked handles.

decisions.title: Unfinished dev server: delete and rebuild lean, or finish the copy
decisions.situation: Jet has a dev server that is meant to show live app previews, browser devtools and the editor helper that powers code completion. It was copied from the old Rust compiler but never finished, so it does not compile and every one of those commands refuses to run. Plain jet dev, which reruns your program on save, already works without it. The vote decides whether to delete the copy and rebuild the editor helper fresh, or to finish the copy.
decisions.gist: Should Jet finish the half-ported dev server, or delete it and rebuild only the editor helper fresh?
decisions.lesson: The dev server is the part of Jet that hosts live app previews, the browser devtools and the editor helper. It was copied from the old Rust compiler but never finished, so all of those commands refuse to run today. Plain jet dev, which reruns a program when you save, already works without it. Whichever wins, the editor helper must work again.
decisions.story: Mia opens a Jet project in her editor and gets no completions, because the editor helper depends on the unfinished dev server. She just wants completions back; she has never used live previews.
decisions.inWild:
$ gopls version
golang.org/x/tools/gopls v0.x
# https://go.dev/gopls
decisions.detail: Census by O0Image-3 on 2026-10-24 ($JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/O0Image/g3/CENSUS.md): Compiler/JetDevserver is a 15.4k-line port of the deleted crates/jet-devserver with 1626 check errors, outside the build. Callers that refuse with E2104: jet dev --canvas, jet run --app/--share, jet self devtools, jet self lsp (JetLSP depends on it). Core/Web/Devserver.jet declares jet_devserver_* routes with no runtime implementation. JetCanvas and JetDebug are orphaned if it is deleted. Card #5931.

options.name: Delete and rebuild lean
options.detail: Delete Compiler/JetDevserver and the jet_devserver_* routes. Rebuild JetLSP so it no longer depends on the dev server. File one card each for live preview (canvas), app sharing and devtools, to be rebuilt on the Jet runtime later.
options.technical: JetLSP is cut loose from JetDevserver; the dead E2104 refusals are replaced by honest not-built-yet errors tied to cards.
options.code:
$ jet self lsp
# starts the editor helper; no dev server needed
$ jet dev --canvas app.jet
Error: live preview is not built yet (tracked card)

options.name: Finish the copy
options.detail: Keep Compiler/JetDevserver and fix it until it type-checks and builds, add the missing jet_devserver_* runtime routes, then switch each refusing command back on.
options.technical: Requires clearing 1626 check errors in Rust-shaped code and implementing the runtime routes.
options.code:
$ jet dev --canvas app.jet
# opens the live preview again
$ jet self lsp
# starts the editor helper through the dev server

comparisons.note: Go keeps its editor helper, gopls, as its own small program, separate from any preview server. See https://go.dev/gopls.

recommendation.why: Nothing works today either way. A fresh, small editor helper returns the most-used feature soonest, and previews get a design that fits Jet instead of the old Rust shape.
gains: The editor helper returns without waiting for previews.

losses.loss: Live previews and devtools stay off for a while.
losses.mitigation: Each gets its own card with a plan, so it is rebuilt when a lane is free.

whyNot.reason: B spends far more work reviving a Rust-shaped design and keeps the editor helper blocked behind it.

recommendation.tradeoff: Previews return later, but on a clean design; the editor helper returns first.

decisions.title: What `jet test` does at the top of a workspace
decisions.situation: A workspace is a folder with several packages inside it. Its top file lists them. At the top today, `jet check`, `test`, `build` and `doc` fail. The error asks you to pick one package. `jet fmt` already formats every package from the top. Inside a package, commands work. But each package then makes its own cache folder, which is a bug. So CI has no single command that checks everything. The vote decides what these commands do at the top.
decisions.gist: What should `jet test` do at the top of a workspace (a folder of packages)?
decisions.lesson: Test every package in one run with one report; `-p app` picks just one.
decisions.story: Ana's team keeps an app and two libraries in one workspace. CI runs `jet test` at the top and gets one report.
decisions.inWild:
Option            Plain `jet test`  New syntax       Like
A every package   tests all         none             Cargo*, Deno
B add a flag      error             --workspace      Cargo, pnpm -r
C list defaults   listed only       default_members  Cargo
D path patterns   error             ./...            Go, Bazel
* when the top folder has no package of its own
decisions.detail:
WHAT WE BUILD
- Top-folder commands plan one build of every package instead of error E2104 (Compiler/JetCli/Source/Cli/Entry.jet:1119; the error is at :1184).
- `jet run` keeps E2104 but counts only packages that can run. Today a library counts.
- `-p` can repeat (Compiler/JetCli/Source/Cli/Front.jet:638).
- Driver: check several packages in one session and reuse shared results. Today each package is its own program.
- `--affected`: new, computed from the build cache's input hashes.

- One report that keeps going, with a line per package and a non-zero exit on failure.
- One `.jet/` at the top for every command (Docs/spec/architecture.md:1575-1579). Today each package makes its own.
- Docs: the five commands in the CLI reference, and the E2104 text.

EVIDENCE
- Probe workspace with a library, an app and a tool (notes/mono_probe.log). At the top, check, build, test, run and doc fail with E2104.
- `jet fmt` at the top succeeds; git then shows all three package.jet files changed.
- Inside packages the commands work, but each package gets its own `.jet/`.

IDS
D-CLI-BARE1=A (syntax-decisions.md:7144). D-JPK-SELECTOR1=C (:7303: repeatable -p, --affected, no pattern syntax). D-MONOREF1 (:5501). D-ECO-MEMBERS1 (:7364). Owner ruling 2026-09-30: one .jet/ at the workspace root (architecture.md:1577).

options.name: Every package, one run
options.detail: At the top, `check`, `test`, `build` and `doc` cover every package at once. Gains: One command checks the whole repository. Shared code is checked once, not once per package. One report lists every failure. Losses: A full run takes longer than one package. The same command does more at the top than in a package.
options.technical:
At the top, `check`, `test`, `build` and `doc` see one build of every package. Shared packages, Core included, are checked once per run. Packages that don't depend on each other run in parallel. A failure doesn't stop the rest. One report lists every failure, and the exit code is non-zero. `-p` can repeat: `-p app -p geometry`. `--affected` runs what changed, plus the packages that use it. A path, as in `jet test packages/app`, picks that package.

Inside a package folder, commands cover that package only. The first output line says what runs, like `testing 3 packages`. All runs share one `.jet/` cache folder at the top. `jet fmt` already covers every package from the top. `jet run` still asks which program to start. It lists only packages that can run.
options.code:
# A: the top means every package
$ jet test                  # every package, one report
$ jet test -p app           # just app
$ jet test --affected       # only what changed

options.name: Add a flag
options.detail: The error stays. `jet test --workspace` runs every package. Gains: Nothing changes for current users. Same as Cargo's `--workspace`. Losses: The first command a newcomer types still fails. Every CI script needs the flag.
options.technical: The same one-run build as A, but only with `--workspace`.
options.code:
# B: the error stays; a flag runs everything
$ jet test                  # error: pick a package
$ jet test --workspace      # every package

options.name: List the defaults
options.detail: The top file lists which packages run from the top. Gains: Slow packages can be left out. Losses: A new package is skipped until someone lists it. Without the list, the top still fails.
options.technical: A `default_members:` field, as in Cargo.
options.code:
# C: the top package.jet lists the defaults
default_members: ["packages/app"]
$ jet test                  # app only

options.name: Path patterns
options.detail: `jet test ./...` runs everything below this folder. Gains: One pattern picks any part of the tree. Losses: A pattern syntax to learn. Plain `jet test` at the top still fails.
options.technical: Patterns as in Go and Bazel.
options.code:
# D: type a pattern
$ jet test ./...            # everything below here
$ jet test                  # still an error

comparisons.note: With no package at the top, every package runs. Otherwise add `--workspace`. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/workspaces.html
comparisons.code:
# Cargo: all, one, or keep going
$ cargo test --workspace
$ cargo test -p app
$ cargo test --no-fail-fast

comparisons.note: `./...` means every package below here. Source: https://pkg.go.dev/cmd/go#hdr-Package_lists_and_patterns
comparisons.code:
# Go: patterns pick packages
$ go test ./...   # every package below here
$ go test         # only this folder

comparisons.note: `-r` runs every package, in order. Source: https://pnpm.io/filtering
comparisons.code:
# pnpm: a flag for all, a filter for some
$ pnpm -r test
$ pnpm --filter "...[origin/main]" test

comparisons.note: `//...` tests everything, with a shared cache. Source: https://bazel.build/run/build#specifying-build-targets
comparisons.code:
# Bazel: all, or one subtree
$ bazel test //...
$ bazel test //app/...

comparisons.note: Runs a task for every project, or only changed ones. Source: https://nx.dev/ci/features/affected
comparisons.code:
# Nx: all, or only what changed
$ nx run-many -t test
$ nx affected -t test

comparisons.note: The top deno.json lists packages; `deno test` covers them. Source: https://docs.deno.com/runtime/fundamentals/workspaces/
comparisons.code:
# Deno: the top covers every package
{ "workspace": ["./app", "./geometry"] }   // deno.json
$ deno test

recommendation.why: People expect the top folder to mean the whole project. `jet fmt` already works this way. One run also shares work between packages.
gains: One command checks everything, as CI needs.
Picking fewer uses `-p`, which already exists.

losses.loss: A full run takes longer than one package.
losses.mitigation: `-p app` runs one package. `--affected` runs only what changed.

losses.loss: The same command does more at the top than in a package.
losses.mitigation: The first output line says what runs, like `testing 3 packages`.

whyNot.reason: The first command people type would still fail.
New packages would be skipped without warning.
It adds a pattern syntax, and plain `jet test` still fails.

recommendation.tradeoff: The top does the whole job by default; one flag narrows it.

whyNot.reason: The first command people type would still fail.
New packages would be skipped without warning.
It adds a pattern syntax, and plain `jet test` still fails.

recommendation.tradeoff: The top does the whole job by default; one flag narrows it.

decisions.title: Where the lock file lives
decisions.situation: A lock file records the exact library versions a project uses, so every computer builds the same program. Today Jet keeps it inside a hidden folder that also holds throwaway build output, and new projects tell git to ignore it. Teammates and CI can then build with different library versions, and deleting the hidden folder silently drops the lock. The owner decides where the lock lives; we recommend a committed file at the project root, so the hidden folder is always safe to delete.
decisions.gist: Where should the lock file live so it is committed and the build folder stays disposable?
decisions.lesson: A lock file records the exact versions a project builds with, so every machine gets the same result. Today Jet keeps it inside `.jet/`, the folder for generated files, and `jet new` tells git to ignore it. The lock also stores a build time, which must move out whichever option wins.
decisions.story: Ben clones a teammate's project and gets a different library version than she tested with, because her lock was never committed.
decisions.inWild:
my-app/
  Cargo.toml
  Cargo.lock   # committed
  target/      # ignored
# Cargo keeps Cargo.lock at the project root and commits it for applications; build output goes to target/. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/guide/cargo-toml-vs-cargo-lock.html
decisions.detail: Audit 2026-10-28 LAY-02, LAY-06: generated .gitignore lists .jet/build/ .jet/lock .jet/cache/ (Compiler/JetCli Host.jet:1478); the lock carries [build.stamp]. Related: D-LOCK1 (spec: commit the lock for executables), D-GENERATED-STORAGE2=B (one top-level .jet), #3421.

options.name: Root jet.lock
options.detail: Move the lock to `jet.lock` at the project root and commit it; `.jet/` holds only throwaway files. Gains: `.gitignore` is one line: `.jet/`. Deleting `.jet/` is always safe. Losses: One more file at the project root.
options.technical: The lock path becomes <root>/jet.lock; [build.stamp] moves to .jet/build/stamp; jet new writes a one-line .gitignore.
options.code:
hello/
  package.jet
  jet.lock     # committed
  .jet/        # ignored, safe to delete

options.name: Cleaned .jet/lock
options.detail: Keep `.jet/lock`, remove machine state from it, and commit it. Gains: No new file at the root. Losses: `.jet/` mixes kept and throwaway files. The `.gitignore` needs exceptions.
options.technical: The lock stays at .jet/lock without [build.stamp]; .gitignore ignores .jet/* except .jet/lock.
options.code:
hello/
  package.jet
  .jet/lock    # committed
  .jet/build/  # ignored

options.name: Never commit the lock
options.detail: Keep the lock as a local file that is never committed. Gains: No lock changes in commits. Losses: Two machines may build different versions.
options.technical: Reverses the spec rule that executables commit their lock.
options.code:
hello/
  package.jet
  .jet/        # ignored, lock rebuilt per machine

comparisons.note: Cargo keeps Cargo.lock at the project root and commits it for applications; build output goes to target/. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/guide/cargo-toml-vs-cargo-lock.html
comparisons.code:
my-app/
  Cargo.toml
  Cargo.lock   # committed
  target/      # ignored

recommendation.why: A root lock is the common habit and makes `.jet/` safe to delete, which is the simplest rule to teach.
gains: Builds repeat across machines, and cleanup is one safe delete.

losses.loss: One more file at the project root.
losses.mitigation: It is one small file, the same habit as Cargo.lock or go.sum.

whyNot.reason: Keeps a committed file inside a folder people delete.
Gives up repeatable builds.

recommendation.tradeoff: One visible root file in exchange for a folder that is always safe to delete.

decisions.title: Optimization flags versus profile settings
decisions.situation: A build profile is a named group of build settings, such as debug or release. Jet already has a profile flag and a release shortcut, and it also has separate flags that change optimization and inlining one at a time. Users meet three ways to ask for a fast build, and the help page grows longer for each. The owner decides whether the separate flags stay; we recommend moving those settings into profiles in the project file and keeping only the profile flag and the release shortcut.
decisions.gist: Should optimization and inlining stay as build flags, or become profile settings only?
decisions.lesson: A profile is a named set of build settings, such as debug or release. Jet already has `--profile` and the `--release` shortcut. It also has `--optimize`, `--opt-level` and `--inline`, which change the same settings one at a time. Whichever option wins, `--release` stays.
decisions.story: Kim wants a fast build and finds three different flags in help. She is unsure which one the team uses.
decisions.inWild:
# Cargo.toml
[profile.release]
opt-level = 3
$ cargo build --release
# Cargo offers --release and --profile; optimization level lives in profile settings. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/profiles.html
decisions.detail: Audit 2026-10-28 CLI-03, CLI-04: jet --help is 419 lines and 249 flags. Ratified: D-CONF-WORD1 and D-BUILD-DEFAULT1 (--profile plus --release sugar); the audit's "--release only" variant would reopen D-CONF-WORD1 and is not offered. Host #4913 (short help). Exact profile field spelling follows the manifest rules.

options.name: Profile settings only
options.detail: Remove `--optimize`, `--opt-level` and `--inline`; set them per profile in package.jet. Gains: One way to ask for a fast build. Help gets shorter. Losses: A one-off experiment needs a profile edit.
options.technical: The three flags leave the option table; profile entries in package.jet carry opt_level and inline.

options.name: Keep every flag
options.detail: Keep all flags as they are. Gains: No change for existing scripts. Losses: Three spellings for one intent. Help stays long.
options.technical: Status quo.
options.code:
$ jet build --release
$ jet build --optimize --inline
$ jet build --profile=release --opt-level=3

comparisons.note: Cargo offers --release and --profile; optimization level lives in profile settings. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/profiles.html

recommendation.why: One way to ask for a fast build is easier to teach and shortens help, and profiles already hold these settings.
gains: Shorter help and one clear spelling.

losses.loss: A one-off experiment needs a profile edit.
losses.mitigation: Add a named profile once, then build with `--profile=<name>`.

whyNot.reason: Keeps three spellings for the same request.

recommendation.tradeoff: Less ad hoc tuning from the command line in exchange for one clear way.

decisions.title: A dataframe in Core or in packages
decisions.situation: A dataframe is a table of named columns that you can filter, group and join, like a spreadsheet inside a program. Jet has decided how files are read into columns, but it has no table type, so analysts loop over rows by hand. Data analysis is a goal for Jet, and every peer language offers a table type. The owner decides whether Core ships one; we recommend a lazy table type in Core built on the shared column format and compute operations.
decisions.gist: Should Core ship a dataframe for table data, or leave it to packages?
decisions.lesson: A dataframe is a table of named columns you can filter, group and join. Jet has decided how files are read into column batches but has no table type to work with them. Whichever option wins, tables run on Jet's shared compute operations rather than a second engine.
decisions.story: Rosa has a sales CSV and wants monthly totals for one region. In Jet today she writes the loop and the grouping herself.
decisions.inWild:
pl.scan_csv("sales.csv")
  .filter(pl.col("region") == "EU")
  .group_by("month").agg(pl.col("amount").sum())
  .collect()
# Polars offers a lazy dataframe over Arrow memory. Source: https://docs.pola.rs/
decisions.detail: Audit 2026-10-28 domain gaps (B12 dataframe half). Ratified context: D-COMPUTE1=D (dataframes integrate through the operation family), D-COLUMNAR-BOUNDARY1, D-DATA-READER1 (scan into column batches). The AI/ML half of B12 is replaced by D-ACCEL-LIB1. Snippets use illustrative method names.

options.name: Dataframe in Core
options.detail: Ship a lazy table type in Core over the shared column batches. Gains: Data analysis works with no extra package. One table type shared by every data package. Losses: Core grows a large API to maintain.
options.technical: core.data.frame wraps the Arrow import and ColumnBatch; operators lower to core.compute operations; evaluation is lazy until print or collect.
options.code:
sales :: data.frame("sales.csv")?
by_month :: sales.filter(region == "EU").group_by(month).sum(amount)
print(by_month)

options.name: Packages only
options.detail: Core keeps column batches; table types come from packages. Gains: Core stays small. Losses: Competing table types that do not work together. Analysts must choose a package first.
options.technical: Core exposes ColumnBatch only.
options.code:
use some_frames
sales :: some_frames.read_csv("sales.csv")?
print(sales.filter(...).group_by(...).sum(...))

comparisons.note: Polars offers a lazy dataframe over Arrow memory. Source: https://docs.pola.rs/

recommendation.why: One shared table type makes data work possible out of the box and lets packages interoperate instead of competing.
gains: Analysts start working without choosing a package.

losses.loss: Core grows a large API to maintain.
losses.mitigation: Start with filter, group, join, sort and select, and measure each against Polars.

whyNot.reason: Splits the ecosystem into table types that cannot work together.

recommendation.tradeoff: A bigger Core in exchange for data analysis that works on day one.

decisions.title: Order for bringing build targets back on the self-hosted compiler
decisions.situation: A build target is a kind of machine or runtime a program can be built for, such as a web browser or a phone chip. On the current compiler, asking for any target other than the local machine fails. Each target is a large piece of work, so the order decides which users are served first. The owner decides that order; we recommend web assembly first, then the ARM chips used by phones and modern laptops, then small embedded boards.
decisions.gist: In what order should build targets return on the self-hosted compiler?
decisions.lesson: A target is the kind of machine a program is built for. On the current compiler, every non-native target answers "not built yet". Earlier support was proven on a compiler that has been retired. Whichever order wins, each target returns with tests that run the built program.
decisions.story: Lin wants to ship a small web service as a WebAssembly component, but `jet build --target` fails today.
decisions.inWild:
$ GOOS=wasip1 GOARCH=wasm go build -o app.wasm
# Go builds for another platform by setting two environment variables. Source: https://go.dev/doc/install/source#environment
decisions.detail: Audit 2026-10-28 TIER-01: --target answers E2104 on the self-hosted CLI; #1914 criteria proven on the Rust path are reopened by draft 12. Order: wasm32-wasip2 (#1914), then aarch64 (#4136), then embedded; e13 Cross Platform is recorded only and not touched here.

options.name: Web, then ARM, then embedded
options.detail: WebAssembly first, then ARM64, then embedded boards. Gains: Web services and browsers are served first. ARM64 covers phones and modern laptops next. Losses: Embedded users wait longest.
options.technical: wasm32-wasip2 (#1914) -> aarch64 (#4136) -> embedded.
options.code:
$ jet build --target=wasm32-wasip2    # first
$ jet build --target=aarch64-linux    # second
$ jet build --target=thumbv7em        # third

options.name: ARM first
options.detail: ARM64 first, then WebAssembly, then embedded boards. Gains: Native phone and laptop builds arrive sooner. Losses: Web deployment waits.
options.technical: aarch64 (#4136) -> wasm32 (#1914) -> embedded.
options.code:
$ jet build --target=aarch64-linux    # first
$ jet build --target=wasm32-wasip2    # second
$ jet build --target=thumbv7em        # third

comparisons.note: Go builds for another platform by setting two environment variables. Source: https://go.dev/doc/install/source#environment

recommendation.why: WebAssembly serves the web and server-side component users first, and an earlier version of it already worked.
gains: The broadest audience gets a working target first.

losses.loss: Embedded users wait longest.
losses.mitigation: Embedded keeps its own card and starts once ARM64 lands.

whyNot.reason: Delays the target with the widest reach.

recommendation.tradeoff: Web first, native ARM second.

decisions.title: New GPUs and accelerators arrive as libraries
decisions.situation: An accelerator is a chip, like a graphics card, that runs number-heavy work much faster than the main processor. Today every accelerator family Jet can use is wired into Jet itself, so supporting a new chip means changing the language. New AI chips appear every year, and users of those chips cannot wait for a language release. The owner decides how new hardware support arrives; we recommend a public interface so a library can add a new device, checked against the main-processor result.
decisions.gist: Should a library be able to add support for a new GPU or accelerator?
decisions.lesson: An accelerator is a chip, like a GPU, that runs number-heavy work fast. Jet's own code knows each GPU family today. The Mojo language lets a hardware maker add a chip by shipping a library. Whichever option wins, results on any device must match the main processor's result.
decisions.story: A startup ships a new AI chip. Its engineers want Jet programs to use it next month, without waiting for a Jet release.
decisions.inWild:
from gpu.host import DeviceContext
var ctx = DeviceContext()
ctx.enqueue_function[scale](input, grid_dim=1, block_dim=64)
# Mojo targets accelerators through libraries written in Mojo, so new hardware support ships as library code. Source: https://docs.modular.com/mojo/manual/gpu/basics
decisions.detail:
Owner direction 2026-10-28: this replaces the audit's "restore AI/ML / re-scope #3955". It builds on ratified D-CORE-BOUNDARY1=A: CPU chip instructions are Core library entries (#4565). It also builds on D-HOST-CAPS1=A: packages add hardware kinds (#4195). D-GPU-PACKAGING1=A, D-COMPUTE1=D and D-COMPUTE-BACKEND1=D apply too. Core owns the compute contract with a CPU reference. Related: #3026, #3028, #4731, #4762, #3955. Snippet names are illustrative.

FutureAudit 2026-10-28 (FUTURE.md T25) refines option A; owner direction folds its D-KERNELIR1 here, no separate ballot. The provider interface covers caps, lower, load, launch, alloc and copy over a public, versioned kernel IR (a subset of the compiler IR). MLIR was weighed and rejected (I6; research avoid-list).

A typed Device value from D-HOST-CAPS1 replaces the string devices in Core/Compute/Solve.jet:83-84; #Kernel stays the restricted subset with a CPU reference (D-COMPUTE-KERNEL-SURFACE1=B). First providers are mined from the Rust-era CUDA, Metal and Vulkan/WebGPU backends (#1144-#1146). Per-vendor backends inside the compiler would contradict D-CORE-BOUNDARY1=A.

options.name: Public device interface
options.detail: A package adds a device by implementing a public interface; it must pass the CPU-reference tests. Gains: New chips arrive without a Jet release. Built-in GPUs use the same interface. Losses: The interface becomes a public promise.
options.technical: A provider interface covers code generation for kernels, memory transfer and launch; providers declare their hardware kind (D-HOST-CAPS1) and must pass the CPU-reference conformance suite before selection.
options.code:
use acme_npu                        // package adds the device
device :: compute.select(.npu)?
out :: device.run(scale, input)?    // checked against CPU result

options.name: Fixed list in Core
options.detail: Core keeps the list of supported device families; new ones need a Jet change. Gains: Full control over every device path. Losses: New chips wait for a Jet release. Core grows with every device family.
options.technical: Status quo.

options.name: Foreign libraries only
options.detail: New chips are reached only by calling their vendor libraries through FFI. Gains: No new interface to design. Losses: No shared compute model or result checks. Every program wires each vendor by hand.
options.technical: Vendors are reached through FFI bindings only; core.compute does not see them.
options.code:
use c.[acme_npu_sdk as npu]
npu.launch("scale", input)

comparisons.note: Mojo targets accelerators through libraries written in Mojo, so new hardware support ships as library code. Source: https://docs.modular.com/mojo/manual/gpu/basics

recommendation.why: A public device interface lets hardware makers add chips themselves, while the CPU-reference tests keep every device's answers correct.
gains: Hardware support grows without waiting for Jet releases.

losses.loss: The interface becomes a public promise.
losses.mitigation: Version the interface, and port the built-in GPUs to it first to prove it.

whyNot.reason: Every new chip waits for a Jet release.
Gives up the shared compute model and its correctness checks.

recommendation.tradeoff: A public interface to maintain in exchange for hardware support that scales with the industry.

decisions.situation: Newcomers type words from languages they already know, such as let, for, while or match. decisions.lesson: Newcomers type words such as `let`, `for`, `while` or `match`. A teaching message names the Jet form to use instead. That work was paused, so these lines get a generic error today. Whichever option wins, any teaching comes from one table with a tested message per row.

decisions.title: Keep inline C as the one inline shape, beside header bindings for libraries
decisions.situation: Jet can call C, so programs can reuse C libraries and write small fast helpers. There are two ways in. A Jet function can hold a C body written inline. Or a C library is read through its header file. An audit proposed removing inline C bodies, so each tool handles one way. A check of today's compiler changes the picture. Inline C builds natively, and Jet writes its C prototype from the Jet signature. So the C compiler catches a mismatch. Reading a header does not yet work in the new compiler. The vote decides whether inline C stays.
decisions.gist: Should a Jet function still be able to hold an inline C body?
decisions.lesson: Yes: your own few lines of C go inline, and a C library uses its header.
decisions.story: Ana writes a script with a three-line C helper inline. It stays one file, and it builds.
decisions.inWild:
Option          Inline C   Inline asm   Like
A keep          yes        yes          Go, Nim
B no inline C   no         yes          Rust, Zig, D
C no inline     no         no           Swift
decisions.detail:
WHAT WE BUILD
- No language change. Keep D-FFI-INLINE1=A as ratified for c, cpp and asm.
- Docs: spec "Inline native functions" (spec.md:2785) states the split: inline for a few lines of your own C, header binding for a library.
- Header import on the self-hosted compiler stays card #4174; jet cc (#1344, D-ADOPT-CC1=B) serves both forms.
- Separate bug card: a plain call to inline C checks without E3103 though the spec requires it.

EVIDENCE
- Compiler/JetCli/Source/Cli/ForeignLink.jet:273-291: Jet writes `ret name(types);` from the Jet signature before the body, so the C compiler rejects a body that disagrees.
- ForeignLink.jet:293-350: each inline body is one translation unit; one strict link refuses unresolved symbols. Compiler/JetBackend/Tests/test-native-inline-c.mjs builds and runs a native inline C program.
- Header import: a probe (deps c@"c", use c.[add as m]) gave E0102; Examples/features/lowlevel/cbind fails check with E1002 and E0067 (bd6, earlier audit).

- Inline C without #Unsafe on the declaration gives E3215 (bd6).

IDS
Keeps D-FFI-INLINE1=A, D-FFI-RAWBODY1, D-FFI-ASM1, D-FFI-CPP1, D-FFI-UNIFY1=A. Audit FFI-01. Host card #4174. Related: D-FFI-UNSAFE1.

options.technical: No language change. Jet writes the C prototype of each body from the Jet signature. So the C compiler rejects a mismatch. Each body compiles as its own C unit, and one strict link refuses unresolved symbols. Header import is finished on the new compiler as already planned. Docs teach the split: your own few lines inline, a library through its header.

options.name: No inline C
options.detail: C lives in its own files, read through a header. C++ and assembly keep inline bodies. Gains: One way to bring in C. Losses: Removes the C path that builds today. A three-line helper needs two extra files.
options.technical: Removes the inline C form. `jet fix` moves each body into a C file with a header. It also adds the package dependency and the use line. It can land only after header import works on the new compiler.

options.name: No inline bodies at all
options.detail: Remove inline bodies for C, C++ and assembly. All foreign code lives in files. Gains: One way for every language. Losses: Removes working inline C and assembly. Even tiny helpers need separate files.

decisions.title: Publishing runs every doc example; coverage is shown, not forced
decisions.situation: A package page helps most when each function shows a working example. In Jet, an example is a code block in a doc comment. `jet test --docs` runs it as a test. The registry already checks gates before it publishes, such as the signature and the name. It checks nothing about examples. So a package can ship with no examples, or with examples that no longer run. The vote decides what publishing checks about examples.

decisions.lesson: Every example must pass to publish, and the page shows how many functions have one.

- Jetpack/Publication/Source/Policy.jet: add an `examples` field to gate_status beside signature, audit, name, liveness and review. Failing doc tests block before artifact or index mutation (Docs/spec/registry-tiers.md:47-53).
- Publish runs the D-TEST4 doc tests (`jet test --docs`; fenced jet blocks in `///`, `EXPR // => VALUE`). `jet test --docs` is not built yet (E2104 in notes/cmd_census.tsv row 100); this gate needs it.
- Registry record: example coverage (passing examples over public functions); shown on the package page and in `jet inspect info`.

- Docs: registry-tiers.md gate list.

EVIDENCE

decisions.title: Checking grows in a straight line with expression size, held by a test
decisions.situation: A type checker works out the type of every expression. In some languages that work explodes on long expressions. Swift can give up on one line of arithmetic. There, one operator can mean many things, chosen by the type its result must have. Jet avoids that design today. But no rule keeps it that way, and no test measures it. A probe found a different limit. Adding up 200 copies of `a` crashes the checker with a stack overflow. The vote decides whether straight-line checking becomes a rule with a test.
decisions.gist: Should checking work grow in a straight line with expression size, as a tested rule?
decisions.lesson: Yes: checking time and depth grow in a straight line, proved by a test.
decisions.story: A generator writes a 5,000-term sum. `jet check` passes in a blink, because a test on every compiler change keeps it so.
decisions.inWild:
Option          Long expression   Result-type picks   Like
A rule + test   checks, linear    never               Go
B best effort   may crash         not ruled out       most compilers
C budget        refused past N    allowed             Swift, TS, Rust
decisions.detail:
WHAT WE BUILD
- Spec: the rule beside D-INFER-LEVEL1 (one pass; expected type read where present; no choice by result type).
- Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Expressions.jet: check left-nested operator chains without recursion depth per term (sema_expr_check_binary :3948, sema_expr_decimal_literal_operand :3825).
- Host gate #4601: a corpus of 1..10,000-term expressions; work counters and stack depth must grow linearly.

EVIDENCE (r14, ballots2/redo/probe/)
- plain_150.jet (150 x `a +`) and lin_150.jet: `jet check` ok.
- plain_200.jet, lin_200.jet and larger: `Stop [E3012]: Stack overflow` in sema_expr_check_binary or sema_expr_decimal_literal_operand, exit 70. This is a compiler crash, which I2 forbids.
- Check time stayed near 100-500 ms up to the crash; the risk shown is depth, not time.

IDS
Consistent with D-INFER-LEVEL1=A and D-TRAIT-OVERLOAD1=A. Does not reopen D-COMPILE-SPEED1 (#4999). FutureAudit 2026-10-28, FUTURE.md T08. File a bug card for the 200-term crash.

options.name: Straight-line rule with a test
options.detail: Checking takes one pass and never picks a function by its result type. A size test runs on every change. Gains: Long and generated code always checks fast. Finds crashes like the 200-term one before users do. Losses: Rules out picking a function by its result type.
options.technical: Expression typing is one pass that reads the expected type where it exists. No function or operator is chosen by the type its result must have. The checker handles long operator chains without deep recursion. The compiler speed gate adds a corpus of expressions from 1 to 10,000 terms. Its work counters and stack depth must grow in a straight line.

options.name: Best effort
options.detail: No rule and no test. Slow or crashing cases are fixed when someone reports them. Gains: No new test to keep. Losses: Nothing stops a later feature from breaking it. Crashes like the 200-term one wait for a user.
options.technical: Today's state. The crash is fixed as an ordinary bug.

options.name: A size budget
options.detail: Past a size or depth budget, the checker stops and asks for a split. Swift and TypeScript do this. Gains: A clear error instead of a crash. Losses: Valid long code is refused. The budget hides slow growth below it.
options.technical: The checker counts steps or depth per expression. Past the budget it reports an error with a fix.

comparisons.note: Result-type overloads make some literal expressions time out. Source: https://www.cocoawithlove.com/blog/2016/07/12/type-checker-issues.html
Deep type instantiation stops at a fixed limit with error 2589. Source: https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/release-notes/typescript-4-5.html
Go has no overloading, so each expression checks in one pass. Source: https://go.dev/doc/faq#overloading
Rust uses result-type inference through traits and sets recursion limits. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/attributes/limits.html

recommendation.why: Jet already avoids the designs that explode. A tested rule keeps it that way. Its first run would have caught the 200-term crash.
gains: Fast checking for any size of code.
Generated code never hits a hidden limit.
Uses the existing compiler speed gate.

losses.loss: Rules out picking a function by its result type.
losses.mitigation: Traits already give one function per operation, and generic calls still read the expected type.

whyNot.reason: It waits for users to find crashes the test finds today.
It refuses valid code instead of checking it.

recommendation.tradeoff: No result-type overloading, for checking that never explodes.

decisions.title: Remote builds speak Jet's own signed protocol, with adapters for existing farms and web stores
decisions.situation: Big teams speed up builds two ways. They share a cache of build results, and they run build steps on a farm of machines. Most farms speak one open protocol, first defined by Bazel. You asked whether Zig copied it. It did not: Zig's build protocol is its own, and it only runs on one machine. Jet's spec already defines signed records for remote results, which that open protocol cannot carry. No wire protocol is chosen yet. The vote picks how Jet talks to remote builders and caches.
decisions.gist: Should remote builds speak Jet's own signed protocol, with adapters for existing build farms?
decisions.lesson: Yes. Jet's protocol carries signed results and Jet's own step names. Existing farms and plain web stores work through adapters, and every result still comes back signed.
decisions.story: Ana's team shares a cache in an ordinary web bucket, because every record is signed and checked on her machine. Later her company's existing farm runs Jet steps through a relay the team runs beside it. Each result comes back signed by that relay, naming the farm.
decisions.inWild:
Option              Core protocol       Existing farms        Like
A Jet's own         signed Jet records  via signing relay     Zig (own), Nix (signed)
B the open protocol Bazel's REAPI       direct                Bazel, Buck2, Pants
C cache only        plain web requests  cache only            Gradle, Turborepo
decisions.detail:
OWNER QUESTION (q3u6bcmb)
Zig made its own. Its compiler server (lib/std/zig/Server.zig) is a small binary message protocol over stdin and stdout between the build runner and the compiler. Messages include error bundles, emit digests, test results, file inputs and timing reports. The build runner adds `--watch`, `--webui`, `--fuzz` and `--time-report`. Zig has no remote cache and no remote execution, and none of this is Bazel's Remote Execution API.

WHY OUR OWN
The open protocol names steps as opaque commands and trusts the farm. Jet's spec (spec.md:4660-4679) requires worker identity and receipts bound to a credential. A stock farm cannot sign those. Copying it would make Jet's typed steps and receipts second-class.

WHAT WE BUILD
- Protocol library `core.build.remote` on the public build-session API: content-addressed blobs, Jet step keys, signed request, result and receipt envelopes (spec.md:4620-4679). `jet remote serve` is a thin command over it.
- Web store adapter: any HTTP or S3-style store holds blobs and signed records. Records are verified locally, so the store needs no trust.

- Farm adapter: `jet remote serve` on a host the team controls, beside an existing farm, relays steps to it over Remote Execution API v2. Each action runs Jet's worker, uploaded as an input blob, so no special farm image is needed.
- The relay holds its own credential and signs every receipt. The receipt names the farm as the trust domain, as D-JPK-REMOTE1=D grants require. So no result reaches a client unsigned.

- `harden: true` can further require receipts from Jet-run workers only; `jet audit` lists which trust domain built each output.
- Adapters are ordinary packages, so anyone can add a peer for another farm or store.

WHY A HAS NO REAL LOSS
- The old loss was unsigned results from farms without Jet's worker image. The relay uploads the worker with each action and signs every receipt, so every farm returns signed, attributed results.
- The relay is one more process only for teams that keep an existing farm; teams on Jet's own servers never run it.

EVIDENCE
- spec.md:4620-4639 defines HMAC-SHA256 request, result, cache-record and CAS-blob envelopes and worker receipts, but no wire protocol.
- `jet remote` exists in r14 help ("manage host-owned remote builders").

IDS
Unchanged: D-JPK-REMOTE1=D (#422: build.remote grants, jet remote bind, no endpoint flags), D-NEST-REMOTECACHE1. Uses D-BUILD-REUSESET1 (`--cache=off` rebuilds locally). FutureAudit 2026-10-28, FUTURE.md T22.

options.name: Jet's own protocol, with adapters
options.detail: Jet's signed records are the wire format, served by `jet remote serve`. Adapters reach plain web stores and existing farms; the farm adapter is a relay that signs every receipt. Gains: every result carries a signed Jet receipt; a cache can live in any web bucket, with no trust in it; teams keep the farm they already run. Losses: none.
options.technical: The protocol is a Core library on the public build API. It moves content-addressed blobs and signed step records keyed by Jet's own step keys. `jet remote serve` runs it on a machine or beside a farm. The web store adapter keeps blobs and records in any HTTP or S3-style store; records are checked locally, so a leaked bucket cannot forge a result. The farm relay speaks the open protocol, ships Jet's worker as an action input, and signs each receipt naming the farm.
options.code:
$ jet remote bind cache s3://corp-builds/jet          # any web store
$ jet remote bind farm jet+grpcs://relay.corp:8980    # relay to the farm
$ jet build --builder farm
1204 steps: 1180 cache hits, 24 run remotely, all receipts signed

options.name: The open protocol at the core
options.detail: Jet speaks Bazel's Remote Execution API directly, for cache and remote steps. Gains: works with existing farms with no adapter. Losses: stock farms cannot sign Jet's receipts; Jet's steps become opaque commands.
options.technical: Jet becomes a client of Remote Execution API v2. Each step becomes a command and an action, named by content hash. A farm is trusted as the trust domain its grant names. Signed receipts ride in result metadata only when the worker is Jet.
options.code:
$ jet remote bind farm grpcs://build.corp:8980
$ jet build --builder farm
1204 steps: 1180 cache hits, 24 run remotely

options.name: Shared cache only
options.detail: Jet shares build results over plain web requests, as Gradle does. It never runs steps remotely. Gains: small and easy to secure. Losses: no remote steps, so cold builds stay slow.
options.technical: Results are stored and fetched by content hash with plain web reads and writes. No remote execution.
options.code:
$ jet remote bind cache https://cache.corp/jet
$ jet build --builder cache
1180 cache hits, 24 built locally

comparisons.note: Its own binary protocol between build runner and compiler, on one machine. Source: https://github.com/ziglang/zig/blob/master/lib/std/zig/Server.zig
comparisons.code:
# Zig: local build runner, its own protocol
$ zig build --watch --webui
$ zig build --time-report

comparisons.note: Defined the Remote Execution API; one flag points at a farm. Source: https://bazel.build/remote/rbe
comparisons.code:
# Bazel
$ bazel build //app --remote_executor=grpcs://farm:8980
INFO: 1180 remote cache hit, 24 remote.

comparisons.note: Meta's build tool speaks the same protocol to the same farms. Source: https://buck2.build/docs/users/remote_execution/
Its own protocol; binary caches are signed, so any web store can host one. Source: https://nix.dev/manual/nix/stable/command-ref/conf-file#conf-trusted-public-keys
comparisons.code:
# nix.conf: a signed cache in a plain web store
substituters = https://cache.corp.example
trusted-public-keys = corp:3k8...=

comparisons.note: The build cache is plain HTTP; there is no remote execution. Source: https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/build_cache.html

recommendation.why: Jet's steps and signed receipts are its own, so its protocol should carry them natively, as Zig and Nix do. A signing relay keeps existing farms usable with no unsigned results. The protocol and every adapter are ordinary libraries.
recommendation.tradeoff: Nothing is given up: existing farms work through a relay, and every result stays signed.
gains: Every result carries a signed Jet receipt.
A cache can live in any web store, with no trust in it.
Teams keep the farms they already run.

whyNot.reason: Stock farms cannot sign Jet's receipts, and Jet's steps become opaque commands.
No remote steps, so cold builds stay slow.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude. Adversarial model family: Claude. Fresh agent: BallotReview. I attacked the trust loss, the cache-only rival and the cited decisions. The build list cited D-JPK-REMOTE1=C, which is the per-command endpoint option; the ratified answer is D, now fixed, and A still wins on reuse of existing farms.

decisions.title: Export a typed Jet config as JSON, YAML or TOML
decisions.situation: Many tools read their settings from JSON, YAML or TOML files. Jet lets a project write configuration in ordinary typed Jet, and can already produce a JSON Schema from a type. Copying those settings into other files by hand repeats them, and the copies drift. The owner decides whether Jet gets a command that writes a checked Jet config value out in those formats. We recommend the command, since the library alone leaves each project writing its own small exporter.
decisions.gist: Should Jet get a command that writes a typed Jet config value out as JSON, YAML or TOML?
decisions.lesson: Configuration is the settings a program or tool reads when it starts. Jet lets you write them as typed Jet values, so mistakes fail early. Other tools need JSON, YAML or TOML files. An export command turns the checked value into those files, so the settings are written once.
decisions.story: Noor keeps a typed Jet config for her service, then hand-copies it into a YAML file for her deployment tool. The copies drift apart.
decisions.inWild:
$ pkl eval -f yaml config.pkl
port: 8080
hosts:
- a.example.com
# Pkl evaluates typed config and renders JSON, YAML or other formats from its command line. Source: https://pkl-lang.org/main/current/pkl-cli/index.html
decisions.detail: FutureAudit 2026-10-28, FUTURE.md T23. Settled and not reopened: D-CONF-PLANE1=A and D-CONF-KEY1=A (one plane of typed facts), D-CORE-JSON-SCHEMA1=A (schema export from codec metadata, #3238), D-SHAPE-ONE1. This ballot is only the command; its spelling is illustrative and counts against the surface budget (D-SURFACE-BUDGET1). Not hosted on #4275, whose ratified scope forbids new ballots. Effect-free, terminating config evaluation is assumed from the comptime rules [INFERENCE].

options.name: Export command
options.detail: One command evaluates a typed config value and writes it as JSON, YAML or TOML. Gains: Settings are written once, in typed Jet. The same output on every project. Losses: One more command.
options.technical: Evaluates a named config value at compile time and encodes it with core.encoding; a schema option writes the JSON Schema from the same codec metadata.
options.code:
$ jet config export app.jet --format yaml
port: 8080
hosts:
- a.example.com

options.name: Library only

decisions.title: Keep a script's approval across comment and format edits
decisions.situation: When you allow a script to use files or the network, Jet remembers that answer for that exact file. Today any change, even fixing a comment, makes Jet ask again. People who are asked too often start saying yes without reading, which defeats the point. The owner decides whether approval survives edits that leave the code unchanged, and whether a real edit can be approved again with one key. We recommend keying on the code itself, and always showing the prompt after a real edit.
decisions.gist: Should a remembered script approval survive edits that change only comments or formatting?
decisions.lesson: Jet remembers your permission answer for one exact script. A fingerprint of the file decides what counts as the same script. A fingerprint of the raw text changes on any edit. A fingerprint of the code's words ignores comments and spacing, so only real code changes ask again.
decisions.story: Ada approved her backup script last week. She fixed a typo in a comment, and Jet asked for permission again as if the script were new.
decisions.inWild:
$ deno run backup.ts
Deno requests write access to "/home/ada/backup".
Allow? [y/n/A]
# Deno remembers nothing between runs: allow flags or a config file are the only way to skip its prompt. Source: https://docs.deno.com/runtime/fundamentals/security/
decisions.detail: Reopens owner ruling #5949 criterion 1 ("editing the file prompts again"; answers remembered per script content hash). Option B is that ruling as written. FutureAudit 2026-10-28, FUTURE.md T11 item 4. Normalized token stream = the lexer's token kinds and texts with comments and whitespace dropped. Option A never approves silently after a code change: the prompt says "same grants as last approved version" and Enter accepts. If the grants differ, the full prompt appears.

options.name: Key on the code; one key after real edits
options.detail: Comment and format edits keep approval; a code edit shows "same grants as before" and Enter accepts. Gains: Fewer prompts, so each one gets read. A code change is never approved silently. Losses: Two fingerprints to explain.
options.technical: Approval key = hash of the normalized token stream (comments and whitespace dropped). A token change shows the grant diff (here none) and needs one key; new grants show the full prompt.
options.code:
$ jet run backup.jet     # comment edited: no prompt
$ jet run backup.jet     # code edited
backup.jet changed; same grants as last approved version
Run it? [Y/n]

options.name: Key on the raw file
options.detail: Any change to the file asks again, as the owner ruling says today. Gains: The simplest rule to explain. Losses: A comment fix costs a full prompt. Frequent prompts teach people to say yes.
options.technical: Approval key = hash of the file bytes (owner ruling #5949 as written).
options.code:
$ jet run backup.jet     # comment edited
backup.jet will: write files ~/backup
Run it? [Y/n/always]

comparisons.note: Deno remembers nothing between runs: allow flags or a config file are the only way to skip its prompt. Source: https://docs.deno.com/runtime/fundamentals/security/
comparisons.code:
$ deno run backup.ts
Deno requests write access to "/home/ada/backup".
Allow? [y/n/A]

recommendation.why: Prompts only protect people who read them; asking again after comment edits trains people to approve blindly, while code edits still always show a prompt.
gains: Approval prompts stay rare and meaningful.

losses.loss: Two fingerprints instead of one.
losses.mitigation: Verbose output names which fingerprint matched and why no prompt appeared.

whyNot.reason: Asks again after edits that cannot change what the script does.

recommendation.tradeoff: A slightly richer rule in exchange for prompts people still read.

decisions.title: Publish packages with short-lived identities, never stored tokens
decisions.situation: To publish a package, a tool must prove it may publish under that name. Most registries use a long-lived secret token, and in 2025 a worm spread through npm by stealing such tokens. Trusted publishing replaces the token with a short-lived identity that a build service issues for one job. The owner decides whether Jet's registry accepts only short-lived identities. We recommend that, with an interactive login that expires within an hour for people publishing from their own machine.
decisions.gist: Should Jet's registry refuse long-lived publish tokens and accept only short-lived identities?
decisions.lesson: To publish a package you prove you own its name. A long-lived token is like a password that works for months, so a thief can reuse it. A short-lived identity comes from a build service for one job and expires within minutes. Signing and the public publish log are already decided.
decisions.story: A worm steals Ana's saved publish token from her laptop and publishes a poisoned version of her package overnight.
decisions.inWild:
permissions:
  id-token: write
steps:
  - run: npm publish   # identity from the CI job, no NPM_TOKEN
# npm trusted publishing lets a GitHub Actions or GitLab CI job publish with an OIDC identity and no token. Source: https://docs.npmjs.com/trusted-publishers
decisions.detail: FutureAudit 2026-10-28, FUTURE.md T15 option B. Already ratified and not reopened: transparency log, sparse TUF metadata and transactional publish (D-JPK-REGISTRY1=D, #423); signing (D-PKGSIGN1); keyless --no-sign (D-PKGSIGN-NOSIGN1=A); trust root (#2199). This ballot is only the upload credential. Short-lived identity = OIDC tokens from configured CI issuers (GitHub, GitLab) bound to repository and workflow, or a device-code login with expiry of at most one hour. Snippet flags are illustrative.

options.name: Short-lived identities only
options.detail: A CI identity or a login that expires within an hour; stored tokens are refused. Gains: Nothing long-lived to steal. The publish log records which job published. Losses: Publishing from a laptop needs a login each session.
options.technical: The registry accepts OIDC tokens from configured issuers, bound to repository and workflow. Each one is recorded in the transparency log. Device-code login issues a credential of at most 1 h; no long-lived API tokens are issued.
options.code:
$ jet registry publish                  # in CI: job identity
published app 1.2.0 by github.com/ana/app release.yml
$ jet registry login                    # laptop: valid 1 hour

options.name: Both kinds
options.detail: Trusted publishing is offered, and long-lived tokens keep working. Gains: Nobody has to change how they publish. Losses: A stolen token still publishes poisoned versions.
options.technical: Both credential kinds accepted; the log marks which was used.
options.code:
$ jet registry publish --token $JET_TOKEN
published app 1.2.0

options.name: Tokens only
options.detail: Keep long-lived tokens as the way to publish. Gains: The simplest registry. Losses: The same risk as the npm worm. No record of which job published.
options.technical: Status quo design.
options.code: $ jet registry publish --token $JET_TOKEN

comparisons.note: npm trusted publishing lets a GitHub Actions or GitLab CI job publish with an OIDC identity and no token. Source: https://docs.npmjs.com/trusted-publishers
comparisons.code:
permissions:
  id-token: write
steps:
  - run: npm publish   # identity from the CI job, no NPM_TOKEN

recommendation.why: Stolen long-lived tokens are how recent registry worms spread; short-lived identities leave nothing worth stealing and record exactly which job published.
gains: A stolen laptop or leaked log cannot publish a package.

losses.loss: Publishing from a laptop needs a fresh login.
losses.mitigation: Login is one command and lasts an hour, enough for a release session.

whyNot.reason: Keeps the token that worms steal, and most people never switch.
Leaves the registry open to the attack that hit npm.

recommendation.tradeoff: A login step for laptop publishing in exchange for no stealable publish secret.

decisions.title: Infrastructure as typed Jet code
decisions.situation: Teams describe servers, databases and networks in tools like Terraform, then apply that description to a cloud. Those tools use their own languages, keep secrets in a state file, and make plans hard to test. A Jet package could describe infrastructure in ordinary typed Jet, with the plan as a value that tests can check. The owner decides whether Jet ships such a package and whether it reuses Terraform's existing provider plugins. We recommend both, after the HTTP library is finished.
decisions.gist: Should Jet ship a first-party infrastructure package that reuses Terraform's provider plugins?
decisions.lesson: Infrastructure as code means you write which servers and databases you want, and a tool makes the cloud match. Terraform does this with its own language and thousands of provider plugins, one per cloud service. Reusing those plugins would give Jet the same reach. Writing the plan in Jet makes it typed and testable.
decisions.story: Raj changes one database setting in a Terraform file. The mistake only shows when apply fails halfway, after two servers have already changed.
decisions.detail: FutureAudit 2026-10-28, FUTURE.md T24. Sequenced after the HTTP client and server (audit card 3: #3665, #4957). Plan = pure value; apply under Net and Secret authority; state = content-addressed lock; Secret values never serialized. The Terraform/OpenTofu plugin protocol is gRPC (tfplugin5/6); licensing of the protocol must be verified [INFERENCE: OpenTofu is MPL-2.0]. Fleet and OS deployment are e9 and out of scope. Related #4195, #5696.

options.name: Package plus Terraform providers
options.detail: A first-party typed package whose resources come from existing Terraform providers. Gains: Thousands of cloud services on day one. Plans are typed values tests can check. Losses: Depends on an outside plugin protocol.
options.technical: Provider schemas imported as typed Jet; the plan evaluates as a pure value; apply talks tfplugin6 gRPC under Net and Secret grants.

options.name: Package with its own providers
options.detail: A first-party package with Jet-written providers for each cloud. Gains: No outside protocol. Losses: Few cloud services for years.
options.technical: First-party providers only.
options.code:
use infra.aws as aws    // provider written in Jet
logs :: aws.S3Bucket{ name: "app-logs" }

options.name: Leave it to the ecosystem
options.detail: No first-party package; community packages may appear. Gains: No first-party cost. Losses: No typed, tested default for teams.
options.technical: Status quo.
options.code: // keep Terraform files beside the Jet app

comparisons.note: Pulumi describes infrastructure in TypeScript, Python or Go and reuses Terraform providers through a bridge. Source: https://www.pulumi.com/docs/iac/concepts/how-pulumi-works/

recommendation.why: A typed plan that tests can check fixes the worst infrastructure failures, and reusing existing providers gives full cloud reach without writing thousands of them.
gains: Services and their infrastructure live in one checked language.

losses.loss: An outside plugin protocol to follow.
losses.mitigation: Pin the protocol version and test providers against recorded plugin replies.

whyNot.reason: Writing a provider for every cloud service would take years.
Teams keep a second, untyped language beside Jet.

recommendation.tradeoff: Dependence on a plugin protocol in exchange for full cloud coverage from day one.

decisions.title: What a library marker body receives at each kind of site, and when it is checked
decisions.situation: A marker declared in a library may run a body that reads facts about the declaration it sits on, adds ordinary code, and may refuse the use. Today that body runs only on structs, top-level functions and text blocks. On an enum, variant, method, field, module or package the marker is accepted and the body silently never runs. The open choice is what the body receives at each kind of site, and when mistakes in it are caught. The recommendation gives nine kinds a typed record, checks the body once where the marker is declared, and makes listing any other kind an error.
decisions.gist: When one marker body can sit on several kinds of declaration, what does it receive, and when is it checked?
decisions.lesson: A marker body is compile-time code that runs once for each place the marker is written; that place is its target. Rust attribute macros receive raw text pieces and parse them. Swift macros receive a parsed declaration and test its kind. C# source generators also test kinds. Jet must say what a body receives and when mistakes are caught.
decisions.story: A library author writes a Route marker for a module and for each function inside it. Today the module use compiles and adds nothing, so a whole group of routes silently vanishes. Under the recommendation the body has one arm for modules and one for functions, and a typo in either arm fails where the marker is declared. A beginner who writes a marker for one kind of site never sees the match.

options.name: A typed record per site, checked once
options.detail:
Nine site kinds get records; a several-kind marker matches on the kind, and the body is checked where declared. Beginners write a one-kind marker and use target directly. Experts list several kinds and write one arm each; a missing arm is an error.

Gains: Mistakes show where the marker is declared. Nine site kinds run library bodies; the rest are errors.

Losses: Several-kind markers need one arm per kind. Nine site records, from type to package, must stay complete.

End effect. A wrong read, such as a field list on a function, fails once at the declaration and names the arm and the record. Nine kinds run the body, and a body that lists any other kind is an error at the declaration. Added items land beside the target, and members are added through an explicit impl block for the owner.
options.technical: A new static checker types a marker body once per declared site kind, at the declaration. With one kind, target is that kind's record. With several, target is a closed site value whose cases are generated from $sites; the type has no source name. Expansion still runs per use, through one site-generic collector. A body that lists a kind without a record is an error at the declaration. Added items join the target's module, and a module target receives them inside itself.

options.name: Same records, checked only at each use
options.detail:
Nine kinds run the body with their records, but reads are checked only when a use expands. Beginners see the same body as today. Experts test every kind themselves, because a wrong read fails only at a use that reaches it.

Gains: Smallest change from today's body rules. No match needed for several kinds.

Losses: A wrong read fails at a user's use site. Untested arms ship broken in libraries.

End effect. Nine kinds run the body, and listing any other kind is an error at the declaration, as in A. A read that does not exist for a kind, such as a field list on a module, fails while expanding that use, inside the user's build.
options.technical: The site-generic collector binds target to the record of each kind, plus a $site member naming the kind. The body stays untyped and is evaluated per use, as today (Derives.jet:1554-1572). A missing member is reported at the use, with the marker declaration named in the detail.

options.name: Bodies only on types, functions and blocks
options.detail:
Other kinds keep marker facts only; a body that lists them is an error at its declaration. Beginners get a clear error instead of silence. Experts act on modules, fields and variants from a hook or the build function instead.

Gains: No new records to build. The silent no-op becomes an error.

Losses: Modules and fields need a second mechanism. Library markers stay weaker than Jet's own.

End effect. Struct, enum, function and text block bodies run. A body that lists a module, field, variant, method or package site is an error naming the build function as the place to act.
options.technical: The collector covers struct, enum and function targets and text blocks. The declaration check rejects any other listed site when the marker has a body, with a fix naming fn build. No module record is added for bodies.

comparisons.note: A Swift peer macro receives any declaration node and must test which kind it got.

recommendation.why: Checking the body where it is declared catches mistakes before any user hits them, and nine site kinds finally run.
gains: Library mistakes surface for the library author.
Nine site kinds run bodies; the other nine are errors.

losses.loss: Several-kind markers write one arm per kind.
losses.mitigation: A missing arm is one error that names the kind and the record it would receive.

losses.loss: Nine site records, from type to package, must stay complete.
losses.mitigation: One producer builds them for every rung, so a gap shows everywhere at once.

whyNot.reason: Mistakes surface in someone else's build, at whichever use reaches the bad read.
Modules and fields would need a different mechanism for the same job, a cliff in the ladder.

recommendation.tradeoff: A trades one match per several-kind marker for errors at the declaration.
