decisions.title: A value forced by a host or fleet file refuses a conflicting flag, as a pin does
decisions.situation: Jet has one law for settings. The nearest source wins, the most explicit run wins, and safety settings only tighten. Two words force a value against later writers. A pin in build code refuses a conflicting flag with an error. A force in a host or fleet file beats the flag with no message. No shipped tool writes host or fleet files yet. So the silent force runs only in tests. The vote decides how a forced host or fleet value treats a conflicting flag.
decisions.gist: Should a host or fleet file that forces a value refuse a conflicting flag?
decisions.lesson: Yes: forcing is pinning, everywhere, and a conflicting flag is an error that names the pin.
decisions.story: An admin pins `optimize` to basic for the fleet. Dev types `--optimize=none` and gets an error naming the fleet file, not a silent build.
decisions.inWild:
Option          Conflicting flag    Message      Like
A pin           refused             error        Firefox, Chrome
B silent force  ignored             none         Nix mkForce
C loud force    ignored             note         no close peer
decisions.detail:
WHAT WE BUILD
- One resolver: policy (Policy.jet:89-138), BuildOptions (BuildOptions.jet:371-393, E2113) and FactLaw (layers with .Force and E3521) move onto the FactLaw contribution law. Required by D-CONF-MERGE1=A under every option.
- Under A: ContributionLayer accepts .Pin at system and fleet layers; a conflicting later writer gets E2113. Two pins on one key at one layer stay E3521. Workspace lock publication checks force_pin for .Pin overlays.

- `jet explain KEY FILE:LINE` prints sources outermost first and marks the winner (#6052 tracks file:line instead of byte spans, Policy.jet:162-169).
- Migration: test fixtures respell .Force as .Pin (Jetpack Tests/Merge.jet:77, JetCli GateProjection fixture). No production writer exists.

DEFECTS FIXED UNDER EVERY OPTION (no vote)
- Sentries direction (#6053): .On is tighter; policy_widens (Policy.jet:286-290) treats .Off as tight, so an inner .On is E0355 today (probe r02).
- Gates in source (#6051): D-GATE-LAW1=A (2026-10-04) supersedes D-ONCE-GATE1=A's five scopes; POLICY_RULES (Policy.jet:119-138) still lists them, and the marker row answers E0930 first (probe r03).

- Two unsafe settings under one word (#6045): the org gate dial (Policy.jet:332-365) and the package path list (Blocks/Policy.jet:135-145). They split into `unsafe:` (dial) and `unsafe_paths: [...]`; .Deny becomes .Forbid. Amends D-TEAMPOLICY1=A's canonical field (SD:7604-7630).

EVIDENCE (r14 jet, drafts7 probes)
- r01: `b.pin(.optimize, .Full)` then `--optimize=none` gives E2113; `--optimize=size` gives E2104 (none, basic or full).
- BuildOptions never reads FactLaw (BuildOptions.jet:371-393 uses Stock, Profile, Code, Flag).

IDS
Under A amends D-CONF-MERGE1=A (host and fleet .Force becomes .Pin with E2113) and D-SETTING-ORDER1=A (pins also in host and fleet files). Keeps D-JOS-PRIORITY-SURFACE2=A's .Default and .Priority(n). Covers #6041 (L-02), #6045, #6051, #6053 and the force word of #6054.

options.name: Forcing is pinning
options.detail: A host or fleet file forces with `.Pin`. A conflicting flag is the same error as a build-code pin. Gains: One word and one behavior for forcing. No flag is ever ignored silently. Losses: A pinned fleet setting can fail a script that passes a flag.
options.technical: One resolver serves policy, build options and settings. Host and fleet layers accept `.Pin`. A later conflicting writer, the command line included, gets E2113 naming the pin. A flag with the same value does not conflict. `.Priority(n)` and `.Default` keep their quiet precedence. `jet explain KEY` lists every source, outermost first, and marks the winner.
options.code:
# A: a fleet pin refuses a conflicting flag
# fleet file: optimize = { value: .Basic, priority: .Pin }
$ jet build --optimize=none
Error [E2113]: `optimize` is pinned to `basic` by the fleet file

options.name: Silent force
options.detail: Keep today's rule: a forced host or fleet value beats the flag. Only `jet explain` shows it. Gains: No ratified rule changes. Losses: A flag can be ignored with no message. Two words force, with two behaviors.
options.technical: The same single resolver. Host and fleet `.Force` beats the command line; `jet explain` records the flag as shadowed.
options.code:
# B: a fleet force wins with no message
# fleet file: optimize = { value: .Basic, priority: .Force }
$ jet build --optimize=none
ok   # built at basic; only jet explain shows why

options.name: Force wins with a note
options.detail: The forced value wins, and the build prints a note naming the file that forced it. Gains: Builds never fail because of a host setting. Losses: A third behavior beside pin and silent force. Notes scroll past in CI logs.
options.technical: As B, but each overridden flag prints one note line naming the forcing source.
options.code:
# C: the force wins and says so
$ jet build --optimize=none
note: `optimize` is forced to `basic` by the fleet file
ok

comparisons.note: mkForce wins silently; a separate query shows which file set it. Source: https://nixos.org/manual/nixos/stable/#sec-option-definitions-setting-priorities
A locked policy cannot be changed by the user, and shows as locked. Source: https://mozilla.github.io/policy-templates/
Mandatory policies override user settings; chrome://policy lists them. Source: https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/
System, global and repo config layer; a later layer always wins, with no force. Source: https://git-scm.com/docs/git-config
comparisons.code:
# Git
$ git config --system core.autocrlf false
$ git -c core.autocrlf=true commit   # the flag wins

recommendation.why: Jet already refuses a flag that conflicts with a pin. Forcing from a host file is the same act, so it should behave the same.
gains: One word, one behavior, at every level.
Every ignored flag becomes a visible error.
Settled before the first writer ships, so no one breaks.

losses.loss: A pinned fleet setting can fail a script that passes a flag.
losses.mitigation: The error names the pin, and a flag with the same value passes.

whyNot.reason: A flag the user typed can be ignored without a word.
It adds a third forcing behavior, and notes are easy to miss.

recommendation.tradeoff: An occasional hard stop, for no flag ever ignored in silence.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude. Adversarial model family: Claude. Fresh agent: BallotReview. I attacked the peer rows and whether a hard stop is worse than a note. Chrome shows forced policies as managed and blocks user changes, so it sits beside Firefox under A, not with silent force; A still wins.

decisions.title: The REPL can use packages, with the same pins and permissions as a script
decisions.situation: A REPL is the prompt where you type code and see each result at once. Jet's REPL is not built yet. The current plan limits it to the standard library. Then nobody can try a package at the prompt. IPython, Deno, Julia and Elixir all allow it. Data work and API exploration mostly happen at such a prompt. The vote decides which packages the REPL may use, and how they are pinned and allowed.
decisions.gist: Should the REPL (the interactive prompt) import packages, like a script can?
decisions.lesson: Yes, with the same version pins and permission prompts a script uses.
decisions.story: Dee types `use textkit#1.4` at the prompt. Jet fetches it once and pins it. `:save slug.jet` writes a script that runs the same tomorrow.
decisions.inWild:
Option            `use textkit` at the prompt   Pinned?       Like
A script rules    fetches, asks once            yes           Deno
B standard only   refused                       n/a           no peer
C project only    only inside a project         project lock  Elixir
Elixir Mix.install and Rust evcxr also fetch at the prompt.
IPython: %pip installs into the whole environment, unpinned.
decisions.detail:
WHAT WE BUILD
- The REPL itself is card #4720 (not built; `jet repl` gives E2104).
- Reuse the inline-dependency resolver (Compiler/JetCli/Source/Cli/ScriptDeps.jet) for each `use` line; fetching is card #4833.
- A session lock in the cache (Compiler/JetCli/Source/Cli/ScriptCache.jet).
- Docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:4217: replace "`jet repl` stays std-only" with this rule.
- Deleted: the standard-library-only gate in the REPL plan.

EVIDENCE
- Probe (commit 8fbf094): `jet repl` gives E2104 "`jet repl` is not built yet".
- `textkit` stands for any registry package.

IDS
Narrows D-REPL18 (syntax-decisions.md:4217). Reuses D-JPK-SCRIPTDEP1=A (inline `use pkg#ver`) and the #5949 ask-once prompt.

options.name: Same rules as a script
options.detail: `use pkg#ver` fetches, pins and asks for permissions once. `:save` writes a pinned script. Gains: Try any package at the prompt. A saved session runs the same later. Losses: A first import waits for fetch and compile. Each session keeps a small lock file in the cache.
options.technical: Each prompt entry is a script body, and bindings carry over. `use pkg#ver` uses the same resolver as a script's inline dependency. The pin goes into a session lock in the cache. Inside a package folder, its locked dependencies import, read-only. A package's permissions join the session through the ask-once prompt. The prompt names the package. `:save` writes the entries and their pins to a file. Offline, only cached packages import.

> use textkit#1.4
> textkit.slug("Hello World")
"hello-world"

options.name: Standard library only
options.detail: Keep the plan: the REPL imports only the standard library. Gains: No fetching or permissions at the prompt. Losses: No package can be tried at the prompt.
options.technical: Today's plan. To try a package, a user writes a script file.

error: the REPL imports only the standard library

options.detail: Inside a package folder, its locked dependencies import. Elsewhere, only the standard library. Gains: No fetching from the prompt. Losses: Outside a project, nobody can try a package. Two rules for what imports.

losses.loss: Each session keeps a small lock file in the cache.

whyNot.reason: Every peer REPL can import packages. Jet would be the only one that cannot.
Two rules, and newcomers outside a project still cannot try a package.

recommendation.tradeoff: A fetch on first use, for a prompt that matches scripts exactly.

decisions.title: Pages, marked methods and single routes share one table on `web.app()`
decisions.situation: A Jet web program can add routes three ways. Pages go on the web app. Marked struct methods and single routes go on a router. Pages and router routes live in separate tables. A clash inside one table fails the check. A page and a router route at the same address pass with no error. The example app writes the same addresses twice. The vote decides whether pages and router routes share one table.
decisions.gist: Should pages, marked methods and single routes share one route table on the web app?
decisions.lesson: Yes: `web.app()` holds every route, so any clash fails the check and one listing shows all.
decisions.story: Leo adds an `/orders/:id` API route beside an `/orders/:id` page. `jet check` names both lines, and he mounts the API under `/api`.
decisions.inWild:
Option            Tables   Cross-table clash   Like
A one table       one      check error         Rails, Phoenix, Next.js

decisions.title: Script mode: a `#!` first line makes a file a script
decisions.situation: A script is a small file you run to do one job. Today every Jet file that runs needs `fn run() { … }`. A three-line script with no wrapper fails with three errors. A `#!` first line also grants every permission today, silently. A new owner ruling ends that: scripts will ask once instead. The owner proposes one switch for both problems: a `#!` first line turns on script mode. In script mode, the statements form the body of `fn run`. The vote decides whether this is the right switch, and what it may change.
decisions.gist: Should a `#!` first line turn on a script mode where statements run without `fn run`?
decisions.lesson: Yes: in a `#!` file, statements become `fn run`, and permissions live on that line.
decisions.story: Ana's script starts with `#!/usr/bin/env jet` and has three lines. Jet asks once to read `name.txt`, then remembers. When the script grows, `jet fix` wraps it into `fn run`.
decisions.inWild:
Option                Hello script   Mode shown by    Like
A #! script mode      2 lines        first line       Deno (#! flags)
B statements anywhere 1 line         nothing          Python, Ruby, C#
C jet script command  1 line         the command      no peer
D .jets extension     1 line         file name        Kotlin, Elixir
E fn run everywhere   4 lines        n/a              Go, Rust, Zig
Every option keeps the same types, checks and imports.
decisions.detail:
WHAT WE BUILD
- One test for script mode: jet_cli_is_script (Compiler/JetCli/Source/Cli/Authority.jet:56), shared by the checker and the CLI.
- Entry: in script mode, build `fn run` from the statements instead of E0621 (Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/CheckProgram.jet:8245-8260; E0621 at :8254). E0620 for imported files (:8253) stays.
- Parser: in script mode, lower-case file-scope bindings join the body in order (Compiler/JetParser/Source/Parser/Entry.jet:850-867). The formatter already interleaves body and items (Compiler/JetParser/Source/Formatter/Formatter.jet:1631-1650).

- Permissions: delete the silent allow-all (Authority.jet:60-67). Flags on the `#!` line apply as typed. The ask-once prompt and its memory are the 2026-10-28 ruling (#5949).
- Fixes: E0621 offers "add a `#!` line" and "wrap into `fn run`". The wrap also moves `#!` permissions into package.jet (Compiler/JetCli/Source/Cli/LspFixes.jet:18).
- Docs: rewrite Docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:349-364; one example showing both shapes.

EVIDENCE
- ballots2/probe/script_today.jet (the program above): `jet check` reports E0621, E0357 and E0622.
- Authority.jet:53-67: a `#!/` file runs as if `-A` were typed.

options.name: Script mode by `#!`
options.detail: A `#!` launch line on line one makes a script. Its statements form `fn run`; its permissions live on that line. Gains: A script is as short as Python, and still fully checked. Line one tells every reader the file runs top to bottom. Fixes the silent allow-everything bug in the same design. Losses: Without `#!`, a bare `print("hi")` file is still an error. A function cannot read a variable from the script body.
options.technical:
Script mode starts when line one begins with `#!/`. Jet already detects this line today. In script mode, statements outside functions form the body of `fn run`. They run in file order. `fn`, `struct`, `use` and ALL_CAPS constants stay declarations. A lower-case `name :: …` is a local of the body. A function cannot read it; the error offers an ALL_CAPS constant or a parameter. A script may write `fn run` itself instead, but not both. Permissions: a `#!` line no longer allows everything.

Flags on that line apply as if typed, as in `#!/usr/bin/env -S jet -A`. Otherwise Jet asks once in a terminal and remembers the answer for this exact code. `jet fix` writes a chosen permission onto the `#!` line. In a normal program, permissions live in package.jet instead. Script mode never changes types, checks, effects, failures or exit codes. The body is `fn run`, so it means the same on every tier.

An imported file still may not hold statements, so imports never run code. To grow a script, delete the `#!` line or import the file. Jet then reports the loose statements. `jet fix` wraps them into `fn run` and moves the `#!` permissions into package.jet. The code itself does not change.

options.name: Statements in any file you run
options.detail: Any file given to `jet run` may hold statements, with or without `#!`. Gains: No first line needed, so hello is one line. Same as Python and Ruby. Losses: Nothing in the file says it runs top to bottom. Reopens the explicit-entry ruling for every file.
options.technical: The file you run may hold statements; imported files still may not. Permissions follow the new ruling, with flags as their only home.

name :: fs.read("name.txt").trim()

options.name: A `jet script` command
options.detail: `jet script hi.jet` allows statements; `jet run hi.jet` does not. Gains: Normal files never change. Losses: One file means two things, chosen by the command. `./hi.jet` still needs `#!` to pick the command.
options.technical: The command, not the file, picks the mode. A `#!` line would have to name `jet script`.

$ jet run hi.jet        # error: needs fn run

options.name: A script file extension
options.detail: A `.jets` file may hold statements, like Kotlin's `.main.kts` files. Gains: The file name shows the mode. Losses: Growing a script means renaming it, and every reference to it. Every tool must learn a second extension.
options.technical: Kotlin (`.main.kts`) and Elixir (`.exs`) work this way.
options.code:

decisions.title: Running commands: `Sh{…}` runs, pipes and fails loudly
decisions.situation: Scripts often run other programs, like git. Jet already has a command literal: `Sh{"git log {rev}"}`. It splits into a program and its arguments, with no shell. A hole like `{rev}` is always one argument, so it cannot inject commands. But the literal cannot run by itself, and pipes need a shell. The easy way to capture output also hides failure. When git fails with code 128, Jet prints nothing and exits 0. The vote decides how a command runs, and what happens when it fails.
decisions.gist: Should the `Sh{…}` command literal run, pipe and fail loudly by itself?
decisions.lesson: Yes: `.text()` runs it with no shell, `|` pipes, and any failure stops the script.
decisions.story: Cy writes `Sh{"git log --oneline {rev} | wc -l"}.text()`. When `rev` is wrong, the script stops with git's own message.
decisions.inWild:
Option         One pipeline                       Loud?  Like
A Sh runs      Sh{"git log | wc -l"}.text()       yes    Bun, zx
B planned      process.pipeline([...])            no     Python
C builder + |  (cmd([..]) | cmd([..])).text()     yes    PowerShell
Bash: `git log | wc -l` loses git's failure without pipefail.
Only A checks the command line before it runs.

WHAT WE BUILD
- Core/Process/Process.jet:24-47 (struct Sh): add run, text, lines and status.

- Core/Process/Process.jet:189-197: the native pipeline route (E2104 today; card #4952).
- Core/Process/Process.jet:80-108 (check): reused for every stage.
- Deleted: getoutput and getstatusoutput (Process.jet:119-127) and call (Process.jet:256-259).

- bench/programs/w07_spawn/main.jet moves to `Sh{…}.text()`. Docs: Docs/spec/spec.md:82-85, syntax-decisions.md:4056-4061, the process section of the core library.

EVIDENCE

- Repo counts (git grep): process.getoutput( 0, process.call( 0, Sh{" 2, process.cmd( 381 in 202 files.

options.name: The literal runs, pipes and fails loudly
options.detail: `Sh{…}` gains `.run()`, `.text()`, `.lines()` and `.status()`. A written `|` pipes. Failure stops the script. Gains: As short as zx, and checked before running. A failed command never looks like success. Losses: A literal `|` argument must be written as a hole. Programs like grep, where code 1 is normal, need `.status()`.
options.technical:
Jet splits the literal when compiling, so programs and pipes are known before running. A hole is never split and never an operator. The only operators are `|`, `<`, `>` and `2>&1`. `.run()` shares the terminal. `.text()` returns the output without the last newline. `.lines()` streams lines. `.status()` returns the exit code with the captured output, and never fails on the code. Any stage that exits non-zero, times out or is killed fails the call.

The error names the program, its code and the last lines of its error output. `process.cmd([...])` gets the same four methods, for arguments built at run time. The permission prompt names each program in the literal. The unchecked helpers `getoutput`, `getstatusoutput` and `call` are deleted. `getoutput` and `call` have no callers today.

options.name: Build the planned form
options.detail: Add `process.run(Sh{…})`, keep the Python-style helpers, and pipe with a list. Gains: No pipe rule inside the literal. Losses: The unchecked helper stays the easy path. Pipes need a list of commands.
options.technical: Builds the existing plan: `process.run(cmd: Sh)` and `process.pipeline([...])`. Checked and unchecked helpers stay side by side, as in Python.

options.name: A builder and a `|` operator
options.detail: `process.cmd([...])` gains a checked `.text()`, and `a | b` joins two commands. Gains: Works the same for fixed and computed arguments. Losses: Longer than A for every command. `|` already means bitwise or on integers.
options.technical: Like PowerShell pipes, but on command values. It needs an operator overload on a library type.

decisions.title: `priv` works on any declaration, not only modules and fields
decisions.situation: Everything in Jet is public by default. Only a private module or a private struct field hides anything. To hide one helper from other packages, an author wraps it in a private module. Then every call needs the module prefix. A promise to add package privacy through the manifest has no form yet. The documented path from internal to public still names a public marker that was removed. The vote decides how one item is hidden, and what package privacy looks like.
decisions.gist: Should `priv` work on any declaration, so one helper can be hidden without a wrapper module?
decisions.lesson: Yes: `priv` on any declaration hides it outside its module; at top level, outside the package.
decisions.story: Mei writes `priv fn pad` in her library. Her own code calls `pad` freely. Other packages get an error naming the `priv` line.
decisions.inWild:
Option            Hide one helper            Like
A priv anywhere   priv fn pad                Kotlin, Swift, Rust
B modules only    wrap in priv module        no peer
C export list     exports: [banner]          Haskell, OCaml .mli
decisions.detail:
WHAT WE BUILD
- Remove E0413 for declarations. `priv` = enclosing module and children; top level = package-only. `priv(package)` on nested declarations; at top level refused with a fix to write `priv`. E0417 on fields stays.
- E0605 names the hidden item and its `priv` line. A `priv` type in a public signature is refused; `pub use` of a `priv` item is refused.
- Loose files: a loose file is its own module, so `priv` hides from path importers; after `jet init` (D-LOOSE-GROW1) it widens to package-only, and `jet init --check` lists those items.

- Lifecycle (D-STRUCT-LIFE1=A, stale since `pub` was removed): `priv` item, public item, `#Deprecated(since:, use:, removed_in:)`, removed. `_name` keeps only its unused and discovery meanings.
- Tools/agent/vis-cutover.mjs:262-281 stops deleting `priv` before non-module declarations.

EVIDENCE (r14 jet)
- Probes q03 and r17: `priv fn` gives E0413 "priv marks only modules and fields"; `priv module helpers` with `helpers.pad` checks clean.
- Audit p07: `_name` has no access meaning; `lib._helper()` is reachable from another package.

IDS
Under A reverses two S18 statements (owner directive 2026-10-07, card #4723): no visibility marker on declarations, and package privacy via the manifest. Under B S18 loses its manifest sentence; under C S18 stands. Hosts #6050 (L-12).

options.name: `priv` on any declaration
options.detail: The module rule for `priv` applies to one item too. At top level, `priv` means package-only. This reverses two lines of the everything-public ruling. Gains: Hiding one helper is one word. One word works on items, modules and fields. Calls keep their plain names. Losses: Any declaration may now carry `priv`, one more word to read.
options.technical: `priv` on any declaration means usable only in the enclosing module and its children. The package top level is its root module, so a top-level `priv` item is package-only. `priv(package)` works on nested items. A `priv` type in a public signature is refused, naming both lines. `jet doc` lists only public items. `jet explain NAME` prints the visibility and the line that set it.

options.name: Modules and fields only
options.detail: Keep today's rule. A `priv(package) module` is the package level, and the manifest promise is dropped. Gains: No change to the ruling beyond one sentence. Losses: One hidden helper needs a wrapper and prefixed calls.
options.technical: E0413 keeps its fix that moves the item into a `priv` module. The sentence promising manifest privacy is deleted.

options.name: The manifest lists exports
options.detail: package.jet gains `exports:`, a list of the names other packages may use. Gains: The public surface is one list in one file. Losses: Visibility lives far from the code it hides. A second mechanism beside `priv` modules and fields.
options.technical: With no `exports:` everything is public. Importers reaching an unlisted name get E0605 naming the manifest line.

Access levels go on any declaration. Source: https://docs.swift.org/swift-book/documentation/the-swift-programming-language/accesscontrol/
Private by default; pub and pub(crate) widen one item. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/visibility-and-privacy.html
A module header lists its exports. Source: https://www.haskell.org/onlinereport/haskell2010/haskellch5.html

# Haskell: Textkit.hs
module Textkit (banner) where
pad s = "  " ++ s

gains: One word for every level of hiding.

losses.mitigation: Public stays the default, so most code never writes it.

whyNot.reason: Hiding one helper still costs a wrapper and a prefix on every call.
It adds a second mechanism, far from the code it hides.

recommendation.tradeoff: One optional word on declarations, for hiding any helper without a wrapper.

decisions.title: Implicit context: scratch memory that cannot dangle, plus the context name, keys and fields
decisions.situation: Jai and Odin give every function a hidden context: the allocator, the logger, and scratch memory that is freed all at once. Jet ratified that context (D-JAI-CONTEXT1) and must now settle how it works. The hard part is scratch memory. Jai frees it with one reset per frame, and a value kept past the reset reads garbage. This vote picks how Jet frees scratch safely, together with the name, key and field rules.
decisions.gist: Should scratch memory rewind when its block ends and move out what leaves, or be reset by hand as in Jai?
decisions.lesson: Scratch memory hands out space by bumping a pointer and frees everything at once. A frame's temporary text and lists then cost almost nothing. In Jai, code resets scratch once per frame, and a value still held after the reset points at reused memory. Jet must rule that out without putting lifetimes in signatures, which D-REGION1 already rejected.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: nothing new to learn. Code that never names scratch allocates as it does today. A library reads `context.allocator` or `context.logger` like any other name.

Expert path: wrap a frame in `#Context(allocator: context.scratch) { ... }`. Everything the frame builds, inside any library, comes from scratch. When the block ends, scratch rewinds. A value that left the block, such as a line pushed onto an older log, was moved into the log's own memory as it was pushed.
decisions.story: Ren writes a game loop. Each frame builds a few hundred labels and throws them away, and one function also pushes a line onto the game's log. In Jai that line would dangle after the reset. Under A it moves into the log as it is pushed, and the labels vanish together at the closing brace.
decisions.detail:
WHAT IS ALREADY RATIFIED
- D-JAI-CONTEXT1=A: code reads typed context fields, packages declare typed keys, reads add the `Context` effect, and scratch is a per-task arena. D-CTX1: `#Context(field: value) { ... }` changes fields for one block and restores them on exit.
- Today only `deadline` takes effect. The allocator and logger are checked and dropped (Compiler/JetIR/Source/BuildTransact.jet:223-228, defect #5030). The task-owned context record landed with #5025 ctx0 (commit 36825b7a15).

THE QUESTION
- The five earlier context ballots (CONTEXT-NAME1, KEYS1, ALLOC1, FIELDS1 and SCRATCH1) are one design, so they return as this one vote. Main withdraws the five when this one goes live.
- Four of their rules have one clear answer, shared by both options below. The real choice is how scratch memory is freed safely.

SHARED: THE NAME AND THE EFFECT
- `context` is a short name for a new Core module, `core.context`, like `print` and `time` today. A local named `context` hides it by the ordinary scoping rule, and `core.context` always reaches it.
- The repository has 1,009 lines declaring something named `context` (query on dev 479d6936df). None needs renaming. A reserved word would force all of them to change.

- Reads add `Context` to the function's effect row. Packages never need it granted, because a read touches no file, socket or device. A budget may still deny it with `!Context`.

SHARED: KEYS
- A package declares a key with a required default, written like a field default: `#ContextKey frame_index: Int{0}`. An optional key writes `#ContextKey user: User?{None}`.
- The ratified spelling had `pub`. That word was removed from Jet (E0411), so the form above drops it.

- A key is an ordinary name. Another package's key is imported with `use game.[frame_index]` and renamed with `as`, like any import, so no dotted labels are needed.
- `#Context(frame_index: n) { ... }` sets it, and `context.get(frame_index)` reads it. A key may not reuse one of the eight field names, so a label never means two things.

SHARED: FIELD TYPES
- `allocator: mem.Allocator` (default: the program allocator). `logger: log.Handler` (Core/Log/Log.jet:382). `deadline: Int?` in epoch milliseconds. `thread: Int`, read-only.
- `on_stop: fn(debug.Stop)` runs before every stop: assert, panic, and bounds or key checks. It replaces the ratified `on_assert`, which covered failed assertions only, so the name says what it does.

- `trace: [debug.Frame]` is captured when read, so it costs nothing until used. Frame names follow `debug_info`, exactly as crash reports already do (spec.md:3722-3725).
- `print: term.PrintStyle` shapes `print` only. String interpolation never reads context, so `-[]>` functions stay pure.

OPTION A: A SCRATCH BLOCK OWNS WHAT IT ALLOCATES
- `#Context(allocator: context.scratch) { ... }` sends every allocation made in the block's extent to scratch, including inside libraries. When the block ends, scratch rewinds to where the block began.
- Nested blocks are nested marks. So `reset`, `mark` and `restore` are not needed, and there is nothing to forget.

- Scratch is one contiguous range of address space per task, reserved on the task's first scratch block. Its pages cost memory only once touched.
- An allocation past the reservation comes from the program allocator. That stays correct, because a heap value never needs to move.

- A value is newer than the block when it lies in scratch above the block's start, or in a stack frame entered after the block began. Each test is one subtract and compare on an address.

A: THE EXITS
- A newer value leaves only by being stored into older data: a binding declared before the block, a global, a link, or anything reached through a `&` parameter.
- It also leaves by `return` from inside the block, by being handed to a task, or inside a closure that outlives the block.

- The block is a statement, not an expression, as `#Context` is today (probe q/b4/ctx/expr.jet gives E0003). A result therefore leaves only through one of these exits.
- At each exit the value first moves into the destination's allocator. It is moved, never duplicated, so the program means what it would without scratch.

- Stores in the block's own text are resolved by the compiler. A store inside a library, such as a callee pushing onto a list passed with `&`, runs the address test.

A: GROWING OLDER CONTAINERS
- A container grows in the allocator that owns it, not the one in context. `&game.log.push(x)` inside the block grows `log` from the program allocator, because `log` is older than the block.
- The owner is read from the container's own address by the same test. No container gains a word, so `[T]` and `String` keep their current size.

- Dropping a scratch value frees nothing. Programs with a reachable scratch block use a free entry that makes the same address test first. Other programs keep today's entry.

A: OTHER RULES
- An installed arena is borrowed for reading until the block ends. So `&arena.reset()` inside the block is the existing E0204 conflict, found at compile time.
- `@` link boxes and their contents always use the program allocator, because a link has no lexical lifetime. Tasks spawned inside the block get the program allocator and their own scratch (D-ALLOC1).

WHAT A COSTS, MEASURED
- Moving one short label out of a block cost 18 ns. Building and freeing the same label on the heap cost 170 ns (q/b4/ctx/cost.jet, `jet run --release`, 1,000,000 labels).
- A moved list moves every element. Relocating a 10,000-label list took 0.11 to 0.12 ms, about 12 ns per label. Building it took 2.3 to 2.7 ms (q/b4/ctx/deep.jet, three runs).

- Jai and Odin code pays the same copy by hand, with `copy_string` or `strings.clone`, when it keeps a temporary. A does it at the exit and never misses one.
- `jet audit copies` lists each exit that can move a value out of scratch, with the value's type. A list exit is marked as moving per element.

- The address test was measured as a proxy: ten million `String` stores through a `&` parameter, with and without one extra compare and branch.
- Over four runs the difference was +77, -32, -90 and -38 ms on about 1,580 ms. That is inside run-to-run noise (q/b4/ctx/store.jet).
- A program with no reachable scratch block emits no test. The build already proves reachability per effect, as E0749 does for denied effects.

A: THE EXPERT WAY OUT
- Code that must never move a value uses an explicit `mem.Arena` and `arena.alloc(v)` views. Views never move, and E0631 and E0632 keep them inside the arena's life at compile time.
- `&arena.reset()` then frees by hand, as Jai's reset does, with zero copies. The cost is managing that lifetime yourself, with no block to do it.

OPTION B: JAI'S RESET, STOPPED IF A VALUE SURVIVES
- The same block sends allocations to scratch, but nothing moves and nothing rewinds. The program calls `&context.scratch.reset()` once per frame, as Jai calls `reset_temporary_storage()`.
- `mark()` and `restore(m)` give nested resets.

- Scratch counts its living values. Each allocation adds one, and each free of a scratch value subtracts one. A reset while any value is alive stops the program and names where that value was made.
- A value meant to outlive the frame must be built outside the block, as in Jai. E0632 catches a read after a reset where the compiler sees both; the rest are run-time stops.

WHY NOT A FULLY STATIC DESIGN
- Rust's bumpalo ties each value to its arena in the type, so every function that returns or stores one needs a lifetime parameter.
- D-REGION1 ratified that such lifetimes never appear in Jet syntax. `arena.alloc(v)` views keep that compile-time rule (E0631, E0632) as the zero-copy expert rung, unchanged in both options.

EACH RULE'S WAY OUT (REWORK item 7)
- A's move at an exit: the expert way out above, at the cost of managing the arena by hand.
- Links and tasks using the program allocator: install an arena inside the task, or hold `arena.alloc` views. Nothing extra is paid.

- A key that repeats a field name: rename it on import with `as`. Nothing extra is paid.
- E0204 on resetting an installed arena has no way out. It is a soundness rule (I1), because the reset would free values the block still uses.

RATIFIED TEXT TO AMEND (flag for Main)
- D-JAI-CONTEXT1=A SCRATCH says scratch has reset, mark and restore, and that scratch values are arena views. Under A, scratch is used only by installing it, and the block replaces all three.
- D-JAI-CONTEXT1=A HANDLER names `on_assert` for failed assertions. Both options rename it `on_stop` and run it for every stop.
- D-JAI-CONTEXT1=A KEYS writes `#ContextKey pub`. `pub` no longer exists (E0411).
- D-CTX1: under A, a block that installs an arena also rewinds it on exit.

PROBE
- q/b4/ctx/pA3.jet is A's program with a local `mem.Arena` in place of `context.scratch`. It runs on dev today and prints the six labels and a log length of 3.
- With `context.scratch`, the only error is E0107 for `context`. With the key declaration, the only errors are E0003 at `#ContextKey` and E0761 for the key label. Those are the features themselves.

IDS
- Builds on D-JAI-CONTEXT1=A, D-CTX1, D-DEADLINE1, D-ALLOC1, D-ALLOC2, D-REGION1, D-MEM-COPYSEM1 and D-ALLOCFAIL1. Card #5025.

options.name: Scratch blocks; what leaves moves out
options.detail: A `#Context(allocator: context.scratch)` block sends every allocation in it to scratch, including inside libraries. Scratch rewinds when the block ends. A value stored into older data, from the block or from any callee, first moves into the destination's own memory. There is no reset call, no mark to forget, and no stop.
options.technical:
Install with `#Context(allocator: context.scratch)` or with any `mem.Arena`. Every arena is one contiguous address reservation per task, with pages committed on touch. The block borrows the arena for reading, so `&arena.reset()` inside it is E0204. Exit rewinds the arena to its entry point, and nested blocks are nested marks.

A value is newer than the block if it lies in the arena above the block's mark, or in a stack frame entered after the block began. Each test is one subtract and compare. Exits are stores into older places, `return`, task hand-offs and escaping closures. The block is a statement, so it has no result value. At an exit the value moves into the destination's allocator, element by element for a list.

An older container grows from its owner's allocator, found by the same address test, so no container gains a word. Dropping a scratch value frees nothing. Stores in the block's text are resolved by the compiler. Stores in callees, and the free entry, run the test only when a scratch block is reachable. Links use the program allocator. The expert way out is `arena.alloc` views with `&arena.reset()`.

options.name: Jai's reset, stopped if a value survives
options.detail: The same block sends allocations to scratch, but nothing moves. The program resets scratch by hand once per frame, as in Jai. Scratch counts its living values, and a reset while one is still alive stops the program and names where it was made. Values to keep are built outside the block.
options.technical: Install as in A, with no rewind on exit. `&context.scratch.reset()`, `mark()` and `&context.scratch.restore(m)` free scratch. Each scratch allocation adds one to a live count; each free of a scratch value subtracts one. A reset or restore with a live value made after that point is a located stop, or E0632 where the compiler sees it. Shared fields, keys, name and effect are as in the detail.

comparisons.note: Temporary storage is freed by `reset_temporary_storage()`, usually once per frame. Nothing checks for a value kept past it. (The Way to Jai, ch. 25A)
comparisons.code:
label := tprint("% at %", name, tick);
reset_temporary_storage();

comparisons.note: `context.temp_allocator` is freed with `free_all`. Nothing checks for a kept value. https://odin-lang.org/docs/overview/#allocators
comparisons.code:
label := fmt.tprintf("%v at %v", name, tick)
free_all(context.temp_allocator)

comparisons.note: An arena is passed explicitly and freed with `deinit`. Nothing checks for a kept value. https://ziglang.org/documentation/master/#Choosing-an-Allocator

recommendation.why: A keeps Jai's frame pattern and its speed, and a kept value can never dangle. The block is the mark, so there is no reset to call or forget. Moving a leaving value costs about a tenth of building it.
gains: No value can outlive its scratch memory, and nothing stops at run time.
Libraries allocate from scratch with no change to their code.
No reset, mark or restore to write or forget.

whyNot.reason: B turns a kept value into a run-time stop, found only by running that path, and makes authors build kept values outside the frame by hand.

recommendation.tradeoff: A value that leaves a scratch block moves once: 18 ns for a short label, against 170 ns to build it on the heap. A list moves per element, about 12 ns each. Programs without scratch blocks pay nothing, and `arena.alloc` views never move.

surface.gist: Should scratch memory rewind when its block ends and move out what leaves, or be reset by hand as in Jai?
surface.lesson: Scratch memory frees everything at once, so a frame's temporary text costs almost nothing. In Jai, a value kept past the reset reads reused memory. Jet must rule that out without lifetimes in signatures.

current.note: The allocator is checked and then ignored, so this block still uses the heap.

wild.note: One reset per frame. A string kept past it dangles.
wild.code:
label := tprint("% at %", name, tick);
reset_temporary_storage();

decisions.title: Core gets no private powers: every list Jet knows is a Core trait that any package can add to
decisions.situation: Jet's compiler keeps many lists of library things it knows by name, such as the checked text kinds SQL and HTML, or the data formats. Core's members of those lists get powers a package cannot reach. D-TEXTHEAD-HOLES1 A, ratified, already fixed this for checked text. This vote decides whether the same rule holds for every list. We recommend yes: each list becomes a Core trait, and Core adds its members exactly as a package would.
decisions.gist: Should every list of library things the compiler knows become a Core trait that Core and packages extend the same way?
decisions.lesson: A list here is a set of library things the compiler knows, such as the kinds of checked text. Today Core's members are written into the compiler, and a package's members are weaker. Under A each list is a Core trait. Core and packages add members with the same `impl`, so they get the same powers.
decisions.story: Mira writes a graph database package. Her users write `graph.Cypher{"...{age}..."}` just as they write `SQL{"...{age}..."}`. Under A her kind checks the query while compiling and sends 18 as a bound value, exactly like SQL. She changed nothing in Jet to get there.
decisions.detail:
Before and after. Today Mira's package can check `Cypher{"..."}` while compiling, but each hole becomes text. Probe probe/ext/arch_a.jet prints `MATCH (p:Person) WHERE p.age > $p RETURN p`, so the 18 is lost. Pasting it instead invites injection. Core's SQL keeps 18 as a bound value only because the compiler knows SQL by name (Facts/Checked.jet:90-101).

With A. The user writes the same literal. Jet runs graph's check while compiling, then calls graph's build. The query goes out as `$p0` with the value 18 beside it. Core's SQL uses the same two members and gains nothing extra. The compiler's TypedHeadKind list is deleted. D-TEXTHEAD-HOLES1 A, ratified, supplies the two members.

Why it matters. A package can match Core, so a database, shell or markup package is as safe as Core's own. Core feels every gap in a trait first, so gaps get fixed for everyone. Name lists also misfire. Facts/Checked.jet:96 tests `name == "SQL"`, so today any type named SQL gets Core's SQL handling.

What A says. Every list of library things in the compiler becomes a Core trait. A member is a type with `impl Member.Trait`, and its settings are trait constants, as D-DECL-TYPES1 A ratified. No new declaration word is added. The compiler reads impls, never library names. lane-check fails any new name list and names the trait to use.

Already moved. D-DECL-TYPES1 A moved markers, effects, facts, derives and Jet's 996 diagnostic rows to Core traits. D-TEXTHEAD-HOLES1 A moved checked text. What remains are smaller lists, such as data formats (Core/Encoding/Encoding.jet:77). The 2026-10-29 census found 1,145 such lists, about 30,700 members, before those two decisions.

What stays closed, on purpose. Grammar and keywords, IR operations, soundness rules, ABI and layout, output kinds, and data fixed by an outside standard, such as Unicode tables. A package adding to these could break the language for everyone. Each has one ledger row with its reason. Opening one takes an owner ballot. Compiler facts stay Prelude-only too (D-DECL-TYPES1 rule 12).

Downsides, designed away. Matches: code never matches over an open list; behavior is a trait method, and the trait's checklist makes every new member complete. Plain data enums stay closed and exhaustive. Speed: Core's impls stay pre-generated into compiler tables (D-OPENTABLE1 D). A package's impls are read once per build, only when imported. A member known while compiling is called directly. One chosen at run time costs one trait-slot call, with no box (Examples/features/traits/trait_value_slots.jet).

Downsides, designed away, continued. Trust: compile-time members are pure (`-[]>`) and run sandboxed (D-META-HOLD1), and laws travel with the trait (D-CORE-LAWS1). A package's failing check is reported in its own name at the user's line, never as a Jet crash. Clashes: members are named by package path. Tools read impls as declarations, without running package code.

Option B, plugins. Each list gets a WebAssembly plugin interface, as Roslyn analyzers and Kotlin compiler plugins work. A plugin can be in any language and can see raw tokens. But it is a second extension system beside impls. Every use is a sandbox call, and the editor sees members only while the plugin runs.

Option C, two tiers. Packages get the open traits, but Core keeps its remaining lists as closed enums, as Swift's standard library keeps private attributes. Core keeps exhaustive matches over its own lists. A package needing a new format must ask for a Core change. Checked text has already left this tier through D-TEXTHEAD-HOLES1 A.

Research. Prettier writes its built-in languages through the same plugin interface outside plugins use (prettier.io/docs/plugins). Elixir protocols stay open to every package, and the build fixes each protocol's impls once (hexdocs.pm/elixir/Protocol.html). Julia's open methods are resolved without a fixed set per build. Loading one package can force thousands of methods to recompile (julialang.org/blog/2020/08/invalidations).

decisions.title: A checked text kind can build a typed value from its parts and holes
decisions.situation: A checked text literal such as `SQL{"… {age} …"}` has fixed text with holes for values. Core's SQL turns each hole into a bound database value instead of pasting it into the text, which is what stops injection. A package's kind cannot do this: today every hole becomes more text. The vote picks how any kind, Core's or a package's, may keep its holes as values. We recommend two optional members on the existing CheckedText trait, so simple kinds stay as they are.
decisions.gist: How should a checked text kind keep its {holes} as typed values instead of pasting them in as text?
decisions.lesson: A checked text literal is fixed text with `{holes}` for values. Pasting a value into text is how injection bugs start, so Core's SQL keeps each hole as a separate bound value. Packages cannot do that today. This vote picks how any text kind may do it. Kinds that only need text, which is most of them, write nothing new.
decisions.story: Mira's graph package defines `Cypher{"…"}`. Her users write `Cypher{"MATCH (p) WHERE p.age > {age} RETURN p"}`. The database must receive `$p0` in the text and the number 18 beside it, never the text `18` pasted in. Core's SQL already works this way; her kind should work the same way, with no second concept to learn.
decisions.detail:
Provenance. Split out of the D-EXTEND-ARCH1 package ballot so the owner votes on the architecture and on this mechanism separately. Ratified D-TEXTHEAD-TYPE1=A made checked text an ordinary String-backed type with one CheckedText impl. This ballot adds how a kind keeps its holes as values. Rebuilt after Main's review: one trait, not a second one.

Today. Core's SQL is `struct SQL { text, values }` built by `__sql_literal(literals: [String], values: [DBValue])` (Core/Db/Db.jet:245-264), which is option A's build kept private. The compiler converts each SQL hole to a DBValue by name (Sema/Expressions/Constructors.jet:1692-1719). A package kind has only `encode_hole`, which must return String (E0112 at Constructors.jet:1151). When a hole is a run-time value, `check` runs while the program runs (Examples/features/text/checked_text_runtime_hole.jet).

The check moves fully to compile time under A. It sees the fixed text with `{}` for each hole, once per literal. A run-time check failure (checked_text_runtime_hole_stop.jet) can no longer happen. A kind whose rule depends on a hole's value, such as a length limit, enforces it in `encode_hole` or `build` instead.

The probes, in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/q/bd/probe/ext. holes_a.jet runs option A's build body as a plain function and prints the `$p0` query. holes_b.jet does the same for option B's steps. trait_defaults2.jet shows default method bodies work today. trait_defaults.jet shows a default associated type is E0003 today. self_static.jet shows `-> Self` from a static trait method is E0108 today (card #6284). zip.jet shows lists have no `enumerate` (E0311), so build keeps one index loop.

Reads with the related ballots. Under D-EXTEND-ARCH1=A, Core's SQL, Sh and HTML become ordinary impls of the winning form, and their compiler lowering is deleted. Under D-EXTEND-ARCH1=C, A or B here serves packages only. Option C here composes only with D-EXTEND-ARCH1=C. D-SQL-SCRIPT1 shows SQL text in scripts; its holes behave as picked here.

options.name: Two optional members on CheckedText
options.detail:
CheckedText keeps its name and its two methods. It gains two optional members. `type Hole` says what a hole becomes; it is text unless the kind says otherwise. `build` receives the fixed parts and the holes and returns the kind's value; unless the kind writes it, it joins them into text as today.

A text kind writes exactly what it writes today. A kind that binds values names its hole type and writes `build`. `check` sees the literal with each hole shown as `{}`, so every literal is checked while compiling, never while running.
options.technical:
Prelude/core/prelude.jet:19-23 gains `type Hole = String` and `fn build(parts: [String], holes: ^[Hole]) -[]> Self { … }` with a default body that joins. `encode_hole` returns `Hole`. Two small language features: a default associated type (today `type Hole = String` in a trait is E0003, probe/ext/trait_defaults.jet) and a static method returning Self (E0108, card #6284). Default method bodies already work (trait_defaults2.jet).

`Kind{"…"}` lowers to `Kind.build(PARTS, [Kind.encode_hole(h1), …])` with PARTS a module constant. `check` runs once per literal at compile time on PARTS joined by `{}`. Core's SQL, Sh and HTML become ordinary impls, and the name-based lowering in Sema/Expressions/Constructors.jet:1692-1719 is deleted. Core has no list `enumerate` or zip today (probe/ext/zip.jet: E0311), so build keeps one index loop.

options.name: Append pieces in order
options.detail:
This is Swift's design. The compiler starts from the kind's empty value, then calls `literal` for each fixed part and the hole step for each hole, in source order. A text kind keeps the default steps, which append text.

Nothing is collected first, and each hole sees all the text before it, which suits HTML escaping by context. A binding kind needs an empty starting value, and its steps change it in place.
options.technical: CheckedText gains `fn literal(&self, part: String) -[]>` and an `&self` form of the hole step, each with a default body. `Kind{"…"}` lowers to `k := Kind{}; &k.literal(p0); &k.encode_hole(h1); …`. Every field needs a default, written `values: [DBValue]{[]}` (probe/ext/holes_b_default.jet; `[DBValue]{}` there is E0003, card #6285). Core's SQL, Sh and HTML builders become appenders. Model: Swift SE-0228.

options.name: Holes stay text
options.detail:
Every package kind keeps today's one hole hook: each hole becomes text, which the kind can quote. The finished text is the value. Core's SQL, shell and HTML kinds keep their compiler support for bound values, separate arguments and context escaping.

This is the smallest rule, and quoting is enough for many small languages. A database or shell package must rely on its quoting being right, and cannot pass values separately.
options.technical: No change. `encode_hole<T: Printable>(value: T) -[]> String` stays the only hole hook (Prelude/core/prelude.jet:22). TypedHeadKind (Facts/Checked.jet:90) keeps SQL, HTML and Sh lowering by name. Consistent only with D-EXTEND-ARCH1=C.

decisions.title: `#FX` above a type bounds everything done in that type's name
decisions.situation: A library author often wants to promise that a whole type is safe, for example that a parser never touches the network or the disk. Today the promise must be written on every method's row. The vote decides whether `#FX` above a type makes that promise once. It would cover the type's methods, its trait impls in any package, and the closures they create. We recommend it.
decisions.gist: Should `#FX` above a type bound everything its methods, trait impls and closures may do?
decisions.lesson: An effect is a kind of power, such as network access. A function promises what it does with its row, like `-[!Net]>`. `#FX` above a block is a ceiling for the code inside it. This vote asks whether a type takes the same ceiling for all code that acts in its name.
decisions.story: Mia publishes `mia_parse`. Her users want to know the parser never reaches the network or the disk before they run it on untrusted notes. She writes `#FX(!Net, !FS)` once, above `Parser`. Months later a contributor adds a `Stylesheet` impl that fetches CSS. The build fails at that line, naming Mia's cap.
decisions.inWild:
-- Haskell: ST's type confines its effects; runST proves none escape.
sumST :: [Int] -> Int
sumST xs = runST $ do
  ref <- newSTRef 0
  mapM_ (\x -> modifySTRef ref (+ x)) xs
  readSTRef ref
decisions.detail:
Provenance. Card c09kjhit. The owner rejected v1, which kept types without a cap of their own. In the owner's words, it threw away the original ask. That ask, after Simon Peyton Jones's work in Haskell, is that a type can limit the effects it may use. v2 makes it the recommendation. It also removes the two costs v1 listed: a third place for promises and a tail rule for generic types.

The one reading. D-DECL-TYPES1 rule 4 says `#FX` above any type means the most that work done in that type's name may do. For an effect type, that work is every function whose row names it. For an ordinary type, option A says the work is its methods, its trait impls in any package, and every closure written inside them.

Generic types need no tail. What a type parameter does belongs to whoever picks it, just as a callback's effects belong to its caller under D-EFF2. So `#FX(IO)` above `Traced<T>` bounds Traced's own code to IO. `Traced<Parser>` does IO plus whatever Parser does, and Parser's part is checked against the caps where `Traced<Parser>` is written. Haskell's monad transformers read the same way: `LoggingT m` adds logging to whatever `m` does.

Why it is sound. Only a type parameter or a function parameter passes effects through, because the caller chose it and sees it. Everything else counts against the cap. A concrete type the methods build and call counts, so no type can launder an effect through another. A trait value in a field counts with its trait's declared row. A function field with a fixed row must fit the cap.

Trait impls in any package. The cap is part of the type's public signature, like a method row. An impl of any trait for the type is checked against it where the impl is written, in whatever package. An inherited default method is checked there too. A `Close` impl is covered, so cleanup cannot reach the network either. Widening a published cap is a semver change, as a row change is under D-EFFECT-OMIT1.

One ladder, not a third place. `#FX` is already the ceiling for a block (spec.md:1825) and, under D-EFFECT-RUNGS1 A, for a module. A type becomes one more rung of the same ladder: block, function, type, module, package. Caps meet, so code obeys every cap above it. A method row may only tighten. `jet explain effects` lists the chain, nearest first.

Cost. The check reads rows the compiler already infers (D-EFFECT-OMIT1). Caps erase before IR, as block caps do today, so generated code is the same with or without them. A generic instance needs no extra check, because each type argument's own work was checked against its own cap. Nothing runs at run time.

Reads with the related ballots. Under D-EFFECT-RUNGS1 A, a type in a capped module obeys both caps. Under RUNGS1 C, the type cap is the only shared ceiling below the package. D-EFFTYPE-USES1 A and D-DECL-TYPES1 rule 4 give `#FX` above an effect type the same reading. D-EFFTYPE-TARGET1 caps whole artifacts and is independent.

Research. Haskell's `ST` type confines mutation, and `runST`'s rank-2 type proves none escapes, at no run-time cost (Launchbury and Peyton Jones, 1994). Monad transformers stack effects so each layer adds its own. Koka and Frank put rows on functions and stay polymorphic in the rest of the row; option A's pass-through reads the same way. Rust has no effect bound on types, only inferred auto traits.

Probes, in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/q/bd/probe/fx2. model.jet is the shown program in today's syntax, without the other package's impl. `jet check model.jet` is ok, because `#FX` above a struct parses and is ignored today. `jet run -A model.jet` is an internal compiler error in `Parser.display` (card to file), so the snippets are checked, not run. `Parser.Stylesheet`, `http.get` and the `T: #FX(...)` bound are illustrative.

options.name: `#FX` above a type bounds its work
options.detail:
`#FX(...)` above a struct, enum or trait is the ceiling for everything done in the type's name. That is its methods, its trait impls in any package, and every closure written inside them. A method row may only tighten it.

What a type parameter or a function parameter does belongs to the caller, as with `via`. So a generic type needs no tail rule, and `Traced<Parser>` does Traced's work plus Parser's. Above a trait, the cap bounds every impl in any package.
options.technical:
The Prelude `marker FX` sites grow from [.Block] to struct, enum and trait. Its D-MARK-SCOPE1 matrix mode is tighten. The check runs on inferred rows (D-EFFECT-OMIT1). Each method, impl method, inherited default method and lambda body must fit the cap, with E0712 naming it. Calls through a type parameter or a function parameter are excluded (D-EFF2 pass-through). Calls on concrete types are counted.

Trait values count with their trait's declared row (D-EFF3). Function-typed fields with a fixed row must fit. An impl is checked where it is written, in any package. The cap joins the public API snapshot. Caps erase before IR.

options.name: Module caps and rows only
options.detail:
A type gets no cap of its own. Its author moves it into its own module and caps the module, which covers the type, its methods and its helpers. A trait keeps its per-method rows, which already bind every impl.

An impl written in another package sits outside the module, so the cap does not check it. Closures follow their module. Generic types use today's open row tails and `via`.
options.technical: Uses D-EFFECT-RUNGS1=A (module `#FX` cap) and D-EFF3 (trait method rows bind impls). No new placement or grammar. A type with its own promise needs its own module line (`#FX(...) module parse`). Generic methods use `-[via f]>` (D-EFF2) and open tails (D-SHAPE8=A). An impl of the type in another package is checked only against that package's own caps and rows.

options.name: Bounds where the type is used
options.detail:
Types carry no promise. A function that needs one asks for it in a generic bound, and the compiler checks the inferred rows of the type's methods. Rust checks its inferred `Send` and `Sync` the same way.

Authors write nothing, and nothing is promised that no one uses. Each caller who needs the promise repeats the bound. A library change can break those callers, because the library never wrote the promise down.
options.technical: New bound form `T: #FX(...)` on generic parameters, checked against the inferred rows of the type's methods and impls (D-EFFECT-OMIT1). Model: Rust auto traits. No marker sites change.

comparisons.note: `ST s` confines mutation to one type, and runST's rank-2 type proves no reference escapes, with no run-time cost. Source: https://hackage.haskell.org/package/base/docs/Control-Monad-ST.html and Launchbury and Peyton Jones, Lazy Functional State Threads (PLDI 1994).
comparisons.code: runST :: (forall s. ST s a) -> a

comparisons.note: A monad transformer adds its own effect to whatever the inner monad does, the reading option A gives a generic type. Source: https://hackage.haskell.org/package/monad-logger
comparisons.code: newtype LoggingT m a = LoggingT { runLoggingT :: (Loc -> LogSource -> LogLevel -> LogStr -> IO ()) -> m a }

comparisons.note: Rows sit on function types and stay open over the rest of the row, so a higher-order function passes its argument's effects through. Source: https://koka-lang.github.io/koka/doc/book.html
comparisons.code: fun map(xs : list<a>, f : a -> e b) : e list<b>

comparisons.note: No effect bounds on types; inferred auto traits such as Send are asked for in bounds (option C). Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/special-types-and-traits.html#auto-traits

recommendation.why: A is the original ask, made safe. One line above a type bounds its methods, its impls anywhere and its closures. It reads like `#FX` on blocks, modules and effect types. Generic types reuse `via`.
gains: A type's promise is written once, on the type, and binds every package.
Generic types need no tail: a parameter's work is the caller's, as with `via`.
One reading of `#FX` from block to package, effect types included.

whyNot.reason: B leaves other packages' impls and a split-out module's helpers outside the promise, and makes authors split modules to state one.
C puts nothing in the library, so every caller repeats the bound and an upgrade can break them silently.

recommendation.tradeoff: A published cap is a promise to users: narrowing it is free, widening it is a breaking change, like a row.

It tried laundering an effect through a concrete type, a trait-value field and an inherited default method, and v2 now counts all three against the cap. surface.gist: Should `#FX` above a type bound everything its methods, trait impls and closures may do?
surface.lesson: An effect is a kind of power, such as network access. A function promises what it does with its row, like `-[!Net]>`. `#FX` above a block is a ceiling for the code inside it. This vote asks whether a type takes the same ceiling for all code that acts in its name.

current.note: Today the promise is repeated on each method's row, and an impl in another package is not held to it.

wild.note: A type can confine the effects of all code run in it: `ST` code can mutate only its own references. Source: Control.Monad.ST.

options.name: `#FX` above a type bounds its work
options.gist: `#FX(...)` above a type bounds its methods, its impls in any package and its closures.
gains: One line promises the whole type, wherever its impls live.
Generic types need no new rule: a type parameter's work is the caller's.
The same `#FX` reading as blocks, modules and effect types.

options.name: Module caps and rows only
options.gist: A type is promised through its module's cap; a trait through its methods' rows.
gains: Nothing new beyond the module cap.
One cap covers the type and its helpers.
losses: An impl of the type in another package is not checked.
A type that needs its own promise must move to its own module.

options.name: Bounds where the type is used
options.gist: Types stay unmarked; code that needs a promise asks for it in a bound.
gains: Authors write nothing.
The promise is checked exactly where it matters.
losses: A new kind of bound for generics.
Each caller repeats the bound, and the library promises nothing.

recommendation.why: A is the original ask, made safe. One line above a type bounds its methods, its impls anywhere and its closures. It reads like `#FX` on blocks, modules and effect types. Generic types reuse `via`.
gains: A type's promise is written once, on the type, and binds every package.
Generic types need no tail: a parameter's work is the caller's, as with `via`.
One reading of `#FX` from block to package, effect types included.

whyNot.reason: B leaves other packages' impls and a split-out module's helpers outside the promise, and makes authors split modules to state one.
C puts nothing in the library, so every caller repeats the bound and an upgrade can break them silently.

recommendation.tradeoff: A published cap is a promise to users: narrowing it is free, widening it is a breaking change, like a row.

decisions.title: A library effect says what it may do with the same `#FX` marker
decisions.situation: A library can name its own effect, such as a graph package's queries, so callers can allow or forbid exactly that. Today such a name can only be a leaf under one built-in effect, like `Net.Query`. Worse, its functions cannot actually use the network: the compiler rejects the very calls the name stands for. One rule matters here: a denial such as `!Net` checks what code really reaches, not what its rows claim. The vote decides how a library effect states what it may do. We recommend the same `#FX` marker used on blocks and modules.
decisions.gist: How should a library's own effect say which basic powers it may use?
decisions.lesson: An effect is a kind of power, such as network access. A library may name its own effect, like `graph.Query`, so a caller can allow or forbid just that. The name must say what it may really do. A denial such as `!Net` checks what code really reaches, not what rows claim, so a hidden network call is still caught.
decisions.story: Ana's reports call the `graph` package. Her lead wants one report that may never run a graph query, while another report may. She wants to write `!graph.Query` on that one function and have the compiler hold it.
decisions.detail:
Provenance. Folded into the D-EFFECT-LIMITS1 package ballot (card c09kjhit), which the owner rejected. Already ratified: the effect tree with roots and leaves (D-EFFTREE1), leaf declarations (D-EFFECT-DECL1=A), denials hold through calls (D-PROP1), and a new user root is E0119.

Probe findings, in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/q/bd/probe/fx. leaf_wrap2.jet: a function under `-[Net.Query]>` calling `net.tcp_listen` is E0740 "uses the effect `Net`, which its signature doesn't allow". deny_leaf_real.jet: the same for `FS.Notes` over `fs.read` (E0740 on `FS.Read`). So a library leaf is a name with nothing behind it today.

uses_a.jet: `#FX(Net)` above `effect Query` gives E0119 "`Query` isn't a known effect", as expected for new syntax. leaf.jet and deny_net.jet: a denial checks real reach, not the declared row. `-[!Net]>` calling a `-[Net]>` function with an empty body checks clean. db_net.jet: `-[!Net]>` calling a `-[DB]>` function checks clean, since DB is its own root.

Side note for existing cards: in leaf_wrap.jet, `print(port()?)` with a bare `?` checked clean. In leaf_wrap2.jet a bare `?` after a binding is E-ERR-PROPAGATE "A bare `?` has no meaning". The cause is not confirmed.

Reads with the related ballots. D-EFFECT-RUNGS1=A puts `#FX` on module lines with the same "at most" meaning, so blocks, modules and effects share one marker. D-EFFTYPE-KERNEL1 option A needs A here: Core declares `DB` and `Log` as library effects over machine powers. D-EFFTYPE-MODEL1 and D-EFFTYPE-TARGET1 are independent of this vote.

options.name: `#FX` above the effect
options.detail:
A package declares `effect Query` with `#FX(...)` above it, the same marker that caps a block or a module. Inside the package, a function whose row says `Query` may do what `Query` stands for, here network calls. Callers write `graph.Query`, like any other package item.

A leaf such as `effect Net.Query` keeps working, with the same rule: a leaf may do at most what its root does. So today's leaves become usable rather than changing shape.
options.technical:
Marker site: `#FX` on an `effect` declaration (D-MARK-SCOPE1 matrix, mode tighten). A positive list only; `!` entries are errors there. Package effects resolve as package items (`graph.Query`); unqualified inside the package. A leaf `Root.Leaf` gets the implicit cap `#FX(Root)`, which fixes E0740 on leaf bodies (probe/fx/leaf_wrap2.jet). Denials keep checking real reach (D-PROP1).

Today `$` marks facts and `#` marks rules: Compiler/Prelude/Effects.jet writes `effect Net $irreversible`. The cap is a rule checked on bodies, so it is spelled with today's rule sigil.

options.name: Leaves only, made usable
options.detail:
A library effect is a leaf under one built-in effect, as today. The one change: a leaf may use its root, so a `Net.Query` function may make network calls.

A library that needs both the network and files cannot say so with one name. Leaves live under shared roots, so two packages can pick the same leaf name.
options.technical: Semantics only: a body under `-[Root.Leaf]>` may use `Root`. No grammar change. D-EFFECT-DECL1 leaf declarations unchanged. Excludes D-EFFTYPE-KERNEL1 option A, which needs multi-power library effects.

options.name: A `uses` clause
options.detail:
The declaration lists its powers after a new `uses` keyword. The meaning matches option A; only the spelling differs.

A reader meets one more keyword, and the same "at most" idea is spelled `#FX(...)` on blocks and modules but `uses` here.
options.technical: New contextual keyword `uses` in `effect` declarations. Same semantics as option A.

comparisons.note: User effects are first-class names; what they do is decided by handlers. Source: https://koka-lang.github.io/koka/doc/book.html
comparisons.code:
effect query
  fun run-query(text : string) : list<person>

comparisons.note: Abilities are declared by libraries and named in function types. Source: https://www.unison-lang.org/docs/fundamentals/abilities/
Capabilities are ordinary values; a library capability wraps the ones it uses. Source: https://docs.scala-lang.org/scala3/reference/experimental/cc.html

recommendation.why: A reuses the one "at most" marker Jet already has, lets a package own its effect's name, and makes today's leaves usable too. It adds a placement, not a concept.
gains: One rule for blocks, modules and effects.
Unblocks Core's own effects in D-EFFTYPE-KERNEL1.

whyNot.reason: B cannot name an effect that needs two powers, and leaf names collide across packages.
C spells the same "at most" idea with a second keyword.

recommendation.tradeoff: Effects gain a marker line above them; a leaf needs none.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude. Adversarial model family: Claude. Fresh agent: Main. A reuses the at-most marker, so a reader learns no new form; the only risk is reading #FX(Net) as granting Net rather than capping it.

decisions.title: The compiler builds in machine powers; Core declares the rest like a library
decisions.situation: Jet has thirteen built-in effects. Some are things the machine does, such as network, files and the clock. Others are services built on those, such as databases and logging. Because a database is its own built-in effect, forbidding the network does not stop a database call that goes over the network. Packages also cannot define effects the way Core does. The vote decides which effects the compiler builds in. We recommend building in only the machine powers and declaring the rest in Core, the way any package would.
decisions.gist: Which effects should the compiler build in, and which should Core declare like a library?
decisions.lesson: An effect is a kind of power, such as network access. Some powers come from the machine: network, files, clock, randomness. Others are services built on them, like a database. If a service is declared over the machine powers it uses, forbidding the network also stops a database that talks over the network.
decisions.story: Ana's offline report reads from the shop database. She writes `!Net` on it so it never waits on the network. Then the team moves the database to a server, and the report still compiles, because a database call is not a network call to the compiler.
decisions.detail:
Provenance. Folded into the D-EFFECT-LIMITS1 package ballot (card c09kjhit), which the owner rejected. Already ratified: the thirteen roots (D-EFF4/5, D-AUTHORITY-ROOTS1), the effect tree (D-EFFTREE1) and leaf declarations (D-EFFECT-DECL1=A). Also settled: the vocabulary is Jet source in Compiler/Prelude/Effects.jet (D-META-ONE1=A), and denials hold through calls (D-PROP1).

Probe, in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/q/bd/probe/fx. kernel_today.jet is today's program: `offline_count` under `-[!Net]>` calls a `-[DB]>` function and checks clean. db_net.jet shows the same with a stub body.

Reads with the related ballots. A needs D-EFFTYPE-USES1=A, which lets an effect declare what it may do. It matches D-EXTEND-ARCH1=A: Core uses the same forms packages use. D-EFFTYPE-TARGET1 takes the machine powers as the facts a target profile lists. D-EFFTYPE-GRANT1 grants these names unchanged.

Open detail inside A, not a vote: the exact caps for `Log` and `Secret` follow their Core drivers. A file logger reaches only FS; a collector also reaches Net.

Side note for existing cards: a `DBConnection` has no query method. Even a first program must build a row policy and call `with_policy` to get a `DBScope` (kernel_today.jet; Core/Db/Db.jet:707-715). That is heavy for the beginner path.

options.name: Machine powers built in, services in Core
options.detail:
The compiler builds in what the machine does: network, files, terminal, clock, randomness, environment, processes, foreign code, graphics card and browser host. Core then declares databases, logging and secrets over those, with the same `#FX` line a package uses.

Users keep writing `-[DB]>` and `!DB`. What changes is that `!Net` now catches a database that talks to a server, while a local database file still passes.
options.technical:
Needs D-EFFTYPE-USES1=A. Compiler/Prelude/Effects.jet keeps the machine roots (Net, FS, IO, Time, Rand, Env, Exec, FFI, GPU, Browser; deny-only Mem, Panic). Core declares `#FX(Net, FS) effect DB`, `#FX(IO, FS, Net) effect Log` and `#FX(Env, FS, Net) effect Secret`, exported through the Prelude so rows keep bare names. Leaves (DB.Read, DB.Write) move with their parent.

Denials keep checking real reach (D-PROP1), so each driver's real calls decide. A server driver written over `core.net` reaches Net. Core's SQLite driver calls C inside vouched `#Unsafe` gates (Core/Db/Db.jet:1374); those stay invisible to callers, as today. A driver over vouched C names its machine reach on its binding.

options.name: Keep thirteen built-in roots
options.detail:
All thirteen effects stay built in, each its own switch. Forbidding one never forbids another.

A team that wants an offline report must forbid both `Net` and `DB`, even when the database is a local file. A package that builds a service like Core's database cannot give it an effect of the same kind.
options.technical: Status quo: D-EFF4/5 roots in Compiler/Prelude/Effects.jet. probe/fx/kernel_today.jet shows `-[!Net]>` calling `-[DB]>` checks clean.

options.name: Everything in Core over foreign calls
options.detail:
The compiler builds in only foreign calls and memory. Core declares network, files and every other effect over foreign calls to the system.

This is the smallest list, but every input and output path now sits under foreign calls. Forbidding foreign code forbids everything, and the switches people use most, like network and files, become library choices rather than facts about the machine.
options.technical: Compiler roots: FFI and deny-only Mem, Panic. Core declares the rest with `#FX(FFI)` or stacks. Package `authority:` and `--deny` lists stay valid but every root becomes a declared effect.

comparisons.note: A small built-in IO underneath; libraries declare abilities on top. Source: https://www.unison-lang.org/docs/fundamentals/abilities/
comparisons.code:
ability Store where
  get : Text -> Optional Text

comparisons.note: Built-in effects such as io, fsys, net, ndet; libraries add their own. Source: https://koka-lang.github.io/koka/doc/book.html
Run permissions name machine powers only: net, read, write, env, run, ffi, sys. Source: https://docs.deno.com/runtime/fundamentals/security/

recommendation.why: A keeps every row users write today and makes `!Net` mean what people expect. Core's services become ordinary declarations, the same form packages use.
gains: Denials follow the machine, not names.
One effect form for Core and packages.

whyNot.reason: B leaves `!Net` blind to database servers and keeps Core's effects out of packages' reach.
C hides every machine power under foreign calls and loses the simple switches.

recommendation.tradeoff: Core gains three short declarations; the compiler's list shrinks to machine powers.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude. Adversarial model family: Claude. Fresh agent: Main. A keeps machine powers in the compiler and declares DB, Log and Secret in Core, so a !Net denial catches a remote database; C-backed drivers must state their reach.

Read Compiler/Prelude/Effects.jet in the dev worktree for today's root list.
