decisions.title: Each build's effect limit is read from its target profile; nothing new to write
decisions.situation: Some builds run where the machine lacks things: a web page with no operating system has no files, and a small board may have no memory allocator. Jet already describes each such machine as a target profile with typed facts. Today those facts do not limit what code may do, so a list allocated under a profile with no allocator checks and builds clean. The vote decides where a build's effect limit comes from. We recommend reading it from the profile's facts, with nothing new to write.
decisions.gist: Where should the effect limit for a no-OS web, GPU or board build come from?
decisions.lesson: An effect is a kind of power, such as file access or allocating memory. A target profile lists what a machine has. If the profile says there is no allocator, code built for it must not allocate. Reading the limit from those facts means a machine is described once, and the compiler checks code against it.
decisions.story: Ana's team ships a small price widget built for a web page with no operating system. Its profile says there is no allocator. A helper that builds a list of labels slipped in, the build passed, and the widget failed at load time.
decisions.detail:
Provenance. Folded into the D-EFFECT-LIMITS1 package ballot (card c09kjhit), which the owner rejected. Reuses the earlier draft at ballots/out/new/D-EFFTYPE-TARGET1.json, with its fact-to-denial table. Already ratified: typed profile modules selected by `targets:` (D-TARGET-SURFACE1=A), facts as the source of truth (D-FREESTAND-FACTS1=A), and required allocator and panic facts (D-TARGET-ALLOC1=A).

D-FREESTAND-FACTS1 rejected effects as the source of what a machine has. Here effects are only derived from facts, never written, so that decision holds.

Probes, in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/q/bd/probe/fx. target_today uses Examples/embedded/heap_free_core/package.jet (profile `web.no_os`, `runtime: "core"`). `use core.files` there is E1006 "`core.files` needs `runtime: hosted`". A list allocation checks clean, and `jet build run.jet` exits 0 with a host ELF binary. target_a/run.jet is option A's program and checks clean today.

Side note for existing cards: `jet build --target=web.no_os run.jet` is E2104 "`jet build --target=web.no_os` is not built yet". Plain `jet build` in a `web.no_os` package produced a host ELF binary rather than refusing.

Reads with the related ballots. D-EFFTYPE-KERNEL1=A keeps the machine powers as compiler roots, which are exactly what profile facts map to. D-EFFECT-RUNGS1 and D-EFFTYPE-MODEL1 cap code by where it lives; this ballot caps it by where it runs. The two combine by intersection.

options.name: Read from the profile's facts
options.detail:
The package already selects its profile. Each fact the profile marks absent becomes a denial for that build: no allocator denies allocation, no sockets denies the network, no file system denies files.

A breach is reported at the line, with the call path from the entry and the missing fact. Hover on the profile line, or `jet explain`, lists every derived denial with its fact.
options.technical:
Keeps D-TARGET-SURFACE1=A (typed profile modules selected by `targets:`) and D-FREESTAND-FACTS1=A (facts are the source of truth). Mapping: allocator absent gives `!Mem.Alloc`; sockets `!Net`; file system `!FS`; entropy `!Rand`; browser DOM `!Browser`; GPU `!GPU`; FFI `!FFI`.

Also: no byte sink gives `!IO`; no clocks `!Time`; no sleep `!Time.Wait`. Facts with no effect (startup, linker, regions, MMIO) map to nothing. Each artifact gets its own limit. Shared code that differs per build branches with `comptime if` on profile facts.

options.name: Written by the package
options.detail:
Each target entry in the package file gets a `deny:` list, written by the team. The profile's facts stay separate.

The limit is visible in one line. But the team repeats what the profile already says, and a denial left out is never checked.
options.technical: New `deny:` field on `targets:` entries, checked like `authority.deny` but per artifact. Profile facts are not consulted.

options.name: No effect limit
options.detail:
Keep what exists: `runtime:` refuses imports of whole libraries the machine cannot support. Anything finer, like one allocation, is not checked until link or load.

Nothing new to learn, but the widget story above keeps happening.
options.technical: Status quo. probe/fx/target_today: `use core.files` under `runtime: "core"` is E1006; a list allocation under `web.no_os` checks and builds clean.

comparisons.note: Platform facts are `cfg` values; `no_std` crates fail at link time when they reach for an allocator. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/conditional-compilation.html
Target facts are compile-time values; using a missing feature fails when it is reached. Source: https://ziglang.org/documentation/master/#Targets
Device-code rules are hard-coded one by one in the compiler. Source: https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-c-programming-guide/

recommendation.why: A turns facts the team already writes into checks, with no new syntax. Each machine is described once, and errors point at the line and the missing fact.
gains: Machine limits are checked at compile time.
No second list to keep in step.

whyNot.reason: B makes teams repeat the profile by hand, and a forgotten line is never checked.
C leaves allocation and similar breaches to fail at load time.

recommendation.tradeoff: The derived limit is not one written line; hover and `jet explain` list it.

decisions.title: `jet add` writes each dependency's grant line; an upgrade that needs more stops with the call path
decisions.situation: Attacks often arrive in an upgrade: a trusted library's new version quietly starts using the network. Jet already has a place in package.jet for what each dependency may do, but nothing writes it, and the compiler refuses any filled-in line today. So a project that allows the network for its own code lets every dependency use it too. The vote decides who writes each dependency's line. We recommend that `jet add` writes it, asking only when the project would gain a power.
decisions.gist: Should `jet add` write what each dependency may do into package.jet, ask first, or leave it?
decisions.lesson: An effect is a kind of power, such as network access. A grant line in package.jet says which powers one dependency may use. If the tool writes that line when you add the dependency, a later version that wants more power stops the build. It names the call that needs the power and offers one command to allow it.
decisions.story: Ana adds a JSON library to her shop. Months later, `jet update` pulls a new version that sends data to a server. Her shop uses the network itself, so nothing in today's package file notices the library's new reach.
decisions.detail:
Provenance. Folded into the D-EFFECT-LIMITS1 package ballot (card c09kjhit), which the owner rejected. Reuses the earlier draft at ballots/out/new/D-EFFTYPE-GRANT1.json. Already ratified: per-dependency provenance in the lock and opt-in enforcement (D-EFFBUDGET1=D), the `grants:` field (D-EFFBUDGET1), and the confirmation prompt shape (D-SCRIPT-CONFIRM1=A).

Probe, in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/q/bd/probe/fx/grant_today. A package.jet with `grants: { json: [] }` gives E1221 "`authority.grants` is not supported by the current compiler package-policy boundary". Today's Examples/features/packages/effect_budget writes only an empty `grants: {}`.

Meaning of a grant line. D-EFFBUDGET1 calls a grant a per-dependency escape from `allow`. Under A, the line is that dependency's whole limit, which covers the escape case and also pins a dependency below `allow`. No project has a non-empty line today, so nothing changes meaning.

Why this matters. Upgrade attacks: event-stream (2018) added a payload through a new dependency; ua-parser-js (2021) and xz-utils (2024) shipped malicious releases of trusted packages.

Reads with the related ballots. D-EFFTYPE-KERNEL1 fixes the names a grant line lists. D-SCRIPT-DESIGNATE1, in the project group, covers what a script grants itself. D-FFI-UNSAFE1 uses the same grant line for a binder's build-time tool.

options.name: `jet add` writes the line
options.detail:
`jet add json` works out what the library uses and writes `json: []` under `grants:`. If that fits what the project already allows, nothing is asked. If it needs a new power, a terminal asks once; without a terminal, the command stops and prints the exact flag to pass.

Each later build and `jet update` checks every granted dependency. A version that reaches further stops with the call path and a one-command fix.
options.technical:
Under `authority.grants`, a listed dependency's limit is its line, replacing `allow` for that dependency. Today non-empty grants are refused (Compiler/JetDriver/Source/Driver/Loader.jet:387-388), so no project changes meaning. Writing grants alone does not turn on `allow` enforcement for the project's own code (D-EFFBUDGET1=D keeps enforcement opt-in).

Prompt shape follows D-SCRIPT-CONFIRM1=A. `--allow` reuses the run flag spelling (`jet run --allow=FS.Read`). Hand-added dependencies without a line keep today's behavior: provenance in the lock. Lines are one per dependency, sorted.

options.name: Ask on every add
options.detail:
Like A, but `jet add` always asks before writing, even when the library needs nothing new.

The question carries no information when the answer is always yes, so people learn to press Enter. Non-interactive use needs a flag on every add.
options.technical: Same grant semantics as A. Adds a confirmation on every `jet add`; `--yes` for scripts.

options.name: Never write
options.detail:
Keep today's rule: the lock records what each dependency uses, and grant lines are written by hand.

The lock shows the change after the fact, if someone reads the diff. Nothing stops the build.
options.technical: Status quo for D-EFFBUDGET1=D provenance; non-empty grants become writable by hand only.

decisions.title: One compile-time mark: `#` marks markers, site values and pastes; everything else is a plain value
decisions.situation: Code that runs while compiling does two things. It reads values, such as a type's fields or the package version. It pastes names into the code it adds, such as a new method's name. Today `$` does both, so a local value named `package` silently hides the package root. D-DECL-TYPES1 A, now ratified, removed every `$` setting. This vote decides how the remaining reads and pastes are spelled. We recommend no `$` at all.
decisions.gist: How should compile-time code read values and paste names into the code it adds, now that `$` settings are gone?
decisions.lesson: A marker's expand runs while compiling and adds code at the marker's site. It reads facts, like a type's fields, and pastes names, like describe_x. If those reads are ordinary values and every paste is marked `#{...}`, the one mark `#` always means the compiler acts right here. Code that reads plainly then behaves plainly.
decisions.story: Leo writes a marker that adds a `stamp()` method and keeps a local value called `package`. Today his generated code prints his local instead of the package name, with no warning. Under A he writes `#package.name`. No local can be spelled with `#`, so nothing can hide it.
decisions.detail:
Provenance. Card c0699zei. The owner rejected v1, which kept `#` for reads and `$` for pastes. He wrote: "I don't love the split and use of $ in general. I feel like there is a more elegant cohesive, idiomatic way to do this we haven't touched on." He asked to design away every downside. His earlier direction (q6c37m9o) made `#` the compile-time mark: capitalized for markers, lower-case for values.

What changed since v1. D-DECL-TYPES1 A, now ratified, removed every `$` setting, such as `$sites`. It also gave every marker `fn expand(self, target: Target)`. So the marked item is now an ordinary parameter. What v1 spelled `#target.name` or `#name` is now the field read `target.name`. That leaves three jobs: reading Jet's values, pasting names and types, and naming the current line.

Today's census, dev 21acbf2fa8. Jet source has 429 `.$` reads or pastes, such as `T.$fields` and `self.$field`. It has 73 `{$x}` pastes inside strings, 26 `fn $name` and 14 `impl $name`. Roots such as `$build.os` and `$package.version` are the rest. Compiler/Prelude/Derives.jet:58 names a generated local `jet_rhs_variant_index`, with a `jet_` prefix, so it cannot collide with user names.

The idea in A. Two observations remove `$`. First, a compile-time value is an ordinary value, as in Zig. A read is a field read, and a value used in added code is copied in as a constant. Second, only names and types need pasting, because a name is not a value. A marks those pastes with `#{...}`, the string-hole braces behind the compile-time mark.

A's one rule for `#`. The mark means the compiler acts where it is written. A capitalized name applies a marker to the item below, as in `#web.Route`. A lower-case name is a value about this spot: `#line`, `#file` and `#package`. Braces paste a name or type here, as in `fn #{method}`. Inside expand, `#line` is the library's line; `target.line` is the user's.

Reads in A. Inside expand, `target.fields`, `target.name` and `field.ty` are plain field reads. Elsewhere, `T.reflect()` returns the same kind of value; it already exists in Examples/features/comptime/reflect.jet. So `Severity.$range` becomes `Severity.reflect().range`. Build facts are one Prelude value, `build`, as in `build.target.os`. It needs no mark, because it is the same wherever it is written. `#package` names the package where it is written, so it keeps the mark.

Pastes in A. A hole pastes a whole name: after a declaration word, after a dot, or where a type goes. It takes a String, a Type, or a reflected item such as a Field, which pastes its name. A hole is never glued to letters. So `pkg#1.4` and `[Int#4]` keep their meaning. A compound name is built as a string first: `method :: "describe_{field.name}"`.

Edge case, types versus values. A value such as `count` is written plainly in added code and copied in as a constant. A value that cannot be a constant, such as an open file, is a compile error at that line. A type is pasted with a hole, `impl #{target}`. The Type value carries its full path, so it never depends on the user's imports.

Edge case, hygiene. Names written in a template resolve in the template's own file. So `Ordering` or `print` in added code mean the library's, and a user's own `Ordering` cannot capture them. A pasted name, such as a handler the user named in the marker's arguments, resolves at the marker's site. A local declared inside added code, such as `value`, is private to that expansion. The `jet_` prefix in Derives.jet becomes unnecessary.

Edge case, name capture and shadowing. A pasted name is meant for the user. If it collides with a user method, the duplicate-name error points at the user's type and notes the marker. Today a local can silently hide a `use` name (probe shadow_use.jet prints "mine"). Inside expand, A makes that E0118, as a hidden inner local already is (shadow_local.jet). So a template value named `web` or `build` cannot hide the package or the Prelude value.

Options B and C. B is A with bare braces, `fn {method}`, and no mark at all. It reads like Swift's syntax interpolation. But in code a bare `{` usually opens a block, so a reader cannot spot a paste at a glance, and no search finds them. C is v1's recommendation adapted: `#` reads Jet's values and `$` pastes. It keeps two marks, and a `$count` paste of a plain value.

Research, quasiquote. Common Lisp's backquote template pastes with `,x` (HyperSpec 2.4.6). It is unhygienic, so authors call gensym for private names. Scheme's syntax-rules is hygienic by default (R7RS 4.3.2). A takes Scheme's default: private locals and definition-site names. The explicit quote form is not needed, because D-DECL-TYPES1 rule 6 already makes the expand body the template.

Research, Rust and Swift. Rust's quote! pastes with `#var` and builds compound names with format_ident! (docs.rs/quote). That is A's mark and A's compound-name rule. Swift macros build syntax from string interpolation, `"func \(raw: name)()"`, and are not hygienic; authors call makeUniqueName (swift-syntax docs). That is B's shape.

Research, Zig. Zig's compile-time values are ordinary values, and build facts come from the ordinary module builtin, as in builtin.os.tag (ziglang.org documentation, comptime). Zig reads a field by computed name with @field(self, name), and the call site with @src(). Zig cannot declare a function with a computed name. A takes Zig's plain values and adds the one paste Zig lacks.

Migration. `jet fix` respells every site once. `T.$x` becomes `T.reflect().x`, or `target.x` inside expand. `$build` becomes `build`, and `$package` becomes `#package`. `$name` pastes become `#{name}`, and `{$x}` inside strings becomes `{x}`. Locals with a `jet_` prefix may drop it. `#line` and `#file` are new; today both are E0003 (probes dollar_line.jet and hash_line.jet).

Reads with the related ballots. D-MARKER-DIAG1, D-MARKER-REFLECT1 and D-MARKER-LADDER1 read `target` as a plain parameter under every option. D-JAI-GENERIC1's `##Pre` keeps its place. D-DECL-TYPES1 rule 6 says `$name pastes a value`. Under A, that clause reads `#{name} pastes a name or type`, a spelling change only.

options.name: `#` marks the compiler; reads are plain values
options.detail:
Compile-time values are ordinary values: `target.fields`, `build.target.os`, `T.reflect().range`. A value used in added code is copied in. Only names and types are pasted, with `#{...}`: `fn #{method}`, `self.#{field}`, `impl #{target}`.

`#` then has one meaning, the compiler acts here: `#Route` applies a marker, `#line` is this line, `#{x}` pastes. Added code is hygienic, so no `$` and no `jet_` prefixes remain.
options.technical: New: hole #{e} in name and type positions of templates, where e is a String, Type or reflected item. New: Prelude value build (target, release). New: #line, #file and #package. Retires every $ read and paste, and {$x} in strings. Template names resolve at the definition site, pasted names at the marker's site, and locals in added code are private. E0118 also covers a local in expand that takes a use or Prelude name. Respells D-COMPILER-NS1=A, D-META-ROOT3=A, D-BUILD-FACT3=A and D-NAME-SPLICE1=B.

options.name: Bare braces paste; no mark at all
options.detail:
Reads are plain values, as in A. A paste is a bare hole, `fn {method}` or `self.{field}`, like a string hole without the quotes.

No mark is needed. But in code `{` usually opens a block or a struct literal, so a reader cannot spot a paste at a glance, and a search for pastes finds every brace.
options.technical: As A, but holes are {e} with no mark. A hole is allowed only after a declaration word, after a dot, or in a type position, where a block cannot start. Hygiene, the build value, #line and the E0118 extension are as in A.

options.name: `#` reads Jet's values; `$` pastes
options.detail:
v1's recommendation, adapted to D-DECL-TYPES1 A. Jet's own values carry `#`: `#build.target.os`, `Severity.#range`. Every paste keeps `$`, including plain values: `$count`, `fn $method`.

Reads and pastes look different. But compile-time code still uses two marks, and `$` stays in the language.
options.technical: Respells roots and facts to # (D-COMPILER-NS1=A, D-META-ROOT3=A, D-BUILD-FACT3=A); D-NAME-SPLICE1=B pastes stay $. Adds #line and #file. A local named like a root is refused, which ends the hiding bug. Templates stay unhygienic, as today.

decisions.title: Read a marker as the typed record its declaration already describes
decisions.situation: A marker often reads another marker on the same item. A `Describe` marker reads the table name from `#store.Table("orders")`, for example. Today it gets a list of marker rows, with names as strings and arguments found by position. The written value, "orders", cannot be read at all while compiling. A typo or a reordered marker returns the wrong row without an error. The marker declaration already lists typed parameters, so Jet knows the record shape. The vote decides how code reads a marker and its arguments. We recommend a typed lookup that returns that record.
decisions.gist: How should code read a marker on an item, and the arguments written in it?
decisions.lesson: A marker declaration like `marker Table(name: String)` lists typed parameters, just like a struct. When other compile-time code looks for `Table` on an item, it can get back a `Table` record and read `.name`. Then a misspelled marker or field is an ordinary error, not a silent miss.
decisions.story: Ada writes a marker that reads `#Table`'s name. A user adds a second marker before `#Table`, and her code reads position 0, which is now the wrong marker. Every generated table name changes without a single error.
decisions.detail:
Provenance. Card c03pi177. This is the reflection question from the D-COMPTIME-MARKERS1 package ballot, asked alone. Spelled with D-META-HASH1 A (`#target`, `#sites`); under another spelling only the marks change.

Today. MarkerInfo rows carry `name`, `args` (each with `name`, `ty` as text, `value`), `sites` and `repeatable` (Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Comptime/Reflection.jet:311-336). `has_marker` takes a string (Sema/Calls/Reflection.jet:229-250). Examples/features/comptime/reflect.jet reads `info.methods[0].markers[0].name` and `info.has_marker("Debug")`.

Probes, in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/q/bd/probe/mk. reflect_args.jet: `has_marker("Table")` and `markers[0].args[0].name` check clean and print "name true", the parameter's name, not the written "orders". reflect_c.jet: reading `markers[0].args[0].value` is E0956 "A derive template binding is not a known-time value", so today no compile-time code can read a written argument. The same file with `markers[0].name` prints "Table" for `#[Table("orders"), TableName]` and "TableName" for `#[TableName, Table("users")]`: the position read shifts silently.

Reads with the related ballots. D-MARKER-LADDER1 A lists every use of a marker as the same record, so `Route.#uses` returns `[Route.Use]` holding a `Route` and its site. D-MARKER-DIAG1 A refuses a bad argument by name. Both hold under every option here.

options.name: Typed lookup
options.detail:
Every marker declaration also declares a record with the same name and fields. `#target.marker(Table)` returns `Table?`: the record if `#Table` is written on the item, otherwise `None`. A repeatable marker returns `[Table]`.

On a type or function named in code, the same read is `Order.#marker(Table)`. A misspelled `Tabel` or `.nmae` is the ordinary unknown-name error.
options.technical: The marker rule's parameter list becomes the record type (MarkerInfo rows already carry name and type per argument, Reflection.jet:311-336). `#sites` and other `#` metadata are not record fields. `has_marker("X")` and string `markers[i].args[j]` reads retire; `jet fix` rewrites them to `marker(X) != None` and field reads. Uses D-META-HASH1 A spelling; under B it reads `target.$marker(Table)`.

options.name: Match the marker list
options.detail:
`#target.markers` stays a list. Each entry can be matched against a marker pattern like `Table(name)`, which binds the arguments with their declared types.

Finding one marker means a loop and a mutable value. A pattern for a marker that is never written on any item still compiles silently.
options.technical: Marker rules become pattern constructors over the MarkerInfo list. `has_marker` stays. Uses D-META-HASH1 A spelling.

options.name: Rows, with values readable
options.detail:
Code keeps asking `has_marker("Table")` and reading `markers[0].args[0]`. The one change is that `.value` becomes readable while compiling.

Nothing checks the string or the position, and values arrive as text.
options.technical: Today's MarkerInfo{name, args: [MarkerArgInfo{name, ty, value}], sites, repeatable} (Reflection.jet:311-336) and `has_marker` (Calls/Reflection.jet:229-250), plus making `args[i].value` a known-time value (today E0956).

comparisons.note: Attributes are classes; `GetCustomAttribute<T>()` returns a typed instance. Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/advanced-topics/reflection-and-attributes/accessing-attributes-by-using-reflection
Annotations are typed interfaces read with `getAnnotation`. Source: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/annotations/
comparisons.code:
Table t = cls.getAnnotation(Table.class);
String n = t.name();

comparisons.note: Derive macros receive raw attribute tokens and parse them by hand, for example with the darling crate. Source: https://docs.rs/darling

recommendation.why: A reuses what the declaration already says: `marker Table(name: String)` is the record. Lookups are one line, typos are errors, and the order of markers no longer matters.
gains: One typed read in place of strings and positions.
Works the same on `#target` and on any named type.

whyNot.reason: B types the arguments but makes every lookup a loop with a mutable value.
C makes values readable but keeps silent misses from typos and shifted positions.

decisions.title: A marker body sees its target in full, plus every type the target names
decisions.situation: A route marker must check that each path hole, like `{id}`, matches a parameter whose type it can parse. Today a function marker body sees only parameter names, an empty module and only the effects written by hand. The build function sees the same function in full. So the route marker cannot check types at all. The vote decides how far one marker body may read. We recommend its whole target, plus every type the target names, through the same records the build function uses.
decisions.gist: How much of the program may one marker body read: its target, what the target names, or everything?
decisions.lesson: A marker body runs once for each item that carries the marker. It needs to know that item fully, including the types of its fields and parameters. It rarely needs the rest of the program. Limiting what a body reads keeps rebuilds small, because a body reruns only when something it read changes.
decisions.story: Mia writes `#web.Route("/orders/{id}")` on a handler whose `id` is an `OrderID`. The route marker cannot see the type, so it accepts the route, and the request fails at run time with a parse error.
decisions.detail:
Provenance. Card c03pi177. This is the reach question from the D-COMPTIME-MARKERS1 package ballot, asked alone. The whole-program listing stays with the root build function (D-METADEPTH2=B). Collecting every use of a marker is split out as D-MARKER-USES1. Whether reading needs a grant is already settled by D-META-OPTIN2=A: read-only facts are standard.

decisions.title: `Route.#uses` lists every use of a marker, read in the marker's own package
decisions.situation: A web library wants one table of every `#web.Route` in the app, so it can serve them all. Today nothing can collect them. A marker body sees only its own item, and only the app's build function may list the whole program. So every app lists its routes again by hand, and a forgotten one is silently never served. The vote decides how a library gathers every use of its own marker. We recommend a typed list of uses that only the marker's own package may read.
decisions.gist: How should a library gather every place its marker is used, such as every route in an app?
decisions.lesson: Some markers only make sense together: every `#Route` belongs in one route table, and every `#Command` in one command list. The library that owns the marker should be able to ask for all its uses as a typed list. Each entry pairs the marker's record with the item it sits on.
decisions.story: Ravi adds `#web.Route("/users")` to a new handler and ships it. The app's hand-written route list never got the new line, so every request to `/users` returns 404.
decisions.detail:
Provenance. Card c03pi177. Split from D-MARKER-LADDER1, which settles how far one body reads. This ballot asks how a library collects every use of its marker. Approved split by Main.

Why only the owner reads. If any package could read any marker's uses, adding a route would change unrelated packages and their rebuilds. Owner-only reading keeps the list a private part of the library's API. The app sees only what the library chooses to expose, here `web.routes()`.

Completeness with separate builds. The uses are known only after the whole program is checked, so a library's route table folds in the app build, never in the library's own build.

Probes, in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/q/bd/probe/mk. uses_c.jet: option C's hand list runs today and prints "/orders -> orders" and "/users -> users". program_today.jet: a marker body cannot list the program (E0956). Examples/features/comptime/distinct_reflect.jet shows the build function listing types with `b.program.types()`.

Reads with the related ballots. `Route.Use.route` is D-MARKER-REFLECT1 A's typed record. The read is written in D-META-HASH1 A's spelling without presuming it: under HASH1=B this is `Route.$uses`, and the meaning is the same. Serving a handler from its `site` is the library's own generated glue, as in D-MARKER-LADDER1 A.

options.name: Typed list, owner reads
options.detail:
`Route.#uses` is a list with one entry per use: `route`, the typed `Route` record, and `site`, the item it sits on. Only code in the package that declares `Route` may read it. The list is complete once the program is checked, so it is filled in while compiling.

The app just writes `#web.Route(...)` on handlers.
options.technical: A `Use` record per marker rule: `{route: M, site: ItemInfo}`, built from the same records as D-MARKER-LADDER1 A. Reading `M.#uses` outside M's package is refused. Its value is fixed after checking, so the call folds to a constant. Spelled with D-META-HASH1 A.

options.name: The app's build function collects
options.detail:
Only the root build function may list the whole program, so the app collects its own routes there and publishes a table.

Every app repeats the same build code, and a library cannot provide the table on its own.
options.technical: Uses D-METADEPTH2=B program listing and D-META-PUBLISH2=A `compiler.generate`. `b.program.types()` exists today (Examples/features/comptime/distinct_reflect.jet); `functions()` would be added.

options.name: The app lists routes by hand
options.detail:
The app writes a constant list of routes beside its handlers, and the library serves that list.

Every path appears twice, and nothing warns when a handler is missing from the list.
options.technical: Today's only working form.

The inventory and linkme crates gather items into one list at link time, outside the language. Source: https://docs.rs/linkme
A source generator reads every attributed method and writes a table while compiling. Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/roslyn-sdk/source-generators-overview

whyNot.reason: B makes every app write the same build code, and libraries cannot ship the table.

recommendation.tradeoff: Only the marker's own package may read its uses, by design.

decisions.title: A library error is a struct that implements the Core trait Diagnostic, with its texts as one-literal methods
decisions.situation: When a marker refuses a use, such as a route path without a leading slash, the user sees an error. Today the library must borrow one of Jet's own codes, so `jet explain` shows an unrelated page. D-DECL-TYPES1 A, now ratified, makes every error a struct that implements a Core trait, Diagnostic. This vote decides where that trait keeps an error's texts: in methods, in trait constants, or in fields with defaults.
decisions.gist: Should a Diagnostic's what, why and fix texts be one-literal methods, trait constants, or fields with defaults?
decisions.lesson: Every Jet error has a code, a short what, a why and a fix, and `jet explain` prints them. Under D-DECL-TYPES1 A, an error is a struct, and the Core trait Diagnostic says what it must provide. Its data lives in fields. The texts need that data, as in route `orders` must start with /.
decisions.story: Noor misspells a route and gets `web.BadPath`, pointing at her own line. `jet explain web.BadPath` prints the library's texts with `{path}` where her route goes. She fixes the path in seconds. The web library's author wrote one struct and three one-line methods.
decisions.detail:
Provenance. Card #6039 (c03pi177). The owner rejected v1, which recommended a new `diagnostic` declaration word. He asked for Diagnostic as a trait, aligned with D-DECL-TYPES1, which he has now ratified with option A. He also asked whether the texts should be fields with defaults or functions. v2 compares both on the merits. Every option here is the Core trait; only where the texts live differs.

What is already settled. D-DECL-TYPES1 A makes an error a struct that implements Diagnostic, with no declaration word (its rules 7 and 13). Its name is its package path, such as web.BadPath. Settings with no data, such as code and severity, are trait constants with defaults. The open question is the three texts, because they read the error's own data.

The deciding fact. In Jet, `{name}` inside a string reads a name in scope. A method has `self` in scope, so `{self.path}` is ordinary, type-checked interpolation. A trait constant and a field default have no `self`. The probes show both fail today with E0107, nothing named `path`. So B must give braces a second meaning, and C cannot put data in a default at all.

Static reading. The foundation registry must read every error's texts without running code. Under A, D-DECL-TYPES1 rule 7 requires each text method's body to be one string literal, and the compiler names any other body. So A and B are equally readable from source. Under C, a raise site may replace a default, so the text a user sees may never appear in the declaration.

jet explain. Under A and B, `jet explain web.BadPath` prints each literal with its holes, shown as `{path}`. Under C it prints only the defaults, which cannot mention the data. Under all three the report points at the user's line, such as app/run.jet:3, with the library line as a note. Today it points inside the library.

Defaults and data. Severity defaults to .Error under every option, as a trait constant in A and B. The value's data is its fields under every option. Under C the texts are fields too, so each raise may restate them, and the same error can read two ways.

Brevity. B is shortest: `what :: "..."` is one short line per text. A writes `fn what(self) -> String { "..." }`, about 25 more characters per text. C is short to declare but long at every raise. A's extra characters buy one meaning for braces, interpolation checked by the existing type checker, and no new rule to learn.

Raising. `reject(BadPath{path: path})` raises any Diagnostic, from a marker's expand or from an ordinary library function that expand calls. It runs only while compiling. An .Error stops that marker's expansion. A .Warning is reported, and the expansion goes on. `#Allow(web.TrailingSlash)` on the user's item silences one warning by name. An .Error cannot be allowed.

Jet's own errors. Under A, each of the 996 Prelude rows becomes a struct with the same three methods and `code :: "E0927"` (rule 13). Jet's errors and library errors then render, explain and allow through one path. No rule of D-DECL-TYPES1 changes under A. B would amend rules 7 and 13; C would amend rule 7 and drop rule 13's fixed texts.

Dropped options. v1's `diagnostic` word is gone, because D-DECL-TYPES1 A retired declaration words. v1's C, inline texts named by the marker, is gone too. It gave two refusals one name, so neither could be explained or allowed alone.

Research. Rust's thiserror writes `#[error("route {path} must start with /")]`, an attribute whose holes name fields. That is B's shape, made possible by a macro that reads the struct. rustc's own diagnostics are structs with fixed message slugs. Swift's DiagnosticMessage is a protocol whose message is a computed property, which is A's shape. Java annotation elements must be constants, which is why C cannot hold data.

Probes, in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/q/bd/probe/diag2. shape_a.jet declares a local Diagnostic trait and BadPath with A's three methods. `jet check` is ok, and `jet run` prints the three report lines with `orders` in place. const_hole.jet and field_default.jet are B's and C's holes; both are E0107 today. Trait constants and the Core trait are proposed, per D-DECL-TYPES1 A.

options.name: Texts are one-literal methods
options.detail:
An error is a struct that implements Diagnostic. Its what, why and fix are methods whose body is one string literal, so `{self.path}` reads a field with ordinary interpolation. Settings with no data, such as code and severity, are trait constants with defaults.

This is D-DECL-TYPES1 A's rule 7 exactly, so nothing ratified changes. `reject(BadPath{path: path})` raises it from expand or a helper. `#Allow(web.TrailingSlash)` silences one warning.
options.technical: Core trait Diagnostic: required fn what(self) -> String, fn why(self) -> String and fn fix(self) -> String. Trait constants: code (default, the type path), severity (default .Error) and lint_name (required when severity is .Lint). Each text body must be one string literal whose holes read self's fields (rule 7). The registry reads the impls as source. reject takes any Diagnostic and runs only while compiling. The report's primary span is the marker's use site.

options.name: Texts are trait constants
options.detail:
An error is a struct that implements Diagnostic, as in A, but its texts are trait constants: `what :: "route {path} must start with /"`. Inside these constants only, `{path}` names a field of the error rather than a name in scope.

Each text is a short line. The braces then mean two things, and this amends D-DECL-TYPES1 rules 7 and 13.
options.technical: Diagnostic's what, why and fix become required String trait constants. New rule: in those three constants, a hole names a field of the implementing type and binds when the value is raised. Replacement rule 7: "A diagnostic's what, why and fix are trait constants whose value is one string literal. Their {field} holes name the type's own fields." Replacement rule 13, row fields: "Each hole in a row's texts becomes a String field. The texts are trait constants."

options.name: Texts are fields with defaults
options.detail:
An error is a struct that implements Diagnostic, and its texts are ordinary String fields with defaults. A default cannot read another field, so a text that names the data is written where the error is raised.

No new rule is needed. But `jet explain` can show only the defaults, and two raises can word the same error differently.
options.technical: Diagnostic requires fields what, why and fix of type String; defaults use the struct form, name: String{"..."}. reject reads the field values. Amends D-DECL-TYPES1 rule 7 to: "A diagnostic's what, why and fix are String fields; their defaults are fixed texts." Rule 13 keeps the rows' texts only as defaults.

comparisons.note: A macro diagnostic is a struct that conforms to DiagnosticMessage; its message is a computed property (option A's shape). Source: https://swiftpackageindex.com/swiftlang/swift-syntax/documentation/swiftdiagnostics/diagnosticmessage
thiserror puts a fixed message on the struct; its holes name fields (option B's shape, by macro). Source: https://docs.rs/thiserror

Roslyn analyzers declare a DiagnosticDescriptor with an ID and a message format with numbered holes. Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/roslyn-sdk/tutorials/how-to-write-csharp-analyzer-code-fix
comparisons.code: new DiagnosticDescriptor("WEB001", "Bad path", "route {0} must start with /", ...)

recommendation.why: A is the trait the owner asked for, exactly as D-DECL-TYPES1 A ratified it. Methods keep one meaning for braces, so holes are checked like any interpolation. Each text is still one literal that jet explain prints.
gains: No ratified rule changes.
Holes are type-checked interpolation of the error's own fields.
Jet's errors and library errors share one shape, explain page and #Allow.

whyNot.reason: B saves about 25 characters per text but gives braces a second meaning inside three constants.
C cannot put data in a default, so texts move to raise sites and explain loses them.

recommendation.tradeoff: Each text is wrapped in a one-line method, `fn what(self) -> String { ... }`, instead of a constant line.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude. Adversarial model family: Claude. Fresh agent: BallotDesign (fresh pass). It argued for B as shorter and found its cost is a second meaning for braces in three constants. It checked that A changes no D-DECL-TYPES1 rule and that the report now points at the user's line.

decisions.title: One view shows every item a marker added, with its source, for the terminal, tests and editor
decisions.situation: When a marker adds a method, the user calls code they never wrote. Today no view shows that code. The templates view lists only names, and it skips any file without a compile-time loop. The derive view names the marker but not what it added. A library author cannot write a test that checks the added code either. The vote decides how users and library authors see the code markers add. We recommend one view that prints each added item with the marker and line that added it.
decisions.gist: How should people see and test the code that a marker adds to their program?
decisions.lesson: A marker such as `#web.Describe` can add methods to your type. When something goes wrong in code you did not write, you need to read it. One view should print each added item as source, labeled with the marker that added it. Library authors should be able to check the same text in a test.
decisions.story: Kai's `Point` suddenly has a `describe_x` method that returns the wrong text. He runs the expand view, sees nothing listed for his file, and has to read the web library's source to guess what it generated.
decisions.detail:
Provenance. Card c03pi177. This is the view question from the D-COMPTIME-MARKERS1 package ballot, asked alone. No new syntax: one inspect lens and one `core.testing` function.

Probes, in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/q/bd/probe/mk. expand_noloop.jet: a marker adds `greeting()` without a `comptime loop`; `jet run` prints "hello", but `--facts templates` reports "0 facts (none in this program)". `--facts derive` prints "Person: AddGreeting" without the method. today_reads.jet with a loop: `--facts templates` lists "impl Point [describe_x]", names only. Bare `jet inspect expand file.jet` is E2104 "not built yet".

Reads with the related ballots. The labels name markers as D-MARKER-REFLECT1 records do. Added code is shown in D-META-HASH1's output spelling, which is plain Jet with nothing left to paste.

options.name: Added items with their source
options.detail:

`testing.expand(source)` returns the same text, so a library can snapshot its own output. Hovering an added method in the editor shows the same block.

The bare all-lens `jet inspect expand` form is E2104 today and is out of scope here.

options.name: Whole expanded file
options.detail:
The view prints the entire file after expansion, with added items inserted where they apply.

Nothing says which lines a marker added, and a test that snapshots the output changes whenever unrelated code changes.
options.technical: A whole-source printer over the expanded tree. `testing.expand` would return the whole file.

options.detail:
The two views stay as they are, and the templates view stops skipping files without a compile-time loop.

Users see that `describe_x` was added, but not what it does.
options.technical: Fix Expand.jet:196-199 to scan every file. No source printing, no `testing.expand`.

decisions.title: `package.jet` is the one project file: `members:` and `environments:` are its fields
decisions.situation: A Jet project describes itself in up to three files. package.jet holds the package. workspace.jet lists member packages, and env.jet lists developer tools. package.jet already accepts the same `members:` and `environments:` fields, so the same fact has two spellings and two places. The env file even uses different words, `packages:` where package.jet says `tools:`. The vote decides whether workspace and environment facts live in package.jet or in their own files. We recommend package.jet alone.
decisions.gist: Should a project's member packages and developer tools live in package.jet, or in their own files?
decisions.lesson: Every Jet project has a package.jet that names it and lists what it needs. A project with several packages also lists its members, and many projects list the tools developers need. If those lists are fields of package.jet, there is one file to read, one shape to learn, and one parser for every tool.
decisions.story: Sam adds `nodejs_22` to the dev tools in package.jet. The team's env.jet still lists the old tools under `packages:`, and that file wins. Sam spends an hour finding out why nothing changed.
decisions.inWild:
# Cargo: one Cargo.toml holds the package and its workspace.
[workspace]
members = ["packages/*"]
decisions.detail:
Provenance. Card c05i2uiq. This is the one-file question from the D-PROJECT-FILE1 package, asked alone. Test profiles are D-TEST-PROFILE1. Growing loose files is D-LOOSE-GROW1. Confirms D-ECO-FILEROOT1=A; overrides the sentence "env.jet and workspace.jet stay canonical" in D-JPK-LEGACY1=A, flagged for the owner.

Probes, in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/q/bd/probe/proj, with the dev jet. one/: a named package.jet with `members:` and `environments:` checks clean, and `jet run packages/shop` prints "shop". root/: a package.jet with no `name:`, holding only `members:` and `environments:`, checks clean today. three/: the same project with workspace.jet and env.jet also checks clean, so both spellings are live.

Counts (git ls-files on dev): 159 env.jet and 22 workspace.jet. 154 of the 181 sit in folders with no package.jet and become 152 nameless root files. 27 merge into 25 existing package.jet files. 78 env.jet files use `packages:`. The largest merged file would be the repo root at 61 lines. The median is 4.

Local values stay out. Secrets are declared by name only; values come from `.env` (allow-listed by `dotenv:`), the shell, or `--set`. Personal tools belong in a developer's own shell setup. A Config listed in `configs:` may hold environments but never `members:` or `build:` (PackageParse.jet:234-240), so each build fact has one owner.

options.name: One package.jet
options.detail:
Members and environments are fields of package.jet. A root folder that only groups packages has a package.jet without `name:`, like Cargo's virtual manifest.

A large team can still split a part out: `configs:` lists other files that hold environments. Editing an environment never invalidates a build.
options.technical: PackageParse.jet:188-217 already parses `members:`, `environments:`, `build:` and `configs:`. env.jet words join `Environment`: `sources`, `languages`, `dotenv`, `imports`, `files`; `packages:` becomes `tools:`. Build keys hash build fields only. `jet fix` moves 181 files (159 env.jet, 22 workspace.jet). A leftover file is an error naming its field.

options.name: Keep three files
options.detail:
Each file keeps one job, as Go splits go.mod and go.work.

To end the duplication, package.jet must stop reading `members:` and `environments:`, and every tool keeps three parsers.
options.technical: Removes the package.jet fields (PackageParse.jet:188-217) and keeps ConfigEval.jet and Host.jet env.jet readers.

options.name: Fold the workspace only
options.detail:
The workspace becomes a package.jet field, but developer tools keep their own file.

The tools list still has its own shape and word, and package.jet loses a field that works today.
options.technical: Retires 22 workspace.jet files; keeps 159 env.jet files and their readers.

comparisons.note: Cargo.toml holds package and workspace; tools live elsewhere. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/workspaces.html
One deno.json holds workspace members, tasks and imports. Source: https://docs.deno.com/runtime/fundamentals/workspaces/
go.mod per module and go.work for the workspace: two files. Source: https://go.dev/ref/mod#workspaces

recommendation.why: A uses fields package.jet already reads, so the project has one file, one vocabulary and one parser. Teams can still split a large part into a listed config file.
gains: No duplicate facts.
One shape to learn.

whyNot.reason: B keeps three shapes and must remove fields that work today.
C keeps the second vocabulary for developer tools.

recommendation.tradeoff: `jet fix` moves the 181 old files once.

decisions.checkInstructions: Use the dev jet from $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/discovery/base/latest with JET_TOOLCHAIN_ROOT set to the dev worktree. In probe/proj/one and probe/proj/root run `jet check`; both pass. In probe/proj/one, `jet run packages/shop` prints "shop".

surface.lesson: Every Jet project has a package.jet that names it and lists what it needs. A project with several packages also lists its members, and many projects list the tools developers need. If those lists are fields of package.jet, there is one file to read, one shape to learn, and one parser for every tool.

current.note: Today the same facts can be written in two places with two vocabularies.

gains: One file and one vocabulary.
Every tool reads one parser.
Nothing new to learn: the fields already parse.

options.name: Keep three files
options.gist: workspace.jet and env.jet stay; package.jet stops accepting the same fields.
gains: Each concern has its own small file.
No migration of the 181 files.
losses: Three shapes: fields, `module workspace` and `module env.dev`.
package.jet's working fields are removed.

options.name: Fold the workspace only
options.gist: Members move into package.jet; env.jet stays as the developer tools file.
gains: Build facts in one file.
Developer tools stay apart from the build.
losses: Two files and two vocabularies remain.
`environments:` in package.jet must be removed.

recommendation.why: A uses fields package.jet already reads, so the project has one file, one vocabulary and one parser. Teams can still split a large part into a listed config file.
gains: No duplicate facts.
One shape to learn.

whyNot.reason: B keeps three shapes and must remove fields that work today.
C keeps the second vocabulary for developer tools.

recommendation.tradeoff: `jet fix` moves the 181 old files once.

decisions.title: `jet init` grows loose files into a package: it writes package.jet and rewrites path imports, showing every edit
decisions.situation: Loose files import each other by path, such as `use "./app/report" as report`. Inside a package all files share one namespace, so path imports are an error there. Adding a package.jet to a folder of loose files therefore breaks every import at once. `jet fix` makes no changes, and `jet init` is not built yet. The vote decides how a folder of loose files becomes a package. We recommend `jet init` doing the whole move, showing every edit and asking about name clashes.
decisions.gist: How should a folder of loose script files become a package?
decisions.lesson: Jet starts small: a few loose files that import each other by path. When a project grows, it becomes a package, and files in a package see each other's names directly. Growing should be one command that writes package.jet and rewrites the imports, never a pile of errors to fix by hand.
decisions.story: Ana's three-file script grows into a tool her team uses. She adds a package.jet, and every file now fails with an import error. She deletes the package.jet and keeps the scripts loose.
decisions.inWild:
$ cargo init
     Created binary (application) package
decisions.detail:
Provenance. Card c0cwk90x. This is the growing question from the D-PROJECT-FILE1 package, asked alone. The default for a package with no name stays split out to #6058.

Probes, in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/q/bd/probe/proj. loose/: the loose files run and print "sales up". grown/: the same files beside `name: "news"` give E0623 "`use \"./app/report\"` imports a file, but this file belongs to a package". `jet fix --all .` prints "no changes made". In loose/, `jet init --check` is E2104 "`jet init` is not built yet".

Reads with the related ballots. Under D-MANIFEST-ONE1 A the written package.jet is the one project file. D-TEST-PROFILE1 adds nothing to `jet init`.

options.name: `jet init` does the move
options.detail:
`jet init` writes package.jet, removes each path import and turns `report.headline()` into `headline()`. It prints the whole plan first; `--check` prints it and writes nothing.

If two files declare the same name, nothing is renamed silently. The plan proposes a name and a terminal asks to accept or type one. Scripts pass `--rename` or `--yes`.
options.technical: Front.jet `jet init` (E2104 today). Rewrites use the compiler's public rename API, the one the editor uses. E0623 and E0624 gain the same fix. Imports captured by a local binding, or `../..` paths outside the root, stop with the line named. Keeps D-ECO-FILEROOT1=A's fold of retired manifests.

options.name: Path imports stay legal
options.detail:
A path import inside a package stays legal, so adding package.jet changes nothing.

But a package now has two ways to reach the same name, which the one-namespace rule was made to remove.
options.technical: Retires E0623 and overrides the 2026-09-30 owner ruling (card #3862) that files of one package share one namespace.

options.name: Rewrite by hand
options.detail:
The user adds package.jet, reads each E0623 error and edits the files.

A larger project meets every broken import together, and clashing names surface only as later errors.
options.technical: Today's state: E0623 with a prose fix; `jet fix --all .` makes no changes.

comparisons.note: `cargo init` turns a folder into a package. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-init.html
`go mod init` writes go.mod; imports then use the module path. Source: https://go.dev/ref/mod#go-mod-init
Deno keeps relative imports everywhere, so nothing changes on growth. Source: https://docs.deno.com/runtime/fundamentals/modules/

recommendation.why: A makes growing a project one safe command. It shows every edit first and never renames a clash without asking.
gains: No broken step between script and package.
One rename engine shared with the editor.

whyNot.reason: B keeps two ways to reach a name inside one package.
C leaves users with every import broken at once.

recommendation.tradeoff: Off a terminal, a clash needs `--rename` or `--yes`.

decisions.checkInstructions: Use the dev jet from $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/discovery/base/latest with JET_TOOLCHAIN_ROOT set to the dev worktree. In probe/proj/loose, `jet run run.jet` prints "sales up". In probe/proj/grown, `jet check` gives E0623.

Growing should be one command that writes package.jet and rewrites the imports, never a pile of errors to fix by hand.

decisions.title: A run's own temp folder is free: files inside the folder `fs.temp_dir` made need no grant
decisions.situation: Many scripts need scratch space: they make a temp folder, write a few files and read them back. Today that is a file write like any other, so a loose script stops with an authority error off a terminal, or asks on one. The folder is new, private and removed at exit, so nothing the user owns is at risk. The vote decides whether a run's own temp folder needs a grant. We recommend it is free, while deny rules still win.
decisions.gist: Should a script need permission to use the temp folder it just made for itself?
decisions.lesson: Jet scripts must be allowed to touch files. But a temp folder made with `fs.temp_dir` is brand new, private to this run and deleted when the run ends. Reading and writing inside it cannot touch anything you own, so Jet can allow it without asking.
decisions.story: Mia's script renders thumbnails into a temp folder. In CI it fails with an authority error about writing files. She adds `-A`, which also lets the script reach the network and her home folder.
decisions.inWild:
// Android: an app's own cache folder needs no permission.
val scratch = File(context.cacheDir, "page.txt")
decisions.detail:
Provenance. Card c0w8kkg9. Split from D-SCRIPT-DESIGNATE1 with Main's approval; that ballot covers paths the user typed. Builds on owner ruling #5949 (ask once, `-A`, basics free).

Probes, in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/q/bd/probe/proj. tmp.jet is the beginner script. Off a terminal it is E1803 "Application authority is undecided for `FS, FS.Read, FS.Write`". With `--allow=FS` it prints "draft". `fs.temp_dir` returns a TempDir with a `path` field today.

Reads with D-SCRIPT-DESIGNATE1 A: typed paths and the run's own temp are the two narrow grants, and both yield to deny rules.

options.name: Own temp is free
options.detail:
When `fs.temp_dir` or `fs.temp_file` makes a folder or file, the run may create, read and write inside it with no grant. The folder sits under a private root for this run and is removed at exit.

Only paths this run made are free. `--deny=FS.Write` or a package `authority.deny` still refuses them. Signatures do not change: `fs.write` still says it writes files.
options.technical: The run records each temp path it creates; the authority preflight (files8_preflight, Core/Files/Files.jet:1631-1656) allows FS.Read and FS.Write beneath a recorded path. Links leaving the folder are refused. `jet inspect rights` shows "own temp" beside each such use. D-AUTHORITY-DENYROW1=A and `--deny` (E1803) are unchanged.

options.name: A grant, as today
options.detail:
Nothing changes. A script that only uses scratch space still needs a file grant.

That grant covers every file the user owns, not just the scratch folder.
options.technical: Today's E1803 path and the `--allow` flag (owner ruling #5949).

options.name: A free `FS.Temp` effect
options.detail:
`fs.temp_dir` and new `TempDir` methods carry `FS.Temp`, which is free by default.

But the ordinary `fs.write` on a temp path still needs FS.Write, so scripts must switch to the new methods.
options.technical: Adds the leaf `FS.Temp` under the D-EFFTREE1 tree and `write`/`read` methods on TempDir (Files.jet:194). `-[!FS]>` still forbids it by subsumption.

comparisons.note: Android apps own their cache folder without permission. Source: https://developer.android.com/training/data-storage/app-specific
Sandboxed macOS apps get their own temporary directory. Source: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/foundation/filemanager/temporarydirectory
Deno needs `--allow-write` even for temp files. Source: https://docs.deno.com/api/deno/~/Deno.makeTempDir

recommendation.why: A lets scripts use scratch space anywhere without widening their rights. Only paths the run made are free, and deny rules still win.
gains: No `-A` for scratch work.
No new API or effect.

whyNot.reason: B pushes scratch-only scripts to grants that cover all user files.
C adds a second set of file methods for one folder.

recommendation.tradeoff: Effect rows still say FS; the run, not the checker, knows which paths are scratch.

surface.lesson: Jet scripts must be allowed to touch files. But a temp folder made with `fs.temp_dir` is brand new, private to this run and deleted when the run ends. Reading and writing inside it cannot touch anything you own, so Jet can allow it without asking.

decisions.title: A path the user typed for a `Path` argument may be read without a prompt; deny rules still win
decisions.situation: A loose script that reads files must be allowed to read them. Off a terminal it stops with an authority error, and on a terminal it asks once. But when the user typed the file name as the script's input, the question is already answered: they chose that file. Desktop systems treat a file picked in an open dialog the same way. The vote decides whether a path the user typed grants access to it. We recommend that a typed `Path` argument grants reading exactly that path, and an `#Output` one grants writing.
decisions.gist: Should a file path the user typed as a script argument be usable without asking again?
decisions.lesson: Jet scripts must be allowed to touch files. When you run `wc.jet --input notes.txt`, you already chose `notes.txt`. If the script declares that argument as a `Path`, Jet can let it read exactly that file and nothing else. Your own deny rules still win.
decisions.story: Bo runs `wc.jet --input notes.txt` in a CI job. It fails with an authority error about reading files, though the only file it reads is the one Bo named. He adds `-A`, which allows everything, including the network.
decisions.detail:
Provenance. Card c0w8kkg9. The private temp folder question is split out as D-SCRIPT-TEMP1, approved by Main. Builds on owner ruling #5949 (ask once, `-A`, basics free) and D-SCRIPT-CONFIRM1=A; neither is reopened.

Probes, in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/q/bd/probe/proj. wcp.jet is the beginner script with `input: Path`. `jet run wcp.jet -- --input notes.txt` off a terminal is E1803 "Application authority is undecided for `FS.Read`". With `--allow=FS.Read` it prints 3. `Path` is accepted as a `#CLI` field and by `fs.read` today.

Why a marker for writing, not a type. `#CLI` fields already take their CLI facts as markers: `#Doc`, `#Env` and `#Short` (Examples/features/cli/typed_entry_args.jet). `#Output` is one more of those. Core has no write-capable path type; Core/Files/Path.jet has only `Path`. A new `OutPath` type would have to be accepted by every `fs` call that takes `String | Path`, and would mean nothing outside entry arguments.

Reads with the related ballots. D-EFFTYPE-GRANT1 A has `jet add` write what a dependency may do; this ballot grants one run one path. Both keep deny rules first. With `--deny=FS.Read` the probe gives E1803 "Application authority denies `FS.Read`".

options.name: Typed paths are granted
options.detail:
After parsing, each typed `Path` argument grants reading exactly that path, or anything under it for a folder. An `#Output` path also grants writing it. Defaults grant nothing; only values the user typed do.

Deny rules always win: `--deny=FS.Read` or a package `authority.deny` still refuses the read. Every other path keeps today's ask-once rule.
options.technical: Entry decode for `#CLI` resolves each `Path` field, following links and `..`, and adds an exact FS.Read grant before `run` starts. `#Output` adds FS.Write and create on that path; `--help` marks it "(written)". An `authority.deny` entry is still a compile-time prohibition (D-AUTHORITY-DENYROW1=A), and `--deny` still wins at run time (E1803). `jet inspect rights` lists each grant with its argument. Builds on owner ruling #5949 and D-SCRIPT-CONFIRM1=A (c06jij4v).

options.name: Ask, naming the argument
options.detail:
Typed paths get no grant. The ask-once prompt says which argument the path came from.

Off a terminal the script still stops, so CI keeps passing broad flags.
options.technical: Today's E1803 and prompt, plus the argument name in the prompt text.

options.name: Grant on the launch line
options.detail:
Users pass `--allow=FS.Read` or approve the prompt.

The flag grants reading any file, which is wider than the one file the user meant.
options.technical: Today's E1803 path and `--allow` flag (owner ruling #5949).

comparisons.note: macOS grants sandboxed apps the files a user picks. Source: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/security/accessing-files-from-the-macos-app-sandbox
Permissions are flags; `--allow-read=notes.txt` narrows to one path but must be typed. Source: https://docs.deno.com/runtime/fundamentals/security/
WASI preopens hand a program only the directories the host passes. Source: https://github.com/WebAssembly/WASI

recommendation.why: A turns the user's own choice into a narrow grant for exactly that path. Deny rules still win, and every other path asks as today.
gains: Narrower than `--allow=FS.Read`.
Scripts work in CI without `-A`.

whyNot.reason: B still stops in CI and asks a question the user already answered.
C grants every file to read just one, which pushes users to `-A`.

recommendation.tradeoff: Only arguments declared as `Path` grant anything.

decisions.title: A foreign row Jet cannot check sits in one `#Unsafe("reason") { }` block in its import module; calls stay plain
decisions.situation: A foreign import row says a C symbol has a given Jet signature. When Jet can read the header, C source or type info, it checks the row. When the library has none of these, the row is only someone's word, and a wrong row corrupts memory. Today such rows are trusted silently and called like any function. The vote decides where that trust is written. We recommend one `#Unsafe("reason")` block around the unchecked rows, so calls stay plain and every promise is listed.
decisions.gist: Where should the promise that an unchecked foreign signature is correct be written?
decisions.lesson: When Jet calls C, it needs each function's exact signature. Jet checks the signature against the header or source whenever it has one. When it has nothing to check against, a person must vouch for it. Jet asks for that once, with a reason, around the rows themselves, so every call stays ordinary.
decisions.story: Sam copies `fn foo_sum(a: I32, b: I32) -> I32` from a PDF manual for a closed library. The real function takes 64-bit values. Nothing marks the row as unchecked, so the crash a month later takes a day to trace.
decisions.detail:
Provenance. Card c08rdp62. This is the vouching question from the D-FFI-UNSAFE1 package, asked alone. C type mapping, C inputs, binder packages and the Rust import form are their own ballots in this group. The owner question q2yczyk8 asks for the best foreign-code experience, starting from the best today; Rust 2024's extern blocks are that baseline for vouching.

Probes, in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/q/bd/probe/ffi. nc/ is a copy of Examples/features/lowlevel/native_c: plain rows with C source check clean. u1/: `#Unsafe("…")` on one row is E3212 "Unknown foreign declaration marker". u2/: an `#Unsafe("…") { }` block of rows is E3212 too.

Cutover. Core's 34 sqlite3 rows and 22 mbedtls rows point at their vendored headers (Core/Vendor), so they become checked and need no vouch. Rows with C source beside them, as in native_c, are checked against that source. `jet fix` wraps any remaining unchecked rows in `#Unsafe("unchecked before D-FFI-VOUCH1")`, so nothing breaks and every one shows in `jet audit`.

Reads with D-FFI-CMAP1, which decides what checked rows may say. With D-FFI-CINPUT1 A, more libraries become checkable, so fewer rows need a vouch.

options.name: Vouch once, at the rows
options.detail:
A row Jet can check against a header, C source or type info needs nothing. A row with nothing to check against goes inside one `#Unsafe("reason") { }` block in its import module. Calls through it are plain.

A row outside any check or vouch is an error with both fixes: point the module at a header, or vouch. `jet audit` lists every vouch with its reason.
options.technical: Adds a block of rows as an `#Unsafe` site, replacing E3212 for that form; D-MARK-SCOPE1=A keeps `#Unsafe` site-bound. A row with no source and no vouch gets a new error with both fixes (no code is assigned yet). Amends D-FFI-CAP1=A (#1889): rows stay directly callable only when checked or vouched. Applies D-UNSAFE-EFFECT=A. Capability-bearing calls (loans, ownership) keep their audited `#Unsafe` region as today.

options.name: Vouch at each call
options.detail:
Rows are written plainly, and each call through an unchecked row sits in an `#Unsafe` block.

The promise is about the row, not the call, so it repeats. Teams write one wrapper per row to keep calls plain.
options.technical: Uses today's statement-position `#Unsafe` blocks (Examples/features/lowlevel/opaque_handles/run.jet) and adds a check that unchecked-row calls sit inside one.

options.name: Keep today: trusted silently
options.detail:
Rows stay as they are, checked or not. `jet audit` reports which rows had nothing to check against.

A reader of the source cannot tell a checked row from a guessed one.
options.technical: Today's behaviour (native_c checks with plain rows), plus an audit report.

comparisons.note: Rust 2024 marks the extern block once; `safe` items need no unsafe at calls. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/edition-guide/rust-2024/unsafe-extern.html
comparisons.code: unsafe extern "C" { pub safe fn abs(x: i32) -> i32; }

comparisons.note: Swift imports C only through headers and module maps, so there are no hand-written rows to trust. Source: https://www.swift.org/documentation/cxx-interop/
Zig's `extern fn` rows are trusted with no marker. Source: https://ziglang.org/documentation/master/#extern

recommendation.why: A writes the promise once, next to the rows it covers. Calls stay plain, and checked rows need nothing at all.
gains: Unchecked rows are visible in source and audit.
No per-call ceremony.

whyNot.reason: B repeats one promise at every call and breeds wrappers.
C hides which signatures were guessed.

recommendation.tradeoff: A library with no header or type info needs one block per import module.

decisions.checkInstructions: Use the dev jet from $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/discovery/base/latest with JET_TOOLCHAIN_ROOT set to the dev worktree, in probe/ffi. `jet check` passes in nc/ and gives E3212 in u1/ and u2/.

surface.lesson: When Jet calls C, it needs each function's exact signature. Jet checks the signature against the header or source whenever it has one. When it has nothing to check against, a person must vouch for it. Jet asks for that once, with a reason, around the rows themselves, so every call stays ordinary.

current.note: Today unchecked rows are trusted silently, and `#Unsafe` is not allowed on rows.

wild.note: Rust 2024 requires `unsafe extern` blocks: the block is the promise, and items marked `safe` are called plainly. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/edition-guide/rust-2024/unsafe-extern.html

options.gist: Unchecked rows sit in one `#Unsafe("reason") { }` block; checked rows and all calls stay plain.
gains: The promise sits next to what it promises.
Calls stay plain.
`jet audit` lists every vouch.

options.name: Vouch at each call
options.gist: Calls through an unchecked row need an `#Unsafe` block around them.
gains: Every risky call is marked where it runs.
losses: The same promise repeats at every call.
Pushes a hand-written wrapper per row.

options.name: Keep today: trusted silently
options.gist: Unchecked rows stay plain; `jet audit` lists them as unchecked.
gains: No change to existing code.
losses: A guessed signature reads like a checked one.
Nothing in the source shows the risk.

recommendation.why: A writes the promise once, next to the rows it covers. Calls stay plain, and checked rows need nothing at all.
gains: Unchecked rows are visible in source and audit.
No per-call ceremony.

whyNot.reason: B repeats one promise at every call and breeds wrappers.
C hides which signatures were guessed.

recommendation.tradeoff: A library with no header or type info needs one block per import module.

decisions.title: C pointers arrive as safe Jet types: a pointer that may be null is `T?`, a counted pointer is a list
decisions.situation: When Jet reads a C header, each C type must become a Jet type. Scalars are easy. Pointers are where C programs crash: a result may be null, and a buffer comes with a separate length. Today a row cannot even say `String?` or a list: both are E3203. The vote decides how C pointers appear in Jet. We recommend Swift's approach, made the default: a pointer that may be null is an optional, and a pointer with a declared length is a list.
decisions.gist: How should C pointers that may be null, or that come with a length, appear in Jet?
decisions.lesson: C passes text and arrays as bare pointers. A pointer can be null, and a buffer's length travels in a separate argument. Jet turns these into the types you already know. A result that may be missing is optional, so you handle it with `??`. A buffer with a length becomes a list, and Jet passes the length for you.
decisions.story: Dev calls `getenv("EDITOR")` on a machine where it is unset. C returns null, and the program crashes inside a string copy, far from the call that caused it.
decisions.inWild:
// Swift: a nullable C result is an optional.
if let home = getenv("HOME") { print(String(cString: home)) }
decisions.detail:
Provenance. Card c08rdp62. This is the C type mapping from the D-FFI-UNSAFE1 package, asked alone. Swift's importer is today's best baseline for this question (owner question q2yczyk8). A takes Swift's mapping and makes the safe reading the default for unannotated pointers.

Probes, in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/q/bd/probe/ffi. u3/: rows returning `String?` and taking `&[I32]` are each E3203 "is not a C-compatible type". nc/ (a copy of native_c) shows today's rows already map `String`, `Bool` and `&I32` out-slots. In h/, `use "c.h" as libc` with a two-line header gives E0102 "Nothing named `abs` exists in this import". The self-hosted header reader is not built yet, and `jet inspect bind` is E2104.

Reads with D-FFI-VOUCH1: a retyping row is checked against the header, so it needs no vouch.

options.name: Safe types by default
options.detail:
A pointer result that may be null, including any unannotated one, is `T?`; `const char*` is `String?`. A pointer marked non-null is plain. A pointer with `counted_by` or `sized_by` is a list, and Jet passes its length. C `bool` is `Bool` and C enums are Jet enums.

When the header is silent but the library never returns null, an `#Import module` row may retype the result as `String`. Jet checks the row against the header, and a null at run time stops with the row named.
options.technical: The c binder (D-CIMPORT1 Clang) reads `_Nullable`/`_Nonnull`, `counted_by`, `sized_by` and `ended_by`. Rows may spell `T?` and `&[T]` (E3203 today). Row retypes are checked by E3205. Pointers with no safe form stay `mem.Ptr<T>` and need `#Unsafe`, as today.

options.name: Only when annotated
options.detail:
Optionals and lists come only from annotations. An unannotated `const char*` result is `String`, and a null result stops the program at the boundary.

Most C headers carry no annotations, so the common case stays unsafe.
options.technical: Same binder reading as A; unannotated pointers map as `_Nonnull` with a boundary check.

options.name: Raw pointers, wrapped by hand
options.detail:
Headers map pointers to `mem.Ptr<T>`, as Zig's C pointers do. Safe wrappers are written by hand.

Every binding needs its own audited wrapper before ordinary code can use it.
options.technical: Uses today's `mem.Ptr<T>` (Examples/features/lowlevel/pointer_cast_deref.jet) for every pointer.

comparisons.note: Nullability becomes optionals; counted pointers become safe spans. Source: https://www.swift.org/documentation/cxx-interop/
`@cImport` gives `[*c]T` C pointers that may be null; wrapping is by hand. Source: https://ziglang.org/documentation/master/#C-Pointers
bindgen emits raw `*const c_char`; safe wrappers are written by hand. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-bindgen/

recommendation.why: A gives C results the types Jet code already uses. A null is handled at the call, and lengths travel with their buffers.
gains: Null crashes move to the call site, as `??`.
Buffers and lengths can't disagree.

whyNot.reason: B leaves the common unannotated case unchecked.
C makes every team write the same unsafe wrappers.

recommendation.tradeoff: A result the header leaves unmarked needs `??` or one retyping row.

decisions.checkInstructions: Use the dev jet from $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/discovery/base/latest with JET_TOOLCHAIN_ROOT set to the dev worktree, in probe/ffi. `jet check` in u3/ gives two E3203 errors.

surface.gist: How should C pointers that may be null, or that come with a length, appear in Jet?
surface.lesson: C passes text and arrays as bare pointers. A pointer can be null, and a buffer's length travels in a separate argument. Jet turns these into the types you already know. A result that may be missing is optional, so you handle it with `??`. A buffer with a length becomes a list, and Jet passes the length for you.

current.note: Today a foreign row cannot spell an optional or a list.

wild.note: Swift maps nullability annotations to optionals and `__counted_by` pointers to safe buffer views. Source: https://www.swift.org/documentation/cxx-interop/ and https://github.com/swiftlang/swift-evolution/blob/main/proposals/0447-span-access-shared-contiguous-storage.md
