options.gist: May-be-null pointers become `T?`; counted pointers become lists; C enums become Jet enums.
gains: Null is handled where it can happen.
No separate length arguments.
Same types as the rest of Jet.

options.name: Only when annotated
options.gist: Only pointers the header marks nullable become `T?`; unannotated ones are plain.
gains: Fewer `??` for old headers.
losses: Most C headers have no annotations, so most nulls go unchecked.
A null still crashes far from the call.

options.name: Raw pointers, wrapped by hand
options.gist: Every C pointer is `mem.Ptr<T>`; users write safe wrappers in `#Unsafe` blocks.
gains: Exactly mirrors C.
No mapping rules to learn.
losses: Every pointer call needs `#Unsafe`.
Each team writes the same wrappers.

recommendation.why: A gives C results the types Jet code already uses. A null is handled at the call, and lengths travel with their buffers.
gains: Null crashes move to the call site, as `??`.
Buffers and lengths can't disagree.

whyNot.reason: B leaves the common unannotated case unchecked.
C makes every team write the same unsafe wrappers.

recommendation.tradeoff: A result the header leaves unmarked needs `??` or one retyping row.

decisions.title: Each foreign-language reader is an ordinary Jet package: a module marker that reads the interface and adds checked declarations
decisions.situation: Jet calls code in 23 languages, from C and Rust to Fortran and Perl. Each language has a reader that turns its interface into Jet declarations. Today the languages are a closed list inside the toolchain, so adding one means changing Jet itself. The owner suggested a binding could just be a single Jet file that is a metaprogram. The vote decides where these readers live. We recommend ordinary Jet packages built on markers, so anyone can add a language and users write the same `use` line.
decisions.gist: Where should the readers that turn another language's interface into Jet live?
decisions.lesson: Calling another language needs a reader that turns its interface into Jet declarations. If each reader is an ordinary Jet package, it is written, tested and shared like any library. The C reader that ships with Jet is one such package, and a new language is one more.
decisions.story: Odin users want to call their libraries from Jet. Today that needs a change to the Jet toolchain and a release. They wait half a year.
decisions.inWild:
# Nim: Futhark is a library macro that reads C headers while compiling.
importc:
  path "/usr/include"
  "raylib.h"
decisions.detail:
Provenance. Card c08rdp62. This is the binder-architecture question from the D-FFI-UNSAFE1 package, asked alone. Owner idea (2026-10-29): "Language bindings could just be a single Jet file that is a metaprogram." Owner question q2yczyk8 asks for the best foreign-code experience.

Ordering. A is the foreign-code instance of D-EXTEND-ARCH1 A, where a domain list becomes declarations any package adds. If that vote picks B, a reader becomes an extension component instead of a marker package. If it picks C, this ballot's B becomes the recommendation. A also needs D-META-PARAMS1 (parameter-list paste) and D-MARKER-DIAG1 (declared diagnostics). `target` and `$` follow today's spelling; under D-META-HASH1=A they read `#target`, and `$` only pastes.

Cost. An earlier probe measured raylib.h, 581 functions, with the dev compiler's trace (q/b4/ffi/rl3/bind.jet). Mapping took 0.7 ms of CPU. Preparing the compile-time code took 56 ms, 34 ms of it loading. That is paid once per change of input, reader version or target. First-party readers ship prebuilt with the toolchain.

Probes, in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/q/bd/probe/ffi. u4/: `use c.[nativeffi]` plus rows checks clean; `c` is a reserved root today (E1002 for local modules). Examples/features/reflection/derive_loop.jet shows today's `comptime loop` emission with `fn $method(self)`; it cannot paste a parameter list.

options.name: Readers are packages
options.detail:
A reader declares a marker on module sites. While compiling it reads the foreign interface and adds checked Jet declarations, using the same `comptime loop` emission markers use today. Its refusals are its own declared diagnostics.

Jet ships today's 23 readers as packages named c, rust, py and so on, so `use "raylib.h" as rl` and `use c.[z]` keep their meaning. Reading an interface is a compiler-owned call in the build sandbox, never a free-running script.
options.technical: Moves the ~22.8k lines under Jetpack/**/Foreign behind a public binder interface and drops the closed ForeignLanguage enum (BinderDescriptor.jet:22) and the root list behind E1002. Needs the parameter-list paste (D-META-PARAMS1) and `diagnostic` declarations (D-MARKER-DIAG1). Output is cached by binder version, input hashes, target and toolchain. A tool-running reader needs an `Exec` grant (D-EFFTYPE-GRANT1). Instance of D-EXTEND-ARCH1 A.

options.name: Readers stay built in
options.detail:
Readers stay inside the toolchain, as today. User code is the same as A.

A language Jet's team has not added cannot be called without hand-written rows.
options.technical: Today's Jetpack Foreign readers and the closed ForeignLanguage enum. Matches D-EXTEND-ARCH1 C.

options.name: Generated files
options.detail:
A generator writes Jet declarations into a file that is committed and imported.

When the header changes, someone must remember to regenerate.
options.technical: The bindgen/c2nim/SWIG model; `jet inspect bind` is E2104 today.
options.code:
// The beginner path
$ jet bind raylib.h --out bindings/raylib.jet
use bindings.raylib as rl
rl.InitWindow(800, 450, "hi")

// The expert path: a new language
$ odin-jet-bind vendor/mathx.odin --out bindings/mathx.jet
use bindings.mathx as mathx

comparisons.note: Futhark reads C headers as a library macro. Source: https://github.com/PMunch/futhark
Zig is moving @cImport from the language into the build system as a package step (accepted proposal 20630). Source: https://github.com/ziglang/zig/issues/20630
bindgen and cxx are crates; bindgen output is often committed. Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-bindgen/

recommendation.why: A makes every language reader an ordinary package while user code stays the same. It is the owner's "a binding is a Jet metaprogram" idea, applied to every language.
gains: New languages without a Jet release.
One way to add a language: write a package.

whyNot.reason: B keeps every new language waiting on Jet's own team.
C brings back stale committed bindings.

recommendation.tradeoff: A third-party reader costs about 57 ms more on a cache miss.

decisions.title: Hand-written imports use one form for every language: the dependency in package.jet, the rows in `#Import module <lang>.<name>`
decisions.situation: Hand-written foreign rows have two spellings today. C uses `#Import module c.z { … }`, with the library named in package.jet. Rust uses its own keyword, `extern rust "base64@0.22" { … }`, with the crate and version written in the source file. `#Import module` accepts only C roots. The vote decides whether Rust, and every other language, joins the C form. We recommend one form, with versions kept in package.jet beside every other dependency.
decisions.gist: Should hand-written imports from Rust use the same form as C?
decisions.lesson: Jet code can call functions from other languages. When you write the signatures yourself, they go in an `#Import module` block. The library's name and version go in package.jet, like any dependency. C and Rust then look the same, and so does any language added later.
decisions.story: Kai bumps the base64 crate in package.jet and the build still uses the old one. The version was also written in an `extern rust` line three folders away.
decisions.detail:
Provenance. Card c08rdp62. This is the Rust import form from the D-FFI-UNSAFE1 package, asked alone. Most languages are read from their own files, as in `use go.handles as handles`; this ballot is only about hand-written rows.

Probes, in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/q/bd/probe/ffi. rd/: `deps: { base64: rust@"base64@0.22" }` is accepted in package.jet. `#Import module rust.base64 { … }` is E0003 "A C module path starts with `c.`, found `rust`". rust.jet, a copy of Examples/features/lowlevel/ffi.jet, parses `extern rust` and stops at E0703 because cargo is not installed.

Counts on dev: 154 `#Import module c` blocks, 48 `extern rust` blocks and 1 `extern c` block in .jet files.

options.name: One form for every language
options.detail:
Every hand-written import names its dependency in package.jet and lists rows in `#Import module <lang>.<name>`. Rust becomes `#Import module rust.base64`, exactly like `#Import module c.z`.

`extern rust` retires. `jet fix` moves each block's crate and version into package.jet and rewrites the block, so no code is lost.
options.technical: Lifts the C-only root check (E0003 "A C module path starts with `c.`") to any foreign root. package.jet already accepts `rust@"base64@0.22"` (probe rd/). 48 `extern rust` blocks and 1 `extern c` block move; the 154 `#Import module c.…` blocks stay. Under D-FFI-BINDER1 A the root names the reader package.

options.name: Keep `extern rust`
options.detail:
Rust keeps `extern rust`, and C keeps `#Import module`.

Readers learn two forms, and a dependency version can live in source as well as package.jet.
options.technical: Today's state (Examples/features/foundations/bridges/run.jet). E0703 when cargo is missing.

options.name: `extern` for every language
options.detail:
Every language uses the `extern` keyword with its dependency in a string.

It unifies the spelling but moves the larger group, and keeps versions in source.
options.technical: Makes `extern <lang>` general (one `extern c` block exists today) and retires the 154 `#Import module c.…` blocks.

comparisons.note: Dependencies and versions live in Cargo.toml only. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/specifying-dependencies.html
One `extern` form for all C symbols; packages live in build.zig.zon. Source: https://ziglang.org/documentation/master/#extern
Package.swift declares dependencies; sources only `import`. Source: https://www.swift.org/documentation/package-manager/

recommendation.why: A gives every language the form C already uses, with versions only in package.jet. It moves 49 blocks, and `jet fix` does it.
gains: One import form to learn.
One place for every version.

whyNot.reason: B keeps two forms and versions hidden in source files.
C rewrites three times as many blocks and keeps versions in source.

recommendation.tradeoff: Existing `extern rust` code changes once, by `jet fix`.

decisions.title: `use` reads C signatures from a header or straight from a C source file, so own C code needs no hand-written rows
decisions.situation: Jet can call C when it knows each function's signature. Headers are the usual source. But a project's own C code is often a single .c file with no header. Today it needs a package entry plus a hand-written row per function, and the copies drift from the C. A closed library may also ship debug type info. The vote decides what `use` can read. We recommend headers and C source, both through the pinned Clang Jet already uses.
decisions.gist: Besides headers, what should Jet read C signatures from?
decisions.lesson: To call C, Jet must know each function's exact signature. A header lists them, and so does the .c file itself. If Jet reads both, you write `use "fast.c" as fast` and call its functions, with no signatures typed by hand.
decisions.story: Ivy has one 200-line C file of image filters. Today she declares a package entry and copies 14 signatures into Jet by hand. When she renames a parameter type in C, the copy silently disagrees.
decisions.inWild:
// Zig: @cImport reads headers; C source compiles with the bundled clang.
const c = @cImport(@cInclude("fast.h"));
decisions.detail:
Provenance. Card c08rdp62. This is the C inputs question from the D-FFI-UNSAFE1 package, asked alone. The baseline is D's ImportC for C source and Zig's bundled clang for building it on any target (owner question q2yczyk8).

Probes, in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/q/bd/probe/ffi. nc/ is a copy of Examples/features/lowlevel/native_c: `deps: { nativeffi: c@"c" }` plus rows checks clean. Its `jet run` here is E2105 "the C compiler is not installed". h/: `use "c.h" as libc` gives E0102 because the self-hosted header reader is not built yet.

Reads with D-FFI-VOUCH1 and D-FFI-CMAP1. Every input is checked and mapped the same way, so a row read from C source is as safe as one read from a header. Debug-info reading (B) can be added later without changing A.

options.name: Headers and C source
options.detail:
`use "src/fast.c" as fast` reads the file with the pinned Clang, builds it for the target and imports its functions, as D's ImportC does. Macros and inline functions come through, as they do from a header.

`#Import module` rows still rename and retype, checked against the file. A closed library with no header keeps vouched rows (D-FFI-VOUCH1).
options.technical: Extends D-CIMPORT1=A's pinned Clang to .c inputs. C source builds join the build cache keyed by file hash and target, and cross-compile with the bundled toolchain, as Zig does. Today's `deps: { x: c@"dir" }` stays for multi-file C libraries.

options.name: Also debug type info
options.detail:
As A, plus `use "libfoo.so" as foo` reads the library's debug type info.

It works only when the vendor ships debug info, needs a reader per platform format, and cannot see macros or inline functions.
options.technical: A plus a DWARF reader (ELF, Mach-O) and a PDB reader (Windows). Can be added later without changing A.

options.name: Headers only
options.detail:
C source is built through a package entry, and each function is a hand-written row.

The rows copy the C signatures and can drift from them.
options.technical: Today's `deps: { x: c@"dir" }` plus rows (Examples/features/lowlevel/native_c).

comparisons.note: ImportC compiles and imports .c files. Source: https://dlang.org/spec/importc.html
Zig reads headers and builds C source with its bundled clang for any target. Source: https://ziglang.org/learn/overview/#zig-is-also-a-c-compiler
bindgen reads headers only; C source builds through the cc crate in build.rs. Source: https://docs.rs/cc

recommendation.why: A reads C signatures wherever source code writes them down, with the one Clang Jet already pins. Own C code needs no copied rows.
gains: No copied signatures for own C code.
Fewer vouches under D-FFI-VOUCH1.

whyNot.reason: B adds two fragile debug-info readers for libraries that rarely ship debug info; it can come later.
C keeps hand-copied signatures that drift.

recommendation.tradeoff: A closed library with no header still needs vouched rows.

void main() { negate(7); }

decisions.title: A marker body pastes a whole parameter list with Jet's spread: `fn $name(...$params)` and `$callee(...$params)`
decisions.situation: Marker bodies add declarations with `comptime loop` and `$` pastes, such as `fn $method(self)`. They can paste a name but not a parameter list. So a marker cannot make a wrapper with the same parameters as the function it marks, and a foreign-language reader cannot add a function of any arity. Jet already spreads lists into calls with `...parts`. The vote decides how a marker pastes a parameter list. We recommend the same spread, inside a template.
decisions.gist: How should a marker body paste a parameter list it read from another function?
decisions.lesson: Markers write code for you. A common job is a wrapper: a function with the same parameters as the marked one, which adds a step and calls it. Jet already spreads a list into a call with `...parts`. Inside a marker, the same `...` spreads a function's parameters into a new signature or call.
decisions.story: Rae writes a `#Logged` marker for her team. It works for functions with no parameters. For the rest she writes one copy of the marker per arity, up to five, and stops there.
decisions.detail:
Provenance. Card c03pi177. The FFI-UNSAFE1 package named this paste as a prerequisite; D-FFI-BINDER1 A needs it. It is asked here, in the markers group, because it is template grammar.

Probes, in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/q/bd/probe/mk. params.jet: `fn $name(...target.$params)` is E0003 "Expected a name for a parameter name, found `...`". params_read.jet: looping `target.$params` and binding `"show_{p.$name}"` is E0956 "A derive template binding is not a known-time value". Today `$params` reflects as a list of strings (FactReads.jet:406), not typed rows. Examples/features/basics/variadics_mixed_lists.jet shows today's call spread, `join(...left, ...right)`.

Reads with D-META-HASH1. Today's spelling reads facts with `target.$params` and pastes with `$params`. Under HASH1=A the reads become `#target.params`, `#target.name` and `#target.result`, while pastes stay `$name`, `...$params` and `$callee(...$params)`. Under HASH1=B or C the binding lines follow that outcome. The meaning is the same in every spelling: bind the list once, then spread the pasted list.

options.name: Spread with `...`
options.detail:
Inside a template, `...` before a pasted parameter list spreads it. In a signature it writes each `name: Type`, and in a call it passes each name. Ordinary parameters may sit beside it, as in `fn $name(log: Logger, ...$params)`.

This is the spread Jet already uses in calls, such as `join(...parts)`. A variadic parameter keeps its own form, `parts: ...String`, after a name.
options.technical: Template-only: a spread in a parameter list is E0003 today. Needs `target.$params` as typed rows (name, type, mode); FactReads.jet:406 returns `[String]` today. Adds `target.$result` for the result type. Used by D-FFI-BINDER1 A.

options.name: Paste the whole signature
options.detail:
A signature value pastes after the name, and an argument value pastes into a call.

A wrapper that adds a parameter, such as a logger, can't be written this way.
options.technical: Adds `$signature` and `$arguments` facts and two paste positions.

options.name: Build functions as values
options.detail:
Declarations are built as data and emitted by a call.

The body has to be built as data too, so a three-line wrapper becomes a tree of values.
options.technical: Adds an `emit` call and Function, Param and Body values beside `comptime loop` templates.

comparisons.note: Decorators forward parameters with `*args, **kw`. Source: https://docs.python.org/3/glossary.html#term-decorator
Proc macros re-emit parsed parameters inside `quote!`. Source: https://docs.rs/quote/latest/quote/macro.quote.html
`@Type` builds types from data; functions are written with `anytype`. Source: https://ziglang.org/documentation/master/#Type

recommendation.why: A reuses the spread Jet already has, so one rule pastes a parameter list in a signature and in a call. Extra parameters still fit beside it.
gains: Wrappers and readers of any arity.
Nothing new to learn beyond `...`.

whyNot.reason: B can only copy a signature whole.
C makes function bodies into data trees.

recommendation.tradeoff: `...` before a parameter list and after a name mean two related things.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude. Adversarial model family: Claude. Fresh agent: Main. A reuses the existing spread to paste a parameter list, so forwarding wrappers need no new construct. B's whole-signature paste can't rename or drop one parameter, and C's emit API is a second way to make functions.

decisions.checkInstructions: Use the dev jet from $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/discovery/base/latest with JET_TOOLCHAIN_ROOT set to the dev worktree, in probe/mk. `jet check params.jet` gives E0003; `jet check params_read.jet` gives E0956.

surface.gist: How should a marker body paste a parameter list it read from another function?
surface.lesson: Markers write code for you. A common job is a wrapper: a function with the same parameters as the marked one, which adds a step and calls it. Jet already spreads a list into a call with `...parts`. Inside a marker, the same `...` spreads a function's parameters into a new signature or call.

current.note: Today a parameter-list paste does not parse.

wild.note: A proc macro re-emits the parsed inputs with `#(#inputs),*`. Source: https://docs.rs/quote/latest/quote/macro.quote.html
wild.code:
let inputs = &sig.inputs;
quote! { fn #name(#inputs) #output { #body } }

options.name: Spread with `...`
options.gist: `...$params` pastes `name: Type` pairs in a signature and the names in a call.
gains: Reuses Jet's existing spread.
Works for any arity.
Extra parameters can sit beside the spread.

proposed.code:

fn $name(...$params) -> $result {      // new
    $callee(...$params)                 // new
}

options.name: Paste the whole signature
options.gist: `fn $name target.$signature { }` copies the parameters and result as one piece.
gains: One paste for the common wrapper.
losses: Can't add or drop a parameter.
Calls still need a separate argument paste.

options.name: Build functions as values
options.gist: The marker builds a `Function` value and calls `emit`, as Zig's `@Type` builds types.
gains: Any shape can be built.
losses: The body must be built as data, not written as code.
A second way to emit beside templates.

proposed.code: emit(Function{ name: name, params: target.$params, body: … })   // new

recommendation.why: A reuses the spread Jet already has, so one rule pastes a parameter list in a signature and in a call. Extra parameters still fit beside it.
gains: Wrappers and readers of any arity.
Nothing new to learn beyond `...`.

whyNot.reason: B can only copy a signature whole.
C makes function bodies into data trees.

recommendation.tradeoff: `...` before a parameter list and after a name mean two related things.

decisions.title: An enum in a fixed array's `#` slot gives one slot per case: `[V2#Direction]`, read as `step[.East]`
decisions.situation: Games and parsers keep one value per enum case: a step per direction, a name per token kind. Today that is a function with a match, or a `[T#4]` read with a number that drifts when a case is added. The `#` slot of a fixed array already parses a type name but gives it no meaning: `[Int#Direction]{10, 20}` is accepted and indexing it fails. The vote decides what an enum in the slot means. We recommend one slot per case, indexed by the case.
decisions.gist: What should `[V2#Direction]`, an enum in a fixed array's size slot, mean?
decisions.lesson: A fixed array `[Int#4]` holds exactly four items. With an enum in the slot, `[V2#Direction]` holds exactly one item per direction. You index it with a direction, `step[.East]`, so it can never be out of range. Add a case to the enum and Jet points at every table that lacks it.
decisions.story: Tom adds `NorthEast` to `Direction`. The `[V2#4]` table still has four rows, and `step[4]` crashes the first time a player moves diagonally.
decisions.inWild:
// Odin: an enumerated array.
step := [Direction]V2{ .North = {0, -1}, .East = {1, 0}, .South = {0, 1}, .West = {-1, 0} }
decisions.detail:
Provenance. Card c05gn07n (#6177); research card #6204. This is the enum table question from the D-ARRAY1 package, asked alone. Ratified and not reopened: D-ARRAY-INIT1=A (`filled`, `from_fn`), D-SHAPE-PLACE1=A (bare place reads, `&place` writes, `~place` copies), D-OOBPROOF1 and the D-MATRIX family.

Probes. On dev, q/b4/arrp/enumlen.jet: `[Int#Direction]{10, 20, 30, 40}` is accepted, and `step[1]` is E0965 "A fixed-list length is not a checked integer measure". q/b4/arrp/constlen.jet: `[Int#V2]{1, 2}` with a struct `V2` runs and prints 2, so the slot accepts any type name today. That needs a refusal whatever this vote picks. probe/arr/fromfn.jet: the ratified `[Int#4].from_fn(…)` (D-ARRAY-INIT1=A) is not built yet and is E0003.

Reads with the rest of the group. D-ARRAY-KEYED1 lets the table be written `{.North: V2{x: 0, y: -1}, …}`. D-ARRAY-INDEX1 puts an index type in the same slot, and D-ARRAY-CAPACITY1 a range. The one reading of the slot is how many items.

options.name: One slot per case
options.detail:
With a fieldless enum in the slot, the array has one item per case, in case order. It is indexed by a case value, never by an Int, so a read can't fail and emits no check.

It is still a fixed array: `len()`, loops, element-wise operators and `[T]` windows all work. It encodes as an object keyed by case name, so reordering cases never misreads stored data.
options.technical: Gives the type slot a meaning (E0965 today). Only fieldless enums; a struct or a field-carrying enum in the slot is an error listing the slot kinds. An Int index is refused; pass the table as a `[T]` window to index by Int. Encoding through the one shape fact (D-SHAPE-ONE1).

options.name: A Core `EnumTable` type
options.detail:
Core gains a named type for enum-indexed tables.

It repeats what fixed arrays already have, such as loops, element-wise operators and windows.
options.technical: A Core struct over `[T#N]` with N from the enum's case count; needs number parameters (#3505) or a compiler intrinsic.

options.name: Keep a function
options.detail:
Per-case values stay a function with a match, which is checked for every case.

There is no table value to iterate, store or edit.
options.technical: Today's form (q/b4/arrp/today.jet). The slot gains a refusal for type names instead of a meaning.

comparisons.note: Enumerated arrays. Source: https://odin-lang.org/docs/overview/#enumerated-arrays
The enum-map crate provides `EnumMap<K, V>` as a library type. Source: https://docs.rs/enum-map
No enum-indexed array; a dictionary or a switch is used. Source: https://docs.swift.org/swift-book/documentation/the-swift-programming-language/enumerations/

recommendation.why: A gives the slot's existing parse a meaning: how many items, one per case. Reads never fail, and a new case is caught at build time.
gains: Tables that can't go out of range.
No second fixed-size type.

whyNot.reason: B adds a second fixed-size type that repeats `[T#N]`.
C leaves no table to loop over, store or edit.

recommendation.tradeoff: An Int index needs the table passed as a `[T]` window.

surface.lesson: A fixed array `[Int#4]` holds exactly four items. With an enum in the slot, `[V2#Direction]` holds exactly one item per direction. You index it with a direction, `step[.East]`, so it can never be out of range. Add a case to the enum and Jet points at every table that lacks it.

gains: `step[.East]` never fails and needs no bounds check.
A new case stops the build at each table lacking it.

losses: A second fixed-size type beside `[T#N]`.

gains: Nothing new.

losses: No table to loop over or pass around.

C leaves no table to loop over, store or edit.

decisions.title: A fixed-array literal may name its positions, `{0: 1, 3..5: 9, else: 0}`, and must cover every position exactly once
decisions.situation: Lookup tables are often mostly one value with a few exceptions: a character class table, an opcode table, a step per direction. Today a fixed-array literal lists every item in order, so a 256-entry table is 256 values, and a reader can't see which position is which. C and Odin let a literal name positions, but fill gaps with zero silently. The vote decides whether Jet literals name positions. We recommend named positions with a coverage check: every position once, gaps only through `else:`.
decisions.gist: Should a fixed-array literal be able to name which position each value goes to?
decisions.lesson: A fixed array literal normally lists every value in order. With keys you write which position gets which value: `{0: 1, 3..5: 9, else: 0}`. Jet checks that every position is covered exactly once, so a forgotten entry is a build error, not a silent zero.
decisions.story: Uma's opcode table has 64 entries in order. She inserts one in the middle and every later opcode shifts by one. The emulator runs, wrongly, for a week.
decisions.inWild:
// C: designated initializers; gaps are silently zero.
int table[8] = { [0] = 1, [3 ... 5] = 9 };
decisions.detail:
Provenance. Card c05gn07n (#6177); research card #6204. This is the keyed literal question from the D-ARRAY1 package, asked alone. Ratified and not reopened: D-ARRAY-INIT1=A (`filled`, `from_fn`), D-SHAPE-PLACE1=A (bare place reads, `&place` writes, `~place` copies), D-OOBPROOF1 and the D-MATRIX family.

decisions.title: A distinct range type in the `#` slot makes an index-typed pool: `[Node#NodeIX]` is read with a `NodeIX` and never checks
decisions.situation: Graphs, free lists and entity pools link items by small integer indexes instead of pointers. The index is only safe if it fits the pool, so every read pays a bounds check, and any Int can be passed by mistake. Jet already has distinct types and range types, but `distinct U16(0..1023)` is refused, and the size slot doesn't take a type. The vote decides whether an index type can size a pool. We recommend it: the pool has one slot per index value, so reads never check.
decisions.gist: Should a pool be sized by its own index type, so reads with that index never need a check?
decisions.lesson: A pool of nodes linked by number is fast but easy to get wrong. Give the index its own type, `NodeIX :: distinct U16(0..1023)`, and size the pool by it, `[Node#NodeIX]`. Every `NodeIX` fits by construction, so `pool[at]` can't go out of range and needs no check.
decisions.story: Pia's pathfinder passes a tile index where a node index belongs. Both are Int, so it compiles and reads garbage. A bounds check catches it only when the tile number happens to be large.

options.name: Pool sized by its index type
options.detail:
A distinct range type starting at 0 may sit in the slot. The pool has one slot per value, so a read with that type never fails, wherever the index came from.

Arithmetic on an index gives an Int, since `at + 1` could leave the pool. Going back is one checked `NodeIX.from_int(i)`. An Int index on the pool is refused; pass it as a `[Node]` window for that.
options.technical: Lifts E0137 for sized carriers when the range fits (research card #6204); at run time the index is its bare carrier. The range must start at 0. Two pools may share an index type; that is memory-safe since the index fits both. The #6204 benchmark links a 1,024-node pool by 2-byte indexes this way.

options.technical: Needs E0137 lifted as in A, plus number parameters (#3505).

options.technical: Today's lists; D-OOBPROOF1 drops checks only where it can prove the range.

decisions.title: A range in the `#` slot makes a capacity list: `[Contact#0..8]` holds up to eight items inline, with no heap
decisions.situation: Physics contacts, small paths and parser lookahead need lists with a known maximum. A `[T]` list allocates on the heap, which hot loops and embedded code avoid. A fixed array has no length of its own. Odin and Rust (arrayvec) have inline lists with a capacity. The vote decides how Jet spells one. We recommend a range in the fixed-array slot: `[T#0..8]` holds from zero to eight items, inline, with the same methods as a list.
decisions.gist: How should a list with a fixed maximum, stored inline with no heap, be written?
decisions.lesson: Sometimes you know a list will never hold more than, say, eight items. `[Contact#0..8]` stores up to eight inline, with no heap allocation, and has `push`, `pop`, `len` and loops like any list. Pushing a ninth stops like an out-of-range index; `try_push` returns an error instead.
decisions.story: Leo's collision code allocates a fresh list per object per frame. The game stutters every few seconds when the allocator compacts.
decisions.detail:
Provenance. Card c05gn07n (#6177); research card #6204. This is the capacity list question from the D-ARRAY1 package, asked alone. Ratified and not reopened: D-ARRAY-INIT1=A (`filled`, `from_fn`), D-SHAPE-PLACE1=A (bare place reads, `&place` writes, `~place` copies), D-OOBPROOF1 and the D-MATRIX family.

options.name: Range in the slot
options.detail:

`push` past the end stops like an out-of-range index; `try_push` returns an error value. A nonzero start, as in `[T#2..8]`, keeps a minimum, and `pop` below it stops the same way.
options.technical: New slot kind (E0003 today). The checks follow the `bounds` setting, and D-OOBPROOF1 drops them where the fit is proven. Odin's `append` instead drops the item and returns a count.

decisions.title: One column of a columnar list is a list place: `ps.x` reads it, `&ps.x` edits it in place
decisions.situation: A columnar list stores each struct field as its own column, so a loop over one field reads packed memory. Jet already has `#Layout(columnar)`, but a column can't be named: `ps.x` is refused, so a solver that wants all x values gets them one item at a time. Odin writes `v.x` for a column. The vote decides how code reaches one column. We recommend the field name: `ps.x` is the column as a `[Float]` place, read bare and edited with `&`.
decisions.gist: How should code reach one column of a columnar list, such as all the x values?
decisions.lesson: A columnar list keeps all the `x` values side by side, then all the `v` values. `ps.x` is that column, a `[Float]` you can pass to any list function. Pass `&ps.x` to let the function edit it in place, with no copy.
decisions.story: Max moves his particles to `#Layout(columnar)` for speed. His solver takes a `[Float]`, so he still copies every x into a new list each frame, and the speed-up vanishes.
decisions.detail:
Provenance. Card c05gn07n (#6177); research card #6204. This is the column question from the D-ARRAY1 package, asked alone. Ratified and not reopened: D-ARRAY-INIT1=A (`filled`, `from_fn`), D-SHAPE-PLACE1=A (bare place reads, `&place` writes, `~place` copies), D-OOBPROOF1 and the D-MATRIX family.

decisions.title: A fixed array passed to a `[T]` parameter is a read window, as a list is; `~a` still copies
decisions.situation: Under D-FIXARR1 a fixed array `[Int#4]` passed to a `[Int]` parameter is copied into a new list. A list passed the same way is a read window, with no copy, under D-SHAPE-PLACE1. So the same call costs an allocation for one and nothing for the other, and hot code avoids fixed arrays to dodge it. The vote decides whether a fixed array passes as a window too. We recommend it: every place reads the same, and `~a` copies when a copy is wanted.
decisions.gist: When a fixed array is passed to a `[T]` parameter, should it be a read window or a copy?
decisions.lesson: A function that takes `[Int]` reads a list without copying it. Today a fixed array `[Int#4]` is copied first. With this change it is read in place too, like any list. If you do want a separate copy, write `~a`.
decisions.story: Kai's audio filter keeps its taps in a `[F32#64]` and passes them to a `[F32]` helper 48,000 times a second. Each call allocates a list, and the profiler shows nothing else.

Probes, in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/q/bd/probe/arr. window2.jet: `total(a)` with `a :: [Int#4]` runs and prints 10. window.jet adds `bump(&a)` to a `&[Int]` parameter that writes `xs[0]`: it runs and prints 10 then 2. window3.jet, the same with a `[Int]` list, prints 2.

Reads with D-SHAPE-PLACE1=A: bare reads, `&` writes and `~` copies, now for fixed arrays too.

options.name: Read window
options.detail:
A fixed array, like a list, is a place, so a bare argument is a read window under D-SHAPE-PLACE1. `&a` passes a write window to a `&[T]` parameter, and `~a` passes a copy.

The callee can't change the length through either window, since a fixed array has none to change.
options.technical: Amends D-FIXARR1's widening copy. Lowering passes pointer and length, as for list windows; the copy path stays for `~a`.

options.name: Keep the copy
options.detail:
The call allocates a list and copies the items.

Hot code converts once and keeps the list.
options.technical: Today's behavior (probe window2.jet prints 10).

options.name: Explicit slice
options.detail:
A whole-array slice gives a window, as Go and Odin do.

The bare call stays a copy, so the obvious spelling is the slow one.

decisions.title: `Mat3.inverse()` and `Mat4.inverse()` return `MatrixError!`, failing on a singular matrix as `Transform.inverse()` already does
decisions.situation: Core has `Mat3` and `Mat4` with products and `transpose()`, but no inverse. Cameras, physics and skinning need one. A singular matrix has no inverse: GLSL returns undefined cells, and Rust's nalgebra returns an Option. Jet's own `Transform.inverse()` already returns an error when the determinant is not finite or within 2.2e-16 of zero. The vote decides what `inverse()` returns for matrices. We recommend the same rule as `Transform`: an error value.
decisions.gist: What should `m.inverse()` return when a matrix has no inverse?
decisions.lesson: Some matrices, such as one that flattens space to a plane, have no inverse. Jet's `inverse()` returns an error in that case, so you handle it with `?` or `??`. A rotation can be undone with `transpose()`, which never fails.
decisions.story: Ana's camera matrix collapses when the zoom hits zero. The inverse fills with infinities, and every object on screen vanishes with no error.
decisions.inWild:

decisions.detail:
Provenance. Card c05gn07n (#6177); research card #6204. This is the matrix inverse question from the D-ARRAY1 package, asked alone. Ratified and not reopened: D-ARRAY-INIT1=A (`filled`, `from_fn`), D-SHAPE-PLACE1=A (bare place reads, `&place` writes, `~place` copies), D-OOBPROOF1 and the D-MATRIX family.

Probes, in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/q/bd/probe/arr. mat.jet: `Mat3.new(…)` and `transpose()` run. `Mat3` has no `identity()` today (Math.jet:857-911), and the call is E0107 "Nothing named `Mat3` exists here". nomethod.jet: a missing static method on a user struct is E0311 "`Box` has no matching static method `missing`", so the Core message is a defect. Core/Math/Math.jet:2040-2042 is `Transform.inverse()` with its singular check.

Reads with the D-MATRIX family, which chose methods (D-MATRIX-SOLVE1=B). Core matrices are column-major already (Math.jet:1601).

decisions.title: Lane-wise comparisons are methods, `a.lanes_lt(b)` → `Lanes<Bool, N>`; `<` and `==` keep returning one Bool
decisions.situation: D-LANES1 ratified `Lanes<T, N>` for vector math. Clamping, masking and branch-free code need a comparison per lane: which lanes of `a` are below `b`. But `if a == b` must stay one Bool, or every equality test breaks. Rust's portable SIMD uses methods such as `simd_lt`; GLSL uses `lessThan`. The vote decides how a lane-wise comparison is written. We recommend methods, `lanes_lt` and siblings, returning a `Lanes<Bool, N>` mask.
decisions.gist: How should a comparison that gives one answer per lane be written?
decisions.lesson: `a < b` asks one question and gives one Bool. Vector code often wants an answer per lane instead. `a.lanes_lt(b)` gives a mask with one Bool per lane. `mask.select(a, b)` picks from `a` where the mask is true. `any()` and `all()` turn a mask back into one Bool.
decisions.story: Sam clamps a particle's four speeds with a loop and an `if` per lane. The loop blocks vectorizing, and the hot path runs four times slower than the C version.
decisions.detail:
Provenance. Card c05gn07n (#6177); research card #6204. This is the lane comparison question from the D-ARRAY1 package, asked alone. Ratified and not reopened: D-ARRAY-INIT1=A (`filled`, `from_fn`), D-SHAPE-PLACE1=A (bare place reads, `&place` writes, `~place` copies), D-OOBPROOF1 and the D-MATRIX family.

Probes, in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/q/bd/probe/arr. lanes.jet: `a + b` on two `[Float#4]` is E0109 today, since fixed-array arithmetic is still being built. eq.jet: `a == b` on the same arrays runs and prints false, the one-Bool answer A keeps. `Lanes` is ratified (D-LANES1=A) but has no Core type yet.

Reads with D-MATRIX-SOLVE1=B, which chose methods for matrix operations.

They work at compile time and on every backend.

Equality of two lane values then needs `.all()`.

decisions.title: Core ships `Quaternion` beside `Vec3` and `Mat3`, built by the ratified literal and rotating a `Vec3` with `q * v`
decisions.situation: 3D games and robotics store rotations as quaternions: four numbers that blend smoothly and never lock up as angles do. Core has `Vec3`, `Mat3` and `Mat4`, and D-LITCARRIER1=D ratified the literal `1 + 2i + 3j + 4k`, but there is no type for it to build. The vote decides whether Core ships one. We recommend a `Quaternion` struct in Core math, with rotation methods, so the ratified literal has a home.
decisions.gist: Should Core ship a `Quaternion` type for 3D rotations?
decisions.lesson: A quaternion is four numbers that describe a 3D rotation. `Quaternion.angle_axis(0.5, up)` makes one, `q * v` rotates a vector, and `a.slerp(b, 0.5)` blends halfway between two rotations. Unlike three angles, blending never jumps or locks.
decisions.story: Ben stores his camera as three angles. Looking straight up, two angles line up, and the camera spins wildly when he nudges the mouse.
decisions.detail:
Provenance. Card c05gn07n (#6177); research card #6204. This is the quaternion question from the D-ARRAY1 package, asked alone. Ratified and not reopened: D-ARRAY-INIT1=A (`filled`, `from_fn`), D-SHAPE-PLACE1=A (bare place reads, `&place` writes, `~place` copies), D-OOBPROOF1 and the D-MATRIX family.

Probes. q/b4/arrp/today.jet runs `Vec3.new(1.0, 1.0, 1.0)` and `v.zyx.x`, printing 1.0. The package probe optA3.jet found `Quaternion` is E0107 today.

Reads with D-LITCARRIER1=D, which ratified the literal, and D-MATRIX-SOLVE1=B, which chose methods.

options.name: Core `Quaternion`
options.detail:
`Quaternion` has parts `w`, `x`, `y` and `z`, `+ - *`, `==`, `conj()`, `length()`, `normalize()` and `identity()`. Rotation adds `angle_axis`, `slerp`, `inverse()` and `Mat3.from_quaternion(q)`, and `q * v` rotates a `Vec3`.

`/` is refused with a hint naming `a * b.inverse()`, because left and right division differ.
options.technical: Core/Math struct over `[Float#4]`, like `Vec4`. The literal `1 + 2i + 3j + 4k` builds it (D-LITCARRIER1=D). Float cells, as all Core math.
options.code:

v :: Vec3.new(1.0, 1.0, 1.0)
print(v.zyx.x)      // 1.0

// The expert path
spin :: Quaternion.angle_axis(0.5, Vec3.new(0.0, 1.0, 0.0))   // new
half :: Quaternion.identity().slerp(spin, 0.5)                 // new
print((half * v).x)

options.name: Rotation matrices only
options.detail:
Rotations stay 3×3 matrices.

Nine numbers drift apart under repeated products, and smooth blending needs extra math.
options.technical: Adds `Mat3.rotation` only.

options.name: A separate package
options.detail:
A community package provides the type.

Core's literal builds nothing until the package is imported.
options.technical: No Core change.

print(v.zyx.x)      // 1.0

// The expert path

spin :: Quaternion.angle_axis(0.5, Vec3.new(0.0, 1.0, 0.0))
print((spin * v).x)

decisions.title: A lambda stored where no type is expected follows the declaration rule: it writes parameter and result types, as `fn square` would
decisions.situation: Most lambdas are passed to a call, which tells them their types. About 219 in Jet's code are stored in a local, where nothing does. decisions.title: A method that changes its receiver is called as `c.bump()` on a changeable value; `grow(&c)` keeps its `&`
decisions.situation: In Jet, `c.n += 1` changes a field with no mark, but `c.bump()`, a method that changes `c`, must be written `&c.bump()`. The vote decides whether the mark before the dot is required. We recommend leaving it to the compiler, as for fields.
decisions.gist: Should calling a method that changes `c` need `&c.bump()`, or just `c.bump()`?
decisions.lesson: A value made with `:=` can change. Calling `c.bump()` on it may change it, just as `c.n += 1` does, and the editor shows a faint `&` there. Passing `c` to another function that changes it still takes `&c`, so changes that leave the line stay visible.

decisions.title: A lambda is the bound value without its name: `(n) { n > 2 }`, leaving out any part the call already fixes
decisions.situation:
A lambda is a small function passed to another function, such as the test in `nums.filter(…)`. Jet writes it today as `n -> n > 2`, a shape no named function uses.

D-DECL-BINDING1 proposes that a function is a binding, `square :: (n: Int) -> Int { n * n }`. This vote decides whether a lambda is exactly that value without the name, or also keeps a short arrow. We recommend one shape. Decide D-DECL-BINDING1 first; this vote holds under each of its outcomes.
decisions.gist: Should every lambda be written exactly as a function binding's value, `(n) { n > 2 }`, with no separate short arrow?
decisions.lesson: A lambda is a function without a name. Under this rule you write it as the value of a function binding: inputs in parentheses, then the body in braces. Types the call already knows may be left out, as in `nums.filter((n) { n > 2 })`.
decisions.explainer:
The two votes fit together. D-DECL-BINDING1 makes `square :: (n: Int) -> Int { n * n }` a function. Dropping `square ::` leaves a lambda, and dropping the types the call gives leaves `(n) { n * n }`.

The only question left is the short arrow. Most lambdas today have a one-expression body, and the arrow is a little shorter there.
decisions.story: Dev passes `n -> n > 2` to `filter`, then wants a log line in it. Today he turns it into `n -> { … }`. Under one shape he adds the line inside the braces he already has.
decisions.detail:
Provenance. Card c0rqt0kq. Version 1 proposed `fn(n) { n * n }` and is kept as D-LAMBDA-SHAPE1.v1.json. The owner asked that the shape align with the binding conversion, which D-DECL-BINDING1 now asks for. Under D-DECL-BINDING1=B both options here gain a leading `fn`. Under D-DECL-BINDING1=C, which keeps `fn name(…)`, the value form is `fn(n) { n > 2 }`, version 1's shape, so the choice here stays the same.

Data, from Main's census (q/b4/lam/census.mjs) rerun on a dev export. There are 4,812 lambdas in 1,197 files. Of these, 3,842 have an expression body and 970 a braced body; 888 have a bare parameter. 2,832 leave at least one parameter type to the call, and 220 are stored in a binding.

Size under A. A bare expression lambda grows by three characters, a parenthesized one by one, and a braced one shrinks by three. Over the corpus that adds 2,813 characters, 0.6 per lambda. Version 1's `fn(…)` form added 12,437. Only the 888 lambdas with a bare parameter and one expression grow by three, and a named function passes with no lambda at all.

Probes in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/SurfaceDesign/probes/m-decl run at o0, o1 and o2. The program in today's spelling is d10_lambda_today.jet, and it prints the commented output on every tier. Main's probe q/b4/lamp/p5.jet shows `(n: Int) -> Int { n * n }` running today as a typed value. With a `print` line added, p10.jet is E0399.

Known defect under both options: a `return` inside a braced lambda passed to `map` is checked against the enclosing function (q/b4/lamp/p12.jet, E0113). Under A a `return` leaves the lambda, as it leaves any function.

Reads with D-LAMBDA-STORED1=A, whose rule stays: a stored lambda with no expected type writes its parameter and result types. Only its spelling changes, from `fn(n: Int)` to `(n: Int)`.

options.name: Exactly the bound value
options.detail:
A lambda is `(params) arrow result failure { body }`, a function binding's value without the name. Parameter, result and failure types may be left out where the expected type gives them. The arrow appears only with a written result or an effect row, as in a named function.

Behavior changes. The arrow lambdas `n -> e` and `(n) -> { … }` are retired, and `jet fix` rewrites them. A `return` inside a lambda leaves the lambda. `(n: Int) -> Int { n * n }` is a function, never a typed value.
options.technical: Parser: in value position, `(` followed by a parameter list and then `{`, `->`, `-[` or a failure rail reads a function, the D-DECL-BINDING1 rule. The arrow-lambda path in Expressions.jet:1152-1304 goes, and E0399 becomes the teaching error for the retired arrow. `jet fix` rewrites 4,812 lambdas, writing the inferred result for the 220 stored ones. Amends D-LAMBDA-IFACE2=A and replaces S46's form.

options.name: The bound value, plus a short arrow
options.detail:
The value form is used as in A. A lambda whose types the call gives, and whose body is one expression, may also be written `n -> n > 2` or `(a, b) -> a + b`.

After `->`, a type followed by `{` reads as a result type, as in a binding's value. So the 40 short lambdas whose body starts with a typed literal `Type{…}` need parentheses around it. Growing a short lambda to two lines changes its head.
options.technical: Keeps the expression arrow path in Expressions.jet:1152-1304 and adds A's value path. `jet fix` rewrites the 970 braced arrow lambdas and parenthesizes 40 typed-literal bodies. Two parse paths decide on the token after `->`.

options.name: The bound value, starting with fn
options.detail:
A lambda is exactly a function binding's value without its name, and like every function value it starts with `fn`: `fn(n) { n > 2 }`. It matches D-DECL-BINDING1 option B, `square :: fn(n: Int) -> Int { n * n }`.

The call still fixes the parameter types, so a passed lambda writes only the names. There is no separate short arrow.
options.technical: Lambda: `fn` `(` params `)` [`-[E]>` | `->` T] `{` body `}`. The params, effect row and result may be left out wherever the call fixes them. The parser sees `fn` and needs no tuple-or-function rule. `n -> e` retires; `jet fix` rewrites it to `fn(n) { e }`.

comparisons.note: One shape: a function literal is a declaration without its name. Source: https://go.dev/ref/spec#Function_literals

comparisons.note: A lambda has its own braces-first shape, apart from `fun`. Source: https://kotlinlang.org/docs/lambdas.html

recommendation.why: C makes a lambda exactly a function value without its name, and `fn` marks every function, named or passed. It matches D-DECL-BINDING1 B, and dropping `fn` later stays a mechanical `jet fix` if it proves redundant.
gains: One shape for named and passed functions.
`fn` marks every function at a glance.
Growing a body keeps its head.
No tuple-or-function parsing rule.

whyNot.reason: A needs a rule to tell `(…)` lambdas from tuples, and adding `fn` back later is far harder than dropping it.
B keeps two spellings for one thing, and a growing body changes its head.

recommendation.tradeoff: Each lambda gains `fn`: two characters per lambda. `jet fix` rewrites every lambda once.

decisions.title: `#Pre` is checked while compiling whenever the values it reads are known; no new mark
decisions.situation: A function states a rule about its arguments with `#Pre(condition, "message")`, checked when the program runs. A call such as `simd_width(6, xs)` can never pass, yet it builds and stops later. The first draft added `##Pre`, a second mark that also made parameters compile-time without saying so. This revision adds nothing to learn. A `#Pre` is decided while compiling whenever the values it reads are known then, the rule you chose for `::` values.
decisions.gist: How should a rule on a function's arguments be checked while compiling, when the call's values are fixed?
decisions.lesson: `#Pre(lanes == 4, "need 4 lanes")` is a rule every call must keep. When a call passes fixed values, such as the number 6, the compiler can work out the answer itself. Under A it does, and a call that can never pass fails to build, on the caller's line, with the author's message.
decisions.story: Ivo calls a library's `simd_width(6, readings)`. Today it builds and ships, then stops on a customer's machine with "need 4 or 8 lanes", a rule the library stated all along. Under A, his build fails on that line with the same message. The library author wrote nothing new.
decisions.detail:
Why the draft was revised. `##Pre` added a second compile-time mark, although D-META-HASH1 A made `#` the one mark. It turned each parameter the rule reads into a compile-time one without a word at the parameter, so each distinct value built its own copy. A run-time value at a call then became an error. That is a hidden cost and behavior change (philosophy principle 8) and a new concept (principle 7).

The rule A uses already exists. D-COMPTIME-WORD1 A, which you ratified, computes every `::` value while compiling whenever it can and falls back to run time otherwise. `comptime` is the one word that requires it. A applies the same rule to `#Pre`: a pure condition over values known while compiling is worked out then. D-PREPOST1 already makes every `#Pre` pure.

What A does at each call. If every value the rule reads is known while compiling, such as a literal, a `::` constant or a `comptime` parameter, the compiler decides the rule. False is a build error on the caller's line, with the message and the values. True means that call carries no run-time check, as a proved check is erased (D-PROVE-SEM1). Otherwise the check runs when the program runs, as today.

If working out the rule runs past the compile-time step budget, the check stays at run time, as a `::` value does; it is never dropped. `#Post` needs nothing new: when a whole call is computed while compiling under D-COMPTIME-WORD1, its `#Post` is checked then too.

Requiring a fixed value. Some functions need the value fixed, for example to pick a vector width. The author writes `comptime lanes: Int`, the ratified spelling (D-COMPTIME-WORD1 A, D-CONSTGEN2 A). Every call then passes a fixed value, so every `#Pre` on it is decided while compiling. The first draft's option B is that case of A, not a separate rule.

Probes on dev, in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/MemDesign-3/probes/pre, on o0, o1 and o2. pre.jet calls `width(6, …)` against `#Pre(lanes == 4, …)`: it builds, prints 6, then stops with E3001 on line 8. The first draft's internal compiler error no longer happens. In early.jet the same call sits in a file constant, `BAD :: width(6, …)`. `jet check` passes and the run stops at startup, so early `::` evaluation is not built yet either.

More probes. prepre.jet: `##Pre` is E0003. lead.jet: a `comptime` parameter is E0003, since it is ratified but not built. ctif2.jet: `comptime if` on a plain parameter is E0989. Census (probes/pre/census.mjs): 26 `#Pre` lines, 5 in Examples and 21 in tests; none in Core.

Overlap. Jet has one contract form, `#Pre` and `#Post` (D-PREPOST1); `#Require` was a placeholder name and was archived. Markers, `comptime` and generic recipes (D-GENERIC-TYPEFN1) keep their meaning. A adds no syntax, no error code beyond the build-time form of the existing contract failure, and no rule for parameters.

Review. Author: Claude (MemDesign-3 lane), revising the Main draft after the owner said he was not happy with it. No fresh adversarial pass has run on this revision.

options.name: `#Pre` is decided while compiling whenever it can be
options.detail:
At each call, if every value the rule reads is known while compiling, the compiler decides it. A call that can never pass is a build error on the caller's line, with the author's message. Other calls are checked when the program runs, as today. No new mark and no parameter changes.

Behavior change: a call with fixed values that breaks a `#Pre` fails to build instead of stopping at run time. A call decided true carries no run-time check.
options.technical: Sema, after argument substitution at each call: if the `#Pre` condition reads only literals, `::` constants and `comptime` parameters, evaluate it in the compile-time engine under the D-COMPTIME-WORD1 step budget. False: the contract-failure error at the call span, with message and values. True: drop that call's entry check, as D-PROVE-SEM1 erases proved checks. Budget exhausted or run-time inputs: keep the run-time check.

options.name: `##Pre` (the first draft)
options.detail:
A doubled mark, `##Pre`, runs the rule while compiling at each distinct call. Every parameter it reads becomes compile-time without a word at the parameter.

A call passing a run-time value is an error, and each distinct value builds its own copy of the function.
options.technical: Parser: `##Name(…)` before a declaration, a second marker form. Sema: the rule runs per distinct call, and the parameters it reads are specialized.

decisions.title: A service worker is an ordinary function: its parameter type is the message type, and `tree.worker` returns `Endpoint<Email>`
decisions.situation: A task group runs `send_email(e)` for each email. Moving that work into a supervised service should keep the same function. Today the service API takes only a function with no parameters, and messages are text the worker reads back itself. The types fall off at exactly the step up from a group. D-SERVICE1 already promises typed workers. The vote decides their shape. We recommend the function itself: its parameter is the message.
decisions.gist: What shape should a typed service worker have?
decisions.lesson: A service runs work that keeps going and restarts when it fails. You write the work as a normal function, like `send_email(e: Email)`. `tree.worker` turns it into an endpoint that only accepts emails, and the service calls the function once for each one sent.
decisions.story: Pia moves `send_email` from a task group into a service so it restarts on failure. She has to rewrite it to take no parameters and parse a string from `tree.receive`.
decisions.inWild:
// Gleam OTP: an actor is a function over a typed message.
fn handle(msg: Email, state: Nil) -> actor.Next(Email, Nil)
decisions.detail:
Provenance. Card c0mhdm27. This is the worker shape question from the D-SERVICE-TYPED1 package, asked alone. D-SERVICE1=D, reaffirmed by the owner on 2026-08-20, already promises typed builders that promote ordinary functions into workers. Hosts card #6048 (ladder audit L-10).

Probes, in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/q/b4/sv/probe, on dev. p1.jet: `service.tree(…)` is E2104 "`service.tree` is not built yet", so no program runs a service today. p2.jet: a worker taking `Email` is E0108 "This needs fn(), but the value is fn(Email)"; messages are `String` today (Core/Service/Service.jet:1378, :1748). p3.jet: the rung below, `task.group` calling `send_email(e)`, runs and prints both lines.

p4.jet: the channel rung, a task looping over `Receiver<Email>`, prints "to ann@example.com" then "done". p6.jet: an enum `if` that misses a case is E0307 "This `if` doesn't cover every case — missing: Remove".

Reads with D-SERVICE-REPLY1, which decides how a worker answers, D-SERVICE-KEEP1, which decides how it keeps data between messages, and D-SERVICE-BATCH1, which decides how it takes many at once. The cutover rewrites the 61 files that call `.worker(`; no user program runs a service today.

options.name: The worker is its function
options.detail:
The runtime calls the function once per message, in order. `tree.send` takes only an `Email`; anything else is the ordinary E0112 argument error.

Several kinds of message are one enum, matched in the function, and a missed case is E0307. A worker with no parameter takes no messages and runs once under restarts.
options.technical: Core/Service/Service.jet: `worker` and `send` become generic over the handler's parameter; the String forms and `tree.receive` go. The runtime half is card #4957, which E2104 names.

options.name: A worker struct; each method is a message
options.detail:
Each method of a `#Worker` struct is one message. `tree.worker` returns a handle whose methods send.

Code moving up from a task group is rewritten into a struct.
options.technical: A new marker, and generated message types per method.

options.name: The worker loops over a typed channel
options.detail:
A worker takes a `Receiver<T>`; `tree.worker` returns the matching sender.

The worker may wait on other sources between messages, but every worker repeats the loop.
options.technical: Workers gain one `Receiver<T>` parameter; the runtime owns the channel across restarts.

comparisons.note: A typed `Subject(msg)` and a handler function. Source: https://hexdocs.pm/gleam_otp/gleam/otp/actor.html
Each grain method is a message. Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/orleans/grains/
A goroutine loops over a typed channel. Source: https://go.dev/tour/concurrency/2

recommendation.why: A keeps the function the task group already calls, so climbing from group to service changes one line. The message type is checked, and no new declaration form is needed.
gains: One function from group to service.
Typed endpoints with no new syntax.

losses.loss: The runtime owns the receive loop.
losses.mitigation: Other sources send into the same endpoint as an enum case.

whyNot.reason: B rewrites plain functions into a new struct form.
C makes every worker write and restart its own loop.

recommendation.tradeoff: A worker can't wait on a second source between messages.

decisions.title: A worker answers by returning a value; `tree.call(pricing, quote)` waits for it and returns `Int ServiceError!`
decisions.situation: Some workers answer: a pricing worker takes a quote and gives back a price. Today a service has no typed answers at all; the caller reads text back with `tree.receive`. Under D-SERVICE-WORKER1=A a worker is an ordinary function, so it already has a result type. The vote decides how a caller gets that result. We recommend `tree.call`, which sends, waits and returns the function's result, or a service error.
decisions.gist: How should a caller get a service worker's answer?
decisions.lesson: If a worker function returns a value, the service sends that value back. Use `tree.call(worker, message)` to send and wait for the answer, the way you would call the function directly. It can fail, for example if the worker crashes, so add `??` or `?`.
decisions.story: Teo's checkout asks a pricing worker for a total. He sends the quote, then reads text back from `tree.receive`, parses it, and hopes no other reply arrived first.
decisions.inWild:
// Elixir GenServer: call waits for the reply.
GenServer.call(pricing, {:price, quote})
decisions.detail:
Provenance. Card c0mhdm27. This is the replies question from the D-SERVICE-TYPED1 package, asked alone. D-SERVICE1=D, reaffirmed by the owner on 2026-08-20, already promises typed builders that promote ordinary functions into workers. Hosts card #6048 (ladder audit L-10).

Probes, in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/q/b4/sv/probe, on dev. p1.jet: `service.tree(…)` is E2104 "`service.tree` is not built yet", so no program runs a service today. p2.jet: a worker taking `Email` is E0108 "This needs fn(), but the value is fn(Email)"; messages are `String` today (Core/Service/Service.jet:1378, :1748). p3.jet: the rung below, `task.group` calling `send_email(e)`, runs and prints both lines.

p5.jet: `price(Quote{sku: "A1", qty: 3})` as a plain function prints 750.

Reads with D-SERVICE-WORKER1, which makes the worker an ordinary function. A batched worker (D-SERVICE-BATCH1) can't reply; that error's fix removes the result or the batch.

options.name: Return the answer; `call` waits
options.detail:
`fn price(q: Quote) -> Int` gives `Endpoint<Quote, Int>`. `tree.call` returns `Int ServiceError!`. `tree.send` on a replying endpoint is an error whose fix is `call`, so no reply is dropped.

A call waits like any wait point, so `#Context(deadline: …)` bounds it. If the worker fails mid-message, the call returns `.Ambiguous`, never a silent retry.
options.technical: Adds `call` and a second type parameter to `Endpoint`. Uses D-SERVICE-DELIVERY1=D (`.Ambiguous`) and D-DEADLINE1. Sema refuses two workers that call each other, as D-SERVICE1=D refuses cycles.

options.name: A reply address in the message
options.detail:
The caller makes a channel, puts its sender in the message and waits on the receiver.

The worker function changes to send its answer instead of returning it.
options.technical: No new endpoint form; uses `channel<T>`.

options.name: No replies
options.detail:
A worker's result type must be empty.

Code that needs an answer sends one back to a worker of its own.
options.technical: Refuses a handler with a result.

A grain method returns `Task<T>`. Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/orleans/grains/

losses.mitigation: Later or repeated answers use a `Sender` in the message, as B.

whyNot.reason: B adds a reply field to every request and lets an answer be forgotten.
C makes every question a pair of workers.

recommendation.tradeoff: A call waits, so a mutual call between two workers is refused.

decisions.title: A worker keeps data between messages as a `&` first parameter; `state:` on the worker line gives its starting value
decisions.situation: A cart worker must remember the cart between messages. Under D-SERVICE-WORKER1=A a worker is an ordinary function, called once per message, so the data needs a home. A plain function already changes data it is lent with `&`. The vote decides where a worker keeps its data. We recommend a `&` first parameter, with the starting value written on the worker line as `state:`. This is Gleam's actor and Elixir's GenServer shape.
decisions.gist: Where should a service worker keep its data between messages?
decisions.lesson: A worker that remembers things takes them as its first parameter, with `&` because it changes them. You give the starting value when you add the worker. Each message then sees the data the last one left.
decisions.story: Ines's cart worker must remember items between messages. With nowhere to keep them, she stores the cart in a shared map and locks it on every message.
decisions.inWild:
// Elixir GenServer: the state is passed in and returned.
def handle_cast({:add, item}, cart), do: {:noreply, [item | cart]}

Provenance. Card c0mhdm27. This is the state between messages question from the D-SERVICE-TYPED1 package, asked alone. D-SERVICE1=D, reaffirmed by the owner on 2026-08-20, already promises typed builders that promote ordinary functions into workers. Hosts card #6048 (ladder audit L-10).

Probes, in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/q/b4/sv/probe, on dev. p1.jet: `service.tree(…)` is E2104 "`service.tree` is not built yet", so no program runs a service today. p2.jet: a worker taking `Email` is E0108 "This needs fn(), but the value is fn(Email)"; messages are `String` today (Core/Service/Service.jet:1378, :1748). p3.jet: the rung below, `task.group` calling `send_email(e)`, runs and prints both lines.

p5.jet: `cart_step(&cart, …)` as a plain function prints 1, 2 and 0 for Add, Add and Clear.

Reads with D-SERVICE-WORKER1 and D-SERVICE-REPLY1: `cart_step` returns `Int`, so `tree.call(cart, msg)` answers with the item count. Under D-RECEIVER-MARK1=A the push reads `cart.items.push(item)` with no `&`.

options.name: `&` first parameter, `state:` start
options.detail:
A handler whose first parameter is `&S` keeps an `S`; `state:` must be given and must be an `S`. Each message sees the last message's changes.

A restart begins again from `state:`, unless the tree declares a snapshot or event log (D-SERVICE-STATE1=D).
options.technical: Sema checks `state:` against the first parameter at the worker line. The runtime holds the value in the worker's own task.

options.name: Return the next value
options.detail:
The worker passes the data in by value and keeps what comes back.

A worker that also answers returns a pair, `(Cart, Int)`.
options.technical: The runtime moves the value in and out each message.

options.name: Keep it outside the worker
options.detail:
Data lives in a `shared` value or a database the worker reaches.

It survives restarts, including a broken value that a restart should have cleared.
options.technical: No change to the worker API.

gains: No lock and no copy per message.
Restarts reset to a known start.

losses.mitigation: Declare a snapshot or event log (D-SERVICE-STATE1=D).

whyNot.reason: B rebuilds the data on every message and pairs it with replies.
C locks every message and can't reset on restart.

recommendation.tradeoff: Only the worker can read its data; others ask it.

decisions.title: `batch: 50, wait: flush` on the worker line hands a `[Email]` handler up to 50 waiting messages; senders still send one `Email`
decisions.situation: Mail providers and databases are much faster in bulk. Senders send one email at a time, but the worker wants fifty at once. Under D-SERVICE-WORKER1=A a worker's parameter is its message, so a `[Email]` parameter alone would mean "one list per message". The vote decides how a worker asks for batches. We recommend two words on the worker line: `batch:` for the most per call and `wait:` for how long to gather.
decisions.gist: How should a service worker receive many waiting messages at once?
decisions.lesson: Sending fifty emails in one request is faster than fifty requests. Write the worker to take a list, and add `batch: 50` when you add it. Senders still send one email; the service gathers up to fifty, waiting at most `wait:` for more.
decisions.story: Ravi's mailer pays one network round trip per email. His provider accepts 50 per request, but the worker only ever sees one message.
decisions.inWild:
// Broadway (Elixir): batchers gather messages for one call.
batchers: [default: [batch_size: 50, batch_timeout: 200]]

decisions.title: jet test mutates changed code on every run, and guided fuzzing finds the input each surviving mutant gets wrong
decisions.situation: A passing test suite can still be weak. Mutation testing checks it: the compiler makes small wrong versions of a function, and a test should fail for each. Fuzzing feeds tests generated inputs and keeps those that reach new branches. Jet has neither; Rust, Go, Java and JavaScript have both. Mutation is usually too slow to leave on, and some mutants cannot be caught. We recommend both, fast enough to run on every jet test.
decisions.gist: Should jet test mutate changed code on every run and hunt each survivor with guided fuzzing?
decisions.lesson: Coverage says a line ran. Mutation says a test would notice if that line were wrong. Guided fuzzing keeps inputs that reach new branches. Together they can show a weak test with the exact input it misses.
decisions.story: Sam edits clamp, and his test still passes. The same `jet test` reports a surviving mutant that returns `n` instead of `low`. It shows `clamp(-1, 0, 3)` as the input that tells them apart. Sam turns it into a property test, and the next run kills the mutant in milliseconds.
decisions.detail:
Provenance. Card c0fvnyiq (#6060), split from #6035 by owner answer Q4 (2026-10-28). Audit/drafts4/BEST-IN-CLASS.md rows Fuzzing and Mutation mark both LOSES. The owner rejected v1 because two losses stood: mutation runs are slow, and equivalent mutants survive. v2 removes both, so mutation can be on by default.

Why it is fast. Stock `mutate: changed` mutates only functions whose IR changed since the last stored run. Their kill results live in the #6035 store, keyed by function and test hashes, so unchanged code is never mutated again. All mutants of a package share one build with a switch, so there is one compile, not one per mutant.

Each mutant runs only the tests that reach its function (D-TEST-AFFECTED1), last killer first, and stops at the first failure. A mutant that loops is cut off at twice the test's normal time. The work grows with the edit, not the package.

Equivalent mutants. A mutant that does exactly what the original does can never be caught, so reporting it is noise. After the compiler folds constants and puts the code in canonical form, a mutant that matches the original is dropped unrun. A mutant that matches another mutant runs once. Research on this check found about 7% of mutants equivalent and 21% duplicates in C programs.

Survivors are then checked. For an effect-free function, the solver behind `jet prove` compares mutant and original. It either proves them equal, and the mutant is dropped as equivalent, or returns an input that tells them apart. Guided fuzzing searches for that input when the solver gives up. In clamp, `n >= high` for `n > high` is proved equivalent, and `return n` gets the witness -1.

What a survivor means. A survivor with a witness is a real gap, shown with the input a test should check. A survivor in effectful code, where neither the solver nor generated inputs may run, is reported as unchecked, not as a gap. Survivors are report rows, never test failures.

How it reads with other ballots. Rows follow the PLAN-6035 naming rule: `--mutate=all`, `mutate: all`. Under D-TEST-PROFILE1 A the profile is the package.jet line shown; under its B it is a `TestProfile` field in test.jet; under its C the flag goes in a CI script. D-CLAIM1=C owns `grade`, `time`, `iterations`, `seed` and `corpus`. Under D-TEST-READS1 mutant rows never reuse a pass.

Research. Trivial Compiler Equivalence (Papadakis and others, ICSE 2015) drops mutants whose compiled code matches. Mutant schemata (Untch, Offutt and Harrold, ISSTA 1993) build all mutants at once. Google runs mutation on every code review, only on changed lines (Petrovic and Ivankovic, ICSE-SEIP 2018). PIT's incremental analysis reuses kill results for unchanged code.

Probes on the dev jet are in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/q/bd/probe/g11/mf. `jet check run.jet` is ok. `jet test` prints "clamps a big number: pass", "stays_in_range: pass" and "2 passed, 0 failed, 0 skipped". `jet test --mutate=all` is E2102 and `--grade=generated` is E2104 today. Report lines marked new are proposed output.

Adversarial pass. Author model family: Claude. Adversarial model family: Claude. Fresh agent: BallotDesign (fresh pass). It found that `n <= low` is not equivalent when low is above high, so the example uses `n >= high`. A fresh clone records a baseline without mutating, CI sets `mutate: all`, and effectful survivors are reported as unchecked.

options.name: Both, on by default
options.detail:
Mutation: `mutate` is a row with three values, stock `changed`, plus `all` and `off`. The compiler makes mutants from typed IR: a flipped comparison, a swapped operator, a changed return, a dropped statement. Mutants equal to the original after folding are dropped unrun. A survivor in an effect-free function is proved equivalent, shown with an input that tells it apart, or marked unchecked.

Fuzzing: `grade: generated` (D-CLAIM1=C) steers generation by branch coverage. It keeps new-branch inputs and shrunk failures under `corpus`, stock testdata/fuzz/<test>/. Later runs replay them as ordinary rows.
options.technical:
Adds the `mutate` row to the PLAN-6035 table: changed (stock), all, off. A mutation pass after sema writes schemata: each site branches on a mutant id, in mutation test builds only. Mutant identity is (function IR hash, site, operator). The kill matrix (mutant, test hash) to verdict lives in the #6035 S4 store. A fresh store records hashes without mutating.

Pruning: canonical IR after constant folding equal to the original or to an earlier mutant. Survivors in -[]> functions go to the D-PROVE-LENS1 solver lens under a bounded budget, then to guided generation. Rows report KILLED, EQUIVALENT, SURVIVED with witness, UNCHECKED or TIMEOUT.

options.name: Mutation on by default, no guided fuzzing
options.detail:
Mutation as in A: changed code only, cached kill results, one build, and equivalent mutants dropped by folding and by the solver. Without guided fuzzing, a survivor gets a witness only when the solver finds one.

`grade: generated` keeps D-CLAIM1's fixed budget of 1,000 inputs per contract, drawn without feedback. Only a shrunk failure is stored and replayed.
options.technical: The `mutate` row, schemata, kill matrix and pruning as in A. No coverage probes in generated runs; no corpus writes beyond the shrunk-failure store.

options.name: Fuzzing only
options.detail: Guided fuzzing as in A. Test strength is judged only by coverage (`--coverage`, D-COV1), which counts lines run, not lines checked.
options.technical: Guided generation and the testdata/fuzz corpus as in A. No mutation pass.

comparisons.note: PIT runs only the tests that cover each mutant, and its incremental analysis reuses kill results for unchanged code. Source: https://pitest.org/quickstart/incremental_analysis/
Stryker builds all mutants into one bundle, switches between them at run time, and can reuse earlier results. Source: https://stryker-mutator.io/docs/stryker-js/incremental/
cargo-mutants builds each mutant separately and can limit a run to a diff. Source: https://mutants.rs/in-diff.html
go test runs coverage-guided fuzz targets and keeps new inputs in testdata/fuzz/. Source: https://go.dev/doc/security/fuzz/

recommendation.why: A is mutation testing fast and quiet enough to leave on. It mutates only changed code, reuses kill results, and drops proved-equivalent mutants. Each real survivor comes with the input a test should check.
gains: Every `jet test` measures the strength of the tests for the code just changed.
A survivor arrives with a witness input, ready to become a test.
Proved-equivalent mutants never reach the report.

whyNot.reason: B leaves generation blind, so fewer survivors get a witness and deep branches stay unreached.
C cannot tell a test that runs a line from one that checks it.

recommendation.tradeoff: Each `jet test` after an edit also runs that edit's mutants: a few test runs per changed function.
