decisions.title: A test that reads files or env vars, through Jet or through foreign code, is reused while what it read is unchanged
decisions.situation: jet test will keep each passing test row in a result store (#6035) and skip it on rerun while nothing it depends on changed. A test that reads a file or an env var always reruns, because the store cannot see those inputs. Go records the reads its own library makes, but not reads made by C code. The vote decides if Jet records reads, including foreign code's. We recommend yes, with no new flag.
decisions.gist: May a test that reads files or env vars, even through C code, be reused when what it read is unchanged?
decisions.lesson: A result is safe to reuse only if every input is unchanged. Jet's effect rows already say which tests can touch files or env vars. Test builds can note every read, whether Jet code or a C library makes it. The reused row then carries the exact list of what it read.
decisions.story: Ana's package has 300 tests that read fixtures from testdata/. Forty of them open a SQLite fixture through core.db, which is C code underneath. Every `jet test` reruns all 300, though she changed one file. With reads recorded, only the 4 tests that read that file rerun. The rest print `pass (cached)`.
decisions.detail:
Provenance. Card c0slmlyv (#6064), split from #6035 as open question Q7 (owner asked to card it, 2026-10-28). Audit/drafts4/BEST-IN-CLASS.md row Result caching marks file and env rows LOSES to Go. The owner rejected v1 because its loss stood: rows that call foreign code never reused. v2 records those reads too.

How foreign reads are seen. An extern whose declared row has no FS or Env reads nothing, so it reuses like pure code. That covers most foreign code, such as math, compression and hashing. For one that may read, the test build routes the C library's file calls through the recorder, as sanitizers intercept calls. So SQLite opening testdata/app.db is recorded like `files.read`.

Why it is sound. On Linux, a syscall filter checks where each file syscall comes from. A file syscall that bypasses the recorder marks the row unseen, and it reruns with the reason shown. On macOS and Windows the recorder sits in the lowest system library, libSystem or ntdll. Neither platform supports raw syscalls, which is why Go moved to libSystem. C code can read `environ` without a call, so an env read by foreign code keys on the whole environment.

What still reruns, and why. Rows with Net, Clock, Random or Process rerun. Their inputs are a server, the time, a seed or a child, none of which the store can hash. That is the meaning of those effects, not a gap in recording. A `.case` row starts processes, so it reruns, as in Go.

Cost. The recorder exists only in test builds; normal and release builds are unchanged. Jet's own reads are recorded at the Core route layer. Foreign reads cost one extra call per open or stat in tests. Hashing reads each recorded file once per run, the same work as Go's test cache.

How it reads with other ballots. `fresh` is an existing jet test flag that PLAN-6035 makes a row: `--fresh`, `fresh: true`, `.fresh(true)`. Under D-TEST-PROFILE1 A, `fresh: true` sits in a package.jet profile; under B it is a `TestProfile` field in test.jet; under C it is the flag. Under D-TEST-MUTFUZZ1, mutant and generated rows never reuse, since each run is new work.

Probes on the dev jet are in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/q/bd/probe/rd2. `jet check run.jet` is ok, and `jet test` passes both tests, the second through core.db's SQLite. probe/rd2mk builds the fixture database. `jet test --fresh` prints the fresh-run note today. The `(cached)` lines and `--explain-reuse` are proposed; no store exists today (spec.md:3528).

Adversarial pass. Author model family: Claude. Adversarial model family: Claude. Fresh agent: BallotDesign (fresh pass). It attacked C code that reads `environ`, makes raw syscalls or maps a file. v2 keys on the whole environment, reruns rows Linux flags, and never stores a file changed mid-run.

options.name: Yes, always, foreign code included
options.detail:
A row whose effect row holds only FS and Env, beyond pure work, is eligible, whether the reads come from Jet or foreign code. While it runs, each read is recorded with a hash of what was returned, including a missing file. The next run reuses the stored pass when every recorded read still matches.

Rows with Net, Clock, Random or Process always rerun. `fresh` (flag, profile field, method) bypasses the store as today.
options.technical:
Adds a read log to the #6035 S4 store entry: (kind, path or name, content hash or absent). Jet reads are recorded in Core Files and Sys at the runtime route layer, under jet test only. Directory listings record a hash of the sorted names. A file that changes during the run is not stored. No new settings row.

Foreign reads: test builds link interceptors for the C library's open, openat, fopen, stat and opendir, as ASan does, at libSystem on macOS and ntdll on Windows. On Linux a seccomp filter compares each file syscall's instruction pointer to the recorder's own call sites; any other caller marks the row unseen. Env read by foreign code keys on the whole environment.

options.name: Opt in per profile
options.detail: The recorder and eligibility rules match A, foreign code included, but they switch on only under a profile, or a run, with `reuse_reads: true`. Stock is false, so a bare `jet test` reruns every file and env test.
options.technical: As A, plus one Bool row `reuse_reads` (`--reuse-reads`, `reuse_reads: true`, `.reuse_reads(true)`) in the PLAN-6035 settings table.

options.name: No, always rerun
options.detail: The #6035 store reuses a row only when its effect row holds none of FS, Env, Net, Clock, Random or Process. Fixture tests always run.
options.technical: No change to the #6035 S4 store.

comparisons.note: go test caches results and records the files and env vars read through package os; reads made by cgo code are not recorded. Source: https://pkg.go.dev/cmd/go#hdr-Test_packages
Bazel reuses a test result when its declared inputs match; undeclared files are absent in the sandbox. Source: https://bazel.build/remote/caching
cargo test has no result cache; every test reruns. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-test.html

recommendation.why: A beats Go's test cache on safety and reach. Effect rows say which rows can read, and test builds record every read, foreign code included. A read the recorder cannot see makes its row rerun. `fresh` is the way out.
gains: Fixture-heavy suites rerun in seconds, including database and C-library tests.
No new setting; `fresh` already exists.

whyNot.reason: B adds a row nearly everyone sets, and the plain path stays slow.
C leaves fixture tests slower than Go's for good.

recommendation.tradeoff: A read recorder in test builds buys exact reuse for every file and env test.

decisions.title: Markers, effects, facts, derives and errors are ordinary types that implement a Core trait
decisions.situation: Jet has special declaration words for markers (the # rules above code), effects (what a function may do), compiler facts, derives and, as proposed, library errors. Each word has its own settings syntax, and none of them can be documented or inspected like an ordinary type. You asked whether they could be ordinary types that implement a Core trait, so one interface lists everything each one must define. The vote decides whether all of them become such types, whether effects and facts stay declared rows, or whether the special words stay.
decisions.gist: Should markers, effects, facts, derives and errors be ordinary types that implement a Core trait instead of special words?
decisions.lesson: Every Jet programmer already knows structs, enums and traits. Declarations written that way get docs, reflection and editor help for free. The trait is the checklist: it lists what each one must provide, and the compiler names anything missing.
decisions.story: Priya writes a storage package. She needs a Bucket effect, a Table marker, an Equatable-style derive and a MissingKey error. Today she learns effect rows, marker parameters with dollar settings, a derive link and a separate error form, and none of them can be inspected like her other types. With trait-backed types she writes structs and impls, and the compiler tells her exactly what each trait still needs.
decisions.inWild: C# attributes are classes; Java annotations are typed records; Scala 3 ties derivation to the type class; Rust error types carry fixed message templates with field holes.
decisions.detail:
Provenance. The owner asked in chat on 2026-10-30: "Should we just make effects & maybe markers types? Like structs as backing?" He wanted a trait for effects as one clear interface with more granularity. Tower question q066hpbq on D-MARKER-DIAG1 asked the same about library errors. His follow-up the same day asked to include facts and derives and do it all correctly the first time. Card #6039.

History. v1 covered markers, effects and library errors and passed one adversarial pass. v2 adds facts, derives and Jet's own diagnostic rows. It reconciles with D-EFFTYPE-USES1 A, D-EFFTYPE-KERNEL1 A and D-MARKER-REFLECT1 A, all ratified on 2026-10-30.

Today, markers (dev cbc43e0c5e). Compiler/Prelude/Markers.jet declares 81 markers as marker Name(params, $sites: [...], ...). The $ parameters are fixed declaration settings: sites, repeatable, owns_menu, inherits, resolution, scopes and companion (Markers.jet:8-21). The repository holds 333 marker declarations in all.

Today, effects and facts. Compiler/Prelude/Effects.jet declares 46 effect rows, such as effect FS.Write $irreversible. A root with leaves is closed (Effects.jet:8). Compiler/Prelude/Facts.jet declares compiler facts as fact Name($holds:, $safe:, $gates:, ...) rows under D-FACTDECL1 A. The repository holds 61 effect declarations.

Today, derives and diagnostics. Compiler/Prelude/Derives.jet writes derive T.Equatable { ... } template bodies. D-CORE-DERIVE-HOME1 A ratified the link marker Equatable($sites: [.Type]) derives Equatable. Compiler/Prelude/Diagnostics.jet holds 996 tab-separated diagnostic rows. Library refusals call reject(code:, what:, why:, fix:) and borrow Jet codes such as E0927. The repository has 100 reject calls.

What A changes. Core gains five traits: Marker, Derive, Effect, Fact and Diagnostic. A marker is a struct whose fields are its arguments. A derive is a trait that implements Derive. An effect is a struct or enum. A compiler fact is a field-less struct. An error is a struct.

What stays. The words marker, effect, fact and derive retire as declaration words. The diagnostic word proposed by D-MARKER-DIAG1 A is never added. Applying a marker, as in #web.Route("/orders") or #[Equatable], is unchanged. Writing an effect row, as in -[FS.Read]>, is unchanged.

The trait constant. This is the one new language capability. A trait may require a named compile-time constant, optionally with a default. An impl supplies it with name :: value. Rust associated consts and Swift static protocol requirements are the proven precedent. A trait constant is a member of its type, so it is snake_case like a field. The ALL_CAPS rule covers module-level constants only.

Settings become constants. Every $ setting becomes a trait constant whose value is a literal, an enum case or a list of them. Marker takes sites, repeatable, owns_menu, inherits, resolution, scopes and companion. Fact takes holds, safe, gates, name, identity and proved_by. Diagnostic takes code, severity and the registry columns. A diagnostic's what, why and fix are ordinary methods (rule 7).

Rule 1, cost. Applying a marker or naming an effect builds its value while compiling. That value costs nothing at run time unless code reads it through reflection. The types stay ordinary, so ordinary code may also construct them.

Rule 2, marker fields. Marker fields hold compile-time values. These are constants or the code-shaped kinds marker parameters take today: Value for an expression such as #Pre's condition, Ident for a name, and Type for a type. Policy's variadic ...PolicySetting becomes a trailing list field. The use site still writes its items as separate arguments.

Rule 2, effect fields. Effect fields must be constants. Effect checking therefore never depends on a run-time value or on code.

Rule 3, effect rows. An effect row names a type, an enum case, or a constant value written as an ordinary struct literal: -[Bucket{name: "photos"}]>. A bare type covers every value, and a case covers that case. A value covers only itself. So a function declared -[Bucket{name: "photos"}]> cannot call one that needs -[Bucket]>.

Rule 3, families. Enum cases are today's closed families. With enum FS { Read Write }, -[FS]> means any case and -[FS.Read]> means one case. Irreversibility is the trait method irreversible(self) -> Bool, default false. So FS.Write can be irreversible while FS.Read is not. Manifest grants and --allow/--deny name a type or case. A value narrows only in source rows.

Rule 4, effect powers. A library effect states the most it may do with #FX above its type, as D-EFFTYPE-USES1 A ratified: #FX(Net) struct Bucket. Its impl Bucket.Effect must sit in the same file as the type. A reader then sees the role next to the #FX.

Rule 4, one reading. #FX above any type means the most that work done in that type's name may do. For an effect type, that work is every function whose row names it. D-EFFTYPE-MODEL1, still open, decides what #FX promises for an ordinary type's own methods. It must keep this one reading.

Rule 4, kernel effects. D-EFFTYPE-KERNEL1 A holds as ratified. The machine powers are Core types the compiler recognizes by identity (rule 10). They are network, files, terminal, clock, randomness, environment, processes, foreign code, graphics card and browser host. Core declares DB, Log and Secret over them with #FX, like any package.

Rule 5, arguments. Marker arguments fill fields in declaration order or by name, as marker parameters do today. Field defaults use the struct form, name: Type{default}.

Rule 6, expand. The marker body becomes the trait method expand(self, target: Target), which runs while compiling. Unlike other methods, its body is a template, as today's marker and derive bodies are. Every declaration written in it is added at the marker's site, including fn and impl $name blocks. $name pastes a value. A helper that should not be pasted is an ordinary function outside the impl.

Rule 6, wrapping. Wrapping markers use the trait method wrap(self, call). Its default passes the call through.

Rule 7, error texts. A diagnostic's name is its package path, such as web.BadPath. Its what, why and fix are methods whose body must be one string literal. Their {self.field} holes may read only the value's own fields. The compiler names any other body. The texts are therefore fixed, so jet explain web.BadPath prints each literal with its holes. #Allow(web.BadPath) names one refusal when severity is .Warning.

Rule 8, reading a marker. Reading a marker returns its value. Inside expand, target.marker(Route) is Route?, and a repeatable marker gives [Route]. D-MARKER-REFLECT1 A's typed lookup is unchanged. The twin record it described is the marker struct itself.

Rule 9, derives. A trait becomes derivable by implementing the Core trait Derive. Derive's one requirement is fn expand(target: Target), a template with no self. Example: impl Equatable.Derive { fn expand(target: Target) { impl $target.Equatable { ... } } }. Writing #[Equatable] or #Equatable on a type applies it. Derive's sites are always types.

Rule 9, the impl head. In an impl head, the name before the dot is the trait itself. It is never the boxed value type that S48 gives a trait name in parameter, field and element positions. Derive is the only trait a trait may implement.

Rule 9, the link. The impl head is the explicit link D-CORE-DERIVE-HOME1 A required. The trait stays only its function contract, and no derive or derives word remains. A derive request carries no data, so it takes no arguments. target.marker(Equatable) answers Bool. Options are separate markers that expand reads. CLI(pack:) and Receipt(name:) stay struct markers that write impls.

Rule 10, Core's own. Core's own markers, effects and facts become Core and Prelude types that the compiler recognizes by identity. Examples are Unsafe, Policy, Net, FFI, Exactness and Rights. D-CORE-ROLE1 A already ratified this mechanism for library types with language meaning. Policy keeps its built-in tightening rule that way.

Rule 11, nesting. inherits and resolution keep today's meaning. .SiteBound and .Override need nothing more. A library marker that sets resolution to .Merge or .Tighten must also implement combine(self, inner: Self) -> Self. That method states how two nested writings join. The trait's checklist names it when missing.

Rule 12, facts. A compiler fact is a field-less struct that implements Fact, with its settings as trait constants. The holds and safe constants are the enum cases of today's rows. The name constant is a string, identity is a Bool, and proved_by is an enum case such as .Ownership.

Rule 12, gates. gates is a list of the Prelude enum Gate. Gate has one case per escape word: .Approx, .Rounded, .Raw, .Wrapping, .Saturating, .Checked, .Detach and .Drop. It also has .Marker(Type) for a marker type. Rights sets gates :: [.Marker(Unsafe), .Marker(Impure), .Marker(Grant)]. Every gate is therefore a checked value, not a bare word.

Rule 12, scope. Facts stay compiler vocabulary declared in the Prelude. A package does not add new facts in this step, because a fact needs a compiler rule that publishes and checks it. The rows' $decision fields are dropped in the cutover, as invariant I7 already requires.

Rule 13, Jet's own errors. Each of the 996 Prelude diagnostic rows becomes a struct that implements Diagnostic. The census is 845 active, 135 retired and 16 reserved rows, and 71 are lints. Jet's errors and library errors then share one shape for jet explain, #Allow and the editor.

Rule 13, row fields. Each hole in a row's texts becomes a String field. Meaning and detail are constant texts. Stage, moment, status and structured fix become enum constants with defaults. A typical row then sets only code, what, why and fix. A lint sets lint_name, which the compiler requires when severity is .Lint.

Rule 13, codes and reading. Codes stay E-numbers, set by code :: "E0927". The type gets a descriptive name, and jet explain accepts either name. Every constant and text is a literal (rule 7). So the foundation registry still reads these impls as source text without running them, as it reads the rows today.

Rule 13, cost. The cost is real. About 1000 one-line rows become about 1000 small struct-and-impl declarations, several thousand lines. jet fix must name each type. Retired and reserved rows convert too, so their codes stay explainable.

Rule 14, one role. A struct or enum implements at most one of Marker, Effect, Fact and Diagnostic. A trait may implement only Derive (rule 9). A type's role is therefore never ambiguous. Marker types are not generic in this step.

Rule 15, groups. A marker group is a struct with no fields whose Marker impl sets the constant group. Example: struct Fast {} with impl Fast.Marker { group :: #[Label("fixed"), Inline(.Always), Scalar] }. D-MARKER-GROUP1's law is unchanged. A group has two or more members and no parameters. Every member's gates and refusals apply at each use.

Folds in, open ballots. D-MARKER-DIAG1: A's Diagnostic trait is its option B plus one rule, that each text method is one string literal. That keeps the texts fixed and removes the reason B lost. D-EFFTYPE-MODEL1 (open): rule 4 fixes the one reading of #FX above a type that it must keep.

Folds in, ratified and kept. D-MARKER-REFLECT1 A keeps its lookup; the record is the marker, and a derive answers Bool. D-EFFTYPE-USES1 A keeps #FX above the effect type. D-EFFTYPE-KERNEL1 A keeps its split, with kernel effects as recognized Core types. D-MARKER-GROUP1 keeps its law (rule 15). D-EXTEND-ARCH1 A already uses the impl Type.Trait shape, as in impl SQL.CheckedText.

Folds in, needing re-ruling. D-MARKER-DECL1 A chose one declaration word for everything applied with #. A keeps the one-form rule but replaces the word with struct plus impl Marker. D-CORE-DERIVE-HOME1 A's explicit link becomes the impl head, so only its spelling changes. D-FACTDECL1 A's fact word retires. D-META-HASH1: the $ settings disappear, which leaves $ only for template pastes.

Research, markers. C# attributes have been ordinary classes deriving System.Attribute since 2002, with [AttributeUsage] naming legal sites. The design is stable and widely used. Java annotations are typed records whose elements must be compile-time constants. That limit matches rule 2 and has not been a practical burden. Java lacked repeatable annotations until Java 8 and needed a wrapper type. A has a repeatable constant from the start.

Research, derives. Kotlin declares annotation class, and Scala annotations extend scala.annotation.Annotation. Rust derive macros are separate items linked to their trait only by name, so a derive and a trait can drift apart. Haskell's DeriveAnyClass and Scala 3's derives clause tie derivation to the type class itself. Rule 9 takes that shape.

Research, errors. Rust's thiserror and miette give errors fixed message templates whose {field} holes name struct fields. rustc's own diagnostics are structs with fixed message slugs. Swift macro diagnostics are structs conforming to the DiagnosticMessage protocol. That is the shape A gives Diagnostic.

Research, effects. Effekt declares effects as interfaces. OCaml 5 effects are constructors of the extensible type Effect.t. Both are ordinary type-system declarations. Koka and Unison use dedicated effect and ability words, which is option C's shape. The known failure to avoid is C# attribute constructors running arbitrary code during reflection at run time. A runs marker code only while compiling.

Migration. One cutover converts everything, and no old spelling remains. jet fix rewrites every marker, effect, fact and derive declaration and every reject(code: ...) call. The Prelude's 81 markers, 46 effects, fact rows, derive bodies and 996 diagnostic rows move to types. The compiler registries read the trait impls instead of the rows.

options.name: Types with Core traits, for all of them
options.detail: A marker is a struct whose fields are its arguments and which implements Marker. A derive is a trait that implements Derive and writes its impl. An effect is a struct or enum that implements Effect, and may carry constant data, so a function can name one bucket known while compiling. A compiler fact is a field-less struct that implements Fact. Every error, Jet's own and a library's, implements Diagnostic with fixed texts. The trait lists what each must provide.
options.technical: Adds the Core traits Marker, Derive, Effect, Fact and Diagnostic, plus the trait constant (name :: value in an impl). Retires the marker, effect, fact and derive words and every $ setting. Marker bodies become expand(self, target), a template. Effect rows accept a type, a case or a constant struct literal. Diagnostic texts are one-literal methods, and Jet's 996 rows become Diagnostic types.

options.name: Types for markers, derives and errors; effects and facts stay rows
options.detail: Markers, derives and errors become trait-backed types as in A. Effects and facts keep their declaration words, so they carry no data and cannot be read as values.
options.technical: Same Marker and Diagnostic traits, derives and trait constants as A. Effects keep the effect word with #FX above it (D-EFFTYPE-USES1 A) and carry no data; facts keep the fact word (D-FACTDECL1 A).

options.name: Keep special declaration words
options.detail: Markers, effects, facts and derives keep their declaration words with $ settings, and library errors get a new diagnostic word.
options.technical: Keeps marker, effect, fact and derive declaration words with the ratified derives link (D-CORE-DERIVE-HOME1 A), and adds diagnostic (D-MARKER-DIAG1 A).

Effects are declared as interfaces, an ordinary type form. Source: https://effekt-lang.org/tour/effects

recommendation.why: A gives every compiler-meaningful declaration one familiar form. The trait is the checklist, so a missing setting is an ordinary compile error. Markers become typed values other code can read, and a derive is tied to its trait by its impl head. Effects can carry constant data, so a function can name one bucket instead of all network access. Errors keep fixed texts, so their help pages still work.
gains: Four declaration words and the $ settings syntax retire.
Docs, visibility and reflection work as for any type.
Effects can be as narrow as one named bucket or host.

losses.loss: Declaring a marker takes three lines instead of one.
losses.mitigation: Only package authors declare markers; users still write #web.Route("/orders"), and jet fix converts every existing declaration.

losses.loss: Jet's own 996 error rows become 996 small types, several thousand lines.
losses.mitigation: jet fix converts them in one pass, and a typical one sets only its code and three texts.

whyNot.reason: B keeps two more declaration forms, so effects and facts carry no data and cannot be read as values.
C keeps five special words with their own settings syntax, and markers still need a twin record to be read.

recommendation.tradeoff: Package authors write a struct and an impl where they wrote one line; in return every declaration is an ordinary type with one checklist, and users' code does not change.

decisions.title: Show, per source line, whether a program's data came from cache, RAM or disk
decisions.situation: You asked how to see when code falls out of the cache and waits on RAM or disk. Linux already lets a normal user count this per source line, and a probe on this machine points straight at the slow line. Jet has no command for it: `jet perf` is registered but not ported. This vote decides how the memory view is asked for and where it is drawn. We recommend a `memory` lens in `jet perf run`, shown in the terminal and in the Canvas code map.
decisions.gist: How should a Jet user ask for, and see, which source lines wait on RAM or disk?
decisions.lesson: A load that misses the small fast caches waits on a slower one, then RAM, and after a page fault, the disk. The chip counts where each load was served. Sampling those counts and mapping them to source lines shows which line waits on what. A lens is what `jet perf run` observes, such as cpu or alloc. A method is how it collects evidence, sampling or counting.
decisions.story: Ana's simulation slows down when the grid gets big. She runs `jet perf run sim.jet --lens=cpu,memory`. The top row is `sim.jet:48  64% time, 51% from RAM`. Line 48 walks the grid column by column. She swaps the loops, runs it again, and the row drops to 3% from RAM.
decisions.detail:
Before and after. Today `jet perf run walk.jet` prints that `jet perf` is not ported (Compiler/JetCli/Source/Cli/Front.jet:1601). The old Rust command never read hardware counters either. Under A the same command with `--lens=cpu,memory` prints a table of source lines. Each row shows time, where its loads were served, and its page faults.

Evidence. On this machine, a normal user sampled the chip's fill-source events for `walk.jet`, built at o2 with line tables. Line 12, the strided loop, took 58% of all refills from L2. The sequential loop took 0.09%. Page-fault counts put list growth on line 21. Disk waits show as major faults: a probe that reads a dropped file counts 16 of them.

What A says. `memory` joins the lens list that D-PERFSESSION1 D ratified (`--lens=cpu,alloc,memory`). It records rows per source range, as D-PROFILE-DETAIL1 A requires, with the source level named: L2, L3, another core's cache, RAM, and disk. dTLB misses and minor faults ride along. `jet perf view` prints the same table from a saved trace.

The code map. D-CODEMAP-VIEW1 A put run-time hotness out of the Canvas code map. A amends that in one narrow way. When the user opens a saved `.jtrace`, the map gains a Memory metric that shades each line by where its data came from. Without a trace, the map is unchanged.

When counters are missing. Some kernels refuse counters to normal users, and virtual machines often hide them. Then the lens prints `unavailable` and the reason, and records no rows. It never prints zeros, retries with other settings or asks for root, as D-PROFILE-METHOD1 A requires. A chip missing from Jet's event table is not this case. Jet's table is generated from the Linux kernel's per-CPU event lists, and an unlisted chip gets the kernel's generic RAM, disk and fault events, with the missing levels named.

Limits stated in the output. Samples can land a few instructions late, and some land in the kernel's page-fault code; those count as outside Jet code. One major fault can bring in many pages through readahead, so it counts waits, not bytes. L1 hits are too frequent to sample and are not shown. Runtime code such as list growth is charged to the Jet line that called it.

Option B. Card #4727 proposed a third method, `--profile-method=memory`. Methods are exclusive under D-PROFILE-METHOD1 A, so one run gives memory rows or time rows, not both. A user who wants to know whether the slow line is the RAM line needs two runs, and the two runs differ.

Option C. The lens as in A, but the code map stays compile-time only. The terminal table and the trace carry everything; nothing changes in Canvas. It is less work, but the map is where a user sees a whole program at once.

Research. Docs/research/2026-10-30-cache-control-and-visibility.md, sections 4 and 5, has the probes and counts. Linux `perf mem`, Intel VTune and AMD uProf all show load sources per line. Cachegrind simulates caches on any host, but runs 20 to 100 times slower and shows a model, not the chip.

Review. Author: Claude (MemDesign lane). No fresh adversarial pass has run on this draft yet.

options.name: A memory lens, in the terminal and the code map
options.detail:
`jet perf run app.jet --lens=memory` records, per source line, where loads were served: L2, L3, another core's cache, RAM or disk. It combines with `cpu` in one run. `jet perf view` prints the table.

Opening the saved trace in `jet dev --canvas` adds a Memory metric to the code map. Missing counters print `unavailable` and the reason, never zeros.
options.technical: Adds `memory` to D-PERFSESSION1's lens list. Linux first: perf_event_open, per thread, user mode, inherited by spawned threads. It samples the CPU model's fill-source events and the page-fault software events. Rows follow D-PROFILE-DETAIL1: source range, lens, level, weight; totals are derived. The trace stores the CPU model and event names. The code-map metric reads only an opened .jtrace (amends D-CODEMAP-VIEW1).

options.name: A third profile method
options.detail:
`jet perf run app.jet --profile-method=memory` replaces sampling by time with sampling by memory events. The table and the code map are as in A.

Methods are exclusive, so time rows need a second run.
options.technical: Extends D-PROFILE-METHOD1's method list to sample|count|memory. Same collection and rows as A, but the method excludes the cpu lens. Comparing time with memory means joining two traces from two runs.

options.name: A memory lens, terminal and trace only
options.detail:
The lens is as in A. The code map stays compile-time only, as D-CODEMAP-VIEW1 A says today.

Users read the terminal table or export the trace to other tools.
options.technical: Same lens and rows as A. No Canvas change; D-CODEMAP-VIEW1 stands unamended.

designAway.loss: Generic cache events are not portable; LLC-load-misses is not supported on this AMD host.
attempts: Use only generic perf events: rejected, the last-level miss count is missing on AMD.
A hand-kept table per CPU family: rejected, a new chip would show nothing until someone edits it.
designAway.result: Jet's fill-source table is generated from the Linux kernel's per-CPU event lists, which chip vendors update before launch. An unlisted chip falls back to the kernel's generic events, so RAM, disk and fault rows still appear, and the output names the missing levels.

designAway.loss: A run-time metric in the code map could clutter the compile-time view.
attempts: Keep the map compile-time only (option C): rejected, the map is where a user scans a whole program.

decisions.title: Huge pages and NUMA placement: the runtime does them itself, measured and visible, and prefetch gets a fair test
decisions.situation: You asked how a program can control the L1, L2 and L3 caches. Three ratified hints cover what code can say: prefetch, a streaming store and the cache-line size. Huge pages and memory placement on multi-socket servers stay outside the program today, and the obvious switch for huge pages stalled a probe for 27 seconds. This vote decides who handles them. We recommend the runtime does it itself, without stalls, and reports what it did.
decisions.gist: Should huge pages and NUMA placement come from the runtime itself, from advice per buffer, or from a program-wide setting?
decisions.lesson: A program cannot choose which cache holds its data; the chip decides. Huge pages make address lookups cheaper, because one lookup entry covers 2 MiB instead of 4 KiB. NUMA means memory attached to one processor socket is faster for the cores on that socket. A background thread does work beside the program, so the program's own threads never wait for it.
decisions.story: Ben's trading server runs on a two-socket machine and keeps a 512 MiB order table. Under A he writes nothing new. The runtime folds the table into huge pages on a background thread, and each worker thread takes memory from its own socket. `jet perf run --lens=memory` shows both, so Ben knows it happened.
decisions.detail:
What a chip lets a program control. It offers hints, not placement. D-CACHE-CONTROL1 A, ratified, already gives code its three useful hints: prefetch, a streaming store, and the line size for padding. Measured here in C, streaming stores made a 256 MiB copy 33% faster, padding made two contended counters 3.7 times faster, and prefetch made a random gather 14% faster.

The prefetch test. D-CACHE-CONTROL1 names its prefetch speed test: a strided grid walk with and without prefetch. That test cannot pass on current chips, which already predict fixed strides. Under every option here, the test becomes an index gather, `xs[idx[i]]`, with and without prefetch. The streaming-store and padding tests stay as ratified.

Huge pages, measured. Jet's runtime heap turns huge pages off on purpose (Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/Alloc.jet:346-356). This machine has transparent huge pages set to `always`, with `defer+madvise` compaction. Filling 512 MiB after MADV_HUGEPAGE took 27.7 seconds, against 0.18 seconds without, and the kernel granted only 4 MiB (probe cprior/thp2.c, mode 1). An earlier run took 6.2 and 7.0 seconds. The stall comes from compaction on the allocating thread.

The design that removes the stall. The heap keeps refusing huge pages when memory is first touched, so no program thread ever compacts. Heap regions of 2 MiB or more are placed on 2 MiB boundaries. A region that stays live is handed to a runtime background thread, which asks the kernel to fold it into huge pages with MADV_COLLAPSE (Linux 6.1 and later). After a refusal the thread waits longer before trying again.

The fold, measured. A refused fold returned in 6 ms on the background thread. The program's own loop ran at the same speed meanwhile, 129 ms against 134 ms (probe cprior/thp2.c, mode 3).

Why the runtime and not the program. Google's TCMalloc moved huge-page handling into the allocator and reported about 7.7% more requests per second across its fleet (Hunter et al., OSDI 2021). Programs that use madvise themselves meet the compaction stall above, which is why Jet's heap opted out. The runtime knows which regions are large and long-lived; the program usually does not.

NUMA. On a machine with one memory node, like this one, the policy does nothing. With several nodes, the runtime keeps each worker thread on one node and gives it heap memory from that node, as the JVM's NUMA mode does for new objects. A buffer much larger than one node's memory is spread across nodes, so no single socket's memory link is the bottleneck. This machine cannot measure NUMA, so its paired cell runs on a two-node machine before the policy turns on.

Visible facts. `jet perf run --lens=memory` (D-PERF-MEMORY1) reports huge pages granted and refused, background fold time, the node count, and the share of local loads. The program can see the same facts at run time through the memory lens's trace. Nothing is silent.

The gate. Each part is a performance surface under AGENTS.md. The huge-page cell is a random walk over a 512 MiB table with the background fold and without. It must win where the kernel grants pages and tie where it refuses, as measured here. The NUMA cell is a multi-worker table build on two nodes.

Cache partitions. Intel CAT, AMD's equivalent and Arm MPAM exist only through the root-only resctrl filesystem, and they change other programs too. No option lets a program claim cache for itself. The memory lens shows when another program evicts this one's data, under every option.

Option B, advice per buffer. `mem.advise(&buffer, .HugePages | .Random | .Sequential | .WillNeed)` passes kernel advice for one buffer. It is safe and a no-op where unsupported. But its main use, huge-page advice, is exactly the call that stalled 27.7 seconds here. A buffer that moves when its list grows loses the advice.

Option C, one program setting. `package.jet` gains `memory: { huge_pages: true, numa: .Local }`, which changes how mem.Heap maps memory. It needs no code change. But it turns huge pages on at first touch for every allocation, which is the measured stall, and it asks the user to know their deployment's hardware.

Research. Docs/research/2026-10-30-cache-control-and-visibility.md, sections 2 and 3, has the earlier measurements. The huge-page fold probe is $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/MemDesign/probes/cprior/thp2.c.

Review. Author: Claude (MemDesign lane). No fresh adversarial pass has run on this draft yet.

decisions.title: A Core allocator trait that user code implements safely, from Core's regions and blocks
decisions.situation: You asked whether users can write their own allocator. Today they cannot write one that Jet uses: no allocator trait exists, and lists and maps always take memory from the runtime heap. Two ratified decisions already speak of "the core allocator trait" without saying what it is. This vote decides its shape. We recommend a trait users implement with no #Unsafe at all, built from safe byte regions and blocks that Core hands out.
decisions.gist: What should the Core allocator trait look like, so users can write allocators that lists, maps and text use?
decisions.lesson: An allocator hands out pieces of memory and takes them back. A trait is a set of methods a type promises to have. Under A, Core hands out a region, a run of bytes, and blocks, pieces of a region. A block is single-use: it can be split, joined or handed back exactly once, so two owners never share bytes.
decisions.story: Kai builds a game engine and wants a free-list allocator over one 64 MiB region. Under A he writes `impl FreeList.mem.Allocator` with three short methods and no #Unsafe. If he hands a block back twice, Jet refuses to compile it. His teammates write `#Context(allocator: pool) { load_level() }`, and every list the loader makes comes from Kai's region.
decisions.detail:
Before and after. Today a user can write a slot pool in safe Jet, and probe a12_user_pool.jet runs it on every tier. But nothing in Jet will ask it for memory. A list's growth calls the runtime heap directly (Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/Collections.jet:186-202). Under A, Kai's type implements `mem.Allocator`, and every list made under `#Context(allocator: pool)` grows inside his region.

Two silent holes today. `impl Counted.NoSuchTraitAnywhere { ... }` compiles and runs on every tier (probe a1d_unknown_trait.jet). `fn takes(a: mem.Allocator)` is accepted, and only the call fails (a1e_trait_call.jet). Whatever wins, an impl of an unknown trait and an unknown type name become errors.

Ratified law already assumes a trait. D-ALLOC-PROGRAM1 A says the program's `allocator:` fact "names any value whose type implements the core allocator trait". D-JAI-CONTEXT1 A makes `context.allocator` readable, and "an unannotated allocation uses context.allocator". Neither says what the trait is. The package parser accepts only `mem.Heap` and `mem.Counting.over(mem.Heap, ...)` (Jetpack/PackageModel/Source/Manifest/Blocks/Allocator.jet:11-23).

The safe building blocks. `mem.Region.reserve(bytes)` asks Core for a run of fresh bytes from the system. `region.take(size, align)` cuts a `mem.Block` from the region's unused end. A block can be split into two, two neighbors can be joined, and its bytes can be read and written as a checked `[U8]` view. Blocks are #SingleUse values, so each is split, joined, released or kept exactly once.

Why that is safe. Only Core makes blocks, and only from bytes no other block covers. Splitting gives two pieces that cannot overlap; joining checks that the two are neighbors. A block handed back is moved, so it cannot be used or handed back again. Rust's `split_at_mut` uses the same idea to give two disjoint halves of one buffer without unsafe code.

What A says. Core declares `trait Allocator` with `allocate`, `release` and `resize`, all in blocks. `allocate` returns a block or AllocError, so failure follows D-ALLOCFAIL1 A. Arena, Bump, Pool, Fixed, Heap and Counting become ordinary impls on regions and blocks, with no private powers. The only #Unsafe call is `mem.Region.adopt(address, bytes)`, which turns memory from outside Core, such as a device mapping or a C buffer, into a region.

A region's life. A region ends when the allocator that owns it ends. Jet's region rule, which views already follow (E0631), refuses a block or collection that would outlive it. That check happens while compiling, so it costs nothing at run time.

Speed. A block is two words, its address and size. Take, split and join are a few compares, and they inline. A call on a known allocator type is direct; a call through `mem.Allocator` or `context.allocator` goes through one trait slot with no box (Examples/features/traits/trait_value_slots.jet). The built-ins move onto blocks only with paired cells that show no loss against today's Arena and Heap.

Edge cases under A. An allocator that more than one task uses must be safe to share, or Jet refuses to pass it into a spawned task. Values given to C with `^` must live in mem.Heap memory, so Jet refuses to hand C a value from another allocator. A user allocator is Jet code, so every tier runs the same code, as I9 requires.

Option B, a safe hook. Users implement `AllocatorHook` with `on_allocate` and `on_release` around a built-in allocator. They can count, cap and log. But they cannot place memory, so a free-list, a slab cache or a GPU staging allocator stays impossible.

Option C, no trait. The built-in set stays closed. D-ALLOC-PROGRAM1 and D-JAI-CONTEXT1 are amended to say "one of the built-in allocators". Users who need a new allocator ask for a Core change. It is the least work, and it answers your question with no.

Research. Docs/research/2026-10-30-custom-allocators-and-soa.md, sections 1 and 2, lists the probes and code facts. Zig passes a pointer and a four-function table, and every allocator handles raw pointers. Rust's Allocator trait is unsafe to implement and has been unstable since 2016. C++ has `std::pmr::memory_resource`, also raw. Each one puts raw memory in every allocator; A keeps it in Core.

Review. Author: Claude (MemDesign lane). No fresh adversarial pass has run on this draft yet.

options.name: A safe trait over Core's regions and blocks
options.detail:
Core hands out regions of bytes and single-use blocks cut from them. `mem.Allocator` has `allocate`, `release` and `resize`, all in blocks, so any type can implement it with no #Unsafe.

Only turning outside memory into a region needs #Unsafe. Lists, maps and text take memory from whichever allocator is in effect.
options.technical: Core adds mem.Region.reserve(bytes), which is safe, and #Unsafe mem.Region.adopt(address, bytes). region.take(size, align) returns mem.Block?. A #SingleUse mem.Block {address, size} has split, join (neighbors only) and a checked [U8] view. The trait: allocate(&self, size, align) -> mem.Block AllocError!; release(&self, block: ^mem.Block); resize(&self, block: &mem.Block, new_size) -> Bool. Built-ins become impls; E0631 covers blocks. Defines D-ALLOC-PROGRAM1's trait.

options.name: A safe hook around built-in allocators
options.detail:
Users implement `AllocatorHook` to watch or refuse requests that a built-in allocator serves. No #Unsafe is ever needed.

Users cannot place memory, so they cannot write a new kind of allocator.
options.technical: trait AllocatorHook { on_allocate(&self, size) -> Bool; on_release(&self, size) }, accepted by every built-in constructor as `hook:`. Built-ins stay compiler-owned. D-ALLOC-PROGRAM1's trait is read as this hook trait.

options.name: No trait; the set stays closed
options.detail:
Jet keeps its fixed set of allocators. The two ratified decisions that mention a trait are reworded to name the built-in set.

A user who needs a new allocator asks for a Core change.

decisions.title: Lists, maps and text take their allocator from the context block, which also gives a value, and remember it at no cost
decisions.situation: You asked how allocators fit with the rest of Jet. The ratified rule says a list, map or text takes memory from the allocator set by a `#Context` block. Today that block is checked and then ignored. This vote decides whether the block stays the only way, and how a collection keeps its allocator once the block ends. We recommend the block only, usable as a value for one list, with each collection remembering its allocator at no memory cost.
decisions.gist: Should a collection get its allocator only from the #Context block, also from an explicit argument, or from its type?
decisions.lesson: An allocator hands out memory. An arena hands out pieces from one big block and frees them all at once, which is fast for per-frame or per-request data. A `#Context(allocator: a)` block sets the allocator for everything inside it, including code in functions it calls. A list that grows needs memory again later, so it must know where to get it.
decisions.story: Lena's game builds a list of visible objects each frame. She writes `visible := #Context(allocator: frame) -> cull(scene)`, and every list the culling code makes comes from the frame arena. The culling code mentions no allocator. At the end of the frame she resets the arena, and Jet has already refused any list that would outlive it.
decisions.inWild:
// Odin: context allocator by default, explicit parameter when wanted (odin-lang.org/docs/overview/#allocators)
context.allocator = arena_allocator
xs := make([dynamic]int)                    // uses context.allocator
ys := make([dynamic]int, allocator = heap)  // explicit, a second way
decisions.detail:
Before and after. Today probe a3_context_list.jet makes a 64-byte arena and pushes 10,000 integers inside `#Context(allocator: arena)`. It prints 10000 on every tier, because all 80,000 bytes came from the runtime heap. Under A the same pushes come from the arena, so the 64-byte arena grows or the push fails with AllocError.

What is ratified. D-JAI-CONTEXT1 A makes the `#Context` block the one way to change context fields for a region of code. It says an unannotated allocation uses `context.allocator`, which defaults to the program allocator. It chose this over Zig's explicit allocator parameters. Card #5030 tracks the fact that the block has no run-time effect today (Compiler/JetIR/Source/BuildTransact.jet:223-236).

The block gives a value. Today `#Context(...)` must be followed by `{` (probes a15_context_stmt.jet and a16_context_bare.jet fail with E0003). Under A the block works like `if` and `loop`. `#Context(allocator: frame) -> expr` runs one expression under that context and gives its value. A `{ ... }` block gives its last value. One list in an arena is one line, and the list is bound outside the block. It is the same block, not a second way, so D-JAI-CONTEXT1 stands unamended.

Collections remember. Each list, map, set and text keeps using the allocator in effect when it was made, even after the block ends. A collection whose allocator ends, such as an arena at `close` or `reset`, cannot be used after that point. Jet checks this while compiling, with the rule views already follow (E0631).

No header word. The list header stays at three words, 24 bytes (Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/Collections.jet:180-202). Every allocator other than the heap takes its memory from Core regions (D-ALLOC-TRAIT1), and the runtime records each region in a page map. Growth and drop already call into the runtime; there it looks up the data address, finds the region's allocator, and treats a miss as the heap. TCMalloc and mimalloc find a block's owner from its address the same way.

Cost under A. Pushes, reads and walks do not change. Only the growth and drop calls gain one page-map lookup, two loads, and for heap lists the first load already says heap. Paired cells must show default-heap lists no slower than today: push-heavy growth, many short-lived lists, and drop of large lists.

Library code under A. A function that needs a particular allocator takes one as a `mem.Allocator` parameter and wraps its work in `#Context`. Functions that only build data take no allocator at all. Their callers decide. Ballot D-ALLOC-TRAIT1 decides what `mem.Allocator` is; under every option there, the built-in allocators take memory from regions.

Option B, also an explicit argument. Constructors in the D-ALLOCFAIL1 family gain `in:`: `List<T>.new(in: a)`, `Map<K, V>.new(in: a)` and `xs.copy(in: a)`. An explicit argument wins over the context for that one collection. It is Odin's model. It is a second way to say the same thing, which D-DEADLINE-ONE1 A removed for deadlines.

Option C, the allocator in the type. `List<Int, mem.Arena>` carries its allocator type, as C++ and Rust do. Calls are direct. But a list from an arena and a list from the heap become different types, so every function that takes a list must be generic over the allocator. Rust has kept this unstable since 2016 for that reason.

Edge cases. A collection made inside a spawned task uses the task's context, which starts as its parent's (D-JAI-CONTEXT1 A). A value passed to C with `^` must come from mem.Heap, so Jet refuses one from an arena. A literal such as `[Int]{1, 2}` follows the context like any other allocation.

Research. Docs/research/2026-10-30-custom-allocators-and-soa.md, sections 1 and 2, has the probes. Odin has both a context allocator and an explicit parameter. Jai pushes allocators through its context. Zig passes them explicitly everywhere. C++ and Rust put them in the container's type. TCMalloc's page map and mimalloc's segments find an owner from an address.

Review. Author: Claude (MemDesign lane). No fresh adversarial pass has run on this draft yet.

options.name: The context block only, as a value too; collections remember
options.detail:
`#Context(allocator: a)` is the one way to choose an allocator. It takes a block or `-> expr`, and gives a value, so one list in an arena is one line.

Each collection keeps its allocator as it grows, found from its address, so headers do not grow. Jet refuses any use after the allocator closes or resets.
options.technical: Implements D-JAI-CONTEXT1's context.allocator for every allocating Core operation. `#Context(...) -> expr` and the block form are expressions. Non-heap allocators take memory from registered Core regions; growth and drop find the allocator through a runtime page map, a miss meaning the heap. Headers stay 24 bytes. The E0631 region rule extends to collections. Fixes #5030 for allocator.
options.code:
use core.mem as mem

fn read_names(path: String) -> [String] { ... }   // knows nothing of arenas

fn run() {
    frame :: mem.Arena.new()
    names := #Context(allocator: frame) -> read_names("names.txt")   // one value
    scores := #Context(allocator: frame) -> [Int]{}                  // one list
    &names.push("zed")              // still grows in frame: the list remembers
    #Context(allocator: frame) {    // the block form, for many lines
        build_index(names, &scores)
    }
    close(^frame)                   // names and scores cannot be used after this
}

options.technical: A, plus an `in: mem.Allocator` parameter on List.new, List.with_capacity, Map.new, Set.new, String.with_capacity, their try_ forms (D-ALLOCFAIL1) and copy. The stored allocator and the region rule are as in A.

decisions.title: Conversion is the generic trait `From(S)`: you write `impl Int.From(Float)`, `To(T)` comes free, braces convert exactly, and a lossy conversion names its rule
decisions.situation: You asked for a generic conversion trait, so a type could write `impl Int.From(Float)` and `impl Int.To(Float)`. Writing both by hand would give one fact two homes, so the vote picks which side you write and which comes free. Every option keeps exact braces, named rounding and overflow rules, and lets your own type convert to and from built-in types. We recommend writing `From`, as Rust does, with `To` derived.
decisions.gist: Which side of a conversion do you write, `From` on the destination or `To` on the source, and which comes free?
decisions.lesson: A conversion has two ends: the type you start from and the type you get. `From(S)` is written on the destination, `To(T)` on the source. Both describe the same arrow, so only one should be written by hand. The other should be worked out by the compiler.
decisions.story: Ana adds a `Celsius` type. In her own module she writes `impl Celsius.From(Float)` and `impl Float.From(Celsius)`. Now `Celsius{reading}` and `Float{c}` both work, and her generic `mean` accepts any `T: To(Float)`, including `Celsius`. When she writes `Int{reading}`, a reading of 3.7 stops at that line instead of silently becoming 3.
decisions.detail:
What happens today. `Int.from_float(3.7)` returns 3 and `Int.from_float(-3.7)` returns -3. `round(1e300)` returns 9223372036854775807 and `round(NaN)` returns 0. `Float.from_int(9007199254740993)` returns 9007199254740992.0 silently, while `Float{9007199254740993}` stops. Each prints the same on o0, o1 and o2.

What a user type can do today. A static `Celsius.from_float` works, and a Core trait such as `Display` can be implemented on `Celsius`. A built-in type cannot be an impl target at all. `impl Float.Describe`, `impl Float { … }` and `fn Float.from_celsius` are each E0301, so no conversion into `Float` can be written. Jet has no overloading: two methods named `from` on one type are E0105.

Generic traits. Ratified build-time generics write a generic trait as a recipe called with parentheses, so your idea is spelled `From(Float)`, not `From<Float>`. Probes show recipes and `prep T` bounds are not built yet. A trait's static method returning `Self` is also rejected today. Every option builds these.

The failure rail. Jet already has one conversion declaration: `impl FileErr -> AppErr { … }` converts a failure as it passes up a call. It is the same arrow as `AppErr.From(FileErr)`. Each option folds it into the chosen trait so Jet keeps one way to declare a conversion. The repository has 156 such lines.

What every option shares. Braces never lose a value: if the conversion would change it, the program stops at that line, and the call form returns the failure instead. A literal in braces, like `Float{0.1}` or `U8{200}`, stays the checked typed literal it is today. A deliberate loss names its rule: `rounding:` takes `.TowardZero`, `.Floor`, `.Ceiling`, `.NearestEven` or `.NearestAway`, and `overflow:` takes `.Saturate` or `.Wrap`. When the written rules make every input succeed, the call has no failure to handle.

The method name and how a call picks. The trait's one method is `from(value: S)`. `Int.from(x)` and `Int{x}` pick the impl whose source is the type of `x`. When `Int` has exactly one `From` impl, a headless value takes that source type. Otherwise a number literal takes its default, `Int` or `Decimal`. Other headless values get an error listing the sources. Jet never searches for a third type.

Other `from_` names. A suffix that names the argument's type becomes `from`, so `Centimeter.from_meter(position)` becomes `Centimeter.from(position)`. Named constructors whose suffix is not a type keep their names, such as `String.from_bytes` and `Secret.from_text`. The census finds 2,889 calls with a built-in type suffix. It finds 3,361 other `from_` calls, which `jet fix` sorts by that rule.

Who may write an impl. `impl T.From(S)` may be written only in the module that declares `T` or the module that declares `S`. That is the rule the failure rail uses today, and the rule Rust and C# use. So `impl Float.From(Celsius)` and `impl Celsius.From(Float)` are both legal next to `Celsius`. A second impl for one pair is E2405, and an impl owned by neither side is E2406. A `From` impl into the default `Err` may still name any source.

Amends. D-SHAPE-CONVERT1: `Target.from_source(x)` becomes `Target.from(x)`, still destination-owned. The #3739 amendment of D-DOTCTOR3: `Int{f}` becomes an exact conversion. D-QUANTITY-CONVERT1: `from_*_rounded(v, mode, digits: n)` becomes `from(v, rounding: mode, digits: n)`. D-ERR-CONV, D-FAIL-CONV1 and D-FAIL-CONV2: the failure rail becomes a `From` impl. S27 and S28: built-in types may be `From` impl targets under the rule above.

options.name: Write `From` on the destination; `To` comes free
options.detail:
Conversion is the Core trait `From(S)`, with one method `from(value: S) -> Self`. You write `impl Celsius.From(Float)` to make a `Celsius` from a `Float`. Then `Celsius{x}` and `Celsius.from(x)` call it.

`To(T)` is never written. It is a bound for generic code: `prep S: To(Float)` means `Float.From(S)` exists. Inside, the code writes `Float{x}`. Writing `impl X.To(Y)` is an error whose fix writes `impl Y.From(X)`.

Every call starts from the type you want, so completion after `Int.` lists the sources. Failures passing up a call use the same impls, as Rust's `?` does.
options.technical:
Core declares `prep fn From(S: Type) -> Trait { trait { fn from(value: S) -> Self Err! } }`. `prep fn To(T: Type) -> Trait` is a derived bound with no members. An impl may narrow the failure or drop it, and may add label-only optional parameters after `value`. Generic code sees only the trait's one parameter.

Core writes the number pairs from BUILTIN_NUMERIC_SOURCES (Registry/BuiltinStatics.jet:175) with the `rounding:` and `overflow:` options. Sema resolves `T{x}` and `T.from(x)` by the head and the type of `x`. Propagation looks up `Target.From(Source)` where it used the failure rail. A builds recipes, `prep` bounds and static `Self` methods, which fail today.

options.name: Write `To` on the source; `From` comes free
options.detail:
Conversion is the Core trait `To(T)`, with one method `to(self) -> T`. You write `impl Celsius.To(Float)` to turn a `Celsius` into a `Float`. Then `c.to(Float)`, `Float{c}` and `Float.from(c)` all call it.

`From(S)` is the derived bound for generic code. Conversions live on the type you start from, so completion after `c.` lists every target. This reverses the ratified rule that conversions live on the destination.
options.technical: Core declares `prep fn To(T: Type) -> Trait { trait { fn to(self) -> T Err! } }` and a derived `From(S)` bound. `T{x}` and `T.from(x)` resolve to `S.To(T)` for the type of `x`. Number pairs move onto their sources, so `Float.To(Int)` carries the rounding options. Ownership and duplicates follow the same rule as A. This amends D-SHAPE-CONVERT1, which rejects source-owned conversions.

options.name: Write either side; one pair, one impl
options.detail:
Both traits can be written by hand. `impl Celsius.From(Float)` and `impl Float.To(Celsius)` declare the same pair, so a program may hold only one of them. Each call form works whichever side was written.

You put each conversion where it reads best. A reader looking for a conversion must check both types.
options.technical: Core declares both traits with members. Sema builds one pair table from both kinds of impl and reports a pair declared twice, by either trait, as E2405. Calls resolve through the pair table. Ownership follows the same rule as A. Core picks one side per number pair.

comparisons.note: You write From; Into comes free. A local type may sit on either side, so `impl From<Celsius> for f64` is legal. Source: doc.rust-lang.org/std/convert/trait.From.html
A user conversion is declared in the source or the target type; two for one pair are ambiguous. Source: learn.microsoft.com, user-defined conversion operators.
comparisons.code:
public static explicit operator Celsius(double v) => new(v);
public static explicit operator double(Celsius c) => c.Degrees;

comparisons.note: Any module may add an initializer to Double, with no ownership rule, so two packages can clash.
comparisons.code:
extension Double { init(_ c: Celsius) { self = c.degrees } }
let d = Double(c)

comparisons.note: Conversions are source-side `toX()` functions, often extension functions anyone may add.
comparisons.code:
fun Celsius.toDouble(): Double = degrees
val d = c.toDouble()

recommendation.why: A is your generic trait with one side written. It keeps the ratified rule that conversions start from the type you want, matches Rust, and folds the failure rail in.
gains: One way to declare a conversion, including failures that pass up a call.
Your types convert to and from built-in types, in your own module.
Generic code can ask for either direction with `From` or `To`.
Braces never lose a value; a loss names its rule.

whyNot.reason: B moves every conversion onto its source, reversing a ratified rule. Number conversions and 156 failure lines would change sides.
C gives one fact two spellings, so a reader must check both types to find a conversion.

recommendation.tradeoff: `jet fix` renames at least 2,889 `from_<type>` calls to `from`, so the source type moves from the name to the argument.

In $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/SurfaceDesign/probes, run run.sh then node summ.mjs on m6313p, m6313q and m6313r. Probe m6313p/p09 shows the silent truncation. decisions.title: Read and set this program's resource limits, and measure what a run used
decisions.situation: A Jet program can cap a child's CPU time, memory and open files, but it cannot read or set its own limits. It cannot turn off crash core dumps or cap a child's stack. After a run it learns CPU seconds but never the peak memory used. This vote decides how limits and usage appear in Core. We recommend the child-limit names Jet already uses, for this program too, and one usage record.
decisions.gist: How should a program read and set its own resource limits, and learn the CPU time and peak memory a run used?
decisions.lesson: A resource limit is a ceiling the operating system enforces, such as 4 GB of memory or no core dump after a crash. Usage is what a run actually took: CPU time and the most memory it ever held. Under A both use Jet's usual units: Duration for time and Int bytes for memory.
decisions.story: Ana's build tool runs 300 compiler jobs. It turns off core dumps once at start-up with `sys.set_core_file_limit(0, 0)`. After each job it prints `receipt.usage` peak memory in megabytes, so the job that grew to 9 GB is named in the report. The same code reads the same units on Linux and macOS.
decisions.inWild:
# Python: raw numbers per platform; ru_maxrss is KiB on Linux but bytes on macOS.
# https://docs.python.org/3/library/resource.html
import resource
resource.setrlimit(resource.RLIMIT_CORE, (0, 0))
print(resource.getrusage(resource.RUSAGE_CHILDREN).ru_maxrss)
// Go: per-child usage on the finished process.
// https://pkg.go.dev/os#ProcessState.SysUsage
usage := cmd.ProcessState.SysUsage().(*syscall.Rusage)
decisions.detail:
Today. ProcessSpec already carries child limits: .cpu_time_limit(Duration), .memory_limit(Int) and .open_file_limit(Int) (Docs/spec/reference/core-library.md:1915-1932). Memory sizes are Int bytes, as for .output_limit. The spawn path installs these as kernel limits in the child (Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/ProcessExecutionLimits.jet:2). It refuses a limit a target cannot enforce.

sys.times() returns CPU seconds for this program and its finished children (Core/Sys/Sys.jet:447). Nothing reads peak memory, nothing reads or sets this program's own limits, and children get no core-file or stack limit. Probe usage_today.jet prints the five times values; no call prints memory.

Who needs it. Tools/agent/cache/safe-jet.sh runs `ulimit -c 0` before every agent probe. release-compiler.mjs and s5-boundary.mjs wrap jobs in `prlimit --core=0 --stack=1073741824`. laneB and laneS read peak memory from the run. Card #5072 criterion 1 asks for get/set of AS, CPU, NOFILE and CORE, and getrusage with max RSS, user and system time.

What A says. Each limit keeps the name its ProcessSpec builder already has. The call sys.memory_limit() reads this program's soft and hard values, and None means unlimited. The call sys.set_memory_limit(soft, hard) sets them, and children inherit them as the OS does.

The same pair exists for cpu_time, open_file, core_file and stack. ProcessSpec gains .core_file_limit and .stack_limit beside its three limits, with the same refusal rule. CPU time is a Duration and every size is Int bytes, the types the builders use today.

One ResourceUsage record carries user time, system time and peak memory. sys.usage(.Self) and sys.usage(.Children) read it for this program. ProcessReceipt.usage carries the exact figure for one child.

Units and portability. Linux reports peak memory in KiB and macOS in bytes. Python exposes the raw field, and its own documentation warns about the difference; psutil exists partly to normalise it. Jet converts once in Core, so peak_memory is bytes everywhere.

Memory is the address-space limit on Linux, the limit ProcessSpec.memory_limit already sets. A target that cannot enforce a limit refuses with an IOError, never a silent no-op, as child limits do today. Windows has no per-process rlimits, so the setters refuse there. Usage works there through GetProcessTimes and the peak working set.

Per-child usage. wait4 already returns the child's rusage on the native runtime (Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/HostProcess.jet:172). ProcessReceipt.usage copies numbers the kernel hands back. sys.usage(.Children) is the sum of all waited children, as the OS keeps it. The receipt field is the precise per-job number a pool needs.

Option B mirrors the C interface, as Python's resource module does: integer RLIMIT_* and RUSAGE_* constants, the RLIM_INFINITY sentinel, and the raw ru_* record. Every caller must handle per-platform units and sentinels, which is the mistake Python's documentation has to warn about.

Option C extends children only: the two new ProcessSpec limits and ProcessReceipt.usage, with no call for this program. It is smaller, but a program still cannot turn off its own core dumps or read its own peak memory. safe-jet.sh's `ulimit -c 0` would have no Jet form.

Research. Python resource (docs.python.org/3/library/resource.html) mirrors getrlimit, setrlimit and getrusage and documents the ru_maxrss unit split. Go returns per-child rusage from ProcessState.SysUsage (pkg.go.dev/os#ProcessState.SysUsage) and keeps setrlimit in syscall. Node exposes process.resourceUsage() for itself only, with maxRSS in KiB (nodejs.org/api/process.html#processresourceusage).

Rust std has neither; the rlimit crate wraps the raw calls. psutil normalises memory to bytes across platforms (psutil.readthedocs.io). Lesson: named limits and fixed units avoid the unit bugs, and per-child usage belongs on the finished child, as Go does.

Effects. Reading is -[Env]>, like sys.cpu_count. Setting is -[Exec]>, the effect process.on_signal and process.exit use for changes to the running program.

options.name: The ProcessSpec limit names, for this program too
options.detail: Each limit keeps its ProcessSpec builder name. sys.memory_limit reads and sys.set_memory_limit sets this program's limit, and the same pair exists for the other four; children inherit them. ProcessSpec gains core-file and stack limits beside its existing three. ResourceUsage holds user time, system time and peak memory in bytes. sys.usage reads it for this program or its finished children, and every receipt carries its own child's figure.
options.technical:
```text
// core.sys, this program; None = unlimited
sys.cpu_time_limit() -[Env]> (soft: Duration?, hard: Duration?) IOError!
sys.memory_limit() -[Env]> (soft: Int?, hard: Int?) IOError!       // bytes
sys.open_file_limit() -[Env]> (soft: Int?, hard: Int?) IOError!

sys.core_file_limit() -[Env]> (soft: Int?, hard: Int?) IOError!    // bytes
sys.stack_limit() -[Env]> (soft: Int?, hard: Int?) IOError!        // bytes
sys.set_cpu_time_limit(soft: Duration?, hard: Duration?) -[Exec]> IOError!

sys.set_memory_limit(soft: Int?, hard: Int?) -[Exec]> IOError!
// likewise set_open_file_limit, set_core_file_limit, set_stack_limit
enum UsageOf { Self, Children }

struct ResourceUsage { user: Duration, system: Duration, peak_memory: Int }   // bytes
sys.usage(of: UsageOf{.Self}) -[Env]> ResourceUsage IOError!

ProcessReceipt.usage: ResourceUsage?   // from wait4; None when the OS reports nothing
ProcessSpec.core_file_limit(value: Int) -> ProcessSpec   // bytes
ProcessSpec.stack_limit(value: Int) -> ProcessSpec       // bytes
```

Names and types follow the existing ProcessSpec builders: Duration for time, Int bytes for sizes, as in .memory_limit and .output_limit. The kernel counts CPU time in whole seconds, so a fractional Duration rounds up. Raising a hard limit without privilege is IOError PermissionDenied.

Unenforceable limits refuse with IOError, as child limits do today. Linux: prlimit64 and getrusage/wait4 syscalls (no C library, D-OS-FLOOR1). macOS: libSystem getrlimit/setrlimit/getrusage; memory refuses as for children. Windows: setters refuse; usage from GetProcessTimes and PROCESS_MEMORY_COUNTERS.PeakWorkingSetSize.
options.code:
use core.sys as sys
use core.process as process

fn run() IOError! -[Exec, Env, Time.Wait]> {
    sys.set_core_file_limit(0, 0)                   // no core dumps from here on
    print(sys.open_file_limit().soft ?? -1)         // e.g. 1024
    spec :: process.cmd(["jet", "build"]).stack_limit(1 << 30)
    receipt :: spec.run()
    usage :: receipt.usage ?? return Ok(())
    print("{usage.peak_memory /% 1_000_000} MB, {usage.user} user")
}

decisions.title: Run many commands at once, at most N at a time, and get every result back in order
decisions.situation: A tool that runs 300 tests or builds has to start many programs, a few at a time. In Jet today that means hand-written tasks, channels and bookkeeping, and the result order, timeouts and clean-up after a crash are easy to get wrong. This vote decides what Core gives for it. We recommend one call that takes the commands and a number, and returns one result per command in the order given.
decisions.gist: How should a program run many commands at most N at a time and collect every result in order?
decisions.lesson: A worker pool runs a list of jobs with at most N running at once; when one finishes, the next starts. Under A this is one Core call. You get one result per command in the order you gave them, and if your program is stopped, the running commands are stopped too.
decisions.story: Ben's checker runs 1,200 example programs with eight at a time. He writes `process.run_all(specs, jobs: 8)` and loops over the results, which come back in his list's order, so his report is the same on every run. When he presses Ctrl+C, the eight running examples stop with his checker and no orphan keeps running.
decisions.inWild:
# Python: a bounded pool; map keeps input order.
# https://docs.python.org/3/library/concurrent.futures.html
with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=8) as pool:
    results = list(pool.map(lambda argv: subprocess.run(argv), jobs))
# GNU parallel: -j bounds the jobs, --keep-order keeps input order.
parallel -j 8 --keep-order ./check {} ::: examples/*
decisions.detail:
Today. Tasks run child processes in parallel: probe pool_today.jet runs ten 0.3 s commands across three task.all lanes in about 1.2 s. But task.all takes a fixed written block, so the number of workers is fixed in the source.

A pool of N from a variable list needs dynamic task spawning with a work channel. A Sender cannot be copied (E0102 on `.clone()`), so each worker needs its own result channel. The caller must then rebuild the order by hand. Clean-up when the caller is cancelled or the program is stopped is left to each tool.

Who needs it. The #5072 tool ports: compiler-diff, goldens-census, run-feature-examples, core-module-check, release-compiler, lost-work-audit and the s5 drivers all run bounded pools of child processes. Today they use Node promise pools or `xargs -P`. Card #5072 criterion 2 asks for a bounded pool, N jobs, per-job timeout, collected exit status, deterministic order, and cancellation on parent exit.

What A says. process.run_all(specs, jobs) starts at most `jobs` children at once, starts the next spec when one finishes, and returns one Result per spec in the order given. A nonzero exit is an Ok receipt, as for spec.run(). A child that cannot start is an Err for that spec only; the other specs still run, so every failure is reported in one pass.

Each spec keeps its own timeout, limits and output modes. A per-job timeout is spec.timeout(d), and output can go to its own file through the ratified file output mode (D-CORE-PROCFILE1=A). jobs defaults to the number of CPUs; below 1 is InvalidInput.

Clean-up. Core already puts every child in its own process group. The calling task may be cancelled: a race loser, a closing task.group, or an expired deadline block. The program may be stopped by a signal or an exit. In every case run_all kills each running child's group and reaps it before it returns or the program ends.

On Linux each child is also started with the parent-death signal, so even a parent killed with SIGKILL takes its children. On Windows each child sits in a Job Object that closes with the parent.

Built on tasks. run_all is ordinary Jet in Core, with one task per slot inside a task.group. It follows the task and deadline rules already ratified and adds no runtime machinery beyond the clean-up hooks.

Option B adds only a primitive: process.wait_any(children) returns the index and receipt of the first child to finish. Callers write the scheduling loop, ordering and clean-up themselves; each tool repeats the same 15 lines.

Option C adds a general bounded parallel map to the task language, `task.map(items, limit: 8) { item -> ... }`, for any work, not just commands. It is new syntax across every tier, and command clean-up would still need A's kill rules.

Research. Python's ThreadPoolExecutor.map keeps input order and bounds workers (docs.python.org/3/library/concurrent.futures.html). GNU parallel's -j and --keep-order are the shell standard (gnu.org/software/parallel). Go's errgroup.SetLimit bounds goroutines but leaves order and process clean-up to the caller (pkg.go.dev/golang.org/x/sync/errgroup).

Rust futures' buffered(n) keeps order; buffer_unordered does not. xargs -P has no order, so outputs interleave and reports change run to run. Lesson: order must be the default, and clean-up must not depend on the caller.

options.name: One call: run_all
options.detail: Core runs the specs at most `jobs` at a time and returns one Result per spec in input order. A nonzero exit is a receipt; a start failure is an error for that spec only. If the caller is cancelled or the program stops, running children are killed and reaped.
options.technical:
```text
process.run_all(specs: [ProcessSpec], jobs: Int{sys.cpu_count()})
    -[Exec, Time.Wait]> [Result<ProcessReceipt, IOError>] IOError!   // IOError only for jobs < 1
```
Implemented in Core/Process with one task per slot in a task.group. Per-spec timeout, limits and stream modes apply unchanged. Cancellation and exit hooks kill each running child's process group (SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after the spec's grace) and reap it. Linux children get PR_SET_PDEATHSIG; Windows children join a kill-on-close Job Object. An authority-bound spec keeps its Capture rule.

options.detail: Core adds one call that waits for whichever child finishes first. The caller starts children, keeps the count under N, puts receipts back in order and kills children on cancellation.
