decisions.title: Sort words the way people read them, the same on every machine
decisions.situation: Jet sorts text by its bytes, so `Zulu` comes before `apple` and `éclair` comes after `zebra`. Tools that print sorted names for people, and code moved from JavaScript or Python that used a locale sort, need dictionary order. Asking the operating system gives a different order on each machine. This vote decides what Core gives; we recommend the Unicode standard's default order, which is also English order, fixed in Jet's own tables.
decisions.gist: Should Core sort text in Unicode dictionary order, the same on every machine, and how?
decisions.lesson: Collation is the rule for putting words in dictionary order: ignore case and accents first, then use them to break ties. Unicode publishes one default rule, and English uses it unchanged. Under A Jet ships that rule with its other Unicode tables, so a sort gives the same order everywhere.
decisions.story: Chen's documentation tool lists 400 command flags. With byte order, `Zulu` comes before `apple` and every flag starting with `_` lands in the middle. He writes `&flags.sort_by(text.collate)` and gets `_x, apple, Banana, éclair, zebra, Zulu`, the order a JavaScript `localeCompare` sort gave, on his laptop and in CI.
decisions.detail:
Today. String `<` and sort() compare UTF-8 bytes, which is code point order and exactly LC_COLLATE=C. Probe collate_today.jet prints [Banana, Zulu, _x, apple, zebra, éclair]. Node's localeCompare gives [_x, apple, Banana, éclair, zebra, Zulu]. GNU sort under LC_ALL=en_US.UTF-8 on the same machine gives [apple, Banana, éclair, _x, zebra, Zulu], because glibc ignores punctuation at the first level. So the host locale and ICU already disagree for English.

Who needs it. Eight #5072 tool ports sort human-facing lists with JavaScript localeCompare: check-agent-doc-flags (ported with an ASCII stand-in), compiler-registries, core-conformance, core-coverage-census, run-feature-examples, test-corpora, native-route-records and classify-native-route-glue. Card #5072 criterion 4 asks for C order for ASCII and a named compare for en_US.

Reconciling ratified law. D-TEXTUNICODE1=A put Unicode algorithms in core.text and said locale collation is an i18n data problem, not v1 core. A keeps that line. It adds only the locale-independent Unicode default order: the Unicode Collation Algorithm with CLDR's root table.

That order is Unicode data, like the normalization and segmentation tables Jet already pins. Per-language rules, such as Swedish putting å after z, stay outside Core. CLDR's English collation has no tailoring, so root order is en and en_US order. C order stays the default `<` and sort().

What A says. text.collate(a, b) returns an Ordering, like `<=>` and every sort_by comparator, so `&names.sort_by(text.collate)` works as written. text.collation_key(value) returns bytes whose plain byte order equals collate.

A key lets the existing sort_by compute one key per item, as Python's strxfrm and ICU sort keys do. Equal keys mean equal text. After the three Unicode levels (letters, accents, case) a final level compares code points, so the order is total and every sort is deterministic.

Data and size. The table comes from CLDR's root allkeys file for Jet's pinned Unicode 17.0.0, vendored beside tests/data/unicode/ucd. The same checksum-verifying generator as the other Unicode assets produces it. Han and unassigned code points use the standard's computed weights, so they need no rows. The table joins a program only when it calls collate or collation_key, as the Unicode names table joins only programs that call text.inspect.

Option B uses the host locale (strcoll and strxfrm under LC_COLLATE). Results differ per machine, as the probe shows, and Jet's Linux builds use no C library (D-OS-FLOOR1=A), so B would have to ship glibc's locale data anyway.

Option C ships every CLDR locale's rules now: text.collate(a, b, locale: "sv"). It answers a wider question than the card asks, adds several megabytes of tailoring data and reverses D-TEXTUNICODE1's i18n line.

Research. ICU and CLDR are the reference implementations used by JavaScript Intl.Collator, Java, Android and Apple platforms (unicode.org/reports/tr10, cldr.unicode.org). Python's locale.strxfrm follows the host locale and differs between Linux and macOS. PostgreSQL moved from glibc to ICU collations after glibc 2.28 changed sort order and silently corrupted indexes (wiki.postgresql.org/wiki/Locale_data_changes). Rust's std has no collation; icu_collator is the ICU4X port. Lesson: pin the data to a Unicode version and never read the host's.

options.name: Unicode's default order, pinned
options.detail: Core adds a compare and a sort key in the Unicode default order from Jet's pinned tables. Byte order stays the default `<` and sort(). Other languages' rules stay outside Core.
options.technical:
```text
text.collate(a: String, b: String) -> Ordering   // like <=>
text.collation_key(value: String) -> [U8]        // byte order == collate order
```
UCA (UTS #10) with the CLDR root table for Unicode 17.0.0. Variable weighting is non-ignorable, the CLDR default. Levels 1-3 are followed by an identical level on NFD code points. So collate is Equal only for canonically equivalent text. Implicit weights for Han and unassigned code points are computed. Asset generated by the Unicode table generator from vendored allkeys_CLDR.txt, verified by checksum, linked only when used.
options.code:
use core.text as text

fn run() {
    names := ["zebra", "Banana", "éclair", "apple", "Zulu", "_x"]
    &names.sort_by(text.collate)
    print(names)   // [_x, apple, Banana, éclair, zebra, Zulu]
    print(text.collate("apple", "Banana"))   // Less
    &names.sort_by((n: String) -> text.collation_key(n))   // same order, one key per item
}

options.name: The machine's locale
options.detail: Core asks the operating system to compare under the current LC_COLLATE setting, as C's strcoll and Python's locale module do.
options.technical: text.collate_host(a, b) -[Env]> Ordering and text.collation_key_host(value) -[Env]> [U8] via strcoll/strxfrm on Unix and CompareStringEx on Windows. Linux builds would need glibc locale data, against D-OS-FLOOR1=A.

options.name: Every language now
options.detail: Core ships the per-language rules from CLDR and takes a locale name. English uses the default order.
options.technical: text.collate(a, b, locale: String{"root"}) -> Ordering and text.collation_key(value, locale) with all CLDR tailorings bundled; unknown locale is an error.

decisions.title: Terminal commands: one `term.execute(...)` call writes a list of screen and mode commands at once, and Jet undoes them on every exit
decisions.situation: Full-screen programs switch the terminal into special modes, move the cursor and clear the screen. Jet has no way to do that today, so you asked for commands like `execute(term.clear_buffer, term.enable_raw_mode, term.hide_cursor)`. We recommend exactly that call, writing all commands at once. Jet also puts the terminal back on every exit, even a crash or Ctrl-C.
decisions.gist: Should terminal programs send screen and mode commands through one `term.execute(...)` call that Jet undoes on every exit?
decisions.lesson: A terminal has hidden settings. Raw mode hands every key to the program at once; the alternate screen is a blank page that hides your shell history. A program that turns these on must turn them off again, or the shell is left broken after it ends.
decisions.story: Ana writes a small file browser. One line, `term.execute(.EnterAlternateScreen, .EnableRawMode, .HideCursor)`, sets up the screen. Her program panics on a bad file name. Under A her shell comes back normal, with the cursor showing and her history intact, and the panic message is readable.
decisions.detail:
What exists today. Core reads and writes lines, sizes the window and wraps text in color codes. Raw mode exists only inside the runtime, used by secret input. There are no commands for the alternate screen, the cursor, clearing, scrolling, mouse, paste, focus, synchronized output, links, clipboard, title or images. Nothing restores the terminal when a program stops. The live-input block is meant to enter raw mode, but a probe shows the terminal settings unchanged inside it.

What other libraries teach. The Rust library crossterm sends a list of command values and writes them as one buffer. The Rust library termion and the Python library blessed undo each mode when its guard ends, which misses signals. The C libraries ncurses and notcurses install signal handlers that restore the terminal before the program dies. The Rust library ratatui added a panic hook for the same reason.

Why one list. A frame of a full-screen program is many small commands. Writing them as one buffer costs one system call and stops the screen from flickering. A list is also data: a program can build a frame with `push` and send it with `execute(...frame)`.

Why automatic undo. Every library that leaves undo to the caller has the same bug reports: a crash leaves the shell in raw mode with no echo. Jet can do better because the runtime already owns the exit path, the signal handlers and the stop report.

What this vote decides. The command list, the undo rule, events, queries and how the pieces fit with color text, key input and child terminals. Child programs on a pseudo-terminal are already decided and work today, so this vote only uses them.

options.name: One command list, written at once, undone on every exit
options.detail:
`term.execute(...)` takes any number of `term.Command` cases and writes them in one go. The cases read like your example: `.ClearBuffer`, `.EnableRawMode`, `.EnterAlternateScreen`, `.HideCursor`, `.MoveTo(col: 3, row: 4)`, `.Print(text)`. A frame can be built as a list and sent with `term.execute(...frame)`.

Every command that changes a lasting setting records its undo. Jet runs those undos when the program returns, exits, panics or stops, and when SIGINT, SIGTERM, SIGHUP or SIGQUIT ends it. On Ctrl-Z it undoes them, and on resume it redoes them. `term.restore()` undoes them early and returns the list, so `term.execute(...undone)` brings them back after running an editor.

`term.events()` delivers keys, mouse clicks, resizes, pastes and focus changes on one channel. `term.keys()` stays the keys-only view. When output is not a terminal, screen commands write nothing and `.Print` writes plain text.
options.technical:
Final enum term.Command. Modes: EnableRawMode, DisableRawMode, CaptureSignalKeys, ReleaseSignalKeys, EnterAlternateScreen, LeaveAlternateScreen, EnableMouse, DisableMouse, EnableBracketedPaste, DisableBracketedPaste, EnableFocusEvents, DisableFocusEvents, EnableLineWrap, DisableLineWrap. Cursor: HideCursor, ShowCursor, MoveTo(col, row), MoveUp(n), MoveDown(n), MoveLeft(n), MoveRight(n), MoveToColumn(col), SaveCursor, RestoreCursor, CursorShape(shape: .Block|.Bar|.Underline, blink: Bool).

Clear: ClearScreen, ClearBuffer (screen and scrollback), ClearLine, ClearToLineEnd, ClearToScreenEnd. Scroll: ScrollUp(n), ScrollDown(n), ScrollRegion(top, bottom), ResetScrollRegion. Text: Print(text: ANSI), SetForeground(TUIColor), SetBackground(TUIColor), ResetStyle. Other: SetTitle(text), Link(url, text), Copy(text), Image(png: [U8], cols, rows), Bell, BeginSynchronizedUpdate, EndSynchronizedUpdate, Bytes(bytes: [U8], undo: [U8]?).

term.execute(commands: ...Command) -[IO]> Unit IOError!. Output bytes go into one buffer; a mode change flushes the pending bytes, applies the setting, then continues, so a typical frame is one write. When the terminal answers mode 2026, a call with two or more output commands is wrapped in a synchronized update. EnableRawMode keeps Ctrl-C and Ctrl-Z as signals, like the live-input block; CaptureSignalKeys delivers them as keys. On a non-terminal, EnableRawMode returns IOError.InvalidInput "raw mode needs a terminal", as secret input does today.

Undo ledger: one process-wide list with a lock. Enabling twice keeps one entry; disabling removes it; DisableX without EnableX writes nothing. Each entry holds precomputed bytes and the saved termios, so the signal and fault handlers only call write and tcsetattr, which are async-signal-safe. Order: scope cleanup, then atexit handlers, then the ledger, then the stop report, so the report prints on a normal screen.

Signals: the handler restores, then re-raises with the default action, so the exit status still names the signal. A program that armed process.on_signal keeps its own handling; the ledger runs when that program exits. On SIGTSTP the ledger restores and the process stops; SIGCONT redoes the entries and sends a Resize event. The commands `jet run` and `jet test` save the terminal settings before starting a program and restore them if it dies from SIGKILL. Calling term.restore() -[IO]> [Command] IOError! returns the commands it undid.

Queries: term.size() -[IO]> TerminalSize IOError! (TIOCGWINSZ; the process TerminalSize record), term.cursor_position() -[IO]> (col: Int, row: Int) IOError! (DSR 6, reply removed through the shared stdin buffer), term.capabilities() gains sync, links, images and kitty_keys flags.

Events: term.events() -[IO]> Receiver<term.Event>, final enum Key(Key) | Mouse(button, kind, col, row, modifiers) | Resize(TerminalSize) | Paste(String) | Focus(gained: Bool). It shares the one decoder and stdin buffer that the incremental-keys decision defines; term.keys() is that receiver filtered to keys. Mouse, paste and focus events arrive only after the matching Enable command. Resize comes from SIGWINCH on Unix and console input events on Windows.

Color text: the checked ANSI type moves from core.tui to core.term, so screen commands and color text live in one module whatever the terminal UI home becomes. ANSI keeps style markup only; its cursor, clearing, alternate-screen and mouse helpers become Command cases. Windows: the runtime turns on virtual-terminal output and input once; raw mode uses the console mode; the same Command cases apply. The live-input block, if kept, enters EnableRawMode and leaves through the same ledger, which also fixes today's no-op.

options.name: A screen guard with one method per action
options.detail:
`term.screen(raw: true, alternate: true, cursor: false)` returns a `Screen` value. Its methods draw: `screen.clear()`, `screen.move_to(3, 4)`, `screen.print(text)`. Nothing reaches the terminal until `screen.flush()`. When the `Screen` value's scope ends, its settings are undone, like a closed file.

This is the termion and blessed style. The guard is visible in the code. Signals, faults and Ctrl-Z do not end a scope, so the guard does not run for them unless the program adds its own handlers.
options.technical: struct term.Screen implements Close; term.screen(raw: Bool, alternate: Bool, cursor: Bool, mouse: Bool, paste: Bool, focus: Bool) -[IO]> Screen IOError!. About forty methods mirror A's cases and append to an internal buffer; flush() writes it. Close undoes in reverse order. No process-wide ledger: undo runs through scope cleanup at return, error and panic only. Events: screen.events() -> Receiver<term.Event>, as in A. A second Screen while one is open returns IOError.

options.name: Codes as checked text, plus one raw-mode switch
options.detail:
Keep screen control inside the already-decided checked color text. Helpers such as `tui.alternateScreen()` and `tui.moveTo(3, 4)` return checked text that the program prints. Raw mode is one function, `term.set_raw(true)`, and the program must call `term.set_raw(false)` itself.

This adds the fewest names. Each print is its own write, and nothing undoes the modes when the program stops.
options.technical: core.tui helpers return ANSI values for every escape sequence in A's list. term.set_raw(on: Bool) -[IO]> Unit IOError! wraps the runtime mode primitive. print writes and flushes per call. No ledger, no signal or fault restore, no events receiver beyond term.keys().
options.code:
use core.term as term
use core.tui as tui

fn run() {
    term.set_raw(true) ?? return
    print(ANSI{"{tui.alternateScreen()}{tui.hideCursor()}{tui.moveTo(3, 4)}hello"})
    key :: term.keys().receive() ?? .Unknown
    print(ANSI{"{tui.mainScreen()}{tui.showCursor()}"})
    term.set_raw(false)
}   // a panic before the last two lines leaves the shell broken

blessed undoes each mode when its with-block ends. Source: https://blessed.readthedocs.io/en/latest/

The shell is never left broken, even after a crash or Ctrl-C.

decisions.title: A `:=` name that is never changed is an error; `jet fix` turns it into `::`
decisions.situation: Jet has two ways to name a value: `::` for one that never changes and `:=` for one that can. Today a `:=` that never changes compiles silently, because the old warning was lost in the move off Rust. You ordered this to be an error. The vote settles exactly what counts as a change, and `jet fix` rewrites the existing sites.
decisions.gist: Which writes keep a `:=` legal, now that a `:=` that never changes is an error?
decisions.lesson: A reader trusts `::` to mean the value stays put. A `:=` that never changes breaks that promise in reverse: it warns the reader of changes that never come. The compiler can see every change, so it can keep the two spellings honest.
decisions.story: Sam writes `names := [String]{}` and later decides not to fill the list. Under A, the build stops with one line: `names` never changes, so declare it with `::`. Sam runs `jet fix`, which swaps the sigil, and the program behaves exactly as before.
decisions.detail:
What Jet does today. `::` never changes and `:=` can (D-BIND1). The warning L0528 is still registered with a safe fix, but no part of the Jet compiler emits it. The Rust checker emitted it until 2026-10-23. Probes show a never-changed `:=` compiles silently on every tier.

What counts as a change today. Plain and compound assignment, field and index writes, `&x` arguments, `&` method calls and writes inside lambdas all need `:=`. On `::` they are E0202, E0205 or E0111. A write through a `Shared` value does not need `:=`.

How many sites change. A heuristic census finds about 6,400 never-written local `:=` lines in 40,600. Most are in the compiler (4,514), then tests (927), Core (468) and Examples (273). Nine module bindings and a few loop headers join them.

What other languages do. Zig made this exact case a compile error in 0.12 and kept it. Rust and Swift warn by default with a machine fix. Kotlin leaves it to an editor hint. Go has no immutable local.

options.name: Any write anywhere in the name's scope counts
options.detail:
Every `:=` name must be written somewhere in its scope, or the build stops with one error. This covers locals, destructured names, state-loop headers, module bindings and `#Persist` bindings.

A write is `=` or a compound assignment to the name, or a write to a field or index rooted at it. Passing `&name` counts, and so does a call to a method that takes `&self`, marked or not. A write inside any lambda, branch, loop, `??` block or compile-time block counts too, even if that code never runs.

Reading the name, moving it with `^`, passing it by value or writing through a `Shared` value is not a write.
options.technical:
The checker looks at the binding's whole scope once, after names and method receivers resolve, with no flow analysis. A new error code replaces the L0528 warning row and keeps its Safe source edit, which swaps `:=` for `::`. For a state-loop header the edit hoists `name :: value` before the loop and keeps the test. Compiler-generated bodies are skipped, as before.

`jet fix` applies the edit to every site in one run. The edit never changes behaviour on any tier.

options.name: Only writes that can run count
options.detail:
The same error and fix, but a write counts only if some path from the name can reach it. A write in `if false { … }` does not count. A lambda that writes counts only if something calls it.

The error follows the code's behaviour more closely, at the cost of depending on what the compiler can prove.
options.technical: The checker runs after constant folding and a local call graph. A write in a branch the folder proves dead, or in a lambda with no call site, is ignored. The fix is the same edit. Whether an error appears can change when an unrelated call or constant elsewhere in the function changes.

options.name: Error for plain locals only
options.detail:
The error applies only to a plain `name := value` inside a function. Module bindings, `#Persist` bindings, state-loop headers and destructured names keep the old warning.

The common case becomes strict and the rarer forms stay soft.
options.technical: The rule of A, applied to plain function locals. The other forms keep L0528 as a warning with the same fix. Two levels exist for one rule.

comparisons.note: Since 0.12 a `var` that is never changed is a compile error that suggests `const`. Source: ziglang.org 0.12.0 release notes.
The `unused_mut` lint warns by default and offers to remove `mut`. Source: doc.rust-lang.org/rustc/lints.
The compiler warns and offers a fix-it to `let`.
Only the editor suggests `val`; the compiler stays quiet. Go has no immutable local at all.
comparisons.code:
var x = 5   // IDE: can be declared as 'val'
// Go: x := 5 has no immutable form

recommendation.why: A is one rule a reader can apply by eye: if the name is written anywhere in its scope, `:=` is right. It matches Zig's error and Rust's lint, and `jet fix` does the whole cutover.
gains: `::` and `:=` always tell the truth.
One rule for every kind of binding.
Errors never move when unrelated code changes.
The fix is safe and automatic.

whyNot.reason: B makes the error depend on what the compiler can prove. Deleting a call elsewhere can break a build that did not change.
C keeps two levels for one rule. Module and loop-header bindings would still lie about changing.

recommendation.tradeoff: A write that can never run still keeps `:=` legal. The reader sees that write on the same screen.

decisions.title: Numbers take their type from where they are used; only a conflicting use needs a conversion
decisions.situation: You asked whether numbers should take their type from their uses in the common cases, with a conversion only where uses conflict. This revision recommends that. A named number such as `rate :: 0.5` acts as if `0.5` were written at each use, as Go's constants do. A variable started from a number, such as `total := 0.0`, takes the type of its first use. Only a conflicting use needs a conversion. A computed value still never shrinks on its own.
decisions.gist: Should a number take its type from where it is used, with a conversion only where uses conflict?
decisions.lesson: A number you type, like 200, means the same thing as a byte, a whole number or a decimal. Picking its type where it is used converts nothing and loses nothing. A value the program computed is different: it may not fit a smaller type, so making it smaller stays a conversion you write.
decisions.story: Ana writes `rate :: 0.5` and `total := 0.0`, adds a list of `Float` prices into `total`, and scales it by `rate`. Today both names are errors until she writes `Float{0.5}` and `Float{0.0}`. Under A the program runs as she wrote it. Later she passes `count := 0` to a function that takes a `U8`, then stores a computed length in `count`. That `Int` conflicts with the `U8` that `count` took, so the error names both lines and offers `U8{line.len()}`.
decisions.detail:
What changes under A. Probes p01 to p14 ran on o0, o1 and o2 with the dev compiler; every tier printed the same thing. `d :: 2.5; half(d)` is E0108 today (p01) and runs under A. `total := 0.0; total += x` with a `Float` x is E0109 today (p04) and runs under A.

`big :: 300; take8(big)` stops at run time today (p03) and becomes a compile error under A. An `Int` the program computed passes into a `U8` parameter today and stops at run time when it does not fit (p07). Under A that is E0108 with the fix `U8{n}`.

The rule for a named number. A `::` name bound to a number literal, or to arithmetic on such names, means that literal at each use. Each use takes the type expected there, exactly as if the literal were written there. With nothing expected, as in `print(rate)`, it takes today's default, `Int` or `Decimal`. A use where the number does not fit, such as 300 as a `U8` or 2.5 as an `Int`, is a compile error. Module constants follow the same rule.

The rule for a variable. A `:=` variable started from a number literal takes one type: the type its first use needs, in source order. A use needs a type when it meets a typed parameter, a typed value, a field or a return. A use with nothing expected, such as `print(total)`, gives it the default.

A later use that needs a different type is a conflict. Its error names the line that set the type, and the fix is a conversion or a head on the first line.

What stays. Values the program computes keep their type, and widening stays implicit (D-INTLIT-WIDTH1=F, D-NUMWIDEN-CROSS1=E). Shrinking a computed value is always written, as `U8{n}` or `U8.from(n, overflow: .Saturate)` (D-CONVERT-TRAIT1). A head such as `U8{200}` stays legal and fixes the type, so every name written with a head keeps its meaning. Empty lists, maps and None still start with their type (D-INFER-LEVEL1=A): they hold no value a use could fit. Checking stays one pass in source order (D-INFER-LINEAR1=A).

Clutter census, Examples and Core without Vendor (1,676 files; probes/infer/census.mjs). Named literals written with a head: 109 `::` names and 231 `:=` variables; 161 of them are `Float{…}`, such as `total := Float{0.0}`. Under A each head becomes optional; under B only the 109 `::` heads do; under C none do.

Bare named literals: 373 `::` names and 1,289 `:=` variables. Under C each one used as a narrower or other kind of number needs a head added, and under B each such variable does. A adds none. Computed values passed through today's implicit narrowing need `U8{n}` under every option. The census cannot see those without the type checker, so the cutover build lists them.

Other languages. Go, Zig and Odin keep a named constant flexible and give a variable its default; Zig even refuses `var total = 0.0` without a type. Swift and Kotlin fix the type where the name is made. Rust lets the uses of a variable decide its type across the whole function. A takes Go's rule for named numbers and a simpler form of Rust's for variables: the first use decides, read top to bottom.

Edge cases. Generic calls with nothing else to go on take the default: `same(limit)` gives `T = Int`. A variable used first inside a loop or a branch takes the type of that use, read in source order. A lambda that captures the variable counts as a use where the lambda is written. Arithmetic on named numbers is exact at compile time, so `KB :: 1024; MB :: KB * KB` is one flexible number. A module-level `:=` variable keeps its start type, since its uses span functions.

Review. Author: Claude (MemDesign-3 lane), revising the SurfaceDesign draft after owner question qcjfku67. No fresh adversarial pass has run on this revision.

options.name: Numbers take their type from their uses
options.detail:
A named number means its literal at each use, so `rate :: 0.5` works as a `Float`, a `Decimal` or an `F32`. A variable started from a number takes the type of its first use, so `total := 0.0` followed by `total += price` is a `Float`. A conflicting use, or a number that does not fit, needs a written conversion.

Behavior changes: `d :: 2.5; half(d)` and the `Float` total now compile. `big :: 300; take8(big)` and a computed `Int` passed to a `U8` move from a run-time stop to a compile error. A counter first used as a `U8` does `U8` arithmetic, so it stops at 255 instead of at the call.
options.technical:
Sema gives a `::` binding of a literal, or of exact arithmetic on such bindings, a literal type. Each use resolves it against the expected type with the existing literal-fit check, and hover shows `number 0.5`. A `:=` binding of a literal gets an open number type. The first use in source order that needs a type closes it, recording that span for later errors.

Uses with no expected type close it to `Int` or `Decimal`. The implicit narrowing at call arguments and returns is removed, so those become E0108 as fields and list items already are. Checking stays one pass.

options.name: Named numbers only, as Go does
options.detail:
A named number means its literal at each use, as in A. A variable takes the default type where it is made, so `total := 0.0` is a `Decimal` and adding a `Float` to it needs `total := Float{0.0}`.

This is Go's, Zig's and Odin's rule.
options.technical: A's literal type for `::` bindings only. A `:=` binding takes `Int` or `Decimal` at once. The implicit narrowing at calls and returns is removed as in A.

options.name: Fixed where it is made
options.detail:
Every name keeps the type it got where it was made: `Int` or `Decimal` for a bare number. Using it as anything else needs a head on that line, which `jet fix` writes.

This was the first draft's recommendation, and Swift and Kotlin work this way.
options.technical: No literal types on bindings. E0108 names the binding's line and carries a safe edit that writes the head. The implicit narrowing at calls and returns is removed as in A.

comparisons.note: An untyped `const` fits any numeric type; a variable made with `:=` takes `int` or `float64`. Source: go.dev/ref/spec#Constants.
comparisons.code:
const rate = 0.5
half32(rate)          // ok
x := 200
takeByte(x)           // error: x is int

comparisons.note: A `::` constant is untyped and fits any width; `x := 0.0` is `f64`. Source: odin-lang.org/docs/overview/#constants.
A `const` number is `comptime_float` or `comptime_int` and fits any type; a `var` needs a written type. Source: ziglang.org/documentation/master/#comptime.
The name takes the literal's default type at once, as in C. Source: docs.swift.org, The Basics, Type Inference.
comparisons.code:
let rate = 0.5        // Double
half32(rate)          // error: Double is not Float

comparisons.note: A variable's type comes from its uses anywhere in the function; conflicting uses are E0308. Source: doc.rust-lang.org/reference/expressions/literal-expr.html.

recommendation.why: A is your direction: numbers take their type from their uses, and only a real conflict needs a conversion. A named number is just its literal; a variable takes its first use's type. Computed values never shrink silently.
gains: The common cases need no head: `rate :: 0.5`, `total := 0.0`.
Up to 340 written heads in Examples and Core become optional.
Only a conflict or a misfit number needs a conversion.

whyNot.reason: B keeps the most common head, `total := Float{0.0}`, and adds one wherever a variable is used as a smaller number.
C adds a head wherever a named number is used as another kind of number, which is the clutter you asked to avoid.

recommendation.tradeoff: A variable started from a bare number takes its type from its first use; a head on its first line still fixes it.

decisions.title: State machines v4: one readable state list for structs and enums, with moves named by their types
decisions.situation: You said v3 was confusing, and that the v2 state list was easier to reason about but needed tweaks. This version keeps the v2 list of states and moves. The same `state { }` block now works in structs and enums, and each method's types name the states it moves between. The `#State` and `#Transition` markers retire. It replaces v3 and folds in D-STATE-PARAM1.
decisions.gist: Should state machines keep v2's readable state list, as one block for structs and enums, with moves named by their types?
decisions.lesson: A state machine is a value that is always in exactly one state, plus rules for which state may come next. Writing the rules as one short list makes the machine easy to read. Writing each move's states in its types lets the compiler check every call.
decisions.story: Mia reads `Draft -> Confirmed, Cancelled` at the top of Order and knows the whole machine. She writes `confirm :: fn(self: ^Order.Draft) -> Order.Confirmed`. When she ships a draft, the error lists the moves a draft allows, and her editor offers them as she types.
decisions.detail:
What you asked. The v3 enum design was hard to reason about. The v2 list was clear but felt disconnected from structs and enums, and its marker was a second syntax. You asked for tweaks that keep the list and make it cohesive and easy to discover.

What changes from v2. One `state { }` block, valid in a struct or an enum, holds every state and arrow. A method's parameter and result types name its states, as in `Order.Draft` to `Order.Confirmed`. That replaces the `#State(-> X)` marker, so states are spelled one way everywhere.

What stays from v2. The `state` word, already ratified for typestate in D-STATE1. The arrow lines, the `Open :: Draft | Confirmed` group line, wrong-state error E0150, and erasure: a struct's state costs nothing when the program runs.

How it serves philosophy.md. Beginner experience (priority 2): one list reads like a diagram, and errors list the legal moves. One mechanism (priority 4): structs and enums share one block and one spelling. Runtime performance (priority 3): struct states are erased.

Discovery in normal use. Hover on a type shows its state list. Typing `o.` lists the moves allowed from o's state first. `jet inspect structure --machines` prints every list with the method on each arrow. Errors name the move, the state needed, the state found and the moves allowed.

options.name: One state list for structs and enums; each method's types name its move
options.detail:
A type lists its states and moves once, in a `state { }` block: `Draft -> Confirmed, Cancelled`. The same block works in a struct and in an enum. In a struct, the states are names the compiler tracks and then erases. In an enum, the states are its cases, with their data.

A move is an ordinary method whose types name its states: `confirm :: fn(self: ^Order.Draft) -> Order.Confirmed`. The build checks that every such method matches an arrow in the list. A constructor's result type names the start state.

Parameters use the same spelling: `Order.Shipped` for one state, `Order.Draft | Order.Confirmed` for a set, and a group such as `Order.Open` from the list. A plain `Order` means any state.

For a value whose state is known only at run time, an enum table narrows it: inside the `.Locked` arm, `door` is a `Door.Locked`. The `#State` and `#Transition` markers retire.
options.technical:
Parsing: `state { }` becomes legal in an enum body, where its names must be cases. A type path `T.State` or `T.Group` is a state type, and `|` joins them. No new token or keyword.

Sema keeps one arrow set per type. A method whose self or result is a state type is a move. Its start and end states must be an arrow, or the build fails naming the missing arrow. Calls are checked as D-STATE1 does today (E0150), and enum arms narrow the tested value.

Struct states erase in codegen, as today. `jet fix` rewrites the 68 files that use the markers.

options.name: The enum is the machine; `#Pre` says where a move starts (v3)
options.detail:
The previous version of this ballot. States are enum cases, moves are methods, and `#Pre(self == .Shut)` names where each move may start. The compiler reads the graph from the method bodies.

There is no list of moves to read. A guarded machine needs a `priv` field and a computed read, and you found it hard to reason about.
options.technical: No parser change. Sema tracks which enum cases a value can be in and proves `#Pre` state conditions at build time. The `state` section and both markers retire.

options.name: The v2 declaration as reviewed, with `#State` markers
options.detail:
The state list as in A, but methods and parameters name states with a `#State(…)` marker, and enums put arrows on their case lines.

States are spelled two ways, as markers on signatures and as types elsewhere, and an enum machine reads differently from a struct machine.
options.technical: Parsing: an enum case line or a `state { }` line may end in `-> To, To`. `#State(-> B)` takes its start set from the lines that list B.

comparisons.note: Typestate is one type per state, and a set needs a hand-written trait; enum moves are unchecked. Source: doc.rust-lang.org/book ch17-03.
An enum with mutating methods; a wrong state is found when it runs, by a guard. Source: docs.swift.org, Enumerations.
States and moves are declared once as a readable table and drawn by tools; illegal events are ignored when they run. Source: stately.ai/docs.
A sealed hierarchy holds the states, so a move's parameter type says where it starts; there is no list of moves. Source: kotlinlang.org, sealed classes.

recommendation.why: A keeps the readable v2 list and makes it one block for structs and enums. States are spelled as types everywhere, and errors and completion show the legal moves. That serves beginner experience and one mechanism.
gains: The whole machine reads as one short list.
Structs and enums share one block and one spelling.
Errors and completion show the legal moves.

whyNot.reason: B has no list of moves to read and adds concepts, which you found hard to reason about.
C spells states two ways and declares enum machines differently from struct machines.

recommendation.tradeoff: Each move method writes its start and end states in its types, which also documents it.

decisions.title: Keep crash locations, live inspection and the memory checker without making every program carry them
decisions.situation: When a Jet program crashes, it prints the function, file and line, and `jet inspect live` can show a running program's tasks. Contributors can also switch on a memory checker that catches bad frees. Today every program carries the code for all three, even hello world: 102 KB of its 437 KB, while C's hello is 17 KB and Zig's is 11 KB. This vote decides how Jet keeps all three without every program paying for them.
decisions.gist: How should every Jet program keep crash locations, live inspection and the memory checker without carrying 102 KB it rarely uses?
decisions.lesson: A crash report names the Jet function, file and line. Today the program finds them by reading its own debug data, with a 50 KB reader. Live inspection writes snapshots that `jet inspect live` shows, with a 37 KB writer. The memory checker guards every heap block when an environment variable asks, with 15 KB of code. The other startup costs go whichever option wins.
decisions.story: Priya ships a small Jet tool to routers with 8 MB of storage. Today even her hello world is 437 KB. Under A, her tool still prints `--> sync.jet:41 in push` when it crashes. `jet inspect live` still shows its tasks. But the 102 KB of helpers are gone from every copy she ships.
decisions.detail:
Before and after. hello world is 437,416 bytes at every optimization level. Docs/audits/2026-10-30-hello-size.md traces each runtime function to the root that keeps it. The crash handler keeps a debug-data reader alive: 50,111 bytes. The live-inspection start keeps a snapshot writer alive: 37,253 bytes, after the unrelated scheduler cost is removed. The memory checker keeps 14,657 bytes alive in every program that allocates, hello included.

The saving under A is about 95 KB, an estimate: the measured 102 KB less a small crash handler, a small raw writer and the checker's start test.

What A does for crashes. The compiler already knows each function's address range, name, file and lines. It writes them as one compact table beside the debug data. A small handler, still installed in every program, looks up the faulting address and prints the same report. The E3012 text, the Fault text, the backtrace option and the exit codes are unchanged.

The table follows the debug data. It sits in a section that `strip` and `debug_info: false` remove, exactly as they remove debug data today. A stripped program prints addresses, as it does now. Its size grows with the program's own functions, so hello pays a few dozen bytes.

What A does for live inspection. JET_OBSERVE=1 still works on every ordinary build, as D-EFF-OBSERVE1 requires. Its file location, owner and permission checks, and its freshness rules, are unchanged. The program records raw, fixed-size facts, and only for features it uses: tasks, channels or events. `jet inspect live` and Canvas turn them into the same view and the same `--json` output.

Process facts, such as CPU time and start time, are read by `jet inspect` from the program's /proc entry. The same user can read that entry without special rights. The snapshot file is a private link between the runtime and `jet inspect` (LiveTransport.jet), not a published format, so changing its contents breaks no user.

What A does for the memory checker. JET_CHECKED_ALLOC=1 is an internal debugging aid for contributors. Under A, jet reads it when it builds a program, as well as when the program starts. A program built without the variable carries only the start test. If the variable is set when such a program starts, it stops before any user code. The message says to build it again with JET_CHECKED_ALLOC=1 set. It never runs unchecked while the variable asks for checking.

Option B keeps the reader, the writer and the memory checker inside every program. Nothing changes for users, but every program pays 102 KB. Hello cannot then get below C or Zig, which card #6328 requires.

decisions.title: Undefined behavior only inside a written #Unchecked block; build settings can no longer remove checks
decisions.situation: You asked that no Jet program have undefined behavior, and then why allowing any would be desirable. Only for speed in one case: a loop the compiler cannot prove stays in range. We measured it. A loop over a list's elements pays nothing for its check, an indexed loop pays 7 to 16 percent, and a raw-pointer read pays about 50 times. We recommend that undefined behavior exist only inside a written `#Unchecked` block within `#Unsafe("reason")`. Option C keeps every check everywhere.
decisions.gist: Where may a Jet program do something the language does not define?
decisions.lesson: Undefined behavior means the language gives a program no meaning at all. A C program that reads past an array may print junk, crash, or appear to work, and the optimizer may assume it never happens. A defined stop is different: Jet halts with a report that names the file and line. Odin defines its arithmetic, but turning off its bounds checks still leaves out-of-range reads undefined.
decisions.story: Priya ships a release build of her game with `bounds: off` to save about ten percent. A level file with one bad index makes the game read a heap address as a tile number. It does not crash; it draws garbage on one player's machine. Under A, she cannot turn checks off for the whole game. She writes `#Unchecked(bounds)` around the one hot loop whose limit she proved, and the bad level stops with a report instead.
decisions.detail:
Your question. Skipping a check is never desirable for its own sake. It buys speed in one case: an index or raw pointer whose range the compiler cannot prove, in a loop that runs millions of times. Rust's `get_unchecked` and Zig's ReleaseFast exist for that case alone. The numbers below show what the check costs in Jet today, so you can weigh A against C.

Measured cost of keeping the check, at o2. Each kernel does 400 million list reads, built once with the stock checks and once with `--bounds=off`, which stands in for `#Unchecked(bounds)`. Runs alternated, 11 each, on a loaded machine; ratios are the fastest checked time over the fastest unchecked time. Every build printed the same answer on o0, o1 and o2.

`loop x in xs -> s += x`, walking the elements: 326 ms against 324 ms, ratio 1.01. It has no index, so it has no check, and it beats every indexed loop below. Eight constant indices into an eight-item list: 1.01 to 1.02.

`loop i in 0..<xs.len() -> s += xs[i]`: 547 against 501 ms, 1.07 to 1.09. `loop i in 0..<n` with `n` a parameter: 1.09. The same loop after one `if n > xs.len()` guard: 1.06 to 1.10. `xs[idx[i]]` with indices read from data: 588 against 508 ms, 1.09 to 1.16.

What the compiler removes today. It removes the checks on constant indices into a short list. It does not yet remove the check in `loop i in 0..<xs.len()`, although every index there is provably in range, and it does not use an earlier guard. Both are optimizer work that needs no new syntax. A data-driven index such as `xs[idx[i]]` can never be proved, so its 9 to 16 percent stays under C.

Raw pointers. Eight raw reads per pass, 400 million in all, take 18.5 s; the same reads through a list index take 0.36 s, about 50 times less. Each raw read calls the runtime check `jet_rt_sentry_check` (Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/Sentry.jet:247-319). It takes a lock and scans every live allocation, so it also grows with the program's heap. No setting skips it today, so the unchecked raw time could not be measured.

Probe ub/bounds_off2.jet indexes `[10, 20, 30]` at positions 3, 4, 7, -1 and 100000000 in a release build with `--bounds=off`. It prints 0, 0, two heap addresses, and then crashes with SIGSEGV. `--bounds=report` reports each one and then does the same reads. Probe bounds_off3.jet writes 99 at position 5 into memory the list does not own, and exits 0. Under A and C, `--bounds=off` is E2102, and these programs stop at the first bad index with E3010.

Where the hole is in the code. The comment at Compiler/JetIR/Source/BuildRoutes.jet:59-61 says that under `report` the access goes on. Both `report` and `off` are listed as check removals (Compiler/JetFoundation/Source/Registry/BuildOptions.jet:46). The build prints a note, and a policy may forbid them (D-GATE-LAW1).

Raw-pointer law. D-MEM-EXPERT1 A says raw-pointer checks stay silent in release builds, and D-RAWPTR2 A says dev and hardened builds check range, liveness and alignment. The build does more than the law today: probes raw_null, raw_past_end and raw_misaligned stop with R0801 in `--profile=release` too. Under A and C, that stays the rule in every profile.

What A promises. A package whose source has no `#Unchecked` has no undefined behavior, except inside foreign code it calls. `#Unchecked(bounds)` skips index and slice checks in its block. `#Unchecked(pointers)` skips raw-pointer range, liveness and alignment checks in its block. Each must sit inside `#Unsafe("reason")`, and `jet audit` lists each one with its reason.

What A removes. The `bounds` build setting and the `--bounds` flag are removed. `jet build --bounds=off` and `--bounds=report` are E2102, with a fix that names `#Unchecked(bounds)`. A `bounds:` field in a package's `build:` block is refused with the same fix. Every example and test that writes it moves to `#Unchecked` or drops it, in one cutover.

Tiers. At o0, Jet keeps every check, even inside `#Unchecked`, so a wrong limit stops while developing. At o1 and o2 the check is skipped. A correct program prints the same output on every tier. The compile-time evaluator always checks, so a bad index in `comptime` code is a build error.

Option B keeps today's law. The promise then reads: no undefined behavior unless the package writes a check-removal setting or `#Unchecked`. This is Odin's model. The weak spot is that one line in a build file changes the meaning of every index in the package.

Option C keeps every check, always. It removes the `bounds` setting as A does, and removes `#Unchecked` too. No Jet code could skip a check, so only foreign code stays outside the promise. Data-driven indexing keeps its 9 to 16 percent, and raw-pointer reads keep their 50-fold cost until the raw check is rebuilt. Rust's safe subset is close to C, but Rust keeps `get_unchecked` inside `unsafe` for the same expert need.

Edge cases. A dependency's `#Unchecked` is held like any `#Unsafe` of a dependency until the root package grants it (D-JAI-EXPERT1). Generic code instantiated from an `#Unchecked` block keeps its checks unless its own body is unchecked. `#Unchecked` outside `#Unsafe` is E0927 with a fix to wrap it. Foreign calls stay outside the promise; D-FFI-VOUCH1 already puts each unchecked foreign row in an `#Unsafe` block.

Amends. D-JAI-BUILDOPT1 loses the `bounds` field. D-JAI-EXPERT1's written gate becomes `#Unchecked` only, no longer a build setting. D-MEM-EXPERT1 and D-RAWPTR2 keep raw-pointer checks in release builds. `#Unchecked(bounds)` is ratified by D-JAI-EXPERT1 and not built yet (probe unchecked_bounds.jet gives E0927).

Research. Docs/research/2026-10-30-defined-behavior.md has the full inventory and the comparison with C, Zig, Rust and Odin. The kernels are in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/MemDesign-3/probes/ub (k_*.jet, time.mjs).

decisions.title: core.math returns the same correctly rounded bits on every platform, tier and at compile time
decisions.situation: You asked that Jet have no behavior that changes from machine to machine. Jet's integer and float arithmetic already give one answer everywhere. The exception is `core.math`: `sin`, `cos`, `exp`, `log`, `pow` and friends call the C library the binary links. Two common C libraries disagree in the last bit for thousands of inputs. We recommend that Jet ship its own correctly rounded math, so every platform gives one answer.
decisions.gist: Should `math.sin(x)` print the same digits on every machine?
decisions.lesson: A float function cannot always return the exact answer, so it returns a nearby float. "Correctly rounded" means it returns the float nearest the true answer. Then there is only one right result. Most C libraries promise less: an error of up to one unit in the last place. So two libraries can both be right and still differ.
decisions.story: Omar's physics test passes on his Linux laptop and fails on the Mac build machine. The two machines print a different last digit for one `math.sin` call, and the simulation drifts after a thousand steps. Under A, both machines print the same digits, so the test result depends only on his code.
decisions.detail:
The probe. probes/libm/d.c ran 200,000 inputs through glibc and musl on one Linux machine. They differ by one unit in the last place on sin 6,328 times, cos 6,096, tan 7,069 and atan2 5,915. They differ on exp 124 times, pow 124 and log 12. cbrt differs 95,062 times, by up to 3 units.

What Jet does today. Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/CompilerNeededMath.jet:1-30 imports `sin` and the rest from C, and its comment says the runtime link supplies libm. Jet's Linux binaries are static and match musl on all six `sin` values checked, on o0, o1 and o2 (probe ub/sin_bits.jet). A macOS or Windows build would link that system's library and could print different digits.

Why it conflicts with ratified law. D-DET1 says a function with an explicit `-[]>` bound is reproducible (Docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:3303). D-CPU-DISPATCH1 A asks copies of one function to give identical bits. Platform math breaks both, and C would make the break official.

What A means. Every elementary function in `core.math` (`sin`, `cos`, `tan`, `asin`, `acos`, `atan`, `atan2`, `exp`, `exp2`, `expm1`, `log`, `log2`, `log10`, `log1p`, `pow`, `cbrt`, `hypot`, `sinh`, `cosh`, `tanh`) returns the correctly rounded `Float` result. The code is written in Jet, ported from the CORE-MATH project's published algorithms (https://core-math.gitlabpages.inria.fr/). The compile-time evaluator runs the same code.

What B means. The same list is written in Jet, ported from musl, which Jet matches on Linux today. Every platform gives musl's bits. Results stay within about one unit of the true answer, as today, but are not always the nearest float.

What C means. Nothing changes in the code. The spec says `core.math` results may differ in the last bit between platforms. D-DET1 and D-CPU-DISPATCH1 get an exception for `core.math`.

Beginner and expert paths. A beginner writes `math.sin(x)` under every option and sees no new syntax. An expert who wants a faster, less exact function writes it in their own package. Under A and B no option or flag switches the math library.

Edge cases. `sqrt` is already correctly rounded by IEEE 754 and by the CPU instruction, so it is unchanged. NaN inputs give a NaN under every option; Jet prints `NaN`. Infinities and signed zeros follow IEEE 754's recommended results. `Float32` versions follow the same rule once they exist.

Amends. A and B amend no decision; they make D-DET1 and D-CPU-DISPATCH1 true for math. C amends D-DET1 and D-CPU-DISPATCH1 with a `core.math` exception.

Prior art. LLVM libc aims for correctly rounded results and imports CORE-MATH code (https://libc.llvm.org/headers/math/index.html). glibc has taken CORE-MATH's single-precision functions (https://sourceware.org/pipermail/libc-alpha/2024-October/160987.html). Zimmermann's accuracy tables compare the major libraries (https://homepages.loria.fr/PZimmermann/papers/glibc241.pdf).

Research. Docs/research/2026-10-30-defined-behavior.md, section "Math library results differ by platform".

decisions.title: jet build --watch rebuilds changed outputs on save, with the same watch engine as run, test and check
decisions.situation: You asked how Jet should compare with Zig's build server. Zig's `zig build --watch` keeps the compiler warm and rebuilds the steps whose input files changed. Jet ratified `--watch` for `jet run`, `jet test` and `jet check` only (D-RUN-WATCH1). Today `jet build --watch` builds once and exits 0 without watching, and says nothing about it. We recommend giving `jet build` the same `--watch` as the other commands.
decisions.gist: Should `jet build` rebuild its outputs each time a file is saved?
decisions.lesson: A watch mode keeps a command running and redoes its work when you save a file. The important part is knowing which files matter. Zig watches exactly the files the compiler read during the last build. Jet already records those files to decide whether a build can be reused, so it can watch the same set.
decisions.story: Lena builds a Jet library that a C program links, and a web bundle a separate server hosts. Neither is run by `jet dev`. She wants both rebuilt each time she saves. Under A she types `jet build --watch` once and sees one line per save, saying what was rebuilt and what was reused.
decisions.inWild:
$ zig build --watch
Build Summary: 3/3 steps succeeded
watching 41 directories, 1 processes
decisions.detail:
Today. Probe: `jet build --watch --output-dir=/tmp/mdw1 ub/shl_63.jet` writes the binary, exits 0 and returns at once. That is a defect under any option, because D-RUN-WATCH1 does not give `jet build` a `--watch`. Under B it becomes E2102; under A and C it works.

What A does. `jet build --watch` builds once, then keeps the compiler session warm and waits. It watches the files the last build read: sources, package.jet, and any file `fn build` read through `embed` or `find`. When one changes, it rebuilds only outputs whose reuse key changed, as D-BUILD-NOCHANGE1 defines the key. It never runs the program.

What A prints. One D-BUILD-NOCHANGE1 receipt line per round, with built and reused counts, then a `watching N files` line. Errors print as usual and the watch goes on. With `--json`, each round streams the same events the session wire carries.

Same engine as run, test and check. D-RUN-WATCH1 says all watch modes share one engine. Today it waits 4 ms for more events, settles for at most 250 ms, and skips saves whose content did not change (Compiler/JetDevserver/Source/WatchService.jet:934-938). A uses it unchanged, so there is no `--debounce` flag.

Setting rows. D-SETTING-ORDER1 says every option has a flag, a package field and a code form. So A adds `--watch` and `--watch=off`, `build: { watch: true }`, and `b.watch(true)` in `fn build`. The stock value is off. The flag wins, so `jet build --watch=off` in CI builds once even if the package says otherwise.

Beginner and expert paths. A beginner types `jet build --watch` and reads one line per save. An expert script uses `jet build --watch --json` and reads one event stream. An editor uses the session wire instead; D-SESSION-UPDATE1 already refuses `--listen=-` with `--watch`.

Edge cases. If `fn build` itself changes, the whole build program reruns. A deleted file counts as a change. A also watches each place where an import or `find` looked and found nothing, so a new file there triggers a rebuild. Output files and `.jet/` are never watched. Ctrl-C exits with 0 if the last round succeeded and 1 if it failed.

What B does. It keeps D-RUN-WATCH1 as written. `jet build --watch` becomes E2102, with a fix naming `jet check --watch` and `jet dev`. Outputs that `jet dev` does not run, such as libraries and bundles, have no rebuild-on-save.

What C does. Everything in A, plus `--debounce=<ms>` as in Zig, and `--ui`, a browser page showing each step's state, like Zig's `--webui`.

Amends. A and C amend D-RUN-WATCH1 by adding `build` to its list. B amends nothing. None changes D-SESSION-*.

Research. Docs/research/2026-10-30-build-server-protocol.md compares Zig's build server, Jai's build loop, and Jet's ratified and built parts.

decisions.title: Builds report each step as it starts and finishes, as two compiler.Event variants
decisions.situation: You asked how Jet should compare with Zig's build server. Zig reports each build step as pending, running, success or failure, and whether each output came from the cache. Jet ratified one public event enum, `compiler.Event`, and said each new variant needs a versioned public decision (D-COMPILER-EVENT1). It has no variant for a build step. We recommend adding two: a step started and a step finished.
decisions.gist: Should tools and terminals see each build step start and finish?
decisions.lesson: A build is many steps: check this package, compile that one, link, copy files. A step is reused when its inputs did not change. Editors, Canvas and scripts want to know which step is running and which were reused, not just the total at the end. A public event is a promise: its name and fields stay stable for tools.
decisions.story: Kenji's build takes forty seconds and he cannot tell why. Under A, the terminal shows `building shop: 12/40 steps (9 reused)` while it runs. His script reads `--json` and finds one link step that takes thirty seconds every time.
decisions.inWild:
# Zig: --webui shows each step's state; the compiler sends emit_digest per output
$ zig build --webui
# Build Server Protocol: build/taskStart, build/taskProgress, build/taskFinish
decisions.detail:
Today. Probe: `jet build --json` prints nothing on a successful build. `jet build --trace` prints compiler phases with time and memory, such as `sema.finalize` and `native.link`. It does not name outputs or steps, or say what was reused.

What a step is. Jet's build graph already lists actions with an id, name, kind, target and a cache-hit field (Core/Build/Build.jet:32-46, `BuildGraphAction`). A step is one of those actions. Nothing new has to be invented to name it.

What A adds. Two variants of `compiler.Event`. `build.step_started` carries the action id, target and kind. `build.step_finished` carries the id, the outcome (`built`, `reused` or `failed`) and the time in milliseconds. A reused step sends only `step_finished`, to keep the stream short.

Where A shows them. `--json` prints one line per event, and the session wire carries them inside a request (D-SESSION-WIRE1). Canvas colors each step. A terminal shows one line that updates, then the D-BUILD-NOCHANGE1 receipt replaces it. Output that is not a terminal gets only the receipt, and `--quiet` hides the line.

Hooks. Because D-COMPILER-EVENT1 uses one enum for hooks and tools, `#On(build.step_finished)` works in build code. A hook can read the result; it cannot change the step.

Beginner and expert paths. A beginner sees one line of progress and a receipt, and writes nothing. An expert reads `--json`, the session wire, or writes a hook.

Edge cases. Steps run in parallel, so events interleave; each carries its id. A failed step's reports come before its `step_finished` event. Cancelling a build sends `failed` for running steps, with the cancel report. With `--watch`, each round starts from step one.

What B does. Nothing new. Tools see `compiler.finished` and the receipt counts at the end. Progress inside a long build is invisible.

What C does. Steps appear in `--trace` text only. There is no public event and no versioned JSON shape, so scripts and Canvas have nothing stable to read.

Amends. A adds two variants to D-COMPILER-EVENT1's enum, which that decision says needs a versioned public change; this ballot is that change. B and C amend nothing.

Research. Docs/research/2026-10-30-build-server-protocol.md compares Zig's build server, the Build Server Protocol and Jet.

Review. Author: Claude (MemDesign lane). No fresh adversarial pass has run on this draft yet.

decisions.title: A sandboxed app sees its machine's shared class, never the machine itself, with no limit on what it asks
decisions.situation: A portable Jet app is compiled on the machine that runs it, so it can use that machine's matrix units, wide vector instructions or GPU. To pick a fast path, its code reads facts about the hardware, and each fact helps a tracker tell machines apart. The approved rule shows a sandboxed app rounded facts about every device, and each hardware package writes its own rounding. We recommend that a portable app see the facts of a machine class that many machines share, with no limit on what it asks.
decisions.gist: What may a sandboxed app learn about the machine it runs on?
decisions.lesson: A fingerprint is a set of facts that together pick out one machine, so a site can follow a user without cookies. Facts are safe to share when many machines give exactly the same ones. A machine class is such a set: a named bundle of hardware facts that a large crowd of machines all meet. Native programs are trusted and keep full hardware facts under every option.
decisions.story: Dana ships a photo app as one portable file. It asks whether the GPU has matrix units, whether there is 16 GiB of memory, and reads the vector width. On her friend's machine the app takes the fast path. Every answer came from the class her friend's machine belongs to, which thousands of other machines share.
decisions.detail:
Today. `$build.os` and `$build.profile` print Linux and dev on o0, o1 and o2 (probe h6b). Reading `$build.cpu`, `$build.hardware` or `$build.arch` is E0107, "Nothing named `$build` exists here" (probes h1, h2, h6). `jet build --target=portable` and every wasm target are E2104, not built yet. No program reads hardware facts today, so no running program changes under any option.

Ratified law. D-HOST-CAPS1=A gives typed hardware descriptions read through `$build.hardware`, and `requires:` and `uses:` on outputs. Packages add hardware kinds with `satisfies` and `coarse` methods. Its explainer says the host grants which facts a bundle sees, by default only coarse classes, and a coarse projection never overstates.

More ratified law. D-PORTABLE1=A compiles the app on the host from checked portable code. D-PORTABLE2=A says facts never grant powers. D-CORE-BOUNDARY1=A and D-CORE-FEATURE-FLOW1=A give every chip path a plain Jet meaning tested equal, so a chip changes speed, not answers.

The gap. The package that defines a hardware kind also writes its `coarse` method. A kind package can return its input unchanged, so a value as precise as a serial number can reach the app. The default also shows every device, and no rule bounds how many facts add up.

Peer evidence. WebGPU says a user agent "must not reveal more than 32 distinguishable configurations or buckets" (W3C WebGPU draft of 27 October 2026, section 2.2). It lets browsers bin hardware limits into buckets (section 2.2.1). Adapter identifiers should be as broad as possible, with details only after user consent (section 2.2.6). A takes the buckets and the consent, but not the fixed count.

Java's Vector API exposes `FloatVector.SPECIES_PREFERRED`, the best vector shape for the current CPU (JEP 529). .NET exposes `Vector.IsHardwareAccelerated` (learn.microsoft.com). Both serve trusted code; neither bounds what untrusted code learns. WebAssembly's relaxed SIMD lets one instruction return different results on different engines, which itself reveals the machine (relaxed-simd Overview, Consistency).

What A means. Jet hosts ship a list of machine classes. A class is a named set of hardware facts, such as a vector width, matrix units and a memory floor. A class enters the list only when a large crowd of machines meets it. In a portable bundle, the host picks the most capable class this machine fully meets. Every `$build.hardware` answer and value the app reads is that class's.

More of A. An app may ask any number of questions and read any value, because all of them together reveal one class and nothing more. No count is fixed: a new class joins the list when enough machines meet it. A fact no class describes answers no, which changes speed only, because every chip path has the same meaning. The user may grant exact facts to one app, such as a benchmark, in the trust store.

What B means. Today's approved rule: a portable app sees the coarse description of every granted device, rounded by each kind's own `coarse` method. What C means. Portable code reads no hardware facts. `requires:` still admits or refuses the app, and Core's automatic chip copies still run, without the app's code seeing which.

Limits under every option. An app can time a loop and guess the chip, as WebGPU section 2.2.3 notes. Classes bound what facts reveal, not what timing reveals. Separate processes, the side-channel hardening D-PORTABLE2 requires for shared processes, and coarse timers are host policy outside this vote. Native outputs are trusted and keep every fact under every option.

Amends. A narrows D-HOST-CAPS1's portable view from each kind's coarse projection to the host's class list. `coarse` stays for descriptions, refusal messages and native code. B amends nothing. C removes hardware facts from portable code. The approved examples spell the branch `prep if`, which is retired; this ballot uses `comptime if`.

Research. Docs/research/2026-10-30-portable-target-capabilities.md. Review: author Claude (MemDesign-2 lane); no fresh adversarial pass has run on this draft yet.

Why no fixed count. A fixed count bounds how many machines a page can tell apart, but it also caps how many hardware facts any app may use. What protects a user is that the crowd sharing their answers is large. A class list keeps every crowd large and lets the list grow with new hardware, so neither the number of questions nor the number of classes needs a cap.

options.name: Shared machine classes, no limit
options.detail:
A portable app reads hardware facts as usual, but every answer and value comes from the machine's class. A class is a named set of facts that a large crowd of machines meets, from a list Jet hosts ship. The host picks the most capable class the machine fully meets.

An app may ask as many questions as it likes, since together they reveal only the class. A fact no class describes answers no, which changes only speed. The user can grant exact facts to one app. Native programs keep every fact.
options.technical: In `form: .Portable` outputs, `$build.hardware` is evaluated against the selected class description, not host observations or a kind's `coarse`. Class selection: the most capable list entry whose every fact the host observed and granted. The class name joins the cache key. The list is host data versioned with the host; an entry needs a published crowd size. A trust-store grant per app hash switches that app to exact facts. `coarse` keeps its role in descriptions, refusals and native builds. Diagnostic code and spelling land under I7.

options.name: Coarse descriptions of every device
options.detail:
A portable app sees the coarse description of every granted device, as the approved rule says. Each hardware kind rounds its own values with its own `coarse` method.

No rule bounds how many facts an app sees in total.
options.technical: No change to D-HOST-CAPS1. `$build.hardware` in portable code exposes the coarse projection of each granted entry, written by each kind's package.

options.name: No hardware facts in portable apps
options.detail:
Portable code cannot read hardware facts. `requires:` still admits or refuses the app at install and launch.

Core's own automatic chip copies still run, chosen by the host without the app's code seeing which one.
options.technical: Amends D-HOST-CAPS1: `$build.hardware` reads are a build error in `form: .Portable` outputs. Requirements and Core multiversioning are unchanged.

comparisons.note: Limits and adapter details are binned; at most 32 distinguishable configurations. Source: W3C WebGPU sections 2.2, 2.2.1, 2.2.6
The Vector API gives any code the preferred vector shape for the CPU. Source: openjdk.org/jeps/529
Any code can ask whether vector hardware is present. Source: learn.microsoft.com, System.Numerics.Vector.IsHardwareAccelerated

recommendation.why: A keeps every fast path an app can name while each user stays in a large crowd, whatever a hardware package's own rounding says. Nothing is capped: apps ask what they need and the class list grows with new hardware. Because every chip path has one meaning, a fact no class describes costs only speed.
gains: No limit on questions or on kinds of machine.
Every user stays inside a large crowd.
Apps may read values, not only yes or no.
A hardware package cannot leak precise values into apps.

whyNot.reason: B trusts every hardware package to round its own values, and nothing keeps the facts an app adds up shared by a crowd.
C stops an app from choosing its own algorithm for the hardware, which A allows without a limit.

recommendation.tradeoff: Brand-new hardware gets its nearest listed class until enough machines share its facts. That costs speed, never answers, and a user can grant one app exact facts.

decisions.title: The same portable app file also runs in a web browser, translated in the page
decisions.situation: Jet's portable app file holds checked Jet code that each machine compiles for itself, which is meant to beat WebAssembly. Browsers run only JavaScript and WebAssembly, so today's approved plan gives the web its own separate build. Then one program ships as two artifacts with two checking paths. We recommend that the same app file also run in a browser, checked and turned into WebAssembly inside the page.
decisions.gist: Should one portable Jet app file run both on a computer and in a browser tab?
decisions.lesson: WebAssembly is the portable code format every browser runs. A host is the program that checks an app file and runs it. Under A, a small Jet host compiled to WebAssembly loads the app file in the page and translates it. In the browser the app runs at WebAssembly speed; outside it, at native speed.
decisions.story: Lee ships a notes app as one file. Colleagues run it from the terminal at native speed. A client opens a link and the same file runs in the browser tab, refused only for the file access a browser page cannot grant.
decisions.detail:
Today. No portable or web output builds. `jet build --target=portable`, `--target=web`, `--target=wasm32-wasip2` and `--target=wasm32-unknown-unknown` all stop with E2104, "is not built yet" (probe w/hello.jet). There is no `.jetapp` code in Compiler/ or Core/. So no shipped program changes under either option.

Ratified law. D-PORTABLE1=A makes the app file versioned, content-hashed portable code that the host verifies and compiles locally. Its text says running in a browser needs a separate adapter. D-PORTABLE2=A adds a machine-code checker for native hosts. D-WASISRV1=A keeps WebAssembly as an export for WASI hosts. D-LEARN-WEB1=A already puts Jet's checker in the page as WebAssembly.

Work in flight. Card #5201 builds a JetIR to JavaScript and WebAssembly back end. Card #5487 (done) runs plugin WebAssembly through JetIR and Jet's own back end, the opposite direction. D-EFFTYPE-TARGET1=A turns a profile's missing facts into denied effects, so a browser profile with no file system denies file access.

Measured cell. The same F32 multiply-add loop, one million values for 400 passes, written in C. Native gcc -O2 took 0.059 s, and 0.044 s with -march=native. Zig's wasm32-wasi build under Wasmtime 48 took 0.122 s with SIMD and 0.324 s without, cold compile included. The machine had load near 90, so treat these as indicative.

The same loop in Jet took 1.72 s at o2 and 2.50 s at o1, minimum of five runs. That native gap is a separate performance finding. So inside a browser the app is bounded by WebAssembly speed. Outside one, local native compilation is what beats WebAssembly.

Peer evidence. Pyodide runs CPython compiled to WebAssembly in the page. Roc's in-browser REPL ships its whole compiler as about 6 MB of WebAssembly (D-LEARN-WEB1 detail). WebAssembly SIMD is fixed at 128 bits, and relaxed SIMD allows engine-dependent results (relaxed-simd Overview, Consistency).

What A means. A Jet host written in Jet, compiled to WebAssembly, loads the app file in the page. It runs the same verifier, compares powers with the page's grants, and translates the checked code to WebAssembly with the same back end as the web export. The browser's engine provides the walls, so the native machine-code checker is not needed there.

More of A. GPU work uses the WebGPU device library. Native-width vector lanes are four F32 values wide in the page. A build may also write a ready-made WebAssembly copy beside the app file, made by the same translator; the page uses it when its hash matches, to skip the in-page translation.

What B means. Today's approved plan. The app file runs only where a Jet host is installed. The web gets a separate `jet build --target=web` from source, with its own artifact.

Amends. A amends D-PORTABLE1's sentence that a browser needs a separate adapter: the adapter becomes the in-page host for the same file. `--target=web` stays as the ready-made copy. B amends nothing.

Research. Docs/research/2026-10-30-portable-target-capabilities.md. Review: author Claude (MemDesign-2 lane); no fresh adversarial pass has run on this draft yet.

options.name: One app file, also in the browser
options.detail:
A small Jet host, compiled to WebAssembly, loads the app file in the page. It checks the file with the same verifier, asks for the page's grants and turns the code into WebAssembly with the same translator as the web build.

A build may also write a ready-made WebAssembly copy beside the app file, which the page uses when its hash matches. Behavior change: an app that needs a power a page cannot grant, such as files, is refused in the browser with the missing fact named.
options.technical:
The host is Jet source built for the browser profile (D-FREESTAND-WASM1), reusing the #5201 back end and the D-PORTABLE1 verifier. Walls come from the WebAssembly engine; D-PORTABLE2's checker applies to native hosts only.

Grants map to page permissions; absent facts deny effects per D-EFFTYPE-TARGET1. `Lanes<F32>` is four wide on SIMD128. Ready-made copies are keyed by app hash and translator version. The loader spelling is illustrative.

options.name: A separate web build
options.detail:
The app file runs only where a Jet host is installed. Browsers get a separate build from source with `jet build --target=web`.

The two artifacts are checked by different paths: the host verifier for the app file, and the compiler for the web build.
options.technical: No change. D-PORTABLE1's separate browser adapter stays a source build through the #5201 back end.

comparisons.note: CPython itself is compiled to WebAssembly and runs ordinary Python in the page. Source: pyodide.org
A JVM class file needs an installed JVM; browsers dropped applets, so the web needs a separate build. Source: openjdk.org/jeps/398

recommendation.why: A makes the portable file the one thing Jet ships: native speed where a Jet host is installed, and WebAssembly speed in any browser. The ready-made copy keeps the web build's small first load.
gains: One artifact runs on computers and in browsers.
One verifier and one translator for both.
A ready-made copy keeps the first page load small.

whyNot.reason: B ships every web program twice, checked two ways, and a browser cannot open the app file itself.

recommendation.tradeoff: The in-page host is a second build of the verifier and translator for the browser profile, which must stay small.
