decisions.title: Text v2: one String type, fixed through `::` and edited in place through `:=`
decisions.situation: You asked for fixed strings plus a way to build text, and said you lean toward one type for simplicity. Today Jet has one type, String. A `::` name never changes, and a `:=` name grows with `+=`, in place when nothing else shares the text. No call can reserve space, insert, remove or truncate. This vote picks between one String with in-place editing, a fixed String plus a second buffer type, and today's model.
decisions.gist: Should Jet keep one String type, where a `:=` name may be edited in place and every other holder keeps its own value?
decisions.lesson: A String is a value, like a number. Giving it to another name gives that name its own text. A `::` name never changes, and a `:=` name may be edited, and no edit ever reaches another holder's copy.
decisions.story: Ana writes a report with `out += "- {item}\n"`, as she would in Python. Later she prints a million CSV rows with one reused line, trimmed and prefixed in place. Under A both are the same String type, and the text she passed to a helper earlier never changes.
decisions.detail:
What Jet does today, probed on O0, O1 and O2. `s :: "a"` then `s += "b"` is E0111. `s := "ab"`, `t :: s`, `s += "c"` prints `abc ab`, so the shared text never changes. The runtime appends in place only for a sole owner (Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/Text.jet:54-58, 357-367). `push`, `clear` and `insert` are E0311, and `String.with_capacity` is E0107.

The memory model already chose this. D-COPY-DEFAULT1=A gives every heap value copy on first write, and removes the sharing test for values the compiler proves unique. Lists already work this way, with edits marked `&xs.push(v)`.

Speed. A `+=` loop runs 6.9 times Rust's cycles at O2 today, from two allocations per text and a runtime call per append. That gap is compiler work under every option. A buffer type would run the same runtime calls.

Jet's own code has 1,449 text locals made with `:= "…"`, of which 405 grow, across 1,397 sites. There are 45 `&String` parameters.

options.name: One String: `::` is fixed, `:=` may be edited in place
options.detail:
String stays the only text type and stays a value. A `::` name never changes. A `:=` name or a `&String` parameter may grow with `+=`. It may also be edited with `&` calls, as lists are: `&s.insert(at, text)`, `&s.remove(from, to)`, `&s.truncate(n)` and `&s.reserve(n)`. `String.with_capacity(n)` and `s.capacity()` join them, and `&s.try_push(x)` is fixed.

Appending stays `+=`, and emptying stays `s = ""`, so no `push` or `clear` is added. Positions count characters, as `len()` and `slice` do.

Behavior changes: none for existing code. D-STR-DECLINE1 is amended to allow these verbs. `s = ""` on a `:=` String nothing else holds now always keeps its storage, which D-STRING-EMPTY1 only allowed.
options.technical:
The verbs are Write-access builtins in BuiltinMethods.jet, like `try_push`. Each runs the existing copy on first write when the text is shared or a literal, then edits in place with geometric growth. For a value proved unique, D-COPY-DEFAULT1 drops the sharing test, so the edit is a plain store.

D-EFF-FORMAT-WRITER1 keeps String as the one public text type, and `out += "{x}"` already streams `x` into `out`. D-CORE-IO-BUF1 stands: `Bytes` stays the byte buffer, and text needs no second buffer.

options.name: A fixed String plus a separate StringBuffer
options.detail:
String keeps no editing calls. `s += x` on a `:=` name still works by giving the name a new String. A new Core type, `StringBuffer`, holds `push`, `insert`, `remove`, `clear`, `truncate`, `reserve` and `with_capacity`. It prints like a String, and `to_string()` makes one.

This matches Java, Go, C# and Dart, and keeps String free of editing verbs. Every text API must pick one of two types, and moving text between them is a conversion call.
options.technical:
StringBuffer is a Core value type written like a list. `to_string()` at its last use hands over storage with no copy (D-DROP-ASAP1). It runs the same append runtime as String `+=`, so it is not faster.

Reopens D-EFF-FORMAT-WRITER1 (String is the one public text type) and D-CORE-IO-BUF1 (the text buffer was deleted). The 5 `try_push` sites move to the buffer.

options.name: Keep today's model
options.detail:
One String, `+=` on `:=` names, and no editing calls. Insert, remove and truncate are written as new Strings built from slices, and reserving space is not possible.

No new names. Every edit other than appending copies the whole text.
options.technical: No change. Each `slice` scans and copies the text today (Text.jet:686-733). The broken `try_push` still needs its own fix.

comparisons.note: One String with value semantics and copy on write. Edits need a `var`; a `let` string never changes. Source: developer.apple.com/documentation/swift/string.
One growable String, edited through `let mut`; `&str` is the fixed view. Source: doc.rust-lang.org/std/string/struct.String.html.
A fixed string, and strings.Builder grows in place. Source: pkg.go.dev/strings#Builder.
comparisons.code:
var b strings.Builder
b.WriteString("x")
out := b.String()

comparisons.note: An immutable String, and StringBuilder edits in place. Source: docs.oracle.com, java.lang.StringBuilder.

recommendation.why: A gives one text type with the guarantee you want from fixed strings: no edit ever reaches text another name holds, and a `::` name never changes. Experts edit in place on the same type, and lists already work this way.
gains: One text type for every API.
No edit reaches another holder's text.
Reserve, insert, remove and truncate in place.
Existing code and decisions stay as they are.

whyNot.reason: B adds a second type and conversions at every hand-off, but no safety, because String values are already never changed under another holder. It runs the same append code, so it is not faster.
C leaves no way to reserve, insert or truncate in place, so experts copy the whole text for each edit.

recommendation.tradeoff: String gains a few editing calls, used only through `:=` names and `&` parameters.

designAway.loss: String gains editing calls that D-STR-DECLINE1 declined.
attempts: Put the calls on a second type, as B does: rejected, it adds a type and conversions for no safety or speed.
designAway.result: D-STR-DECLINE1 declined them because they would change an immutable String. Here no value changes under another holder: edits act on a `:=` name or `&` parameter, as list edits do. `push` and `clear` stay declined, since `+=` and `s = ""` cover them.

designAway.loss: Editing a shared String copies it once, and the copy is not written in the code.
attempts: Require `.copy()` before editing a shared String: rejected, D-COPY-DEFAULT1 already chose copy on first write for every heap value, lists included.
designAway.result: The copy happens at most once, on the first edit, and never for a value the compiler proves unique, which is the usual `out := ""` case.

designAway.loss: A `::` String could look fixed only by convention.

decisions.title: The name of Jet's one text type: `String` or `Text`
decisions.situation: Jet has one text type, and the board has ruled that it stays one type. You asked why it is called String and not Text. The word string comes from logic and linguistics, where a string is a row of symbols. Early text-processing languages took the word in the 1950s and 1960s, and almost every language since has kept it. The type appears 81,344 times in Jet's own code. We recommend keeping String.
decisions.gist: Should Jet's one text type keep the name `String`, or be renamed `Text`?
decisions.lesson: A string is a row of symbols, as in a string of beads. Logicians used the word by 1918, and the first text-processing languages, COMIT and SNOBOL, made it the programmer's word. Nearly every language since says String. Text is plainer English, and Haskell's text library, Unison and Dhall use it.
decisions.story: Kai comes from Python and writes `fn greet(name: String)`. Under A that is right with no explanation. Under B the compiler says String is unknown and offers Text, and Kai learns the new word once.
decisions.detail:
History. "String" meant things in a row for centuries, and 19th-century typesetters measured a compositor's "string" of type. Logic took the word for a row of marks: C. I. Lewis wrote of "strings of recognisable marks" in 1918.

Computing took it from there. COMIT (Yngve, late 1950s) and SNOBOL (Farber, Griswold and Polonsky, 1964) were the first string-processing languages. ALGOL 60's report names quoted literals strings, in section 2.6.

From then on the word stuck. PL/I had character strings and bit strings, BASIC had string variables, and C++, Java, C#, Python, Go, Swift, Kotlin, Rust and JavaScript all name the type string or String.

Where Text appears. Pascal used `text` for a text file, not a value. Haskell's Prelude String is a list of characters, so the faster library type is Data.Text. Unison and Dhall name their built-in type Text, and SQL databases have a TEXT column.

So Text usually marks a newer design choice, such as Haskell's packed text over a list. Jet's String is already packed UTF-8, so Text would not mark a difference.

Today in Jet. The census counts 81,344 mentions of `String` in 17,636 Jet files: Compiler 36,082, Core 6,730, Examples 2,169, tests 9,488, Jetpack 24,309 and Tools 2,566. A parameter typed `Text` is E0119 today (probe m6342c/p_Text.jet).

D-TEXT-FIXED1=A (2026-10-30) ruled one text type, fixed through `::` and edited through `:=`. So this vote names only that one type, and no buffer type needs a name.

Review. Authors: Claude (SurfaceDesign lanes); v3 adds the history from card 6379 and drops the buffer-type branch. No fresh adversarial pass has run on this draft.

decisions.title: Name the "this program" case of sys.usage `.Program`; amends D-CORE-RLIMIT1
decisions.situation: D-CORE-RLIMIT1 (ratified A) gives `sys.usage(of:)` two cases, written `enum UsageOf { Self, Children }`. A probe of that line failed with E0003, and it looked as if `Self` cannot name a case. It can: the error came from the commas, since Jet separates cases with spaces or new lines. The question left is only the word. We recommend `.Program`, because every other line of the ratified ballot already says "this program".
decisions.gist: What should the "this program" case of `sys.usage(of:)` be called?
decisions.lesson: `sys.usage(of:)` reports CPU time and peak memory, either for the running program or for its finished children. The case name is what a reader sees at the call, as in `sys.usage(of: .Program)`. `Self` already has a meaning in Jet: the type an `impl` block is about.
decisions.story: Ana's build tool prints its own peak memory with `sys.usage(of: .Program)` and the children's with `sys.usage(of: .Children)`. A reader new to Jet reads both calls aloud and knows which is which without opening the docs. Nothing else in her code changes between the options.
decisions.detail:
What the probes show. Probes of_self, of_program and of_current in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/MemDesign-3/probes/rlimit write `enum UsageOf { X Children }` and match on `.X`. All three print the same two lines on o0, o1 and o2. Probe kw_type shows the word `Type` works as a case too. The comma form, `enum UsageOf { Program, Children }`, fails with E0003 for every name (probe comma.jet).

So no parser change is needed for any option. ToolsJet's probe usage_of.jet failed because it copied the ratified technical text, which writes commas. Every option below corrects that text to `enum UsageOf { X Children }`, the form Core uses, for example `enum PathPlatform { Unix Windows }` in Core/Files/Runtime/KernelPathComponents.jet:6.

Why the word matters. In Jet, `Self` inside an `impl` block means that block's type. A case named `Self` gives the word a second meaning: inside `impl UsageOf`, `Self.Self` names the case of the type. Probe self_noimpl shows `.Self` and `UsageOf.Self` both work at a call. The parser accepts it; the question is how it reads.

Other names. `.Program` matches the ratified text, which says "this program" for every limit and usage call. `.Current` is shorter, but it does not say current what: program, thread or task. C, Python and Go say `RUSAGE_SELF`, so `.Self` is familiar to C programmers.

Scope. Only the case name and the ratified text change. The calls, units and the rest of D-CORE-RLIMIT1 A stay as ratified. Nothing is built yet, so no code or test moves.

decisions.title: Rotate the working seed once B1 lands; the HTTP client (#3665) keeps gating the release
decisions.situation: The compiler that builds Jet, called the seed, is a0_021. It cannot read trait constants, so Core cannot use them. The diagnostic types you approved, such as `jet.UnusedParameter`, need them in Core. You ruled that the next seed, a0_022, waits for the HTTP client port (#3665), which has 9 of 10 criteria open. We recommend rotating the working seed as soon as trait constants land, with the usual checks, and keeping #3665 as the gate for the release.
decisions.gist: Should the working seed rotate before the HTTP client port lands?
decisions.lesson: Jet builds itself. Core and the compiler are compiled by an earlier, trusted compiler called the seed. New syntax can reach Core only after a seed that understands it replaces the old one. A release is a seed published for others to download (D-SEED-DIST1); none is published yet.
decisions.story: DeclTypes finishes B1, which teaches the parser trait constants. B3 is ready: every Jet diagnostic becomes a type with its `jet.` name. The build fails, because a0_021 compiles Core and reads `code: String` in a trait as E0003. Under A, Main rotates the seed that evening and B3 lands. The release still waits for the HTTP client.
decisions.detail:
What is blocked today. Four pieces of work need a seed newer than a0_021. DeclTypes B3 and its later batches put trait constants in Core (#6039 C9 to C14). IrTypes has a Core alias, `Name<T> :: Type`, staged for golden transform_source_identity (#6176). The `__coded_stop` migration of Server.jet and Web.jet waits as g3b. #6279 C4 deletes the email bootstrap file at the first rotation past a0_021.

Why a0_022 waits now. The HttpDest landing note ($JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/land/HttpDest-g1.msg, line 8) records your ruling. Two Jetpack test rows, foundation_fetch and the Public-client test, fail until the Jet HTTP client port lands. Those rows fail because their source calls a client that is not written yet, so they fail the same way under any seed.

How a rotation is checked today (ROTATION.md in each seed folder). The candidate is built from a clean dev export with no Rust in the chain. It must rebuild itself to the same bytes, s2 equal to s3. Its full golden suite must be no worse than the current seed's, your rule of 2026-10-22. a0_021 took 9 minutes of wall time for these steps.

What A adds. Before the chain, a collect-all preflight checks Core and the compiler with the candidate and lists every error at once, as seed-preflight.sh does with keep-going. Any row stops the rotation. Every earlier seed stays on disk (a0_005 to a0_021), and current.env names the active one, so switching back is one line.

What A changes. The working seed and the release become two separate events. The seed rotates whenever the checks pass and new Core syntax needs it. A release, the seed published for download under D-SEED-DIST1, still waits for #3665. Your ruling keeps its effect: nothing is released before the HTTP client is in Jet.

Option B keeps the hold. All four pieces of work wait for #3665, a P0 card with 9 open criteria spanning Core HTTP, sockets, TLS and server framing. Option C lands B3 without trait constants by keeping each diagnostic's name in a compiler table, then moves them into Core after the rotation. That is a second cutover and a temporary twin of the table, which AGENTS.md forbids.

Probe. trait_const.jet in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/MemDesign-3/probes/seed declares a trait constant and reads it. Both a0_021 and today's dev compiler stop with two E0003 errors. B1 has not landed on dev yet, so A's rotation starts after it does.

decisions.title: A link hook returns a build action Jet runs, chosen per output by an ordinary setting
decisions.situation: Some programs need a different linker than Jet's, such as a web game linked with a WebAssembly linker. Others need a step after linking, such as shrinking, signing or adding an icon. Jet already agreed that build code may hook these moments. It did not settle what a hook hands back or how a package picks which outputs use it. We recommend that a hook returns a declared build command that Jet runs, picked per output by an ordinary setting.
decisions.gist: How may a build replace one output's link step and process the file it writes?
decisions.lesson: Linking joins compiled pieces into one program file. A build action is a command Jet runs with declared inputs, outputs and powers, so Jet can cache, show and audit it. A hook is a function Jet calls at a set moment. Under A the hook describes an action, and Jet runs it.
decisions.story: Kim's game has a desktop output and a web output. Only the web one should link with wasm-ld and then shrink with wasm-opt. Under A she names those two hooks in the web output's settings. The desktop output builds as before, and `jet inspect build` shows the exact commands.
decisions.detail:
Ruled already. D-JAI-EVENTS1=A (2026-10-17) added `build.link(LinkInputs) -> Artifact`, `build.before_write` and `build.after_write`. They run as build actions with declared Exec and FS powers, one link hook per target, listed by the root. On #5009 (2026-10-30) the owner asked for a ballot on replacing one output's link step and post-processing the written file.

What A does at link time. A `#On(build.link)` function receives LinkInputs: object files, libraries, link arguments, the output path, and `default`, the action Jet would run itself. It returns a BuildAction (D-BUILDACTION1): argv, declared inputs and outputs, and powers. Jet runs it in place of its own link, checks the declared file was written, caches it and records it.

After linking. A `#On(build.before_write)` function receives the linked file and returns a BuildAction that turns it into the final file: strip, shrink, sign, or add an icon or manifest. Several run in the listed order. `#On(build.after_write)` stays read-only and returns findings. Hooks never write files themselves, so every byte of the output came from a declared action.

Choosing outputs. `link: default | <hook>` and `post_link: [<hook>, …]` are two rows of the one option table (D-SETTING-ORDER1). Each has a flag (`--link=default`), an output field (`options:`), a profile field and a handle method, `b.output("game_web").link(wasmtools.link)`. A hook that no output names never runs. Per D-JAI-CONFIG1, the row is fixed once linking starts.

A plain linker swap needs no hook. The toolchain's `linker:` field (D-BUILD-CORE1) and `add_link_args` (D-JAI-CONFIG1) still cover a different linker binary or extra flags. The hook is for a different command shape or extra steps after linking.

Policy and audit. `policy: { forbid: [link, post_link] }` refuses both rows for a package or a whole project. A hook from a dependency is held until a `jet trust grant`, as every dependency hook already is (D-HOOK-STAGES1, D-JPK-BUILDSCRIPT1). `jet inspect build` shows each output's link action, its argv, its powers and the line that chose it.

Failure. A link or post-link action that fails, or does not write its declared file, is one registered build diagnostic. It names the output, the hook and the setting line, and includes the command's error output.

Size (D-SIZE-PAYUSE1). Hooks run at build time and link nothing into the program, so programs that do not use them are byte-for-byte unchanged. `LinkInputs.default` carries all of Jet's link arguments, so a hook that edits one keeps the rest. Size reports read the file after the last post-link step.

What B does. The rows are the same, but the hook runs the linker itself under its declared powers and returns the file, as D-JAI-EVENTS1's signature reads. Jet sees only the result. It cannot show the command, and it caches the step only by the hook's own inputs.

What C does. Hooks return actions as in A, but there are no option rows. A link hook listed by the root package applies to every executable output, and picking one output means testing its name inside the hook.

Peers. Jai's `use_custom_link_command` hands the object files to the build program, which links them itself (focus first.jai). Cargo offers a per-target linker setting and `-C link-arg`, but no step after the build. Bazel and Buck2 model linking as a declared action inside a rule. Zig exposes the link step in its build graph.

Amends D-JAI-EVENTS1=A (link and before_write return a BuildAction; outputs pick hooks through option rows) and D-HOOK-STAGES1=A (two rows join the build table). Companion proposal section 7 has the full design.

decisions.title: Pillar 9: primitives first, pareto wrappers on top, options not siblings, with a review checklist and an api lint group
decisions.situation: Core often documents only convenience wrappers, while the function that does the work is undocumented and takes a bare true or false flag. In twenty areas a need one step past a wrapper has no documented route. Variants of one job become separate names, such as encode_url and encode_url_padded, which cannot be combined. A current house rule asks for those separate names. The vote decides whether a new philosophy pillar replaces that rule. We recommend the pillar, a review checklist and a lint group.
decisions.gist: Should Core APIs be complete documented primitives with a few wrappers on top, and options instead of sibling names?
decisions.lesson: A wrapper makes the common case short, but if it is the only documented door, the next case needs copied code. Libraries that age well document the general function and add a few shortcuts over it. Python's base64 takes an `altchars` option, and Go's encoder takes a padding setting, rather than adding a name per variant.
decisions.story: Kai needs unpadded standard base64 for a token. Core documents encode, encode_url and encode_url_padded, but none fits. Under A he writes `base64.encode(data, padding: .Omit)`, one documented call.
decisions.inWild:
# Python: one function, a variant is an option
import base64
base64.b64encode(data, altchars=b"-_")
decisions.detail:
Today. A full audit of Core and Jetpack counts 20 areas where the documented names are only wrappers. The worker behind them is public but undocumented, with a positional `Bool`. Base64.jet:277 `encode_alphabet(data, alphabet: String, padded: Bool)` and Regex.jet:380 `replace_n(..., first_only: Bool)` are two.

The call tools exist but go unused. 100 of 9,067 Core parameters have a default, 2 functions are variadic, and 2 documented top-level functions use a `*` zone. Lint L2401 for positional `Bool` parameters is registered but never fires.

The house rules contradict each other. Law 9 (D-STDLIB-OPTPARAM1=A) says sibling names stay the house style and forbids a mode parameter. Review row L9 on the same page asks for one root method with a label-only option enum. Law D3 says defaulted options replace overload families.

What A does. Philosophy gains pillar 9. Every API area has a complete documented primitives layer and a few wrappers for common work. A wrapper is a one-step composition of public primitives. Variants that differ only in policy are labelled, defaulted, typed options on one function.

A sibling name stays right when the job differs: a different result type, failure type, safety level, effect row or call shape. For example `read` and `read_bytes` return different types, and `replace_all_with` takes a callback.

Enforcement under A. An eight-question API review checklist goes in the contributing docs, and the review record gains its answers. A new `api` lint group in `jet lint` holds the mechanical rules, starting with L2401, constant siblings, string policies and long positional lists.

The lints are ordinary compiler-library clients, so any package can turn them on, as D-STDRUBRIC1=A's lints-first rule asks. Law 9 is replaced and D-STDLIB-OPTPARAM1=A is superseded.

Moves under A. Promote the base64, log and regex workers to documented primitives and fold their wrappers into options. Wire the api lint group and make L2401 fire. Four further audit cards rest on laws already ratified and do not wait on this vote.

Out of scope. Options after a variadic parameter are a separate language vote on the same day. Alias spellings, public `__` hooks and per-call timeouts are already decided elsewhere.

Peers. Python's `base64.b64encode(s, altchars=)` and `re.sub(count=)` use options. Go uses `base64.StdEncoding.WithPadding(base64.NoPadding)`. Rust's base64 crate takes an engine value with a padding setting.

Review. Author: Claude (SurfaceDesign lane), from MemDesign's proposal and audit for card 6367. No fresh adversarial pass has run on this draft.

decisions.title: One report channel for a library's compile-time checks
decisions.situation: Libraries can check code while it compiles in two ratified ways. A hook returns plain warnings about a whole function. A marker check calls `reject` with a full library error, but only on the marker's line. A house rule like "never keep an entity past a frame" needs an error on the bad call, with a why and a fix. The owner decides whether both ways share one report type that can point inside the checked code. We recommend that, with an optional location.
decisions.gist: Should a house rule's report be a real error that points at the bad line, through the same channel `reject` uses?
decisions.lesson: Jet has two ratified ways for a library to report while compiling. A hook finding is a message-only warning at a whole declaration. `reject` raises a full library error, with what, why and fix, but only at the marker's line. Neither can say "this call, here, is an error". Whichever option wins, `reject` and hook findings still need to be built.
decisions.story: Priya keeps a game engine with one house rule: never keep an entity past the end of a frame. Her check runs over the whole codebase while compiling and finds the bad call. The report is a plain warning on the function's first line, and a 200-line function hides the call.
decisions.inWild:
// Jai metaprogram check (Jonathan Blow, youtu.be/ZF1m1DsW3Rg 07:57-08:35)
compiler_report("Don't hold an Entity pointer across a frame; see wiki/frames", loc = node.location);
decisions.detail: Source: card #6377, Blow talk 07:57-08:35 (youtu.be/ZF1m1DsW3Rg), report Docs/research/blow-error-reporting-talk-2026-10-30.md. Related law: D-MARKER-DIAG1=A (#6039, library Diagnostic and `reject`). D-HOOK-STAGES1=A: hook findings are L1401 warnings, and deny gives E1293. D-JAI-EVENTS1=A: settled and finished stages also return findings. D-META-COMPILER1=A: its Error event observes diagnostics and does not raise them. Build card: #6388. Probe t11_reject.jet: `reject` is E0102 today on jet 03c64ad0c4.

options.name: One report type, placed anywhere in the checked code
options.detail:
A hook may return a finding built from a library error value, the same kind of value `reject` takes. That value brings its own code, severity, what, why and fix. Both calls take an optional `at:` naming a spot inside the code being checked, such as one call.

Without `at:`, nothing moves. A hook finding sits on its declaration, and a `reject` sits on the marker's line. With `at:`, that line becomes a note under the report.

A message-only hook finding stays a warning, exactly as ratified. A team's policy can still turn any warning into an error. A dependency's hook that can raise errors says so in its grant request.
options.technical:
`compiler.finding` gains an overload `finding(err: impl Diagnostic, at: Span?)`, beside the ratified `finding(d, msg)`. `reject(err, at: Span?)` gains the same parameter. Severity comes from the Diagnostic's `severity` constant (D-MARKER-DIAG1=A), so an error-severity finding fails the build without a deny policy.

`at:` accepts only a span taken from the invocation's own payload: the hook's declaration or the marked item. Any other span is a registered error. Each direct named call in the `compiler.declared` payload carries its span as `d.call_sites: [compiler.CallSite{name, span}]`; this ballot adds that list beside the ratified `d.calls` names.

This amends D-MARKER-DIAG1's sentence "primary span is the marker's use site" to add "unless `at:` names a span inside the marked item". The D-HOOK-STAGES1 grant text lists "findings and errors" when a hook module builds Diagnostic findings. Merge identity is the finding's package-qualified code plus span: the Diagnostic's `code`, or `lint_name` when its severity is .Lint; message-only findings keep their hook/lint identity. `#Allow` on the item that holds the span silences warnings, as today.

options.name: Keep the two ratified channels
options.detail: Hook findings stay message-only warnings on a declaration. A team that wants an error adds the lint to its deny policy. `reject` stays the only library error, always on the marker's line.
options.technical: No change to D-HOOK-STAGES1=A (L1401 findings, deny gives E1293) or D-MARKER-DIAG1=A (primary span is the marker's use site).

options.name: Only `reject` gains a location
options.detail: `reject` takes an optional `at:` naming a spot inside the marked item. Hook findings stay message-only warnings on a declaration.
options.technical: Amends only D-MARKER-DIAG1=A, as in A. D-HOOK-STAGES1=A findings are unchanged.

comparisons.note: compiler_report takes a location, so metaprogram checks point at any node.
A macro error carries a span chosen by the macro author.
A rule reports at any node, and the rule's metadata sets its severity.

recommendation.why: Blow's house rule needs an error that names the bad line and explains itself. One report type gives hooks and markers the same power, with no second mechanism.
gains: House rules read like Jet's own errors.
One report type to learn, render and look up.

whyNot.reason: It leaves house rules as vague warnings on the wrong line, which is the exact problem in the story.
It fixes markers only, while the codebase-wide rule in Blow's example is a hook.

recommendation.tradeoff: None remains. A dependency's hook can raise errors only after a grant that says so, just as a dependency's marker can already `reject`.

decisions.title: Whether a library's error can carry its own help link
decisions.situation: Every error Jet prints ends with a help line that links to a page about that error. Libraries can now define their own errors, such as a game engine refusing code that keeps an entity past a frame. Those errors have a what, a why and a fix, but no way to give a link, so they end without help. The owner decides what a library error shows on that line. We recommend an optional link on the error type, always printed beside the explain command.
decisions.gist: Every Jet error ends with a help link. What should a library's own error show there?
decisions.lesson: Jet's own errors end with a `More:` line linking to a page about that error code. Libraries can define their own errors with a what, a why and a fix, but they have no way to give a link. Whichever option wins, library errors still need to be built.
decisions.story: Priya's engine refuses code that keeps an entity past a frame. The why and fix fit in two lines, but the reasoning needs a page with diagrams. Her team's wiki has that page, and she wants every report to point at it.

// Blow's metaprogram check links to a web page (youtu.be/ZF1m1DsW3Rg 07:57-08:14)
"Hey, you're not supposed to do this in this code base ... here's the link to the web page"
decisions.detail: Source: card #6377, Blow talk 07:57-08:14 (youtu.be/ZF1m1DsW3Rg), report Docs/research/blow-error-reporting-talk-2026-10-30.md. Related law: D-DIAG-URL1=B (every diagnostic carries a link), D-MARKER-DIAG1=A (#6039, library Diagnostic trait), D-HOOK-STAGES1=A (hook findings are L1401). Build card: #6388. Probe t01_cascade.jet shows today's `More:` line on jet 03c64ad0c4.

options.name: Optional link, plus the explain command
options.detail:
The Diagnostic trait gains an optional constant `more`, an https address. The report prints `More: <more>` and then `(or: jet explain game.FrameHold)`. Without `more`, the report prints `More: jet explain game.FrameHold`.

A third-party page can go dead later. The explain command reads the library's own texts from the installed package, so it still works offline and after the page is gone.

Today a hook finding is message-only and keeps its L1401 code, which already links to Jet's page. If D-REJECT-AT1 adopts Diagnostic findings, they print that value's `more`.
options.technical:
Trait constant `more: String?` with default None, beside `code`, `severity` and `lint_name` (D-MARKER-DIAG1=A). The registry check refuses an address that is not https. Machine output carries `more` and `explain` as two fields, not prose (D-DIAG-URL1 review note).

This amends D-DIAG-URL1=B, which fixes the line as `More: jet-lang.dev/e/<CODE>`. For package codes, A prints `More: <more>  (or: jet explain <code>)`, or `More: jet explain <code>` when there is no link. Jet's own codes keep the ratified line.

`jet explain <package code>` prints what, why and fix from the package's Diagnostic impl, which card #6388 already plans. Message-only hook findings (D-HOOK-STAGES1=A) keep the L1401 line. If D-REJECT-AT1 adopts Diagnostic findings, they print that value's `more` through this same path.

options.name: No link for library errors
options.detail: Library errors print no `More:` line. Only Jet's own codes link. Hook findings keep only their L1401 link.
options.technical: The Diagnostic trait stays as D-MARKER-DIAG1=A ratified it: what, why, fix, code, severity and lint name. The renderer omits the `More:` line when the code is not a Jet registry code.
options.code:
Error [game.FrameHold]: `player` is kept past the frame
 Why: entities may be freed when the frame ends
 Fix: store the entity id

options.name: One link pattern per package
options.detail: The package file gains `error_docs`. Every error code of that package links to that address followed by the code.
options.technical: Package field `error_docs: String?`, an https prefix. The renderer prints `More: <error_docs><code>`. Without the field, no `More:` line is printed.
options.code:
package { name: "game", error_docs: "https://wiki.example.com/e/" }
// More: https://wiki.example.com/e/game.FrameHold

comparisons.note: Every lint ends with a link to its page.
Each rule's metadata can carry its own docs URL, shown by editors.

recommendation.why: It matches the ratified rule that every error ends with a link. It lets a house rule point at the page that explains it.
gains: Library errors read like Jet's own.
No library is forced to host pages.

whyNot.reason: It breaks the ratified rule that every error carries a link, and hides the explanation Blow's example relies on.
It forces one address layout on every package, even when the explanation already lives elsewhere.

recommendation.tradeoff: None remains. A library without a page, or with a page that later vanishes, still gets a working `jet explain` line.

decisions.title: Users build tensors through core.compute functions; a Tensor's storage is private to Core
decisions.situation: A Tensor must remember two receipts: why it sits on its device, and what its last transfer moved. Today Tensor is a record with five fields that user code can name, read and overwrite. There is no place for the receipts, and user code can forge a placement. The vote decides where the receipts live and whether user code keeps the Tensor literal. We recommend that tensors come only from core.compute functions.
decisions.gist: Should user code keep writing Tensor{...} literals, or build every tensor through core.compute?
decisions.lesson: A tensor is numbers in a shape, placed on a device. core.compute already builds every tensor a program needs, with checks: zeros, full, from_list, matrix, eye, reshape. A literal skips those checks and lets code claim a device or a profile the data never had.
decisions.story: Ana loads a model on the CPU and moves it to CUDA. She prints transfer_show to see how many bytes moved. Under A the receipt comes from the move itself, because no code outside Core can write a Tensor's fields.
decisions.inWild:
# NumPy: arrays come from constructors, not from field literals
import numpy as np
a = np.zeros((2, 2))
b = np.array([1.0, 2.0]).reshape(2, 1)
decisions.detail:
Today, measured on f3bfe8ca7b plus wave 2 (lane GoldC p0 build, probe tmp/pv). The registry row CoreRecordLiteralRow Tensor is not core_only (CoreRecordRows.jet:1015). So user code may write `Tensor{shape:, data:, device:, numeric_profile:, requested:}`. The same rows let user code read and assign every field: `a.requested = "Metal"` changes what `compute.placement(a)` reports. Tensor has no ==, Display or Debug today (E0312, E0915, E0112).

Law. core-library.md:4285-4287 makes the registered compute vocabulary the sole owner of tensors, devices, streams and receipts. Lines 4288-4292 say placement and receipts use the real provider. Lines 4308-4309 and 4327 fix the signatures of transfer, transfer_show and deserialize.

What needs the storage. transfer_show reports the last transfer's receipt, else the placement (Rust oracle Compute.rs:8398-8403). transfer and deserialize set the placement reason (Compute.rs:8374-8378, 9935). The Rust oracle kept both per tensor and compared them in equality (Compute.rs:4034-4042).

Elsewhere. NumPy, PyTorch and Rust ndarray build arrays only through constructors and keep the storage private. PyTorch changes a device only through .to(), which returns a new tensor. None of them offers a literal that names storage fields. Jet's own ComputeDevice and ComputeStream already follow that rule.

Five fixture files use the literal. Two are the corpus files core/compute/solve/dense.jet and lu.jet. Three are the tier copies of the core_compute_solve case fixture, which also read `.data`. No file under Core (outside Compute.jet), Examples or Docs reads `.numeric_profile` or `.requested`.

ComputeDevice, ComputeStream and SparseTensor are already opaque: user code gets E0119 on a literal and E0302 on a field read. Main approved private storage for them; they are not on this ballot.

options.name: Tensors come only from core.compute functions
options.detail:
The Tensor literal and its fields become private to Core, like ComputeDevice and ComputeStream today. User code builds tensors with zeros, ones, full, from_list, vec, matrix, eye and reshape, and reads them with shape, to_list, device and placement.

Core keeps the receipts in fields no user code can reach.
options.technical: CoreRecordLiteralRow Tensor gets core_only true (existing form, as TextError and RangeError). Field rows gain a core_only flag, so non-Core reads and writes report E0302. CompilerOwned Tensor row adds reason and transfer. The five fixture files switch to compute.full / from_list + reshape; their expected output is unchanged.
options.code:
a :: compute.from_list([1.0, 2.0]) ?? panic("a")
m :: compute.reshape(a, [2, 1]) ?? panic("shape")
moved :: compute.transfer(m, compute.device_cpu()) ?? panic("move")
print(compute.transfer_show(moved))
// Transfer(from=CPU, to=CPU, bytes=0, fallback=none)

options.name: Hidden receipt fields the literal never names
options.detail:
Tensor gains two fields, the placement reason and the last transfer receipt. User code cannot name, read or write them. A user literal still lists the five fields of today, and the two hidden fields start empty.

The five named fields stay readable and writable by user code, as today.
options.technical: New registry form: a CoreRecordFieldRow with core_only true and a literal default (""). Sema rejects a non-Core read, write or literal mention with E0302 or E0119. CompilerOwned Tensor row grows to seven fields; the literal lowers the two defaults. The five public fields keep their rows.

options.name: Receipts travel as separate return values
options.detail:
Tensor stays exactly as today. transfer returns the moved tensor together with its receipt, and transfer_show takes that receipt. deserialize returns the tensor together with its placement reason.

The Tensor literal and its five fields stay open to user code.
options.technical: New registered record TransferReceipt{from, to, bytes, fallback}, opaque to users. transfer(tensor, target) -> (Tensor, TransferReceipt) !ComputeError; transfer_show(receipt: TransferReceipt) -> String; deserialize(text) -> (Tensor, String) !ComputeError. Amends core-library.md:4308-4309 and :4327.
options.code:
a :: compute.from_list([1.0, 2.0]) ?? panic("a")
(moved, receipt) :: compute.transfer(a, compute.device_cpu()) ?? panic("move")
print(compute.transfer_show(receipt))
// Transfer(from=CPU, to=CPU, bytes=0, fallback=none)
(back, reason) :: compute.deserialize(text) ?? panic("read")

comparisons.note: Arrays come from constructors such as np.array, np.zeros and np.full. Shape and dtype are set through checked calls, not a field literal. Source: numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/routines.array-creation.html.
A tensor's device is read through t.device and changed only by t.to(device), which returns a new tensor. Source: pytorch.org/docs/stable/tensor_attributes.html.
comparisons.code:
t = torch.ones(2, 2)
g = t.to("cuda")
g.device   # cuda:0

comparisons.note: Array fields are private; arrays are built with Array::from_shape_vec, zeros or from_elem, which check the shape. Source: docs.rs/ndarray (ArrayBase).

recommendation.why: A gives tensors one owner, as the spec already says. Every tensor passes the same checks, and receipts cannot be forged. ComputeDevice and ComputeStream already follow this rule, as do NumPy, PyTorch and Rust ndarray.
gains: Every tensor is checked when it is made.
Receipts always describe what really happened.
One rule for every compute type.

whyNot.reason: B adds a new registry form for hidden fields and still lets user code write device and requested, so placement can still be forged.
C changes three public signatures and makes every caller carry a receipt it may not want. The open literal stays.

recommendation.tradeoff: Five test fixtures switch from a Tensor literal to compute.full or from_list. Their expected output does not change.

decisions.title: Release builds carry a crash report of addresses and a build id, 840 bytes in hello; Jet's tools add the names
decisions.situation:
Every Jet program catches a crash and prints where it happened. Today that report is about 30 KB. The last draft rebuilt it in 2,197 bytes, and you asked us to start from hand-written assembly and justify every byte above it.

We did. Hello's floor is 253 bytes. The release report now prints the signal, the build id and the frame addresses in 840 bytes, so release hello is 1,185 bytes. Names and lines come from the side file through `jet crash`, and dev and test builds keep today's full text.
decisions.gist: Should release builds carry an 840-byte crash report of addresses and a build id, with Jet's tools adding the names?
decisions.lesson: When a native program touches memory it must not, the system stops it with a signal. A crash report catches the signal and prints where it happened. Turning an address into a function name and line needs a table. That table can stay in the program, or live in a side file that a tool reads later.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. The floor is hello written by hand in assembly: 253 bytes, with a non-executable stack. A frame address is where each active function will return to. A build id is a 20-byte hash in the binary that names its side file, the file holding names and lines. `jet crash` reads a pasted report, finds that side file by build id and prints names and lines.

E3012 is Jet's stack overflow stop. A dev build is what `jet run`, `jet test` and `jet dev` make; a release build is `jet build --release`.
decisions.story: Ana ships a status tool to tiny devices. Hello-sized tools were 134 KB with a 30 KB crash report; the release report is now 840 bytes. When a Jet bug crashes one device, the report gives the signal, the build id and four addresses. She pastes it into `jet crash` and gets the function names and lines, exactly as `jet run` would have printed them.
decisions.detail:
The floor. Hello written by hand is 253 bytes: ELF header, one code segment, a non-executable stack, the SIGPIPE ignore, the write loop, exit and the text. The proposal measured it with asm-floor.mjs (Docs/proposals/hello-size-architecture-2026-10-30.md).

What the release report keeps. It catches SIGSEGV, SIGBUS, SIGILL and SIGFPE. It prints the signal line exactly as today, then the build id and the frame addresses. Then it re-raises the signal, so the exit status and any core dump are unchanged. A stack overflow still stops with E3012 and exit 70, with the faulting address.

What it leaves to the side file. Finding the function and line, reading the source line and printing the snippet move into `jet crash`. So does the Why and Fix text, which `jet crash` prints from the code alone. In hello this removes 1,357 bytes of code and text and the 67-byte table. In the release HTTP server the table alone is 91,771 bytes.

Measured. The prototype in ballot/rep/report.S builds every variant, links them and runs each fault. Today's text with names is 2,197 bytes. The release report is 1,139 bytes and 926 when the stack bound is proven. Hello's form, single-threaded with no Secret or buffered output, is 840 bytes with no writable data.

Hello's budget above the floor, 932 bytes. Build id note and header, 92. Installing the four handlers, 62. Capturing the signal, address and frame, 71. Choosing and printing the signal line, 239, of which 160 is the four lines' text. The template printer and stderr writer, 134. Re-raising the signal, 37. Printing the build id, 92. Walking the frames and printing addresses in hex, 205.

Paid only when a program uses the feature, measured by variant. Code that can overflow the stack pays 200 bytes and one 8-byte word for E3012 and the alternate stack. Threads pay 27 and a word for the one-report claim. Secret pays 27 and a word to scrub on a crash; buffered stdout pays 14 and a word to flush it. The first word adds a 56-byte writable segment header in a program with none. The backtrace mode is a build option fixed in the code, so it costs nothing.

Why each part stays. Without the handler a Jet bug prints only "Segmentation fault", and the user cannot tell Jet's bug from theirs. The addresses and build id are the least that lets `jet crash` name the frames. Every other byte prints them or restores the exit status.

Dev builds. `jet run`, `jet test` and `jet dev` build with names inside, so they print today's full text: 2,197 bytes of report plus the table. Every golden test of crash text stays byte for byte, as the 16 parity cases in report/check.mjs showed.

Peers. Zig's ReleaseSmall hello is 10,720 bytes and C with musl at -Os is 17,696; neither has a crash handler. Rust and Go print no Jet-style frames. Release Jet hello at 1,185 bytes is smaller than both and still reports.

Landing. The compiler emits the report as machine code with relocations to the build id, as the prototype links it. It replaces Fault.jet in plan stage S3. The release form needs the Fault report section of Docs/spec/diagnostics.md to gain the build id line and the address frames.

options.name: Release builds print addresses and a build id; Jet's tools add names
options.detail:
Release builds carry the small report: the signal line, the build id and the frame addresses. Hello is 1,185 bytes, 932 above the hand-written floor, and every byte is justified by what it prints.

A program pays more only for the features it uses: stack overflow, threads, Secret or buffered output. `jet crash` turns a pasted report into today's full text from the side file. `jet run`, `jet test` and `jet dev` print today's full text directly.
options.technical: The compiler emits the report as machine code, chosen per program from five facts. They are the build kind, a proven stack bound, threads, Secret and buffered stdout, and they select E3012, the claim word, the scrub and the flush. Frames come from the frame-pointer chain, and Jet images are fixed-address, so the addresses are the side file's. Release builds load no location table. Dev builds emit the 2,197-byte full report and its table.

options.name: Every build keeps the full report and its table inside
options.detail:
Every build, release included, prints today's full text with names, lines and source. The report is 2,197 bytes plus the location table, which loads with the program.

Hello is about 2,599 bytes, 2,346 above the floor. The release HTTP server carries a 91,771-byte table that the program reads only when it crashes.
options.technical: The compiler emits the 2,197-byte report in every build, reading the .debug_jetline format from a loaded table found by two link symbols. Programs with a proven stack bound omit E3012 (1,345 bytes).

options.name: One-line note in programs that cannot crash
options.detail:
Programs whose code cannot crash, by a compiler proof, carry a one-line note naming the signal. Hello is 504 bytes. Every other program keeps a full report.

When Jet itself has a bug in such a program, the note shows no frames, and the user must rebuild with `--backtrace=full` and crash again.
options.technical: Link the full report only when the reference graph has recursion, an unbounded stack, unsafe code or FFI. Otherwise install a 257-byte fixed-text handler that writes one line and re-raises the signal.

comparisons.note: Release modes without safety checks link no crash handler. Source: zig 0.16 std/debug.zig, `default_enable_segfault_handler = runtime_safety and have_segfault_handling_support`.
comparisons.code:

// a crash ends with the system's message and the signal status

comparisons.note: A native crash writes a tombstone: the signal, the fault address, each frame's address and the library's build id. `ndk-stack` adds names from the unstripped libraries.
The standard library catches stack overflow only; any other crash gets the system's message. Source: library/std/src/sys/pal/unix/stack_overflow.rs.
comparisons.code:
// a stack overflow: thread 'main' has overflowed its stack
// any other crash: Segmentation fault (core dumped)

comparisons.note: Every binary carries the runtime's crash traceback with names; hello is 1.6 MB. Source: go.dev/doc/diagnostics.
comparisons.code:
// panic: runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference
// goroutine 1 [running]: main.main() /src/hello.go:5 +0x1d

Each feature's bytes appear only in programs using that feature.

decisions.title: The native ray library keeps raylib's names but draws on explicit window and frame values
decisions.situation: Jet is building `ray`, its own game library written in Jet, meant to feel like raylib and beat it. Raylib keeps one hidden global window, so drawing calls take no window and tests cannot run two windows or check pixels. Its colors and keys are plain integers, so a wrong key compiles. This vote fixes the public shape of `ray`: its names, how a program reaches the window and frame, and its types for colors and keys.
decisions.gist: Should `ray` keep raylib's function names but call them on window and frame values, with typed colors and keys?
decisions.lesson: Raylib programs open one window, then draw each frame between begin and end calls on hidden global state. A frame value makes that state visible: the loop hands you the frame, and drawing calls hang off it. A headless window draws the same pixels into memory, so a test can check them exactly.
decisions.story: Mia ports a raylib tutorial. `DrawRectangle(10, 10, 50, 50, RED)` becomes `frame.draw_rectangle(10, 10, 50, 50, .Red)`. Her test opens a headless window, draws one frame, and checks the screenshot's checksum.
decisions.detail:
Today. core.game.raylib exposes 18 functions with raylib-style global drawing: `begin_drawing(window)`, then `draw_rectangle(...)` with no window. Keys and gamepad buttons are strings checked at run time (Core/Game/Raylib.jet:124-176). The library is headless on the native runtime.

What A does. `ray.init_window(w, h, title)` returns a `Window`. `ray.headless_window(w, h)` returns the same type, drawing into memory. `loop frame in win.frames()` runs once per frame and presents when the body ends. The loop stops when the user closes the window.

Names. Every raylib function keeps its name in snake_case and its argument order. Drawing calls hang off `frame`, window and input calls off `win`, and loaders off `ray`. So `DrawCircle(x, y, r, c)` is `frame.draw_circle(x, y, r, c)` and `IsKeyDown(KEY_A)` is `win.is_key_down(.A)`.

Types. `Color` is a struct with raylib's named colors as constants, so `.Red` and `Color{r: 1, g: 2, b: 3, a: 255}` both work. `Key`, `MouseButton` and `GamepadButton` are enums, so a misspelled key is a compile error. Raylib's `Vector2` and `Rectangle` are structs; integer and float overloads both exist.

Effects. Drawing on a frame only writes memory, so it carries no effect and runs in any function or thread. Opening a window, presenting, reading input and playing sound carry `GPU`. Loading files adds `FS`.

Headless capture. `win.load_image_from_screen()` is raylib's own name and returns an `Image`. `image.checksum()` gives a stable hash of its RGBA bytes. The software rasterizer draws identical pixels on every tier and host, so goldens can assert it.

Multi-window. Each `Window` owns its framebuffer, so two headless windows can render in one test, which raylib cannot do.

Peers. Raylib's 70-plus language bindings mostly keep its names, often generated from raylib_api.json. Rust raylib-rs moved drawing onto a `RaylibDrawHandle` from `rl.begin_drawing(&thread)`, the same idea as the frame value. Pygame and LÖVE keep global state, a common complaint when testing.

Edge cases. Drawing outside the framebuffer clips. A frame used after its loop iteration is a compile error, because `frame` is a loop-scoped borrow. `win.frames()` on a closed window yields nothing.

decisions.title: How a derived encode writes an optional field that holds None
decisions.situation: A #Codable struct can have an optional field, like `nickname: String?`. When it holds None, the derived encode can leave the key out, or write it with a null value. The encoder leaves it out today, as the Rust encoder did. One golden expects null, and no spec line says which is right. Industry practice is split by library default, but the style guides and the most common settings leave the key out. We recommend leaving it out, as today.
decisions.gist: When an optional field holds None, does encode leave the key out or write null?
decisions.lesson: A derived encode turns a struct into a tree of keys and values. A format such as JSON or TOML then writes that tree as text. An optional field holds a value or None. JSON can spell None as null. TOML has no null at all, so it can only leave the key out.
decisions.explainer:
You asked what is most common and what the best practice is. Library defaults split. Swift's synthesized Codable, Protocol Buffers' JSON form and JavaScript's JSON.stringify leave an absent optional out. Rust serde, Go encoding/json, Java Jackson and .NET System.Text.Json write null by default.

Each of those four ships a switch to leave the key out, and that switch is the usual setting. The written best practice is the Google JSON Style Guide: drop an empty or null property unless there is a strong reason to keep it. So Jet's default matches the best practice, with no switch to learn.
decisions.story: Ada saves a customer with no nickname and reads the JSON back. Under A she sees no nickname key. Under B she sees "nickname":null. Then she saves the same customer as TOML. Under A the key is missing again. Under B TOML needs a separate rule, because it has no null.
decisions.detail:
Today. The derived encode adds one key per field and adds nothing for an optional field that holds None. The Jet derive says so in Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Registration/SerdeItems.jet lines 421-442. The Rust derive it ports said the same in crates/jet-sema/src/Sema/Registration/Serde.rs lines 1270-1275, at c9129d174d^.

The golden. Examples/features/serde/field_metadata_edges expects `"nickname":null` on lines 2 and 3 of its output. That file was written in a6265a2225 on 2026-10-07. The Rust rule that leaves the key out landed earlier, in c0c5493a97 on 2026-09-29.

A second golden line is not part of this vote. Line 5 expects `found Null`, but the Jet and Rust decoders say `found null`. The Rust word list is DynKind.rs line 5, and Core/Encoding/Encoding.jet line 339 matches it. That line changes to `found null` under either option.

Industry writers. Swift's synthesized Codable encodes an optional with encodeIfPresent, so nil leaves the key out. Proto3 JSON leaves an unset optional field out. JSON.stringify leaves out a property whose value is undefined. Rust serde, Go encoding/json, Jackson and System.Text.Json write null by default.

Their switches. Each of those four has a one-line switch to leave the key out. They are skip_serializing_if, omitempty, JsonInclude NON_NULL and WhenWritingNull. Spring Boot exposes the Jackson one as an application setting. The Google JSON Style Guide says to drop an empty or null property unless there is a strong semantic reason for it.

Industry readers. A missing key reads as None by default in serde, Go, Jackson, System.Text.Json, Swift, proto3 JSON and JavaScript. Two readers differ. Pydantic v2 treats `Optional[str]` with no default as required. Kotlinx.serialization treats a nullable property with no default as required. Both document the fix on the reader side: give the field a None or null default.

Decoding in Jet. Both options read a missing key and a null value as None, so a JSON round trip gives back the same struct either way. A probe on this tree printed `true true true` for a missing key, a null key and a null nested record.

TOML. TOML has no null. Core/Encoding/Toml.jet line 713 writes a null leaf as an empty string. Under B a None nickname would be written as `nickname = ""`. A probe decoded that back as Val(""), not None. So B also needs TOML to drop null keys, or the round trip breaks.

Schemas. A #PublishedSchema decode first tries the current shape, and a missing optional key already passes that check. So neither option changes migration matching for records that decode today.

Who changes. Under A, the golden's lines 2 and 3 drop the nickname key, and no code changes. Under B, the derive writes Dyn.Null for None, and TOML gains a rule that drops null keys. Every encoded record with a None field also grows by one key.

options.name: Leave an absent optional field off the wire
options.detail: An optional field that holds None adds no key. JSON, YAML, TOML and CBOR all write the same set of keys. Jet's decoder reads a missing key and a null value alike, so nothing a Jet program writes or reads changes. This is what the encoder does today, and it matches the Google JSON Style Guide.
options.technical: No compiler or Core change. SerdeItems.jet 421-442 keeps its pattern switch on Val. Golden field_metadata_edges lines 2 and 3 lose `"nickname":null`. The decode side already maps a missing key and a null value to None.

options.name: Write an absent optional field as null
options.detail: An optional field that holds None is written with a null value. JSON and YAML show every declared key. TOML has no null, so it must drop those keys or write a wrong value. Every record with a None field grows by one key per empty field.
options.technical: The derive pushes (key, Dyn.Null) for None in SerdeItems.jet 439-442. Toml.jet stops writing a null leaf as an empty string and drops the key instead. Golden lines 2 and 3 stay as they are.

comparisons.note: A None field is written as null by default. The common opt-out is skip_serializing_if = "Option::is_none". Source: serde.rs/attr-skip-serializing.html.
The synthesized encode calls encodeIfPresent for an optional, so nil leaves the key out. This is option A, with no switch.
An unset optional field is left out of the JSON form by default. Source: protobuf.dev/programming-guides/json, the field presence rules.
A nil pointer is written as null unless the field tag says omitempty, which is the common setting.

recommendation.why: A matches the written best practice and the default of Swift and proto3 JSON. It writes None the same way in every format, including TOML, which has no null. B changes the encoder, needs a TOML rule, and grows records.
gains: No compiler or Core change.
Every format writes None the same way, including TOML.
It is the style-guide rule and Swift's default, with no switch to learn.

losses.loss: A reader that demands every key rejects a record without one.
losses.mitigation: JSON has two spellings of no value, so some reader always wants the other; that reader gives its field a None default.

whyNot.reason: B needs a separate TOML rule, or a None comes back as an empty string. It also grows every record that has a None field, and goes against the style guide.

recommendation.tradeoff: Under A, a foreign reader that demands every key needs a None default on its side. Jet readers and the common foreign readers need nothing.

It hunted for downsides left on A and for open questions, and found the owner's industry question unanswered, a misleading claim that no reader needs the key, and single examples. Each option now has a simple and a complex example, the industry survey is in detail, and the one irreducible reader-side loss carries its reason and mitigation.

decisions.title: `jet audit foreign <entry.jet>` proves a program calls no foreign code and needs no dynamic loader
decisions.situation: Card 5035 asks that the Jet game example make no call into C, and that `jet audit` show it. No Jet command reports this today. `jet audit <file.jet>` reports implicit copies, and the old Rust compiler's audit only checked the lockfile. This vote picks where the foreign-code report lives. We recommend a new `foreign` subject of `jet audit`, next to `copies` and `memory`.
decisions.gist: Where should Jet report that a program has no foreign code: `jet audit foreign`, `jet inspect foreign`, or `jet build --json`?
decisions.lesson: Foreign code is code Jet did not compile from Jet source: a C library, an inline C body, or a Rust helper. A program with none links as one static file, and no dynamic loader runs before it. The checker already knows each foreign declaration and the `FFI` effects a program reaches. The built file shows whether the operating system must load anything else.
decisions.story: Ana ships the Jet game example to a locked-down kiosk. She runs `jet audit foreign Examples/features/game/raylib_indexed/run.jet` and reads `foreign code: none`, `dynamic loader: none`. Her review closes without reading the runtime source.
decisions.inWild:
# Rust: list the C libraries a crate links
cargo tree -e normal,build | grep -- '-sys'

# Any ELF: does it need a dynamic loader?
readelf -l ./app | grep INTERP
readelf -d ./app | grep NEEDED
decisions.detail:
Today. `jet audit` has three subjects: `copies`, `memory`, and a bare `.jet` file that means `copies` (Docs/spec/reference/cli.md:767-781). No command lists foreign declarations, reached `FFI` effects or the built file's loader needs together. Readers must combine `jet inspect rights`, `readelf` and source search.

What A does. `jet audit foreign [--json] [<entry.jet>]` checks and builds the entry. It reports four facts. They are the foreign declarations (`#Import(c)`, `#FFI(c)`, Rust helpers) with their sites, and the `FFI` effects the entry reaches. They also include the C libraries the link adds, and the built file's loader needs. The last line reads `foreign code: none` only when all four are empty. The exit code is 0 when the report runs, so a CI script reads the verdict from `--json`.

Why audit. `jet audit copies` and `jet audit memory` already answer "does this program do X anywhere" for one entry, and the card names `jet audit`.

Why check the built file. A declaration list cannot see a loader that the link step adds. Reading the ELF program headers proves what the operating system will do.

Effects. The command reads files and runs the native build into a temporary folder. It never runs the program.

Edge cases. A Core module that wraps a vendored C library, such as SQLite, counts as foreign when the program imports it. A web or interpreter target has no ELF file, so the loader line reads `not built for this target`.

decisions.title: Jet publishes one small, complete set of FFI building blocks, and every binding is made from them
decisions.situation: Every Jet binding to another language is built from a few low-level steps, such as a type's C layout, a symbol lookup, a call and a callback. Today those steps live inside the compiler. A user who needs one writes C by hand, for example to open a library chosen at run time. The FFI proposal for card #6366 asks for a public, documented set, so every wrapper is a recipe you can repeat. We recommend the complete set in a new `core.ffi` package, with unsafe steps behind `#Unsafe("reason")`.
decisions.gist: Should Jet publish the low-level FFI steps that every binding is built from?
decisions.lesson: A foreign function interface (FFI) lets a program call code written in another language. Easy forms, like importing a C header, are built from small steps. Examples are a type's memory layout, a symbol's address, a call and a callback. If those steps are public, an expert can do anything a wrapper does. If they are hidden, the expert must leave the language.
decisions.story: Priya's audio app loads effect plugins that users drop into a folder, so the library name is only known at run time. Today she writes 40 lines of C with dlopen and dlsym and imports that file. Under A she writes the same thing in Jet with `ffi.Library.open` and one `#Unsafe` block, and `jet audit` lists it.
decisions.detail:
What the proposal says. Docs/proposals/ffi-perfect-boundary-2026-10-30.md section 4 lists about twelve building blocks. Every wrapper must expand into them, and `jet inspect bind <name>` must show that expansion. If a reader needs a step the list cannot express, that is a bug in the list, not a reason for a private hook.

What Jet has today. D-RAWPTR2 gave public raw pointers behind `#Unsafe`. D-FFI-BINDER1 made readers ordinary packages that call `foreign.read`. Layout and ABI queries, dynamic symbols, closures as callbacks, errno capture and user-written conversions are compiler-private or missing (proposal section 9, row "Public primitives layer").

What A means. A new package `core.ffi` holds the full set. Compile-time queries are safe: `ffi.layout<T>(target:)` and `ffi.abi(target:)`, plus `Contract` values with `read`, `merge`, `verify` and `hash`.

A's run-time steps are `ffi.Library.open(path)`, `lib.symbol<Sig>(name)` and `FnPtr<Sig>` calls. Closures pass to C through `ffi.thunk(f)`. Error capture uses `.Errno`, `.LastError`, `.NSError` or `.HResult`. Unwind policy and thread affinity are set per row. Async foreign code bridges through `ffi.completion<T>()`, and conversions through the `Marshal` trait.

A's safety rule. A step that can break memory safety is callable only inside `#Unsafe("reason")`. That covers opening a library, taking a symbol by name, and handing over a raw callback pointer. Creating a thunk, capturing errno and asking a layout are safe.

What B means. Only the compile-time half is public: `layout`, `abi` and `Contract`. Reader packages can use them. Run-time steps stay inside the compiler. An expert who needs a run-time library, a closure callback or errno writes a C file and imports it with `use "src/x.c"` (D-FFI-CINPUT1).

What C means. Nothing new is public. Readers keep `foreign.read`, experts keep inline C and C files, and each new need becomes a compiler change.

Beginner and expert paths. A beginner writes `use "png.h" as png` under every option and never sees `core.ffi`. An expert under A climbs one rung at a time: the wrapper, then `jet inspect bind` to see its steps, then the same steps by hand.

Edge cases. A symbol that is missing at run time returns an error from `lib.symbol`, and a weak symbol declared optional returns `T?`. A wrong signature on `lib.symbol` is undefined behaviour, which is why it needs `#Unsafe`. The hardened profile (D-HARDENED1) checks those calls at the edge.

More edge cases. A thunk is an owned value, so dropping it unregisters the callback. A C API that keeps a callback beyond the call needs a `retained` fact or a vouch. On the web target `ffi.Library.open` is a compile error naming the target, because browsers cannot load native code.

Amends. A and B amend no ratified decision. They extend D-RAWPTR2 and D-FFI-BINDER1. C leaves the proposal's "no cliff" goal (G5) unmet.

Prior art. Java's FFM API is a complete public set (Linker, FunctionDescriptor, MemoryLayout, Arena), and jextract is the wrapper on top (https://openjdk.org/jeps/454). .NET shows its generated marshalling code and accepts custom marshallers (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/native-interop/custom-marshalling-source-generation). LuaJIT and Python cffi expose the steps with no safety.

Review. Author: Claude (BugSweep lane), from the #6366 proposal. No fresh adversarial pass has run on this draft yet.

decisions.title: Release builds ship only the bytes that run; debug info goes to a side file Jet keeps
decisions.situation:
A release build is the binary people ship. Today it also carries 662 KB that the running program never reads: debugger info, a symbol table and the crash table. In the 3.12 MB release HTTP server that is 21% of the file.

You asked whether this inflates deliverables, and it does. We now recommend that a release binary carries only its code and data, plus a 36-byte build id. Everything else goes to a side file that Jet files in a local symbol store under that id. Jet's tools read the store, so crash reports, gdb and profilers still show names and lines.
decisions.gist: Should a release binary carry only the bytes that run, with debug info in a side file that Jet keeps and finds by build id?
decisions.lesson: Debug info maps machine code back to source. A program never reads it while it runs; only tools do, such as a debugger, a profiler or a crash report reader. So it can live in a second file, if the tools can always find the right one. A build id is a hash of the binary stored inside it, so a tool can match the binary to its exact debug file.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A release build is `jet build --release`. Debugger info is DWARF, read by gdb, lldb, perf and addr2line. The symbol table (.symtab) names every function for those tools. The crash table (.debug_jetline) is Jet's own list of function names and lines, read by the crash report.

A side file holds those three next to the binary. A build id is a 20-byte hash in a note the loader maps, so it is also in every core dump. The symbol store is a folder, .jet/symbols, laid out the way gdb's debug-file-directory expects. Debuginfod is the HTTP protocol gdb uses to fetch debug files by build id.
decisions.story: Ana ships an HTTP server built with `jet build --release`. It is 2.46 MB, and nothing in it is debug info. One night it crashes on a server. The report gives the build id and the addresses, and she pastes it into `jet crash`, which prints the usual Jet report with names and lines. A week later it hangs, and `jet debug` attaches gdb with the side file found by build id.
decisions.detail:
What a release binary holds today. Measured on the stage-1 compiler of this lane's tree (jet 3f14a7012aa876f1), `jet build --release` of http_server.jet gives 3,124,896 bytes. The loaded code and data are 2,463,080 of that. The rest is never read by the running program.

The non-running bytes. DWARF is 337,800 bytes: .debug_info 146,123, .debug_line 150,573, .debug_loclists 40,686 and .debug_abbrev 418. The symbol table is 231,704: .symtab 129,624 and .strtab 102,080. The crash table is 91,771. Section names and headers are the remaining 541.

Each variant, measured with binutils on that file. Without DWARF: 2,771,016. Without DWARF and the crash table, keeping symbols: 2,679,160. With nothing but code and data: 2,463,080, that is 661,816 bytes or 21.2% smaller.

The build id. A GNU build-id note is 36 bytes: a 12-byte header, "GNU" and a 20-byte hash. It needs one PT_NOTE program header, 56 bytes, so loaders and core dumps carry it. That is 92 bytes in all, computed from the ELF layout; Jet writes no note today.

The side file. objcopy --only-keep-debug writes all three tables into one file of 647,128 bytes. With its DWARF sections zlib-compressed, the form gdb reads directly, it is 398,080. Under xz it is 186,184.

How tools find it. gdb looks for .build-id/xx/rest.debug under its debug-file-directory and asks debuginfod servers by build id. The previous version of this ballot observed with gdb 17.2 that a side file restores `break http_server.jet:28` and `info args`. perf reads the same build-id layout.

Why a rebuild can stand in for a lost store. Jet's compiler is deterministic: the stage-2 and stage-3 compilers of every chain build are byte-identical. Rebuilding the same source with the same compiler therefore gives the same build id and side file. User programs go through the same code generator and linker, so this is inferred for them, not yet measured.

The crash report. D-RT-DEFECT-REPORT1 makes the in-program report print the signal, the build id and the frame addresses. Under `jet run`, `jet test` and `jet dev`, Jet prints today's full report from the side file instead. So a beginner sees no change.

What else stays. The unwind table (.eh_frame, 63,048 bytes) is loaded and used by the runtime, so it is not debug info and is not part of this vote. The 2026-10-09 owner rule kept .symtab in every binary; this ballot replaces that default for release builds.

Bug fixed under every option. `debug_info: false` must drop the debug records of Core and the runtime too. Today it removes only the package's own and leaves 342,701 bytes in the release HTTP server.

options.name: Ship only the bytes that run; debug info in a side file Jet keeps
options.detail:
A release binary holds its code, data and a 36-byte build id: 2,463,172 bytes for the HTTP server, 21% smaller than today. The build also writes http_server.debug beside it and files a copy in .jet/symbols under the build id.

Jet's tools find the side file by that id. `jet run`, `jet test` and `jet dev` print the full crash report with names, lines and source. `jet crash` turns a pasted report from a shipped binary into the same text. `jet debug` starts gdb or lldb with the side file, for a binary, a core dump or a running process.

For a machine that cannot see the store, `jet symbols serve` serves it over debuginfod, which gdb reads. A lost store is rebuilt from the same source, because Jet builds are deterministic and the build id proves the match.
options.technical:
debug_info gets a third value, `split`, the stock under `--release`; plain `jet build`, `jet run`, `jet dev` and `jet test` keep `true`. With `split`, StaticLink writes DWARF, .symtab and .debug_jetline to `<name>.debug`, writes a .note.gnu.build-id under one PT_NOTE, and leaves no section headers beyond what the loader needs.

The store is .jet/symbols/.build-id/xx/rest.debug, the layout gdb's debug-file-directory reads. Its DWARF sections are zlib-compressed, 398 KB for the HTTP server. `jet clean` keeps side files whose build id appears in a release record. `backtrace: full` stays legal with `split`. The `debug_info: false` fix applies here too.

Release binaries keep DWARF, the symbol table and the crash table, as today. The HTTP server is 3,124,896 bytes, 662 KB more than A. gdb, perf and the crash report work on the shipped file alone, with no store and no side file.

Every deliverable pays those bytes even though the program never reads them. The expert who wants a small file sets `debug_info: false` and loses names everywhere.
options.technical: No change to the build options table or the linker. StaticLink keeps writing the DWARF sections, .debug_jetline, .symtab and .strtab, pruned to live functions. The `debug_info: false` fix still applies.

options.detail:
Release binaries drop DWARF and keep the symbol table and the crash table. The HTTP server is 2,771,016 bytes, 308 KB more than A. The crash report and perf name functions on the shipped file, but gdb cannot break on a line or show variables.

Debugging a shipped binary by line needs a rebuild with `debug_info: true` and a repeat of the problem.
options.technical: The `debug_info` row gets a value `crash_table`, the stock under `--release`. StaticLink writes .debug_jetline, .symtab and .strtab and skips the four DWARF sections. The `debug_info: false` fix still applies.

comparisons.note: Release builds write DWARF to a .dSYM bundle. Crash reports carry the binary's UUID and are symbolized later with the matching .dSYM.
Fedora and Debian ship stripped binaries. gdb fetches each debug file by build id from a debuginfod server.
`go build` keeps DWARF and symbols in every binary. A smaller file needs `-ldflags="-s -w"`, which drops them with no side file.
comparisons.code:
$ go build ./cmd/server                    # DWARF kept
$ go build -ldflags="-s -w" ./cmd/server   # dropped

comparisons.note: Since Cargo 1.77 the release profile strips debug info unless it sets `debug = true`. `split-debuginfo` can write it to a side file instead.

recommendation.why: A ships only the bytes that run, 21% less for the HTTP server, and keeps every debugging path. Jet's tools find the side file by build id, so crash reports and gdb still show names and lines.
gains: The HTTP server ships 662 KB smaller, with no debug info at all.
jet run and jet crash print today's full crash report, names and lines.
gdb, perf and core dumps find the side file by build id.

losses.loss: A host with neither the store nor a debuginfod link shows addresses only.
losses.mitigation: The names are the 662 KB removed; jet crash, jet symbols serve or a deterministic rebuild restores them.

whyNot.reason: Every deliverable carries 662 KB that the program never reads, about a fifth of the HTTP server.
It still ships 308 KB of tables, and gdb loses lines and variables anyway.

recommendation.tradeoff: Debugging a shipped binary needs the store, a debuginfod link, or a rebuild of the same source. Jet's tools find all three by build id.
