decisions.title: What does a derive with no trait become when the derive word retires?
decisions.situation: D-DECL-TYPES1 A makes a derive a trait that implements Derive: impl Equatable.Derive { fn expand(target: Target) { ... } }. But every user derive in the repository today is a provider with no trait at all. For example, derive T.DebugText adds a debug_string method, derive T.FieldNames adds one method per field, and derive T.LayoutFacts adds only constants. There are 40 such declarations in 37 files: 8 examples, 3 perf constructs, and the rest tests. None of them names a trait, so impl X.Derive has nothing to attach to.
decisions.gist: Should a derive that has no trait become a marker that writes the code?
decisions.lesson: A derive writes code onto a type when you mark it, as in #DebugText struct Point. Under D-DECL-TYPES1 A, a derive belongs to a trait. A marker can also write code onto the item it marks, through its expand template (rule 6).
decisions.story: Lee's package has derive T.FieldNames, which writes field_x and field_y methods onto any struct marked #FieldNames. The method names depend on the fields, so no fixed trait can describe them. When the derive word retires, Lee needs a form that still writes those methods.
decisions.detail:
WHAT IS ALREADY RATIFIED

D-DECL-TYPES1 A rule 9: a trait becomes derivable by implementing Derive, whose one requirement is fn expand(target: Target). The derive and derives words retire. Rule 6: a marker's expand(self, target: Target) is a template, and every declaration in it, including impl $name blocks, is added at the marker's site. Rule 9 also keeps CLI(pack:) and Receipt(name:) as struct markers that write impls.

WHAT IS OPEN

No rule says what jet fix writes for a derive with no trait. The Prelude's two derives, Equatable and Comparable, are compiler-known traits and are not affected.

CENSUS

At dev 2d8aea4762: 40 user derive declarations in 37 files, all trait-less. Some write a fixed method (DebugText), some write methods with pasted names (FieldNames), and some write only constants (LayoutFacts).

options.name: A marker struct that writes the code
options.detail: A derive with no trait becomes a marker: a field-less struct with impl Marker { sites :: [.Type] } and an expand template that writes impl $target { ... }. Writing #DebugText on a type is unchanged. A derive whose name is a trait becomes impl X.Derive, as rule 9 says. jet fix picks the form by checking whether a trait of that name exists.
options.technical: Uses only ratified forms (rule 6 markers, rule 9 derives). The derive orphan rule (E2711) and the derive collision checks apply to the trait form only; a provider that becomes a marker follows the marker rules. Their UI snapshots change wording.

options.name: jet fix writes a trait for it
options.detail: jet fix writes a new trait from the methods the derive adds (trait DebugText { fn debug_string(self) -> String }) and turns the derive into impl DebugText.Derive. A derive whose methods depend on the fields (FieldNames) or that adds only constants (LayoutFacts) has no fixed method list, so it still becomes a marker as in A.
options.technical: Adds a trait per provider with a fixed method list. Two forms remain for user code that writes methods onto a type, and jet fix must decide which one applies to each provider.

options.name: Keep a trait-less derive form
options.detail: A provider keeps a derive form without a trait, such as impl Derive for a field-less struct named after the request. Derive then has two shapes, one with a trait and one without.
options.technical: Needs a new rule for Derive on a struct, against rule 14 (a struct implements at most one of the four roles, and Derive is the trait-only role).

recommendation.why: A uses only forms that are already ratified. A derive stays tied to a trait, and code that just writes methods onto a type is a marker, which rule 6 already lets write impl blocks.
gains: No new trait or new rule.
One mechanical fix, chosen by whether a trait of that name exists.

losses.loss: Derive-only checks (the orphan rule E2711 and the derive collision checks) no longer apply to these 40 providers.
losses.mitigation: The marker rules cover the same sites, and expand output is checked like any other code.

whyNot.reason: B invents traits nobody asked for, and still needs A for providers with pasted names or only constants.
C gives Derive a second shape and breaks rule 14.

recommendation.tradeoff: Derive-only checks stop applying to trait-less providers, in exchange for using only ratified forms.

decisions.title: Where does a module's and a package's metadata live, and how do you set it?
decisions.situation: A package and a module each have a body: metadata fields first, then bindings. package.jet and module.jet are bodies with implicit braces; in any other file you write name :: package { ... } or name :: module { ... } and the metadata goes inside the braces. Every example uses the planned binding form, where every named thing is a constant bound with ::. The options differ only in how you read the fields.
decisions.gist: Should a module's metadata fields be read directly, as pricing.category, or only through #module(pricing)?
decisions.lesson: A module groups functions under one name, such as pricing. A package is a project with a package.jet file. Both have metadata: a name, a file, docs, a version and a license. This vote decides how you set and read it.
decisions.story: Mia's shop has a pricing module and an old discount module she wants to retire. Her About screen shows her version, authors and the version of the json package she uses. She marks discount as deprecated so its callers get a warning.
decisions.inWild:
Python: a module keeps its metadata in reserved double-underscore names, such as __name__, __doc__ and __file__.
Rust: Cargo exposes package fields such as CARGO_PKG_VERSION as text, one macro read per field.
Jai: a module is a constant, Basic :: #import "Basic", and module settings are written where it is imported.
decisions.detail:
YOUR RULE

A package in package.jet and a module in module.jet are implicitly wrapped in braces: the whole file is the body. A package or module written in any other file wraps its body in braces, as name :: package { ... } or name :: module { ... }. The metadata and optional fields go in the body, first, followed by the bindings. Both options follow this rule exactly; they differ only in how you read the fields.

THE FORM EVERY EXAMPLE USES

D-DECL-BINDING1=B is ratified: every named thing is a constant bound with ::. A function is total :: fn(text: String) -> Int { ... }, a type is Module :: struct { ... }, and a module bound in a file is discount :: module { ... }. The file-module line, module pricing, stays as that ruling kept it, and finds pricing.jet or pricing/module.jet as today. Lambdas are fn(n) { n + 1 } (D-LAMBDA-SHAPE1=C). None of the proposed forms is built yet, so every proposed example is marked not built.

THE BODY

A package body or module body holds field lines first, then bindings. A field line is name: value, the line form package.jet already uses. A binding is name :: value or name := value.

- package.jet: the file is the package body. Its field lines are today's package.jet lines.

- pricing/module.jet: the file is the module body. category: "billing" at its top sets a field.

- Any other file: discount :: module { category: "billing" ... total :: fn ... } and tool :: package { name: "tool" ... }. The fields go inside the braces, first.

A module's fields are those of the built-in type Module: name, file, doc, package, maturity, category and deprecated. name, file, doc and package are filled by the compiler. maturity, category and deprecated have defaults, so you opt in only to the ones you want. A package's fields are the Package fields package.jet has today, plus authors.

WHAT A MEANS

The fields are the module's own. You read pricing.category, and describe(pricing) passes the module to a function that takes a Module. You read your own package as #package.version and a dependency's as json.package.version.

WHY NOT B, READ THROUGH #module

B writes the bodies and field lines exactly as A, but reads a module's fields only as #module(pricing).category. A module member may then use any name, so nothing is renamed. The cost is a second, longer read form, and a module no longer passes as a Module itself.

THE CLASH RULE IN A, EXACTLY

In every module body, the seven names name, file, doc, package, maturity, category and deprecated are fields. A binding in a module body with one of those names is the generic duplicate-name error, E0105, which lists the module's fields.

Nothing else is touched: locals, parameters, struct fields, methods, types and struct members may use all seven names. Package fields never clash, because they are read through package or #package. The list is closed; your own metadata is an ordinary constant, such as OWNER :: "billing team".

Today 9 module-level items use name or file, out of 59,105, including Core/Files/Path.jet:102 and Core/Sys/Sys.jet:286; jet fix renames them and their callers once.

FIELD LINES

Field lines come first in the body: at the top of package.jet or module.jet, after the /// comment, or right after the opening brace. Each field is written at most once, and the value must have the field's type, so category: 3 is a type error.

Writing a compiler-filled field, such as name: "x", is the generic error for a read-only field. Any other name, such as limit: 5, is the generic error that lists the legal forms: name :: value, name := value, or a field line.

EDGE CASES

- deprecated makes every use from another module warn, as #Deprecated warns today. It never fails the build.

- A module's doc is the /// comment at the top of module.jet, or the one above name :: module { ... }.

- A function that takes Module sees only the seven fields, as a trait value sees only its trait's members.

- A dependency's Package is read-only. json.package.authority shows json's rules; only json's own build applies them.

- Old package.jet files keep working, because every new field has a default.

- Module and Package live in core.meta, not the Prelude. Reading their fields needs no import; naming the type does, as run.jet's use line shows.

- Every field is known while building. Metadata ships in the program only where code reads it.

BEGINNER AND EXPERT

A beginner writes no field lines in a module, because every field has a default, and prints #package.version on an About screen. An expert opts in to category, maturity or deprecated and passes modules to tools that take a Module.

WHAT RUNS TODAY

Probes are in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Research/ballots-2026-11-05/modvalue and modvalue3, run with the pinned compiler (jet@0.0.1#006bccd5).

- f01 and f05: a category: "billing" line is an error today, at file top and inside a module. The line form is free.

- f02 and f03: square :: fn(...) and pricing :: module { ... } are not built yet; both are parse errors today.

- f07: a repeated module-level name is E0105, "defined twice".

- m01_today prints 3, standard rules, m01_today and 0.0.0. Only $package.name and $package.version are readable; $package.license is E0107.

- Today module pricing finds pricing.jet, then pricing/module.jet (Compiler/JetDriver Loader.jet:2276-2287).

RATIFIED DECISIONS IT TOUCHES

All code is in D-DECL-BINDING1=B and D-LAMBDA-SHAPE1=C form. Both options use D-ECO-FILEROOT1 for the Package value. B adds #module(m) beside the ratified #package (D-META-HASH1=A). D-MARK-META1=B's law that behavior-free metadata is a #Meta field still holds for functions and types; for packages and modules the metadata is a field of the body. Choice point C2 of Docs/proposals/effect-types-2026-10-29.md is answered: modules are first-class values.

options.name: A module's fields are read directly
options.detail: A package or module body holds its metadata fields first: implicit braces in package.jet and module.jet, explicit braces in any other file. You read pricing.category, and a module passes as a Module. The seven field names are taken in module bodies, so 9 items are renamed once.
options.technical: Sema gives each module the fields of core.meta.Module, filled from the file or binding, owning package, /// comment and the body's field lines. A field line is name: value at the top of a body, before any binding, checked against the field type. A binding in a module body named like a field is E0105. Package is PackageFacts' fields plus authors. #package is that value. All values are known while building.

options.name: Same bodies, fields read only through #module
options.detail: Bodies and field lines are exactly as in A, but a module's fields are read as #module(pricing).category. A module member may use any name, so nothing is renamed. Every outside read is longer, and a module does not pass as a Module itself.
options.technical: As A for bodies, field lines and types. The fields are not members of the module type. #module(m) is a new form that returns m's Module value; bare #module is the module where it is written. Nothing is reserved.

comparisons.note: Python reserves double-underscore names for module metadata, a naming rule like A's taken names. This file prints the three lines shown.
Cargo exposes package fields as text, one macro per field. Code cannot read a module's docs.

recommendation.why: One mechanism: the metadata are the body's own typed fields with defaults, written first in the body and read as plain fields. A module then passes as a Module value.
gains: Package and module metadata are typed fields with defaults, written first in the body.
One body rule: implicit braces in package.jet and module.jet, explicit braces anywhere else.
One plain read, pricing.category, the same as any field.

losses.loss: Seven field names are taken at module level, so 9 items are renamed once today.
losses.mitigation: Irreducible for direct reads; jet fix renames them, and the list is closed.

whyNot.reason: B frees the seven names, but every outside read becomes #module(pricing), a second form.

recommendation.tradeoff: Seven names taken in module bodies, for metadata you read like any field.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude. Adversarial model family: Claude. Fresh agent: Main. Every example now follows the owner's body rule: implicit braces in package.jet and module.jet, braces in any other file, metadata first. C wrote metadata as markers outside the body, which that rule excludes, so it was removed.

surface.lesson: A package or module body holds metadata fields first, then bindings. package.jet and module.jet have implicit braces; any other file writes name :: module { ... }.

options.gist: Fields first in the body; read pricing.category.

One plain read.

options.name: Read through #module
options.gist: Same bodies; read #module(pricing).category.
gains: No names taken.
losses: A second, longer read form.

gains: Typed fields with defaults, opt-in.

decisions.title: How should Jet offer both ways to take a value out of a place it writes?
decisions.situation: Both of your answers are kept. The old manual option is now the manual form, and the old call option is now the beginner form. The new A and B only decide where the calls live. This revision makes the two forms one mechanism with two spellings. The beginner calls are written with the manual form, and one rule checks both. Only one choice is left: whether the beginner calls need an import.
decisions.gist: Should swap and replace work with no import, or only after use core.mem?
decisions.lesson: A parameter marked & lends the caller's place to the function, which may change it; the caller still owns it. ^x moves a value, leaving the old place empty. swap(&a, &b) exchanges two places, and replace(&place, value) puts in a new value and returns the old one.
decisions.story: Mia is new to Jet and writes swap(&d.front, &d.back) and replace(&self.head, None). Her teammate Raj writes the same moves by hand in a hot loop. Both compile to the same moves, and neither copies a list.
decisions.inWild:
Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Expressions/Places.jet:193-199 refuses ^ on every read or write parameter at a binding (E0201).
Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Calls/Checking.jet:583-584 lets a write parameter's field move into a call whose result refills it. That path closes the value twice when the call stops (probe stop_refill.jet).
Compiler/JetCli/Source/Cli/AdaptiveTable.jet:103-107 already refills before anything that may stop, by hand, on a local.
Docs/spec/spec.md:1534-1535: Cell.replace(value) returns the old value, the spelling replace follows.
Rust: std::mem::swap, std::mem::replace, Option::take; the take_mut crate aborts the process on a panic inside the gap.
decisions.detail:
WHAT IS ALREADY RATIFIED

The mark ^place is the exact move, and any later use of the moved place is E0121. The same mark on borrowed storage is E0201 (D-COPY-DEFAULT1 A). &place is the exclusive write window, and the caller keeps ownership (D-SHAPE-PLACE1 A). The mark sits on the place, as in swap(&d.front, &d.back) and &s.pop_all() (D-CAP-RECEIVER1 D).

A stop runs the cleanup of every frame it leaves (D-FAIL-EXIT1). A function can deny Panic with -[!Panic]> (D-NOPANIC1 D). A task's join can report that the task stopped, so code after the group still runs (D-TASK-WINDOW1 A).

```jet
struct Deque {
    front: [Int]
    back: [Int]
}

fn flip(d: &Deque) {
    t :: d.front.copy()      // today: a copy, because ^d.front is E0201
    d.front = d.back.copy()
    d.back = t
}

fn run() {
    d := Deque{front: [1], back: [2, 3]}
    flip(&d)
    print(d.front.len())
}
```

THE OWNER'S ANSWER

Both forms are valid. The call is the beginner form, and the move and refill written out is the manual form.

ONE MECHANISM, TWO SPELLINGS

core.mem gains swap(&a, &b) and replace(&place, value), which returns the old value. Both are ordinary Jet functions whose bodies use the manual form, so a call and the hand-written moves are the same moves. The compiler checks one rule, for both.

```jet
// In Core (core.mem): the beginner calls are written with the manual form.
fn swap<T>(a: &T, b: &T) -[!Panic]> {
    t :: ^a
    a = ^b
    b = ^t
}

fn replace<T>(place: &T, value: ^T) -[!Panic]> T {
    old :: ^place
    place = ^value
    old
}
```

THE RULE FOR THE MANUAL FORM

^ on a & parameter, a field below one, or a named write window opens a gap. The function must put a value back before anything can see the gap. Inside the gap, a read of the place is E0121, as today.

A return, break, next, ? or ?? exit inside the gap is E0201 at the exit, with a note at the move. Both arms of an if or match must refill, or neither. A loop body closes its own gap in the same pass.

STOPS INSIDE THE GAP

A stop is a panic, a trap, or a cancellation at a wait. If one comes while the moved value is still whole in a local, the stop path moves it back first. Then the cleanup and any defer run, so the caller finds a whole value.

If the moved value is no longer whole in a local when something can stop, nothing is left to put back. That is E0201 at that point, as at a call that takes the value with ^. The fix offers two ways out. One is to put a stand-in first, as in old :: replace(&self.conn, .Idle). The other is to mark the callee -[!Panic]> with no wait in it.

WHAT EACH FORM GUARANTEES

The call never leaves a place empty. The manual form copies nothing, and the compiler proves every exit is refilled. After a stop, the caller always holds a whole value.

THE BEGINNER FORM IS THE DEFAULT

The tour and jet explain E0201 teach the calls first. When the manual form is refused, the fix rewrites it to swap or replace. The manual form needs no opt-in line. The ^ mark is the explicit opt-in, at the exact place, as D-COPY-DEFAULT1 defines it. A gate would refuse a safe program, and the owner's #6066 direction says only #Unsafe opts out.

PLACES THAT MIGHT OVERLAP

swap needs two places that cannot be one place. Two fields, two locals, or two fixed list positions such as rows[0] and rows[1] work today. The same place twice, two list positions picked at run time, or two map keys are E0204.

The way out is the list's or map's own swap, which this ballot adds: &rows.swap(i, j) and &m.swap(a, b). They check at run time, and the same position twice does nothing. The E0204 fix writes that call. Lists have no swap method today (E0311).

PINNED PLACES

While a pin into node is live, swap(&node, &other) is E0220, and the fix says to go through the pin. A Pin<Node> is not a Node, so swap(&pinned, &other) is E0112. Fields still swap through a pin, as in swap(&pinned.payload, &other.payload), because the address stays put. The manual form ^node beside a live pin stays E0219. The rule changes none of these.

WHY NOT METHODS

A value method a.swap(&b) would have to exist on every type. A replace method would clash with the replace that String, Regex, LocalDate and Cell already have. Free functions keep one meaning per name.

A BUG THIS RULE FIXES

Today self.r = next(^self.r) on &self is accepted. If next stops, the value is closed twice (probe stop_refill.jet prints "close a" twice on O0 and O1; #6066 c10). The gap rule refuses it unless next cannot stop. A repo scan finds 8 sites of that shape to check.

COST

The normal path is unchanged: a call is the same moves, and at O0 it is one call. Only stop paths inside a gap gain a move back. Existing programs keep compiling, except the 8 sites above if their callee can stop.

THE QUESTION

Should the beginner calls work with no import, as swap and replace, or only after use core.mem, as mem.swap and mem.replace?

options.name: swap and replace need no import
options.detail: Both forms are valid. The beginner calls swap(&a, &b) and replace(&place, value) are ambient, with no import. They live in core.mem and the prelude names them, as it names read_file and channel. A user function named swap or replace still wins, so existing code keeps compiling.
options.technical:
core.mem gains swap<T> and replace<T>, both -[!Panic]>, with the manual form as their bodies. The prelude adds pub use core.mem.[swap, replace], two names on the closed list of D-PRELUDE-LAW1. #NoPrelude files write mem.swap after use core.mem. List and Map gain swap(i, j) and swap(a, b) as Core methods.

Sema tracks each gap in the moved-place state behind E0121. An exit inside a gap is E0201, and so is handing the value to a call that can stop. Each E0201 fix offers swap or replace. IR gives every stop path inside a gap a move back from the local that holds the value.

options.name: swap and replace come from use core.mem
options.detail: Both forms are valid, with the same rule and the same guarantees as A. The beginner calls are written mem.swap and mem.replace after use core.mem. The prelude does not change. The E0201 fix adds the import line when it is missing.
options.technical: As A, without the prelude alias. core.mem is also the module behind the low-level rung, so the import puts a beginner one line from Ptr and the allocators. Ptr and the allocators still need #Unsafe for their operations (E3101).

recommendation.why: A gives the beginner form with no ceremony, which makes it the easy default. One rule checks both forms, because the calls are written with the manual form. It fixes today's double close too.
gains: A beginner swaps or takes with one call and no import, and never sees an empty place.
An expert writes the moves by hand with no copy, and the compiler proves every exit is refilled.
A stop inside a gap leaves the caller a whole value, which also fixes today's double close.

decisions.title: Can tasks in a task group write separate parts of one list?
decisions.situation: A task.group waits for all of its tasks before its block ends. Today a task in the group cannot capture a write window into a local list, even when the two windows do not overlap. So splitting work across tasks means copying each half out and writing the results back. The program is safe when the windows do not overlap and the group ends before the list does. The vote decides whether such tasks may write their window directly.
decisions.gist: May each task in a group write its own, separate part of a list the block owns?
decisions.lesson: &v.split_write(mid) gives two write windows, left and right, that cannot overlap. task { … } starts work that the enclosing task.group joins before its block ends. Today a task may only capture owned values, so a window is refused with E0631.
decisions.story: Lee splits a pixel buffer in two and wants one task to brighten each half in place. Today Jet makes him copy both halves into owned lists, run the tasks, and copy the results back.
decisions.inWild:
Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Expressions/Lambdas.jet:2171-2184 refuses a view capture that is a write window or cannot be materialized (E0631).
Compiler/JetIR/Source/BuildExpr.jet:6297-6300 already holds a written alias by address so a scoped task's writes land on the owner.
Rust: std::thread::scope with split_at_mut gives each thread one &mut half.
decisions.detail:
WHAT IS ALREADY RATIFIED

One crossing prover answers every concurrent boundary, and each refusal names what cannot cross, the boundary and the fix. A task.group joins every task before its block ends. split_write returns two non-overlapping write windows.

```jet
task.group g {
    { left: a, right: b } :: &v.split_write(2) ?? panic("split")
    left :: task { a[0] = a[0] + 1 }   // today: E0631
    right :: task { b[0] = b[0] + 1 }
    ^left.join() ?? panic("left")
    ^right.join() ?? panic("right")
}
```

THE QUESTION

Should a task in a group be allowed to capture a write window, or a read view, whose owner outlives the group?

options.name: Tasks in a group may write windows into a list that outlives the group
options.detail: A task inside a task.group may capture a read view or a write window when the owner of the storage lives longer than the group. Two live tasks may not hold overlapping windows where either writes, and nothing outside the tasks may touch the owner until the group ends. The element type must still be sendable. Callers do not change.
options.technical: The crossing prover admits a view or window capture into a task whose innermost group scope ends inside the owner's scope. The capture becomes a loan held until the group's join, so the existing loan-conflict checks (E0204, E0212) refuse a second overlapping write window and any use of the owner inside the group. IR holds the window by address, as it already does for written aliases.

options.name: Tasks keep taking owned values
options.detail: No change. A task works on an owned copy and returns its result, which the block writes back.
options.technical: No change.

recommendation.why: A accepts a safe and common parallel pattern without copies, and the existing loan checks keep overlapping writes out. The group's join is what makes it safe, and the group is already required.
gains: Parallel in-place work on one buffer, with no copy in or out.
No new syntax; split_write and task.group already exist.

losses.loss: The crossing prover gains a scoped case to reason about.
losses.mitigation: The case is one rule: the group ends inside the owner's scope; everything else reuses loan checks.

whyNot.reason: B copies both halves in and out, for a program that is already safe.

recommendation.tradeoff: One scoped rule in the prover, for zero-copy parallel writes.

decisions.title: Can a function return a write window onto one map value?
decisions.situation: A function can already return a write window onto one list element, written &lib.books[i..i], and the caller edits it through the window. There is no such window onto one map value, so a helper that finds or creates a map entry and hands it back for editing cannot be written. The vote decides whether &map[key] can be returned as a one-value write window.
decisions.gist: May &map[key] be returned as a write window, like &list[i..i]?
decisions.lesson: ViewMut<T> is a write window over values of type T in some owner. &books[i..i] is a window over one Book. from map in the result type names the owner the window points into. While the window is live, the owner cannot change shape.
decisions.story: Sam keeps groups of ids in a map and wants slot(&groups, key) to return the list for a key so callers can push into it. Today the return is refused, so every caller repeats the lookup.
decisions.detail:
WHAT IS ALREADY RATIFIED

A returned view uses View or ViewMut with public provenance and no lifetime syntax, and there is no second view mechanism. A one-element list window is written i..i. A live window blocks any change to its owner's shape (E0212).

```jet
fn edit_at(lib: &Library, i: Int) -> ViewMut<Book> { &lib.books[i..i] }

fn run() {
    dune :: edit_at(&lib, 0)
    dune[0].pages += 10
}
```

THE QUESTION

Should &map[key] at a ViewMut<V> destination be a one-value window onto that map entry?

options.name: &map[key] is a one-value window
options.detail: Where a ViewMut<V> is expected, &map[key] is a window over that one map value, used as w[0] like a one-element list window. A missing key fails the same way map[key] does. While the window is live the map cannot gain or lose entries.
options.technical: Sema types &map[key] at a ViewMut<V> destination as a window with provenance on the map, and records the loan that the list window records, so E0212 covers adds and removes. IR builds the window header from the entry's value address with length 1, the same shape as ir_list_window.

options.name: No map windows; pass the map and the key
options.detail: No change. A helper takes the map and the key and does the edit itself.
options.technical: No change.

recommendation.why: A extends the ratified window to the one owner that lacks it, with the same spelling and the same loan rule, so entry-style helpers can be written.
gains: Find-or-create helpers that hand back an editable value.
One window rule for lists and maps.

losses.loss: A map entry window is written w[0], like a list window.
losses.mitigation: It is the same rule as &list[i..i], which the example already teaches.

whyNot.reason: B forces every edit into the helper, so callers cannot keep a handle to the value.

recommendation.tradeoff: One more owner kind for windows, for entry-style helpers.

decisions.title: Can += and the other compound updates target a list or map slot?
decisions.situation: Today counts[key] += 1 and xs[0] += 1 are refused with E0164, while counts[key] = counts[key] + 1 and xs[0] = xs[0] + 1 are accepted and mean the same thing. The refusal was meant to stop a read of a missing map key, but the long form does that same read. The vote decides whether compound updates may target an indexed slot.
decisions.gist: Should xs[i] += 1 and counts[key] += 1 be allowed, meaning the same as the long form?
decisions.lesson: x += 1 means x = x + 1. Reading map[key] stops the program when the key is missing, and reading xs[i] stops it when i is out of range. map.get(key) ?? 0 reads a key that may be missing without stopping.
decisions.story: Ana counts words with counts[w] += 1 and gets E0164, then writes counts[w] = counts[w] + 1, which compiles and fails the same way on a missing key.
decisions.inWild:
Docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:259-265 S17: direct indexed compound updates remain E0164 (copy, update, then store).
prep/c6066/bal/idx_a.jet today: E0164 at 4:11 and 5:7; prep/c6066/bal/idx_c.jet (long form) runs: 2, 2.
Rust, Python, Swift and C# accept v[i] += 1 and m[k] += 1.
decisions.detail:
WHAT IS ALREADY RATIFIED

Compound updates work on mutable names, & parameters and fields, including fields reached through list elements. Direct indexed compound updates are E0164. An indexed read stops on a missing map key or an out-of-range index.

```jet
counts := [String: Int]{"a": 1}
counts["a"] = counts["a"] + 1   // accepted today
counts["a"] += 1                 // E0164 today
```

THE QUESTION

Should a compound update on an indexed slot be allowed, with the meaning of the long form?

options.name: Allow it on lists and maps
options.detail: xs[i] op= v and map[key] op= v mean xs[i] = xs[i] op v and map[key] = map[key] op v, with one lookup. They stop where the long form stops. E0164 is retired.
options.technical: Sema checks the slot as a write place of the indexed collection and lowers to one element address, then a load, the operator and a store. The missing-key and out-of-range stops are the ones the indexed read already has.

options.name: Allow it on lists only
options.detail: xs[i] op= v is allowed. A map slot keeps E0164, so a count that may start missing is written with get(key) ?? 0.
options.technical: As A for lists. E0164 stays for map slots, with its total-update fix.

options.name: Keep E0164
options.detail: No change. Indexed slots use the long form.
options.technical: No change.

recommendation.why: The refusal does not prevent the stop it was meant to prevent, because the long form it suggests does the same read. A removes a rule that only costs keystrokes and matches every mainstream language.
gains: The shortest form works on every place.
One lookup instead of two.

losses.loss: counts[w] += 1 on a missing key stops at run time.
losses.mitigation: The long form already does; map.get(w) ?? 0 remains the total form, and a lint can suggest it.

whyNot.reason: B keeps a map rule that the accepted long form already bypasses.
C refuses a safe program for no safety gain.

recommendation.tradeoff: A run-time stop on a missing key, the same as the long form, for the short form everywhere.

decisions.title: Is a reflected field's type read as `f.type` or as `f.ty`?
decisions.situation: Already ratified: a marker is a struct with `impl Marker`, and its `expand(self, target: Target)` reads the marked type as plain values, such as `target.fields`. Each field in that list is a ratified record with a name, a type, a default and an offset. One ratified record names the type field `type`, and gives the same name to parameters, captures, settings and values. Two other ratified records write `field.ty` when they show a field read. A marker author has to know which name to write.
decisions.gist: When a `Describe` marker prints `size: Float` for each field, does it read `f.type` or `f.ty`?
decisions.lesson: Every reflected record should name its type the same way, so one spelling is right everywhere.
decisions.story: Mia writes a Describe marker that prints each field as `name: Type`. She reads the field list, then needs the field's type.

Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Comptime/Reflection.jet:811 today's field record has a `ty` entry holding type text
Examples/: no example reads a reflected field's `.ty` today
probe p8_typefield.jet: `type` is accepted as a field name (prints 3)
decisions.detail:
ALREADY RATIFIED, IN CODE

struct Describe { impl Marker { sites :: [.Type]  fn expand(self, target: Target) { ... } } }
Inside expand, target.fields is a list of field records. Elsewhere T.reflect() returns the same kind of value.

THE TWO SIDES

D-META-REFLECT2 A (2026-09-21): "FieldInfo has identity: DeclarationHandle, name: String, type: TypeId, ...". ParameterInfo, CaptureInfo, SettingInfo and ValueInfo also use type. D-MARKER-LADDER1 A writes p.type for parameters.

D-META-HASH1 A (2026-10-30): "Inside expand, target.fields, target.name and field.ty are plain field reads". D-ENUM-CASEMETA1 A (2026-09-12): "FieldInfo.ty is the payload field's Type handle".

WHO IS AFFECTED

No example or test reads a reflected field's type by either name today. Only the compiler's own record changes, under either option.

WHAT A DOES

Every reflected record uses type. The two field.ty mentions are amended. Today's ty entry is renamed in the same cutover that retires the $ reads.

options.name: `type`, as in the full schema

options.technical: FieldInfo.type: TypeId, as D-META-REFLECT2 A lists. D-META-HASH1 A and D-ENUM-CASEMETA1 A field.ty mentions are amended to field.type. The compiler's ty entry (Comptime/Reflection.jet:811 and siblings) is renamed in the #4276 [24] cutover. `type` is a legal field name (probe p8).

options.name: `ty` everywhere
options.detail: Every reflected record names its type `ty`, as today's compiler record and the two later mentions do. The full schema's `type` fields on fields, parameters, captures, settings and values are renamed.
options.technical: FieldInfo.ty, ParameterInfo.ty, CaptureInfo.ty, SettingInfo.ty and ValueInfo.ty, all TypeId. D-META-REFLECT2 A's schema text is amended. The compiler's ty entry keeps its name and changes from text to TypeId.

recommendation.why: A keeps the only record that defines the whole schema, and it uses one plain word across every reflected record. No app or example changes under either option.

decisions.title: What the header of Jet's own errors names: the type, the E-code, or both
decisions.situation: Every Jet error is now a type with a name, such as jet.ValueTypeMismatch, and a code, such as E0112 (D-DECL-TYPES1 rule 13). Batch 2 (37eae4f5d6) changed the first line of every Jet report from Error [E0112] to Error [jet.ValueTypeMismatch], about 2,700 snapshot headers. The rest of the report still uses the code: the More: link, the closing jet explain hint and the JSON code field. Library errors have only a name, and print it as Error [web.BadPath] (D-MARKER-DIAG1). No decision says what the header of Jet's own errors shows. The vote decides that, and whether the link and hint follow it.
decisions.gist: Should a Jet error's first line name the error type, its E-code, or both?
decisions.lesson: Each Jet error has two identifiers: a stable code like E0112 and a type name like jet.ValueTypeMismatch. The first line of a report shows one of them in brackets. You write the name in #Allow(jet.FloatMoney), and jet explain accepts either. Library errors have only a name.
decisions.story: Mia gets Error [jet.ValueTypeMismatch] in her build log. The More: line under it says jet-lang.dev/e/E0112 and the last line says run jet explain E0112. She wonders whether these are three different errors. Later a warning tells her to write #Allow with a name, but the warning's link shows an L-code.
decisions.inWild:
Probe $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/prep/hdr/hdr.jet on 37eae4f5d6: one jet check prints Error [E1003] and Error [jet.ValueTypeMismatch] together. More: shows E1003 and E0112, and the hint says run `jet explain E1003`.
Compiler/JetFoundation/Source/Registry/Diagnostics.jet:363-368 diagnostic_display_name: a row with a runtime stage keeps its E-code in the header. That is 24 snapshot headers, E0123, E0128 and E1003 among them, even at compile time.
Compiler/JetFoundation/Source/Diagnostics/Render.jet:330 header; :356 More: link by code, skipped for dotted library codes.
Compiler/JetFoundation/Source/Registry/Explain.jet:29 jet explain accepts the code, then the name; its title line prints only the code.
jet check --json: "code":"E1003" and no name field.
tests/ui/gate_law/allow_reason_cannot_suppress_itself.jet:1 #Allow(jet.AllowReason, ...); tests/ui_lint/*.warn headers are Warning [jet.X].
Compiler/Prelude/Diagnostics.jet:4440-4446 a lint carries a third identifier: FloatMoney has code L0504 and lint_name float_money.
Docs/site/dist/e/: 910 E-code pages, 65 L, 3 R, 27 legacy E-SLUG pages, none by name.
rustc: error[E0308]: mismatched types; lints print a name: #[warn(unused_variables)] on by default.
TypeScript: error TS2322. Clippy and ESLint name the rule: clippy::needless_return, no-unused-vars. Elm heads each error with a name: -- TYPE MISMATCH --.
decisions.detail:
WHAT IS ALREADY RATIFIED

D-DECL-TYPES1 A rule 13: each Jet error type keeps code :: "E0xxx". D-MARKER-DIAG1 A: a library error's code is its type path by default. Its header shows Error [web.BadPath], #Allow(web.TrailingSlash) silences a lint by name, and jet explain web.BadPath works. D-DIAG-URL1 B: every error ends with a More: line, written as More: jet-lang.dev/e/<CODE>. D-DIAG-LIBLINK1 A: a library error prints More: <its link> (or: jet explain <name>), or More: jet explain <name> when it has no link. Jet's own errors keep the ratified line.

WHAT IS TRUE TODAY (37eae4f5d6)

The header prints the name, except for the 24 rows the runtime can also raise, which print the code; one run can mix both. More:, the closing hint and JSON code all use the E-code. JSON has no name field, so a tool that reads JSON cannot write the #Allow name without calling jet explain. Names and codes are one to one: 1,006 rows give 1,006 codes and as many names. A name is about 23 characters long with jet. (36 at most); a code is 5.

WHAT EACH OPTION COSTS IN SNAPSHOTS

A: about 2,800 More: lines and 41 hints change, plus the runtime's report strings and the docs site's page names (old E-code addresses redirect). B: only the 24 mixed headers. C: about 2,700 headers return to codes. D and E: about 2,700 headers again, and E also changes the 2,800 More: lines. Every change is mechanical: a bless plus a generator rerun.

SEARCH

Jet's E0001-E0799 overlap rustc's numbers, so a search for E0107 or E0308 finds Rust pages (rustc E0107 is a wrong count of generic arguments; Jet E0107 is an unknown name). A dotted name such as jet.UnknownName belongs to Jet alone.

UNDER EVERY OPTION

The 24 runtime-stage rows follow the same rule as the rest. JSON reports gain a name field beside code, so agents can key on either. jet explain keeps accepting both.

options.name: The name everywhere, with the code kept as an alias
options.detail: The header, the More: link and the closing hint all show the type name. The link becomes jet-lang.dev/e/jet.ValueTypeMismatch, the same shape a library error's explain line uses. The E-code stays as the type's stable code: JSON carries both, jet explain E0112 still works, and the old E0112 address redirects. Runtime reports print the name as well.
options.technical: diagnostic_display_name (Diagnostics.jet:363) returns row.name for every row, and the runtime-stage exception goes. Render.jet:356 links by name. The explain hint prints the name. jet.report/v3 gains name. Runtime report strings (TrapMessages.jet, ServicesMessages.jet, report.S) print names. The site generator writes /e/<name> pages and E-code redirects. This amends D-DIAG-URL1 B's line shape from <CODE> to <name>, and D-DIAG-LIBLINK1's sentence that Jet's codes keep the ratified line.

decisions.title: With reflect(Rock), which types keep run-time type info by default?
decisions.situation: You asked that reflect take the type itself, as print(reflect(Rock)), with no .of. This revision does that under every option. reflect(Rock) gives the type's record, and reflect(rock) gives one value's record. reflect(Rock{}) stays legal: it reflects a new Rock built from its defaults, so it shows values as well as the type. The open question is unchanged. Already ratified: a program that never reflects gets no type-info table, and only types a program asks about keep info. A build setting copies Jai's three words, full, reachable and none, and none of them means only what was asked about. Recommended A adds that word, requested, as the default.
decisions.gist: When a game reflects a rock but never a door, does the door's type info ship?
decisions.lesson: reflect(Rock) reads a type, and reflect(rock) reads one value. Run-time type info is kept only for what a program asks about, and the build setting must say so.
decisions.story: Bo ships a small game. Its level editor calls reflect(rock) to list a rock's fields, and nothing ever reflects Door. He wants the release build to carry only what the editor uses, and a full table in a debug build.
decisions.inWild:

probes/D-REFLECT-TYPEINFO1/r02_reflect_type_arg.jet: reflect(Rock) is E0803 today, "reflect is Unknown, not a function".
probes/D-REFLECT-TYPEINFO1/r03, r04 and r08: a bare type name used as a value crashes the compiler, a defect found 2026-11-04.
probes/D-REFLECT-TYPEINFO1/r10: [Int] and Int? already parse as call arguments; Box<Int> parses but loses its <Int>.
Jai: type_info(Rock) and Zig: @typeInfo(Rock) take the type itself.
Compiler/JetIR/Source/BuildRoutes.jet:4976-5021: per-call-site records, no global table today.
decisions.detail:
THE SPELLING YOU ASKED FOR

Every option uses one call, reflect, so any vote adopts it. reflect(Rock) gives the type's record: its name, path, fields and markers. reflect(rock) gives one value's record: each field with its value, and .type, which is reflect(Rock).

print(reflect(Rock)) prints the type's shape, struct Rock { size: Float, hard: Bool }. print(reflect(rock)) prints the value, Rock { size: 1.5, hard: true }.

WHAT reflect(Rock{}) MEANS

It is legal and means the value form. Rock{} builds a new Rock from its defaults, and reflect reads that value. So reflect(Rock{}).type is reflect(Rock), and its fields also carry 1.0 and true.

It is not refused, because refusing one kind of argument would be a special case. If a field has no default, Rock{} is E0303 today, and that stays (probe r09). When code reads only .type from it, a lint offers reflect(Rock).

HOW THE ARGUMENT IS READ

Name lookup decides, as it does for every name. A type spelling, such as Rock, [Int], Int?, Box<Int> or a generic T, names a type. Anything else is a value. The parser already accepts these as call arguments, though it drops Box's <Int> today (probe r10).

In generic code, reflect(T) replaces T.reflect(), and each copy reads its own T.

TYPES STAY TYPES

A type is still not an ordinary value. t :: Rock stays an error, and its fix offers reflect(Rock); today it crashes the compiler. User functions take types through <T>, so reflect is the one call that takes a type.

An effect row already takes either a type or a constant struct literal (D-DECL-TYPES1 A). The earlier @TYPE(T) and @VALUE(value) forms also passed types and values as arguments (D-META-REFLECT2).

MIGRATION

jet fix rewrites reflect.of(x) to reflect(x), 44 lines in 21 files today. It rewrites T.reflect() to reflect(T), 34 lines in 25 files. It deletes the alias line use reflect :: core.reflect. The core.reflect module keeps its record types.

The spelling amends D-METAREFLECT1, D-NAME-REFLECT1, D-ANY-JAI1's of entry and D-META-HASH1's template reads. The record shapes, the type field (D-REFLECT-FIELDTYPE1) and read-only reflection stay. No file declares a function named reflect.

WHAT IS ALREADY DECIDED ABOUT KEEPING INFO

D-META-REFLECT2 A: run time exposes type and value facts kept for requested roots. Dead-code removal must keep requested facts without keeping unrelated ones by default. A program without run-time reflection gets no new table.

D-JAI-BUILDOPT1 A: every Jai build-setting family becomes a typed Build field. Its list includes type_info full, reachable or none. It names no default.

THE CONFLICT

The ratified default, requested roots only, is not one of the three words. In Jai, reachable keeps every type the program uses, which is wider. Choosing any of the three words as the default breaks one record.

WHAT COUNTS AS A REQUEST

A reflect call that runs while the program runs requests that type's record and the types its fields reach. reflect(Rock) used only while building requests nothing at run time.

WHAT A DOES

The setting gets a fourth word, requested, and it is the default. reachable and full widen it for debug or tool builds. none turns any reflect call that runs while the program runs into a compile error naming the setting.

COST

Under A, a program with one reflect(rock) call carries records only for Rock's field graph. Paired size cells compare requested against full on the same game.

GENERIC CODE

Under A and C, a reflect call in generic code asks about each type the code is used with. So fn show<T>(x: T) that calls reflect(x), used only with Rock, keeps Rock's info and not Door's.

Amends D-JAI-BUILDOPT1 A's list; D-META-REFLECT2 A unchanged. The reflect(x) spelling is shared by every option.

recommendation.why: A keeps the ratified rule that unused reflection costs nothing, and still gives Jai's wider settings to builds that want them. The default is what is already promised, and reflect(Rock) reads the way you asked.

decisions.title: How does a level editor change a field it knows only by name?
decisions.situation: You asked us to engineer away the downsides of the recommendation, which were a #Patchable word on every editable type and work not yet built. The engine's own entity marker now includes #Patchable, so an entity type writes nothing extra, and build work no longer counts as a loss. Typos, nested fields, private fields and undo now each get a defined result with a readable error. The reflection write stays as B and the marker template as C, both unchanged.
decisions.gist: Does the editor set Rock's size by name through a typed patch, a reflection write, or marker code?
decisions.lesson: An editor knows a field only by its name, such as size, and must change it on any entity. Reflection reads fields today. #Patchable gives a type a typed patch, apply and undo.
decisions.story: Ana's level editor shows the fields of the selected entity. A designer types 2.0 into Rock's size, then 0.5 into its tint's red part. The editor does not know the Rock type, only the field path and the text.
decisions.inWild:
Bevy: every component an editor may change derives Reflect, and engines bundle that into their own component derive.
Unity: SerializedObject.FindProperty("size") sets a field by name through engine metadata.
Jai: an editor writes a member through its byte offset from the type table.
decisions.detail:
YOUR QUESTION

You asked to engineer away A's two downsides. Both are gone.

"Each editable type writes #Patchable." The engine already needs its own entity marker, so it can register, save and list each entity type. D-MARKER-GROUP1=A lets that marker be a fixed group, and the engine's group includes Patchable. Rock writes #engine.Entity, the one line it writes under every option, and gets Patchable with it.

"The Patchable bound and Patch.parse are not built yet." That is build work. Ranking never counts build work, and B and C need unbuilt pieces too.

WHY THE OPT-IN ITSELF STAYS

The opt-in is the guarantee, not a cost. Without it, any function holding a changeable reference could change any field of any type by name, which is B. With the group, consent costs no extra word: the author writes #engine.Entity, hover lists its members, and edit<T: Patchable> shows it in the engine's signature.

WHAT A DOES, EXACTLY

#Patchable already gives Rock a Rock.Patch with every field optional, plus apply, diff and merge (D-PATCH1). A adds one generated method: value.parse_patch(path, text) -> T.Patch PatchError!.

It finds the field named by the path, parses the text with that field's own parse, and returns a patch with that one field set. apply then makes the change. The engine's edit is one line.

For undo, the engine keeps T.diff(before, after), the old values of the changed fields. Applying it restores them.

EDGE CASES

- A typo fails with PatchError, whose text is "no field `sise` on Rock; did you mean `size`?".

- Bad text fails with "`abc` is not a Float, for `size`". The value is unchanged.

- A dotted path such as tint.r walks into a field whose type is Patchable. The patch holds the whole new tint, so diff and undo work unchanged.

- A field whose type has no parse and is not Patchable fails with "`shape` cannot be set from text", and hover on the marker lists such fields.

- A priv field fails with "`hp` is private to Rock". Only the type's own module may write it.

- A computed field is not in Patch (D-PATCH1), so it fails as unknown, with a note that it is computed.

- A type with type parameters cannot be Patchable (E0336), and a field holding a reference or function is refused (E0337). The error points at the field on the #engine.Entity line, so callbacks stay outside entity data.

- A type the engine does not mark cannot be changed by name. The error at edit offers to add #engine.Entity.

BEGINNER AND EXPERT

A beginner writes #engine.Entity on a type and never sees Patchable. The editor just works. An expert writes the engine: edit is one line, and an undo stack keeps one patch per edit. Expert code may also read the PatchError to show the designer why an edit failed.

WHAT IS BUILT TODAY

Probes are in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Research/ballots-2026-11-05/edit, run with the pinned compiler (jet@0.0.1#006bccd5).

- e01: #Patchable apply and diff set and undo size; it prints 2.0, then 1.0.

- e02: a marker group in the ratified form, group :: #[Patchable, Equatable], is not built yet (E0003).

- e03: the old marker Entity = #[…] form is retired (E0381), and its fix writes the ratified form.

Earlier probes from the 2026-11-04 revision: a T: Patchable bound is not built yet (E0904), and a Patch cannot be read from text today (E0905). fn keep<T>(value: &T) cannot write value.size today (E0302). Reflection already reads priv fields.

WHY NOT B

B is easy to read, but it lets any generic function change any field of any type by name, so a signature no longer tells you which values it may change. It reaches priv fields, since reflection already reads them, so it needs a new refusal. It keeps field records while the program runs.

B also needs three amendments. D-METADEPTH1/2 says "read-only reflection + derives" and "No mutation". D-ANY-JAI1 says the core.reflect floor has no "string-named field mutation", and that get and set "remain declined". D-ENUM-CASEMETA1=A says "There is no new get, read, cast, write-by-name, or constructor operation".

WHY NOT C

The engine's marker writes an Edit impl with one typed branch per field. It changes no rule, but each write hides in a template, the hardest code here to read. Templates and #{…} pastes are not built yet.

DROPPED

The JSON round trip stays dropped. Every edit paid a full encode and decode.

COST WHILE RUNNING

parse_patch compares the path with each field name once, then does the typed apply. It is left out of the program when nothing calls it. No field records are kept while running.

RATIFIED DECISIONS IT TOUCHES

A amends no ratified rule. It extends D-PATCH1 with parse_patch and PatchError, the way Codable decode already fills fields by name. It uses D-MARKER-GROUP1=A for the engine's group and D-DECL-TYPES1=A for the T: Patchable bound.

options.name: Build a typed patch from a field path
options.detail: The engine's entity marker is a group that includes #Patchable, so entity types write nothing extra. #Patchable gains value.parse_patch(path, text), which builds a typed patch for one field or dotted path. The engine applies it with the existing apply, and undo is the existing diff. Failures say exactly what went wrong.
options.technical:
Extends D-PATCH1: #Patchable also synthesizes value.parse_patch(path: String, text: String) -> T.Patch PatchError!, one branch per patchable field, using each field type's parse. A dotted path recurses into Patchable field types and stores the whole new field value. PatchError implements Diagnostic, with UnknownField (nearest name), BadText, NoParse, Private and Computed cases.

The engine's Entity marker is a D-MARKER-GROUP1=A group (unbuilt: E0003 today). The T: Patchable bound comes from D-DECL-TYPES1=A's derive-as-trait rule (unbuilt: E0904 today). No Core reflection change and no ratified rule amended.

options.name: Reflection writes a field
options.detail: A reflected value can set a field by name: reflect.of(&value).field(name)?.set_text(text). The engine needs no marker on the type. Any holder of a changeable reference can write any field of any type, and three ratified rules are reversed.
options.technical: Adds a write through a borrowed reflected value, a by-name field lookup and a text setter that calls the field type's parse. Amends D-METADEPTH1/2, D-ANY-JAI1's declined list and D-ENUM-CASEMETA1=A. Adds a priv-field refusal outside the type's module and needs field records kept while running.

options.name: The marker writes setter code
options.detail: The engine's Entity marker writes an Edit impl for every entity type: one typed branch per field. The editor calls it through the trait. Core reflection stays read only, but the write hides in a template.
options.technical: No Core change. Uses expand, #{…} pastes and a loop over target.fields unrolled while compiling. Each branch calls its field type's parse. Templates and pastes are unbuilt today.

recommendation.why: A keeps B's short engine code and gives a typed, visible write. The engine's one entity marker carries the opt-in, so types write nothing extra. Every failure says why, undo is the existing diff, and no ratified rule changes.
gains: Engine code is one line, as readable as B.

C hides each write in a template, the hardest code here to read.

recommendation.tradeoff: The engine marks its entity types once, for typed edits with clear errors and free undo.

decisions.detail:
THE PROBLEM

Mia has many structs and wants each to print a one-line summary, such as Point has 2 fields, without writing it by hand. By hand she repeats the method in every struct, and the count goes stale when she adds a field. This file runs today:

```jet
// By hand: the same method in every struct. Runs today (probe x03_by_hand).
struct Point {
    x: Int
    y: Int

    fn describe(self) -> String { "Point has 2 fields" }
}

struct Order {
    id: Int
    total: Int
    paid: Bool

    fn describe(self) -> String { "Order has 3 fields" }
}

fn run() {
    print(Point{x: 1, y: 2}.describe())                       // Point has 2 fields
    print(Order{id: 7, total: 30, paid: true}.describe())     // Order has 3 fields
}
```

THE FIX THAT RUNS TODAY

One Describe marker writes describe() for every struct it marks. Its expand reads the struct's name and field count, and the impl block inside it is added to that struct. Option A's code is the whole file. It runs today and prints Point has 2 fields, then Order has 3 fields.

WHAT THIS BALLOT ASKS

A library marker runs inside the compiler while Mia's program builds. Mia should not have to trust a library with her files or the network. So card #6129 publishes one list of every place library code runs inside the compiler, each with a row saying what it may read. Her editor shows that row on hover.

The question is how that list writes the marker's entry. A writes the expand method exactly as the author writes it. B writes a function that returns a syntax value, which changes how every marker is written.

WHY NO VOTE IS NEEDED

The ratified rules already answer it. D-DECL-TYPES1=A rule 6 makes a marker's body the trait method expand(self, target: Target), whose body is a template. Rule 9 makes a derive fn expand(target: Target). D-CTCODEGEN1 makes added code re-enter the compiler as source. D-DERIVE-PROVIDER1=A (2026-11-04) keeps that form for derives without a trait.

The disagreeing text is Docs/proposals/effect-types-2026-10-29.md, section 9.1, lines 367-368, which list fn(Site) -[Compiler.Read]> Syntax and fn(TypeInfo) -[Compiler.Read]> Syntax. Its header says "Nothing here is ratified." Card #6129 criterion 44 already records amending section 9.1 to the ratified methods. Approving A changes no rule and closes this ballot.

THE LIST UNDER A

Each entry is the code its author writes, plus its row. Marker expansion is Marker.expand(self, target: Target) -[Compiler.Read]>, with a template body. A derive is Derive.expand(target: Target) -[Compiler.Read]>, with a template body. Lint, code generation and build actions keep their section 9.1 entries, which are already the functions their authors write.

WHAT B WOULD MEAN

Option B's code is the same program under B, as a whole file. It does not run, because Site, Syntax and the row are not built. Each marker would build its method from calls such as Syntax.method, instead of writing the method as code. Every existing marker and derive body would change.

WHAT RUNS TODAY

Probes are in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Research/ballots-2026-11-05/expand, run with the pinned compiler (jet@0.0.1#006bccd5).

- x03_by_hand prints Point has 2 fields and Order has 3 fields, with describe() written in each struct.

- x04_marker_two prints the same two lines from one Describe marker. It is option A's code.

- x05_surface_a is the short A file on the summary card, and prints Point has 2 fields.

- x02_expand_reads_file: a marker whose expand reads a file is refused with E0956, "A derive template binding is not a known-time value". The published row will say the same thing in the list.

EDGE CASES

- $tname and {$names} are today's splice spelling. D-META-HASH1=A moves splices to # (card #4276 c22), jet fix rewrites them, and nothing else in these files changes.

- A marker that needs outside data, such as a file, uses the separate impure preparation entry. That entry has its own row and needs --gate impure=allow.

- A derive takes no self, because a derive request carries no data.

- The name of the row's effect, written Compiler.Read here, is settled by card #6129 itself, as criterion 44 says.

- Target is the same value T.reflect() returns for the marked item.

BEGINNER AND EXPERT

A beginner writes #Describe above a struct and calls describe(). They never see expand or the list. An expert writes expand as a template, and tools show its row on hover. Neither path changes under A.

WHY NOT B

B rewrites every marker and derive body to build syntax values, as Swift macros do. It reopens D-DECL-TYPES1 rules 6 and 9 and needs a Syntax builder. D-CTCODEGEN1 would then require each syntax value to be printed back to source before it re-enters the compiler.

DROPPED

An earlier option kept the template but published a Syntax result in the list. Nobody writes or sees that value, so it described the code wrongly. It stays dropped.

decisions.title: Comment glyph: keep // or move comments to ##
decisions.situation: Jet starts a comment with two slashes, and a doc comment, which tools show as help, with three. The owner asked whether two hash signs would be better, since that frees the slash and the hash already marks compile-time work. Nothing planned needs the double slash, but Python's 7 // 2 compiles today and silently keeps 7, while two hashes would sit beside markers and rewrite every comment. We recommend keeping two slashes and adding a warning that catches the Python habit.
decisions.gist: Should Jet comments start with ## instead of //?
decisions.lesson: A comment is text the compiler skips. Jet starts one with //, and a doc comment, shown as help, with ///. A single # marks places where the compiler acts, such as #Inline. The vote: move comments to ##, freeing //, or keep //.
decisions.story: Mia learned Python first. She writes half :: 7 // 2, the program runs, and half is 7 instead of 3. Ben came from Rust and types // and /// without thinking. The owner wants # to feel like Jet's meta mark. This vote decides which glyph comments use, and how Mia is protected.
decisions.inWild:
// Odin, Swift, Rust, C, C# and Jai mark compiler work with # and keep // for comments.
share :: #force_inline proc(total, people: int) -> int { return total / people } // Odin
print(#file, #line) // Swift
# Python, shell, Ruby, Nim and Nix use # for comments and nothing else.
half = 7 // 2  # Python: // is floor division, so half is 3
## Nim: a doc comment. In C macros, a ## b pastes two tokens.
decisions.detail:
WHAT IS ALREADY DECIDED

S5 makes // the line comment and nested /* */ the block comment (ratified 2026-06-15). S49 makes /// the doc comment, which jet doc shows and jet test --docs runs. The registry rows are COMMENT_PREFIX and BLOCK_COMMENT_OPEN and BLOCK_COMMENT_CLOSE in Compiler/JetFoundation/Data/Syntax/CoreSurface.jet:188-195.

D-META-HASH1 A (2026-10-30) defines # as the one compile-time mark: markers such as #Inline, site values such as #line, and pastes such as #{x}. Its stated meaning is that the compiler acts here. D-PRE-COMPILE1 A (2026-10-31) rejected a doubled-hash form, ##Pre. Whole-number division was ratified as /% on 2026-08-05.

TODAY

Probes ran on the admitted compiler at commit 1f70b8d4. Probe c14 is the ballot program; it runs, prints 333 and passes jet fmt --check. Probe c11, half :: 7 // 2, prints 7 with no diagnostic. Probes c02 and c12 show that ## is an error today (E0003), so the glyph is free. Probe c04 shows a #! line after byte 0 is E0042.

WHAT THE SLASH WOULD FREE

The single / is never a comment, so division and the positional-only parameter zone already use it (probe c08). Only // and /* are taken. Python's floor division is the one strong rival meaning for //, and Jet already spells it /% (1,057 uses). Regex is the typed literal Regex{"..."}, and paths are typed native values. No ratified or open decision needs //, /* or slash literals.

CENSUS

Tracked .jet files under Compiler, Core, Examples, tests and Jetpack hold 94,746 comment tokens in 7,815 of 17,255 files. That is 90,855 full-line comments, 1,140 trailing comments and 2,698 doc lines. There are 17 block comments and 14,325 # tokens in code. 829 comments begin with #, mostly card references such as // #4828, and 28 are commented-out markers.

EDGE CASES

A commented-out marker stays readable either way: // #Inline or ## #Inline. A #{x} or #line inside a comment is plain text in both options (probe c13). The shebang rule does not change. Under B, a doc line that holds a markdown heading reads ### ## Examples; the corpus has none today. Nim's #[ ]# block form would collide with the #[A, B] marker list, so B drops block comments; only 17 exist.

BEGINNER PATH

A newcomer writes // for a note and /// above a function to document it, as in Rust, Swift, C# and Zig. A Python habit such as 7 // 2 gets a warning with the /% fix under A, or an error under B.

EXPERT PATH

Experts keep nested /* */ to fence off a region under A, or use the editor's toggle-comment key under B. Machine-read comments such as doctest // => lines keep working under A. Under B they are renamed to ## =>.

NOT ON THE BALLOT

Single # comments, as in Python and shell, would need every marker, [T#N], pkg#1.2.0 and #!Name moved to another glyph. That reverses the owner's own # rulings, so the research note studies it but the ballot does not offer it. Spending a freed // on floor division would reopen /% and belongs to a later ballot if B wins.

Research note: Docs/research/2026-11-04-comment-sigil.md (drafted at $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Research/comments/).

options.name: Keep //, and warn on Python's //
options.detail: Comments stay as they are: // for a line, /// for a doc comment and nested /* */ for a block. One new warning catches the Python habit. It fires when the code before // ends a number expression and the comment text is itself a number expression whose names exist here. The fix shows /%.
options.technical:
Lexer, parser, registry and editors are unchanged. The warning lives where types and scope are known, after type checking. It needs three things on one line. A number-typed expression ends right before a line comment. The comment text parses as an expression of number type. Every name in it resolves in scope. The structured fix replaces // with /%.

Lexical rules are not enough. The census in floor-warn-census.mjs flags 367, 146 or 61 corpus lines under three lexical rules. All 61 lines under the tightest rule are labels, such as return false // WB3. Each fails the typed rule, because it ends in a Bool or a unit call, or because it names something not in scope.

options.name: Two hashes
options.detail: A comment starts with ## and a space, and a doc comment with ### and a space. Four or more hashes make a plain divider comment. Block comments are removed, as in Python and Zig. A ## followed by a letter is an error, so ##Inline cannot silently drop a marker. // and /* become teaching errors, and a // b points to /%.
options.technical:
Lexer: ## followed by a space, a tab or the line end is a line comment. ### followed by the same is a doc comment. Four or more # make a plain comment. ## followed by anything else is a new error saying a marker uses one #. # stays one token everywhere else, so markers, [T#N], pkg#1.2.0, #line and #{x} keep working. The byte-zero shebang rule stays, and the config-file exception for :// is deleted.

Registry: COMMENT_PREFIX becomes ##, a doc row ### is added, and the block rows are removed. One lexer-driven jet fix rewrites 94,746 comment tokens in 7,815 files, 17 block comments and about 630 lines in 40 Markdown files.

The same cutover updates about 30 hand-written comment scanners, five machine-read comment forms, both TextMate grammars, the tree-sitter grammar, Zed and VS Code settings, and the self-host fixtures.
options.code:
### Splits a bill evenly.
#Inline fn share(total: Int, people: Int) -> Int {
    ## whole-number division drops the cents
    total /% people  ## #4828: round up later
}

fn run() {
    half :: 7 // 2
    print(share(1000, 3))
}

## jet check:
##   Error: Jet comments start with "##", not "//"
##     --> run.jet:8:15
##   Fix: whole-number division is "/%": half :: 7 /% 2
##   (a "##Inline" with no space is also an error: a marker uses one "#")

comparisons.note: Odin marks compiler directives with # and keeps // and nested /* */ for comments. Source: odin-lang.org/docs/overview.
Swift uses # for compiler-supplied values and macros, and // and /// for comments.
Rust attributes start with #, and comments use // and ///. Its lexer must tell a #! shebang from a #![ attribute on the first line.
Nim comments use #, doc comments ##, and nested blocks #[ ]#. Pragmas in {. .}, not #, mark compiler work. Source: nim-lang.org/docs/manual.html.
comparisons.code:
proc share*(total, people: int): int {.inline.} =
  ## Splits a bill evenly.
  # whole-number division drops the cents
  total div people

comparisons.note: In C macros, a doubled ## pastes two tokens. C readers know ## as paste, which Jet spells #{x}.
comparisons.code:
#define FIELD(name) int field_ ## name;  // ## pastes tokens
FIELD(total)  // expands to: int field_total;

comparisons.note: Both use # for comments. That frees // for floor division in Python and for merging records in Nix. Neither uses # for anything else.
comparisons.code:
half = 7 // 2              # Python: half is 3
defaults // { port = 8080; }  # Nix: merge two records

recommendation.why: Nothing planned needs //, because whole-number division is already /%. Keeping // matches every language that uses # for compiler work, and # keeps meaning that the compiler acts here.
gains: No rewrite, and every editor already knows //.
Comments never look like markers.

losses.loss: Python's 7 // 2 compiles and keeps only 7.
losses.mitigation: A new warning fires when a number is followed by // and a number expression, and shows /%.

losses.loss: On German and Nordic keyboards, / needs Shift.
losses.mitigation: Most of those keyboards need Shift or AltGr for # too, and editors toggle comments with one shortcut.

whyNot.reason: Two hashes put comments beside markers and rewrite 95,000 lines to free a glyph nothing needs.

recommendation.tradeoff: Keep the familiar comment and one meaning for #, and give up the thematic fit of ##.

decisions.title: Ask whether a Pool id still names a live entry: pool.has(id)
decisions.situation: A Pool is Jet's box for game objects such as monsters. Adding a monster gives you an id, a small ticket for its spot in the box. A monster can remember its target by id. When the target dies and is removed, reading through that old id stops the program, and today there is no way to ask first. We recommend pool.has(id): it answers yes or no, copies nothing, and the read after it still checks, so an old id can never reach the wrong monster.
decisions.gist: Should Pool answer whether an id still names a live entry?
decisions.lesson: An id holds a spot number and a count. Removing an entry bumps the spot's count, so an old id never reaches a new monster that reuses the spot. Reading through an old id stops the program. A yes-or-no check lets a chasing monster forget a dead target instead.
decisions.story: Ana's imp chases a target it holds by id. Between two game ticks the target dies and is removed. On the next tick the imp must hit the target if it still exists, or else forget it. Every option runs the same program and prints 90, then true. No option may hit a new monster that took over the old spot.
decisions.inWild:
Rust's slotmap crate, a widely used generational arena, offers contains_key(id) -> bool beside indexing. Source: https://docs.rs/slotmap/latest/slotmap/struct.SlotMap.html#method.contains_key

In C the same check is written by hand: the spot number is in range and the spot's count matches the id's count.
decisions.detail:
RATIFIED RULES

Docs/spec/spec.md:1569-1576 and Docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:2848-2856 (D-POOLID-API1) give Pool add, indexing, ids and remove. Ids are copyable and comparable. Indexing a stale id stops the program; remove returns an optional value. add, remove and pool[id] = v need a writable pool: a := binding or a & parameter. D-HAS-VERB1=A makes has the membership word for lists, sets and map keys. 

D-FNVAL-WRITE1=A lets a function type carry & and ^ input marks, which makes option B's write callback legal. D-WRITE-TAKE1=A gives replace(&place, value) and swap on any place, including pool[id].

WHAT THE CODE DOES TODAY

Compiler/JetIR/Source/BuildPools.jet:111-129 (ir_pool_find) computes one live bit: the spot number is below the pool length and the spot's count equals the id's count. remove (:133-155) and indexing (:192-217) both use that bit. Indexing stops with 'this ID no longer refers to a live value — its pool slot was removed' (:207). Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Calls/SharedOwner.jet:378-429 checks add, remove and ids; has is unknown, E0102.

Probes, rechecked on 2559996f at O0 and O2: opus_pool_today prints 60, then stops with E3001 after removal. opus_pool_has_today fails with E0102. opus_pool_reuse shows a stale id still stops after a new entry takes the spot, and removing it again returns None. opus_pool_shape runs every line of option A except has and prints 90, then true.

HOW A'S DOWNSIDES ARE DESIGNED AWAY

The earlier draft listed two losses for A and a third caveat. Each now has a concrete answer.

1. Two checks (has, then index). has returns the same live bit that indexing computes, so the extra cost is one length compare and one count compare on a spot just read. It never reads or copies the monster. Code that already knows an id is live indexes directly.

2. The answer could go stale before the read. Only code that holds the pool for writing can remove an entry (spec.md:1574-1576). So between has and the read, only code written on that path can remove it. If it does, the read still checks and stops. It never reaches a newer monster in the same spot.

3. Ids carry no pool identity. In review61_edges an id from one pool read 300 from another. This is true of indexing and remove today and of every option. It is shared, not a cost of A. A pool stamp in ids would fix it for all options and needs its own card.

WHY B CHANGED

The earlier B returned a copy. A copy cannot write the target back, costs a full copy and does not work for entries that cannot be copied. With D-FNVAL-WRITE1=A, the honest alternative is a write callback, which removes A's two-step gap. So B is now that design.

KNOWN DEFECTS, NOT VOTES

review61_id_eq fails with E0312 even for id == id, against the comparable-id rule; option C needs it fixed. review61_edges removes an entry through a read-only Pool parameter, against spec E0202. That defect weakens A's staleness argument until fixed and needs a defect card whatever the vote.

STALE IDS AND REUSE

has(id) is false exactly when remove(id) would return None: spot out of range or count mismatch. Reusing a spot never makes an old id live again. The count is a 64-bit number, so wraparound needs 2^63 removals of one spot.

BEGINNER AND EXPERT

Beginners call has right before indexing. Experts who know an id is live index directly and keep the safety check. Proposed examples use the ratified name-first declaration spelling (D-DECL-BINDING1=B); probes use the current spelling.

options.name: pool.has(id) -> Bool
options.detail: Ask whether the pool still has a live entry for this id. Read and write the entry with pool[id], as today. The read still checks, so a stale answer stops the program and never reaches the wrong monster.
options.technical: has returns the live bit that indexing already computes: spot in range and matching count. It is false exactly when remove(id) would return None. It neither reads nor copies the entry. Sema gains one Pool method beside add, remove and ids; the lowering reuses ir_pool_find.

options.name: pool.edit(id, action) -> Bool
options.detail: Run an action on the entry if it is live, and return whether it ran. Check and write happen in one step. While the action runs, the pool is busy, so the action cannot touch other monsters in it.
options.technical: action has type fn(&T), allowed by D-FNVAL-WRITE1=A. edit checks once, lends the entry to the action and returns true, or returns false for a stale id. The pool is borrowed for writing during the call, so a lambda that also uses the pool is refused. It adds a second way to write an entry beside indexing.

options.name: No new API: search pool.ids()
options.detail: Take a fresh list of live ids and compare the target with each one. Pool gets no new method.
options.technical: Uses only ratified operations. It needs id == id, which fails today with E0312; that bug fix needs no vote. Each check builds a list and scans it, so a tick with many chasers does work that grows with chasers times entries.

comparisons.note: slotmap pairs a yes-or-no check with indexing, and indexing a removed key panics. Source: https://docs.rs/slotmap/latest/slotmap/struct.SlotMap.html
The same check written by hand over a spot table.

recommendation.why: A asks one yes-or-no question with the word maps and sets already use. It copies nothing, keeps pool[id] as the one way to read and write, and the read still checks, so the worst case is a clear stop.
gains: A dead target is forgotten instead of stopping the game.
No copy, no callback, no new way to write.
The same has word as maps and sets.

losses.loss: The check and the read are two steps.
losses.mitigation: Only code you write between them can remove the entry. If it does, the read stops clearly, never reaching the wrong monster.

losses.loss: has and the read both check the id.
losses.mitigation: The second check is two number compares on the spot just read. Code that knows an id is live indexes directly.

whyNot.reason: B closes the two-step gap, but the action cannot touch other monsters and every write needs a callback.
C needs no new method, but every check builds and scans a list of all monsters each tick.
