decisions.title: Run normal exit cleanup before process replacement, with an explicit skip setting
decisions.situation: Process replacement hands the running program over to another one, like a shell's exec. The approved call skips cleanup, and the seed does not implement that call yet. Running cleanup first would finish logs and restore the terminal, but cleanup cannot be undone if startup fails or deletes an input file. We recommend normal cleanup by default with an explicit skip setting, while stating that irreversible cost without calling it rare.
decisions.gist: Should process replacement run normal cleanup first, with an explicit opt-out for resource-sensitive handoffs?
decisions.lesson: Every option hands the same launcher to sh, which exits 3. A prepares the command, then runs normal exit cleanup before handing over. Checks can catch errors early, but cannot guarantee startup. One cost remains: cleanup is irreversible, including deleted temporary inputs. Use explicit kept handles or .cleanup(.Skip) when the target needs those resources.
decisions.story: Priya's launcher records a tool choice and leaves a full-screen picker before handing over. She wants its log finished and terminal restored without writing a second cleanup path.
decisions.inWild:
# POSIX shell; source and exercised results are in detail.
exec sh -c 'exit 3'
# Same process, exit 3; the old shell's EXIT trap does not run.
decisions.detail:
WHAT THIS AMENDS

D-CORE-PROCREPLACE1=A ratified spec.replace_process(), skip-cleanup and a Windows waiting stand-in. A changes default cleanup and post-cleanup errors; B keeps that approval. Retain -[Exec, Time.Wait]> Never IOError!, admitting Exec before preparation or cleanup. D-JAI-DEFER1=A supplies one reverse-order cleanup list; D-TERM-COMMANDS1=A supplies terminal restoration. Reuse the ordinary exit boundary, not a second cleanup mechanism.

PREPARE, THEN COMMIT

Reject ratified incompatible settings before side effects: Capture/Stream, terminal, detached, timeout, output_limit and under. Retain cwd, environment, supported limits and explicit keep_open ownership under D-CORE-PROCINHERIT1=A. Unset stdin stays closed. Pin launch data and kept handles outside frames cleanup destroys. Resolve using the spec's PATH/cwd and check what can be validated without changing the caller. Preparation failure returns IOError without exit cleanup.

After preparation, A commits to normal cleanup and terminal restoration. Launch data and kept handles survive; flush writers without closing transferred handles. Start only after cleanup succeeds. A reported startup failure after commitment prints once and exits 127 for missing program/interpreter, otherwise 126, without repeated cleanup. Cleanup failure follows existing exit-failure policy and never starts the target. Cleanup can remove files or cancel work; it cannot be rolled back.

NO AUTOMATIC TEMPORARY RETENTION

The prior draft scanned argument strings and cancelled temporary-path deletion. That misses --input=path, script/config dependencies, environment references, symlink aliases and arbitrary deferred deletes. It also changes ownership and can leave unowned files. Remove that mechanism: temporary owners keep normal deletion semantics.

Targets needing temporary content use existing explicit keep_open ownership and an open-handle path where supported, or .Skip when the original pathname must survive. No new file-lifetime API is hidden here.

PREFLIGHT IS NOT A PROOF

Opening an executable protects that file against replacement/unlinking, not its interpreter, loader, libraries or later permission/resource checks. Path-based starts and scripts have different constraints. Do not substitute a script interpreter manually and claim unchanged semantics. Linux execveat of a script with a close-on-exec descriptor can fail ENOENT; inheriting it can leak a descriptor. Use the approved launch and kept-handle contracts, not a prescribed syscall trick. No Jet measurement establishes failure frequency.

SKIP AND FAIR B

spec.cleanup(.Skip).replace_process() keeps skip-cleanup behavior: no defers, resource cleanup or exit handlers; output still flushes. This suits deliberate terminal/resource inheritance. A defaults to .Run. The setting applies to replacement, not run/spawn.

B keeps skip as the sole contract. Callers can finish resource scopes and restore the terminal explicitly; not every launcher needs to duplicate all cleanup. Ordinary reported launch errors return as approved. Neither option can recover from kernel failure after the old image is already destroyed.

ONE COST REMAINS

Cleanup is irreversible: late startup failure ends the launcher, and cleanup may delete inputs the target needs. Use explicit kept handles where suitable or .Skip for resource-sensitive handoffs. This is not engineered away or proven negligible for every launcher.

WINDOWS AND TIERS

Keep Windows start/wait/exit with the child's status. A cleans once before start; B skips. Add no descendant-killing policy. One runtime contract covers O0/O1/O2, memory execution and file fallback under D-EXEC-RELAUNCH1=A and D-EXEC-NOEXEC1=A. Web refuses Exec before cleanup.

Future acceptance covers rejected settings, normal cleanup/defer order, terminal restoration, kept writers/handles, temporary-path deletion, scripts, missing interpreter/loader, cleanup failure, late startup failure, signals and the Windows stand-in. These are not completed checks.

CHECKED EVIDENCE

exec_now.jet ran a child and exited 3; exec_replace.jet failed E0102. HostProcess.jet:72-85 uses a root stop for cleanup. RouteAFiles.jet:694-698 describes last-owner temporary-file deletion. ProcessExecutionPrepare.jet:192-278 contains relaunch and argv/env preparation, not the old draft's complete preflight. Shell probes skipped EXIT traps on successful exec (3) and missing executable (127).

PRIMARY SOURCES

Linux execve documents permission, interpreter, I/O, resource and format failures, including failure after image teardown: https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/execve.2.html. execveat documents script-descriptor limitations: https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/execveat.2.html. No proposed replacement implementation or late-failure rate was exercised.

decisions.title: Keep moving-source intent in env.jet and exact versions in the lock only
decisions.situation: An automatic package source says which updates the developer wants, while a lock file records the exact selected version. The approved refresh rule also writes that result into the environment declaration, and a reported refresh produced a line the next run rejected. The current development source guards against unparseable writeback, but still contains the rewrite path. We recommend making the lock the sole exact-version authority and leaving the developer's file untouched.
decisions.gist: Should refreshes leave env.jet untouched and record exact versions only in the lock?
decisions.lesson: env.jet says omp@jetpack#auto; the lock records the exact version chosen. A keeps that split and removes refresh writeback. The exact version remains readable in the lock, and outdated includes it even for current packages. B also keeps one authoritative lock, but writes a human-readable version comment into env.jet after each refresh.
decisions.story: Lena marked omp to update automatically. A refresh changed her declaration, and the next environment preparation rejected a line she had never written.
decisions.inWild: Ordinary stable cargo update updates Cargo.lock while preserving Cargo.toml version requirements: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-update.html. The documented nightly --breaking mode can modify requirements, so this is not a claim that every possible Cargo update mode never rewrites the manifest.
decisions.detail:
WHAT THIS AMENDS

D-CHANNEL-AUTO1=A names the automatic tier and says refreshed pins propagate into the manifest. This vote replaces only that writeback contract for moving sources, including manual update of #latest. Pinned/manual/automatic policy meanings stay unchanged. AUTO1's example used a prefix marker; the current source-ref spelling is the suffix omp@jetpack#auto. That spelling difference is not another choice here.

REPORTED FAILURE, NOT A NEW REPRO

The supplied report says a refresh rewrote omp@jetpack#auto to omp#1.2.3@nixpkgs#auto and the next preparation failed E0968. This review did not rerun the reported failure. RefSpec.jet:614-619 rejects # in the target before @; :767-777 also rejects direct @nixpkgs. The moving selector does not have an independent exact-pin slot, so the proposed writeback cannot express both meanings in the existing grammar.

WHAT THE DEVELOPMENT CODE ACTUALLY DOES

ChannelResolution.jet:145-158 constructs the rewritten ref, then returns without writing when ProviderRef.classify rejects it at :155. This guards the demonstrated malformed shape. Do not claim every possible resolver result is rejected or the entire writer is proven dead: cli_exact_upstream at :257-259 passes through any colon-containing fixture value. The source still calls the writer before recording the lock at :106-115; manual update does so in UpdateCommand.jet:219-225. This is source evidence, not an exercised end-to-end refresh.

A'S CONTRACT

Refresh/update never modify env.jet. Remove cli_rewrite_channel_manifest, cli_manifest_channel_ref and their writeback-only error/report paths; retain resolution and lock errors. The lock remains the sole authoritative exact resolution. ChannelResolution.jet:125-133 reads the locked exact source for the table; automatic policy can refresh it first, so saying build/run/env only read and never resolve would be false. The selected exact source must be locked before realization; existing offline, CI and trust behavior stays unchanged.

UpdateCommand.jet:261-278 currently prints exact versions on stale rows but only current on equal rows. A prints the locked exact version on both and includes it when freshness lookup fails, labeling freshness unknown rather than current. A failed network request is not evidence of freshness. Offline readers can inspect the lock directly; this vote does not promise outdated already works offline.

STRONG B WITHOUT A SECOND PIN AUTHORITY

B uses exactly the same lock and resolution behavior, but refreshes a tool-owned comment beside the declaration showing the locked result. Comments never affect resolution or override the lock; outdated remains authoritative reporting. A stale comment is merely a stale annotation, not a pin-conflict error. This is a real convenience option for reading one file, without adding selector grammar or a second pins field. Both options resolve the same omp version.

WHY THE OLD B AND C WERE REMOVED

Duplicating an authoritative exact pin in a selector or pins field adds reconciliation and a second mechanism for the same meaning. A derived comment offers the visibility benefit without another semantic authority. No new source-ref syntax, lock format or retired-spelling rewrite is approved.

NO REMAINING VERSION-VISIBILITY LOSS

The exact version stays in its canonical lock home and is included in freshness reporting. Not copying it into a hand-written declaration is the intended separation, not an unresolved runtime cost. Lock sharing remains necessary for reproducibility under both options, as it already was.

ACCEPTANCE

Prove byte-for-byte env.jet preservation on automatic and manual refresh, changed/unchanged locks, malformed old writeback shapes, locked/current/unknown report rows, and missing-lock or write failures. These are future checks; no package refresh or new reporter ran in this review.

decisions.title: Core declares the runtime functions it calls with a checked #Import(jet), bound only to the runtime's published #Export(jet) surface
decisions.situation: Core calls runtime functions that no Jet source declares. Core/Time/Time.jet calls core.time.__sleep_ns(duration.ns), and only a row in Compiler/Prelude/Core.jet binds it to jet_std_time_sleep_duration_ns. Dev 97ec15f323 has 1057 such rows naming 575 runtime symbols. The runtime defines 3216 #Export(c) functions, so most exports are internals that Core never binds. The runtime side is typed Jet already: HostTime.jet:214 exports jet_std_time_sleep_duration_ns(nanos: I64). Packages bind C symbols with `#Import(c) name: fn(…) -> T = "symbol"`, a gated unsafe region. `#Import(jet)` does not parse today (E0081). Card #6151 needs one ratified, safe way for any package to declare such a leaf, so the compiler tables and module-name gates can go.
decisions.gist: How does Jet source, Core included, declare a function the Jet runtime provides, so that the call is checked, safe and keeps its effects?
decisions.lesson: A pairs the runtime's export with the package's import, using the marker Jet already has for foreign symbols. The runtime marks what it publishes `#Export(jet)` and writes the effects there. A package writes `#Import(jet) name: fn(…) -[Effects]> T = "symbol"`, and the compiler checks both signatures, effects included. A declaration can then neither drop an effect nor reach an internal runtime function. Internal functions stay `#Export(c)`, reachable only through `#Import(c)` inside `#Unsafe`. The cost is one cutover of 575 symbols and an export manifest inside jet.
decisions.story: Core's sleep is ordinary Jet: `sleep: fn(duration: Duration) Never! -[Time.Wait]> { __sleep_ns(duration.ns) }`, and `__sleep_ns` is declared one line above it, not hidden in a compiler table. Mia writes a metrics package and wants the runtime's monotonic clock. She writes the same one-line import Core uses, the compiler checks it against what the runtime publishes, and her package's authority line must still grant Time. When she copies a symbol that the runtime keeps internal, the compiler refuses it and points at the published list.
decisions.inWild: Rust binds foreign symbols in `extern` blocks renamed with #[link_name], and every call is `unsafe` (https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/items/external-blocks.html). Zig's `extern fn` binds by name and trusts the declaration (https://ziglang.org/documentation/master/#extern). Swift's unofficial @_silgen_name binds a declaration to a runtime symbol without a check (https://github.com/swiftlang/swift/blob/main/docs/ReferenceGuides/UnderscoredAttributes.md). Go's //go:linkname let packages reach runtime internals, and Go 1.23 began restricting it because those internals could no longer change (https://go.dev/doc/go1.23#linker). None checks a declaration against the provider's signature.
decisions.detail:
WHAT VOTING A INCLUDES

1. Runtime side. A runtime function published to Jet code is written `#Export(jet) symbol: fn(params) -[Effects]> T Failure! { … }`. `#Export(c)` stays for the C ABI and for internals. Published signatures obey a Jet-safe boundary law: typed handles, no raw pointers, no bare handle ids.

2. Package side. A package writes `#Import(jet) name: fn(params) -[Effects]> T Failure! = "symbol"`, a bodiless declaration like `#Import(c)`. The symbol must be a published export. Types must match under the Int-to-I64 marshalling law. Effects and failure must be identical. Each mismatch is one registered diagnostic with a UI snapshot (#6151 c3).

3. Calls. A call needs no `#Unsafe`. Its effects come from the declaration, so the package's authority must grant them. `jet inspect` shows the same effects for a Core call and a user call (c33). Visibility is ordinary: a `__` name is module-private (c5, c6).

4. Internals. An unpublished runtime symbol is reachable only as `#Import(c)` inside `#Unsafe("reason")`. That is today's expert path, with its sentry and ratchet row. Core uses it for handle internals as vetted standard-library code (I1).

5. Manifest. jet generates the export manifest when it builds its runtime pack, embeds it, and ships it with each release. A chain drift check compares it with the runtime sources. The web tier links the same published symbols from the shared runtime (I9). A target that cannot provide an export reports it through the existing target-capability rule.

6. Cutover. The 575 bound symbols move to `#Export(jet)`, with effects taken from today's Core wrappers. Each dispatcher row becomes an `#Import(jet)` declaration in its Core module. The dispatcher tables and member-keyed Route*.jet tables are deleted (c11). Core and user leaves lower to one IR call shape (c12).

NEW SPELLINGS (I7). The marker argument `jet` on `#Import` and `#Export`. Both markers and the `= "symbol"` form already exist.

REVIEW FINDINGS. The draft let a declaration choose its own effects, which bypasses authority; A now checks effects against the export. The draft let any package bind any of 3216 exports; A now publishes a deliberate surface. Measured counts replaced the draft's estimate of 2,000 rows. Option D was added.

LIMITS. Runtime-side effects are asserted by vetted runtime code, not proved. Web provision of every published export is required by I9 but not yet measured.

options.detail: The runtime marks what it publishes and writes the effects there; packages import by symbol with the same marker they use for C. The compiler checks types, effects and failure on both sides. Internal runtime functions stay #Export(c), reachable only through #Import(c) inside #Unsafe.

Sema: a manifest of #Export(jet) signatures (generated with the runtime pack, embedded in jet) checks each import; calls carry the declaration's effects. Codegen: one foreign-call IR shape for every leaf.

options.name: A separate #Host marker, with the same checks

options.technical: Every published runtime export is renamed to the law in one cutover. Moving a Core function to another module renames its runtime symbol (an ABI change), and one runtime function cannot serve two Jet names.

options.name: A generated runtime module; no leaf declarations at all
options.detail: jet generates a module `jet.runtime` from the #Export(jet) manifest. Core and packages write `use rt: jet.runtime` and call `rt.jet_std_time_sleep_duration_ns(d.ns)`. Nothing can drift, because nothing is hand-written.
options.technical: No new marker on the import side. Callers see C-style symbol names, and every package sees the whole published surface. #6151 c1 and c3 (a declaration that can disagree) have no subject and would need rewording.

options.name: The runtime is an ordinary library
options.detail: The runtime package jet_runtime ships prebuilt with the compiler, and any package, Core included, uses it like any other library. Its public functions have Jet names, Jet types and their own inferred effects. Private functions stay unreachable through ordinary visibility. There is no marker, no symbol string and no manifest, because the declaration is the runtime's own code.
options.technical: The compiler loads the runtime package interface from the toolchain, the way it reads any precompiled dependency. Calls lower to direct calls into the one shared runtime library, so every tier runs the same code. The dispatcher rows in the compiler go away. A few runtime helpers written in C keep a C import inside the runtime, under #Unsafe. #Export(c) stays only for the C ABI used by generated code and foreign hosts.

use rt: jet.runtime.time
sleep: fn(duration: Duration) Never! -[Time.Wait]> { rt.sleep_ns(duration.ns) }

recommendation.why: Core uses only what any package can use, and nothing can drift because the declaration is the runtime's own code.
gains: Core leaves are ordinary declared Jet; the compiler's Core tables and member-keyed route tables go.
Any package can bind a published runtime service safely, with its effects enforced by authority.
The runtime's internal functions stay changeable, because only #Export(jet) is a public contract.

losses.mitigation: The rename is mechanical, and the compiler's check of every caller proves it complete.

Same checks as A, but a second marker for the meaning #Import already has (an I8 cost) with its own parser, formatter and sema path.
Ties runtime symbol names to Core module paths: moving a function becomes an ABI change, one runtime function cannot serve two Jet names, and all published symbols are renamed.
No drift, but C-style names leak into every caller, Core keeps no readable leaf declarations, and #6151 c1/c3 lose their subject.

decisions.title: Every effect is allowed by default; written code denies, and a run warns when its effects change
decisions.gist: What may a Jet program do when nobody has written any authority?
decisions.lesson: Every effect is allowed unless code denies it. Jet knows a program's effects before it starts, so a run lists them up front, and lists them again whenever they change. A written authority row is a ceiling and silences the notice for what it lists.
decisions.story: Ana writes a script that reads a file and calls an API. She runs it and sees one line naming what it does, then it runs. Next week a dependency update adds process launching, and the next run names the new effect. Her team adds an authority row to the package, and anything outside that row fails at check time.
decisions.inWild: Deno denies by default and prompts at first access, so most users pass -A. Node allows everything unless started with --permission. Python, Go and Rust have no authority model at all.
decisions.detail:
Option A is the owner's proposal with four refinements. First, the notice repeats when the effect set changes. Second, a written authority row is a ceiling and silences the notice for what it lists. Third, jetpack reports a dependency whose effects widen, and --locked refuses it. Fourth, code run straight from a URL or the registry asks before its first run.

Option B is the proposal as first stated: a notice on the first run only.

Option C keeps today's model, where undecided effects prompt in a terminal and stop without one.

options.name: Allow by default, warn on change, ceilings
options.detail: Every effect is allowed unless denied. The run lists effects before the program starts and again when they change. Authority rows are ceilings, jetpack reports dependency widening, and remote code asks first.
options.code:
$ jet run tool.jet
note: tool.jet reads files and connects to the network (-A hides this)

options.name: Allow by default, warn on first run
options.detail: Every effect is allowed unless denied, and the first run lists the effects once.
options.code:
$ jet run tool.jet
note: first run: tool.jet reads files and connects to the network

options.name: Keep the prompt
options.detail: Undecided effects prompt in a terminal and stop without one.
options.code:
$ jet run tool.jet
tool.jet reads files and connects to the network. Run it? [Y/n/always]

recommendation.why: No friction for beginners, and nothing changes silently: a new effect, from your code or a dependency, is always named.
recommendation.tradeoff: A run is never blocked by default; protection comes from written ceilings and the change notice.

whyNot.reason: A dependency update that adds an effect would never be noticed after the first run.
Prompts train people to answer yes, and stop every run without a terminal.

losses.loss: Unreviewed local code runs with the user's full authority.
losses.mitigation: The notice names every effect before the program starts, and ceilings stop what a team denies.

decisions.title: What `Int{f}` means when f is a Float
decisions.gist: What should `Int{f}` do with a Float, and how do experts pick the exact rounding and overflow behavior they need?
decisions.lesson: Conversions are written `Type{value}`, and `Float{n}` already stops when the result would be inexact. Across languages and fields, the agreed practice is that the default never loses information silently. The rounding direction is always named. An out-of-range value stops, returns a value you can check, or saturates because you asked. Fields disagree on rounding (games want floor, statistics and money want ties-to-even, everyday arithmetic wants ties-away, audio and pixels want saturation), so no single silent default serves them all.
decisions.story:
Ana has `pos: Float` and wants a list index. She writes `Int{pos}`; when pos is 2.0 she gets 2, and when it is 2.5 the program stops. The message offers `math.floor`, `math.trunc`, `math.ceil`, `math.round` and `math.round_even`. She picks `Int{math.floor(pos)}`.

Ben writes an audio mixer and wants out-of-range samples clipped, never a stop: he writes `I16.saturating_from(sample * 32767.0)`. Chen totals invoice lines and writes `math.round_even(cents)`, the rounding accountants and IEEE 754 use.
decisions.inWild:
IEEE 754-2019 section 5.8 defines one float-to-integer conversion per rounding direction: toward zero, down, up, nearest-even and nearest-away. Each signals invalid operation on NaN, infinity or out of range, never a silent value (https://standards.ieee.org/ieee/754/6210/).

Julia: `Int(2.5)` throws InexactError and `Int(2.0)` is 2. Rounding is named: `trunc(Int, x)`, `floor(Int, x)`, `ceil(Int, x)` and `round(Int, x)`. `round` is ties-to-even unless a RoundingMode says otherwise, and out of range throws (https://docs.julialang.org/en/v1/manual/mathematical-operations/#Rounding-functions). This is option A's design.

Swift: `Int(3.7)` truncates and traps on NaN, infinity or out of range. `Int(exactly: 3.5)` is nil. `x.rounded(.toNearestOrEven)` names any of six rounding rules (https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swift/floatingpointroundingrule).

Rust: `f as i64` truncates and saturates, and NaN becomes 0; before 1.45 it was undefined behavior. `to_int_unchecked` is the unsafe fast form. `round_ties_even` arrived in 1.77, because `round` is ties-away (https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/expressions/operator-expr.html#numeric-cast). Java and Kotlin `toInt()` also truncate and saturate with NaN as 0.

Python `int(3.7)` truncates and raises on NaN and infinity. Its `round()` is ties-to-even. NumPy, R and C# `Math.Round` also default to ties-to-even. Go `int(f)` truncates and is implementation-defined out of range.
decisions.detail:
WHAT A INCLUDES

1. `Int{f}` is exact. A whole, finite Float inside Int converts; a fraction, NaN, infinity or an out-of-range value stops the program with a registered error naming each rounding function. A literal body is checked at compile time: `Int{3.0}` is 3, `Int{3.5}` is an error.

2. Every rounding direction is named. `Int{math.trunc(f)}`, `Int{math.floor(f)}` and `Int{math.ceil(f)}` use the existing Float functions. `math.round(f) -> Int` keeps ties-away-from-zero (2.5 is 3, -2.5 is -3). New `math.round_even(f) -> Int` rounds ties to even (2.5 is 2, 3.5 is 4), the IEEE 754 default used by statistics and money.

3. `math.round` stops on NaN, infinity or an out-of-range value. Today it returns 0 for NaN and silently clamps, which breaks the rule in item 1. `math.round_even` behaves the same way.

4. The recoverable form stays: `Int.from_float(f)` truncates and returns None on NaN, infinity or out of range.

5. Saturation is an explicit opt-in. New `Int.saturating_from(f)` truncates toward zero, clamps to the type's range and maps NaN to 0, and never stops. Every integer head has it: `U8.saturating_from(f)` for a pixel, `I16.saturating_from(f)` for an audio sample.

6. Cost. `Int{math.floor(f)}` must compile to the CPU's round and convert instructions plus one range check, and the check disappears when the optimizer proves the range. That is why no unchecked `#Unsafe` form is proposed: the check costs one compare.

7. `I64{f}`, `U8{f}` and the other integer heads follow the same rules as `Int{f}`. `Float{n}`, `F32{f}` and integer-to-integer heads do not change.

BEGINNER PATH: `Int{f}`, and the stop message teaches the named roundings. EXPERT PATH: pick the exact rounding (`trunc`, `floor`, `ceil`, `round`, `round_even`) and the exact failure handling (stop with `Int{...}`, None with `from_float`, clamp with `saturating_from`).

EDGE CASES: -0.0 converts to 0. 9223372036854775807.0 is out of range, because the nearest Float is 2^63. A subnormal is not whole, so it stops unless it is rounded first.

options.name: Exact by default, every rounding and overflow behavior named
options.detail: `Int{f}` converts a whole number and stops otherwise. trunc, floor, ceil, round (ties away) and round_even (ties to even) pick the rounding. `from_float` returns None and `saturating_from` clamps. `math.round` stops on NaN and out of range instead of returning 0 or clamping.
options.code:
idx: Int{pos}                  // 2.0 -> 2; 2.5 stops
cell: Int{math.floor(-2.5)}    // -3
cents: math.round_even(2.5)    // 2
sample: I16.saturating_from(4.0e4)  // 32767
maybe: Int.from_float(pos) ?? 0

options.name: Truncate and stop (Swift, Python)
options.detail: `Int{f}` truncates toward zero and stops only on NaN, infinity or a value outside Int.

options.name: Truncate and saturate, never stop (Rust `as`, Java, Kotlin)
options.detail: `Int{f}` truncates toward zero, clamps to the type's range and maps NaN to 0. It never stops.

recommendation.why: It is the shared best practice: the default never loses information silently, as in IEEE 754, Julia and Jet's own `Float{n}`. Fields disagree on rounding and overflow, so each choice is named instead of guessed. Beginners get the short spelling with a teaching stop; experts get each IEEE rounding direction and each failure style explicitly.
recommendation.tradeoff: A fraction is caught when the program runs, not at check time, because the checker cannot know whether a Float value is whole. Literal bodies are still checked at compile time.
gains: `Int{f}` works, with the same rule as `Float{n}`.
Every rounding a field needs is one named call, including ties-to-even, which Jet lacks today.
Audio, pixel and sensor code gets saturation explicitly, without a stop.
`math.round` no longer turns NaN into 0 silently.

losses.loss: Code that wants truncation writes `Int{math.trunc(f)}` instead of a bare `Int{f}`.
losses.mitigation: The stop message names each rounding, and `jet fix` offers them.

losses.loss: Three failure styles exist: stop, None and clamp.
losses.mitigation: They differ only in failure handling, like indexing versus `.get()`. Beginners meet only `Int{f}`.

losses.loss: `math.round` stopping on NaN changes current behavior.
losses.mitigation: Every in-repository caller is migrated in the same cutover; code that wants a fallback writes `Int.from_float`.

whyNot.reason: Silent truncation is a classic bug: `Int{-0.5}` is 0 and `Int{2.9999}` is 2, with no sign a fraction was dropped. Games also need floor, not truncation, for negative coordinates.

Silent clamping and NaN as 0 turn bad data into plausible numbers; Rust kept `as` only for compatibility and added explicit forms. Saturation belongs to the code that asks for it, which A gives as `saturating_from`.

surface.gist: What should `Int{f}` do, and how do experts pick the exact rounding and overflow?
surface.lesson: Best practice everywhere: never lose information silently, and name the rounding, because fields disagree.

current.note: Today Int{f} is an error; from_float truncates and returns None; math.round turns NaN into 0 and clamps.
current.code:
lo: Int{pos}                  // E0112
lo: Int.from_float(pos) ?? 0  // works

wild.note: Julia's `Int(x)` is exact; every rounding is named.
wild.code:
Int(2.0)          # 2
Int(2.5)          # InexactError
floor(Int, -2.5)  # -3
round(Int, 2.5)   # 2 (ties to even)

options.name: Exact default, named control
options.gist: Int{f} is exact; trunc, floor, ceil, round, round_even and saturating_from give experts each behavior.
gains: Your spelling
Never loses a fraction silently
Ties-to-even and saturation available
losses: Fractions are caught at run time

options.name: Truncate
options.gist: Int{f} drops the fraction, stops on NaN.
gains: Short
losses: Silent loss of the fraction

proposed.code: idx: Int{2.7}  // 2

options.name: Saturate
options.gist: Int{f} truncates and clamps; NaN is 0; never stops.
gains: Never stops
losses: Bad data becomes plausible numbers

proposed.code: nan: Int{math.NAN}  // 0

recommendation.why: The default never loses information, and every field's rounding and overflow is one named call.
gains: Int{f} works
Matches Float{n}
Experts control rounding and overflow exactly

losses.loss: Truncation is written out.
losses.mitigation: The stop message and jet fix offer each rounding.

whyNot.reason: Drops fractions silently.
Turns NaN and overflow into plausible numbers.

recommendation.tradeoff: Fractions are caught when the program runs, not at check time.

decisions.title: Transpile Jet to any language through a target trait that a library implements
decisions.situation: Transpiling means writing a Jet program as the same program in another language, such as C, Rust, JavaScript or Lua. You asked for targets that anyone can add: each target is an ordinary Jet library that implements one trait. The hard part is keeping Jet's meaning. Overflow checks, bounds checks, cleanup and error stops must behave the same in every language. You are asked what a target library receives from the compiler, what it must implement, and how much of the output it may shape. Seeding and bootstrapping the compiler are a separate, later question on their own card.
decisions.gist: What does a transpilation target implement, and what does it receive from the compiler, so that a library can add any language while the program keeps one meaning?
decisions.lesson: A target can only keep Jet's meaning if every check is already an explicit step when it receives the program. A target that receives the source tree must re-implement every check itself, and that is where languages drift apart. Haxe is the known example: its Int behaves differently on different targets.
decisions.story:
Ana's team has a Lua game engine and wants her Jet pathfinding code inside it. She adds the community `lua` target package to her project and runs `jet build --to lua path.jet`. She gets `path.lua` plus `jet_runtime.lua`, and the engine loads them like any other module.

An overflow in her code stops with the same message in Lua as in `jet run`, because the target spelled checks the compiler had already made explicit. Ben writes that `lua` target in about 2,000 lines of Jet. He implements the required trait methods, then overrides the hooks for records and loops so the output reads like ordinary Lua. `jet test --to lua` runs every executable example through his target and compares the output with `jet run`.
decisions.inWild:
Haxe compiles one language to JavaScript, C++, C#, Java, Python, Lua and PHP. Reflaxe lets a library add a target from Haxe's typed syntax tree (https://github.com/SomeRanDev/reflaxe). Integer width and overflow differ between Haxe targets (https://haxe.org/manual/types-basic-types.html).

Fable compiles F# to JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, Rust and Dart from the typed tree. Its documentation lists behavior that differs per target, such as numeric types and reflection (https://fable.io/docs/).

Kotlin lowers every platform from one shared IR, and its JVM, JavaScript, Wasm and Native back ends consume that IR (https://kotlinlang.org/docs/multiplatform.html).

Nim, Gleam and Scala.js each ship a fixed set of first-party back ends, and third parties cannot add a language (https://nim-lang.org/docs/backends.html, https://gleam.run/documentation/).

LLVM lets anyone add a machine target by implementing its target classes. Emscripten and wasm2c turn low-level code into JavaScript or C that is correct but hard to read.
decisions.detail:
WHAT VOTING A INCLUDES

1. One trait. `core.compiler.target.Target` is a public, versioned trait. A target is any Jet package with a type that implements it. First-party targets are ordinary implementations with no special access.

2. What a target receives. It receives the checked program after one shared pass that makes every meaning explicit. That covers overflow checks, big-integer spills, bounds checks, cleanup, error stops and the stop protocol. Jet's own runtime (Prelude and Core) arrives the same way and is transpiled by the same target.

3. What a target must implement. Required methods spell a closed list of explicit operations (arithmetic, memory, calls, branches, loops and returns). A small set of host leaves gives the target language's system calls, clock, memory and threads. Each operation has a conformance test.

4. Idiom hooks. Optional hooks let a target spell records, enums, functions, loops, strings and errors in the target language's own style. Each hook receives the already explicit form and has a default built from the required methods. A target can therefore start plain and grow idiomatic, and a hook can never drop a check.

5. Capabilities first. A target declares what it can spell, such as threads, 64-bit integers, tail calls or SIMD. A program that needs something missing gets a registered error naming the target before anything is written.

6. One meaning. `jet test --to <target>` runs every executable example through the target and compares stdout, stderr and the exit code with `jet run`. A target is listed as conforming only when that passes.

7. Command. `jet build --to <target> file.jet` writes the program's files. `c` and `rust` are the first-party targets; any other name is a target package listed in the project's dependencies.

8. Order. The shared explicit pass and the public program view land first, because today the x86-64 and web code writers still decide some meaning themselves. Then the trait and the C target, then Rust, then third-party targets.

WHAT VOTING A DOES NOT INCLUDE

Seeding and bootstrapping the compiler, which are on their own frozen card. Native code writers for new machine architectures. Speed claims for transpiled code.

EDGE CASES

Languages without fixed 64-bit integers, such as JavaScript or Lua, spell `Int` through host leaves, so overflow still stops at the same values. Garbage-collected languages still run Jet's cleanup at the same points, because cleanup is an explicit step. C's undefined behavior is avoided because the C target spells only operations C defines exactly. A target without threads rejects programs that spawn them, with the capability error. Compile-time code runs in the compiler before transpiling, and only its results are written.

options.name: A trait over the explicit program, with optional idiom hooks (recommended)
options.detail: A target implements required methods for a closed list of explicit operations and host leaves, and may override idiom hooks that shape readable output. The runtime is transpiled through the same target. Conformance runs every executable example.
options.technical: Prerequisite: one shared IR pass moves exact-Int spills, fixed-width traps and the stop protocol out of the x86-64 and web selectors. Then core.compiler exposes a versioned, read-only program view. Target: trait has required op methods, a host-leaf table and hooks with defaults. Capabilities are registered diagnostics checked before any output. `jet test --to` drives the example corpus.

options.name: A trait over the checked source tree (Haxe with Reflaxe, Fable)
options.detail: A target receives the typed, checked syntax tree and writes idiomatic code directly. Each target re-implements Jet's checks, cleanup and error behavior. The conformance suite catches what it gets wrong.
options.technical: core.compiler exposes the checked tree and its types. Target: trait has one method per syntax node. Prelude and Core are transpiled from source by the same target, so every target re-spells overflow, bounds and stop semantics.

options.name: A trait over the explicit program, with no idiom hooks
options.detail: Like A, but a target spells only the explicit operations. Output is correct and portable but reads like machine code, as Emscripten and wasm2c output does.
options.technical: Same prerequisite and program view as A, with no hook layer. Target: trait has the op methods and host leaves only.

options.name: First-party targets only, with no public trait (Nim, Gleam)
options.detail: The compiler ships C and Rust writers. Nobody outside the compiler can add a language.
options.technical: The C and Rust writers live in Compiler/ beside the x86-64 and web writers and read the internal IR directly.

recommendation.why: It is the only option where any language can be added by a library and the program still keeps one meaning. Every check is explicit before a target sees it, and idiom hooks cannot remove a check.
gains: Any language can be added by an ordinary Jet package.
Overflow, bounds, cleanup and error stops behave the same in every target, proven by the example corpus.
Targets can start plain and become idiomatic one hook at a time.

losses.loss: Targets wait for the shared explicit pass and the public program view.
losses.mitigation: Both also remove duplicated meaning from the x86-64 and web writers, so the work pays off even before the first target.

losses.loss: The trait is a public contract that changes as the compiler grows.
losses.mitigation: It is versioned with the compiler library, and first-party targets change in the same commit, so breakage shows up at once.

losses.loss: Output without hooks reads like low-level code.
losses.mitigation: The C and Rust targets ship with hooks for records, enums, functions and loops.

whyNot.reason: Every target re-implements Jet's checks by hand, so meaning drifts between languages, as it does in Haxe and Fable.
It keeps the meaning but gives up readable output, which is much of why teams want transpiled code.
It rules out the library-defined targets you asked for.

recommendation.tradeoff: A delays third-party targets until the explicit pass and the public program view exist, in exchange for one meaning in every language.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude. Adversarial model family: Claude. Fresh agent: PortsLead-2. It reviewed the earlier seed draft and found that each writer still decides exact-Int, trap and stop meaning; fixing that is option A's first step. A fresh review of this re-scoped revision is pending and is the build card's first criterion.

decisions.title: Core gets files.sync_filesystem: one durable flush for a whole tree of writes
decisions.gist: How does Jet code make a tree of many new files durable without one disk flush per file?
decisions.lesson: core.files.fsync makes one file durable. Writing a tree of thousands of files and calling fsync on each one costs a journal commit per file. sync_filesystem flushes the whole filesystem that holds a path in one call, so a writer can create every file, flush once, and only then publish the tree with a rename.
decisions.story: Jetpack installs a toolchain of about 1,900 files. Today it calls fsync on every file and directory before it publishes the tree, and a cold install takes 45 minutes on a normal ext4 disk. With sync_filesystem it writes every file, flushes once, and renames the finished tree into place. A crash before the flush still leaves no published tree, and the install takes a few minutes.
decisions.inWild: Linux has syncfs(2), which flushes one filesystem. Go exposes it as unix.Syncfs in golang.org/x/sys, and Rust as nix::unistd::syncfs or rustix::fs::syncfs; neither standard library has it. Python has os.sync(), which flushes every filesystem. Package managers either fsync per file, like dpkg, which sorts its writes so the commits batch, or skip durability, like pip and npm.
decisions.detail:
Option A adds one public function beside fsync in Core/Files/Files.jet: sync_filesystem(path) IOError! -[FS.Write]>. On Linux it calls syncfs(2) on the filesystem that holds path. Elsewhere it calls sync(2), which flushes every filesystem in one call. Where the host has neither, it returns IOError and the caller keeps per-file fsync. Jetpack writes every object, flushes once, and renames the tree into place. A failed flush fails the publish, so a crash never publishes a partial tree.

Option B adds a higher-level fsync_tree(dir) that fsyncs every file under dir from several threads at once, so the journal batches the commits. It adds no new kind of flush, but it still does one fsync per file, and its speed depends on the filesystem's batching.

Option C adds no API and keeps per-file fsync. A cold toolchain install stays at about 45 minutes, and the clean-clone proof (#6096 c65) stays near 2 hours.

options.name: Add sync_filesystem(path)
options.detail: One public Core function: a single flush of the filesystem that holds path (syncfs(2) on Linux, sync(2) elsewhere, IOError where neither exists). The store flushes once before its publish rename.
options.code:
use { files: core.files }

loop object in objects -> files.write(object.path, object.bytes) ?? return Err(err)
files.sync_filesystem(staging) ?? return Err(err)
files.rename(staging, published) ?? return Err(err)

options.name: Add fsync_tree(dir)
options.detail: One public Core function that fsyncs every file and directory under dir in parallel, so the journal can batch the commits. Still one fsync per file.
options.code:
use { files: core.files }

loop object in objects -> files.write(object.path, object.bytes) ?? return Err(err)
files.fsync_tree(staging) ?? return Err(err)
files.rename(staging, published) ?? return Err(err)

options.name: No new API
options.detail: Keep fsync per file. Installs stay slow.

recommendation.why: One call replaces thousands of journal commits, and the write-flush-rename order keeps the same crash guarantee. It maps directly to the operating system's own primitive.
recommendation.tradeoff: The flush also covers unrelated dirty data on the same filesystem, so one call can take longer than a single fsync on a busy disk.

whyNot.reason: It still does one flush per file; batching helps only on some filesystems and adds a thread pool to a file API.
A cold toolchain install stays at 45 minutes and dominates every clean-clone proof.

losses.loss: On hosts without syncfs(2), sync(2) flushes every filesystem, not just one.
losses.mitigation: It is still one call per publish, and the docs say which flush each host uses.

surface.gist: How does Jet code make a tree of many new files durable without one disk flush per file?
surface.lesson: fsync flushes one file. sync_filesystem flushes the whole filesystem holding a path in one call. Write every file, flush once, then publish with a rename.

current.note: Today each file needs its own fsync.

wild.note: Go exposes Linux syncfs in golang.org/x/sys.
wild.code:
fd, _ := unix.Open(dir, unix.O_RDONLY, 0)
unix.Syncfs(fd)

options.name: sync_filesystem(path)
options.gist: One flush for the whole filesystem.
gains: One call per tree
Maps to syncfs(2)
losses: Also flushes unrelated dirty data

proposed.code:
files.sync_filesystem(staging) ?? return Err(err)
files.rename(staging, published) ?? return Err(err)

options.name: fsync_tree(dir)
options.gist: Parallel fsync of every file.
gains: No new kind of flush
losses: Still a flush per file
Speed depends on the filesystem

proposed.code: files.fsync_tree(staging) ?? return Err(err)

options.name: No new API
options.gist: Keep per-file fsync.
gains: Nothing to add
losses: 45-minute cold installs

proposed.code: files.fsync(object.path) ?? return Err(err)

recommendation.why: One call replaces thousands of journal commits with the same crash guarantee.
gains: Cold installs drop from about 45 minutes to a few
Same write-flush-rename crash safety

losses.loss: Flushes unrelated dirty data on the same filesystem.
losses.mitigation: Still one call per publish.

whyNot.reason: Still one flush per file.
Installs stay at 45 minutes.

recommendation.tradeoff: A wider flush in exchange for one call.

decisions.title: A build step can run a program the same build makes, built for this machine, with each file declared where it is passed
decisions.situation: A build function is a short Jet program that tells `jet build` what a project makes. Today it can list programs and simple steps. But a step cannot run a program the same build makes. It cannot run longer than 30 seconds, and it cannot read files outside its own folder. So the Jet repository keeps its real build in separate scripts that run one after another. They cover the compiler's self-check, the runtime pack, the Jetpack engine and the generated tables, and a stale table already broke a landing. You are asked how far a build function should reach. We recommend letting a step run what the build makes, inside the build graph Jet already has, with time limits and a timing record.
decisions.gist: How far should a build function reach: running programs it builds, long steps, other folders, and timing records?
decisions.lesson: A build function describes steps, and `jet build` runs them, reuses unchanged ones and seals each one off from the machine. Today a step may only use tools the machine already has, so anything that needs a freshly built program lives in scripts. Letting a step run a program the same build makes, as Zig and Bazel do, moves those scripts into the build and keeps reuse and sealing.
decisions.story:
Adding one value to a Core enum means running Tools/agent/CoreSourceRows.jet by hand to rewrite the generated row tables. Forgetting it fails the next landing, as a stale CoreEnumRows did on 2026-11-07. The packages suite builds its own Jetpack engine, which takes 3 minutes on a quiet machine and 13 under load. The self-host chain, the runtime pack and the release are separate Jet scripts that run one after another.

With this change, Compiler/build.jet says all of it once. The table generator is a program the build makes and then runs, so the tables are never stale. The engine is built once and reused by the test suite. The self-host stages are steps whose tool is the previous stage, so an unchanged stage is reused. Every build leaves a record of what ran and how long each part took.
decisions.inWild: Zig's build.zig is the closest match. `b.addRunArtifact(exe)` makes a step that runs a program the same build compiles. `addFileArg` and `addOutputFileArg` declare a file and pass it in one call. A tool is built for `b.graph.host`, the machine running the build. Steps run in parallel, and `zig build --summary all` prints each step's time. Bazel and Buck2 build the programs a rule runs for the machine that runs it. CMake turns a target named in a command into its built file. Jai runs its build program with `#run` and runs commands directly, with no reuse or sealing. Cargo runs `build.rs` before compiling a crate, unsealed.
decisions.detail:
Option A has three parts: files, steps and records.

Files. A BuildFile is a file or folder the build knows. The call `b.host(target)` is a target built for the machine running the build. The call `b.image(target)` is the same target built for the build's selected platform. The call `b.jet()` is the compiler running the build. The call `b.found(probe)` is the path a probe found. The call `b.dependency(name).file(path)` is a file inside a package that package.jet lists.

Why both host and image. In a native build they are one file, built once, because their options match. In a cross build such as `jet build --target web` they differ. A step that runs gen needs the host build. A step that packs the shipped compiler needs the image. One call would have to guess which one a step meant.

The host rule. A tool always runs on the machine running the build. So `b.host(target)` takes that machine's os and arch and ignores the cross options. Every other option, such as optimize, follows the build. A target that is both a tool and a shipped program builds twice in a cross build. The host copy goes under `.jet/build/host/` and is never installed.

Host edge cases. A host-only tool in a cross build builds for the host only. A tool that cannot build for the host is refused before anything runs. That happens when its source needs a web-only feature, or when the native backend cannot write images for this machine. The registered error names the tool, the host and the reason. A web image used as a tool is refused the same way, since a sandbox cannot run it.

Steps. The call `b.run(name, tool, caps)` takes a BuildFile as its tool and returns a BuildAction. Its arguments are added one call at a time, and each call that passes a file also declares it. The call `.input(path)` declares a source file or folder and passes its path. The call `.output(path)` declares an output, passes its path and returns its BuildFile.

More step calls. The call `.file(file)` passes a BuildFile that a target or another step makes. The call `.arg(text)` passes plain text. Each file call takes an optional `flag:` such as `flag: "--in="`, for tools that want one joined argument. The calls `.reads(path)` and `.writes(path)` declare files the tool uses without being told their names.

No undeclared argument file. The only way to pass a file is a call that declares it. The call `.arg(text)` refuses text that names a file in the package, and the fix points to `.input`. A step that never passes or declares an output it writes fails, because only declared outputs leave the sealed folder.

One step call replaces `b.action`. A machine tool is `b.found` of a find_program probe. The trailing toolchain and signing arguments of `b.action` become `.toolchain(t)` and `.sign(s)`. Every `b.action` caller migrates in the same change.

Time limits are Durations, written with the Time unit literals such as `30s` and `10min`. The call `.timeout(10min)` sets one step's limit. A new build option `action_timeout` sets the default, 30s when unset. It gets a new Duration kind: profile field `action_timeout: 10min`, flag `--action-timeout=10min`, call `b.action_timeout(10min)`. A zero or negative limit is refused.

Order and failure. The executor treats targets and steps as one graph. Everything whose inputs are ready runs at once, up to `--threads`. A target compiles once its steps finish. A step waits for its tool and its files. A failure stops only what depends on it, and every failure is reported in one pass.

Step edge cases. A tool built from its own step's output is a cycle, refused before anything runs. A step past its limit fails with a registered error naming the step and the limit. A rebuilt tool has a new digest, so its steps run again. Two steps that declare the same output are refused. An output that would overwrite a committed file is refused, as generated sources already are.

Records. Every `jet build` writes `.jet/build/receipt.json`, the core.build BuildGraph it built. It also writes `.jet/build/times.json`, a new core.build BuildTimes value. Each row holds a target or step name, its kind, its wall time and whether it was reused. Times stay out of BuildGraph, so receipt_diff still finds equal graphs equal. The command `jet inspect build --times` prints the record.

Beginner path: nothing changes. The calls `b.add_executable` and `b.default` stay the whole build. A first generator adds one `b.run` with an input and an output. Expert path: each self-host stage is a step whose tool is the previous stage's output. A last step compares two stages byte for byte, and receipts and times are diffed between commits.

Option B makes the build function run things immediately, like Jai. The call `b.compile(name, sources)` builds a program for the host and returns its path. The call `b.exec(argv)` runs a command at once, unsealed. Nothing is reused unless the build code checks for itself. Commands run one after another, and `jet inspect build` cannot list steps without running them.

Option C adds nothing. Most criteria of card #6682 close as out of scope. The scripts stay: Tools/agent/Chain.jet, Tools/packaging/PrebuildRuntime.jet, and the CoreSourceRows.jet check in the precommit.

options.name: Steps can run what the build makes
options.detail: Add BuildFile values (b.host, b.image, b.jet, b.found, dependency files) and one step call, b.run, whose argument calls declare each file where they pass it. Tools build for the machine running the build. Limits are Durations. b.run replaces b.action. The executor runs one parallel graph, and every build writes receipt.json and times.json.

options.name: An eager build program, like Jai
options.detail: Add b.compile(name, sources) -> String, which builds a host program now and returns its file, and b.exec(argv), which runs now, unsealed. The build function reads like a script. Nothing is reused, sealed or run in parallel unless the build code does it itself.

options.name: No new API; keep the scripts
options.detail: The Build API stays as it is. The repository keeps its build in Jet scripts that run jet and the programs it makes, one after another.

comparisons.note: Naming the target gen in COMMAND passes its built file and orders the step after it. Files are still written twice, in OUTPUT or DEPENDS and in COMMAND. Its best case: one build file drives Make, Ninja and IDEs, and DEPFILE adds inputs found while running, which A lacks. Cross builds need a separate host build of gen, which A makes for you.
comparisons.code:
add_executable(gen gen.c)
add_custom_command(OUTPUT rows.c
  COMMAND gen ${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/rows.tsv rows.c
  DEPENDS gen rows.tsv)
add_executable(app main.c rows.c)

comparisons.note: A genrule lists the programs it runs as tools, and Bazel builds them for the machine that runs the step, as A's host rule does. Its best case goes further than A: steps run remotely and share results across machines, and the sandbox is strict. A runs every step locally.
comparisons.code:
genrule(
    name = "rows",
    srcs = ["rows.tsv"],
    outs = ["rows.jet"],
    tools = [":gen"],
    cmd = "$(location :gen) $(SRCS) $@",
)

comparisons.note: This is the model for A. One call declares a file and passes it, a tool is built for the host, steps run in parallel, and the summary prints times. Zig does not seal steps from the machine, which A does. Zig can also check a step's output directly with expectStdOutEqual.

A build.rs program runs before its crate compiles, and its build-dependencies are built for the host. Its best case: rerun-if-changed lets the script name inputs it discovers while running, which A cannot. It is unsealed and can only feed its own crate.

The exe macro builds gen for the machine that runs the step. Inside rules, an output is declared where it is passed, as A does. Its best case goes further than A: remote execution, and dynamic outputs that let one step's result shape later steps.

recommendation.why: It moves every script the card names into the build graph Jet already has. Steps keep reuse, sealing and parallel runs, and beginner builds do not change. Most of the machinery exists: the executor already models tool paths, mounts and probe results.
recommendation.tradeoff: About a dozen new Build calls, a Duration option kind and the retirement of b.action, in exchange for one build graph for the whole project.

whyNot.reason: Every build reruns everything, unsealed and one step at a time. `jet inspect build` cannot list steps without running them, and reuse becomes each project's own code.
The scripts stay, generated tables can still go stale, and the packages suite keeps building its own engine.

losses.loss: More Build calls to learn.
losses.mitigation: Beginner builds do not change. The new calls appear only when a step runs a program the build makes, and the docs show one example per call.

losses.loss: Every b.action caller must move to b.run.
losses.mitigation: The callers are about 50 test fixtures and docs, all in this repository. They move in the same change, and each move is mechanical.

losses.loss: A sealed step needs the built tool's files bound in.
losses.mitigation: The executor already binds declared toolchain mounts read-only. A built tool adds its file and runtime pack the same way.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude. Adversarial model family: Claude. Fresh agent: Main. It found no host rule for tools, arguments that listed each file twice, an Int time limit, and no comparisons; the redesign fixes each.

surface.gist: How far should a build function reach: running programs it builds, long steps, other folders, and timing records?
surface.lesson: A build function lists steps, and `jet build` runs them, reuses unchanged ones and seals each off. Today a step may only use tools already on the machine, so work needing a freshly built program lives in scripts. Letting a step run what the build makes moves those scripts into the build.

current.note: Today gen cannot run, every file is written twice, and steps stop at 30 seconds.

wild.note: Zig builds gen for this machine, runs it, and compiles its output into the app.

options.name: Steps can run what the build makes
options.gist: One graph: build gen for this machine, run it sealed, reuse it when unchanged.
gains: Generated tables can never be stale
Each file is declared where it is passed
Every build records how long each part took
losses: More Build calls
Every b.action caller moves to b.run

options.name: An eager build program, like Jai
options.gist: Each line builds or runs at once, like a script.
gains: Reads like an ordinary script
losses: Nothing is reused or sealed
Steps run one at a time
Steps cannot be listed without running them

options.name: No new API; keep the scripts
options.gist: The build function stays small; scripts do the rest.
gains: Nothing new to learn
losses: Generated tables can go stale
Scripts run one after another

recommendation.why: It moves the scripts into the build graph Jet already has. Steps keep reuse, sealing and parallel runs, tools build for this machine, and beginner builds do not change.
gains: One build graph for the whole project
Unchanged steps are reused
Beginner builds stay the same

losses.loss: More Build calls to learn.
losses.mitigation: They appear only when a step runs a built program.

losses.loss: Every b.action caller moves to b.run.
losses.mitigation: About 50 test fixtures and docs in this repository move in the same change.

decisions.title: Run code straight from a URL or the registry, asking before its first run
decisions.situation: D-AUTH-DEFAULT1 refinement (4) says code run straight from a URL or the registry asks before its first run (card #6614 c8). Q25a=B asked for a ballot on the command itself. Today `jet run` takes local paths only, and `jet X` resolves a command, a job, a retired spelling, a path, then `jet-X` on PATH (D-JET-VERBS1). Jet already fetches remote code in one place: a script's inline `pkg#1.4` dependency. It is resolved through the signed registry index, verified, stored in the Hangar by content hash and pinned in `<script>.jet.lock` (D-JPK-SCRIPTDEP1). This ballot picks the command that runs remote code, what it fetches and pins, and how the first-run question behaves with and without a terminal.
decisions.gist: How do you run a Jet program that lives at a URL or in the registry?
decisions.lesson: `jet run` also takes an https URL or a registry package. Jet fetches it, checks it, pins its exact bytes, and asks once before the first run, naming what the program can do. Later runs of the same bytes are silent. Changed bytes or new effects ask again.
decisions.explainer:
The question happens after Jet fetches and checks the code and before its first instruction. Jet knows every effect a program can reach before it starts, so the question names them all at once.

Pinning is by content. A registry package is pinned by its signed index entry and artifact hash. A URL is pinned by the hash of the bytes fetched the first time. Nothing is fetched again silently: `--update` re-resolves, and `--locked` refuses any change.

Fetching never runs code. Nothing is written to the current folder. The fetched code lives in the Hangar store, and a small per-user record under `$XDG_STATE_HOME/jet/remote` keeps the pin and the effects the user said yes to.
decisions.story: Sam sees a log-cleaning tool in a blog post. He types `jet run https://example.org/tool.jet`. Jet shows where it came from, its hash and that it reads files and connects to the network, then asks. He says yes and it runs. Next week the author changes the file, and Jet asks again before running the new bytes. In CI, the same command stops and names the `-A` flag to use.
decisions.inWild: npx asks "Need to install the following packages. Ok to proceed?" in a terminal and fails in CI without --yes. Deno runs a URL directly and pins hashes with a lockfile, then prompts per permission while the program runs. Go runs `go run pkg@version` against a checksum database with no question.
decisions.detail:
Option A adds a remote target to `jet run`: an `https://` URL, `name#1.4.2`, `name#1.4` or a bare `name` that is not a local path. A local path always wins. Plain `http://` is refused. In a terminal Jet asks `Run it? [y/N]`, and only `y` runs. Without a terminal it stops before running and its Fix names `jet run -A <target>`.

Under A, `-A` skips the question, `--allow=R` skips it when R covers the effects, and `--deny=R` still wins. `--sha256=<hex>` pins a URL's first fetch, and `--locked` refuses any re-resolution.

Option B adds a separate verb, `jet x <target>`, with the same fetch, pin and question.

Option C has no remote run form. `jet fetch <target>` stores the code and prints a local path, and the first `jet run` of that path asks.

options.name: `jet run` takes a URL or package
options.detail: `jet run` accepts an https URL or a registry package as its target. It fetches, verifies and pins the code, then asks once in a terminal before the first run. Every run flag works as it does for a local file.
options.code:
$ jet run https://example.org/tool.jet
tool.jet from example.org (sha256 3f9a…), new to this machine
it reads files and connects to the network
Run it? [y/N] y
cleaned 12 log files

options.name: A separate `jet x` verb
options.detail: A new top-level verb runs remote code with the same fetch, pin and question. `jet run` stays local-only.
options.code:
$ jet x https://example.org/tool.jet
tool.jet from example.org (sha256 3f9a…), new to this machine
it reads files and connects to the network
Run it? [y/N] y
cleaned 12 log files

options.name: Fetch first, then run the path
options.detail: `jet fetch` stores the code and prints its local path. The first `jet run` of that path asks.
options.code:
$ jet fetch https://example.org/tool.jet
~/.local/share/jet/hangar/3f9a…/tool.jet
$ jet run ~/.local/share/jet/hangar/3f9a…/tool.jet
it reads files and connects to the network
Run it? [y/N] y
cleaned 12 log files

comparisons.note: npx runs a registry package by name and asks before installing it in a terminal. In CI it fails unless you pass --yes.
comparisons.code:
$ npx cowsay hi
Need to install the following packages:
cowsay@1.6.0
Ok to proceed? (y)

comparisons.note: Deno runs a URL directly. A lockfile pins the hashes, and it prompts for each permission while the program runs.
comparisons.code:
$ deno run https://example.org/tool.ts
⚠ Deno requests read access to "logs". Allow? [y/n/A]

comparisons.note: Go runs a module at an exact version and checks it against a public checksum database. It never asks.

recommendation.why: It is one run command: flags, entry selection and authority work as for a local file. It reuses the `#version` selector, the Hangar store, the signed index and the lock record. The question is the change notice turned into a question.
recommendation.tradeoff: `jet run` gains a second kind of target, so a bare word that is not a local path may reach the registry.

whyNot.reason: It adds a second run command whose flags must mirror `jet run`, and it takes a top-level word from every project's job names.
It takes two steps for the common case, and the printed store path is long and opaque.

losses.loss: A typo in a bare package name could reach the registry instead of failing locally.
losses.mitigation: The question shows the source and hash before anything runs, and `name#version` or `./name` makes the intent explicit.

decisions.checkInstructions: Try each option's command on the same remote tool.jet. Check that nothing runs before the question, that CI stops with a Fix naming -A, and that changed bytes ask again.

surface.gist: How do you run a Jet program that lives at a URL or in the registry?
surface.lesson: `jet run` also takes a URL or a registry package. Jet fetches it, pins its exact bytes and asks once before the first run. Changed bytes ask again.

current.note: Today `jet run` takes local files only.
current.code:
$ jet run https://example.org/tool.jet
error: no file https://example.org/tool.jet

wild.note: npx asks before installing in a terminal and fails in CI without --yes.
wild.code:
$ npx cowsay hi
Need to install the following packages:
cowsay@1.6.0
Ok to proceed? (y)

options.name: `jet run` takes a URL
options.gist: One run command for local and remote code.
gains: One command to learn
Every run flag works
losses: Bare names may reach the registry

proposed.code:
$ jet run https://example.org/tool.jet
it reads files and connects to the network
Run it? [y/N]

options.name: A `jet x` verb
options.gist: A separate verb for remote code.
gains: Remote runs stand out
losses: Second run command
Takes a job name

proposed.code:
$ jet x https://example.org/tool.jet
it reads files and connects to the network
Run it? [y/N]

options.name: Fetch, then run
options.gist: Store the code first, then run its path.
gains: No new run target
losses: Two steps
Long store path

proposed.code:
$ jet fetch https://example.org/tool.jet
~/.local/share/jet/hangar/3f9a…/tool.jet
$ jet run ~/.local/share/jet/hangar/3f9a…/tool.jet
Run it? [y/N]

recommendation.why: One run command, and remote code is pinned and named before it runs.
gains: Same flags as local runs
Pinned by content

losses.loss: Bare names may reach the registry.
losses.mitigation: The question shows source and hash first.

whyNot.reason: Two run commands to keep in step.
Two steps and an opaque path.

recommendation.tradeoff: `jet run` gains remote targets; local paths still win.

decisions.title: Port the editor server now and keep the unbuilt dev server out of the package tests until `jet dev` is rebuilt
decisions.situation: Two tool packages in the compiler tree, the editor server JetLSP and the dev server JetDevserver, are Rust code rewritten line by line into Jet syntax. Neither has ever compiled. Together they are about 48,000 lines. No command runs them today: `jet self lsp` and `jet dev` both report that they are not built yet. The full test profile still runs every package, so both fail it. The clean-clone gate for the Rust removal goal cannot pass while they fail. This vote decides what to port now and what the full profile runs meanwhile.
decisions.gist: Should Jet port the editor server now and keep the unbuilt dev server out of the package tests until `jet dev` is rebuilt?
decisions.lesson: The full test profile compiles and tests every package in the tree, including tools no command uses yet. A package that cannot compile fails the whole profile. Jet already handles a frozen tree this way: the owner names it, the profile skips it as one visible row, and nothing deletes it.
decisions.story: Ana clones Jet on a machine with no Rust and runs the full test profile. Today it fails on four rows for two packages she never uses. With A, the editor server builds and passes, and the dev server shows as one skipped row naming its card.
decisions.inWild:
// Compiler/test.jet today: only JetOS is frozen
FROZEN_TREES: [String]{"Jetpack/JetOS"}
decisions.detail:
Today. Compiler/JetLSP is 18.7k lines in 113 files and reports 565 problems. About 480 of them come from its dependency on Compiler/JetDevserver. JetDevserver is 29.9k lines in 79 files and reports 480 problems. It uses Rust's standard library names (sync, net, io), unwrap and the old error-propagation operator. Four known-failing rows name card 6650. A fifth, the corpus check for retired failure spellings, names card 6582: its 278 lines are all in JetDevserver.

What A does. Port JetLSP against current Core and drop its JetDevserver dependency. It uses the editor host module (EditorHost.jet, 801 lines) and its five method-name constants, and those move into JetLSP. Add Compiler/JetDevserver to FROZEN_TREES in Compiler/test.jet. Teach package_dirs to skip frozen trees, and have the corpus spelling check skip them too. Remove the JetDevserver and #6582 known-failing rows at once, and the JetLSP rows when its port lands. Cost: about 12-20 agent-hours for JetLSP, plus about 1 for the freeze.

What B does. Port both packages. No suite change. Cost: about 45-60 agent-hours. JetDevserver also needs Core sockets and threads it may not have yet.

What C does. Freeze both trees as in A and port neither now. Cost: about 1 agent-hour.

What the gate then proves. With A, every package under Compiler/ and Jetpack/ builds and passes except JetDevserver, shown as one skipped row. With B, every package builds and passes. With C, the same as A minus JetLSP.
