decisions.title: The default shape and system-frame opt-in
decisions.situation: The owner requires a Jet-drawn window frame by default. The pictures offer a 46-unit Unified header and a 34-unit Classic bar. A compact notes canvas benefits from Classic's extra space; a header with actions may benefit from Unified's height. This ballot chooses the default, the available presets, and one explicit System opt-in. System is a request, not a promise that every compositor draws decorations. The examples remain one Notes program. They do not prove working window controls or header embedding.
decisions.gist: Which Jet frame should be the default, and should frame: .System request the host frame?
decisions.lesson: Unified is taller; Classic saves vertical space. Either needs accessible controls and host integration. System requests host decorations, falling back to Jet when unavailable.
decisions.story: Ada opens the same Notes canvas with each default. Unified reserves more height above it; Classic reserves less. She can request the host frame explicitly. Neither choice edits her document or recolors her pixels.
decisions.inWild:
GNOME headerbars combine app controls with window controls and respect the system button layout. Their centering policy can be loose or strict. StyleManager exposes accent, dark appearance and high contrast. Jet must supply its own equivalent behavior without restoring GTK.

KDE/Breeze supports user button layouts, fonts, scale changes and configurable title alignment. It extends edge targets for easy pointing. A fixed Jet layout gives up some desktop integration; Breeze is not simply a left-aligned Windows bar.

Windows 11 supports compact captions and taller search headers, RTL, text scaling and high contrast. Mica is an opaque wallpaper-derived material with solid fallbacks, not a generic blur. Snap layouts need native caption integration or correct custom hit testing. Jet's PNGs establish none of those behaviors.

macOS uses system window controls, including traffic lights at the upper left. Apple advises against copying native frames imperfectly. A Jet-drawn cross-desktop style is an intentional trade, not evidence of matching macOS behavior.

Chrome's Linux frame handles leading and trailing controls, tiling, shadows and input margins. Electron can combine custom content with native controls and safe areas. Flutter's Linux runner uses a GTK window; a headerbar is optional in its template. Flutter's input host handles touch and stylus separately. Custom drawing does not make those responsibilities disappear.

The decoration protocol negotiates who draws the frame, not its shape, title alignment or colors. Settings supplies appearance preferences, not a full desktop palette or button layout. These are different services, not competing ways to set an accent.
decisions.detail:
These are proposals, not implemented public settings. The owner requires a Jet-drawn default, Atkinson Hyperlegible Next, deletion of GTK, and retention of TUI and null. No new spelling is authorized before ratification. No claim about another ballot's ratification is made here.

Images 01–09 under $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/WaylandLead/mockups/out were inspected. They are static drawings, not interactive windows. The repaired sample keeps one Notes program and a deliberately white pixel canvas. Appearance settings do not recolor those raw pixels. Accent has no visible effect until an accented role, such as a focused frame control, is shown.

All four ballots share these proposed release requirements. Normal text must meet 4.5:1; essential control marks, boundaries and focus cues must meet 3:1. Use readable normal title colors even on unfocused windows; unfocused is not the same as disabled. Disabled controls alone may use the WCAG exception. Do not signal selection or danger by hue alone.

Use a solid two-unit focus ring with a two-unit gap for fields and buttons, including window controls. It must remain visible and unobscured in every state. Frame controls have nonoverlapping rectangular hit regions, at least 24 by 24 logical units. Touch and pen get at least 44 by 44, growing the bar when needed. Painted glyph size is not hit-target size.

Every action needs an accessible name and keyboard route through the window menu. F6 cycles content and frame focus; Tab and Shift+Tab cycle frame controls. Shift+F10 on the focused frame opens its menu. Alt+Space opens it when the host delivers that shortcut. Enter activates; Escape dismisses and restores prior focus. Arrow keys move or resize; Enter commits and Escape cancels.

The menu exposes move, resize, minimize, maximize, restore and close. Close uses the ordinary close-request event; maximize and minimize remain host requests, not guaranteed state changes. Disable unavailable actions rather than silently doing nothing. Pointer, touch and pen activate on release inside; moving out cancels. Only empty header space drags. Do not emulate a refused compositor move by painting at guessed screen coordinates.

Higher contrast overrides decorative colors, including pinned accents. Proposed light high contrast is white background, black text and boundaries; dark is the reverse. Focus uses the foreground color. Selected controls invert foreground and background and retain a check or position cue. Theme changes are immediate, with no fades or motion, including when reduced motion is requested.

Title, controls and hit testing use logical coordinates, rasterized at the current device scale. A scale change rebuilds frame assets and input transforms together. Images at 1x and 2x are not fractional-scale evidence. Test 1.25x, 1.5x and mixed-output moves, text enlargement, narrow widths, fullscreen, maximization and partial tiling before claiming parity.

Jet controls default to the physical right, ordered minimize, maximize, close. This differs from macOS and some user layouts. Title direction does not silently move controls. System decoration delegates placement and behavior to the host. On Jet frames, text direction determines logical start; controls reserve space first. No common portal key supplies button layout. Desktop-layout customization remains a named integration gap, not a promise from these PNGs.

Tiling alone must not imply maximization or a restore glyph. Use restore only while maximized; fullscreen hides the frame. Remove shadows on tiled edges and prevent shadow-only pixels intercepting neighboring windows. A compositor refusing client-side decoration wins negotiation: never draw two frames. Without a decoration manager, clients may self-decorate; this is not a compositor lacking CSD support.

Wayland is the pending graphical backend considered here. TUI and null keep their existing non-window meaning and gain no fake title bar. Headless pixel windows have no host frame. Future X11, Windows and macOS hosts are design requirements below, not claims of implemented backends. Web chrome remains outside these ballots.

Proposed signature addition: frame: UIFrame?{None}. Proposed enum UIFrame has Unified, Classic and System; one-shape options omit the other Jet value. Omitted or None means this option's default. Existing width and height continue to mean content size, excluding frame and shadow. This is one frame selection mechanism; do not add another native_frame boolean.

Beginner: omit frame. Expert: ui.open(width: 640, height: 400, title: "Notes", frame: .System). On Wayland, System requests server_side and draws no Jet frame only after the compositor confirms it. If absent or refused, draw this option's default Jet shape. Both Jet shapes request client_side, but honor an enforced server_side answer. Reconfigure without transient double decoration.

Future native hosts: System keeps the window manager's X11 decorations, Windows caption controls, or macOS system titlebar and traffic lights. Jet shape settings affect Jet drawings only. System titles, controls and placement remain host-owned; theme and accent do not promise to recolor them. An unsupported graphical host returns UIError.Unsupported("display backend unavailable"), not a fake System frame. Headless, TUI and null draw none.

Unified paints a 46-unit bar, 12-unit corner radii and 28-unit circles. Classic paints 34 units, 8-unit corners and 46-unit-wide full-height buttons. These are baseline visuals, not rigid accessible hit regions. Header embedding is not demonstrated by the sample and no public slot spelling is proposed here. Two presets must share window actions, not duplicate their semantics.

Both shape-only choices remain real alternatives. Full customization does not by itself require every named preset, and no approved rule proving otherwise was supplied. The missing Classic-only choice is now D. Native-default and frameless-default alternatives are excluded because the owner's Jet-drawn default is binding.

decisions.title: Title alignment in Jet-drawn frames
decisions.situation: A Jet-drawn frame needs a rule for placing its title. The existing comparison treats physical left as universally readable and centered titles as losing both ends. Image 09 instead shows both keeping the start and trimming the end. Strict centering can leave unused space beside an uneven button group; centering within available space avoids that waste. This ballot compares those layouts on the same Notes canvas. It also defines RTL behavior and leaves system-drawn titles to the host.
decisions.gist: Should Jet titles follow text start, stay centered, or center when space permits?
decisions.lesson: Start follows reading direction. Strict centering balances the whole window. Adaptive centering keeps the midpoint when possible, shifting only to avoid occupied regions.
decisions.story: Grace opens the same long report title in each layout. All preserve its full accessible name. Only the painted position and available width differ; no option edits the title string.

Proposed argument title_align: UITitleAlign?{None}, with Start, Centre and AdaptiveCentre. A defaults to Start, B to Centre, C to AdaptiveCentre. None uses that default. decisions.title: Where Jet gets its accent seed
decisions.situation: An accent marks choices, focus and primary actions. Jet's own colors are black and red (site tokens: ground #0B0B0D, red #E8232A, hot red #FF3B41). The earlier mockups show blue, teal and violet accents, and they do not read desktop settings. The Settings portal can publish an accent; some hosts or versions supply none. This ballot chooses whether to follow that preference live, ignore it by default, or sample it once. All choices keep the same accessibility checks and allow an explicit pinned seed. Respecting a desktop accent is useful, but cannot promise an exact toolkit match or unchanged brand pixels.
decisions.gist: Should Jet follow the desktop accent live, use Jet red, or sample the desktop once?
decisions.lesson: One seed supplies accent roles, not every color. Text, marks and focus need separate contrast checks. Apps may pin a seed without disabling accessibility.
decisions.story: Ken picks teal for his desktop. The same Notes frame can follow it, keep Jet red, or retain the opening accent after a later change. The white content canvas stays white in every option.
decisions.inWild:
GNOME headerbars combine app controls with window controls and respect the system button layout. Their centering policy can be loose or strict. StyleManager exposes accent, dark appearance and high contrast. Jet must supply its own equivalent behavior without restoring GTK.

KDE/Breeze supports user button layouts, fonts, scale changes and configurable title alignment. It extends edge targets for easy pointing. A fixed Jet layout gives up some desktop integration; Breeze is not simply a left-aligned Windows bar.

Windows 11 supports compact captions and taller search headers, RTL, text scaling and high contrast. Mica is an opaque wallpaper-derived material with solid fallbacks, not a generic blur. Snap layouts need native caption integration or correct custom hit testing. Jet's PNGs establish none of those behaviors.

macOS uses system window controls, including traffic lights at the upper left. Apple advises against copying native frames imperfectly. A Jet-drawn cross-desktop style is an intentional trade, not evidence of matching macOS behavior.

Chrome's Linux frame handles leading and trailing controls, tiling, shadows and input margins. Electron can combine custom content with native controls and safe areas. Flutter's Linux runner uses a GTK window; a headerbar is optional in its template. Flutter's input host handles touch and stylus separately. Custom drawing does not make those responsibilities disappear.

decisions.detail:
These are proposals, not implemented public settings. The owner requires a Jet-drawn default, Atkinson Hyperlegible Next, deletion of GTK, and retention of TUI and null. No new spelling is authorized before ratification. No claim about another ballot's ratification is made here.

Images 01–09 under $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/WaylandLead/mockups/out were inspected. They are static drawings, not interactive windows. The repaired sample keeps one Notes program and a deliberately white pixel canvas. Appearance settings do not recolor those raw pixels. Accent has no visible effect until an accented role, such as a focused frame control, is shown.

All four ballots share these proposed release requirements. Normal text must meet 4.5:1; essential control marks, boundaries and focus cues must meet 3:1. Use readable normal title colors even on unfocused windows; unfocused is not the same as disabled. Disabled controls alone may use the WCAG exception. Do not signal selection or danger by hue alone.

Use a solid two-unit focus ring with a two-unit gap for fields and buttons, including window controls. It must remain visible and unobscured in every state. Frame controls have nonoverlapping rectangular hit regions, at least 24 by 24 logical units. Touch and pen get at least 44 by 44, growing the bar when needed. Painted glyph size is not hit-target size.

Every action needs an accessible name and keyboard route through the window menu. F6 cycles content and frame focus; Tab and Shift+Tab cycle frame controls. Shift+F10 on the focused frame opens its menu. Alt+Space opens it when the host delivers that shortcut. Enter activates; Escape dismisses and restores prior focus. Arrow keys move or resize; Enter commits and Escape cancels.

The menu exposes move, resize, minimize, maximize, restore and close. Close uses the ordinary close-request event; maximize and minimize remain host requests, not guaranteed state changes. Disable unavailable actions rather than silently doing nothing. Pointer, touch and pen activate on release inside; moving out cancels. Only empty header space drags. Do not emulate a refused compositor move by painting at guessed screen coordinates.

Higher contrast overrides decorative colors, including pinned accents. Proposed light high contrast is white background, black text and boundaries; dark is the reverse. Focus uses the foreground color. Selected controls invert foreground and background and retain a check or position cue. Theme changes are immediate, with no fades or motion, including when reduced motion is requested.

Title, controls and hit testing use logical coordinates, rasterized at the current device scale. A scale change rebuilds frame assets and input transforms together. Images at 1x and 2x are not fractional-scale evidence. Test 1.25x, 1.5x and mixed-output moves, text enlargement, narrow widths, fullscreen, maximization and partial tiling before claiming parity.

Jet controls default to the physical right, ordered minimize, maximize, close. This differs from macOS and some user layouts. Title direction does not silently move controls. System decoration delegates placement and behavior to the host. On Jet frames, text direction determines logical start; controls reserve space first. No common portal key supplies button layout. Desktop-layout customization remains a named integration gap, not a promise from these PNGs.

Tiling alone must not imply maximization or a restore glyph. Use restore only while maximized; fullscreen hides the frame. Remove shadows on tiled edges and prevent shadow-only pixels intercepting neighboring windows. A compositor refusing client-side decoration wins negotiation: never draw two frames. Without a decoration manager, clients may self-decorate; this is not a compositor lacking CSD support.

Wayland is the pending graphical backend considered here. TUI and null keep their existing non-window meaning and gain no fake title bar. Headless pixel windows have no host frame. Future X11, Windows and macOS hosts are design requirements below, not claims of implemented backends. Web chrome remains outside these ballots.

Proposed argument accent: UIAccent?{None}. Proposed enum UIAccent has Desktop, JetRed and Color(U32), with Color storing opaque 0xAARRGGBB. The alpha byte must be FF; otherwise opening returns UIError.Invalid("accent requires opaque AARRGGBB"). There is no untyped color-or-enum overload. A defaults to Desktop, B to JetRed, C samples Desktop once. Explicit Desktop always follows live; explicit JetRed or Color pins the seed.

For a fixed teal seed, pass accent: .Color(U32{0xFF0B8A7A}). Omit accent for the option's default, or pass .Desktop to resume live following. One RGB seed does not contain separate light and dark palettes.

JetRed seeds are Jet's brand tokens: #E8232A in light and #FF3B41 in dark. Desktop uses one portal RGB seed, not an invented light/dark pair. Color uses its one seed in both themes. The raw seed is not a guarantee of pixel-identical branding: every option uses the same accessible role resolver. Pinning must not disable higher contrast.

Proposed resolver: decode sRGB, then derive roles in linear light. For accent fills, first require 3:1 against their adjacent base surface. If needed, mix toward black in light mode or white in dark mode. Choose the first passing step among 0 through 255, in increments of 1/255. Quantize to sRGB bytes before measuring. Choose black or white on-accent text by the larger contrast ratio; ties choose black.

Derive hover and pressed from the resolved seed using the pictured mixes, then apply the same contrast checks to each final state. Focus is a separate semantic role from fill, resolved against its own adjacent surface by the same algorithm. A text-on-fill check does not establish a visible focus ring. Marks and switch thumbs use the resolved on-accent color, not unconditional white. Higher contrast uses the shared black/white palette instead.

Measured from mock.jet: white on light blue is 4.4987:1, below 4.5 without rounding. White on light teal #0B8A7A is 4.2591:1. The dark switch's white thumb on blue is 2.5850:1. The shown pictures therefore do not prove the proposed resolver. Source tokens and exact computations are in contrast.json; regenerate pictures after the resolver is implemented.

Accent does not control danger, every decorative icon, every avatar, or arbitrary app pixels. It controls the accent roles, not every color in the window. A portal accent can differ from a toolkit's restricted accent palette. No universal Windows or macOS app behavior is asserted.

Proposed portal contract: org.freedesktop.appearance/color-scheme is uint32: 1 dark, 2 light, 0 or unknown light fallback. accent-color is an sRGB triple of doubles in [0,1]. Missing, malformed, nonfinite or out-of-range accent values mean Jet red. Neither desktop name nor wallpaper is a substitute for these values.

Use one appearance service for accent, theme, contrast and reduced motion, feeding one resolved style record. ReadAll works with version 1; ReadOne requires version 2. Subscribe to SettingChanged before the initial snapshot, then reconcile queued changes. There is no guarantee of zero-latency delivery or of support for every key. Unknown contrast or reduced-motion values mean no preference.

Portal absence, permission errors or disconnect must not prevent opening a window. Use the stated fallback; on service return, reread preferences for Desktop settings. Apply valid changes together at a frame boundary, retaining focus, text, selection and scroll. Pinned settings ignore their matching preference only; accessibility settings still apply. Connection setup, bus authentication, message routing, signal subscriptions and service restarts cost more than two calls.

decisions.title: How Jet follows light and dark preference
decisions.situation: The desktop can publish a light or dark preference through Settings. Jet's pictures show two palettes, not a working settings reader or live redraw. This ballot compares live following, a fixed light default with opt-in following, and a snapshot at opening. Each opens the same Notes canvas and permits explicit Light or Dark. Raw pixels remain app-owned, so a white canvas will not turn dark on its own. The choice must also define absent portals, unknown values and changes during input. Owner direction 2026-11-09: follow the desktop, with a dark fallback, by default.
decisions.gist: Should Jet follow light and dark live, default to light, or sample the desktop once?
decisions.lesson: Following chooses a palette, not the meaning of app pixels. Live changes need one event and coherent redraw. High contrast and reduced motion remain independent.
decisions.story: User changes his desktop to dark while Notes is open. A live-following frame changes at its next update; a pinned or sampled frame does not. The white document pixels stay app-owned, and keyboard focus is preserved.

Proposed argument theme: UITheme?{None}; enum UITheme { Desktop, Light, Dark }. A defaults to Desktop live. B defaults to Light. C samples Desktop at opening. Explicit Desktop always follows live; Light and Dark pin appearance. No separate follow_theme boolean or second observer API is introduced.

This ballot proposes adding UIEvent.ThemeChanged(UITheme), carrying only resolved Light or Dark. Deliver it once before the first frame using a newly resolved scheme, not on duplicate portal values. The appearance service updates the frame and styled widgets together, then queues the event and redraw. A raw-pixel app may inspect that event to redraw its own content, but nothing can infer the meaning of its arbitrary colors. The sample deliberately presents white in both themes. No portal or no preference means Dark. Unknown color-scheme values mean no preference, which uses the Dark fallback. decisions.title: The command that lists the effect caps in force at a site, nearest first
decisions.situation: The effect-rung and type-rung rulings promise `jet explain effects` (every cap in force, nearest first) and `jet explain effects --caps` (each module cap with its file and line), card #6551. They do not fix the site it explains or its JSON shape, and today the command is E2104 (not built). The ratified CLI has `jet explain marker <file>:<line>` for one site and `jet explain log [<file|dir>]` for a listing with file and line. `jet explain <ref> --json` uses the `jet.report/v1` envelope. `jet inspect rights [TARGET]` lists every callable's declared and inferred rows against the application authority. The owner answered Q27 with option A on 2026-11-08; this ballot records that form with its alternatives and costs.
decisions.gist: How do you ask Jet which effect limits apply to a line of code?
decisions.lesson: `jet explain effects` prints every limit in force at a site, nearest first: the `#FX` block, the function row, the module cap, the package row and the run. Each line names the file and line that wrote it, and the last line names the effects the site reaches.
decisions.explainer:
A site is `<file>:<line>`, the innermost scope at that line. A bare `<file>` is that file's module, plus its `run` if it has one. No site means the entry `jet run` would pick, with the same selection rules and the same errors when it is ambiguous.

The output has one line per rung, nearest first. The rungs are `block` (an `#FX` region), `function` (the `-[…]>` row or `-[!E]>` denials) and `module` (`#FX` on the module). Then come `package` (the `authority` row or `deny`) and `run` (everything allowed unless denied; `--deny` wins). A rung that writes nothing prints `(none written)`, so the ladder is always the same shape. The last line names the effects the site reaches, each with the first call that reaches it, which is the same chain E0749 prints.

`--caps` lists every module cap in the project, or under a given file or directory, as `file:line  #FX(…)  module`, sorted by path then line. `--json` uses the `jet.report/v1` envelope. The command shares one walker with `jet inspect rights`; it is the explain view of the same facts.
decisions.story: Ana's `jet check` stops with E0749 in `push`. She runs `jet explain effects Source/sync.jet:14`. Jet lists the block cap, the function row, the module cap and the package deny, each with its file and line. It shows that the line reaches `Net.HTTP.Get` through `http.get`. She sees the module cap is the one that leaves it out and widens it.
decisions.inWild: Rust's `cargo tree -e features` prints which features are on and why, but only for features. Deno's `deno info` lists a module's permissions requests only at run time. AWS IAM's policy simulator shows, for one action, every policy that allows or denies it, nearest first, with the deciding statement.
decisions.detail:
Option A is `jet explain effects [<file>[:<line>]] [--caps] [--json]`, the form ruled in Q27. A line outside any function starts at the module rung. A line inside a lambda gets its own `function` rung, then the enclosing function. A line inside `comptime` adds a `comptime` rung for the `#Impure` gate. A file with no `package.jet` shows `package (none written)`.

A line past the end of the file, or `:0`, gets the existing `jet explain marker` refusal and its code. Generated code maps to the user site that produced it, as diagnostics do. A line holding more than one function explains the first one that starts on it; no column form is proposed. `--caps` with `:line` is a usage error.

Option B folds the ladder into `jet inspect rights [TARGET]`, with `file:line` targets and a `--caps` filter.

Option C names a function instead of a line: `jet explain effects <module>.<function>`.

decisions.title: Should Core add the four basic Bessel functions?
decisions.situation: Wave calculations use special mathematical functions called Bessel functions. Jet has no public calls for the four basic ones, so a simulation using them cannot yet use Core alone. Beginners need a dependable default, while experts need a clear accuracy promise. Choose Core or a package, correct or faithful rounding, or deferral. We recommend correctly rounded Core functions because of Jet's Core-parity and accuracy direction, not evidence that they are cheap.
decisions.gist: Should Core add the four basic Bessel functions?
decisions.lesson: Correct rounding returns the nearest float, with ties going to even. Faithful rounding permits either float beside the exact answer. A fixed faithful algorithm can also be repeatable. Core's ratified elementary-math direction is correct rounding; this vote sets the Bessel contract.
decisions.story: A developer ports a wave simulation that calls j0, j1, y0 and y1. The same inputs must give the same bits on every supported machine and execution mode.
decisions.detail:
D-MATH-BITS1 outcome A says each Core math function is correctly rounded, but its detailed implementation list names elementary functions, not Bessel. A extends that direction explicitly. B scopes a faithful exception for these four F64 calls; no existing Bessel API is weakened. I9 requires one shared meaning at O0, O1, O2, compile time and web where applicable. No option permits host-dependent answers or an accuracy flag.

The scope is j0, j1, y0 and y1 for Float and F32. Integer-order jn and yn are excluded, so the combined POSIX census row cannot become fully covered. This vote closes neither #6700 nor #6688.

All shipping options share these proposed edge rules: J0 is even and J1 odd for finite real inputs; J0(+-0)=1 and J1(+-0)=+-0. Y0/Y1(+-0)=-infinity. Negative nonzero Y arguments and all quiet/signaling NaN inputs return fixed positive quiet NaN: binary64 0x7ff8000000000000, binary32 0x7fc00000. This is not math.canonicalize's payload-preserving behavior.

J0/J1(+-infinity)=+0; Y0/Y1(+infinity)=+0; Y0/Y1(-infinity)=fixed quiet NaN. Gradual underflow applies; any zero from a nonzero finite result has the exact result's sign. Overflow is nearest-even even for B/F's F64 route. Y1 can overflow negatively near zero. No host errno, traps or floating-environment dependence. CR forms evaluate the function of the exact input and round once to the destination type; B/F use bracketing within the finite range.

CORE-MATH has no fixed-format Bessel implementation in the inspected binary32/64 tree, but has a Sollya adapter. Harrison 2009 supplies zero-distance analysis, not a complete CR midpoint proof. MPFR supplies rounded Bessel values. Inspected FLINT/Arb ball-arithmetic source is further certification prior art, not an executed fixed-format CR kernel. Go ships the four calls in math; Julia's Bessels.jl shows specialist packaging.

Beginners and experts use the same calls. Experts can use their own explicitly chosen domain-specific approximation package, not a second Core accuracy mode. D/F require installation and version pinning; C explicitly defers this Core-parity scope and offers no first-party Bessel path.

A/B/D/F would be implemented in Jet without new external runtime dependencies; source reuse still needs license review. The markdown and third review give sources, proof/tests and executed witnesses. Shipping-option Jet snippets are proposals; C shows a verified rejection. No delivery date, coefficient count, speed or proof-cost estimate is established.

options.name: Correctly rounded Core functions in Jet
options.detail: Add the four calls to Core and explicitly extend the correct-rounding direction to them. Implement in Jet using certified numerical methods. No new external dependency is authorized.
options.technical: Proposed j0(x: Float) -> Float and same-name F32 -> F32, likewise j1, y0 and y1. Certified adaptive precision is a candidate, not a ready fallback: it may require substantial multiprecision infrastructure. Prove termination, bounds and exact cases. No fixed fallback width or hard-case search is prescribed.

options.name: Faithful F64 Core functions
options.detail: Use the same calls, with faithful F64 and correctly rounded F32 results. Explicitly scope an exception to D-MATH-BITS1's general accuracy direction for these four F64 calls. Implement in Jet without a new external dependency. There is no existing Bessel API to downgrade.
options.technical: For representable-range finite results, faithful means either bracketing float, or the exact float when representable. Fix one canonical algorithm. Common edge rules also fix NaNs, zero signs and nearest-even overflow. Faithfulness can avoid resolving rounding midpoints, so may save work, but no Jet cost saving is measured. CR F32 still needs proof: midpoint-gated narrowing can work with faithful F64, but its midpoint cases and corrections must be certified for that kernel. A later CR upgrade can change some bits.

options.name: Defer the four functions
options.detail: Add no Bessel calls in this scope. Keep the POSIX gap visible. Explicitly defer this part of the Core-parity goal; do not treat remaining math work as complete.
options.technical: No implementation campaign is authorized for these calls. Retain the gap and absent-call checks. This frees this scope's implementation effort for other work, but leaves no first-party Bessel path. It neither closes another card nor authorizes a host fallback.

options.name: Correctly rounded battery
options.detail: Put the four calls in one opt-in numerical package, not Core. Specialist grouping and independent releases may help scientific users. It changes the Core boundary and needs explicit approval against the standard-library parity goal.
options.technical: Proposed package import numerics.bessel; same four names and Float/F32 contracts as A. Implement in Jet without a new external dependency. No duplicate Core aliases. Package placement does not remove numerical proof cost. Test installation, discovery, version pinning and every applicable execution tier.

options.name: MPFR-backed Core functions
options.detail: Use MPFR and GMP for the same correctly rounded calls. This explicitly approves new dependencies and an exception to the no-C order. Distribution obligations and all applicable targets must be resolved before shipping.
options.technical: Same public API as A. Pin MPFR/GMP behind one approved bridge. Establish target exponents, gradual underflow and no double rounding; map MPFR's NaN representation to the chosen Jet contract. Include compile time and web; no native-only or host-libm fallback. Measure scratch memory, allocation, latency and distribution size; no fast-libm performance is assumed.

options.name: Faithful numerical battery
options.detail: Keep Core unchanged and provide one opt-in numerics.bessel package with faithful F64 and correctly rounded F32 results. This combines specialist releases with B's possible midpoint savings, without weakening an existing Core function.
options.technical: Same proposed import and names as D; exactly B's accuracy, overflow, NaN and signed-zero contract, including one canonical algorithm on every applicable tier. Implement in Jet, with no new external dependency. Approve the Core-boundary exception explicitly. Installation, pinning, proof and performance tests still apply; no duplicate Core alias or accuracy switch.

recommendation.why: A follows Jet's Core-parity and correct-rounding direction. Go's math library supports Core placement; specialist packages support D/F. This is a policy preference, not a measured cost win.
gains: One nearest-even answer.
No new runtime dependency.

losses.loss: Proof, multiprecision infrastructure and speed costs remain unmeasured.
losses.mitigation: Require certified bounds, termination, and measured time, memory and size before shipping; promise no completion date.

whyNot.reason: May avoid midpoint work, but its weaker guarantee has no measured Jet saving yet.
Saves this scope's implementation effort, but leaves the first-party capability absent.
Independent releases suit specialists, but depart from Jet's Core-parity goal and add setup.
Existing rounded algorithms reduce numerical invention, but conflict with the no-C order without an explicit exception.
Combines specialist releases and possible midpoint savings, but leaves Core parity unmet and gives a weaker F64 guarantee.

recommendation.tradeoff: A funds numerical research rather than claiming a ready fixed-format upstream kernel exists. Existing algorithms may inform a port, with license review. Shipping waits for proof and performance evidence.

decisions.title: Remember command flags in a separate commands block with flat registry keys
decisions.situation: The owner ruling recorded on #6606 requires one flag registry and command.flag keys. Explicit flags win over package values, which win over user values. Destructive flags cannot be remembered. The package already declares typed program settings in settings:. This vote chooses a separate commands: block, nested command maps, or mixed entries in settings:. All examples below are proposals, not features proven by the seed accepting a manifest.
decisions.gist: Should remembered command flags use flat registry keys in their own commands: block?
decisions.lesson: A program setting declares a typed value for the program. A command setting supplies a default for jet itself. Keeping them apart need not require nested maps.
decisions.explainer: The recorded ruling is #6606's 2026-11-08 log, Q24 A. It settles registry keys, precedence and destructive-flag refusal, not every rule in this proposal. Build profiles and command defaults must feed the same option resolver, including pins and existing value checks. A separate block is organization, not a second settings engine.
decisions.story: Ada wants jet fmt to check instead of writing. She keeps the program's cache_slots declaration and adds one remembered flag. Her own color preference goes in the user file. Each option below represents those same values.
decisions.inWild:
# npm .npmrc: tool settings, separate from package.json program config
save-exact=true

# git: sectioned keys, not a section for every command
[pull]
    rebase = true

# Cargo.toml: checked-in compiler profile
[profile.dev]
opt-level = 1

# .cargo/config.toml: local/user tool defaults
[build]
jobs = 4
decisions.detail:
Settled scope: use one registry, command.flag keys, and explicit flag > package > user. Reject destructive defaults with a registered diagnostic. Source: Tools/tower/.tower/tower.json, card #6606, log dated 2026-11-08. Operand refusal and the rules below are proposed common terms, not quotations from Q24.

Proposed file: $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/jet/settings.jet, falling back to $HOME/.config/jet/settings.jet when XDG_CONFIG_HOME is absent or empty. Reject relative XDG_CONFIG_HOME. Missing files supply no values; unreadable or malformed present files fail with their location. Read data only: configuration must not execute code. No system file, include chain or environment-value layer is added.

Proposed package lookup: use an explicitly selected workspace member, otherwise the nearest package.jet above the working directory. Do not merge ancestor package files. Apply that same rule to -e and stdin source; outside a package only user values apply. Dependencies cannot contribute command defaults. Relative path values resolve against their declaring file, not a later invocation's directory.

Each registry row owns its value parser, allowed values, repeat behavior and persistence classification. Do not reduce durations, integers and enumerated build options to unchecked strings. Repeated lists replace lower layers; [] clears a list. false is a value, not absence. Duplicate normalized keys fail. Short flags share their long flag's key; global flags get keys only on commands accepting them.

Remembered build flags occupy the existing flag layer below explicit flags and above profiles and build code. A build pin still rejects a conflicting default. The resolver must retain origin information, not inject text into argv. Unknown keys, wrong values and forbidden persistence fail before command effects, naming file and line. An explicit override cannot hide invalid stored configuration.

Persistence is not authority. Operands, help/version actions, destructive confirmations and authority-expanding or safety-disabling overrides must not become ambient grants. Classify no_sign as security-sensitive, not a harmless example. Existing authority and gate policy still applies. This classification extends the common proposal beyond Q24's destructive-flag exclusion and needs approval with this vote.

A package default can affect compiled behavior: run.optimize and run.bounds are not merely display preferences. Both forms must resolve once through the existing option and authority rules. --verbose should show effective keys, winning origins and overridden sources, redacting secrets. No claim is made that these reports exist today.

Seed a0_042 probes: typed settings compile; a mixed fmt.check entry fails because it lacks a type and default. Both commands: shapes were accepted by a trivial run, but that proves no flag was applied. A user commands: file did not make fmt check; it still rewrote an unformatted scratch file. Implementation proof must compare the command's actual effect.

I8 review: A and B keep program declarations separate. C can also use one resolver, so sharing a block is not itself an I8 violation. None may create independent profile/CLI validation or bypass pins. Beginners use defaults; experts inspect the origin and explicitly override through existing flags.

Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/config.html and https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/profiles.html. Cargo merges ancestor config and arrays, supports environment and --config overrides, and allows profiles in Cargo.toml and config. Jet's replacement lists and two file scopes are simpler but less flexible.

Sources: https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/v11/configuring-npm/npmrc/ and https://git-scm.com/docs/git-config. npm has project, user, global and builtin files plus environment settings. Git has system, global, local, worktree and command scopes, origin reports, conditional includes and protected configuration. Neither promises a one-to-one key for every CLI flag.

Sources: https://docs.deno.com/runtime/fundamentals/configuration/ and https://docs.deno.com/runtime/reference/deno_json/#permissions. Deno combines tool fields and tasks in deno.json. Tasks preserve whole commands; named permission sets require -P selection. They are stronger for named workflows and explicit grants, but are not ambient per-command defaults. Jet should not copy them as a second meaning for the same setting.

options.name: Flat registry keys in commands:
options.detail: Add commands: in package.jet and the user file. Its quoted keys are the exact dotted registry keys. settings: remains typed program declarations. This is the added option.
options.technical: One map parser resolves each full key against the registry. No nested-versus-flat aliases are accepted. Migrate every consumer of overlapping defaults into the same resolver; build profiles remain a lower layer, not a second engine.

options.name: Nested command maps in commands:
options.detail: Add commands: with a map for each command word. The user file has the same structure. This is the original option A.
options.technical: Flatten only this chosen structure into registry keys, then use the shared resolver. A subcommand/flag name collision must be rejected by the registry before shipping. Do not also accept flat keys as aliases.

options.name: Dotted command keys beside typed settings
options.detail: Keep one settings: block. Typed declarations describe program values; quoted dotted entries supply CLI defaults. This is the original option B. It avoids a new top-level field but mixes two entry forms.
options.technical: Distinguish entries by declared shape, not by banning a program setting named fmt. Typed settings remain visible to $build.settings; command keys do not. Both forms still use the same command resolver as A.

comparisons.note: Separate config and manifest roles, but profiles can appear in both. Config tables are not simply one per command. Ancestor merging and --config exceed this proposal's scope. Sources are in detail.
.npmrc supplies typed supported tool keys at several scopes; package.json config supplies script values separately. Not every flag is a durable setting.
Sectioned configuration has explicit scopes and origin reporting. Protected configuration prevents some repository values becoming security policy. Sections are not universally commands.
Tool fields and named tasks share deno.json. Permission sets are selected explicitly with -P. Tasks can express pipelines but do not directly change plain fmt defaults.

recommendation.why: A keeps program declarations separate and writes the registry key unchanged. It avoids nested command collisions without inventing another resolver.
gains: Exact registry keys work in both files.
Program declarations keep their existing shape.

losses.loss: One new manifest field.
losses.mitigation: Accept only commands: for CLI defaults; keep one registry and resolver.

losses.loss: Ambient defaults can surprise scripts and CI.
losses.mitigation: Report origins, isolate test homes, and reject ambient authority or destructive confirmations.

losses.loss: Fewer scopes than Cargo or git.
losses.mitigation: Keep lookup deterministic; use existing profiles for named build choices.

whyNot.reason: B groups commands well, but nests keys and can collide with subcommand names.
C avoids a field, but mixes declarations and defaults in the same block.

recommendation.tradeoff: One extra block buys clear ownership, not extra settings semantics. The persistence classifications are part of this proposal.

decisions.title: The phase read is spelled #phase, a value about the spot where code is evaluated
decisions.situation: Some helpers run while Jet compiles and again in the finished program. A table made early can call the same helper that the program calls later. The helper may need to print only in the finished program. Jet planned a phase read, but its old dollar spelling is retired and neither replacement works today. We recommend #phase, with three answers and an ordinary if, and update five stale criteria across four cards.
decisions.gist: How should code ask whether it is running while compiling, while building, or in the finished program?
decisions.lesson: A phase is the time at which a piece of code runs. Jet has three: while compiling (a comptime block), while building (the build function), and in the finished program. A helper can be called in more than one phase. Reading the phase lets it skip work that only makes sense in one of them, such as printing.
decisions.explainer: Words used here. Compiling is when Jet turns source into a program. A comptime block is code Jet must run while compiling. The build function is the fn named build that makes the outputs. Run time is when the finished program runs. A site value is a hash name that Jet fills in for the spot where it is written or evaluated, such as #line. A plain value is an ordinary name whose value is the same in every file, such as build.target.os.
decisions.story: Mia writes a square helper that prints each call. She also fills a lookup table with it while compiling. An unguarded print needs an explicit compile-time effects gate today. She wants the helper to print only in the finished program, without granting that gate.
decisions.detail:
D-META-HASH1=A is ratified and retires every dollar read and paste, but does not name a replacement for $phase. This vote supplies one. D-COMPTIME-WORD1=A names Phase.Comptime and distinguishes required early evaluation from an optional early try.

Observed with admitted jet: p1 and p2 give E0107 for $phase. p4 gives E0927 for #line and #phase. p10 prints [1, 4, 9] and 16. p11 gives E3410 for an unguarded compile-time print. BallotReview/phase-type.jet gives E0107 for Phase. p9 instead proves comptime if works, printing linux branch.

Registry entries are not implementations: CoreSurface.jet:139 has FACT_ROOT_PHASE; Spellings.jet:35 lists $phase. AST/Comptime.jet does not declare a source Phase enum.

Proposed A: Prelude Phase: enum { Comptime, Build, Runtime }, read only through #phase. Explicit comptime evaluation, including marker expansion, reads Comptime. Ordinary build-entry execution and its helpers read Build. Finished-program execution reads Runtime. Generated code reads its own execution phase. Explicit comptime inside build reads Comptime. Direct, indirect and recursive calls must agree across O0, O1, O2 and applicable web output (I9).

Before compile-time ambient-effect checks, drop only phase-proven unreachable branches in that copy. Runtime rows retain runtime effects; a pure runtime caller cannot hide IO. Check names and types in every branch. Zero-cost folding, including callbacks, is an acceptance condition, not a measurement.

Reject phase reads reached from comptime if conditions, including through helpers, with a registered error and a plain-if fix. Ordinary if inside comptime is allowed and reads Comptime. Preserve WORD1's distinction: a local optional early try reaching phase falls back to runtime; a required file constant reads Comptime or fails. #phase is not part of #here.

B puts the same read on build, whose Prelude name a user build function can hide (p7 establishes Prelude shadowing). C's Boolean loses the Build distinction. E keeps a function surface without losing any phase. D shares the arithmetic and accepts an explicit trace flag; it needs no duplicated body. BallotReview/phase-explicit.jet already prints [1, 4, 9], square 4 and 16 with D.

Read-only board check: #3520 c23 replaces $phase with the chosen read; #6281 c51 and #6206 c4 replace $build.os with build.target.os. #6039 c6 uses the ratified marker struct/expand shape; c26 uses impl #{target}. These are five criteria across four cards. Keep their behavioral acceptance terms.

Beginners calling libraries need no phase read. Shared-helper authors use one ordinary if. Experts keep normal effect rows and explicit gates: phase grants no permission. Add syntax, errors, UI snapshots, explain text and cross-tier goldens together. A, B, C and E are proposals, not working syntax today.

options.name: #phase, a site value
options.detail: `#phase` is a Phase value that Jet fills in for each compiled copy: `.Comptime`, `.Build` or `.Runtime`. A plain `if` on it folds away. `comptime if #phase` is an error with a fix.
options.technical: Add a site-value row #phase and Prelude Phase: enum { Comptime, Build, Runtime }. Substitute by execution phase, including indirect calls. Fold only phase-proven unreachable effects for the required compile-time copy; preserve runtime effect rows and check names/types in all branches. Reject phase reads reached from comptime if conditions, not ordinary if inside comptime blocks. Preserve D-COMPTIME-WORD1's local-try fallback and required file-constant rule.

options.name: build.phase, a field of the build value
options.detail: The phase is a field of the plain `build` value that HASH1 adds, next to `build.target.os`. Same results as A where `build` is not hidden.
options.technical: Add phase: Phase to the proposed Prelude build value, with A's phase and effect rules. Top-level names can hide Prelude names today (p7); the proposed build qualification and resolution must be specified before implementing B.

options.name: in_comptime(), a Prelude function
options.detail: A Prelude function returns true while compiling and false otherwise, as in Zig and C++. Build code reads true, so it cannot be told apart from a comptime block.
options.technical: Prelude `in_comptime: fn() -> Bool`, substituted per copy like A. The comptime-if trap gets the same registered error. No Phase enum is exposed.

options.name: No phase read
options.detail: No implicit read exists. Share the arithmetic and pass an explicit trace flag. Callers choose whether to print; no helper body is duplicated.
options.technical: Delete FACT_ROOT_PHASE from the public registry and amend the phase-read provisions of D-COMPTIME-WORD1. Ordinary parameters and existing effects remain the only mechanism.

options.name: phase(), a three-case Prelude function
options.detail: A Prelude function returns the same three-case Phase as A. It preserves the Build distinction without a hash name.
options.technical: phase: fn() -> Phase is a compiler-substituted read with A's phase, effects, folding and comptime-if checks. This replaces, rather than accompanies, #phase.

comparisons.note: `@inComptime()` returns whether it ran in a comptime context; the result is a compile-time constant (ziglang.org/documentation/master, @inComptime).
`std::is_constant_evaluated()` always returns true as the condition of `if constexpr`; C++23 adds `if consteval` to avoid the trap (cppreference, is_constant_evaluated, Notes).
comparisons.code: if consteval { /* compile time */ } else { std::printf("square\n"); }

comparisons.note: `__ctfe` is true during compile-time evaluation; it cannot be read in a static if, and every use is evaluated statically at no run-time cost (dlang.org/spec/function.html).

recommendation.why: The phase is a fact about where code is evaluated, so it belongs with #line in the hash family. A names three phases, folds away while running, and turns the known trap into an error with a fix.
gains: One spelling family: hash names are facts about a spot.
Build code can be told apart from comptime code.
The always-true trap is an error with a fix.

losses.loss: One more hash name to learn.
losses.mitigation: Only helper authors need it; hover and jet explain describe each phase.

whyNot.reason: The build value is the same everywhere but the phase is not, and a build file's own build function hides it.
The Boolean cannot distinguish build execution from explicit compile-time evaluation; E shows that a function need not lose that information.
It shares the implementation, but every caller must choose a flag rather than inheriting the execution phase.
It preserves all three phases, but presents an execution-site fact as an ordinary zero-argument call; A makes the special read visible.

recommendation.tradeoff: One explicit site read; zero-cost folding is an implementation acceptance condition, not measured performance.

decisions.title: Run quick, build fast code, and use one short flag for a quicker build
decisions.situation: The owner ruled that jet run defaults to O0, jet build defaults to full optimization, and a flag selects the quicker basic build. That also ends automatic promotion of reused scripts. The current option registry still sets build to basic. The admitted compiler accepts -O1 without refusing it, but the flag has no registered meaning yet. This vote chooses the quick-build spelling and its interactions with profiles and remembered settings. We recommend -O1, with -O0 and -O2 mapped to the same existing optimize option.
decisions.gist: Should jet build default to full, with -O1 as the quick-compile flag and no background rebuild of reused scripts?
decisions.lesson: A compiler can stop early and start the program sooner, or keep working and make the program run faster. Jet runs scripts with the quick choice and builds programs you keep with the slow, thorough one. A flag picks the middle level when compile time matters more.
decisions.explainer: Optimization levels change speed, not program meaning (I9). The registry currently defaults run, dev and test to none, and build to basic. All options below change build to full and delete automatic promotion. Explicit overrides still select another level; they never change a future run through background work.
decisions.story: Ada uses jet run while writing her log script. When it is done she types jet build for full optimization. While iterating on a large build, she chooses -O1 instead. The level is explicit and never changes because of prior runs.
decisions.inWild:
# GCC's documented numbered optimization flag
cc -O1 tool.c -o tool

# Cargo exposes optimization through profiles
cargo run
cargo build --release
# Cargo.toml can set profile.dev.opt-level = 1
decisions.detail:
Read-only authority check: #6087 c11 records the 2026-11-09 direction: run at O0 from memory, build default full, one basic-build flag, replacing RUN-TIER1 promotion. The default and deletion are fixed direction, not choices reopened by this ballot.

Current source: BuildOptions.jet:47 maps none/basic/full to O0/O1/O2, stock_build basic and stock_run none. ScriptCache.jet:62-69 declares background full promotion and JET_RUN_FULL_BUILD. The admitted jet run -O1 on BallotReview/build-probe.jet prints review-build-ok; this proves acceptance, not O1 selection. Front.jet:591-592 skips single-dash words in its unknown-long-flag check. Refusing unknown short flags is a proposed/in-review change, not observed current behavior here.

Author measurements are dated evidence, not universal bounds. buildbench-results.json records three cold builds per level and workload under load 11-13. w04 basic/full medians are 750/830 ms wall, 1650/2070 ms CPU, and 575072/646752 bytes. Its binary medians are 3060/2710 ms. Validate builds are 810/870 ms wall and 1850/2400 ms CPU. The largest reported edit delta is 120 ms. A larger compiler workload is not measured here.

The benchmark compares identical workload outputs and exit status, not equal hashes or complete correctness. Its Validate binary exits 1 at both levels on a ballot with gaps; do not describe that as successful ballot validation. Tiny w01/w14 builds show 40 ms at both levels at the timer's resolution. These observations do not establish a general CPU or memory ceiling.

A maps -O0/-O1/-O2 to the existing optimize values none/basic/full. They share the long flag's option key, parser, profile precedence, pin checks and cache identity. Equal duplicates coalesce; conflicting explicit optimization values give E2104 independent of order. A flag against a different pin gives E2113. The short forms are alternate spellings, not a second optimization mechanism.

All choices preserve release as full plus split debug information. An explicit optimization flag overrides the profile with a note, so -O1 with --release means basic plus split debug info. Define stock debug explicitly as none, rather than inheriting the changed build default. Package profiles still replace stock profiles by name. Settings remember optimize through the existing shared key; no quick-specific key is added.

Cutover covers native Jet and C/C++ entries, web dev preview, test/golden tier selectors and bootstrap commands. Make every intentional O1 build explicit. Do not promise byte-identical outputs from a flag edit: reproducibility must be checked on the actual seed and source. Moving an explicitly basic ship profile to full is not implied by changing the command default.

Kept programs use their effective optimization level in the cache identity. Delete promotion, its environment variable, locks and markers. Reject or rebuild old promoted slots that do not match the requested level. An explicit jet run --optimize=full remains full across reruns; an unmodified default run remains O0. No implicit background compile may change either.

Update I9 to name defaults: O0 for run/dev/test/comptime, O2 for build/release, with explicit build-option overrides except for comptime. Preserve one meaning across levels. Beginners use run then build. Experts pick the quick-build flag, profiles or existing settings. Register help and diagnostics together, and prove precedence, pins, both argv orders, stale slots and cross-tier output before claiming delivery.

options.name: Full builds, -O1 for a quicker one, no background rebuild
options.detail: jet build defaults to full. -O0, -O1 and -O2 are short forms of --optimize on every command that takes it. jet run, jet -e, jet run -, jet dev and jet test stay at none, and a reused script keeps its none program.
options.technical: Set the optimize row's stock_build to full. Add three short-flag rows derived from the row's values, and keep refusing every other unowned single-dash word with E2102. Delete the background build, JET_RUN_FULL_BUILD and its locks and markers. Then update the debug profile, the C entry level, the web preview, the golden o1 tier, the self-host stages and the I9 text.
options.code:
jet run tool.jet             # none, reruns reuse it
jet build tool.jet           # full
jet build -O1 tool.jet       # basic, quicker compile
jet build --release tool.jet # full, split debug info
jet run -O2 job.jet          # full, from memory

options.name: Full builds, --optimize=basic as the only spelling
options.detail: The same as A, but no short flag is added. The quicker build is jet build --optimize=basic, or a remembered build.optimize setting. The 59 tier test steps already spell the long flag.
options.technical: The same as A without the three short rows. Unowned single-dash words, -O1 among them, stay refused with E2102. The golden o1 tier passes --optimize=basic.
options.code:
jet build tool.jet                   # full
jet build --optimize=basic tool.jet  # basic
jet run --optimize=full job.jet      # full

options.name: Full builds with --basic
options.detail: The same defaults and no background promotion, with a descriptive --basic flag for the quicker compile.
options.technical: Register --basic as the basic value of the same optimize option. It shares the long flag's precedence, duplicates, pins and settings. No separate Boolean or optimization key.
options.code:
jet run tool.jet                    # none
jet build tool.jet                  # full
jet build --basic tool.jet          # basic
jet build --basic --release tool.jet # basic, split debug info

options.name: Full builds, with a quick stock profile
options.detail: jet build defaults to full, and a new stock profile, quick, selects basic. jet build --profile=quick is the quicker build. jet run stays at none with no background rebuild.
options.technical: Add a stock quick profile beside release and debug, and refuse unowned single-dash words. A package profile named quick would replace the stock one. --release and --profile=quick can't be combined, because one profile wins.
options.code:
jet build tool.jet                 # full
jet build --profile=quick tool.jet # basic

comparisons.note: gcc and clang spell the level as one short flag. The default is O0, and -O1, -O2 and -O3 raise it.
comparisons.code:
cc -O1 tool.c -o tool
cc -O2 tool.c -o tool

comparisons.note: Cargo exposes dev and release profiles and lets a project set opt-level in its manifest (Cargo reference, Profiles).

recommendation.why: A carries out the ruling with the spelling the owner named and the one many developers know from C compilers. A typed -O1 then does what a C user expects, instead of an E2102 refusal. Deleting the background rebuild keeps jet run at the O0 level I9 names.
gains: Programs built to keep get the full optimizer with no flag.
A quicker build uses the three-character -O1 flag.
jet run does no background optimization, and its level never depends on run history.

losses.loss: Full builds can cost more compiler work; the author's w04 and Validate samples used about 25-30 percent more CPU.
losses.mitigation: Choose basic explicitly when compile speed matters; these small samples are not an upper bound.

losses.loss: Three new flag rows join the CLI surface.
losses.mitigation: They are derived from the optimize row's values, so they never drift from --optimize, and they share its settings key.

losses.loss: Removing automatic promotion can slow long reused scripts relative to a promoted full image.
losses.mitigation: Explicit --optimize=full or a built executable selects full without hidden future work.

whyNot.reason: B has no new spelling, but --optimize=basic is 16 characters rather than the three-character -O1.
--basic is readable, but -O1 is shorter and aligns with familiar numbered optimization levels.
D can't combine with --release, and a package's own quick profile would silently change what the stock flag means.

recommendation.tradeoff: A spends some CPU on every default build for faster programs, and adds three short flags for the quick path. The meaning is the same on every level under each option.

decisions.title: One metaprogramming ladder: Meta effects follow the rule of every effect, compiler control is one passed value, and macros stay out
decisions.situation: While Jet compiles a program, code can act on that program in growing steps. It can read types, add new code through markers, and finally rewrite function bodies through a compiler value. Four earlier votes each set up part of this ladder, and they now disagree. One turns the strong steps on with a package flag, one gives macros to everyone, one adds expert permissions that start off, and one removes macros again. Since then Jet ruled that every effect is allowed unless written code denies it, and that effects are ordinary types. This vote picks one ladder that fits those rules, so the board can build it.
decisions.gist: Which one set of rules should decide who may add or rewrite code while a program compiles?
decisions.lesson: Metaprogramming is code that writes or changes code while Jet compiles. An effect is a kind of outside action a function takes, such as using the network. Jet now allows every effect unless written code denies it, and names new effects when a run starts. The question is whether adding and rewriting code follow that same rule, or a rule of their own.
decisions.explainer: Words used here. A marker is a hash name above a declaration, such as #Traced, whose expand code can add new code. The Compiler value is an object that lets code watch the compile and rewrite function bodies. A rewrite replaces a function's body with new checked code. A macro is a function whose body is pasted into the caller's code. An authority row in package.jet lists effects to allow or deny. A grant line limits what one dependency may do.
decisions.story: Ines wants every function marked #Traced to log when it starts and ends. She installs a trace library and passes it her build's compiler value. Today four rulings disagree on what else she must write: a package flag, an expert line, or nothing. She also wonders whether a macro would have been the simpler tool. She wants one rule, the same one her network calls follow.
decisions.detail:
Ratification checked read-only: OPTIN2 authorizes root-approved registration. CODE1 authorizes macros. COMPILER1's ratified detail explicitly removes them and restores the user-macro ban; its A option alone omits that explanation. HOLD1 adds package authorization. AUTH-DEFAULT1 later allows effects unless denied. HASH1 retires dollar pastes. This vote explicitly reconciles those contracts.

Exercised earlier: l1 prints hello and 2; l2 prints start sum, done sum and 5; l3 reports E1221 for Meta.Generate; l4 prints l4 with the package flag accepted. l2 contains no defer. BallotReview/defer.jet separately reports E0003 for general defer. DEFER1=A ratifies reverse-order cleanup on every exit but is not implemented by that probe.

A declares Meta in Core's compiler library, not the machine-only kernel list. Its empty #FX ceiling grants no host power. Generate, Include, Rewrite, Types and Raw are nominal compiler-operation cases. Adding a type from text checks Generate, Types and Raw together. Host work retains machine effects and #Impure gates. No Meta alias hides FS, Exec or FFI.

Only root-package source can call b.compiler(output), using loader/lock identity, not a caller-supplied name. Forwarding Build cannot bypass that check. Compiler recipients can retain and forward control during that build; record every handoff. Stale values fail closed. Root and organization denials and locked dependency rewrite consent apply to every deferred action.

Retain COMPILER1's #code constructor. HASH1 copies ordinary values plainly, so trace.enter(name) captures the early String; only Code body insertion uses the proposed #{f.body} extension. Ordinary meta.add(code) and meta.rewrite_body(f, code) calls avoid a second special trailing-template-block convention. Name/type pastes retain HASH1 hygiene.

The same program in the options has a marked load_level with early return, fallible read and cleanup. trace registers first; timer registers second and wraps outside trace. Under the proposed DEFER1 meaning, every exit prints time start, enter, exit, time stop. This is a design expectation, not current executable output. C also shows explicit macro wrapping, which can leave the caller; closures cannot promise that behavior.

B keeps A's flat effect family but adds HOLD1-style authorization of Compiler possession. It needs neither expert attributes nor a third effect level. D is traceable through root registration and import alone remains inert. Its difference is provider registration/trust state instead of value delegation.

#3526 c1 changes opt-in to possession plus per-action Meta checks. c2 keeps root/external denials. c3 keeps import, possession and registration distinct. c4 freezes authority and consent when build returns and includes them in provenance/cache identity. c5 keeps host, credentials, consent and Unsafe independent. c6 keeps issued declaration identities and replaces target-record spelling with CROSSPKG1's locked-package allow_rewrite consent.

c7/c8 reopen syntax/spec rows for the replacement surface; c9/c10 retain grammar and UI snapshot obligations. c11 keeps no-value, import-only, authorized-value, dependency request, forwarded Build, denial, policy and unknown-root/no-TTY fixtures. No source/header/cache/subprocess self-enablement may succeed. c12 keeps stale-handle refusal and checked backend options.

c13 keeps advanced type factories, deterministic identity and layout under Meta.Types. This does not forbid ordinary type declarations, generic instantiation, or marker-generated declared types without a Compiler value. All applicable effects still check. c14 keeps hygienic Code and scoped meta.add(code, scope:); call-site register_expansion leaves with macros, as COMPILER1 explicitly rules.

c15 keeps atomic rechecking of all a handler's actions and affected callers; a failed handler publishes none. Generated Unsafe is never authorized. c16 keeps revision-aware dependencies, changed-authority invalidation and fresh host effects on cache hits. c17 records the complete producer/handoff chain. c18 maps project checkers to read/report handlers that cannot suppress Core diagnostics.

c19 retains foreign evidence receipts and opaque-evidence refusal through the existing FFI contract. c20 remains with GENERIC1 for explicit specialization, while procedure-of-call identity remains SITE1. No other behavior is deleted merely by retiring an API. #5023 has three bookkeeping criteria, not macro rows to close. B adds its authorization fixture; C restores call expansion; D retains OPTIN2 criteria.

Handlers share PREP-FUEL1's budget and the existing round-17 limit. Budget/round exhaustion is an error with no partial publication. Cache keys cover source, compiler, reflected inputs, lock, authority and consent. The language server follows the same handlers. Beginners apply markers; experts delegate one Compiler value and inspect later handoffs. None of these proposed APIs is claimed as implemented by l1-l4.

options.detail: Meta is a flat ordinary effect family, allowed unless denied. Only the root's own source makes Compiler; passing it delegates control. Recipient libraries can forward it, so later handoffs stay visible in provenance. No macros.
options.technical: Proposed Meta: enum { Generate, Include, Rewrite, Types, Raw } implementing Effect, declared in Core's compiler package under D-EFFTYPE-KERNEL1, not in Prelude/Effects.jet. Retain COMPILER1's #code constructor with HASH1 hygiene, and explicitly extend #{e} to paste Code inside it. All #3526 acceptance obligations remain; no behavior is removed merely by deleting its old API spelling.

options.name: As A, but strong steps need one package line

decisions.title: Require an early marker expression with Jet's existing #run, not a new sigil
decisions.situation: A library sometimes needs a bad argument rejected before the program starts. An ordinary precondition can check a runtime input, so it does not require that early answer. The owner asked for a cohesive way to choose early checking without turning every argument into a generic parameter. Jet already has a request for required early evaluation: #run. Choose whether to reuse that request inside marker expressions or add a general marker-wide mode. We recommend #run on the expression whose answer must be known, with ordinary calls unchanged.
decisions.gist: Should marker expressions use the same #run request as every other required early expression?
decisions.lesson: #Pre says what must be true. #run says when its expression must have an answer: while building. Combining them keeps those meanings instead of inventing another hash. It does not run the whole function early.
decisions.explainer: A required check fails the build when inputs are unavailable or evaluation cannot complete. A number parameter is a compile-time generic value. Distinct generic instances need not imply distinct emitted machine bodies if the compiler can share them safely.
decisions.story: Ola requires a lane count of four or eight before accepting a call, while the list itself remains runtime data. Every option adds [1,2,3,4] to 10. The example tests a contract, not SIMD performance.
decisions.inWild: Zig's comptime expressions and parameters make an early requirement explicit. C++ constant evaluation likewise differs from merely hoping an optimizer folds an expression. These are documented comparisons, not peer performance measurements.
decisions.detail:
Revision 3 answers q3ybwski, q8sdri5o and q1x848xv together. Required early call validation is the job, not duck typing or currying. F writes #Pre(#run { lanes == 4 || lanes == 8 }, "need 4 or 8"). Parentheses belong to Pre; #run owns its braced expression. No new sigil, parameter grammar or build-error operation is needed.

Marker application and code generation happen while building, but a Pre predicate describes each invocation's inputs. Post describes its result. Under F, required evaluation happens at that contract's normal instantiation point. For Pre, substitute checked caller argument facts first, then use the canonical required evaluator. Do not evaluate an unbound parameter once while reading the declaration.

A false early Pre is a build error under D-PRE-COMPILE1=A. Unavailable inputs, invalid operations, refused effects and exhausted budgets are separate errors, never runtime fallback. Ordinary Pre retains its approved early-if-possible behavior. Unread arguments stay runtime values. Requiring a fact does not make the body parameter generic, permit type shaping, or execute the body early.

F's reach is general expression staging. #Post(#run { result > 0 }, "positive") needs an actual permitted early result fact or fails. User-marker delayed predicates use the same #run at their documented instantiation point. #Memo(bound: #run compute_bound()) requires an early bound. #Layout(c, align(#run alignment())) requires an early alignment. Already early expressions gain no power by repeating #run.

Legal sites, schemas and authority do not change. #Unsafe(#run reason()) computes a reason, not an unsafe action. Runtime allocators and callbacks cannot become build-time resources by wrapping them. Non-expression arguments cannot accept value regions. Every expression-bearing marker follows the same rule; other markers are unaffected. Verifying a Kernel or generating declarations does not run their target code.

Forwarding preserves checked requirements and their dependent argument facts. Known literals or pure early expressions discharge them at outer calls. Unknown runtime wrappers cannot hide them. Interfaces, methods, defaults and generic instances retain the same obligation. A plain callable or foreign callback cannot erase unresolved requirements: bind the arguments or preserve a contract-bearing callable type. Recursion keeps canonical budgets.

Beginner path: ordinary #Pre, ordinary parameters and ordinary calls. Expert path: add #run only to the expression requiring an early answer. Use number parameters separately when a value must shape types. Tools show required caller facts on the signature; the body keeps ordinary parameter semantics.

Compiler/JetFoundation/Data/Syntax/Spellings.jet:26-38 registers current comptime value regions, explicit comptime parameters and $ facts. MathLayout.jet:756-759 owns the requirement word. D-META-SPELL1=A ratifies #run for required regions; D-META-HASH2=A ratifies #build and related filled-in values. A build: fn entry orchestrates a build, not arbitrary early application execution. Facts describe values, not evaluation requests.

Independent t17a a0.0.43 probes, jet run -: comptime { 2 + 2 } prints 4; <comptime N: Int> sum<4> prints 10. #run's value block gets E0733; $build.profile gets E0003. Pre containing a comptime value block is refused, including E0391. Ordinary false Pre prints before, then stops E3005. These prove implementation gaps, not working F syntax.

A is the owner's general ## alternative. It stages all dynamic expressions owned by a marker application, including user markers, at the documented checking point. Post needs early result proof. Runtime-resource or unknown obligations fail; already early markers gain nothing. This adds marker-wide grammar, unlike F's selective expression request. It is not restricted to Pre.

B's early number parameter is sound and useful for type shaping. It changes call organization when only predicate knownness is needed. It is not recommended merely because generic machinery exists. All options share one bounded pure evaluator; no machine-body duplication per count is assumed.

Adversarial verdict: F holds as a cohesive proposal, not current implementation. First try ordinary Pre: it cannot require knownness. Then reuse #run on the deferred expression that needs it. This removes a Pre-only switch. Forwarding and callable-erasure limits remain real and must appear in interfaces and diagnostics. No zero-cost or universal-proof claim is made. Breaking cutovers follow D-LANG-MIGRATE1=A's registered rewrites without retired-syntax teaching.
