decisions.title: Sized booleans for C APIs: one ffi.Bool<U32> wrapper in core.ffi
decisions.gist: How should Jet code hold a C API's 4-byte true-or-false field, such as VkBool32 or Win32 BOOL?
decisions.lesson: Some C APIs store true or false in a fixed-width integer, such as Vulkan's 32-bit VkBool32. A shared struct must match the foreign field's size and alignment. Using an ordinary Bool can change later offsets.
decisions.story: Kai binds Vulkan's 32-bit feature flags. Using ordinary Bool fields risks wrong offsets, so he currently stores U32 and compares with zero. He wants the representation to say it is a Boolean.
decisions.inWild: Vulkan defines VkBool32 as uint32_t and requires inputs of 0 or 1 (https://docs.vulkan.org/refpages/latest/refpages/source/VkBool32.html). Keeping that integer in bindings is a strong zero-wrapper alternative; a wrapper can instead make Bool conversion explicit. The C declaration alone does not distinguish a boolean typedef from an ordinary integer typedef.
decisions.detail:
Exercised with admitted jet: b1.jet gives E0119 for B32; b2.jet prints true using U32 != 0. BallotReview/integer-condition.jet gives E0110 for if on U32. Thus C does not silently accept a forgotten condition comparison. ForeignLink.jet:406 maps Bool to _Bool for inline C scalars; that is not proof of every foreign layout or of C bool's size on every ABI.

A adds an ordinary exact-representation core.ffi wrapper under PRIMS1. ffi.Bool<T> accepts fixed-width signed or unsigned integers, preserving T's size, alignment and scalar call/return ABI. Win32 BOOL's signed storage must not be silently replaced with unsigned storage. Structs, arrays, pointers, callbacks and by-value arguments/results all need foreign round-trip proofs; matching size alone is insufficient.

get() returns false for zero and true for nonzero without modifying the stored bits. Constructing from Bool stores 0 or 1. Equality and hashing use the normalized Bool together, so 1 and 2 compare/hash consistently. Fixed-width storage has no invalid Bool bit pattern; never reinterpret noncanonical integers as native Bool. Unsupported T is a registered error.

The binder wraps only declarations whose Boolean meaning is established by a supported schema or explicit binding annotation. It cannot infer Boolean intent from an arbitrary int typedef. Vulkan inputs must still be 0 or 1; its outputs are specified as 0 or 1, so a returned 2 is not a valid Vulkan example. General C BOOL-style nonzero truth is a different API contract.

B adds four compiler-known names. C retains exact integer storage and explicit comparisons, already checked as Bool conditions by Jet. A's benefit is readable typed conversion, not repairing an existing truthiness hole. Plain code keeps Bool; experts choose exact storage through the same public FFI representation mechanism. No new built-in type or binder-only privilege is authorized.

recommendation.why: C structs get the exact size and still read as true or false. Only foreign code sees it, so the beginner's type list stays Int, Float, Bool and String.
gains: Exact C layout with Bool reads.

losses.loss: Reads need .get() instead of using the field directly.
losses.mitigation: An if or && on the field gives an error whose fix adds .get().

whyNot.reason: Four built-in names that only C bindings need, in every program's type list.
C is ABI-simple and already rejects an integer condition; it repeats the zero comparison instead of naming the Boolean representation.

recommendation.tradeoff: A library wrapper with a .get() call instead of new built-in types.

decisions.title: Run-time type values: a comparable reflect.TypeKey in core.reflect
decisions.gist: How should a running Jet program name a type as a value, for example to key a map by type?
decisions.lesson: A type-keyed table needs a value identifying the exact type. Jet's current reflection gives display names and paths, which are strings, not an exact portable identity contract.
decisions.story: Rui keeps component counts by type. A reflected path works for his small program, but he wants exact identity across generic instances and separately loaded packages, without relying on display text.
decisions.inWild: Rust's opaque TypeId is comparable and hashable, with release-dependent hash/order and no stable layout (https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/any/struct.TypeId.html). Its documentation warns that identity-based abstractions still need correct variance. A Jet key must similarly be more than a hash of a printable path.
decisions.detail:
Exercised: t1 prints Point, t1.Point, Int and true; t2 reports E0107 for TypeId; t3's string-keyed map prints 2. Core/Reflect/Reflect.jet has text inspection, while typed of is compiler-projected. Calls/Reflection.jet:48-57 builds display paths from module path and name, even replacing hyphens with underscores. That is not a globally unique or persistent type identity proof.

A adds an opaque TypeKey projection of the compiler's existing canonical type identity, not a second identity registry inferred from display strings. reflect.key<T>() and reflect.of(x).key() agree for x's static concrete type T. Existing reflect.of visibility/secret/display restrictions remain; key<T>() itself does not render a value. A key for Any names the box type; Any.key() separately names its stored concrete payload.

Aliases share the underlying identity; distinct nominal types differ even with identical layout or path text. Generic type/value arguments and complete callable types participate in the existing canonical identity. Two separately loaded package identities cannot collide merely because their paths match. Hash collisions must still compare full identity. Keys cannot be forged from integers, pointers or strings, and equality alone grants no value access or cast authority.

Keys are meaningful only within one linked program/session identity domain. Do not serialize them as a cross-build protocol. No Encode/Decode or integer conversion is provided, but Display remains printable, so lack of Encode cannot prevent users saving its text. Paths are diagnostic names, not promised stable schema IDs. Applications needing persistence must own versioned schema identifiers.

Dynamically loaded metadata must outlive retained keys; unload/reload must not reuse an identity for a different type or leave dangling display pointers. Use the same managed descriptor lifetime as reflection and Any. This metadata retention is a real cost; exact key comparison is not a measured speedup over string maps. No per-key heap allocation is required for statically linked types.

B makes Type a runtime value kind and must explicitly reconcile compile-time type contracts; an archived decision is not authority to dismiss it. C can compute both map keys from reflect.of rather than type path literals, avoiding the draft's alleged unavoidable typo. C still lacks an exact identity guarantee. Beginners need neither API; experts get exact comparison without a new top-level language value kind.

options.name: TypeKey in core.reflect
options.detail: An opaque key projects canonical type identity. Same concrete type means equal keys; different nominal types or generic instances remain distinct. Keys are session-local, not a persistent schema format.

options.name: A built-in Type value
options.detail: Type is a built-in value kind, and type_of(x) returns it, as in Jai and Odin.

options.name: Keep path strings
options.detail: No new value. Programs key by reflect.of(x).path(), as t3.jet does today.

recommendation.why: A small key covers maps keyed by type and checked unboxing. It lives in the reflection library next to type_name and path, so the language gains no new value kind.
gains: Exact opaque identity rather than display-name identity.
No new built-in value kind.

losses.loss: Keys are not a persistent or cross-program schema identifier and may retain type metadata.
losses.mitigation: Expose no serialization conversion; print a diagnostic path, and keep descriptor lifetimes managed by the shared reflection mechanism.

whyNot.reason: B is a broader runtime-Type design, not forbidden by an archived record; A meets this exact-identity use without making all types runtime values.
C can avoid path typos by deriving keys from values, but display paths still have no exact identity guarantee.

recommendation.tradeoff: A library key fixed per build instead of a built-in Type value.

decisions.title: Pointer-sized integers for C layouts: ffi.USize and ffi.ISize in core.ffi
decisions.situation:
A C library describes sizes and offsets with size_t, ssize_t, ptrdiff_t, uintptr_t and intptr_t. Their width depends on the target: 64 bits on x86-64 and AArch64, and 32 bits on wasm32. Jet has no type for them today, so both hand bindings and the header binder write U64 or I64, which is wrong on a 32-bit target.

This ballot adds two target-sized types to the ratified FFI building-block package, the way sized booleans were added. It leaves Int as Jet's one everyday integer. Keeping today's fixed widths is option C.
decisions.gist: Should core.ffi add USize and ISize, sized to the target, so a C binding is right on 32-bit and 64-bit targets?
decisions.lesson: C programs describe memory sizes with types whose width depends on the machine. A binding that guesses the width gets the struct layout wrong on other machines. This vote decides how Jet bindings name those types, without changing the Int that everyday code uses.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A binding is Jet code that describes a C library's functions and structs. A layout is the size and position of each field in memory. The target is the machine a program is built for.

A pointer-sized integer is as wide as a memory address on the target: 64 bits on most desktops, 32 bits on wasm32.
decisions.story: Noor binds a C buffer whose length is a size_t. She writes U64, and the binding works on her laptop. Built for wasm32, every field after the length sits four bytes off.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. How Jet code names C's target-sized integers in bindings and #Layout(c) structs. It does not change Int, list lengths or indexes.

Today, on the t6c compiler (dev 76955986d0), every probe matches the seed. Probe u02 writes USize{8} and gets E0119, UnknownType: there is no type called USize. Probe u03 declares a #Layout(c) struct with a U64 length, converts it with Int{b.len}, and prints count 3.

Probe u01 converts U64{18446744073709551615} with I64{big} and stops with E3010, value doesn't fit in destination type, rc 70. Probe u04 calls I64.from_u64 on the same value and gets an error result: value doesn't fit in destination type. Conversions are checked; the -1 results reported in Docs/research/2026-10-30-type-conversions.md no longer happen.

The binder hard-codes the 64-bit answer. Dev's C header binder maps size_t and uintptr_t to U64, and ssize_t and intptr_t to I64, on every target (Jetpack PackageModel Foreign/C/HeaderParser.jet:521-522). It has no row for ptrdiff_t. So a generated binding is wrong on wasm32 today, not only a hand one.

The rule under A. core.ffi gains two types. ffi.USize is the target's unsigned pointer-sized integer, and ffi.ISize the signed one. On x86-64 and AArch64 they are 64 bits; on wasm32 they are 32 bits. Their width, sign, alignment and calling-convention class come from the target's C facts, not from the host compiling the program.

Which C names map to them. The binder resolves size_t, ssize_t, uintptr_t, ptrdiff_t and intptr_t separately from the target's C facts, replacing HeaderParser's fixed rows. It uses ffi.USize or ffi.ISize only when the width, sign, alignment and calling class match exactly. On a target where they differ, such as one where uintptr_t is wider than size_t, the binder emits the exact fixed-width type and says why.

Arithmetic. ffi.USize and ffi.ISize are fixed-width integers, so they share D-FIXED-WRAP1's rules: + stops on overflow, and wrapping(...), saturating(...) and checked(...) are the explicit forms. A binding can add offsets and compare lengths without leaving the type.

Into Int and back. The conversions are the ones probes u01 and u04 exercise. Int{n} stops if the value does not fit, and checked(Int{n}) returns an outcome you can handle, per D-FIXED-WRAP1, which retires today's I64.from_u64. ffi.USize{i} from a negative Int stops, and so does a narrowing on a 32-bit target. No conversion ever wraps or drops high bits.

Migration. Regenerated bindings change size_t from U64 to ffi.USize. On x86-64 and AArch64 the width, alignment and calling class are identical, so no 64-bit layout changes. Int{b.len} keeps working. Code that mixes the field with U64 values gets a type error, and jet fix writes the U64{…} conversion.

Why the overflow case is rare. An ffi.USize that measures real memory, a length or an offset, always fits Int, because no target's address space reaches 2^63 bytes. The value that does not fit is a sentinel such as SIZE_MAX, which C uses for not found. Compare it with ffi.USize.MAX before converting, as the C code does.

Addresses. Holding an address in ffi.USize grants no right to read it; turning it back into a pointer stays an unsafe step under D-FFI-PRIMS1 and #Unsafe(reason). All tiers, the interpreter, the JIT and native builds, use the same target facts, so a layout and a conversion behave the same everywhere.

Delivery proof, part of building A: compare size, sign, alignment and calling class with the C compiler for structs, arrays, by-value arguments and results, and callbacks, on x86-64, AArch64 and wasm32. The wasm32-wasip2 build is not implemented on the seed (E2104, #6418), so A's 32-bit claims are a contract for that target, not a measurement.

Beginner path. Everyday code never sees these types: counts, lengths and indexes stay Int. Generated bindings use ffi.USize where C says size_t, and one checked conversion turns it into an Int.

Expert path. A hand-written binding uses ffi.USize and ffi.ISize directly and gets the right layout on every supported target from one source. Sentinels are compared in ffi.USize before conversion.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. A conversion from ffi.USize to Int can fail. For real sizes it cannot, as above; for sentinels, the comparison comes first. The checked conversion stops with file and line, never with a wrong number.

Two more names in core.ffi. They follow ffi.Bool<U32>'s pattern, so a binder or reader already knows where C-only types live.

Other options. B builds USize and ISize into the language and makes them the type of lengths and indexes, as Rust does. C keeps today's form: the binder writes the exact fixed width, U64 or U32, per target, and hand bindings choose it themselves. D adds one name per C typedef, ffi.SizeT, ffi.PtrDiffT, ffi.UIntPtrT and ffi.IntPtrT, as Rust's libc crate does.

B mixes Int and USize in every program that touches a list, which is the conversion noise Rust users know. C needs one hand binding per target width. D is exact for every typedef but gives four names where every supported target needs two.

options.name: ffi.USize and ffi.ISize in core.ffi
options.detail: Two target-sized types in core.ffi for bindings and C layouts. Int stays the everyday integer, and checked conversions cross between them.
options.technical: Extends D-FFI-PRIMS1=A like D-PRIM-BOOLSIZE1=A. Width, sign, alignment and calling class come from target C facts. The binder maps size_t, ssize_t, uintptr_t, ptrdiff_t and intptr_t separately, replacing HeaderParser.jet's fixed U64/I64 rows, and uses the alias only on an exact match. D-FIXED-WRAP1 arithmetic; existing checked conversions.

options.name: Built-in USize as the type of lengths
options.detail: USize and ISize are built in, and list lengths and indexes use USize, as in Rust.
options.technical: Adds two primitive types and changes len() and indexing to USize across Core. Every program that mixes lengths with Int arithmetic converts.

options.name: Keep fixed widths per target
options.detail: No new type. The binder learns to write U64 or U32 from the target's C facts; today it writes U64 everywhere. A hand binding chooses the width for each target it supports.
options.technical: No change to core.ffi. HeaderParser.jet's fixed rows become target lookups. Hand bindings that support several widths need one declaration per width, chosen by #if on the target.

options.name: One name per C typedef
options.detail: core.ffi adds ffi.SizeT, ffi.PtrDiffT, ffi.UIntPtrT and ffi.IntPtrT, each exactly its C typedef on the target.
options.technical: Four target-derived types, distinct even where they share a width, as Rust's libc crate names them. No mapping rule is needed in the binder.

recommendation.why: A makes C layouts right on every supported target from one binding source. Everyday Jet keeps one Int, and conversions stay checked.
gains: One binding source is right on 64-bit and 32-bit targets.
Int stays the only integer everyday code uses.
Arithmetic and conversions reuse the checked rules that exist today.

losses.loss: A sentinel such as SIZE_MAX does not fit Int.
losses.mitigation: Compare it with ffi.USize.MAX before converting; real sizes always fit.

whyNot.reason: B puts USize into every program that touches a list, with conversions everywhere.
C needs a separate hand binding for each target width.
D gives four names where every supported target needs two.

recommendation.tradeoff: Two C-only types in core.ffi, in return for layouts that are right on every target.

decisions.title: Should hiding an arbitrary concrete type require explicit Any construction?
decisions.situation: Should hiding an arbitrary concrete type require explicit Any construction? A plugin may return a type its host has never named, yet the host may need that exact type later. Our small example stores 14 and recovers it to print 14. Ordinary typed storage covers known cases, but does not settle open concrete recovery. We recommend an explicit box using ordinary trait ownership, not another dynamic value system.
decisions.gist: Should hiding an arbitrary concrete type require explicit Any construction?
decisions.lesson: Any hides a concrete type but keeps its checked identity. A trait instead exposes shared operations; an enum lists known alternatives. Hiding a type must never hide its cleanup, lifetime, permissions or secrecy.
decisions.explainer: A carrier owns a hidden payload and remembers its exact type. A duty names how a value must finish. Erasure may hide the concrete type, but cannot hide duties, effects or safety facts.
decisions.story: Lin stores 14, then recovers and prints it. All options do that job; only the Any options admit previously unnamed plugin types.
decisions.inWild: Checked borrowed recovery; illustrative excerpt from the documented Any API, not executed here.
decisions.detail:
origin/dev:Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Expressions/Constructors.jet:721-734 constructs the existing TraitBox. Both Any choices extend that identity and ownership route. The enum choice uses ordinary enum checking; it adds no erasure mechanism.

A adds a Core Any trait carrier and Any{value} construction. A proposed .Int(n) pattern on that carrier checks exact canonical identity and lends the payload within its arm. An open carrier requires else. No display-name comparison, arbitrary cast or second Dyn representation is allowed. E has identical recovery but admits ordinary implicit trait coercion. B deliberately has no arbitrary concrete recovery; an enum or a shared behavioral trait remains the better design when sufficient.

Beginners keep concrete types, enums or behavioral traits. Experts use Any only for genuine open recovery. Preserve transitive loans, allocator provenance, secrecy tags and callable effects. A nontransferable payload stays nontransferable. Ordinary trait-interface facts retain sendability, finishing obligations and normalized cleanup/failure effects; do not create Any.Send, Any.Owes or parallel duty syntax. Full resource payload support is required, not a data-only implementation. Reject unrepresentable loans or obligation-erasing callable conversions rather than treating them as plain data.

Consuming extraction: take<T>(&&self) -> T TakeMismatch<Self>!. TakeMismatch<C> is an ordinary error struct with original: C. On mismatch it retains the unchanged carrier and every obligation; on success ownership and duties transfer to T. Construction failure preserves source ownership and drops partial storage once. Containers enforce duties per element. Unwinding settles owned payloads once; plugin code stays loaded while its values or loans survive. Hiding a secret-selected type preserves the control-flow tag on its identity test. No inline-size or allocation-elimination promise is part of this vote.

Fresh review, 2026-11-11. Removed invented carrier families and the duplicate data box; restored dot-prefixed patterns and retained mismatch, secrecy and plugin lifetime obligations.

reports.title: Rust Any identity and lifetime limits

decisions.title: Read-only fields: a public computed field over a priv stored field, with writes refused
decisions.situation: A file lock exposes the path it names, and the library documentation intends callers only to read it. The checker currently accepts a write to that Core field, but running the program fails in the compiler backend before the lock is taken. Ordinary user structs do allow public-field writes. Jet also has computed fields that can read private storage without exposing a writable field. Their literal-write error exists, but assignment checking is incomplete. We recommend finishing that existing rule and using a private stored path behind a public computed path, rather than adding a setter qualifier.
decisions.gist: How should a field be readable everywhere but writable only inside its own module, such as a lock's path?
decisions.lesson: Field visibility and write access are different. A public field can be edited only through a mutable owner or write view; priv also restricts which module may access it. A public computed getter can expose a value without exposing storage to write.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A module is a file or a name: module { … } block; its code owns the types it declares. priv before a field hides it outside that module. A computed field, name: Type -> formula, is read like a field but holds no value of its own; its formula reads other fields.

Forging means building or changing a value so it claims something untrue. A lock whose path was rewritten forges a claim about which file is locked.
decisions.story: Sam's backup helper tries to overwrite a lock's path. He wants a normal compiler error explaining that the field is read-only, not a backend failure, while print(lock.path) keeps working.
decisions.inWild: Kotlin separates getter and setter visibility: a public var can have private set (https://kotlinlang.org/docs/properties.html). This preserves stored-field organization. Jet's working private-field/reader-method probe r4 offers a different organization without a new setter qualifier.
decisions.detail:
Exercised admitted jet: r1 gives E0605; r2 gives E0414. r3 prints /tmp/app.lock then /etc/passwd for a user struct. r4 and r5 print /tmp/app.lock through a method and computed getter. r8 prints true then /tmp/next.lock after an internal backing-field edit. r9 gives E0339 for the computed literal field and E0605 for explicitly setting private storage.

r6, r7 and r10 pass jet check but jet run reports an internal backend failure for their field writes. r7 is a real FileLock and was run from BallotReview/field-run, not the repository. Therefore the draft must not say a Core lock currently takes effect and then successfully changes its reported path. This is a checker/backend gap, not proven runtime mutation.

E0339's declaration covers computed fields in literals or direct assignments. Constructors.jet:628 checks the literal case. Finish assignment-place checking under every ballot option, independently of the handle API choice (I2/I3 and #6468 c3). A computed field is not writable even inside its defining module; that module changes the separate stored field.

A uses private storage plus a public computed projection. Reject direct and compound assignment, destructive take and write loans into computed properties before lowering, including nested/indexed projections. Plain reads follow existing ownership, copy and view rules; do not promise zero String copies without IR evidence. Keep constructors private where hidden handles enforce provider ownership.

Current Core paths are stored fields on TempDir, TempFile, FileLock, FileReader, FileWriter, Directory and MappedFile. Cutover must cover their constructors, host projections and in-repo readers, not just source declarations. The corpus currently reports E0302, E0205 and E0605: its write owners are immutable. To require E0339 unchanged, check computed-target validity before ordinary mutability; also add mutable-owner tests so E0205 cannot hide the actual gap.

B narrows setter permission on a stored field. That is distinct from computing a value with no stored place, so its benefit is one declaration, ordinary internal writes and unchanged storage metadata. Its cost is another permission qualifier and enforcement across every write/loan path; it is not automatically forbidden by I8. D is an ordinary private field plus reader and remains a working alternative. C retains public mutable path but must still fix computed-field checking, document the changed promise and remove only the explicitly voted forge-by-write expectations.

#6468 c1 is this choice; c2 applies the chosen API to named handles and corresponding tests; c3's sema refusal is unconditional. The corpus is an acceptance target, not an observed pass under unimplemented A. Beginner reads stay .path under A/B/C; D changes them to .path(). Experts retain explicit provider methods and normal ownership checks. No new accessor evaluator or special Core-only protection is authorized.

options.name: A computed field over a priv field
options.detail: No new syntax: a public computed getter reads private storage. No code assigns the getter itself, even inside its module; provider code edits the backing field.
options.technical: Finish E0339 computed-place validation independently of this vote. Migrate all named handle storage, constructors and host projections. Test direct/compound/nested writes, write loans and destructive takes from storage. Consuming an ordinary materialized getter result remains legal. Add mutable-owner cases and define diagnostic priority for the existing immutable-owner corpus.

options.name: A priv(set) qualifier
options.detail: priv(set) path: String reads anywhere and writes only in the type's module, like Swift's private(set).
options.technical: The grammar accepts set as a second priv qualifier on fields only. Reads follow the type's visibility. Writes and literal entries outside the type's module are E0605 with a write message. The syntax registry gains a set qualifier row.

options.name: Keep path writable; drop the write rows
options.detail: path remains publicly writable through a mutable owner. The docs change, and only the specifically voted write expectations leave the corpus. Existing computed-property bugs still must be fixed.
options.technical: Retain public stored paths and implement valid Core-handle lowering without changing checks or allowing forging of the private handle. Fix computed-field assignment checking under #6468 c3 regardless. This option relaxes a path-reporting API promise; it does not authorize descriptor forgery.

options.name: A priv field and a path() method
options.detail: The field is hidden, and a method returns a copy, as in Rust's tempfile crate.
options.technical: Core renames each stored field and adds path: fn(self) -> String. Every caller, doc row and corpus row changes from .path to .path(). r4 shows the form works today.

comparisons.note: Setter visibility can be narrower than getter visibility (Kotlin Properties, backing fields/getters/setters).

recommendation.why: A reuses computed getters and private storage, keeping .path reads unchanged. Computed-write validation is already owed; the vote chooses the handle API, not whether backend crashes are acceptable.
gains: No new syntax: computed fields already exist and are taught.
Existing read call sites remain unchanged; the corpus remains an acceptance target.
Computed-field writes are refused by sema under every option.

losses.loss: Each read-only field needs two names, the hidden stored one and the public one.
losses.mitigation: The pattern is two lines, and E0339's fix text shows it.

whyNot.reason: B preserves stored-field identity and uses one declaration, but adds a setter-permission qualifier. A reuses existing getters where that extra storage permission surface is unnecessary.
C lets any caller make a lock name a file it does not hold, and the backend still needs new work to lower the writes.
D changes every .path reader to a call, and reading becomes a method where the rest of Core reads fields.

recommendation.tradeoff: Two names per read-only field instead of a new qualifier.

decisions.title: Package-private helpers: priv in Core and every package, with __ kept for generated names
decisions.gist: How should any package, Core included, mark a helper that only its own code may call?
decisions.lesson: User source cannot spell double-underscore names, while Core currently takes a generated-source lexer route. Explicit visibility should instead follow the same declaration rule in ordinary packages.
decisions.story: Ana writes a text library whose public functions share a pad helper. She wants pad hidden from the library's users, the same way Core hides its own helpers.
decisions.inWild: Rust's pub(crate) makes an item visible inside its crate (https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/visibility-and-privacy.html). That is explicit visibility, not a compiler-library lexer exemption.
decisions.detail:
Exercised: p1 gives E0067 for __pad; p2 E0413 for item priv; p3 E0067 for __decode_dyn; p4 E0605 for greeter.text.pad. p4 never runs its earlier greet line. A separate BallotReview/helpers-good app prints two spaces then hello using the public dependency function.

Loader citations were stale. Current Loader.jet:3763-3796 selects a Core parse job. User source uses lex_threads at :3699; Core uses lex_generated_threads at :3811 and filters members/tests at :3824-3827. Payload.jet:951-956 implements the reserved-name flag. A prefix rename alone cannot remove every Core parse decision.

VIS-ITEM1=A is ratified, unimplemented in p2. Item priv means enclosing module plus children; package-root priv is package-only. Nested priv(package) widens to the package. A applies that rule uniformly and keeps __ reserved in authored source. Compiler hygiene uses issued identities, never a prefix as permission.

Classify declarations before migration. True private helpers use priv; public FFI/library primitives remain public. Only the five already-ratified CORE-PRIVATE-SEAM1 entrypoints use priv(toolchain) modules. That qualifier is module-only, not a blanket new privilege for every generated call. Migrate source declarations, semantic callers and registry references together; external ABI symbols are not automatically helper source names.

A also unifies authored-source lexing/parsing. Move ownership/member/test selection to ordinary declared mechanisms rather than an is-Core syntax mode. #6151 c35 is not met by a rename alone. c36 replaces its stale __ wording with the chosen visibility and proves inside/outside behavior in ordinary and Core dependencies.

B can avoid duplicate mechanisms: __ becomes the single package-private item spelling, replacing overlapping item priv/priv(package) uses; priv remains for narrower module/field access. Generated names remain hygienic without another reserved text prefix. B's cost is a wider visibility cutover and access meaning carried by names, not loss of hygiene.

C retains a protected toolchain setting and a source-mode exception. Self-written package metadata must not confer installed-toolchain identity. Choosing C amends c35 rather than satisfying uniformity. Its exception must be explicit.

No unverified helper count or mechanical-rename promise is used. Resolve collisions by declaration identity. Beginners use explicit privacy; experts retain existing module/package visibility and only the ratified toolchain seam scope. A/B/C remain proposals, not behavior proved by p1-p4.

options.name: priv everywhere; __ only for generated names
options.detail: Use ratified item priv in Core and user packages; keep __ reserved in authored source. Unify parser decisions too, not just spellings.

options.name: __ means package-private everywhere
options.detail: __ becomes the single package-private item spelling, replacing overlapping forms. priv remains for narrower visibility; generated names use hygienic identities.

options.name: A toolchain-only package setting
options.detail: The __ prefix stays reserved. Core's exemption becomes a package setting that only toolchain packages may set; users keep priv.

recommendation.why: A reuses ratified visibility and removes authored-source grammar privilege without a new naming convention. The Core parse route must also be unified; renaming alone is insufficient.
gains: One spelling and one error for package-only helpers.
Shared authored-source grammar and visibility, retaining only the existing toolchain seam scope.

losses.loss: A declaration, caller and registry cutover is needed; some names collide.
losses.mitigation: Classify helpers, public primitives and protected seams, then rename by semantic identity with all callers.

whyNot.reason: B can retire duplicate forms, but carries visibility in names and requires a broader visibility cutover.
C keeps two lexer modes and a rule users cannot use, so Core still differs from user packages.

recommendation.tradeoff: A one-time Core rename for one visibility spelling everywhere.

Same error everywhere.

losses.mitigation: Classify declarations and migrate semantic callers/registries, not a blind prefix replacement.

Core keeps a rule users cannot use.

decisions.title: One comptime block that makes everything inside it run while building
decisions.situation:
You asked to write comptime once around a group. Today a required value uses name: comptime { value }. Function-scope statement blocks run while building but do not export names. A top-level block gets E0621; a later CELLS read gets E0107.

Plain constants can already fold as an optimization. Ratified D-COMPTIME-WORD1 extends tries and requires early file constants; it does not require one word for every local value. This ballot concerns grouping required evaluation and build-only declarations, not a promise of smaller binaries.
decisions.gist: Should one comptime block make everything inside it run while building, with its names readable after it?
decisions.lesson: Required build-time results use explicit comptime; opportunistic folding is different. The choices group named results, restrict grouping to declarations, add a namespace, retain separate bindings, or return one record from a scoped block.
decisions.story: Ada computes cells, rows and a label, then checks a limit. A would group required computation and export named results. Existing dead-code removal can already omit her helper; an explicit build-only region instead prevents accidental runtime use. Another choice returns one record from a scoped value block without exporting its internal names.
decisions.inWild:
Nim separates a grouped const section from static statements that require compile-time execution (https://nim-lang.org/docs/manual.html#statements-and-expressions-const-section).

Racket's begin-for-syntax raises forms' phase rather than exporting ordinary runtime values (https://docs.racket-lang.org/reference/begin.html). Its phase separation is useful, but is not the same contract as A's exported stored values.
decisions.detail:
Exercised current behavior. Option D prints 144, grid-144 and 4 columns. Its final emitted IR contains run and stop-poll calls, not square: the claim that square necessarily ships is false. A file-scope block gets E0621/E0107; a local post-block read gets E0107; comptime module gets E0003. A multi-statement record-valued comptime block gets E0391 today, so E is a real extension, not a current workaround.

A proposes a standing region at file, module or function scope. Direct immutable bindings are required compile-time values exposed in the enclosing scope after the region. Nested if/loop/block bindings stay nested. Mutable scratch bindings remain local. Ordinary casing and visibility apply; the region grants no new export or shadowing privilege. Local regions cannot read runtime inputs; generic-local regions evaluate per specialization, never per runtime call.

At file/module scope, functions and types declared in the region are build-only declarations, not executed function bodies. Required evaluation invokes their bodies normally. E0944 rejects runtime references, callable/closure escape and stored values whose representation depends on a build-only type. Ordinary shared types live outside. Inner mutable state must be serialized into independent storable results; live loans/handles cannot escape.

Top-level regions run once per compilation instance, including checks when their containing module is loaded even if their result is unused. Regions' imperative statements run in source order. Bindings may depend on ordinary file constants through the existing dependency graph; a cycle through a region is an error, never partial execution. Local regions do not mutate runtime variables or return/break out of runtime control flow.

No evaluation engine, effect rule or limit changes. D-COMPTIME-WORD1's per-binding budgets remain per binding, not a new shared-block allowance. Standalone region statements use one required-evaluation budget. Existing #StepLimit rules apply. Runtime barriers, required-input classification, #Impure grants and dependency-consent checks cannot be bypassed by an outer block. Diagnostics point at the failing binding or statement. The same recorded facts feed every tier.

Plain use is not added inside the region. Import with existing comptime use in the enclosing declaration scope. A nested comptime is redundant but retains the same meaning; any new warning needs a registered code, removal edit and snapshot before delivery. A region used as a value retains lexical scope and returns only its final value.

B exposes file/module bindings but preserves local statement-block scope. Its best case is phase grouping without changing existing local lexical behavior. C adds a qualified compile-time module; checks run when first used, so an unused module does not promise its checks ran. It trades unqualified access for namespace isolation. D retains current spelling plus ratified WORD1 and USE1; helpers need not ship. None needs a second evaluation mechanism.

E instead completes multi-statement value blocks. One external record type carries the stored results; internal names and scratch state remain lexical. A final record exports several results with one comptime word. It cannot replace a standalone file check without a containing binding, but avoids changing the owner's scope law. Its example includes the same size check and runtime output.

A/B amend the 2026-09-30 scope rule only for their stated positions. C adds a declaration position. E lifts the current E0391 limitation without changing name scope. All use existing comptime vocabulary, so no keyword is added. Diagnostic and grammar-position counts must reflect the chosen option; no measured binary-size or timing gain is claimed.

Beginner path: one region for named results under A, or one stored record under E. Expert path: explicit build-only helpers with USE1 or region phase checks, while ordinary helpers remain dual-use. Acceptance requires collisions, captures, generics, cycles, effect failures, budgets, host/target layout and callable/type escape witnesses.

options.name: A standing comptime block shares its names, everywhere
options.detail: Write comptime once in a file, module or function. Direct immutable results become enclosing-scope bindings; scratch state stays local. Functions/types declared in a file/module region are build-only.
options.technical:
Add standing regions in declaration positions; retain statement positions. Only direct immutable result bindings enter the enclosing scope; nested names and mutable scratch remain lexical. File/module helper declarations are build-only. Extend E0944 to direct and indirect phase escapes and non-storable result types.

Reject plain use with a fix to an enclosing comptime use. Register any redundant-keyword warning with an exact removal edit and snapshot. Migration preserves every old binding's references: rename collisions with their scoped uses, or rewrite the old block as explicit result bindings. Never silently change which declaration a name resolves to.

options.name: Standing blocks in files and modules only
options.detail: The same block, but only among file and module declarations. Inside a function, names bound in a comptime statement still stay inside it, so each local value keeps its own word.
options.technical: As A at file/module scope; local statement blocks keep lexical scope. This preserves existing local behavior and avoids exporting local names. Only new declaration positions expose direct immutable bindings.

options.name: A compile-time module
options.detail: Group build-time code in a named module marked comptime. Every member is computed while building, and code reads them as grid.CELLS. Function bodies are unchanged.
options.technical: Parser: comptime before module in a module declaration; today that is E0003. Sema: every immutable member is a required compile-time binding; functions and types are build-only, with E0944 at runtime references. Names are always qualified, so nothing leaks into the file scope. Checks run when the module is first used.

options.name: One word per value
options.detail: Keep today's rule. Plain file constants are computed early once D-COMPTIME-WORD1 is built, and every other build-time value, check or helper keeps its own comptime word.
options.technical: No new grouping form beyond ratified WORD1 and USE1. Dead-code removal may already omit build-only callees, as this example's emitted IR does. Separate required values and statement checks retain their existing scope.

options.name: One scoped value block returning a record
options.detail: Complete multi-statement comptime value blocks. Bind one record outside; internal names remain inside. One word computes several outputs and runs the same check without changing scope.
options.technical: Lift E0391 for multi-statement values, using the existing required evaluator, final-value rule and WORD1 storable-value/budget checks. No new name-export or module mechanism. Helpers can remain ordinary or use existing build-only imports.

recommendation.why: A directly groups named required results in every scope and forbids accidental runtime helper use. E is a strong simpler alternative when one record result suffices; binary size is not a demonstrated advantage of A.
recommendation.tradeoff: A standing block now leaks its names, so it reads differently from a block used as a value, which keeps them inside.

whyNot.reason: B preserves local lexical scope but does not group multiple externally readable local results without separate value bindings.
C provides namespace isolation and build-only members, at the cost of qualification and lazy checks for unused modules.
D keeps separate required bindings. WORD1 already removes unnecessary words where opportunistic early evaluation is enough; helpers need not ship.
E preserves lexical scope and groups results with one word, but readers use record fields and it does not add a bare file-level check region.

losses.loss: It amends your 2026-09-30 rule that names stay inside a block.
losses.mitigation: Only standing blocks change; a block used as a value keeps its names, and the cutover renames every collision.

losses.loss: Functions and types in a block cannot be used at run time.
losses.mitigation: E0944 names the item and offers moving it outside the block, where both sides can use it.

decisions.title: jet check and jet build lower every function body; jet run and jet dev lower only what they reach
decisions.situation:
Lowering turns checked code into the compiler's simpler internal form, and that step can find faults of its own. Today jet check never lowers, so it cannot report those faults. jet build lowers the package's own functions, reached or not.

The owner asked for a strict check that finds every error, reached or not. An earlier draft proposed lowering only reached code everywhere. This ballot has check and build lower everything, while run and dev lower only what they reach.
decisions.gist: Should jet check and jet build lower every function, reached or not, so every error shows in one run?
decisions.lesson: Lowering turns checked code into the simpler form the machine-code step reads, and it can find errors of its own. Today jet check never lowers, so it cannot report those errors. This vote decides which commands lower every function and which lower only what the program uses.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. Checking reads source and finds type and name errors. Lowering rewrites each checked function into the compiler's internal form, called IR, and an IR lint checks that form. A reached function is one the program can call from its entry.

A dependency is a package your package uses.
decisions.story: Sam's package has greet and an unused helper with a fault only lowering finds. jet check says ok. Months later a caller reaches the helper, and the build fails in code nobody has touched.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. Which commands lower which function bodies. Every command still checks every declaration, and dead_code still decides what the final program keeps. Where handle layouts come from is D-CORE-LAYOUT1, and either outcome there combines with this one.

Today, re-measured on the t6c compiler (dev 76955986d0) with jet check --trace=FILE on G6Lead's probe s02, a 17-line program that pulls in Core. The trace has no lower, ir.build or ir.lint phase, so jet check cannot report any fault that only lowering finds, in any package.

jet build --trace on the same probe lowers 761 items; lower, IR build and IR lint take about 21 ms of 1,018 ms of CPU, about 2%. G6Lead measured the same shape on the seed: 654 items under both --dead-code=remove and keep, about 12 ms of 467 ms.

So jet build already lowers the entry package's own bodies whether they are reached or not. Unreached Core bodies are pruned by jet_driver_prunable_core_modules in Compiler/JetDriver/Source/Driver/Pipeline.jet, with exclusions for build-time-only and test modules.

What lowering covers under every option. Generic functions are lowered once per concrete type list (JetIR Build.jet:328), so a generic body that nothing instantiates is lowered by no command. Bodies under a false #if target condition are lowered only by jet check --target for that target. A cannot remove either limit; it finds strictly more than C or D.

The cost on Compiler/, the largest package, as G6Lead measured it on the seed. jet check Compiler takes 20.3 s wall, 10.8 s of phase CPU and 5.5 GB peak memory. A dev build lowers 28,955 items; IR build takes about 1.0 to 1.3 s of CPU, and the build peaks at 6.8 GB. So adding lowering and IR lint to jet check Compiler costs about 1.4 s of CPU, about 13%, and about 1.3 GB as built today.

The rule under A. jet check and jet build lower every function body of the packages being checked, the entry package and workspace members, reached or not. They report every lowering and IR lint error together with every other error, collect-all. jet check stops after IR lint: no optimization, no machine code and no link.

Dependencies are lowered by reach in every command, because their own jet check lowered all their bodies when they were published or built. jet run and jet dev lower by reach in every package, which keeps card c0w1wcfc's c17 for the commands where speed matters most.

Engineering away the cost. First, lowering runs in parallel per function, under --threads. Second, each function's IR is linted and then freed before the next, so peak memory grows by the largest function per thread, not by 1.3 GB. Third, lowered bodies are cached by the content of the function and its callees, so a repeated check lowers only what changed.

With the cache, a warm jet check Compiler after a one-function edit lowers that function and its changed callees. The 13% applies only to a cold check with an empty cache, such as a first clone or CI without a cache. None of these three steps exists yet; they are part of building A.

What remains after the engineering. A cold jet check of a very large package pays the parallel lowering time: about 1.4 s of CPU on Compiler/, spread over the compiler threads. jet run and jet dev pay nothing, because they lower by reach.

The same program under each option is the Greeter package: greet is called, and never_called is not. Under A, jet check Greeter lowers both. jet run run.jet lowers greet only. Under C, nothing lowers never_called until something calls it.

Beginner path. jet check is the command that finds everything; jet run starts fast. A fault in an unused helper appears in jet check's list the day it is written, not the day someone calls the helper.

Expert path. --threads bounds lowering's parallelism. A team auditing its dependency tree runs jet check inside each dependency, or uses B's switch if you choose it. --trace shows lower and ir.lint as separate phases with their cost.

Other options. B is A plus one expert switch, jet check --all-deps, which also lowers every dependency body for a full audit. C is the posted draft: reach-based lowering in every command, check included, so a fault is found only once the body is reached. D keeps today's rule: check never lowers, build lowers own bodies, and only eligible Core modules prune.

B adds a flag whose findings belong to other packages' authors, since their own check already lowers those bodies. C reports a fault late and far from where it was written. D leaves jet check unable to report any lowering fault.

decisions.title: #run, #if and #loop replace the comptime word, with every ratified meaning kept
decisions.situation: Your 2026-11-09 review asks that # mark what is for the compiler and that the comptime word go. This ballot changes spelling only. A respells D-COMPTIME-WORD1's word and the forms ratified in D-PREP-SURFACE2, D-PREP-LOCAL1, D-PREP-BRANCH1, D-PREP-FN1, D-COMPTIME-USE1 and D-CONSTGEN2. It reverses the choice in D-PREP-BRANCH1 and D-PREP-FN1 of a word over their # option. It respells the regions of D-COMPTIME-BLOCK1=A without changing their scope. D-META-PHASE1, D-META-LADDER1, D-META-HASH1 and D-BUILD-TIER1 stay as ratified.
decisions.gist: Should #run, #if and #loop replace the comptime word in every form, keeping what each form does?
decisions.lesson: Jet can do work while it compiles: build a table, choose code for one system, or repeat declarations for several types. Today the word comptime asks for that, while # already marks markers, site values and pastes. This vote decides whether those requests use # too.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A request asks the compiler to do something while building. A value region computes one value and gives it back. A standing region is a block whose results stay visible after it, as D-COMPTIME-BLOCK1 ratified.

A declaration modifier changes one declaration, such as the hook that turns a number literal into a Rational. A number parameter is a whole number fixed for each generic copy, such as the 4 in Ring<4>.
decisions.story: Ada already writes #Test, #line and the ratified #phase. When she wants a table built while compiling, she must learn a separate word, comptime, with braces around a single call. She would like one mark for everything the compiler does for her.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. Only how the existing requests are spelled. Each form keeps the meaning its ratified decision gives it: what runs while building, the budget, the effects allowed, and which names it sees. The staging and Call questions belong to D-META-HASH2 and are not decided here.

Today, on seed a0_042. Probe t01 uses a value, a statement region, two branches, a loop of declarations and a literal hook, and prints six lines. Examples/Metaprogramming/Comptime/ComptimeUse shows the build-only import. The tested new spellings are refused: #run reports E0733 as an unknown tag, and #if and #loop report E0003.

Some ratified forms are not built in any spelling yet. A multi-statement value region is E0391 today (t02). A parenthesized region is also E0391 (ms/s03); the attempted function expression gets E0003 and E0391 (ms/s02). These are building gaps, so they count for no option. The ballot specifies every form as ratified, not as the seed limits it.

The three kinds of #run under A. Where #run stands decides its kind, as the ratified comptime forms specify. First, a declaration modifier: #run directly before a declaration's name, as in the literal hook, with D-PREP-FN1's legal sites and purity checks. #run use is D-COMPTIME-USE1's build-only import, in both its forms.

Second, a standing region: #run { } on its own line in a file, module or function body. It follows D-COMPTIME-BLOCK1 to the letter. Its direct immutable results become bindings of the enclosing scope, mutable scratch and nested names stay inside, and file and module helpers are build-only, with E0944 for any escape.

Third, a value region: #run in a value position, meaning the right of a binding, an argument, a list element or an operand. #run { } there has its own scope and gives back its last expression, as D-PREP-SURFACE2 ratified, including blocks with several statements.

The unbraced operand rule. Without braces, #run takes exactly one operand: a name, a literal, a parenthesized expression, or a call, member, index or constructor chain on one. So TABLE: #run build_squares(5) is legal. Anything larger needs braces or parentheses: #run a + b is an error whose fix offers #run { a + b } or (#run a) + b.

How the rule treats each case. f(#run g(1), x) computes only g(1). Postfix ! inside the operand makes a failure a build error, under the existing required-evaluation failure contract. A fallback is binary, so #run { load() ?? DEFAULT } and (#run load()) ?? x are the two spellings, and each says what it means.

Functions and closures. D-COMPTIME-WORD1 says functions are storable, and closures are storable when their captures are. A value region keeps that rule. A lambda expression needs a braced value region. A reference to a standing file/module region's build-only helper still cannot escape, under BLOCK1 and E0944.

Why a misread boundary cannot change a result silently. A value region cannot see runtime locals: probe ms/s01 shows comptime { build(3) + y }, with y a runtime local, reported as E0107. The operand rule makes the boundary visible anyway. A function that branches on #phase still does what D-META-PHASE1 says for each copy.

#if and #loop. #if takes every form comptime if takes: a condition with a block, else, else #if, and the matching table #if x == { arms }. It keeps D-PREP-BRANCH1's checks: the arm not taken gets name checks only. Probe ms/s07 shows an unknown name there reported as E0107, and ms/s05 shows a type error there accepted.

#loop takes the pattern, in and closed list that comptime loop takes, in the same places. D-META-PHASE1 is unchanged: a #phase read reached from an #if condition is refused with a fix to a plain if, which folds per copy and checks every arm.

Number parameters. <N: Int> drops the word. Under D-CONSTGEN2's restriction, a parameter whose right side resolves to the core Int, through aliases and by declaration identity, is a number parameter. A trait on the right, as in <T: Comparable>, is a bound. Any other type is an error that says only Int may be a number parameter.

Defaults, inference, identity and the refusal of runtime arguments stay as D-CONSTGEN2 says. A user type named Int is not the core Int, so it cannot make a number parameter by accident. Hover in the editor names the parameter's kind.

The # family. As D-META-HASH1 ratified: # then a lower-case word is a request or a site value, such as #run, #if, #loop, #line or #phase. # then { is a paste. # then a capital letter is a marker, such as #Test. Inside a fixed-size type such as [Int#N], # keeps its size meaning.

What does not change. Automatic early evaluation of immutable values under D-COMPTIME-WORD1 stays; #run requires early evaluation, as comptime does. D-META-LADDER1's #code, Code insertion and Compiler effects stay, and so does D-META-HASH1's hygiene. D-BUILD-TIER1's defaults stay. D-META-PHASE1 keeps #phase, its cases, its crossing checks and the local-try fallback.

Retiring the word. comptime stops being a keyword and becomes an ordinary name, as prep did. Old code that writes comptime gets one registered retirement error with a checked fix. The fix works on parsed nodes, keeps comments and source locations, and renames by declaration identity, never by text.

What the fix does, form by form. A value comptime { e } becomes #run e only when e is a single operand with no comment inside; otherwise it becomes #run { e }. A standing comptime { } becomes #run { }. comptime if, comptime loop and comptime use become #if, #loop and #run use. comptime before a declaration becomes #run. <comptime N: Int> becomes <N: Int>.

Migration changes spelling, not binding identity. BLOCK1 already requires a checked scope migration preserving every old reference. The spelling fix must compose with that migration; neither step may silently rebind a name.

A parsed migration inventory, including examples, tests, diagnostics and prose, is required in the cutover. No regex total proves the number of safe edits. No jet fix for this respelling exists yet; it is part of building A.

Beginner path. The first build-time value is TABLE: #run make_table(). The first system choice is #if build.target.os == { … }. Errors keep their codes and print the new spelling.

Expert path. Standing regions, multi-statement value regions and number parameters keep every ratified rule; only the word changes. Templates through #loop and D-META-LADDER1's Code keep their positions.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. A reader must know where an unbraced #run ends; the operand rule limits it to one call or name, and anything larger needs braces. A number parameter has no word of its own; the core Int on its right marks it, and hover names it. Both are real reading costs; no reading-cost comparison was measured.

Respelling touches many sites and much prose. The checked fix handles code, and Docs change in the same pass. #run, #if and #loop are three words where comptime was one; all three share the # mark, and #if and #loop match the plain if and loop the reader already knows.

Other options. B keeps the ratified word and its braces. C keeps the word but lets a plain if select arms when its condition is known while building, which changes checking, not only spelling. D marks the one word as #comptime. E uses A's short requests but always braces values and marks number parameters as <#run N: Int>.

Option C in full. A plain if whose condition is known while building selects its arm, like comptime if today. The arm not taken gets name checks only, and its effects leave the effect row. Today a plain if on a constant checks the types of both arms: probe ms/s06 reports a type error in the arm not taken.

So under C, every existing plain if on a constant loses type checks on its other arm. Whether an arm is type-checked then depends on how its condition is computed. C must also exempt #phase. A condition that reads #phase stays D-META-PHASE1's fold, checking every arm per copy, because a phase-dependent selection of source arms is what that decision forbids.

Boundary cases. Prefix operators, including a negative number or logical not, require braces or a parenthesized operand. Calls and their nested arguments belong to the operand. Binary operators outside that operand require grouping around #run when meant to run later. Value-region scope never becomes standing-region scope just because its contents span several lines.

decisions.title: Return memory-allocation failure by default; stop only when the caller explicitly chooses to
decisions.situation: Growing a list sometimes needs more memory, and that request can fail. In the tested compiler, try_push lets the caller handle failure, while plain push cannot be handled that way. Choosing different names throughout a library makes recovery easy to miss. Returning an error preserves the choice to stop without forcing every caller to stop. We recommend one recoverable operation by default, using ordinary error handling for propagation or an explicit stop.
decisions.gist: Should memory requests return ordinary errors by default, with stopping an explicit choice?
decisions.lesson: Recovery means the program gets a chance to decide, not that it can always continue. A server may reject one request; a tiny command may stop. Return the same error in both cases and let the boundary choose.
decisions.explainer: Words used here. An allocation is a request for memory, such as a list growing. AllocError is Core's error for a refused one. A contract is the part of a signature that names the errors a function can fail with. A handler is ?? or an arm table on a call.
decisions.story: Rin appends three numbers. Success prints 3 under every option. If memory is refused, she wants either a normal error or an explicit stop, not behavior selected by whether a handler happens to surround the call.
decisions.inWild: Rust offers try_reserve alongside stopping allocation APIs. Zig makes allocation failure an ordinary error. C++ can throw bad_alloc. These are different policies, not evidence that recovery is free or always successful.
decisions.detail:
Recommendation changes from A to C. Recoverability preserves choices, but it is not always cheaper or useful. Emergency reporting, cleanup and foreign callbacks may be unable to recover. A program that cannot continue can explicitly stop at its error boundary. An external operating-system kill cannot become a returned error.

C gives every potentially allocating operation a stable AllocError route, including implicit text, literal, capture and temporary allocations. Reuse ordinary automatic propagation, not dynamic exceptions. Unannotated functions infer failure; typed domains admit or convert it. Never! must prove or handle failure. The standard conversion into the ordinary report family must not allocate; its current absence is build work.

Stopping is explicit: push(value) ?? panic("no memory") selects one call, or load() ?? panic(...) selects a larger boundary. Strict no-failure code uses Never! and proves or handles failure. No package flag silently changes a callee's contract. A stop is not a proof of infallibility.

Observed on t17a a0.0.43 with jet run -: handled rows.try_push(7) followed by print(rows.len()) prints 1. Handled plain push gets E0405. Unhandled try_push in ordinary run gets E2402 for missing AllocError-to-Err conversion. These prove success and typing, not exhaustion recovery. Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Expressions/Control.jet:911-918 implements ordinary propagation refusal and missing-conversion diagnostics.

Failure guarantees: failed growth leaves the collection unchanged. Never retry evaluated arguments. Clean moved values and partial destinations once. Error return does not undo prior I/O. Error construction, transfer and emergency rendering need bounded nonallocating storage. Cleanup cannot depend on exhausted memory. Forced-failure tests must establish these properties before delivery; successful probes do not.

A's best case is minimal beginner code, but C already has inference and propagation. A changes failure typing with surrounding handlers and needs special optional-return rules. B is sound and explicit over one primitive, not an I8 violation merely because it has two names. E is appropriate where recovery cannot be supported, but cannot reject one server request and continue.

The old dynamic-scope option was removed. Silently making Never! callees fail needs a separate contract change and is unnecessary here.

Adversarial verdict: C holds as a cohesive policy, not a measured cost win. First reduce plumbing through ordinary inference and propagation. Then choose stopping once at the application boundary. Static contracts still widen and real failure paths occupy bytes. Remove proved-impossible branches and measure remaining cost against a reference with the same recovery promise. Migration follows D-LANG-MIGRATE1=A's registered rewrites without retired-name teaching in errors.

decisions.title: Show library promise changes during ordinary checks, and calculate the minimum release version
decisions.situation: A library makes promises to programs that use it. Those promises include what its functions need permission to do, not just their argument types. Adding a clock read inside a greeting function can change that promise without changing its written signature. The probe runs that function successfully; it does not demonstrate an early API-change gate. Choose whether ordinary checks should show such changes and whether publishing should calculate the version. We recommend a generated promise file checked during development, with a calculated minimum release version.
decisions.gist: Should ordinary checks show library promise changes and calculate the minimum release version?
decisions.lesson: An API is the part of a library other programs use. Think of package.api as its generated promise sheet. A source edit can change that sheet. Reviewing the difference makes the change visible before a release surprises users.
decisions.explainer: Words used here. The public surface is everything another package can call or name. A version bump is how a library signals change: major means breaking, minor means added, patch means fixed. An effect is a power like reading the clock.
decisions.story: Ana publishes greeting as 1.0.0, then adds a clock read. Every option runs the same greeting. They differ in when Ana sees the changed promise and who chooses the next version.
decisions.inWild: TypeScript API Extractor generates a committed API report and distinguishes local updates from read-only validation. It makes public changes reviewable, but does not claim that a signature report proves every behavioral promise.
decisions.detail:
A beginner writes ordinary library functions and runs jet check. For a declared library output, A derives package.api from the compiler's existing public API rows. A harmless internal edit changes no rows. An added public function appears as an addition. A newly required clock effect is shown as a breaking promise change, including the path through helpers. Executable-only packages need no promise file merely because functions default to public.

Concrete proposed sequence: start at released 1.0.0; change greeting from a fixed message to a clock-stamped message; jet check shows that greeting now needs Time. A breaking change fails until jet check --accept-api records the new generated baseline. Commit source and package.api together. Later jet registry publish compares fresh checked source against the immutable released 1.0.0 receipt and calculates a minimum of 2.0.0. Accepting the local baseline never resets release history.

For compatible additions, a successful local check updates the generated view with a visible note. jet check --locked is always read-only and refuses missing or stale views. Failed or partial checks never replace the last complete file. Use atomic replacement and one deterministic row order so concurrent checks cannot corrupt the view. The file is generated, not a second authored contract.

Experts can raise the calculated minimum for behavior the rows cannot detect. C has the same early gate but retains deliberate author version selection, with the calculated minimum enforced at publish. This is a real release-planning benefit, not permission to choose an invalid version. The first release uses the declared starting version. Pre-release and supported release-line selection keep their existing version semantics; the calculation compares against the selected released line.

Include public types, names, solved effects, error sets, layout and checked ownership contracts. Adding a publicly exhaustible enum or error case can break callers. A narrower effect is compatible only where actual type and reflection rules prove it. Record compiler/schema identity and supported target/configuration coverage. Publication refuses missing coverage or incomparable old receipts, rather than guessing patch compatibility. Runtime behavior not represented by the rows still needs human review.

Evidence: t17a a0.0.43, jet run - on the clock-stamped greeting, exits 0 and prints a clock-stamped hello. Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/PublicApi.jet:49-79 gathers public functions; its canonical sorter is at 32-44. This source establishes a reusable row mechanism, not that A's commands or file policy already work. Old check-versus-doc timing claims were removed: they do not measure the proposed gate.

Adversarial verdict: A holds for reviewable static promises, not complete compatibility. First remove extra compilation by reusing the check's own rows. Second remove needless manual edits by generating compatible changes and accepting breaking ones explicitly. Comparing rows and checking a target matrix still costs time; measure that cost rather than call it free. An author can still approve a harmful API change, and behavior-only breakage still needs an intentional larger version.

decisions.title: One-liners move under their own verb, jet eval, with every power of today's jet -e
decisions.situation:
Your 2026-11-09 review suggested that one-liners move off the bare jet command and under their own verb, jet eval. Today there are two half-tools. jet -e reads input and accepts semicolons, but refuses a final if. jet eval prints a final if, but reads no input, refuses semicolons and prints () after print.

A amends D-SCRIPT-ONELINER1=A, which ratified one jet -e flag, and reverses D-CLI-FOLD1=A's fold of eval into jet run --eval. The other five folds and D-CLI-ALIAS1=A's one-spelling rule stay. Keeping the ratified forms is option B.
decisions.gist: Should one-liners run as jet eval 'code', one verb with every power of today's jet -e, retiring jet -e?
decisions.lesson: A one-liner is a short program typed straight into the terminal, such as counting the lines of a file. Today Jet has two ways to run one, and each lacks something the other has. This vote decides whether one verb, jet eval, does all of it.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A verb is the word after jet, such as run or check. A flag is an option that starts with a dash, such as -e. Standard input, or stdin, is text piped into a command.

The final value is what the last line of the code works out to, which a one-liner prints for you.
decisions.story: Ada pipes a log into jet eval to count its lines, and gets 0. She switches to jet -e, which counts 2, then adds an if at the end and gets an error. The help for each says nothing about the other.
decisions.inWild:
# Perl, Ruby and Node: one flag on the main command.
perl -ne 'print if /error/' app.log
node -e 'console.log(1 + 2)'

# Deno: its own verb.
deno eval 'console.log(1 + 2)'
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. The command that runs code typed on the command line, and what that command can do. The Core names a one-liner uses, such as input, words() and input.csv(T), stay as D-SCRIPT-ONELINER1 ratified them.

Today, on seed a0_042, jet -e. Piping two lines into jet -e 'input.to_list().len()' prints 2. jet -e 'x := 2; x += 1; x * 10' prints 30. jet -e 'if 1 > 0 -> "yes" else -> "no"' is E0003, because the code becomes a run body where a bare if value is not a statement. jet run -e works the same way.

Today, jet eval. It exists, and its help says Evaluate pure Jet and print the value. jet eval '1 + 2' prints 3, the map example prints [2, 4, 6] on one line, and the final if prints "yes" with quotes. --json prints a jet.status/v1 object with the value, and jet eval hello.jet runs the file.

Its gaps: the same piped input gives 0, because eval reads no stdin. The semicolon form is E0373. jet eval 'print("hi")' prints hi and then (), and --pure does not refuse print. In both commands, core.files and other Core modules are E0107 without a use line, which a one-liner has no room for.

Other spellings today. jet run - reads a program from stdin and works. jet hello.jet runs a file. jet '1 + 2' and jet print are E2101 UnknownCommand with exit code 2, so the bare command never ran code.

The rule under A. jet eval 'code' is the one way to run a one-liner. The code is the body of a run function, checked like a file, with the files and arguments after it. input is the lines of those files or of stdin, as D-SCRIPT-ONELINER1 says.

What jet eval gains over both commands today. Semicolons separate statements, as jet -e allows. A final expression of any kind, an if or a match included, is the final value, as jet eval allows. A unit final value prints nothing, so print never adds (). Core modules resolve by full name, core.files, with no use line.

Printing the final value. A list or a stream prints one item per line, and a string prints without quotes, as D-SCRIPT-ONELINER1 ratified and jet -e does today (probe cli3). So the map example prints 2, 4 and 6 on three lines. --json prints today's jet.status/v1 object with the value.

Effects and --pure. jet eval has jet run's default authority and flags, -A, --allow and --deny, so a one-liner may read and write files and says so in its effects note. --pure refuses any effect, print included, with the effect named. jet eval file.jet stays a short form of jet run file.jet.

What is retired. jet -e and jet run -e become teaching errors in D-CLI-ALIAS1's retired-spelling table, each naming jet eval with the same code. jet run - stays, because it reads a whole program, not a one-liner. D-CLI-FOLD1's jet run --eval is never built.

Migration, counted over the seed's git-tracked files. jet -e is mentioned 94 times in 28 files, jet eval 197 times in 54 files, and jet run - 36 times. The retired forms print the new spelling, and docs and tests move in one cutover with no alias period, as D-CLI-ALIAS1 requires.

Beginner path. Type jet eval and the code. It prints the answer, reads whatever is piped in, and says which effects it used. jet help eval lists input, words() and the other one-liner names.

Expert path. jet eval --json returns the value as structured data for scripts. --pure checks that a snippet touches nothing. --allow and --deny bound what a pasted one-liner may do, with the same flags as jet run.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. jet eval is five letters longer to type than jet -e. A shell alias covers that for heavy users, and the verb is listed in jet help, where a flag on the bare command is not.

People and scripts that type jet -e meet a teaching error. It prints the jet eval form of the same command, and the docs that teach jet -e change in the same cutover.

Other options. B keeps the ratified forms: jet -e on the bare command, plus D-CLI-FOLD1's jet run --eval once built. C is jet run -e only, the Perl, Ruby and Node style of a flag on the run command. D keeps two tools: jet eval for expressions and jet run -e for statements and input.

B and C put a one-liner behind a flag that jet help does not show as a command. D keeps the split that made Ada switch tools, with two sets of rules to remember.
