decisions.title: A typed collection head takes a loop and builds that collection directly: Set<String>{loop …}, [String:Int]{loop … -> k: v}
decisions.situation:
A loop with an arrow builds a list, such as loop w in words -> w.len(). The ratified rule says a loop always gives a list. A set then goes through a conversion, and a map is filled by a second loop.

The review asked for a loop that builds a set or a map directly. This ballot lets the type written before braces take a loop. A bare loop stays a list; keeping today's rule is option B.
decisions.gist: Should a typed collection head take a loop, so Set<String>{loop …} and [String:Int]{loop … -> k: v} build directly?
decisions.lesson: A loop with an arrow builds a list of its results. Sometimes you want a set, which drops repeats, or a map from keys to values. Today that takes a conversion or a second loop. This vote decides whether the loop can build them directly.
decisions.explainer: Words used here. A comprehension is a loop that gives a collection. A typed head is the type written before braces, as in [Int]{1, 2}. A set holds each value once; a map pairs keys with values.
decisions.story: Mae counts distinct words in a log. In Python she writes {w for w in words}. In Jet today she writes Set.from around the loop, and for a map she writes an empty map and a second loop. Under A she writes the type and the loop.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. Whether a loop can build a set or a map in one expression, and how it is spelled. A bare loop with -> stays a list.

Today, on the t6c compiler (dev 76955986d0). Probe c02 does it the ratified way. A loop gives the list [5, 3, 5, 3], Set.from around a loop gives 3 items, and a second loop fills a map of 3 keys. Probe c05 already accepts a typed list head, [Int]{loop … -> w.len()}.

Probe c04 writes Set<String>{loop w in words -> w}. It parses, and fails E0108: this needs Set<String>, but the value is [String]. Probe c01 adds [String:Int]{loop w in words -> w: w.len()}, which gets E0107 because key: value is not a loop body.

Probe c06 shows a terminal: (loop …).to_set() runs and gives 3. to_map does not exist, E0311.

The rule under A. A typed collection head may hold one loop in place of its items. The loop's results go into that collection in loop order, through the FromIterator protocol of D-ITER-COLLECT1=A, so any user collection works the same way.

A map's loop body yields key: value, the map literal's own item form. The key is an expression, as it is in a map literal today: probe c07 writes [String: Int]{w: 5} with w bound to apple and prints [apple]. A later key replaces an earlier one, as the map assignment loop in c02 does.

User collections. A struct literal's braces hold name: value fields and never start with loop, so Bag<String>{loop …} cannot be misread as a struct literal. The head is a collection head exactly when the type implements FromIterator.

What stays. A bare loop still gives a list and still ignores the expected type, so D-COMPREHENSION1's rule that context never changes a loop's result holds. The head is written on the same line, so a reader always sees the destination.

Census on dev, comment lines included. 1,057 lines in 301 Jet files bind or pass a loop with ->, all unchanged. Set.from around a loop appears 3 times and .to_set() 7 times, which jet fix may rewrite to a head; Map.from appears nowhere. No file writes a loop inside a typed head today.

Beginner path. A loop gives a list; write Set<String>{…} around it for a set. Expert path. Any collection that implements FromIterator takes a loop in its head, with no extra method.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. A typed head now holds either items or one loop. Mixing them, as [Int]{0, loop …}, is a build error with a fix to concatenate, so a head is never half literal and half loop.

A map loop that repeats a key keeps the last value without a word. That matches map assignment and Python. A program that must refuse repeats uses a loop with an explicit check.

Other options. B keeps today's rule. C is Rust's collect, naming the destination after the loop. D is Python's: braces around a loop make a set, and key: value makes a map. E is Kotlin's to_set and to_map terminals.

Their best cases. B adds nothing. C works for any destination. D is shortest. E is a plain method. Their costs: B needs a second loop for maps. C puts the type last. D collides with Jet's block braces. E needs pair values and a to_ method per collection.

decisions.title: Core loads a trait implementation only when a program reaches both its type and its trait, and Core's modules sit in checked layers
decisions.situation:
On seed a0_042, a five-line program that imports core.tasks makes jet check load 62 Core source files: 3.2 MB and 47,088 lines from 12 Core areas. It peaks at 277 MB and takes about a second. With no import, the same check takes 10 ms and 28 MB.

The chain runs through trait implementations: Time's decode implementation names core.encoding, which names core.files, which names system, process, testing and mem. Your review proposed two rules to cut it.
decisions.gist: Should Core load an implementation only when both its type and its trait are used, and keep its modules in checked layers?
decisions.lesson: A program that uses one small part of Jet's core library today pulls in most of the rest. Each part's extras point at other parts. This vote decides two rules: extras load only when used, and lower parts may not lean on higher ones.
decisions.explainer: Words used here. Core is Jet's built-in library. A trait is a promise of methods, like Decode. An implementation keeps that promise for one type. A layer is a group of Core modules that may use only lower groups.
decisions.story: Kim's script imports core.tasks to run two jobs at once. Its check takes a second and loads file, crypto and encoding code she never calls. Under A the decode chain to those modules stays unloaded.
decisions.inWild:
// Go keeps its standard library layered with a test, go/build/deps_test.go:
// "unicode/utf8 < strconv < fmt < os" and so on; a forbidden import fails the build.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. Two rules for Core. They change what loads and which imports Core may write; no public API changes.

Today, on seed a0_042. Probe c01 imports core.tasks and starts one task. Its jet check trace shows 62 Core source files from 12 areas: Tasks, Text, Math, Prelude, Time, Encoding, Files, Process, Sys, Testing, Mem and Crypto.

That is 3.2 MB of source, 277 MB at peak and about a second, on a warm second run too. Probe c02, with no import, loads none and checks in 10 ms at 28 MB.

The chain. Time.jet line 1723 is ZonedDateTime's decode implementation, and it names core.encoding. Math.jet line 15423 does the same for Decimal. Encoding's Cbor.jet imports core.files, and Files names sys, process, testing and mem.

Rule 1, the reach rule. The implementation of a trait for a type is loaded and checked for a program only when the program reaches both the type and the trait. Reaching means naming or calling it, directly or through something else reached.

A generic function that requires the trait reaches it. The implementation stays where it is written, beside its type. Under rule 1, c01 names no decode trait. Unless something it calls does, Time's decode implementation and the encoding chain stay unloaded.

Rule 2, layers. Every Core area sits in one of four layers. Layer 0 is the prelude, with mem, rt, reflect, meta and sync. Layer 1 is data: text, math, collections, time, encoding, regex, units, data, compute, crypto, log and event.

Layer 2 is system: sys, files, net, process, tasks, term, watcher, args, perf, testing, plugin, mod, archive, font and vendor. Layer 3 is services: http, db, ui, web, app, auth, service, jobs, game, reactive, tui, devtools, build and compiler.

A module may name its own layer or a lower one. The table lives in Core's package.jet, and jet check on Core reports each upward name as a registered error, with the file, line and the two layers.

Census on the seed, Core .jet files, comment lines skipped. Under that table, Core has 78 upward references in 16 files across 13 area pairs. Crypto naming files is 31 of them and encoding naming files is 27.

Most upward references are file adapters, such as encoding to or from a file. They move up to the files module, which implements the encoding stream trait for its own reader and writer. Rule 1 then loads them only for programs that use both.

Files names core.testing for the fault hooks of D-TESTFAULT1=A. Those hooks move down into the prelude layer, beside the effect carrier they guard.

Ratified decisions. D-BUILD-COREUNIT1=A checks Core whole once per compiler and target, and a warm run reads back only what its program needs. Rule 1 is what makes that read-back small, so the two fit. D-EFF-CORE-INIT1=A already makes a Core import start nothing.

Beginner path. Nothing to learn: imports work as today, and small programs check faster. Expert path. A Core author sees the layer error when a lower module names a higher one, and jet inspect structure with --core shows what a program loaded and why.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. The 78 upward references must move before the check turns on. The check lists every one in a single run, and most are file adapters that move as a group.

What remains. A Core author must place a new module in a layer, and some helpers end up one layer lower than their natural home. The table is one reviewed list in package.jet.

Other options. B keeps today's ball and relies on D-BUILD-COREUNIT1=A's cache. C adopts the reach rule only. D adopts the layers only. E splits Core into separate packages with declared dependencies, as Rust's core, alloc and std do.

Their best cases. B costs nothing now. C gets most of the load cut with no moves. D gets an enforced shape with no loader change. E makes each dependency a package fact. Their costs: B keeps every program reading the ball; C lets the cycles regrow; D still loads unused implementations; E reverses D-BUILD-COREUNIT1=A.

decisions.title: Runtime carriers are ordinary declarations, and the compiler's handle table goes
decisions.situation:
Some Core types hold an object the runtime made, such as an open file. Today a compiler table, RuntimeHandles.jet, says how each one copies, compares and prints, found by bare name or a Core path prefix. Card c0w1wcfc's c18 requires that BuildTypes.jet have no such Core prefix test.

D-HOST-LEAF1=E made the runtime an ordinary library. This ballot decides where a carrier's facts come from. It amends the registry clause of D-PRIVATE-NATIVE-CARRIER1=A; keeping the table is options B and D.
decisions.gist: Should a Core carrier's copy, equality and text come from its own declaration, so the compiler's handle table can go?
decisions.lesson: Some Core types hold something the runtime made, such as an open file. The compiler must know whether such a value copies, compares and prints. This vote decides whether that knowledge lives in the type's own declaration, under rules every package uses, or in a hidden compiler table.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A carrier is a Core type whose value holds a runtime object, such as an open file. A row is one entry in the compiler's table. A derive is a power Jet gives a type from its fields, such as ==.

A refusal mark, such as #!Equatable, turns a derive off for one type.
decisions.story: Sam names his own type Reader. Today the compiler's table has a bare row named Reader, and only a later check keeps it from Sam's type. Under A no table exists: Sam's Reader has his fields and nothing else.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. Where a carrier's copy, cleanup, equality and text come from. Lowering is D-CORE-LOWER1; the runtime boundary itself is D-HOST-LEAF1=E, unchanged.

Today, on seed a0_042. RuntimeHandles.jet has 470 rows naming 364 distinct runtime objects. 184 rows are keyed by a Core path, 12 by a double-underscore name, and the other 274 by a bare name, mostly second keys for the same type.

Probe y07 is the same program in today's form. It prints stdin copies compare true, entries compare false, the DirEntry text, and user reader 3 true. The StdinHandle row says it neither copies nor compares, yet the program does both: Core's declaration wins. The table and the declaration already disagree.

Every capability already has an ordinary form, shown by probes on the seed. Probe y01 copies a struct with private fields and gets an independent copy, and prints a record as Entry { name: n, path: a/n, is_dir: false }. Probe y02 refuses == with #!Equatable, E0312. Probe y06 refuses default text with #!Printable, E0915.

Probe y04 gives a handle a Close impl, moves it, and closes it once, after moved. #!Debug refuses the debug text. #!Copyable is ratified by D-GENERIC-CLOSE-COPY1 but not built: probe y03 gets E0931.

The rule under A. A carrier is an ordinary struct, in Core or in jet_runtime, and its declaration is the only source of its facts. The compiler reads no table and tests no name or prefix, so c18 is met. A user type named Reader is its own declaration and gets only its own fields.

Copying. A carrier whose state is plain Jet fields copies them, so each copy has its own cursor, as today's clone routines do by copying bytes and position. Under D-COPY-DEFAULT1 that copy is made on first write, which is cheaper than today's eager clone.

Sharing and owning. A carrier that shares one runtime object holds it in Shared, which closes it once when the last holder goes. A carrier that owns a descriptor holds a jet_runtime handle type with a Close impl. A struct with a Close part is not copyable, so the one-owner rule follows from the field.

That closes the copying hole a raw number would open. A descriptor is never a bare Int in a copyable struct: it lives in a typed handle with Close, so a copy cannot alias it. A carrier with no cleanup that must still have one owner uses #!Copyable.

Equality and text. A row with eq false becomes #!Equatable. show false becomes #!Printable, and debug false becomes #!Debug. display true becomes an impl Display. The table's 12 distinct capability combinations all map to these marks, one to one.

Privacy and identity. D-PRIVATE-NATIVE-CARRIER1's opacity stays: a priv field cannot be read or forged outside its module, E0605. Its registry clause goes. Layout and version come from jet_runtime's precompiled interface, as for any dependency, and the toolchain pins that version.

Every tier and build time. The same declarations run in the interpreter, the JIT, native builds and build-time evaluation, because HOST-LEAF1 uses one runtime library. A carrier still cannot be stored in a build-time constant; that refusal, E0956, stays.

Delivery proof, part of building A. For each of the 364 runtime objects, a test pins independent copy or sharing, close count on every exit, equality and text, on o0, o1, o2 and at build time. A row is deleted only when its test passes against the declaration.

Beginner path. Nothing to learn: Core's types copy, compare and print as their declarations say, and hover shows it. Expert path. Write a carrier in your own package with the same fields, handles and refusal marks Core uses, and get the same facts.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. The cutover touches 364 runtime objects. A generator writes each declaration's marks from its row once, since the combinations map one to one. The bare-name rows are second keys and need no type of their own.

What remains. Carriers whose state lives in raw allocations today must move that state into Jet fields or a typed handle, which is porting work per object. #!Copyable must be built before the one-owner carriers without cleanup can move.

Other options. B keeps the table but keys each row by exact declaration, so no name or prefix test remains. C imports C handle types with a new #Handle marker. D keeps today's table and tests, and revises c18. E puts a #Runtime marker on each declaration, which any package may use, and takes the other facts from derives.

Their best cases. B is the smallest change and keeps every clone routine. C lets any package bind a C handle directly. D needs no work. E keeps the runtime routines while removing the table. B and D keep a second source of truth, the disagreement y07 shows.

options.detail: Each carrier is an ordinary struct. Copying, cleanup, equality and text follow from its fields, Close and refusal marks. The table and every name and prefix test go.
options.technical: Amends D-PRIVATE-NATIVE-CARRIER1=A's registry clause; keeps its E0605 opacity. Descriptors live in jet_runtime handle types with Close; shared objects in Shared. Row flags map to #!Equatable, #!Printable, #!Debug, #!Copyable and impl Display. Layout from the runtime's precompiled interface per HOST-LEAF1. Per-object tests gate each row's deletion.

options.technical: No change. c18 is revised. Rows and declarations can disagree; the declaration wins where BuildTypes.jet keeps the source shape.

decisions.title: One migration block is the only description of a type's history, used for stored data, messages, live reload, database rows and service handoff
decisions.situation:
Jet's migration block already moves old stored data: on seed a0_042, decoding old JSON with name gives display_name. D-LIVE-PERSIST1=A runs the same steps on live state. Two ratified designs describe their own step: D-DB-SCHEMA1=A's declared step for tables and D-SERVICE-UPGRADE1=D's typed migrate function.

decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. Whether D-DB-SCHEMA1=A's declared step and D-SERVICE-UPGRADE1=D's migrate function are both the migration block. Disk, wire and live state already share it.

Today, on seed a0_042. Probe d01 declares UserRecord with migration rename name -> display_name. It decodes old JSON with a name field and prints user: Ana, age: 30. That is D-MIGRATE4=A's chain in decode.

Census on the seed. 15 files hold a migration block. No Examples file uses #Table, and no Jet source names ForwardOnly or DualWrite. So the database and service halves are not built.

What must exist first. D-DB-SCHEMA1=A's #Table records and D-SERVICE-UPGRADE1=D's generation handoff. A decides only what they read when they are built.

What A does for tables. A #Table record that is also #PublishedSchema takes its schema steps from its migration block. A rename becomes a column rename and an added field with a default becomes a column with that default.

A removal drops the column, and a change via a converter rewrites each row. D-DB-SCHEMA1=A's derived migration is printed from the block and still reviewed.

What A does for services. D-SERVICE-UPGRADE1=D's migrate function is generated from the block, and each step gets that decision's class. A rename or an added field with a default is Reversible, with its inverse generated.

A removal, or a change with only a forward converter, is ForwardOnly. A change becomes Reversible when the block also writes a back converter, for example change score: Int -> MemberRank via { .. } back { .. }.

Ratified decisions. A keeps D-MIGRATE1 to D-MIGRATE4, D-LIVE-PERSIST1=A, D-BOUND-EVOLVE1=A and D-SELFVER1=A. It fills in D-DB-SCHEMA1=A's declared step and D-SERVICE-UPGRADE1=D's migrate function without changing their outcomes. The back converter is a new clause of the block.

Beginner path. A beginner writes one migration line and every place follows. Expert path. jet inspect schema status, which exists today for saved schema versions, would also list tables and services, and the back converter turns a forward-only step into a reversible one.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. A table or service may need a step the block cannot say, such as a backfill from another table. Such steps stay ordinary code that D-DB-SCHEMA1=A already allows, listed after the block's steps.

What remains. The block gains one clause, back, used only when a team wants rollback.

Other options. B lets each place keep its own step, as ratified today. C shares the block for tables but keeps the service's own migrate function. D replaces the block with ordinary conversion functions between versioned types.

Their best cases. B lets each design pick its best form. C covers the common database case with no service coupling. D needs no special syntax. Their costs: B writes one rename up to three times. C still writes it twice for services. D reverses the ratified migration block and makes every old version a type to keep.

decisions.title: Effect arguments name a scope, such as a folder, a host or a device, with one covers rule from Core's scope types
decisions.situation:
Ratified D-DECL-TYPES1=A makes an effect a struct whose fields carry constant data, matched by equality. In installment 3 Main proposed one covers rule, so rows, grants and denials share one spelling, such as FS.Read("templates/"). That question is still open with you.

BallotReview3 marked the posted draft NOT CLEAN: an arbitrary covers function has no sound laws, and memory budgets are not scopes. This ballot keeps arguments to scopes and leaves budgets as they are. Keeping equality only is option E.
decisions.gist: Should effect arguments name scopes, a folder, a host or a device, with one covers rule for rows, grants and denials?
decisions.lesson: An effect says what a function may do, such as read files. Today it cannot say which files. An argument narrows it: reading templates/ only. This vote decides whether those arguments are allowed, how a wide permission covers a narrow need, and where the check happens.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A row is the effect list on a function, written -[FS.Read]>. A grant, in package.jet, says what a dependency may do. A denial is a ! entry that forbids an effect.

A scope is what an argument names: a folder, a host or a device. Covers means a wider scope includes a narrower one, as templates/ includes templates/home.html.
decisions.story: Sam adds a template library to a shop. It should read only the templates folder and call only api.example.com. Today Sam can grant it all files and all network, or pass a flag on every run.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. Whether effect arguments may name scopes, how coverage between scopes is defined, and how rows, grants and denials use them. Memory and copy budgets, such as !Mem.Alloc(above: 64), are not scopes; they keep today's aggregate rule, unchanged by every option.

Today, on seed a0_042, re-running G6Lead's probes. e01's !Mem.Alloc(above: N) row runs and prints 1. e04's bare FS.Read row reads logo. e03's FS.Read("assets/") row, e07's !Net("api.example.com") denial and e08's !Mem.Copy(above: 64) give Expected , between effects in the row. e02's constant struct effect, ratified by DECL-TYPES1, fails the same way.

Scoping today is per run and per process. e09 reads logo and secret normally. With jet run --allow=FS.Read:assets it prints logo, then refused. That comes from CLI/Authority.jet and a Linux Landlock rule installed at launch, for the whole process, not per dependency.

Why budgets stay out. BallotReview3's memory probes show a budget adds up: one 40-byte reservation passes !Mem.Alloc(above: 64), and two give E0921. A covers rule treats a repeated need as one, so it would lose the second 40. Budgets therefore keep their own summing rule in Effects/Checks.jet.

The rule under A, part 1: scope types. Core defines three scope kinds, each with fixed laws. fs.Path covers by whole path components after normalization, so templates/ covers templates/home.html but not templates2/. net.Host covers by exact match after lower-casing and IDNA, so api.example.com never covers evilapi.example.com. Every other field covers by equality, as DECL-TYPES1 already says.

Part 2: one covers rule. An effect instance covers another of the same type when every field covers the matching field. A bare type, FS.Read with no argument, covers every instance. Because each field law is fixed by Core, coverage is reflexive, transitive and always terminates; no library code runs to decide it.

Part 3: library effects. A library declares its own effect as a struct whose fields use these scope types, such as Bucket: struct { name: String } with impl Effect. It gets the same covers rule with no extra code. Device arguments use HOST-CAPS1's hardware kinds, so GPU(acme_npu.Kind) names a library-declared kind; the provider work stays ACCEL-LIB1's.

Part 4: rows. A function's row is inferred from what it calls, and arguments come from constant values in the calls. files.read("templates/{name}.html") infers FS.Read("templates/"), its longest constant prefix. A path known only at run time infers bare FS.Read. Core's file and network functions publish which parameter names the scope, and libraries may publish the same.

Part 5: grants. A dependency's inferred row must be covered by its grant in package.jet, checked at build time. A bare need under a narrow grant is allowed only through mediated calls. The file or network function checks the actual path or host against the grant when it runs, and refuses the rest with an error value.

Part 6: denials. A need covered by a denial is a build error. A need that only overlaps one, such as reading all of assets/ with assets/secret/ denied, builds, and the mediated call refuses the denied part at run time. A need disjoint from the denial is unaffected.

Who is checked at run time. A callback runs with the authority of the package that wrote it. A task started by a dependency inherits that dependency's grant. Foreign code and subprocesses are not mediated, so a dependency that uses them needs the FFI or process grant, which covers everything; package.jet shows that.

Engineering away the downsides. The unsound covers function is gone: coverage comes from three fixed laws. The host-suffix attack is gone: hosts match exactly. Budgets keep their summing rule. Inference costs nothing extra to write, because arguments come from constants already in the calls.

What remains. Run-time mediation adds one check per mediated file or network call, only in a dependency whose grant is narrower than its row. Its cost is not measured; the mitigation is that a dependency whose row is statically covered pays nothing.

Census over Core, Compiler, Jetpack, Tools, Examples and tests. Argued rows in Jet source today are memory budgets, such as !Mem.Alloc(above: N) in 13 rows, and Fail with an error type. No program writes a scoped FS or Net row, so no program changes meaning; grants with arguments are new.

The same program under every option is templ, a library that reads templates/ and calls api.example.com, and a shop that grants it exactly that. Each option shows templ's row.

Beginner path. Write no rows at all: they are inferred, and jet check shows what each dependency may do, folder and host included. Expert path. Write a scope in a grant or a denial, or declare a library effect whose fields use fs.Path or net.Host.

Other options. B allows arguments only in grants and denials, never in rows, checked only at run time, as Deno does. C keeps today's form: arguments only on memory budgets, and scoping by a run flag. D lets each effect define its own covers function in ordinary code. E keeps DECL-TYPES1 as ratified: constant arguments matched by equality only.

B gives up build-time checking of what a dependency may do. C cannot name a folder in a grant. D runs library code to decide coverage, which has no guaranteed laws and may not terminate. E cannot say that templates/ covers templates/home.html, so every file would need its own grant.

decisions.title: Compiler packages read the toolchain's Core sources while building, through a toolchain: path prefix allowed only inside the toolchain tree
decisions.situation:
Jet's compiler needs facts from its own core library's source files, such as the list of effects. Today a script copies those facts into nine compiler files, about 1.2 MB, each stamped with a checksum. Every core edit means running the script again, and 509 commits since October touched those copies.

The compiler cannot read the core files itself while it is built. A build-time file read must name a path below the reading file, and the core library sits beside the compiler, not below it.

We recommend A: a toolchain: prefix names a file from the top of the Jet source tree, and only packages inside that tree may use it. Every other package keeps today's rule.
decisions.gist: Should compiler packages embed the toolchain's Core sources through a toolchain: path prefix allowed only inside the toolchain tree?
decisions.lesson: Jet's compiler needs facts from its own core library's source files. Today a script copies those facts into compiler files, and every core edit means running it again. This vote decides how the compiler can read those files directly while it is built.
decisions.explainer: Words used here. embed_file reads a file while building and makes its text a constant. The toolchain tree is the directory holding Core/ and Compiler/Prelude/. A generated file is one a script writes.
decisions.story: Ivy adds an effect to Effects.jet. Under A, the next compiler build reads the file itself. No regenerate step, no SHA header to refresh, no stale table.
decisions.inWild:
// Rust reaches files above the crate with a path macro:
include_str!(concat!(env!("CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR"), "/../core/effects.rs"))
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. How a compiler package names a toolchain source at build time. The embed rules of D-CTIO1 and D-CTFIND1 otherwise stay.

Scope, measured on dev c460ba91e5. The generator Tools/agent/CoreSourceRows.jet writes twelve files (CoreSourceRows.jet:2908-2921). Nine are derived tables in compiler and Jetpack packages: 1,240,667 bytes, touched by 509 commits since 2026-10-01. The earlier draft counted only five of them, 279,898 bytes. CoreCallRows.jet alone is 895,709 bytes.

What stays generated under every option. Core/EmbeddedSources.jet, the in-place rows of Core/Compiler/Lang.jet and Compiler/Prelude/Core.jet, and one section of the core-library reference. They are Core or docs, not compiler tables.

Probes with the a0.0.43 compiler. A file beside the reader embeds. A path with .. is E0957 even inside one package, by design. The spellings core: and toolchain: are both E0955 today: A is not built. The ratified #run spelling is E0733, so the code shown uses today's comptime { } block.

Cost, measured. Embedding a 279 KB copy of Core.jet and counting its 116 module rows at build time adds 44 ms and 21 MB to a cold check. A cached check takes about 1 ms more. The whole generator takes 3.09 s and 414 MB today.

Staleness, measured. A cached build notices an edit to the embedded file: the count went 116, then 117 after one added row, then 116 after the revert. The driver records each read's SHA-256 (JetDriver ComptimeInputs.jet:54-57) and the cache keys on it.

A defect found. The spec says every embed records its SHA-256 in .jet/lock (spec.md:539). On a0.0.43 a package that embeds a file builds and runs, and no .jet/lock is written. A's first build criterion is that lock record.

What A does. embed_file and find accept a toolchain: prefix, as in embed_file("toolchain:Compiler/Prelude/Effects.jet"). The rest is a literal path from the toolchain root, with no .. and no absolute form, so E0957's rules still apply after the prefix.

Resolution. The prefix reads the tree the compile already takes Core from: JET_TOOLCHAIN_ROOT, else the nearest directory above the input that holds Core/ and Compiler/Prelude/ (Request.jet:300). So the tables always describe the Core the new compiler is compiled against. There is no built-in-copy fallback, so the jet binary does not grow.

The gate. The prefix is allowed only in a package whose directory lies inside that tree. Anywhere else it is a new registered error, so Core's file layout never becomes a public interface. When JET_TOOLCHAIN_ROOT names a different tree, the error names both directories.

Derived rows. A pure copy, such as the effect source, is an embed and runs no code. Row tables are computed by a function over the embedded text, in the package that needs them. The generator keeps only its four non-compiler outputs.

Ratified decisions. A keeps D-CTFIND1 and D-CTFIND2 and adds no ambient name, so D-PRELUDE-LAW1 holds. It fits D-BUILD-COREUNIT1=A: Core stays one compiler-known unit. It amends D-CTIO1 by one sentence: for a package inside the toolchain tree, the project is that tree. The compiler workspace already treats it so, naming ../Examples and ../tests in Compiler/package.jet:43-47.

Peers. Go's embed refuses .. and files outside the module; Zig refuses an embed outside the package path. Rust's include_str! reads any relative path. Go's own compiler keeps a checked-in generated builtin.go, which is D at scale.

Beginner path. Nothing changes; ordinary packages never see the prefix. Expert path. A compiler author embeds the source and derives rows in Jet, with no generator step.

Other options. B adds one workspace grant in Compiler/package.jet, toolchain_reads, listing globs; members inherit it. C gives Core a package.jet and makes it a path dependency. D keeps today's generated files. B still needs A's location check, or any package could write the grant.

decisions.title: A function's error contract is written String ! ParseError
decisions.situation:
A function that can fail with a named error writes it after the result with a trailing mark: -> String ParseError!. That is the only place in the grammar where two types sit side by side joined by a space. Your review proposed String ! ParseError.

The suffix form was ratified as D-TYPE-SUFFIX1=A; A amends its error half and keeps its optional half. Keeping today's form is option B. D-SIG-ARROW1's unit form follows whichever wins.
decisions.gist: Should a function's error contract be written String ! ParseError instead of String ParseError!?
decisions.lesson: A function that can fail says which error it fails with. Today that is written after the result type with a trailing mark, so two type names sit side by side. This vote picks how the result and its error are joined.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A contract is the part of a signature that says which errors a function can fail with. A union, such as DBError | TimeoutError, means either one.

Writing no contract means the default error, Err; most code never writes one.
decisions.story: Ben reads -> String ParseError! and asks whether ParseError is a second result. Under A he reads -> String ! ParseError: a String, or a ParseError. The mark sits between the two, so the eye splits them without counting spaces.
decisions.inWild:
// Zig: an error union joins the error set and the payload with !.
fn parseDigits(text: []const u8) ParseError![]const u8 { ... }
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. How a signature joins its result and its named error. The default contract stays unwritten, and which errors exist and how they convert is unchanged.

Today, on seed a0_042. Probe e01 writes -> String ParseError! and prints 42 then bad. Probe e03 writes a union, -> String (DBError | TimeoutError)!, and prints row 3 then failed. Probe e04 writes a failing unit function as save: fn(n: Int) SaveError! and prints saved 5 then full.

Probe e02 writes -> String ! ParseError and gets E0003, whose fix text talks about a unit-fallible signature. Probe e05 shows ! already beside a contract in three roles: !strict, !=, and the -[!Panic]> denial, and prints true.

The rule under A. A contract is written after the result as ! and the error: -> String ! ParseError. The mark has a space on each side, and the formatter keeps it. It binds looser than |, so a union needs no parentheses: -> String ! DBError | TimeoutError.

A failing unit function writes nothing before the mark: -> ! SaveError, read as returns nothing, or fails with SaveError. With an effect row it is -[FS.Write]> ! SaveError. The default stays unwritten, and Err pins it: -> Int ! Err. A function that cannot fail writes -> Int ! Never.

Function types use the same form: fn(String) -> Int ! ParseError. A contract is still only legal in a signature, never in a field or a generic argument, as D-TYPE-SUFFIX1 ruled. Optional results keep their suffix: -> Entry? ! DBError.

Why the reading stays clear. In type position ! has no other meaning. Not is a value operator, != is its own token, and a denial sits inside -[ ]> with no space after !. A spaced ! between a type and an error can only be a contract, so the parser needs no lookahead.

The mark is the same one the error wore before, moved between the two names. A reader who knows Err! reads ! ParseError at once.

What A removes. The two-types-by-a-space form goes. So does D-TYPE-SUFFIX1's rule that A | B! must be written (A | B)!, since ! now binds loosest. E0003's misleading text for e02 becomes a retirement error for the old form, with a fix that rewrites it.

Census on the seed. Signature lines with a contract, comments skipped, in Core, Compiler, Jetpack, Tools, Examples and tests: 39,940. Of these, 29,920 write Never!, 9,371 a named error, 564 Err! and 85 a union; 7,031 put the error first. Contract lines in Examples are a small share; the bulk is generated Core and Compiler signatures.

Migration. jet fix rewrites every contract from the parse tree, not from text, in the same cut as D-SIG-ARROW1's reorder. One tool pass covers both. Grammars, highlighting, the spec and snapshots move in that cut too.

Beginner path. Write no contract; calls propagate errors. Expert path. Write -> T ! E for a named error, ! E1 | E2 for several, and ! Never to promise none.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. About 40,000 signature lines change. The rewrite is mechanical and lands with D-SIG-ARROW1's cut, so files move once, not twice.

A unit contract starts with the mark, -> ! SaveError, which could read as not at a glance. The space after ! is required and the formatter enforces it. A !SaveError written without the space is refused with a fix, so the denial look-alike never compiles.

What remains. Lines get two characters longer, about one percent of a typical signature. The Never contract is the largest share; whether Core should keep writing it is a separate question for the generated-signature cards.

Other options. B keeps today's suffix. C is Zig's error union, error first: -> ParseError!String. D is Swift's typed throws: -> String throws ParseError. E is Rust's Result: -> Result<String, ParseError>.

Their best cases. B costs nothing and is ratified. C is proven in Zig and puts the error where the eye lands first. D reads as English. E needs no special grammar at all. Their costs: B keeps two types joined by a space. C puts the result last, against D-SIG-ARROW1's result-first order.

D adds a reserved word against your fewer-keywords steer. E turns the default Err route into a type every beginner must write or infer.

decisions.title: Retire the fence <: … :>: loops and lists cover repeated statements, and #loop covers repeated declarations
decisions.situation:
A fence repeats the statement around it once per entry: show(<: "left", "right" :>, <: 1, 2 :>) is two calls. It was ratified as D-EACH1=C, and its spelling as D-FENCE2=A, so eight task handles could be written in four characters.

Your review called it the least guessable form and asked whether #loop and #{…} make it unneeded. A retires it, reversing those decisions; keeping it is option B.
decisions.gist: Should the fence <: … :> go, with loops, lists and #loop doing the repeating it does today?
decisions.lesson: A fence makes one written line stand for several copies, one per entry between <: and :>. Loops and lists also repeat work, and #loop repeats declarations while building. This vote decides whether Jet still needs the fence.
decisions.explainer: Words used here. A fence is <: a, b :> inside a statement; the statement runs once per entry. A binding fence names several values at once, as <: t1..t8 :>. #loop repeats declarations while the program builds, and #{…} pastes a name.
decisions.story: Lena reads show(<: "left", "right" :>, <: 1, 2 :>) in a code review and has to look up what it does. Under A the same code is two calls, or a loop over two pairs, and needs no lookup.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. Whether the fence stays in the language. Loops, lists, #loop and #{…} are unchanged; D-META-SPELL1=A and D-META-HASH1=A already ratified them.

Today, on seed a0_042. Probe f01 uses a binding fence with numbered names, an expression fence, a lock-step pair of fences and a fence in an assignment. It prints 7, 7, 7, left=1, right=2 and 60.

Probe f02 writes the same program in plain Jet: three bindings, three prints, two calls and a loop over a list. It prints the same six lines. Probe f03 writes the lock-step pair as a loop over two named pairs and prints left=1 and right=2.

Census on the seed, .jet files only, comment lines skipped. Fence lines: 67 in 22 files. 41 are in the compiler's own fence parser, formatter and tests; 12 are in tests and 11 in the FencedNames example. Core and Jetpack have none, so no library or program uses it.

The rule under A. The fence and its tokens go. A repeated statement becomes a loop over a list, or the copies written out. Several values become a list. Repeated declarations use #loop with #{…}, as ratified.

jet fix rewrites every fence to the copies it stands for, since a fence is defined as those copies. So the rewrite never changes meaning. Where the copies are three or more, it writes a loop over a list instead.

What goes. The fence parser, its formatter rows, its diagnostics and their UI snapshots, the numbered-name expansion that jump-to-definition had to look through, and the <: and :> tokens. :> stops needing its double job beside the retired-arrow error.

Beginner path. One way to repeat: a loop. Expert path. #loop for declarations, and a list of handles for tasks, which D-FANOUT3 already waits on together.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. The case D-EACH1 was ratified for, eight task handles at the spawn and the wait, now uses a list. A list of handles is one line to spawn and one to wait, and it needs no numbered names.

Text search for t5 found nothing under the fence; with a list it is handles[4], which search and jump-to-definition handle without special rules.

What remains. A short lock-step call such as show(<: "left", "right" :>, <: 1, 2 :>) becomes two lines or a loop over pairs. The fence's visual pairing with <> goes; <> itself stays under D-PIPE1=A.

Other options. B keeps the fence. C keeps expression fences and drops binding fences and numbered names. D drops the fence and lets #loop in a function body write one copy per entry, as Zig's inline for does.

Their best cases. B is built and shortest. C keeps the call-site use and drops the part that hides names from search. D gives build-time repetition one spelling everywhere.

Their costs. B keeps the least guessable form. C keeps a form with no users outside its tests. D makes #loop in a body mean unrolling, while ratified D-META-SPELL1=A gives it today's comptime loop meaning: it runs while building.

decisions.title: May a foreign-library permission name one locked library instead of every library in that language?
decisions.situation: May a foreign-library permission name one locked library instead of every library in that language? Calling a native library brings outside code into the program. Our example calls the C absolute-value function and prints 7. A broad permission also admits unrelated C libraries, even when their behavior differs. We recommend narrowing the existing foreign permission by locked library identity, while keeping evidence and isolation separate.
decisions.gist: May a foreign-library permission name one locked library instead of every library in that language?
decisions.lesson: A permission says which outside library is admitted. Its checked contract says what that library does. Neither a name nor an effect list stops native code from issuing system calls.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A binding is the #Import block that gives C functions Jet signatures. An effect is something a call does to the world, such as reading files. A row is the list of effects a call may use.

A grant allows effects, either for the package's own code or for one dependency. A written allow list is a ceiling: code may use only what it lists.
decisions.story: Lee calls the same absolute-value function in both options. The result is 7; the difference is whether another C library shares the permission.
decisions.inWild: Illustrative native call; library-specific permission does not contain the library after loading.
decisions.detail:
origin/dev:Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Effects/Checks.jet:1750-1760 adds the foreign effect root and preserves opaque reach. Both choices reuse that effect solver. origin/dev:Compiler/Prelude/Effects.jet:71-98 owns the FFI family.

Foreign function interface (FFI) permission and evidence-backed behavior are separate questions. D-FFI-CONTRACT1=A and D-FFI-FACTS1=A already require one artifact-bound contract and the strongest justified safe shape. They are shared obligations, not options to disable accurate facts. This ballot now asks only about library-specific grants.

A explicitly extends the existing FFI.C value spelling into manifest allow/deny and command grants. It amends D-DECL-TYPES1 rule 3, which otherwise limits value narrowing to source rows. Resolve the local dependency key to its locked artifact identity; equal keys in different packages confer no shared authority. The `c` binding in both panes denotes the same toolchain C library. B preserves broad FFI.C grants. It still uses every justified contract fact; it does not force unknown effects where evidence exists.

Beginners use generated bindings whose required grant is shown with the dependency. Experts inspect evidence or select existing isolated placement. Unknown native reach stays conservative. An empty declared row alone proves nothing. Callback, retained-callback and cleanup effects join through the same descriptor; stale evidence fails admission. In-process trust is not enforcement. A separate process alone does not deny files or network. Unsupported mediation must refuse, never silently choose in-process execution.

The existing descriptor supplies the function contract under both options; this vote adds no import-arrow syntax and requires no duplicate handwritten effect database. The intended C ABI mapping must be established by that descriptor before executing the panes. No native call, containment or fixed ABI layout is claimed from the ordinary-function syntax probe.

Fresh review, 2026-11-11. Separated already-settled effect evidence from the remaining grant gate and made the required value-grant amendment explicit.

decisions.title: Keep jet explain and jet inspect as ratified, and add a per-line view of the run-time checks a build keeps, with a promise that none remains
decisions.situation:
Jet has two ratified commands for compiler knowledge. jet explain answers about one thing, and jet inspect shows a whole plane. The review asks to fold both into jet explain, and to show every run-time check the compiler could not remove.

Today jet explain effects answers per line. No command says which index on a line still carries a bounds check. This ballot keeps both commands and adds that view, plus a marker that refuses any kept check.
decisions.gist: Should Jet keep its two inspection verbs and add a per-line view of kept run-time checks, plus a promise that none remains?
decisions.lesson: Jet adds a safety check where it cannot prove an index fits. That keeps programs safe but costs a little speed. This vote decides whether you can see each check that stayed, and ask Jet to refuse any in a hot loop.
decisions.explainer: Words used here. A bounds check tests an index against a list's length while the program runs. A kept check is one the compiler could not prove away. A promise is a #Policy marker that the build enforces.
decisions.story: Dana's game loop is slow. Under A, jet explain checks shows the one index the compiler could not prove, and #Policy(checks: .Forbid) keeps new checks out of the loop.
decisions.inWild:
// Swift and Rust leave this to reading assembly:
$ cargo asm my_crate::sum_first
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. Whether to keep D-CLI-ONE1=A's two verbs, and whether to add a view and a promise for kept run-time checks. The review's query questions are covered at the end.

The verbs today, on the t6c compiler (dev 76955986d0). jet help inspect lists 28 subcommand words, including the plane views, decisions, expand, audit, query, impact and semindex. jet explain takes a code, a fact, a marker, a policy key, or effects at a file and line.

Kept checks today. Probe g01 indexes xs[i] with i below a parameter n, so the index is not proven. jet inspect decisions lists vectorized sum reductions and a stepped index guarded before the loop. It names no kept bounds check. jet explain effects g01_sum.jet:5 reports effects only.

A name collision, engineered away. On t6c, jet explain checks g01_sum.jet:5 is read as a package name and fails E1274, no package record. jet explain matches its fixed topics, log, effects and marker, before package names, and A adds checks to that list. A policy key followed by a file already routes to the policy explanation, so the view also prints the checks policy in force, as explain effects prints caps.

One answer on every build profile. The view lists the checks sema could not prove, which never depend on the profile. It then marks which of them the optimizer removed on the profile asked for, with --profile. The promise judges only sema's list, so a function that passes in a debug build passes in a release build.

The facts exist. The IR builder records which list accesses sema proved in bounds and lowers those with no check. IR.jet's loop proof rows count proven and unchecked accesses. No command prints them per line for a user.

What A does. A keeps both ratified verbs. It adds jet explain checks with a file and an optional line, beside jet explain effects. For each line it lists each bounds check and other trap check the build kept, each implicit copy and each allocation, with the reason it stayed.

For g01 line 5 the reason reads: xs[i], i is below n, and n is not known to be at most xs.len(). The fix names the proven form, such as loop over xs or a test against xs.len() first.

The promise. #Policy(checks: .Forbid) on a function or block makes each kept check inside it an error with the same line and reason. It joins the policy ladder as a new key, beside the no_alloc promise of D-NOALLOC-SEM1.

The promise uses only proofs sema makes today. D-OOBPROOF1=A's refinement-based proofs would remove more checks once refinement types land; A does not wait for them.

Census on t6c. The repository has no per-line check report. jet inspect audit copies already counts implicit copies, and prints implicit read-view copies: 0 for g01.

Query questions from 8.10. Which functions touch this name: jet inspect impact g01_sum.jet sum_first lists one caller. What can fail: jet inspect semindex prints each function's failure contract. What changed in meaning: jet review v1.jet v2.jet prints effect and authority changes. These exist, so 8.10 needs no new verb.

Tracing from effects. Callable policies already wrap calls, and CallablePolicies.jet applies #Policy(trace(...)). A span on every effect call is a separate ballot.

Ratified decisions. A keeps D-CLI-ONE1=A, uses D-PACKAGE-POLICY-SCOPE1=A's ladder and D-LEDGER1=D's one query, and does not depend on D-OOBPROOF1=A. Option C would reverse D-CLI-ONE1=A.

Beginner path. A beginner never needs the view; a slow loop leads to one command. Expert path. The promise keeps a hot loop free of checks, and the error says why each one stayed.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. The promise can reject code that is correct but unproven. The error names the proven form, and #Policy(checks: .Forbid) applies only where it is written.

What remains. The view adds one more jet explain topic. It sits beside jet explain effects and reads the same way.

Other options. B keeps the ratified verbs with no view or promise. C folds jet inspect, audit and expand into jet explain topics, as the review asks. D adds the view but not the promise.

Their best cases. B adds nothing. C gives one word to learn. D shows the checks without new errors. Their costs: B leaves kept checks invisible. C moves 28 words that D-CLI-ONE1=A just placed. D cannot keep a hot loop clean.

decisions.title: Every breaking language change lands with a rewrite registered in jet fix; errors still never teach retired spellings
decisions.situation:
Jet changes its spelling often before 1.0, and the repository migrates itself with one-off scripts. Users' code gets no rewrite. A file that still writes the retired word prep gets an error saying there is no type called prep, and jet fix makes no change.

Today an owner rule says retired spellings get no teaching message and no jet fix rewrite, and it holds until this vote. D-TEACH-RECONCILE1=A already bars teaching. The recommendation keeps that bar and adds rewrites only, which changes the rule's rewrite half.
decisions.gist: Should every breaking language change land with a jet fix rewrite, so old code moves forward in one command?
decisions.lesson: When Jet changes how something is written, old programs stop compiling. This vote decides whether each such change must ship with an automatic rewrite. Then jet fix updates old code instead of leaving a confusing error.
decisions.explainer: Words used here. A breaking change makes code that compiled before stop compiling. A rewrite is a saved, replayable edit that turns the old form into the new one. A codemod plan is Jet's existing file format for such edits.
decisions.story: Chen opens a project he last touched in October. Under A, jet check gives the ordinary error and says the project was locked with an older jet. jet fix rewrites the old word, and one command later the project builds.
decisions.inWild:
// Rust ships each edition's rewrites in the compiler:
$ cargo fix --edition
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. Whether a breaking language change may land without a rewrite users can run. Library items already have one: D-STRUCT-LIFE1=A and D-DEPRECATE-INLINE1=A. This is the language half.

The rule in force. On 2026-11-10 Main recorded the owner rule on cards #6622 and #6281. Until this ballot is decided, retired spellings get the generic error, no teaching text and no jet fix rewrite. D-TEACH-RECONCILE1=A, ratified on 2026-11-05, already says no teaching of retired Jet spellings anywhere.

So the ballot has two halves. Teaching, a message that names the retired word and its new form, is settled against by D-TEACH-RECONCILE1=A. Rewriting, jet fix editing old code on request, is the open question. A adds rewrites and keeps the teaching bar. E adds both and would reverse D-TEACH-RECONCILE1=A for Jet's own spellings.

Today, on the a0.0.43 compiler (dev c460ba91e5). Commit 5a467902a3 retired prep, and its message says the rewrite was a script in a scratch directory. Probe m05 writes LIMIT: prep { 2 + 3 } and gets E0119, there is no type called prep. jet fix --dry-run prints no changes made, with or without --edition=2026.

jet fix --edition=2027 fails E2104: this jet migrates to edition 2026 only. The next spelling change is already ratified: D-META-SPELL1=A replaces comptime with #run. Probe m06, comptime { 2 + 3 }, still prints 5. Probe m07, #run { 2 + 3 }, fails E0733, no tag called run, and suggests the unrelated tag PII.

How often spelling breaks. Since 2026-09-10, 131 commits that touch the parser or checker say retire. comptime appears 2,816 times in 1,013 Jet files, the size of the next migration. History holds 30 respell commits and 284 that mention a codemod. All 22 codemod plan files in the tree sit under tests.

What A does. Each breaking language change adds one rewrite file in a new Compiler/Migrations directory. The file uses the codemod plan format of D-CODEMOD-BATCH1=A. Its name carries the decision ID and the toolchain version that made the change.

jet fix applies every rewrite between the toolchain recorded in .jet/lock and the running one, in order. jet new already writes that record: a fresh project's lock has toolchain = a0.0.43 and a [[toolchain]] section. A file with no lock names its start: jet fix --since 0.4 file.jet.

Rewrites chain. When D-META-SPELL1=A lands, its rewrite turns comptime into #run, so jet fix on prep code applies both in order. A rewrite that cannot be automatic is marked manual; jet fix lists each such site in its own report and changes nothing there.

No teaching, by design. Under A the old word keeps the generic error, which names no retired form. A failing check adds one toolchain line only when the project's lock is older than the running jet. The line reads: this project was locked with a0.0.41; jet fix --dry-run shows 3 pending rewrites.

That line names no spelling, old or new, so it is not teaching under D-TEACH-RECONCILE1=A. It compares two version strings and counts rewrite files, only on failure, so a clean build pays nothing. A project with no lock gets no line.

The landing rule. A change that breaks code lands together with its rewrite. Its fixture holds the old spelling, and the suite requires the result to check clean. A change of meaning under an unchanged spelling counts too: its fixture must print the same output before and after jet fix. The repository migrates itself with the same file users get.

After the 1.0 boundary, the same files become edition migrations that jet fix --edition reads. That matches the release policy: breaking changes need an edition bump and jet fix. A keeps D-REL5, so source is rewritten only by jet fix, on request, and D-CODEMOD1=A and D-CODEMOD-BATCH1=A as the format.

Beginner path. Old code fails with the ordinary error and the toolchain line; jet fix updates it in one command. Expert path. Each rewrite is a reviewable file with a fixture, and jet fix --dry-run shows every edit first.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. Each breaking change costs its author one rewrite file and one fixture. The repository already writes that script for its own migration; A checks it in. A user whose project has no lock sees no toolchain line and must know to run jet fix --since.

What remains. A rewrite is only as good as its fixture. A missed form leaves the ordinary error, and jet fix --dry-run lists which rewrites ran, so a user can report the gap. A project made without jet new has no toolchain record until a build writes one.

Other options. B keeps today's practice and the owner rule as it stands. C keeps a teaching error for each retired spelling but no rewrite, like Python 3's print message. D waits for editions: no rewrite rule before 1.0. E is A plus a hint naming the retired form and its rewrite.

Their best cases. B costs nothing and lets spelling move fastest. C tells users exactly what to write. D follows the release policy as written. E tells users why their code broke. Their costs. B strands old code. C and E reverse D-TEACH-RECONCILE1=A for Jet's spellings. C also leaves every edit to the user. D strands everything written before 1.0.

recommendation.why: Old code moves forward in one command, and the repository migrates itself with the file users get. A keeps D-TEACH-RECONCILE1=A: no message names a retired spelling.
gains: Old code updates in one command.
The repository uses the users' rewrite.
No teaching text; D-TEACH-RECONCILE1=A stands.

C reverses D-TEACH-RECONCILE1=A and leaves every edit to the user.
D strands everything written before 1.0.
E reverses D-TEACH-RECONCILE1=A for Jet's own spellings to name the old word.

recommendation.tradeoff: One rewrite file per breaking change, and errors that never name a retired word, for old code that never strands.

decisions.title: A named number adapts like the literal it names; a variable takes the type its function needs only where the default is refused
decisions.situation:
A number literal adapts to where it goes: half(3.0) passes a Float. A module constant does too: GRAVITY: 9.81 passes to a Float parameter. A local name does not: after y: 2.5, half(y) is an error, because y is an exact Decimal by default.

The review asked that naming a number not change what it is. This ballot lets local names adapt the way literals and constants already do. The exact default and the rule that precision is lost only at a written step stay as ratified.
decisions.gist: Should a local name for a number adapt the way the literal and module constants already do, so half(y) just works?
decisions.lesson: Jet's plain decimal numbers are exact by default, and Float is the fast approximate kind games use. A written 2.5 becomes a Float where a Float is needed. A name for it, y: 2.5, does not. This vote decides whether naming a number keeps that.
decisions.explainer: Words used here. A literal is a number written in code, such as 2.5. Decimal is Jet's exact default for written decimals; Float is approximate binary. A binding gives a value a name: y: 2.5 cannot change, speed := 2.5 can.
decisions.story: Jo writes a game. half(3.0) works, so she names it: y: 3.0, then half(y), and gets E0112 saying y is a Decimal. The fix text suggests Float{3.4}. Under A her code runs as written.
decisions.inWild:
// Go: a named constant is untyped until used, like the literal.
const y = 2.5
var f float32 = y   // fine: y adapts
var g float64 = y   // fine too
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. What type a name for a number has. Number types, the exact default of D-TYPE2-DEFAULT1=A, and the rule that precision is lost only at a spelled step are unchanged.

Today, on the t6c compiler (dev 76955986d0), every probe matches the seed. Probe l01 passes 3.0 to half and gets 1.5; naming it y: 2.5 and calling half(y) is E0112. Probe l08 passes a module constant GRAVITY: 9.81 to the same kind of parameter and prints 4.905. So module constants already adapt, and local names do not.

Probe l04 writes speed := 2.5 and speed = step(speed, 0.5): E0112. Probe l06 passes n: 200 to a U8 parameter: E0108, while the literal 200 works. Probe l07 multiplies a local Decimal by a Float: E0131.

Today's ways out. Probe l10 writes Float{2.5} into each value and prints 1.25, 3.0, 200. Probe l09 converts with y.to_float(). Probe l03 shows approx refuses a Decimal; it is for whole numbers.

The rule under A, for a name that cannot change. A local binding whose value is a number literal, or arithmetic on such literals and constants, adapts at each use exactly as the literal would there. That is the rule module constants follow today.

The rule under A, for a name that can change. A local := binding of such a value keeps today's default, Int or Decimal. Only where that default is refused does it take the type the use needs, at the binding.

If two uses need different types, the error names both lines. So a program that compiles today never changes meaning; A only accepts programs that are errors today.

Names built from names. b: y * 2, where y is an adapting name, adapts too, because it is arithmetic on literals once y is replaced. A closure that captures y captures the literal. A generic parameter that decides nothing gives the default, Decimal, exactly as the literal 2.5 would there.

Why the precision law holds. A name behaves exactly as its literal written at the use, which the compiler already converts with its exactness check. No value at run time loses precision without a spelled step, as D-TYPE2-EXACT1=A requires.

Census on dev, git grep -cE over Jet files, indented lines only, so comments and module lines are skipped. Local bindings that write Float, F32 or F64 into a literal: 827 in 190 files. Local bindings that write a fixed-width integer type into a literal: 2,910 in 429 files. Under A, jet fix may drop the type where a use decides it.

Module number constants, which already adapt: 4,592 lines in 495 files, all unchanged. Plain whole-number := bindings: 7,085, which keep Int unless today they are errors. Bare decimal-literal locals, the cases A reaches directly: 39 in 33 files.

Beginner path. Name a number and use it; it fits where it goes. Expert path. Write Float{2.5} or F32{2.5} to fix a type on purpose; hover shows which line decided a name's type.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. A later line can decide a variable's type, so speed / 3 above it becomes Float division. This happens only where the default would be an error, and hover names the deciding line.

E0112's fix text today always says Float{3.4}. Under A the error remains for real conflicts, and its text names both uses with their own numbers.

What remains. A reader of speed := 2.5 cannot tell its type from that line alone when a later use decides it. That is Rust's rule for every number binding; A applies it only where the default fails.

Other options. B keeps today's rule. C is Go's: names that cannot change adapt, variables keep the default. D makes decimal literals Float by default, as Swift and Python do, and writes exact numbers as Decimal. E is Rust's: every use decides one type for the binding.

Their best cases. B tells a reader every type at the binding. C covers constants with no inference. D makes games simplest. E is the most uniform.

Their costs. B makes naming change meaning. C leaves the speed := 2.5 case an error. D reverses the exact world of D-TYPE2-DEFAULT1. E changes programs that compile today, such as y / 3 becoming Float division.

decisions.title: A wrapping marker gets call: Call<R>, with the arguments already bound, checked once where it is declared
decisions.situation:
A wrapping marker runs its own code around each call of the function it marks, for example to retry it. Jet already agreed that wrappers exist, the order they run in, and that a wrapper never changes a function's signature. Nothing fixes what the wrapper's handle on the call looks like.

Today that handle is the function itself, so a wrapper must pass the function's own arguments and only fits functions it knows. Its body is checked again at every use. We recommend A: the arguments are already attached, so one wrapper fits any function and is checked once.
decisions.gist: Should a wrapping marker's call have its arguments already bound, so one wrapper works on any function and is checked once?
decisions.lesson: A wrapping marker runs code around a function, such as retrying it, timing it or logging it. To do that it needs a way to call the function it wraps. This vote decides what that call looks like, so a wrapper written once works on any function.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A marker is a # name with a capital letter, such as #Retry. A wrapping marker runs its own code around each call to the function it marks. call is the handle it uses to run that function.

The arguments are bound when the values the caller passed are already attached to call.
decisions.story: Lena writes a Retry wrapper and marks fetch(id). Today the wrapper must write call(id), so it works only for functions with an id. Under A it writes call(), and the same Retry marks any function.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. The type of call in wrap, when the wrapper's body is checked, and whether it may call more than once. Attachment through markers, #Policy and apply() stays as D-CALLPOLICY1 says. Staging is D-META-STAGING1 and spelling is ratified D-META-SPELL1=A and D-META-HASH2.

Today, with the t6c compiler on dev 76955986d0, the same as the seed. Probe w02 is Examples/Basics/Functions/CallablePolicies.jet, today's policy declarations with wrap(call). It prints nine lines, and audit:outer:audit:inner:ok shows the outer wrapper runs first. Probe w01 writes wrap in impl Marker and gets E0907: Marker has only expand today.

Probe w03 wraps a function that returns Int with a wrapper that returns a String. The error, E0113, ReturnTypeMismatch, points into the wrapper's body and names a generated function: the body is checked again at each use, like a template.

Probe w04 calls call() twice in a wrapper on bump(n: Int). It gets E0766, MissingArgument, twice: call is bump itself, so the wrapper must write call(n), and a wrapper written once cannot forward the arguments of a function it has never seen.

The rule under A. call has the Core type Call<R>, where R is the wrapped function's result, its error or None included. The arguments are bound before wrap runs, so call() takes none. It runs the next inner wrapper, then the body, in D-CALLPOLICY1's chain order. wrap returns R.

Checked once. The wrapper's body is checked where it is declared, against Call<R> with R generic, as D-MARKER-TARGETS1 checks marker bodies. At each use the compiler checks only that the function's result fits the wrapper's R, such as R? for Retry. A mismatch is an error at the marker, naming the function's result.

Calling more than once. A wrapper may call call() zero, one or more times: zero returns early, as a cache does. A wrapper that may call more than once declares repeats: true, beside sites. It may then mark only functions whose parameters, self included, are borrowed or copyable, so each call sees the same arguments.

Using it on a function that takes an argument by move is an error naming the parameter, with the fix to borrow it. Arguments are cleaned up once, by the caller, after wrap returns.

What a wrapper may read. self holds the marker's arguments, and self.function is D-META-REFLECT2's FunctionInfo for the marked function, so a wrapper can log its name. It cannot read or change the argument values; a marker that needs them adds code through expand instead.

What stays ratified. CALLPOLICY1's law holds: the wrapper's own effects and errors must be covered by the marked function's row, checked at each use. A wrap edits no body, so it needs no Compiler value under D-META-LADDER1; the marker written on the declaration is the visible authority.

Effects inside the once-checked body. Call<R> carries the marked function's effect row with it, and call() performs exactly that row, which the function already declares. So the body needs no effect of its own to call it, and each use checks only what the wrapper adds, as CALLPOLICY1 requires.

Call cannot outlive wrap. Its bound arguments belong to the caller's frame, so storing call, returning it, or moving it into another task is the ordinary borrow error. The arguments are cleaned up once, by the caller, after wrap returns, so no option leaves them dangling.

Census on dev 76955986d0 over Core, Compiler, Jetpack, Tools, Examples and tests, raw matching lines in Jet files. Policy declarations: 7 in 5 files. wrap(call): 18 lines in 11 files. #Policy(: 88 lines in 71 files. Every user wrap(call) body in Examples and tests writes call() with no arguments, so their text is kept.

Beginner path. Use a wrapper: #Retry(attempts: 3) above a function. Expert path. Write one: a struct with impl Marker and wrap. It is checked once, and it works on any function whose result fits.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. A wrapper cannot read argument values. The add rung, expand, can add code that reads them, so nothing is lost. A repeating wrapper cannot mark a function that consumes an argument, which is the price of calling it twice. The error names the parameter and the fix.

Other options. B keeps today's form: call is the function itself, and the body is checked at each use. C is Java's around advice: Call<A, R> exposes the arguments as call.args, and call.with(args) passes changed ones. D removes wrapping, as Rust and Go do: a retry is a plain function taking a closure. E is Python's: wrap returns any function, so a wrapper may change the signature.

Their best cases. B needs no work and lets a wrapper meant for one function use its arguments. C lets a wrapper sanitize arguments. D has no hidden control flow. E is the most flexible. D and E reverse ratified laws: D the wrap rung of DECL-TYPES1, E the signature law of CALLPOLICY1.

Body checked at declaration with R generic, per MARKER-TARGETS1; each use checks result fit, effect and error cover. Call is a borrow of the wrap frame and cannot escape it. repeats: true requires borrowed or copyable parameters. self.function is REFLECT2's FunctionInfo.
