decisions.title: Name C23's one-rounding narrowing arithmetic in core.math: f32_add, f32_sub, f32_mul, f32_div, f32_fma and f32_sqrt
decisions.situation:
Jet's math module aims to cover every function in C's math library, and six are still missing. C23 added them: they take two large approximate numbers and round the exact answer once to the small type, F32. Today the only way to write that in Jet adds in the large type and then shrinks, which rounds twice and is sometimes one step off.

The code behind the six is the same under every option; only the names are open. People porting C or writing emulators need them, while everyone else keeps writing F32 arithmetic and is already right. We recommend A: f32_add and its five siblings, named by the result type, with C's names taught by Jet's one foreign-name error.
decisions.gist: What should core.math call the six operations that round a Float sum, product or root once to F32?
decisions.lesson: F32 is the smaller approximate number type; Float is the larger. Adding two Floats and then shrinking the answer to F32 rounds twice, and once in a while that lands one step off. C23 added six operations that round only once. This vote picks their Jet names.
decisions.explainer: Words used here. Rounding picks the nearest number the type can hold. Rounding twice can land one step away from the nearest. Narrowing means shrinking a Float to an F32. core.math is Jet's math module.
decisions.story: Lee ports a C physics tool that adds in double and stores float vertices with fadd. Under A, Jet's error for fadd says Jet calls it math.f32_add, jet fix rewrites the call, and the port gives the same bits as the C build.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. The names of six core.math functions. The behavior is fixed by the C23 standard and by D-MATH-BITS1=A, so it is the same under every option.

Exact behavior, every option. Each takes Float operands and returns the F32 nearest the exact result, ties to even. The six are add, subtract, multiply, divide, fused multiply-add (a times b plus c, rounded once) and square root.

Overflow gives infinity, a NaN operand gives NaN, and the square root of a negative number gives NaN. Every tier and compile time give the same bits, per D-MATH-BITS1=A.

The code is an exact Float operation with its error term, then a sticky-bit fix before the one narrowing. C's l forms collapse, because Float is Jet's widest format. faddl is the same call as fadd, and daddl is plain Float addition.

Today, with the t6c compiler on dev 76955986d0. Probe n01 builds a Float a exactly halfway between two F32 values and a tiny b that tips the exact sum above it. F32{a + b} gives bits 1065353216, which is 1.0; the once-rounded answer is 1065353217.

Probe n05 shows that approx can't stand in: it only opts an integer crossing out of its check, so it is E0109 on a Float. Probe n04 shows that neither f32_add nor fadd exists yet, E1004. The seed compiler gave the same results.

Probe n07 shows the beginner case is already right. When both operands are F32 values, F32 of the Float sum equals the direct F32 sum. Float has more than twice F32's digits, so add, subtract, multiply, divide and square root are exact there.

So the six matter only when the operands carry more than F32 precision, as in a C port or an emulator. That makes them an expert path. The beginner keeps writing F32 arithmetic or F32{…} and is right.

How core.math names C's functions today. Probe n02 runs fabs, fdim and fma under C's names; in those the leading f means floating, and the result stays Float. Probe n06 shows pown and fmaximum are respelled pow_n and maximum, and E1004 suggests those by spelling.

core.math also still ships C aliases beside Jet names: nextafter beside next_after, expm1 beside exp_m1, log1p beside ln_1p, and muladd beside fma. D-CORE-ONE-NAME1=A deletes such aliases and teaches the foreign name instead. Probe n08 shows that table is not built yet: json.loads and a list's contains still check clean.

Census on dev, .jet files, comment lines skipped. F32 appears on 359 lines in 101 files. The C narrowing names appear once, in LibcCensus.

What A adds. core.math gets f32_add, f32_sub, f32_mul and f32_div, each taking two Floats, plus f32_fma(a, b, c) and f32_sqrt(a). Each returns F32. The name starts with the result type, like IEEE 754's formatOf operations. Completion lists the six together.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. It isn't C's spelling. D-CORE-ONE-NAME1=A already gives Jet one table of foreign names and one diagnostic with a jet fix rewrite. A adds rows to it: fadd and faddl teach math.f32_add, and daddl teaches plain Float addition. So a C name costs one automatic fix, and no second lookup is added.

What remains. F32{a + b} on Float operands still rounds twice, with no warning. That is not a wrong answer: it is the correct F32 of the Float sum. It equals the once-rounded sum whenever the operands are F32 values, because Float carries at least 2 times 24 plus 2 bits. The F32 page and the f32_add docs name the one case where the two differ.

Ratified decisions. D-MATHLIB2=A makes core.math free functions the one callable surface, with no duplicate spellings. D-CORE-ONE-NAME1=A makes foreign names taught, never aliased, and D-FLOATW1 makes core.math width-generic. A and B follow all three; C amends D-MATHLIB2=A, and D adds a language rule instead of names.

Other options at their best. B uses C's names, so ports need no renaming. C makes them Float methods, found from a Float value. D makes F32{a + b} itself round once, so the obvious spelling becomes the right one.

Their costs. B puts fadd, which narrows, beside fabs and fdim, which don't. C adds six methods, which needs amending D-MATHLIB2=A. D changes what F32{a + b} means today, and naming a + b on its own line changes the result.

options.name: f32_add, f32_sub, f32_mul, f32_div, f32_fma, f32_sqrt
options.detail: Six core.math functions named result type first. C's names are taught foreign names with an automatic fix.
options.technical: core.math.f32_add(a: Float, b: Float) -> F32; likewise f32_sub, f32_mul, f32_div; f32_fma(a, b, c: Float) -> F32; f32_sqrt(a: Float) -> F32. Exact operation plus error term, sticky fix, one narrowing. LibcCensus row 113's 18 C names become rows in D-CORE-ONE-NAME1's foreign-name table: the f and l forms teach the six, and the d forms teach Float operators.

options.name: C's names: fadd, fsub, fmul, fdiv, ffma, fsqrt
options.detail: The C23 spellings, so C code ports with no renaming.
options.technical: core.math.fadd(a: Float, b: Float) -> F32 and so on, beside the existing fabs, fdim and fmod, which return Float. The l forms become taught names for the six, and the d forms teach Float operators, through D-CORE-ONE-NAME1's table.

options.name: Float methods: add_to_f32 and the rest
options.detail: Methods on Float, found by typing a dot after a Float value.
options.technical: Float.add_to_f32(self, other: Float) -> F32; likewise sub_to_f32, mul_to_f32, div_to_f32, fma_to_f32(b, c), sqrt_to_f32(). Amends D-MATHLIB2=A, which keeps core.math free functions as the one callable surface.

options.name: F32{a + b} rounds once
options.detail: No new names. An F32 head around one Float operation rounds the exact result once.
options.technical: Sema rule: F32{x op y} with Float operands and op one of + - * /, and F32{math.fma(a, b, c)} and F32{math.sqrt(x)}, lower to the one-rounding operation. Any other body rounds twice, as today.

comparisons.note: Narrowing functions named by result.
formatOf operations, named by destination format.
No named form; convert after the operation.
No named form; cast after the operation.

recommendation.why: A names the F32 result first, so the narrowing shows in the name. It keeps core.math's free-function rule, and Jet's one foreign-name table teaches C's names with an automatic fix.
gains: The name shows the narrowing.
Keeps D-MATHLIB2=A's one callable surface.
C's names lead to it through D-CORE-ONE-NAME1's table, and jet fix rewrites them.

losses.loss: A C port renames each call once.
losses.mitigation: The foreign-name diagnostic carries the fix, and jet fix applies it across a project.

losses.loss: F32{a + b} on Float operands still rounds twice, with no warning.
losses.mitigation: It is the correct F32 of the Float sum and equals the once-rounded sum for F32 operands; the F32 page and f32_add docs name the case.

whyNot.reason: B saves the rename, but puts fadd, which narrows, beside fabs and fdim, which keep Float.
C amends D-MATHLIB2=A for six rare methods.
D changes today's F32{a + b}, and naming the sum changes the result.

recommendation.tradeoff: C porters run one automatic fix from fadd to f32_add, for a name that shows the narrowing.

decisions.title: The values the compiler fills in are spelled with #: #build, #here and #caller
decisions.situation:
Some values are filled in by the compiler: the build being made, the place in the source, and the place a function was called from. An earlier decision spelled the build as a plain name, build, and the places as hash line and hash file. It named nothing for the caller's place.

Your review approved one rule: a hash marks everything the compiler fills in, written #build, #here and #caller. A plain build is hidden inside any file that defines a function named build, as every build file does. We recommend A, that one rule.
decisions.gist: Should the build, this place and the caller's place be read as #build, #here and #caller?
decisions.lesson: A program can ask the compiler what it is building and where a line sits in the source. A logger uses the caller's place to say where a message came from. This vote decides how those values are spelled, so a reader sees at once that the compiler filled them in.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A site value is a value the compiler fills in for the spot where it is written, such as the line number. The caller's site is the place a function was called from. The build value describes what is being built: target system, profile, settings and stamp.

A marker is a # name with a capital letter, such as #Test.
decisions.story: Ines writes a build function named build, as every package's build file does. Inside it she reads build.target.os and gets her own function, not the build being made. Under A she writes #build.target.os, and no name of hers can hide it.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. Only how three compiler-filled values are spelled, where #caller may be written, and the # form of the orphaned $program root. What the values contain stays as D-BUILD-FACT3 and D-JAI-SITE1 ratified. #package and #phase stay as HASH1 and D-META-PHASE1 ratified. Reflection stays reflect(x) per D-REFLECT-TYPEINFO1. Staging and wrapping are their own ballots, D-META-STAGING1 and D-MARKER-CALL1.

Today, with the t6c compiler on dev 76955986d0, the same as the seed. Probe h03 is the same program in today's spelling: a logger whose at parameter defaults to $caller, a branch on $build.os, and $build.profile. It prints 8: on linux, then dev, then 12: done, so the caller's line reaches the logger.

Probe h01 shows that #if does not parse yet (E0003), which D-META-SPELL1=A changes once built. Probe h02 writes #build.profile and #caller: E0087, MarkerLibraryCasing, and E0927, UnknownAppliedRule. Probe h05 writes HASH1's plain build.profile and gets E0107, UnknownName. Probe h04 prints #line and #file and gets E0915, MissingDisplay: both read as Unit. No option here is built.

Two new probes. h06 calls the logger directly and through a function value, f: log. It prints 7: direct and 9: through a value, so a caller default already fills at each call, even through a value. h07 declares build: fn() -> Int beside $build.profile and prints dev then 1: a marked read and a function named build coexist today.

Why a plain name is fragile here. A package's build file defines a function named build, the entry point D-BUILDENTRY1 ratified. On dev, 181 lines in 180 Jet files of Core, Compiler, Jetpack, Tools, Examples and tests declare build: fn(, Compiler/build.jet among them. Inside those files a plain build value would be hidden by the function.

The rule under A. #build is the build value, with D-BUILD-FACT3's contents: target, profile, settings and stamp. #here is a SourceLocation for the spot where it is written, with file, line, column and enclosing function, per JAI-SITE1. It replaces HASH1's #line and #file, which become #here.line and #here.file: one record, not three names.

#caller is a SourceLocation for the call. It may be written only as a parameter default, as JAI-SITE1 ratified, so each call that leaves the parameter out passes its own place. A wrapper forwards the place by declaring the same default and passing it on. Anywhere else #caller is an error whose fix adds that parameter.

All six are plain values once read, with #package, #phase and #program. #build.profile can be stored, compared, passed and printed like any value; # only says who filled it in. No user name can hide them, because a # name cannot be declared. Under #if, #build.target.os selects an arm while building, as D-META-SPELL1=A says.

The casing rule that keeps # unambiguous. A lowercase # name is a compiler-filled value, and a capitalised one is a marker, as #Test. That is the split E0087's casing check already enforces. So #build can never be read as a marker, and no marker can be named build.

The sixth root. Today's parser also accepts $program, which D-SCRIPT-SCRIPTDIR1 ratified as $program.dir beside $here.dir. HASH1 retired it with no successor under every option. Under A it becomes #program, and #here keeps .dir, so every root has one # form. Under B it would need a plain program name, hideable like build.

#caller stays legal only as a parameter default. Today's second place, inside an #Expand macro, left with macros under D-META-COMPILER1 and D-META-LADDER1.

Census on dev, raw matching lines in Jet files of the same roots. $build is on 183 lines in 76 files, $here 25 in 15, $caller 55 in 20, $package 51 in 26, $phase 22 in 11 and $program 10 in 6. #line and #file appear nowhere. Under A each maps one to one, so the respelling is a token rename with a checked fix.

Beginner path. Print #build.profile to see the profile, and add at: SourceLocation{#caller} to a helper to learn who called it. Everything filled in by the compiler starts with #, so a search for # finds it.

Expert path. Wrappers forward #caller through their own default. Build files read #build freely, even inside a function named build. Code that needs only the line reads #here.line.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. A changes HASH1's ratified spelling before HASH1 is built, so no program breaks that does not already use the $ forms, and those need renaming under every option but E. The rename is one to one, so the fix is mechanical and checked.

#build is one character longer than build. Most reads sit in #if lines or in build files, where the mark also tells the reader the arm is chosen while building. Dropping #line and #file costs five characters per read; one record keeps line, file and column together for loggers.

Other options. B keeps HASH1 as ratified: plain build, #line and #file, adding only #caller so JAI-SITE1's caller place has a successor. C is Swift's rule: #line written as a parameter default is the caller's line, so no #caller is needed. D is Rust's: a #TrackCaller marker lets SourceLocation.caller() return the caller's place. E keeps today's $ spelling, which HASH1 retired.

Their best cases. B needs no new rule for build and keeps three ratified names. C adds no name at all and is proven in Swift. D keeps call sites free of extra parameters and is proven in Rust. E needs no work. B and C still leave the build value hidden in every file that defines a build function.

D-SCRIPT-SCRIPTDIR1's $program becomes #program. Lowercase # names are compiler values, capitalised ones markers. #package and #phase unchanged. The $ forms map one to one under a checked fix.

options.name: Keep HASH1, add #caller
options.detail: Plain build, #line and #file stay as ratified. #caller is added as a parameter default so the caller's place has a successor.
options.technical: D-META-HASH1=A unchanged. Adds #caller with D-JAI-SITE1's SourceLocation, legal only as a parameter default. A function named build hides the Prelude value in its file.

options.name: Swift's defaults
options.detail: #line and #file written as a parameter default mean the caller's line and file. No #caller, and build stays plain.
options.technical: D-META-HASH1=A plus one rule: a site value in a parameter default is filled at the call. No SourceLocation record at call sites; each part is its own parameter.

options.name: Rust's TrackCaller marker
options.detail: A #TrackCaller marker on a function makes SourceLocation.caller() return the caller's place inside it. Build stays plain.
options.technical: D-META-HASH1=A plus a Core marker and a Core function. The marker adds a hidden location parameter, so calls through a function value carry it too.

options.name: Today's $ spelling
options.detail: $build, $here and $caller stay as they work today.
options.technical: Reverses D-META-HASH1=A's retirement of $ reads for these three. No respelling.

comparisons.note: #line and #file are filled at the call when they are parameter defaults.
comparisons.code: func log(_ m: String, line: Int = #line) { }

comparisons.note: #[track_caller] lets Location::caller() see the caller.
@src() gives the place where it is written; there is no caller form.

recommendation.why: A gives every compiler-filled value one mark that no name can hide. The $ forms rename one to one. One record replaces three place names.
gains: No function named build can hide the build value.
Every compiler-filled value starts with #.
One SourceLocation record for this place and the caller's.

losses.loss: It amends HASH1's ratified build and #line spellings.
losses.mitigation: Neither is built yet; the $ forms rename one to one under a checked fix.

whyNot.reason: B leaves build hidden in the 180 files that declare a build function.
C splits the place into separate parameters and keeps the hidden build.
D adds a marker and a hidden parameter for what a default already does.
E keeps $ reads, which HASH1 retired.

recommendation.tradeoff: One character more per build read, in return for a value no name can hide.

decisions.title: A marker that reflects a type sees every member other markers add to it
decisions.situation:
A marker can read a type while building and can add members to it. When two markers sit on one type, or one marker reads a type another changes, the answer depends on when the read happens. Nothing agreed so far fixes that moment.

Today a marker sees only the members written in the source, in either order. We recommend A: every read sees the finished type, and stacked markers give the same code in any order.
decisions.gist: Should a marker reading a type see the members other markers add to it, whatever order they are written in?
decisions.lesson: Markers can write code for you, such as a method that turns a type into JSON. A marker that reads a type's members needs to know whether another marker's additions count. This vote decides what such a read sees, so stacked markers give the same result in any order.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A marker is a # name with a capital letter that runs code while building, such as #Json. Its expansion is the code it adds. To reflect a type is to read its fields, methods and markers while building.

Stacked markers are several markers on one declaration, written #[A, B].
decisions.story: Omar puts #Timestamps and #Json on Order. Timestamps adds a created_at method; Json lists methods to write. Today Json never sees created_at, in either order, and nothing says why.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. What a reflected read made while building sees: in marker expansions, #run values and D-HOOK-STAGES1's declared hook. Checked code after building already sees the finished program. Spelling is settled by D-META-SPELL1=A and D-META-HASH1; wrapping is D-MARKER-CALL1.

Today, with the t6c compiler on dev 76955986d0, the same as the seed. Probe s01 is the same program in today's $ spelling. AddHello adds a hello method; CountMethods counts the target's methods. It prints first sees 0 and second sees 0: inside an expansion, a marker sees only written members, in either order.

Probe s02 reads the same count from a compile-time value after expansion and prints hello, then reflect sees 1: the added method counts there. Probe s03 removes the marker and prints reflect sees 0. So today has two stages: expansions see the written program, and later values see the expanded one.

The rule under A. Every reflected read sees the finished type, whatever order markers are written in. The compiler records what each expansion reads: which type, and which part, such as fields, methods, markers or layout. A read never sees the reader's own additions.

When an expansion adds to a part another expansion already read, the compiler runs the reader again with the new state and replaces its old output. It repeats until nothing read has changed. Expansions are pure apart from the code they add, and D-HOOK-STAGES1 snapshots their file inputs, so a rerun gives the same answer for the same state.

When the answers cannot settle. If a rerun withdraws a member that another expansion already read, the markers disagree, for example one adds b only when a is missing and the other adds a when b exists. That is an error naming both markers, the type and the part, with the chain of reads.

Reruns count against the existing compile-time step budget from D-COMPTIME-WORD1, so a loop ends in that error, not a hang. jet inspect shows each expansion's reads and additions, so the chain can be followed.

What stays ratified. D-META-LADDER1's rewriting through the Compiler value, and D-META-CONTROL2's checked change sets, run after expansion on the finished program, as today. Layout reads wait for the fields they measure, through the same reruns. D-META-REFLECT2's records are unchanged.

Census on dev 76955986d0 over Core, Compiler, Jetpack, Tools, Examples and tests, raw matches in Jet files. There are 73 marker expansions, written expand: fn(, in 65 files. Those files hold 102 reads of fields, methods or markers, with or without $, in 21 files.

There are 45 reflect() calls in 28 files. Stacked markers, a #[ list with two or more names, appear on 268 lines in 163 files.

No expansion in the census reads a member another marker adds, because today none can see one. So A changes no existing result: every read that today sees only written members sees the same members under A, until a second marker adds to that part.

Beginner path. Stack markers in any order; the generated code is the same. A marker that lists methods lists all of them. Expert path. Write markers that build on each other's output. A disagreement is a named error with the chain, not a silent difference.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. Reruns cost build time. Only readers of a part that changed rerun. No expansion today sees another marker's additions, so existing programs need no rerun, and a program pays only where it builds on another marker.

The cost that remains. Two markers that each add only when the other's member is absent can settle in two ways. The compiler then runs them in a fixed order of their full names, never written order, so reordering a stack or moving a declaration cannot change the output. jet inspect shows the chain. Such a pair is rare and is a design smell in any language.

Other options. B keeps today's two stages: expansions see written members only, and later values see everything. C runs stacked markers in written order, as Python's decorators do, so each sees what earlier ones added. D is Rust's: a marker reads only the tokens written on its own item.

E is Zig's: a read of a type first finishes every marker on that type, on demand, and a loop is an error. A marker may then add members only to its own target. Each option's best case: B and D need no reruns; C is easy to explain; E needs no rerun but forbids adding to another type.

options.name: Reads see the finished type
options.detail: Every reflected read sees every member other markers add, in any order. The compiler reruns a reader when a part it read changes, and a disagreement is a named error.
options.technical: Read sets are recorded per type and part: fields, methods, markers, impls and layout. A read excludes the reader's own output. Readers rerun until stable; withdrawal of a read member is an error with the chain. Where two stable answers exist, readers run in the order of their full names, not written order. Reruns count against the existing step budget. LADDER1 rewrites and CONTROL2 change sets run after, unchanged.

options.name: Two stages, as today
options.detail: Expansions see written members only. #run values and checked code see the expanded program.
options.technical: Today's behavior, probes s01 and s02. No reruns. A marker that needs another's output cannot get it.

options.name: Written order
options.detail: Stacked markers run left to right, and each sees what earlier ones added. Declarations expand in source order.
options.technical: One pass in source order. Moving a marker or a declaration can change generated code. No reruns.

options.name: Rust's tokens only
options.detail: A marker reads only the text written on its own item. Reflecting other types while expanding is an error.
options.technical: Removes reflect from expansions; target is the written item. #run values and checked code keep full reflection.

options.name: Zig's on demand
options.detail: Reading a type first finishes every marker on that type. A marker may add members only to its own target, and a loop is an error.
options.technical: Demand-driven expansion per type; a cycle is an error. Forbids impl blocks for any type but the target from inside an expansion.

comparisons.note: A derive or attribute macro sees only the tokens of its item.
@typeInfo analyzes a type on demand; a dependency loop is a compile error.
Stacked decorators apply bottom to top, each to the previous result.

recommendation.why: A makes stacked markers give the same result in any order. Markers can build on each other's output. A disagreement is a named error, never a silent difference.
gains: Stacked markers give the same code in any order.
A marker can build on another marker's members.
No existing result changes.

losses.loss: Reruns cost build time where a part is both read and added to.
losses.mitigation: Only those readers rerun; existing programs need none, and jet inspect shows the chain.

losses.loss: Two markers that each add only when the other's member is absent settle by a fixed order of their names.
losses.mitigation: Written order never matters, the build stays repeatable, and jet inspect shows both markers and the part.

whyNot.reason: B hides every marker's additions from every other marker.
C makes generated code depend on the order markers are written.
D removes reflection from expansions, so a marker cannot read a field's type.
E forbids a marker from adding to any type but its target.

recommendation.tradeoff: Some reruns while building, in return for markers whose order does not matter.

decisions.title: Every module-level value is computed while building, and one that fails or has effects is a build error
decisions.situation:
A value written at the top of a file belongs to the whole program. The rules already say a fixed value there is worked out while building, and a failure is a build error. Today's compiler has not built that yet, so a failing value still builds and stops the program later.

Three kinds of top-level value are still left out of that rule. A shared holder is built the first time it is used, and a foreign call is run once at startup. A value kept across reloads may only be a plain number. This ballot asks whether all three are worked out while building too, so no code runs before the program starts.
decisions.gist: Should every module-level value, including shared holders, foreign calls and reload-kept values, be computed while building?
decisions.lesson: A value written outside any function belongs to the whole file. Most such values are already worked out while building, so a mistake shows up before the program runs. This vote decides whether the last few exceptions follow the same rule.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A module-level value is a name: value written outside every function. Computing while building means the compiler works the value out and stores the result in the program. An effect is something a function does to the world, such as reading a file.

A shared holder is a value that several tasks lock and change. A foreign call runs code from another language. A pinned build input is a file the build reads and records by hash, so the same build always sees the same bytes.

Under A, every top-level value is worked out while building. One that stops, reads the world or cannot be stored is a build error with three fixes: move the work into run, make it a function, or use a pinned build input.

Under B, the ratified rules stay as written. Fixed values and plain changeable values are already worked out while building. A shared holder is still built on first use, a foreign call still runs at startup, and a reload-kept value stays a plain number.

C runs every top-level value at startup, as Go does. D computes each one when it is first read, as Swift does.
decisions.story: Ada's game keeps a shared high-score table and a reload-kept list of best runs at the top of a file. Today the table is built when first touched, and the list must start as a plain number. Under A both are stored in the program, ready before run.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. When the three remaining kinds of top-level value are computed: shared and Atomic holders, foreign-call values, and #Persist initializers. It also restates the whole file-scope rule in one place. Values inside functions keep the ratified tries and quiet fallback, and a file of statements is unaffected.

Ratified law today. D-COMPTIME-WORD1=A already rules that a file-scope immutable value is computed while building, and that a fallback reason there is an error, with E0952 for an exhausted budget. D-JAI-COMPTIME1=A bakes storable changeable globals the same way, but leaves #Persist unchanged.

Still outside that rule. D-CORE-GLOBAL-STATE1=A builds a module Shared holder once, on first access. D-FFI-COMPTIME2=A computes a foreign row once at startup when it cannot fold. #Persist initializers keep E0622, scalar literals only. A closes all three; B keeps them.

Dev has not built the file-scope rule yet, on the t6c compiler (dev 76955986d0). Probe m01 has BAD: 10 / zero(): jet check passes, and jet run stops with E3010 at run time. Probe m07 wraps it in comptime, and jet check reports E3010 at build time. Probe m04's print runs before run.

More dev facts. m03 reads a file and m05 reads the environment at module level, and both build. m11 gets E0622 even for count := square(3), so baked changeable globals are unbuilt too. m12 writes a #Persist shared holder from two tasks and prints dark light. m14's #Persist best := [Int]{} is E0622.

Spelling. #run is D-META-SPELL1=A's ratified spelling, and an unbraced #run takes one call. Dev still spells it comptime { }, and m10's #run embed_file(...) is E0733 today. The embed_file read is recorded with its SHA-256 in the comptime input lock, which is the pinned build input.

The rule under A. Every module-level initializer runs in the build-time engine with the target's facts, as if written with #run. The result is stored in the program, and every tier reads that stored value. Dependencies are computed first, and a cycle is one registered error. No user code runs before run.

Build errors under A, all reported at once. A stop, such as divided by zero. An exhausted budget, E0952, fixed with #StepLimit or a function. An effect: a file, the clock, the environment, the network or print. A value that cannot be stored, such as a file handle. A foreign row that cannot fold.

The three fixes the error offers. Move the work into run and pass the value on. Make it lazy explicitly: a function, marked #Memo when pure, so the first result is kept. For outside data, use a pinned build input: #run embed_file("config.txt"), or a hashed net.fetch. Probe m06 runs all three fix forms today, in today's spelling.

Shared and Atomic holders. A module holder with storable contents is computed while building, and its lock starts as a zeroed word in the program's data, as Rust's const Mutex::new does. This is the one place a shared cell is stored. Inside any other value it stays unstorable, as D-COMPTIME-WORD1 rules.

Each controlled test world starts from its own copy of the baked holder, where today it builds its own cell on entry. So tests still never share a holder with the process default. A retained cell keeps its live value across a reload, as D-CORE-GLOBAL-STATE1 rules.

#Persist values. A storable initializer such as #Persist best := [Int]{} is baked like any changeable global, which lifts E0622 there. jet dev computes a changed initializer at its next build, and a #Persist binding keeps its live value across the reload, as today.

Foreign rows. A foreign row at file scope folds while building when it passes D-FFI-COMPTIME2's fold gate. Otherwise it is the build error, with the same fixes. Foreign rows inside functions keep the startup-once fallback.

What this settles. Nothing runs before run, so loading a library runs none of its code. Every tier reads one stored value, so a value cannot fail on one tier and not another. Startup order disappears, because there is no startup work.

Census on dev, over Core, Compiler, Jetpack, Tools, Examples and tests, package files excluded. 13,519 module value bindings in 2,678 files; 1,284 contain a call. 21 call a files, env, net, sys, time or process function. Seven are pure time functions, and twelve already sit inside comptime, testing its refusals or its hashed fetch.

The last two read the environment at module level: StartupConstants.jet in Examples and one constant-folding fixture. They are build errors under A and under B, because the ratified rule already refuses them. 29 shared module holders in 25 files and 14 #Persist bindings change only in when they are built. embed_file or embed_bytes appears 444 times.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. Each effectful module value must move, and its build error names the effect and the three fixes. jet fix moves a value into run when only run reads it. When other functions read it, the fix refuses and explains how to pass it, as D-ENTRY-EXPLICIT2 requires.

A heavy initializer makes builds slower, where it might otherwise run at startup or on first use. Outcomes are cached per package version, target and compiler, as D-COMPTIME-WORD1 rules, so only a changed initializer is recomputed. #StepLimit bounds the cost, and each build prints the total bytes of stored values.

A large stored value grows the program file. A zero-filled holder or buffer goes in zero-filled data, which costs no file bytes. Anything too large to store is a #Memo function instead.

Other options at their best. B needs no amendment, and a holder nobody touches costs nothing. C is Go's simple startup order. D is lazy, like Rust's LazyLock or Swift's globals, and a value never read is never computed.

Their costs. B keeps two hidden run-time steps and literal-only #Persist. C runs effects before run, so loading a library can touch files and the network. D checks a flag on every read and moves failures to the first read, after the program has started.

decisions.title: A plain module variable is owned by the main task, and the compiler refuses any task that touches it
decisions.situation:
Today a changeable value at the top of a file can be declared, but any function that writes it is refused, even run. The error suggests a shared holder instead. Games and scripts want a plain variable that functions read and write.

The owner asked for one without a written effect on every function. This ballot lets functions write it, and has the compiler refuse any task that touches it. Keeping today's rule is option B.
decisions.gist: May a function read and write a plain module variable directly, with the compiler refusing any task that touches it?
decisions.lesson: A module variable is a name at the top of a file that the program changes as it runs, such as a game's score. This vote decides whether functions may change it directly, and how Jet keeps two tasks from changing it at once.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A module variable is a := name declared at the top of a file. The main task is the one that runs run. A task is work started with task, which may run at the same time as other tasks.

To touch a variable is to read or write it, directly or through a function you call.
decisions.story: Lena writes a small game. Her score lives at the top of the file, and hit adds to it. Today Jet refuses the write and tells her to wrap the score in Shared. Under A it just works. If she later starts hit as a task, the error names score and the path to it.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. Whether functions may read and write a plain module variable, and the rule that keeps that free of data races. Survival across a hot reload is D-PERSIST-ONLY1. How a module value is first computed is D-MODULE-BUILD1.

Today, on the t6c compiler (dev 76955986d0). Probe m01 declares score := 0 and writes it from hit; it gets E0111, module state, so a function can't change it directly. Probe m02 shows even run cannot assign it. Probe m03 marks it #Persist, and the write works and prints score 7.

Probe m05 writes the #Persist binding from a task and from run at the same time. It compiles and runs, so today's grant already allows the race E0111 exists to stop. Probe m04 uses the holder E0111 suggests, written from a function and a task, and prints score 7. D-PERSIST-BORROW1=A keeps ordinary module bindings read-only from functions, which A reverses.

The rule under A, in six parts. One: a := name at file scope is a module variable. Any function that can see it reads and writes it directly. Its first value is computed while building, as D-MODULE-BUILD1 rules.

Two: the compiler infers which module variables each function touches, through calls, closures and function values. Hover and docs show it. It is never written in a signature.

Three: the main task owns every module variable. Starting a task whose work touches one, or sending a closure that touches one to a task, is a build error. It names the variable and the call path and offers two fixes: pass the value in, or keep it in Shared.

So no data race is possible: only the main task ever runs code that touches a module variable. The fact is deny-only, like Panic and Mem. Nobody writes State on a function; a ceiling may write !State to promise no module state, and that denial is optional.

Four: function values carry the fact in their type, as they carry inferred effects. A helper that starts f as a task requires f to be free of module state, so passing a touching closure fails at the caller's line. A dynamic call counts as touching whatever any of its possible targets touch.

Five: no write behind a reader's back. Holding a borrow of a module variable, such as looping over enemies, while calling a function that writes the same variable is a build error naming that call. It is the rule locals already follow, made static because touches are known.

Six: packages and tests. A library's module variables belong to the main task of the program using it, and a public function's touches appear in its docs. jet test gives each test its own copy of every module variable, as D-CORE-GLOBAL-STATE1=A gives each test world its own shared cell. Each test is the main task of its world, so tests stay parallel.

Files of statements. D-FILE-STATEMENTS1, still open, makes a top-level binding in a file of statements a local of that program, which functions do not see. A keeps that: this rule governs := bindings in files with run: fn and in libraries. So one line never switches between a local and a module variable under this ballot.

Hot reload. Under D-JAI-COMPTIME1=A a module variable keeps its live value across a swap unless its starting value changed. #Persist also keeps it across a stop and start, as D-DEV-STATE1=A rules, and under D-PERSIST-ONLY1 that is all #Persist means. The runtime's own raw words keep the #Unsafe escape E0111 offers today, with their stated reasons.

Census on dev, over Core, Compiler, Jetpack, Tools, Examples and tests, package files excluded. File-scope := bindings: 164 in 93 files, 125 of them in 63 Compiler/JetRuntime files, where writes sit in #Unsafe blocks. #Persist bindings: 14 in 14 files, all scalar literals. shared module holders: 29 in 25 files.

None of these breaks under A. The holders stay correct, and each may become a plain variable when no task touches it.

Beginner path. Write score := 0 and change it from any function. Expert path. Write !State on a ceiling to promise a function never touches module state, and ask jet inspect which functions touch which variable.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. A task cannot touch a module variable at all, even to read it. That is the price of no races. Fixed module values written with : stay readable from every task, and under D-MUT-NEVER1=A a := that nothing changes is already an error. So only values that really change are owned.

For those, the error says which variable and the call path, and offers Shared, the cross-task holder, so the fix is one line.

Inference across packages could make a library change break a caller, if a function starts touching a variable. The touch fact is part of the public surface, so docs and hover show it, and jet update reports a dependency whose public function newly touches module state.

What remains. In test builds, a module variable is reached through the test's world, one extra load per access. Release and jet run builds keep the plain address, so only the test tier pays it.

Other options. B keeps today: functions read but never write module state, and every write goes through Shared. C is Swift's way: a marker names the owner on the variable and on every function that touches it. D is Go's: plain variables, with a race detector for tests. E is Rust's thread_local: each task gets its own copy.

Their best cases. B needs no new rule and makes every shared write visible. C makes ownership explicit where it is declared. D has zero friction. E never refuses a program. Their costs: B and C add ceremony to the common single-task case, D allows real races, and E silently loses a task's writes.

Touch sets are deny-only facts on function types, like Panic and Mem; task spawn requires none. Static exclusivity on borrows across touching calls. #Unsafe raw writes stay.

Closes the race today's #Persist grant allows.

losses.mitigation: Fixed : values stay readable everywhere; the error names the variable and path and offers Shared, a one-line fix.

losses.loss: In test builds, a module variable access costs one extra load.
losses.mitigation: It buys a private copy per test, so tests stay parallel; other builds keep the plain address.

whyNot.reason: B makes the common single-task case wrap every counter in Shared.
C writes an owner the compiler can infer on every declaration.
D allows real races and finds them only when a test hits one.
E silently drops a task's writes, which surprises everyone.

decisions.title: Byte streams gain read_into, which appends what arrives to a caller-owned buffer, so a steady read loop allocates nothing
decisions.situation:
Every read from a network connection hands back a fresh piece of memory holding the bytes. The runtime fills its own reusable block, then copies the bytes into a new list for the caller. The web server and the encrypted-connection reader then append that list to a buffer they already own.

So each read asks for memory and copies twice. The recommendation is A: a read form that appends straight into a buffer the caller owns, so a steady read loop stops asking for memory.
decisions.gist: Should byte streams gain read_into, which appends what arrives to a buffer the caller owns, so steady reads allocate nothing?
decisions.lesson: Reading from a network connection today hands back a fresh piece of memory each time. Busy servers read thousands of times a second. This vote decides whether Jet adds a way to read into memory the program already holds.
decisions.explainer: Words used here. A buffer is a byte list a program keeps and reuses. A short read returns fewer bytes than the limit. Allocation is asking for new memory.
decisions.story: Ana's proxy forwards traffic in a loop. Under A, she keeps one buffer, clears it after each forward, and the loop asks for no new memory once it has warmed up.
decisions.inWild:
// Go: Read fills a slice the caller owns.
n, err := conn.Read(buf)
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. Whether byte streams get a read form that writes into a caller's buffer, and its shape. read(limit) stays.

Today, with the a0.0.43 compiler (dev c460ba91e5). Probe r02 reads a local TCP pair in a loop of server.read(4096) and prints read 4. Probe r03 calls server.read_into(buffer, 4096) and gets E0102, TCPStream has no method read_into.

Where the cost is. net_tcp_read_result in Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/NetHandleRoutes.jet:67-118 now reuses a per-stream read block (net_read_buffer_take, :175). It still allocates a 48-byte scratch per call (:78). net_read_publish_bytes (:208-211) allocates an exact-size list and copies the bytes into it.

The hot callers on dev. Core/Http/Server.jet:1217 and 1226, Core/Http/Client.jet:735 and 746, Core/Net/Tls.jet:1104 and Core/Net/Net.jet:287. Tls.jet:1106 extends its own rx buffer with each result, the exact append A performs in place.

The per-stream block reuse that an earlier draft called pending has landed on dev. It removed the limit-sized allocation, but the exact-size list and its copy remain, so D's internal-reuse path is already spent.

Measured on a0.0.43, built programs, five runs each. 100,000 rounds of a 4,096-byte write and read on a local TCP pair take 1.09 s median (m1), about 11 µs a round. Appending each chunk to a held buffer, as TLS does, measures the same within noise (m2, 0.98 s).

Copying a 4,096-byte list 100,000 times takes 0.026 s median (m3), about 0.26 µs. So the list and copy A removes are about 2% of a local read round. Peak memory stayed near 14.5 MB in every run.

The case for A is therefore a loop that asks for no memory, which D-FREESTAND-ALLOCAPI1=A asks of Core and which devices need. It is not raw speed.

The paired cell. A arrives with a two-program cell in the canonical performance manifest, as AGENTS.md requires of a surface added for performance. One program loops on read(4096); its twin does the same work with read_into into one held buffer.

The pair records wall time, allocations per read and peak memory. Ratification waits until read_into strictly beats read on it; any loss stays on a card.

What A does. n: stream.read_into(buffer, limit) appends at most limit bytes to the end of buffer and returns the count, 0 at end of stream. A limit below 1 is an invalid-input error, so 0 always means end of stream. A deadline form, read_into(buffer, limit, deadline:), matches read's.

It takes buffer by & as the parameter declares, so the call passes plain buffer. Bytes go straight from the socket into buffer's spare room, and the read's scratch lives with the stream. The list grows only when that room is short. TCP, Unix and TLS streams and file readers get the same method.

Clear already keeps a byte list's room when the list is not shared (Compiler/JetIR/Source/BuildExpr.jet:3093-3117). So a loop that clears buffer after use stops allocating after the first reads. If the loop hands the bytes somewhere that keeps them, clear gives buffer fresh room; the kept bytes need their own memory anyway.

Precedent. Core's encoders already read this way through a private core.encoding.__read_into, used by Csv.jet, Stream.jet and Xml.jet. A makes the same move public, without that helper's empty-list rule.

Ratified decisions. A fits D-FREESTAND-ALLOCAPI1=A, which prefers caller-owned buffers in Core. It keeps D-NETIO-CONTRACT1=A and D-NETIO-CONTRACT2=B: the Reader trait keeps exactly read, and read_into is an inherent method.

Beginner path. Keep writing chunk: stream.read(4096); nothing changes. Expert path. Hold one buffer and call read_into in the loop; the HTTP server and TLS reader switch the same way.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. Generic Reader code cannot call read_into. The four hot stream types cover the measured callers, and a trait default can follow later without breaking them.

What remains. A buffer that is never cleared keeps growing. That is the caller's list, visible in their code, and the limit caps each read.

Other options. B fills from index 0 up to the buffer's length, as TlsLead first drafted and as Go does. C adds read_into to the Reader trait for every Core byte source. D adds nothing and relies on internal reuse.

Their best cases. B matches Go and Rust slices. C makes middleware generic. D adds no surface. Their costs: B needs a zero-filled buffer, which Core can only build by pushing bytes, and appenders still copy. C amends D-NETIO-CONTRACT2's trait law. D keeps one allocation and copy per read.

decisions.title: No warnings: jet fmt rewrites style, tidy errors never stop jet run or jet dev, and jet check and jet build list them and fail
decisions.situation:
The owner agreed that Jet should have no warnings: a finding is an error or nothing. The owner added a builder-friendly rule. Tidiness never stops jet run or jet dev, while jet check and jet build list everything and fail, so the list is a to-do list.

The ratified rule says warnings and lints never fail a build by default. This ballot reverses it and changes how four ratified checks report their findings, without changing what they find. Keeping today's rule is option B.
decisions.gist: Should Jet drop warnings, so jet fmt fixes style and jet check fails on untidy code that jet run still runs?
decisions.lesson: A warning is a message that says something may be wrong but lets the program build anyway. People learn to ignore them, and real problems hide among them. This vote decides whether Jet keeps warnings, or makes each finding a style fix, a listed error, or nothing.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A lint is a check for code that works but is probably not what was meant, such as an import nothing uses. Style is how code is laid out and spelled when the meaning is the same.

A tidy error is a new kind of finding under A. It never stops jet run, jet dev or jet test, and it makes jet check and jet build fail.
decisions.story: Ada's game runs, and jet check prints four warnings and says ok. She ships it. Months later the warnings number two hundred, and the one that mattered, a never-read result, is lost among them.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. How findings that are not plain errors reach the user, and which commands fail on them. It does not change what any check finds. Real errors, where a program has no single meaning, stop every command as today.

Today, on the t6c compiler (dev 76955986d0). Probe n01 has an unused import, an unused local, a final return, a positional Bool argument and an unused private function. jet run prints TOTAL 6 and exits 0. jet check prints four warnings, now shown by name: PositionalBoolParameter, RedundantFinalReturn, UnusedLocalBinding and UnusedImport. It ends ok with 4 warnings and exits 0; jet build prints none and exits 0.

No unused-function finding fires for the unused helper in a loose file. Probe n02, a := that never changes, gets no finding at all, so D-MUT-NEVER1's ratified error is still not built. Probe n03 writes loud: true at the call, and PositionalBoolParameter still fires on the declaration.

Under A, every current lint goes to exactly one of three places. First, style: a rewrite with one certain result goes to jet fmt, which applies it. Second, tidy errors: a finding that needs a person's choice is listed with its fix. Third, advice that is not about wrong code leaves the diagnostic stream and becomes a report command.

Style moves to jet fmt. Examples are a redundant final return (L0530), a redundant unit binding (L0531), compound assignment (L0503) and a positional Bool argument (L2401). For L2401, jet fmt writes the parameter's label at each call, as n03 shows by hand, and the declaration lint is deleted. Style never fails any command; jet fmt --check exists for CI.

Tidy errors keep their code, Why and Fix. Examples are unused imports, locals, parameters and private functions (L0101 to L0104), unreachable arms and code, a constant loop condition, a discarded value, a zero divisor, and floats compared with ==. D-MUT-NEVER1's never-changed :=, D-MEMBER-LIVE1's unread fields and D-IDENT-CHARS1's look-alike names become tidy errors too.

D-SHAPE-INTERNAL1's one unsuppressible warning on pub _name becomes an unsuppressible tidy error. Tidy errors are reported with error severity in the editor, and in JSON output they carry kind tidy, so a tool can tell them from real errors.

Advice becomes reports. Performance hints such as growth in a loop (L0505), hidden allocation (L0506) and whole-file reads (L2501) leave the diagnostic stream. So do complexity (L2902), undocumented public items (L2201) and doctor advice (L2101). They move under jet lint, which already takes --complexity and --a11y, and which fails only when --max is given.

Which command does what under A. jet run, jet dev and jet test never stop or print for tidy errors; jet dev's status line shows their count. jet check and jet build list every tidy error with every real error, collect-all, and exit 1 if there is any. The list is the to-do list the owner asked for.

Whose to-do list. Tidy errors are listed only for the packages being checked or built: the entry package and workspace members. A dependency's tidy errors never fail its consumer; its own jet check lists them for its author. Findings inside code made by #run, derives or templates are reported at the written template when it is in the package, and dropped otherwise.

Saying a finding is intended. #Allow(jet.Name, "reason") is a marker that exists today, with 52 uses on dev, such as #Allow(jet.RedundantFinalReturn, ...). It removes one tidy error at one site, and its reason is required. The build report lists every #Allow, so a reviewer sees each exception. Real errors and unsuppressible tidy errors ignore it.

Migration. Compiler/Prelude/Diagnostics.jet registers 69 L and W codes on dev, and DiagnosticRows.jet mirrors the same 69. Each code gets one of the three places in the cutover, by the rule above. On the seed, docs mentioned L and W codes 14,182 times, mostly in generated pages that regenerate.

Existing code that warns today will fail jet check and jet build under A. The first run lists every item, so a package sees its whole to-do list at once. jet fix applies every fix that is certain, such as deleting an unused import, and jet fmt applies style.

Beginner path. jet run always runs a program that has a meaning, however untidy. Before sharing it, jet check lists what to clean, each item with its fix, and the list ends at zero.

Expert path. CI runs jet check, jet build and jet fmt --check; all three must pass. #Allow(jet.Name, "reason") records a deliberate exception, and jet lint --complexity or --a11y with --max adds stricter reports where a team wants them.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. A package that builds today with warnings fails jet build after the cutover. jet fix and jet fmt clear the certain items in one run, and jet run keeps working while the rest is cleaned.

A half-finished edit with an unused local cannot pass jet check, even when the author means to finish it later. The author either names it _name, as the fix says, or keeps running with jet run and jet dev, which never stop for it.

Other options. B keeps D-LINTPOLICY1: warnings stay, and they never fail a build. C is Go's rule: unused imports and locals are real errors in every command, jet run included, and other checks move to a separate vet command. D is Rust's rule: warnings stay by default, and a project setting or flag turns every warning into a failure for CI.

C is the strictest, and it stops a quick experiment for an unused name, which the owner's rule says tidiness must never do. D keeps warnings for people who do not turn on the setting, so the ignored-warnings problem stays for most users.

decisions.title: #Persist means only that a value survives a hot reload, and writes follow the one module-variable rule
decisions.situation:
The owner agreed that #Persist should mean only that a value survives a reload. Today the marker also makes the value writable from functions and lets it be handed to a write parameter. No other module value gets either right.

This ballot removes both write rights from the marker. Who may change a module value is then one rule for every module value. That rule is decided by the open module-variable ballot, so the two are coupled, and the cutover waits for it. Keeping today's grant is option B.
decisions.gist: Should #Persist only keep a value across a hot reload, leaving who may change it to the module-variable rule?
decisions.lesson: jet dev can swap in edited code while a game keeps running. #Persist marks a value, such as a score, that keeps its contents through that swap. Today the marker also decides who may change the value. This vote decides whether it does only the first job.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A hot reload is jet dev replacing changed code in a running program. A module variable is a name := value written outside every function.

A write parameter, written &Int, lets a function change the caller's value. A shared holder, written shared Score{…}, is a value several tasks may change safely.
decisions.story: Ada marks her score #Persist so playtests keep it through edits. She then marks an unrelated counter #Persist too, only because that is the one way a function may change it. Now the counter also survives reloads, which she never wanted.
decisions.inWild:
; Clojure: defonce survives a reload; the atom does the writes.
(defonce score (atom 0))
(swap! score inc)
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. Only what the #Persist marker grants. It does not decide whether functions may write a plain module variable; that is the open module-variable proposal. Survival itself, its identity by module path and name, the announced restart on a layout change and D-LIVE-PERSIST1's migrations stay as ratified.

Today, on the t6c compiler (dev 76955986d0), every probe p01 to p11 matches the seed. Probe p01 writes a plain score := 0 from a function and gets E0111, whose fix offers a shared holder, #Persist, or #Unsafe. Probe p07 shows that run itself cannot write a plain module variable either. Probe p02 marks the binding #Persist, and the same write works and prints score 1.

Probe p03 hands a #Persist binding to a function taking total: &Int, and it prints score 1; today's call site writes add_point(score) with no &. Probe p04 hands a local of run the same way, and it works. Probe p06 hands a plain module variable the same way and gets E0223, PersistentMutableBorrow. Probe p05 reads a #Persist value without writing it and prints best 10.

Probe p09 builds a module-level holder, SCORE: shared Count{value: 0}, writes SCORE.value += 1 from a function, and prints score 1. Probe p08 marks the same holder #Persist and gets E0622, ModuleGlobalNotLiteral, so D-CORE-GLOBAL-STATE1's persisted holder is ratified but not built. The open D-MODULE-BUILD1=A lifts E0622 for storable initializers. E0111's fix shows the holder with a lowercase name, which fails the constant casing rule.

What survival means, exactly. Under D-JAI-COMPTIME1=A, a jet dev swap already keeps every module variable's live value unless its starting value changed. #Persist adds the two cases a plain value loses. It is kept when its starting value is edited, and kept across a jet dev restart as D-DEV-STATE1=A rules, while its name and type still fit.

The rule under A. #Persist grants survival and nothing else. It grants no write access and no write parameter passing. A #Persist binding is written exactly where a plain module variable of the same kind may be written, and refused with the same error where one may not.

With today's module rule, a function cannot write a #Persist scalar. The form for changing pinned state is a holder: #Persist SCORE: shared Score{value: 0}, written SCORE.value += 1, in today's holder spelling. Probe p08 shows it is not built yet. Survival comes from the marker and safe writes come from the holder, as Clojure's defonce and atom split them.

If the open module-variable ballot passes as recommended, score := 0 becomes writable from functions on the main task, and #Persist score := 0 is writable by that same rule. A task still cannot touch it, which closes the race today's grant allows: a task can write a #Persist score while run does. No marker then changes who may write.

The coupling, engineered so no game loses pinned state. A's cutover lands in the same change as the module-variable outcome. If you accept the proposal, the write grant moves from the marker to the plain rule, and no #Persist program changes. If not, the cutover lands with D-CORE-GLOBAL-STATE1's persisted holder built, and jet fix rewrites each written #Persist scalar into a holder.

D-PERSIST-BORROW1's write parameter rule follows the same law. A #Persist binding may be handed to a &Int parameter exactly when a plain module variable may. Today that is E0223 for both; the module-variable outcome decides it for both at once.

Error texts. E0111's fix drops the or mark it #Persist choice from both of its copies, because the marker no longer grants writes. Its holder example is written SCORE: shared Count{value: 0}, with the constant casing; if D-SHARED-TYPE1 respells holders, the text follows it. E0223 stops naming #Persist as the exception.

Migration, a census on dev. There are 14 #Persist module bindings, all scalar; one is Examples/Tooling/DevLoop/Persist.jet and the rest are tests. #Persist appears 62 times in 32 Jet files, mostly Compiler source and fixtures, and 55 times in 18 Markdown files. On the seed, 10 of the bindings were written by a function in the same file.

Beginner path. Mark game state #Persist to keep it while editing. Change it the same way as any module value; the error that refuses a write names the holder, and later the plain variable, as the fix.

Expert path. Survival and write access are separate decisions, so a cache can be persisted read-only, and a holder can be shared between tasks without surviving reloads. Each property is visible in one place.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. Until the module-variable outcome lands, a written #Persist scalar needs a holder, which is longer than score += 1. The cutover never lands before the holder or the plain rule is built, and jet fix writes the holder.

A holder for a scalar needs a one-field struct today, because probe p10 shows shared 0 refuses SCORE += 1 and printing. That scalar ergonomics question is part of the open module-state proposal, and A does not depend on its answer.

Other options. B keeps D-PERSIST-DEVSTATE1: #Persist both survives reloads and grants writes. C is Elm's model: no module value survives; run keeps its state in a local, and jet dev hands run's state value to the reloaded code. D is a Smalltalk or Lisp image: every module variable survives a reload, with no marker.

C changes how every game is written, since state must flow through run and its callees. D keeps stale values the author meant to reset, such as a constant table they just edited.

decisions.title: Keep <> in every pipe step, and let E0438's fix write it into the missing first slot
decisions.situation:
A pipe step is a line starting with |>, and <> inside it stands for the value from the line above. The ratified rule says every step writes <> at least once; a step without it is an error.

The review asked whether a step without <> should pass the value as the first argument, as Elixir does. The owner kept <>, because it marks where piped data goes. A keeps the rule and makes the error's fix write <> for you; B is the review's proposal.
decisions.gist: Should a pipe step keep writing <>, or should a call step without <> take the value as its first argument?
decisions.lesson: A pipe passes a value down a chain of steps. Jet marks where the value lands with <>, as in |> add(<>, 10). Some languages drop the mark and put the value first. This vote decides whether Jet's steps keep the mark.
decisions.explainer: Words used here. A pipe step is a line starting with |>. <> stands for the value from the step above. E0438 is the error for a step that never uses <>. A fix is the rewrite an error offers to apply for you.
decisions.story: Ivo writes |> double() and |> add(10) out of Elixir habit and gets E0438 twice. Under A, jet fix turns the first into double(<>). For add, both slots take an Int, so his editor offers add(<>, 10) first, and a later reader sees exactly where the value went.
decisions.inWild:
# Elixir: the value is the first argument of each call step.
3
|> double()
|> add(10)
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. Whether a pipe step may leave out <>. Pipes themselves, the <> glyph and the ?? return fallback of D-PIPE1=A are unchanged.

Today, on the t6c compiler (dev 76955986d0), as on the seed. Probe p02 writes 3 |> double(<>) |> add(<>, 10) and prints 16, and 3 |> add(10, <>) prints 13. Probe p01 writes |> double, |> double() and |> add(10), and each is E0438, PipeStepWithoutValue. Its fix today is general: write <> where the value goes, or end the pipe before this step.

Probe p03 writes |> print("done") in the middle of a pipe. That is also E0438, and here the error is doing its job: the step ignored the value, which is almost always a mistake.

The rule under A. Every step writes <>, as ratified, and E0438's fix gets exact. A bare function name of one parameter becomes name(<>). A call exactly one argument short becomes a call with <> in the one slot whose parameter accepts the value's type. A name that is only a method of the value's type becomes <>.name(…).

No silent wrong placement. jet fix applies the fix only when exactly one placement fits. When several slots accept the type, as in add(10) with two Int parameters, the error lists each placement. The editor offers each, first slot first, and jet fix leaves the site for a person. Otherwise the fix stays the general one.

So the typing cost of the mark becomes one jet fix, and the reader still sees where the value lands in every step.

Census on dev, unchanged from the seed. Pipes are rare. 13 lines in 4 Jet files start with a step. Outside the compiler's message strings, 18 steps sit in 7 files. 5 pass <> as the whole first argument and 5 call a method on it there, as Int.parse(<>.trim()). 4 put it in a condition, a lambda or a comparison, and 4 are error tests with no <>.

So 9 of the 14 working steps would need <> even under a first-argument rule, and those steps would mix two styles.

Beginner path. Write <> where the value goes; if you forget, jet fix writes it. Expert path. The same rule everywhere: a step is any expression, and <> may appear more than once or deep inside.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. A step written the Elixir way fails once. The improved fix rewrites it exactly, so the cost is one command, not a lookup.

What remains. The common first-argument step carries two characters, <> and a comma, that Elixir leaves out. That is the price of the mark you chose to keep.

Other options. B is the review's proposal, guarded: a call one argument short takes the value first, so a complete call like print("done") still fails. C is Elixir's rule unguarded. D is F#'s bare function name. E fills the last argument, as OCaml and F# do.

Their best cases. B shortens 5 steps with no silent change to a complete call. C is the shortest. D reads cleanly for one-argument functions. E suits curried libraries.

Their costs. B leaves no mark, so a reader must know the callee's arity to see where the value goes. C turns a forgotten value into a silent wrong call. D adds a second step form. E puts the value where Jet's argument order rarely expects it.

options.name: Keep <>; a better fix
options.detail: Every step writes <>, as ratified. E0438's fix writes <> into the one slot that fits, and offers each slot when several do.
options.technical: D-PIPE1=A unchanged. E0438 fix: a bare one-parameter name gets (<>); a call with exactly one required argument missing gets <> in the one slot that accepts the piped type; a method-only name gets <>.name(…). jet fix applies it only when one placement fits; with several, the editor offers each and jet fix leaves the site.

options.name: First argument, guarded

options.technical: Reverses D-PIPE1=A's every-step clause. A complete call gains an argument; E0438 remains only for non-call steps.

options.name: Bare function name

options.technical: F#'s point-free step. A second step form beside expressions with <>.

A forgotten value is still caught.
The Elixir habit costs one jet fix.

losses.mitigation: jet fix inserts it; it is the mark you chose to keep.

whyNot.reason: B hides where the value goes behind the callee's arity.
C turns a forgotten value into a silent wrong call.

recommendation.tradeoff: Two characters per step, for a visible value everywhere.
