decisions.title: Types as values and type switches, amending the ratified TypeKey
decisions.situation:
A ratified rule gives a running program an opaque key object that carries a type's exact identity; it is not built yet. The owner later asked why types as values would be a downside, since they allow switches on types. This ballot offers that: a type's own name becomes a value of type Type where a Type is expected.

Option A amends the ratified key and two reflection rules: that types stay types, and that one reflect call handles every value. Options B and F keep the ratified key. The owner's question is not itself a ratification.
decisions.gist: Should a type name be usable as a value of type Type, so programs can key maps and switch on types?
decisions.lesson: A running program sometimes needs to treat a type as data: count game components by type, or pick a handler for each kind of message. Today Jet has an approved but unbuilt key object for that. This vote decides whether the type's own name can be that value instead, with a switch on it.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A type's identity is what makes two types the same or different; Box<Int> and Box<String> differ, and two names for one type agree. A type switch picks an arm by a type's identity. It does not convert a value.

A descriptor is the small record a running program keeps for one type's identity. Type info, under D-REFLECT-TYPEINFO1, is the larger record of fields and methods kept for reflection.
decisions.story: Rui writes a game whose systems count components by type and describe each kind. Today the display path of a value's type is his only key, and probe k07 shows Box<Int> and Box<String> print the same path. He wants to write counts[Position] and a switch on the type.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. Whether a running program names a type with a Type value whose source spelling is the type's own name, and switches on it. It amends D-PRIM-TYPEKEY1=A, which chose an opaque reflect.TypeKey. It also amends two rules of D-REFLECT-TYPEINFO1: types stay types, and one reflect call handles every value. Options B and F keep the key as ratified.

Today, on the t6c compiler (dev 76955986d0), as on the seed. Generic type switches work: k01's if T == { } prints a different line for each component type, and k02 and k03 fail with E0003 without else. k07 shows reflect.of(x).path() is the same for Box<Int> and Box<String>. t: Rock is E0636, TypeAsValue (p09), and type_of is E0102 (k08, p08).

More facts on t6c. The ratified TypeKey is not built: dev has no TypeKey or reflect.key in any Jet file. A user type named Type is legal (k05), and a local declaration can shadow a Prelude name such as Dyn (k04). p05 shows a closed enum switch with no else. None of these probes runs A, B's key or E.

The rule under A. Type is a Prelude type whose values are type identities. A bare type name is a Type value only where a Type is expected. Those places are a parameter, field or result of type Type, a [Type: V] map key and a [Type] list element. They also include the other side of == with a Type, and a switch pattern on a Type.

Anywhere else a bare type name stays a type, so t: Rock is still E0636. Its fix offers Rock{…} for a value, or Type{Rock} for a Type value, the same typed-literal form as U8{1}. So a missing constructor brace can never bind a Type by accident, but a Type-accepting call still accepts any type identity, whether intended or not.

Identity. Two Type values are equal when they name the same type, as D-PRIM-TYPEKEY1 already requires. Aliases agree. Nominal types differ even with equal fields. Generic instances differ by their arguments. A function type's identity is its full signature, as D-META-REFLECT2's CallableSignature records it: parameter types and passing modes, result, error contract, effect row, calling convention and generic bindings.

Callable identity reuses canonical sema equality, including labels, zones, access modes, view provenance and identity-bearing policies. Defaults remain facts, not evaluated identity inputs. A Type value grants no authority: it cannot construct, cast, call, or reach private members. It is a plain value that compares, hashes, prints and can be sent between tasks.

type_of. type_of(x) gives the static type of x, worked out while compiling. Its argument must be a name or a field path such as p or p.pos. A call or other expression is an error whose fix is to bind the value first. So type_of reads no value, borrows nothing, runs nothing and has no effects.

Erased values. For a value whose static type is an erased carrier, such as Dyn, a trait value or the Any of D-PRIM-ANY1, type_of gives the carrier's type, never the payload's. The payload's identity comes from the carrier itself, as box.type under D-PRIM-ANY1. So one name never means two different things.

Type switches. if t == { Position -> … else -> … } on a Type value compares identity at run time, arm by arm. Type is an open set, so else is required, as for generic switches today. A duplicate arm is an error. The switch binds no payload; taking a payload out of an erased value is the Any ballot's job. if T == { } on a generic parameter stays a compile-time choice.

Printing and names. print(t) shows the type's full package path, such as game.Position or game.Box<Int>. When two linked packages share a path, such as two versions of one package, the display adds the version. Equality never compares display text, so a display collision cannot make two types equal. Version alone may not distinguish separately loaded packages with equal name and version; display also needs a package-identity qualifier then.

Reflection, an explicit amendment. D-REFLECT-TYPEINFO1 lets one reflect call handle every value. A amends that for one written type: reflect(t), where t is written with static type Type, is a compile error. The error says t names a type, and offers t.info() for the type it names, or reflect(Type) for the info of Type itself.

Inside generic code, reflect(x) on a parameter of type T keeps its value meaning even when T is Type. It then gives the info of Type itself, an opaque Prelude type with no public fields. So a generic helper never reads a Type value as if it were the type it names.

The schema. t.info() returns the same reflection value that reflect(T) returns for the type t names, or an InfoError. InfoError has two cases, each naming the type and its package. NotKept means the image that declares the type kept no info for it. Unloaded means that package's code has been released. The Type value itself is inspected with print(t), ==, hashing, and reflect(Type).

The strongest same-call alternative makes reflect(t) reflect the type t names, with no second operation. It is shorter. But then either reflect's meaning depends on whether the call sits in generic code, or a generic helper reads a Type value as a Position. A refuses only the written case that would mislead. E shares A's rule; B and F leave reflect unchanged.

A Type value is one word. It is the same 56-bit key of canonical identity that dev's trait values already carry in their first word (JetIR BuildTraits.jet), and the key D-PRIM-ANY1's box checks. Equality is one compare, and hashing reads the word. Two identities sharing a key stop the build, and keys of separately built packages are compared at load.

What the program keeps, by setting. Each type that becomes a Type value keeps a descriptor holding its key and display path, under every setting including none. Fields and methods are not in it. Under none, t.info() is a registered compile error naming the type_info setting.

Under requested, the default, reflect calls keep what D-REFLECT-TYPEINFO1 says. A program that calls t.info() also keeps the type info of every type that becomes a Type value somewhere in it. The build report lists those types and their sizes, so the cost is visible. reachable and full keep their ratified retention rules.

Descriptors across packages. Each type identity has one descriptor per process. The linker merges descriptors by identity: canonical package identity including checked content, module path, declaration revision, then generic type and value arguments, recursively. A package loaded while running adds its descriptors to the process table and reuses any that already exist.

Packages loaded while running. Each image, the program or a loaded package, keeps type info by its own build's rules. A package built for loading keeps info for every type it exports or makes into a Type value, since its loader may call t.info(). Its build report lists that cost. Kept info includes the field type graph, transitively, as D-REFLECT-TYPEINFO1's type graphs do.

Privacy. t.info() shows the members visible to the calling code: public members always, and package-private ones only when the caller is in the type's own package. The check compares package identities at run time, so a Type value from a loaded package grants no new access.

Code lifetime. A type info value holds method, default and body references into its package's code, and so does a function value. The loader counts these references for each loaded package. Unloading retires a package at once for new lookups, but its code and info stay resident until that count reaches zero. Type values hold only descriptors, so they never keep code alive.

After release, t.info() on that package's types returns Unloaded, and no stale method reference can run. Descriptors are never freed, so unloading cannot leave a Type value pointing at nothing. Identity is session-local, as D-PRIM-TYPEKEY1 says: it is not a format to store or send between processes.

Hot reload. A type's identity includes its declaration revision and the identities of its field types, recursively; mutually recursive types are hashed as one group. When Position's shape changes, every type that holds a Position, such as Box<Position>, gets a new identity too. A type whose transitive field types are unchanged keeps its identity.

The real cost of never freeing descriptors, and its bound. Only hot reload grows the table: a reload that changes no type's shape adds nothing, and a release program never reloads. As an unmeasured estimate, 1,000 reloads that each change 50 types keep 50,000 descriptors of a key and a path, a few megabytes.

A jet dev restart frees them, and D-DEV-STATE1=A keeps every #Persist value across that restart. A loaded package adds its descriptors once per distinct identity, so loading the same package again adds none.

The name Type. A user declaration named Type shadows the Prelude Type in its own module, as k04 shows for Dyn; core.Type stays reachable. The census finds one user declaration named Type, in Compiler. jet fix offers a rename, by declaration identity.

Migration from the ratified key. reflect.TypeKey becomes Type, reflect.key<T>() becomes T in a Type context or Type{T}, and reflect.of(x).key() becomes type_of(x). The old names are removed in the same change, with no aliases. The census finds no use of TypeKey or reflect.key in code, because the key is not built, so the code migration is empty.

Other counts, by git grep -c on dev. There are 59 calls to reflect.of in 29 files, which keep working, and 6 mentions of type_of in 3 files. The seed's census found 12 generic type switches, which keep working. These are regex counts.

Beginner path. Write counts[Position] = 2 and if t == { Position -> … }. If you write t: Rock by mistake, the error offers Rock{…} or Type{Rock}.

Expert path. Function types, generic instances and types from loaded packages all have exact identity. The build report lists what t.info() keeps, and type_info none forbids it. t.info() returns NotKept or Unloaded instead of guessing, and an unloaded package's code stays resident while any info or function value still refers to it.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. A program that calls t.info() keeps type info for every type it makes into a Type value. The build report names that cost, and generic reflect(T) avoids it. Descriptors are never freed, so repeated hot reloads grow memory without bound until the dev process restarts.

Type joins the Prelude, so a user type named Type now shadows it; that affects one declaration in the tree. A bare type name is a value in some places and a type in others. Those places are exactly where a Type is expected, and every other place reports E0636 with both fixes. reflect(t) on a written Type is refused, so reflection gains a second operation, t.info().

Option B in full. Keep D-PRIM-TYPEKEY1=A: reflect.TypeKey, reflect.key<T>() and reflect.of(x).key(), with the same exact identity, session-local meaning and descriptor lifetime. Branching uses chains of if key == comparisons; there is no type switch on a key. Nothing is migrated, and type names never appear in value position.

Option C repeals D-PRIM-TYPEKEY1. Maps are keyed by display paths from reflect.of(x).path(), derived rather than typed by hand. Two types with the same path collide, as k07 shows for generic instances. D also repeals the runtime key and keeps only generic switches on type parameters, so a runtime registry falls back to paths.

Option E. Runtime Type handles and type switches through a library constructor: reflect.type<T>() makes a reflect.Type, and type_of(x) returns one. Type names stay types except in switch patterns. It shares A's identity, retention and descriptor rules, and replaces TypeKey rather than living beside it.

Alternative F separates two choices that A bundles: exact-key switching and bare type names as values. Its only new surface is a checked comparison table on TypeKey. Its descriptors and lifetime are the ratified key mechanism, not another type representation.

options.name: A type name is a Type value wherever a Type is expected
options.detail: counts[Position] = 2 and describe(Position) pass the type itself, and if t == { Position -> … } switches on it. Elsewhere a type name stays a type, and Type{Rock} makes a Type value explicitly. type_of(p) gives the static type of a name or field.
options.technical: Amends D-PRIM-TYPEKEY1=A and two D-REFLECT-TYPEINFO1 rules: types stay types, and one reflect call for every value. reflect(t) on a written Type is refused, and t.info() returns info or an InfoError, NotKept or Unloaded. Prelude Type keeps D-PRIM-TYPEKEY1's identity, including full callable signatures and transitive field identities. Bare names are Type values only in Type contexts. Descriptors are linker-merged, never freed and kept under every type_info setting; loaded code stays resident while info or function values refer to it.

options.name: Keep the ratified reflect.TypeKey
options.detail: Build D-PRIM-TYPEKEY1=A as ratified. An opaque key from reflect.key<T>() or reflect.of(x).key() gives exact identity for maps and comparisons, and type names never become values. Branching uses if chains on keys.
options.technical: No decision changes. The key has D-PRIM-TYPEKEY1's exact identity, session-local meaning and managed descriptor lifetime. There is no runtime type switch; comparisons are explicit.

options.name: Repeal exact keys; key maps by display path
options.detail: Drop the ratified key. Maps and comparisons use the display path from reflect.of(x).path(), derived rather than typed by hand. There is no new value kind, but different types can share a path.
options.technical: Repeals D-PRIM-TYPEKEY1. Path equality cannot tell generic instances apart (probe k07) or two packages with the same path. Run-time reflection is still governed by D-REFLECT-TYPEINFO1.

options.name: Compile-time type switches only
options.detail: Keep switches on generic type parameters, which work today, and drop the runtime key. A runtime registry uses display paths, as in C.
options.technical: Repeals D-PRIM-TYPEKEY1's runtime key, not D-REFLECT-TYPEINFO1's run-time reflection. A generic switch cannot serve a registry built while the program runs.

options.name: Runtime type handles made by a library call
options.detail: reflect.type<T>() makes a reflect.Type, type_of(x) returns one, and if t == { Position -> … } switches on it. Type names stay types everywhere except switch patterns.
options.technical: Replaces TypeKey with reflect.Type, sharing A's identity, descriptor and retention rules. No Prelude name is added and no type name appears in value position outside a switch pattern.

options.name: Keep TypeKey and add a checked key switch
options.detail: Keep the ratified opaque TypeKey and its constructors. Add an identity switch using explicit key expressions, without adding Type or making bare type names values.
options.technical: Extend key comparison tables, not the identity mechanism. Evaluate the subject once. Arm keys are build-known reflect.key<T>() expressions; compare canonical identity, reject duplicate keys, and require else. No payload is bound. Keep TYPEKEY1 and REFLECT-TYPEINFO1 retention unchanged.

comparisons.note: TypeId is an explicit library identity made by TypeId::of; it is not a display path. Source: doc.rust-lang.org/std/any/struct.TypeId.html.
comparisons.code:
let mut counts: HashMap<TypeId, i32> = HashMap::new();
counts.insert(TypeId::of::<Position>(), 2);

comparisons.note: A type switch inspects the dynamic type an interface holds; reflect.Type values compare by identity. Source: go.dev/ref/spec#Type_switches.

decisions.title: Should an unresolved scratch-memory escape be refused rather than silently copied?
decisions.situation: Should an unresolved scratch-memory escape be refused rather than silently copied? Scratch memory holds temporary work that is cleared together. Noor joins two temporary names into text that must survive. Building that text in its final storage can avoid a copy, but uncertain destinations need a stated rule. We recommend final placement first and an explicit repair when a no-copy escape cannot be proved.
decisions.gist: Should an unresolved scratch-memory escape be refused rather than silently copied?
decisions.lesson: Build the finished result where it will live. Moving ownership is not necessarily copying bytes. A surviving reference into cleared scratch is invalid under either option.
decisions.explainer: An escape is a surviving dependency on arena storage, not every value created during a block. Scalars, old values and stable resource handles can leave when their owned graph contains no arena dependency. Copying bytes cannot duplicate a resource's identity or finishing duty.
decisions.story: Noor joins ada and lin, closes the arena and prints ada;lin. Both choices produce the same text; only their fallback for uncertain lifetimes differs.
decisions.inWild: Illustrative Standard ML join; MLKit infers storage from lifetimes, with no Jet performance claim.
decisions.detail:
origin/dev:Compiler/JetIR/Source/BuildTransact.jet:253-260 evaluates context guards and releases non-deadline guards. Both options extend this existing Context allocation route, not an extra `_in` API family.

D-CONTEXT1=A already requires safe scratch rewind and relocation of survivors. Final-destination construction is a valid optimization under that contract, not a new allocation selector. The remaining owner gate is whether automatic relocation remains a permitted fallback. F amends that fallback; E keeps it. Neither option requires an avoidable copy merely to cross a brace.

F propagates destination and retention facts through ordinary checked calls and interfaces. Known temporary allocations use the selected arena. A surviving owned graph is built directly in its destination or transfers compatible storage. A true conflict is refused; move creation outside scratch or explicitly copy a copyable graph into proved final storage. E uses the same placement analysis but may relocate when needed. E can therefore accept some programs F refuses; that is a real ergonomic advantage, not a slower implementation by definition.

Beginners use the default allocator. Experts install the existing arena context, inspect placement and choose explicit repairs for uncertain lifetimes. Follow the entire reachable graph, including captures, interior aliases, shared cells, retaining stores and task handoffs. A stable resource identity cannot be copied or relocated as bytes. Older containers keep their allocator. Partial construction, errors and cancellation settle owned values exactly once before rewind. No implicit arena-lifetime extension is allowed.

The printed join only tests the computation. The inspected guard lowering is not actual allocator routing. Before any no-copy or speed claim, measure allocations, copy counts and peak storage on both a returned text and a retaining-container workload. No performance superiority is asserted here.

Fresh review, 2026-11-11. Made the actual amendment explicit and gave the ratified policy the same placement optimization; removed mandatory-copy and duplicate allocator-API alternatives.

decisions.title: Should compact outcome handling keep the ordinary pattern-table head or use a shorter general head?
decisions.situation: Should compact outcome handling keep the ordinary pattern-table head or use a shorter general head? A lookup may return a value, no match or an error. Kai needs three different answers without repeating the lookup. Both choices make that same pattern table fit on one line and retire the result-only short form. We recommend adding compact layout to the existing table, without another expression head.
decisions.gist: Should compact outcome handling keep the ordinary pattern-table head or use a shorter general head?
decisions.lesson: Missing data is different from a failed lookup. List each outcome when they need different answers. Compact and expanded tables must use the same patterns, ownership checks and control-flow rules.
decisions.explainer: Words used here. A result is a value or an error. An arm table is if subject == { … } with one arm per case. A single-arm if tests one case, as in if r == .Ok(n) -> …. The ?? fallback gives a value when the result is an error.
decisions.story: Kai calls lookup for -1, 0 and 7. Every choice prints -1, 0 and 7 after exactly one lookup per input.
decisions.inWild: Illustrative comma-separated general match for the same three outcomes.
decisions.detail:
origin/dev:Compiler/JetParser/Source/Parser/ExpressionForms/ResultHandlers.jet:1-3 and :99-105 already lower the short handler to ordinary pattern branches. Both options extend that canonical pattern route; neither adds a second result evaluator.

C adds comma separators and optional trailing commas to ordinary pattern tables. F additionally permits `subject ? { arms }` as a general short head. Both retire the result-only `? name -> ... ! name -> ...` spelling in a coordinated cutover, explicitly amending D-RESULT-DECON2=B. The compact feature is general to enums, not only error carriers. Ordinary automatic propagation and ?? remain unchanged.

The shared program uses the ratified flat Int? Problem! cases: .Val, .None and .Err. There is no nested .Ok(.Val(...)) carrier. Evaluate the subject once, run only the selected arm and retain branch-local bindings. Return, break and next retain their enclosing targets; no callback is inserted. Ordinary move/borrow, cleanup, finishing duties and secrecy tags apply.

Beginners use propagation or ?? for simple fallbacks. Experts expand the same table for multi-step arms. Closed sets list every case explicitly; an else arm cannot hide a newly added closed case. Open sets keep the existing else requirement. Missing and duplicate arms use the same checker. Format by width and comments; do not maintain separate compact and expanded AST meanings.

The strongest smaller change was already option C. The prior recommendation preferred a new head mainly because it was shorter, without evidence that the existing head imposed meaningful friction. C supplies the compact three-outcome expression without that extra spelling. F remains a genuine organization alternative under I8, not a second runtime mechanism. The migration must preserve subject evaluation, control targets, binding hygiene and drop timing.

Fresh review, 2026-11-11. Changed the recommendation to the strongest smaller extension and removed the false second-runtime-mechanism framing.

decisions.title: Fixed-time rules for the Secret tag, from the checker to the final machine code
decisions.situation:
Code that handles keys must take the same time and touch the same memory whatever the key is. Otherwise an attacker who times it learns the key. Today Jet follows a Secret label through the program but checks nothing about timing, so an early-exit compare of a secret runs as written. This matters most to people who write crypto and login code, and it protects every program that uses theirs.

You are deciding whether the Secret label also makes the compiler refuse secret-dependent branches, lookups, divisions and stops, checked down to the final machine code. We recommend A: it does, and it rewrites simple secret branches into fixed-time code instead of refusing them.

One cost cannot be removed. On a chip whose maker publishes no fixed-time guarantee, or whose switch only the operating system can set, Jet checks its own code but cannot confirm the chip. The build report says so, and the hardened profile refuses such hosts.
decisions.gist: Should the Secret tag forbid secret-dependent branches, indexes, divisions and stops, checked down to the final machine code?
decisions.lesson: A timing leak needs no bug in the math, only a branch, a memory lookup, a division or a stop that depends on a secret. A compiler can refuse those only if it knows which values are secret, follows them everywhere, and checks the code it finally emits.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A tag is a label the compiler follows through the program, written #Secret before a value or a type. A secrecy tag protects what a value says; Secret, Credential and PII are secrecy tags. An integrity tag, such as Input, protects where a value goes.

A branch is an if, a loop test or a match. A stop is a run-time halt, such as an overflow. Fixed time means the work does not depend on a value. To scrub is to release a tag on purpose, in a function marked #Scrub.
decisions.story: Ana writes the check for the tag that proves a message was not changed. Her first version compares byte by byte and returns at the first mismatch. Correct-answer tests can miss this leak. An attacker sends forged tags and times the replies; a slower reply means one more byte was right. Today Jet accepts her code (c07), and nothing stops a later optimizer from turning a careful version back into a branch. Under A her first version compiles and runs in fixed time, because the compiler rewrites the early exit.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. Whether values with a fixed-time tag, Secret first, may steer branches, addresses, divisions, shifts, allocation sizes or stops, and how far down the compiler checks it. Protection of memory is D-MEM-WIPE1's ratified duty, and disclosure sinks are D-SECRETEDGE1's. This ballot changes neither; it adds timing.

No starting assurance is claimed. Core tags nothing #Secret today (census: 0 uses), so no checker sees its keys. Its crypto code is written with masks, and its tests check results, not timing. Nothing here claims that today's TLS or crypto code is constant-time.

Today, on the t6c compiler (dev 76955986d0), with the same results as seed a0_042. Ana's early-exit compare, a secret table index, a secret divisor, a secret shift amount and a loop counted by a secret all check and run (c07). A Secret condition that picks untagged text reaches process.cmd with no report (c01, BallotReview4's attack).

A Credential condition does the same (c06), though passing the token itself is E0721. A secret U8 plus one prints 1, then stops with E3010 at 255, exit 70 (c02). A compare over a shorter input stops with E3010 (c03). Under #Arithmetic(.Wrapping) the same addition prints 0 (c05).

Flow fixes under every option. The tag checker loses tags in seven known ways, and ratified tags promise all of them. Stores into a list, field or & parameter must tag the container. A loop body must be walked until its tags stop changing. A call must walk its callee with the argument tags, receivers included. A branch's condition must tag its results. Every option below fixes all seven.

Implicit flow, exactly. A branch on a secrecy tag sets a control tag for its arms. Every value an arm produces, assigns outside itself, stores or writes through & gets that tag. A call made in the arm is a use of each sink the tag denies. If an arm can leave by return, break, continue, ? or !, everything after the branch is under the control tag too.

Integrity tags such as Input get no control tag, because a branch on untrusted input that picks a constant query injects nothing. A tag says which kind it is with a new tag-only Marker constant, protects, of the Prelude enum TagProtects { Secrecy, Integrity }. Its default is .Secrecy, the stricter kind. The Prelude sets Input to .Integrity, and Secret, Credential and PII to .Secrecy.

Run-time stops and loops that never end are not tracked for leak-only tags; that residue is named below. Migration: no tag on the seed is declared in D-TAG-MARKER1's form yet (no .TypeUse site), so only the four Prelude tags need constants. A user tag that omits protects gets implicit flow, and one that omits timing gets no timing rule.

Alias, call and capture flow. A loan of a tagged value is tagged, and a write through it tags the owner. A callee is checked once per pattern of argument tags, cached, with recursion solved to a fixed point. Generic code is checked per instance. A closure that captures a tagged value tags its results.

Function and trait values. A function value cannot be walked, so passing a fixed-time value to one is refused unless its type names the tag, as in fn(#Secret U8) -> #Secret U8. A function becomes such a value only when its checked summary for that tag pattern has no refusal and tags its results at least as the type says.

A trait method called through a trait value with a fixed-time argument follows the same rule: its signature must name the tag. Every impl is checked against that signature where it is declared. Under C, the function type must also say #ConstantTime, so only marked functions fit it; naming a Secret parameter is not enough.

Exported callbacks. A Jet function exported to foreign code may take a fixed-time parameter only with #Unsafe and a reason, listed in the build report, because its foreign caller is not checked. Its body is checked as usual.

Separate compilation. Each package's checked interface carries a tag summary for each public function: which argument tags reach which results and sinks, and whether it is fixed-time safe for each tag pattern. Callers in other packages use the summary instead of the body. The summary is part of the package's checked content identity, so a changed body changes the identity.

Loaded code. A package loaded while running is reached only through function and trait values, whose types name the tags. The loader refuses a package whose checked summaries do not satisfy those types. Two boundaries stay outside the promise, and are named: a tampered binary, and foreign code behind an audited extern.

Under A, a tag declares fixed time with a second tag-only constant, timing, of the Prelude enum TagTiming { Free, Fixed }, default .Free. Branch, index and divide are not effects, so they stay out of D-TAG-MARKER1's #FX denial row. The Prelude Secret gets timing: .Fixed. Credential and PII keep .Free, because tokens and personal data are parsed by code that branches on their text.

Several tags. A value may carry more than one tag. It follows the timing rules if any of its tags is .Fixed, and gets implicit flow if any is .Secrecy. A branch's results carry the union of its arms' tags plus its control tag; a container's element tags and its own tag are kept apart.

What is refused for a fixed-time value, with E0737. In control: an if, while or loop-until condition, a match subject, the left side of && or ||, and the subject of ??, ? or !. In addressing: a range bound or loop count, a list index, map key or slice bound. Also either operand of / or %, a shift or rotate amount, an allocation size or capacity, and a call target.

Widths, with E0738. A fixed-time scalar must be a fixed-width integer or a Bool. A fixed-time value may be any container of such scalars: a struct, a fixed or growable array, a String's bytes, or an Any payload. Int and Float, and any type that holds them, are refused. Int's exact routes branch on the value's size, and some hardware slows down on very small floats.

Stops, with E0739. Plain arithmetic on a fixed-time value would stop on overflow, and whether it stops depends on the secret. So the plain Stop policy and checked(...) are refused for fixed-time operands. wrapping(...), saturating(...) and #Overflow(.Wrapping) are accepted, all from ratified D-FIXED-WRAP1; saturating lowers to masks. A narrowing conversion T{x} follows the same rule.

Code that needs to know whether a sum overflowed computes the carry bit with masks, as ConstTime.jet does today, and keeps it as a #Secret Bool. That closes the overflow-stop attack: next_counter must write wrapping(k + U8{1}), which gives 0 for 255 and never stops.

What stays allowed. Comparisons such as == and < on fixed-time values give a fixed-time Bool, lowered to a branch-free compare. Bit operations, wrapping and saturating arithmetic, and selection by mask are allowed. A bounds check with a public index on a list of public length stays, because its stop depends only on public data.

Secret branches that are rewritten, not refused. A branch on a fixed-time value compiles when both arms are total. Total means no stop, no loop with a secret count, no call with an effect, no allocation, and writes only to locals and & places. The compiler runs both arms and picks each result with a mask, as FaCT does. An early return or break in such a branch becomes a secret flag, and the code after it runs with its writes masked.

If the code an early exit would skip is not total, the early exit is refused. A function with a rewritten branch returns a fixed-time value, so check_fast below returns #Secret Bool. The build report lists every rewritten branch by line. Every other secret branch is refused with E0737, which names the first part of the arm that blocks the rewrite: the call, the allocation, the stop or the secret count.

The rewrite is not trusted for timing. The final-code validator below checks its output like any other code, so a rewrite bug is an internal compiler error, not a leak. Tier parity checks its answers: the forced interpreter runs the branch as written, and both tiers must agree.

Public lengths. Allocation sizes are never secret, so every buffer's capacity is public. [#Secret U8] tags each element, and its length and is_empty are public too. #Secret [U8] and #Secret String tag the whole value, so their length is secret and only their capacity is public. TlsLead's probe p4 shows the whole-value length is tagged today.

A public length stays public only while no secret decides it. So push, pop, insert, remove, truncate or extend on a [#Secret U8] is refused under a secret control tag, with E0737, and their count arguments must be public. A call made under a control tag is checked as if each write it makes through & were inside that branch.

The length fact lives in the type, so it travels with every loan, parameter and capture. Turning #Secret [U8] into [#Secret U8] declares its length public, so it is done only in a #Scrub(Secret) function, listed for review. The other direction is a plain widening.

The seed accepts [#Secret U8] as a type but drops the element tag: a byte read from it reaches process.cmd with no report (c04). A builds element tags.

Comparing unequal lengths. Core's crypto.equal(expected: [#Secret U8], got: [U8]) -> Bool returns false at once when the lengths differ, which reveals only public lengths. Otherwise it reads every byte, combines the differences with masks, and reveals one Bool through its scrub. That closes the short-compare attack.

The attack's own hand-written loop is refused when expected is #Secret [U8], because its range bound is secret. With [#Secret U8] the loop compiles, and the stop on a short input depends only on public lengths; crypto.equal is the fix.

Declassifying. #Scrub(Secret) is the only place a fixed-time value becomes public, as D-SECRETEDGE1 already lists. A scrub lifts the timing and disclosure rules from its result only. It never ends D-MEM-WIPE1's protection of the values it read, and Credential and PII keep that duty in every option. Core ships reveal for one Bool and the outputs of seal, sign and public-key derivation.

Secret text. Code over a #Secret String or #Secret [U8] works over the public capacity with masks and never stops at the secret length. Core's fixed-time operations on them are move, drop, copy, crypto.equal and its decoders for base64, hex and PEM. Any other String method reached with one is checked like any helper, and its first refused line reports E0737.

Secret input. A keeps D-MEM-WIPE1's spelling, #Secret (sys.get("SIGNING_KEY") ?? return). The tag applies to the read itself, so the value is protected and fixed-time from its first copy, with type #Secret String; key.bytes() gives #Secret [U8]. Core's decoders take tagged input and return tagged output, so no parser sees untagged secret text.

Boxes and enums. A #Secret Any has secret contents and a public payload type, so type tests and take compare public identity and bind #Secret T. A box, or an enum whose cleanup depends on its variant, may not be made inside a Secret branch, with E0737: dropping it would choose cleanup by a secret. Other variants chosen there become secret, and matching them is refused.

Foreign code. Jet cannot see a foreign body, so passing a fixed-time value to an extern function is refused. An extern may accept one only when its declaration names the tag on that parameter and carries #Unsafe with a reason; each such crossing is listed in the build report. This matches D-MEM-WIPE1's audited owning receivers.

Keeping the tag to the end. Today the IR builder strips tags (BuildTypes.jet:21, ir_untag), so the optimizer sees plain integers. Under A, a fixed bit rides every slot, temporary and register that holds a fixed-time value. Inlining, SSA, copy coalescing and scalar replacement keep the bit. An IR check after every optimizer pass, in every build mode, refuses a branch, address, divide, variable shift or call target that reads a fixed slot.

The leakage model. For code holding fixed-time values, A promises that the executed instruction sequence, every memory address and every branch outcome are independent of those values. Every instruction that reads one is in its target's table. The attacker may time the program and watch caches and branch predictors from the same machine.

Excluded, and named. Power and electromagnetic readings, frequency changes driven by power use, speculative execution, and the timing of the operating system and other processes. A does not promise identical wall time. Jasmin's separate speculative check is a stronger model that A does not offer.

The per-target tables. Each supported target ships a table of exact instruction forms, and each entry cites the vendor document revision that names it; a form without a citation is not listed. The admitted classes are add and subtract with carry, bitwise logic, shifts and rotates by a public amount, multiply, compare and test, conditional select and set, and moves.

Never admitted with fixed-time operands: division and remainder, branches on flags set from them, and loads or stores at addresses they decide. Bit scans, population counts and runtime-helper calls are refused too. Intel's data operand independent timing list governs x86-64, and Arm's DIT list governs AArch64. Compares lower to setcc or cset, and selection to cmov, csel or masks.

Admission on AArch64. Where the CPU reports FEAT_DIT, a function that holds fixed values sets the DIT bit on entry and restores it on exit; an ordinary program may do this itself. DIT is per-thread state, saved with the thread, so thread creation, moves between cores and signal handlers need nothing more. A foreign call made while DIT is set keeps it set.

Admission on x86-64. Intel's DOIT guidance (ID 768873, updated 2025-09-10) covers Core processors before Ice Lake and Atom processors before Gracemont. It says they run the listed instructions as if the mode were on, so those hosts are confirmed. Ice Lake, Gracemont and later need the DOITM bit of a model-specific register. Only the operating system can write it, and Intel advises against setting it for the whole machine. Those hosts are confirmed only where the operating system reports the bit on.

Intel also says some vector forms depend on the MXCSR setting; the x86-64 table leaves those out. This repair read Intel's page but found no AMD list, so AMD processors are unconfirmed until AMD publishes one; the probe machine's Ryzen 9 7950X3D is one of them. A WebAssembly engine is always unconfirmed, because it compiles the module again.

What an unconfirmed host does. By default the program runs, as programs built with BoringSSL, subtle or Go's crypto/subtle run on the same chip. The code half of the promise still holds, because the checker, the IR check and the validator all ran. The build report names each target whose hosts may be unconfirmed. sys.timing_host() returns .Confirmed, or .Unconfirmed with the missing control, so a server can log it or stop.

Under the hardened profile, policy: { harden: true } or --profile=hardened, an unconfirmed host refuses to start a program holding fixed-time values, and the error names the missing control. This adds one check to the ratified hardening fact of D-MEM-GUARANTEE1 and D-HARDENED1; it adds no new switch.

Final-code validation. After register allocation, a validator reads the final instructions of every function that holds fixed values. It follows fixed values through registers, condition flags and spill slots, whose addresses are frame offsets and so public. It checks that only listed instructions read them, and that none feeds a branch, an address, a divide or a variable shift.

Compiler-made code is covered the same way. Inline copies, wide multiplies and stack probes are checked as instructions, and a runtime-helper call with a fixed operand fails validation. Unwinding, cancellation and early exits run only on public conditions, since stops on fixed values are refused, and their wipes loop over public capacities.

A failed validation after sema is an internal compiler error, exit 101 under I2/I3, and no program is emitted. The emitted-code test from #6694 c10 (a) stays as a test of this validator. The checker rules are the same on every tier, and the fixed bit, IR check and validator run at O0, O1 and O2, including jet dev's JIT.

Fail closed, in two separate cases. A target without D-MEM-WIPE1's memory protection already refuses sensitive values under that ratified decision. Every supported target ships a timing table; wasm32-wasip2's covers the WebAssembly instructions Jet emits, which are only arithmetic and bit operations on fixed values. No target is carved out, so I9 holds. A new target gets its timing table before it is supported, as it gets its other tables.

Allocation and memory. A fixed-time value cannot size an allocation, so allocation, growth and allocation failure depend only on public data. Storage for fixed-time values is D-MEM-WIPE1's protected storage, wiped and kept out of swap and crash output. The 270 manual wipe calls in 23 files of Core, Compiler and Examples stay until D-MEM-WIPE1 is built.

Helper coverage. There is no allow list: every function reached with a fixed-time value is checked, Core included. ConstTime.jet has 38 functions, and 18 take Int parameters. BallotReview4 found that memmove_left, memcpy_offset and memcmp_partial handle secret offsets and skip counts as Int. Under A those become #Secret U64, with their totals and ranges public.

Build-time code. The timing rules apply to code in the shipped program; build-time code runs on the build machine and is not timed. A build-time result may not carry a secrecy tag, because the program image is not protected storage. That makes it a non-storable result type under D-COMPTIME-BLOCK1's E0944. It follows from D-MEM-WIPE1 and narrows neither D-COMPTIME-BLOCK1 nor D-META-PHASE1.

Beginner path. Use core.crypto's seal, open, sign, verify and equal, and never write a tag. A natural early-exit compare of a tagged key compiles and runs in fixed time. A secret branch that prints or allocates gives E0737, whose fix names the masked form or crypto.equal.

Expert path. Tag key material once as [#Secret U8] or #Secret U64, write the primitive with bit operations, wrapping arithmetic, mask selection or total branches, and publish results only through #Scrub(Secret) functions. The build report lists every scrub, every rewritten branch and every foreign crossing. The hardened profile adds the host check.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. A secret branch with an effect, a secret index and a secret loop count are still refused, because no rewrite can hide an address or an effect. E0737 names the part that blocks the rewrite, and Core ships crypto.equal and fixed-time decoders for base64, hex and PEM. Secret arithmetic must name wrapping or saturating, and E0739's fix writes it.

The one cost that cannot be removed. On an unconfirmed host the chip's half of the promise is unknown, because its maker publishes no list or only the operating system can set the switch. Mitigation: AArch64 sets DIT itself, older Intel is covered by Intel's statement, the build report and sys.timing_host() say which hosts are unconfirmed, and the hardened profile refuses them.

Two smaller costs. Leak-only tags do not track run-time stops or endless loops in their branches, and timing and termination can reveal more than a branch outcome; a tag that needs that sets timing: .Fixed. Callees are checked again for each pattern of argument tags, and the summaries are cached.

Other options. B adds core.ct types, such as ct.U8 and ct.Bool, that are always Secret and whose comparisons give a ct.Bool that no if accepts. Operators work on them, and they share A's lowering, validator and host policy. C applies A's timing rules only inside functions marked #ConstantTime, with the same whole-program tag flow. D adds no timing rule; an emitted-code test covers listed Core functions.

E is A without the rewrite: every secret branch is refused, so Ana's early-exit compare must be written with masks. The trusted compiler stays smaller, and no code runs work the source seems to skip.

F is the strictest form, the draft this repair replaced. Every unconfirmed host refuses to start a program holding fixed-time values, and wasm32-wasip2 cannot build one. D-WASISRV1 ratified wasm32-wasip2 as a full server target with no carve-out under I9, so F needs you to approve an I9 exception. A, B, C and E keep the target.

The forced interpreter is a test path, not a deployment target. It gives the same results, makes no timing promise, and says so when it starts.

options.name: Fixed-time rules on the Secret tag, with simple secret branches rewritten
options.detail: Secret gains fixed time. A secret branch whose arms are total is rewritten to run both arms and pick by mask, so natural code works. A secret branch with an effect is refused. So are a secret index, division, shift amount, allocation size or call target, secret Int and Float, and arithmetic that could stop on a secret. A validator checks the final instructions on every target. Unconfirmed hosts run and are reported; the hardened profile refuses them.
options.technical:
Tag-only constants timing: TagTiming and protects: TagProtects, set on the Prelude tags. FaCT-style predication of total secret branches and early exits before lowering, listed in the build report. E0737, E0738 and E0739 at the line, with tag summaries in each package's checked interface. A fixed bit replaces ir_untag for fixed tags and is checked after every pass.

Cited per-target tables, wasm32-wasip2's included, and a final-instruction validator. Host admission follows each vendor's statement, with sys.timing_host(), and harden refuses unconfirmed hosts. No I9 exception. D-MEM-WIPE1, D-SECRETEDGE1, D-TAG-MARKER1, D-COMPTIME-BLOCK1 and D-META-PHASE1 unchanged.

options.name: A family of always-secret integer types
options.detail: core.ct adds U8, U32, U64 and Bool types that are always Secret. Their arithmetic wraps, their comparisons give a ct.Bool, and no if, index or division accepts one. Operators work on them. The type system alone refuses a secret branch. Host and target policy are A's.
options.technical: ct types carry the Secret tag, so disclosure and protection rules apply unchanged, and A's flow fixes still cover Credential and PII. Lowering, the final-instruction validator, the tables and the host policy are A's; no branch is rewritten. Wrapper primitives still need checked lowering; calls and conversions must not launder secrecy. Generic code over U8 does not accept ct.U8 unless written over both.

options.name: Timing rules inside #ConstantTime functions
options.detail: A function marked #ConstantTime gets A's timing rules and rewrite, with the same whole-program tag flow. A marked function may pass fixed-time values only to marked callees. Unmarked code may branch on a secret, and the result keeps its tag.
options.technical: The strongest scoped design: tags flow across functions, fields and lists as in A, and only the timing refusals are scoped. The rewrite, fixed bit, validator and host policy apply to marked functions. Key parsers need no fixed-time rewrite, but an unmarked early-exit compare compiles and leaks.

options.name: No timing rule, and an emitted-code test
options.detail: No new language rule. The seven flow fixes, D-MEM-WIPE1 protection and D-SECRETEDGE1 sinks still apply. A test builds each listed Core primitive in every build mode and fails if its machine code branches on, indexes by or divides by a secret.
options.technical: The #6694 c10 (a) test is the only timing check. User code and unlisted Core code are not checked, and secret arithmetic keeps the Stop policy.

options.name: A, with every secret branch refused instead of rewritten
options.detail: As A, but no secret branch is rewritten. Every if, loop test or match on a secret is refused with E0737, so early exits must be written with masks. Host and target policy are A's.
options.technical: A without the predication pass. The fixed bit, tables, validator, admission and hardened check are A's. The trusted compiler is smaller, and source never hides work that always runs.

options.name: A, failing closed on every unconfirmed host and on server WebAssembly
options.detail: As A, but a program holding fixed-time values refuses to start on any unconfirmed host, and wasm32-wasip2 cannot build one. This is the draft the repair replaced, and it needs an I9 exception.
options.technical: A's rules, rewrite, tables and validator, with admission always fail-closed. Ice Lake and later Intel without DOITM, AMD without a published list, and every WebAssembly engine are refused. Asks for an I9 exception against D-WASISRV1's no-carve-out server target.

comparisons.note: BoringSSL uses masks, optimization barriers and optional Valgrind secret-flow validation. These are real defenses, not a language-level guarantee, and it runs on every host without checking the CPU mode. Source: crypto/internal.h.
The subtle crate's Choice and ConditionallySelectable hide values behind an optimization barrier; it is a library promise, not a compiler check.
comparisons.code:
let c: Choice = a.ct_eq(&b);
let v = u8::conditional_select(&x, &y, c);

comparisons.note: crypto/subtle.WithDataIndependentTiming runs a function with the CPU's fixed-time mode on. It sets DIT on arm64 and does nothing on other architectures, so x86-64 hosts run unconfirmed. A's default matches it and adds the report and the hardened refusal. Source: crypto/subtle/dit.go, Go 1.24 release notes.

A research language with secret and public types. It rewrites secret branches, early returns included, into masked operations, and refuses secret indexes. A's rewrite follows it. Source: Cauligi et al., PLDI 2019.
comparisons.code:
secret uint8 x = ...;
if (x == 0) { y = 1; }   // rewritten to a select

comparisons.note: Programs state security contracts; the checker runs after lowering, has a DOIT mode, and offers a separate speculative model that A lacks. Source: Almeida et al., CCS 2017; Barthe et al., CCS 2021.
comparisons.code: fn eq(reg u64 a, reg u64 b) -> reg u64 { ... }

recommendation.why: A uses the Secret tag Jet already follows, so ordinary operators keep working. Simple secret branches are rewritten into fixed-time code, and only what no rewrite can hide is refused. It checks the final instructions on every supported target, keeps every target, and reports hosts it cannot confirm.
gains: Ana's early-exit compare compiles and runs in fixed time; a secret overflow is refused.
No optimizer change can add a secret branch, because the final instructions are checked.
The same tag carries disclosure, protection and timing, so secret means one thing.
Every ratified target stays, with no I9 exception and no narrowing of build-time code.

losses.loss: On an unconfirmed host, such as AMD without a published list or newer Intel without the operating-system switch, the chip's half of the promise is unknown. This cannot be removed.
losses.mitigation: AArch64 sets DIT itself, older Intel is covered by Intel's statement, the build report and sys.timing_host() name unconfirmed hosts, and the hardened profile refuses them.

losses.loss: A secret branch with an effect, a secret index and a secret loop count are still refused.
losses.mitigation: E0737 names the blocking part, and Core ships crypto.equal and fixed-time decoders for base64, hex and PEM.

losses.loss: Leak-only tags such as Credential do not track stops or endless loops in their branches.
losses.mitigation: A tag that needs that sets timing: .Fixed.

whyNot.reason: B makes the timing distinction explicit, but natural branch code is a type error, and generic code over U8 needs a second version or a shared trait.
C keeps tags across functions, but an unmarked early-exit compare compiles and leaks, so safety is opt-in.
D checks only listed Core functions after the build, and secret arithmetic can still stop on a secret.
E keeps the compiler smaller, but every natural early exit must be rewritten by hand with masks.
F refuses to start on AMD and newer Intel hosts by default and needs an I9 exception for server WebAssembly.

recommendation.tradeoff: Stricter rules for effects and addresses in secret code, in return for a timing promise that holds through every optimizer pass on every target. The chip's half is confirmed where vendors allow it and reported where they do not.

surface.gist: Should the Secret tag forbid secret-dependent branches, indexes, divisions and stops, checked down to the final machine code?
surface.lesson: A timing leak needs only a branch, a memory lookup, a division or a stop that depends on a secret. A compiler can refuse those only if it follows secret values everywhere and checks the code it finally emits.

decisions.title: Let safe tree-building helpers work without letting shared objects keep each other alive forever
decisions.situation: Shared objects stay alive while another owner points to them. A loop of owning links can therefore keep unused objects alive forever. The compiler refuses a simple tree built through a helper in the probe, even though building the child directly works. This affects reusable code as well as memory safety. Choose how much the compiler should prove before accepting a write. We recommend better write checks, with collection still an explicit choice for real loops.
decisions.gist: Should safe tree-building helpers work without enabling hidden collection?
decisions.lesson: Think of owning links as people holding each other's tickets: a circle never gives its tickets back. A weak link is an address, not another ticket. A tree needs no circle of owners. The question is how to distinguish that tree from a real circle.
decisions.explainer: Reachability includes owned containers, erased payloads and callback captures, not only visible Shared fields. A collector also needs exact external-root accounting and safe cleanup. A graph sketch alone proves neither.
decisions.story: Ada wants a root with one child. Today putting child creation in make_child makes the tested program fail. She should not have to give up reusable helpers to get a safe tree.
decisions.inWild: Rust documents strong Rc loops as possible leaks and offers Weak links. That is useful explicit control, but safe Jet promises leak freedom too. Source comparison, not a Rust execution claim.
decisions.detail:
Same job in every option: create a root, create a child through a helper, attach it, and print 1. Every code pane is proposed canonical Jet. Shared{value} is the owner's ratified construction spelling; the available compiler still requires the old keyword for this probe. Beginners keep ordinary owned values; shared ownership is needed only when several owners need the same object. Experts use weak back-links or the existing explicit collection policy for real loops.

Observed on the t17a a0.0.43 compiler with jet run -: the helper program, written with the compiler's shared keyword, fails E0221 at root.kids.push(kid.copy()). Replacing that argument with a freshly constructed child prints 1, exit 0. This checks a false refusal, not a collector or a memory-leak measurement. Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/SharedCycles.jet:151-159 accepts some fresh expressions, including lambdas; that shortcut is not evidence that captured ownership is harmless. No old retained-feed claim is carried forward without a new run.

A checks writes, not recursive type declarations. Track the owned graph through aliases, containers, captures, erased payloads and reachable calls. Publish checked summaries with ordinary interfaces. Unknown reach means not proved, not a fabricated exact loop. A store is accepted only if it cannot create an uncollected owning loop. Later mutation must preserve that proof. This is greater acceptance where proved, not a promise to decide every possible program.

A, B and C retain D-GC-OPTIN1=A: opted types may participate in collection; unopted cycles remain forbidden. Every participant in a collected owning loop must meet that policy. Collection must eventually reclaim unreachable loops, account for external roots, and honor the existing consuming cleanup and task rules. No resurrection hook or second cleanup protocol is introduced. Cyclic resources that need to call dying neighbors must be settled before collection.

B explicitly reverses #6281's companion memory card c2 requirement that refusal occur at writes, not declarations. C preserves write-site checking but leaves the helper refusal. D explicitly replaces collection opt-in; it is not already authorized. Allowing safe-code leaks was removed as a misleading normal alternative: it violates I1 unless the owner separately changes that invariant.

Adversarial verdict: A holds only within stated proof limits. Two attempts remove conservative refusals: propagate helper summaries and track aliases after calls. Neither makes arbitrary mutable graphs decidable. When proof is missing, name the uncertain link and offer weak links, IDs or explicit collection rather than unsafe acceptance. B and C are genuinely simpler; D is genuinely more convenient for arbitrary loops but adds collection where the owner currently forbids it. No speed or zero-pause claim is made.

options.name: Prove safe writes, including helpers
options.detail: Accept the helper-built tree when its links are proved safe. Keep collection explicit for actual loops.
options.technical: One ownership checker, with complete alias and call summaries; no hidden runtime cycle test or automatic collector.

options.name: Refuse potentially circular types
options.detail: Refuse this recursive owning type before any write. The job must use IDs or a different representation, or explicitly opt its types into collection.
options.technical: Includes hidden captures and erasure in the type rule. Reverses the ratified write-site requirement; not merely an implementation shortcut.

options.name: Keep conservative write checks
options.detail: Repair every safety hole, but keep refusing helper writes the current checker cannot understand. The child can be constructed directly at the push.
options.technical: Soundness repair is required regardless of precision. This option does not retain unchecked capture loops.

options.name: Automatically collect possible loops

decisions.title: The shared keyword is retired, and Shared{value} builds a shared cell
decisions.situation:
The owner's language review ruled that the shared keyword goes and that Shared{value} is the spelling. Today counter: shared Counter{hits: 0} builds a lock-guarded cell of type Shared<Counter>. That spelling was ratified, with the rule that shared expr constructs the cell.

A amends only that construction form. Plain field access, one atomic step per statement, #Transact, the Shared<T> type and the sharing menu stay, respelled. Keeping the keyword is option B.
decisions.gist: Should a shared cell be built as Shared{Counter{hits: 0}}, retiring the shared keyword and the Shared.new leftover?
decisions.lesson: A shared cell lets several tasks read and change one value safely, one statement at a time. Today a keyword builds it, while its type is written Shared<Counter>. This vote decides whether the type's own name builds it, the way other Jet values are built.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A task is work that runs alongside other work. A shared cell is a value that several tasks may use at once; a lock inside it lets one statement in at a time.

Shared<Counter> is the type of a shared cell that holds a Counter. A keyword is a word the language reserves for its own grammar.
decisions.story: Ada sees Shared<Counter> in a parameter and writes Shared{Counter{hits: 0}} to make one. The compiler says it needs Shared but got Counter. The working spelling is the lowercase word shared, which she would not have guessed from the type.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. Only how a shared cell is written when it is built. What a shared cell does, how its fields are read and written, how several steps commit under #Transact, and how lock order is checked do not change.

Today, on the t6c compiler (dev 76955986d0), every probe matches the seed. Probe h01 builds counter: shared Counter{hits: 0}, passes it to two tasks, and prints 1, 2 and hits 2. Probe h02 writes Shared{Counter{hits: 0}} and probe h03 writes Shared<Counter>{Counter{hits: 0}}; both are E0108, This needs Shared, but the value is Counter.

Probe h04 uses shared as a local name, and it works and prints shared 3, so the word is already contextual. Probe h05 writes Shared.new(Counter{hits: 0}) and it works and prints hits 1. E1115 RetiredSharedNew is registered for that form, with status Retired, so it never fires.

The rule under A. Shared{value} builds a cell that holds exactly one value, and its element type is inferred from that value. Shared<Counter>{value} names the element type, for when the value alone does not settle it. The value moves into the cell, and cloning the cell clones its handle, as today.

Why braces. In Jet a type name followed by braces builds a value of that type: Counter{hits: 0} builds a struct, and [Int]{1, 2} builds a list from its elements. Shared{value} is the list form with one element. The project's rule says a construct is a word, a marker or a library name. A shared cell is a runtime value with a type, so its library name builds it.

What is refused, each with a fix. Shared{} and a cell with two values say a cell holds one value. A field list such as Shared{hits: 0} says to build the value first, and its fix writes Shared{Counter{hits: 0}} when the expected type names Counter. E0108 for a Counter where a Shared<Counter> is needed gains the fix: wrap it as Shared{value}.

Retiring the old spellings. shared expr becomes one registered retirement error whose fix rewrites it to Shared{expr} by parse node. shared becomes an ordinary name everywhere; it leaves the reserved list, and the KW_SHARED spelling and its four references are deleted. Shared.new(value) gets E1115 back with an active status and the same fix.

Fix texts that spell the keyword are updated. E0111's fix today shows score: shared Count{value: 0}, which itself fails, because a module constant needs an ALL_CAPS name (probe p09). Under A it shows SCORE: Shared{Count{value: 0}}. E1101's menu becomes: give it (^), freeze it (freeze), or share it (Shared{value}).

D-CORE-GLOBAL-STATE1=A writes a module-level shared holder with the keyword; under A the same holder is written #Persist STORE: Shared{Storage{...}}. Probe p09 shows today's module-level holder works: SCORE: shared Count{value: 0} is written by a function and prints score 1.

Scalars are unchanged by this ballot. Probe p10 shows shared 0 builds a Shared<Int>, but SCORE += 1 and printing it are refused today. Under A, Shared{0} builds the same Shared<Int> with the same rules, so wrapping a scalar in a struct stays the working form.

Migration. The seed's census script counted 402 constructions: tests 149, Compiler 134, Core 59, Jetpack 26, Examples 16, Tools 7 and Docs code blocks 11, plus 23 prose mentions. On dev, git grep -cE for shared followed by a capital, digit, bracket or paren finds 413 in Jet files, comments included. Shared.new( appears 9 times. jet fix rewrites every construction in one run.

Beginner path. The type a parameter asks for, Shared<Counter>, is also how to build one: Shared{Counter{hits: 0}}. There is one spelling to learn, and the old one prints the new one in its fix.

Expert path. Shared<Counter>{make_counter()} pins the element type when a generic value would infer something else. Expert guards, Condition, #Transact and freeze are unchanged, and a cell inside a struct field or a list is built the same way.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. Shared{Counter{hits: 0}} has one more pair of braces than shared Counter{hits: 0}. The braces show where the held value starts and ends, which the keyword left to the reader's sense of precedence.

402 constructions and the docs that teach the keyword must change. jet fix rewrites them by parse node, and the retirement error teaches the new form to anyone who types the old one.

Other options. B keeps the keyword as D-CONC-SHARE1 ratified. C is Rust's style, Shared.new(value), which works today through h05's leftover path. D is a marker on the binding, #Shared counter: Counter{hits: 0}, at its best case: no new construction syntax, and the binding reads as a Counter that tasks may share.

D hides a change of type behind a marker: the binding's type is Shared<Counter>, yet it is written as a Counter. Under the project's rule, markers carry compile-time properties of a declaration, not the type of a runtime value. C adds a second way to build values next to the brace form every other type uses.

One construction form across open ballots. Jet's conversions and typed literals already use braces: Int{b.len}, U8{1}, and Type{Rock} in the open type-value ballot. The open Any ballot spells its box Any(value). If both pass, the box follows this ballot's form, Any{value} and Any.Owes{value}, so every wrapper is built the same way; its type patterns keep parentheses.

decisions.title: The arrow always comes first after the parameters, and the error-first unit order is retired
decisions.situation:
The owner's language review agreed that the arrow should always come before the result, and that the error-first order should be invalid. Today a function that returns a value writes its arrow first. A unit function that can fail writes its error first, or has no arrow at all.

A later ruling already writes a failing unit function as -> ! SaveError, which assumes the arrow-first order. A reverses the ratified error-first order and keeps one arrow and the fused effect arrow. Keeping the error-first order is option B.
decisions.gist: Should every signature put its arrow before the result and the error, so a failing unit function writes -> ! IOError?
decisions.lesson: After a function's inputs come up to three things: what it may touch, what it returns, and how it can fail. Today their order depends on whether the function returns a value. This vote decides whether one order holds for every function.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. The effect arrow, such as -[FS.Write]>, lists what a function may touch; -> is the arrow with no effects listed. The result is the type a function returns on success.

The error contract, such as ! IOError, names how the function can fail, and ! Never says it cannot. A unit function returns no value.
decisions.story: Ada writes load with the arrow first and copies its shape for save, which returns nothing. The compiler refuses the arrow before a unit contract and tells her to write the error first. She now keeps two orders in her head for one idea.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. Only the order of the parts that follow a function's parameters. Which effects, results and errors a function has, and how they are checked, do not change. Lambdas keep D-LAMBDA-IFACE2's rule: they write no result or error type, and their arrow starts the body.

Today, on the t6c compiler (dev 76955986d0), probes are written in today's built spelling, String IOError!, and match the seed. Probe s01 writes load arrow first, save error first and check_name with no arrow; it runs and prints hello. Probe s02 writes save as -[FS.Write]> IOError! and check_name as -> IOError!.

Both lines of s02 are E0003: a unit-fallible error contract comes before the effect arrow, and a unit-fallible signature has no ->. Probe s03 tries the Swift order for a value and gets E0080, because a type may follow the arrow only where the result goes. Probe s04 shows -> Never! refused like s02. Probe s05 shows the same rule inside a function type.

The rule under A. After the parameters, a signature has either nothing or exactly one arrow, -> or -[Effects]>. After the arrow come the optional result type and then the optional error contract, in that order. A unit function that can fail writes the arrow and then the contract alone.

Every form under A. With nothing to say, fn(x) { } has no arrow. Pure forms: fn(x) -> Int, fn(x) -> Int ! ParseError, fn(x) -> ! IOError and fn(x) -> ! Never. With effects the arrow is -[FS]> in the same position: -[FS]> { }, -[FS]> String ! IOError and -[FS]> ! IOError. The empty row -[]> works the same way.

Function types read the same way, so fn(String) -[FS.Write]> ! IOError is a parameter type. Trait methods and extern declarations follow the same order. The entry point keeps its default: run: fn() { } is fallible with Err, and an expert pins it as run: fn() -> ! Err.

Reading a contract. After the arrow, a spaced ! starts the error contract; a type before it is the result. So -> ! IOError is a unit function that can fail, -> String ! IOError returns a String or fails, and -> String cannot fail. A lone type with no ! is the result.

Spelling. D-ERR-CONTRACT1=A, ratified, writes the error contract as String ! ParseError, and its own unit example is save: fn(n: Int) -> ! ParseError. So that ruling already assumes this order, and its retirement of String ParseError! lands with this ballot's cut. One jet fix run applies both.

That spelling is not built yet. On t6c, probe s09 writes -> String ! SaveError and gets E0003 at the result, so every probe here uses today's String IOError! spelling. The programs in this ballot show the ratified spelling.

What becomes an error. Today's error-first order fn(x) IOError! -[FS]> and the arrowless contract fn(x) IOError! both become one registered retirement error. Its fix moves the contract after an arrow and respells it: -> ! IOError or -[FS]> ! IOError. A bare -> with nothing after it, and -> Unit, stay illegal, as D-SIG-AFTER1 says.

The four E0003 texts that teach the old order are deleted with their fixes; the census finds exactly four, in Compiler, tests and Docs. The retirement fix works on parsed nodes, keeps comments and source locations, and moves only the contract and arrow tokens. It rewrites function types inside parameters, fields and aliases too.

Migration, from the census script re-run on dev. Error first with an effect row: 1,606 signatures (Core 605, Jetpack 698, Compiler 114, Tools 123, tests 45, Examples 9, Docs 12). Arrowless unit-fallible, not Never: 1,807. Arrowless Never!: 3,859. So A changes about 7,272 signatures.

Value signatures with effects, a result and an error already use A's order: 2,250 of them, and they change only in D-ERR-CONTRACT1's respelling. The counts come from regular expressions over source text, so they are estimates; the fix works on the parse tree and reports each edit. The owner's review figures for Core came from a different count.

Beginner path. One sentence covers every function: after the inputs, write an arrow, then what it returns, then how it fails. A function with nothing to say after its inputs has no arrow. The retirement error prints the rewritten line beside the old one.

Expert path. Function types, trait methods, extern declarations and generic signatures share the one order, so a signature copied into a type annotation needs no edit. Effect rows, error unions such as ! DbError | TimeoutError, and ! Never all sit where they sit for a value function.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. About 5,700 unit functions that can fail gain an arrow, 3,859 of them Never functions. jet fix writes the arrow in one run, and the formatter never removes it. A failing unit function is three characters longer, the arrow and its space; that is the price of one order.

Readers and tools that learned the old order meet the retirement error. It is registered, so jet fix applies it across a package in one run, and the error names the new order on the exact line.

Other options. B keeps the error-first order: unit signatures that can fail put the error first or have no arrow, and value signatures put the arrow first. Under the ratified spelling that reads fn(p) ! IOError -[FS.Write]>, and B would also amend D-ERR-CONTRACT1's unit example, -> ! SaveError.

C is Swift's order for every function: the error contract before the arrow, then the result, as in fn(p) ! IOError -[FS.Read]> String. D moves only the effect form, so -[FS]> ! IOError is required and a pure fn(x) ! IOError keeps no arrow.

C moves the 2,250 value signatures with effects and errors, and every pure value signature with an error. It reverses D-SIG-AFTER1's rule that the result follows the one arrow. D changes the fewest lines, 1,606, but keeps two shapes for a unit function that can fail, chosen by whether it has effects.
