decisions.title: Teach three ways to hold changing state: a plain value, Shared across tasks, and a Pool with IDs for graphs
decisions.situation:
Jet has seven ways to hold a value that changes: a plain value, Shared, Pool with ID, Cell, Atomic, guards and Weak, beside #Persist and module state. The docs and examples show them as peers, so a beginner must choose among seven.

The owner's language review proposed teaching three, with the rest kept for experts. This is a teaching rule, not a language change, and it extends the ratified short-path rule for examples.
decisions.gist: Should Jet's beginner path teach three ways to hold changing state, with Cell, Atomic, guards and Weak kept for experts?
decisions.lesson: A program's values change as it runs: a score goes up, tasks count hits, a tree grows. Jet has seven tools for holding such values. Most programs need only three. This vote decides which tools a beginner is taught first.
decisions.explainer: Words used here. A holder is how a value that changes is kept. Shared lets tasks change one value safely. A Pool stores many values and hands out IDs, so a tree can point both ways. Cell, Atomic, guards and Weak are finer tools.
decisions.story: Sam counts hits from two tasks. Coming from Java, he reaches for Atomic, and Jet answers E1102: Atomic can't cross into a task. Under A the first page on changing state shows him Shared, which works.
decisions.inWild:
// Go's advice: share memory by communicating.
results := make(chan int)
go func() { results <- work() }()
total += <-results
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. Which holders the beginner path teaches, and in what order. No holder is added or removed; experts keep every one.

Today, on the t6c compiler (dev 76955986d0), every probe matches the seed. Probe s01 uses the three proposed holders: a plain score, a shared hit count changed by two tasks, and a Pool tree with a parent ID. It prints score 10, tasks 2, hits 2, leaf leaf.

Probe s02 writes the same program with Cell and Atomic, as a reader from Java or Rust would. Cell works. Atomic<Int> passed to a task is E1102, and its Why says the compiler has no registered ownership facts for Atomic.

So that refusal is a missing registration, not a rule, and this ballot does not lean on it. Probe s03 writes Go's way: tasks return values, and it prints score 10, hits 2.

Census on dev, Jet files in Examples, comment lines skipped, by git grep. shared or Shared is on 43 lines, Pool< or ID< on 10, guard_edit, guard_read, guard_write and guard.value on 12. Cell is on 4, Weak or downgrade on 4, #Persist on 1 and Atomic on 0. So the examples already lean toward the three.

What A changes. The guide's chapter on changing state teaches three holders, in order. First a plain value, the default. Then Shared, for one value changed by several tasks. Then a Pool with IDs, for graphs and trees.

Cell, Atomic, guards, Weak, #Persist and module-state rules move to an expert chapter, each with the problem it solves. Examples/Memory keeps the three at its top level and moves the rest under an Expert folder.

A registry check makes it stick. When a beginner holder solves the problem, an error's first fix names it. An expert holder may come first only when none of the three solves it, and then the fix links its chapter.

The check lists today's rows to reword. E0111 suggests the shared keyword with a lowercase module name, which itself fails; under A it shows the ALL_CAPS module holder, a Shared. E1102 suggests rebuilding an owned copy, and under A it names Shared first.

What stays. Every holder keeps its API: D-SHARED-API1, D-POOLID-API1 and D-SHAREDGUARD1 are unchanged. Expert pages link from each error that needs them.

Beginner path. Change a plain value; share it across tasks with Shared; build a graph with a Pool. Expert path. Cell for change behind a read-only view, Atomic for lock-free counters, guards for holding a lock, Weak for back links, #Persist for state across reloads.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. A reader from Rust or Java looks for Atomic first. Every error that mentions Atomic links the expert chapter, and E1102 names Shared as the fix for a value several tasks change.

What remains. Shared costs a lock where Atomic would not. For a beginner's counter that cost is small, and the expert chapter shows when Atomic is worth it, once its ownership facts are registered.

Other options. B keeps today's peers. C teaches two, a plain value and Shared, and builds graphs from shared nodes with Weak back links. D teaches one, a plain value, and has tasks return results, as Go and Erlang advise; Shared and Pool become expert.

Their best cases. B hides nothing. C is one holder fewer. D is the smallest first step. Their costs: B leaves the beginner to pick among seven. C teaches Weak, the hardest part, to beginners. D leaves no beginner answer for a value several tasks must change.

decisions.title: One strictness field in package.jet names four levels, script, app, library and hardened, each a fixed bundle of today's policy keys
decisions.situation:
Jet already has many separate rigor settings: 20 scoped policy keys, 10 package policy fields, the authority block and named test profiles. A team that wants a careful package must know which ones to turn on.

A probe package that turns on harden, sentries, a lint and an authority list runs. A package that writes one strictness level is refused as an unknown field.
decisions.gist: Should package.jet get one strictness field whose four levels turn on fixed bundles of today's policy keys?
decisions.lesson: Jet can check a program more or less strictly, but each check is its own setting. This vote decides whether one word in package.jet picks a level. Each level turns on a fixed set of the existing checks.
decisions.explainer: Words used here. A policy key is one package.jet setting, such as harden: true. The authority block lists the powers a package may use. A sentry is a runtime check kept in the built program.
decisions.story: Ben's team ships a parser that other teams depend on. Under A he writes strictness: .Library, and jet check refuses any change to a public function's effects or errors that would break those teams.
decisions.inWild:
// TypeScript: one switch turns on a family of checks.
{ "compilerOptions": { "strict": true } }
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. Whether one field names a level, and what each level turns on. Every level is built from checks that exist today.

Today, on the t6c compiler (dev 76955986d0), every probe matches the seed. Policy.jet lists 20 scoped policy keys, such as unsafe, check_removal, sentries and lint_allow. package.jet's policy block also takes contain, harden, unsafe, expert, deps, claims, licenses, sources, exceptions and lints. The authority block holds allow, deny and grants.

Probe today sets policy to harden, sentries .On and a lint deny, plus an authority allow list, and prints 42. Probe dial writes strictness: .Library and gets E1215: strictness is not part of the Package vocabulary.

What A does. package.jet gets one field, strictness, with four values. A missing field keeps today's behavior exactly, so no existing program changes.

jet new writes no level, so a first program meets no new check. The cli and web templates, which ship programs to other people, write strictness: .App with their allow list already filled in.

.Script is today's default: effects are inferred and summarized, and no manifest is needed. .App adds the authority requirement. The package must have an authority allow list, which turns on D-EFFBUDGET1=D's opt-in enforcement. The error offers the inferred list as its fix.

.Library adds a stable public surface. A change to a public function's types, effects or errors that would break callers is refused until the author accepts it. The inferred signature is what is checked, so nothing new is written in source, as D-HONEST-SIG1=A says.

Where that surface lives. If the open API ballot passes, it is package.api, and .Library turns on its --locked check in every jet check. If it fails, .Library requires written effects and errors on public items instead, with the inferred text as the fix.

.Hardened adds the safety keys. It sets harden: true from D-MEM-GUARANTEE1=A, sentries .On and unsafe .Obligations from D-UNSAFE-OBLIG1=A. It also makes jet test run D-HARDENED1=A's hardened profile.

Levels only tighten. A package may add any key on top of its level. To loosen a key the level sets, the package picks a lower level and adds the keys it wants. This keeps D-PACKAGE-POLICY-SCOPE1=A's rule that policy only tightens.

jet explain strictness lists each level's keys, and jet inspect guarantees prints the level a package chose. The levels are fixed lists in one Jet table, so a new key joins a level by one row.

Ratified decisions. A uses D-PACKAGE-POLICY-SCOPE1=A, D-EFFBUDGET1=D, D-EFFECTS-BLOCK1=B, D-MEM-GUARANTEE1=A, D-UNSAFE-OBLIG1=A and D-HARDENED1=A unchanged. D-MATURITY1=B's #Hardened marker is a doc label on an item; the .Hardened level is a package setting.

Census on dev, by git ls-files and git grep. The repository holds 2,490 package.jet files, 2,173 of them in tests. 207 write an allow list, and 51 write a policy block. None of them changes under A, because a missing field keeps today's behavior.

Beginner path. A first program never sees the field, since jet new writes none. Expert path. One word picks a level, and extra keys tighten further; jet explain strictness lists what each level turns on.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. A team that wants .Hardened minus one key must drop a level and add keys back. jet explain strictness prints the exact key list to copy.

What remains. The levels are a fixed judgment about which checks belong together. A team with a different judgment writes the keys one by one, as it does today.

Other options. B keeps separate keys. C is one strict: true switch, as TypeScript has. D puts the level on the build profile, so one package builds at different levels.

Their best cases. B adds nothing to learn. C is the simplest name. D lets a nightly build run harder checks than a daily one. Their costs: B leaves the team to find the keys. C has only two levels. D lets a published package's level differ by build.

losses.mitigation: jet explain strictness prints the key list to copy.

D lets a package's level differ by build.

recommendation.tradeoff: A fixed bundle per level, for one word that names how careful a package is.

decisions.title: A build target is an ordinary Core type that implements Machine, so a package can add a board
decisions.situation:
A target describes the machine a build is for: its instruction set, memory, and services such as a clock or a serial port. Today the compiler holds a fixed table of machines, and a package names one by a string. A board the table lacks cannot be added by a package, and one table board quietly builds code for the wrong chip.

The owner asked for a target to be an ordinary Core type implementing a trait, declared by a library. That changes an earlier ruling, which made targets typed modules; keeping that ruling is option C. We recommend A: a board is a type implementing Machine, with one checked record of facts.

One limit holds under every option: a package can describe a board, but a chip family needs a code generator inside the compiler. Jet has two today, x86-64 and WebAssembly.
decisions.gist: Should a build target be a type implementing Machine, with one typed facts record, so a package can add a board?
decisions.lesson: Programs for small devices must know the machine: how much memory it has, whether it has a clock, how it reports a crash. This vote decides how that machine is described, so a board maker can ship it as an ordinary package instead of waiting for a compiler change.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A target is the machine a build is for. A fact is one thing known about it, such as its pointer size. A service is something the machine provides, such as a clock; its provider is the function that does it.

An emitter is the part of the compiler that writes machine code for one instruction set. A denial forbids an effect for a build.
decisions.story: Kofi's company makes an x86-64 sensor gateway and an Arm sensor board. Today he asks the Jet team to add each to the compiler's table. Under A he publishes acme with both types, and jet check validates every fact. His customers build the gateway today, and the board build stops with a clear message until Jet has an Arm code generator.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. How a target is declared and selected, and the one record of facts every option shares. What each fact means stays as ratified in D-FREESTAND-FACTS1, D-TARGET-ALLOC1, D-TARGET-MEMORY1, D-TARGET-LINKER1 and D-EFFTYPE-TARGET1.

Today, with the t6c compiler on dev 76955986d0. Probe pkg_lib selects the profile board.sensor_v1, whose table triple is thumbv7em-none-eabihf, and builds an x86-64 ELF file. Its first bytes are 7f 45 4c 46 and its machine field is 0x3e. The board's facts do not reach code generation. Examples' package files spell profiles in a second vocabulary, web.no_os against the driver's wasm.no-os.

Probe t_web builds with --target web and now prints words Web, as D-BUILD-TOOLCHAIN1=A requires. The seed printed words Linux; that building bug is fixed on dev.

Probes p6 to p8 show the shape A uses already works for user traits. p6 prints a struct's trait constants, thumbv7em-none-eabihf 32 32 32. p7 prints 32 64 with a default constant. p8 leaves a required constant out and gets E0933, MissingTraitConstant.

The rule under A. core.target declares the trait Machine with one required constant, facts, of type MachineFacts. A target is a struct with no fields that implements Machine. Core declares its own machines this way, the host machines and web among them, and a package declares a board the same way.

A package selects a machine by type in targets:, and code reads it as build.target, spelled as D-META-HASH1 ratifies. Hosted single-file programs never name a machine, as D-TARGET-SURFACE1 requires: the host machine is implied.

The record. MachineFacts maps one to one onto the compiler's TargetMachine record today. Required: triple, os, layout, allocator and panic. layout carries pointer and word size, cache line, endianness and atomic width, and is checked against the triple's ABI rather than assumed. os is one of the owner's #6206 list: Linux, MacOS, Windows, Web, Wasm or Freestanding.

The rest default to absent. Machine parts: memory regions, linker input, MMIO, volatile access, startup entry, vectors and placement. Services: the wall and monotonic clocks, zone data, sleep, entropy, scheduler and byte sink read, write and report. Host features: sockets, files, processes, environment, browser DOM, GPU and FFI. Hardware facts, programmers and audit carry over.

Today's HostedDefault arms are gone. Core's host machines state each service explicitly, so no fact is hidden behind a default. This one record is the #6206 c24 capability union, declared once, so no second closed list exists.

Providers. A present service names a provider function, as provider(uart_write). The compiler fills in the rest of D-FREESTAND-FACTS1's contract. Identity is the function's full path, and the digest and provenance come from its package's locked digest. ABI and limits come from the function's signature and declared limits.

A bad provider is today's E3312. A missing allocator is E3303, a missing or host-only service E3311, MMIO E3313, and every other missing fact E3314. Those codes and their texts exist today.

Denials. Each absent service becomes a denial for that build, per D-EFFTYPE-TARGET1. No allocator denies Mem.Alloc; no sockets, Net; no files, FS; no entropy, Rand; no sleep, Time.Wait; no processes, Exec; no environment, Env. Browser is present only on Web.

Partial services are checked per operation, as the compiler does today. A board with a write-only byte sink allows print and refuses a read with E3311 at that line, naming the machine and the missing service. One clock allows only its own reads.

Staging. Each artifact's code and every #if in it see that artifact's build.target. Build code also reads build.target as the target, and reads the machine it runs on as build.host, per D-BUILD-TOOLCHAIN1. A machine is checked when its package is checked, even if no application selects it.

Scope. A package may declare a machine for any triple Jet's layout table knows, Arm and AArch64 included, and jet check validates it. Building a machine whose triple has no emitter stops before code generation. A new registered error beside E3302 names the triple and the emitters Jet has: x86-64 and Wasm today. So pkg_lib's silent x86-64 build becomes that stop.

Census of the cutover on dev, Jet sources only. Six package.jet files in Examples/LowLevel/Embedded name a profile by string. Compiler/JetFoundation/Source/Target/TargetMachine.jet builds the machines from literals. The driver's list, the loader, the checker, Jetpack's Targets.jet parser, the embedded battery and Flash.jet read those names. 129 $build reads in 57 files keep working, respelled with HASH1.

Beginner path. Write nothing: a single-file program builds for the host. To build for a board, add one line to package.jet naming the board's type, and errors name the machine and the missing service.

Expert path. Declare a board as a struct implementing Machine with one MachineFacts record. Share a pure function that builds the record when several boards differ in one fact. Check the package with jet check, and every fact is validated before any application selects it.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. Each configuration is its own type. A pure facts builder shared by several types keeps each one three lines long, and D is the option that takes configuration as a value.

The trait is named Machine, not the steer's Target. Target already names Core's codegen-family enum (Lang.jet:193) and the declaration every marker expansion receives (Core/Compiler/Compiler.jet:39). Another meaning would collide in every marker body, and probe p4b shows a user trait named Target beside #Target(Web) checks with no warning. A amends D-TARGET-SURFACE1's module wording; option C keeps it.

What remains. No option can add an instruction set from a package: a chip family needs an emitter in the compiler. Under A the board is declared and checked anyway, and the build stop names the missing emitter. Deriving each provider's digest from the lock is compiler work, reusing digests the lock already records.

Other options. B adds a target keyword whose braces hold the same record. C keeps the ratified typed module with a facts field. D takes a value of a type implementing Machine, with facts(self), so boards are configured by fields. E keeps today's compiler table selected by name, as Swift's closed platform list does.

Their best cases. B reads like a declaration of its own and can lower to A's checks. C needs no amendment and checks the module when its package is checked. D configures a board without a type per configuration, at the cost of putting the value into build cache keys. E needs no work.

options.name: A type implementing Machine
options.detail: A target is a struct with no fields that implements core.target.Machine, whose one required constant is a MachineFacts record. A package selects it by type.
options.technical: Amends D-TARGET-SURFACE1=A's module wording. MachineFacts maps TargetMachine one to one; triple, os, layout, allocator and panic are required, the rest absent by default. Providers get identity and digest from the lock. Denials per EFFTYPE-TARGET1, per-operation checks for partial services. Any layout-known triple may be declared; building one with no emitter is a registered stop naming the triple.

options.name: A target keyword
options.detail: A new declaration word, target Name { }, whose braces hold the same MachineFacts fields.
options.technical: Adds target as a reserved word. Lowers to A's Machine and MachineFacts, so the checks are shared. Selection, denials and scope as A.

options.name: Keep the ratified typed module
options.detail: A target is a module with a facts field of type MachineFacts, as D-TARGET-SURFACE1 ratified. A package selects the module.
options.technical: D-TARGET-SURFACE1=A unchanged. The module's facts are checked when its package is checked. Same record, providers, denials and scope as A; generic code cannot take a machine as a type.

options.name: A value implementing Machine
options.detail: A package selects a value, such as acme.Sensor{flash_kib: 256}, whose type implements Machine with facts(self).
options.technical: Machine requires a pure facts(self) -> MachineFacts. The selected value is evaluated while building and enters the build cache key. Same record and checks as A.

options.name: Today's compiler table
options.detail: The compiler holds a closed table of machines, and a package names one by string. A new board needs a compiler change.
options.technical: Today's behavior: six machines in TargetMachine.jet, selected by profile string. Two name vocabularies, Jetpack's and the driver's. Reverses D-TARGET-SURFACE1's typed profiles.

comparisons.note: std.Target is a plain struct that build code makes; code reads builtin.target.
A custom target is a compiler-validated JSON file; its format is unstable.
Platforms are a closed list in the compiler.

recommendation.why: A lets a board maker ship a machine as an ordinary package. It adds no keyword and checks every fact before any application selects it.
gains: A new board is a package, checked before any application selects it.
One MachineFacts record replaces the table and both name lists.
A missing fact is today's E0933, and a missing service names the machine.

decisions.title: TCP writes keep the ratified Writer law, mark the short count must-use, and retire the five free-function spellings
decisions.situation:
A network connection in Jet can be written eight ways. Three of them may send only the first part of the bytes and report how many went. Today a program can call one of those three, ignore the count, and compile and run. A partial send then passes unnoticed.

We recommend A. The counted write keeps its count, and ignoring it becomes a build error that points to the write-everything call. The five old free-function spellings retire. On today's code almost nothing breaks: no stream write outside those five functions ignores its count.
decisions.gist: Should TCP writes keep write's short count, make dropping it an error, and retire the five free-function spellings?
decisions.lesson: A network write may send only part of your bytes and tell you how many went. Jet has eight ways to write to a connection, and three can stop early. This vote picks the spellings to keep and how Jet stops a silent partial write.
decisions.explainer: Words used here. A short count is a write that reports sending fewer bytes than asked. Must-use means the compiler refuses a call whose result is ignored. Write-everything means the call loops until all bytes are sent.
decisions.story: Ben sends a 2 MB reply with client.write(bytes) and ignores the count. Under A, the build stops on that line and tells him to call write_all, which sends every byte.
decisions.inWild:
// Rust: write may be short; clippy flags an unused count.
stream.write_all(b"ping")?;
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. Which TCP write spellings remain, and what happens when a caller drops a short count. Reading, Unix sockets and TLS keep their own names.

The ratified law. D-NETIO-CONTRACT2=B, with option A's laws, says write may return any positive prefix count and write_all loops until done. Compiler/Prelude/Traits.jet's Writer trait has exactly write -> Int and write_all.

Where they live. The methods are sema builtins in Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Calls/NetworkHandles.jet:99-104. The free functions are in Core/Net/Net.jet:282-313, each a one-line call to a method.

Census on dev 76955986d0. net.send has 0 callers. tcp_write has 1, tcp_write_bytes 1, tcp_write_all_bytes 50 in 27 files, tcp_write_text 20 in 8 files. Method calls: write_all 187 in 116 files, write_text 49 in 35 files.

Dropped counts today. A statement-start .write( on a stream-named receiver appears 3 times on dev. Two are inside the retiring send and tcp_write_bytes (Net.jet:283, 304); the third, in TrustGate.jet:172, already writes .drop(reason). So A's new error breaks no caller outside the code it retires.

Probes with the t6c compiler. t02 opens a local TCP pair, calls client.write with the count dropped, then write_all, and prints got pingpong. t01 shows a dropped pure result is E0433, but write has effects, so that rule does not apply.

Probe t03 marks an effectful function #MustUse, and the dropped call is E0419. Probe t04 marks a trait method #MustUse and drops it through an impl and through a generic bound: both compile and run. The marker is accepted on a trait method and ignored, a building bug.

Probe t05 gives #MustUse a reason and gets E0930: the marker's signature is MustUse(), so today its fix line cannot name write_all.

A ninth spelling hides in the checker. TCPStream.write also accepts a String and writes its UTF-8 bytes (NetworkHandles.jet:318-320), returning a byte count that can split a character. Its one caller is net.send, which retires.

What A does. TCPStream.write takes bytes only, keeps its count and is must-use, so a dropped count is E0419 with a fix line naming write_all. write_all and write_text stay the write-everything forms for bytes and text. Writer.write in Compiler/Prelude/Traits.jet gains #MustUse, so files and TLS match.

Compiler work A needs. #MustUse gains an optional fix text, MustUse(fix: String), shown on E0419's fix line, as Rust's must_use takes a reason. A trait method's #MustUse applies to every impl and to calls through a bound, which fixes t04. The builtin write rows at NetworkHandles.jet:99-100 carry the same flag.

The five free functions go, each with a jet fix rewrite under D-CODEMOD1=A. tcp_write and tcp_write_text become write_text, tcp_write_all_bytes becomes write_all, tcp_write_bytes becomes write, and send(s, text) becomes s.write(text.bytes()). Each rewrite calls what the function called, so it keeps behavior and applies unattended.

Ratified decisions. A keeps D-NETIO-CONTRACT1=A and D-NETIO-CONTRACT2=B's write law. It uses D-DISCARD1=A's must-use rule as it stands and D-MARK-DISCARD1=A's .drop(reason) for a deliberate discard.

Beginner path. Write stream.write_all(bytes) or stream.write_text(text). If you reach for write and drop the count, the error points to write_all. Expert path. n: stream.write(bytes) keeps the count for a hand-rolled send loop.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. Code that drops write's count stops compiling; on dev that is no caller outside the retiring functions. For other code, jet fix offers write_all as a needs-review edit, since it sends the rest of the bytes too. jet fix --all applies it.

What remains. The plain name write stays the partial form, which surprises Go programmers. The E0419 fix line names write_all at the moment of surprise.

Other options. B amends D-NETIO-CONTRACT2: write writes everything, as Go's io.Writer does, and write_some returns a count. C keeps all eight names and makes each write everything. D keeps today's surface.

Their best cases. B gives the short name the safe meaning. C breaks no caller. D costs nothing. Their costs: B changes the Writer law for files and TLS too. C keeps eight spellings for two jobs. D leaves the silent partial write.

decisions.title: A task group can ask for a larger stack; programs otherwise get the system's stack size
decisions.situation:
Today every task in every Jet program gets a stack of at least 192 MiB, a size chosen for the compiler's own deep recursion. The main thread gets the normal system size, so the same deep call works in a task and stops on the main thread.

The plan is to give programs the normal size everywhere, while the compiler keeps its large stacks. The open question is how the compiler asks for them: a task-group argument, a process-wide call, a package setting, a private back door, or no change.

Whatever is chosen must not leak into programs the compiler starts, and must not need a privilege other packages lack. We recommend A: a task group can ask for a bigger stack, and one deep function uses the depth mark Jet already ratified.
decisions.gist: How should the compiler get its large worker stacks once ordinary programs stop getting 192 MiB for every task?
decisions.lesson: A stack is the memory a thread uses for calls in progress. Today every task gets a very large one because the compiler needs it. This vote decides how the compiler keeps its large stacks while ordinary programs get the normal size.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A stack is the memory that holds calls in progress; deep recursion needs a big one. The soft stack limit is the size the operating system offers, usually 8 MiB.

A worker is a thread that runs tasks, and a fiber is a task with its own small stack on a worker. A task group is the task.group block that owns the tasks started in it.
decisions.story: Mia's program recurses deeply in a task. Today it works, because every task gets 192 MiB, but the same call on the main thread stops. Under A both stop at the same depth. The stop names the fix: mark the function with the depth it needs, and it works in both places on every build level.
decisions.inWild:
// Rust: the thread that needs a big stack asks for it.
std::thread::Builder::new().stack_size(192 << 20).spawn(compile)?;
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. How the compiler gets the stack size its recursive passes need, once ordinary programs get a stack chosen for programs. The runtime's default and the docs follow from the choice.

Today, with the t6c compiler on dev 76955986d0. Thread.jet's thread_stack_bytes gives each worker and fiber the larger of the soft stack limit and 192 MiB. It is capped at 8 GiB and at a hundredth of a finite address-space limit. The main thread keeps the soft limit, 16 MiB on the probe machine.

Probe t01 recurses 3,000,000 calls deep on the main thread, and jet run stops it with Stop [E3012]: Stack overflow in depth. Probe t02 makes the same call in a task and prints task 3000000, because the task got 192 MiB. On the seed compiler jet run also ran t01 to the end; t6c now runs the program's main thread with every stack default (Host.jet:3383).

Probe t03 writes task.group deep(stack: …) and gets E0003, task-group parameter stack is not supported. Probe t04 calls core.sys.__thread_stack_floor from user code and gets E0067. Probe t06 writes #MaxDepth(3000001) and gets E0927: the ratified depth mark is not built yet.

The rule under A, for one deep function. D-RESOURCE-LIMIT1=A and D-STACKBOUND1=A already ratified #MaxDepth(n): every build level reserves room for n waiting calls when the entry or task starts. That is the fix A's stop suggests when the overflow repeats one function, as in Mia's program. It gives the same depth on every tier.

The rule under A, for other deep code. task.group gains a stack argument next to limit. Every task started in that group runs on a stack of at least that many bytes. A group opened inside one of those tasks uses the same size, unless it names its own. The bytes give a depth that depends on the machine, as D-RESOURCE-LIMIT1=A allows for unmarked code.

Without a mark or a stack argument, a task gets the soft stack limit, at least 8 MiB, the same room the main thread gets. That meets the card's goal, and the runtime docs state both numbers.

Nothing outside the group changes. The process's stack limit is never written, so no child process inherits anything: not jet dev's program, not a jet test binary, not a core.process spawn. Other groups in the same program keep the default.

The compiler. Host.jet already compiles inside task.group compile_stack. Its deep code is many functions calling each other, so one mark cannot size it. Under A that line asks for 192 MiB, and the compiler's internal groups inherit it. D-COMPILE-STACK1=A already says jet::compile runs on a worker with an explicit stack size; A gives that size a public spelling.

A needs no double-underscore exception, no C import and no package field. Any package can do what the compiler does, which is the rule card c0w1wcfc asks for.

Limits and refusals, following D-RESOURCE-LIMIT1=A. A literal size the target can never supply is a build error. A request that the address-space limit cannot cover is cut to a hundredth of it, as today, and the stop report names the request and the cut.

A target whose tasks share one fixed stack, such as web, refuses a stack argument at build time, naming the target. The argument reserves address space without touching memory, as today's 192 MiB does, so resident memory does not grow until the stack is used.

What building A takes. The parser and checker accept stack beside limit. The runtime keeps one fiber pool per stack size instead of one size per process. Alloc.jet's arena bands read each thread's real stack size instead of assuming 192 MiB. E3012's fix text names #MaxDepth or the group's stack argument.

Beginner path. Nothing to write. Tasks and the main thread get the same room, so a recursion that works on one works on the other. If one function needs more, the stop writes the #MaxDepth line for it. Expert path. Ask a group for more with stack:, and see the computed worst case with jet inspect memory under D-STACKBOUND1=A.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. A program that relied on 192 MiB in its tasks now stops with E3012. The stop names the fix: #MaxDepth on the function that repeats, or the stack argument on the group. Until #MaxDepth is built, it names only the stack argument, so the default should change after #MaxDepth lands.

The census on dev counts task.group headers outside comments: 195 in 146 files, 24 of them with an argument list such as limit:. Only the compiler's compile_stack group is known to need more than the default. The suite's compiler_stack cases and every example's golden output prove the rest under an 8 MiB limit before the default changes.

What remains. Two fiber pools in one process, one per size, keep some idle stacks of each size. That is address space, not resident memory; the cost is bounded by the pool's existing cap.

Other options. B adds a public core.sys call that raises the floor for every worker in the process. C adds a package.jet field fixed at build time. D lets Compiler packages call Core's double-underscore functions. E keeps 192 MiB for every program and retires c6. F makes the compiler's passes iterative so nothing needs more (#5910).

Their best cases. B is one call and is already drafted. C needs no code in Host.jet. D is the smallest change. E costs nothing and keeps every deep task working. F is the cleanest end state, with no stack request at all.

Their costs. B and C act on the whole process, not on the code that needs it. D gives one set of packages a privilege, against D-SHAPE-DUNDER2=A and D-CORE-HELPERS1=A. E keeps the compiler's size in every program. F has no date; until then it is E.

E3012 suggests #MaxDepth(n) for one repeating function, else stack:. Gives D-COMPILE-STACK1=A's explicit worker stack a public form.

gains: Programs get the normal stack size, as c6 asks.
The compiler uses the same public form as any package.
No child process inherits a changed limit.
A deep function marked with #MaxDepth gets the same depth on every tier.

losses.mitigation: The stop names #MaxDepth or the group's stack argument; goldens under 8 MiB prove the change first.

losses.loss: #MaxDepth is ratified but not built (probe t06, E0927), so the best fix is missing today.
losses.mitigation: The default changes after #MaxDepth lands; until then E3012 names the stack argument.

losses.loss: One fiber pool per requested stack size.
losses.mitigation: Idle stacks are reserved address space, not resident memory, under the pool's existing cap.

whyNot.reason: B raises every worker in the process, not just the code that needs it.
C fixes a process-wide size in the package file, far from the code.
D gives Compiler packages a privilege the ratified naming rules forbid.
E keeps the compiler's stack size in every program.
F has no date, and until then it is E.

recommendation.tradeoff: A small new argument on task.group, in return for program-sized stacks and no privileged route.

decisions.title: A WebSocket route kind on the HTTP mux: the server validates and upgrades, and the handler gets the request and the connection
decisions.situation:
A WebSocket starts as a web request and then becomes a two-way connection. In Jet today, a server handler makes that switch itself and must still return a web response, which the server throws away. The handler also writes its own error replies for a bad handshake.

There is a bigger catch. The server answers one connection at a time, so while one WebSocket stays open, no other client is served (probe w04). That breaks the ratified server design, D-HTTP-SERVER2=A, and its fix serves every option.

The recommendation is A: a WebSocket route kind. The server checks the handshake, and the handler returns nothing.
decisions.gist: Should the HTTP mux gain a WebSocket route whose handler gets the connection and returns nothing, instead of a fake response?
decisions.lesson: A WebSocket starts as an ordinary web request and then becomes a two-way connection. Today a handler must still hand back a web response that nobody sees. This vote decides how a Jet server says a route is a WebSocket.
decisions.explainer: Words used here. Upgrade is the step where a web request becomes a WebSocket. The mux is the server's table of routes. A handler is the function a route calls.
decisions.story: Lee writes a chat route. Under A, mux.websocket("/chat", chat) is the whole setup. Bad handshakes get a 400 before chat runs, chat never invents a response, and once the server serves connections side by side, as ratified, a second user joins while the first talks.
decisions.inWild:
// Axum: the upgrade extractor hands the socket to a callback.
ws.on_upgrade(|socket| handle(socket))
decisions.detail:
This vote chooses WebSocket route registration and the handler result. A is proposed, not built. Independently reran w01-w04 on a0.0.43: echo works, websocket registration is E0102, the proposed handler body checks, and GET waits behind an open socket.

A registers mux.websocket(pattern, handler) and #Server.WebSocket(pattern) over the same route table. The handler receives HTTPRequest and WsConn and returns Unit on the WsError rail. Authentication and Origin policy run before the handshake. Use the existing handshake validator once, not a second route-specific validator.

A owns GET for that pattern; another equivalent GET registration is a conflict. Plain GET without upgrade headers returns 400. HEAD must never upgrade; it returns 405. OPTIONS lists GET. OpenAPI records GET with handshake responses, including 101, not the later frame protocol.

The shared upgrade operation must own a transport, not a plain socket descriptor. Carry plain TCP or TLS through that same operation. Rejecting all secure WebSocket servers at bind is a dropped feature, not a fix. This transport repair is required for every option and is not evidence that A is better.

The server must meet ratified concurrency and shutdown rules under every option. Upgraded tasks remain in the server's connection budget and cancellation scope until closed. A task ending normally closes cleanly; application failure uses 1011 only while writable. Preserve protocol close codes and peer closure, and never send a second HTTP response after 101.

B returns an explicit switched response after manual upgrade. C uses an optional response; None without a completed upgrade must be an error, not a silent hang. D keeps the unused response. E returns a typed response-or-upgrade outcome with an owned callback, allowing one handler type and ordinary HTTP denial responses.

Beginner path: A's one route line and socket handler. Expert path: the same upgrade operation supports custom servers; mixed HTTP and WebSocket behavior is E's strongest case. Both require one ownership state and one handshake implementation.

options.technical: One route-table adapter and handshake implementation for TCP and TLS. Run authentication and Origin policy before upgrade. Own GET; reject equivalent GET registrations; HEAD returns 405 without upgrade, OPTIONS lists GET. Keep upgraded tasks inside existing server limits and shutdown. Preserve protocol close codes; application failure may send 1011 only before transport closure. OpenAPI describes handshake responses only.

decisions.title: How should a trait be implemented for Pair<T> only when T has another trait?
decisions.situation:
A generic type such as Pair<T> holds values of any type T. Sometimes a trait makes sense for Pair<T> only when T can do something itself. For example, a pair can describe its total price only when each half has a price.

Jet has no way to say this today. An impl block names the type bare, and its methods cannot add a bound to the type's T. The workaround is a separate wrapper type. This ballot picks where that condition is written, or decides that Jet keeps the wrapper.
decisions.gist: Where should Jet write a condition such as 'only when T is Priced' on a trait impl for a generic type?
decisions.lesson: A trait is a set of methods a type promises to have. An impl block keeps that promise for one type. A generic type like Pair<T> works for any T. A conditional impl keeps the promise only for some T, such as every T that is Priced. Calling the method on another Pair is an error at the call.
decisions.explainer:
Today, impl Pair.Describe { … } promises Describe for every Pair. Inside it, a method may use only what every T can do. So calling self.left.price() fails with E0901, because not every T has price.

Writing the bound in the head, impl Pair<T: Priced>.Describe, fails with E0003: an impl names the type bare. Adding <T: Priced> to the method makes a new T that has nothing to do with the pair's T, so the call fails with E0904.

Putting the bound on the type, Pair: struct<T: Priced>, works, but then every Pair needs a Priced T. A Pair<Int> could no longer exist.

Option A writes the condition in the impl head: impl Pair<T: Priced>.Describe { … }. The head names the type's own parameter and adds a bound to it. Inside the block, T is Priced, so self.left.price() checks.

Option B keeps the bare head and adds a trailing clause: impl Pair.Describe when T: Priced { … }. The meaning is the same as A, with a different spelling.

Option C adds nothing. A program writes a wrapper type, PricedPair<T: Priced>, and implements Describe on it. Callers wrap a Pair before they describe it.

Under A and B a call on a Pair whose T is not Priced is an error at the call. p.describe() on a Pair<Int> reports E0905, the type doesn't implement the required trait, naming Describe and the unmet bound Int: Priced. The same error stops show(p) when show needs Describe.

Overlap. Two impls of one trait for one type may not both apply to the same T. A bare impl Pair.Describe and a conditional impl Pair<T: Priced>.Describe overlap for every Priced T, so having both is E0908, a duplicate trait impl. Two conditional impls with different bounds also overlap, because one T could meet both bounds. So they are E0908 too.

The orphan rule does not change. The module must own the trait or the type, exactly as for a bare impl.
decisions.story: Rosa has a Pair<T> type for two items in a shopping cart. She wants pairs of priced items to describe their total, and her generic show function to accept them. Jet tells her an impl names the type bare. Her only choice today is a second type that wraps every Pair she wants to show.
decisions.detail:
Probes were run on dev 76955986d0 with the t6c compiler, as #6281 c58 asks. The files are p/c58/a.jet, b.jet and c.jet in the G1Lead-4 lane.

Probe a writes impl Pair<T: Priced>.Describe and gets E0003: impl Pair takes no type parameters. The why text says an impl of a generic type names the type bare.

Probe b writes impl Pair.Describe with a describe method that calls self.left.price(). It gets E0901: calling price needs Priced.

Probe c adds <T: Priced> to the describe method. The method's T is a fresh parameter, so p.describe() gets E0904: Jet can't figure out what T should be.

A bound on the type, Pair: struct<T: Priced>, holds for every Pair, so it does not express only when.

So the answer to c58 is that current law cannot express a conditional impl. This ballot is the missing form that c58 names.

What is the same in A and B. Sema reads the bound on the impl head's parameter as a condition on the impl row. Bound satisfaction, sema_type_bound_satisfied_nominal, then also checks the impl's own bounds against the actual type arguments. Method lookup on a Pair<Int> receiver finds the row, checks the condition and reports E0905 when it fails.

Coherence. Two impl rows of one trait whose targets resolve to one nominal overlap unless their conditions can never both hold. Jet cannot prove two traits are disjoint, so any pair of rows overlaps and E0908 reports the second. A bare row is a row with no condition.

Reproduced in this lane with the same compiler, probes/ic. a_head_bound gets E0003, b_bare_head gets E0901, and c_wrapper runs and prints pair costs 7. d_two_impls, two bare impls of one trait, gets E0908 today, the rule A extends. e_missing_impl passes a Pair<Int> to show and gets E0905, the error A reports.

Generic callers. Inside a function with U: Priced, a Pair<U> meets the condition, because the check reads U's declared bounds. Inside a function whose U has no bound, Pair<U>.describe() is E0905 naming the missing U: Priced, and the fix adds that bound.

Several parameters. For a type with two parameters, such as Entry: struct<K, V>, the head lists every parameter in order and bounds only some: impl Entry<K, V: Priced>.Describe. A head that lists parameters with no bound at all stays E0003, whose fix writes the bare head.

What A does not add. A head with a concrete argument, such as impl Pair<Int>.Describe, stays E0003; a type parameter is required in each place. The head's parameter list is the same form the struct declares, Pair: struct<T: Priced>, so nothing new is spelled.

options.name: The bound goes in the impl head
options.detail: impl Pair<T: Priced>.Describe { … } implements Describe for every Pair whose T is Priced. Inside the block, T is Priced. The bare head impl Pair.Describe still means every Pair. A call on a Pair<Int> is E0905, and a bare and a conditional impl of one trait together are E0908.
options.technical:
The parser accepts type parameters with bounds after the target in an impl head and stores them on ImplDef. The head lists every parameter of the type, in order, by its declared name, and at least one carries a bound. Otherwise E0003 names the expected list or, with no bound, writes the bare head.

Registration records the bounds on the impl row. Bound satisfaction and method lookup check them against the actual type arguments, reading a type parameter's declared bounds in generic code; a failure is E0905 naming the unmet bound. Coherence treats every pair of impl rows of one trait for one nominal as overlapping, so a second one is E0908. The formatter prints the head as written.

options.name: A trailing when clause
options.detail: impl Pair.Describe when T: Priced { … } has the same meaning as A. The head stays bare, and the condition follows it as a clause. Calls, overlap and errors are the same as under A.
options.technical: The parser accepts a when clause after the impl head, as a list of bounds on the target type's parameters. Names must be the type's own parameters, or E0003 names them. Registration, bound satisfaction, method lookup, E0905 and E0908 are the same as under A. The formatter prints the clause on the head line.

options.name: No conditional impls; use a wrapper type
options.detail: Jet keeps today's rule. A program declares a wrapper, PricedPair<T: Priced>, and implements Describe on it. Callers wrap a Pair before they describe it. E0003 keeps its current text, and its fix names the wrapper.
options.technical: No compiler change except the teaching. E0003 for a bounded impl head gains a fix that names the wrapper form. The c58 golden records the wrapper as the answer.

comparisons.note: The bound sits on the impl's own type parameter, as in option A.
Conditional conformance uses a trailing where clause, as in option B.
An instance context names the condition before the instance head.
comparisons.code:
instance Priced t => Describe (Pair t) where
    describe (Pair l r) = show (price l + price r)

recommendation.why: A puts the condition where the type is named, next to the parameter it limits. It reads like a generic function's bound, which Jet already writes as <T: Priced>, so there is nothing new to learn.
gains: Pairs of priced items describe themselves with no wrapper type.
The bound looks the same as a generic function's bound.
A call on the wrong Pair gets one clear error at the call.

losses.loss: The impl head grows a new form.
losses.mitigation: The form is the one generic functions already use, and the bare head keeps its meaning.

losses.loss: Two impls of one trait with different bounds cannot coexist.
losses.mitigation: Rust and Swift refuse the same overlap. E0908 names both impls, and a second trait covers the rare case.

whyNot.reason: A when clause is a second way to write a bound, while Jet writes every other bound inside angle brackets.
A wrapper type is boilerplate at every call, and it is the workaround this ballot exists to remove.

recommendation.tradeoff: One more form in the impl head, for conditional impls that read like every other bound.

decisions.title: Give Core the host's time zone, and let format selectors take a computed number
decisions.situation:
Jet aims for scripts that are no longer than the tools they replace. A trace viewer written for Node has 915 words, and the shortest faithful Jet version has 1000. Most of the gap is a header that shows the time of day.

Node asks the machine for its time zone in one call, while each Jet script must find the zone by hand. A smaller part is that a padded column cannot take its width from the data. Unpadded hours are already decided, so this ballot asks only about the zone and computed widths.
decisions.gist: Should Core tell a program the machine's time zone, and should format selectors accept a computed number?
decisions.lesson: A time zone turns an instant into a wall-clock time. The host zone is the one the machine is set to. A script that shows the time to a person wants it, while a program that must print the same everywhere names its zone.
decisions.explainer:
Today a Jet script finds the host zone itself. It reads the TZ variable, else the system zone link, else it uses UTC. Even with the decided unpadded-hour code, that lookup costs the twin 29 words, and every such script repeats it.

Under A, time.host_zone() returns the machine's zone, and an instant's in_host_zone() shows it there. Both declare that they read the environment and files, as zone(name) already does. The header becomes one interpolation.

The host rule is the one glibc and Go use. An unset TZ means the system setting, and an empty TZ means UTC. A set TZ loses one leading colon, then names a zone, or a zone file when it starts with a slash. Anything that does not resolve gives the zone named UTC.

Under A, every selector number may also be any Int expression: Pad, PadLeft, Fixed, Grouped, Sci, Percent and Hex. A negative number acts as zero. So a column as wide as its longest entry uses the selector, as fixed columns already do.

B adds the zone but keeps literal selector numbers. C adds only host_zone(), so callers write in_zone(time.host_zone()). D adds nothing and leaves the twin at 942 words.
decisions.story: Lee ports a watch-mode trace viewer from Node. Its header shows the wall-clock time, and the Jet version needs a zone lookup by hand to print 6:09:27 AM. Under A the header is one interpolation, and the column sized by the data is one selector.
decisions.detail:
Counts are whitespace-separated words, the gauntlet's source metric. The original viewer has 915. Compact.jet, the twin built from existing forms, has 1000. Projected.jet, with the A spellings, has 908. B gives 912 and C gives 908. The review's variants are in the lane's probes/lc/counts folder.

The no-pad flag is not on this ballot. The ratified one-percent-code ruling already gives every numeric code the GNU flag, so %-I prints 6. With that flag and nothing else, the twin has 942 words, and that is D.

From 942, the host zone saves 30 words and the computed width saves 4. Computed widths alone give 938. So the zone is the part that closes the gap, and the width supplies the slack.

Dev does not have the flag yet. On the t6c compiler, format and strftime copy %-I through as text, and format_checked refuses it. The twin reaches its count only after that ratified work lands, under every option.

Selectors today. {word:Pad(width)} and {x:Fixed(digits)} are refused with 'Expected width inside :Pad( )'. The parser's one number reader serves all seven numbered selectors, so A widens them together. The IR builder already passes the number as an operand of the helper call. A literal stays a constant, so existing output does not change.

The change touches the parser's number reader, the selector's tree node, the source formatter, the tree dump and the IR builder. Every tier runs that IR, so the tiers agree, as the selector ruling requires. The pad helpers already treat a zero or negative width as no padding, and a probe confirms it.

Zones today. zone(name) refuses a leading colon and any absolute path, and knows no POSIX rule string. The twin's hand rule picks the system zone when TZ is empty, but Node, glibc and Go use UTC. A uses UTC there, so the twin matches the original in one more case.

Limits common to every option. A POSIX rule string in TZ gives UTC, where glibc and Node honor it. Day and month names are English, where Node follows the host locale. Selector padding counts characters, not terminal columns.

A Core defect the review found, outside this ballot. zone(name) reads a TZif table but not the rule footer at its end. So New York shows standard time in July 2045, where Node and date show daylight time. The fix needs a POSIX rule reader, and TZ rule strings would then work for free.

Census on dev. Ten lines in eight files pass a computed width to a pad call, mostly package-tool tables. Selector numbers appear on 103 lines in 36 files, all literals. Four lines call in_zone, and one reads the system zone link by hand.

options.name: Host zone and computed selector numbers
options.detail: Add time.host_zone() -[Env, FS.Read]> Zone and DateTime.in_host_zone() -[Env, FS.Read]> ZonedDateTime. Let every selector number take any Int expression.
options.technical: host_zone() applies the host rule, then zone(name) or a direct zone-file read. in_host_zone() is in_zone(host_zone()). Web asks the browser's Intl zone, and Windows maps its zone setting to the IANA name with the CLDR table. Selector numbers parse as expressions, check as Int and run after the value. The twin projects to 908.
options.code:
print("{esc}[2J{esc}[H{time.now().in_host_zone().format("%-I:%M:%S %p")}  {path}")
lines.push("{row.kind:Pad(width)} {count:PadLeft(7)}")

options.name: Host zone; selector numbers stay literal
options.detail: A without computed selector numbers. Columns sized by the data keep writing pad_end(width, " ").
options.technical: The twin projects to 912 of 915, three words of slack. The selector parser does not change.
options.code:
print("{esc}[2J{esc}[H{time.now().in_host_zone().format("%-I:%M:%S %p")}  {path}")
lines.push("{row.kind.pad_end(width, " ")} {count:PadLeft(7)}")

options.name: Host zone function only, plus computed selector numbers
options.detail: Add time.host_zone() and computed selector numbers, with no in_host_zone() shortcut. Callers write in_zone(time.host_zone()).
options.technical: One fewer method on DateTime. The count equals A's, 908, because a dotted chain is one word. The longer chain is what most callers would write.
options.code:
print("{esc}[2J{esc}[H{time.now().in_zone(time.host_zone()).format("%-I:%M:%S %p")}  {path}")
lines.push("{row.kind:Pad(width)} {count:PadLeft(7)}")

options.name: No new Core; keep finding the zone by hand
options.detail: Scripts keep the TZ and system-link lookup. With the decided no-pad flag it is a 29-word function. The twin stays at 942 against 915.
options.technical: No API is added. Every script that shows local time repeats the lookup, and the hand rule picks the system zone for an empty TZ, unlike its peers.
options.code:
name := (sys.get("TZ") ?? "").remove_prefix(":")
if name == "" -> name = (files.read_link("/etc/localtime") ?? "").split_once("zoneinfo/")?.after ?? "UTC"
time.now().in_zone(time.zone(name) ?? time.utc()).format("%-I:%M:%S %p")
lines.push("{row.kind.pad_end(width, " ")} {count:PadLeft(7)}")

comparisons.note: Date methods use the host zone. toLocaleTimeString also uses the host locale, so its text varies by machine. This is the original's spelling.
time.Local is TZ, else the system zone file, else UTC, and an empty TZ is UTC. That is A's rule. Layouts spell the unpadded hour as 3.
LocalDate and LocalTime are zone-free, as Jet's are, so the host zone is named systemDefault rather than local.
Local::now() reads the host zone. %-I is the GNU no-pad flag Jet has already adopted.
astimezone() with no argument uses the host zone. Format specs take computed widths.

recommendation.why: Showing the clock in the machine's zone is ordinary script work, and every peer does it in one call. Jet already has zones and patterns, and lacks only the host lookup. A computed column width is the normal table case, and the selector path already passes its number at run time.
gains: The twin projects to 908 of 915 words.
One host rule for every script, the same as glibc and Go, including an empty TZ.
Columns sized by the data use the selector form, and so do computed decimal places.
The names avoid Local, which Jet's zone-free LocalDate and LocalTime already use.

losses.loss: in_host_zone() output depends on the machine. This cannot be removed, because it is the feature.

decisions.title: The place values: #here is where code is written, and a #caller default is the place of each call
decisions.situation:
Jet can tell a function where it was called from, and code where it is written. A logger uses this to print the caller's line, and a check helper to name the failing claim's line.

Today both are spelled with a dollar sign, which a ratified ruling retires. That ruling names hash line and hash file, but nothing for the caller's place. This vote picks the new spelling and closes three traps found while probing.
decisions.gist: Should the two place values be spelled #here and #caller, with assert and panic using the same caller default?
decisions.lesson: A log line is more useful when it says which line wrote it. Jet fills that place in for you, so the logger does not need it passed by hand. This vote decides how that filled-in place is written, now that its old spelling is retired.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A source location is the file, line, column, function and module of a place in code. It displays as file:line:column.

A parameter default is the value a parameter takes when a call leaves it out, written at: SourceLocation{...}. A site value is a value the compiler fills in, marked with #.
decisions.story: Ravi writes a check helper for his tests. It prints the caller's line, but when a claim fails, the stop report names the helper's own assert line instead. He has no way to pass the place on.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. How Jet spells the two place values that are $here and $caller today, now that the ratified one-mark ruling retires every $. It also settles their edge rules.

D-META-HASH1=A names #line, #file and #package as site values. It names no successor for the caller's place. #line and #file cover two of the five fields today's record carries.

Today, on the t6c compiler (dev 76955986d0). $here is a SourceLocation record: file, line, column, function and module, displayed as file:line:column. Probe s01 prints here 13:11 in run, module s01_today.

$caller is legal only as a parameter default, written at: SourceLocation{$caller}. Each call that leaves at out passes its own place. In s01 the direct log prints line 11, and the forwarding warn prints line 12.

The fill rule also holds for methods and pipes, where s04 prints lines 16 and 17. It holds for a generic function called from a lambda (s06, function run) and for a call through a function value (s12).

Anywhere else, $caller is E2427, CallerSiteMisplaced (s03). D-JAI-SITE1=A also allows it inside an #Expand macro, but sema has no such case, and #Expand left with macros under D-META-COMPILER1.

Three traps today. $here written as a default names the declaration, so both calls in s02 print line 2. At module level, $here has an empty function (s09). assert reports its own line, never the caller's (s08).

Census on dev, by git grep for $here and $caller. Jet code has 22 caller defaults: Core/Log 14, Core/Http 3, Examples 3 and tests 2. It has 4 $here reads: Examples 1 and tests 3.

The compiler side holds the parser's root list, sema's site checks in five files, the loader's SourceLocation alias, the syntax tables and E2427's texts. Four editor grammars and 16 Markdown lines in 5 files follow. The $here in Tools/perf is a shell variable.

Core/Log reads at.module to filter records, and the HTTP route check requires its at default to be $caller. Both need one record with a module, not separate line and file values.

The rule under A. #here is the SourceLocation of the place where it is written. #caller, written as a parameter default, is the place of each call that leaves that parameter out. Both are constants and never fail.

#line and #file become #here.line and #here.file. Neither is built: probe mh/h04 gets E0915 for #line, and s05 gets E0927 for #caller. No code uses them, so one record serves every place read. #package stays, since it names a package.

D-SCRIPT-SCRIPTDIR1=A, ratified after the one-mark ruling, still spells $here.file and $here.dir as package-relative Path values. Under A those members ride on #here unchanged, so the record gains dir and file becomes a Path, as ratified.

Edge rules under A. #caller anywhere but a default keeps E2427, respelled, with its fix: declare at: SourceLocation{#caller} and read at. Inside a lambda, the function field is the enclosing named function, as s06 shows today.

#here written as a parameter default becomes an error whose fix writes #caller. Today that default silently names the declaration (s02). No code on dev writes it, so the error refuses only the trap.

A wrapper forwards its caller's place by declaring the same default and passing at: at, as today. A call through a function value fills the call's place, as s12 shows. At module level the function field stays empty.

The one-mechanism check. assert, assert_eq and panic gain the same trailing at: SourceLocation{#caller}. A plain assert(ok) still reports its own line. The check helper above passes at: at, so the stop names its caller.

With that, every place Jet reports comes from one record and one fill rule. There is no second channel for stops, no hidden parameter, and no name whose meaning depends on where it is written.

Lowercase # names are compiler values and capitalised ones are markers, the split E0087 already enforces. So #here and #caller cannot be read as markers, and no user name can hide them.

Migration. jet fix rewrites $here to #here and $caller to #caller one to one: 26 Jet uses, then the compiler's tables, diagnostics, grammars and docs. The retired $ forms get that fix.

Relation to the open hash-spelling ballot, D-META-HASH2. Its option A writes the same #here and #caller. This ballot decides the place values and their edge rules alone, so that ballot can settle build separately.

Beginner path. Call log("starting") and the message names its line; nobody writes #caller to use a logger. Write spot: #here to ask where a line is.

Expert path. Declare at: SourceLocation{#caller} on a helper and pass at: at down to log or assert. Read at.module to filter by module, and build a SourceLocation by hand in tests.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. A wrapper that forgets at: at names itself, not its caller. The printed place names the wrapper's own function, so the slip shows on the first run.

assert, assert_eq and panic gain a parameter. Existing calls do not change, since the default fills it; only the stop report reads it.

Other options. B makes here and caller plain Prelude values, like build. Its best case is no mark at all: a reader sees an ordinary name.

B's cost. A default resolves where its function is declared, and a module function named caller is legal; s11 prints 42 from one. So a plain caller can be hidden, silently changing every default in that file.

B also adds a plain value that is filled at each call, which no other value does. And it reverses D-META-HASH1's rule that compiler-filled site values carry #.

C folds both into one name: only #here, and a #here default means the call's place, as a Swift #line default does. Its best case is one name fewer.

C's cost. One token means two places by position, and a reader of at: SourceLocation{#here} must know the rule to know which. It also flips s02's meaning without a word changing.

D is Rust's track_caller. A #TrackCaller marker adds a hidden place parameter, SourceLocation.caller() reads it, and calls between marked functions forward it. Its best case is no at parameter and nothing to forget.

D's cost. The place travels in a parameter no signature shows, so function values and package interfaces must carry it. It adds a second way into a function next to defaults, which the one-mechanism rule refuses.

options.name: #here and a #caller default
options.detail: #here is where code is written; a #caller default is each call's place. #line and #file become fields of #here. assert, assert_eq and panic take the same default.
options.technical: Respells D-JAI-SITE1=A's roots under D-META-HASH1=A, and amends HASH1's #line and #file to #here.line and #here.file. #here as a default is refused with a fix to #caller. E2427 respelled. Stops read an at: SourceLocation{#caller} parameter.

options.name: Plain Prelude values here and caller
options.detail: here and caller are ordinary Prelude names, like build. A caller default is filled at each call.
options.technical: Reverses D-META-HASH1=A's # mark for site values. Prelude names are shadowable, so a file's own caller or here hides them. A call-filled plain value is a new kind of value.

options.name: One #here; a default means the call
options.detail: Only #here exists. Written as a parameter default, it is the place of each call, as in Swift. Elsewhere it is where it is written.
options.technical: D-META-HASH1=A plus #here, with Swift's default rule. No #caller. Today's $here default meaning flips.

options.name: A #TrackCaller marker
options.detail: A marked function receives its caller's place in a hidden parameter, read with SourceLocation.caller(). Calls between marked functions forward it.
options.technical: Core marker and Core function, as in Rust. Function types and package interfaces carry the hidden parameter. #here as in A.

comparisons.note: A #line or #file default is filled at the call.
comparisons.code: func log(_ m: String, line: Int = #line) { }

comparisons.note: #[track_caller] adds a hidden location parameter.
comparisons.code:
#[track_caller]
fn check(ok: bool) { let at = Location::caller(); }

comparisons.note: source_location::current() as a default is the call's place.
comparisons.code: void log(std::string_view m, std::source_location at = std::source_location::current());

recommendation.why: A gives both places one record, one mark and one fill rule, and stops use it too. No name can hide it, and no position changes its meaning.
gains: Logs, checks and stops name the caller through one mechanism.
The $here default trap becomes an error with a fix.
26 Jet uses respell one to one.

losses.loss: A wrapper that forgets at: at names itself, not its caller.
losses.mitigation: The printed function names the wrapper, so the slip shows on the first run.

losses.loss: #line and #file, ratified but unbuilt, become #here.line and #here.file.
losses.mitigation: No code uses them, and one record serves every place read.

whyNot.reason: B's plain caller can be hidden by a file's own name, silently changing its defaults.
C gives one token two meanings by position and flips today's default meaning.
D adds a hidden parameter, a second way into a function next to defaults.

recommendation.tradeoff: Forwarding stays written as at: at, in return for one visible mechanism.

decisions.title: Public routes for a custom HTTP method: mux.custom(token, path, handler) and #Server.Custom(token, path)
decisions.situation:
HTTP lets a server accept methods beyond the nine standard ones, such as PURGE for caches or PROPFIND for WebDAV. Jet's server already reads such a request and answers 405 with an Allow list. But public code cannot register a route for one.

Each standard method has its own call, like mux.get, plus a struct marker like #Server.Get. The one call that takes a method value is mux.__route, and the compiler refuses that name in user code. So card #6206 cannot meet its rule that a custom-method route checks and serves.

We recommend A: mux.custom("PURGE", path, handler) and #Server.Custom("PURGE", path), named for the Custom case of the Method enum. The compiler checks the token while building.
decisions.gist: Should a custom HTTP method get its own route call, mux.custom(token, path, handler), named for the Method enum's Custom case?
decisions.lesson: A web server answers requests by method, such as GET or POST. HTTP also allows other methods, such as PURGE. Jet's server can already receive them, but your code has no public way to route one. This vote picks how you write that route.
decisions.explainer: Words used here. A method is the verb at the start of an HTTP request, such as GET. A custom method is any other valid token, such as PURGE; HTTP calls it an extension method. A mux is Jet's route table; a router is the same table with fully checked contracts. A marker such as #Server.Get tags a struct method as a route. A token is the HTTP word grammar: letters, digits and a few symbols, with no spaces.
decisions.story: Sam runs a cache in front of an API. The CDN sends PURGE /cache/:key to drop one entry. Under A, Sam writes mux.custom("PURGE", "/cache/:key", purge) next to mux.get. A typo with a space fails the build, and the route shows in the Allow header and the OpenAPI document.
decisions.detail:
This vote chooses extension-method registration on muxes, routers and mounted structs. All options are proposals, not implemented APIs.

Reran r01-r07 on a0.0.43. PURGE reaches a 405 with Allow. The attempted public registration forms are refused. CONNECT documentation and Method.custom exit 101. A module-constant router path is refused.

A adds custom(token, path, handler) and #Server.Custom(token, path) over one route table. Preserve the exact case-sensitive RFC 9110 token in dispatch, duplicate keys, Allow, operation IDs and OpenAPI. Refuse only exact standard tokens such as GET, already registered by mux.get. Lowercase get is a distinct method, not a typo to rewrite.

Check literal and constant tokens while building, and dynamic mux tokens at registration before changing the table. Routers and markers need static tokens. Invalid tokens need registered Jet diagnostics and snapshots. OpenAPI 3.2 additionalOperations describes extension methods and CONNECT. Downstream 3.1-only tools may not support it.

B replaces per-verb calls with one route(Method, path, handler) and #Server.Route marker. Migrate all callers and remove per-verb registration. Its typed standard cases are a genuine strength. Fix Method.custom regardless of the vote; its defect is not a design objection.

C replaces per-verb registration with one method-and-path pattern grammar. D dispatches inside a catch-all. D needs explicit method metadata for accurate Allow and OpenAPI, recreating registration.

options.name: custom verb named for the Custom case
options.detail: mux.custom(token, path, handler), router.custom and #Server.Custom(token, path); static tokens are checked while building, dynamic mux tokens at registration.
options.technical: Derive custom from Method.Custom and lower through the existing route table. Preserve exact case throughout; refuse only exact standard tokens. Reuse one token validator for build-time and registration checks. Render extension methods and CONNECT under OpenAPI 3.2 additionalOperations; downstream 3.1-only tools may not support them.

options.name: route taking a Method value
options.detail: mux.route(method, path, handler), with method an http.Method such as .Custom("PURGE").
options.technical: One canonical route(Method, path, handler) and #Server.Route marker for all methods. Migrate and remove per-verb registration in one cutover; both forms lower to the same table. Typed standard cases prevent spelling mistakes, but Custom still contains a string requiring validation. Fix Method.custom's independently reproduced backend defect; do not score that defect as a design loss.
options.code:
mux.route(.Get, "/cache/:key", hit)
mux.route(.Custom("PURGE"), "/cache/:key", purge)
#Server.Route(.Custom("PURGE"), "/cache/:key")

options.name: method inside the pattern
options.detail: One method-and-path pattern API replaces per-verb registration.
options.technical: Migrate per-verb callers and markers in one cutover. Share the existing path parser after the method separator. No parallel registration API remains.
options.code:

mux.handle("PURGE /cache/:key", purge)

options.name: catch-all route
options.detail: mux.any(path, handler); the handler checks request.method itself.
options.technical: Like Axum's any: the route matches every method, so the mux cannot answer 405 or list Allow for it, and the document cannot name the method.

comparisons.note: ServeMux patterns may start with any valid method token.
MapMethods takes a list of method strings.
One method per name in Node's method list, plus app.all.
MethodFilter has ten fixed methods; others need any, which sends no Allow header.

recommendation.why: A extends the existing verb-family organization without migrating standard routes. Literal and constant tokens are checked while building; dynamic mux tokens are checked at registration. All forms share one exact-case route table.
gains: A custom-method route checks and serves, closing #6206 c35.
One spelling per method: the verb list stays derived from the Method enum.
405 answers, Allow lists and OpenAPI include the custom route.

losses.loss: The method is a string argument, not a typed value.
losses.mitigation: The build checks the token's grammar and refuses standard names; named constants, which E2805 already promises, give it one spelling.

losses.loss: OpenAPI 3.1 has no slot for an extension method.
losses.mitigation: Such routes render under OpenAPI 3.2's additionalOperations, and only documents with one carry the 3.2.0 stamp.

losses.loss: One more call on mux and router, and one more marker.
losses.mitigation: Both come from the Method enum's Custom case, like the other verbs, so no second list exists.

whyNot.reason: A unified Method-based cutover is coherent and typed. It requires migrating standard routes; A keeps their organization. The backend defect is a shared repair, not a design objection.
A clean-cutover pattern API is coherent, but method and path become two grammars within one string.
D loses 405, Allow and the document entry, and moves dispatch into the handler.

recommendation.tradeoff: A string token checked while building, for one route call per Method case.
