decisions.title: Build-time reads of walked and data-named files
decisions.situation:
Card #5072 c28 moves five generated Core-declaration tables into build-time code. That code must read files named by a directory walk or by another file's text. On a0.0.43, find returns paths, but embed_file and embed_bytes accept literals only (E0957). A parent import outside a script's authorized root also fails (E0602).

We recommend A: accept build-time String arguments for the existing reads and find, without widening their file authority. E is the smaller change: computed embeds, literal globs. Both cover c28. The ratified toolchain: direction stands; neither proposal works on the seed yet.
decisions.gist: Should existing build-time reads accept computed paths, and should find accept computed globs too?
decisions.lesson: Jet can embed files while compiling. Today their paths must be literals. A table builder needs to read files named by a walk or by another file. This vote picks that read rule. Recording every read in .jet/lock is required but not working on the seed.
decisions.explainer: A build-time read is embed_file or embed_bytes inside #run. find(glob) returns sorted paths. A data-named read gets its path from another file. toolchain: is the ratified prefix for compiler packages reading toolchain sources. Proposed examples use #run; seed probes use comptime. The lock is a required output, not an access grant or a sandbox.
decisions.story: Lee keeps recipes in Markdown files. Under A she writes loop path in find("recipes/*.md") -> embed_file(path). A new file joins the next build's table. The same code works under E, whose glob stays literal. A path outside the existing authority is rejected.
decisions.detail:
A amends D-CTIO1's literal clause and the literal-glob restriction. E changes only the embeds. Neither reopens D-EMBED-TOOLCHAIN1=A. Relative paths remain relative to the embedding file, not the package root. toolchain: keeps its ratified authority check. No absolute path, parent component, symlink escape or ambient file API is enabled.

Independent seed runs confirm E0957 for computed text, bytes and find arguments; sorted results; empty matches; and E0955 for invalid UTF-8 text and symlinks. b.find and b.embed already accept computed String values. The former's literal-only diagnostic is misleading, not an AST literal check.

The traced generator input set has 284 files (19.4 MB), including 42 runtime units and 13 syntax files. Literal-embed adaptations produced matching hashes for CoreCallRows and all twelve views. These are host-only probes, not the five-table package cutover or a cross-target proof. The report records cold-build costs; no option has an end-to-end implementation benchmark.

Implementation is more than deleting sema's literal check. Today's typed host call stores a String and IR emits ConstText. Sema must check a build-time String expression and own the evaluated path-law check. IR lowers checked operations; the rooted host transport remains the security backstop. Preserve the Core-reader authority boundary rather than silently granting Core find.

All options need per-read digests, sorted glob membership including empty results, correct invalidation and watches, and target/toolchain-aware identity. Reusing bytes is a proposed bounded evaluation snapshot, not an existing cache. Key it by root, embedding directory and normalized path. Detect concurrent changes rather than mixing different file versions. Lock diffs show reads after execution; untrusted builds still need external isolation.

The option examples are same-derivation sketches: core_source_rows, pick and core_call_records stand for shared parser work, not new APIs. The complete executable derivation probes use literal embeds because the seed cannot implement any proposed option. The generated baseline stays until the chosen mechanism, shared parser and all cutover proofs pass.

options.name: Computed embeds and globs
options.detail: embed_file, embed_bytes and find accept build-time String values. Apply the existing path law to the value. No new name.
options.technical: Sema checks the argument type, phase and common normalized path law, including evaluated values. Typed calls and IR carry the argument expression instead of ConstText. Evaluation invokes sema-owned validation before rooted transport. E0957 quotes a rejected value; E0955 covers read or UTF-8 failure. Beginner: existing literal embeds. Expert: data-derived paths and globs. The complete record, watch and snapshot contract in the report applies.

options.name: Content globs
options.detail: embed_files(glob) returns [(path: String, text: String)]; embed_files_bytes(glob) returns [(path: String, bytes: [U8])]. Patterns and scalar embeds stay literal-only.
options.technical: Two names need D-PRELUDE-LAW1 admission. Both bulk calls must use the same canonical reader and path law, not duplicate file policy (I8). A static bound is a real review benefit. Data-named reads select from a superset. Invalid UTF-8 fails the text call with E0955; bytes require no UTF-8. Sorted results and empty matches follow find. Beginner: scalar embed, then a content glob. Expert: choose a bounded source set.
options.code:
CORE_CALLS: #run {
    core: embed_file("toolchain:Compiler/Prelude/Core.jet")
    units: embed_files("toolchain:Core/*/Runtime/**/*.jet")
    sources: embed_files("toolchain:Core/**/*.jet")
    owned: loop row in core_source_rows(core) -> pick(sources, "toolchain:{row.path}")
    core_call_records(core, units, owned) ?? panic(err.message)
}

options.name: Computed reads bounded by find
options.detail: Computed embeds must match a literal find already executed in the same evaluation. Literal embeds keep their existing authority.
options.technical: Track normalized matched identities, not bare path spellings. Reject an unmatched computed read with E0957. This adds authority state and call-order dependence, not another reader. Beginner: literal embeds. Expert: run a bounding find before computed reads. The example's Core bound may include files it never uses. Reusing bytes can remove repeated I/O but not the order rule.
options.code:
CORE_CALLS: #run {
    core: embed_file("toolchain:Compiler/Prelude/Core.jet")
    bound: find("toolchain:Core/**/*.jet")
    units: loop path in find("toolchain:Core/*/Runtime/**/*.jet") -> (path: path, text: embed_file(path))
    owned: loop row in core_source_rows(core) -> (path: row.path, text: embed_file("toolchain:{row.path}"))
    core_call_records(core, units, owned) ?? panic(err.message)
}

options.name: Declared input ceiling
options.detail: package.jet declares comptime_inputs globs. Computed reads and walks must stay inside that ceiling; literals retain today's rule. Reading code is A's.
options.technical: A new manifest key contributes to package identity. Reject values outside the ceiling with E0957. The ceiling is distinct from the actual read set and need not change for every new file. Beginner: literal embeds need no field. Expert: choose a narrow ceiling. Costs: another authority surface, manifest maintenance, and wider restrictions if authors use broad roots to avoid maintenance.

options.name: Computed embeds; literal globs
options.detail: embed_file and embed_bytes accept build-time String values. find keeps its literal-only argument. This covers the same c28 program as A.
options.technical: Use A's checked expression, rooted reader and recording contract for embeds without widening find's source restriction. Beginner: existing literal embeds. Expert: data-named embeds work directly; a data-named walk needs a broad literal find and filtering. This is the smallest semantic expansion the traced generator requires. It does not add C's matched-set requirement.

comparisons.note: The implementation resolves a constant-string value and rejects an embed outside the module path. This is a source comparison, not a local Zig execution.
Literal package-relative patterns bound an embed.FS. Computed names read inside it. Patterns exclude parent components and symlinks; empty matches fail. Source comparison only.
A build script is a cached host program. It can derive table literals directly, not only emit include_str! calls. Authors declare invalidation paths. Source comparison only.

recommendation.why: A keeps one value-argument rule across existing operations and matches the computed-value build host. E is equally sufficient for c28 and changes less. Prefer A for consistency, not because these tables prove a need for computed globs. This recommends a direction, not implementation approval.
gains: One argument rule for literal, walked and data-named paths.
No new ambient name.
No superset read is required just to authorize a computed embed.

losses.mitigation: Reproducer: probes/empty_glob.sh. Record and revalidate empty membership before cache reuse; c25 and the cutover must cover this.

A real source ceiling, but mutable authority state and a call-order rule.
A useful manifest ceiling, but another policy surface. The ceiling and actual reads are different facts, not duplication by definition.
Equally sufficient and smaller for c28. A avoids differing rules for computed paths and globs; that consistency gain is not a performance claim.

decisions.title: Make hidden environment controls normal flags and settings, and list their effective values
decisions.situation: Jet reads environment variables that can quietly change checking, optimization and reporting. A command copied from a teammate can therefore behave differently because of an invisible shell setting. Some controls already have flags, but several inspected code paths still read variables directly. Choose the flag and setting names and where to list the effective values. We recommend normal descriptive flags, the existing command-setting naming rule, and a read-only env vars listing. This extends the existing environment command group instead of replacing its project-shell behavior.
decisions.gist: Should hidden controls become normal settings with a read-only effective-value listing?
decisions.lesson: A flag changes one run; a project setting records intent; an environment variable is only an override of that same setting. The listing should show the winner and why it won, without printing secrets or starting a project shell.
decisions.story: Mia checks a tiny program while recording a compiler trace. Every option checks the same program and reports where the trace setting came from, whether it came from the project, a variable or a flag.
decisions.inWild: Go env lists effective values and go env -w stores user defaults. Cargo maps many config keys to CARGO_* variables and lets command-line config override them. Python exposes implementation controls through -X. Zig build exposes project options through -D. Jet should reuse its own typed setting table rather than imitate four unrelated syntaxes.
decisions.detail:
Scope is #6606 c4/c6/c7. Reuse D-SETTING-ORDER1=A and Compiler/JetCli/Source/Cli/CommandSettings.jet:66-74's command-qualified keys. A flag's dashes become underscores: package check: { trace: "trace.json" } is check.trace. User settings use the same key. No new settings file. Existing --set keeps its typed program-input meaning.

A's exact names, part one: --keep-going / keep_going; --keep-going-report=PATH / keep_going_report; repeated --keep-going-skip=ITEM / keep_going_skip; --trace[=PATH] / trace; --trace-detail=functions|phases / trace_detail. Repeated CLI list values append within that invocation; a higher layer replaces a lower list.

Part two: repeated --opt-dump=FUNCTION / opt_dump; repeated --opt-disable=PASS / opt_disable; --opt-verify / opt_verify; --opt-ssa-stress / opt_ssa_stress; --gc-trace=PATH / gc_trace; --phase-counters / phase_counters; --memory-ledger=PATH / memory_ledger. Prefix suffixes with each supporting command's dispatch path, such as check.opt_verify and run.gc_trace. Share one row across supporting command families.

Bool flags take bare true or =off; settings use Bool. Lists are typed string arrays. Paths are strings, relative to invocation directory across every layer. --trace selects stderr, --trace=PATH a file, --trace=off disables it; write ./off for a file named off. Its setting accepts true, path string or false. Reject invalid values, unknown passes and unsupported combinations. Preserve registered defaults and dependencies between controls.

Other c4 rows use their canonical setting suffix with underscores changed to flag dashes. Retain existing flag-backed names, especially --trace rather than --trace-file. The c3 census must classify every row and resolve collisions before cutover. A genuinely new meaning or collision needs an owner choice, never a guessed fallback or omitted row. Test hooks and transport fields do not automatically become public controls.

A lists with jet env vars [--command=COMMAND] [--json]. It resolves controls without realizing environments, fetching or launching children. For a hypothetical invocation, append -- TARGET_FLAGS after --command; parse those using the target command's normal flag registry. Never pretend that flags from a previous process were persisted. Without hypothetical flags, list current settings/environment/default resolution.

Rows include variable name, kind, command-qualified setting, effective typed value, winning source and location, variable presence and shadowed environment input. Redact secrets before either renderer, including credentials inside paths or URLs. An unset optional is null. Without a command filter show all applicable command-qualified rows. This is not a dump of unrelated user-program environment values.

Precedence: default, source marker, approved project/user setting layers, entry code, environment override, explicit flag. This adds environment below flags; pins refuse conflicting environment overrides too. Authority flags remain never-persisted under c2. No setting or environment variable can mint --allow, gate, token or trust approval. Report secret presence without value.

B prefixes every A flag suffix with control- and every setting suffix with control_, replacing existing names. Example: --control-trace and check.control_trace. Types, defaults, authority, lists and precedence remain identical. Its listing is jet inspect controls with the same command filter, JSON and hypothetical-flags forms. It groups expert controls but requires broader renaming; neither option retains aliases.

Observed on t17a a0.0.43: help identifies env as the project-shell group and inspect env as typed config-read inspection. jet env --json reaches E1271 for an unlocked project source, not a pure control listing. Request.jet reads keep-going and tracing variables; InspectDecisions.jet:49-50 reads optimizer variables. This targeted observation is not a complete census.

Adversarial verdict: A holds as one setting mechanism. First reuse existing names rather than aliases. Then make inspection read-only and independent of activation, with hypothetical flags explicit. Environment contamination remains visible rather than removed. Go's -w would duplicate Jet settings, so omit it. Cargo's mapping is partial; Jet must cover every owned read. Zig -D and Python -X justify visible controls, not overloading Jet's program inputs.

decisions.title: One typed fact query in core.compiler, with inspect as its command-line view
decisions.situation: Jet records rules, facts about a checked program, and evidence from a run. Those records live for different lengths of time, so they should not be squeezed into one mutable table. The owner already approved one typed way to read them, but did not name its public entry point. The tested ledger import and inspect facts command are unavailable. Choose the API and command spelling, without reopening the three-store design. We recommend one query in core.compiler and a command that renders its exact results.
decisions.gist: Should a core.compiler query and inspect command share one typed fact result?
decisions.lesson: The rulebook, a checked program and a run receipt are different shelves. One librarian can answer questions about all three without mixing them up. An empty answer must mean there are no matching rows, not that the librarian never opened the shelf.
decisions.story: A tool counts the marker-rule facts in the schema. Every option answers that same question from the same schema snapshot. Experts can use the same query for a particular checked program or run receipt.
decisions.inWild: A command-line view and a library view can share one typed implementation. Jet's approved compiler-as-library design already requires this direction; a CLI subprocess should not be the only way a build-time Jet tool reads its own checked facts.
decisions.detail:
D-META-REG1=A approves shared schema machinery; D-LEDGER1=D retains schema, checked-program and run-evidence stores behind one typed query. This ballot names its public views. It adds no fourth store, mutable compiler heap or second evidence grader. Read-only queries need no Meta mutation effect.

Canonical API: core.compiler.query(source: FactSource, kind: FactKind, at: QueryTime?{None}, limit: Int?{None}) -> [Fact] MetadataError!. FactSource is Schema(SchemaSnapshot), Program(ProgramInfo) or Run(RunReceipt). Each supplies an explicit immutable authorized snapshot, not a forged name or ambient current program. Omitted time selects that snapshot's complete recorded view; omitted limit requests all authorized matching rows.

Fact is a tagged projection of SchemaFact, ProgramFact or RunFact, preserving canonical typed fields and source identity. FactKind comes from the executable schema. QueryTime selects the approved temporal view, not a schema column. Only claims have evidence grades. Rights retain their existing gate kind and provenance without grades.

Reuse D-META-REFLECT2=A's MetadataError: Unavailable, Unsupported, Stale, Invalid, Denied or Truncated. Empty success means checked emptiness. Missing stages, private facts and absent runs never become empty success. Explicit limits return Truncated instead of a partial list claiming completeness. Identity and order stay canonical across every consumer.

CLI: jet inspect facts --store=schema|program|run --kind=K [SOURCE] [--json]. Schema selects the running toolchain's schema; no SOURCE is allowed. Program requires a target source, checked into a snapshot through the normal pipeline. Run requires an explicit receipt path, validated by the ordinary receipt reader. No default latest run. A failed program check cannot publish recovered rows as valid facts. Both renderers include schema/snapshot identity and completeness.

Beginner path: inspect answers a concrete question. Expert path: ordinary Jet imports core.compiler and reads an authorized immutable source, including permitted #run code. A read snapshot confers no Compiler mutation authority; D-META-COMPILER1's powerful passed control handle keeps its distinct purpose. No new global ledger namespace or discovery mechanism.

B publicly exposes only the Core query; internal consumers still share it. C publicly exposes only the CLI; its internal typed query remains shared, but user Jet libraries must cross a subprocess/JSON boundary. That gives up the library-first ladder, not the three-store rule.

Observed on t17a a0.0.43: core.compiler.ledger import gets E1001. inspect facts with schema/kind/JSON arguments gets E2101. The inspected Core/Compiler/Compiler.jet contains small typed records and extension points, not this query. These targeted reads are not an API census. The ratified_p12 d_meta_reg1_contract path was absent here and not executed.

Adversarial verdict: A holds as multiple views of one query. First require explicit immutable sources instead of ambient mutable state. Then keep CLI rendering outside the typed reader. Lists cost memory; reuse immutable storage where legal and honor explicit limits. Missing/stale facts remain failures. No proposed query or performance advantage was exercised.

decisions.title: Read a declaration's source location from its existing reflection record
decisions.situation: Tools need to say where a type, field or function was declared. The location where a query is written is not that declaration's location. Jet already has reflection records and a common SourceLocation record, but the tested reflection result lacks the proposed location field. Choose how to read that declaration location without confusing it with value provenance or caller location. We recommend a location member on the ordinary reflection record. It reuses reflection instead of inventing another compiler-filled sigil.
decisions.gist: Should declaration locations be ordinary members of existing reflection records?
decisions.lesson: #here says where this expression is written; #caller says where the caller called. A declaration location says where Point or helper was defined. A tracked value's origin answers yet another question: where its data came from.
decisions.story: A tool prints Point at line 3 and helper at line 7 of one source file. Every option asks about those same declarations, not about the later query lines.
decisions.inWild: Jet's existing reflection records already carry checked source spans. Its SourceLocation record already supplies file, line and column for site information. The cohesive extension derives a location from that same checked source, rather than creating another source-tracking system.
decisions.detail:
#3520 c24 requires declaration/field/method positions as D-JAI-SITE1 SourceLocation. D-META-HASH1=A selects ordinary reflection; D-META-HASH2=A owns #here/#caller. A adds location: SourceLocation? to type, callable, field and method records. C uses declared_at with that same type. B's #origin returns the same optional record. None means known absence of a source declaration; unavailable analysis still fails the existing reflection query with MetadataError.

The location identifies the declaration-name token in the checked snapshot. Reuse SourceLocation's line, column and path conventions, not another coordinate scheme. Generic instances point to their definition, not a random call. Alias type reflection follows existing resolved-type identity; no new alias-handle syntax is introduced here. Overloads require existing typed selection, never the first same-named declaration.

Derive the member from canonical SourceSpan and SourceId; do not maintain another location store. Generated declarations point into checked generated source and retain existing expansion provenance for navigation. No fallback to #here or fabricated line zero. Snapshot digests remain valid identities even when a mutable disk file changes.

Only the compile-time access required by c24 is authorized here. Do not retain source metadata at runtime just for an early line query. Existing visibility, authority and retention rules apply. Private paths and generated text remain protected. No implicit source reopen to repair stale metadata.

Beginner path: read location and handle known absence, as the complete panes show. Expert path: iterate fields/methods with the same member while using snapshot and expansion metadata. #here/#caller remain use/call sites. Tracked value origin remains data provenance, possibly ambiguous; it is not declaration identity.

B is a new parameterized compiler root, unlike #here's lexical read, but must still use the same checked metadata. It creates no runtime type lookup or extra authority. C is a strong ordinary-field alternative whose name emphasizes the declaration. A uses the common location vocabulary throughout reflected records. Optionality and errors are identical in every option.

Observed on t17a a0.0.43: early Point.reflect() metadata prints struct for kind. INFO.location.line gets E0302. Ordinary runtime Point.reflect() gets E0311, not proof that early reflection is absent. Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Comptime/Reflection.jet:817-826, 891-906 and 1477-1505 expose field/method/type spans; 89-93 builds offset spans. These are reuse points, not a working location projection.

Adversarial verdict: A holds as a checked-source view. First reuse span and location records. Then preserve identity and expansion provenance instead of silently substituting the query site. Cache snapshot line tables rather than scan text per query. Known absent declarations remain None, never invented positions. No proposed exact-line golden was executed; the named witness file was absent here. The panes supply its complete proposed source with Point at line 3 and helper at line 7.

decisions.title: Should a reusable type choice be an alias body or an ordinary type-returning function?
decisions.situation: Should a reusable type choice be an alias body or an ordinary type-returning function? A library wants small storage inline and larger storage in a growing list. Mia uses both and prints their counts, 2 then 3. An ordinary alias names one shape but does not express this checked choice. We recommend extending aliases with the existing required early evaluator and trait bounds, without creating a wrapper type.
decisions.gist: Should a reusable type choice be an alias body or an ordinary type-returning function?
decisions.lesson: An alias is another name for an existing type. A bound requires that chosen type to implement a trait. The choice happens while building; the resulting value has no runtime selection wrapper.
decisions.story: Mia stores two numbers inline and three in a growing list. Both recipes hide that storage choice and print 2, then 3.
decisions.inWild: Illustrative early type-returning function, the broader alternative here.
decisions.detail:
origin/dev:Compiler/JetParser/Source/Parser/Declarations/Types.jet:51-85 classifies transparent generic aliases. origin/dev:Compiler/JetFoundation/Data/Syntax/Spellings.jet:27-32 supplies early evaluation and number parameters. Both options reuse those generic identities and the ordinary trait checker.

D-ALIAS-GENERIC1=A authorizes generic aliases; D-META-SPELL1=A supplies #run for required early work. D-GENERIC-TYPEFN1 is archived; the later alias decision preserves angle-bracket generics and does not approve either computed form. A proposes `Name<parameters>: Bound #run { type-expression }`. B proposes `#run name: fn(parameters) -> Type<Bound>` and constant calls in type positions. Both run the same canonical early evaluator, never an alias-specific interpreter.

The shared Inline and Heap implementations below are deliberately retained. A generic-implementation failure in the shared baseline must not be hidden by changing the workload. The proposed result retains exact Inline<2> identity: passing it where that type is required needs no conversion. B preserves the same identity through its type-valued result. No fresh nominal identity, allocation or emitted runtime branch is authorized.

Beginners use the recipe as an ordinary type. Experts supply bounds and explicit value parameters. Check every reachable return type against Store, including an unused choice; generic branches need sufficient declared constraints rather than an invented universal proof. Refuse non-types, runtime conditions, invalid capacities and cycles with their declaration path. Conditions may use permitted pure early constants, not ambient host state. Keep ordinary evaluation budgets and diagnostics.

A keeps the new capability at aliases. B is a real stronger option: reusable type values and type-returning functions beyond alias selection. It is not intrinsically a second evaluator, slower or less safe. Both introduce public syntax and therefore remain an owner gate. Explicit concrete constructors remain available under either choice; removing the already requested recipe is not a same-capability alternative.

Fresh review, 2026-11-11. Kept the full shared workload and its generic-implementation failure; corrected archived authority and retained general type functions as a fair stronger alternative.

decisions.title: Should inherited print defaults be simple fields or typed formatter callbacks?
decisions.situation: Should inherited print defaults be simple fields or typed formatter callbacks? Jet already chose a block-carried print style, separate from string interpolation. Mia wants 255 and a list shown as four-digit hexadecimal inside one block. Both choices leave prepared text unchanged and restore ordinary output afterward. We recommend simple typed fields that reuse the existing number formatter, with explicit formatting for unusual output.
decisions.gist: Should inherited print defaults be simple fields or typed formatter callbacks?
decisions.lesson: A print style supplies defaults only when print formats a value. Prepared strings are already text and remain unchanged. The existing context carries the style through a block and restores it on exit.
decisions.story: Mia prints 00ff, a list of padded hexadecimal numbers and x = 255 inside the block. Both styles produce those same lines.
decisions.inWild: The existing explicit formatter supplies the same numeric rules.
decisions.detail:
origin/dev:Core/Text/Fmt.jet:13-17 and :42-43 own radix and decimal formatting. origin/dev:Compiler/JetIR/Source/BuildTransact.jet:253-260 is the Context installation path both choices extend. D-CONTEXT1=A already names term.PrintStyle.

D-CONTEXT1=A already settles context.print; removing it is not routine completion. This gate chooses its public members. A proposes PrintBase with Binary, Octal, Decimal and Hex. PrintStyle has int_base: PrintBase, int_min_digits: Int, float_digits: Int?, list_separator: String and field_names: Bool. Defaults are Decimal, zero, None, comma-space and true. Reuse existing radix/sign padding and decimal rounding; do not create a second formatter.

B instead supplies integer: fn(Int) -[]> String mem.AllocError! and floating: fn(Float) -[]> String mem.AllocError!, plus the same separator and field-name fields. Results are final text. Under D-ALLOC-FAIL1=C, formatting allocation uses ordinary recoverable errors, not a false Never promise. Reject other callback effects, including Context reads, so callbacks cannot recursively print. Both choices share one recursive walk; no Any callback or runtime reflection API is added.

Beginners omit the style and keep existing output. Experts override selected fields or explicitly format a prepared String. Context remains task-owned, restores on normal and early exits and copies into spawned tasks under the existing context rule. A style read adds Context; the read itself needs no machine permission. Printing still needs its ordinary output authority. Interpolation, Debug, to_string and eprint are unchanged by this field. Custom Debug text is opaque.

Normalize negative minimum width and precision as existing formatting does. Preserve signed and fixed-width values without truncating to machine integers. Cover non-finite floats, nested containers and empty lists. list_separator affects list and tuple elements; field_names affects generated struct labels, not custom text. Very large requested output has real memory cost and the normal allocation-failure route. Data fields cannot express arbitrary callback behavior; explicit formatting is the existing expert escape, not a hidden second style mechanism.

Fresh review, 2026-11-11. Removed the settled no-context alternative, corrected imports to separate rows, and preserved recoverable allocation errors in the typed callback contract.

decisions.title: Declare package lint findings and structured fixes without a second diagnostic mechanism
decisions.situation: The research sketch uses a declaration spelling that Jet does not have. It also assigns a built-in numeric code to a package lint and gives no activation or safe-edit contract. A package needs a declared finding and an optional checked fix. We recommend keeping Diagnostic as the finding value and using checked compiler events for discovery. A dedicated registration trait remains a fair alternative, not another diagnostic carrier.
decisions.gist: How should packages declare lint findings and structured fixes?
decisions.lesson: Finding text and an edit are different values. Keep human help in fix; validate structured edits separately. Importing a package must not silently enable its policy.
decisions.story: A library opts into NoPrintInLib. Every option finds the same resolved print call and offers the same deliberate logging edit.
decisions.inWild: A dedicated registration trait can offer a compact authoring surface.
decisions.detail:
D-DECL-TYPES1 supplies Diagnostic with literal what/why/fix. D-API-COMPOSE1 favors one general operation and typed options, not sibling rewrite APIs. D-NO-WARNINGS1 distinguishes style rewrites, tidy errors and optional reports: do not invent warning severity or make style a new failing lint tier. Tidy findings fail check/build, not run/dev/test; reports use lint. 

Fixes are opt-in and may change behavior only with explicit authorization. Printing to logging is not inherently behavior-preserving. Detect symbol aliases and shadowing, refuse unsafe argument duplication and incompatible logger calls, and reject stale or overlapping edits atomically. Recheck before writing. Proposed APIs are UNCHECKED; no package lint execution is claimed.

options.name: Diagnostic values; checked rewrites
options.gist: Use one diagnostic carrier and checked compiler events.
options.detail: Keep Diagnostic as the only finding carrier. Add tier and structured_fix; fix remains literal help text. A root build subscriber traverses checked calls and emits NoPrintInLib only for the resolved print symbol in the opted-in library. syntax.rewrite takes resolved callable identities and preserves argument subtrees. It requires compatible argument and return types. Dependents do not activate a lint merely by importing its package. Beginners enable the package lint group once; experts register a checked event subscriber.

options.name: Lint trait; same diagnostic carrier
options.gist: A dedicated Lint trait registers traversal, not another error type.
options.detail: Lint is a registration trait whose find method consumes a checked call and returns an optional Diagnostic value. It does not replace Diagnostic, change command failure policy, or invent warning severity. Activate it explicitly for the same library as A. Use A’s checked rewrite value and the same finding texts. Its convenience is a one-place declaration; its cost is a second way to register checked-code traversal.

options.name: Diagnostic values; string patterns
options.gist: Use one carrier with parse-checked pattern and template strings.
options.detail: Use A’s Diagnostic carrier and explicit subscriber activation, but structured_fix is syntax.rewrite("print($x)", "log.info($x)"). These strings are a proposed pattern language, not Jet source. Parse both at declaration time; require every replacement hole to bind once in the pattern. Resolve names by symbol identity, preserve trivia and source spans, and reject rewrites that change evaluation order or cannot recheck. This is not automatic safe conversion from stdout to logging.

recommendation.why: Keep one Diagnostic value and reuse compiler-event registration. Make the structured fix a separately checked value, not a replacement for literal help text.
gains: One reporting mechanism

losses.loss: The checked-edit API is new.
losses.mitigation: Refuse stale, overlapping or untypeable edits before changing source.

whyNot.reason: A separate discovery trait is coherent, but duplicates compiler-event registration for this use.
Concise, but string holes duplicate checked-node matching and require a new binding and hygiene contract.

recommendation.tradeoff: Choose the stated contract, not an unmeasured implementation advantage.

decisions.title: How should an opt-in deep check be written?
decisions.situation: A deep check walks data to find a bug, such as a wrong stored tree size. The approved design keeps it off until --deep-checks selects it. Its original marker was #DebugOnly(.deep). A later ruling replaced #DebugOnly with #Off(.Release), leaving the deep spelling unsettled. The selection and safety rules are not being voted on again. Choose a spelling that preserves them. We recommend adding .DeepDisabled to #Off: the block is off when deep checks do not select it. This keeps one presence marker. #On(.Deep) reads more directly, but adds another marker and changes the earlier one-marker direction.
decisions.gist: How should code mark an expensive check that stays off until requested?
decisions.lesson: A deep check inspects data for a bug. It stays off until --deep-checks selects it, even in development. Jet must still check its types while off. Today's #Off(.Release) removes ordinary code in release builds. The choice is how to name the deep-check block, not whether its safety rules apply.
decisions.explainer:
Expected command results after implementation, identical for all five choices. Run these from the tree package beside run.jet. These are requirements, not observations of proposed syntax.

```text
jet run -A run.jet
stdout: 4\n
stderr: empty
exit: 0

jet run -A --deep-checks run.jet
jet run -A --deep-checks=tree run.jet
jet run -A --deep-checks=tree.run run.jet
stdout: empty, for each selected command
stderr first line: Stop [E3001]: `panic: tree size is wrong`
exit: 70, for each selected command

jet run -A --deep-checks=tree.leaf run.jet
stdout: empty
stderr: E2121, a blocking check-free-scope report
exit: 1
```

The selected command results stay the same with --profile release. -A suppresses authority notices; it does not enable deep checks or override a written Panic denial. Full report source excerpts depend on the chosen header's line positions; they must be snapshotted when implemented.
decisions.story: Ana's three-node tree wrongly records four nodes. She wants a full walk while hunting the bug, without paying for that walk on normal runs.
decisions.inWild:
# Python illustration of the same three-node tree, not a library quotation.
import sys

def deep_consistent(tree):
    children, cached_size = tree
    return all(deep_consistent(child) for child in children) and cached_size == 1 + sum(child[1] for child in children)

tree = ([([], 1), ([], 1)], 4)
if '--deep-checks' in sys.argv:
    assert deep_consistent(tree), 'tree size is wrong'
print(tree[1])
# No flag: stdout 4, exit 0. Flag: AssertionError, exit 1.
# This is an ordinary runtime branch, not Jet's checked removal contract.
decisions.detail:
All five choices are proposals, not working deep-check syntax. Each code pane shows the same complete run.jet. Beside it, package.jet contains name: "tree" and version: "0.1.0", on separate lines. Only the check header changes. The check walks the same corrupt tree and has the same required output under every choice.

The shared contract is D-DEEP-CHECK1=A, ratified September 11. No switch means off in every profile. --deep-checks selects all authored deep checks in the program and its Jet libraries, not foreign libraries or separate build tools. --deep-checks=tree selects this package; --deep-checks=tree.run selects this declaration, not its callers or callees. Paths use dots, not the retired ::. Several scopes take their union. An empty, unknown or check-free scope blocks compilation, even beside a bare switch.

Each selected block may read captured state and mutate only fresh, nonescaping locals. External effects are rejected transitively. Local helper returns and local loop control remain allowed; return, propagation, break or next cannot leave the check. No ownership transfer, initialization, permission, refinement or optimizer assumption escapes it. Assert may stop, but the block grants no Panic permission. Disabled checks contribute no reachable Panic or memory effects. Required contracts and safety checks stay on. Selection is independent of release eligibility.

Every option needs the same compiler plumbing. CLI and embedded callers share one typed request. Selection belongs to the authored declaration, including private methods and anonymous bodies under their nearest named function. Overloads and generic instances with the same authored name are selected together. Diagnostics name matched declarations. Sessions retain their creation-time selection; changing it starts another session. Compiled-out code needs recompilation; compatible units may be reused, while unverifiable prebuilt identities need admitted source or a blocking refusal, even with checks off.

Current source: origin/dev Core/Compiler/Lang.jet:24-28 declares only BuildCondition.Release. Compiler/Prelude/Markers.jet declares Off at Statement and Block sites. Compiler/JetFoundation/Data/Syntax/CoreSurface.jet registers Off and also #here and #caller. The parser emits Stmt.Switched; sema's Off arm checks the body in isolated state and emits TStmt.DebugOnly for .Release. JetIR then omits it for release. That internal name does not make #DebugOnly legal source. Adding any condition still requires generalizing that path, not just declaring an enum case.

The earlier D-OFF-RELEASE1=A ruling explicitly chose one conditional-presence marker. New options must say when they amend that direction. SUB G6Decl-44 stages only spelling-independent selection and diagnostics E2119-E2121; it is not proof that any proposed body runs. Proposed diagnostic reuse and removal costs below are design requirements, not observed behavior. Beginner and expert paths are stated per option; the expert selection and safety rules above never change.

options.name: #Off(.DeepDisabled)
options.detail: Add one BuildCondition case to the existing marker. DeepDisabled means this site's deep check was not selected. Beginner: write this header and use --deep-checks. Expert: use the same header with declaration scopes; no second presence marker is introduced. The negative condition is longer and requires care when reading it.
options.technical:
The proposed BuildCondition.DeepDisabled is evaluated per authored site, not once for the whole build. It removes this block when unselected, regardless of profile. .Release and bare Off retain their current meanings. Reuse Stmt.Switched and the isolated checking/removal path, with the shared deep restrictions.

Cost: one condition case, registry and marker-argument updates, generalized selection/removal, plus all shared deep-check work. No measured compile-time or runtime advantage is claimed. Enabled checks pay for the walk; disabled checks must emit no branch or body at any level.

Edge cases: two Off markers on one statement remain refused. DeepDisabled is valid only for a deep-check body, not a general escape from read-only rules. Nesting under Off(.Release) can suppress an otherwise selected check in release, so document both conditions rather than promising it runs there. Statement and Block sites stay; expression and item uses are refused. This extends the closed condition menu but keeps the ratified one-marker direction.

options.name: #On(.Deep)
options.detail: Add an affirmative marker. Beginner: the header says the check is on only when selected. Expert: target declarations with the same switches as A. It reads directly but asks the owner to amend the earlier one-marker direction. It can share A's semantic path; two spellings do not require two implementations.
options.technical:
Propose On at Statement and Block sites and BuildCondition.Deep, with the same isolated deep checker and removal path as A. Cost: a new marker, condition case, registry/parser wiring and shared implementation work. There is no measured cost comparison with A.

Edge cases: this option refuses On(.Release), Off(.Deep) and two presence markers on one statement. Those refusals are proposed, not today's E0344 behavior for On. Expression and item uses are refused. Nested Off(.Release) can still erase an enabled deep block. The new spelling amends D-OFF-RELEASE1's one-marker direction. Sharing the underlying mechanism is required by I8; a second independent selector or checker is not authorized.

options.name: #DeepCheck
options.detail: Name the purpose rather than the build condition. Beginner: one short word with no condition to learn. Expert: declaration targeting and all shared rules stay unchanged. This is the clearest domain name, but adds a marker beside Off and amends the earlier one-marker direction.
options.technical:
Propose DeepCheck at Statement and Block sites, lowered into the shared switched-body path. It needs no BuildCondition case. Cost: one marker and registry/parser wiring, plus shared checking, selection and removal work. Its shorter source spelling is not proof of faster compilation.

Edge cases: arguments are refused; item and expression uses are refused. DeepCheck plus Off on one statement is refused, while nesting keeps both conditions. No ordinary check, required contract or arbitrary effectful debug block is silently converted. This changes the one-marker surface direction but need not violate I8 if it has exactly one semantic path.

options.name: Restore #DebugOnly(.deep)
options.detail: Use the spelling originally approved for deep checks. Beginner: old deep-check examples remain recognizable. Expert: targeting stays identical. It revives a retired name, and DebugOnly is misleading because selected checks may run in release. Bare DebugOnly would remain refused, not become an alias.
options.technical:
This explicitly amends D-OFF-RELEASE1's retirement. Register only the deep form and lower it through the same switched-body path. Cost: marker and argument registration, parser changes and shared work. Lowercase .deep needs an explicit argument rule; do not claim it follows the current BuildCondition menu.

Edge cases: bare DebugOnly stays refused with Off(.Release) as its repair. Other arguments are refused. Two presence markers on one statement, expression uses and item uses are refused. The argument-sensitive retirement rule is additional teaching and diagnostic work, but does not mean one accepted name has two runtime meanings. Selected checks remain legal in release unless an enclosing condition removes them.

options.name: if checks.deep(at: #here)
options.detail: Use an ordinary-looking call with an explicit site. Beginner: familiar if syntax, but a new checks API must be learned and imported. Expert: the site can identify the authored declaration without a hidden caller-dependent function. It still needs special branch rules to satisfy the already approved deep-check contract.
options.technical:
The checks module and deep function are proposed, not existing Core APIs. #here already supplies a SourceLocation with function and module; #caller is also an existing parameter-default mechanism. Thus an ordinary function can receive site information. A Boolean need not have one value throughout a build. The draft's impossibility argument was false.

Site information alone does not mark a checked diagnostic region. Ordinary if allows outward writes and effects and does not promise branch removal at every level. To keep this a spelling-only choice, recognize only this direct condition as a deep site and lower its then branch through the same isolated checker/removal as A. Cost: a new Core API, exact-call recognition and shared work. Purely ordinary if without those rules is not equivalent and would need reopening D-DEEP-CHECK1.

Edge cases: this option refuses a stored result, negation, a compound condition, an else arm, a forwarded or forged site, and indirect calls as deep-check spellings. That is extra expression policy; these are proposed refusals, not current diagnostics. A wrapper's #caller default could capture a site, but does not remove the need for branch-region recognition. Function identity alone also cannot identify each check site for artifact identities.

recommendation.why: Off(.DeepDisabled) extends the existing presence marker instead of introducing a second one. Its longer negative name buys consistency with the ratified direction. All choices still need the same deep safety and selection work.
gains: One presence marker
No revived retirement or call-sensitive branch rules

losses.loss: The negative condition is longer and less direct.
losses.mitigation: Teach it as off unless selected, show the exact command beside it, and keep its condition meaning consistent with Off.

whyNot.reason: It reads well, but adds a marker and explicitly amends the earlier one-marker direction.
The purpose is clearest, but another marker is not necessary to express this build condition.
It revives a retired name whose debug-only promise is false in release.
Site passing is feasible, but ordinary-looking if needs special restrictions and guaranteed removal to preserve the approved behavior.

recommendation.tradeoff: Prefer one marker and a longer condition over the shorter affirmative or purpose-specific names. This is a readability judgment, not a measured speed claim.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude Opus. Adversarial model family: OpenAI. Fresh agent: Review3. Added the missing Off condition and corrected the claim that a function cannot receive its source site; all five options now name costs and the same behavior. Replaced unsupported implementation and diagnostic promises with proposals, restored shared edge cases, and recommend one presence marker rather than the original On recommendation.

decisions.checkInstructions:
First verify this payload with the ballot validator. After the vote, implement only the chosen spelling and the complete shared contract. Prove valid and corrupt trees, default off, global and dotted scopes, union, every malformed or unmatched occurrence, and an embedded caller. Prove type errors while off, read-only captures, no external effects, no escaped facts, local versus outward control flow, Panic denial and required contracts.

Exercise every entry point, optimization level and applicable target. Check session immutability, resolved-site artifact identities and missing-source refusals. Validate each spelling's proposed pairing and attachment diagnostics with snapshots. Do not count rejection of unsupported syntax as behavior coverage.

decisions.title: Which permission covers the host reads used by TLS?
decisions.situation: HTTPS uses TLS to protect a connection. Jet's TLS code samples the clock, gets OS entropy, and can read environment variables and certificate files. Its host calls currently report Net, so denying FS, Rand or Env does not reject those TLS operations. This is a choice about the meaning of declared program effects, not a promise that the whole process makes no file or clock calls. The original draft recommended treating grants and denials differently inside the engine. This review instead recommends declaring the host effects normally. Beginners can still omit an authority list and use inference. Written ceilings become longer, but they do not need an engine-only permission rule. The alternatives below retain the same client and server workload.
decisions.gist: Should TLS declare its host reads, or should Net cover them?
decisions.lesson: An effect describes an operation the program may reach. A grant permits it; a denial prohibits it. TLS uses more than sockets: its default client also reads trust settings and certificates. We must decide whether Net includes those operations. Effect checking is not itself an OS sandbox or a ban on runtime housekeeping.
decisions.story: Mia downloads a price list over HTTPS. Her package permits Net but denies files. She needs to know whether that excludes certificate files too, and how to limit secret paths without disabling certificate verification.
decisions.detail:
Source scope is origin/dev plus the staged TlsLead-3rows patch to RuntimeEffectRows.jet. Initial source reads used origin/dev at 0d9e4b845ffd6d6afb8a7a7b910b72804911c472. During review it advanced to 5142789ba45286ed2c54763832210193c1bd7030, adding the split table. The staged patch adds removed_when; it was read, not applied or executed. Seed-b5 is the published probe compiler, not a compiler rebuilt from either revision. Future-option outcomes are proposed contracts, not implementation receipts.

Core/Net/Tls.jet:836-855 reads SSL_CERT_FILE and SSL_CERT_DIR. Nonempty overrides replace distribution defaults. Otherwise six bundle paths are tried until roots load, then /etc/ssl/certs if none loaded. The directory loader at 810-828 enumerates files, not only hash names. CustomOnly PEM avoids this loader at runtime; path-based custom roots still read files. Static inference can include both branches.

Core/Net/Tls.jet:620-628 seeds a context from 48 bytes of OS entropy. Client and server contexts use it. Core/Net/SSL/Defs.jet ssl_time samples the wall clock through the TLS host leaf. Generated CoreCallRows.jet:703-709 classifies seven TLS host leaves as Net: wall sample, entropy, file read, directory open/list/close, and environment read.

The later origin/dev row_splits table has five TLS-related symbols. The staged patch gives all five one removal condition, but some also encode non-TLS differences. Removing the TLS classification does not justify deleting wall-clock Time/pure, entropy Rand/pure or directory-close Read/Write splits. The rowSplitOutcomes table specifies all five symbols for each option. The staged condition also omits Env; the TLS inventory includes it.

Seed-b5 checked Net-only clients, including deny FS and deny Rand/Env. Controlled localhost HTTPS runs returned 200 under those policies. Combining deny FS/Rand/Env with a function denial covering the actual CA file also returned 200. scoped-denied-live.trace:384-385 shows a 48-byte getrandom and that CA content open. These connections used certificate verification, not an insecure bypass. No example.com status was used as proof.

The server checked with Net, FS.Read and Time, including deny Rand. A live server under that denial served hello to curl trusting its generated certificate. server-live.trace:361-363 shows 48-byte entropy requests. The application read its certificate and key before passing text to server.tls. This current server path loads no client trust store; that says nothing about future mutual TLS.

Controls distinguish the meanings. An ordinary files.read under allow Net fails E0749. Reserved __host_read_bytes access fails E0067. A DB-row function can read a file, but its caller's !FS rejects it. Core's service declarations and Effects/Checks.jet:1803-1815 support that library rule, not an existing privileged kernel Net boundary. The original recommendation therefore needs more than a claim of reuse.

Package scoped denials fail E1221 today, so path examples use function rows. A dynamic files.read under !FS.Read("server.pem") returned PermissionDenied. The equivalent TLS CA open succeeded. Runtime Authority.jet arms resource checks through scope publishers; TLS wiring and permission-error propagation are required work. Existing path checks document a check/open race needing kernel confinement.

Written allow acknowledges effects. The Net-only live client printed no notice; the no-authority client printed the network notice. Time.Wait needs no grant, but deny Time also denies Time.Wait and already fails E0749 today. Do not mistake that wait rejection for newly enforced certificate-clock authority.

Every option concerns this named TLS inventory, not all process syscalls. The trace also opened /etc/hosts during networking. Compiler, loader, allocator, resolver and native FFI boundaries need separate treatment before claiming complete confinement. Parsing a secret only as certificates does not make access, timing, errors or resource use harmless. This review does not certify secret erasure: no memory-lifetime proof ran.

Each option shows the same GET and server in separate files, with a controlled matching certificate. Only E adds configuration arguments. Production URLs do not guarantee status 200. Denied CA overrides must not fall back silently; preserve permission errors through TLS and HTTP. Test directories, links, relative paths, working-directory changes, callbacks and task inheritance. No option may disable hostname/date checks or substitute deterministic production entropy.

In-memory roots can avoid runtime file and environment reads without proving a file-free static row. A server key remains an ordinary file read unless supplied in memory. Embedded targets missing trustworthy time, entropy or files need explicit inputs or honest unsupported-capability errors, never invented clocks or skipped verification. These Linux seed probes establish no applicable-tier parity.

Migration for A touches TLS host leaves, declared TLS/HTTP rows and callers. It also affects service dependency lists, generated registries, split conditions, authority fixtures, diagnostics, examples and notices. Exact additions follow the call graph, not a blanket requirement for Env on every server. Beginners can still omit allow lists. No speed result or counted repository-wide migration estimate is claimed.

options.name: Declare the host effects normally
options.detail: This was option C in the author draft. The default client's written ceiling lists Net, Time, Rand, Env and FS.Read. Beginners can omit the ceiling and let inference report unacknowledged effects. Experts get ordinary grant and denial rules, with no TLS-only privilege. Proposed: Net alone fails E0749 for the default client; denied FS, Rand or Env rejects it. Scoped file denials build when not statically covered and are enforced on the actual TLS paths.
options.technical:
Reclassify actual TLS host ingress under ordinary Time, Rand.Draw, Env and FS.Read. Propagate the solved rows through Core rather than special-casing Net. Preserve Time.Wait separately. Route TLS file and directory ingress through the existing scope-publisher checks and preserve permission errors through HTTP.

Cost: more written grants and a full caller/registry/test cutover. A file-free configuration can still inherit a conservative FS row; precision requires separate entry paths or existing effect-polymorphic machinery, not pretending runtime branch choice is a static proof. Review new host-read dependencies when Core changes.

I8: one effect mechanism for grants, denials, inference and scopes. Service-effect declarations remain the existing library abstraction; update their listed machine dependencies where needed. No engine-exclusive authority exemption is introduced.

options.name: Cover engine reads for grants, not denials
options.detail: This is the original recommendation, now an alternative. Net alone admits the engine reads, but FS/Rand/Env denials still reject them. Beginner grants stay short. Experts must understand two views of the same call: a covering root for ceilings and actual leaves for denials. These are proposed semantics, not today's service-effect behavior for Net.
options.technical:
Retain both the protocol permission and actual host-effect provenance at each covered boundary. Denials, nested scopes and dependency sandbox checks must keep the latter through wrappers, callbacks and tasks. Explain output must show that provenance, even when Net acknowledges the grant. The read set must be bounded to protocol work; no arbitrary user read can borrow that coverage.

Cost is not established as one checker rule. Kernel roots and library service effects have different declaration paths today. This needs an owner-approved, generally expressible rule rather than a Core-only hook; its exact public boundary contract remains a pre-build review gate. Scoped enforcement and error propagation cost the same work as A. No performance advantage has been measured.

options.name: Treat the reads as Net completely
options.detail: This retains current TLS classification. Net permits the engine reads, and FS/Rand/Env denials do not apply to them. Beginner and explicit-grant paths stay short. Experts must accept that FS means declared program file operations, excluding this trust-store work. That is a coherent narrower contract if stated plainly, not proof of zero host file reads.
options.technical:
Specify the exclusion explicitly and keep TLS host rows under Net. Retain the five TLS-related splits and replace the staged removal condition with an explicit retained-policy rationale. rowSplitOutcomes gives this option's action for every symbol. Low implementation cost is not zero work: document the boundary, add regressions and expose protocol-internal reads in tools.

Best case: a narrow network service consumes a trust source without exposing arbitrary raw bytes to its caller. Cost: Net still permits reads of paths selected by CA environment variables. Parsing may fail after a secret file was read. FS and Rand denials cannot certify absence of these TLS operations.

options.name: Expand Net into an inspectable grant set
options.detail: Add a named Net host-read set that explain output expands. It contains Time, Rand.Draw, Env and FS.Read, and Net grants those rights normally throughout the package. This avoids an engine-only exception and keeps one-word grants. Denials still win. The price is broader authority: code holding Net can now read ordinary files too.
options.technical:
The named set is declaration metadata, not an extra grant or second runtime policy. Extend the canonical effect dependency relation to kernel protocol grants and display the transitive set in jet explain effects and machine-readable authority facts. Dependencies are fixed and reviewed, never inferred into a silently growing grant from an arbitrary implementation change. Denials inspect actual solved leaves using A's classification and scoped ingress.

Expert ceilings cannot use Net while excluding its ordinary positive host rights except by explicit denials. A host-scoped Net grant must not turn into an unexplained unrestricted FS grant: explain output must expose that widening. This option deliberately chooses broad implied grants, unlike B's engine-only coverage. It requires owner approval for that changed meaning and the shared dependency relation.

options.name: Declare a host-read ceiling on TLS configuration
options.detail: Use A's actual effect rows and add a TLS configuration ceiling. A default System setting permits the standard host-read set within the caller's authority. An explicit list can narrow it, never grant rights the caller lacks. Beginners keep defaults; experts review each connection's settings. This is extra configuration, not a substitute for package denials. The API below is proposed, not present on seed-b5.
options.technical:
Proposed TLSHostReads is an enum System or Only([String]); ClientConfig.host_reads defaults to System. Only entries are checked using canonical authority-right parsing and intersection, not a new permission matcher. Unknown or nongrantable entries are configuration errors before connection setup. Strings here describe existing rights; they are not code-level decision IDs.

System resolves the fixed TLS host inventory; it never overrides package, task or function restrictions. Both modes keep conservative actual effect rows, so changing a value does not silently remove static obligations. Propagate the ceiling to every deferred handshake operation, including entropy and clocks, and to server context creation at bind. Key-file reads in the application remain outside this TLS ceiling.

This materially extends HTTP/TLS APIs and adds a per-connection restriction carrier. The existing config has trust selection but not this host-read field. It does not itself supply a missing embedded clock or entropy source. A capability-provider version would need a separately complete API and lifetime review; merely putting an Authority handle in an escaping config would conflict with today's scoped-handle rules. I8 requires this to remain an explicit narrower view of the one authority mechanism.

options.name: Name TLS separately under Net
options.detail: Add Net.TLS to the secure-operation rows, while retaining A's actual host leaves. Net still covers its descendant, so existing Net grants cover the protocol but not unrelated host reads. Beginners infer effects; experts may deny Net.TLS while keeping plaintext networking. This makes TLS visible but does not by itself solve the host-read question.
options.technical:
Register the protocol leaf and report it on TLS handshakes and stream operations. TCP transport still requires Net; granting only Net.TLS does not grant all sockets. Keeping Net plus Net.TLS is not two authorization mechanisms: ordinary ancestor/descendant coverage applies. Host reads retain their ordinary leaves and scope checks from A.

A generic HTTP entry that can reach HTTPS conservatively carries Net.TLS even when a particular runtime URL is HTTP. Exact separation would require separate entry paths or a proven existing static specialization. This option adds useful protocol denial vocabulary but does not shorten the host grant list. Making Net.TLS imply host reads instead would choose B or D's additional coverage policy, not solve it by naming a leaf.

comparisons.note: Deno offers runtime host/path permissions, explicit deny precedence, prompts, query APIs and permission audit logs. These are real deployment controls that static rows alone do not provide. Its documented permission boundary excludes some runtime-internal I/O, and its default Rust TLS root store is embedded Mozilla roots. Thus HTTPS is not evidence that Deno secretly reads an OS CA directory.

A Wasm guest can use only linked host imports; WASI filesystem access is capability-based and restricts the files and directories supplied to it. This is stronger isolation than a source row by itself. TLS implemented inside the guest needs suitable imports; TLS supplied as a host service puts internal reads across that trust boundary. WASI does not settle Jet's naming policy.

Pony passes unforgeable object references as authority rather than relying on permission lists. Austral describes linear capability values, granular directory access and a root capability at entry. Their best case is explicit delegation to a narrow service or resource, including no access without a capability. Their trusted FFI wrappers still need auditing; reference capabilities for concurrency are not the same as object authority.

Koka infers effects and supports polymorphic rows and handlers, keeping much annotation out of ordinary code. Effekt offers contextual effect polymorphism with effects handled at the call site's lexical scope. Neither cited model is itself a filesystem deny-list sandbox. Their lesson is that a concise higher-level operation need not force every caller to handwrite a long list.

Historically it offered least-privilege checks with privileged library regions, allowing internal reads without granting callers arbitrary files. JEP 486 documents both that benefit's mechanism and its maintenance burden; it disabled the Security Manager in JDK 24. This is a warning about boundary complexity, not proof that permissions or B cannot work.

Effect handlers express modular control flow, concurrency and asynchronous I/O without requiring effect annotations everywhere. OCaml explicitly does not statically guarantee that all performed effects are handled; an unmatched operation raises Effect.Unhandled. These handlers are neither Jet denial rows nor an OS capability policy. Do not compare them as a failed attempt at the same sandbox.

recommendation.why: Use ordinary host-effect rows first. Inference keeps the unwritten beginner path short, while explicit ceilings and denials share one meaning. The service-effect analogy does not justify privileged kernel Net boundaries. Explain output should expose actual TLS host dependencies under every option, not hide them to keep a notice short.
gains: One grant and denial mechanism
TLS host dependencies remain visible
No engine-only authority privilege

losses.loss: Explicit HTTPS ceilings need more rights.
losses.mitigation: Keep inference for beginners and show the missing rights with the call chain; do not recommend granting all rights to silence an error.

losses.loss: Conservative rows can reject a file-free TLS configuration under deny FS.
losses.mitigation: State that limit; use separately checked file-free entry paths when required, without disabling verification or pretending a runtime branch is a static proof.

losses.loss: Scoped TLS reads and permission errors need a real cutover.
losses.mitigation: Reuse the ordinary scope checks, preserve refusals through TLS and HTTP, and gate the implementation on focused runtime and tier evidence.

whyNot.reason: It preserves concise grants and meaningful denials, but its engine-only privilege rule is not already implemented by kernel Net. A general boundary contract is missing.
It has the lowest code-change cost and a coherent service boundary, but excludes actual TLS reads from the denials reviewers want to enforce.
Inspectable implied grants are stronger than invisible exceptions, but Net would also authorize ordinary file and environment reads throughout the package.
A useful expert restriction, but it adds API and runtime state without replacing the actual effect rows or supplying embedded capabilities.
A useful protocol distinction, but it adds a name rather than resolving how host reads are authorized.

recommendation.tradeoff: This changes the original recommendation and lettering: original C is A, original A is B, and original B is C. It favors one checkable meaning over minimal explicit permission lists. No claim of performance superiority, complete sandboxing or completed implementation is approved.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude (Opus). Adversarial model family: GPT. Fresh agent: BallotHostReads. Fresh review: yes; claimReviews records each verdict and evidence, correcting stale exceptions, notice behavior and the service-effect analogy. Recommend ordinary rows, not the original engine privilege; future contracts remain unbuilt and require a passing audit.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Validate this payload without writing Tower. A passing schema is not a passing implementation or an adversarial design audit. Post it only as an open policy choice with the evidence limits intact. AGENTS requires the chosen build direction to name a passing dated audit before construction.

For A, prove client failures under Net-only and deny FS/Rand/Env, and server failure under deny Rand. Exercise an in-memory trust path separately from the default system path. Test !Time carefully because it already rejects Time.Wait. Keep ordinary Net-only file reads rejected.

For scope enforcement, use a real CA under the denied path, require no content open, and retain the permission error through TLS and HTTP. Cover CA overrides, directories, symlinks, nested tasks and denial precedence without silent fallback. Test notices both with and without explicit allow; test explain output's actual dependencies.

For B or D, first approve and review the shared coverage contract under I8, including scopes and dependency sandbox intersection. For E, first review its exact API and carrier lifetime. For F, test plaintext versus TLS denial and conservative URL branches. For C, document and test the explicit internal-I/O exclusion.

For every selected option, update all affected Core rows, generated registries, authority examples, tests and docs in one cutover. Exercise every applicable tier and honest missing-capability outcomes. Do not build this review's proposed semantics merely because the ballot validator has no gaps.

surface.gist: Should TLS declare its host reads, or should Net cover them?
surface.lesson: TLS reads clocks, entropy and sometimes certificate files. Today those operations report Net, so file and random denials miss them. This is about program effects, not banning every process syscall. Beginners can omit permission lists and use inference. We recommend ordinary host-effect rows rather than an engine-only privilege rule.

current.note: Observed on a trusted local endpoint: the client still returned 200.
