decisions.title: Where the effect for reading a task's context lives
decisions.situation: Reading a task's deadline or thread index adds Context to a function's effects. Two earlier votes require that dependency to remain visible. The kernel vote lists twelve built-in roots, but the compiler now has thirteen, including Context. We recommend declaring Context in Core while keeping its name and read effect. This is not just moving a declaration: authority checks must still distinguish a context dependency from permission to touch the machine. Keeping a runtime-context root is a credible alternative, but needs an explicit amendment to the twelve-root rule. This vote does not remove context reads at compile time: an earlier vote expressly permits reading the build's root context.
decisions.gist: Should Context be an effect declared somewhere, or an implicit input to every function, as in Jai?
decisions.lesson: Reading context touches no machine and needs no permission. Jai passes its context to every procedure as a hidden argument, and reading it is ordinary. Options A to E keep a visible Context effect and differ only in where it is declared. F follows Jai: context is an implicit input, so a function stays deterministic in its arguments plus its context. #Memo keys on the context it reads. C callbacks get no context unless they install one.
decisions.story: Priya's helper checks the deadline installed by its caller. She can omit its effect row; her reviewer can inspect the inferred Context dependency. A package that must not depend on that ambient input can deny Context. The question is where to declare that effect, not whether to make Priya write a row.
decisions.detail:
Authority checked on origin/dev at 271be24d15. Docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:9102,9186,9298 records A for the three cited decisions, but contains only their index entries. Their full clauses were checked read-only in Tower, not inferred from that index. D-EFFTYPE-KERNEL1 option A technical lists ten machine roots plus deny-only Mem and Panic. D-JAI-CONTEXT1 EFFECT and D-CONTEXT1 SHARED require Context on reads. The latter also requires no grant and permits denial.

Important correction: D-JAI-CONTEXT1 PREP says build-time reads see the build's root context, with no scratch unless set. It does not prescribe numeric thread id zero. The current runtime assigns zero to the first/main thread. Seed-b5 prints zero for a prepared thread read and None for a prepared deadline. Those results are consistent with the contract, not evidence of a defect. The older Mem-only wording in D-RIGHTS1 must be reconciled with the later specific permission; this ballot does not reverse PREP.

Commit 1e1fff240f added Context to Compiler/Prelude/Effects.jet:123-125. The generated Effect enum at Compiler/JetFoundation/Source/Registry/EffectRoots.jet:5 has thirteen cases. Policy/Authority.jet:42-47 exempts Context by name. Driver/Pipeline.jet:4795 separately inserts it into package budgets. The beginner floor at Policy/Authority.jet:24 does not contain Context.

Core/Compiler/Meta.jet:11-20 demonstrates a bare #FX declaration, and Registry/EffectVocabulary.jet:25 reads all three effect sources while building. That proves the declaration form, not A's complete behavior. Core effect bounds can admit their listed machine effects (Effects/Checks.jet:741-762). Keeping a nominal Context dependency and granting no machine permission are distinct jobs.

Seed-b5 probes cover both fields, inferred and written rows, an authority ceiling, denial, spawned tasks, nested restoration, compile-time values, and write-only Context blocks. A direct empty-row read gets E3401, but its text misleadingly calls the field read `call`. Env.Context is accepted as an open path today but does not cover Context: the same reader gets E0740. A is proposed, not a cutover tested with a rebuilt compiler.

Owner ranking, Docs/spec/philosophy.md:28-54: safety, beginner experience, runtime performance, one mechanism, implementation simplicity and compile speed, then ecosystem breadth. A, B and E keep the same beginner path. No option has a measured performance advantage here. A is preferred for preserving ratified boundaries, not because twelve is inherently simpler than thirteen.

options.name: Core declares Context with no machine power
options.detail:
Move the declaration to Core/Effects/Effects.jet under bare #FX, retaining bare Context rows. A read still records a nominal Context dependency even with an empty machine list. A package can deny it; an allow ceiling need not list it. Neither a direct read nor a call reaching one becomes pure.

Beginner: omit the row. Expert: write Context or !Context, or a package deny. Spawned deadlines and dynamic thread identity remain unchanged. A block that only installs a deadline is not itself a Context read. Prepared reads see the build root, not the eventual runtime caller.

This is a proposed cutover. Reuse the vocabulary and effect checks, and derive no-grant treatment from declaration provenance plus its machine list. Do not test kernel emptiness alone: today's machine roots also have empty kernel arrays. Do not add a Context-only purity walker or a private Core declaration form.
options.technical:
Move the Prelude declaration and regenerate EffectRoots plus affected Prelude and core.compiler.lang projections. Preserve Expressions/Places.jet's intrinsic Context fact. Replace the named grant exemption and Driver budget insertion with consistent library-effect authority handling. Empty kernel means no machine permission, not no dependency.

Migration includes generated root consumers, maximal rows, effect parsing, authority and notice paths, snapshots, examples and specs. Keep the existing runtime carrier and app spelling. The landing proof must cover direct and transitive reads, function values, generic and trait calls, denials, ceilings and build-root reads. None of this is proved by the Meta declaration alone.

options.name: Ratify the thirteenth runtime root
options.detail:
Keep today's built-in Context root and named no-grant rule. Amend the kernel contract explicitly: built-in primitives include task-runtime state, not only the enumerated machine powers. Reading a running thread index is plausibly a runtime primitive; external I/O is not the only useful effect.

Beginner and expert code are the same as A. No declaration or app migration is needed, but the twelve-root specification changes. This keeps the existing separate grant exception and package-budget insertion. It does not fix the generic `call` diagnostic.

Spawn, block restoration and build-root reads keep their current meaning. B is a valid owner choice after an explicit amendment, not something agents may silently infer from the implementation.
options.technical: Current Prelude/Effects.jet:123-125 and generated EffectRoots.jet:5. Foundation Policy/Authority.jet:42-47 exempts Context from grants; Driver/Pipeline.jet:4795 adds it to package ceilings. Context is not deny-only in the purity-check sense. Making it deny-only would hide a dependency that the earlier ballots require tracking.

options.name: Remove the Context read effect
options.detail:
Allow ambient reads without adding an effect. This is a reversal of the two ratified read-effect clauses, not merely relocating a declaration. Pure rows could then depend on the task's deadline or running thread. The benefit is shorter explicit signatures, not fewer beginner annotations: inference already avoids those.

Context-read denials disappear. Context-dependent memoization or constant folding would require a different contract; do not assert that either is already broken by this unimplemented option. Prepared reads would still see the build root under the existing PREP clause. Forbidding them instead would require another owner amendment.

Spawn propagation and Context blocks remain. Remove obsolete effect names, grant rules, budget entries and diagnostics in one cutover; migrate written rows, tests, snapshots and documentation. The underlying ambient-input semantics remain even after their effect label is gone.
options.technical: Remove the intrinsic effect recording at Expressions/Places.jet:766 and remove the Context root and authority special cases. Keep ContextRead lowering and the task carrier. Update the purity contract explicitly. This option does not make ambient state an ordinary argument or a mathematical pure input.

options.name: Env.Context on the beginner floor
options.detail:
Keep the dependency but rename it Env.Context. Add that leaf to the ordinary floor, like Exec.Args, while allowing denial. Twelve roots remain. Treating task context as input to a task has a coherent rationale, but Env currently describes process environment variables.

Beginner inference is unchanged. Experts rename rows and denials. A deny of Env also blocks context reads, and a deny of Env.Context blocks only this leaf. Excluding only environment-variable access would need a separate Env leaf and migration; this option does not invent one silently.

Spawned tasks, block restoration and build-root reads keep their meaning. The spelling parses today because Env has no declared leaves, but it does not authorize the current Context intrinsic. Converting Env to a closed enum is unnecessary and would close other open leaf paths.
options.technical: Keep Env as the existing root; declare its new leaf through the existing effect-leaf mechanism rather than adding a new root. Record Env.Context for reads and use the ordinary floor across budget and notice checks. Remove Context everywhere in the same cutover. Audit open Env leaf uses before making the vocabulary closed. Amend the earlier ballots' exact Context name.

options.name: Context stays built in, using the ordinary floor
options.detail:
Keep the built-in Context root but put it on the existing beginner floor instead of using a separate no-grant exception. This separates two questions the draft had bundled: declaration location and default authority. No new syntax or renamed app row is needed.

Beginner, expert, spawn, block and build-root behavior match B. Use one ordinary floor relation for package ceilings and invocation notices; do not leave the Context-only predicate beside it. A deny still wins. Context remains a dependency for pure-row checking, unlike deny-only Mem.

Cost: amend the twelve-root kernel contract, update the floor contract and its closed-list guard, migrate authority tests and inspect output. It may be the cleaner choice if the owner prefers Context as a runtime primitive. It is not today's authority implementation, although the app code already runs.
options.technical: Retain Prelude/Effects.jet's Context declaration. Add Context to AUTHORITY_AMBIENT_BASIC_EFFECTS and remove its special grant branch and separate Driver budget insertion. Check all consumers of the floor and effect notices together. Amend the floor invariant openly instead of bypassing its executable guard.

options.name: Context is an implicit input to every function, as in Jai
options.detail:
Every Jet function receives the task context as an implicit input, the way Jai passes its context to every procedure. Reading it is not an effect. It adds nothing to a row, and nobody writes, grants or denies it. `Context` is no longer an effect name.

A function's result depends on its arguments and its context, so it is deterministic in both. A pure `-[]>` function may read context.

`#Memo` keys its cache on the arguments plus the context fields the function can reach. A result computed under one deadline is never reused under another.

A C callback, like Jai's #c_call, receives no context. Reading context there is a registered error until the callback installs one. Using a context field is separate from reading it: time left until a deadline reads the clock, which stays Time.
options.technical:
Context becomes an implicit parameter of every Jet-convention function, which matches how the runtime already threads the task context. Remove the Context root from EffectRoots, the grant exemption at Policy/Authority.jet:42-47, the budget insertion at Driver/Pipeline.jet:4795 and the deny path.

The read inference at Expressions/Places.jet stays, but only as a sema fact naming the context fields a function can reach. #Memo uses it as the extra cache key. A function that can reach no context read keys on its arguments alone, so it pays nothing.

Where sema cannot bound the reach, as with an unknown function value, #Memo keys on the whole context. The C-callback check stays in sema as a calling-convention fact with a registered diagnostic.

Migrate every -[Context]> row, deny entry, snapshot, example and spec line in one cutover. This amends the read-effect clauses of D-JAI-CONTEXT1 and D-CONTEXT1. The convenience they ratified, Jai-style context without forwarding parameters, is unchanged.

comparisons.note: Jai's context supplies allocator, temporary storage, logger, print settings and thread index without forwarding parameters. push_context overrides it for a region; #add_context extends it. That is the convenience Jet is retaining, not evidence for any effect-root location. Source: Jai Community Library, Advanced, Context section; community documentation, not an executed Jai probe.
comparisons.limit: The source does not establish an effect-row guarantee, a Jet-style deny policy or comparative performance. No Jai compiler was run.

comparisons.note: Odin passes a scoped context pointer with its ordinary calling convention, letting libraries use substituted allocators and logging without extra parameters. It also has a contextless convention, so the draft's claim about every procedure was false. Context reads are not Jet-style dependency rows. Sources: Overview, Implicit context system and Calling conventions.
comparisons.limit: user_index is an application value, not a deadline or physical worker index. The comparison is about plumbing only; no Odin compiler was run.

comparisons.note: Koka infers effect rows and supports user-defined effects and handlers. A reader effect can make ambient access visible and locally supply its value. It also supports implicit parameters: argument inference and tracked effects are distinct choices, not synonyms. Sources: Koka book sections 3.2 and 3.4, plus its implicits release notes.
comparisons.limit: Handlers can replace an operation's interpretation; Jet's #FX declaration only bounds permitted effects. No speed or safety superiority is claimed and no Koka compiler was run.

comparisons.note: Effekt offers lexically scoped handlers and contextual effect polymorphism. Callback effects can remain handled at their call site without explicit row-variable plumbing. Its name-based implicit value and block parameters are another convenience for forwarding dependencies. These are not all one dynamically inherited task context. Sources: effect-polymorphism and name-based-implicits pages.
comparisons.code:
def foo(?context: String): Unit =
  println(s"Called from ${context}")
comparisons.limit: The empty requirement set in Effekt's contextual callback type is not Jet's absolute pure-row assertion. No Effekt compiler was run.

comparisons.note: Context function types such as ExecutionContext ?=> T synthesize context arguments and allow explicit using arguments. They expose a typed dependency without manual forwarding at every call. They are not, by themselves, an effect or purity checker, a sandbox grant, or a task-context inheritance policy. Source: Scala 3 reference, Context Functions.

import scala.concurrent.ExecutionContext
type Executable[T] = ExecutionContext ?=> T
comparisons.limit: This is a library-plumbing alternative, not proof that a root belongs in Core. No Scala compiler was run.

comparisons.note: Go recommends context.Context as an explicit first parameter and supports deadlines, cancellation and request values across goroutines. Callers may derive and pass independent contexts. That makes propagation visible but costs forwarding parameters. The draft overstated signature guarantees: a function can capture or store a context without accepting one. Source: context.go:34-54,72-76,118-163.
comparisons.limit: This helper returns zero for no deadline to match Jet's example. Go's Context does not supply a Jet worker index or an effect-row denial. No Go compiler was run.

Core declaration uses the existing effect form.

F follows Jai and the owner's stated view that context is an input. It drops the package deny, adds a context key to #Memo where context is read, and amends two ratified clauses. A vote for F authorizes the direction; its build card's first criterion is the passing cross-family adversarial review.

decisions.title: Which permission covers the small reads that only make unique names or inspect the running program?
decisions.situation: Some library operations quietly read a small fact from the computer while they work. A safe file save picks a throwaway name from the process number, and a temporary folder name mixes in the clock. Starting another program looks it up on PATH, and the scheduler reads files about its own process. Today none of these reads is listed under its own permission, so denying Env, Rand or Time does not stop them. They never change what a program computes: they only keep names from colliding, find the program to start, or watch the program itself. You are asked how a denial should treat them. We recommend writing them into the effect rules as part of the operation's own permission, so a denial means exactly what the rules say.
decisions.gist: Should name-making and self-inspection reads count under the operation's own permission?
decisions.lesson: A permission (an effect) names what code may touch: files, the clock, the environment. A denial says the program must never touch it. A few library steps read tiny facts only to make a unique throwaway name, to find the program being started, or to inspect the running program. The question is whether those steps belong to the operation's permission or need their own.
decisions.story: Sam's backup tool may write files, and he runs it with Env, Rand and Time denied. It saves notes.txt with a safe write that first writes a hidden temporary file. Sam wants the save to keep working, and he wants the deny list to mean exactly what it says.
decisions.detail:
The four reads come from Docs/spec/reference/host-reads.md. H6 is the clock sample and TMPDIR for a temporary name (core.files mkdtemp, files_temp_path and the temp_* constructors, -[FS]>). H7 is the process id in an atomic write's candidate name `.jet_tmp_<pid>_<sequence>` (core.files and core.crypto, FS.Write). H7 also covers a core.service store's temporary name (core.service __host_pid).

H9 is PATH from the logical environment, read to resolve a command (runtime ProcessExecutionAuthority.jet, Exec). H10 is the process's own /proc/self and cgroup files (scheduler monitor, process scopes, Unix-socket paths, test reads; no row).

The reads that can change a result are already declared. They are core.service's clock, entropy and working directory (H3), the terminal-capability variables (H5) and path.home (H8). core.files mktemp already declares -[FS, Env, Time]> for H6's reads. Until this ballot is ruled, host-reads.md lists the four rows as open. No page or diagnostic claims that a denial blocks every host read of its kind.

options.name: Count them under the operation's own permission, written into the rules
options.detail:
spec.md "Effects" gains one rule. A read that only makes a collision-avoiding name, finds the program an Exec call starts, or inspects the running process belongs to the calling operation's effect. The temporary-name and atomic-write reads are part of FS.Write, the PATH lookup is part of Exec, and /proc/self reads are part of whatever call makes them.

host-reads.md lists each read by name under that rule. A new host read must either fit the rule or declare its own effect. Nothing changes for programs. A name such a read makes is documented as unspecified, so a program that prints it sees a different name each run under every option.

options.name: Declare Env, Rand or Time on each operation that makes such a read
options.detail: write_atomic, the temp_* constructors and mkdtemp declare Env and Time next to FS; core.process starts declare Env for PATH; every scheduler and process-scope entry declares FS.Read for /proc/self. A written authority row that allows only FS no longer covers a safe save.

options.name: Remove the reads where possible
options.detail: Temporary and atomic-write names come from a per-process counter, seeded once by one start-up read that the runtime declares with its other start-up controls. No file operation reads the clock or the process id. PATH lookup and /proc/self reads can't be removed, because finding the program is the start and the scheduler must watch its own threads, so those two still need option A's rule.

recommendation.why: These reads can't change what a program computes or prints beyond a throwaway name, so a denial that refused them would only break safe saves and program starts. Writing the rule down keeps every denial honest, because the rules list exactly which reads it covers.
recommendation.tradeoff: A denial of Env does not stop the process-id read inside a safe save. The effect rules say so by name, and that read can't leak anything into the program's results.

It rewrites file naming and still needs option A's rule for PATH and the process's own files, so it adds work without removing the rule.

decisions.title: Large build-time data the program reads: store it smaller by a fixed rule, keep it raw, or compress it when asked
decisions.situation: Some programs build a large table while compiling and then read it while running. This vote decides how Jet stores such data in the executable file. Today Jet copies every byte in, so two fifty-million-byte values make a hundred-million-byte program. Hand-written code does better in one case: a long run of one repeated byte, which it rebuilds instead of storing. Irregular data, which is what real lookup tables hold, stays raw in every language measured. You are asked whether Jet stores runs as a short recipe, whether it also compresses other data, and what turns that on. We recommend A: one fixed rule that stores long runs as a recipe, keeps everything else raw, and never compresses behind the author's back.
decisions.gist: For large build-time data a program reads while running, should Jet store it smaller, and what switches that on?
decisions.lesson: Storing a value smaller and reading it quickly usually pull against each other. A long run of one repeated byte is the exception: a few bytes describe it, and rebuilding it is faster than reading it from the file. Real tables are irregular. Compressing them saves file bytes but costs decoding time and private memory on every run, so the cost belongs where the author can see it.
decisions.explainer:
Raw means the exact bytes sit in the executable file. Read-only pages are mapped from that file; every running copy shares them, and the system can drop them under memory pressure without writing anything. Private memory is memory one process filled itself; it is never shared and can only be reclaimed by writing it to swap.

Zero-fill memory is handed out already zeroed and costs no file bytes. A run is a whole value made of one byte, or one short pattern, repeated. Decoding rebuilds the original bytes from a compressed form. Cycles means run time; bytes means file and memory size.
decisions.story: A developer builds two values while compiling: a table of Collatz step counts for fifty million numbers, and a rule line of fifty million dashes. The program looks up one number's step count and prints the whole rule line. Every option uses this same program and prints the same output; option D adds one marker word. Real tables from Jet's own library are measured in the detail, because the dash line is the rare case.
decisions.inWild: C, C++, Rust, and Zig keep constant data raw in read-only data. Measured here, gcc, clang, and Rust stored fifty million zero bytes in the file when the array was declared constant. A plain, non-constant C array of zeros goes to zero-fill memory instead, in a 16,024-byte file. Linkers compress only debug sections, never data the program loads. Whole-program packers such as UPX are a separate outside tool. Embedded font libraries such as u8g2 compress glyphs in their own code and decode one glyph per draw. None of the compilers measured here compresses data the program reads.
decisions.detail:
Settled baseline. Card #6769 already decided three things, and no option here reopens them. Build-time bytes that nothing reads are not emitted. The length of a constant folds to a number. Data that is read lives raw in read-only pages. This vote covers only large data the program reads while running: may Jet store it smaller, and what switches that on?

Same complete program. COUNT is 50,000,000. STEPS is a build-time table of Collatz step counts, one irregular byte per number. RULE is fifty million dashes, one byte repeated. Both use the ratified forced build-time form, NAME: #run value. The program reads one byte of STEPS for the number on the command line, then prints every byte of RULE. Only the storage of the two values differs between options.

Measured today on seed-b13 with --optimize=full (probe review/spelling.jet). The build took 12.04 s with a 4,105,916 KiB peak, and the executable is 100,123,056 bytes. Both values sit in a writable segment, so read-only placement has not reached this seed. Running with 27 prints "27 takes 111 steps" and the dashes in 0.01 s or less. Its peak was 48.6 to 49.0 MB. An index of 60000000 stops with E3010.

Every native tier behaves the same today (review/tiers-rerun.txt, agreeing with tiers.txt). Optimize none, basic, and full, each with small false and true, produced images of 100,123,056 to 100,123,312 bytes. All six gave identical output digests for 27 and for 49999999. So --small changes nothing about stored data today; it only limits inlining.

The web build wrote a 100,006,747-byte app.wasm; neither run executed the web build. A rerun of zero.jet stored ten million zero bytes as file bytes, in a 10,065,936-byte image.

Measured storage costs, using C probes on the same bytes (rss.txt, rerun in review/rss-rerun.txt). Reading one byte of STEPS kept raw takes 0.01 ms and adds almost no memory. Reading all of it took 24 to 28 ms in the first run and 65 ms in the rerun, on a busier machine. It holds 50,000,000 bytes of file pages. A second running copy shares them, halving each copy's share. Under memory pressure the kernel dropped them without writing anything.

Compressing STEPS changes that (decode.txt, rerun in review/decode-rerun.txt). zstd level 19 stores 17,101,885 bytes, 2.92 times smaller, and decodes in 62 to 63 ms. LZ4 HC level 12 stores 23,975,076 bytes, 2.09 times smaller, and decodes in 14.6 to 15.0 ms. That is about 1.25 ms per megabyte for zstd and 0.3 ms for LZ4. Both decode the whole table even for a one-byte read, and leave 48.9 MB of private memory per process.

Real tables, measured (review/realdata.txt and review/decode-real.txt). The review took five. Three come from Jet's library: the Unicode name index (1,487,610 bytes), the collation elements (500,849), and the built-in font (65,068). The others are a CRC-32 table (1,024) and a flat table with one category byte per code point (1,114,112). None of the five is a run as a whole value. So A stores all five raw, exactly as today. The dash line in the story is the rare case.

Compression does better on real tables, and costs less because they are smaller. zstd shrinks the name index 5.09 times, decoding in 1.57 ms, and the collation elements 1.92 times, in 0.55 ms. In the flat category table, 10 of 17 aligned 64 KiB blocks hold one byte. zstd shrinks it 336 times, to 3,313 bytes, decoding in 0.29 ms. Jet's own table generator avoids that waste in the source, storing 1,398 seven-byte ranges.

RULE is different, because it can be rebuilt faster than it can be read (emit.txt, rerun in review/emit-rerun.txt). Writing fifty million dashes to a file from raw bytes took 17.5 to 20.3 ms in the first run and 27.6 to 28.7 ms in the rerun. Filling a fresh buffer and writing it took 17.5 to 19.4 ms, then 11.2 to 14.3 ms, with 48.9 MB of private memory.

Writing one 64 KiB buffer over and over took 12.4 to 13.7 ms, then 8.1 to 8.8 ms, with about 0.2 MB. So printing from raw bytes took 1.3 to 3.5 times as long as streaming. The order held in both runs while machine load moved the times. Reading fifty million zero-fill bytes took 0.72 to 0.90 ms and added no memory.

Where the owner's rule draws the line. The owner ruled that size never moves evaluation to run time. Under every option, the build evaluates each value completely, and the compiler looks only at the finished bytes. At run time Jet may then only place bytes the build already knows: copy them, fill them from a pattern, or stream them. It never calls the author's code and never computes anything new.

Placing bytes is the same kind of work the system loader does when it reads file pages, and a browser does when it copies data segments. Filling RULE measured 3.5 to 4.9 ms, faster than reading the same bytes raw. By this line, decoding compressed bytes is placement too, so C and D do not break the owner's rule. They are judged on their cost instead.

The performance gate decides this vote. Jet must match hand-optimized code in both cycles and bytes. For irregular data that is read, the fastest hand-written code keeps it raw, so raw is the bar. For a repeated byte, hand-written code generates it and never stores it, so raw storage fails on both bytes and time. Where a build must be smallest, hand-written code compresses in its own code and pays the decode where it can see it.

A hand-coder could also skip the table and compute one number's steps directly. That is an algorithm choice the author makes in the source. This vote covers only how the compiler stores data the source asks it to keep.

Web. A WebAssembly module's active data segments are copied into linear memory at start, so stored bytes become private memory there anyway. Web memory has no read-only pages. Servers already compress downloads with Content-Encoding. Brotli shrinks today's app.wasm to 17,025,105 bytes and gzip to 18,825,738, with no Jet feature. zstd on STEPS alone gives 17,101,885, so compressing inside the module saves about nothing on the wire and adds a decode.

Embedded. Microcontrollers such as the RP2040 run code and read-only data straight from flash, with only 264 kB of RAM. Decoding a whole table into RAM, as C and D do, fails for any table larger than that. Flash-tight code instead decodes a small piece on each read, as u8g2 does per glyph. That is a data-format choice in the author's code, which A leaves open. Jet has no embedded back end yet, only x86-64 and web, so none of this is measured in Jet.

The author's own path has a gap today. Under A, an author who wants a table smaller compresses it at build time and decodes it at run time with core.archive.zstd. But Core's zstd and gzip encoders write stored blocks only, so that build-time step shrinks nothing. A now includes the fix, a real zstd encoder in Core. It is a library change, not a language change.

Whole-program packing was considered and dropped as an option. zstd level 19 shrinks today's image to 17,138,559 bytes, and decoding it took 70 ms, paid on every start. That decodes both values and the code, even when the program reads one byte. The UPX manual says packed programs do not share memory between running copies. It is also an outside tool any author can already run, so it needs no language decision.

Peers, measured here. gcc 15.3 and clang 21 at -O2 kept both constant C arrays raw in .rodata, about 100,000,000 bytes, including fifty million zero bytes. Rust 1.99 did the same, in a 100,526,064-byte file. A plain, non-constant C zero array went to .bss instead: 16,024 bytes with gcc and 15,968 with clang (review/bss.txt). Zig 0.16 kept the dash array raw but emitted no zero array when its only use was one indexed read.

So B matches the peers only for arrays declared constant; a C author who wants zeros free drops the const. The only compression option ld 2.46 lists is --compress-debug-sections, for debug data, default none.

Build cost, a separate defect. Building this program took 12.04 s with a 4.1 GB peak. The same Collatz table built while running took 1.24 to 1.29 s with a 596 MB peak (review/runtime.txt). So Jet's build-time evaluation spent about nine times the time and seven times the memory of running the same code. No option here changes that, so it needs its own card, outside this vote.

Build-time limits, for context only. Jet stops one build-time call after 10,000,000 fuel units, about 5 seconds, with error E0952. gcc caps constexpr loops at 262,144 iterations, clang at 1,048,576 steps, and Zig at 1,000 backward branches unless raised. C++20 constexpr allocations cannot survive into the program, and Rust cannot call str repeat in a constant. No option changes these limits.

REVISION AFTER THE OWNER'S REQUEST (2026-11-12)

The owner asked for A's remaining downsides to be designed away. A carried four costs. Two are gone, and the other two shrink to costs that hand-written code pays as well.

Almost-runs, such as a run with one changed byte, stay raw. That never makes a file larger than today, so it is not a loss and is no longer listed.

Core's encoders shrinking nothing was a cost of A, because A sends authors who want compression to their own code. A now includes the fix: core.archive.zstd gains a real encoder. Compressing at build time with zstd.compress and decoding with zstd.decompress then works with no outside tool. The decode cost is a line the author wrote, where the author can see it.

A run used whole filled unshared memory on more uses than it needed to. A now runs length, loops, slices, comparisons, searches and hashing on the pattern itself. Only handing the whole value to a function that takes [U8], or to foreign code, still fills it, once. Hand-written code that needs those bytes at one address pays the same fill.

Irregular tables staying full size cannot be removed without compressing. Compressing costs decode time and unshared memory on every run, as the C and D measurements show. A keeps such tables as fast as hand-written code and makes the choice an informed one. jet inspect decisions lists each large raw value, and --estimate shows its zstd size.

Attack on the revision. Pattern-aware operations add code paths, so a wrong one could print different bytes. That code is linked only into programs that hold a pattern value, as the fill and stream code already is. The proof table gains one row per operation: identical output to raw bytes on every tier. The encoder must round-trip every real table measured here through Core's existing decoder. All of this is proposed and UNCHECKED.

options.name: Fixed storage rule, no switch
options.gist: Keep irregular data raw and read-only, store long runs as a recipe, and never compress.
options.detail:
The compiler applies one fixed storage rule to every value it emits, in every build and every tier. There is no switch, attribute, or setting. The rule looks only at the finished bytes of a whole value, never at how the source wrote it. A value of at least 64 KiB whose bytes repeat one pattern of at most 64 bytes is stored as that pattern and a length. A value of all zero bytes is the same case, kept as zero-fill memory that costs no file bytes.

Everything else stays raw in read-only pages, exactly as hand-written code keeps it. jet inspect decisions lists each value stored as a pattern, with its length, so the rule is easy to check.

How a pattern value is used. Reading one item, like RULE[i], becomes a bounds check and a lookup in the pattern at every optimization level. Its length is a constant. Looping over it, slicing it, comparing it, searching it and hashing it also work on the pattern, and a slice of a pattern is a pattern. Printing it, or writing it to a file or socket, streams from one reused 64 KiB buffer. Copying it into a new value writes the pattern straight into the new value.

Any other use needs the bytes at one fixed address, for example handing RULE to a function that takes [U8]. For that use the value is filled once, the first time. Its address space is reserved when the program loads, like a C array of zeros, so the fill cannot run out of memory partway through a run. The fill runs under a one-time guard, so racing threads wait for one fill.

The probe review/fillonce.c models this. Eight racing threads filled 50,000,000 bytes once, in 3.5 to 4.2 ms, and a later write faulted because the pages were read-only. Under a 30 MB address-space limit, both it and a raw 50 MB table failed at load, before any code ran. The guard is checked where the value is taken, not on every read. Checked per read, it measured 1.04 to 1.14 ns against 0.27 to 0.29 ns.

For the ballot program, the file would hold STEPS raw plus a few bytes for RULE, about 50.1 MB instead of 100.1 MB. Printing RULE would match the measured 64 KiB buffer case. Both projections are proposed and UNCHECKED.

Beginners write nothing new and get the smaller file automatically. Experts get a predictable rule: a long whole-value run is nearly free, everything else costs its size, and nothing is compressed behind their back.

The author's own path. A includes a real encoder for core.archive.zstd, so an author compresses a table at build time with zstd.compress and decodes it with zstd.decompress, with no outside tool. jet inspect decisions lists each large raw value, and with --estimate shows the size zstd would give it. The estimate runs only when asked, so builds pay nothing.

Edge cases. A run with one different byte is not a run, so it stays raw, which is never worse than today. A value under 64 KiB stays raw, so at most 64 KiB of a run is ever stored in full. Long runs inside a mixed value also stay raw, as in the flat category table; the hand-written fix there is a two-stage table in the source. An index past the end stops with E3010, as measured with 60000000.
options.technical:
Proposed, unimplemented. Classification runs once per data row of the shared IR module, after evaluation. Both writers read that mark: the x86-64 object writer and the web module writer. On native targets a zero row becomes reserved zero-fill memory. A pattern row gets a page-aligned reservation, filled once under an acquire-release guard and then made read-only. On the web, linear memory starts zeroed, so a zero row needs no data segment, and a pattern row is filled with memory.fill on first use.

Web memory has no read-only pages, so there the language's own immutability is the only guard, as it is for raw data on the web today. Item reads, length, loops, slices, comparisons, searches and hashing are lowered to the pattern at every optimization level, so memory use matches across O0, O1, O2, and web.

Only an argument passed to a function that takes [U8], or to foreign code, takes the guarded fill. Streaming is one library path in print and in file and socket writes. The fill and stream code is linked only into programs that hold a pattern value.

Considered and not adopted: filling every pattern value at start, which needs no guard but charges every run. Also mapping one stored tile of the file many times, which needs no private memory but works only on some systems, hits loader limits, and is impossible on the web. Proof after implementation: identical output digests on every tier, file bytes never above raw, and the C stream and fill probes as the bar.

Shared with the author's path: core.archive.zstd gains an encoder that writes compressed blocks, where today's writes stored blocks only. jet inspect decisions gains --estimate, which compresses each large raw value with that encoder and prints the stored and estimated sizes.

options.name: Raw and read-only, always
options.gist: Keep every byte the program reads raw in read-only pages, with nothing added.
options.detail:
Every value the program reads stays raw in read-only pages, byte for byte. This is the settled baseline with nothing added. It matches gcc, clang, and Rust for arrays declared constant, as measured. The ballot program's file holds 100,000,000 bytes of data. Beginners and experts do nothing new. An author who wants RULE small must make it depend on run-time input, so that it is built while running.

Gain: the simplest rule, with every page shared between running copies and dropped freely under memory pressure. Loss: long runs cost their full size. RULE adds 50,000,000 file bytes, and printing it took 1.3 to 3.5 times as long as streaming from the 64 KiB buffer, across two runs. Zero runs cost file bytes too, as the ten-million-zero probe showed, while a plain C zero array costs none.

Edge cases match A for irregular data. An index past the end stops with E3010. This option fails the gate for repeated data on both bytes and time.
options.technical: No new compiler work beyond the settled read-only placement, which seed-b13 does not have yet. Output, tiers, and the web build behave as measured today, with the data pages made read-only.

options.name: Fixed rule, plus compression in small builds
options.gist: Do everything in A, and compress large irregular data when the build asks for small.
options.detail:
Everything in A, plus one more step in builds marked small. The existing spelling turns it on: jet build --small, or small: true in a package build profile. Large irregular values, from 1 MiB up, are stored compressed with zstd. The whole value is decoded on first use into memory reserved at load, under A's one-time guard. The program's source and output never change.

Today small only limits inlining, so this gives the existing switch a new meaning. The cost grows with size: about 1.25 ms per megabyte with zstd, measured. STEPS shrinks from 50,000,000 to 17,101,885 bytes, and first use costs about 62 ms, even for one byte, plus 48.9 MB of private memory. Jet's Unicode name index shrinks 5.09 times and decodes in 1.57 ms. Raw needs 0.01 ms for one byte.

Beginners get smaller files when they ask for small, and pay start-up time they may not notice. Experts can reason about it, but the cost moves from disk to every run, for every large table in the build at once. On the web, servers already compress downloads to about the same size. On microcontrollers, decoding a whole table into RAM fails once the table is larger than RAM. Decoding in blocks would make one-byte reads cheaper but adds work to every read.
options.technical: Proposed, unimplemented. Every small build that holds a compressed value carries a decoder in its runtime. The compiler also needs a real encoder, which Core lacks today. Each value needs a reservation made at load and a one-time guard for threads. The compiler, not the author, fixes the codec: zstd for size, where LZ4 would decode four times faster but store 40 percent more.

options.name: Fixed rule, plus compression on marked values
options.gist: Do everything in A, and compress one value when its declaration carries #Compressed.
options.detail:
Everything in A, plus one new storage marker. Writing #Compressed before a build-time value stores it compressed, in every build and every tier. It is decoded whole on first use, into memory reserved at load, under A's one-time guard. Output never changes. The marker would join #Static and #Inline, the existing marks for how a constant is stored.

The cost is per value, and visible where the value is declared. For STEPS it is C's cost: 17,101,885 bytes in the file, then about 62 ms and 48.9 MB of private memory at first use, even for one byte. For a smaller table it is smaller: 1.57 ms for the Unicode name index. Unmarked values follow A.

Beginners never meet it. Experts choose it per table, and --small keeps its meaning. It is new syntax, which is why it needs this vote. It does what an author can already write with embed_bytes and core.archive.zstd, once Core has a real encoder. On microcontrollers it has C's problem: a whole table must fit in RAM.
options.technical: Proposed, unimplemented. The marker is legal only on a build-time value of at least 64 KiB; anywhere else it is a compile error. The compiler carries a real encoder, and every program with a marked value carries a decoder. jet inspect decisions lists each marked value with its stored and decoded sizes.

recommendation.why: A matches hand-optimized code in both measures. It keeps irregular data raw, which is what the fastest hand-written code does. It stores long runs as a recipe, which measured smaller and faster than raw. It needs no switch, so every build and tier behave alike. Compression saves file bytes only by spending time and memory on every run, so A leaves it to the author's own code, where that cost is visible.
gains: Long runs cost almost no file bytes, with no switch
Irregular data reads as fast as hand-written code
One storage rule in every build and tier
Authors who want compression get a real Core encoder and a size estimate

losses.loss: A run handed whole to a function that takes [U8], or to foreign code, fills unshared memory once.
losses.mitigation: Hand-written code that needs those bytes pays the same fill. Item reads, length, loops, slices, comparisons, searches, hashing, printing and copies work on the pattern and never fill it. Its memory is reserved at load, so the fill cannot fail partway through a run.

losses.loss: Irregular data, which real lookup tables are, stays full size unless the author compresses it.
losses.mitigation: That matches today and the fastest C and Rust. A adds a real zstd encoder to Core, so compressing is two calls with no outside tool. jet inspect decisions --estimate shows what each large table would save.

whyNot.reason: Simplest, but stores long runs at full size, failing the gate on bytes and time.
Saves file bytes, but every small build pays about 1.25 ms per megabyte and the same amount of private memory, even for one byte. It also changes what --small means.
Puts the cost on the one value the author marks, but adds syntax for what the author's own code can do, and still decodes the whole table.

recommendation.tradeoff: Files shrink by themselves only where bytes are cheap to rebuild. Irregular data stays at full size, at full speed, until the author chooses to compress it in code that shows the decode cost.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude Opus. Adversarial model family: Claude Opus. Fresh agent: ReviewComptimeSize. Reran the seed builds on every tier and web, the C storage, decode, and emit probes, and added probes for real tables, guarded fill, zero arrays, and run-time table cost. Repaired the spelling, noisy timings, the peer zero claim, the shared-writer and O0 parity claims, A's fill failure and threading, C's cost scale, the Core encoder gap, and added option D.

decisions.checkInstructions:
All probes live in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/ballots/probes/D-COMPTIME-SIZE1; source env.sh for tool paths. The adversarial review's probes and outputs are in its review directory.

Jet: build review/spelling.jet with --optimize=full, run it with 27, 49999999, and 60000000, and read its segments with readelf -lW. review/tiers.sh writes tiers-rerun.txt for six native tiers and the web build, with download sizes. zero.jet stores ten million zero bytes. review/runtime.jet builds the same table while running.

C: gen.c writes the payloads. rss.sh, decode.c, and emit.c write rss.txt, decode.txt, and emit.txt, and the review's rerun files hold the second run. review/realdata.py extracts five real tables; decode on review/real/*.bin writes decode-real.txt. review/fillonce.c models A's guarded fill. review/bss.c and exec-limit.txt cover zero arrays and failure at load. codecs.sh, peers.sh, and peers2.sh write their text files.

The A, C, and D behaviors are proposed and UNCHECKED. After implementation, prove identical output digests on every tier, file bytes never above raw, and RULE printing within the emit.c stream bar. Validate this payload with Tools/agent/ballots/Validate.jet.

The 2026-11-12 revision adds pattern-aware length, loops, slices, comparisons, searches and hashing, a real zstd encoder in Core, and jet inspect decisions --estimate, all proposed and UNCHECKED. After implementation, prove each pattern-aware operation gives the same output as raw bytes on every tier. Round-trip the five real tables through the new encoder and Core's decoder.

decisions.title: C callbacks and context: refuse reads, or allow scoped installation
decisions.situation: C may call a Jet callback immediately, later, or on another thread. A callback cannot assume that thread carries the registering task's context. The ratified context vote allows pure Jet functions to read context, but says a C callback must install one first. Today's callback checker rejects the installation block too. The named example gets two errors; neither explains context, and one calls the read an impure call to `call`. We recommend dropping the installation clause and passing needed values explicitly, or choosing the callback before calling C. The alternative permits scoped installation, but must define foreign-thread entry and restoration. It can inherit an active Jet context on synchronous entry; it cannot recover a finished task's context.
decisions.gist: Should C callbacks refuse context reads, or allow a scoped context block?
decisions.lesson: A C callback does not carry the context of the task that registered it. Even if C calls it on a Jet thread, that need not be the registering task. Passing a value explicitly preserves a snapshot, not a live task. Installing a context supplies local values and defaults; it does not revive a task.
decisions.explainer: Context holds task settings. Seed-b13 implements reads of deadline and thread; the broader field list is a ratified contract, not all working today. A callback is a C-compatible function value, not a closure carrying task state. D-CABI-CALLBACK1 bans captures, heap allocation, mutable static or thread-local state, scheduler access and panic-capable paths. #Context overrides named fields for a lexical block and restores them on exit.
decisions.story: A developer passes `late` to C. It returns x unchanged when no deadline is installed, otherwise x + 1. Both options start with exactly named.jet. Both refuse its uninstalled read. A repairs it by selecting a context-free callback before calling C. B also offers an installation block, but a fixed installed deadline changes the program's input.
decisions.inWild: The Way to Jai, section 29.7, shows a #c_call callback creating a Context and using push_context before calling log and print. Section 25 explains defaults and scoped restoration. This is B's strongest case: ordinary procedures can use the installed services. Jet's present callback subset bans such calls, so that benefit is not delivered by B alone. These are documentary examples, not independently compiled Jai results.
decisions.detail:
Scope. This ballot resolves #5025 c20 under D-CONTEXT-EFFECT1=F, ratified 2026-11-12. Tower contains F's full text; the supplied checkout's syntax-decisions.md does not yet contain F. D-CABI-CALLBACK1's contract is at Docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:4360-4367. A drops F's installation clause; B defines it and explicitly amends the callback contract.

Both choices retain F's no-effect context reads, pure Jet readers and context-aware #Memo keys. Card #5025 c16 and c17 require context-reaching locals to remain run-time code and context-reaching module values to keep E0643. These are requirements, not proof that F has shipped. The supplied adversarial review is still an inbox patch, not a landed audit.

Observed checks. All seven supplied probes were independently checked with seed-b13, identity jet@a0.0.45#6c8af19f74a2cb887fbb0f82ff7d830bb3236ac00549aefc4906413ed8ed461a. No C library was linked or executed. No compiler commit is inferred from this identity.

plain.jet: accepted. named.jet: E3203 NonCAbiType and E3401 ImpureCallInPureContext. The latter says `late` calls the impure function `call`, although its location is the deadline read. Neither explains context. This matches #5025 c11's diagnostic defect.

lambda.jet: E3203 and E0747 CallbackEffectBoundExceeded, explicitly naming the Context effect. Thus the claim that today's errors never mention context holds only for named.jet, not all callbacks.

install.jet: E3203 alone. It installs deadline 5 but does not read it. It proves installation is rejected, not that installed reads work. helper.jet: E3203 and E3401 naming `which`.

arg.jet and choose.jet: accepted by check only. choose.jet preserves x and the C declaration while selecting stay or bump from the deadline's presence before entry. arg.jet repurposes the existing x slot as a presence flag. It gives the same printed result for this x=1 example, but is not a general way to pass both x and a deadline.

Code basis. Callback checking is identical in the supplied checkout and $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/G12Docs/w at Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Calls/Checking.jet:406-450. It rejects calls, field/place expressions, #Context and even conditional expressions. B must admit the conditional in its installed example explicitly; merely removing the #Context refusal is insufficient.

The source snapshot under G12Docs/w contains context reads at Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Expressions/Places.jet:752-768. The supplied checkout lacks this addition. In that snapshot Context is recorded at line 766. Under F, removal of that effect should remove the context-caused row errors [INFERENCE, not a rebuilt result]. The syntax-subset refusal still needs a dedicated explanation.

Runtime limits. In G12Docs/w, Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/Context.jet:25 reads the current record via the thread control block. Thread.jet:102-106 sets GS; lines 115-126 allocate a block and assign a real thread index. These runtime files match seed-b13's provenance hashes. This does not establish that every foreign thread starts on Jet's zero word. Bootstrap explicitly clears a potentially stale inherited base before using it (lines 141-152). No rejected callback was forced past sema, and no foreign-thread crash is claimed.

Shared diagnostic contract, proposed. At conversion to a C callback, report one registered context-specific diagnostic with labels on the read and conversion. Apply it to named functions and capture-free lambdas. Suppress duplicate row/subset reports caused by that read, not independent errors. A Jet-only call to the same function remains legal under F. Reuse F's reached-context fact; do not add another effect or a second reach analysis.

Explicit-input alternative, available under either choice. Read the needed fields in Jet and pass C-safe scalar snapshots through arguments the C API actually provides. A hidden context pointer is forbidden; an explicit argument is not. A user-data pointer requires its API's lifetime and unsafe-boundary rules; this ballot proves no general safe context-object transport. If C offers no suitable argument, choose between static callbacks as choose.jet does. This is A's existing argument mechanism, not a distinct third semantic option.

Beginner path. The error explains that C does not carry the registering task's context. Show choose.jet for this exact C signature. Offer explicit scalar arguments only when the actual API supplies them. Under B also offer #Context(deadline: value), explaining that this supplies a new deadline rather than discovering the caller's.

Expert path. Under A, keep payload and context metadata separate where the C API permits, or select a static callback. Under B the same repairs work, plus scoped installation and real executing-thread identity inside the block. Neither choice authorizes captures, user allocation, helper calls or scheduling from the callback.

Proposed edge contracts, not executed runtime results:

1. Direct and lambda reads outside an installed block are refused under both choices. A refuses installed reads too. Under B an install value cannot itself read context before the block opens. Reads after exit are refused again.

2. On synchronous entry to an attached Jet thread, B overrides its active context and restores it on every ordinary return. Unmentioned fields inherit. On a newly attached foreign thread they use library-root defaults. These are invocation-time values, never a promise about the registering task. A refuses reads even on attached threads.

3. Concurrent calls share no writable context frame. B's attachment ownership must distinguish a new attachment from an existing one; inner entries must never detach the outer entry's thread. Nested #Context blocks restore in reverse order. Do not read a foreign GS pointer to decide whether it is live.

4. After the registering task ends, the function pointer remains valid for the program lifetime. Neither choice retains its task record. Copied scalar metadata can survive; borrowed task storage cannot be smuggled through user data. B creates a fresh root if no attachment is active. Library retention and shutdown rules still apply.

5. A deadline is an absolute timestamp, not a ticking remaining-time value. Expiring during a callback does not change its presence or interrupt the callback under this proposal. Reading a clock still needs Time, which the empty row forbids. A precomputed presence flag can therefore be stale for cancellation purposes. Neither choice adds cancellation, joining or preemption.

6. A C-to-Jet-callback-to-C call is refused: both choices retain the ban on callback calls. Reentrancy allowed by the callback ABI does not itself permit such a body. If ordinary calls are later admitted, restoration and reached-context checks must cover the whole nested chain. The D-FFI-CALLBACK3 text in Docs/proposals/ffi-perfect-boundary-2026-10-31.md is a proposal, not ratification.

7. context.thread is the executing attachment's index, not the registering task's identity. A refuses it. B must preserve this meaning with distinct live attachment indices, never a fabricated zero. An index need not persist across detach and reattach.

8. #Export entry points are outside this function-value conversion ballot. Their root-context contract is not evidence that arbitrary callback entry is already attached. Neither choice changes that contract.

9. Foreign longjmp across a Jet frame, signal-handler entry, and library calls after runtime shutdown are not authorized by either choice. B's cleanup guarantee covers supported returns, not skipped frames.

I8. A introduces no transport mechanism or runtime behavior. B must use the existing scoped override and thread-attachment mechanism, not a second callback context store. Its additional entry policy and runtime safety exceptions are real surface costs, not proof that #Context inherently has two meanings.

options.name: Drop the clause; pass inputs explicitly
options.gist: Keep callbacks context-free and explain the refusal at the C boundary.
options.detail:
F's callback sentence becomes: "A C callback receives no implicit task context. A function value that reaches a context read cannot become a C callback; the conversion gets a registered diagnostic." D-CABI-CALLBACK1 stays unchanged.

The shared named.jet program is refused. Its fix for this C signature is choose.jet: read deadline presence before the call and select stay or bump. Explicit scalar metadata is another repair only if the C API has an appropriate argument. The callback's payload must not silently be replaced by that metadata.

Gain: no callback attachment, context lifetime or restoration policy. Loss: callbacks cannot use the ambient context convenience available to ordinary Jet code. Some C APIs provide neither user data nor enough argument slots. Selecting static callbacks works for this finite choice, not arbitrary dynamic context. A does not pretend to solve that wider FFI problem.
options.technical: Proposed, unimplemented. Register a context-specific diagnostic with what/why/fix and UI snapshots for named and lambda conversions. Use F's single reached-context fact, including transitive reach if callback calls are ever admitted. Independent subset errors remain E3203. This is a compile-time rule, not a new effect, hidden parameter or runtime attachment. No measured speed advantage is claimed.

options.name: Permit scoped installation at callback entry
options.gist: Allow #Context inside callbacks, with defined attachment and restoration.
options.detail:
F's callback sentence becomes: "A C callback receives no registering-task context. Context reads require a lexical #Context block in that callback; the block supplies a scoped current context." This explicitly amends D-CABI-CALLBACK1's no-thread-local-state rule for the scoped context and runtime attachment bookkeeping only.

At the first block on an unattached thread, obtain an attachment scoped to the callback invocation. Start from the library root, override named fields, and restore them on exit. An already attached thread keeps its current record and real thread index. Unmentioned fields inherit that active record. Only an invocation that created an attachment releases it, on return after restoring all active blocks. Nothing retains the registering task.

Admit ordinary #Context fields and scoped reads when their initialization, use and cleanup meet the remaining callback safety rules. Admit the pure conditional used below. No captures, user heap allocation, helper calls or scheduling become legal. A field operation requiring allocation, such as an allocating trace capture, remains refused; the diagnostic must explain that independent restriction. Installation does not authorize calling a logger or allocating scratch. The same original program is refused because its read is outside a block.

Gain: one familiar scoped override, root defaults on foreign threads, active-context inheritance on Jet threads and real thread identity. It preserves a path toward calling context-aware libraries, but that needs a separate callback-call amendment. Loss: thread-sensitive inheritance, attachment ownership, restoration and initialization failure become part of this small callback feature. A fixed installed deadline does not preserve the original caller-dependent computation.
options.technical:
Proposed, unimplemented. Extend the existing thread-attachment mechanism with a scoped, allocation-free lease; do not create a callback-only TLS store. A fresh lease's control block and root live in the invocation frame. Its live index comes from the runtime's index allocator, not a constant zero. Existing attachments are borrowed, never freed by the callback. Concurrent leases have separate frames; nested leases release only what they own.

Preserve and restore the prior platform TLS state without dereferencing an untrusted inherited base. No stack pointer may remain in TLS or the live registry after return. Registration and context-value lowering must remain heap-free. An initialization failure stops with a registered runtime error before executing the block, never unwinds through C. This is an explicit exception to the callback's panic-free entry guarantee, not permission for panic-capable user code.

Today's jet_rt_thread_attach allocates, and jet_rt_thread_detach frees and performs scheduler/TLS cleanup. Calling that pair unchanged is not this design. The scoped lease must be a rung of that same attachment mechanism and preserve the no-user-scheduler rule. #Context still means override and restore, not capture the registering context.

The current Linux backend changes GS with arch_prctl; extra attachment work is real, but no fixed syscall count or performance number is established here. Already attached entries need no fresh attachment. Require a matched two-program measurement before claiming a cost advantage for any new performance surface.

Register the same outside-block diagnostic as A, plus snapshots for reads in install values and after exit. Prove installed conditional reads, early return restoration, fresh/attached threads, simultaneous calls and reentrant ownership on every applicable tier. Admit only operations proven allocation-free and panic-free within the body; merely accepting #Context in the syntax walker is insufficient.

recommendation.why: A is the smaller semantic surface under the present callback restrictions: it needs no new thread-entry policy or runtime safety exception. Prefer explicit inputs or static callback selection. This is not proof that installation is useless, impossible or slower by a measured amount.
gains: Keeps the existing callback safety contract
Adds no callback context lifetime or attachment work
Explains the context-specific refusal

losses.loss: Callbacks lose ordinary Jet code's ambient context convenience.
losses.mitigation: Pass scalar snapshots where the C API supports them. For this exact signature, choose.jet preserves x by selecting the callback before entry.

losses.loss: Some C APIs cannot transport arbitrary task settings.
losses.mitigation: Name this limit rather than inventing a hidden pointer or claiming static selection solves arbitrary state. B supplies defaults and overrides, not retained task context.

losses.loss: If callback calls are later admitted, context-aware libraries will need an entry policy.
losses.mitigation: Review installation with that broader callback amendment. A does not foreclose it; B alone still bans the calls that make Jai's pattern useful.

whyNot.reason: Scoped installation is coherent and can inherit active values or defaults. For this call-free subset, its entry, identity and failure policy buys little beyond explicit scalar inputs.

recommendation.tradeoff: Keep today's safety boundary, while accepting that explicit snapshots cannot recreate a live task or fit every C API.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude Opus. Adversarial model family: GPT. Fresh agent: SolBallotContextCB. A holds within limits; checked all seven probes and corrected inheritance, transport, thread safety, runtime citations and unsupported cost claims. B is a defined amendment, not working code; explicit arguments are covered without a duplicate option.
