decisions.title: Script helpers and the script's own variables
decisions.situation: A script is a Jet file of plain statements that runs top to bottom, with no `run: fn` wrapper. Scripts often define small helper functions. Today a helper can't use the script's own variables: if the script says `count := 0`, a helper that adds to `count` is refused. The same lines work inside `run: fn`, so the rule surprises beginners and makes scripts longer than Python or JavaScript. This vote decides whether helpers may use all script variables, only the unchanging ones, none, or whether they become file-wide variables. We recommend all of them: Jet passes each variable a helper uses as a parameter it fills in for you, and catches a too-early call before the script runs.
decisions.gist: May a helper function in a script file use the variables the script's own lines set up?
decisions.lesson: A script's lines run top to bottom, and its helpers are named functions. Today a helper can't use the script's variables. That comes from how the compiler builds scripts, not from a user need. Python, JavaScript, Lua, Swift and Kotlin let script functions use script variables. Jet can do the same and still catch a too-early call before running, as Swift already does for its nested functions.
decisions.explainer:
A script file holds top-level statements and no `run: fn`; Jet runs its lines in order. A helper is a function declared in a script with `name: fn(…) {…}`. A script variable is a value the script's lines set up, either fixed, `limit: 3`, or changeable, `count := 0`. A closure is an unnamed `fn() {…}` stored in a variable; it can use the variables around it.

A `&` parameter lets a function change the caller's variable. A parameter after `*` must be passed by name, as in `note("fig", count: tally)`. A task is code that runs at the same time as the rest of the program.
decisions.story: Maya writes a short script that counts the words it notes. She adds a helper, `note`, that adds one to `count` and prints progress against `limit`. Jet refuses it twice and tells her to pass `count` as a parameter. She moves the same lines into `run: fn`, and they work, which confuses her more. Every option below uses her exact program. A and D print three lines, B keeps today's errors, and C keeps the errors about `count`.
decisions.inWild:
Python: functions read module names when called; changing one needs `global`; a too-early call is a NameError at run time (run here, Python 3.13).
JavaScript (Node 24 module): function declarations read and change module `let` names; a too-early call throws a ReferenceError at run time (run here).
Lua 5.4: a function sees a `local` declared above it; above the declaration the same name silently means a global (manual, not run).
Swift: names at the top of the entry file are globals every function can use; only one file may hold top-level code (book, not run).
Swift nested functions: they read and change the enclosing function's variables. The compiler refuses one that would capture a variable before its declaration ('closure captures … before it is declared'; compiler diagnostic, not run).
Kotlin scripts: the script compiles into a class, so its functions can use its top-level values (scripting proposal, not run).
Rust: a `fn` written inside a function can't use that function's locals, and error E0434 says to use a closure, like Jet today (error index, not run).
Ruby: `def` starts a new scope, so methods cannot see top-level locals, like Jet today (Ruby FAQ, not run).
decisions.detail:
Scope. This vote decides one rule: may a named function declared at the top of a script file use the script's variables? A script file holds top-level statements and no `run: fn`. The one-entry rule is unchanged: a file is a script or has `run: fn`, never both (E0621, probe p19). Scripts are never imported (E0620, probe p20_import). ALL_CAPS constants already reach every function (probe p03).

Code. sema_script_entry turns a script's statements into a generated `run: fn` (Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/CheckProgram.jet:9141-9191). Bindings that are mutable or snake_case move into that body as script variables (:9193-9199). Named functions stay module functions outside that body (:9153-9174). A function naming a script variable gets E0107 jet.UnknownName: 'Pass `name` as a parameter' (Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Diagnostics.jet:325-341). Docs/spec/spec.md:304-308 states the rule; tests/ui/script_local_unseen_by_function.jet pins it.

History. The ratified script-mode ballot D-SCRIPT-TOPLEVEL1 listed 'A function cannot read a variable from the script body' as a loss of its winning option. A later ruling made top-level bindings locals of the generated entry. The owner has since said that a function not seeing the script's variables does not make sense. The rule follows from compiling helpers as separate module functions, not from a user need.

Probes. Every current-behavior claim was run on seed-b13 in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/ballots/probes/D-SCRIPT-HELPERS1. The file results.txt there holds the full output. Script files:

```
p01 helper reads `total: 5`              -> E0107 "`total` is a local of this file's top-level statements, which a function can't see"
p02 closure `show := fn() {...}` reads it -> 5
p03 helper reads `LIMIT: 3`              -> 3
p04 helper writes `count := 0`           -> E0107
p05 closure writes `count` twice         -> 2
p06 closure made above `total: 5`        -> E0107 with the same "function can't see" text
p07 helper called above `total: 5`       -> E0107
p08 helper recursion fact(5)             -> 120
p09 closure recursion                    -> E0804 RecursiveLambda and E0102
p10 call above two helpers, one calling the other -> HI!
p11 helper as a map callback             -> [2, 4, 6]
p12 closure reading `factor` in map      -> [3, 6, 9]
p13 closure writing `count`, given to each -> 0 (the write is lost)
p14 task reads `total: 5`                -> 10
p15 task reads `count := 5`              -> 10
p17 `run: fn` file, function writes module `count` -> E0111 "module state"
p18 module value from process.args()     -> E0643 (module values are made while building)
q15 task writes `count`                  -> E1101 ConcurrentCaptureNotOwned
p20 another file imports the script      -> E0620, plus E0357 on `total`
s01 shared program                       -> E0107 on `count`, lines 4 and 5
s02 shared program with parameters       -> 1/3 apple, 2/3 pear, done: 2
s04 shared program with a closure        -> the same three lines
s06 two script variables in one string       -> only the first is reported
s07 generic helper fn<T>, called above it -> 4
q14 jet test on a script with #Test      -> 1 passed
q17 `&Int` parameter in a script         -> 5, then 2
q18 closure reads `total := 1`, then `total = 9` -> 1
```

Inside `run: fn`, a nested `name: fn` is a closure. These probes show what a closure does today:

```
p16, s03 nested helper reads locals      -> 5; the shared program prints all three lines
q05 nested helper writes `count`         -> 2
q02 nested helper made above `total`     -> E0107 "Nothing named `total` exists here"
q03 call above the nested helper         -> E0102
q04 helper made after `total`, called    -> 5
q06 nested recursion                     -> E0804 and E0102
q07 nested helper calls one made below   -> E0102 (q07b, made above: HI!)
q08 nested reader as a map callback      -> [3, 6, 9]
q09 nested writer given to each          -> 0 (the write is lost)
q10 task calls a nested reader           -> 10
q11 task writes `count` directly         -> E1101
q12 task calls a nested writer           -> 0 (the write is lost, no error)
q13 nested generic fn<T>                 -> E0003
q16 nested reader, total 1 then 9        -> 1
```

Review probes. The adversarial review added r01-r10 in the same folder. Most write out by hand the call that A's rewrite would make; the rest check a rule A must keep:

```
r01 add(count, count): read Int and `&Int` of one name   -> 2 (allowed)
r02 append_all(items, items): read list and `&` list     -> E0204 "`items` is already shared in this call"
r03 f := bump, where bump has a `&` parameter            -> E0227 MarkedFunctionValue
r04 task calls bump(count), `&` parameter                -> E1101
r05 script helper makes its own `count := 5`             -> 5, then 0
r06 the same lines inside `run: fn`                      -> E0118 NameAlreadyTaken
r07 nested parameter named `count` inside `run: fn`      -> E0118
r08 #Test reads `total`                                  -> jet run: 5; jet test: E0107
r09 jet test on a script whose lines panic               -> 1 passed; the lines don't run
r10 bump(count, count): two `&` of one name              -> E0204
```

Why A is not a plain closure. A first draft made every helper a closure. The probes show that would take away what script helpers have today: recursion (p08), calls in any order (p10), generics (s07) and use as values (p11). It would also bring stale reads (q16) and lost writes (q09, q12). So A keeps helpers as real functions. The compiler hands each helper the script variables it uses, as extra parameters at each call.

Writes through values. A helper that changes a name carries a `&` extra parameter. Jet already keeps any function with a `&` parameter callable only directly (E0227, r03; spec.md:1127-1128). So A reuses E0227, with text naming the write through an extra parameter. In a task the `&` extra parameter is a captured write, E1101 (r04). Neither error can go without letting a function value hide a write, which E0227 exists to stop.

Shared and changed in one call. Jet refuses one call that shares a list and also changes it (E0204, r02, r10). Under A, `append_all(items)` is that call when the helper also changes `items`. The error must name the write through an extra parameter, and the spec's fix, `append_all(items.copy())`, works (spec.md:1482-1483). A plain number is fine (r01). Python and Node allow this sharing; Jet keeps its rule.

Same spelling inside a helper. Inside `run: fn` a nested helper may not reuse an outer name as a parameter or local (E0118, r06, r07). Scripts that follow today's fix, a parameter named `count` (s02), and helpers with their own `count := 5` (r05) compile now. A keeps them compiling: a helper's own parameter or local hides the script variable. A local also gets a tidy error, because `count := count + 1` in a helper makes a new name and leaves the script's `count` alone.

Stored helper values. A helper used as a value becomes an ordinary closure that holds its read extra parameters, made at that point. Passed straight to `map`, it sees the current values. Stored and called after the script changes a `:=` name, it shows the old value, as a stored closure does today (q18). Direct calls always see the current value.

Recursion. Helpers that call each other share one list of extra parameters. If `even` calls `odd` and only `odd` changes `count`, both carry `&count`. Then `even` is callable only directly too, and the E0227 text names the chain: `even` calls `odd`, which changes `count`.

Order. The check runs on the script's own lines: each call, each use of a helper as a value, each task, and each closure made there that calls a helper. Every name the helper reaches, through any helper it calls, must be bound above that line. The check is cautious: a call is refused even when the branch reading the name would not run. Reading a name a script line already moved is E0121 at the call.

Tests. `jet test` doesn't run a script's lines (r09), so a test has no script variables (r08). A test passes a helper's extra parameters by name, as in `note("fig", count: tally, limit: 3)`, with its own values. Leaving one out is E0107, naming the parameter. On seed-b14, probe s1_label_only shows `jet test` passing a test that calls a helper with a label-only `&Int` parameter this way.

Tools. `jet fmt` changes nothing, because the source doesn't change. Hover and `jet inspect expand --facts callable-signature` list each helper's extra parameters, marked read or change, beside its written parameters. Find-references and rename for `count` include the helpers that use it. Every error caused by a extra parameter names the input and the line that binds it.

Speed and tiers. After the rewrite a call is the s02 call, with one extra argument per name reached. So it costs what hand-written parameters cost; nothing is measured yet. One pointer to all script variables would pass less on long chains, but every call that also passes a script variable would then clash under E0204. So A passes names one by one. The rewrite happens in the checker, before code generation, so O0, O1, O2 and web run the same calls.

One mechanism? A adds no new runtime mechanism: extra parameters are ordinary read and `&` parameters, checked by E0204, E0227, E1101 and E0121. Users do meet two ways to reach outer names. A closure holds names from when it is made (q16, q18); a script helper takes them at each call. The split is real and named. It shows only when a `:=` name changes between making a closure and calling it.

What doesn't carry over. Lines move from `run: fn` into a script unchanged, except the q16 pattern, which prints 1 inside `run: fn` and would print 9 in a script. Moving script helpers into `run: fn` loses recursion, any-order calls and generics (q06, q07, q13), and s02-style parameters become E0118 (r07). Methods in a script get no extra parameters and keep E0107, because a method can be called through a trait where the call site isn't known.

Edge cases. Each row is a script file; A, C and D are proposed and UNCHECKED, B is today's probed result:

```
case                                            A (proposed)                  B (today)                          C (proposed)                D (proposed)
1 helper reads `total`, called below it         5                             E0107 (p01)                        5                           5
2 helper above `total: 5`, called below it      5                             E0107 (p01, p07)                   5                           5
```

Peers run here. Python 3.13 and Node 24 ran peers/python_helpers.py and peers/node_helpers.mjs. Python printed `NameError: name 'total' is not defined` for a too-early call, then 5 and 2. Writing without `global` raised UnboundLocalError. Node printed `ReferenceError: Cannot access 'total' before initialization`, then 5, 2 and 5, so a callback's writes land. Lua, Swift, Kotlin, Rust and Ruby are cited from their documentation below and were not run.

Right and wrong ways. Python and JavaScript let helpers use script variables, but report a too-early call only when that line runs. Lua silently reads a global when the function sits above the `local`. Ruby and Rust refuse, like Jet today; users switch to closures, blocks or constants. Swift nested functions already reject a capture before its declaration at compile time, so A's order check follows known practice. A takes the reach of Python and JavaScript and moves their run-time failure to compile time.

Option D. Swift makes top-level names of its entry file into globals. In Jet that is an exception to two rules. Module values are made while building (E0643, p18), and a function may not change module state, because every task can reach it (E0111, p17). D's extra gains over A are writing callbacks and stored helpers that see later changes. Both need a function value to hide a write, which E0227 refuses. Keeping Jet's checks needs A's per-helper analysis, and then D's gains disappear.

Separate defects found, outside this vote. A closure that writes a captured `:=` local loses the write when given as a callback (p13 and q09 print 0). A task that calls such a closure compiles and loses the write (q12), while a direct write is E1101 (q11). A closure made above a script variable gets the 'function can't see' text (p06), though the cause is order. In one interpolated string only the first unknown script variable is reported (s01, s06).

More defects. The spec says a closure that only reads a name has 'shared read access' (spec.md:1169), yet q16 and q18 print the old value 1 after `total = 9`. The spec or the closure code must change. `jet run` accepts a #Test body that `jet test` rejects (r08).

Shared work. A and C both need the order check, the extra-parameter rewrite and the same-spelling rule with its tidy error. They also need new E0107, E0204 and E0227 text, the hover and inspect rows, and UI cases for every table row on every tier. D needs the order check plus exceptions to E0111, E0643 and E0227. B needs none of that.

REVISION AFTER THE OWNER'S QUESTION (2026-11-12)

The owner found the terms confusing and rejected A because its downsides were not designed away. The ballot now uses plain words. A script variable is a value the script's own lines set up. An extra parameter is what the earlier draft called a hidden input or hidden argument.

The model is now one sentence. For each script variable a helper uses, Jet gives the helper an extra parameter with that variable's name, after `*`, so it is passed by name. Inside the script, Jet fills it in at every call. This is a mechanism Jet already has, label-only parameters, not a new kind of hidden state.

What was designed away. Tests could not call a helper that uses script variables. Now a test passes them by name, with its own values, so every helper is testable. A signature that hid inputs is gone too: hover, inspect and the docs show the extra parameters as part of the helper's signature, `note(word: String, *, count: &Int, limit: Int)`.

Two former losses were not losses of A. A call that shares a list and also changes it is refused under E0204 whether the parameter is written or filled in, so it is shared Jet behavior. A stored helper value keeps the values from when it was made, as every stored function value in Jet does (Examples/Basics/Functions/ClosureCaptureModes.jet).

The one place A and `run: fn` still differ is a defect, not a design. A nested helper inside `run: fn` that reads a variable after it changes prints the old value (q16). The spec says such a closure has shared read access, which would print the new value. Fixing that defect makes both print 9. It is listed under the separate defects above.

WHAT REMAINS

A helper that changes a script variable can only be called directly. Handing it to `each` or running it as a task would let a function value hide a change, which E0227 and E1101 exist to stop. Writes from a task would also race with the script. The error rewrites the call as a loop, and helpers that only read pass freely.

A method declared in a script gets no extra parameters, because a method can be called through a trait, where no script is in reach. The error names the variable and offers a helper function or a written parameter.

Attack on the revision. Passing by name in a test is ordinary label-only argument passing, and probe s1_label_only passed it in `jet test`.

The same labeled `&` call written in the script's own lines hits an internal compiler error on seed-b14 under `jet run`. That is a separate defect, and the fix belongs to any option. A call that names a parameter the helper doesn't have is an ordinary unknown-label error. Inside the script a caller may still pass one by name, and that value wins, which is how label-only parameters behave today.

options.name: Helpers use the script's variables
options.gist: Each script variable a helper uses becomes a parameter Jet fills in; a test passes it by name; a too-early call fails to compile.
options.detail:
A function declared at the top of a script may use the script's variables, as the script's own lines do. The shared program prints `1/3 apple`, `2/3 pear` and `done: 2`.

How it works. For each script variable a helper uses, Jet gives it an extra parameter with that variable's name, passed by name. Inside the script, Jet fills it in at every call. A helper reads the variable's value when it is called, and its changes land on the script's variable. Hover shows the full signature, `note(word: String, *, count: &Int, limit: Int)`.

Anywhere else, such as a test, the caller passes them by name: `note("fig", count: tally, limit: 3)`. So every helper can be tested. A call that runs before a variable it needs is set is a compile error. Helpers stay ordinary functions: they recurse, call each other in any order, and can be generic.

One limit stays. A helper that changes a script variable can only be called directly. Handing it to `each` or running it as a task is refused, as for any function that changes its caller's variable, and the error offers a loop. Methods in a script get no extra parameters.

Gain: lines written inside `run: fn` work in a script too, with earlier errors than Python or JavaScript.
options.technical:
Proposed, UNCHECKED. The checker computes, for each script helper, the script variables it reaches, and adds one label-only parameter for each,, including through helpers it calls. Helpers that call each other share one list. Each call passes them as extra parameters. A name the helper or its callees change goes as `&`. Any other goes as an ordinary read parameter, which shares the value without copying it (r02's E0204 text says 'already shared'). After the rewrite every call is the explicit form of probe s02.

Existing rules then apply unchanged, with text naming the extra parameter. E0227 covers a changing helper used as a value (r03), and E1101 one called in a task (r04). E0204 covers a call that also passes the changed name (r02, r10). E0121 covers a read of a name a script line already moved. A helper used as a value becomes a closure holding its read inputs, made at that point, under the closure rules (spec.md:1167-1186).

The order check reuses E0107, with text naming the helper, the call chain, the name and its binding line. A helper's own parameter or local hides a script variable of the same spelling; a local also gets a tidy error (it stops jet check and jet build, not jet run). Methods get no extra parameters. A `#Test` body is not script code, so it passes the extra parameters by name, as any caller outside the script's lines does.

The rewrite runs in the checker, before code generation, so O0, O1, O2 and web run the same calls. Hover, find-references and `jet inspect expand --facts callable-signature` show the extra parameters. The change is additive. Today any helper that names a script variable fails (p01, p04), and helpers that reuse a script variable's spelling (r05, s02) keep their meaning.

options.name: Keep today's rule
options.gist: Helpers see only their parameters, ALL_CAPS constants and other declarations.
options.detail:
Keep E0107. The shared program fails with two errors on `count` (probe s01). Beginners fix it with parameters: `note: fn(word: String, count: &Int, limit: Int)` called as `note("apple", count, limit)` prints the three lines (s02). The other fix is a closure, `note := fn(word: String) {…}`, which also prints them (s04).

Experts get signatures that list every input. Closures have limits: they can't recurse (p09), must be made below the names they use (p06), and copy values they only read (q18 prints 1 after `total = 9`). Gain: no new rule. Loss: lines that work inside `run: fn` (s03) fail in a script, and every call repeats the script's variables.
options.technical: Current behavior, probed on seed-b13. No change to CheckProgram.jet or Diagnostics.jet. The closure defects listed in detail (lost writes, misleading E0107 text, stale reads) need fixing under every option.

options.name: Helpers see only fixed variables
options.gist: Helpers read script variables set with `:`; variables set with `:=` still need parameters.
options.detail:
Helpers may read script variables bound with `:`, which never change, but not names bound with `:=`. In the shared program `limit` works, and `count` is refused on lines 4 and 5. The fix passes `count` as an `&Int` parameter, as probe s05 does. The order check from A applies.

Beginners meet two kinds of script variables that act differently in helpers. Experts get helpers that never change script state, so any helper may run in a task or be passed as a value. Gain: no write through an extra parameters. Loss: counters and totals, the common case, still need parameters, and tests still can't call a helper that reads script variables.
options.technical: Proposed, UNCHECKED. The same extra-parameter rewrite as A, limited to script variables that are not mutable, with A's rules for same spellings, tests and order. A `:=` local named in a helper keeps E0107, with new text naming its `:=` binding.

options.name: Script variables become file-wide variables
options.gist: Every script variable lives for the whole run, like Swift's top-level names; any function, value or task can reach it.
options.detail:
Every name the script binds lives for the whole run, the way Swift treats the top-level names of its entry file. Helpers read and change it directly, with no extra parameters. The shared program prints the same three lines. A helper passed as a callback can change `count`, as in Node, and a stored helper sees later changes.

Beginners get Node's behavior. Experts lose two of Jet's guarantees. A function value can hide a write, so a call that passes `items` while a callback appends to it can't be checked. A task could read `count` while the script changes it. Gain: writing callbacks. Loss: those guarantees, or A's analysis added back, which removes the gain.
options.technical: Proposed, UNCHECKED. Each script variable a function names becomes file storage, set when its line runs; A's order check still refuses a too-early use. This is an exception to two rules. Module values are made while building (E0643, p18), and a function may not change module state (E0111, p17). A writing callback is a function value that hides a write, which E0227 refuses (r03). Keeping E0204, E0227 and E1101 needs the same per-helper analysis as A.

recommendation.why: A removes a rule that exists only because helpers are compiled outside the script's body. Each script variable a helper uses becomes a parameter Jet fills in, a kind of parameter Jet already has. Lines written inside `run: fn` then work in a script, tests can call every helper, and Jet reports a too-early call before running. Every program that compiles today keeps its meaning.
gains: Fewer parameters in scripts
Too-early calls caught before running
Tests call any helper by passing its variables by name
No current program changes meaning

losses.loss: A helper that changes a script variable can only be called directly, not handed to `each` or run as a task.
losses.mitigation: This is Jet's rule for any function that changes its caller's variable (E0227, E1101); it stops hidden changes and races. The error rewrites the call as a loop, and helpers that only read pass freely.

losses.loss: A method declared in a script can't use script variables.
losses.mitigation: A method can be called through a trait, where no script is in reach. The error names the variable and offers a helper function or a written parameter.

whyNot.reason: It keeps a rule made by the compiler's build steps, and the same lines that work inside `run: fn` fail in a script.
It fixes reading, but counters and totals, the most common case, still need parameters.
Its only gains over A, writing callbacks and stored helpers that see later changes, need a function value to hide a change. Keeping Jet's checks against that turns D back into A.

recommendation.tradeoff: Script helpers get parameters Jet fills in, in exchange for shorter scripts with earlier errors. A helper that changes a script variable is called directly, and methods keep written parameters.

decisions.title: Names for the parts of a plugin's tuple result
decisions.situation: A Jet program can load a WebAssembly plugin and call the functions it exports. A plugin built in another language may return a tuple, such as a pair of numbers, whose parts have no names. Jet has no tuples like that. Every Jet record names its members, written in braces as {min: 1, max: 9}, and a destructure binds each member by its name. Ratified rules keep that, and make written member order part of a record's type. So a host can't read a plugin's tuple result today. This vote decides how that result appears in Jet. We recommend naming the parts part0 and part1, in the plugin's order, which the host renames in one line.
decisions.gist: How should a Jet program read a plugin result that is a tuple whose parts have no names?
decisions.lesson: WebAssembly components describe their functions in WIT. WIT has records, whose fields have names, and tuples, whose parts are known only by position. Jet has records only: every member has a name. So a WIT tuple needs names before Jet can read it. Rust, JavaScript and Python read such tuples by position, because their own tuples are positional. Go, C and C# give the parts made-up names, such as F0, f0 and Item1. The Component Model itself labels tuple parts 0, 1, and so on.
decisions.explainer:
A plugin is a WebAssembly component that a Jet program loads and calls like an object. WIT is the language that lists a component's functions and types. A WIT tuple, written `tuple<s64, s64>`, is a fixed group of values known by position; `s64` is a 64-bit integer, Jet's `Int`. A WIT record is a group whose fields have names.

A Jet record, written `{left: Int, right: Int}`, is a group whose members have names, kept in the order written. This ballot says record for Jet's side and tuple only for the plugin's positional group. A destructure, written `{left, right}: value`, binds each member by its name. `{part0: left}: value` binds the member part0 to the new name left.
decisions.story: Ana's Jet program loads a geometry plugin written in Rust. Its function `pair` returns `tuple<s64, s64>`, two corner values, 7 and -9. Ana wants to print them. Every option below uses her program and the same plugin. Options A, B and D print `7 -9`. Option C refuses the call until the plugin's author changes `pair` to return a record.
decisions.inWild:
Rust (wasmtime `bindgen!` on the host, wit-bindgen in the guest): `tuple<s64, s64>` becomes `(i64, i64)`, read as `.0` and `.1` or by a positional pattern. Checked in the wasmtime-wit-bindgen 25.0.3 source; wasmtime 48 ran the test guest and printed `(7, -9)`.
JavaScript (jco): a tuple becomes an array such as `[7n, -9n]`, read by index. Checked in jco's generator source, not run.
Python (componentize-py): a tuple becomes a Python tuple, read by index or unpacking. From documentation only, not checked.
Go (wit-bindgen-go, package cm): a tuple becomes `cm.Tuple[int64, int64]`, a struct whose fields are named `F0` and `F1`. Checked in the cm package source, which stops at 16 parts.
C# (wit-bindgen): a tuple becomes a value tuple `(long, long)`, whose members are `Item1` and `Item2`. Checked in the generator source; a one-part tuple becomes its bare value.
C (wit-bindgen): a tuple becomes a struct whose fields are named `f0` and `f1`. Checked in the generator source, not run.
decisions.detail:
Scope. This vote decides one rule: the Jet type a host sees for a Component tuple, wherever a tuple appears in a plugin export's signature. It does not change tuples written in Jet source. It does not change what a Jet sandbox exports either. Jet sandboxes cannot export tuples (D-PLUGIN-EXPORT1), so tuples reach a host only from components built in other languages.

The rule today. S73 says tuples have named members only, with no positional tuples and no `.0` (Docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:1254-1255). A tuple destructure selects each member by name (Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Statements.jet:5182-5198). Its E0313 text says "a tuple destructure binds each member by its name, never by position" (:5270). The ratified naming ladder, D-NAME-SIGIL1, gives a leading `_` one meaning, internal or discarded. It says compiler-made visible names use `__jet_` (syntax-decisions.md:7862-7869).

The rule being built. D-RECORD-BRACE1 A (2026-11-06) moves every record to braces, `{x: 1}`, retires paren tuples and makes one-member records legal. D-RECORD-ORDER1 A, the same day, makes written member order part of a record's type, and uses it for comparison, printing and encoding. Neither adds positional binding or optional names.

Neither is built yet: on seed-b14 the brace type `{part0: Int, part1: Int}` is a parse error (E0080), and `{part0: 7}` is E0119 (probes t1 and t2). The paren record `(left: 7, right: -9)` still destructures by name and prints `7 -9` (probe t4). The S73 text in the spec still describes paren tuples sorted by name.

What the probe showed. Before card #5971 c25, the plugin interface reader refused a tuple result as E1260 (unsupported Component value `tuple`). The first c25 draft gave the tuple's members empty names. Probe g3-fold3 then failed `(left, right): guest.pair()` with E0313 "`left` isn't a member of (: Int, : Int)". Its fix text offered `(, ): …`, which nobody can write. The output is in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Lander/probe/out/g3-fold3/7.out.

Code. The interface reader maps each export's Component types to Jet types (Compiler/JetPlugin/Source/Plugin/Interface.jet, staged in G3Core-golden1b-r2 and not yet on dev). The checker turns that Jet type into a descriptor that tells code generation where each value lands (Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Calls/Plugin.jet).

The runtime writes one word per tuple part in Component order. Code generation stores each word into the member its label names (Compiler/JetIR/Source/BuildRoutes.jet, ir_route_tuple_order). Today a record sorts its members by name (S73), so every option with names needs that label map, and it already exists. Under D-RECORD-ORDER1 the members keep Component order instead, and the label map still places each word.

Review probes. These ran on the seed-b13 compiler in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/probe/ReviewComponentTuple. The first draft spelled the parts `_0` and `_1`. Member access `pair._0` and the rename `{ _0: left, _1: right }: …` work and print `7 -9`. A local named `_0` fails E0357, so `(_0, _1): …` and `loop (_0, _1) in list` don't compile. A signature that writes `(_0: Int, _1: Int)` draws two L0601 warnings, because `_0` reads as soft-public.

The E0313 fix text for that tuple offers `(_0, _1): …`, which fails E0357. It also offers `{ _0: name, _1: name }: …`, which fails E0118 because `name` repeats, a fault for every tuple. The same probes spelled `part0` and `part1` pass `jet check` with no warnings. `(part0, part1): …`, the rename, a loop over a list of pairs and nested access all print the expected values.

Other evidence. The renaming destructure `{ x: a, y: b }: p` ships in Examples/Basics/Tuples.jet:13. A loop header can't rename members, so a list of tuples destructures there only under the given names. The only positional destructure is the built-in VJPRun pair, and the checker names its parts `value` and `pull` (Statements.jet:5155-5165 and 5239-5250). That precedent uses ordinary words, not `_` names. The draft cited EditActions.jet:364 for `_0`; that devserver file is untranslated and proves nothing, so the probes replace it.

Edge cases. Each row is one plugin signature. Every option is proposed and UNCHECKED except where a row cites a probe or today. Card #5971 c25 builds only a top-level result tuple of scalars. Nested tuples, lists of tuples and tuple parameters stay E1260 until built, and each option fixes the type they will get then.

```
case                                 A (part0, part1)                          B (positional)            C (records only)            D (host struct)
1 tuple<s64, s64> result             {part0: Int, part1: Int}                  (Int, Int)                E1260: return a record      Corners { left, right }
2 tuple<s64>, one part               {part0: Int}, a one-member record         (Int), clashes with ( )   E1260                       a one-field struct
3 tuple<>, no parts                  refused by the Component Model, which requires at least one part (every option)
4 tuple<tuple<s64, s64>, s64>        {part0: {part0: Int, part1: Int}, part1: Int}  nested positional  E1260                  nested structs
5 list<tuple<string, string>>        [{part0: String, part1: String}]          [(String, String)]        E1260                       [Entry]
6 tuple parameter                    host passes {part0: 1, part1: 2}          host passes (1, 2)        E1260                       host passes a struct
7 destructure with the wrong count   E0315 count mismatch                      E0315                     not reached                 struct fields, no count
8 declared shape differs from guest  does not arise                            does not arise            does not arise              new compile error, like E3205
9 tuple of 11 or more parts          kept in Component order                   works                     E1260                       works
10 record { left: s64, right: s64 }  E1260, separate work                      E1260, separate work      {left: Int, right: Int}     E1260, separate work
11 record with a field named part0   mapped by Component position, not name   same                      same                        same
12 Jet sandbox exports a tuple       E1260 (D-PLUGIN-EXPORT1)                  same                      same                        same
```

Row notes. Row 2: today a one-member record can't be written: `{part0: 7}` is E0119 on seed-b14 (probe t2), and a paren literal needs two members (E0003). D-RECORD-BRACE1 makes `{part0: 7}` legal, so a one-part result is read and built like any record. Row 9: under D-RECORD-ORDER1 the members keep Component order, so `part2` prints before `part10`. Today's rule sorts members by name instead (S73). Each value lands in its own member either way, because code generation stores by label.

Beginners and experts. Under A a beginner sees `{part0: Int, part1: Int}` in hover and errors; hover was not run. The repaired E0313 fix text offers `{ part0: left, part1: right }: …`, filled with the names the user wrote. An expert reads `pair.part0` directly.

Under B a beginner writes `(left, right)` as in Rust or Python. An expert must remember that positional tuples exist only at this boundary and convert before passing one on. The VJPRun exemption keys on a type the compiler owns by name. A plugin tuple is structural, so it can't reuse that exemption without a new wrapper type.

Under C a beginner who can't change the plugin is stuck. An expert can wrap the plugin in a second component that returns a record. Under D everyone declares a struct and an overlay before the first call, and gets meaningful names and a checked contract.

Peers. Rust, JavaScript and Python read WIT tuples by position because their own tuples are positional. Go, C and C# have no positional form in their structs, so their bindings invent names. The Component Model defines a tuple as a record labeled "0", "1" (CanonicalABI.md, despecialize), which `part0` mirrors as a legal Jet name. None of the peers asks the host to restate names. Jet's C boundary does, through an `#Import c.<lib>` overlay (D-FFI-UNIFY1), which D reuses.

Where tuples appear. WASI 0.2.12 uses tuples in 9 function signatures and 2 type aliases. Examples are environment variables and HTTP header lists as `list<tuple<string, string>>`, and `insecure-seed` returning `tuple<u64, u64>`. All are host imports, not plugin exports, so none is in this vote's scope today. How often hand-written plugin exports return tuples was not measured. Jet's C boundary already refuses tuples outright (E3203), a precedent for C.

Shared work. Every option needs c25's lift through the return area, staged as G3Core-c25b and held for this vote. Its case covers member access only. It has not run, and no case tests a destructure. The staged patch spells the parts `_0`. Moving to `part0` changes Interface.jet's name text, the checker's position decoding, one spec sentence and the case's `pair._0`.

A as repaired carries each part's Component position in the interface fact instead of decoding it from the name. Records need that fact anyway, since a WIT record may legally name a field `part0`. The staged runtime already lifts records of scalars. A also repairs E0313's fix text to fill in the user's own names in order.

B needs a positional tuple kind in types, destructure by position, hover text and UI snapshots. C needs new E1260 fix text and the reader's record mapping; the runtime record lift is already staged. D needs an `#Import plugin.<artifact>` root, a check of the overlay against the component, the tuple-to-struct mapping, a mismatch error and UI snapshots.

REVISION AFTER THE OWNER'S QUESTION (2026-11-12)

The owner asked whether Jet tuples are positional with optional names. They are not. The latest ratified guidance is D-RECORD-BRACE1 A and D-RECORD-ORDER1 A, both 2026-11-06. Every group of values names its members, in braces, and a destructure binds by name. Written member order becomes part of the type. The earlier draft predated both and spelled records with parentheses; it now uses braces.

What was designed away. Two of A's four costs came from rules those votes replace. `part10` sorting before `part2` is gone, because members keep the plugin's order. A one-part tuple that could be read but not built is gone, because one-member records become legal. Learning one more naming rule is not a separate cost: part N is the Component Model's own label N with a word in front.

Terms. The ballot now says record for Jet's side and tuple only for the plugin's positional group, so the two never share a word.

What remains. The plugin carries no names, so the parts can't say what they mean. Under named-only records the host must type the names it wants once. A makes that one line, `{part0: left, part1: right}: guest.pair()`. When a host writes `{left, right}: guest.pair()`, E0313's repaired fix text offers exactly that line, and jet fix applies it. This is the floor for any named-only design: the names have to come from somewhere, and only the host or the plugin's author has them.

Outside this vote. If Jet's records became positional with optional names everywhere, plugin tuples would need no names at all. That reopens D-RECORD-BRACE1 for every Jet program, so it needs its own ballot; it can't be decided here for plugins alone. B shows why a plugin-only exception is worse: it creates two kinds of group with two destructure rules.

Attack on the revision. A now depends on D-RECORD-ORDER1 for Component order in printing and comparison. Until that lands, the label map still stores each word correctly, and only printed and sorted order differ. The `part` prefix can't clash with a WIT record field, because record fields map by Component position, not by name (row 11).

options.name: Parts are named part0, part1, and so on
options.gist: A Component tuple becomes a Jet named tuple whose members are `part0`, `part1`, in Component order.
options.detail:
The part at position N is the member `partN`, counting from 0 as the Component Model's own labels do, and the members keep the plugin's order. Ana writes `{part0: left, part1: right}: guest.pair()`, or `{part0, part1}: guest.pair()`, or reads `pair.part0`. The program prints `7 -9`. Nested tuples and lists of tuples follow the same rule, as Go's and C's bindings do. The names are ordinary snake_case words, so they pass every naming rule and lint.

Beginners meet `part0` in hover and in the E0313 fix text, which writes the rename with their own names. Experts read members directly. Gain: one rule for every tuple, any length, in the plugin's order, with no new syntax. Loss: the names say nothing about meaning, so a host renames them in one line.
options.technical:
Staged as G3Core-c25b with the spelling `_0`, held. That spelling broke D-NAME-SIGIL1, where a leading `_` means internal. It also drew L0601 in signatures and failed E0357 as a local, so `(_0, _1): …` could not compile.

Repair: Interface.jet names each part `part{index}` and records its Component position in the interface fact. The checker orders the descriptor's fields by that position, not by decoding names, so a WIT record field named `part0` can't be misread. ir_plugin_invoke_words passes the member names as labels, and ir_route_store_tuple stores each word in the member its label names. E0313's fix text fills in the user's own names in order, and jet fix applies it.

The member order follows D-RECORD-ORDER1 once built; the label map stores each word correctly before then.

options.name: Positional tuples for plugin results only
options.gist: A Component tuple becomes a positional Jet tuple `(Int, Int)` that destructures by position.
options.detail:
Plugin results get a tuple kind with unnamed parts. Ana writes `(left, right): guest.pair()` and the program prints `7 -9`, as in Rust. The kind exists only for values that come from a plugin, so S73 gains an exception.

Beginners write what Rust and Python users expect. Experts learn that a destructure means two things: by name for Jet tuples, by position for plugin tuples. A plugin tuple can't be passed where a named tuple is expected without rebuilding it. Gain: no invented names. Loss: two tuple kinds, and the rule that destructures never bind by position breaks.
options.technical:
Proposed, UNCHECKED. The type system gains a positional tuple kind, or a flag on Type.Tuple, that only the interface reader creates. The destructure in Statements.jet binds such a tuple by position instead of by name. Hover, error text and the type printer need a spelling for it, such as `(Int, Int)`; a one-part `(Int)` reads as plain grouping. Member access stays refused, since S73 bans `.0`. Code generation can reuse the same word layout.

Statements.jet already exempts one pair from the by-name rule: VJPRun, a type the compiler owns by name (:5155-5165). A plugin tuple is structural and looks like any Jet tuple of the same shape, so B can't reuse that exemption. It needs a new type kind.

options.name: Refuse tuples; plugins return records
options.gist: A Component tuple stays E1260; a guest returns a WIT record, whose field names Jet uses.
options.detail:
A tuple anywhere in an export's signature stays E1260, and the fix text asks for a record. A WIT record such as `record corners { left: s64, right: s64 }` becomes the Jet record `{left: Int, right: Int}`. Ana's program fails until the plugin's author changes `pair`. Then `{left, right}: guest.pair()` prints `7 -9`.

Beginners who own the plugin get the best names. Beginners using someone else's plugin can't fix it. Experts can wrap the plugin in a component that returns a record. Gain: every name comes from the plugin's author. Loss: a host that can't change the plugin has no fix, and card #5971 c25 as written can't be met.
options.technical:
Proposed, UNCHECKED. The interface reader keeps tuple as an unsupported kind, so the E1260 text names `tuple` and its fix suggests a record. Jet's C boundary already refuses tuples the same way (E3203). The staged c25b runtime already lifts a record of scalars. The remaining work is the reader's mapping from a WIT record's fields to a Jet record, folding `-` to `_` as export names already do. Card #5971 c25's criterion would be amended to the refusal.

WASI's own tuples, such as HTTP header lists, are host imports and outside this vote. How many real plugin exports return tuples was not measured.

options.name: The host declares a struct for the result
options.gist: The host declares a struct and an overlay; the plugin's tuple fills the struct's fields in declaration order.
options.detail:
Jet hosts have no declaration of a plugin's signatures today; the checker reads them from the component. D adds an optional overlay, like the `#Import c.<lib>` overlay that already lets a host override a generated C binding. Ana declares a struct `Corners` with fields `left` and `right`, then writes `#Import plugin.guest: module { pair: fn() -> Corners }`. The tuple fills the fields in declaration order, and the program prints `7 -9`.

Beginners must write the struct and overlay before the first call. Experts get meaningful names and a contract checked against the component. Gain: no invented names. Loss: two sources for one interface and new syntax. Without an overlay a tuple still needs A, B or C.
options.technical:
Proposed, UNCHECKED. The draft mapped a trait method's tuple result by written order. Under D-RECORD-ORDER1 a record's written order will be part of its type, but D still uses a struct, which gives the result a name and a place to check the contract. A struct's declaration order already does: the checker maps struct fields to Component record fields by declaration index (Calls/Plugin.jet:134-143).

Reused: the overlay model of D-FFI-UNIFY1, where an overlay wins over the generated binding and an incompatible one is E3205. New: an `#Import plugin.<artifact>` root naming guest.wasm, the check against the component, and the tuple-to-struct mapping. D could also be added later on top of A, as an optional overlay.

recommendation.why: A keeps Jet's record rule whole: every member has a name, from one fixed rule with no new syntax. The names follow the Component Model's own labels and Go's and C's bindings, and pass every naming rule. They keep the plugin's order, so any tuple reads and prints as the plugin wrote it.
gains: No new syntax, no exception to the record rule, and no naming-rule exception
One naming rule for every tuple, any length, in the plugin's order
One-part tuples are ordinary one-member records

losses.loss: The names `part0` and `part1` say nothing about what the values mean.
losses.mitigation: One line renames them, `{part0: left, part1: right}: guest.pair()`. Writing `{left, right}` gets a fix that writes that line, and jet fix applies it. The plugin carries no names to use instead.

whyNot.reason: It adds a second kind of group and makes a destructure bind by position in one place, breaking the ratified rule that every member is named.
A host that can't change the plugin has no fix, and card #5971 c25 as written can't be met. WASI's own tuples are host imports, so the cost to real plugin exports is unmeasured.
It adds a second source for the plugin's interface and new syntax, and without an overlay a tuple still needs another rule. It can be added later on top of A as an optional overlay.

recommendation.tradeoff: One cost remains: the host types the names it wants once, because the plugin has none. In exchange, one rule reads every tuple, in the plugin's order, with no new syntax.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude Opus. Adversarial model family: Claude Opus. Fresh agent: ReviewComponentTuple. Seed probes showed `_0` breaks D-NAME-SIGIL1, draws L0601 and fails E0357 as a local, so A became `part0` with a repaired fix text. D became a struct overlay because S73 erases written order, and C's wasi-http claim and several citations were corrected.

decisions.title: How a build names a field's type when it declares a struct with meta.add_struct
decisions.situation: A build can declare a new struct while it runs, by calling meta.add_struct with a list of fields. Each field record has a name and a type. Today the type is text, such as "I64", which the build host turns into source for the new struct. That text check only blocks a few characters, so the type "I64, extra: String" quietly adds a second field. The ratified rule also passes a reflected field's type, which reflection gives as a TypeId, not text, so the rule contradicts itself. This vote decides what a field's type is: a TypeId, text, or either. We recommend a TypeId, written in the build file when it can see the type, and looked up by text when it can't.
decisions.gist: When a build declares a struct with meta.add_struct, is each field's type a TypeId, a text spelling, or either?
decisions.lesson: A type passed as a value keeps its identity and is checked where it is written. A type passed as text is checked only when the build runs, and it is read again in the new struct's module, where its name can mean a different type.
decisions.explainer:
A TypeId is the compiler's name for one checked type. Reflection gives one for every field, as field.type. Programs cannot make a TypeId from text; under A they can only ask the compiler for one it already issued.

A text spelling is a String such as "I64" or "[Point]". The build host pastes it into source for the new struct when the build runs.

The build function and the app can live in separate files. A build file sees only the types it declares or imports. A type only the app declares is invisible to it, unless both files import the module that declares it.

A type written as a value means a type name where a value is expected, such as String in CompilerField{name: "label", type: String}. Any other spelling goes in braces, as in TypeId{[String]}. D-PRIM-TYPEKEY2 A ratifies both spellings for a Type value, Rock and Type{Box<Int>}. Neither is built yet.

A lookup by text, meta.find_type("Point"), asks the compiler for the TypeId of one type the app declares. It returns that identity or None, and the text itself never becomes source.
decisions.story: A build reads the fields of a struct called Source, drops one, and renames another. It adds two hand-written fields, label of type String and tags of type [String]. It also adds a field at of type Point, which only the app declares, so the build file can't name it. It then declares a new struct, Shape, from that list with meta.add_struct. Every option builds the same Shape; they differ in how the hand-written, app-only and reflected types are written.
decisions.inWild: Zig builds a struct type at compile time with @Type, and each field's type is a type value, never a string. That works inside one compilation. Across the build-to-app split, Zig's build.zig passes values to the app by generating Zig source text (std.Build.Step.Options), so Zig also falls back to text there. C++26 reflection (P2996) declares a struct with define_aggregate, and each member's type is a reflection value such as ^^int. Rust procedural macros emit types as token streams, which the compiler checks only after expansion, like a text spelling. These outside facts were not re-checked for this ballot.
decisions.detail:
The ratified row reads: meta.add_struct(name, fields, scope: module) declares the struct name of fields, a list of CompilerField{name:, type:} records. Their names and types may be computed, as in a reflected field's f.type. The build host refuses a type that is not one type's spelling.

D-META-REFLECT2 A (2026-09-21) says FieldInfo's type is a TypeId, an opaque compiler-issued identity that user code cannot make from casts or strings. D-REFLECT-FIELDTYPE1 A named that field type. So the row's own example passes a TypeId into a String slot, which the checker refuses (E0108).

On dev today the two CompilerField rows disagree. The core.compiler index field row says TypeId (commit G6Decl-72), the literal row says String, and a build that writes a literal crashed the IR. The staged fix G6Meta-addstruct1 makes both rows String. It fills the index with the printed type name and has reflected sites write field.type.name. Every other type in that index stays a TypeId.

The host's check is a block-list of characters (jet_driver_meta_type_text_plain in Compiler/JetDriver/Source/Driver/BuildAdapter.jet), not a type parser. Probe inject: the type "I64, extra: String" passed it. The generated struct got a second field, extra, and the app printed a value stored there. So the row's promise that the host refuses non-type text fails today.

A TypeId's name is the type as its declaring module wrote it (type_name in Compiler/JetFoundation/Source/Types/Types.jet). The checker resolves such a name relative to the module that reads it. The new struct lives in a different module, which reads the name again in its own scope. A printed name can then fail to resolve there, or name a different type with the same short name.

Some printed forms are display-only and do not parse at all, such as a quantity's Quantity<dimension, base; identity>. Probe roundtrip: "Point", "Int?", "[String:Int]" and "fn(Int) -> Int" worked as text. The spellings "geo.Point" and "[geo.Point]" for a dependency's type crashed the compiler.

Text can name types a build file cannot see. Probe split: a separate build.jet named the app-only type "Point" and the app printed 9. In that build file, the bare name Point is E0107. Probe forward: a second add_struct named the struct an earlier call made, "Inner", and also "[Inner]" and "Inner?"; the app printed 7.

Type written as a value is not built for any type. Probe typevalue: Type itself is E0119, and Point passed as an argument is E0636. [Point] parses as a list literal, and Int? parses as Int followed by the ? operator. Type arguments, as in name_of<[Point]>(), accept every spelling today.

Migration under A is mechanical. jet fix writes a String literal as a bare name or a braced spelling when the text, read from the build file, names the same type the host finds in the app. Every other literal, and every computed text, becomes meta.find_type(text) with a failure for None.

In this repository the edit is small. Four test files write literal types, all I64 or I32, and jet fix rewrites them. The bad_type case computes its text and moves to find_type, which returns None for it. The typed and raw_denied cases already pass field.type. No example or Core file builds a CompilerField.

REVISION AFTER THE OWNER'S QUESTION (2026-11-12)

The owner called the TypeId direction solid and asked for its downsides to be designed away. The earlier A carried five costs. Four are gone, and one remains with a mitigation.

Computed type text, a type only the app declares, and a list of a struct made earlier in the build all failed under the earlier A. They now go through one lookup, meta.find_type(text). It returns a TypeId the compiler issued, or None. The text never reaches the new struct's source; only the identity it found does.

Function types needed a one-line alias, and compound spellings relied on name lookup to tell a type from a list literal. Braces remove both. TypeId{fn(Int) -> Int} and TypeId{[String]} reuse the ratified Type{Box<Int>} form. A type inside braces parses like a type argument, and probe typepos shows type arguments accept every spelling today. In a bare value position, [Point] reads as a list and Int? as the ? operator (probe typevalue).

The checker work for bare names and braces was listed as a loss. It is shared build work, and difficulty never ranks an option. The split between Type and TypeId predates this ballot. Both values now take the same two spellings, and the expected type picks one, so nothing new is learned.

ATTACKING THE LOOKUP

Forging. D-META-REFLECT2 A says user code can't make a TypeId from casts or strings, so that no program forges an identity. find_type returns only the identity of a type the compiler already declared, or None, so it forges nothing. A amends that sentence to allow this one lookup.

Injection. find_type reads exactly one type spelling. The text "I64, extra: String", which adds a field today (probe inject), returns None.

Scope. Names resolve as the app's root module sees them, plus every struct this build has already made, so "[Inner]" works after Inner is made. A short name that two modules declare finds nothing, and the build writes the module path, as in shapes.Point. The host still refuses, when the build runs, a type the new struct's module is not allowed to see.

Timing. The build already reads the app's declared types through b.program.packages() (spec.md, fn build), so a lookup needs nothing the build lacks. find_type, the braced form and add_struct's returned TypeId are proposed and UNCHECKED.

WHAT REMAINS

A type named by text is checked only when the build runs. That cost can't be removed, because the text exists only then, as with a config file. It is minimized: find_type returns None, so the build must handle a miss, and written and reflected types never take this path.

options.name: A TypeId, written in the build file or looked up by text
options.gist: CompilerField.type is a TypeId. Reflected types pass as is, written types are checked where written, and other types are looked up by text.
options.detail:
CompilerField.type becomes a TypeId. A reflected field's type passes as is. So does a field list from the core.compiler index, whose types are already TypeIds on dev.

A type the build file can see is written there, and checked there. A plain name such as String or geo.Point is written bare where a TypeId is expected. Any other spelling uses braces: TypeId{[String]}, TypeId{Int?} or TypeId{fn(Int) -> Int}. These are the two spellings D-PRIM-TYPEKEY2 A already ratified for a Type value.

A type the build file can't name is looked up by text. meta.find_type("Point") returns the TypeId of that one type, or None. It reads exactly one type spelling and resolves names as the app's root module sees them, plus every struct this build already made. So it covers a type only the app declares, "[Inner]" after an earlier add_struct, and type names read from a config file.

The text is never pasted into source. meta.add_struct returns the new struct's TypeId, so a later call can use it directly. The host writes each field from its TypeId. It still refuses, when the build runs, a type the new struct's module is not allowed to see. A misspelled written type is a check error at the call, and a String where a TypeId is expected is E0108.

options.name: A text spelling, as today
options.gist: CompilerField.type stays a String the build host reads. Reflected sites write field.type.name.
options.detail:
CompilerField.type stays a String. A hand-written type is its spelling in quotes, and a reflected field passes field.type.name. Any type the app can see can be named, including a type only the app declares and a struct an earlier call made. A reaches the same types through its lookup, but keeps the identity it finds.

B must replace the host's block-list with a parser that accepts exactly one type, to close the hole probe inject found. That repair is part of this option. Errors still come only when the build runs.

A reflected type loses its identity on the way. Its printed name is read again in the new module, where it can fail to resolve or name a different type. The index's CompilerField.type is then the only String type in an index of TypeIds.

options.name: Either a TypeId or a text spelling
options.gist: CompilerField.type accepts a TypeId or a String. Reflected sites pass field.type; hand-written types stay quoted.
options.detail:
CompilerField.type accepts either, so the field needs a union type, TypeId | String. A reflected field passes field.type, a TypeId. A hand-written type is a quoted spelling, which the host reads when the build runs.

Two ways to name the same type stay in one field, against I8. The text path keeps every cost of B, including the parser repair.

recommendation.why: A keeps every type's identity from reflection to the new struct, and checks a written type where it is written. Text is only ever looked up, never pasted into source, so the hole that added a field cannot occur. Every type in the core.compiler index stays a TypeId.
gains: Reflected and index field lists pass through unchanged
A misspelled written type is a check error at the call, in the editor too
Config text, app-only types and structs made earlier still work, by lookup
No text a build supplies is pasted into source

losses.loss: A type named by text, from a config file or known only to the app, is checked only when the build runs.
losses.mitigation: find_type returns None for a miss, so the build must handle it, and its text can never add a field. Written and reflected types never take this path.

whyNot.reason: B pastes text that is read again in another module, where a reflected type's name can mean a different type. Every mistake shows up only when the build runs.
C keeps two ways to name one type in one field, against I8, and its text path keeps every cost of B.

recommendation.tradeoff: One cost remains. A type named by text is checked when the build runs, and the build must handle a miss. Every other type keeps its identity and is checked where it is written.
