decisions.title: Whether a C callback can ever read the task context
decisions.situation: The ratified context rule says a C callback receives no context, and that reading context there is an error until the callback installs one. The adversarial review found that the second half cannot happen. The callback rule only admits a small foreign-thread-safe subset, and that subset refuses every #Context block. A foreign thread also has no context record to install into. So the clause names a form nobody can write. This vote picks one rule. Either the clause is dropped and a callback never reads context, or the callback rule gains a form that attaches a context for a callback. We recommend dropping it.
decisions.gist: Should a C callback never read context, or gain a form that installs one first?
decisions.lesson: A C callback runs on whatever thread the C library chooses. Jet code there has no task, so it has no task context to read. Giving it one means building a context record on a thread Jet does not own.
decisions.story: A program hands a comparison function to a C sort routine. The comparison runs on the C library's thread. A helper it might call reads context.deadline to decide how long to wait. Option A refuses that read when the program is checked. Option B lets the callback open a #Context block, which builds a fresh root context for the call, so the read sees no deadline.
decisions.inWild: Jai marks a C-callable procedure #c_call. It receives no context, and it must push one with push_context before it calls code that needs it. Go's cgo callbacks run Go code on a thread Go attaches on entry, and a callback gets no request context unless it is passed explicitly. These outside facts were not re-checked for this ballot.
decisions.detail:
D-CONTEXT-EFFECT1=F says: a C callback, like Jai's #c_call, receives no context; reading context there is a registered error until the callback installs one. D-CABI-CALLBACK1=A admits a callback only from a checked foreign-thread-safe subset. Sema checks that subset in Calls/Checking.jet, and it refuses #Context blocks. On a foreign thread the runtime has no control block, so there is no current context record.

Today a context read in a callback is refused through the generic subset error, E3203. F asks for a registered error that names the context read.

options.name: A callback never reads context
options.detail: Drop "until the callback installs one". A C callback reads no context, directly or through anything it calls. Sema refuses a read with a registered error that names the context field and the callback. The subset stays as D-CABI-CALLBACK1 ratified it. If the subset later admits calls, the same reach fact that keys #Memo also refuses a callee that reaches a read.

options.name: A callback may install a context first
options.detail: Amend D-CABI-CALLBACK1: a callback may open a #Context block as its outermost statement. Entering it attaches a fresh root context record to the foreign thread for the call, and leaving it detaches the record. Reads inside see that record: thread from the attach, deadline None unless the block sets one. Reads outside it are refused with the same registered error as A.

recommendation.why: A states the rule the code already enforces, with a clearer error. B needs a context record on a thread Jet does not own, and a block form the callback subset refuses for good reasons.
recommendation.tradeoff: A callback cannot reuse code that reads context. It must take what it needs as arguments.
gains: One rule with no new form.
The error names the context read.

losses.loss: Callback code cannot call helpers that read context.
losses.mitigation: Pass the value in an argument, or read it before handing the callback over.

whyNot.reason: It adds a runtime attach path for one rare need and widens the callback subset.

surface.gist: Should a C callback never read context, or gain a form that installs one first?
surface.lesson: A C callback runs on a thread the C library picks. Jet has no task there, so there is no context to read. Giving it one means building a context on a thread Jet does not own.

current.note: The rule says reads are refused until the callback installs a context, but no install form exists.

wild.note: A #c_call procedure has no context and must push one before calling code that needs it.

options.name: A callback never reads context
options.gist: Drop the install clause. Any read in a callback is a named error.
gains: Matches what the code already enforces.
losses: Callbacks cannot call helpers that read context.

options.name: A callback may install a context first
options.gist: An outer #Context block attaches a fresh context for the call.
gains: Callbacks can reuse code that reads context.
losses: Adds a runtime attach path on foreign threads.

recommendation.why: A callback runs on a foreign thread that has no context record. The callback subset already refuses #Context blocks, so A only states that rule.
gains: One rule and no new form.

losses.loss: Callback code cannot read context through helpers.
losses.mitigation: Pass the needed value in as an argument.

whyNot.reason: A runtime attach path for a rare need.

recommendation.tradeoff: A helper shared with callback code must take its settings as arguments.

decisions.title: How a Jet tool sends Chrome debugger commands to one page and reads where it paused
decisions.situation: Card #5072 moves repo tooling from Node to Jet. The Jet twin of the source-map check must pause a page at a breakpoint and report the line where it stopped. Jet's browser library can send Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP) commands, but only to the browser as a whole, never to one page. Its events keep only a name and a few network facts, so a pause carries no line. The live half of the check therefore cannot move to Jet today. This vote decides how a Jet tool reaches one page's debugger and reads where it paused. We recommend A: a CDP handle for one page, plus named debugger facts on events.
decisions.gist: How should a Jet tool send Chrome debugger commands to one page and read where the page paused?
decisions.lesson: A browser library can hand events to a program as raw protocol data or as a fixed set of named facts. Raw data serves every later need, but carries page content past the library's redaction. Named facts stay small and safe, but each new need is a new accessor.
decisions.explainer:
CDP is Chrome's debugging protocol. A command such as Debugger.enable goes to one target, usually a page, through that page's session. An event such as Debugger.paused comes back with JSON params. A pause lists the call frames, each with a function name and a 0-based line.

Jet's browser library, core.web.browser, speaks WebDriver BiDi to the browser. Chromium's BiDi server passes CDP through a command named goog:cdp.sendCommand. The library's protocol("cdp") handle uses it, but sends no session, so its commands reach the browser rather than a page.

The library turns each event into a BrowserEvent. It keeps the event's kind and named facts: request id, request method, status code, and url_hash. A hash is a fixed-length fingerprint of the text, so the URL itself is not stored. A program can compare a hash with the hash of a string it already knows.

The beginner path is a test that opens a page with page.goto, finds elements with page.get_by_role and clicks them, and reads page.text(). It needs no protocol, and it is the same in every option. The expert path is a tool that needs a CDP feature the library does not wrap. Every option changes only the expert path.
decisions.story: The source-map check serves a built web app and finds the generated app.js line that the source map assigns to a Jet statement. It sets a breakpoint there, loads the page and waits for the pause. It checks that the top frame is render, jet_main or empty. It prints the paused line plus one, and whether Chrome reported app.js.map. Each option writes that live half as one function, live(port, line). The map decoding is plain Jet in every option and is not shown.
decisions.inWild: Puppeteer gives each page its own CDP session with page.createCDPSession(). session.send runs a command, and session.on hands raw event params to the program. Playwright's context.newCDPSession(page) works the same way, on Chromium only. Both pass raw JSON to the program and redact nothing. Selenium 4 sends CDP commands through chromedriver with execute_cdp_cmd and reads no events that way. These outside facts were not re-checked for this ballot.
decisions.detail:
Commands today. BrowserProtocol.send in Core/Web/Browser.jet (line 579) sends goog:cdp.sendCommand with a method and params and no session. The BiDi handle refuses every goog:cdp method (line 573), and so does Browser.subscribe for goog:cdp events (line 216). So no hand-built command can reach a page's debugger. That chromium-bidi takes the page session as a field beside method and params is [INFERENCE] from its schema, not run live.

Events today. __cdp_event_facts (line 1177) keeps only the request id, request method, url_hash and status. A #Test near line 1993 pins that a Debugger.paused event has every fact empty. Docs/spec/architecture.md says the trace never holds payloads and events carry named facts. Command replies are not redacted: send returns the full reply JSON (lines 575 and 580).

Limits today. The event queue holds 256 events and drops the oldest first (C_EVENT_LIMIT, line 1058). The trace holds 8 KiB and also drops the oldest first. Every script the library runs in the page also fires Debugger.scriptParsed, so a long session can push out the event a tool wants.

Hashes today. browser.fact_hash is not public. A probe calling browser.fact_hash("app.js.map") fails with E1004, core.web.browser has no item fact_hash. So no caller can compare url_hash with a known URL today. The hash is 64-bit FNV-1a. It keeps strings out of logs, but anyone who guesses a string can confirm it.

Navigation. page.goto waits for the load to complete (line 339). A breakpoint that fires during the load blocks it, so goto would time out first. Every option navigates with CDP Page.navigate, which returns at once, as the original did.

The original is Tools/web-test/sourcemap.mjs before commit 70532ccd85. It used its own CDP pipe in Tools/canvas-test/driver.mjs, attached to the page with a flattened session. It printed pausedGeneratedLine and scriptParsedMapUrl. It asserted the paused line is within one of the expected line, and the function name is render, jet_main or empty.

Edge cases. A closed page: the page handle in A and B checks page_live (line 1366) before every send and returns closed. A pause left open blocks the page, so each program resumes before it closes. Frames from another site in an iframe run in their own target, which the page session does not reach; this is a stated limit. Sharing the session chromedriver itself uses for the page is [INFERENCE] and is the build card's first live proof.

Migration. No code uses this surface yet. The only caller is the source-map twin under card #5072. Option D restores the deleted Node file.

options.name: A CDP handle for one page, and named debugger facts on events
options.gist: page.protocol("cdp") sends to that page. A pause and a parsed script add named facts to the event; nothing else of the event is kept.
options.detail:
New public items, six in all. BrowserPage.protocol(kind) returns a BrowserProtocol for that page, and accepts only "cdp". "bidi" is refused, because BiDi commands already name their page, and a second BiDi handle would be a second way to send them (I8).

On first use the handle asks chromedriver for the page's session with goog:cdp.getSession. That method joins the protocol allowlist (C_BIDI_2024_11) behind the same CDP check as goog:cdp.sendCommand. Every send then carries the session, which never leaves Core. Its subscribe names this page, so next_event yields only this page's events.

BrowserEvent gains frame_line(), frame_column() and frame_function_hash(), from the top frame of Debugger.paused. It also gains source_map_url_hash() from Debugger.scriptParsed, and url_hash() is filled from that event's url. browser.fact_hash(text) becomes public, so a program can compare any hash fact with a string it knows.

The beginner path does not change. Each further debugger fact, such as scope values or other frames, needs its own ballot.

options.name: A CDP handle for one page, and the raw debugger event
options.gist: page.protocol("cdp") sends to that page. A debugger event carries its raw params as JSON text, which the tool decodes into its own struct.
options.detail:
BrowserPage.protocol("cdp") is the same as in A.

BrowserEvent gains payload(), the event's CDP params as JSON text. It is filled only for Debugger events and is never written to the trace. A payload over 64 KiB arrives empty, and payload_truncated() says so. The cap matters because the queue counts events, not bytes, and a pause with deep scopes can run to tens of KiB.

The tool decodes the text with json.parse and decode into structs it declares with #Rename(.Camel). That decode was probed and runs. Two accessors serve every debugger field, now and later.

The cost is the event rule: events stop being named facts for one protocol domain. A second domain that asks for raw events, such as network bodies, then has no principled refusal.

options.name: The tool speaks CDP itself over a WebSocket
options.gist: No Core change. The tool starts the pinned Chromium, connects with core.net.ws and writes its own small CDP client, as the original did in Node.
options.detail:
The tool finds the pinned Chromium with browser.locked("chromium") and starts it with --remote-debugging-port=0. It reads the port from the DevToolsActivePort file and connects with ws.connect. It then attaches to a page and matches replies to commands by id. The whole program below type-checks today on the dev compiler.

The tool can read every field. But it is a second CDP client beside Core's checked one, and other ported tools would copy it. It skips the protocol check, the trace and the redaction. The public WsConn.recv has no timeout, so a hung browser hangs the tool. The tool must start, poll and stop Chromium itself.

options.name: Defer: keep the live half in Node
options.gist: No new API. Restore sourcemap.mjs for the live half; the Jet twin keeps only the static half.
options.detail:
The deleted Node file comes back beside Tools/web-test/SourceMap.jet. The Jet twin checks the static half: the fetches, the map decoding and the wasm section. Criterion c3 of card #5072 stays open on this ballot.

A stand-in that runs page script, such as reading new Error().stack, is not an option. No page script can see a debugger pause or Chrome's scriptParsed event, so it would print the same line while testing something else.

recommendation.why: A is the only option that reaches the page through Core's one checked CDP handle while events stay named facts. The twin prints the original's two fields: the paused line from frame_line(), and the map flag by comparing hashes.
gains: Commands reach the page, and no session id or payload reaches the caller
Events stay named facts, and the trace stays free of page content
A public fact_hash also lets programs compare the existing url_hash

losses.loss: Six new public items: one method, four event accessors and fact_hash.
losses.mitigation: Each answers one need the original had. The accessors are documented together as the debugger group, apart from the network facts.

losses.loss: Each further debugger fact, such as scope values or other frames, needs its own ballot.
losses.mitigation: Option B stays available as a later ballot if real tools need many such facts. One ballot per fact keeps each addition reviewed.

losses.loss: fact_hash lets a program match a string, but gives no secrecy.
losses.mitigation: The docs say so plainly. The hash's job is keeping strings out of the trace and logs, which it still does.

losses.loss: BrowserEvent stays one flat struct that grows a field per fact.
losses.mitigation: Unset facts are empty, as network facts are on a pause today. Splitting the struct would break next_event for every caller.

losses.loss: Sharing chromedriver's own page session with the debugger is unproven.
losses.mitigation: The build card's first proof is a live run of A's program against the gauntlet fixture, before any other work.

whyNot.reason: B ends the rule that events carry named facts, for one domain at first. The next domain that asks for raw events then has no principled refusal.
C adds a second CDP client that skips the protocol check, the trace and the redaction. Its recv has no timeout, and other tools would copy it.
D keeps Node for this check and leaves card #5072's criterion open, so the move to Jet stays unfinished.

recommendation.tradeoff: Events stay named facts and the trace stays clean. In exchange, every new debugger fact is a small reviewed addition.

Checked against Core/Web/Browser.jet and probes, the draft had a private fact_hash, a goto that times out mid-pause, and an asserted function name. Repairs: public fact_hash, Page.navigate, no page BiDi handle (I8), a 64 KiB cap on B, and the own-client and defer options.

proposed.code:
// New: a CDP handle for this page only.
cdp: page.protocol("cdp")
cdp.subscribe("Debugger.paused")
_: cdp.send("Debugger.enable", "{{}}")
_: cdp.send("Debugger.setBreakpointByUrl", breakpoint)
_: cdp.send("Page.navigate", "{{\"url\":\"{url}\"}}")
event: cdp.next_event(browser.timeout(20000))
// New: named facts from the pause; the rest of the event is dropped.
paused_line: event.frame_line() + 1
in_render: event.frame_function_hash() == browser.fact_hash("render")
_: cdp.send("Debugger.resume", "{{}}")

decisions.title: Which public Core API the web battery calls once the web app layer leaves Core
decisions.situation: Card #6445 moves the web app layer out of Core into the first-party web battery (D-WEB-HOME1=A). Core gets no private powers, so the battery may call only public Core API. Today that layer reaches the runtime through names only Core may use. They are the live-query store and its WebSocket publish, the process-wide shared cell, the startup environment, a coded runtime stop and private HTTP fields. Eleven compiler rules also key on the core.web module name. This vote decides which public Core API replaces those private calls. We recommend A: host powers stay in Core modules that own them, and the battery becomes plain Jet.
decisions.gist: When the web app layer leaves Core, which public Core API should the web battery call for the powers it uses privately today?
decisions.lesson: A library outside the standard library can only use what the standard library makes public. Moving code out forces a choice: publish general tools anyone may use, publish narrow ones that keep each power in its owner, or let first-party packages keep private access.
decisions.explainer:
Core is Jet's standard library, compiled with the toolchain. Names that start with two underscores are Core-private. A package that uses one fails to compile with E0067.

The web app layer is Core/Web: pages, forms, router, store, tables, live queries and browser storage, about 7,100 lines. It also holds core.web.browser, the browser automation library. The battery is Jetpack/Provider/Batteries/web, a package that ships with Jet; `jet add web` adds it.

The beginner path is the same in every option. A program writes `use web`, calls web.app(), adds routes and serves. Only the battery's own source and the compiler rules behind it change. The expert path is someone writing their own battery that needs the same powers. Option C gives them the most, A gives them what Core modules already own, and B gives them nothing new.
decisions.inWild: Next.js and Remix are npm packages, not part of Node; they use only public Node APIs plus their own compiler plugins. Phoenix LiveView is a Hex package on top of Phoenix.PubSub, a public publish-subscribe library. Bun exposes server.publish(topic, data) as public API for WebSocket topics. These outside facts were not re-checked for this ballot.
decisions.detail:
The private calls in Core/Web today, by count. core.mem.__process_shared (8, browser storage). core.sys.__startup_env (3) and __env_value (1, browser automation). core.net.ws.__connect (2) and core.web.browser.__ws_set_timeout (2, browser automation). core.web.__live_load, __live_replace and __live_publish (1 each, the live store). core.web.__contract_stop (1, OpenAPI). Private core.http fields: __router_mux, mux.__route, server.__state and app.__state.

The live store is shared. Core's app module (Core/App/App.jet) uses core.web for live bindings and sync sessions. So app cannot stay in Core while the store leaves.

The runtime bindings behind the live store are jet.runtime.web live_load, live_replace and live_publish. They are priv, and Guest.jet sema_guest_runtime_binding admits only the generated Core interface and the runtime package.

The compiler rules keyed on core.web, each to become a marker or trait. One: web.form lowering, Calls/Http.jet:590-716. Two: App route checks, Calls/Methods.jet:1304, 1315 and 1345. Three: the table.column schema check E2475, Calls/Core.jet:1549 and Direct.jet:1926. Four: web.openapi(mux), Calls/Http.jet:789-803.

Five: live, subscribe, push, invalidate and sync, Calls/Live.jet:61 and Http.jet:807. Six: the CLI web graph matching web.app, store, form and query.live by name, WebGraph.jet:512-1002 and Entry.jet:911. Seven: runtime handle rows for core.web types, RuntimeHandles.jet:225-273. Eight: effect rows, CoreDeclarations/Calls.jet:444, 493 and 549, and Taint.jet:319 and 342.

Nine: thread-confined browser types, Ownership/Crossings.jet:144. Ten: fixed signature rows, CorePlatformSignatures.jet:308-312 and 635-658, and all of WebCoreSignatures.jet. Eleven: ring rows, Rings/RingLayer.jet:17 and 100-111.

Rule four goes away with #6055 c2, which removes server.mux(). Under every option except D, rules one, two, three and six become markers the battery declares. Under A and C, rules seven, eight and ten shrink to the rows of the Core modules that stay.

Migration. The card's owner order applies: `use core.web` becomes an ordinary unknown module, with no teaching error or fix. About 470 files mention core.web today, 230 of them conformance cases.

options.name: Host powers stay in the Core modules that own them; the battery is plain Jet
options.gist: Browser automation and the browser host calls move to core.browser, the live store moves to app, and the battery calls only their public API.
options.detail:
Three moves inside Core, and no new general primitive.

One. core.web.browser becomes core.browser with its members unchanged. It keeps its private calls (startup environment, WebSocket connect and timeout), because it stays in Core.

Two. The browser host calls move beside it. core.web.on(path: String, title: String, handler: fn(WebEvent)) -[Browser]> and core.web.value(key: String) -[Browser]> String become core.browser.host.on and core.browser.host.value. core.web.storage.local and .session become core.browser.storage.local and .session, with get(key: String) -> String?, set(key: String, value: String), remove(key: String) and clear(). Storage keeps core.mem.__process_shared, because it stays in Core.

Three. The live store moves into Core's app module, which already presents it. Live<T, E>, app.live, app.subscribe, app.push, app.invalidate, app.state(binding: Live<T, E>) -> Loadable<T, E> and app.live_stats() -> String keep their signatures. The jet.runtime.web bindings stay priv and move under app. The battery calls app.invalidate and never sees the cell.

OpenAPI no longer stops the program. web.openapi(site: App) returns String OpenAPIError!, an ordinary typed error, instead of the E2805 stop. The battery's App owns its route table under D-ROUTE-ONE1=A, so it needs none of core.http's private fields.

Compiler rules become four markers the battery declares: #Form on a model struct, #RouteTable on App, #ColumnOf on table.column's name parameter, and #WebApp on web.app(). The checks behind them stay compiler code, keyed on the marker instead of the module name.

options.name: First-party batteries may declare runtime bindings
options.gist: The battery declares its own jet.runtime bindings, as Core does today, and keeps its private calls under its own names.
options.detail:
sema_guest_runtime_binding also admits packages under Jetpack/Provider/Batteries. The battery declares #Import(c) priv live_load: fn() -> [U8] = "jet_web_live_store_load", and likewise live_replace and live_publish, and calls them directly.

The other private Core calls get battery copies in the same way: the process-wide cell, the startup environment and the WebSocket connect. Browser automation and browser storage move into the battery with the rest of core.web.

The live store is shared with Core's app module, which cannot depend on a package. So the live store and app's live and sync functions move into the battery too, and app keeps only auth.

Compiler rules become the same four markers as A.

The cost is a second trust tier. First-party batteries can do what no other package can, so a third-party battery can never match the web battery. The runtime's binding rules, which today cover only Core, now cover Jetpack.

options.name: Core publishes general primitives; the battery builds the rest
options.gist: Core makes the process-wide cell, WebSocket topic publish and startup environment public; the battery rebuilds the live store and storage on them.
options.detail:
Three new public Core functions. core.mem.process_shared<T>(init: fn() -> T) -> Shared<T> returns one value per process, made on first use. core.http.server.publish(topic: String, event: String) -[Net]> sends an event to every WebSocket joined to a topic, as Bun's server.publish does. core.sys.startup_env() -> [String: String] is the environment as the process started.

The battery then holds everything core.web holds today: browser automation, browser storage and the live store. Core's app module cannot use a package, so its live and sync functions move into the battery, and app keeps only auth. The live store uses process_shared for its cell instead of the runtime's compare-and-replace cell. That is a lock instead of a lock-free retry, [INFERENCE] slower under contention and not measured.

OpenAPI returns a typed error, as in A. Compiler rules become the same four markers as A.

Any program may now hold hidden process-wide state with process_shared, which Core keeps private today. publish reaches every connection on a topic from anywhere in the program.

options.name: Defer: core.web stays in Core until v1 release preparation
options.gist: No new API. #6445 waits, and the web app layer keeps its private access.
options.detail:
core.web stays where it is. The battery keeps calling `use core_web: core.web` as it does today. Card #6445 stays open until v1 release preparation (#6068). Work that the card names as sequenced after it, the image pipeline of #4695, continues on core.web and moves with it later.

Nothing breaks and nothing is built now. The cost is that Core keeps a 7,100-line app framework with eleven compiler rules keyed on its name, against the ratified D-WEB-HOME1=A.

recommendation.why: A moves the layer out without giving any package a private power and without publishing a general hidden-state tool. Each private call stays in the one Core module that owns its concept, and the battery uses that module's public face.
gains: The battery compiles as an ordinary package; a third-party battery could do the same
No new general primitive: process-wide state and runtime bindings stay inside Core
Core's app module keeps live queries and sync, so app programs do not change

losses.loss: Core gains core.browser, core.browser.host and core.browser.storage, and keeps about 2,400 lines of browser code.
losses.mitigation: Browser automation is a test tool used outside web apps, and the host calls are Core's browser boundary. Neither belongs to the app framework the card moves.

losses.loss: web.openapi now returns a typed error, a signature change for its callers.
losses.mitigation: Registered routes already reject a bad contract at compile time, so callers handle an error that only hand-built contracts can raise.

losses.loss: Four new markers, each with compiler checks behind it.
losses.mitigation: Each replaces a check that exists today keyed on the module name, so no new check is added.

losses.loss: Programs that wrote web.live must write app.live.
losses.mitigation: The owner order for #6445 moves every in-repo caller in the same change, with no teaching error.

losses.loss: A frees the battery from private HTTP fields only once App owns its route table, which #6055 c2 has not built yet.
losses.mitigation: #6055 c2 lands first, on core.web where it lives today, and #6445 moves the finished table.

whyNot.reason: B makes first-party batteries a privileged tier that no other package can match, and moves app's live and sync out of Core.
C makes hidden process-wide state and program-wide publish public for every program, and moves app's live and sync out of Core.
D leaves a 7,100-line framework in Core against the ratified D-WEB-HOME1=A and keeps #6445 open.

recommendation.tradeoff: The battery gets no special access, but Core keeps the browser module and the live store under its own names.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude Opus. Adversarial model family: Claude Opus. Fresh agent: Main. Checked against Core/App/App.jet, which already forwards state and live_stats to core.web, and Core/Web (6,974 lines); the claims hold. One gap: A needs the App route table of #6055 c2 first, now a stated loss.

decisions.title: Core's file readers and writers for JSON, CBOR, CSV, XML and sealed files keep their paths under a six-group layer table
decisions.situation:
D-CORE-LAYERS1=A puts Core in four checked layers and says file adapters move to files. It also says neither rule changes an import or an API.

On dev a17e4f4491 those two promises conflict. The census counts source lines that name a higher module. Under the ratified table, 63 such lines remain once the staged moves land. Forty-nine are in public file adapters, such as json.reader over a FileReader. They can't move to files without new import paths.
decisions.gist: How should Core keep its file readers and writers when the ratified layer table and the no-API-change promise conflict?
decisions.lesson: Jet's core library is being sorted into layers, where lower parts may not use higher ones. Readers that turn a file into JSON or CBOR events sit in a low layer but use files, which sit higher. This vote picks a fix: reorder the layers, move the readers to new names, or add a new interface.
decisions.explainer: Words used here. Core is Jet's built-in library. A layer is a group of Core modules that may use only its own or lower groups. An adapter is a function that connects a format, like JSON, to a file. A path is the import name, like core.encoding.json.
decisions.story: Ana streams a large catalog.json with json.reader over an open file. Under A her program is unchanged. Under B she imports core.files.json instead. Under C her call is unchanged, but Core gains two new public traits.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. How the Core layer check of D-CORE-LAYERS1=A turns on without breaking its promise of no import or API change.

The census. Every Core .jet line naming another Core module was counted by module, with comment lines skipped. Private parts count as their owner. It counts lines, not names. On dev a17e4f4491, the ratified table gives 67 upward lines in 20 module pairs. A staged change clears 4 of them: sync, rt, meta and the TLS test vectors. That leaves 63.

The counts in one sentence: the 63 upward lines sit in 30 public names and the private code beside them, and 49 of the lines are in file adapters. This census has no count of 58. The table below splits the 63 by kind, with what each option does.

```text
kind                                  lines  public  A        B                   C
encoding codecs naming files             27      21  reorder  core.files.<codec>  traits, no move
crypto sealed files naming files         20       3  reorder  core.files.crypto   moves as in B
data's file readers                       2       2  reorder  core.files.data     traits, no move
data and CSV naming db's SQL type         7       1  reorder  core.db.csv_query   moves as in B
data reading PATH through sys             2       2  reorder  core.process        moves as in B
Hex and ETF naming archive                2       0  reorder  private move        private move
WebSocket upgrade naming HTTPRequest      2       1  reorder  core.http           moves as in B
crypto naming tasks                       1       0  reorder  with sealed files   with sealed files
total                                    63      30  0 move   30 move             7 move
```

Why they can't simply move. The adapters are public: json.reader, cbor.writer, csv.reader, crypto.file_seal and others take a FileReader, FileWriter or Path. Moving them to files changes their import path.

The SQL type lives in core.db, which names core.web, so db can't sit low. WebSocket's public upgrade takes an HTTPRequest.

Option A reorders the table into six groups. Files, sys, process, tasks and term sit just above the data layer. The codecs, crypto, compute and archive sit above them, and data with CSV join services. Core.encoding's root, which holds Dyn, stays in the data layer beside time and math.

Under A, 3 upward lines remain, and none is public. Sys's hostname uses net. Two private encoding parts hold the JSON and CBOR file engines. Hostname's read moves into sys. The engines move into parts owned by the json and cbor modules.

Option B keeps the ratified table and moves 30 public names to new paths under core.files, core.db, core.http and core.process.

Option C keeps the table and adds public ByteSource and ByteSink traits that FileReader and FileWriter implement. C still moves 7 names that are not byte streams. They are crypto's file_seal, file_open and FileCryptoError, data's status and require_bridge, csv.query and ws.upgrade.

C's routing work, measured with git grep on a17e4f4491. 75 compiler lines in 20 files name FileReader or FileWriter beside a stream or codec. The largest are StreamHandles.jet 21, RuntimeRoutes.jet 9 codec handle fields, CoreHostSignatures.jet 6, Statements.jet 5, the runtime's Encoding.jet 5, RuntimeInterface.jet 5 and CoreValueSignatures.jet 4. In Core, 36 lines in 8 Encoding and Data files change. Those routes become trait-dispatched.

The load cost of A. A program loads a Core module with every module it names. Under A, json, jsonl, cbor, csv, xml and crypto still name core.files. So any program that imports one loads files, sys, process and term. Under B or C, json names no files, and json.parse loads none of them.

Measured today, with seed b13 on a17e4f4491, before any layer move. A 5-line json.parse program loads 29 Core units, 1.95 MB of Core source, at a 252 MB peak. base64.encode loads 28 units, 1.86 MB, at 240 MB. files.exists loads 28 units, 1.86 MB, at 234 MB. All three load files today, because core.encoding's own Stream and CborStream parts name it.

The files chain is files, its path kernel, sys, process and term: 5 Core units and 0.29 MB of the 1.95 MB. Under B or C, json.parse skips them. Under A it keeps them, about 15% of its Core source. Probe g11-adapt1 measures the same three programs on the build with A's staged moves.

Why A still wins. It keeps the no-API-change promise, and it leaves C open. FileReader would implement ByteSource, so making json.reader generic later breaks no caller. B's 30 path changes can't be undone that way. The 0.29 MB is source the compiler parses and checks today; precompiled Core, now in progress, removes that per-compile work.

Decode chain. Under every option, time and math keep their decode implementations beside Dyn. The chain from tasks to files is cut, which is what D-CORE-LAYERS1 set out to do.

options.name: Six groups; adapters stay
options.detail: Amend the ratified table to six groups. Files and the system basics sit below the codecs, crypto and archive; data and CSV join services. No public path changes.
options.technical:
The layers in Core/package.jet, lowest first, one line each.

Prelude: prelude, mem, rt, reflect, meta, sync.
Data: text, math, collections, time, regex, units, log, event, encoding.
OS: sys, files, process, tasks, term.
Formats: encoding.base32, encoding.base64, encoding.binary, encoding.cbor, encoding.eetf, encoding.hex, encoding.ini, encoding.json, encoding.jsonl, encoding.toml, encoding.validate, encoding.xml, encoding.yaml, crypto, compute, archive.
System: net, watcher, args, perf, testing, plugin, mod, font, vendor, git.
Services: http, net.ws, db, data, encoding.csv, ui, web, app, auth, service, jobs, game, reactive, tui, devtools, build, compiler, target.

The longest listed name decides a module's layer. The census on a17e4f4491 finds 7 upward names, and the staged moves clear 4 of them. Three private moves remain. sys.hostname owns the hostname read, and net.gethostname calls it. The CborStream part is re-owned by core.encoding.cbor. The JSON and JSONL FileReader engines leave Stream.jet for a part owned by core.encoding.json.

options.name: Adapters move to new paths
options.detail: Keep the ratified four layers. The file adapters move under core.files, and the other upward public names move up beside what they use. Thirty public names change path.
options.technical:
Public moves, old path to new path. core.encoding.json.{reader, reader_allow_duplicates, writer, JSONReader, JSONWriter} go to core.files.json. core.encoding.jsonl.{reader, writer, JSONLReader, JSONLWriter} go to core.files.jsonl. core.encoding.cbor.{reader, writer, CBORReader, CBORWriter} go to core.files.cbor.

core.encoding.csv.{reader, writer, CSVReader, CSVWriter} go to core.files.csv. core.encoding.xml.{reader, writer, XMLReader, XMLWriter} go to core.files.xml. core.crypto.{file_seal, file_open, FileCryptoError} go to core.files.crypto. core.data.{csv_reader, json_reader} go to core.files.data.

core.data.{status, require_bridge} go to core.process. core.encoding.csv.query becomes core.db.csv_query. core.net.ws.upgrade becomes core.http.ws_upgrade. Private moves: data's SQL query goes to core.db with its compiler route. Hex's CRC-32 and ETF's inflate kernels move into the data layer. Docs, examples and tests follow each path.

options.name: Byte stream traits
options.detail: Keep the ratified four layers. Add public ByteSource and ByteSink traits in the data layer; FileReader and FileWriter implement them in files. The stream adapters take any source or sink, as in Go's encoding/json and Rust's serde_json.
options.technical:
core.encoding gains ByteSource (read_into, read_byte) and ByteSink (write_bytes, write_text, flush). The 11 codec constructors, data's 2 readers and the 10 reader and writer types become generic over them. Their paths stay.

Today the compiler routes FileReader and FileWriter by name. git grep on a17e4f4491 finds 75 such lines in 20 compiler files beside a stream or codec. They include StreamHandles.jet 21, RuntimeRoutes.jet 9 and the runtime's Encoding.jet 5. Those become trait-dispatched routes, and 36 Core lines in 8 files change.

Crypto's sealed files need atomic temp files, hard links and removal, which a byte sink doesn't cover. They still move, as do csv.query, ws.upgrade, data.status and require_bridge: 7 public names, as in B.

comparisons.note: Codecs take io.Reader; os.File implements it. Source: https://pkg.go.dev/encoding/json#NewDecoder
serde_json reads any io::Read, including std::fs::File. Source: https://docs.rs/serde_json/latest/serde_json/fn.from_reader.html
json.load takes any object with a read method. Source: https://docs.python.org/3/library/json.html#json.load

recommendation.why: A keeps the promise of no import or API change and cuts the same decode chain. It costs an amended table and three private moves. Codec users still load the files chain, about 0.29 MB of Core source. B breaks 30 public paths. C, the Go and Rust design, adds public API and 75 compiler routing lines and still moves 7 names. A leaves C open later with no break.
gains: No public path or signature changes.
Three private moves, then the check turns on.
Time and math still never load files.

losses.loss: Amends the ratified four-layer table to six groups.
losses.mitigation: Each group is still one reviewed row in Core's package.jet.

losses.loss: Data and CSV sit with services, above files.
losses.mitigation: Both already use SQL from core.db, which is a service.

losses.loss: Any json, jsonl, cbor, csv, xml or crypto import still loads files, sys, process and term: 5 Core units, 0.29 MB of source.
losses.mitigation: Precompiled Core removes their parse and check; C can still come later without breaking a caller.

whyNot.reason: B moves 30 public names, breaking every program and doc that imports them.
C is the mainstream design, but it adds two public traits and 75 compiler routing lines, and still moves 7 names. It can follow A later without breaking a caller.

recommendation.tradeoff: Six table groups instead of four, for no change to any public import.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude Opus. Adversarial model family: Claude Opus. Fresh agent: Main. The first draft hid that A keeps codec users loading core.files, and it was unfair to C, which is the Go and Rust design. The revision measures that load and states both as losses.

decisions.title: Rounding a Float to an Int: make every rounding a Float and convert with Int{}, keep only round_even a Float, or make round_even return an Int
decisions.situation: D-FLOAT-INT1=A puts math.round_even beside math.round as a way to get an Int, and the card text says round_even(f) returns an Int. Today math.round_even is the C23 roundeven function: it takes a Float and returns the nearest whole Float, ties to even. A test pins it bit for bit against musl, and the libc census maps C's roundeven to it. 42 lines of Jet code call it, 35 of them inside Core/Math/Math.jet. math.trunc, math.floor and math.ceil also return a whole Float, but math.round returns an Int. The exact Int{f} conversion is now built, so Int{math.round_even(f)} already gives the Int. This vote decides which roundings return an Int.
decisions.gist: Should every rounding return a whole Float that Int{} converts, or should math.round_even return an Int as the card says?

decisions.title: Memory a program still holds and keeps growing: count it as the program's data, make it carry a visible mark, or forbid it in safe code
decisions.situation: Safe Jet promises that a program does not leak memory. A leak here means memory nothing can reach any more but that is still taken. Jet frees such memory by rule. A program can still keep data it can reach and let it grow without end. Two examples are a cache told to keep every answer and a global list it appends to forever. The memory audit for the no-leak promise must say whether that growth breaks the promise. You are asked whether growing data the program can still read counts as a leak. We recommend treating it as the program's own data and keeping the existing marks that show where it can grow.
decisions.gist: Does memory a program can still reach, but lets grow without a bound, break safe Jet's no-leak promise?
decisions.lesson: A leak is memory a program lost track of but never gave back. Retention is memory the program still holds on purpose, such as a cache or a log. Jet already frees lost memory by rule. This vote decides whether unbounded retention also counts against the promise.
decisions.explainer: Words used here. Reachable means some live name, global, task or cache can still get to the memory. A bound is a cap on how many entries a store keeps. #Memo marks a function whose answers are kept and reused. Shared{...} is a value many places can read and change.
decisions.story: Ana writes a log service. It keeps every line in a global list so a status page can show them all. After a week the process uses 2 GB. Under A this is Ana's data: the leak checker at exit reports nothing, and she caps the list herself. Under B the global needs a #Grows mark before it builds, so a reviewer sees it. Under C the global list does not build at all, and the log must live inside run.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. The memory audit (Docs/audits/2026-11-12-safe-jet-memory-retention.md) lists each construct that can keep memory alive and the rule that frees it. Three constructs can grow without a bound while still reachable, so no rule can free them. They are #Memo(bound: none), a module Shared{...} global holding a growable collection, and a collection owned by a task that never ends.

Today. spec.md: a #Memo function keeps 128 results by default and #Memo(bound: none) makes it unbounded; Examples/Memory/Memoize.jet uses bound: none. A module global `NAME: Shared{value}` holds one process-wide cell of literal data, and the program may push to a list inside it. A seed run of the example program below builds, prints `kept 100000 lines` and exits 0. No diagnostic marks the global.

The leak witness. #6567 c7 adds a runtime check that counts live allocations at exit on O0, O1 and O2. Under A and B it drops globals, memo stores and task results first, then counts; under C nothing unbounded can exist to drop.

What stays the same under every option. Lost memory is still freed by rule: E0221 rejects strong Shared cycles, Weak back-edges break the ones a program needs, channels are bounded, and #Memo is bounded by default.

options.name: Reachable data is the program's own; marks show where it grows
options.detail: The no-leak promise covers memory nothing can reach. Data a live global, cache or task still reaches is the program's own, as in Rust, Go and Swift. The places that can grow without a bound stay visible in the source. A #Memo cache is capped at 128 unless it says bound: none. A growing global is a named Shared{...} at module level. The leak witness drops every global and cache at exit, then counts what is left, so retention never hides a real leak.
options.technical: No language change. Docs/spec/spec.md gains one sentence under memory safety: the no-leak guarantee covers unreachable allocations; reachable retention, including #Memo(bound: none) and module Shared globals, is program data. #6567 c7's witness frees module globals, memo stores and joined task results before it counts live blocks. The audit's B1 row cites this decision.

options.name: Unbounded growth needs a visible mark
options.detail: A module global whose Shared value holds a list, map or set must carry a new #Grows mark. #Memo(bound: none) is already such a mark and stays. Without #Grows the global is a compile error that names the mark. A reviewer can search for #Grows and bound: none to find every store that can grow without end.
options.technical: New marker #Grows on module globals. A new registered diagnostic, with a ui snapshot, rejects an unmarked module Shared global that holds a collection. spec.md and syntax-decisions.md gain rows, and every existing module Shared global that holds a collection migrates. The witness behaves as in A.

options.name: No unbounded store in safe code
options.detail: #Memo(bound: none) is removed; a cache gives a number. A module Shared{...} global may hold only fixed-size data, so a list that keeps growing must live inside run or a task. Every store that can grow is then owned by a function and freed when it returns.
options.technical: Remove bound: none from #Memo (spec.md, syntax-decisions.md, Compiler/Prelude/Markers.jet, sema FunctionHeaders.jet) and migrate Examples/Memory/Memoize.jet. A new registered diagnostic rejects a module Shared global whose type holds a list, map, set or String, with a ui snapshot. Migrate existing globals that hold collections.

comparisons.note: A static collection may grow without end; Rust's safety promise is about freed and dangling memory, not growth.
A package-level slice grows freely; the garbage collector frees only what nothing reaches.
ARC frees unreachable objects; a global array that keeps growing is the program's data.

recommendation.why: A keeps the promise exact: Jet frees by rule every byte the program can no longer reach. Each store that can grow without a bound is already visible in the source. It matches Rust, Go and Swift, needs no new mark, and leaves every program that builds today unchanged.
gains: The promise has one exact meaning: nothing unreachable stays allocated.
No new mark, diagnostic or migration.
Each unbounded store is visible: bound: none or a module Shared global.
The exit leak witness still catches real leaks, because it frees globals and caches first.

losses.loss: A program can still grow a global list until the system runs out of memory.
losses.mitigation: No language can stop growth of data the program still reads. Under A the place it grows is a named module global or a bound: none cache, so a search finds it.

whyNot.reason: B adds a second mark beside bound: none for the same meaning and a migration, and a global still grows once marked.
C removes bound: none, which programs use for exact caches, and forces shared logs and tables into run, where they grow just the same.

recommendation.tradeoff: No new rule, in exchange for leaving growth of reachable data to the program, as every mainstream language does.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude Opus. Adversarial model family: Claude Opus. Fresh agent: Main. I tried to break the claim that every unbounded store is already visible; module Shared globals and bound: none are the only unbounded roots in safe code, so the claim holds.

surface.gist: Does memory a program still reaches, but lets grow forever, break the no-leak promise?
surface.lesson: A leak is memory a program lost but never gave back; Jet frees that by rule. Retention is memory still held on purpose, like a cache or a log. This vote decides whether retention that grows without end counts as a leak.

current.note: Today a global list may grow forever, and bound: none makes a cache unbounded.

wild.note: A static list may grow forever; it is not a leak.
wild.code:

LOG.lock().unwrap().push(line);

options.name: It is the program's data
options.gist: The promise covers lost memory; visible marks show growth.
gains: One exact meaning of leak.
No new mark or migration.
losses: A global list can still grow until memory runs out.

proposed.code:

#Memo(bound: none) label: fn(n: Int) -[]> String { "line {n}" }

options.name: Growth needs a mark
options.gist: A growing global needs #Grows before it builds.
gains: Every growing global is marked.
losses: A second mark beside bound: none.
Existing globals migrate.

proposed.code:

#Memo(bound: none) label: fn(n: Int) -[]> String { "line {n}" }

options.name: Forbid it
options.gist: No bound: none; globals hold fixed-size data only.
gains: No global can grow.
losses: Exact caches lose bound: none.
Logs move into run and grow there.

recommendation.why: Jet frees every unreachable byte by rule, and each unbounded store is already visible, as in Rust, Go and Swift.
gains: One exact meaning of leak.
No program changes.

losses.loss: Reachable data can still grow without end.
losses.mitigation: It grows only in a named global or a bound: none cache, which a search finds.

whyNot.reason: A second mark for what bound: none already says.
Removes exact caches; logs grow in run anyway.

recommendation.tradeoff: No new rule, and growth of held data stays the program's choice.

decisions.title: Background tasks still alive when run returns: cancel them with a short grace, keep today's rule, forbid them, or end the process at once
decisions.situation: A background task is work a program starts with detach() and does not wait for. When run returns, such a task can still be alive. Today a waiting task, such as a ticker that sleeps between ticks, stops the program with error E3013 and exit status 70. A task stuck in a loop that never waits keeps the process alive forever. Past 4,096 tasks, waiting ones are not even cleaned up. This matters for servers, tickers and anyone who wants a clean, prompt exit. You are asked what happens to background tasks when run returns. We recommend cancelling every one, giving them one second to clean up, and then exiting with run's own status.
decisions.gist: When run returns, what should happen to background tasks: cancel with a grace, today's rule, forbid them, or exit at once?
decisions.lesson: A background task is work started with detach() that nobody waits for. When the main function run ends, some of that work may still be going. Jet must stop it cleanly, treat it as an error, forbid it, or simply end the process. This vote picks one rule.
decisions.explainer: Words used here. A task is work that runs alongside the rest of the program. detach() lets a task go on without anyone waiting for it. Cancel asks a task to stop, and a task notices only at its next wait, such as a sleep, a channel read or a network read. Cleanup is the code that runs as a value goes away, such as closing or flushing a file.
decisions.story: Kai starts a ticker task that wakes every second to refresh a cache, and detaches it. When run finishes, the program prints run returns. Today it then stops with E3013 and exit status 70. Under A the ticker is cancelled at its sleep, cleans up and the program exits 0 at once. Under B Kai must keep the handle, cancel it and join it. Under C, detach() is gone, so he must do the same. Under D the process ends the moment run returns, and the ticker's cleanup never runs.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. What the runtime does with detached tasks that are still alive when run returns.

Today, parked tasks. After run returns, main_exit_cleanup in Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/Main.jet looks for tasks parked on a wait. If it finds any, it reports E3013 (Parked tasks remain at process exit). It cancels the tasks it can reach so they unwind, and the process exits 70. Tasks past the registry cap (OBSERVE_TASK_CAP, 4,096) are neither reported nor unwound. A seed run of the ticker program prints run returns, then E3013 with the ticker blocked on its sleep, and exits 70.

Today, running tasks. If no task is parked, jet_scheduler_drain_after_exit waits until no task is queued or running. A seed run of a program whose detached task runs `loop { n += 1 }` never exits; it was killed after 10 seconds.

Cancellation reaches only waits. In spec.md, cancellation is preemptive at wait points: channel send and receive, time.sleep, join, select and I/O. There is no check on loop back-edges. A seed run that cancels and then joins a task looping on `n += 1` also never returns. tasks.yield_now() is a wait point, so a loop that calls it can be cancelled.

The rest of the spec. A cancelled task unwinds and runs Drop-backed cleanup. #Shield defers cancellation until its block exits. Dropping a handle without joining or detaching is L1101, so every detach is an explicit choice.

Why it matters for memory. #6567's leak witness counts live allocations at exit. A task that is not unwound keeps its frame and captures, so the witness must either see every task unwound or leave task frames out.

options.name: Cancel every background task, wait up to one second, then exit
options.detail: When run returns, the runtime cancels every task still alive. A waiting task stops at its wait at once, runs its cleanup, closes its files and frees its memory, with no cap on how many. The exit waits until every cancelled task has unwound, or for one second, whichever comes first. A task still running after that second is in a loop that never waits. It is abandoned, the process exits, and the system takes its memory back. The exit status is run's.
options.technical: Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/Main.jet: after run returns, cancel every live task through the task registry, with no OBSERVE_TASK_CAP limit. Drain until no task is queued, ready or running, or until 1 s of monotonic time has passed, then exit. Retire E3013's exit report: its registry row, explainer page and runtime_e3013 ui snapshot, which becomes a case that exits 0. The leak witness counts after the drain and names each abandoned task instead of counting its frame. spec.md gains the rule.

options.name: Keep today's rule and close its gap
options.detail: A waiting background task still stops the program with E3013 and exit status 70, after it is cancelled and cleaned up. A task in a loop that never waits still keeps the process alive forever. The 4,096-task cap goes, so every waiting task is reported and cleaned up. A program with a ticker keeps its handle, cancels it and joins it before run returns.
options.technical: Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/Main.jet and Observe.jet: lift OBSERVE_TASK_CAP from the exit report and unwind. No other change; E3013 stays.

options.name: No task may outlive run
options.detail: detach() is removed. Every task handle is joined, so every task ends before the function that started it returns. A ticker is kept, cancelled and joined. A server that serves each connection in its own task joins those tasks through a group. A joined task in a loop that never waits still never ends.
options.technical: Remove Task.detach from Core and the sema rule that lets it discharge L1101. Retire the detach forms of E1103 and E1106, and migrate every detach() caller (Core/Http/Server.jet and others) to task groups. spec.md D-DETACH1 is superseded.

options.name: End the process the moment run returns
options.detail: This is the model of Go and of Rust's standard threads. When run returns, the process exits at once with run's status. Background tasks stop where they are, without cancelling and without cleanup, and the system takes their memory back. Nothing can hang the exit, and nothing waits.
options.technical: Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/Main.jet: after run returns and the main task's own cleanup, flush stdout and exit without draining the scheduler. Retire E3013's exit report and the exit unwind. The leak witness leaves every live task's frame and captures out of its count. spec.md gains the rule.

comparisons.note: When main returns, the process ends; goroutines stop at once and their deferred calls do not run.
When main returns, the process exits; spawned threads stop without running their destructors.
Runtime shutdown drops spawned tasks at their await points and runs their destructors; a task that never awaits blocks a blocking shutdown, so shutdown_timeout bounds it.
asyncio.run cancels the tasks still pending when main returns and waits for them to unwind.

recommendation.why: A gives every program a clean exit with run's status. Every task that waits, which is almost every background task, cleans up and frees its memory at once. A loop that never waits can delay the exit by at most one second, so nothing hangs. It is Tokio's shutdown_timeout as the default.
gains: A ticker or server task no longer turns a normal exit into status 70.
Every waiting task's cleanup runs at exit, with no 4,096 cap.
No exit hangs: a loop that never waits costs at most one second.
No new syntax; detach() keeps its meaning of not waiting.

losses.loss: Background work still in progress at exit is cut short.
losses.mitigation: Join the task when its work must finish, or put that work in #Shield, which finishes before the cancel lands.

losses.loss: A loop that never waits is abandoned after one second without its cleanup.
losses.mitigation: Its memory goes back to the system and the leak witness names the task. Calling tasks.yield_now() in the loop makes it cancellable.

losses.loss: E3013 no longer reports a background task stuck on a wait at exit.
losses.mitigation: A task whose end matters is joined, and L1101 already forces that choice.

whyNot.reason: B keeps stopping normal programs with ticker or server tasks with status 70, and a loop that never waits still hangs the exit.
C removes detach(), which servers and tickers use, and a joined loop that never waits still hangs.
D is fastest, but it skips every background task's cleanup, so files go unflushed and connections unclosed, and the leak witness cannot see task memory.

recommendation.tradeoff: Up to one second of exit for a loop that never waits, in exchange for cleanup in every task that waits.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude Opus. Adversarial model family: Claude Opus. Fresh agent: Main. The first draft hid that a task looping without a wait never reaches a cancel point, and it omitted the Go and Rust std exit. The revision checks that hang on the seed, adds a 1 s grace to A, and adds D.

surface.gist: When run returns, should background tasks be cancelled with a grace, stop the program, be forbidden, or just die?
surface.lesson: A background task is work started with detach() that nobody waits for. When run ends, some may still be going. Today a waiting one stops the program with status 70, and a loop that never waits hangs it. This vote picks the rule.

Nothing can hang it.
losses: No task cleanup; files go unflushed.

recommendation.why: Every waiting task cleans up at once. A loop that never waits costs at most one second, so the exit is clean and never hangs.
gains: No status 70 from tickers.
No exit hangs.

losses.loss: Unfinished background work is cut short.
losses.mitigation: Join it, or wrap it in #Shield so it finishes first.

whyNot.reason: Normal programs keep exiting 70.
Removes detach(); loops still hang.
Skips all task cleanup.

recommendation.tradeoff: At most one second of exit, for cleanup in every waiting task.

decisions.title: Sending on a closed channel: return the Closed error that receive uses, return a SendError that hands the value back, stop the program, or keep dropping it
decisions.situation: Today sender.send(v) returns nothing. When the receiver is closed or gone, the runtime drops v and returns as if the send worked, so the program never learns the value was lost. The other end already reports this case: receiver.receive() returns T !Closed once every sender is closed. Card #3239 c61 says sender.send(v) returns SendError! and a closed send is that error. That changes public API. 405 lines of Jet code contain .send(. This vote decides what a send on a closed channel does.
decisions.gist: When a program sends on a channel whose receiver is closed, should send return an error, stop the program, or keep dropping the value?
decisions.lesson: A channel has two ends. The sender puts values in and the receiver takes them out. If the receiver closes first, the sender has nowhere to put the value. Today Jet throws the value away and says nothing. This vote picks what happens instead.
decisions.explainer: Words used here. A closed channel is one whose receiver called close() or was dropped. Closed is the error receive already returns when every sender is gone. Jet has no ? operator: a fallible call propagates by itself. Where the function's error type can't take the failure, a bare call is a compile error (E2402), so the caller handles it with ?? or declares a conversion.
decisions.story: Ana runs a worker task that sends results to a logger task. The logger stops early. Today her worker keeps sending and every result vanishes. Under A or B her send line fails, and she writes ?? to stop the worker. Under C her program stops with a located message. Under D nothing changes.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. What Sender.send returns, and what it does when the channel's receiver is closed or dropped.

Today's send. Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Calls/Concurrency.jet types sender.send(v) as Unit. Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/Channel.jet jet_rt_native_sender_send breaks out of its loop when the channel is closed or has no receiver left, then drops the value it was given. The caller cannot tell. The spec says send moves its value into the channel and says nothing about a closed channel.

Today's receive. receive() -> T !Closed. Closed is a built-in error type with one case.

What the card says. #3239 c61 reads: core.tasks has no sentinel or silent rail: sender.send(v) returns SendError! and a send on a closed channel is that error (never -1).

How many lines this touches. 405 lines contain .send(; 404 are not comments, in 217 files. 122 of those already handle a result with ??; they are HTTP requests, services and browser calls, not channel sends. So at most 282 lines are channel sends. 161 lines call send on a value named sender, tx, or ending in _sender or _tx.

What a bare send does under A and B. A fallible call propagates by itself. Inside a function whose error type can't take Closed, a bare call is refused with E2402 (jet.MissingErrorConversion); that includes a plain run: fn(), and no impl Closed -> Err exists. Each such line gains ?? or its function declares a conversion. Inside a function that already fails with Closed, a bare send propagates the failure, which is handled, not silent.

A and B make send fallible. A reuses Closed. B adds SendError<T>, which carries the unsent value back. C keeps send returning nothing and stops the program with a located message. D keeps today's silent drop and writes it into the spec.

options.name: send returns Closed!, the error receive uses
options.detail: sender.send(v) returns Unit !Closed. A send on a closed channel, or one with no receiver left, returns Closed and drops v. The program sees the loss and chooses what to do. Both ends of a channel then report the same error.
options.technical: Concurrency.jet: the SenderSend node gets type Unit !Closed. Channel.jet: jet_rt_native_sender_send returns 0 when accepted and 1 when closed, and the IR builds the Closed error from it. A cancelled send still unwinds, as a cancelled receive does. Update spec.md Channels, core-library.md, the goldens that send, and every channel send line (at most 282) that E2402 then refuses.

options.name: send returns SendError<T>!, which hands the value back
options.detail: sender.send(v) returns Unit !SendError<T>. The error carries the value that was not sent, in err.value, as Rust's SendError does. The card names this type. The program can log the value or send it elsewhere.
options.technical: Add SendError<T>: struct { value: T } to core.tasks, a generic type marked #Error with one field. Concurrency.jet types SenderSend as Unit !SendError<T>. Channel.jet keeps the slot when the send fails and moves it into the error instead of dropping it. Update spec.md, core-library.md, the goldens that send, and the same channel send lines as A.

options.name: send stops the program
options.detail: sender.send(v) still returns nothing. A send on a closed channel stops the program with a message naming the send line, as an index out of range does. No caller changes. A program that must survive an early-closed receiver has to check before it sends.
options.technical: Channel.jet: when the send loop finds the channel closed, call the runtime stop with a new located code instead of dropping the slot. Register the stop code and add a UI snapshot. No sema or call-site change. Update spec.md Channels.

options.name: Keep dropping, and write it down
options.detail: sender.send(v) still returns nothing and still drops v on a closed channel. The spec states this. The card's rule that nothing is dropped silently is removed for send.
options.technical: No code change. spec.md Channels gains one sentence: a send on a closed channel drops its value. Card #3239 c61 text loses its send clause.

comparisons.note: std::sync::mpsc send returns Err(SendError(value)) once the receiver is dropped, handing the value back.
Sending on a closed channel panics. A receiver that just stops reading makes the sender block forever.
comparisons.code: ch <- 7 // panics if ch is closed

comparisons.note: Channel.send throws ClosedSendChannelException; trySend returns a failed result instead.

recommendation.why: A makes the loss visible with the error Jet already has for the other end, so both ends of a channel report Closed. Handing the value back only helps a program that can retry, and a closed channel never reopens. The ratified try_send already hands the value back when the channel is full.
gains: No send loses a value without the program being told.
One error, Closed, for both ends of a channel.
No new public type.

losses.loss: Up to 282 channel send lines change: each one in a function that can't fail with Closed gains ?? or a declared conversion.
losses.mitigation: The compiler refuses each such bare send with E2402, so none is missed; a send in a function that already fails with Closed propagates.

losses.loss: The unsent value is dropped, so a program cannot recover it from a closed send.
losses.mitigation: A closed channel never reopens, so the value has nowhere to go. try_send hands it back when the channel is only full.

losses.loss: The card's SendError name is not used.
losses.mitigation: The card text changes to Closed!, and its rule that no send is silent still holds.

whyNot.reason: B adds a generic public error type to hand back a value that can never be delivered on that channel.
C turns a common shutdown race, a consumer finishing first, into a crash, and gives the program no way to handle it.
D keeps the silent loss the card exists to remove.

recommendation.tradeoff: Up to 282 send lines gain ?? or a conversion, in exchange for no send ever losing a value unseen.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude Opus. Adversarial model family: Claude Opus. Fresh agent: Main. I challenged two claims: that err is bound in the fallback of a send, and that an unhandled send cannot be silently missed. Seed probes confirm both: E2402 refuses a bare unhandled send, and a bare send inside a Closed fn propagates.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Count the lines that contain .send( in the Jet repository with git grep -n -F '.send(' c367fdfe56 -- '*.jet'; it lists 405 lines.

Run git grep -n -P '^(?!\s*//).*\.send\(' c367fdfe56 -- '*.jet'; it lists 404 non-comment lines in 217 files (add -l and count for the files).

Count the lines that already handle a result, which are not channel sends. Run git grep -n -P '^(?!\s*//).*\.send\([^)]*\)\s*\?\?' c367fdfe56 -- '*.jet'; it lists 122 lines, so at most 282 are channel sends.

Count the sends on a value named like a sender. Run git grep -n -P '^(?!\s*//).*\b(sender|tx|[a-z_]*_sender|[a-z_]*_tx|sender[0-9]*)\.send\(' c367fdfe56 -- '*.jet'; it lists 161 lines.

Today's silent drop is in Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/Channel.jet, in jet_rt_native_sender_send. When the channel is closed or has no receiver, its loop breaks and coll_slot_drop drops the value.

The seed (b14) proves the handling claims with the programs in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/ballots/probes/D-SEND-ERROR1. jet run err_in_fallback.jet prints no receiver; kept 7, then done, so err names the failure inside a ?? fallback.

jet check bare_closed_call.jet, a bare call of a Unit !Closed function in run: fn(), is refused with E2402 (jet.MissingErrorConversion). jet run closed_propagates.jet prints closed, then done: a bare call inside a function that fails with Closed propagates.

Validate this payload with Tools/agent/ballots/Validate.jet.

surface.gist: Should a send on a closed channel return an error, stop the program, or keep dropping the value?
surface.lesson: A channel has a sender end and a receiver end. If the receiver closes first, today's send throws the value away and says nothing. This vote picks what happens instead.

current.note: send returns nothing; on a closed channel the value is dropped unseen.

sender.send(7)
print("done")   // the 7 is gone

options.gist: send returns the Closed error that receive already uses.
gains: No value is lost unseen.
One error for both ends.

proposed.code: sender.send(7) ?? print("no receiver")

options.name: Return SendError
options.gist: send returns an error that carries the value back.
gains: The value comes back.
Matches the card and Rust.
losses: New public generic type.
Up to 282 send lines gain ?? or a conversion.

proposed.code: sender.send(7) ?? print("kept {err.value}")

options.name: Stop the program
options.gist: send stays the same, but a closed send stops with a message.
gains: No call line changes.
losses: An early-closed receiver crashes the sender.

proposed.code: sender.send(7)   // stops: send on a closed channel

options.name: Keep dropping
options.gist: Write today's silent drop into the spec.
gains: No change at all.
losses: Values still vanish unseen.

recommendation.why: The loss becomes visible with the error Jet already has, and a closed channel never reopens, so handing the value back buys nothing.
gains: No value is lost unseen.
No new public type.

losses.loss: Up to 282 send lines gain ?? or a conversion.
losses.mitigation: The compiler refuses every unhandled send with E2402.

A consumer finishing first crashes the program.
