decisions.title: A guard table over one enum: a jet lint report, an error, retire L0302, an error for if tables only, a jet fmt rewrite, or a tidy error
decisions.situation: L0302 is a warning. It fires when every head of an if table, or of an if/else-if chain, tests the same enum value with a pattern, and it suggests the subject table if value == { … } instead. D-IFGUARD1 ratified it as a recommendation. D-NO-WARNINGS1 then ruled that Jet has no warnings. Card #6326 c4 says L0302 becomes a jet fmt rewrite or a registered error, or is retired. The repository has 18 such sites outside the tests, and 11 of them end in else. A subject table over an enum must name every case and cannot keep an else (E0641). So an error leaves those 11 sites one rewrite: list every remaining case. This vote decides what L0302 becomes.
decisions.gist: When every branch of an if chain tests the same enum, should Jet say nothing, suggest a table in a report, refuse the code, or rewrite it?
decisions.lesson: An enum is a type with a fixed list of cases. Jet has two ways to branch on one. A chain of if tests checks the cases one at a time and may end in else. A subject table names the value once and must list every case. Jet suggests the table today with a warning, and Jet is dropping warnings.
decisions.explainer: Words used here. A guard table is if { … } whose arms are true-or-false tests, tried in order. An if/else-if chain is the same thing written with else if. A subject table is if value == { … }: each arm is a case of value, and over an enum it must name every case, with no else (E0641). A jet lint report is a list that jet lint prints on request; it never fails jet check or jet build.
decisions.story:
Ana writes area(shape) as if shape == .Circle(r) { … } else if shape == .Square(s) { … } else { … }. Today jet check warns L0302 and runs her program. Under A, jet check says nothing and jet lint --dispatch lists the suggestion. Under B, jet check fails until she writes a table naming Circle, Square, Line and Dot. Under C, nothing is ever said. Under D, her chain is fine, but an if { … } table with no else would fail. Under E, jet fmt rewrites chains that have no else.

Under F, her program runs, but jet check fails until she writes the table or an #Allow with a reason.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. What happens to L0302 (jet.SameEnumGuardTable). It is the warning that suggests a subject table when every head of a guard table or chain tests the same enum value.

The two rules that meet here. D-IFGUARD1 says the subjectless table is not a lesser way to branch, and has L0302 recommend exhaustive subject dispatch. D-NO-WARNINGS1 says Jet has no warnings. A finding becomes a jet fmt rewrite, a tidy error, or a jet lint report. Card #6326 c4 names a fmt rewrite, a registered error, or retirement.

What L0302 fires on today. On the seed, the probe chain/main.jet gets L0302 on all three of its functions. They are an if/else-if chain ending in else, a chain whose first head adds && r > 10, and an if { … } table with no else. A head joined with || is not a pattern test, so it does not fire. Option and result values do not fire: they are not closed enums the rule counts.

What the subject table demands. Over an enum, if value == { … } names every case, and an else there is E0641. The probe subject/main.jet shows it. So the subject form of a chain that ends in else names every case the else stood for, and a head with && becomes a nested if.

Where it fires in the repository. A scan of base 98469bf0cf finds 17 chains and 1 if table outside the tests: 18 sites, 11 ending in else. Two of the others have a head with &&. The seed's check of the JetSema package reports exactly the 5 JetSema sites the scan lists. The enums include Type, Expr, Item and NodeKind, which have dozens of cases. Five test fixtures exist to show L0302.

One more warning, BranchArmTable, also fires on both chains in the probe. It has its own D-NO-WARNINGS1 cutover, and this ballot does not decide it.

The same program under each option. chain/main.jet's area function is the program every option's code shows.

Beginner path. A beginner writes the chain they think in. Under A, C, D and E it runs and passes jet check. Under B, jet check fails, and the fix writes the table for them.

Expert path. Under A an expert runs jet lint --dispatch to find chains worth turning into tables. Under B every chain over one enum is a table, so adding a case makes the compiler stop at each one.

Where F sits. D-NO-WARNINGS1 has three places: a jet fmt rewrite, a tidy error, and a jet lint report. A is the report and F is the tidy error. B is a real error that stops every command. Against A, F makes every chain a to-do item that jet check fails on, so beginners see it too. Against B, F never stops jet run, and #Allow keeps a chain whose else is deliberate. F needs the tidy kind built for compiler diagnostics first.

options.name: Move the advice to a jet lint report
options.detail: jet check, jet build and jet run say nothing about a guard table or chain over one enum. jet lint --dispatch <file> lists each one with the subject table it suggests, and fails only when --max is given. This is the place D-NO-WARNINGS1 gives advice that is not about wrong code. No source site changes.
options.technical: L0302 keeps its code, name and texts and leaves the diagnostic stream: sema records the finding for the lint host instead of pushing a warning. jet lint gains a --dispatch category beside --a11y and --complexity. The five L0302 test fixtures become jet lint --dispatch snapshots. The D-IFGUARD1 sentence in syntax-decisions.md names the report. The 18 sites stay as written.

options.name: Make it an error, and name every case
options.detail: A guard table or chain whose every head opens with a pattern test of one enum value is the error E0644 in every command. Its fix rewrites it as if value == { … } naming every case. An else's body goes to the cases it stood for. A head with && becomes a nested if in its case. Adding a case to the enum then stops the compiler at every such site.
options.technical: Register E0644 (jet.GuardTableNeedsSubject) with what, why, fix and a SourceEdit fix that writes the cases, as E0641's does, and retire L0302. Sema reports it through sema_error. Rewrite the 18 sites: 11 name every case their else stood for, over Type, Expr, Item, NodeKind and smaller enums, and 2 move a && condition into a nested if. The five fixtures become E0644 error snapshots.

options.name: Retire L0302
options.detail: Nothing is ever said about a guard table or chain over one enum. A chain, an if table and a subject table are equal choices, and only the subject table checks that every case is named. No source site changes.
options.technical: L0302 becomes a Retired registry row that names this decision, and its sema check is deleted. The 18 test, lint-policy and spec files that name L0302 or same_enum_guard_table are deleted or move to another lint. The D-IFGUARD1 sentence about L0302 is removed.

options.name: An error only for an if { } table with no else
options.detail: if { … } with no else whose every head tests one enum is the error E0644, with B's fix. if/else-if chains and tables with an else stay legal and silent. The error catches a table that quietly does nothing for the cases it leaves out.
options.technical: B's E0644, raised only for a subjectless table with no else arm; L0302 retires. No source site changes: the one if table outside the tests has an else. The five fixtures become E0644 snapshots, and the rest of L0302's references go as in C.

options.name: jet fmt rewrites a chain with no else
options.detail: jet fmt turns a chain or if table over one enum that has no else and no && into a subject table, adding the cases it leaves out with an empty body. A chain that ends in else, or whose head adds &&, stays legal as written. Nothing is reported.
options.technical: jet fmt reads the syntax only, so it cannot know which cases an enum has. This rewrite needs the checked program to list them, which makes it a jet fix edit that fmt invokes, not the plain formatter rewrite D-NO-WARNINGS1 describes. L0302 retires. 5 source sites are rewritten; the 11 ending in else and the 2 with && stay.

options.name: A tidy error
options.detail: L0302 becomes a tidy error, D-NO-WARNINGS1's middle place. jet run, jet dev and jet test never stop for it. jet check and jet build list it with its fix and fail. #Allow(jet.SameEnumGuardTable, "reason") keeps one chain as written. Each of the 18 sites is either rewritten as a table naming every case or carries an #Allow with its reason.
options.technical: No tidy kind exists in Compiler/Prelude/Diagnostics.jet today. Only package lints raised through meta.report have a Tidy tier. F builds the tidy kind for compiler diagnostics. It shows as an error in the editor and as kind tidy in JSON. Only jet check and jet build list it and fail. D-NO-WARNINGS1 already needs that mechanism for its other L codes, so the cost is shared. Each of the 18 sites then gets an #Allow or the rewrite.

comparisons.note: An if-let chain over one enum gets no lint. Only match must name every case, and match may use _.
comparisons.code: if let Shape::Circle(r) = shape { 3 * r * r } else { 0 }

comparisons.note: An if case chain is legal and silent. A switch over an enum must be exhaustive, and default is allowed.
comparisons.code: if case .circle(let r) = shape { return 3 * r * r } else { return 0 }

comparisons.note: An if chain with is checks is legal. A when used as a value over a sealed class must be exhaustive.
comparisons.code: if (shape is Circle) 3 * shape.r * shape.r else 0

comparisons.note: D-NO-WARNINGS1 gives advice three homes. A uses the report, B a plain error, F a tidy error. Only A leaves a beginner unaware, since she never runs jet lint --dispatch.

recommendation.why: L0302 is advice about how to write a correct program, and D-NO-WARNINGS1 already sends advice to jet lint reports. A keeps the advice for anyone who asks, fails no build, and changes no source line. An error would fall hardest where the chain is the clearer code.
gains: No source line changes, and no build fails for a style of branching D-IFGUARD1 ratified as equal.
The advice stays available to an author who wants every enum branch to be a table.
It follows D-NO-WARNINGS1's own rule for advice.

losses.loss: A chain ending in else still hides a case added to the enum later.
losses.mitigation: jet lint --dispatch lists every such chain, and a team that wants them gone can run it with --max in CI.

losses.loss: jet lint gains one more category to build and document.
losses.mitigation: It reuses the existing lint host beside --a11y and --complexity, and the finding's texts already exist.

losses.loss: A beginner never runs jet lint --dispatch, so for a beginner A behaves the same as C: the advice is never seen.
losses.mitigation: Their chain is still correct code. A subject table is the form the guide teaches, and jet lint --dispatch is there for anyone who wants every chain listed.

whyNot.reason: Eleven sites would list every case of enums with dozens of cases to replace one else, and the two && heads become nested ifs. A Bool helper such as shape.is_circle() still escapes the rule.
C drops advice D-IFGUARD1 chose to give, when D-NO-WARNINGS1 already has a place for it at no cost to builds.
D is an error for a form no source uses, and it is silent on the chains where a missing case most often hides.
jet fmt cannot list an enum's cases without the checker, and E leaves the 11 else-ended chains, the riskiest ones, untouched.
A chain with an else is correct code, so F fails jet check on code that is not wrong. 18 sites then carry an #Allow or name every case. F also waits on the tidy kind, which does not exist yet.

recommendation.tradeoff: Chains over one enum stay legal and silent in builds, in exchange for no forced rewrites and the advice kept on request.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude Opus. Adversarial model family: Claude Opus. Fresh agent: Main. Main checked the claims against dev code and the seed, and added the missing tidy-error option F with its true cost. A states its loss: a beginner never runs jet lint --dispatch.

decisions.checkInstructions:
The scanner is chainscan.awk in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/ballots/probes/D-GUARD-LINT1. In a checkout of 98469bf0cf, run git ls-files -z -- "*.jet" | xargs -0 awk -f chainscan.awk. It prints 17 if/else-if chains, and 10 of them show else=1. None is under tests.

The one if { } table outside the tests is Compiler/JetIR/Source/BuildRoutes.jet:1374, and it ends in else. That makes 18 sites, 11 ending in else. The chains whose first head adds && are X64Select.jet:2615 in JetIR and Web/Select.jet:1404 in JetWeb.

The scan agrees with the compiler where both ran. The seed (b14) jet check of Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Statements.jet checks the whole JetSema package. It reports SameEnumGuardTable at exactly the 5 JetSema lines the scan lists.

Count the files that name the lint with git grep -l -e L0302 -e same_enum_guard_table -e SameEnumGuardTable 98469bf0cf. Leave out Docs/site, Docs/audits, Docs/research and Tools/tower. decisions.title: Where a user reads the declared target machines and their dossiers: a new `jet inspect target [machine]` view, a section of `jet self doctor --target`, or no command at all
decisions.situation: A target machine is a named kind of computer Jet can build for, like hosted (a normal Linux PC) or wasm.no-os (WebAssembly with no operating system). Each one has a dossier, a fact sheet that says what it gives a program: a heap, a clock, random numbers, a place to print, and the ways it runs. Today no command lists the machines or shows a sheet. The compiler refuses one kind of misuse: a web build that starts other programs or calls C is stopped at the call. Nothing tells a user that wasm.no-os has no clock. This vote decides where the list and the sheets are shown. We recommend a read-only view: `jet inspect target` lists the machines, and `jet inspect target <machine>` shows one sheet.
decisions.gist: Where should a user list the target machines and read what one provides: a new `jet inspect target` view, the `jet self doctor --target` health check, or nowhere on the command line?
decisions.lesson: Jet can build one program for different kinds of computers. Each kind has a fact sheet that says what the program can use there, such as a clock or random numbers. This vote picks the command that lists those computers and shows a sheet.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A target machine is a named build destination that Jet knows: hosted, wasm.browser, wasm.wasi, wasm.no-os and two boards. A capability is one thing the machine gives a program, written like Time.Wall (the wall clock) or Rand.Entropy (random numbers). A dossier is the full fact sheet for one machine.

An effect is a kind of outside action a function performs, like Exec (starting another program). An inspect view is a read-only `jet inspect <name>` command that shows compiler facts and changes nothing. `jet self doctor` is the health check that tests whether the toolchain works on this computer.
decisions.story:
Lena writes a sensor program for a WebAssembly chip with no operating system. First she wants the exact machine name, then whether that machine has a clock.

Under A she runs `jet inspect target`, sees wasm.no-os in the list, then runs `jet inspect target wasm.no-os` and reads `lacks: ... Time.Wall ...`. Under B she runs `jet self doctor --target wasm.no-os` and finds the same line after the toolchain checks; doctor has no list. Under C she has no command. The checker only stops web builds that start programs or call C, so nothing tells her the chip has no clock.

decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. Which user command, if any, lists the declared target machines and shows one machine's dossier, and in what shape.

Today's facts. The compiler holds every declared machine in its machine table (Pipeline.jet JET_DRIVER_TARGET_MACHINE_NAMES and jet_driver_target_machine_by_name). Each machine carries an audit policy. The policy's dossier lens says whether its dossier may be shown (AuditPolicy.dossier_lens). Every part of the dossier already has a Jet JSON writer in Compiler/JetFoundation/Source/Target. No command lists the machines or prints a dossier.

Today's commands. `jet self doctor --target <machine>` only checks that the name is a declared machine. It prints `[ok  ] <machine>: declared target machine (<triple>)` in its `cross` section (Doctor.jet jet_cli_doctor_check_cross_target). A wrong name gets E3302 with the list of names. No `jet targets` command exists. `jet inspect build` takes `--target` only as a build flag for its gates. The other inspect views (memory, choices) each came through a ballot.

What the checker already says. E1123 (jet.TargetDeniedEffect) is the one target refusal that runs today (Sema TargetDenials.jet). It runs in the checker when the build selects the browser machine. A `build: fn` output with `os: web` selects it (Request.jet build_os, Pipeline.jet jet_driver_selected_target_machine).

E1123 in detail. The checker walks every function the entry reaches.

Where it reports. It reports E1123 where Exec or FFI.C first enters the program's own code: a use in its body, or its call into Core. Only the browser machine denies effects (jet_target_machine_denied_effects is empty for every other machine). The cases pin it at `jet build` (cross/build_fn_checks_each_target_against_its_own_row) and in the checker's ui suite (target_denied_effect_e1123). `jet check --target web` does not select the browser machine yet (known failure #5201).

What no command says. E3311 (Target `wasm.no-os` lacks the required `Time.Wall` capability) is written and unit-tested in JetFoundation (jet_target_machine_validate). No driver or checker path calls it. So no check names a missing clock, entropy source or allocator on a no-OS machine.

What the card asks. #6663 c1 reads: a user-visible target dossier view exists (e.g. jet inspect target <name> --json) built from AuditPolicy.dossier_lens, with a case pinning its output.

The same dossier under every option. A machine whose audit policy drops the dossier lens shows no dossier. The JSON fields are name, triple, environment, provider_identity, linker, allocator, panic, memory and mmio_capability. Then come time_wall, time_monotonic, time_zone_data, time_sleep, entropy, scheduler, byte_sink and startup. Last come provider_facts, hardware, programmers, execution {aot, dev} and audit.

Other tools. rustc lists names (`--print target-list`) and prints one target's facts (`--print cfg`, and `--print target-spec-json` on nightly). zig targets prints every target and the host's facts as one JSON document. go tool dist list -json lists every OS and architecture pair. Every one of them can list all targets. The first draft of A could not, so A now lists the machines when no name is given.

The docs rule. AGENTS.md forbids hand-kept catalogs and committed generated output in docs. Reference output is generated on demand. So the docs cannot carry a per-machine capability table; they can only point at a command that prints it.

A ready build exists for A. It is the held submission G5DevX-dossier5, which replaces G5DevX-dossier4. It holds jet_target_machine_dossier_json and the inspect view with its list. It adds the help and completion rows, a case that pins the list and two dossiers, and a Jet test for the dossier lens.

decisions.title: Mapped files: keep borrowed bytes stable by holding the file or copying it, copy always, copy on every read, or let the bytes change
decisions.situation: A mapped file is a file the program reads as if it were already in memory. files.map(path) gives Jet code a borrowed view of the bytes with no copy. Today another program can change those bytes while the view is borrowed. One probe read 3, another process wrote the file, and the same borrowed byte then read 9. If the other program shrinks the file, the next read kills the process with SIGBUS. Safe Jet promises that a borrowed value does not change under you, so this breaks the promise. It matters to anyone who maps large files for speed. This vote decides what a safe mapped view sees when another program writes or shrinks the file. We recommend A: the runtime holds the file so writers wait, and copies the bytes when it can't.
decisions.gist: When another program writes a file that Jet has mapped, should the borrowed bytes stay as they were, be copied up front, be copied on each read, or change?
decisions.lesson: Mapping a file lets a program read a huge file without loading it first: the operating system brings in each page when the program touches it. The bytes still belong to the file, so another program can change them while Jet is reading. Jet's rule is that a borrowed view never changes under you. This vote picks how mapped files keep that rule.
decisions.explainer: Words used here. A view is a borrowed window into bytes someone else owns; it is not a copy. A lease is a Linux promise to the program that holds it: before another process may write or shrink the file, the kernel tells the holder and makes the writer wait. Copying means reading the bytes into the program's own memory, which costs time and memory equal to the file's size.
decisions.story: Mia's log tool maps a 2 GiB log and scans it for errors. One night a rotation script truncates the log mid-scan. Today her tool dies with SIGBUS. Under A the script waits a moment while Jet copies, and the scan finishes. Under B the tool never mapped: it spent a second and 2 GiB copying first. Under C each read copies, and a read past the new end stops with a message. Under D her scan sees whatever the file says at each moment.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. What a safe borrowed view from files.map sees when another process writes or truncates the file, and where zero-copy mapping lives.

Today's map. Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/CompilerMapped.jet jet_std_files_map opens the file read-only, takes a shared flock (advisory, so non-Jet writers ignore it), and calls mmap with PROT_READ and MAP_PRIVATE. A private mapping is not a snapshot on Linux: pages not yet copied show the file's current bytes. The in-process writer check (jet_std_files_writer_refusal) only refuses this program's own writes.

What the card says. #6706 c1: a safe borrowed view must not observe a byte change made by another process after the borrow, or the safe API no longer hands out such a view. c2: a truncation during safe access gives a typed error or a registered fault, never a raw SIGBUS.

Uses today. Six Jet files call files.map: two examples, one perf tool, one case, one run test and one UI snapshot. The view API (window, window_len, lines) is pinned by Examples/Systems/Files/FilesMapViews.jet, which returns views through Option, Result, tuples, lists and Shared guards.

Probes. The probes are in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/ballots/probes/D-MMAP-STABLE1. today.jet, option_b.jet and option_c.jet are one program under three spellings, run on the b14 seed. lease_probe.py shows option A's Linux mechanism with real leases, and lease_probe.py stall shows the kernel's deadline. copy_cost.py measures what a copy costs.

How Linux leases work. fcntl(2) F_SETLEASE: a writer's open or truncate blocks, and the kernel signals the holder, SIGIO unless F_SETSIG names another signal. The holder has /proc/sys/fs/lease-break-time seconds, 45 by default, before the kernel removes the lease itself and lets the writer in. Only the file's owner or a CAP_LEASE process may take one, and not while anyone has it open for writing.

Other hosts. Windows opens without FILE_SHARE_WRITE, and SetEndOfFile already fails on a file with a mapped view. macOS and FreeBSD have no lease call. Web has no mmap; files.map returns a typed IOError today.

Sources. memmap2: docs.rs/memmap2/latest/memmap2/struct.Mmap.html (Safety). Go: pkg.go.dev/syscall#Mmap, pkg.go.dev/runtime/debug#SetPanicOnFault and pkg.go.dev/golang.org/x/exp/mmap. Java: docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/nio/MappedByteBuffer.html. .NET: learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/standard/io/memory-mapped-files and learn.microsoft.com/windows/win32/api/fileapi/nf-fileapi-setendoffile. Linux: man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/fcntl.2.html (Leases).

options.name: Stable map: hold the file where the OS can, copy where it can't
options.detail:
files.map keeps zero-copy views and makes them stable. On a local Linux filesystem the runtime takes a read lease on the file. When another process opens it for writing or shrinks it, the kernel makes that process wait and tells Jet. Jet copies the mapped bytes into its own memory at the same address and releases the lease. The views keep their address and their old bytes.

Where no lease is possible, the map is a copy from the start, so the meaning is the same everywhere. If a copy can't finish before the kernel's deadline, the Jet program stops with a message; it never reads changed bytes.
options.technical:
Which files get a lease. At map time fstatfs picks the path. Local Linux filesystems (ext4, xfs, btrfs, tmpfs, f2fs, bcachefs) get a lease. NFS, SMB, FUSE, 9p, Ceph and overlayfs files are copied at map time: there a lease is refused or misses writes from other machines and FUSE daemons. A refused lease (a writer already open, a file not owned) also copies.

The signal. jet_std_files_map opens read-only, sets F_SETSIG to SIGRTMAX (64), takes F_SETLEASE F_RDLCK, then calls mmap. Its handler only records si_fd and wakes the runtime's signal thread. Native images link musl statically, and the build passes over a glibc libc.a, so FFI.C code never brings in glibc's threads. musl keeps 32 (timers), 33 (SIGCANCEL) and 34 (synccall) below the SIGRTMIN (35) it reports; 64 is none of them.

Keeping 64 for the runtime. Safe code can't subscribe to it: process.signals takes only the named POSIX signals, with no real-time kinds. #Unsafe reset_signal refuses 64. C code linked through FFI.C can still install its own handler, so files.map reads the action back with rt_sigaction first. If 64 isn't the runtime's handler, that map is a copy.

The copy. The signal thread copies each live map of that file into anonymous memory, mremaps the copy over the mapped address (MREMAP_FIXED) and releases the lease. Program threads keep reading meanwhile, because the writer is still held back.

The deadline. The runtime reads lease-break-time at map time. If the copy isn't done one second before it, the program stops with a registered message while the writer still waits. At the probe's 0.36 s per cached GiB, 45 s covers about 120 GiB; from a 200 MB/s disk, about 8 GiB.

Memory. A map-time copy larger than the host's available memory (MemAvailable on Linux) fails files.map with a typed IOError. A break-time copy that can't get its memory is the same registered stop.

Other hosts. Windows opens without FILE_SHARE_WRITE; a file already open for writing is copied. macOS, FreeBSD and web copy at map time. Truncation can no longer fault a safe view, which also meets c2 for safe code.

options.name: The safe map is a copy; zero-copy mapping moves behind #Unsafe
options.detail: files.map(path) reads the whole file into the program's memory, as files.read_bytes does, and keeps the MappedFile API (window, lines, len). Views are stable because they borrow the copy. Zero-copy mapping becomes an expert call inside #Unsafe that hands out raw reads, never a safe view.
options.technical: jet_std_files_map reads the file into an owned buffer instead of calling mmap; the drop frees the buffer. Add an #Unsafe raw map in core.files whose reads go through checked raw access and whose truncation fault is c2's registered stop. Update spec.md, core-library.md and the files.map examples. Web gets the same copy, so every tier has one meaning.

options.name: VolatileBytes: no borrowed views; every read copies
options.detail: files.map returns a map that never lends a view. mapped.read(start, count) copies the bytes it asks for at that moment, and lines() yields copied lines. Searching and counting run inside the runtime over the live pages, so scans stay zero-copy. Two reads can disagree if another program wrote in between. A read past a shrunk end stops with a registered message.
options.technical: MappedFile loses window, window_len and the View<U8> lines iterator; it gains read(start, count) -> [U8] !IOError, a copying lines() and runtime scan kernels (find, count, checksum) that read the mapping. c2's registered SIGBUS stop is required. FilesMapViews and the view-provenance cases for maps are deleted.

options.name: Keep views and let them change: a mapped view is shared with other programs
options.detail: files.map keeps today's zero-copy views. The spec states that another program may change a mapped file's bytes at any time, so a mapped view can read different values at different moments. The compiler never assumes a mapped byte stays the same between reads. A read after a shrink stops with a registered message.
options.technical: No API change. Sema marks map views as externally mutable, so no optimization reuses a loaded mapped byte. c2's registered SIGBUS stop is required. Card #6706 c1 is rewritten to accept change.

comparisons.note: memmap2 marks every file-backed map constructor unsafe, because the map is undefined behavior if the file is modified in or out of process; the caller must prevent that.
comparisons.code: let map = unsafe { Mmap::map(&file)? }; // UB if the file changes

comparisons.note: syscall.Mmap returns a plain byte slice that shows other processes' writes. A read after truncation crashes the program unless debug.SetPanicOnFault turns the fault into a panic. x/exp/mmap's ReaderAt copies on each ReadAt.
comparisons.code:
m, _ := syscall.Mmap(fd, 0, size, syscall.PROT_READ, syscall.MAP_SHARED)
first := m[0] // may change later

comparisons.note: MappedByteBuffer documents that its content can change at any time when the file changes, and that touching a truncated region throws an unspecified exception, possibly later.
comparisons.code:
MappedByteBuffer buf = ch.map(MapMode.READ_ONLY, 0, ch.size());
byte first = buf.get(0); // may change

comparisons.note: MemoryMappedFile views of a file show other processes' writes; sharing is the point of the type. On Windows, SetEndOfFile fails while a view is mapped, so a truncation can't happen there.

recommendation.why: A keeps both the promise and the speed where the OS can hold the file: local Linux filesystems and Windows. Everywhere else it copies, with the same meaning. Its costs fall on other programs' writers, which wait for one copy, and on a huge map under a writer, which stops with a message instead of reading changed bytes.
gains: A borrowed mapped byte never changes, on every host.
Zero-copy maps on local Linux filesystems and Windows: a 1 GiB map opened in 0.05 ms in the probe.
A shrink by another program can no longer fault a safe view, so card c2 holds for safe code.
No change to any Jet program that maps files today.

losses.loss: Many maps are a copy: on macOS, FreeBSD and web, on Linux network and FUSE filesystems, and for a file the program doesn't own or another program has open for writing. In the probe, 1 GiB cost 0.36 s and 1056 MiB of memory. There a file larger than available memory can't be mapped.
losses.mitigation: The meaning is the same as a zero-copy map, so no program changes. A file too large to copy gives a typed IOError from files.map, not an out-of-memory kill. An #Unsafe raw map stays for experts who need zero copy anyway.

losses.loss: Other programs pay. A program that opens the mapped file for writing waits while Jet copies: 18-32 ms for 64 MiB in the probe, about 0.36 s per cached GiB. A Jet program reading a log can stall the logger. A non-blocking open, like coreutils truncate, fails once with EAGAIN.
losses.mitigation: It happens once per map: after the copy the lease is gone. A program that must never stall a writer reads with files.read_bytes or files.open.

losses.loss: On Windows, other programs can't open the file for writing at all while the map lives; they get a sharing violation.
losses.mitigation: Deny-write sharing is ordinary Windows behavior, and a file another program already has open for writing is copied instead.

losses.loss: A copy that can't finish before the kernel's lease break time (45 s by default), or can't get its memory, stops the Jet program. That is about 120 GiB from the page cache, or 8 GiB from a 200 MB/s disk.
losses.mitigation: The stop is a registered, located message, and it comes while the writer still waits, so no view ever reads changed bytes. Smaller maps never reach it.

losses.loss: The runtime reserves real-time signal 64 (SIGRTMAX) for lease breaks.
losses.mitigation: Images link musl, whose own signals are 32-34, so nothing collides. Safe code can't subscribe to 64, #Unsafe reset_signal refuses it, and a C handler on 64 turns that map into a copy.

whyNot.reason: B pays the full copy on every host for every map, and a file larger than available memory can't be mapped at all. It never stalls another program.
C removes borrowed views from maps, so every line a program keeps is a copy, and two reads can disagree.
D gives up Jet's promise that a borrowed value doesn't change under you.

recommendation.tradeoff: Copies where no hold exists, a wait for the first writer and a stop for a huge map under a writer, for stable zero-copy views on local Linux disks and Windows.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude Opus. Adversarial model family: Claude Opus. Fresh agent: Main. Main reviewed five attacks: lease-break timing, filesystems, cost to other writers, per-OS behavior and peers; each is probed or stated in A losses. The lease signal moved to SIGRTMAX after Main found the collision with libc reserved real-time signals.

decisions.title: Cancelling a task that has a task group open: cancel the group's children too, let them finish first, or keep today's lost cancel
decisions.situation: A task group is a block that starts several tasks and waits for all of them at its closing brace. Today, cancelling a task that is waiting at such a brace does not reach the tasks inside the group. Those children run to their end, and then the cancelled task carries on as if nothing happened, so its join reports success and the cancel is lost. A child that waits forever, such as a server loop, makes that cancel hang for good. This matters for anyone who stops a job made of parallel parts: a crawler, a fan-out request, a test that times out. You are asked what a cancel does to the children of a group the cancelled task has open. We recommend that it cancels them, waits for their cleanup, and then the task stops as cancelled.
decisions.gist: What should cancelling a task do to the tasks inside a group that task has open?
decisions.lesson: A task group waits for every task it started before its block ends. When the task that opened the group is cancelled, the children can be cancelled with it. They can instead be left to finish before the cancel lands. Or they can be left alone as today, where the cancel is lost.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A task is work that runs alongside the rest of the program. A task group is a block, written task.group name { ... }, that starts child tasks and waits for all of them at its closing brace.

Cancel asks a task to stop. The task notices at its next wait, such as a sleep, a channel read, a network read or waiting for another task. It then unwinds: it leaves its functions and runs its cleanup on the way out. Join waits for a task and gives back its result, or a failure such as Cancelled.
decisions.story:
Mia's command-line tool fetches twenty pages in a task group, inside a job task. When the user presses Ctrl-C, or her two-second time limit runs out, she cancels the job. Today the twenty fetches keep going to the end. Then the job prints that all pages were fetched, and its join says it succeeded.

Under A the fetches stop at their next network wait, close their connections, and the job's join reports Cancelled within moments. Under B the job waits for all twenty fetches, then reports Cancelled. Under C nothing changes.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. What happens to the children of a task.group block when the task that opened the block is cancelled while the block is open.

What the rules say today. spec.md, Task completion and cancellation: cancellation lands at wait points, and task join is one of them (D-CANCELMODEL1=C). spec.md, Structured tasks and combinators: the group owns and joins every child created in its body (D-CONC-SPAWN1=D). task.all cancels remaining children on a failure, and task.race and task.any cancel the losers.

D-NURSERY1=A says work created inside the scope must finish, be cancelled, or report an error before the scope exits, without choosing which. No ratified rule says whether cancelling the opener reaches the group's children. process.on_signal cancels every live task, which is a separate path.

What the code does today. Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/TaskGroup.jet task_group_close cancels the group's children only when the closing task's deadline has expired (status 2). Otherwise it calls task_drain on each child, and task_drain (Task.jet) is a plain futex wait with no cancellation check. So the closing brace is not a stop point for the opener.

The combinators already cancel their children when the waiting task is cancelled: task_selection_wait_check delivers the cancel and task_selection_drain(handles, count, true) cancels every child.

Seed run. Seed b14, at --optimize=none. A parent task opens a group whose one child sleeps 3 s. run cancels the parent after 100 ms and joins it. Output: child finished its sleep, then parent closed its group, then parent joined Ok, and the join took at least 2 s. The cancel was lost, and the parent's code after the group ran.

Relation to other ballots. D-TASK-SLICE1=A makes loop turns stop points, so under option A a busy child also stops promptly. D-EXIT-TASKS1 covers detached tasks at process exit. Detached tasks are not group children and are untouched here.

options.name: Cancel flows down to the group's children
options.detail:
Cancelling a task also cancels every child of each task group it has open, and their own groups' children, all the way down. Each child stops at its next wait and runs its cleanup. The group's closing brace still waits for all of them, so no child outlives its group. Then the cancelled task itself unwinds, and its join reports Cancelled.

A child that must finish a step it started puts that step in #Shield, which already delays a cancel until the step is done. This is what task.all, task.race and task.any already do with their children, and what a group already does when its deadline passes.

The cost of A. A child stopped in the middle of a step that is not in #Shield leaves that step half done: a file half written, a request half sent. Its cleanup still runs, so the file is closed and the connection dropped, but the half-done work is not undone. Steps that must not stop halfway go in #Shield.
options.technical:
The cancel of a task walks the groups it has open and cancels each unfinished child (scheduler_control_cancel), recursively. This is what task_group_close already does under an expired deadline. A task records its open groups, so a cancel that arrives while it is already parked at the closing brace still reaches them.

task_group_close cancels the children when the closer is cancelled and not shielded, waits for all of them, then delivers the pending cancel so the closer unwinds as Cancelled. A closer inside #Shield keeps today's behaviour until the shield ends. spec.md gains one sentence in Task completion and cancellation and one in Structured tasks and combinators.

Cost. A cancel walks only the unfinished descendants in open groups: one step per such task, paid once per cancel. Each group's child list is read under that group's own lock, and the cancels are sent after the lock is released, as the deadline path already does. A task that is never cancelled pays one list push and one pop per task.group block, to record the open group.

options.name: Children finish first, then the cancel lands
options.detail:
The group's children are not cancelled. They run to their own end, the closing brace waits for them as it does today, and then the cancelled task unwinds and its join reports Cancelled. The cancel is no longer lost, but it takes as long as the slowest child. A child that waits forever, such as a server's accept loop, makes the cancel hang, so the author must stop such children by hand through a channel or a flag.

B keeps the ratified rule that waiting for a task is a stop point; it only delays the cancel.
options.technical: task_group_close keeps task_drain without cancelling children, then delivers the closer's pending cancel. Group children differ from task.all, task.race and task.any children, which are cancelled. B does not amend D-CANCELMODEL1=C: the cancel still lands at the closing brace, which is a task join, only after the children end.

options.name: Keep today's behaviour
options.detail: The group's closing brace is not a stop point. The children run to their end, and then the cancelled task carries on with the code after the group as if it had never been cancelled. Its join reports success. A child that waits forever hangs the cancel. Choosing C amends a ratified rule: today waiting for a task is a place where a cancel lands, and C makes the group's closing brace an exception.
options.technical: No change to task_group_close or task_drain. spec.md must then name the group's closing brace as an exception to task join being a wait point. C amends the ratified D-CANCELMODEL1=C, which lists task join among the wait points where a cancel lands.

comparisons.note: Cancelling a task cancels every child task in its task groups; children check at their next await.
comparisons.code: job.cancel()   // the group's addTask children are cancelled too

comparisons.note: Cancelling a parent Job cancels all of its children, and the parent completes only after they finish unwinding.
comparisons.code:
val job = launch { coroutineScope { launch { fetch("a") }; launch { fetch("b") } } }
job.cancel()

comparisons.note: Cancelling a scope cancels everything inside it, including every task in a nursery opened there.
comparisons.code:
with trio.move_on_after(2):
    async with trio.open_nursery() as n:
        n.start_soon(fetch, "a")
        n.start_soon(fetch, "b")

comparisons.note: Cancellation is explicit. A context's cancel reaches every context derived from it (pkg.go.dev/context: "When a Context is canceled, all Contexts derived from it are also canceled"). But a goroutine sees it only if it was passed that context and checks Done(). A goroutine that was not passed it runs on. This is the strongest case for B or C: nothing stops without being told in the code. Go also has no group that must outlive its children, so a forgotten goroutine is a leak, not a hang.
comparisons.code:
ctx, cancel := context.WithCancel(parent)
go fetch(ctx, "a")   // stops only if fetch checks ctx.Done()
go fetch(ctx, "b")
cancel()

comparisons.note: StructuredTaskScope (JEP 453, preview; docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/util/concurrent/StructuredTaskScope.html). shutdown() interrupts every unfinished subtask, and join() and close() wait for all of them. An owner interrupted while waiting in join() gets InterruptedException, and closing the scope then shuts it down, so the subtasks are interrupted and awaited, as in A.

recommendation.why: A cancel means the whole job stops, children included, and nothing outlives its group. It matches how Jet's own task.all, task.race and task.any already treat their children, and how Swift, Kotlin and Trio treat groups.
gains: A cancelled job stops promptly, with every child's cleanup run.
The cancel is never lost: the join reports Cancelled.
A child that waits forever no longer hangs a cancel.
Groups and task.all, task.race and task.any follow one rule.

losses.loss: A child's unfinished work is cut short when its group's opener is cancelled.
losses.mitigation: Work that must outlive the job is started with detach() instead, so it is not a group child.

losses.loss: A child stopped mid-step outside #Shield leaves that step half done, such as a half-written file or a half-sent request.
losses.mitigation: Steps that must not stop halfway go in #Shield, which already delays a cancel until the step ends. Cleanup still runs either way, so files close and connections drop.

losses.loss: Each cancel walks the unfinished tasks in open groups.
losses.mitigation: The walk is one step per unfinished descendant, paid once per cancel, with each group's lock held only to copy its list. Tasks never cancelled pay one push and pop per group.

whyNot.reason: B keeps the cancel but makes it wait for the slowest child, and a child that waits forever hangs it. It also gives groups a different rule from task.all, task.race and task.any. Go's explicit style favours B, but Go has no group that must wait for its children, so it never hangs.
C silently loses the cancel and reports success for a job that was asked to stop. It also amends the ratified rule that waiting for a task is a stop point.

recommendation.tradeoff: A child's in-progress work stops with its job, and #Shield keeps the steps that must finish.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude Opus. Adversarial model family: Claude Opus. Fresh agent: Main. Main attacked A against Go explicit contexts and Java StructuredTaskScope, the cancel-walk cost, and work cut mid-step outside Shield; each is now stated as a cost with its mitigation. C is shown to amend D-CANCELMODEL1, and B delays but keeps the cancel.

surface.gist: When a task with an open task group is cancelled, what happens to the group's tasks?
surface.lesson: A task group waits for all the tasks it started. Today, cancelling the task that opened it does not reach those tasks: they run to the end, and the cancel is then lost. This vote picks what a cancel does to them.

gains: The whole job stops promptly, with cleanup.
The join reports Cancelled.
losses: Unfinished work inside the group is cut short.

options.name: Let them finish first
options.gist: The group's tasks run to their end; then the job stops as cancelled.
gains: The cancel is no longer lost.
losses: The cancel waits for the slowest task.
A task that waits forever hangs it.

options.name: Keep today's behaviour
options.gist: The group's tasks finish and the job carries on as if not cancelled.
gains: No change.
losses: The cancel is lost and the join succeeds.
A task that waits forever hangs it.
It amends the rule that joins are stop points.

recommendation.why: A cancel stops the whole job, nothing outlives its group, and groups follow the same rule as task.all, task.race and task.any.
gains: Prompt stop with every task's cleanup.
The cancel is never lost.

losses.loss: A child stopped mid-step can leave half-done work.
losses.mitigation: Put steps that must finish in #Shield; cleanup still runs either way.

The cancel is silently lost, against the rule that joins are stop points.

questions.text: How do other languages handle this? What are the tradeoffs for each approach?
questions.answer: Most modern toolchains use Option A — one binary, tool subcommands: Deno (deno fmt/lint/lsp), Gleam (gleam format/lsp), Ruff (ruff format/check/server), Bun. The recurring exception is the LSP, shipped as a separate artifact by Zig (ZLS), Go (gopls), and Rust (rust-analyzer) because editors spawn it long-lived on its own cadence. Rust's fmt/clippy are separate binaries (B) but hidden behind cargo subcommands and version-locked via rustup. Pure plugin (C) has no real precedent for compiled-language toolchains. Tradeoffs: A = one install, tooling can never disagree with the compiler, bigger binary, no independent patch cadence; B = independent releases + smaller core but version-skew risk and N artifacts; C = max flexibility, runtime ABI surface, no prior art, fights one-source-of-truth. Jet-specific: fmt/lint/lsp all need the real lexer/parser/sema (I2/I3), so under B/C they must link the same front end as a shared lib and stay version-locked anyway — getting separation's costs without its benefits. Prior art + that constraint both point at A, reserving the LSP as the one piece that could become a separate artifact later. Full table added to the D-TOOL-SPLIT card in docs/ballots/decision-ballots.md.

questions.text: I still have absolutely no clue what this means. Give me a user story with example code so I can learn what you mean
questions.answer: Ratified A (2026-06-20). Not a language feature — a naming clash inside our own spec docs. Two ratified decisions both coined "Layer 2": S26 (derive ladder: built-in derives) and S60 (capability tier: compile-time pure eval + data embedding). A keeps both numbers and adds one cross-reference sentence on S60 so the next reader can tell them apart. No code, no rename. Compile-time embedding work files under S60.

questions.text: I am leaning B but want to understand the practical tradeoofs of going with B & C respectively
questions.answer: Ratified B (2026-06-20). B (stdlib Guard value: scope.guard(() => {…})) delivers ~95% of C's value — cleanup on every exit path including the ? early return — for zero new syntax and zero ratification, running on existing Drop + lambda machinery, and keeps Jet's one-cleanup-story (RAII) intact. C (a defer keyword) adds a second cleanup mechanism plus the Go leak-by-omission bug class S63 was chosen to avoid; its only unique win is errdefer-style partial rollback, not yet proven. B doesn't foreclose C — add the keyword later on evidence. defer (C) stays declined (D-SUGAR5); user-definable Drop remains the long-term roadmap item.

questions.text: 1) Isnt sharing not supportable with the borrow checker? Wouldnt that be a mutable borrow which can only have 1, but immutable can have many? I dont get the point, refresh me on the memory capability model. How does it play into the borrow checker system? What is auto inferred for beginners but can be specified for experts?
questions.answer: `share` is shared *ownership* (Rc/Arc), not a shared mutable borrow — so the borrow-checker rule still holds: mutable XOR shared. The four capabilities map onto it directly: `view` = `&T` (many readers ok), `edit` = `&mut T` (exactly one, exclusive), `take` = move (ownership transfer), `share` = `Rc<T>`/`Arc<T>` (many owners, READ-only — no mutation, so no conflict with the one-mutable rule). `share` exists for graph/tree shapes where a single owner is awkward; it buys multiple readers by giving up mutation, exactly mirroring &T. Beginners write none of this — the compiler infers the narrowest capability from how the value is used; experts annotate it to pin intent or widen sharing. Full capability↔borrow-checker table is on the D-CAP2 card.

questions.text: How is a supportive of the experts? That is one of the major points for jet -> a beginner friendly automagical side & an expert exposed full control side
questions.answer: Reframed so it serves experts directly: ship BOTH. A (scope-inferred regions) is the beginner default — the compiler places allocations automatically. B (`region r { … }`) is the explicit expert tier — you name a region and allocate into it deliberately, e.g. two arenas live side by side and you choose which one each value lands in. The beginner never sees a region; the expert gets full manual placement. Now RATIFIED (D-REGION1 = A+B together, 2026-06-21). Worked two-arena example is on the card.

questions.text: I'm leaning towards A, but how is bloat/buildup addressed? For large codebases, how will users be able to avoid 3k lines of code that are just migrations?
questions.answer: Bloat is bounded by published-API surface × support window, NOT codebase size, via four bounds: (1) only `#PublishedSchema` types accrue migrations — internal types never do; (2) migrations live in `migrations/`, are build-tier, and cost zero at runtime; (3) you keep migrations only back to your declared support floor; (4) `jet schema squash` collapses old chains into a fresh baseline snapshot. So a large codebase with a few published types stays tiny. Now RATIFIED (D-MIGRATE1 = A) and the rename-only slice is implemented end-to-end + verified green; the squash/baseline tooling and other ops are tracked as follow-on D-MIGRATE2.

questions.text: Please reform the ballot using a2 & c beta (#context) as the baseline. Give me grammar options to pick from using those two choices. That is what I want to pick but need to ensure I like the syntax/grammar
questions.answer: Reformed and now RATIFIED. A2+Cβ fixed as the baseline; the grammar pick resolved to G2 — `#context(field: value) { … }`, reusing Jet's single `name: value` spelling (S61/S29), with `=` staying reassign-only. No single-field shorthand; bundle-spread deferred. Shipped as the c74 Smart Context feature.

questions.text: Option D but I dont want to defer the full implementation if avoidable. We are close to epoch 3 anyway, so what should we do to get this working? Propose a new approach in this decision.
questions.answer: Proposed Option D+ so nothing is deferred: an interpreter seam now (Phase 1) plus a Cranelift JIT this Epoch-3 (Phase 2, tiered — interpreter tier-0, Cranelift tier-1). I6 still holds because Cranelift is runtime-side, never in Source/. This needs your approval of the runtime-side Cranelift dependency (same posture as the regex dep). Recommendation: D+. Decision still open pending your call on the dep.

questions.text: How does this interplay with experts that will want to use low level memory controls like references and pointers?
questions.answer: The tiers compose rather than conflict. `view`/`edit` ARE the safe references an expert wants (`&T`/`&mut T`) — capabilities are the safe-reference surface, not a wall in front of it. The drop below that layer is a raw `Ptr<T>` via `use core.mem` inside a `#Unsafe`/`#Audit` region, where the guarantees are explicitly suspended. The two bridge at the function boundary: public params stay safe capabilities, and the raw-pointer work is a localized `#Unsafe` block inside. Worked `checksum(buf: view [U8])` example added to the D-CAP3/D-CAP2 card. Decision still open.

questions.text: How is this affected when no type is written (inferred type)?
questions.answer: Capabilities are a parameter concept and parameters carry types, so an omitted capability is simply inferred — there is no token to place when no type is written, and the capability rides the type. Rule: no type written ⇒ capability inferred too; you never get a dangling capability. This reinforces option A (type + capability written together in one place). The only spot you'd write an inferred-type parameter is a lambda, where you write the type alongside precisely to pin a capability. Decision still open.

questions.text: I think the $ is fine for me, but what about people trying to use the language globally? Is having such a commonly needed symbol an issue? What if people dont have that symbol? How likely is that? Is it a reasonable concern or not a big deal
questions.answer: Not a blocker. `$` is plain ASCII and universal on physical keyboards; Jet already left the ISO-646-invariant subset behind by depending on `# @ { } [ ]`, so `$` adds nothing new. Programmers type `$` constantly (shell/PHP/JS) and no mainstream language uses it as a binding operator, so no conflicting habit. Answered in the D-BIND2 card; rec stands at A (`$=`); decision stays open for your pick.

questions.text: Please update this card so it isnt called "raw mode" AND we will have a separate library for TUI. This gives experts control but also provides batteries included TUI development features out of the box. Please update this question accordingly & give me alternatives to "raw mode"

questions.text: What are the downsides of recommendation A? In practice does this cause friction? How do new users know what to do? Will this make it harder to use the system for simpler projects or beginner projects?
questions.answer: Honest answer: A's only real cost is key custody, and it lands entirely on PUBLISHERS — never on consumers, never on beginners, never on simple projects. (1) Consuming a package (the common case + every beginner): zero friction — `jet add` verifies the signature silently and only ever speaks on a MISMATCH (a normal Jet diagnostic, not crypto). Strictly better than checksum-only for the same effort. (2) Simpler/local/unpublished projects: nothing changes — signing is only on the registry-publish path; path/git/unpublished deps are never signed or asked about. (3) Publishing (the one place friction exists): mitigated by the dual-facet rule — `jet publish` auto-generates+stores a keypair on first publish (no separate keygen on the magic path), then prints one line nudging `jet key backup`. The beginner's required action is the command they were already running. What stays genuinely hard is key LOSS/THEFT/ROTATION — the inherent cost of authenticity. Prior art is a warning: PyPI REMOVED GPG signing in 2023 (nobody verified, so publisher pain bought nothing); npm/Go/crates.io all moved authenticity OFF author-managed keys; Maven Central's mandatory GPG is the canonical 'publishing is painful' complaint. Lesson: never make key management mandatory or visible on the magic path. Bearing on the decision: this argues for A as an OPT-IN / non-blocking layer with SHA-256 checksum (B) as the always-on floor — `require_signed` stays an org policy, OFF by default — not a hard gate that refuses unsigned packages. That keeps A's unique win (offline authorship proof) while spending friction only on publishers who opt in. Full Owner Q&A block added to the D-PKGSIGN1 card.

questions.text: What is really the issue with full jai? Build systems allow arbitrary code execution, but this just keeps it within the language. Play devil's advocate & tell me what we would lose out on by going with option a vs full jai. Consider every level of use case (beginner/college student/enterprise/etc.)
questions.answer: Full writeup is on the D-METADEPTH1 ballot card as Owner Q5. Steel-manning C: one language/debugger/syntax (no second toolchain) and a genuinely higher ceiling — rewrite decls, schema-driven codegen, DSLs — that A (read + derive) gives up. BUT 'inside the language' only removes a TOOLCHAIN seam, not Jai's two real costs: (1) local reasoning dies — if any macro can rewrite any decl you can't read code and know what it does; grep/go-to-def/'what did it expand to' all degrade (the proc-macro tax), bending I3/I8 and D-CTCODEGEN1=A (generated code re-enters sema, never injected). (2) It's still arbitrary build-time code execution + non-reproducibility — identical whether in-language or in build.rs; keeping it in-language removes the very seam you'd sandbox/audit it through, so it makes supply-chain RISK worse, not better. By use case: BEGINNER loses ~nothing (and C only adds footguns — a struct no longer trustworthy at face value); LEARNER trades metaprogramming exercises for the guarantee that reading code = understanding it (A wins for learning the language, C only for learning metaprogramming); POWER USER loses custom rules/DSLs/schema-codegen — the genuine cost, mitigated by S56 derives + blessed first-class rules (#(net) effects enforce 'no panic in net', typestate enforces state rules) + the B rung (rejection-lint); ENTERPRISE flips entirely — frictionless idiomatic compile-time exec is exactly the xz/SolarWinds/npm-postinstall attack surface, so a Jai-style Jet gets banned or heavily sandboxed and reproducibility (D-CTEFFECT1) dies. Decisive point: A⊂B⊂C is a LADDER. A is the floor, not the ceiling — we can vote UP later (B for rejection rules, C only post-self-host) with no redesign, because nothing in A forecloses them; the reverse is impossible (you can't un-ship macros — the ecosystem locks you in, see Rust). So A is the only rung that is safe-by-default for beginners, auditable-by-default for enterprise, AND forward-compatible. Recommendation stays A; the live decision is how far up the ladder v1 goes (Owner Q1/Q2: ship B's rejection-lint now or defer).

questions.text: How does jai handle this? Show me a detailed comparison between jet & c3 so I can see what this looks like in practice. What about jai's "#run" directive? How do we do that in jet? How can we scope to a code block?
questions.answer: Full writeup on the D-CTMARKER1 ballot card as Owner Q3 (with a Jet↔C3 table and the Jai #run breakdown). Jai's #run does two jobs: (a) bake a compile-time value into the binary (X :: #run f();), and (b) a free-standing #run { … } block of arbitrary build-time statements that can even generate source via add_build_string — and it is UNGATED (any I/O, no reproducibility wall). Jet already has (a): a `comptime` binding IS #run-for-a-value (`comptime ICONS = pack(@embed("icons/"))`), but GATED — comptime runs only the curated pure-Core whitelist (D-CTCORE1), and world-touching effects are hashed-reproducible (Tier 1 @embed/find/fetch(…,sha256:)) or behind #Impure (Tier 2) per D-CTEFFECT1. Jai's source-generating add_build_string is exactly what D-CTCODEGEN1=A (generated code re-enters lexer→parser→sema, never injected) and D-METADEPTH1=A (reflection/derives only, no user macros) deliberately fence off — so Jet gives you #run's POWER (compute at build time, derive code) without #run's FOOTGUNS (ungated RCE + post-sema injection). C3 vs Jet in practice = the same program with C3's `$` sigil vs Jet's `comptime` keyword: $crc/comptime crc, $if/comptime if, $foreach/comptime loop — identical for everything EXCEPT a build-time statement BLOCK, which Jet does NOT have today (only comptime bindings + comptime if; 'no comptime blocks'). That is the genuine gap and the real thing to add. Sharpened recommendation: add a keyword-spelled `comptime { … }` block (Jet's gated equivalent of Jai's free-standing #run {}, consistent with comptime if) and reserve `$` for the metaprogramming SPLICE site only (rec C: $name = a comptime value woven into runtime/generated code) — Jai's full reach behind Jet's reproducible-by-default wall, no $if/comptime-if I8 fork. Added Owner Q4 to the card to pick the block form. Decision stays open.

1) This was more a request for comprehensive and native builtin support for inline assembly and easy way to see generated assembly from jet source

questions.answer:
Final integration: D-CODE-INSPECT2 recommends A: direct source assembly emission while preserving the ratified explicit capture workflow. B is the explicit alternative that removes retained capture. Fresh review found that capture was already ratified, not merely a new proposal; removing it must be an honest owner amendment.

The earlier Astra recommendation is preserved below as attributed design advice, not the final recommendation or ratification. The final source-view and three native-assembly ballots have completed independent beginner/adversarial review and pass the ballot readiness checker. Astra answer — openai-codex/gpt-6-astra. This is a design recommendation, not a claim that the proposed commands already ship.

1. Native inline assembly and generated assembly viewing are separate needs. Keep the ratified #FFI(asm), core.mem and audited #Unsafe gates. Complete typed operands/results, register directions/classes, constants, symbols, local control flow, machine effects, target facts and applicable native execution modes through that one compiler contract. For ordinary Jet, propose jet emit --asm FILE: compile current source when needed and show compiler-emitted assembly without starting the application or requiring a prior recording. Propose jet inspect code for exact existing artifacts or identified live code. Source compilation may still perform its authorized compile-time/build work. #3016 owns this viewer.

2. The earlier ballot put recording infrastructure in the way. Remove the proposed --capture-code, --run and --generation workflow from this revision. questions.text: Do not like either option. How is this handled elsewhere for other languages? I like the idea of one top level .jet folder that also includes things like build folder for anything generated by jet to keep things clean and tidy without polluting top level dir
questions.answer:
Yes. One top-level .jet directory is a reasonable design. My earlier ballot treated a local directory as clutter, but your concern is scattered directories, not one organized directory.

Other tools handle this in several ways:

- Rust/Cargo puts build outputs in workspace-root target/ by default. It separates profiles and target platforms below that root. [Cargo documentation](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/build-cache.html).
- Dart shares .dart_tool/ for project tool caches. Its build tools use .dart_tool/build/. Downloaded packages remain in a shared user cache. Not every Dart output lives in .dart_tool/. [Dart documentation](https://dart.dev/tools/pub/package-layout#project-specific-caching-for-tools).
- Java/Kotlin with Gradle uses .gradle/ for project caches and build/ for build products. Shared caches also exist under the user's home directory. [Gradle documentation](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/directory_layout.html).
- .NET offers an opt-in artifacts/ directory containing every project's build outputs, grouped by kind and project. This is the closest direct precedent for gathering build outputs under one configurable root. [.NET documentation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/sdk/artifacts-output).

I revised B to mean one top-level .jet directory for all default project-generated files, including .jet/build/, .jet/cache/, and .jet/generated/. Existing records, receipts, reports, and locks also remain below that root. Nested source files share the root rather than creating their own directories. Default top-level build/ and .jet-build/ disappear.

Generated does not mean disposable. Saved replay claims, required evidence, and reproducibility metadata keep their protection. Routine cleanup and version-control ignore rules must target disposable contents, not all of .jet. Shared downloads, user credentials, application data, and explicitly requested export destinations remain separate.

The retained limitation is write permission: required local build output needs a writable destination. Optional cache and history writes keep their existing best-effort behavior.

I now recommend the expanded B. I updated the ballot and card #3421, but left the decision open for your ratification. No generated files were moved or deleted. The comparisons come from official documentation read on 2026-09-15; they are not newly executed peer builds.

questions.text: Dont we already reserve/use dunders for compiler stuff in jet? Why not just use that as a namespace? then build info, package info, compiler info can all be dunders and not pollute user namespaces and still be shorter than compiler.{...} format?
questions.answer:
Short answer: yes, Jet already reserves every name that starts with two underscores, but only as hidden machine space, not as a public namespace. Writing `__build` or `__package` in your code today is error E0067 ("double-underscore names belong to the compiler and tools"). The compiler uses that space for generated names (`__jet_...`) and internal markers such as `__core_intrinsic`.

Using dunders for build, package, and compiler info would work and is shorter than `compiler.build.os`. The costs: the same visual lane would then hold both hidden internals and a public API, and the two reservation rules (D-SHAPE-DUNDER2 and D-NAME-SIGIL1) must be amended with a closed list such as `__compiler`, `__build`, `__package`. Python is the usual precedent, but Python dunders are user-visible hooks, not compiler facts.

This is already option B on the family ballot D-COMPILER-NS1 (`__compiler.build.os`, `__compiler.type(T)`). Since `prep if`, `prep fn`, and `<prep N: Int>` are now ratified, that ballot really decides how compiler facts are spelled. I added your other idea there as option D: `$build.os`, `$package.version`, `$type(T)`. The recommendation stays A (`compiler.build.os`) because these facts are rare, and rare things can afford a clear word (friction in proportion to how common something is). `$` also already means an environment variable in config files and was Jet's first, retired compile-time mark.

Evidence: crates/jet-lexer/src/Lexer/Scan.rs:624-634 (E0067); crates/jet-foundation/src/Syntax/predicates.rs:430-447 (every `__name` is reserved); crates/jet-foundation/src/Syntax.rs:62-64 (`__core_intrinsic` is compiler-only); Docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:6708-6720 (D-SHAPE-DUNDER2, D-NAME-SIGIL1); crates/jet-foundation/src/Syntax/core_surface.rs:126-141 (retired `$` compile-time mark); Docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:6818 (D-ONCE-DOLLAR1: `$NAME` is a config environment variable); https://docs.python.org/3/reference/datamodel.html#special-method-names.

questions.text: I like the idea of being safer with 6to4 and Teredo ipv6 being private but why would we NOT want to use IANA conforming registry like python other than it taking more upfront work?
questions.answer:
Use IANA, but for the right question. The IANA special-purpose registries answer "is this address globally reachable?". They do not answer "is it safe for my server to fetch?" (SSRF safety).

IANA marks 6to4 (2002::/16) and Teredo (2001::/32) as N/A, not False. So treating them as not public is a stricter safety policy, not an IANA fact. Python's ipaddress follows IANA plus its own exceptions: current docs mark 2002::/16 and most of 2001::/23 private, and gh-113171 fixed missing ranges in 2024. The tables change over time. NAT64 (64:ff9b::/96) is globally reachable per IANA, yet it can reach private IPv4 hosts.

So one overloaded "public" meaning is the real risk. Recommendation: `is_global` follows a dated, versioned copy of the IANA tables (reachability); a separate `is_public_destination` policy, stricter (denies 6to4, Teredo, NAT64-to-private, and so on), guards HTTP fetches and provider downloads.

Evidence: Core/net/ip.jet:62-83,448-455; crates/jet-net/src/lib.rs:651-713; https://www.iana.org/assignments/iana-ipv6-special-registry/iana-ipv6-special-registry.xhtml; https://www.iana.org/assignments/iana-ipv4-special-registry/; https://docs.python.org/3/library/ipaddress.html#ipaddress.IPv4Address.is_global; https://github.com/python/cpython/issues/113171; https://github.com/python/cpython/pull/118177.

questions.text: I think parallel default wouldn't be a terrible idea with magic for beginners but it could make debugging difficult and make things less predictable with effective data races. So we would need a non default version as well for full expert control.
questions.answer:
Agree, and parallel by default does not create data races here. The scheduler (ResourceSchedule) only runs systems together when their checked access sets do not overlap: reads with reads, writes on disjoint resources or regions. Unknown aliases are treated as conflicts, and a system that needs parallel access with unknown or conflicting writes is rejected. Tests cover read/read, overlap, unknown alias, conflicting writes, and disjoint regions.

What can still vary: which system finishes first, the order of emitted commands, events, and logs, and float sums that combine in a different order. Fix these by merging commands and events in a fixed order (system declaration order) at the end of each stage.

Expert control, using the choose-explain-pin rule: Auto groups disjoint systems; `jet inspect` or `schedule.explain()` shows why; a Serial pin runs one at a time for debugging and fully repeatable runs; a Parallel pin fails compilation when facts become incomplete or conflicting. Bevy offers similar ambiguity reports.

Note: game callbacks still run directly today; D-SYSSCHED1 is open.

Evidence: crates/jet-foundation/src/ResourceSchedule.rs:62-114,289-306,772-829,1377-1497,1941-2017; crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/CoreLib/Top/Game.rs:303-352; Docs/proposals/memory-model-foundations-2026-09-27.md:376-392; https://docs.rs/bevy/latest/bevy/ecs/schedule/.

questions.text: I want to support both reactive & timed, please update accordingly
questions.answer:
Done. Option A is now both, sharing one key queue.

Timed: term.read_key_within(wait) returns a key, or None when the wait runs out. Closed input is an error, so a loop cannot spin.
Reactive: term.keys() returns a Receiver<Key> that joins the wait table beside process.signals and after arms. This is the same shape as the ratified D-CORE-PROCSIGNAL1=A.

Both calls take keys from one queue that #Live owns. A receiver reads input only while the program waits on it, so each key goes to exactly one reader and none is lost. That removes a trap in Rust crossterm, which offers both styles but forbids mixing them. It also keeps one mechanism (I8): the timed call is the beginner path, and the receiver is the expert path.

Options are re-lettered. B is receiver only, where a time limit is an after arm. C is the earlier timed-only option. The earlier poll-then-read option is dropped, because the timed call already returns the key in one step. Recommendation: A. Its one loss is that two spellings can wait for a key with a time limit.
