questions.text: why would this be a side effect? it is a piece of context implicitly included in all functions? i dont see why that would be an environmental effect or otherwise it is a core part of the language itself
questions.answer:
You're right that it isn't an environmental effect. Reading the context touches no file, socket or device, and it needs no permission. Under today's rules a package never grants it.
The row entry tracks a dependency, not a power. A function that reads context.deadline or context.thread depends on an input its arguments don't show. Three checks rely on knowing that:
1. #Memo caches a result by its arguments (E0938). A memoized function that reads the deadline would hand back a result computed under a different deadline.
2. A pure -[]> function promises its result depends only on its arguments.
3. A C callback has no task context to read.
The effect row is simply the tool Jet already has for inferring "what does this function depend on" through calls, function values, generics and traits. So the earlier votes reused it, plus a package deny.
If you see context as part of the language itself, I've added option F to the ballot. Context reads never appear in rows and aren't effects, so nobody writes, grants or denies them, and a function with a written `-[IO]>` row can read context freely. The compiler still infers context reads internally, so pure, #Memo and C-callback functions are still refused with a clear message.
F drops the package-level deny and amends the read-effect clauses of D-JAI-CONTEXT1 and D-CONTEXT1. A to E all keep the visible Context row; they differ only in where it is declared. F's cross-family adversarial review hasn't been done yet.

questions.text: What would be the tradeoffs of encoding & compression? wouldnt that be part of building a binary anyway? We are trying to win against every other language and hit hand optimized machine code level for bin size, speed, performance, etc. How do other languages handle this? Sweeping it under the rug rather than fixing it doesnt seem like a good solution
questions.answer:
You're right, and the recommendation (A, a report) was wrong. Reporting the cost leaves it in place. Here is the full answer, and what changes.

1. This program shouldn't carry the data at all. It only uses the two lengths. Hand-written machine code for it prints 100000000 and holds no string bytes. Zig, Rust and C++ get there as well: the length of a constant is itself a constant, so the bytes nothing reads are never emitted. Jet today stores both 50 MB runs and then rescans them at run time to count characters. That's an optimizer defect, not a policy question, so it gets fixed without a ballot: #6769 c4 (fold the length) and a new c5 (bytes no run-time code reads are not emitted; this program's binary must come out about as small as the version that reads the size at run time, 136 KB).

2. Data the program really reads goes in read-only pages, raw. That's what every peer does (C, C++, Rust, Go, Zig): constants sit uncompressed in .rodata. The kernel maps those pages from the file on demand, so only the pages actually touched use RAM, they're shared between processes running the same binary, and they can be dropped and reloaded without swap. Today Jet puts them in writable .data, which loses the sharing; #6769 c3 fixes that.

3. Compression is not part of building a binary in any mainstream toolchain. Compilers and linkers don't compress code or data; the one exception is debug sections (`--compress-debug-sections=zstd`), which never load at run time. Packers like UPX are a separate, opt-in step. The trade-offs:
- Size: large wins on repetitive data (50 MB of "x" compresses to a few bytes), about 2-4x on typical tables, nothing on data that's already dense.
- Speed: the data must be decoded before use. zstd decodes at roughly 1-2 GB/s per core and LZ4 at about 4 GB/s, so 50 MB costs tens of milliseconds at startup or at first use.
- Memory: decoded data lives in private anonymous memory. It's always resident, counted in RSS, never shared between processes, and can't be dropped without swap. Raw read-only data can be all of those things.
So compression swaps disk bytes for RAM and startup time. Under the gate (Jet must match hand-optimized code on cycles and bytes), it loses for data that is read, except where disk or download size is the actual target, such as embedded or web.

4. How the peers handle huge compile-time values: C++ can't keep a compile-time heap string at run time at all (allocations during constant evaluation must be freed before evaluation ends), and clang and GCC cap evaluation steps. Rust's const evaluation can't build a String. Zig can build a large array at compile time, needs an explicit evaluation budget for long loops, and stores the result raw. None compress it.

What I'm doing: c3, c4 and c5 on #6769 are built as fixes, with no vote. I'm withdrawing this ballot's current options and rewriting it around the only real choice left: whether Jet offers compressed storage for large read data, for size-targeted builds only (embedded, web), and how that's switched on. It comes back to you with measured numbers for each option, after an adversarial review.

questions.text: typeid seems like a solid direction but needs downsides engineered away
questions.answer: Agreed, and revised. The ballot keeps TypeId and removes four of its five costs. Type text computed from data, types only the app declares, and lists of a struct made earlier in the same build now go through one lookup, meta.find_type("Point"). It returns the compiler's identity for that one type, or None, and the text is never pasted into source, so "I64, extra: String" can no longer add a field. Written types use the two spellings a Type value already has: a bare name such as String, or braces for anything else, such as TypeId{[String]} or TypeId{fn(Int) -> Int}. So function types no longer need an alias. The checker work is now listed as build work, not a cost, and the Type-versus-TypeId split is older than this ballot. One cost remains, because the text only exists while the build runs: a type named by text is checked then. The lookup returns None for a miss, so the build must handle it. Written and reflected types never take this path. One note: the lookup loosens the ratified sentence that no string can make a TypeId. It can only find a type the compiler already declared, so it can't forge one.

questions.text: i thought jet tuples ARE positional with optional names? is that not the latest guidance? also, the recommended option does not have downsides engineered away so it is immediately rejected on both grounds
questions.answer: No. The latest guidance is the pair of record votes you ratified on 2026-11-06. Every group of values names its members and is written in braces, {min: 1, max: 9}. Paren tuples retire, and a destructure binds by name: {min, max}: bounds(xs). Written member order is now part of the type and decides comparison and printing. Neither vote adds positional binding or optional names. Neither is built yet: on today's compiler the brace spelling is still a parse error, and the old paren form (left: 7, right: -9) still works and destructures by name. You were right that the ballot was stale. It predated both votes, and with them two of A's costs disappear. Parts keep the plugin's order, so part10 no longer sorts before part2, and a one-part tuple becomes the one-member record {part0: 7}. The ballot now says record for Jet's side and tuple only for the plugin's positional group. One cost remains, and no named-only design can remove it: the plugin supplies no names, so the host types the names it wants once, {part0: left, part1: right}: guest.pair(). Writing {left, right} gets an error whose fix writes that line, and jet fix applies it. If you want Jet records to be positional with optional names everywhere, that reopens the brace-record vote for every program, so it needs its own ballot. Say so and it will be drafted; this question then goes away.

questions.text: the terminology youre using is confusing me, but either way, the downsides are not engineered away for the recommended option, therefore rejected
questions.answer: Sorry for the jargon. The ballot now uses two plain terms. A script variable is a value the script's own lines set up, such as count := 0. An extra parameter replaces what the draft called a hidden input. The whole idea is now one sentence: for each script variable a helper uses, Jet gives the helper a parameter with that name, passed by name, and the script fills it in at every call. That reuses Jet's existing label-only parameters, so tests can now call every helper by passing the variables themselves: note("fig", count: tally, limit: 3). Today's compiler already runs that form in a test. The same labeled call in the script's own lines currently crashes the compiler, a separate bug the ballot now lists. Hover shows the full signature. Two former costs were ordinary Jet rules that apply to written parameters too, so they are no longer listed. The one place a script and run: fn would differ is a closure bug, now listed separately. Two small costs remain, each kept for safety. A helper that changes a script variable can only be called directly, not handed to each or run as a task, because a function value must not hide a change or race. The error rewrites the call as a loop. Methods in a script can't use script variables, because a method can be called through a trait; the error offers a helper function.

questions.text: please do your best to engineer away the remaining downsides for the recommended option
questions.answer: Revised. A's four costs are down to two, and both are costs hand-written code pays too. Almost-runs staying raw is no longer listed, since it never makes a file bigger than today. The missing Core encoder is now part of A: core.archive.zstd gains a real encoder, so an author compresses a table at build time and decodes it at run time with no outside tool. A stored run now stays a short recipe for its length, loops, slices, comparisons, searches, hashing, printing and copies. Only handing the whole value to a function that takes [U8], or to foreign code, fills it into memory once, as hand-written code would. Irregular tables, which real lookup tables are, still stay full size unless the author compresses them. Compressing them automatically would cost decode time and unshared memory on every run. jet inspect decisions --estimate now shows what each large table would save, so the author decides with numbers.

Valen (https://verdagon.dev/blog/golden-spike-reviving-vale-valen) replaces Vale's generational references with Nick Smith's group borrowing (https://verdagon.dev/blog/group-borrowing; original gist https://gist.github.com/nmsmith/cdaa94aa74e8e0611221e65db8e41f7b). Mutable aliases to the same object stay valid; a mutation invalidates only references into its independently replaceable contents (child groups); signatures name which groups a function may mutate. Smith reports Mojo 1.0 adopted a variation as 'Interior Origins' (unverified here). For Jet this would let attack(&a, &d) accept the same entity twice without a runtime check, but it relaxes the exclusivity of & and needs an owner ballot after #4247 ships the runtime-check baseline and a paired cell exists.
