papercuts.resolution: Fixed on master: both stack-overflow tests (failed_action_replaces_stale_rebuild_provenance, action_generated_jet_reenters_frontend_before_runtime_codegen) now pass, re-run today single-threaded

papercuts.text: master has pre-existing jet-pkg-model unit test failures unrelated to manifest work (confirmed on master HEAD in main checkout, cargo test -p jet-pkg-model): LintPolicy::tests::undenied_lint_stays_a_warning (looks like a genuine test bug -- asserts empty output but its deny list includes the exact lint code it fires), Manifest::tests::latest_edition_is_last_supported_and_drives_banner, Overlay::tests::keyed_overrides_merge_typed_environment_by_priority, PhpBind::tests (3), PowerShellBind::tests::rejects_generated_powershell_helper_and_alias_collisions, plus an apparently-flaky FFI::http_server_tls_persist_tests::session_preserves_pipelined_leftover_bytes.
papercuts.resolution: Superseded: jet-pkg-model tests now fail earlier (Prelude Email.rs JetAbsent compile error); tracked as card #1608 including re-check of the originally named unit failures

papercuts.text: rustfmt not on PATH in either 'nix develop' or 'nix develop .#full' devshell (cargo fmt / rustfmt --check both fail with 'not found'); D-CI2's rustfmt gate can't be wired until flake.nix adds the rustfmt component.
papercuts.resolution: Fixed: pkgs.rustfmt added to both default and full devshells in flake.nix; rustfmt now on PATH via jet-env

papercuts.text: tower card criteria has no reopen/unmeet verb — once --meet sets a criterion to met, only --verify can move it further; a builder who discovers a criterion was falsely marked met (found via fresh review) has no CLI way to set it back to open, only to overwrite evidence text while status stays met.
papercuts.resolution: Implemented: tower card criteria --unmeet n --evidence why --by X reopens a falsely-met criterion (clears metBy/verifiedBy); CLI + API + tests

papercuts.text: jet run caches per-file under ~/.cache/jet/run as well as ~/.cache/jet/build; clearing only build still serves a stale quick-run result and looks like a real failure
papercuts.resolution: Documented: verify skill fresh-binary-smoke section + memory now say rm -rf ~/.cache/jet (build AND run) — clearing only build serves a stale quick-run result

papercuts.text: /tmp is tmpfs (RAM+swap-backed). An e4 agent set CARGO_TARGET_DIR=/tmp/jet-e4-target (15GB) plus 5GB scratchpad targets/logs; this filled 24GB swap and caused kernel OOM kills on the owner's machine. Never put cargo target dirs or multi-GB logs in /tmp; use a disk path and clean up session outputs.
papercuts.resolution: Fixed: jet-env rejects /tmp CARGO_TARGET_DIR, AGENTS.md documents the tmpfs trap, scripts/agent/tmp-guard.sh auto-cleans and blocks under memory pressure

papercuts.text: tests/comptime_diff.rs numbered rustc artifacts by per-test case index, so two tests both using index 0 raced for one output path and failed as a fake I2 miscompile; fixed on bd3/reader

CARGO_TARGET_DIR=<main>/target shared across worktrees caused a real build break (E0599: no variant ComptimeSplice for jet::AST::Expr in Source/CmdProve.rs) even though the variant exists in my worktree's own crates/jet-foundation/src/AST/expressions.rs — reproducible on retry, not transient. Likely stale rlib reuse across worktrees with divergent AST enum shapes. Fell back to the worktree-local target dir to unblock.

Shared CARGO_TARGET_DIR across worktrees poisons builds: concurrent cargo from worktrees/dollar and worktrees/profile made my build fail with 'no variant ComptimeSplice in jet_foundation::AST::Expr' on unmodified code. Different sources, one target dir, whoever writes last wins. Agents need per-worktree target dirs.

Sharing CARGO_TARGET_DIR across git worktrees lets another worktree's build replace target/debug/jet and shared dep artifacts mid-session: a stale binary made a working sema fix look broken, and a lib test failed with 'no variant named ComptimeName in jet_lexer::AST::Expr' from another branch's artifacts. Build and run in one command, or verify the binary is yours.

git stash push -- <one-file> with no local changes to that file reports 'No local changes to save' but a following git stash pop still pops whatever is on TOP of the stash stack (an unrelated old stash from a prior session) and can conflict — hit this in the main repo's stash list (foreign-eval-builtins, foreign-wip-during-1478-abi-fix, cleanup-session entries pre-date this session). Resolved safely by restoring the one conflicted file to HEAD; stash entries left untouched. Avoid stash push/pop entirely when just wanting a scoped before/after diff — use git show HEAD:<path> instead.

tower CLI resolves .tower from cwd, so running it from a worktree silently reads the worktree's stale tracked copy instead of the canonical main board; agents in worktrees must export TOWER_DATA=<main>/plugins/tower/.tower

A worktree whose branch predates the canonical-board redirect ships a vendored plugins/tower/app/paths.mjs without canonicalDataDir, so tower card add run from that worktree writes to the stale worktree .tower and mints a card number that already exists on the real board, with no warning. Run the main checkout's plugins/tower/tower.mjs for every board write from a worktree.
tower card criteria <ref> --list errors with 'unknown flag for card: --list' although the CLI help documents it; workaround is card show <ref>, which prints the same checklist
tower help advertises 'card criteria --unmeet n' but cli.mjs has no unmeet flag — falsely-met criteria cannot be reopened via CLI

Full-workspace cargo check for jet-sema blocked repeatedly (multiple minutes) by a concurrent agent's in-flight jet-comptime refactor (DataLite.rs deletion / core_calls.rs signature change) leaving apply_data_line_call call sites mismatched (E0061) — not my card's files, can't fix without stepping on their WIP.
tower card has no 'show' or 'log' subcommand and no --text/--note flag; a card log line is 'tower card update <ref> --by X --log "..."', which tower help does not list under card update.

Repo build was red/flaky mid-task from concurrent wave-6 edits to jet-foundation/jet-lexer/jet-parser (TokKind::KwWhile/KwFor missing, Type::Quantity non-exhaustive matches) landing and clearing repeatedly; unrelated to cards #1660/#1747/#1751. A concurrent agent also swept my uncommitted files for those 3 cards into commit 52a7573fb via a broad add-all, so 'never touch another task's paths' was violated by someone else, not me.

tests/decisions.rs::ratified_decisions_enforced fails: S57 in SURFACE_IN_SYNTAX_RS has no matching /// S57 doc comment in Syntax.rs — core_surface.rs COMPTIME_MARK now carries D-META-STAGE1=B instead (metaprogramming rework). Pre-existing, unrelated to cards #1668-1670.

tests/compute_views.rs AOT tests (tensor_slice_and_mutable_view_run_through_aot, tensor_stored_range_uses_the_same_owned_and_mutable_window_law) fail with 'Tensor mutable view requires exclusive backing storage' panic (exit 70); JIT (jet run) produces correct output for the same source. Unrelated to card #1662 (Compute.rs last touched 2026-08-04, no compute-views/Tensor-refcount code in this diff).
card criteria --list is documented but rejected by the current CLI flag table; plain card criteria <ref> lists items

tower card criteria --list documented in tower help but rejected as unknown flag at runtime; no free-text 'tower card log' command exists either -- progress notes have to go through criteria --meet --evidence or card update --body.

FFI/lowlevel examples (ffi, inline_asm, inline_c) falsely decline E0956 when 'jet run' is invoked outside scripts/agent/jet-env's nix PATH (no cc/rustc/clang) - backend.rs's bind_bundle_ffi can't build the runtime bridge cdylib and silently falls back to the interpreter, which lacks ExternCall. Same binary passes cleanly under jet-env. Hit repeatedly on card #1763 (bd14/bd15/bd16/orchestrator probes); always reproduce FFI/lowlevel examples via jet-env, never a bare shell.
tower help documents card criteria --list, but tower rejects the flag; card show was required to inspect criteria.
rustfmt --check could not run: rustfmt is not installed in the sandbox; no formatter proof available.
scripts/agent/jet-env rg fails before command: read-only ~/.cache/nix/fetcher-cache-v4.sqlite; direct rg fallback used.
tower card criteria #1687 --list rejected documented --list flag as unknown; card show still exposes criteria.
Managed sandbox blocks scripts/agent/jet-env at the Nix daemon socket; cached Nix-store cargo/rustc fallback required for checks and proofs.
scripts/agent/jet-env cannot connect to /nix/var/nix/daemon-socket/socket in the sandbox; focused project commands need approved escalation.
sandboxed scripts/agent/jet-env cannot reach /nix/var/nix/daemon-socket; focused proof requires escalation.
scripts/agent/jet-env cannot reach the Nix daemon socket in this sandbox; nix develop --offline is the working project-command fallback.
scripts/agent/jet-env cannot reach the Nix daemon in the managed sandbox; elevated retry is policy-rejected, so local cargo fallback is required.
Jet proof commands are blocked in this sandbox: jet-env cannot access the nix daemon socket, escalation is rejected, and host cargo is unavailable.
tower help documents card criteria REF --list, but that exact command is rejected as an unknown tower card flag.
The pinned jet-env shell exposes neither rustfmt nor cargo fmt, so an agent cannot run a scoped Rust formatting check there.
scripts/agent/jet-env cargo check cannot reach the Nix daemon socket under sandbox; local cargo fallback lacks a complete linker/sysroot.

Worktree-isolated agents (spawned already sandboxed to .claude/worktrees/agent-*) cannot do git ops in the shared builder worktree: any bash command that cd's to .claude/worktrees/builder and runs git is hard-refused by the sandbox ('git operations must target its own worktree'), even for builder-sync.sh --release itself if cd'd there first. builder-sync.sh succeeds (claims the lock) but is then unusable for git in that session. Card #1850: fell back to the agent's own isolated worktree per the exit-75 contingency, and released the builder lock via the script's bare 'rm -f' path (no cd needed) so it didn't sit claimed.

tower card add/update --blocked-by accepts '#N' and the lane renders 'Blocked by #N', but lint's orphan-blockers rule only resolves internal card ids, so every '#N' blocker reads as dangling; pass the card id from 'card show --json'.

codex workers launched in a linked worktree under .claude/worktrees cannot reach the nix daemon socket (EPERM on /nix/var/nix/daemon-socket/socket) so every scripts/agent/jet-env command dies before cargo starts, and git metadata is read-only so the required commit fails. Hit three workers in one session (cards 1801, 1864, 1650/1775/1844). Workers then report fallback-toolchain greens the orchestrator cannot trust, or leave work staged and uncommitted. The sandbox writable_roots entry for the main .git does not cover a linked worktree's own git dir.

Adding /nix/var/nix to a codex worker's sandbox_workspace_write.writable_roots breaks bwrap outright: every shell launch dies with 'bwrap: Cant mkdir /nix/var/nix/.git: Permission denied', including pwd. One worker burned 55k tokens and ran nothing. It was an attempted fix for the daemon-socket EPERM that blocks jet-env in worker sandboxes; it makes things strictly worse. Known-good roots are the repo .git plus ~/.cache/nix, which still hit the socket EPERM intermittently but recover.

codex exec workers launched with cwd inside .claude/worktrees/* sometimes apply_patch by absolute path into the MAIN clone (two lanes in one wave); worktree .git pointer resolves there. Briefs now carry an absolute-path ban + orchestrator must diff-check the main tree before every merge.
codex-rescue task agent deterministically fails immediately: configured model claude-sonnet-4-0 returns 404; seven parallel read-only milestone prep jobs all failed identically
codex-rescue task dispatch deterministically fails before work because it requests unavailable model claude-sonnet-4-0; ten parallel lanes failed identically
task codex-rescue dispatch deterministically fails before running with unavailable model claude-sonnet-4-0; direct codex exec -p luna works.
verify/check instructions invoke check-unsafe-ratchet.mjs --check, but the script rejects --check; plain invocation is the actual check mode.
Codex 0.144.5 repeatedly logs 'failed to load models cache: missing field base_instructions at line 95 column 5' on Luna launches; runs continue, but every transcript gains error noise.
Every Luna codex exec warns twice that agent role default lacks a description; fix ~/.codex agent role config to remove deterministic launch noise.
card list --epoch/--milestone --json deterministically exits 5 with jq-style 'cannot use null as iterable' when current E3 card data contains nullable fields; blocks queue inspection.
codex-rescue task agent deterministically fails before work: configured model claude-sonnet-4-0 returns 404 not_found; use direct Luna codex exec fallback.
codex-rescue task agent fails immediately with 404 model claude-sonnet-4-0; use working default task agent or direct Luna runtime instead.
codex-rescue subagent fails immediately with 404 model claude-sonnet-4-0, preventing fresh milestone review; agent profile needs a live model.

codex/Luna account usage limit exhausted until 2026-08-19 23:30; the burndown skill mandates Luna as the sole implementer, so all five dispatches died in 10s. Implementation fleet switched to Claude task subagents under the same source-only discipline (no builds, orchestrator owns proof).

Corpus-gate and three-way batteries write per-stem AOT crate scratch into TMPDIR, which is /tmp and RAM-backed tmpfs here; 745 dirs reached 26G of 31G and drove swap to 22G of 24G. jet-env rejects a /tmp CARGO_TARGET_DIR but nothing redirects the nix-shell TMPDIR. Export TMPDIR to a disk path such as ~/.cache/jet-scratch before long gate runs; scripts/agent/tmp-guard.sh reclaims most of it after the fact.
codex-rescue harness agent type broken: every spawn fails instantly with 404 model: claude-sonnet-4-0 not found; fell back to scout agents for research fan-out
card add minted blank criterion rows on #2056-#2061 (criteria arrays with empty text) — closure guard becomes unsatisfiable-as-intended; the CLI/store should reject empty criterion text at add time.

scripts/agent/jet-env run from a cwd outside the repo prints '/tmp/nix-shell.XXXX: line 2233: <cwd>/scripts/agent/clean-nix-tmp.sh: No such file or directory' on every invocation because it resolves the cleanup script relative to cwd, not the repo. Harmless but noisy; hits every agent that runs jet-env against scratch dirs.

lane-dispatch.mjs brief could not target sidequest cards: cards() hardcoded card list --epoch $LANE_EPOCH and sidequest cards carry no epoch, so explicit card numbers returned (nothing to brief). Fixed in-session with LANE_EPOCH=all support.

Full ballot adversarial summaries cannot satisfy both contracts: store.mjs requires the two-sentence Author/Adversarial model-family prefix and also caps every reviewPass at two sentences, leaving no sentence for the evidence summary required by tower-ballot/SKILL.md.

tower decision add linked D-TYPEDSQL-SINK1 to planning card c0gsgsir but left the card in planning, while tower-ballot/SKILL.md says the card flips to deciding automatically; a manual card update was required.

scripts/agent/jet-env bash tools/ci/test-compiled-workload-gate.sh deterministically fails its Node stdin canary with ENOENT stat '-~/Projects/Github/jet' because the script reads process.argv[1] instead of argv[2].

scripts/agent/jet-env env TMPDIR=$HOME/.cache/jet-test-scratch node tools/ci/compiled-workload-runner.mjs deterministically rejected the mandated disk scratch because it compared scratch against os.tmpdir(), which honors TMPDIR and became the same disk path; fixed the guard to reject Linux /tmp specifically.

tools/ci/compiled-workload-runner.mjs passed node --check and its self-check but every production run crashed at startup because jetToolInfo and jetToolVersion were referenced without definitions; restored both from the canonical toolchainIdentity helper.

tools/ci/compiled-workload-runner.mjs staged every runtime argv=input-root fixture inside the Jet package before compilation while peer builds received no input; systems-file-index then failed E1334 on its hostile symlink tree before measurement. Fixed staging so only the declared build-input authority embeds input at compile time.

scripts/agent/proof-parallel.sh documents mixing SUITE and --crate targets, but cargo test --no-run applies each --test name to every -p crate and fails deterministically: no test target named fresh_agent_t4 in jet-foundation. Split suite/crate build invocations internally.

scripts/agent/jet-env cargo test --test build_entry deterministically reports E3505 because the default devShell omits pkgs.bubblewrap even though build-entry tests require it; flake.nix adds bubblewrap only to devShells.full.

scripts/agent/check-agent-doc-flags.mjs deterministically rejects the documented scripts/agent/core-conformance.mjs --check invocation because its static flag scanner detects no accepted flags for that script, although --check is the script's actual interface.

The HTML skill checker rejects ordinary source-citation hyperlinks as external resources: .agents/skills/html/scripts/check.mjs:67 matches any http(s) string, including <a href="https://compcert.org/man/manual001.html">. Running its documented command on the eight foundations-and-trust pages flags all seven citation-bearing areas; exact argv/output is in ~/.cache/jet-luna/foundations-20260904/html-checker.initial.json. Citations are required by the report contract and are not loaded asset dependencies. Keep citation links; distinguish actual script/style/font/image dependencies in this check.

HTML checker proseRun at .agents/skills/html/scripts/check.mjs:53 crosses paragraph/container boundaries. Four 45-word paragraphs arranged as two separate sibling pairs produce a false three-paragraph wall: regex captures contain 1,2,1 paragraph elements. The corrected 01-foundations report has zero actual long sibling triples in Chromium, yet the documented checker still flags it. Exact checker argv/output: ~/.cache/jet-luna/foundations-20260904/html-checker.corrected.json; minimal fixture result and actual DOM evidence: prose-check-counterexample.json in the same directory. Count real sibling elements rather than allowing a capture to span multiple paragraphs.

scripts/agent/jet-env node scripts/agent/check-skill-consolidation.mjs fails with SKILL CHECK FAIL: orchestration OMP-first rule is missing. checkAuthority pins an old exact sentence, although docs/agents/orchestration.md currently mandates OMP task/hub. This is a prose-matching false positive, not a missing dispatch rule. Addressed with the B7 checker integration on #2931; do not rewrite the gated policy file to satisfy the stale sentence.

scripts/agent/jet-env node scripts/agent/dx-benchmark-matrix.mjs --check --manifest tools/agent-eval/dx/manifest.json exits 78: SETUP: dx benchmark matrix: games references unknown profile unreal. The canonical manifest lists that comparator but has no matching profile. Relocation preserves the profile table; this prevents benchmark qualification, not file loading.

scripts/agent/jet-env node scripts/agent/fresh-agent-domain-run.mjs --check --manifest tools/agent-eval/dx/manifest.json --capsule tools/agent-eval/jet-context-capsule.md --llms llms.text exits 78: SETUP: assert is not defined. validateScenario and validateMethodTask call assert without importing it. Added node:assert/strict during the cleanup consumer smoke; recording the tooling defect rather than silently bypassing it.

Two user-authorized direct Claude reviews of the FFI report and ballots timed out with exit 124, at 240 seconds and 150 seconds. The retry disabled MCP integrations and hooks; it ended error_during_execution/aborted_streaming without reviewer analysis. Full ballots remain drafts. Exact receipts are ~/.cache/jet-luna/ffi-20260905/adversarial-review-first.json and adversarial-review.json. Cause is unverified; do not count these as completed reviews.

E0113 for `fn half(n: Int) -> Int { n / 2 }` says "promises to return Int, but this returns Fraction" with Fix "Use Int here"; the fix should name the integer-division spelling or conversion. Observed 2026-09-28, mine-for-jet playlist run.
E0107 for `core.files.read(...)` without an import suggests "Add use core as core"; the natural fix is `use core.files` then `files.read`. Observed 2026-09-28, mine-for-jet playlist run.

E1803 Why prints raw key=value facts (required_effects=...; granted_effects=...; undecided_effects=...) and the terminal prompt prints a JSON array: authority required for ["FS","FS.Read"]. Plain prose would read better. Observed 2026-09-28, mine-for-jet playlist run.

briefings.title: Gaps against hand-written code: every identified root (2026-11-11 late evening)
briefings.body:
# Gaps against hand-written code: every identified root (2026-11-11, late evening)

This revision replaces briefing0o7180b. Every number is measured unless marked as an estimate. Nothing below has landed yet: each fix is staged or held, and lands only on a measured win under the paired rule at the end.

## 1. Hot-loop instructions (CodegenCeiling kernels)

Jet against hand-written, in loop instructions: list_sum 254/5, gather 273/8, point 213/9, collatz 180/11, byte_count 119/7, stride 71/6.

|#|Root|Cost (list_sum / gather)|Fix|
|---|---|---|---|
|R1|Versioning re-versions its own fallback loop after inlining: three guarded copies plus the original|132 / 120|G9: list_sum 254→122, gather 273→153, about −40% on every kernel. Held; re-judged under the paired rule|
|R2|The cold bounds-stop path (19 instructions) is laid out inside the loop body|0 / 76|next SUB; G12 and G14 move fail arms out of hot code in general|
|R3|Each pass re-runs big-integer guards on the index and the sum, because `i += 1` isn't accepted as a stepped index|42 / 42|next SUB|
|R4|An error return after `ret` jumps back into the epilogue and forms a false loop|10 / 10, in every kernel|next SUB|
|R5|The fallback loop spills to stack slots and tests the same values twice|about 31 / 40|after R2|
|R6|The length is reloaded every pass|4 / 8|last|
|R7|The exact-integer fallback is a second copy of the loop, where hand code uses one `jo` to a shared cold path|the remaining gap|design in progress|

After R1–R4 the estimate is list_sum about 81 and gather about 40. Reaching 5 and 8 needs R7. The gate itself doesn't change.

Other code-generation roots, each with a staged fix:

- G10r2: r8 and r9 don't hold values across exact-integer paths, causing extra spills.
- G12/G14: fail arms are laid out in hot code, and aggregate copies read every field.
- G13: short byte runs become text through a store-forwarding stall.
- G15: `||` and `&&` chains build a boolean instead of branching once per link.
- G17: a one-byte find runs the general search.
- G18: a runtime stop that never returns is treated as a call.
- G19: a jcc that only skips a jmp. It caused 45% of regexlogscan's branch misses, and the +7.5% regression.
- G22: inlining weighs cold fail paths as hot.
- G25: the overflow check on `x + 1` stays when a dominating `x < y` rules it out.
- G33: a multiply by a constant loads the constant into a register first.
- G16/G21: time parsing boxes an Option needlessly and doesn't inline a two-digit helper.
- G11: slices of unchanged text are allocated and copied, where they could be frame views.

## 2. Binary size (hello: 31,439 B against hand-written 1,453 B with the same features)

38 bytes are the program. The rest is the runtime floor every program links.

|Root|Hand (B)|Jet (B)|Fix|
|---|---:|---:|---|
|The crash receipt writer is reached through overflow checks that can't fire|0|12,080|G23|
|The fault report maps the executable to find a build ID that is at a fixed address|858|3,584|G26, about −1.3 KB|
|A startup refusal path for stops that can't happen in a one-thread start|0|2,501|G30|
|A 12 KiB stdout buffer, a TCGETS probe and an exit flush, though hello's print writes directly|82|1,827|G27, about −1.6 KB, −12 KiB RSS and −2 syscalls|
|A general-purpose out-of-memory writer|259|1,662|G31|
|Argument registration through globals|78|824|not yet staged|
|Every numeric stop text is linked into every module|—|about 4 KB|G32|
|Data that no function reaches is kept|—|—|G20|

The call-graph estimate for G23+G26+G27 is about 21.5 KB of code down to about 7.4 KB. Not yet measured.

Three size items change behavior and will go on owner ballots:

- the 3,832 B gap before the code page, which keeps code on its own page;
- the test-read recorder armed at every start (468 B plus an environment scan);
- the crash receipt and fault report (14.6 KB), which only a new public flag such as `--minimal` could drop.

## 3. Run-time memory

- hello maps a 12 KiB stdout buffer it never uses (G27).
- Per-program peak memory against hand-written code hasn't been rooted for any other cell yet.

## 4. Compile time and compiler memory

A cold script costs about 1.8 s and 250 MB against the shell's 30 ms.

- All of Core is loaded: a bare `math.sqrt` pulled 1,785 functions from 39 modules. G8Scope-38..45 make loading follow use. With -45 the count is 1,364 functions and the check takes 734 ms instead of 915 ms. The target is a few dozen functions.
- Parsing runs at 136k lines/s, about 220× short of 30M. Lexing is 45% of parsing, and float bignum conversion is 22% of lexing.
- `jet check` peaks at 6–9 GB on the compiler roots. Its cause isn't found yet. #6527 c11 caps a root at 3 GB and is G8Scope-3's next item.

## Not yet rooted

Only the seven kernels, hello, sieve (whose +16.8% was startup and page-fault variance with identical code) and regexlogscan are rooted. nbody, wordfreq, csvtransform and the other cells are measured against hand-written references but not yet broken down.

## Proof integrity tonight

Four false-credit vectors have been found and closed:

1. b4–b7 deferred proofs were credited without being read (90 credits). The jq fix and a canary case closed it.
2. PortBars didn't check a timed run's exit code. ScriptAPI-63 closes it.
3. `jet test` exits 0 for SKIP-HOST and KNOWN-FAILING rows. The PASS-only judge and a known-failing canary close it. Audit3 found 25 zero-pass lines; no met criterion rested on one.
4. Meet lines were labeled with a criterion they didn't run. Each meet line now names its proof's source.

Only #6129 c64 had to be reopened.

Two more findings:

- I4: 397 of 977 registered diagnostic codes have no UI snapshot. Card #6752.
- Hosts: the 38 host-skipped rows get chromium, firefox and 16 toolchains, installed after b9's self-check.

## Measurement rule (adopted tonight)

Per cell:

- instructions:u may rise by at most 0.1%;
- the claimed static win (loop instructions or bytes) must be shown;
- cycles are judged by 10 ABBA pairs on one pinned CPU, and a regression is at least 8 of 10 pairs slower with a median above +1%;
- a consistent loss under 1% lands only with that loss recorded in the gains file and on #6414.

## Releases

b8's admission failed on a census parser defect: tallies ending in ", 0 skipped" read as unfinished. The fix e7d517a402 is in b9, so the next a0.0.N comes from b9. b9 built in 74 s and its self-check is running. The newest admitted release is still a0.0.44.

briefings.title: Gaps against hand-written code and cold-script cost: update (2026-11-11 night)
briefings.body:
# Gaps against hand-written code and cold-script cost: update (2026-11-11 night)

This revision replaces briefing0i2ghnn. Every number below is measured, except where a line says it is an estimate.

## Proof incident: deferred credits on b4–b7 (fixed)

Since b4, the Lander credited every merged deferred proof (case, ui and golden lines merged into one run per profile) as a pass without reading it. The script read the results with a JSON tool that was not on its PATH, so the results table came out empty and every member was credited.

- Scope: 90 credits across 58 submissions (b4 17, b5 33, b6 12, b7 28). On b7 the merged runs actually held 52 case FAILs, 4 ICE ERRORs (exit 101) and 4 REFUSED, plus 3 ui FAILs.
- Tower impact: none of Main's meets cited a merged b4–b7 credit; they rest on pre-landing proved lines or b2/b3 deferred passes. Four adjacent meets were rechecked on seed-b7. Three hold. #6129 c64 (a pure fn cannot write held state) had regressed and was reopened; G8Scope-44 fixes it, and c64 is met again only from b9's proved line.
- The four ICEs (I2) came from G6Meta-55: the build-entry comptime input route refused while a host was installed. G6Meta-67 fixes it: the host serves the read, and with no host the error is E0956, never 101.
- Every flipped credit was reset, every owner got one fail list, and every false-passed line reruns in full on b8.
- A guard against recurrence: an always-failing canary case now rides every merged run. If it reads as a pass, the deferred step fails red.

A second measurement defect of the same kind: PortBars never checked a timed run's exit code, so roots-sh "passed" speed at 14.3 ms when every timed run was an instant refusal. A real cold run is about 1.8 s and 250 MB against the shell script's 30 ms, so speed still fails. ScriptAPI-63 makes a wrong exit fail the bar as not measured and re-judges every tool entry.

## Hello world: per-feature cost, hand vs Jet

The ceiling reference now carries the smallest hand-written version of every feature Jet's hello pays for (Tools/perf/asm-parity hello ref.S, 1,453 B):

|Feature|Hand (B)|Jet (B)|
|---|---:|---:|
|Startup|78|824|
|Refusal / defect stop|0|2,501|
|Checked allocation|259|1,662|
|Fault report|858|3,584+|
|Print|82|1,827|
|Crash receipt|0|12,080|

Jet hello is 31,439 B on b4. These submissions cut it, each landing only on a measured win:

- G23: runtime bookkeeping uses wrapping arithmetic, so no overflow stop is reachable from it.
- G26: the fault report enters through the linker.
- G27: a lazy stdout buffer, set up on the first buffered write, with no startup mmap or terminal probe.
- G30: the startup refusal writes its bytes straight to stderr, and the arguments check is installed only for programs that read arguments.

With G23, G26 and G27, release hello code should fall from about 21.5 KB to about 7.4 KB. That is a call-graph estimate, not a measurement; the third measurement window measures it.

## Codegen ceiling kernels (b4)

Jet against hand-written, in loop instructions: list_sum 254/5, gather 273/8, stride 71/6, collatz 180/11, point 213/9, byte_count 119/7.

The second measurement window measured two submissions:

- G9 cuts loop instructions 12–50% on all seven kernels, and isum is 1,600 B smaller. Its sieve time read +14.5% against a control of −4.9%. Instruction counts are identical, so it is being re-measured as 20 repeated runs against a control-vs-control spread. It lands only if sieve falls inside that spread.
- G11 (the clone path) is 416–1,152 B smaller on every cell, with time within the control (+2.0% against +3.1%). It lands on size only if every cell's time is within its control's noise.

G10r failed its runtime lowering; G10r2 fixes the cause (a non-slot value read as a slot) and is measured first in the third window. Also queued there: G12–G22 (store-forward stalls, compare-and-branch for `||` and `&&`, one-byte find, jcc fusion for the regexlogscan regression, and the cold-arm inline cost).

## Cold scripts and compile speed

Jet compiles from cold on every run, with no cache. Measured on Roots.jet: 0.67 s wall, 1.13 CPU-s and 287 MB. Parsing runs at 136k lines/s, about 220× short of the 30M lines/s target.

Landed or staged load-by-use steps:

- G8Scope-38: the first root loads 60 modules instead of 101.
- G8Scope-39: runtime units load by use.
- G8Scope-40: unreached constants are skipped.
- G8Scope-41: the route set is built from compiler tables.
- G8Scope-42: reached words come from the tokens, which removes a second byte pass.
- G8Scope-45 (step 3): core.math's types, methods, F32 forms and precise families load by use. A program calling only `math.sqrt` goes from 1,785 to 1,364 functions and from 39 to 31 modules, and checks in 734 ms instead of 915 ms. It lands only on a cold-compile win across sqrt1, Roots.jet and MathAudit, with no cell worse.

The target remains a few dozen functions for a bare `math.sqrt`, and then lexing (45% of parsing, with float bignum at 22% of lexing).

Every switch of a tool script to its Jet version stays blocked on speed until this closes: a small tool still pays about 1.8 s of compile per run.

## Memory

`jet check` OOM: on seed-b6, 8 compiler and test roots were killed at a 6 GB cap (JetBackend/Tests, JetCli, JetCli/Commands and its Tests, two JetCli fixtures, and JetDriver/Tests). #6527 c11 now requires a per-root peak of 3 GB or less. It is G8Scope-3's next item.

## Releases

The newest admitted release is a0.0.44, from the train before b1. b8 (776b3d1191) is published, and its admission as the next a0.0.N is queued after its deferred pass. a0.0.44 cannot build current Core, so the admission uses a boot seed from b8.

briefings.title: Gaps against hand-written code and cold-script cost: update (2026-11-11 evening)
briefings.body:
# Gaps against hand-written code and cold-script cost: update (2026-11-11 evening)

This revision adds today's measured results and the newly found roots. The earlier gap table (`briefing06136p6`) still stands for anything not listed here. All timings are best of 5 runs, alternated, on one pinned CPU against a same-source base, with a control column (the base measured again) that shows the noise floor.

## Landed: G6, the allocator leaves

`jet_rt_free_8` and `jet_rt_alloc_8` no longer save registers they don't need. free_8 went from 119 to 110 instructions with no spills; alloc_8 from 88 to 82, with 5 pushes down to 3.

| benchmark | change | control |
|---|---|---|
| wordfreq | -6.1% | +0.4% |
| logreport | -6.5% | -0.5% |
| tokensplit | -5.2% | +0.8% |
| csvtransform | -2.3% | -2.9% (noise) |
| geomean | -4.6% | -1.7% |

Binaries are 1.0% smaller in every cell. RSS is unchanged.

## Held, then fixed: frame-view substrings (G7, now G11)

G7 cut logreport by 29.8% and tokensplit by 10.4%, but slowed csvtransform by 3.5%, so it was held. The cause was that inlining the view copy into `string_clone` made every clone save 5 registers instead of 1. csvtransform clones about 15M times and uses no views, and clone's share of its time rose from 6.0% to 9.5%. G11 keeps clone's hot path as it was before G7. The +768 KiB RSS reading was noise: page faults and peak matched across 3 runs. G11 is being measured now.

## New codegen gate

`Tools/perf/CodegenCeiling.jet` counts the hot-loop instructions of 9 kernels and fails on any increase. Every compiler, IR or runtime change must pass it. Seed-b4 counts against hand-written code:

| kernel | Jet | hand-written |
|---|---|---|
| list_sum | 254 (11 loop copies) | 5 |
| gather | 273 | 8 |
| collatz | 180 | 11 |
| point | 213 | 9 |
| byte_count | 119 | 7 |
| stride | 71 | 6 |

The roots are below. Each fix is staged and goes through the quiet measurement window; it lands only on a measured win with no cell worse than the noise.

- **Loop copies copied again (G9).** Versioning re-copied an inlined callee's already versioned loop; list_sum ends up with 11 loops.
- **Registers refused (G10).** r8 and r9 were refused to any value live across a checked Int op, because its rare overflow path calls a function. Loops doing Int math had 5 registers and reloaded the list's base and length on every pass.
- **Fail arms inline (G12).** Bounds and unwrap failure paths sat inside hot loops; they move after the function's return.
- **Store-forwarding stalls (G13, G14).** Short text built byte by byte and then read as one word stalls the CPU: 57% of text checking in wordfreq, and 7.9% in date parsing.
- **`||` and `&&` chains (G15).** Each link becomes a compare and a branch; the two-digit date parser was 9.6% of logreport's date parsing.
- **Boxed results (G16).** Date parsing boxed its result on every line; the fast path no longer does.
- **Not a root.** The repeated 62-bit range checks in fib are in the general copy, which runs only for n of 2^60 and up, and are needed there; the hot copy is already minimal.

## Cold script cost (#6527 c10), and why the tool twins fail their speed bars

A small Jet script that uses only files, process and sys cost 1.90 s and 357 MB from cold on b5, and type-checked 101 Core modules.

| root | fix | effect |
|---|---|---|
| core.files calls a test-only fault hook, pulling in core.testing, all of Crypto, Encoding and random | G8Scope-38 | 101 → 60 modules; peak 357 → 272 MB. A second script: 388 → 290 MB, CPU 2.17 → 1.51 s |
| runtime units were reached whole, so one `utf8_bytes` call loaded every Unicode table | G8Scope-39 | 58 → 43 modules; Core source parsed -12.5% |
| any `.abs` or `.pow` opens all of core.math (499 functions plus most compile-time constants) | in progress | |

After root 1, the same script takes 0.67 s wall, 1.13 s CPU and 287 MB peak:

| phase | wall ms | CPU ms |
|---|---|---|
| load (parsing) | 280 | 370 |
| sema finalize | 160 | 440 |
| register | 80 | 170 |
| comptime | 30 | 150 |
| sema check | 20 | 30 |

**Parsing is an architecture gap.** Each cold script lexes and parses about 38,000 lines of Core (2.8 MB) to use a few hundred. That runs at 136k lines/s wall, about 220 times short of the 30M lines/s target. Lexing is 45% of parse time. Float literals go through bignum math, which is 22% of lexing. Each byte read is an un-inlined, bounds-checked call. The parser re-skips trivia on every token read.

The plan has no cache, per the cold-compile rule:
1. Each Core module is reached by name.
2. Lazy declaration parsing: lex once, record each declaration's span, and parse a body only when something reaches it. `jet check` still reports every diagnostic.
3. The lexer's cheap wins: inlined byte access, an exact float fast path, and skipping trivia once per token.

## Open ballots raised today

- **D-NET-HOSTREADS1.** Does Net cover the host reads TLS needs (clock, entropy, CA files)? On b5, an HTTPS client still works after it denies FS, Rand and Env. The reviewed recommendation is explicit host-effect rows.
- **D-CONTEXT-EFFECT1.** Is `Context` a 13th built-in effect root, as in the code, or a Core-declared effect inside the ratified 12?

briefings.title: Codegen gaps against hand-written machine code (2026-11-11 measurement)
briefings.body:
# Codegen and runtime gaps against hand-written machine code

Measured 2026-11-11 14:48–14:51 on a quiet machine (other jobs paused, heavy lock held, CPU 8 pinned). Each wall time is the best of 5, with the compilers interleaved and a b3-against-b3 control. Per-program noise is up to ±4.4%. Every binary printed the expected output. Raw data: `$JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/G11Speed/poc/gains.md` (tool: `Tools/perf/asm-parity/asm-parity.mjs --candidate`, landed 0e48c3e0d6).

## The prototype result

The candidate is b3 plus G11Speed-G1: plain retain/release while the process has one thread, and a bounded List length so indexed loops drop their checks.

| | candidate vs b3 |
|---|---|
| Time, geometric mean | +1.4%, no gain beyond noise |
| Peak memory | −0.3% |
| Binary size | −0.4% |
| Regressions | sieve +16.8%, regexlogscan +7.5% |

G1 does not land as it stands. b3 against a0.0.44 is also flat (+0.8%).

## Where the gaps are: b3 against the hand-written reference

| program | time × ceiling | Jet RSS KiB | ref RSS KiB | Jet bytes | ref bytes |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| csvtransform | **78.1** | 198,248 | 8,524 | 400,927 | 4,393 |
| logreport | **18.7** | 264 | 14,132 | 335,919 | 5,629 |
| wordfreq | **11.3** | 16,776 | 15,200 | 206,415 | 1,669 |
| embeddeddata | 8.9 | 24,712 | 11,576 | 214,511 | 3,058 |
| regexlogscan | 8.7 | 1,080 | 41,896 | 648,655 | 3,053 |
| tensormap | 6.9 | 439,032 | 393,248 | 240,223 | 647 |
| nbody | 3.8 | 0 | 0 | 152,367 | 2,358 |
| regexfindall | 3.5 | 8,904 | 4,096 | 198,543 | 1,411 |
| binparse | 3.2 | 20,616 | 8,452 | 246,191 | 1,376 |
| sieve | 3.1 | 4,880 | 0 | 116,687 | 1,208 |
| fft | 2.5 | 788 | 0 | 352,671 | 1,756 |
| sensorring | 2.3 | 0 | 0 | 119,759 | 1,732 |
| bulkrename | 1.2 | 1,092 | 2,080 | 748,287 | 1,491 |
| isum | 1.2 | 79,944 | 78,152 | 114,287 | 632 |
| collatz | 1.1 | 0 | 0 | 117,423 | 480 |
| hello | 1.05 | 0 | 0 | 31,439 | 504 |
| w11fetch | 1.05 | 4,468 | 0 | 4,710,255 | 1,225 |
| fib | 0.83 | 0 | 0 | 103,823 | 456 |
| taskfile | 0.77 | 276 | 12,320 | 542,911 | 4,407 |
| **geometric mean** | **3.30** | | | | |

The Jet columns are the candidate; b3's numbers are within noise of them. RSS under a few hundred KiB reads 0.

**Size is the widest gap.** Every Jet binary carries a floor of about 30–100 KB, and typical programs are 100–700 KB against 0.5–5 KB by hand.

## Roots found so far

Each comes from a single profile of one benchmark binary.

1. **Store-forwarding stall on short fresh text.** About 52% of wordfreq. The text-validity check and the string hash read the last 8 bytes as one word right after the bytes were written one at a time. Fix: read a tail under 8 bytes byte by byte. Being written as G11Speed-G3; it is general (from_bytes, hashing short keys and fields).
2. **Atomic reference counts in single-threaded code.** About 17% of csvtransform: string clone is 24.9% of cycles, and 67% of that is `lock xadd`. G1 removed the lock, but its in-flight counter costs as much again. Next: a cheaper sole-thread test.
3. **Every substring is an owned copy.** In logreport, alloc+free are 20.2%, plus builder, copy and drop: `split_once` copies both halves, so three splits per line copy the rest of the line three times. In csvtransform it is 14.6% plus mem_move. In logreport's `parse_rfc3339` (14.6%), `bytes()` copies and checks the bounds of each byte. Fix: a substring shares its parent's buffer, an internal representation change with no API or syntax change. A design is due before coding: how memory is freed, and how a small slice is kept from pinning a huge parent.
4. **The binary size floor.** Not yet analyzed: what is linked into hello that hello does not use.
5. **Redundant integer checks.** Seen in fib's objdump: each Int operation repeats an `add rdx,rdx; jo` small-integer check several times on the same value. Not yet costed.

## Why fib and taskfile beat the "ceiling"

Both references are weaker than Jet, so they are not ceilings yet. AGENTS.md requires the best known technique, so both will be raised.

- **fib (0.83×).** `fib/ref.S` calls itself for every leaf. Jet b3 tests `n < 2` at the call site and skips the call (objdump of `run_fib`), so it makes about half as many calls. The reference is a plain transliteration. The new reference keeps the recursion the cell measures but uses call-site leaf checks and any further unrolling hand asm would use. Jet still pays redundant overflow checks (root 5), so a proper reference should beat it.
- **taskfile (0.77×).** `taskfile/ref.S` reserves one lazy 4 GiB anonymous mapping and writes areas far apart in it (rows at 32 MiB, text at 96 MiB, keys at 1 GiB, output at 1.5 GiB). With transparent huge pages set to `always`, each touched area likely faults in a zeroed 2 MiB page. It reaches 12,320 KiB RSS against Jet's 276 KiB, and pays it in each of the 6 process steps the cell runs. The page-fault counts are still to be confirmed. The new reference sizes its areas to the input.

## What happens next

G11Speed-2 does these in order:
1. G3, the short-tail fix.
2. Raise the fib and taskfile references.
3. Substrings share their parent's buffer.
4. A cheap sole-thread test for reference counts.
5. The sieve and regexlogscan regressions.
6. The size floor.

In parallel, `Tools/perf/CodegenCeiling.jet` is a static check, required for any change to codegen or the runtime, so closed gaps cannot reopen (#6414 c15, c30). This briefing is updated as each root is measured.

briefings.title: Language review: correction (much of the compile-time proposal is already ratified, not built)
briefings.body:
# Language review: correction after the first adversarial review

This corrects the briefing "Language review: all installments". The full file, with this note at its top, is in the home directory as jet-language-review.md.

The adversarial reviewer went through the `#` ballot (D-META-HASH2) against Tower and the compiler and marked it
NOT CLEAN. Three of its findings correct things I told you, so they change how to read sections 3 and 8 below:

1. **Much of what I proposed for compile time is already ratified, just not built.** I worked from the spec and
   registry, which still show the old forms. Tower already holds decisions for: no `$` and `#{name}` splices
   (D-META-HASH1); markers as types with typed arguments, including the wrap power (D-DECL-TYPES1); one
   reflection entry `reflect(type-or-value)` with its record types (D-TYPEINFO1, D-META-REFLECT2); and who may
   rewrite code, through a compiler value that only the root package creates (D-META-LADDER1). So `#info(x)` would
   duplicate the ratified `reflect(x)`, and "markers take arguments" needs building, not deciding.
2. **My one-line rule was too strong.** "No `#` means it runs in your program" is false as written: module
   constants, generic parameters and build functions are build-time with no `#`. The honest rule is narrower:
   an explicit request to the compiler carries `#`.
3. **Two parts of my proposal conflict with what you ratified.** Dropping the host gates for build-time effects,
   and letting a marker's presence authorize a wrap, both go against D-META-LADDER1.

The reviewer added an option it prefers to mine as drafted: **a spelling-only cutover** (`#run`, `#if`, `#loop`
replace the `comptime` word) that keeps every ratified contract as it is. My reading now: the compile-time area
feels weak and messy mostly because roughly ten ratified decisions are unbuilt and the spec, registry and guide
still show the old language. The fastest real improvement is to build what is ratified and add the spelling
cutover, not to redesign. The ballot is being repaired to say this plainly, with the same real programs under
every option. Section 3 below is kept as written so you can see what I proposed; read it with this note.

The same caution applies to the rest of this file: I did not check Tower's ratified decisions before writing
it, so some items in sections 4 to 8 may also be decided already. Each one is checked against Tower before it
becomes a ballot.

briefings.title: Language review: all installments, for your answers by item number
briefings.body:
# Jet language review: installments 3 to 8

Written 2026-11-09 by Main for the owner to read on return. Installments 1 and 2 and every answer so far are in
`$JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/language-review.md`.

**How to answer:** every item has a number. Reply with numbers, for example "4.1 yes, 5.2 yes, 8.3 tell me more,
6.4 no". Anything you approve becomes a ballot or a criterion; nothing here is built yet.

**How this was made:** from a fresh view, as you asked. I did not read old audits, proposals or reports, and I left
speed out. I read the spec sections that say what Jet is today and ran small programs on the current compiler
(seed a0_042). Where a claim was run it says "checked"; where I am going by the spec or by judgment it says so.

Marks: **[N]** near, buildable in months on today's compiler. **[F]** far, a year or more, or it needs other
pieces first.

---

## Where we stand

| Decided | State |
|---|---|
| A file of top-level statements just runs | Ruling, #6281 c128. ScriptLead is building it. Top-level bindings are locals of the program, in order. |
| The arrow always comes before the result; error-first signatures are invalid | Ruling, #6281 c127 (455 Core signatures to migrate). |
| No warnings; tidiness never stops `jet run`, and `jet check` / `jet build` list everything | Ruling, #6281 c129. |
| `shared` is a type: `Shared{value}`; the keyword goes | Ruling, #6281 c130. |
| A module-level `name: value` is always evaluated while building; failure is a build error | Ruling, #6281 c132. |
| `#Persist` means only "survives hot reload" | Ruling, on #6281. |
| `#` means "for the compiler"; `#run`, `#if`, `#loop`; `#{name}` splices; `comptime` and `$` go; `use` stays a word | Approved in direction. Ballot **D-META-HASH2** is being drafted, then reviewed. See the note below. |
| One type-level rule for cycles in shared state | Approved as a proposal. Ballot **D-SHARED-CYCLE2** is drafted and with the reviewer. See the note below. |
| A block in which ordinary collections allocate from an arena | Approved as a proposal. Ballot D-REGION-ALLOC1 is being drafted. |
| Withdrawn after your answers | Call-site `&` marks; removing `<>`; `is` for arm tables; `State` as a written effect. |

**Two of these reopen decisions you already ratified.** I worked from a fresh view and did not know; the agent
drafting the ballots found them. You said everything ratified is open in this review, but you should see what
you would be reversing:
- **D-META-HASH1, ratified 2026-10-30.** It already decided "no `$` at all" and `#{name}` for splices, so on
  those two points today's proposal agrees with you. It differs on three: HASH1 made compiler facts plain values
  (`build.target.os`, `T.reflect()`) and site values `#line`, `#file`, `#package`; today's proposal writes
  `#build`, `#info(x)`, `#here`. HASH1 is not built yet: the spec and registry still show `$`. The new ballot
  shows HASH1 exactly as ratified as one of its options.
- **D-SHARED-CYCLE1, ratified as option C** (card #6066, with a criterion already met). Today's type-level
  rule would reverse it. The new ballot says so.
- The arena-block ballot (D-REGION-ALLOC1, drafted, with the reviewer) builds on two ratified decisions about
  allocation context and shows them as an option.

**Still waiting for your answer from installments 1 and 2:**

| # | Question | My recommendation |
|---|---|---|
| O1 | A plain module variable: `score := 0` at file scope that any function reads and writes directly, owned by the main task; the compiler refuses to start a task that touches it | Yes. It is what games and scripts need, and it stays race-free. |
| O2 | `String ParseError!` becomes `String ! ParseError` | Yes. Two types joined by a space is the only such place in the grammar. |
| O3 | Delete the second result-branch form `r ? ok -> … ! error -> …` | Yes. The arm table already does it, and `?` and `!` keep one meaning each. |
| O4 | `fn(…) { … }` is a value in any scope (today `add: fn() { … }` inside a function is an error; checked) | Yes. |
| O5 | Replace the `try_new` / `try_push` / `try_insert` twins with one scope in which allocation failure is an error value | Yes, but it needs design. Expert-only. |
| O6 | One-liners move under their own verb, `jet eval '…'`, as you suggested | Yes. |
| O7 | Markers get the fourth power, wrap (retry, cache, trace) | Offer it in the ballot with and without. I lean yes, with `jet expand` showing the result. |
| O8 | Effects take arguments: `FS.Read("assets/")`, `GPU(.Vulkan)` | Yes, limited to build-time constants. Own ballot, D-EFFECT-ARGS1. |

---

## 3. Compile time: the whole design on one page

You asked for a big rework here. The `#` proposal you approved is its base. This is the full shape, so you can
judge it as one thing.

**3.1 One rule.** No `#`: it runs in your program. `#`: it is addressed to the compiler.

| Kind | Looks like | Set |
|---|---|---|
| Directive: "do this while building" | `#run`, `#if`, `#loop` | Small and closed |
| Marker: "this has a property" | `#Test`, `#Unsafe("…")`, `#Retry(times: 3)` | Open; libraries declare their own |
| Question to the compiler | `#build`, `#package`, `#here`, `#caller`, `#phase`, `#info(x)` | Small and closed |
| Splice | `#{name}` | One form |

**3.2 A marker is a type; its fields are its arguments.** Typed, named, with defaults. Its `impl Marker` block
gives it meaning, as a ladder: tag, check, add, wrap (O7). A whole-program query, "everything marked with this",
is what route tables, test lists, command lists and a game's system list are built from.

**3.3 One reflection record.** `#info(x)` returns one typed record for a type, function or value. The build
function gets the same record, and the run-time `reflect.of(value)` returns the part that exists at run time.
Today there are four ways to read these facts.

**3.4 One way to generate code.** Typed templates of ordinary items. Never strings, never rewriting code the
user wrote. `derive`, marker bodies and the build function's generation become one mechanism.

**3.5 Build-time code obeys the ordinary effect rules.** Pure by default. Pinned inputs (`embed_file`,
`fetch(url, sha256:)`) are recorded in the lock. Anything else needs a grant from the package, the same grant
mechanism run time uses. `#Impure`, the gate flag and the tier table go.

**3.6 Literal hooks, one mechanism for every embedded language. [N]** SQL, regex, CSS, HTML, format strings and
paths all need the same thing: text that is checked while building and becomes a typed value. Jet already has
checked text types and a build-time literal hook. I would make that the single way to embed a language: a type
declares a build-time parser for its literal, written in ordinary Jet. Then CSS is a library, not a language
feature, and the CSS ballot that failed review today is replaced by something general. (From the spec; not run.)

**3.7 The fence `<: … :>`.** It is the least guessable form in the language. I have not studied it. With
`#loop` and `#{…}` in place I would check whether it is still needed, and cut it if not.

**3.8 What I would not add.** Types as ordinary values (Zig's way: it removes generics but makes signatures hard
to read); string macros; anything that rewrites existing code. Generics with trait bounds, plus `#info` and
templates, cover the ground with code a reader can follow.

---

## 4. Everyday semantics: numbers and small things

**4.1 Number literals should adapt, the way Go's constants do. [N]** Checked: Jet's number defaults are right
for beginners. `Int` does not overflow (9223372036854775807 + 1 prints 9223372036854775808), `7 / 2` is 3.5,
`0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3` is true, and `"héllo".len()` is 5.

The friction, also checked: a literal adapts to what it is passed to, but a named one does not.

```jet
half: fn(x: Float) -> Float { x * 0.5 }

print(half(3.0))    // works: the literal becomes a Float
y: 2.5
print(half(y))      // error E0112: y is a Decimal
```

Naming a number should not change what it is. Proposal:
- An immutable binding of a number literal (`y: 2.5`, `GRAVITY: 9.81`) has no fixed type until it is used, and
  each use adapts, exactly as the literal would.
- A mutable one (`speed := 2.5`) takes its type from how the function uses it, and falls back to Decimal or Int
  only when nothing decides.

This matters most for games and numeric code, where almost every number is a Float. Cost: a little more
inference, and the error message must say which use fixed the type.

**4.2 Ranges are right.** `..` is inclusive and `..<` stops short. Checked: `loop i in 0..xs.len()` is refused
with a message that offers three correct forms. Keep.

**4.3 Two small defects, found by running the spec's examples.** Both are now a criterion on #6281.
- The spec's three-part loop, `loop i := 0, i < 3, i + 1 -> print(i)`, does not parse.
- The E0112 fix text says `Float{3.4}` whatever the number was.

**4.4 Teach three ways to hold changing state, not seven.** After your `Shared` ruling: a plain value (the
default), `Shared{…}` (across tasks), and `Pool` with `ID` (graphs). `Cell`, `Atomic` and guards stay for
experts and leave the beginner path. This is documentation, not a language change.

**4.5 One question I could not answer by reading.** Is an `Int` field in a struct a machine word or a big
number, and what does a game developer write to get a plain 32-bit or 64-bit field? If the answer is "write
`I32`", that is fine; it just needs to be the first thing the game guide says.

---

## 5. Modularity and scale

**5.1 Core is one connected ball. [N]** Evidence from today: `use tasks: core.tasks` loads 64 Core modules
(2.7 MB of source). The chain: the time module's encode and decode implementations are always live; they load
encoding; that loads files, math and memory; then system, process, text, testing and crypto follow. Two rules
fix the cause:
- A trait implementation is loaded only when the program uses both the type and the trait.
- Core gets layers, and a lower layer may not import a higher one: Prelude; then data (text, math, collections,
  time); then system (files, net, process); then services (HTTP, database, UI). A check enforces it.

**5.2 A public API should not change silently. [N]** Jet infers effects and errors from function bodies. That
is right inside a package. At a package's public edge it means an edit to a body can change the public
signature with no one noticing. Core already has a surface ledger with a check. Proposal: every package gets
one. `jet check` compares the public surface (types, effects, errors, markers) with the committed ledger; a
difference is an error until the ledger is updated; and the size of the difference gives the version bump, so
the version number is computed, not chosen.

**5.3 One strictness dial per package. [N]** Script, app, library, hardened. Each step turns on more: a
library must write its public types, effects and errors; hardened forbids panics and unchecked operations. Jet
has the pieces as separate policies and profiles (I have not checked how many). One named dial is easier to
teach, and it is the "ladder, not cliff" pillar applied to rigor.

**5.4 The compiler runs its own migrations. Do this first. [N]** Today's rulings mean rewriting thousands of
sites: 455 signatures, every `shared`, every `comptime` and `$`. The closed-set `else` rule alone touched 4,520
sites in 783 files, with a tool one agent wrote for that job. Rule: every breaking change to the language
registers its rewrite in `jet fix`, so one command updates any code base, the repository's and a user's.
Libraries get the same power for their own APIs: `#Deprecated(replace: …)` with a typed rewrite, so upgrading a
package updates your call sites. Breaking changes that fix themselves are what make it affordable to keep
improving the language, before and after v1.

**5.5 The library test.** For every mechanism, ask: could Core's own use of it be written by a library? Markers,
effects, targets, literal hooks and allocators should all pass. Where the compiler still knows a Core type by
name, that is a defect. One ballot on this is held for the rework (D-TYPE-FACTS1).

**5.6 One verb for "tell me about my program". [N]** There are `jet explain`, `jet inspect`, `jet audit` and
`jet expand`, each showing compiler knowledge. I would fold them into one family, `jet explain <topic>`:
effects, copies, checks, the expansion of a marker, the layout of a type. (Seen in the spec; I have not counted
the flags.)

---

## 6. FFI and incremental adoption

**6.1 What exists.** The spec lists foreign interfaces for 22 languages, from C, C++, Rust, Python, JavaScript
and Go to COBOL, Ada and COM, plus schema binders. I have not tested their depth.

**6.2 The missing direction: Jet called from other languages. [N]** I did not find it in the spec's FFI
section. It is the adoption wedge: nobody rewrites an application, but many will write one new module in a
better language. Proposal: `jet build --lib` produces a C-callable library and its header, and from the same
public surface a Python wheel and an npm package (JVM and .NET later). Types map through the existing binders
run in reverse. The library's effects become the permissions its documentation states. Your module-level ruling
helps here: with no code running before `run`, loading a Jet library has no hidden start-up step.

**6.3 The adoption ladder for an existing code base.**
1. Use `jet` around it: as the script, build and test tool (`jet run x.c` already works).
2. Call the existing code from Jet (exists).
3. Write one new module in Jet and call it from the host (6.2).
4. Move files over one at a time. **[N to F]** `jet port file.c` writes the Jet version, with `#Unsafe` blocks
   wherever it could not prove safety, and generates the tests that show the two behave the same. The repository
   already built this proof for itself: the paired-tool entries with identical-output cases. That mechanism is a
   product feature, not just a house rule.

**6.4 Foreign code under the effect system.** Today a foreign call is one coarse effect. With arguments (O8) it
can name the library: `FFI.C("sqlite3")`. **[F]** Further out: run an untrusted foreign library compiled to
WebAssembly inside the process, holding only the effects it was granted.

**6.5 Zero-copy data exchange. [N to F]** For data and machine-learning work the entry point is a Jet function
called from a Python notebook. That needs Jet's views to map onto Arrow and the Python buffer protocol without
copying.

**6.6 Out of scope for now:** a stable binary interface between Jet libraries. Source packages are enough
until the language stops changing.

---

## 7. What each domain needs

Core already has modules for most of these (App, Web, Ui, Game, Db, Http, Compute, Data, Units and more). I
listed the folders; I did not test their depth. This table is my judgment of what decides adoption and what I
would close first.

| Domain | What decides adoption | Jet's asset today | Close first |
|---|---|---|---|
| Scripts and command-line tools | Starts instantly; one file; no setup | `jet run`, effects that announce themselves | A file of statements (decided); adapting numbers (4.1); `jet eval` (O6); start-up time (the gauntlet's job) |
| Back-end services | Safe dependencies; database; deploys | Effects and grants; tasks; HTTP, TLS and SQL written in Jet | Queries checked while building (8.7); tracing from effects with no code (8.5); least-privilege dependencies (8.8) |
| Web front end | Small downloads; fast edit-and-see loop | Web, Reactive and Ui modules; `jet dev` | CSS and HTML as checked text (3.6) |
| Games | Globals; Floats; frame memory; hot reload | Value semantics; `Pool` and `ID`; `#Persist` | Plain module variables (O1); adapting numbers (4.1); arena blocks (approved); layout markers (8.9); `#System` lists from marker queries (3.2) |
| Data, numeric, machine learning | Works from a notebook; arrays; accelerators | Units, Data and Compute modules | Called from Python with no copies (6.2, 6.5); shapes in types and kernels (8.2, 8.11) |
| Systems and embedded | No runtime surprises; small; auditable | No C underneath; `#Unsafe` with reasons; "no allocation" and "no panic" promises | Targets declared by libraries (ballot being drafted); the report of remaining run-time checks (8.5) |
| Desktop and mobile apps | One code base; looks right; accessible | The single UI framework direction | Not examined |
| Operations and infrastructure | One static binary; safer than shell | No C; permission-scoped scripts | `jet eval`; process and pipe ergonomics (not examined) |
| Teaching | Install in one step; errors that teach | Diagnostics with a fix on every error | One downloadable binary instead of Nix |

---

## 8. Trailblazing ideas, ranked

Each one grows out of something Jet already has that other languages lack: effects the compiler tracks, value
semantics, typed migrations, and a compiler that can answer questions about the program.

**8.1 Breaking changes that fix themselves. [N]** Item 5.4. First, because it pays for everything else.

**8.2 "Where can this run?" as a fact the compiler infers. [N, then F]** This is the Mojo question, answered
Jet's way. The compiler already knows whether a function is pure, whether it allocates, whether it can panic and
which target facts it reads. A function that is pure, allocation-free and bounded can run on any device: SIMD
lanes, many cores, a GPU, an accelerator that does not exist yet. So eligibility is inferred, like effects, and
never annotated: no shader dialect, no second language for kernels. A target is a library-declared type that
states what it can run; `jet explain` says why a function is or is not eligible for it. A new chip becomes a
package. Near: the eligibility fact and CPU SIMD and multi-core. Far: GPU and accelerator back ends.

**8.3 Record and replay, and simulated worlds, from the effect boundary. [N, then F]** Every touch of the
outside world goes through thirteen effect roots. So the runtime can record every result that came in (`jet run
--record`) and replay the run exactly: a bug report ships its recording, and a recording becomes a test. The
same boundary can be handed a simulated world: a fake clock, a network that drops packets, a disk that fails on
the ninth write. That is the testing method behind the most reliable databases, available to every Jet program
with no test doubles written. Near: single-task record and replay. Far: deterministic task scheduling.

**8.4 A public surface the compiler guards, and versions it computes. [N]** Item 5.2. Others do this for types.
Jet can include effects and errors, so "this update started using the network" is a version change the tool
sees.

**8.5 The glass box. [N]** The compiler knows every run-time check it could not remove (bounds, ranges,
overflow), every copy, every allocation and every outside-world call. Show them per line through `jet explain`,
and let a region demand none: "no check remains here" joins the existing "no allocation" and "no panic"
promises. The same knowledge gives tracing for free: a span around every effect call, with no code written.

**8.6 One evolution mechanism for data on disk, on the wire and in memory. [F]** Jet has typed migrations for
schemas and `#Persist` for hot reload. They are the same idea: a type's history is part of the type. Unified,
one declared migration moves data on disk, messages from an older peer and live state across a code reload;
later, a new version of a running service can take over the old one's state with no downtime.

**8.7 The database as typed collections. [N to F]** Jet now has a SQL engine written in Jet. So a table can be
a typed collection, a query an ordinary Jet expression checked against the schema while building, and the
schema's history the migrations of 8.6. No mapping layer and no query strings.

**8.8 Least privilege for dependencies and for AI-written code. [N, after O8]** "This package may read
`./templates` and reach `api.example.com`, and nothing else", checked while building. The same mechanism runs
code an AI agent wrote with a hard ceiling and no sandbox process. In an era of generated code, a language whose
permissions are part of the type system is the safe place to run it.

**8.9 Layout as a marker. [N to F]** `#Layout(.SoA)` on a list of structs: you write ordinary struct code and
the storage is columns. Games and data code both want it; other languages bolt it on or drop it. It would also
be the proof that library markers (3.2) are powerful enough, because it should be a library.

**8.10 The program as a database you can query. [N]** "Which functions touch this state?", "what can fail
here, and where does each error come from?", "what changed in meaning between these two commits?". With `#info`
as one record this is a small step, and it gives merges and code review that work on declarations, not on
lines.

**8.11 Shapes in types, and derivatives as a library. [F]** Arrays whose dimensions are build-time parameters,
so a shape mismatch is a compile error; automatic differentiation generated from `#info`, not built into the
compiler. Together with 8.2 this is the machine-learning story without a second language.

**8.12 Tasks that can move. [F]** A task whose captured values are sendable and encodable could run in another
process or on another machine, and its effects say what that place must allow. The rules that make tasks safe
today are most of what is needed.

---

## 9. The order I would build in

1. Migrations in `jet fix` (5.4), because every item below rewrites code.
2. The `#` rework with markers as types (section 3), then literal hooks (3.6).
3. Adapting numbers (4.1) and the plain module variable (O1): the two biggest everyday frictions I found.
4. `jet build --lib` with the Python wheel (6.2): the adoption wedge.
5. The guarded public surface (5.2) and the Core layering rules (5.1).
6. Record and replay (8.3) and the glass box (8.5): the two trailblazing items that are near and that nobody
   else can copy quickly, because they rest on the effect system.

## 10. What I did not check

- The depth of any Core module or foreign binder; I only know they exist.
- Whether a pure function may read module state today.
- How `#Persist` variables behave across tasks.
- What a user-declared marker can do today (the ballot starts by probing it).
- The fence `<: … :>` beyond its one-line description.
- How many policies and profiles exist behind the strictness dial (5.3), and how the explain, inspect, audit
  and expand commands overlap (5.6).

---

## Appendix: installments 1 and 2, as discussed

### Installment 1: syntax and semantic coherence

| # | Finding | Proposal | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1.1 | A write is invisible at the call: `bump(score)` | `&` on write arguments | Dropped: messy in the odd cases. A `:` name can never be changed by a call; only a `:=` name can. |
| 1.2 | `print("hi")` alone in a file is an error | A file of statements just runs | Decided. |
| 1.3 | Two signature orders (1,258 arrow-first, 455 error-first in Core) | The arrow always comes before the result | Decided. |
| 1.4 | `String ParseError!`: two types joined by a space | `String ! ParseError` | Open: O2. |
| 1.5 | Three implicit names: `it`, `<>`, `err` | Drop `<>` | Withdrawn: `<>` marks where piped data goes and pairs with the fence. |
| 1.6 | A second way to branch on a result: `r ? ok -> … ! error -> …` | Delete it | Open: O3. |
| 1.7 | `==` that destructures and binds in arm tables | `is` | Withdrawn after testing: every case behaves as a reader would guess. |
| 1.8 | Compile time has too many spellings | Rework | Section 3. |
| 1.9 | Style lints as warnings | No warnings | Decided, with the builder-friendly rule. |

Also from installment 1: one-liners under their own verb (O6); a comprehension should build a set or map directly;
a pipe step with no `<>` should pass the value as the first argument (not checked whether it does today).

### Installment 2: memory and reasoning

| # | Finding | Proposal | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2.1 | Value semantics (checked: after `b: a` and `a.push(4)`, `b` still has 3 items) | Keep; it is the strongest part of Jet | Keep. |
| 2.2 | Shared mutable state: many holders, and a cycle rule nobody can predict | One type-level rule; teach `Pool` and `ID` | Approved as a proposal: ballot D-SHARED-CYCLE2. |
| 2.3 | `add: fn() { … }` inside a function is an error (checked) | `fn(…)` is a value in any scope | Open: O4. |
| 2.4 | `try_new`, `try_push`, `try_insert` double the API | One scope where allocation failure is an error value | Open: O5. |
| 2.5 | No way to give ordinary code arena memory | A block in which ordinary collections allocate from an arena | Approved as a proposal: ballot D-REGION-ALLOC1. |
| 2.6 | Module-level mutable state is a trap: `score := 0` can be declared but no function may write it (checked) | First a `State` effect (withdrawn: friction for games); now a plain module variable owned by the main task | Open: O1. |

Leave alone: `name: value` everywhere; one `if` and one `loop`; read by default with `&` and `&&`; effects as
inferred permissions; errors as values; explicit `.copy()` and `.move()`; views with inferred owners instead of
lifetimes; tasks that must be joined or detached; `freeze`; no async/await; raw pointers only inside `#Unsafe`.

sections.title: #6376 — What five years of language release notes teach Jet
sections.body:
## #6376 — What five years of language release notes teach Jet

**Plain answer.** From 2021 to 2026, the language changes that worked were safe by default, had a measured cost, and came with a mechanical migration. The ones that failed put annotations on correct code, blocked the runtime in ways users could not see, or offered safety that a second path could skip.
Jet already follows most of these lessons. Probes found five real gaps: SQL and HTML injection through public fields, tasks stalled by OS waits, 192 MiB worker stacks that crash 32 trivial tasks under a 4 GB limit, a `jet fix` that breaks code, and one wrong error text.
One owner choice remains: how `jet fix` should move callers when a deprecated function's replacement takes different arguments (ballot D-DEPRECATE-INLINE1).

Full catalogue: `Docs/research/2026-10-30-language-release-notes.md`. It covers 25 languages, with a table per language: version, change, how it went in practice with its source, Jet today, and Jet's action and why.

### Source and method

- Official release notes, JEPs, PEPs and team blogs for C, C++, Rust, Go, Zig, Swift, Kotlin, Java, C#, Python, JS/TS, Ruby, PHP, Dart, Elixir/Erlang, Haskell, OCaml, Julia, Odin, Nim, V, Lua, Gleam, Mojo and Carbon, 2021–2026.
- Jet state: published `jet` 03c64ad0c4, dev worktree at 59213de00f, and Tower decisions and cards read on 2026-10-30.
- 18 probe files in the card's scratch probe set (rel/, not kept in the repository), all run on 03c64ad0c4 (`small/` holds the 8-, 16- and 32-task variants of r08, and `fixcopy/` the file `jet fix` edited). r07, the C-call variant of r08, could not resolve its C header in this environment. The shell's soft address-space limit is 4 GB; the two runs that raised it to 16 GB are marked.

### Lessons, with Jet's position

1. **Safe defaults win when the cost is measured.**
   - Go 1.22's per-iteration loop variables caused no production problems at Google.
   - Hardened libc++ cost Google 0.30% and found over 1,000 bugs.
   - Jet already captures per iteration (probe r04 prints `1`) and checks bounds by default.
2. **Breaks survive only with a mechanical fix.** Rust 2024 shipped `cargo fix`, Go 1.26 added `//go:fix inline`, and Mojo 1.0 shipped deprecated aliases and fix-its. Zig 0.15's "Writergate" broke every I/O caller with only hand migration.
   - Jet has the rule (#6068), but `jet fix` turned a compiling `double(4)` into a broken `scaled(4)` (r11).
3. **Withdrawn features died of cost or leaks.** Java string templates were withdrawn, Dart macros cancelled, Go error syntax abandoned, V's autofree is still "avoid using it", and Python 3.14.5 reverted its new GC.
   - Jet already avoids these: metaprograms cannot rewrite code, there are no glob imports, and there is no `async`.
4. **Concurrency must not punish correct code or block silently.**
   - Swift 6's checks flagged correct globals, and 6.2 changed the defaults.
   - Java virtual threads pinned their carrier threads until JEP 491.
   - Jet has the same blocking hole for OS waits (r08: a ready task waited 3.02 s).
5. **A safety type needs one door.** Java refused plain interpolation into templates, and Python's t-strings are not strings.
   - Jet refuses a plain String as SQL (E0149), but `SQL{text: s, values: []}` and `HTML{markup: s}` build both from any runtime string. r01f returns every row for `x' OR '1'='1`.

### Gaps found (cards in `answers/6376-cards.json`)

1. **Checked SQL and HTML built through their public fields** (r01e, r01f, r10). Make the fields private and keep `.raw` as the single, listed door.
2. **OS waits and foreign calls hold the worker** (r08, `HostProcess.jet:166-177`). This goes against D-ASYNCRT1=A's "blocking calls yield automatically".
3. **At least 192 MiB of stack per worker** (`Thread.jet:353-370`). Failing to start one is reported as a program panic (r09: 32 trivial tasks, exit 70 under a 4 GB limit; `done` at 16 GB).
4. **`jet fix` applies a rename that breaks the call**, and L2001 promises automatic migration anyway (r11).
5. **E0111 on a loop variable** says it "was made with `::`" and suggests `i := ...` (r06).

Criterion for an existing card: **#5026** (general defer). `return`, `break`, `next` and `?` inside a defer must get their registered codes. Today r03b gets E0003 "Expected a value", plus a follow-on error. Evidence: C's defer TS 25755 and Python's PEP 765.

Evidence for an open ballot: **#6332 / D-MODULE-WRITE1**. Swift 6 → 6.2 and Lua 5.5 show that the rule must not make single-task code carry concurrency annotations. r05 prints `2` today with no diagnostic.

Already filed, re-confirmed: #6374 (`String + String` gives a number-type error, r01b).

### Owner choice

- **D-DEPRECATE-INLINE1** (card #6405): `answers/ballots/D-DEPRECATE-INLINE1.json`, PLAIN OK and READY. When a deprecated function's replacement takes different arguments, how does `jet fix` move callers?
  - A (recommended): three steps in order. Inline the old body when it is a one-line wrapper, as Go 1.26 does. Otherwise use the author's call pattern from the marker. Otherwise leave the call and print the exact edit.
  - B: rename only.
  - C: a call pattern for every migration.

sections.title: #6377 — Jonathan Blow on error reporting, source locations and stack traces
sections.body:
## #6377 — Jonathan Blow on error reporting, source locations and stack traces

**Plain answer.** Jet already does much of what the talk asks for. It has no error cascades from one unknown name, it reports all files, every error ends with a help link, and failure trails show each hop.
The probes found four real gaps. A missing `}` gets blamed on the wrong block. A compile-time stop points at the `comptime` block, not at the failing line. A panic shows only its innermost frame. One error message suggests a spelling the compiler refuses.
Two owner choices come from the talk's metaprogram example: whether a house rule's report can be a real error at the bad line, and whether a library error may carry its own link.

Full catalogue: `Docs/research/2026-10-30-blow-error-reporting-talk.md`. It has 33 timestamped rows, each with what Jet does today and what Jet should do.

### Source and method

- Talk: "Why Compilers Bury the Real Error", Jonathan Blow Clips, 2026-10-15, 12:37 (<https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZF1m1DsW3Rg>), a clip of <https://youtube.com/watch?v=MnctEW1oL-E&t=8847s>.
- Mined with mine-for-jet-v2. Capture root: the mining run for #6377 (local capture, not kept). It holds 4 segments, 37 ledger items and 29 claims (23 micro, 6 macro).
  `check_coverage.mjs` passes. Density is 2.93 ledger items per minute against a floor of 1.
- Jet state: digest at master 1eef4640ad, dev 03c64ad0c4, Tower revision 86436.
  Probes are in the card's scratch probe set (trace/, not kept in the repository) and ran on the published `jet` 03c64ad0c4.
- Recall audit: PASS by a fresh reviewer. Seed `6377-r1-kestrel` sampled segments 01 (00:00–03:40) and 02 (03:40–07:36).
  The reviewer re-mined 22 concepts with 0 misses and 0 disputed mappings, and `check_coverage.mjs --audit` exited 0 (`recall-audit.json`).

### What Jet already does well (probe evidence)

- **No cascade from one unknown name** (talk 00:30–01:53, "poison values"). t01 uses an unknown name in three later lines and gets exactly one E0107.
