sections.title: Projects and packages: one clean model for Jet's config files
sections.body:
# Projects and packages: one clean model for Jet's config files

Status: proposal for card #6368, 2026-10-30. Design only; nothing here is built.
Reads with: `Docs/research/2026-10-30-project-package-config-today.md` (the map of today's files, fields, words and confusions, and the peer comparison).
Owner choices: six ballots, listed in section 11. The workspace-to-project rename is already the owner's ruling and is not balloted.

## Summary

Jet's config is confusing because one file does four jobs and one fact has several homes. This proposal gives every fact exactly one home, chosen by one question.

- **Two kinds of folder.** A **package** is code that others can depend on: it has a `package.jet`. A **project** is the folder you work in, usually the repository root: it owns `project.jet`, the committed `jet.lock` and the disposable `.jet/` folder. A small program is both at once and needs only `package.jet`, or no file at all.
- **One question sorts every fact.** *Would someone who depends on this package need it?* Yes: `package.jet` (name, version, deps, outputs, the effects it needs, its lint rules). No, it is about how we work here: `project.jet` (which packages are in the project, build and test profiles, dev tools, toolchain pin, overrides, team policy). Only for this one run: a command-line flag.
- **Facts are data, work is code.** `package.jet` and `project.jet` hold values only. Code that computes or runs lives in three fixed files beside `package.jet`: `build.jet` holds `fn build`, `test.jet` holds `fn test`, `dev.jet` holds `fn dev`. Nothing is found by searching.
- **Primitives first, wrappers on top.** The data files and the entry code make the same Core values (`Output`, `Action`, `BuildOptions`, `TestProfile`, `Environment`). One primitive call, `b.add(...outputs)`, can add any output; `b.add_executable("app", "run.jet", "util.jet", deps: [log])` is a one-line wrapper over it. Calls use positional arguments for what every call needs, a variadic tail for lists you type inline, and labels for every option.
- **One settings order.** stock → project → package (source markers, `package.jet`, `build.jet`) → flag. A pin anywhere, or a project `forbid`, refuses any conflicting value and names both lines.
- **"Workspace" leaves the package system.** No file, field, flag or message uses it. It keeps only its Jai meaning: one compilation with its own build options.
- **Custom linking (#5009).** A link hook returns a typed build action that Jet runs in place of its own link step for the outputs whose `link` option names it. A write hook may post-process the written file the same way. Both are option rows, so every one can be set, audited, pinned and forbidden. Programs that do not use them pay zero bytes.
- **Migration.** About 420 files change, almost all in `tests/` and `Examples/`. `jet fix` makes every move. A leftover old spelling is an error that names its new home.

## 1. The nouns

| Noun | What it is | Its file | Published? |
|---|---|---|---|
| **module** | a source file or folder of source files | any `.jet` | with its package |
| **package** | the unit you name, version, depend on and publish | `package.jet` (or an inline `package { }` block in a one-file program) | yes |
| **output** | one thing a package makes: one of the nine kinds of D-TARGET-ONE1 (Executable, Service, Library, Check, Bundle, Environment, Image, System, Fleet) | an `outputs:` entry or a `b.add(...)` call | with its package |
| **project** | the folder you work in: its packages, profiles, tools, lock, cache and policy | `project.jet` (optional), `jet.lock`, `.jet/` | never |

Rules that make these exact:

1. **Every command runs in exactly one project.** The project root is the nearest folder upward that holds `project.jet`. With no `project.jet`, it is the folder of the nearest `package.jet` (or the lone file's folder). So a one-package program is a project without writing one.
2. **A package belongs to one project.** A multi-package project lists its packages in `project.jet` `packages:`. A `package.jet` never lists other packages.
3. **Projects do not nest.** A `project.jet` inside another project's folder makes its own project; the outer project cannot list packages inside it. The error names both files.
4. **Nothing in `project.jet` is ever published or read by a consumer.** When your package is someone else's dependency, your `project.jet` does not exist for them. Cargo already behaves this way for profiles ("Profile settings defined in dependencies will be ignored", [Cargo profiles](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/profiles.html)); Jet makes it visible by giving those facts their own file.

The ladder (philosophy pillar 4) keeps every rung:

| Rung | Files | When |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | `hello.jet` | a script; `jet run hello.jet` (D-ECO14) |
| 1 | `hello.jet` with a `package { }` block | a one-file program that needs a name, deps or effects |
| 2 | `package.jet` + source files (+ `build.jet`, `test.jet`, `dev.jet` when needed) | a package |
| 3 | `project.jet` + packages | custom profiles, dev tools, team policy, or more than one package |

Moving up a rung never rewrites a fact: the same field, with the same text, moves to the next file. `jet fix` and `jet init` do the move (D-LOOSE-GROW1).

## 2. Which file? The beginner's rule

Ask, in order:

1. **Is it only for this run?** → a flag (`jet build --profile release`, `--set port=9090`).
2. **Is it work, meaning code that computes something or runs a tool?** → `build.jet`, `test.jet` or `dev.jet`, beside the `package.jet` it serves.
3. **Would someone who depends on or installs this package need it?** → `package.jet`. Otherwise → `project.jet`.

That is the whole rule. Each line below is "X goes in F because …".

| Fact | File | Because |
|---|---|---|
| name, version, edition, license, description, repository | `package.jet` | it identifies the package to everyone who uses it |
| `jet: "0.4"` (the toolchain range the package needs) | `package.jet` | a consumer's toolchain must satisfy it |
| a dependency, `deps: { http: "1.4" }` | `package.jet` | the package does not compile without it |
| "every package here uses the same `http` version" | `project.jet` `catalog:`, and `deps: { http: project }` in each package | it is a team agreement; each package opts in explicitly |
| an output, `outputs: { app: .Executable{ entry: run } }` | `package.jet` | it is what the package makes |
| an output's own needs, such as `os: web` for a web build or a C library to link | `package.jet`, in that output's `options:` | the output is wrong without it, whoever builds it |
| which output bare `jet run` picks, `defaults: { run: cli }` | `package.jet` | it is a choice among the package's own outputs |
| effects the code uses, `authority: { allow: [IO] }`, and grants to its deps | `package.jet` | a consumer must approve them |
| effects `build.jet` needs (today `build: { allow: … }`) | `package.jet` `authority: { build: [FS, Exec] }` | a consumer runs that build code too |
| lint and code rules for this package (`policy:`, `boundaries:`) | `package.jet` | they describe this package's code |
| a test suite that is plain data (a golden folder), `suites:` | `package.jet` | the suite is part of the package, like an output |
| a test suite that needs code (a fuzz driver) | `test.jet`, `t.suite(...)` | it is work |
| generated code, a code-made output, a custom tool step | `build.jet` | it is work |
| dev-loop behaviour of one service (port, watch, reload) | `dev.jet`, or that output's `options:` | it belongs to that output |
| the packages in this repo, `packages:` | `project.jet` | a consumer never sees your repo layout |
| `version`, `edition`, `license` that every package shares | `project.jet` | a package that leaves one out takes the project's (D-CORE-HEADER1, now written in one place) |
| build profiles, `release: BuildOptions{ optimize: full }` | `project.jet` `profiles:` | how you choose to build; a consumer's build never reads yours |
| test profiles, `quick: TestProfile{ suites: [tests], time_limit: 60s }` | `project.jet` `profiles:` | how you choose to test; same namespace as build profiles (D-TEST-PROFILE1) |
| which profile bare `jet build` / `jet test` uses | `project.jet` `defaults:` | a team choice |
| dev tools, shells and local services (today `env.jet`) | `project.jet` `environments:` | they serve the people working here |
| the exact toolchain the team builds with | `project.jet` `toolchain:`; the resolved version goes in `jet.lock` | a team choice; `package.jet` `jet:` is only the range consumers need |
| a local replacement for a dependency (overlay, patch) | `project.jet` `overlays:` | it must never leak to consumers |
| team policy: forbid an option or effect, pin a value, allow a dependency's hooks | `project.jet` `policy:` | it is a ceiling over every package here |
| the resolved dependency graph and toolchain | `jet.lock` (written by Jet, committed) | D-LOCKFILE1 |
| build output, cache, generated files | `.jet/` (disposable, git-ignored) | D-WORKSPACE-CMD1 |
| `optimize: size` just this once | a flag | rule 1 |

`policy:` exists at both levels with the same shape: the package's block governs that package's code, the project's block is a ceiling over every package. The stricter one wins, and a conflict names both lines. `defaults:` also exists at both levels, but each level picks only among its own things: a package picks among its outputs, a project picks a package and profiles.

Large teams that want to split `project.jet` do not need a `configs:` mechanism. Both data files are Jet values, so a field can take a value from an ordinary module of the project: `environments: team_envs.all`. The special `Config{}` records and `configs:` lists retire.

## 3. Code files: `build.jet`, `test.jet`, `dev.jet`

- `fn build(b: Build)` lives in `build.jet`, `fn test(t: Test)` in `test.jet`, `fn dev(d: Dev)` in `dev.jet`, each beside its `package.jet`. One of each per package at most (D-CONF-ENTRY1's count rule, kept).
- The only other home is a program with no `package.jet` (rungs 0 and 1): there, everything is in the one file.
- `project.jet` has no entry functions. A project builds by building its packages, in dependency order (D-WORKSPACE-CMD1). A thing made from several packages, such as a release bundle, is an output of a small package that depends on them.
- `package.jet` and `project.jet` hold values only, so `jet env`, editors and policy checks read them without running project code (D-JPK-DEVCOMPOSE1).

Why fixed homes, when D-CONF-ENTRY1 allowed any file: `fn build`, `fn test` and `fn dev` run on the developer's machine, before the program exists, with powers such as `Exec` and `FS`. A reviewer must be able to see from a diff that build-time code changed. Cargo (`build.rs`), Zig (`build.zig`), Gradle (`build.gradle.kts`) and Bazel (`BUILD`) all give build code one name for this reason. It also removes discovery: today `Examples/features/tooling/build_entry_discovery` needs a README to say where its build lives.

`jet new --template overrides` stubs change from "replace the stock default" to the shape D-ENTRY-SHAPE1 ratified: the entry sets values, then the stock work runs once.

## 4. How settings combine

One list replaces the three in force today (D-CONF-MERGE1, D-SETTING-ORDER1, and D-BUILD-REUSESET1's root layer). Later wins:

1. **stock**: Jet's defaults and the stock profiles;
2. **project**: `project.jet`, including the profile selected by `--profile` or `defaults:`;
3. **package**: source markers, then `package.jet`, then `build.jet`, for that package's outputs. Inside this layer an output's own `options:` beat package-wide values (D-SETTING-ORDER1);
4. **deployment**: environment, system and fleet layers, for Image, System and Fleet outputs only (D-CONF-MERGE1);
5. **flag**: the command line.

Two rules sit across the list:

- **Pin.** `b.pin(...)`, a `pin:` in `package.jet`, or a `pin:` in `project.jet` policy fixes a value. Any other layer that sets a different value is an error naming both lines (D-JAI-BUILDOPT1). A package pins what its output cannot work without; a project pins what the team requires.
- **Forbid.** `project.jet` `policy: { forbid: [...] }` names options or effects that no layer in the project may set. The error names the policy line (the owner's build-options ruling: project or package policy can forbid any option).

Why the project sits under the package: the project sets the team's defaults and profiles, and a package's stated need for one of its outputs must not be overridden silently by a team default. When the project must win, it pins, and the conflict becomes a visible error instead of a silent override. This is D-BUILD-REUSESET1's order, with the profile moved into the project.

`jet explain setting optimize --output app` prints every layer that set the value, with file and line.

## 5. Composition: primitives first, wrappers on top

The owner's rule for every API applies here first: a strong set of primitives that can express everything, then high-quality wrappers for the common cases. In config this means:

### 5.1 One set of values

Data files and entry code build the same Core values, so a fact moves between them unchanged:

| Value | Written in data as | Made in code by |
|---|---|---|
| `Output` (nine kinds) | `outputs: { app: .Executable{ entry: run } }` | `b.add(.Executable{ name: "app", entry: run })` |
| `BuildOptions` | `profiles: { release: BuildOptions{ optimize: full } }` | `b.options()`, `b.profile("release")` |
| `TestProfile` | `profiles: { quick: TestProfile{ suites: [tests] } }` | `t.profile("quick")` |
| `Environment` | `environments: { dev: Environment{ tools: ["git"] } }` | (data only; `jet env` never runs code) |
| `Action` | `options: { link: wasm.link }` (a function that returns one) | `b.action("stamp", run: [...], inputs: [...], outputs: [...])` |
| `Generated` | — | `b.generate("table") { ... }` (D-BUILD-GENVALUE1) |

### 5.2 The primitives

- `b.add(outputs: ...Output) -> [Output]`: add any outputs. A library can return `Output` values from ordinary functions and the caller adds them: `b.add(...web.targets("game", "editor"))`. This is the call every `add_*` wrapper reduces to.
- `b.output(name) -> &Output`: change a data-made or code-made output until the plan is sealed (D-TARGET-ONE1, D-JAI-CONFIG1).
- `b.action(name, *, run:, inputs:, outputs:, allow:, …)` → `Action`: every field of a declared build action, by label (D-BUILD-CORE1, D-BUILDACTION1).
- `b.generate(name) { … }` → `Generated`: the generated code as a value. It can be passed anywhere a source is, so nobody types `.jet/generated/...` paths again.
- `b.pin(...)` and the generated setting methods, one per option row (D-SETTING-ORDER1).

### 5.3 The wrappers

Each wrapper is an ordinary Core function whose body is one primitive call. It has no power the primitive lacks, and its doc comment shows the expansion. `jet explain` prints it.

```jet
// Core/Build: a wrapper is one line over the primitive
fn add_executable(b: &Build, name: String, sources: ...Source, *,
                  deps: [Package]{[]}, options: BuildOptions{}, entry: Entry?{None}) -> Output BuildError! {
    b.add(.Executable{ name: name, sources: sources, deps: deps, options: options, entry: entry })[0]
}
```

The data files are the zero-code wrapper: an `outputs:` entry is the literal form of the value `b.add` takes. The stock defaults are the zero-file wrapper: no `package.jet` means `run.jet` is the program.

### 5.4 Argument shape rules for config and build APIs

These follow Jet's call rules (S61, D-CALLPOS1, D-VARIADIC1) and use them on purpose:

1. **What every call needs is positional:** the name, then the main input.
2. **A list you would type inline is a variadic tail:** sources, command arguments, suites. `b.add_executable("app", "run.jet", "util.jet")`, not `["run.jet", "util.jet"]`. Spread passes an existing list: `b.add_executable("app", ...find("src/**/*.jet"))`.
3. **Every option is label-only with a default:** `deps:`, `options:`, `entry:`, `link:`. Callers never count positions.
4. **No arity families.** One signature per method, never "5 or 7 to 15 positional arguments".
5. **A wrapper is one primitive call** (5.3).

Today the build handle breaks all five. The checker rejects every label with E0764 "`Build.{method}` takes positional arguments … the build method contract does not declare labels or variadic slots" (`Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Calls/Build.jet:148`). `b.action` takes "5 or 7 to 15" positional arguments, and `add_*` takes "3 to 7" (`Build.jet:94-96`). D-BUILD-CORE1 already ratified labels; this section adds the variadic tail and the primitive.

Rule 2 needs one small language change. Jet requires a variadic parameter to be last (E1310), and a variadic after `*` becomes label-only. So `fn f(name: String, sources: ...String, *, deps: [String]{[]})` is E1310 today, and `fn g(name: String, *, deps: [String]{[]}, sources: ...String)` makes the call `g("app", "run.jet", deps: ["core"])` an E0769 (probed on dev; section 12). Python ([PEP 3102](https://peps.python.org/pep-3102/)), Swift ([Functions: variadic parameters](https://docs.swift.org/swift-book/documentation/the-swift-programming-language/functions/#Variadic-Parameters)) and Kotlin ([vararg](https://kotlinlang.org/docs/functions.html#variable-number-of-arguments-varargs)) all allow named parameters after a variadic one. Ballot D-CALL-VARTAIL1 asks whether label-only parameters may follow a variadic tail.

## 6. Before and after: four real projects

### 6.1 Hello

Before (`jet new hello` today, `Host.jet:1529-1531,1607,1618`):

```text
hello/package.jet   name, version, jet, description: "", license, repository: "",
                    authority: { allow: [IO, Mem.Alloc] }, deps: {}
hello/run.jet       fn run() { print("hello") }
hello/.jet/lock     written, and git-ignored by .gitignore
hello/.gitignore    .jet/build/  .jet/lock  .jet/cache/
```

After:

```text
hello/package.jet   name: "hello"
                    version: "0.1.0"
                    authority: { allow: [IO] }
hello/run.jet       fn run() { print("hello") }
hello/jet.lock      written by Jet, committed (D-LOCKFILE1)
hello/.gitignore    .jet/
```

No `project.jet`: the package folder is the project. Smaller still, `hello.jet` alone runs with `jet run hello.jet`. Changes: the lock is committed at the root, as ratified; empty placeholder fields are not written.

### 6.2 A library with tests

Before (D-TEST-PROFILE1's ratified shape, which today's parser rejects with E1206):

```jet
// textkit/package.jet
name: "textkit"
version: "0.3.0"
edition: "2026"
license: "MIT"
deps: { unicode: { git: "https://example.com/unicode", tag: "v1.2.0" } }
outputs: { textkit: .Library{ entry: textkit } }
build: { release: Build{ optimize: full } }
test: {
    quick: TestProfile{ suites: [tests], time_limit: 60s }
    full: TestProfile{ suites: [tests, golden], optimize: [none, full] }
}
suites: { golden: TestSuite{ golden_corpus: "tests/golden" } }
defaults: { test: quick }

// textkit/test.jet
fn test(t: Test) {
    t.suite("fuzz", fuzz_driver(seed: 7))
    t.run()
}
```

After:

```jet
// textkit/package.jet: what textkit is, needs and makes
name: "textkit"
version: "0.3.0"
edition: "2026"
license: "MIT"
deps: { unicode: { git: "https://example.com/unicode", tag: "v1.2.0" } }
outputs: { textkit: .Library{ entry: textkit } }
suites: { golden: TestSuite{ golden_corpus: "tests/golden" } }

// textkit/project.jet: how this team builds and tests it
profiles: {
    release: BuildOptions{ optimize: full }
    quick: TestProfile{ suites: [tests], time_limit: 60s }
    full: TestProfile{ suites: [tests, golden, fuzz], optimize: [none, full] }
}
defaults: { test: quick }

// textkit/test.jet: only the suite that needs code
fn test(t: Test) {
    t.suite("fuzz", fuzz_driver(seed: 7))
    t.run()
}
```

What a consumer of `textkit` sees is now exactly `package.jet`. The profiles stop looking like part of the library. `Build{ … }` becomes `BuildOptions{ … }` (D-ENTRY-NAMES1). A team that never customizes profiles has no `project.jet`.

### 6.3 A multi-package project: the Jet compiler

Before:

```jet
// env.jet (repo root): two of its environments
module env.compiler {
    sources: { default: NixOS/nixpkgs/nixos-unstable@github }
    packages: [ default.[ cargo, rustc, gcc, clang, lld, git, ripgrep, … ] ]
    prompt: "jet-compiler"
}

// Compiler/package.jet: a package named "compiler" that is also the root of 13 others
name: "compiler"
version: "0.0.1"
edition: "2026"
members: [ "JetFoundation", "JetLexer", …, "JetCli" ]

// Compiler/build.jet: makes the jet executable out of another package's file
fn build(b: Build) {
    jet :: b.add_executable("jet", ["JetCli/run.jet"], [])
    b.default(jet)
}

// Compiler/JetCli/package.jet
name: "jet_cli"
version: "0.0.1"
edition: "2026"
deps: { jet_foundation: ../JetFoundation, … }
authority: { allow: [Env, Exec, …] }
```

After:

```jet
// project.jet (repo root): the repo is the project
packages: [
    ...find("Compiler/*"),
    ...find("Jetpack/*"),
]
version: "0.0.1"
edition: "2026"
environments: {
    compiler: Environment{
        sources: { default: NixOS/nixpkgs/nixos-unstable@github }
        tools: [ default.[ cargo, rustc, gcc, clang, lld, git, ripgrep, … ] ]
        prompt: "jet-compiler"
    }
}

// Compiler/JetCli/package.jet: the package that owns the code owns the output
name: "jet_cli"
deps: { jet_foundation: ../JetFoundation, … }
outputs: { jet: .Executable{ entry: run } }
authority: { allow: [Env, Exec, …] }
```

`env.jet`, `Compiler/package.jet` and `Compiler/build.jet` are gone. `jet build` at the root builds every package; `jet build jet` builds the one output; `jet run jet -- --version` runs it. Members take `version` and `edition` from the project. The package named "compiler", which had no code of its own, no longer exists. That ends the case where a named root silently skips its own code (bug B1, section 12).

### 6.4 A project with build-time code generation

Before (`Examples/features/tooling/build_write_generated`):

```jet
// package.jet
name: "build_write_generated_example"
version: "0.1.0"
edition: "2026"
build: {
    inspect: Build{ write_generated: on },
}

// build.jet
fn build(b: Build) {
    b.generate("table") {
        fn table_size() -> Int { 5 }
    }
    app :: b.add_executable("run", ["run.jet", ".jet/generated/build_write_generated_example/table.jet"], [])
    b.default(app)
}
```

After:

```jet
// package.jet
name: "build_write_generated_example"
version: "0.1.0"
edition: "2026"

// project.jet
profiles: { inspect: BuildOptions{ write_generated: on } }

// build.jet
fn build(b: Build) {
    table :: b.generate("table") {
        fn table_size() -> Int { 5 }
    }
    app :: b.add_executable("run", "run.jet", table)
    b.default(app)
}

// The same build written with the primitive only:
fn build(b: Build) {
    table :: b.generate("table") {
        fn table_size() -> Int { 5 }
    }
    b.default(b.add(.Executable{ name: "run", sources: ["run.jet", table] })[0])
}
```

The generated code is a value, so the build no longer names a path inside `.jet/`, and the cache layout can change without breaking it. The trailing `[]` (an empty positional action list) is gone. The two spellings build the identical plan; `jet inspect build` cannot tell them apart.

## 7. Custom link and post-link steps (#5009)

D-JAI-EVENTS1=A (2026-10-17) added the stages `build.link(LinkInputs) -> Artifact`, `build.before_write(Artifact) -> replacement` and `build.after_write(Artifact) -> findings`, run as build actions. The owner asked for a ballot on whether a typed build action may replace one output's link step and post-process the written file. In this model the answer fits in three pieces:

1. **The hook returns a typed action; Jet runs it.** A `#On(build.link)` function receives `LinkInputs`: the object files, libraries, link arguments, the output path, and `default`, the exact `Action` Jet would run. It returns an `Action` (D-BUILDACTION1): a declared command with inputs, outputs and `Exec`/`FS` capabilities. Jet runs it in place of its own link step, checks that it wrote the declared file, and records it. A `#On(build.before_write)` function returns an `Action` that turns the linked file into the final one (strip, compress, patch). `#On(build.after_write)` stays read-only and returns findings. Hooks never write files themselves, so every byte that reaches the output came from a declared, cached, recorded action.
2. **Which outputs use it is an option row.** `link: default | <hook>` and `post_link: [<hook>, …]` are rows of the one option table, so each has a flag (`--link=default`), a `package.jet` field (an output's `options:`), a `project.jet` profile field and a handle method (`b.output("game").link(wasm.link)`). Owner directive #4913 holds: no option without all three. Experts get full control: `LinkInputs.default` is the stock command, so a hook can edit one argument and keep everything else.
3. **Policy and audit.** `project.jet` or `package.jet` `policy: { forbid: [link, post_link] }` refuses both. A dependency's hook runs only if `project.jet` policy allows that package's hooks (D-HOOK-STAGES1's grant rule). `jet inspect build` shows, per output, the link action's argv, its capabilities, and the line that chose it.

**Binary size (D-SIZE-PAYUSE1).** Hooks run at build time and nothing is linked into the program, so a program that does not use them is byte-for-byte unchanged. `LinkInputs.default` is the stock link command with all of Jet's link arguments, so a hook that edits one argument keeps the rest, including the ones that keep the file small. The build record reports the artifact size after the last post-link step, so size reports measure the file that actually ships.

```jet
// wasmtools/link.jet: a hook package
#On(build.link)
fn link(i: build.LinkInputs) -> Action {
    Action{
        run: ["wasm-ld", "--no-entry", "--export-all", ...i.objects, "-o", i.output],
        inputs: i.objects,
        outputs: [i.output],
        allow: [.Exec],
    }
}

#On(build.before_write)
fn optimize(a: build.Artifact) -> Action {
    Action{ run: ["wasm-opt", "-Oz", a.path, "-o", a.next], inputs: [a.path], outputs: [a.next], allow: [.Exec] }
}

// game/package.jet: only the web output links with wasm-ld
outputs: {
    game_web: .Executable{ entry: run, options: { os: web, link: wasmtools.link, post_link: [wasmtools.optimize] } }
}

// project.jet: the team allows hooks from this one dependency
policy: { hooks: [wasmtools] }
```

Ballot D-LINK-STEP1 has the options and the same program under each.

## 8. Words

- **project**: the folder you work in (section 1). It replaces "workspace" in the package system, in CLI help and diagnostics, and in Canvas's `"mode": "workspace"` (`Docs/spec/reference/canvas-workspace-architecture.md`).
- **workspace**: only its Jai meaning, one compilation with its own build options (`compiler_create_workspace`). In Jet that is one output built under one set of options (D-JAI-CONFIG1). No file, field or flag uses the word.
- **Jetspace** (D-ECO-ROOTNAME2=D) retires: "the project" names the checked graph of a project's packages.
- **packages:** is the `project.jet` field that lists packages (it replaces `members:`). The old `package.jet` `packages:` map of output kinds folds into `outputs:`.
- **profile**: a named `BuildOptions` or `TestProfile`, written only in `project.jet` `profiles:`. A platform preset in `targets:` says `platform:`, not `profile:`.
- **build**: the command, the `Build` handle and `build.jet`. The `build:` field retires (profiles moved), and so does `Build{ … }` as a record (D-ENTRY-NAMES1).
- **target**: the platform only (D-TARGET-ONE1).

Ballot D-PROJECT-WORDS1 settles the words that follow from the rename.

## 9. Migration and the `jet fix` story

Counts are `git ls-files` at `e784bb1ffe`.

| Today | After | Files | `jet fix` |
|---|---|---|---|
| `workspace.jet` (`module workspace { members: X }`, overlays) | `project.jet` (`packages: X`, `overlays:`) | 22 | rename and reshape; a `fn` inside moves to its package's `build.jet`/`run.jet` |
| `env.jet` (`module env.<n> { packages: … }`) | `project.jet` `environments: { <n>: Environment{ tools: … } }` | 159 | merge; 154 sit where no `package.jet` exists and become `project.jet` files, not nameless packages |
| `members:` in `package.jet` | `project.jet` `packages:` | 5 | move; a named root with no code of its own is deleted after its outputs move to the package that owns the code |
| `build:` profiles in `package.jet` (35) and inline blocks (3) | `project.jet` `profiles:`; `build: { allow: }` → `authority: { build: }` | 38 | move; `Build{}` → `BuildOptions{}` |
| profile keys of `defaults:` | `project.jet` `defaults:` | ≤ 18 | split by key |
| `packages:` output map in `package.jet` | `outputs:` | 80 | rewrite each entry as an output value |
| `config.jet`, `configs:` files, `Config{}` records | the field's home in `package.jet` or `project.jet` | 32 + 5 | inline by field |
| `fn build`/`fn test`/`fn dev` outside its home, in a package with `package.jet` | `build.jet` / `test.jet` / `dev.jet` | 38 (21 in `run.jet`, 8 in `main.jet`, 3 in `package.jet`, 2 in `tools/build_entry.jet`, 4 others) | move the function; same package, so names still resolve |
| committed `.jet/lock` | `jet.lock` | 22 | move; `.gitignore` becomes `.jet/` |
| `pkg.jet` | `package.jet` | 5 | rename (already retired) |
| `jet new` templates and stubs | the new shapes | code | rewrite (`Host.jet:1513-1531`) |

Total: about 420 files, almost all fixtures under `tests/` and `Examples/`. Core's 604 inline `package { }` blocks are unchanged except 3 with `build:` and 3 with `configs:`. The 29 entry functions already in their home and the 104 in one-file programs do not move.

`jet fix` is mechanical for every row: each rewrite moves text between files without changing its meaning, and `jet fix --dry-run` prints the moves. After the cutover, every old spelling is a registered error that names its new home and the fix, for example: "`members:` belongs in project.jet as `packages:`. Run `jet fix`." There are no aliases and no fallback reads (clean cutover).

## 12. Bugs and drift found while probing

Probes ran on dev `e784bb1ffe` with the base compiler. Repros are in the research doc, section 6.

- **B1. A named root with members skips its own code.** Root `package.jet` with `name: "p3"`, `members: ["a"]` and an `outputs:` app; root `run.jet` refers to an undefined name; member `a/run.jet` prints "hi". `jet check .` and bare `jet check` print "ok: …/a/run.jet has no problems"; `jet run` prints `hi`. Only `jet check run.jet` reports E0107. Expected: check every package, including the root, and run the root's own default.
- **B2. E1206 for `test:` explains the wrong thing.** Its "Why" line says "Identity is bare `name:` and `version:` … there is no `identity:` or `payload:` wrapper".
- **B3. One mistake, two codes.** Two `fn build` in one package (`build.jet` and `tools/build.jet`): `jet check .` gives E0105 "Imported names share the module namespace", `jet build` gives E3520 "Two build entries for the package".
- **B4. Members listed twice are accepted.** A root with `members: ["a"]` in `package.jet` and `module workspace { members: ["a"] }` in `workspace.jet` checks clean.
- **Drift D1.** `jet new` writes `.jet/lock` and git-ignores it, against D-LOCKFILE1 (committed root `jet.lock`).
- **Drift D2.** `jet new --template overrides` stubs say "replace the stock default", against D-ENTRY-SHAPE1.
- **Drift D3.** Six `.jet/last-run/*` files are committed under `Examples/features/tooling/build_entry_discovery`, though `.jet/` is disposable.
- **Language gap.** A variadic cannot be followed by label-only parameters (E1310), and a variadic after `*` is label-only (E0769). Not a bug; D-CALL-VARTAIL1 asks the owner.

Peer facts and citations are in the research doc, section 7. Additional: [PEP 3102 keyword-only arguments](https://peps.python.org/pep-3102/); [Swift functions, variadic parameters](https://docs.swift.org/swift-book/documentation/the-swift-programming-language/functions/#Variadic-Parameters); [Kotlin varargs](https://kotlinlang.org/docs/functions.html#variable-number-of-arguments-varargs). Repo: `Jetpack/PackageModel/Source/Manifest/PackageParse.jet`, `Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Calls/Build.jet`, `Compiler/JetCli/Source/Cli/{Entry,Host,Request}.jet`, `Docs/audits/jai-parity-2026-10-16.md` §D, `Docs/proposals/build-programs-and-compiler-events-2026-10-22.md`.

sections.title: A greenfield FFI design, and what Jet should adopt
sections.body:
# A greenfield FFI design, and what Jet should adopt

Card #6366. Status: proposal. Owner choices are in the ballots listed in §9.
They are not decided here.

## Plain summary

- **The idea.** Every foreign boundary is described once, as a *boundary
  contract*. That is a typed list of functions and types, plus the facts a C
  header cannot say: who owns memory, how long a view lives, how errors come
  back, which thread may call, and whether a call is async.
- **Readers and writers.** A reader package builds the contract from whatever
  the other side has (a C header, a Rust crate, a `.d.ts`, a WIT file, a JVM
  class, Windows metadata, a GPU shader). A writer package turns the same
  contract into bindings for whoever calls *us*. Both directions share one
  model, so N languages cost N readers plus N writers, not N×N bridges.
- **Two layers.** A small, complete, unsafe *primitives* layer can express
  every boundary: layout, symbols, calls, memory, callbacks, errors, threads,
  async, isolation. Pareto *wrappers* sit on top: `use "png.h" as png`,
  `#Export`, and typed imports for Rust, Python and JS. Every wrapper
  expands into primitives that you can inspect, so the expert path is a ladder,
  not a cliff.
- **Safe by default.** A call is safe when its facts are checked, vouched for
  in a named `#Unsafe("reason")`, or *isolated*. Isolated means the same import
  runs in a wasm sandbox or a separate process, with no source changes.
- **Zero cost.** A crossing whose types already match costs one direct call.
  When the foreign source is visible, the optimizer can inline across the
  boundary.
- **For Jet.** Most of this is already ratified: header import, C source import,
  binder packages, ownership sigils at the border, vouches, both embedding
  artifacts, and the hardened profile. The new pieces are a public primitives
  layer, isolation as a placement option, and rich exports. Each is one ballot.
  Inline C stays, and becomes a thin wrapper over C-source import, which
  removes the "two ways to bring in C" loss that D-FFI-ONE1 recorded.

This builds on, and does not replace, the boundary audit
[`Docs/audits/ffi-owned-source-and-boundaries.md`](../audits/ffi-owned-source-and-boundaries.md)
(#2933), which covers project arrangements and workflows. This document is the
mechanism underneath them.

---

## 1. What "perfect" means: ten testable goals

| # | Goal | Test |
|---|------|------|
| G1 | **Any to any.** Call out to, and be called from, C, C++, Rust, Zig, Swift, Objective‑C, Java/Kotlin, C#, Python, JS/wasm, GPU kernels and OS ABIs. | Every language has a reader and a writer, or a documented reason why not. |
| G2 | **Zero cost when shapes match.** | A blittable call compiles to the same machine code as a C-to-C call. |
| G3 | **Safe by default, total control when asked.** | No safe code can corrupt memory through a binding. Every unchecked fact is a named, auditable vouch. |
| G4 | **No hand-written glue for the common case.** | One line binds a library. Zero lines of marshalling. |
| G5 | **No cliff.** | Every wrapper is a documented composition of public primitives (philosophy: *Ladders, Not Cliffs*). |
| G6 | **Facts, not guesses.** | Each fact (ownership, length, nullability, error style) carries its provenance. Unknown facts get the conservative projection, never a guessed one. |
| G7 | **One meaning everywhere.** | The same import behaves the same at every tier, on the web, and in compile-time code (I9). |
| G8 | **Versioned.** | A library upgrade that breaks the contract fails at build time or at load time, with a diff. It never shows up as a crash. |
| G9 | **Debuggable.** | Mixed-language backtraces, boundary tracing, and hardened checks at the edges. |
| G10 | **Placement independent.** | The same import can run in-process, in a wasm sandbox, or in another process. Only one option changes. |

No shipping system meets more than four of these goals today (§2).

## 2. State of the art

Each row lists the idea worth taking and the gap that stops it being the
answer. Sources are in §10.

| System | Model | Best idea | Gap |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Zig** `@cImport` / translate‑c | Compile-time header translation with a bundled Clang | The compiler is also a C compiler, so C and Zig cross-compile and link with no extra toolchain. | C only. No ownership or length facts. `@cImport` is moving to the build system (0.16 notes) because compile-time import tied the language to Clang's life cycle [Z1,Z2]. |
| **Rust bindgen / cxx / UniFFI / PyO3 / Diplomat** | Build step (bindgen), bridge macros (cxx), IDL or proc-macro (UniFFI, Diplomat), per-host crate (PyO3) | cxx: a safe *bridge* language that is checked on both sides. UniFFI and Diplomat: **one description, many host languages**. Rust 2024 `unsafe extern` lets each item be marked `safe` [R1–R6]. | Five tools with five models. Outward bindings come from Rust only. The stable ABI (`crabi`) is still experimental [R7]. |
| **Swift ↔ C/C++/ObjC** | Clang importer in the compiler | Imports headers directly. Clang *API notes* refine imported facts without editing the header. Non-escapable types and lifetime annotations make C++ views safe [S1–S3]. | Safety rests on annotations that most libraries lack. Template and virtual-class support is partial [S4]. |
| **Kotlin/Native cinterop, Swift export** | `.def` file plus a build-time tool | A declarative definition file that holds options, headers and filters. Direct Swift export without ObjC headers [K1–K3]. | Build step only. ObjC import is still Beta. |
| **.NET P/Invoke → `LibraryImport`** | Source generator at compile time | Marshalling code is *generated and visible*, works with AOT, and is extensible through custom marshallers [N1,N2]. `UnmanagedCallersOnly` handles the reverse direction. | One direction at a time. No lifetime facts. |
| **Java FFM (Panama)** | Runtime linker API plus `jextract` | A complete *primitives* API (Linker, FunctionDescriptor, MemoryLayout, Arena) with jextract as the wrapper. `captureCallState` reads errno. Confined arenas bound lifetimes [J1–J3]. | Verbose without jextract. Safety is a runtime check, not a type. |
| **LuaJIT FFI** | Parse C declarations at run time | The JIT compiles FFI calls inline. Close to zero overhead from a dynamic language [L1]. | No safety at all. C only. |
| **Python cffi / ctypes** | ABI mode (dlopen) or API mode (compile a shim) | Offers *both* modes behind one declaration language [P1,P2]. | Copies by default. No ownership model. |
| **Nim** `importc` / `importcpp` | Pragmas on declarations | Pattern strings for C++ calls (`#.method(@)`) reach templates without a shim [M1]. | Nothing is checked. A wrong pattern means undefined behaviour. |
| **Odin** `foreign` blocks / **Jai** `#foreign` | Declarations in the source, link by name | The shortest syntax there is. Calling convention and library on the block [O1,JA1]. | Hand-written. Nothing is read from headers. |
| **D** ImportC / `extern(C++)` | Compiler compiles C directly | `import foo;` on a `.c` file. Matches C++ mangling and vtables for single inheritance [D1,D2]. | C++ templates must be mirrored by hand. |
| **Carbon** | `import Cpp library "x.h"` | C++ interop is a *design mandate*. Bidirectional, with no wrapper layer [C1,C2]. | Experimental. |
| **Mojo** | Python objects in Mojo, plus `PythonModuleBuilder` for exports | Both directions with a single builder [MO1]. | CPython only. Exports are built by hand. |
| **GraalVM polyglot** | Shared VM, interop protocol | One object protocol across JS, Python, Ruby, Java and LLVM bitcode [G1]. | Needs the Graal VM. Not a native ABI. |
| **wasm Component Model / WIT** | IDL plus canonical ABI | **A language-neutral contract with resources (owned handles), results, and since WASI 0.3, async `future`/`stream`** [W1–W3]. Isolation comes free. | Copies across the boundary. Sandboxed only. |
| **WinRT / win32metadata** | Machine-readable metadata, then projections | Windows APIs described once, projected into C#, C++ and Rust [WM1]. | Windows only. |
| **RLBox** (Firefox) | Compile C libraries to wasm, then back to native | *Isolation without rewriting*: the same library is sandboxed, with "tainted" types at the edge [RB1]. | C++ only. Annotations by hand. |
| **Arrow C Data / DLPack** | ABI-stable structs for columns and tensors | Zero-copy data exchange across every runtime [A1,A2]. | Data only, no calls. |
| **Clang `-fbounds-safety`** | `counted_by` / `sized_by` annotations | Length facts live in the C header itself, so any reader can use them [B1]. | Only as good as adoption. |

**The pattern:** the best systems separate a *contract* (WIT, winmd, UniFFI
UDL, cxx bridge) from *projections*. The best ergonomics come from reading
sources the user already has (Zig, Swift, D, Carbon). The best expert control
comes from a public primitives API (Java FFM). Nobody combines all three, and
nobody makes placement (in-process versus sandbox) a single option.

## 3. The design in one picture

```
 foreign sources          readers (packages)        contract           writers (packages)        callers
 C/C++/ObjC headers ─┐                          ┌─ functions, types ─┐  C header ─────────────┐
 C/C++ source        ├─► c, cpp, objc ──────────┤  + facts with      ├─► C++ RAII header        │
 Rust crate (rustdoc)├─► rust                   │    provenance:     ├─► Swift package          │
 Swift .swiftinterface► swift                   │  ownership, life-  ├─► Kotlin/JVM (FFM, JNI)  ├─► any host
 JVM class / .NET md ├─► jvm, dotnet            │  time, length,     ├─► C# LibraryImport       │
 .pyi / .d.ts / WIT  ├─► python, js, wit        │  errors, threads,  ├─► Python ext (abi3)      │
 winmd / SDK .tbd    ├─► os                     │  async, effects,   ├─► Node-API / JS + WIT    │
 SPIR-V / PTX / WGSL ┘─► gpu                    └─ version, purity ──┘  Rust crate, WIT world ──┘
                                     ▲                     │
                                     │        lowered by the primitives layer
                       overlays (API-notes style)          ▼
                                            layout · symbol · call · memory · thunk ·
                                            error capture · thread attach · async bridge ·
                                            marshal · isolate
```

There are four layers. Each one is written only in terms of the layer below.

1. **Primitives (L0).** The complete, unsafe vocabulary (§4).
2. **Contract (L1).** Plain data: the rows and their facts. Readers produce it,
   overlays refine it, writers and the lowering pass consume it (§5).
3. **Readers and writers (L2).** Ordinary packages that run at compile time.
   They are sandboxed and have pinned tool versions (§6).
4. **Wrappers (L3).** The pareto one-liners (§7).

## 4. Layer 0: the primitives (complete set)

Every primitive is public. The ones that can break memory safety are callable
only inside `#Unsafe("reason")`. The comptime-only ones are safe. Together they
must express every boundary in G1. If a reader needs something they cannot
express, that is a bug in L0, not a reason for a private hook.

| Primitive | Purpose | Safe? |
|---|---|---|
| `layout<T>(target:)` → `Layout` (size, align, field offsets, bitfields, padding) | Ask the exact per-target layout. Pick a layout with `#Layout(.C | .Packed(n) | .Explicit | .Std430 | .Scalar)`. | yes (comptime) |
| `abi(target:)` → `CallConv` classifier (SysV x86‑64, Win64, AAPCS64, Apple arm64, RISC‑V, wasm32, Swift, Rust‑C, `.Vectorcall`, …) | Shows how each argument is passed (register, stack, sret, split). Used for the Apple arm64 rule that variadic arguments always go on the stack [AP1]. | yes (comptime) |
| `symbol<Sig>(name, from:)` (static), `Library.open(path)` and `lib.symbol<Sig>(name)` (dynamic) | Get the address of a foreign function or global. Weak or optional symbols return `T?`. | link: yes; dynamic: `#Unsafe` |
| `FnPtr<Sig>` call; `call_variadic(fp, fixed, extra: ...CArg)` | Direct call through a typed signature. C default argument promotions are applied by the compiler. `va_list` is a type. | `#Unsafe` unless the row is checked |
| Raw memory: `Ptr<T>`, offset, cast, `alloc_raw` / `free_raw`, `view(ptr, count)` | The memory model, with provenance kept. | `#Unsafe` |
| `thunk(f, conv:)` → `Callback<Sig>` (code pointer + context + owned registration) | Pass closures to C as a (function, user data) pair. `trampoline(f)` covers APIs that take no user data, using a fixed pool. | creating: yes; handing over a raw pointer: `#Unsafe` |
| `capture: [.Errno, .LastError, .NSError, .HResult]` on a call | Read thread-local error state atomically with the call (as in Java `captureCallState`). | yes |
| `unwind: .Abort | .Catch(.Cpp) | .Catch(.RustPanic) | .Propagate` | What happens when a foreign exception reaches the edge. The default is `.Abort`, because unwinding through frames that do not expect it is undefined behaviour (Rust `C-unwind` [R8]). | yes |
| `attach()` and `affinity(.Any | .Main | .Creator)` | Foreign threads enter the runtime automatically through thunks. Affinity is checked when a call is made. | yes |
| `completion<T>()` → (token, Future) and `poll_bridge(handle)` | Turn callback-style or poll-style foreign async into Jet tasks, and the reverse. | yes |
| `Marshal<F>` trait: `lower`, `lift`, `release`, and `BLITTABLE: Bool` | User-extensible conversion. Every built-in projection is a `Marshal` impl. | impl: yes; raw parts: `#Unsafe` |
| `Contract` values: `read`, `merge(overlay)`, `verify(lib)`, `hash` | The L1 data, available at compile time to every package. | yes |
| `isolate(contract, placement: .InProcess | .Wasm | .Process)` | Run the same contract behind a sandbox. Arguments are copied or shared according to their facts. | yes |

Why this set is complete: a boundary needs (a) a shape (layout and ABI),
(b) a target (symbol), (c) a transfer (call, memory, marshal), (d) the reverse
transfer (thunk, attach), (e) the out-of-band channels (error capture, unwind,
async), and (f) a trust decision (contract, isolate). Each primitive covers
exactly one of these.

## 5. Layer 1: the boundary contract

A contract is a list of rows: functions, types, constants and globals. Each
row has a signature plus **facts**. Every fact records where it came from:

| Provenance | Meaning | Callable from safe code? |
|---|---|---|
| `Read` | Stated by the source: a `counted_by`, `_Nonnull`, a Rust `&`, a WIT `own<T>`, Java `@NonNull`, or a `.d.ts` type. | yes |
| `Proved` | Checked by analysis. The C source is visible and the fact holds. | yes |
| `Vouched` | Written by a person inside `#Unsafe("reason") { … }`. Listed by `jet audit`. | yes, at the vouch |
| `Observed` | Asserted at run time by the hardened profile (D-HARDENED1). | adds checks only |
| `Unknown` | Nothing is known. | **only through the conservative projection** (copy in, copy out, opaque handle, `T?`) or isolation |

Fact kinds, one vocabulary for every language:

- **Ownership.** Lend for this call (`&`), give away (`^`), returns owned (with
  a `#Close(fn)` release), returns borrowed from parameter *p*, shared
  (refcounted: ObjC ARC, COM, `Arc`, `shared_ptr`).
- **Lifetime.** A view is valid while *p* lives, until the next call on *p*, or
  only for this call. This is the Swift `@lifetime` and non-escapable model [S2].
- **Length and termination.** `counted_by(n)`, `sized_by(n)`,
  NUL-terminated, sentinel-terminated.
- **Nullability and encoding.** Nullable or not. UTF-8, UTF-16, Latin-1,
  OS-native path, or raw bytes.
- **Errors.** Return code with a success set, status plus out-parameter, errno,
  `GetLastError`, `NSError**`, `HRESULT`, C++ exception, Rust panic, JS throw,
  Python exception. Each maps to a typed `T E!` result.
- **Threads.** Thread-safe, main-thread only, same thread as the creator,
  reentrant or not.
- **Async.** Completion callback (which argument, called how many times),
  promise or future, stream.
- **Effects and purity.** The Jet effects the call performs (`Net`, `FS`, …).
  `pure` allows compile-time evaluation and common-subexpression elimination.
- **Version.** Introduced in, deprecated in, optional symbol.

**Overlays** are the Clang API-notes idea generalised [S5]. A user module can
add or correct facts and rename rows without touching the foreign source. The
overlay wins, and a fact the overlay changes from `Read` to `Vouched` becomes
an audit entry. (In Jet this is `#Import module c.png { … }`, D-FFI-CMAP1 and
D-FFI-VOUCH1.)

**The conservative projection** is what makes "safe by default" real without
blocking work:

| Unknown fact | Safe projection |
|---|---|
| Pointer with no length | Opaque `Handle` (no indexing) |
| Pointer that might be null | `T?` |
| `char*` with no encoding | `Bytes` (copied) |
| Returned pointer with no owner | Borrowed for this call only. It is copied out before the call returns. |
| Callback with no thread fact | Delivered on the caller's executor through a queue |
| Error style unknown | Plain return value, with an audit note |

## 6. Layer 2: readers and writers

Readers and writers are ordinary packages written with comptime and the L0/L1
API. The compiler has no private hooks for them; this is philosophy's *The
Language Is A Library*. They run sandboxed with pinned tool versions, and their
output is cached by content (reader version, inputs, target). The same reader
runs as a build step (`jet bind`) when a team wants to commit or vendor the
result. **One mechanism serves both compile-time import and build-step
generation**, which answers the problem behind Zig's move of `@cImport` into
the build system [Z1].

| Language | Reader input | How a call crosses | Writer output (being called) |
|---|---|---|---|
| C | Headers and source, through a pinned Clang. Constant macros are evaluated. Function-like macros are instantiated as tiny typed C shims. | Direct C ABI | `.h`, plus `counted_by` and nullability annotations |
| C++ | Clang AST. Templates are instantiated on demand in a generated shim. Overloads are folded by label. Virtual classes can be subclassed through vtable thunks. | C ABI shim. Exceptions are caught in the shim. Inlined at O2 when the source is visible. | A C++ header of RAII classes over the C ABI (the cxx/Diplomat pattern [R2,R5]) |
| Objective‑C | Clang plus nullability, `NS_SWIFT_NAME`, ARC rules | Typed `objc_msgSend` per selector. Blocks are thunks. Retain and release map to ownership. | An ObjC header with `NS_*` annotations |
| Swift | `.swiftinterface`, using library-evolution layout rules [SW1] | The Swift calling convention on Apple targets, or `@_cdecl` shims elsewhere | A Swift package (C module plus a Swift overlay) |
| Rust | rustdoc JSON, plus a generated `extern "C"` shim crate. `crabi` when it is stable [R7]. | C ABI. Panics are caught in the shim (`C-unwind`). | A crate with an `unsafe extern` block whose items are marked `safe` [R6], plus safe wrappers |
| Zig | Exported C-ABI declarations | Direct C ABI | A `.h` (Zig consumes C headers) |
| Java/Kotlin | Class files and Kotlin metadata | An embedded JVM through JNI invocation, or a JVM sidecar | FFM bindings (jextract-shaped) on desktop and server, JNI on Android |
| C# / .NET | ECMA‑335 metadata | Hosting through `hostfxr`, or NativeAOT exports | A `LibraryImport` partial class with generated marshallers |
| Python | `.pyi` plus the C-API, HPy, or a supervised worker | In-process (CPython stable ABI), or isolated | A stable-ABI (`abi3`) extension module |
| JS / TS | `.d.ts` | Browser: direct imports. Native: an embedded engine in a wasm component. | Node-API addon, ES module plus wasm, a WIT world for jco |
| wasm components | WIT | Canonical ABI. Async uses WASI 0.3 `future`/`stream` [W2]. | A WIT world and a component |
| GPU | SPIR-V reflection, PTX, WGSL, Metal libraries | Launch descriptors and buffer-binding layouts (std430/scalar). DLPack or Arrow for zero-copy tensors and columns [A1,A2]. | SPIR-V/PTX modules with generated host bindings |
| OS ABIs | Linux syscall tables. winmd (Win32/WinRT/COM) [WM1]. Apple SDK headers and `.tbd` files. | Raw syscalls on Linux only, where that ABI is stable. Otherwise libc, ntdll or libSystem. COM vtables with refcounts mapped to ownership. | Not applicable |

**Embedding when we are called.** The writer emits an `init(capabilities)`
entry and lazy per-thread attach. The capability list comes from one contract,
for both a native library and a component (Jet already ratified this as
D-EMBED2=C).

**Garbage-collected hosts (JVM, CLR, JS, Python).** Foreign references become
owned handles with a `#Close` that releases a global reference. Nothing
collects cycles across two heaps. The writer documents weak handles for back
references, and the hardened profile reports leaked handles.

## 7. Layer 3: the pareto wrappers

| Need (most common first) | Wrapper | Expands to |
|---|---|---|
| Use a C library | `use "png.h" as png` | C reader → contract → lowering. Safe rows are callable, the rest need a vouch or isolation. |
| A few lines of C | an inline foreign body on a `fn` | An anonymous C source unit read by the **same** C reader. The prototype comes from the Jet signature. |
| Fix or rename imported rows | `#Import module c.png { … }` | An L1 overlay |
| Vouch for an unchecked row | `#Unsafe("reason") { fn … = "sym" }` | A `Vouched` fact plus an audit entry |
| Use a Rust, Python, JS or C++ package | `#Import module rust.serde_json`, `use py.numpy`, … | A reader package, a contract, and a placement |
| Sandbox an untrusted library | `use "libxml2.h" as xml, isolate: .Wasm` | `isolate(contract, .Wasm)`. No call site changes. |
| Be called from another language | `#Export` plus `bindings: [c, python, swift]` | Writer packages over the same contract |
| Share tensors or columns | `Tensor.from_dlpack(x)` / `.to_arrow()` | `Marshal` impls over DLPack and Arrow |

Every wrapper shows its expansion through `jet inspect bind <name>`. That
command prints the row, each fact and its provenance, the projection used, and
the primitives it lowered to.

## 8. Cross-cutting rules

**Zero cost (G2).** A crossing whose `Marshal` impls are all `BLITTABLE` is
one call instruction, with no prologue and no runtime transition. Jet has no GC
and no safepoints, so the JDK `critical` and .NET `SuppressGCTransition`
tricks are not needed [J4,N3]. Only thunks entered by foreign threads pay for
an attach check, which is one thread-local load. When C or C++ source is
visible, the pinned Clang emits LLVM IR into the optimizing tier's module, so
the optimizer can inline across languages (the Rust linker-plugin LTO
precedent [R9]). Inlining is an optimization, never a change of meaning (I9).

**Strings and buffers.** A lend (`&`) of `String` or `[T]` passes
pointer plus length with no copy. A NUL-terminated parameter gets a stack copy
only when the Jet value is not already terminated. Returned views are
zero-copy when a lifetime fact links them to a living owner, and copied
otherwise.

**C variadics.** Typed per call site. The compiler applies default promotions
and the ABI's variadic rule; on Apple arm64 every variadic argument goes on the
stack [AP1]. `printf`-style rows with a `format` attribute are format-checked
at compile time.

**Macros.** Constant macros are evaluated by Clang. A function-like macro
becomes a typed shim, `static inline T name(params) { return MACRO(params); }`,
compiled by the same Clang. Its parameter types come from an overlay, or are
inferred when the macro body is a single call. A statement macro that cannot
be typed is reported, not guessed.

**C++.** Classes are owned handles whose destructor runs as `close`. Movable
types map to `^`. Templates are instantiated on demand in a shim; explicit
`instantiate:` is for libraries with no visible use. Overloads fold into labels,
and ambiguity is a compile error. `std::string_view` and `std::span` become
lifetime-bound views. `unique_ptr` maps to an owned value, `shared_ptr` to a
shared one. Exceptions become `T CppError!`.

**Callbacks.** A closure lowers to a (code, context) pair. Registration returns
an owned token, and dropping the token unregisters it. A callback that a C API
keeps beyond the call needs a `retained` fact: either `Read` (with a matching
unregister) or `Vouched`.

**Threads.** Main-thread-only APIs (UIKit, AppKit, most GUI toolkits) carry
`affinity(.Main)`, and calling them off the main thread is a compile error
where it can be proved and a checked trap otherwise. Foreign threads that enter
Jet are attached on first entry and detached at thread exit.

**Async.** Callback-style APIs turn into `async` functions through
`completion<T>()`. A Jet `async` export becomes the host's native form: a JS
Promise, a Swift `async` function, a Kotlin `suspend` function, a .NET `Task`,
or a WIT `future<T>` [W2].

**Versioning.** Every contract has a hash, and the bound library is verified
at link or load time (symbols present, interface hash equal). `jet build`
diffs the contract against the last frozen one (`api: stable`) and reports
breaking changes. Foreign structs whose size can change between versions are
accessed through generated accessors, so an upgrade cannot shift field offsets
under compiled code (Swift library evolution [SW1]). Optional symbols are `T?`.

**Debugging.** Every tier emits DWARF, so backtraces mix languages. `--trace-ffi=png.*`
logs each crossing with its lowered arguments and results.
The hardened profile checks vouched facts at the edges. An isolated placement
turns the boundary into a message boundary, which can be recorded and replayed.

## 9. Adoption analysis: the design mapped onto Jet

The verdicts are: **Fits** (already ratified, or implementation under a ratified
rule), **Extends** (new capability that is consistent with ratified rules), and
**Replaces** (changes a ratified rule; needs an owner ballot).

| Idea | Jet today | Verdict | Migration | Owner ballot |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Contract plus readers as packages | D-FFI-UNIFY1, D-FFI-BINDER1 (23 readers, about 22.8k lines), D-CIMPORT1 (pinned Clang), the `jet-ffi-descriptor-v1` stamp | Fits; the descriptor grows into the full fact vocabulary | Medium: descriptor schema v2, readers fill in more facts | none (implementation) |
| Facts with provenance; conservative projection | D-FFI-CMAP1 (nullable → `T?`, `counted_by` → lists), D-FFI-VOUCH1 (vouch blocks, `jet audit`), D-HARDENED1 | Fits; `Proved` and `Observed` become explicit labels | Small | none |
| Ownership across the border | D-FFI-CAP1 (`&`, `^`, `#Close` at the border) | Fits exactly | none | none |
| Public primitives layer (§4) | D-RAWPTR2 raw pointers; `jet_builtins` (D-CORE-BUILTINS1); readers use `foreign.read`; layout and ABI queries, dynamic symbols, thunks, error capture and `Marshal` are compiler-private or missing | **Extends** | Medium: about 12 primitives, most of them already exist internally | **D-FFI-PRIMS1** |
| Inline C as a wrapper over C-source import | D-FFI-ONE1=A keeps inline `#FFI(c)` bodies with the prototype written from the Jet signature. Its recorded loss is "two ways to bring in C". | Fits. The inline body is lowered as an anonymous unit through the D-FFI-CINPUT1 reader, so there is one mechanism and the recorded loss goes away. Syntax is unchanged. | Small, compiler-internal | none: implementation under I8 |
| `#Unsafe` and I1 | The only escape hatch. Vouches name a reason. | Fits. Isolation adds a third safe route that needs no vouch. | none | (see the next row) |
| Isolation as a placement option | Python and JS already run in supervised workers or JS-on-wasm (D-FFI-JS1). Plugins are sandboxed components (D-PLUGIN*). C libraries are in-process only. | **Extends** | Medium: a wasm-compiled C path through the pinned Clang (`wasm32-wasip2`), plus a process host | **D-FFI-ISOLATE1** |
| One meaning across tiers (I9; D-EXEC1, amended by D-EXEC3) | The comptime evaluator refuses foreign calls by name | Extends. `pure` rows run at compile time through the wasm placement, so they are deterministic and sandboxed. The web tier compiles the same C to wasm32. | Comes with the isolation work | covered by D-FFI-ISOLATE1 |
| Wasm and web | D-PORTABLE-WEB1, D-WASISRV1, WIT for plugins, D-EMBED2=C | Fits. WIT becomes one reader and one writer of the contract. WASI 0.3 async maps onto `completion`. | Small | none |
| Rich exports (being called) | `#Export(c)` allows C primitives only (spec, Embedding artifacts). D-EMBED2=C lists `bindings: [c, python]`. | **Extends**: records, lists, strings, errors, callbacks, handles and async, projected per language by writer packages | Medium to large: one writer per language, C first | **D-FFI-EXPORT2** |
| Zero-cost and cross-language inlining | O2 goes through LLVM. D-EXEC3 limits runtime-function inlining to the runtime's own source. | Fits. Visible C and C++ source is lowered to LLVM IR in the O2 module. | Small to medium | none |
| GPU | D-ACCEL-LIB1 (devices as libraries with CPU reference), D-GPU-COMPUTE-LAUNCH1, D-GPU-DEVICE-OPS1 | Fits. Adds std430/scalar layouts to `layout`, a SPIR-V/PTX reflection reader, and DLPack/Arrow `Marshal` impls. | Medium | none now |
| C++ depth | D-FFI-CPP1 (opaque classes, `CppError`, on-demand templates) | Fits. Adds lifetime-bound views and vtable subclassing. | Medium | none |
| Versioning | `api: stable` (D-CAP4), descriptor stamp, E3208 | Fits. Adds load-time verification and resilient accessors. | Small | none |
| Debugging | `jet inspect bind`, D-HARDENED1 | Fits. Adds `--trace-ffi` and mixed DWARF backtraces. | Small | none |

**Net effect on ratified decisions.** Nothing ratified is reversed. D-FFI-ONE1's
recorded loss goes away through implementation. Three ballots add capability:
D-FFI-PRIMS1, D-FFI-ISOLATE1 and D-FFI-EXPORT2. The ballot JSON files are in the
lane's `ballot/` directory.

## 10. Sources
