## 7. How peers draw the lines

| System | Package data | Build code | Multi-package root | Profiles and flags | Lock |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cargo | `Cargo.toml` `[package]`, `[dependencies]` | `build.rs`, one fixed file per package | `[workspace]` in the root `Cargo.toml`; a root without `[package]` is a "virtual manifest" | `[profile.*]` honoured only at the workspace root; `.cargo/config.toml` per machine or repo | `Cargo.lock` at the root |
| Go | `go.mod` | none; `go generate` runs by hand and its output is committed | `go.work`, a separate file, "generally inadvisable to commit" | build tags and flags only | `go.sum` |
| Zig | `build.zig.zon`, "metadata specifically pertaining to build.zig" | `build.zig`, real Zig code that builds a step graph | none; a package is the unit | `b.standardOptimizeOption` and `-D` flags declared in `build.zig` | hashes inside `build.zig.zon` |
| SwiftPM | `Package.swift`: Swift code that builds one declarative `Package` value | plugins (build-tool and command plugins), separate packages | none (Xcode workspaces are an IDE concept) | `swift build -c release`; `swiftSettings` per target | `Package.resolved` |
| Bazel | `MODULE.bazel` (identity and deps) | `BUILD` files (Starlark, restricted) and `.bzl` rules | the repository root marked by `MODULE.bazel`; the `WORKSPACE` file was disabled by default in Bazel 8 | `.bazelrc` named configs (`--config=release`) | `MODULE.bazel.lock` |
| Buck2 | `BUCK` files | Starlark rules | cells in `.buckconfig` | `.buckconfig`, modifiers | — |
| Nix flakes | `flake.nix` `inputs` | `flake.nix` `outputs`, a function of the inputs | none; one flake per repo is the norm | outputs per system | `flake.lock` |
| npm | `package.json` | `scripts` strings | `"workspaces"` globs inside the root `package.json` | none | `package-lock.json` |
| pnpm | `package.json` | `scripts` | `pnpm-workspace.yaml`, a separate file that also holds shared version "catalogs" | `.npmrc` | `pnpm-lock.yaml` |
| Gradle | `build.gradle(.kts)` per project | the same file, real Kotlin or Groovy; shared logic in convention plugins (`build-logic`) | `settings.gradle(.kts)`, a separate file that lists included projects | `gradle.properties`; version catalog `libs.versions.toml` | dependency locking, opt-in |
| Jai | none | the metaprogram (`first.jai` / `build.jai`), real Jai code run by the compiler | none | `Build_Options` per workspace | none |

What each teaches Jet:

- **Cargo** proves the split between package facts and checkout facts is real. It enforces it silently ("Cargo only looks at the profile settings in the `Cargo.toml` manifest at the root of the workspace. Profile settings defined in dependencies will be ignored", [profiles](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/profiles.html)). It also shows the cost of one file for two roles: a root `Cargo.toml` can be a package, a workspace or both, and its docs need a "root package" vs "virtual manifest" section to explain the difference ([workspaces](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/workspaces.html)). `[workspace.package]` and `[workspace.dependencies]` add opt-in inheritance (`version.workspace = true`): explicit, per field. `build.rs` has one fixed name ([build scripts](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/build-scripts.html)).
- **Go** keeps the module file free of checkout concerns and puts multi-module work in `go.work` ([Go modules reference, Workspaces](https://go.dev/ref/mod#workspaces)). It is the cleanest split, but it gives up build code entirely, which Jet will not do.
- **Zig** uses a data file for identity and dependencies and a code file for the build graph, and names the data file after the code file to show they belong together ([build.zig.zon](https://github.com/ziglang/zig/blob/master/doc/build.zig.zon.md), [Zig build system](https://ziglang.org/learn/build-system/)). Options are declared in code (`b.option`), then set by `-D` flags: one mechanism.
- **SwiftPM** writes the manifest as code that builds one declarative value ([PackageDescription](https://docs.swift.org/swiftpm/documentation/packagedescription)). This is close to Jet's "data file is Jet values" design. Plugins extend the build without making the manifest imperative ([Plugins](https://github.com/swiftlang/swift-package-manager/blob/main/Documentation/Plugins.md)).
- **Bazel** splits three concerns into three file kinds: identity and deps (`MODULE.bazel`, [modules](https://bazel.build/external/module)), targets (`BUILD`, [BUILD files](https://bazel.build/concepts/build-files)) and invocation flags (`.bazelrc`, [bazelrc](https://bazel.build/run/bazelrc)). It replaced its `WORKSPACE` file because of its "shortcomings"; "the WORKSPACE file is already disabled in Bazel 8" ([Bzlmod migration](https://bazel.build/versions/8.1.1/external/migration)). Bazel's lesson for Jet is the cost of a word and file that grew several jobs.
- **Buck2** names the multi-repo root a "cell" in `.buckconfig` and keeps targets in `BUCK` files ([Buck2 docs](https://buck2.build/docs/)).
- **Nix flakes** put inputs and outputs in one file, outputs as a function of inputs, with a committed lock ([nix flake](https://nix.dev/manual/nix/latest/command-ref/new-cli/nix3-flake)). One file is clear when it holds one project; it does not attempt multi-package grouping.
- **npm** puts `"workspaces"` inside the root `package.json` ([npm workspaces](https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/using-npm/workspaces)); **pnpm** moved it to its own `pnpm-workspace.yaml` ([pnpm workspaces](https://pnpm.io/workspaces)) and added "catalogs", "a workspace feature for defining dependency version ranges as reusable constants" ([catalogs](https://pnpm.io/catalogs)).
- **Gradle** has a separate settings file for the build as a whole and a build file per project ([multi-project builds](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/multi_project_builds_intermediate.html), [organizing projects](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/organizing_gradle_projects.html)). Shared logic moves into convention plugins, and shared versions into a catalog ([version catalogs](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/version_catalogs.html)). Note the naming trap: Gradle calls each sub-unit a "project", which is Jet's package. Jet's docs must define the word once and keep it.
- **Jai** has no package or project file. One metaprogram creates workspaces, sets each one's options and drives the compiler ([The Way to Jai](https://github.com/Ivo-Balbaert/The_Way_to_Jai) ch. 30; `focus` [`first.jai`](https://github.com/focus-editor/focus/blob/main/first.jai)). It is the strongest primitive layer of any peer and has no wrappers at all, so every project re-writes the same message loop (`jai-parity-2026-10-16.md` line 91).

The pattern across peers:

1. The ones that scale keep "what this package is and needs" apart from "how this checkout builds it": Cargo by a root-only rule, Go, pnpm and Gradle by a separate root file, Bazel by three file kinds.
2. Where build code exists, it has one fixed home: `build.rs`, `build.zig`, `build.gradle.kts`, `BUILD`, `first.jai`.
3. The data file and the code file meet through shared value types, not by repeating facts: Zig's `b.dependency("x")` reads `.zon`; SwiftPM's manifest is a value.
4. Shared versions and options across many packages are an explicit, opt-in feature of the root (Cargo `workspace = true`, pnpm catalogs, Gradle catalogs), not silent inheritance.

## 8. What a cleaner system must do

These requirements come from sections 4–7 and from `Docs/spec/philosophy.md` (ladders, not cliffs; one mechanism; enterprise auditability; the language is a library). The proposal answers each one.

- **R1. Two nouns, two files, no overlap.** One noun and one file for the unit others depend on (package). One noun and one file for the folder people work in (project). No file means both.
- **R2. One home per fact.** Every field has exactly one file it may appear in. A beginner can sort any fact with one question.
- **R3. One home per entry function.** `fn build`, `fn test` and `fn dev` each have one fixed file name, found without discovery rules.
- **R4. One settings order.** One list of layers, with pins and policy forbids stated on the same list.
- **R5. Explicit inheritance.** A package states what it takes from its project, or the project states what it gives. No hidden layer.
- **R6. Composition.** Data files and entry code build the same Core values. The primitive (`b.add(output)`, a typed action) can express everything; the wrappers (`outputs:` entries, `b.add_executable`) cover the common cases and expand to the primitive.
- **R7. One meaning per word.** "Workspace" leaves the package system; "build", "target" and "profile" each keep one meaning.
- **R8. A mechanical migration.** `jet fix` moves every file and field, and a leftover old spelling is an error that names the fix.

sections.body:
# Project, package and config files today: a map and what confuses people

Status: research, for card #6368. Written 2026-10-30 against dev `e784bb1ffe`.
Companion proposal: `Docs/proposals/project-package-config-2026-10-30.md`.

## Summary

Jet has no single answer to "where does this setting go?" today. The same fact can be written in two to six places, the same word means three or four different things, and several ratified rulings disagree with each other and with the code.

- **Files.** Twelve file names carry configuration or command code: `package.jet`, `pkg.jet` (retired but still read), `workspace.jet`, `env.jet`, `config.jet`, `build.jet`, `test.jet`, `dev.jet`, `bench.jet`, `run.jet`, `.jet/lock` and the ratified-but-unbuilt `jet.lock`. On top of those come an inline `package { }` block and freely named `configs:` files. `fn build` can sit in any file of a package, including `tools/build_entry.jet` and `workspace.jet`.
- **Fields.** `package.jet` accepts 25 top-level fields. They mix four kinds of fact: what the package *is* (name, version), what it *needs* (deps, effects), what it *makes* (outputs), and how *this checkout* works (profiles, members, environments, toolchain, policy ceilings). Nothing in the file tells you which kind a field is.
- **Words.** "Workspace" means the monorepo root (`workspace.jet`), the editor window (Canvas), and, in Jai, one compilation with its own options. The owner has ruled that it moves to "project". "Profile", "target", "build" and "package" are each overloaded too.
- **Rulings.** Three rulings named the root differently (Package, Jetspace, workspace). Two rulings place `fn build` differently. Two rulings order settings layers differently. Today's D-MANIFEST-ONE1 folds `workspace.jet` and `env.jet` into `package.jet`, which makes one file mean both "a package" and "a group of packages".
- **A real bug from that overlap.** A root `package.jet` with a `name:`, its own `run.jet` and `members:` silently skips its own code: `jet check` passes with a broken root `run.jet`, and `jet run` runs a member's program instead (probe P3 below).
- **Peers.** Every peer that scales well separates "what a package is" from "how this checkout builds" (Cargo by root-only profiles, Go by `go.work`, pnpm by `pnpm-workspace.yaml`, Gradle by `settings.gradle`, Bazel by `MODULE.bazel` + `BUILD` + `.bazelrc`). Zig, SwiftPM, Gradle and Nix all let real code drive the build, but keep one fixed file for it. Bazel retired its `WORKSPACE` file in Bazel 8.

Section 8 turns these findings into eight requirements that the proposal answers.

## 1. Every file that carries configuration

Counts are `git ls-files` at `e784bb1ffe`. "Read by" names the code that gives the file meaning.

| File | What it holds today | Count | Read by | Ruling state |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `package.jet` | identity, deps, outputs, profiles, settings, policy, members, and more (section 2) | 2310 | `Jetpack/PackageModel/Source/Manifest/PackageParse.jet` (one parser, 521 lines) | D-CONF-PLANE1, D-MANIFEST-ONE1 |
| inline `package { }` block | the same fields, inside a source file (all of `Core/` uses it, e.g. `Core/Build/Build.jet:1-10`) | 604 files | same parser | D-ECO-INLINEPACKAGE1; may not coexist with `package.jet` |
| `pkg.jet` | retired name for `package.jet`, still a project marker | 5 | `JetCli/Source/Cli/Request.jet:232`, `Entry.jet:74` | retired, still recognised |
| `workspace.jet` | `module workspace { members: … }`, overlays, sometimes `fn build` or even `fn run` | 22 | `JetFoundation/Data/Syntax/JetpackConfig.jet:484`, `Entry.jet:70` | D-WORKSPACE1=B said "no workspace file"; D-MANIFEST-ONE1=A folds it into `package.jet` (not built) |
| `env.jet` | `module env.<name> { sources: … packages: … prompt: … }`: dev tools and source aliases | 159 | `JetpackConfig.jet:469` | D-MANIFEST-ONE1=A folds it into `package.jet environments:` (not built) |
| `config.jet` and `configs:` files | `NAME :: Config{ … }` records: deps, environments, even `outputs:` (`Examples/features/tooling/compiler_api_package/config/release.jet`) | 30 + 2 users of `configs:` | `PackageParse.jet` (E: ConfigMembers forbids members, build, settings) | D-MANIFEST-ONE1 keeps `configs:` for env-only files |
| `build.jet` | `fn build(b: Build)`; `jet new` writes a commented stub | 27 | `JetCli/Source/Cli/Entry.jet:72`, `Loader.jet:2613` | D-CONF-ENTRY1: one per package, any file |
| `test.jet` | `fn test(t: Test)` | 8 | same | D-TEST-PROFILE1: only for code suites |
| `dev.jet` | `fn dev(d: Dev)` | 6 | same | D-ENTRY-SHAPE1 |
| `bench.jet` | old bench entry | 3 | none (Bench handle retired, D-ENTRY-NAMES1) | stale |
| `run.jet` | the stock program entry, `fn run()` | 1695 | `Entry.jet:77` | D-ECO14 |
| `.jet/lock` | toolchain pin, build stamp, dependency graph | 22 committed; `jet new` writes and git-ignores it | `Host.jet:1607,1618`, `InspectProvenance.jet:308` | D-LOCKFILE1=A moved it to a committed root `jet.lock` (not built) |
| `jet.lock` | the ratified lock | 0 | none yet | D-LOCKFILE1=A |
| `.jet/` | build output, cache, generated code, last-run records | 6 committed `.jet/last-run/*` files in `Examples/features/tooling/build_entry_discovery` | everything | D-WORKSPACE-CMD1: one `.jet/` at the root, disposable |
| `project.jet` | one stray fixture | 1 | none | none |

The command code that `fn build` holds can live in any file of a package. A census of top-level `fn build|test|dev(` declarations finds them in `main.jet` (55 files), `run.jet` (36), `build.jet` (25), `workspace.jet` (3), `package.jet` (3) and others, such as `tools/build_entry.jet`.

`JetCli/Source/Cli/Entry.jet:72-74` reserves nine names that user code cannot use as module files: `run.jet`, `build.jet`, `dev.jet`, `test.jet`, `package.jet`, `pkg.jet`, `env.jet`, `config.jet` and `workspace.jet`.

## 2. Every field of `package.jet`

The parser's switch (`PackageParse.jet:160-215`) accepts these fields. The census column counts `package.jet` files (not inline blocks) that use the field. The last column sorts each field by the question it answers. That sorting is this document's own, and it drives the proposal.

| Field | Meaning | Files | Kind of fact |
|---|---|---|---|
| `name`, `version` | identity | 2305, 2265 | what the package **is** |
| `edition`, `jet`, `source` | language edition, toolchain requirement, source root | 389, 92, few | is |
| `description`, `license`, `repository` | publishing metadata | 114, 109, 95 | is |
| `deps` | dependencies | 177 | what it **needs** |
| `authority` | effects the package may use, grants to its deps, trust | 1494 | needs |
| `boundaries` | which modules may import which | 7 | needs (code rules) |
| `policy` | lints and code rules (`lints: { deny: [auto_derive] }`, `check_removal: .Forbid`, `sentries`) | 47 | needs (code rules) |
| `allocator`, `runtime` | program allocator and runtime flavour | 5, 12 | what it **makes** |
| `outputs` | the things the package makes (nine kinds, D-TARGET-ONE1) | 94 | makes |
| `packages` | an older map of output kinds (`packages: { backend: library }`) | 80 | makes (second home) |
| `targets` | platform profiles (`targets: { machine: { profile: "hosted" } }`) | 6 | makes (and a third meaning of "target") |
| `settings` | typed knobs the package declares | 8 | makes |
| `build` | named build profiles, plus `allow:` for build-time effects | 35 | how **we work** |
| `defaults` | which output `jet run` uses; which profile bare commands use | 18 | how we work |
| `dev`, `services` | dev-loop policy, local services | few | how we work |
| `environments` | dev tools and shells | 1 | how we work |
| `members` | the packages this root groups | 5 | how we work |
| `configs` | extra files holding `Config{}` records | 2 | how we work |
| `test`, `suites` | ratified by D-TEST-PROFILE1, not accepted yet (E1206) | 0 | how we work |
| `dev_deps`, `patch`, `workspace` | reserved; must be empty | 0 | — |
| `grants` | retired, moved under `authority:` | 0 | — |

One more spelling sits beside these: a `package.jet` may also declare the package's single `fn build`, and an inline `NAME :: Config{ … }` record.

The fourth kind ("how we work") is the trouble. None of these fields describe the package to someone who depends on it. They describe one checkout, one team or one machine. Cargo reached the same split and enforces it by ignoring a dependency's profiles (section 7).

## 3. Every concept and word

| Word | Meanings in use today | Where |
|---|---|---|
| package | (1) the unit with a `package.jet`; (2) the root noun for a group of packages (D-ECO-ROOTNAME1=I); (3) the old `packages:` output map; (4) env.jet `packages:`, which means tools | ratified rulings, `PackageParse.jet:186`, `env.jet` files |
| workspace | (1) the monorepo root and `workspace.jet` (D-WORKSPACE-CMD1, D-BUILD-REUSESET1, spec "Workspace overlays" §2360); (2) the Canvas editor window (`Docs/spec/reference/canvas-workspace-architecture.md`); (3) in Jai, one compilation with its own build options (`compiler_create_workspace`) | owner ruling on #6368: rename (1) to project |
| Jetspace | the whole checked graph (D-ECO-ROOTNAME2=D) | ratified, never used in code |
| project | the folder the CLI and Canvas call "the project" (`project-navigation.js`, `Request.jet:232 JET_CLI_PROJECT_MARKERS`) | used informally everywhere, defined nowhere |
| member | a package listed by a root | `members:` in `package.jet` or in `module workspace` |
| output | a thing a package makes (D-TARGET-ONE1) | `outputs:`, `b.add_*`, `b.output(name)` |
| target | (1) the platform (D-TARGET-ONE1); (2) the `targets:` platform-profile field; (3) old meaning "a thing to build", still in `Core/Build/Build.jet` `BuildGraphTarget`; (4) the field name `target`, which is an error | parser, Core, flags |
| profile | (1) a named bundle of build options (D-CONF-WORD1); (2) a test profile (D-TEST-PROFILE1, same namespace); (3) a target platform profile (`targets: { … profile: "hosted" }`); (4) env presets (renamed by D-CONF-WORD1) | `build:`, `test:`, `targets:` |
| build | (1) the `build:` profiles field; (2) `Build{ … }`, the profile constructor (until `BuildOptions` lands, D-ENTRY-NAMES1); (3) `Build`, the handle in `fn build(b: Build)`; (4) `build.jet`; (5) `jet build`; (6) the `build.*` hook stages | `Examples/features/tooling/build_link_inputs` uses (1), (2), (3) and (4) together |
| config | (1) `Config{}` records; (2) `config.jet`; (3) `configs:` | parser |
| settings / options | (1) `settings:`, knobs a package declares; (2) build options (`BuildOptions`, D-SETTING-ORDER1's one option table) | spec, rulings |
| policy / authority / grants / boundaries | four blocks about what is allowed: code rules, effects, effect grants, import rules | `package.jet` |
| environment | dev tools and shells: `env.jet`, `environments:`, `Config{ environments: }` | three homes |
| lock | `.jet/lock` (code, git-ignored by `jet new`) and `jet.lock` (ratified, committed) | two homes |

## 4. The rulings in force, and where they disagree

| Ruling | Says | Conflicts with |
|---|---|---|
| D-WORKSPACE1=B (06-25) | Reuse the package file; no workspace manifest | 22 `workspace.jet` files, spec §3905 ("`workspace.jet` supplies workspace membership") |
| D-ECO-ROOTNAME1=I | The root noun is "Package" | D-ECO-ROOTNAME2=D ("Jetspace"), D-WORKSPACE-CMD1 and D-BUILD-REUSESET1 ("workspace"), the owner's "project" |
| D-BUILDSCOPE1=A (07-19) | `fn build` lives in the unit's existing definition file at every rung (single file, `pkg.jet`, `workspace.jet`) | D-CONF-ENTRY1=A: any file of the package; `jet new` writes `build.jet` |
| D-CONF-SPLIT1=A | Facts in text, actions in `fn build` | D-ENTRY-SHAPE1=A: `fn dev` sets facts in code (`d.port(8080)`); D-TARGET-ONE1=A: outputs from data and from code |
| D-CONF-MERGE1=A | declaration < profile < workspace < environment < system < fleet < CLI | D-SETTING-ORDER1=A: stock < source marker < `package.jet` < entry code < flag; D-BUILD-REUSESET1=A adds a root layer between stock and each member |
| D-SETTING-ORDER1=A, owner directive #4913 | every option row has a flag, a package field and a handle method | D-OPTFLAG1=A removed `--optimize`, `--opt-level` and `--inline` in favour of profiles |
| D-TEST-PROFILE1=A | named test runs are data in `package.jet` (`test:`), code suites in `test.jet` | the parser rejects `test:` (probe P1); `jet new`'s `test.jet` stub still says "replace the stock default" |
| D-LOCKFILE1=A | `<root>/jet.lock`, committed | `jet new` writes `.jet/lock` and git-ignores it (probe P4) |
| D-MANIFEST-ONE1=A (10-30) | `package.jet` is the one project file; a root without `name:` is a virtual root | makes a `package.jet` mean "a package" or "a group" depending on one missing field; keeps `configs:` files |
| D-ENTRY-NAMES1=A | `Build` is the handle; the profile record is `BuildOptions` | 35 `package.jet` files still use `Build{ … }` as the profile record |

## 5. The confusions, with examples

Each confusion names a real file or probe. They are ordered by how often a newcomer meets them.

**C1. One project, many homes.** `Examples/features/tooling/build_entry_discovery` is one small project spread over seven configuration places: `package.jet` (identity, authority), `workspace.jet` (members, and also `fn run`), `tools/build_entry.jet` (the root's `fn build`, found "package-wide" per its `tools/README.md`), `packages/foundation/tools/build.jet` (a member's `fn build`), two member `package.jet` files, and six committed `.jet/last-run/*` files. Nothing in `package.jet` points at any of the others. A reader must know the discovery rules to find the build.

**C2. A root is both a package and a group.** `Compiler/package.jet` has `name: "compiler"`, a version and 13 `members:`. Its comment says `jet build Compiler/` runs `build.jet`, which builds an executable from the JetCli member. So is `compiler` a package with code, a group, or both? Probe P3 shows the cost: a named root with `members:` and its own `run.jet` is silently skipped by `jet check` and `jet run` (bug B1).

**C3. One fact, several homes.**
- Members: `members:` in `package.jet`, or `module workspace { members: }` in `workspace.jet`. Probe P3 accepts both at once, listing the same member twice, with no warning.
- Environments: `env.jet` `module env.<name>`, `Config{ environments: }` in a `configs:` file (`Examples/jetpack/epoch5/config/dev.jet`), or `environments:` in `package.jet`.
- Outputs: `outputs:`, the older `packages:` map, `Config{ outputs: }` in a configs file, or `b.add_*` in `fn build`.
- The entry function: any file of the package. The census found `fn build`, `fn test` or `fn dev` in `main.jet`, `run.jet`, `build.jet`, `workspace.jet`, `package.jet` and `tools/build_entry.jet` (section 1).
- The lock: `.jet/lock` or `jet.lock`.

**C4. Three syntaxes for one kind of data.** Top-level `field: value` (`package.jet`), `module workspace { field: value }` (`workspace.jet`, `env.jet`), and `NAME :: Config{ field: value }` (`config.jet`). A fourth, the inline `package { }` block, holds the first syntax inside a source file. The output constructor is spelled `.Executable{ … }` in `package.jet` and `Executable{ … }` in a configs file.

**C5. "Workspace" collides with Jai.** In Jai a workspace is one compilation with its own build options, created by `compiler_create_workspace` ([The Way to Jai, ch. 30](https://github.com/Ivo-Balbaert/The_Way_to_Jai); `Docs/audits/jai-parity-2026-10-16.md` §D). Jet's equivalent of that is one output with its options (D-JAI-CONFIG1). Jet uses the same word for the monorepo root, and Canvas uses it for the editor window. A user reading Jai material and Jet material at once meets two meanings for the word.

**C6. "Build" names six things.** `Examples/features/tooling/build_link_inputs/package.jet` writes `build: { vendored: Build{ optimize: none, link_args: ["-Lvendor"], os: linux } }`. Its `build.jet` writes `fn build(b: Build)`. Here `build:` is a profile map, `Build{}` is a profile record, `Build` is a handle and `build.jet` is a file, all in one example.

**C7. "Target" and "profile" are overloaded.** `targets: { machine: { profile: "hosted" } }` uses both words in a third and a fourth sense. A field named `target` is an unknown-field error. Test profiles and build profiles share one namespace (D-TEST-PROFILE1) but live under different fields.

**C8. Facts and code overlap without a rule.** D-CONF-SPLIT1 says "facts in text, actions in code". Yet the default output is `defaults: { run: cli }` or `b.default(x)`, a profile is `build: { … }` or `b.profile(…)`, an option is a field or a handle call, and a test suite is `suites:` data or `t.suite(…)`. Each pair is ratified. No rule says which to pick, so two teams write the same project two ways.

**C9. The settings order has two versions and a hidden layer.** D-CONF-MERGE1 lists seven layers, D-SETTING-ORDER1 lists five, and D-BUILD-REUSESET1 adds the root's `package.jet` as a layer under each member. A member's effective `optimize` depends on which ruling the implementation follows.

**C10. Inheritance has three different rules.** Members inherit `version`, `edition` and `license` from the root (D-CORE-HEADER1), build settings from the root (D-BUILD-REUSESET1), and policy ceilings through the grant chain (D-BUILDSCOPE1). They do not inherit deps, lints or outputs. A member cannot tell what it inherits without reading three rulings.

**C11. What publishes and what does not is unstated.** A library's `build:` profiles, `environments:`, `members:` and `defaults:` mean nothing to a consumer, but they sit beside `name:` and `deps:` in the file that gets published. Nothing says whether a consumer's build honours them. Cargo answers this explicitly ("Profile settings defined in dependencies will be ignored", [Cargo profiles](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/profiles.html)).

**C12. Command files are named by convention only, and their stubs are stale.** `jet new --template overrides` writes `build.jet`, `dev.jet` and `test.jet` stubs that say "Uncomment one `fn build` to replace the stock default" (`Host.jet:1514-1516`). D-ENTRY-SHAPE1 says entries set values and never replace the stock work. Nine file names are reserved (section 1), so a module cannot be called `test.jet` or `config.jet`.

**C13. Four blocks say what is allowed.** `policy:` (lints, code rules), `authority:` (effects, grants, trust), `boundaries:` (imports) and `build: { allow: }` (build-time effects, parsed inside the profiles map by `BuildProfiles.jet:310`). The project's ceiling ("this team never allows `unchecked`") has no home of its own; it sits in the root's `package.jet` beside the package's own needs.

**C14. Errors point the wrong way.** Probe P1's E1206 for `test:` says "Identity is bare `name:` and `version:` at the top level — there is no `identity:` or `payload:` wrapper", which has nothing to do with `test:` (bug B2). Probe P5's duplicate `fn build` is E0105 "Imported names share the module namespace" from `jet check` but E3520 "Two build entries" from `jet build` (bug B3).

## 6. Probes

Run with `JET_COMPILER_IDENTITY="jet@0.1.0#probe" JET_TOOLCHAIN_ROOT=<export of e784bb1ffe> $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/discovery/base/latest/jet`.

| Probe | Input | Result |
|---|---|---|
| P1 | `package.jet` with `test: { quick: TestProfile{ suites: [tests], time_limit: 60s } }` | `E1206 Unknown field test:`; the "Why" line talks about identity wrappers |
| P2 | `build: { small: .{ optimize: size } }` | `E1206 … remove the dot before {` |
| P3 | root `package.jet` with `name: "p3"`, `members: ["a"]`, an `outputs:` app and a `run.jet` containing an undefined name; `workspace.jet` also listing `a`; member `a` prints "hi" | `jet check .` and bare `jet check`: "ok: …/a/run.jet has no problems". `jet run`: prints `hi` (the member's program). `jet check run.jet`: E0107 for the root file. Removing `workspace.jet` changes nothing. |
| P4 | `jet new demo` | writes `demo/.jet/lock` and a `.gitignore` containing `.jet/lock` |
| P5 | `build.jet` and `tools/build.jet` both declaring `fn build` | `jet check .`: E0105 at `build.jet:1:4`; `jet build`: E3520 |

## 7. How peers draw the lines

| System | Package data | Build code | Multi-package root | Profiles and flags | Lock |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cargo | `Cargo.toml` `[package]`, `[dependencies]` | `build.rs`, one fixed file per package | `[workspace]` in the root `Cargo.toml`; a root without `[package]` is a "virtual manifest" | `[profile.*]` honoured only at the workspace root; `.cargo/config.toml` per machine or repo | `Cargo.lock` at the root |
| Go | `go.mod` | none; `go generate` runs by hand and its output is committed | `go.work`, a separate file, "generally inadvisable to commit" | build tags and flags only | `go.sum` |
| Zig | `build.zig.zon`, "metadata specifically pertaining to build.zig" | `build.zig`, real Zig code that builds a step graph | none; a package is the unit | `b.standardOptimizeOption` and `-D` flags declared in `build.zig` | hashes inside `build.zig.zon` |
| SwiftPM | `Package.swift`: Swift code that builds one declarative `Package` value | plugins (build-tool and command plugins), separate packages | none (Xcode workspaces are an IDE concept) | `swift build -c release`; `swiftSettings` per target | `Package.resolved` |
| Bazel | `MODULE.bazel` (identity and deps) | `BUILD` files (Starlark, restricted) and `.bzl` rules | the repository root marked by `MODULE.bazel`; the `WORKSPACE` file was disabled by default in Bazel 8 | `.bazelrc` named configs (`--config=release`) | `MODULE.bazel.lock` |
| Buck2 | `BUCK` files | Starlark rules | cells in `.buckconfig` | `.buckconfig`, modifiers | — |
| Nix flakes | `flake.nix` `inputs` | `flake.nix` `outputs`, a function of the inputs | none; one flake per repo is the norm | outputs per system | `flake.lock` |
| npm | `package.json` | `scripts` strings | `"workspaces"` globs inside the root `package.json` | none | `package-lock.json` |
| pnpm | `package.json` | `scripts` | `pnpm-workspace.yaml`, a separate file that also holds shared version "catalogs" | `.npmrc` | `pnpm-lock.yaml` |
| Gradle | `build.gradle(.kts)` per project | the same file, real Kotlin or Groovy; shared logic in convention plugins (`build-logic`) | `settings.gradle(.kts)`, a separate file that lists included projects | `gradle.properties`; version catalog `libs.versions.toml` | dependency locking, opt-in |
| Jai | none | the metaprogram (`first.jai` / `build.jai`), real Jai code run by the compiler | none | `Build_Options` per workspace | none |

What each teaches Jet:

- **Cargo** proves the split between package facts and checkout facts is real. It enforces it silently ("Cargo only looks at the profile settings in the `Cargo.toml` manifest at the root of the workspace. Profile settings defined in dependencies will be ignored", [profiles](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/profiles.html)). It also shows the cost of one file for two roles: a root `Cargo.toml` can be a package, a workspace or both, and its docs need a "root package" vs "virtual manifest" section to explain the difference ([workspaces](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/workspaces.html)). `[workspace.package]` and `[workspace.dependencies]` add opt-in inheritance (`version.workspace = true`): explicit, per field. `build.rs` has one fixed name ([build scripts](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/build-scripts.html)).
- **Go** keeps the module file free of checkout concerns and puts multi-module work in `go.work` ([Go modules reference, Workspaces](https://go.dev/ref/mod#workspaces)). It is the cleanest split, but it gives up build code entirely, which Jet will not do.
- **Zig** uses a data file for identity and dependencies and a code file for the build graph, and names the data file after the code file to show they belong together ([build.zig.zon](https://github.com/ziglang/zig/blob/master/doc/build.zig.zon.md), [Zig build system](https://ziglang.org/learn/build-system/)). Options are declared in code (`b.option`), then set by `-D` flags: one mechanism.
- **SwiftPM** writes the manifest as code that builds one declarative value ([PackageDescription](https://docs.swift.org/swiftpm/documentation/packagedescription)). This is close to Jet's "data file is Jet values" design. Plugins extend the build without making the manifest imperative ([Plugins](https://github.com/swiftlang/swift-package-manager/blob/main/Documentation/Plugins.md)).
- **Bazel** splits three concerns into three file kinds: identity and deps (`MODULE.bazel`, [modules](https://bazel.build/external/module)), targets (`BUILD`, [BUILD files](https://bazel.build/concepts/build-files)) and invocation flags (`.bazelrc`, [bazelrc](https://bazel.build/run/bazelrc)). It replaced its `WORKSPACE` file because of its "shortcomings"; "the WORKSPACE file is already disabled in Bazel 8" ([Bzlmod migration](https://bazel.build/versions/8.1.1/external/migration)). Bazel's lesson for Jet is the cost of a word and file that grew several jobs.
- **Buck2** names the multi-repo root a "cell" in `.buckconfig` and keeps targets in `BUCK` files ([Buck2 docs](https://buck2.build/docs/)).
- **Nix flakes** put inputs and outputs in one file, outputs as a function of inputs, with a committed lock ([nix flake](https://nix.dev/manual/nix/latest/command-ref/new-cli/nix3-flake)). One file is clear when it holds one project; it does not attempt multi-package grouping.
- **npm** puts `"workspaces"` inside the root `package.json` ([npm workspaces](https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/using-npm/workspaces)); **pnpm** moved it to its own `pnpm-workspace.yaml` ([pnpm workspaces](https://pnpm.io/workspaces)) and added "catalogs", "a workspace feature for defining dependency version ranges as reusable constants" ([catalogs](https://pnpm.io/catalogs)).
- **Gradle** has a separate settings file for the build as a whole and a build file per project ([multi-project builds](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/multi_project_builds_intermediate.html), [organizing projects](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/organizing_gradle_projects.html)). Shared logic moves into convention plugins, and shared versions into a catalog ([version catalogs](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/version_catalogs.html)). Note the naming trap: Gradle calls each sub-unit a "project", which is Jet's package. Jet's docs must define the word once and keep it.
- **Jai** has no package or project file. One metaprogram creates workspaces, sets each one's options and drives the compiler ([The Way to Jai](https://github.com/Ivo-Balbaert/The_Way_to_Jai) ch. 30; `focus` [`first.jai`](https://github.com/focus-editor/focus/blob/main/first.jai)). It is the strongest primitive layer of any peer and has no wrappers at all, so every project re-writes the same message loop (`jai-parity-2026-10-16.md` line 91).

The pattern across peers:

1. The ones that scale keep "what this package is and needs" apart from "how this checkout builds it": Cargo by a root-only rule, Go, pnpm and Gradle by a separate root file, Bazel by three file kinds.
2. Where build code exists, it has one fixed home: `build.rs`, `build.zig`, `build.gradle.kts`, `BUILD`, `first.jai`.
3. The data file and the code file meet through shared value types, not by repeating facts: Zig's `b.dependency("x")` reads `.zon`; SwiftPM's manifest is a value.
4. Shared versions and options across many packages are an explicit, opt-in feature of the root (Cargo `workspace = true`, pnpm catalogs, Gradle catalogs), not silent inheritance.

## 8. What a cleaner system must do

These requirements come from sections 4–7 and from `Docs/spec/philosophy.md` (ladders, not cliffs; one mechanism; enterprise auditability; the language is a library). The proposal answers each one.

- **R1. Two nouns, two files, no overlap.** One noun and one file for the unit others depend on (package). One noun and one file for the folder people work in (project). No file means both.
- **R2. One home per fact.** Every field has exactly one file it may appear in. A beginner can sort any fact with one question.
- **R3. One home per entry function.** `fn build`, `fn test` and `fn dev` each have one fixed file name, found without discovery rules.
- **R4. One settings order.** One list of layers, with pins and policy forbids stated on the same list.
- **R5. Explicit inheritance.** A package states what it takes from its project, or the project states what it gives. No hidden layer.
- **R6. Composition.** Data files and entry code build the same Core values. The primitive (`b.add(output)`, a typed action) can express everything; the wrappers (`outputs:` entries, `b.add_executable`) cover the common cases and expand to the primitive.
- **R7. One meaning per word.** "Workspace" leaves the package system; "build", "target" and "profile" each keep one meaning.
- **R8. A mechanical migration.** `jet fix` moves every file and field, and a leftover old spelling is an error that names the fix.

sections.title: One text type, fixed through `::` and edited through `:=` (card #6342)
sections.body:
# One text type, fixed through `::` and edited through `:=` (card #6342)

Date: 2026-10-30. Lane: SurfaceDesign-2. Dev: 4e514f96e1.

The owner asked for a fresh look at strings. Strings should be fixed, and text
should be easy to build, perhaps like Odin's string builder. The owner floated
`Text` as a name. He later said he leans toward one type for simplicity, with
growth explicit and visible.

This note maps today's `String`, measures what it costs against Rust, surveys
peers, and proposes a model and a name. It ends with the migration size, the
`jet fix` rule for each option, and paired perf cells. Two ballots carry the
owner choices: D-TEXT-FIXED1 (the model) and D-TEXT-NAMES1 (the name).

## 1. What `String` is today

### 1.1 The value is already fixed

Every probe below ran with the dev compiler on O0, O1 and O2 and gave the same
result on all three. The probe sources are in
`$JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/SurfaceDesign/probes/m6342` and `m6342b`, generated by
`gen6342.mjs` and `gen6342b.mjs`.

| probe | code | result |
|---|---|---|
| s01 | `s :: "a"` then `s += "b"` | E0111: made with `::`, so it can't change |
| s02 | `s := ""`, five `s += "{i}"` | `01234` |
| s03 | `s := "ab"`, `t :: s`, `s += "c"` | `abc ab`: the shared text is untouched |
| s10 | `s = ""` then `s += "d"` | `d` |
| s11 | `fn fill(out: &String) { out += "ab" }` | `xab` |
| s12 | `p.name += "b"` on a struct field | `ab` |
| s13 | `xs[0] += "!"` on a list item | E0164: compound assignment can't target an indexed slot |
| s14 | `s += "x"` on a plain parameter | E0111 |
| s17 | `t :: s.copy()` then `s += "c"` | `abc ab` |
| s18 | a lambda that does `s += x` | `ab` |
| s38 | `s = "{s}{i},"` four times | `0,1,2,3,` |
| b16 | `t := s` from a `^String` parameter, then `t += "!"` | `hi!` |

So no operation changes a `String` value that another name holds. `+=` changes
the name, like `n += 1`. The runtime says so directly: text is immutable once
published, and only a sole owner is written in place
(Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/Text.jet:54-58). `jet_rt_string_append` appends in
place only when the owner is unique and not a literal. Otherwise it builds a
fresh text (Text.jet:357-367).

The owner-notes digest of 2026-10-07 answered this question once already. It
said a `::` string is fixed and a `:=` string is the builder, and recommended
one type (Docs/audits/2026-10-07-owner-notes-digest.md:413-436). The owner has
now asked again and leans toward one type, so this note keeps a second type as
a ballot option with its costs stated.

### 1.2 What is missing

| probe | code | result |
|---|---|---|
| s08 | `s.push("c")` | E0311: `push` isn't a method |
| s09 | `s.clear()` | E0311 |
| s16 | `s.insert(1, "b")` | E0311 |
| s15 | `String.with_capacity(64)` | E0107: nothing named `String` exists here |
| b06 | `&s.try_push("c")` in `run` | E2402: can't convert `AllocError` into `Err` |
| s45 | `&s.try_push("c") ?? panic(..)` | internal compiler error, exit 101 |
| s05 | `a + b` on two Strings | E0109 (S8: no `+` on text) |
| s06, s07 | `s[0]`, `s[0] = 'z'` | E0503 |
| s36 | `Bytes.with_capacity(16)` | E2104: `Bytes` is not built yet |
| m6342c | `fn show(t: Text)`, and the same with `StringBuffer` and `StringBuilder` | E0119: there's no type called `Text` (and so on) |

The only editing method is `try_push`. It is declared as a write in
Compiler/JetFoundation/Source/Registry/BuiltinMethods.jet:82-182, and every
other String method is a read. In practice it cannot be called (s45, b05, b06).
D-CORE-IO-BUF1 named `Bytes` as the growable buffer, but `Bytes` does not
build today (s36).

D-STR-DECLINE1=C declined the mutation verbs `clear`, `push`, `pop`, `remove`
and `write` because they "clash with immutable String". D-STRING-EMPTY1=A
chose `s = ""` over a `clear` method. D-EFF-FORMAT-WRITER1=A says "String
remains the one public text type".

### 1.3 Representation and its costs

A heap text is a 32-byte block `[count][data, len, cap]` from
`jet_rt_alloc_8`, and the bytes live in a second allocation
(Text.jet:54-63, 74-77). So every fresh text costs two allocations. Literals
are static headers with cap 0 (Text.jet:67-72).

`len()` counts Unicode scalars (S41, Docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:1657-1658).
Its body is `receiver.chars().len()`, which builds a list of every character
first (Core/Text/String.jet:15-17).

`slice(a, b)` takes scalar positions. The runtime first counts every scalar of
the whole text, then walks to `a`, then to `b`, then copies the bytes
(Text.jet:686-733, 98-100). D-FOUND-VIEW1=A promised views everywhere, but a
slice is a scan plus a copy.

`trim`, `after` and `before` are zero-copy when the call is bound with `::` to a
local, on a local or parameter (Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Ownership/StringViews.jet:1-8;
spec.md:1375-1396). Its Jet-level type stays `String`. At a return or a field,
`View<str>` states that a value is such a window
(Examples/features/memory/returned_views.jet:4-30), and returning one works
(probe b13). Passing `s.trim()` to a `View<str>` parameter is E0112 (probe
b04); no example uses `View<str>` as a parameter type.

### 1.4 Measured cost against Rust

The machine is shared and its load average was 60 to 95 on 32 cores during the
runs. Wall time was useless, so every kernel ran three times under `perf stat`.
The tables keep the minimum user-space cycles and instructions, in millions.

Jet kernels: `probes/k6342/*.jet` (from `gen6342k.mjs`). Rust peers:
`probes/r6342/kernels.rs`, built with rustc 1.97.1 at `-C opt-level=3`.
Harness: `probes/pstat.sh`. Results: `probes/pstat6342.tsv`.

Each cell is millions of user cycles / millions of user instructions. The last
two columns divide Jet O2 by Rust O3.

| kernel | Jet O0 | Jet O1 | Jet O2 | Rust O0 | Rust O3 | Rust O3 + overflow checks | cycles O2/O3 | instructions O2/O3 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `append_plus_eq` | 622 / 3,597 | 995 / 3,591 | 799 / 3,570 | 431 / 1,057 | 116 / 335 | 69 / 335 | 6.89 | 10.66 |
| `append_self_interp` | 1,129 / 3,597 | 1,031 / 3,591 | 951 / 3,571 | did not finish | did not finish | did not finish | n/a | n/a |
| `fresh_small` | 1,549 / 7,048 | 1,462 / 6,943 | 1,914 / 6,475 | 2,413 / 6,630 | 317 / 919 | 284 / 948 | 6.04 | 7.05 |
| `len_loop` | 822 / 4,825 | 1,171 / 4,824 | 1,143 / 4,821 | 63 / 189 | 39 / 149 | 39 / 149 | 29.31 | 32.36 |
| `bytes_len_loop` | 9 / 30 | 5 / 29 | 8 / 27 | 11 / 19 | 1 / 3 | 2 / 3 | 8.00 | 9.00 |
| `slice_loop` | 74,898 / 352,158 | 66,501 / 352,150 | 72,329 / 352,116 | 94 / 232 | 6 / 32 | 6 / 33 | 12,054.83 | 11,003.62 |
| `trim_loop` | 523 / 2,566 | 550 / 2,558 | 521 / 2,548 | 1,934 / 3,628 | 108 / 244 | 51 / 246 | 4.82 | 10.44 |
| `split_join` | 4,835 / 20,687 | 4,136 / 20,687 | 3,735 / 20,686 | 2,489 / 8,970 | 285 / 1,198 | 273 / 1,204 | 13.11 | 17.27 |
| `share_append` | 4 / 21 | 4 / 21 | 6 / 20 | 3 / 9 | 1 / 1 | 1 / 1 | 6.00 | 20.00 |

Reading the table:

- Every kernel that finished printed the same output in Jet and Rust. No
  kernel meets the 1.05 gate (AGENTS.md:149-154) at O2.
- `append_self_interp` writes `s = "{s}{i % 97},"` a million times. Jet costs the same as
  `append_plus_eq`, so it appends in place. The Rust peer, `s = format!("{}{},", s, i % 97)`,
  copies the whole text each step and did not finish within 150 seconds.
- `len_loop` needs 32 times Rust's instructions, because `String.len()` builds
  a `[Char]` list first (Core/Text/String.jet:15-17); Rust counts with
  `chars().count()`. Counting bytes instead,
  `bytes_len_loop` is 9 times Rust, at tiny absolute cost.
- `slice_loop` is the worst row, about 11,000 times Rust's instructions. Each
  slice counts every scalar of the text and then copies (Text.jet:686-733).
- Appending (`append_plus_eq`, 10.66) and building small fresh strings
  (`fresh_small`, 7.05) cost 7 to 11 times Rust. These are the costs the
  one-type design must close with `reserve` and in-place growth.
- `trim_loop` is 10.44 and `split_join` 17.27 times Rust's instructions.
  `share_append` is too small to read: 20 against 1 million instructions.

## 2. Peers

| language | fixed text | growable text | `+=` on fixed text | source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Go | `string` (immutable byte slice) | `strings.Builder` | yes, builds a new string | pkg.go.dev/strings#Builder |
| Java | `String` | `StringBuilder` | yes, new string | docs.oracle.com java.lang.StringBuilder |
| C# | `string` | `StringBuilder` | yes, new string | learn.microsoft.com System.Text.StringBuilder |
| Dart | `String` | `StringBuffer` | yes, new string | api.dart.dev dart:core StringBuffer |
| Kotlin | `String` | `StringBuilder`, `buildString {}` | yes, new string | kotlinlang.org |
| Odin | `string` (pointer and length) | `strings.Builder` | no | pkg.odin-lang.org/core/strings |
| Zig | `[]const u8` | `std.ArrayList(u8)` with a writer | no | ziglang.org/documentation/0.15.2 |
| Rust | `&str` (view) | `String` | `String += &str` appends in place | doc.rust-lang.org/std/string |
| Swift | `String` and `Substring` share storage | `var String` grows in place | yes, in place | docs.swift.org Substring |
| Mojo | `StringSlice` (view) | `String` grows in place | yes | mojolang.org/docs/std/collections/string |

Two families exist. Go, Java, C#, Dart and Kotlin pair a fixed `String` with a
separate builder, and `+=` on the fixed type gives the name a new value. Rust,
Swift and Mojo make the main `String` growable and add a view type. Odin and
Zig have a fixed slice and a growable buffer, and no `+=`.

Jet's semantics sit closest to Swift: the value never changes under another
holder, a `:=` name may grow, and a sole owner appends in place, as CPython also
does for `str`. Swift adds in-place editing on `var` strings through copy on
write, which is what option A of D-TEXT-FIXED1 adds to Jet.

## 3. The design

### 3.1 Model (ballot D-TEXT-FIXED1)

Option A, recommended: one `String`, which stays a value. A `::` name never
changes. A `:=` name or a `&String` parameter may grow with `+=`. It may also
be edited in place with `&` calls, as lists are: `&s.insert(at, text)`,
`&s.remove(from, to)`, `&s.truncate(n)` and `&s.reserve(n)`.
`String.with_capacity(n)` and `s.capacity()` join them, and `&s.try_push(x)`
is fixed. Appending stays `+=` and emptying stays `s = ""`, so no `push` or
`clear` is added.

This is Swift's model: one value-type String with copy on write, where a `let`
name never changes and a `var` name may be edited. Jet already chose the memory
side. D-COPY-DEFAULT1=A gives every heap value copy on first write, and drops
the sharing test for values the compiler proves unique. Probe s03 shows the
value rule today: `s := "ab"`, `t :: s`, `s += "c"` prints `abc ab`.

Fixed is checked, not a convention. `s += "b"` on a `::` name is E0111, and
`&xs.push(2)` on a `::` list is E0202 (probe `m6342c/q1_fixed_list_push.jet`).
The new String calls get the same check.

Option B is the two-type design that v1 of the ballot recommended: String keeps
no editing calls, and a separate `StringBuffer` edits in place. It matches Java,
Go, C# and Dart, and keeps D-STR-DECLINE1 as it is. It adds no safety, because
no edit can reach a String another name holds under A either. It adds no speed,
because a buffer runs the same append code as `+=`. It costs a second type,
conversions at every hand-off, and reopens D-EFF-FORMAT-WRITER1 and
D-CORE-IO-BUF1. Option C keeps today's model with no editing calls.

A amends D-STR-DECLINE1, which declined mutation verbs because they "clash with
immutable String". Under A no value changes under another holder, so the reason
no longer applies to these calls. `push` and `clear` stay declined. A also
turns D-STRING-EMPTY1's permission into a rule: `s = ""` on a `:=` String that
nothing else holds keeps its storage on every tier.

### 3.2 Name (ballot D-TEXT-NAMES1)

With one type, the vote is that type's name. Option A, recommended, keeps
`String`. Option B renames it `Text`. If D-TEXT-FIXED1 picks a second type, A
names it `StringBuffer` and B names it `TextBuffer`.

The text type is the most common type in Jet code, so its name should be the one
newcomers already type. Python, Java, Go, C#, Kotlin, Swift, Dart and
JavaScript all call it `String` or `string`. Renaming it touches 81,344
mentions. The earlier idea of `Text` fixed and `String` growable needs two
types, so it falls away with one.

## 4. Migration and the `jet fix` rule

Census scripts: `$JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/SurfaceDesign/b2/census6342.mjs` (raw
mentions) and `census6342b.mjs` (text locals and their writes). Both scan
`*.jet` under Compiler, Core, Examples, tests, Jetpack and Tools, skipping
whole-line comments. They are regex counts, so they are close but not exact.

| kind | Compiler | Core | Examples | tests | Jetpack | Tools | total |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `.jet` files | 1,632 | 170 | 1,508 | 12,825 | 767 | 734 | 17,636 |
| `String` mentions | 36,082 | 6,730 | 2,169 | 9,488 | 24,309 | 2,566 | 81,344 |
| `name: String` params and fields | 14,305 | 3,750 | 1,063 | 2,986 | 12,767 | 1,405 | 36,276 |
| `[String]` | 12,404 | 1,024 | 249 | 3,509 | 5,995 | 597 | 23,778 |
| text locals `x := "…"` | 628 | 171 | 43 | 235 | 270 | 102 | 1,449 |
| of those, appended to | 157 | 82 | 22 | 30 | 87 | 27 | 405 |
| `x += …` sites on them | 63 | 66 | 17 | 11 | 0 | 4 | 161 |
| `x = "{x}…"` sites on them | 442 | 359 | 19 | 24 | 336 | 56 | 1,236 |
| `x = ""` resets on them | 9 | 8 | 0 | 9 | 11 | 2 | 39 |
| `&String` parameters | 19 | 1 | 4 | 15 | 5 | 1 | 45 |
| appends through `&String` | 7 | 39 | 4 | 1 | 6 | 2 | 59 |
| `.try_push(` | 0 | 0 | 1 | 4 | 0 | 0 | 5 |
| `.slice(` | 397 | 60 | 31 | 53 | 35 | 76 | 652 |
| `.trim/.after/.before(` | 639 | 91 | 119 | 258 | 1,020 | 142 | 2,269 |
| `.len()` (all types) | 13,156 | 4,070 | 947 | 2,452 | 4,430 | 1,162 | 26,217 |
| interpolated literals | 21,382 | 2,026 | 3,327 | 8,438 | 10,831 | 2,571 | 48,575 |

The card estimated about 2,250 String uses in Examples; the census finds 2,169.

`jet fix` rule per option:

- D-TEXT-FIXED1 A: none. The 5 `try_push` sites keep working once the internal
  error is fixed. No fix is needed for `+=`, `s = ""` or `&String`. Code that
  rebuilds text from slices may adopt `insert` and `truncate` by hand.
- D-TEXT-FIXED1 B: rewrite the 5 `try_push` sites to a `StringBuffer`.
- D-TEXT-FIXED1 C: none.
- D-TEXT-NAMES1 A: none.
- D-TEXT-NAMES1 B: rename the `String` type by symbol in all 17,636 files, the
  spec, guides and diagnostic texts, in one cutover with no alias.

## 5. Compiler criteria (no owner choice)

These hold under every option and need no ballot. Each one names the file to
change and the cell that proves it.

1. One allocation per fresh text: header and bytes together, so `"{a}{b}"`
   costs one `jet_rt_alloc` instead of two (Text.jet:54-63, 74-77). Cell:
   `text/string_fresh`.
2. `len()` without a list: a scalar count that walks the bytes once, with no
   allocation (Core/Text/String.jet:15-17). Cell: `text/len_loop` (new).
3. An all-ASCII flag set when text is built. For ASCII text, `len()` is the
   byte count and scalar positions are byte offsets, so `slice` and `insert`
   positions cost nothing to find. Cells: `text/len_loop`, `text/slice_loop`.
4. `slice` without the full scan: walk only to the end position, never count
   the whole text first (Text.jet:690-733). Cell: `text/slice_loop` (new).
5. Views wherever D-FOUND-VIEW1 promised them: `slice`, `trim`, `after`,
   `before`, `split` and `lines` return zero-copy windows in every read
   position, not only a `::` binding. Storing one still copies, as that
   decision says. Cells: `text/trim_loop` (new), `text/split_join`.
6. `try_push` lowers instead of failing the IR build. Repro: probe s45.
7. Capacity from the allocator's size class, so a String needs no separate
   `cap` word and `+=` still grows geometrically. Cell: `text/self_append`.
8. Under D-TEXT-FIXED1 A, `s = ""` on a sole-owner `:=` String keeps its
   storage on every tier, and each edit call on a value proved unique has no
   sharing test. Cell: `text/edit_rows` (new).

## 6. Paired perf cells

AGENTS.md:171-174 says a surface added for performance needs a paired
two-program cell against the plain spelling it replaces. Ratification waits
until the surface strictly beats the plain form. AGENTS.md:151-154 sets the
Rust gate: Jet/Rust at or below 1.05 is parity, and every other peer must be
beaten outright.

| cell | plain form | surface or peer form | proves |
|---|---|---|---|
| `text/edit_rows` (new) | `line = ""`, `line += "{cell},"`, `line = "> {line}"` per row | `&line.truncate(..)`, `&line.insert(0, "> ")` on a reused `:=` String | in-place edits beat rebuilding text (D-TEXT-FIXED1 A) |
| `text/insert` (new) | `s = "{s.slice(0, k)}x{s.slice(k, n)}"` | `&s.insert(k, "x")` | in-place insert beats two slices and a concat |
| `text/self_append` vs `text/self_append_builder` (exist) | `s = "{s}…"` | list of pieces joined | already paired; add a `String.with_capacity` plus `+=` third arm |
| `text/string_fresh` (exists) | Jet | Rust `String` built per call | criterion 1 |
| `text/len_loop` (new) | Jet `s.len()` | Rust `s.chars().count()` | criteria 2 and 3 |
| `text/slice_loop` (new) | Jet `s.slice(a, b)` | Rust `&s[a..b]` | criteria 3, 4 and 5 |
| `text/trim_loop` (new) | Jet `padded.trim()` | Rust `padded.trim()` | criterion 5 |
| `text/split_join` (exists) | Jet | Rust `split(',').collect().join(";")` | criterion 5 |

Each new cell's Jet source and Rust peer is already written:
`probes/k6342/*.jet` and `probes/r6342/kernels.rs`, one kernel per argument.

## 7. Bugs found

1. `&s.try_push("c") ?? panic("no memory")` is an internal compiler error on
   O0, O1 and O2: "ir.build unlowered: mutating builtin TryStringPush on
   String". Repro: `probes/m6342/s45_amp_method_on_string.jet`.
2. `Bytes.with_capacity(16)` is E2104, "`Bytes` is not built yet", although
   D-CORE-IO-BUF1=A names `Bytes` as the growable buffer. Repro:
   `probes/m6342/s36_bytes_builder.jet`.
3. `s.len()` builds a list of every character to count them
   (Core/Text/String.jet:15-17). See the `len_loop` row in section 1.4.
4. `s.slice(a, b)` counts every scalar of the whole text and then copies
   (Text.jet:686-733), against D-FOUND-VIEW1=A. See the `slice_loop` row.
5. An unknown parameter type gives E0119 and then a second error, E0112
   "`print` doesn't know how to show `Text`", for the same unknown name.
   Repro: `jet check probes/m6342c/p_Text.jet`.

## 8. Decisions consulted

D-STRING-EMPTY1=A, D-FOUND-VIEW1=A, D-EFF-FORMAT-WRITER1=A, D-CORE-IO-BUF1=A,
D-CORE-STRING-HOME1=A, D-STR-DECLINE1=C, D-COPY-DEFAULT1=A, D-COPY-WORD1=A,
D-COPY-MOVE-SPELL1=A, D-MEM-LOCALRC1=A, D-ALLOC-SITE1=A, D-LIST-PLUS1=A,
D-STR-ESCAPE1=A, D-RAWSTR1=A, D-TEXTHEAD-HOLES1=A, D-LINK-SIBLING1=A,
D-PARAM-CONST1=A, D-FREESTAND-ALLOCAPI1=A, D-STR-AFTER1=A, D-FMT-INTERP1=A,
D-FMT-INTERP2=A, D-FMT-INTERP3=B, D-DISPLAYDBG2=A, D-TEXTUNICODE1=A,
D-GRAPHEME1=B, D-BYTESDECODE1=A, D-API-LEN1=A, D-ARRAY-CAPACITY1=A,
D-DROP-ASAP1=A, D-SCRIPT-FIND1 (open: text search returns a character index),
D-SCRIPT-SLOTADD1 (open: it would allow `xs[i] += v` on list slots, the E0164
of probe s13).

Spec rules: S8 (interpolation, no `+`), S20 (escapes) and S41 (`len` counts
scalars, no `s[i]`), Docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:1647-1668. Zero-copy string
views: Docs/spec/spec.md:1375-1396.

sections.title: Declarations as bindings, and the lambda shape
sections.body:
# Declarations as bindings, and the lambda shape

Cards #4735 (D-DECL-FORM2, now D-DECL-BINDING1) and #6251 (D-LAMBDA-SHAPE1,
D-LAMBDA-STORED1). Design note for two ballots. Nothing here is implemented.

The owner asked that the lambda shape align with "the planned conversion to the
Jai-style bindings", where a function is declared as `my_function :: (...)`.
No Tower decision or card ratifies that conversion. D-DECL-FORM2=A (2026-10-07)
ratified the opposite: `struct Point` and `fn double` keep their leading word.
So the conversion needs its own vote, D-DECL-BINDING1, and D-LAMBDA-SHAPE1 is
rewritten to follow it.

## 1. Tower decisions that bear on this

- D-DECL-FORM2=A, card c04j9ahx: named structs, enums, traits, functions and
  modules start with their word; `Point :: struct { … }` is refused with a fix.
  D-DECL-BINDING1=A reverses it.
- D-LAMBDA-SHAPE1, open, card c0rqt0kq: version 1 proposed `fn(n) { n * n }`.
  Version 2 asks whether a lambda is exactly the bound value `(n) { n * n }`.
- D-LAMBDA-STORED1=A: a lambda stored with no expected type writes parameter
  and result types. The rule stays; only the spelling changes.
- D-LAMBDA-IFACE2=A: a lambda writes no result type. Both new ballots amend it.
- D-LAMBDA-INFER1=A and D-LAMBDAINFER1=A: parameter types may be left out when
  the expected type gives them. Unchanged.
- D-CALLABLE-ONE1=A: one callable shape, "a function is a named lambda".
  D-DECL-BINDING1=A makes that literal.
- D-SIG-AFTER1=A: one arrow after the inputs, braces on every named body, and
  `-> Point {` always opens the body. The head shape stays; the name moves.
- D-GENERIC-TYPEFN1=A: generics are prep parameters and `prep fn` recipes.
  Under D-DECL-BINDING1=A a recipe is `Pair :: prep (T: Type) -> Type { … }`.
- D-BIND-BARE1=A: only `::` and `:=` bind. Unchanged.
- D-CASE-LAW1=A: fixed module-level bindings are SCREAMING_SNAKE. A amends it,
  so a function binding stays snake_case and a type binding PascalCase.
- D-ALIAS-BIND2=B (keep `alias`) and D-VIS-REEXPORT1=A (`clamp ::
  core.math.clamp`) already put the name first. Unchanged.
- D-MOD1 (spec-only import): `module math { … }` becomes `math :: module { … }`
  under A; the file form `module math;` stays.
- D-TUPLE-DESTRUCT1=A: tuples have named members, `(x: 1, y: 2)`. This is the
  value a function head must be told apart from.
- D-DOTCTOR3=A: `Type{ body }` is a typed literal. It is why
  `(n: Int) -> Int { n * n }` runs today as a typed value.
- D-CALLVALUE1=B and D-MARKER-DECL1=A: unchanged; markers stay above the
  binding.

## 2. What happens today

Probes live in `$JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/SurfaceDesign/probes/m-decl`. Each ran
with the dev jet at `--optimize=none` and `full`, and d8 and d10 also at
`basic`.

- `d1_lambda_today.jet`: `square :: (n: Int) -> n * n`, `n -> n * 2` and
  `(n) -> { n + 1 }` all run.
- `d2_tuple.jet`: `p :: (x: 1, y: 2)` is a tuple and prints 3.
- `d3_bind_fn.jet`: a module-level `square :: (n: Int) -> Int { n * n }` is
  E0357, "Constant `square` must be ALL_CAPS".
- `d4_point_struct_bind.jet`: `Point :: struct { x: Int }` is E0003.
- `d5_fn_value.jet`: a `:=` lambda can be reassigned and prints 3.
- `d6_local_recur.jet`: a local lambda calling itself is E0804.
- `d7_fn_literal.jet`: `fn(n) { n * n }` as a value is E0003.
- `d8_program_today.jet`: the D-DECL-BINDING1 program in today's spelling,
  minus the generic parts, prints 7, 4.0, [1, 4, 9], [1, 4, 9], 2, 120 and 7.
- `d10_lambda_today.jet`: the D-LAMBDA-SHAPE1 program in today's spelling
  prints [3, 4], [10, 20, 30, 40], [9, 16], `> done` and [3, 5, 7, 9].

Writing the program surfaced two checks worth knowing. `#Inline(Always)` on a
function that is also passed as a value is E0918. An error enum named in a
failure rail needs `#Error`, or the result is E2417.

## 3. The design

Every named thing is `name :: value`. A function value is
`(params) arrow result failure { body }`: today's head without `fn` and the
name. A type is `struct { … }`, `enum { … }`, `trait { … }` or another type on
the right. A lambda is the same value without a name, leaving out what the
call gives: `nums.map((n) { n * n })`.

A parenthesized list is a function only when `{`, `->`, `-[` or a failure rail
follows its `)`. So `origin :: (x: 0, y: 0)` stays a tuple, and
`Pt :: (x: Int, y: Int)` stays a tuple type. In `if` and `loop` heads the test
is off, as Rust does for struct literals. A scan of every `.jet` file found no
`if (name) {` or `loop (name) {` head in Jet code.

Inside a type body, `x: Int` is a field and `norm1 :: (self) -> Int { … }` a
method. `Shape.area :: (self) -> Float { … }` adds one outside, replacing
`fn Shape.area`. `impl Type { … }` keeps its head, because it names nothing
new. `::` binds a fixed function that may call itself; `:=` binds a changeable
function value that may not. `fn` remains only in function types.

D-DECL-BINDING1 also shows Odin's form, `square :: fn(n: Int) -> Int { … }`,
and keeping the words. D-LAMBDA-SHAPE1 v2 shows keeping a short arrow beside
the value form. Ballots: `$JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/SurfaceDesign/ballot/`
`D-DECL-BINDING1.json` and `D-LAMBDA-SHAPE1.json`.

## 4. Size of the change

`$JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/SurfaceDesign/b2/census-decl.mjs` over a dev export of 17,636 `.jet` files counted:

| site | count | under A |
|---|---|---|
| `fn name(` heads | 62,347 | `name :: (` |
| of those, indented members | 49,924 | `name :: (` inside the body |
| `struct Name` heads | 7,168 | `Name :: struct` |
| `enum Name` heads | 1,889 | `Name :: enum` |
| `trait Name` heads | 183 | `Name :: trait` |
| inline `module name {` | 576 | `name :: module {` |
| `impl` blocks | 1,612 | unchanged |
| `fn(` function types | 773 | unchanged |
| markers before a function | 4,808 | unchanged, above the binding |

Main's lambda census (`$JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/q/b4/lam/census.mjs`), rerun
on the same export, counts 4,812 lambdas in 1,197 files. Of these, 3,842 have
an expression body, 888 a bare parameter, and 220 are stored in a binding.
Version 1's `fn(…) { … }` form adds 12,437 characters. The bound-value form
adds 2,813, or 0.6 per lambda, because braced lambdas shrink.

## 5. Sources

- Jai: Docs/research/jai-vs-jet-syntax-briefing-2026-09-16.html:234-238 and
  https://github.com/Ivo-Balbaert/The_Way_to_Jai
- Odin: https://odin-lang.org/docs/overview/#procedures
- Zig, RFC to bind functions with `const`: https://github.com/ziglang/zig/issues/1717
- JavaScript arrow functions:
  https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Functions/Arrow_functions
- Kotlin lambdas: https://kotlinlang.org/docs/lambdas.html
- Earlier Jet review: Docs/research/jai-vs-jet-fable-brief-2026-09-16.md:106

sections.title: Working back from the speed of light (card #6343)
sections.body:
# Working back from the speed of light (card #6343)

Date: 2026-10-30. Lane: SurfaceDesign-2. Dev: 4e514f96e1.

The owner asked us to work backwards from the machine's physical limits to
what Jet must support and generate, and to be faster than Rust, tail calls
included. This note takes each hardware limit in turn. For each it says what
the hardware allows, what Jet does today, what Rust, Zig, C, Mojo and Odin
guarantee, and what Jet must guarantee.

Most answers are compiler work, not language surface. Those become numbered
criteria in section 5, for codegen cards. One answer needs an owner choice:
whether tail calls are jumps on every build level. Ballot D-TAIL-CALL1
carries it.

## 1. Method

The probe machine is an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X3D (Zen 4, 16 cores, 32 threads,
AVX-512). Its load average ran from 40 to 95 during the runs, so wall time
was useless. Every kernel ran three times under `perf stat -e
cycles:u,instructions:u`, and the tables keep the minimum of each.
Instruction counts are exact; cycle counts still carry some noise from the
shared caches.

- Jet kernels: `$JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/SurfaceDesign/probes/k6343/*.jet`,
  built at `--optimize=none`, `basic` and `full` (O0, O1, O2) with the dev
  compiler, toolchain root an export of 4e514f96e1.
- Rust peers: `probes/r6343/kernels.rs`, one binary, the kernel picked by
  argument. Built with rustc 1.97.1 at opt-level 0, at opt-level 3, and at
  opt-level 3 with `-C overflow-checks=on`. Inputs pass through `black_box`.
- Harness: `probes/pstat.sh`. Raw table: `probes/pstat6343.tsv`.

Hardware figures come from AMD's Software Optimization Guide for Zen 4,
publication 57647 revision 1.01 (cited below as SOG).

## 2. Measured kernels

Each cell is millions of user cycles / millions of user instructions. The last
two columns divide Jet O2 by Rust O3. The AGENTS.md gate (AGENTS.md:149-154)
is a Jet/Rust ratio at or below 1.05. Every finished kernel printed the same
output in Jet and Rust. `tail2` stops in Jet, so its ratio columns say
"stops". Each figure is the lowest of three runs, taken with `perf stat`
on a loaded 32-core machine.

| kernel | Jet O0 | Jet O1 | Jet O2 | Rust O0 | Rust O3 | Rust O3 + overflow checks | cycles O2/O3 | instructions O2/O3 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `loop_int` | 5,652 / 31,110 | 6,418 / 28,310 | 2,707 / 16,402 | 14,438 / 30,400 | 1,853 / 5,200 | 1,850 / 7,600 | 1.46 | 3.15 |
| `loop_i64` | 6,682 / 27,110 | 5,906 / 23,910 | 3,558 / 18,310 | 8,014 / 30,400 | 1,415 / 5,200 | 1,472 / 7,600 | 2.51 | 3.52 |
| `sum_index` | 2,009 / 13,472 | 1,759 / 12,132 | 2,182 / 11,542 | 6,892 / 20,040 | 236 / 500 | 442 / 1,350 | 9.25 | 23.08 |
| `sum_iter` | 1,562 / 8,712 | 1,135 / 7,132 | 1,035 / 6,572 | 2,412 / 9,240 | 270 / 500 | 293 / 1,350 | 3.83 | 13.14 |
| `axpy` | 4,524 / 27,008 | 3,630 / 20,572 | 2,758 / 16,992 | 5,284 / 16,356 | 505 / 750 | 542 / 750 | 5.46 | 22.66 |
| `inline_small` | 4,471 / 30,202 | 3,038 / 18,885 | 1,660 / 10,519 | 5,622 / 20,742 | 873 / 2,788 | 620 / 3,259 | 1.90 | 3.77 |
| `struct_ret` | 2,528 / 14,226 | 2,078 / 12,676 | 2,018 / 11,827 | 1,203 / 4,400 | 473 / 1,275 | 473 / 1,275 | 4.27 | 9.28 |
| `option_ret` | 942 / 5,885 | 837 / 4,902 | 537 / 3,319 | 1,490 / 5,450 | 201 / 784 | 212 / 900 | 2.67 | 4.23 |
| `fib` | 362 / 1,809 | 266 / 1,495 | 269 / 1,495 | 198 / 672 | 75 / 302 | 152 / 433 | 3.59 | 4.95 |
| `dispatch` | 5,351 / 16,620 | 3,161 / 14,932 | 2,778 / 9,440 | 4,065 / 14,638 | 925 / 3,175 | 776 / 3,488 | 3.00 | 2.97 |
| `matmul` | 1,101 / 6,056 | 833 / 5,157 | 490 / 2,337 | 2,133 / 5,457 | 20 / 102 | 25 / 102 | 24.50 | 22.91 |
| `byte_count` | 4,174 / 23,900 | 3,098 / 15,041 | 3,006 / 11,622 | 7,617 / 30,410 | 1,084 / 3,364 | 1,114 / 4,872 | 2.77 | 3.45 |
| `closure_map` | 1,876 / 9,818 | 2,837 / 9,124 | 2,076 / 8,776 | 5,191 / 11,019 | 188 / 553 | 184 / 603 | 11.04 | 15.87 |
| `tail2` | 645 / 1,353 | 464 / 1,110 | 504 / 1,110 | 310 / 527 | 6 / 25 | 62 / 185 | stops | stops |

Reading the table:

- No kernel meets the 1.05 gate at O2. The closest in cycles are `loop_int`
  (1.46) and `inline_small` (1.90). In instructions every kernel needs at
  least three times Rust's count.
- The worst gaps are loops over lists: `matmul`, `sum_index`, `axpy`,
  `sum_iter` and `closure_map`, at 13 to 23 times Rust's instructions. Each
  step pays a bounds check, `Int` tests and scalar code, where Rust
  vectorizes and removes the checks.
- Quick runs already beat Rust's debug builds on most kernels. Jet O0 used
  fewer cycles than Rust O0 on 10 of the 13 finished kernels. Rust O0 won on
  `struct_ret`, `fib` and `dispatch`.
- O2 adds nothing over O1 on `fib` and `tail2`: the instruction counts are
  identical.
- Rust with overflow checks on is the fair peer for checked arithmetic. It
  costs 1.46 times plain Rust's instructions on `loop_int` and 2.7 times on
  `sum_index`; Jet costs 3.15 and 23.08 times.
- `tail2` is not a finished run in Jet. It prints the first result, then
  stops with E3012 in `is_even(10000000)` on every level. Rust O3 finishes in
  25 million instructions because LLVM turned both recursions into loops.
  Rust O0 overflows its stack.
- Cycle counts carry noise from the loaded machine; for example Jet O2
  `sum_index` shows more cycles than O1 with fewer instructions.
- The first `dispatch` peer used Rust's truncating `%`, and printed a
  different total. Jet's `%` on `Int` is the floor modulo (`-7 % 3` is 2), so
  the peer now uses `rem_euclid`, and both print 967383. The `dispatch` row
  comes from that rerun (probe `probes/m6343/mod.jet` prints 2 and -4).

## 3. The limits, one by one

### 3.1 Instruction throughput

**Hardware.** Zen 4 dispatches up to 6 macro ops per cycle and keeps up to
320 in flight (SOG sections 2.9.8 and 2.10.3). A loop's speed is set by how many
instructions each step needs, and by the longest chain of dependent ones.

**Jet today.** `loop_int` needs 3.15 times Rust's instructions at O2, and
`inline_small` 3.77 times. Every `Int` operation carries a small-or-big test
(D-INTBIG1=A: "arithmetic carries a small-versus-big check"). The O2 code of
`axpy` holds about seven `add`/`jo` pairs per step. The fixed-width `I64` loop
is slower than the `Int` loop (18,310 against 16,402 million instructions),
because each `I64{i}` conversion and each `I64` operation is checked too.

**Peers.** Rust release builds turn overflow checks off by default, so `+`
wraps silently (Cargo book, profiles: `overflow-checks` defaults to false in
release). C makes signed overflow undefined, so the compiler assumes it never
happens. Zig checks overflow in Debug and ReleaseSafe and assumes it away in
ReleaseFast (ziglang.org/documentation/0.15.2, Build Mode). This note did not
check Odin's or Mojo's overflow rules.

**What Jet must guarantee.** Exact `Int` and checked fixed widths stay; they
are ratified safety. The compiler must then remove the checks it can prove
away, so a counted loop costs what Rust's costs. Rust with overflow checks on
is the honest peer for checked arithmetic: `loop_int` costs 7,600 million
instructions there, against Jet's 16,402. Range analysis (P-RANGE in
Docs/research/ir-optimization-inventory-2026-10-21.md:257-259) is the
missing pass.

### 3.2 Memory bandwidth and latency

**Hardware.** The L1 data cache serves three memory operations per cycle, at
most two of them 256-bit loads (SOG section 2.6.2). A main-memory miss costs
hundreds of cycles, so a stream must be sequential and prefetchable.

**Jet today.** `byte_count` scans a 64 MB list of `U8`. `sum_iter` and
`sum_index` scan 80 MB of `Int`. Even so, their instruction ratios (table
above) show the loop body, not memory, is the limit today. Two layout costs
show up as well: optionals and small records returned from functions
(`option_ret`, `struct_ret`).

**Peers.** Rust, Zig and C store plain values inline and return small structs
in registers under the platform C ABI. Rust's `Option<i64>` is two words with
no heap use.

**What Jet must guarantee.** Values in lists, optionals, results and records
are stored inline (D-MEM-UNBOX1=A). Layout control for experts is ratified
(D-JAI-LAYOUT1=A), and so are cache hints (D-CACHE-CONTROL1=A). The compiler
criteria are box elimination for optionals (P-BOX, inventory:270-271) and
register returns for small records (G2, inventory:246).

### 3.3 Caches

**Hardware.** 32 KB of L1 data, 1 MB of L2 per core, and 96 MB of L3 on this
part (SOG sections 2.6.2 to 2.6.4; `lscpu` on the probe machine). Each cache line is 64
bytes.

**Jet today.** A fresh `String` is two allocations: a 32-byte header and the
bytes (Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/Text.jet:54-63, 74-77). That doubles
allocator traffic and splits each text over two lines. `matmul` keeps three
300 by 300 `Float` lists, 2.2 MB in all, so they spill out of L2 into L3. Rust
runs the same layout in 20 million cycles, so Jet's gap there is in the loop
body, not the cache.

**What Jet must guarantee.** Nothing new at the surface. Note #6342
(Docs/research/2026-10-30-fixed-text-and-buffer.md) lists the text layout
criteria.

### 3.4 Branch prediction

**Hardware.** A mispredicted branch costs 11 to 18 cycles, 13 in the common
case (SOG section 2.8). A predictable branch costs almost nothing, so checks
that never fail are cheap if they sit off the hot path.

**Jet today.** `if op == { … }` on an enum compiles to a chain of compares,
one arm per `If` (Compiler/JetIR/Source/BuildExpr.jet:3552-3553). Jet has no
jump table. `dispatch` measures the cost. Bounds and overflow stops in `axpy`
are inline in the loop body, each behind a forward branch.

**Peers.** Rust, C (Clang), Zig and Odin compile through LLVM, which lowers a
dense `match` or `switch` to a jump table when that is cheaper than compares.

**What Jet must guarantee.** Nothing at the surface: `if x == { … }` already
says everything a jump table needs. The criteria are a jump table for dense
enum and integer matches, and stop paths moved out of line.

### 3.5 SIMD width

**Hardware.** Zen 4 runs AVX-512 by issuing each 512-bit operation over two
cycles on 256-bit paths, so peak FLOPS match 256-bit code (SOG section 2.11).
Four `Float`s per operation per pipe is the floor a loop should reach.

**Jet today.** Jet has no vectorizer (P-VEC, inventory:281). `axpy` at O2
uses scalar `movsd`, `mulsd` and `addsd`. It needs 22.66 times Rust's
instructions. Before the loop it copies `dst` when the list might be shared:
a uniqueness test, then `jet_rt_alloc_8` and `jet_rt_mem_move`.

**Peers.** Rust and C vectorize through LLVM, helped by `&mut` being
`noalias` in Rust and by `restrict` in C. Zig has `@Vector`, Mojo makes
`SIMD[type, width]` its base numeric type, and Odin has `#simd`.

**What Jet must guarantee.** Already ratified: auto-vectorization by default
with an opt-out (D-SIMD3=B), one lane type family (D-LANES1=A) and checked
native intrinsics (D-SIMD-NATIVE1=A). Jet's `&` is exclusive
(D-MEMREF-EXCL1=A), and plain parameters cannot be written (D-PARAM-CONST1=A).
So Jet can promise the "no alias" fact that Rust gets from `&mut`, on every
call, with no annotation. The vectorizer must use it.

Float reductions are the one trap. Adding Floats in a different order changes
the result, and I9 (AGENTS.md:135-147) forbids a result that depends on the
build level. A vectorized Float sum must keep the source order, or the
program must ask for lanes. Integer sums can be reordered freely.

### 3.6 Call overhead

**Hardware.** A call and return cost a few cycles plus any registers saved,
restored or spilled around them. Inlining removes all of it and opens the
callee to the caller's optimizations.

**Jet today.** `fib(35)` needs 4.95 times Rust's instructions and 3.96 times
its cycles at O2. Each call and return also costs a fetch bubble (SOG
section 2.8.1.3.3). Jet's inliner skips any callee over 40 IR
instructions at O1 and 60 at O2 (inventory:198), and does not honour
`#Inline(Always)` (P-IA, inventory:272). Every `Int` argument carries a drop
after the call, because an `Int` may own heap digits.

**Tail calls.** A call that is the last thing a function does can reuse the
caller's frame. D-DROP-ASAP1=A promised this: "Emit tail calls as jumps when
no visible drop is pending". D-RESOURCE-LIMIT1=A says "Only O2 may remove
recursive calls". Today no level does it. `walk(10000000, 0)` and
`is_even(10000000)` stop with E3012 on O0, O1 and O2. The O2 code of `walk`
is `call tail2_walk` followed by `call jet_rt_int_drop`. The drop is the
pending work that blocks the jump.

Rust has no stable guarantee. `become` is nightly only and "incomplete"
(doc.rust-lang.org/std/keyword.become.html). Rust O3 turns `walk` into a loop
by choice, but Rust O0 overflows. Clang's `[[clang::musttail]]` and GCC 15's
same attribute guarantee the jump or refuse to compile: a GCC 15.3 build at
`-O0` ran `walk(10000000, 0)` to completion (`probes/c6343/mt.c`). Zig has
`@call(.always_tail, f, args)`. Scheme requires proper tail calls of every
implementation (R7RS section 3.5).

Guaranteed tail calls are a place where Jet can beat stable Rust. Interpreters
and parsers written as small functions that jump to each other keep their
state in registers. The upb protobuf parser reached over 2 GB/s that way
(blog.reverberate.org, 2021-04-21, "Parsing Protobuf at 2+GB/s").

**What Jet must guarantee.** Ballot D-TAIL-CALL1 recommends that every tail
call is a jump on every level, with a lint naming any call that cannot jump.
With ASAP drop, an `Int` argument's digits are freed before the jump, so the
drop no longer blocks it.

### 3.7 Code size

**Hardware.** The op cache holds 6.75 K macro ops and the L1 instruction
cache 32 KB (SOG section 2.9.1). Hot code that fits runs from the op cache at
up to 9 ops per cycle.

**Jet today.** Inline overflow and bounds stops bloat hot loops. The
inventory records O1 code 4.5 percent and O2 code 9.6 percent larger than O0
over 280 programs (inventory:216-221).

**What Jet must guarantee.** Nothing at the surface. The criterion is that
stop paths and cold calls move out of the loop body, so hot loops fit in the
op cache.

## 4. Peer guarantees

| guarantee | Rust | Zig | C | Mojo | Odin | Jet (ratified) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| integer overflow | wraps in release, panics in debug | checked except ReleaseFast | signed is undefined | not checked | not checked | exact `Int` (D-INTBIG1); fixed widths trap |
| bounds checks | always, optimizer removes | except ReleaseFast | none | not checked | default on, `#no_bounds_check` per block | always; proofs remove (D-OOBPROOF1) |
| no-alias facts | `&mut` is noalias | `noalias` keyword | `restrict` | not checked | not checked | `&` exclusive (D-MEMREF-EXCL1) |
| guaranteed tail calls | nightly `become` only | `.always_tail` | Clang and GCC 15 `musttail` | not checked | not checked | promised (D-DROP-ASAP1), not built |
| SIMD | auto plus `std::arch` | `@Vector` | auto plus intrinsics | `SIMD` type | `#simd` arrays | auto plus lanes (D-SIMD3, D-LANES1) |
| destruction | end of scope | manual, `defer` | manual | at last use | manual, `defer` | at last use (D-DROP-ASAP1) |
| forced inlining | `#[inline(always)]` | `inline fn` | `always_inline` | `@always_inline` | `#force_inline` | `#Inline(Always)` (D-INLINE-PARAM1), not honoured |

Sources: Cargo book profiles (doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/profiles.html);
Zig 0.15.2 documentation, Build Mode and `@call`; Clang AttributeReference,
`musttail`; Mojo manual, "Value destruction" (mojolang.org/docs/manual/lifecycle/death);
Odin overview and directives (odin-lang.org/docs/overview, /docs/directives).

## 5. Compiler criteria (no owner choice)
